papers.title: Fabric anisotropy, entropy, and flowability of dense suspensions: The case of fresh concrete
papers.abstract: The paper examines the evolution of fabric anisotropy in fresh concrete for two distinct flow regimes: free flow under gravity and driven shear flow. Fabric anisotropy is seen to increase during gravity flow, resulting in a lowering of the Shannon entropy of the contact normal distribution, which in turn facilitates flow. Anisotropic, fabric-dependent stress tensors are examined to understand the meso-scale mechanics driving this behavior. The fabric-dependent tensor σ¯c, associated with anisotropy in the contact normal distribution, is found to play a critical role in the reorientation of interface normals. The forces driving the buildup in anisotropy, however, reduce sharply following the onset of a limit instability. Subsequently, the fabric becomes more isotropic, which induces an increase in entropy and a reduction in flowability. The fabric dependence of the yield stress is examined, and anisotropic stress tensors contributing to higher yield stress in certain mixes are identified. Compared to gravity flow, the buildup in anisotropy is smaller in the case of shear flow and is largely induced through preferential densification along the principal compressive direction and preferential failure along the principal tensile direction. No significant reorientation of the interface normals occurs, and σ¯c remains negligibly small throughout the duration of the flow. The results suggest that the formation of favorable fabric anisotropies in dense suspensions during free gravity flow can be hindered in the presence of constraints.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of the vortex ring state for side-by-side propellers in descent flight
papers.abstract: The present paper describes an experimental wind tunnel campaign aimed at investigating the aerodynamic interactions between two side-by-side (SBS) propeller models operating in Vortex Ring State (VRS) conditions. Load measurements and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) were employed in this comprehensive test campaign. Several configurations were considered, varying the tip-to-tip distance between the SBS propellers (i.e., with aligned propeller disks) in both co-rotating and counter-rotating configurations. The test results enabled characterization of the mutual aerodynamic influence between the two SBS propellers, providing insight into the loss of performance that occurs when the propellers enter this specific descent flight condition. Moreover, PIV measurements provided a detailed characterization of the velocity flow field and the dimensions of the vortical structures associated with VRS occurrence across the different configurations tested.

papers.title: Impact dynamics of successive droplets impinging on a superhydrophobic surface
papers.abstract: The impact behavior of multiple droplets is frequently encountered in practical applications such as anti-icing and spray cooling. In this study, the lattice Boltzmann method is employed to study the successive impact of two droplets on a superhydrophobic surface. The effects of horizontal distance between droplet centers (l*), the impact time interval (Δt*), and the Weber number (We) on impact dynamics are systematically investigated. During the spreading phase, inertial forces dominate, rendering the process largely independent of l*, Δt*, and We. In contrast, the receding dynamics exhibit significant sensitivity to these parameters. A small l* leads to asymmetric impact, resulting in three distinct spreading stages and a notable increase in contact time. The parameter Δt* governs the timing at which the trailing droplet interacts with the liquid film generated by the leading droplet, thereby influencing the duration of the second spreading event. Increasing We enhances both the spreading diameter and rate, while higher We values reduce contact time by accelerating the receding process. Based on the interaction patterns between the leading and trailing droplets, four distinct impact regimes (I–IV) are identified, and corresponding three-dimensional phase diagrams of We–l*–Δt* are constructed. Contact time is strongly dependent on the impact regime: it is significantly prolonged in regime IV and stabilizes in regime III, while elevated We values contribute to the reduction of contact time. This work advances the fundamental understanding of sequential droplet impact dynamics and provides a theoretical foundation for the effective control of contact time in engineering applications.

papers.title: Aerodynamic forces and vortex-induced vibration characteristics of bark-inspired surface textures on stay cables
papers.abstract: Inspired by the natural texture of tree bark, its unique grooved structure may regulate boundary layer flow and help suppress flow separation. To explore biomimetic aerodynamic measures for reducing wind-induced vibrations of stay cables, this study introduced bark-inspired surface textures into the design of external sheaths. Wind tunnel experiments were conducted to investigate the aerodynamic forces and vortex-induced vibration characteristics of stay cables with different bark-like textures. The results show that at a Reynolds number of 1 × 105, the minimum drag coefficient of bark-inspired stay cables is reduced by 13% compared to that of smooth stay cables under different wind angles. The bark texture increases the Reynolds number at which the stay cable enters the critical regime, and the rate of drag coefficient reduction in the critical regime is greater than that of the smooth cable. Additionally, the bark texture enhances the lift force on the cable, and in the subcritical regime, the fluctuating lift coefficient increases monotonically with Reynolds number. The bark texture reduces the onset wind speed for cable vibration, but has little effect on the resonance amplitude. Bark-inspired stay cables exhibit a pronounced sensitivity to added damping. Within low damping ratios relevant to practical stay cables, the peak resonance amplitude is reduced by up to 73.7%. When combined with appropriately tuned dampers, bark-inspired surface textures enable a hybrid mitigation strategy that effectively suppresses vortex-induced vibrations. Moreover, the bark texture increases the negative pressure on the leeward side of the cable and reduces the maximum vorticity in the wake.

papers.title: Influence of plate wettability and inclination angle on bubble dynamics and acoustics
papers.abstract: The interaction between bubbles and solid boundaries is fundamental to optimizing multiphase flow processes. This study experimentally investigates the coupling effects of surface wettability and plate inclination on bubble dynamics and acoustic signatures using synchronized high-speed imaging and hydrophone measurements. Experimental results demonstrate that hydrophobic surfaces promote rapid bubble coalescence into expansive gas films, which subsequently release strip-like secondary bubbles upon detachment. Under inclined conditions, hydrophobic surfaces exhibit significantly higher bubble sliding velocities compared to hydrophilic ones. Acoustically, the sound pressure amplitude during bubble detachment is governed by the competition between edge anchoring and inertial effects. Despite their smaller detachment volume, bubbles on hydrophilic plates generate higher acoustic amplitudes than those on hydrophobic plates, because strong contact line pinning intensifies the neck contraction. Conversely, at steeper inclinations (α = 28°), elevated sliding velocities augment inertial forces, thereby disrupting the neck rupture process and attenuating the acoustic signal. These findings provide new insights into near-wall bubble kinetics and validate passive acoustic monitoring as a robust tool for characterizing bubble–surface interactions.

papers.title: Wettability-regulated dynamics of floating spheres: From jet entrapment to inertial repulsion
papers.abstract: The attachment of a liquid jet to a convex surface is a well-established phenomenon that typically results in fluid adherence. This study reports a distinct regime demonstrating that the wettability of the floating curved surface is a key parameter determining whether the impinging jet and the curved surface undergo attraction or repulsion. On the hydrophilic sphere, flow attachment creates a restoring force that traps and centers the sphere beneath the jet. Conversely, the superhydrophobic sphere induces rapid fluid rebound and reflection, which inverts the momentum transfer and generates a significant repulsive force. Experimental analysis using high-speed imaging and force measurements reveals that this superhydrophobic repulsion is governed by the jet's impact location and inertial momentum flux. Theoretical models based on elastic collision and momentum conservation are derived, which agree with the experiments. These findings identify superhydrophobicity as a passive mechanism for the manipulation of the motion of floating objects.

papers.title: Migration dynamics and hydrodynamic resistance of elastic vesicles in deformable stenosed arteries: A fluid–structure interaction study
papers.abstract: Understanding vesicle dynamics in stenosed arteries is essential for interpreting pathological hemodynamics relevant to cardiovascular health and drug delivery. This study presents a coupled arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian and phase-field model to simulate elastic vesicle transport through a deformable stenosed artery, resolving two-way fluid–structure interactions under physiologically relevant conditions. We systematically examine the influence of stenosis geometry, severity, wall stiffness, vesicle size, membrane elasticity, and fluid rheology. Results reveal that stenosis shape strongly modulates flow and vesicle dynamics. Elliptical stenosis induces the highest vesicle velocity, pressure, and arterial wall deformation and also the greatest hydraulic resistance due to abrupt narrowing and reduced lubrication film thickness. In contrast, sinusoidal stenosis maintains sustained shear interaction along the stenotic length, leading to a 64% increase in wall shear stress and a 13.7% increase in vesicle membrane strain energy while preserving a thicker lubrication layer and exhibiting the lowest hydraulic resistance, which may mitigate hemolysis and vesicle–wall adhesion. Increasing stenosis severity from 30% to 80% causes strong nonlinear amplification of vesicle velocity (≈99%), pressure (≈111%), wall shear stress (≈125%), membrane stress (≈207.5%), and strain energy (≈659%), accompanied by a substantial reduction in lubrication film thickness (≈53%), migration (≈39%), and relaxation time (≈10%). Arterial wall stiffening further intensifies vesicle transport, increasing vesicle velocity and pressure by approximately 64.2% and 89.5%, respectively, while rigid arterial walls result in a nearly 36-fold increase in vesicle strain energy and a 7.65-fold rise in hydraulic resistance. Vesicle size and membrane elasticity significantly influence deformation dynamics: larger vesicles and stiffer membranes experience sharper stress concentrations and thinner lubrication layers, whereas softer membranes store greater elastic energy and exhibit slower recovery. Additionally, shear-thinning blood rheology enhances near-wall velocity gradients, leading to elevated pressure and wall shear stress levels. Overall, this study bridges a critical gap in modeling vesicle dynamics within deformable stenosed microchannels and provides quantitative insight into cardiovascular biomechanics, atherosclerosis-related transport phenomena, and the optimization of vesicle-based drug delivery systems.

papers.title: A compressible linear theory of Richtmyer–Meshkov unstable interfaces propagating along cylindrical tubes
papers.abstract: We develop a linear compressible theory for Richtmyer–Meshkov unstable interfaces propagating along cylindrical tubes. In contrast to classical planar periodic systems, the cylindrical geometry introduces non-periodic boundary conditions and produces distinct features in interface morphology and growth dynamics. Using a complete eigenfunction expansion based on Bessel modes, we derive the linear evolution equations for arbitrary initial interface shapes and study the growth rates and mode amplitudes. The analysis reveals qualitatively new fingering patterns, including substructures associated with each fundamental mode, which is a feature absent in periodic geometries. We also identify a universal scaling relation that collapses the growth rates and amplitudes of all cylindrical-tube fundamental modes onto a single curve and provides a direct mapping to the two-dimensional periodic case. The results of this study form a key step toward a comprehensive quantitative nonlinear theory of Richtmyer–Meshkov unstable interfaces between compressible fluids of arbitrary density ratios in cylindrical geometries from early to late times.

papers.title: Distinct flow instability mechanisms in a variable cycle engine fan: Decoupling analysis of backpressure at the different outlets
papers.abstract: Variable cycle engines (VCEs) are the core technology of the next-generation military aero-engines. As a key component of VCEs, the compression system is one of the critical factors restricting the overall performance of the VCEs. To investigate the flow instability mechanisms of the compression system in VCEs under different throttling modes, a dual-flow fan was selected as the research object in this study. By employing a throttling method that fixes the backpressure at one outlet while gradually increasing the backpressure at the other outlet, this study systematically studied the flow instability mechanisms of the dual-flow fan under different throttling modes. The results indicate that the flow instability mechanisms of the dual-flow fan differ significantly depending on the throttling mode. During bypass flow throttling, the flow instability originates in the front fan (F-Fan), whereas during core flow throttling, the initial instability position shifts to the aft fan in the inner bypass. The key criterion for determining whether the initial instability position is located in the F-Fan is whether the static pressure at the F-Fan outlet exceeds “F-Fan instability static pressure” (obtained by calculating the F-Fan separately). Furthermore, the initial instability position in the studied dual-flow fan is independent of the outlet backpressure of the initial operating condition. Specifically, during bypass flow throttling, the flow instability always occurs in the F-Fan, and during core flow throttling, it always occurs in the aft fan. This study further refines the theoretical framework for flow instability in VCE compression systems and provides valuable insights for addressing potential stability issues and designing flow control strategies.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics of nonplanar quadrotors with rotor failure
papers.abstract: This study investigates the aerodynamic performance of a nonplanar quadrotor subject to one rotor failure. Experiments (α = 0°–50°) and computational fluid dynamics simulations reveal a counter-intuitive “Aerodynamic Relief” phenomenon, where the gains in Thrust Coefficient and Figure of Merit for the remaining rotors reach or approach their peak values at α = 20°. Numerical analysis elucidates that this relief effect stems from a geometric threshold that triggers a topological transition from a “blocked” to a “vented” state. At this critical angle, the tilted geometry effectively “directs” the high-momentum downwash away from adjacent disks and the central airframe, facilitating significant blockage release. This redirection triggers a pressure-gradient-driven flow and lateral stream tube expansion into the failure void. This flow reconfiguration reduces induced velocity and redistributes blade loading, where a substantial load surge at the blade tips (r/R = 0.95) outweighs inboard (r/R = 0.75) unloading. These findings provide a fluid dynamic basis for utilizing passive flow control to enhance fault tolerance unmanned aerial vehicle.

papers.title: Linear and nonlinear rheology of unentangled telechelic ionomers: Effects of cation species
papers.abstract: This work aims to investigate the effects of counterion species, including sodium, cesium, and zinc ions, in unentangled telechelic ionomers based on carboxylate groups on linear viscoelasticity and nonlinear rheological responses in both shear and extensional flows. The linear viscoelastic response of the telechelic ionomers reveals the presence of “superbridges” structures composed of linearly associated sequences of ionomer chains. During nonlinear shear response, the sodium-containing ionomer demonstrates a more significant stress decay after the overshoot compared to the prepolymer and the cesium/zinc-containing ionomers. This could be due to the stress-bearing network strand being sufficiently stretched when the ions are pulled out from the strong ionic aggregates of carboxylate sodium, leading to a stronger chain retraction following the strain-induced rupture of aggregates. In addition, compared to prepolymers, the ionomers neutralized by various cations display stronger damping responses, and the damping behavior is highly dependent on the association strength of cation species. In extensional flow, the sodium-containing ionomer shows more significant strain hardening compared to other ionomers as expected, also due to its stronger ionic aggregates. These findings highlight the significant impact of the association strength of cation species on the rheological behavior of these polymers, which offers valuable insights for optimizing the processability of these materials.

papers.title: Electromagnetic effects of magnetic field deformation on a hypersonic shock
papers.abstract: In reentry environments, the magnetic Reynolds number can exceed unity within the shock layer. Consequently, the low magnetic Reynolds number approximation (LMHD), which neglects magnetic field deformation, may yield inaccurate predictions of electromagnetic effects. To investigate this, we study the impact of an applied magnetic field on thermochemical nonequilibrium flow in a hypersonic moving shock environment. A thermochemical nonequilibrium three-temperature model and resistive magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) model, which account for magnetic field deformation, were employed. Numerical stiffness upstream of the shock was effectively mitigated by accounting for photoionization effects. Analysis of a moving shock at an altitude of 70 km and Mach number 40 under perpendicular magnetic fields confirmed that magnetic field deformation is non-negligible. This deformation supplied momentum and energy to the flow via the Lorentz force and Joule heating, accelerating the shock speed and increasing the temperature. Notably, as the magnetic field strength increased, the control efficiency via electromagnetic effects decreased once the flow entered the submagnetoacoustic region. Furthermore, the results confirmed that the LMHD model fails to satisfy Galilean invariance, resulting in frame-dependent predictions of the Lorentz force. Although the LMHD model can approximate RMHD results via a Galilean transformation under limited conditions, these findings underscore the need to account for magnetic field deformation in hypersonic environments. These results demonstrate that magnetic field deformation cannot be neglected for the precise prediction of electromagnetic effects in hypersonic shock environments.

papers.title: Investigation of deflagration characteristics of lean premixed hydrogen–air mixtures in a semi-confined duct
papers.abstract: To evaluate the hazards of lean premixed hydrogen explosions, multiple experimental conditions were investigated in a small-scale duct. The effects of lean hydrogen equivalence ratio, obstacle blockage ratio, and number of obstacles on flame propagation and overpressure were systematically examined. The results show that at low equivalence ratios, flame propagation transitions sequentially through hemispherical, finger, planar, and distorted tulip stages. However, at 0.65 and 0.7 equivalence ratios, only hemispherical and finger-phase flames are observed, which is due to increasing laminar flame speed. Deflagration behavior was strongly influenced by the hydrogen equivalence ratio. Accordingly, fundamental fuel parameters, flame instability, and chemical kinetics at different equivalence ratios were analyzed. Furthermore, the greater the obstacle blockage ratio, the greater the turbulence generated, which significantly increases the combustion rate of the mixture and overpressure. Consequently, both deflagration intensity and maximum overpressure significantly increased.

papers.title: Principal aerodynamic mechanisms in phonatory flow
papers.abstract: This article presents high-fidelity simulations of fully coupled interaction between a slightly compressible fluid and the compliant vocal folds through which it flows. The focus here is identification of the dominant aerodynamic mechanisms in phonation. The modified Immersed Finite Element Method is used to compute self-sustained vibration of three-layer, viscoelastic model vocal folds with a skewed elliptical shape. Simulations, performed for Reh= 2350 and reduced frequency f*= 0.11, and driven by a lung pressure of 1 kPa, were used to estimate terms of the integral mass conservation, momentum, and mechanical energy equations, as well the Bernoulli equation. The vocal folds vibrated at 227 Hz, with subharmonic modulation. Analysis of the surface motion showed three modes that captured >99% of the energy. Analysis using the integral equations shows that the aerodynamics is essentially described by a balance between pressure drag on the vocal folds and the pressure force pushing fluid through the vocal folds. Furthermore, it was shown that fluid dynamic friction is always negligible compared to the pressure forces. Flow work comprised the energetic input, and the primary output was the work on the vocal folds (21% of input), with losses comprising 70% of input. Analysis of the Bernoulli equation shows that the flow is inherently unsteady at the beginning and end of a vibration cycle, when the vocal folds are nearly closed, and that, in the jet flow region, the unsteady and convective accelerations nearly offset one another. These results are consistent with those from driven wall experiments.

papers.title: Quantifying transition predictability: Statistical mapping from initial disturbances to transition onset
papers.abstract: Laminar–turbulent transition in boundary layers remains a fundamental challenge, governed by the interplay between external disturbances and nonlinear interactions of perturbations. Quantitative links between similar disturbances and similar transition positions, however, remain elusive. A data-driven framework is proposed to connect the initial disturbance characteristics with transition behavior and to identify the universal features underlying the transition process. Large-scale datasets of flat-plate boundary-layer transition (K-type and H-type) were generated using the nonlinear parabolized stability equations. K-means clustering quantified correlations between initial conditions [frequency, spanwise wavenumber, and two-dimensional (2D)/three-dimensional (3D) amplitudes] and transition onset, defined by the rise in the skin-friction coefficient Cf. A modified Residual Network (ResNet) 18, trained with clustering-derived pseudo-labels, combined with Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping, identified transition-relevant features. The results show that similar initial conditions yield clustered transition locations (Pearson correlation coefficient r=0.834; maximum entropy 1.062), indicating strong predictability, while dissimilar conditions may lead to similar transitions (r=0.019), revealing a many-to-one mapping. K-type and H-type transitions share core dynamics, including 2D Tollmien–Schlichting waves, Λ-vortices, and spanwise periodicity. The Convolutional Neural Network achieved 97% validation accuracy. This study establishes bidirectional correlations between initial disturbances and transition responses, and reveals universal structural features of the transition, offering a quantitative foundation for data-driven prediction and control of boundary-layer transition.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of the thermodynamic and hydrodynamic effects on viscous fingering in partially miscible systems
papers.abstract: The displacement of a more viscous fluid by a less viscous fluid in porous media or Hele–Shaw cells exhibits fingerlike interfacial patterns known as viscous fingering (VF). Classically, VF dynamics are divided into two categories depending on whether the fluids are fully miscible or immiscible. Recently, attention has been drawn to a third category, namely, VF in partially miscible systems. Our previous numerical study showed that, in such systems, VF patterns can transition to multiple droplet patterns with certain values of parameters. In the present work, we numerically investigate the effects of seven key parameters on partially miscible VF dynamics: (i) Péclet number, (ii) log-mobility ratio, (iii) Korteweg force, (iv) interfacial energy, (v) and (vi) two transport parameters governing mass transfer, and (vii) a parameter for the bulk free energy. We find that fingering patterns are primarily governed by the hydrodynamic parameters (i) and (ii) and the chemical–thermodynamic parameters (iii) and (iv), whereas droplet patterns are mainly controlled by the chemical–thermodynamic parameters (v), (vi), and (vii). This parametric study contributes to improved prediction and control of processes such as enhanced oil recovery and CO2 sequestration, where partially miscible systems arise under high temperature and pressure.

papers.title: Rigid body rotation and chiral reorientation combine in filamentous E. coli swimming in low-Re flows
papers.abstract: When treated with doses of antibiotics below the minimum inhibitory concentration, bacterial cell division turns off, but cell growth does not. As a result, rod-like bacteria, including E. coli, can elongate many times their original length without increasing their width. The swimming behavior of these filamentous bacteria through small channels may provide insights into how bacteria that survive antibiotic treatment can reach channel walls. Such swimming behaviors in settings like hospital tubing may signal precursors to adhesion, biofilm formation, and infection. Despite the importance of understanding the behavior of bacteria not killed by antibiotics, the hydrodynamics of filamentous bacteria swimming in external flows has not received much attention. We study the swimming behavior of stressed, filamentous E. coli. In quiescence, highly elongated E. coli swim with a sinusoidal undulating motion, suggesting rigid body rotation of long, rigid, buckled cell bodies. In low Reynolds number pressure-driven flows through a microchannel, the undulating motion becomes irregular; it may even stop and start within a particular bacterial trajectory. We refer to this behavior in flow as “wiggling.” Rigid body rotation persists in flow, appearing as a high-frequency change in body orientation on top of a slower one. Chiral reorientation can explain the slower reorientation frequency. We quantify swimming behaviors in two different flow rates and observe rheotaxis in addition to the preferential orientation of bacterial bodies. Faster flow constrains wiggling bacteria trajectories and orientations compared to those observed in slower flow, with rheotaxis taking bacteria toward the wall. Interestingly, not all bacteria in flow wiggle. Populations of non-motile “non-wiggling” filamentous E. coli follow streamlines, without preferential alignment of their orientation. Non-motile bacteria do not behave like chiral rods propelled and rotated by flagellar bundles, but like rigid rods. Motility slows the swimmers in comparison. Differentiating these two populations may have important implications for understanding consequences of motility loss that inevitably occurs as bacteria die.

papers.title: Magnetohydrodynamic hybrid blood nanofluid flow and heat transfer in a bifurcated stenosed artery with slip effects
papers.abstract: Atherosclerosis is a chronic disease caused by the accumulation of plaques on arterial walls, leading to wall damage and narrowing of vessels that supply blood to body tissues. This paper provides a computational aspect for magnetohydrodynamic (MHD), slip, and no-slip hybrid nanofluid flow through a stenosed bifurcated artery. A hybrid nanofluid containing iron oxide and gold nanoparticles suspended in blood is developed to analyze the influence of an externally generated transverse magnetic field on flow regulation. The nonlinear partial differential equations of the model are solved by employing the Galerkin finite element method, which is implemented in COMSOL Multiphysics. The impacts of magnetic field strength, slip and no-slip boundary constraints, and nanoparticle concentration affect velocity, pressure, and thermal distributions. The results indicate that the presence of magnetic field suppresses velocity fluctuations and stabilizes flow, while the hybrid nanoparticles enhance heat transfer and promote smoother uniform velocity profiles. This slip boundary condition significantly reduces wall shear stress compared with the no-slip constraint and allows for more physiologically realistic flow. With respect to the MHD and hybrid nanoparticles, the recirculation zones are further suppressed, resulting in the recovery of flow symmetry. Biomedical applications of gold and iron oxide nanoparticles are categorized into three main areas: targeted drug delivery field, localized hyperthermia, and improved therapy for arterial diseases such as atherosclerosis and thrombosis.

papers.title: Velocity field reconstruction of buoyancy-driven convection flow based on synthetic temperature data of background-oriented schlieren technique
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a cost-effective data assimilation framework for reconstructing the velocity field in turbulent natural convection within enclosed geometries. Accurate flow characterization often faces challenges due to unknown or inaccessible thermal boundary conditions. The proposed method combines experimental measurements with numerical simulations by introducing the measured data as a source term in the Navier–Stokes equations. This approach eliminates the need for explicit thermal boundary conditions, which are often unavailable in practical experiments. To validate the proposed method, synthetic background-oriented schlieren data are generated for both laminar and turbulent natural convection benchmarks. For the laminar differentially heated cavity, the framework demonstrates high reconstruction accuracy and robustness against Gaussian noise and near-wall data loss. For turbulent convection, benchmark data from the European Research Community on Flow, Turbulence and Combustion Classic Database are utilized, and the Reynolds stress model (RSM) serves as the ground truth to evaluate the reconstruction performance of three eddy-viscosity turbulence models: k–ε, k–ω, and k–ω shear stress transport. Results indicate that the k–ω family model achieves the best agreement, successfully reproducing complex flow topologies, including secondary corner vortices inherent to the RSM benchmark. Furthermore, a computational performance analysis reveals that the proposed framework, implementing a Coupled pressure–velocity algorithm, significantly mitigates source term stiffness, reducing computation time by approximately 12.5 times compared to traditional computational fluid dynamics. These findings confirm that the framework offers a reliable and efficient approach for integrating optical measurements into thermal–fluid analysis.

papers.title: Droplet impact characteristics on sinusoidal wavy micro-structured hydrophobic surfaces
papers.abstract: The dynamics of an impacting droplet can be controlled by microstructuring the surface. This work presents a numerical investigation of droplet impact characteristics on a hydrophobic surface microstructured with sinusoidal wavy patterns. The effects of amplitude and wavelength of the wavy surfaces on droplet deformation are analyzed for different impact velocities. A dynamic contact angle model is incorporated into the numerical method to track the three-phase contact line accurately. The influence of the Weber number on the wettability transition is analyzed, and the flow characteristics inside the droplet at different flow regimes are explained. A regime map is prepared to show the transition between different regimes for different surface attributes and Weber numbers. The initial contact of the impacting droplet with the surface is influenced by the amplitude and wavelength of the roughness element, leading to different wettability states. The Wenzel (wetting), Cassie (non-wetting), and mixed wetting states affect the droplet's spreading, recoiling, and rebound characteristics. The Cassie state of a plane surface is transformed into the Wenzel state due to microstructuring the surface with small amplitude and wavelength. A further increase in amplitude and wavelength leads to a transition from the Wenzel state to a mixed state, and finally from the mixed state to the Cassie state. The amplitude-controlled mixed state results in partial rebound of the droplet, whereas the wavelength-controlled state results in partial rebound and rebound with droplet breakup. The study may aid in designing droplet retention surfaces required for practical applications.

papers.title: Modeling and experimental investigation of compression and jamming behavior in shear thickening fluids
papers.abstract: Shear thickening fluid (STF) is a class of smart fluid that transitions from a liquid to a solid-like state when subjected to external forces. This solid-like state, known as the jamming state, has led to widespread applications in protective fields. However, the mechanisms by which STF, when integrated into structural forms with very thin liquid layers, enhances the mechanical performance of the structure remain underexplored. This study aims to investigate the transition between the jamming and liquid states of STF under compression. Plane compression tests reveal a critical loading speed for the state transition of STF. When the loading speed is lower than 30 mm/min, the STF responds predominantly in a liquid-like flow regime. In contrast, loading speeds above 30 mm/min trigger a transition into the jamming state. Additionally, a new theoretical model is developed to describe STF's compression response, considering the spatial distribution of the different states within the material. By combining theoretical and experimental results, the analysis identifies normal stress and the high-viscosity area ratio (HVAR) as key indicators for distinguishing the different states of STF. The occurrence of the jamming state is found to require an initial normal stress greater than 5 Pa and an initial HVAR exceeding 5%. This study enhances the understanding of the jamming mechanism in STF and provides theoretical support for the design of protective structures utilizing STF's solid–liquid phase transition characteristics.

papers.title: Impact dynamics of viscous droplets on inclined patterned superhydrophobic surfaces
papers.abstract: Bio-inspired doubly re-entrant surfaces exhibit exceptional droplet repellency; however, the impact dynamics of viscous droplets and the distinct roles of normal and tangential velocity components during droplet impact remain insufficiently explored. To address this, we fabricated surfaces featuring four distinct microscale patterns. The repellency of these surfaces to three impacting viscous droplets (viscosity range: 1–20 mPa s) was systematically evaluated. By varying the normal and tangential velocity components while maintaining a constant impact speed of 3 m/s, we achieved a wide range of normal and tangential Weber numbers, from 0 to 368. Results show markedly different maximum spreading ratios between rebound-capable and non-rebound surfaces, primarily governed by initial pinning conditions. On rebound-enabled surfaces (samples I and II), the redistribution of momentum from normal to tangential directions leads to opposing spreading behaviors in inertial vs viscous droplets. This divergence, which contrasts with prior theoretical models, arises from dynamic shifts in the balance between sliding velocity and viscous depinning forces. Through suspension pressure analysis, we further demonstrate that capillary forces can be optimally utilized at inclination angles below 60°. Moreover, we extend the conventional inertial–capillary contact time scaling model by incorporating a correction coefficient that accounts for viscous effects. This modification effectively normalizes the spreading dynamics of viscous droplets to a nearly constant value at a certain impact velocity. These insights contribute to the rational design of patterned superhydrophobic surfaces for applications such as anti-icing systems and microfluidic precision droplet control.

papers.title: Diffusive stabilization of density-driven instability in contaminated aquifers: Analytical and numerical study
papers.abstract: Density-driven convective instabilities in porous media control the migration of contaminant plumes in aquifers. We present a comprehensive theoretical and numerical study of miscible Rayleigh–Taylor instability in unbounded porous media, where diffusion acts as a strong stabilizing mechanism that delays instability onset. Using a modified quasi-steady state approximation, we derive analytical expressions for the critical time and the wavelength of maximum growth. The analytical solution is obtained using a piecewise-linear approximation of the diffusive concentration profile. Despite this simplification, the theory accurately predicts the critical time for instability onset. Direct numerical simulations validate the theory in critical time prediction and agreement in growth rates during the linear regime. The results provide quantitative criteria for assessing when density-driven instabilities become significant in contaminated aquifers, informing monitoring network design, remediation strategy selection, and long-term risk assessment for groundwater protection.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of cavitation dynamics at mesoscale and microscale in swirled and non-swirled venturi tubes
papers.abstract: Hydrodynamic cavitation has been widely used in various applications, namely, peening, surface cleaning, and wastewater treatment. Recent studies have demonstrated that introducing swirl in hydrodynamic cavitation can substantially enhance process efficiency. However, a knowledge gap remains regarding the comparative characteristics of hydrodynamic cavitation in swirled and non-swirled flows at the mesoscale and microscale. In this study, we utilize shadowgraph and high-speed phase-contrast x-ray imaging techniques alongside spectral proper orthogonal decomposition to resolve such characteristics in venturi tubes. The analyses show that imposing swirl reduces the hydraulic power delivered by the pump to initiate cavitation by 71.9%. It also makes the cavitating length of the flow less dependent on the operating condition. Investigations indicate that the non-swirled venturi tube is dominated by sheet cavitation followed by cloud cavitation. Introducing swirl shifts the cavitation toward the cloud regime established at the center of the tube while changing the coherent motions of the cavitating flow. In non-swirled flow, coherent motions are dominated by disk-like structures, while in the swirled flow, they include helical and double-helical coherent structures. Both mesoscale and microscale analyses reveal that swirl shifts the cavitation dynamics toward low-frequency coherent motions. Microscale results suggest that microbubbles from cavitation cloud collapse could trigger cavitation when they are involved in high-velocity motions.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of drag coefficient and hydrodynamics of bubbly flow in two-scale bubble column
papers.abstract: Bubbly flow inside a lab-scale bubble column reactor with continuous air feedstock is numerically predicted by presenting the two-fluid model approach coupled with the RNG k–ε method in which the motion of the gas and liquid phases are tracked in the Eulerian–Eulerian frameworks. After validation, the visualization of the hydrodynamics and drag coefficient to bubble diameter ratio (Cd/db) is analyzed, together with the comprehensive discussion of the impacts of the inter-phase interaction forces, apparatus geometrics, and operating parameters. The results indicate that considering both drag and lift forces simultaneously provides improved simulation accuracy, especially in the lower portion of the apparatus. The value of Cd/db increases with increasing height to depth (H/D) ratio of the bubble column. Increasing sparger numbers intensifies liquid circulation but slightly decreases gas holdup. Larger bubbles suppress stagnation zones and improve mixing efficiency. The normalized drag coefficient Cd/db increases with both gas superficial velocity and column aspect ratio, reflecting stronger bubble–liquid momentum coupling under enhanced aeration. Insights into the properties of multiphase interactions in reactors provide a theoretical basis for optimizing fluid dynamics in industrial processes.

papers.title: Broadband low-frequency acoustic absorption using a compact tapered helical duct
papers.abstract: We propose a tapered helical duct absorber with power-law geometric gradients to control low-frequency acoustic waves in a fluid medium. The structure functions as a non-uniform acoustic waveguide, achieving both graded impedance matching and an extended propagation path for enhanced wave energy dissipation. The absorber is modeled using the transfer matrix method and validated through finite element simulations and experiments on two samples with different geometric parameters. The numerical and experimental results agree well with theoretical predictions. Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate that a concurrent power-law decrease in pitch and increase in diameter synergistically improves low-frequency attenuation and broadens the effective bandwidth, through enhanced impedance matching and a prolonged acoustic path. This work provides a fluid-dynamic perspective on the design of compact waveguide structures for efficient acoustic energy control in confined environments.

papers.title: Experimental characterization of multimodal flow features in cavity-induced flapping jets
papers.abstract: In this study, the flow features of flapping jets previously proposed are systematically characterized. Instantaneous pressure fields across cavities were measured using fast-response pressure-sensitive paint and denoised. The jet oscillations were primarily induced by the instability of the shear layer and the propagation of compression waves generated by vortex impact on the trailing edge. A spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) analysis was also performed, the dominant spatial modes at spectral peaks were extracted. SPOD revealed that the dominant frequency was generated by the feedback flapping motion. The first-mode frequency transitioned from the first feedback flapping mode to the transverse acoustic resonance mode with increasing cavity length. The harmonics associated with the first mode of feedback flapping motion were generated by large-scale axisymmetric vortex shedding. Subharmonic modes at approximately half the first-mode frequency were observed for all cavity lengths, exhibiting symmetric flow structures. The pressure oscillations generated by three flapping jet devices with different scales were measured, and the dimensionless spectra were derived for various normalized cavity lengths. A modified prediction model reproduced the spectral peaks at various pressure ratios with higher accuracy than the previous model. The spectral peaks corresponding to the first and second modes of feedback flapping motion and the transverse acoustic resonance modes were identified. The effect of the Reynolds number and the pressure ratio on the oscillation frequency was investigated. The Reynolds number and pressure ratio affect high-order mode energy, oscillation thresholds, and mode transitions but have only a slight effect on dimensionless peak frequencies.

papers.title: The impact of rear cover plate cutting on the degree of gas–liquid mixing in centrifugal pumps
papers.abstract: To enhance the conveying capacity of semi-open gas–liquid centrifugal pumps under high inlet gas volume fraction (IGVF), a systematic investigation was conducted to reveal the mechanisms by which different rear cover plate cutting designs affect the gas–liquid mixing degree. At low IGVF (≤9%), the performance of the original pump Y1 outperforms the modified rear cover plate pumps SL1 (Slice Plan 1) and SL2 (Slice Plan 2). In contrast, at high IGVF (>9%), the performance of pumps SL1 and SL2 was found to be significantly better than the pump Y1. The analysis of gas–liquid mixing degree (λ) showed that, at IGVF = 12%, the λ value of pump SL1 reached 0.86. For pumps SL2 and Y1, the λ values were 0.76 and 0.846, respectively. It was thereby demonstrated that the rear cover plate cutting configurations enabled more thorough gas–liquid mixing. At different blade heights (Span), the energy dissipation degree (σ) of pump SL1 was found to be the lowest. That of pump SL2 was higher than SL1 but still lower than Y1. The energy dissipation degree of the original pump Y1 was significantly higher than those of the two optimized models. Compared to the original model, at an IGVF of 12%, SL1 shows increases in pump head and hydraulic efficiency by 7.01 m and 12.7%, respectively, with corresponding increases of 6.47 m and11.8% for SL2. This study provided valuable implications for improving the mixing uniformity, pump head, and hydraulic efficiency of centrifugal pump operating under high IGVF conditions.

papers.title: Dawn–dusk asymmetry of MLT middle- and low-latitude temperature responses to super geomagnetic storms
papers.abstract: At high latitudes, storm-time temperature enhancements in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT, ∼90–110 km) typically exhibit a pronounced dawn–dusk asymmetry, characterized by weaker warming on the dawn side and stronger warming on the dusk side. However, whether similar patterns and their underlying mechanisms extend to mid- and low latitudes remains unclear. Using the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model, this study investigates the atmospheric dynamical and thermodynamical variations during the Mother's Day superstorm (10–14 May 2024). The simulations reveal that in the mid- to low-latitude MLT regions, the dawn side warms by over 40 K while the dusk side stays under 20 K, with the Southern Hemisphere warming more overall but the Northern Hemisphere exhibiting a sharper dawn–dusk contrast. These results agree well with measurements from the Sounding of the Atmosphere using Broadband Emission Radiometry instrument aboard the Thermosphere, Ionosphere, Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics satellite. Moreover, the simulations further reveal that the pronounced dawn-side heating is driven by steady, storm-induced downward winds powered by a continuous equatorward meridional flow that persists even as the storm weakens, whereas dusk-side downflows are brief and reverse during recovery due to competing wind patterns. To our knowledge, this study is the first to identify the physical mechanisms underlying the opposing dawn–dusk asymmetry in storm-time MLT temperature responses at mid-low and high latitudes, offering new insight into MLT dynamics under extreme space weather and potentially facilitating the advancement of predictive models.

papers.title: Bouncing dynamics of impacting unequal-sized sessile droplets: An atom-level study
papers.abstract: The dynamic behavior of nanodroplets impacting unequal-sized sessile droplets has a wide range of applications in engineering, including anti-erosion, anti-icing, and self-cleaning. This study employs molecular dynamics simulation to investigate the dynamic behavior of a nanodroplet impacting another unequal-sized sessile droplet. The time evolutions of the spreading factors are used to analyze the particular dynamic behaviors and elucidate the underlying physics. A new extended scaling law βmax ∼ ηWe1/2Re1/5 characterizes the relationship between the maximum spreading radius βmax and the ratio of droplet radius η, Weber number We, and Reynolds number Re. The ratio of the contact time of unequal-sized droplet impact to that of a single droplet impact decreases with the increase in η, with a slope of −1/2 when η < 1 and −20/7 when η > 1. The two conditions intersect at 1.414 when η = 1, representing equal-sized droplet-on-droplet impact, which agrees with previous macro-scale droplet impact studies. Two boundaries are identified to discriminate among three outcomes: deposition, bouncing, and splashing, which are highly dependent on both the impacting velocities and the ratio of droplet radius. The conclusion of this article can lay a theoretical foundation for effectively manipulating nanoscale droplets. The research findings can provide theoretical guidance for engineering fields such as anti-icing coating design, micro-droplet printing, and spray cooling.

papers.title: Topology of direct simulation Monte Carlo constitutive relations for neural network-accelerated finite-volume solutions of velocity-shear flows
papers.abstract: A novel framework for modeling non-equilibrium gas flows was recently introduced by Garg et al. [“Neural network-based finite volume method and direct simulation Monte Carlo solutions of non-equilibrium shock flow guided by nonlinear coupled constitutive relations,” Phys. Fluids 36, 106113 (2024) and “Fast neural network-based direct simulation Monte Carlo solutions of shock flow of diatomic gases with vibrational modes,” Phys. Fluids 37, 076105 (2025)], in which a pre-trained deep neural network (DNN) machine learning (ML) model of constitutive relations, learned from direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) data, was embedded into a finite volume method (FVM) solver, enabling the accurate reproduction of shock structures at a fraction of the computational cost. Both studies, however, focused solely on the compressive flow regime. The present study extends this framework to the velocity-shear flow regime for monatomic gases. Using DSMC data (up to Mach number 20, Knudsen number 50) for one-dimensional Couette flow, the topology of the constraints in the constitutive relations governing viscous stresses and heat fluxes is analyzed and compared with that of the nonlinear coupled constitutive relation (NCCR) theory. Building on this topological analysis, a comprehensive FVM-DSMC-ML framework is developed that integrates a DNN-based model of DSMC constitutive relations, specifically designed for velocity-shear dominated flows, within the FVM approach. The DNN model incorporates DSMC data to ensure generality and accuracy. The FVM-DSMC-ML framework also employs the modified Maxwell and Smoluchowski boundary conditions introduced by Myong [“Theoretical description of the gaseous Knudsen layer in Couette flow based on the second-order constitutive and slip-jump models,” Phys. Fluids 28, 012002 (2016)], whose coefficients are further refined using DSMC data. The resulting FVM-DSMC-ML solver demonstrates excellent agreement with DSMC predictions while reducing computational cost to approximately 1/15 that of conventional DSMC simulations. This study provides new physical insight into non-equilibrium velocity-shear flows and represents an important advance toward data-driven constitutive modeling in such regimes.

papers.title: Optical flow image warping method based on a Runge–Kutta deformation field
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measurements in complex flows are fundamentally limited by systematic errors induced by particle trajectory curvature, which are inadequately modeled by conventional straight-line displacement assumptions. To address this limitation, we propose a Runge–Kutta forward diffeomorphic deformation interrogation (RK-FDDI) framework that explicitly incorporates curved particle trajectories into the image warping process, in which displacement compensation is performed along particle trajectories rather than being approximated by instantaneous velocity vectors. A hybrid-norm adaptive step-size strategy is further introduced to balance global flow smoothness and local curvature intensity. The deformation-compensated images are progressively refined via optical-flow iterations, allowing subpixel in-plane motion compensation and enhanced recovery of fine-scale flow structures. Extensive evaluations were conducted on synthetic particle image pairs generated from multiple flow fields, spanning various curvature intensities, particle concentrations, and particle diameters. Compared with forward-difference interrogation with post-correction (FDI2CDI) and forward diffeomorphic deformation interrogation (FDDI), RK-FDDI demonstrates improved robustness and higher accuracy. In the sea surface flow, the root mean square error is reduced by 21.89% and 20.71% relative to FDI2CDI and FDDI, respectively. As the curvature increases, RK-FDDI suppresses the error growth observed in FDDI, achieving a maximum reduction of 25.7%. RK-FDDI maintains consistently low errors across different particle concentrations and particle diameters, with particularly improved performance at a concentration of six particles per interrogation window and particle diameters around three pixels. Furthermore, experimental validation based on a 2D PIV system shows that RK-FDDI reliably recovers flow features in real measurements, confirming its applicability to achieve high-accuracy velocity reconstruction for complex flows.

papers.title: Atomistic simulation of the combustion of pyrolysis gases derived from silicone-modified phenolic nanocomposites
papers.abstract: This study employs reactive molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the gas-phase combustion behavior of pyrolysis gases released from silicone-modified phenolic nanocomposites under high-temperature conditions relevant to atmospheric and Martian reentry. The effects of composite density, ambient oxygen content, and environmental gases (atomic O/N, O2, CO2) on combustion kinetics and reaction pathways are systematically analyzed. Results reveal that lower-density composites exhibit more intense gas-phase combustion, releasing greater heat and producing more low-molecular-weight hydrocarbons. Key reaction pathways for H2, CH4, H2O, and CO formation are identified, and activation energies for dominant mechanisms are quantified. Surface effects promote the emission of gaseous products, while volume ablation favors solid residue formation. These findings provide atomic-scale insights into pyrolysis gas combustion, supporting the development of high-fidelity ablation models for thermal protection systems.

papers.title: Reacting hydrogen jet in crossflow—Flame dynamics under acoustic forcing
papers.abstract: This paper presents an experimental study of reacting hydrogen jet in crossflow (JIC). High-speed shadowgraph images are used to capture flame dynamics. The flame jet is first compared with non-reacting helium JIC. It is observed that the vortical structures that are present densely in helium jets are significantly reduced in the hydrogen jet. Furthermore, unforced jets with various velocity ratios are studied. It is noted that jet penetration increases with the jet to crossflow momentum ratio. Proper orthogonal decomposition analysis is used to characterize the spatiotemporal behavior of the reacting jet. Furthermore, the jet is acoustically forced with a range of frequencies and it is observed that the flame response is more prominent for higher forcing frequencies. This aspect is further explored using Kelvin–Helmholtz instability analysis. It is noticed that a higher velocity ratio produces stronger interaction with the crossflow, which dampens the effect of forcing. A novel interface tracking method is used to characterize the shear layer instability from shadowgraphy images. This is perhaps the first attempt where high-speed shadowgraphy images are used to obtain quantitative information on the shear layer, which also compares well with theoretical analysis. This paper also presents the first experimental study of forced hydrogen flame jet in crossflow configuration.

papers.title: Tail-like vortical structures in extreme turbulent kinetic energy dissipation events of wall turbulence
papers.abstract: Structural environment of extreme turbulent kinetic energy dissipation events in turbulent channel flows is studied at friction Reynolds numbers Reτ = 180, 395, and 640 using direct numerical simulation. Extreme events were identified by applying a connected-component labeling framework with spatiotemporal tracking, ensuring unbiased sampling. The vortical motions surrounding these events were characterized using the Rortex criterion, which suppresses the shear contamination and provides directional information about local rotation. The analysis revealed a previously unreported tail-like vortical structure that consistently accompanies extreme dissipation events. This structure exhibits a preferential orientation, negative spanwise Rortex dominance, and a strong association with sweep motions characterized by positive streamwise and negative wall-normal fluctuations. The results refine the classical view of quasi-streamwise vortices by demonstrating their entanglement with secondary tail structures during intermittency.

papers.title: Heat transfer characteristics of supercritical carbon dioxide flowing in vertical mini square channels
papers.abstract: In the common square channels of printed circuit heat exchangers, the unique thermophysical properties of supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) lead to the poor prediction effect of the existing heat transfer correlations for circular channels, and different flow directions also affect the heat transfer coefficient. To address these gaps, this work experimentally investigates heated sCO2 flow in a 1.6 × 1.6 mm2 vertical square channel. The operating ranges are system pressure p = 7.4–8.4 MPa, mass flux G = 1000–2000 kg/(m2 s), and heat flux q = 100–200 kW/m2. Based on the distribution characteristics of the heat transfer curve, the sCO2 flow heat transfer was divided into three regions: liquid-like, two-phase-like, and vapor-like. The effects of thermal–hydraulic parameters, as well as buoyancy and thermal acceleration effects, on convective heat transfer are systematically analyzed. The results indicate that the heat transfer coefficient for upward flow is higher than for downward flow, while both buoyancy and thermal acceleration have only minor influences. Existing heat transfer correlations are further evaluated, and a new heat transfer predictive correlation for vertical mini square channels on sCO2 was established. The deviation between the predicted value and experimental data is within −20% to +30%.

papers.title: Solute dispersion in laminar Hadley circulation
papers.abstract: We investigate the role of the Hadley circulation in the dispersion of passive pollutant gases released into the atmosphere by various sources (e.g., industrial chimneys, volcanic eruptions, etc.) and dispersion of passive non-buoyant particulate matter, treated mathematically as a passive scalar (solute). Following earlier studies, to mimic Hadley circulation, we consider buoyancy-driven circulation due to differentially heated sidewalls in a rectangular box. To include pollution sources, a slug source of finite spatial extent and a point source characterized by an impulse function are considered. The absorption at the bottom wall is introduced to represent the absorption of pollutant gases by natural sinks (e.g., trees) along the Earth's surface. To solve the concentration convection–diffusion equation, well-established Gill's methodology is employed, which allows analytical solutions for the transport coefficients, mean, and local concentration at arbitrary timescales. The results obtained by Gill's methodology in the large time limit are validated by the homogenization approach. Our analysis finds that owing to the inverted S-shaped velocity profile, the initial slug source height a and point source height h strongly affect the fate of the pollutants. The exchange coefficient K0 is higher for smaller a and h owing to the ready availability of the solute near the lower wall for absorption. This rapidly reduces the solute concentration in the environment, thereby decreasing prolonged exposure of human beings. The velocity changes from upstream (−x) to downstream (+x) at the half height of the fluid. Due to this, if the solute source is in y>0.5 (y<0.5), then in the small time limit, the solute will be convected downstream (upstream), thereby changing the sign of the convection coefficient K1. Similarly, the diffusion transport coefficient or effective diffusivity (K2) is highest in the short time limit if the initial source location is in the region where the velocity gradient is high. This is due to the larger contribution by the shear-enhanced diffusion to the diffusivity. These results regarding transport coefficients collectively affect mean concentration, with short-time behavior dominated by convection, while large-time behavior is dominated by diffusion. The contour plots for the local concentration further shed light on the dispersion of the solute in the transverse (y) and longitudinal (x) directions.

papers.title: Particle-induced micro-convection and heat transfer enhancement in nanofluids: Roles of Brownian motion and aggregation
papers.abstract: Particle dynamics play a pivotal role in the heat transfer performance of nanofluids, yet the mechanisms of particle-induced disturbances remain insufficiently understood and actively debated. A particle-scale perspective is essential for elucidating how Brownian motion and aggregation modulate fluid convection and heat transfer. In this study, the discrete element method coupled with the lattice Boltzmann method and immersed moving boundary is employed to resolve particle motion and its effects on convective heat transfer. Analysis of the Péclet (Pe) and Nusselt (Nu) numbers across different flow regions and inlet velocities reveals that the contribution of particle-induced disturbances is inversely proportional to fluid velocity. Heat transfer is markedly enhanced in boundary layers with low fluid velocity, achieving up to a 33.3% increase in Nu, where particle motion disrupts weak gradients and strengthens local fluctuations. In contrast, the effect becomes negligible in central regions or at high inlet velocities, where bulk convection dominates. Moreover, variations in the Brownian number (Br) and adhesion number (Ad) demonstrate that strong Brownian motion leads to dispersed particles, which promote widespread velocity fluctuations, whereas large-scale aggregation suppresses them. Finally, a phase diagram of convective heat transfer that integrates the two governing dimensions of fluid velocity (Pe0) and particle dynamics (Br and Ad) is proposed, providing insight into the conditions under which particle-induced disturbances predominantly influence convective heat transfer in nanofluids.

papers.title: Flow topology and wake calming mechanisms in a hybrid wind–solar system
papers.abstract: This study investigates the coupled aerodynamic interference between a vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) array and a parabolic trough condenser (TC) array in a hybrid wind–solar system. Combining wind tunnel testing and high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics with a hybrid RNG (renormalization group) k–ε/LES (large eddy simulation) approach, we analyze the three-dimensional wind field under varying TC elevation angles (30°, 60°, and 90°). Results show that the TC angle governs the internal flow regime: A low angle (30°) induces strong ground-channeling acceleration but high spatial heterogeneity, while a high angle (90°) yields a more uniform flow with a concentrated wake. Crucially, a universal “wake calming effect” is identified, but with a redefined physical mechanism. Topological analysis (Q-criterion) reveals a “structural breakdown” phenomenon, where the upstream VAWT wake shatters the large-scale coherent gap vortices of the TC array into disjointed eddies. Power spectral density quantitatively confirms that while the dominant low-frequency shedding is suppressed, the turbulent energy is redistributed to broadband scales (spectral broadening). This process facilitates momentum injection from the freestream into the stagnation zones, effectively transforming the VAWT from a passive obstacle into an active flow stabilizer. This study reveals the fluid-mechanic coupling mechanisms, providing critical insights for optimizing hybrid system layouts to mitigate aerodynamic impacts and improve overall performance and safety.

papers.title: Wake field characteristics of a toroidal propeller under different advance coefficients
papers.abstract: This study employs Improved Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation to investigate the open-water wake characteristics of a novel toroidal propeller. Following validation against cavitation tunnel data, numerical simulations were conducted at advance coefficients of J = 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 to analyze the wake field, focusing on vortex evolution and topology. Dynamic Mode Decomposition was subsequently applied to extract coherent spatiotemporal modes from the downstream flow. The results reveal that the closed-loop tip induces strong shear, generating symmetric alternating high- and low-velocity axial streaks at the slipstream boundary. Notably, the tip vortex manifests as a distinct double-layer anti-phase pulsation at the Blade Passage Frequency. As the advance coefficient increases, the hydrodynamic load shifts toward the tip. Consequently, at a low advance coefficient (J = 0.4), secondary vortices formed by the merging of blade wakes surround and destabilize the main tip vortex. Conversely, at a high advance coefficient (J = 1.2), extended blade vortices interact with the hub vortex, inducing significant instability in the hub region.

papers.title: A unified pore-scale multiphysics model for the integrated soot transport-deposition-oxidation in catalytic diesel particulate filters
papers.abstract: Understanding the intricate interplay between soot dynamics and chemical reactions within catalytic diesel particulate filters (CDPF) is crucial for enhancing both filtration efficiency and regeneration performance. In this paper, we establish a unified pore-scale multiphysics model based on the Eulerian–Lagrangian framework to comprehensively resolve the transport, deposition, and oxidation of soot. Distinguishing itself from conventional empirical correlations and stochastic-based approximations, the system models soot deposition through fundamental physical principles, integrating elastic deformation and surface adhesion mechanics at the particle–wall interface. Simultaneously, it incorporates a robust oxidation model that accounts for the competitive kinetics of both O2 and NO2 pathways, enabling comprehensive coverage of all CDPF operating regimes. Validated against three classical benchmark cases, the model demonstrates superior accuracy in capturing interfacial mass transfer and particle-wall interactions. Simulation under a typical CDPF low-temperature operating condition emphasizes the pivotal role of NO2 and a catalyst in promoting regeneration and reveals complex synergistic and competitive effects between distinct reaction pathways. Notably, the reaction rate of direct O2 pathway is accelerated by a factor of 87 in the presence of the catalyst. For ultra-fine soot particles (50 nm), the Brownian motion and thermophoretic forces directly dictate the deposition efficiency. Their strong thermal sensitivity also underscores the necessity for an integrated soot transport-deposition-oxidation framework. To support further research, the model implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/zhangyujing2001/CDPF_Multiphysics_Model.git [Y. Zhang, Y. Zhang, L. Fang, D. Lou, P. Tan, and Z. Hu (2026). “Data for ‘A unified pore-scale multiphysics model for the integrated soot transport-deposition-oxidation in catalytic diesel particulate filters,’” GitHub. https://github.com/zhangyujing2001/CDPF_Multiphysics_Model].

papers.title: Flow-field and pressure distribution characteristics of the Coandă-effect-based nodule collector
papers.abstract: Coandă-effect-based nodule collectors generate vertical pressure gradient through a convex curved-wall structure to enable the detachment and collection of nodule particles, which demonstrates considerable potential for engineering applications. The Large Eddy Simulation (LES) method was verified and employed to conduct a comprehensive numerical investigation on the flow field generated by this kind of collector under different bottom clearances h, jet velocities v, and moving speeds V. The results indicate that a high-velocity and low-pressure zone forms within the narrow region near the curved-wall, accompanied by the presence of numerous vortex structures in the vicinity of the seabed and the rear wall. The disturbance zone exhibits a distinct triangular morphology in planform. Along the streamwise direction, the extremum of the vertical pressure difference |ΔPz0|max under different v consistently occurs near x/h = 0.5, while the effective high-pressure zone is vertically confined to the region where z/h > −0.19. It is recommended that the operational h be matched to the specific working conditions. The influence of h on |ΔPz0|max exhibits an oscillatory behavior, while the effects of v and V follow well-defined quadratic and cubic relationships, respectively. These findings reveal the flow field characteristics of Coandă-effect-based collectors and provide practical guidance for the selection of operational parameters in deep-sea nodule collecting.

papers.title: Hydro-mechanical coupling modeling on drainage-induced seepage field in deeply buried tunnels
papers.abstract: In water-rich geological formations, drainage systems play a vital role in controlling external water pressures and managing seepage flow in deeply buried tunnels. This study develops a hydro-mechanical coupling model that incorporates stress-dependent fracture permeability to quantify water pressure distributions on tunnel linings and characterize seepage behavior. The grouting–lining interface is modeled as a rock mass discontinuity, enabling three-dimensional analysis of fracture permeability under coupled stress–seepage conditions. The parametric study systematically examines three key design parameters: drainage hole number, drainage hole length, and groundwater head level. Results reveal a three-stage pattern of external water pressure reduction with increasing drainage hole quantity (reduced radial hole spacing): beginning with a gradual decline, followed by an accelerated decrease, and ultimately reaching a stabilized state. Seepage flow rates exhibit a progressive deceleration trend before stabilizing. While borehole penetration depth has limited impact on water pressure reduction, it significantly influences seepage flow rate within the drainage networks. The analysis reveals distinct spatial patterns in the distribution of lining pressure. It is observed that the maximum external water pressure on the tunnel lining demonstrates an approximately linear decrease as the groundwater level declines. A comparative analysis of external water pressure calculation results between 3D and 2D numerical models reveals that the 3D model predicts higher lining pressure values. These findings provide valuable guidance for optimizing drainage hole design in the construction of large-scale, deeply buried tunnels in water-rich strata.

papers.title: Thermal and kinetic energy dissipation rates in vertical convection over rough sidewalls
papers.abstract: Adding roughness elements to walls is an effective method for enhancing heat transfer. However, the mechanism governing heat transfer variations, specifically the distribution and variation of energy dissipation remain unclear, particularly in vertical convection (VC). This study investigates how rough elements on the sidewalls affect both thermal and kinetic energy dissipations in vertical convection. Two-dimensional direct numerical simulations are conducted over a range of roughness heights and Rayleigh numbers. The results identify distinct critical roughness heights for thermal and kinetic energy dissipations, and illustrate the probability density function of them across the entire domain, demonstrating markedly different responses of thermal and kinetic energy dissipations to roughness modulation. By examining the spatial distribution of temperature and velocity fields, as well as the thermal and kinetic energy dissipations in the boundary layer and bulk, we identify the underlying mechanisms responsible for these differences. These findings provide new insights into how wall roughness modulates heat transfer and flow structures in vertical convection.

papers.title: A second opinion on the Weissenberg effect: The role of the second normal–stress difference in rod-climbing effect
papers.abstract: The Weissenberg (rod-climbing) effect, i.e., the rise of a viscoelastic fluid along a thin rotating rod, has long served as a canonical demonstration of elasticity and normal–stress differences in complex fluids. The effect is most commonly attributed to the first normal–stress difference N1, which induces tensile hoop stresses that draw fluid upward along the rod. The second normal–stress difference N2, in contrast, is often presumed negligible or dynamically unimportant. However, many polymer solutions and industrial fluids, such as suspensions, exhibit N2 of appreciable magnitude, and modern constitutive models predict that it can significantly modify free-surface stresses and thereby the climbing behavior. In this work, we perform high-resolution axisymmetric simulations of the Linear Phan–Thien–Tanner model to systematically isolate the influence of N2 on rod climbing. We show that increasing the magnitude of N2 progressively weakens the climbing response and ultimately reverses it, producing rod-descending once the normal–stress ratio exceeds a critical value ψ0≈0.25. Larger N2 also destabilizes the flow, promoting early onset (in terms of the rotation speed) of bubble formation, subcritical Hopf oscillations, and fully asymmetric three-dimensional motion that culminates in rupture. By mapping these regimes in the (Wi,ψ0) parameter space, where Wi is the Weissenberg number, we reconcile discrepancies among perturbation theory, experiments, and numerical simulations. These results establish N2 as a crucial control parameter governing free-surface stability in viscoelastic liquids.

papers.title: Film cooling behavior from shaped holes on a curved wall under nonuniform pressure gradients
papers.abstract: Film cooling over curved surfaces subjected to variable pressure gradients exhibits complex near-wall flow dynamics, which are strongly influenced by the local pressure gradient distribution and the mainstream flow structure. In this study, the film cooling response of different hole geometries on a single curved surface exposed to a highly nonuniform three-dimensional mainstream is investigated using numerical simulations, with particular emphasis on the coolant-to-mainstream pressure ratio (RP). The upstream region is dominated by a strong adverse pressure gradient (SAPG), which suppresses coolant discharge, induces near-wall recirculation, and leads to unstable and direction-sensitive jets' behavior for cylindrical holes. As RP increases, several holes remain susceptible to jet bifurcation, lift-off, and reverse entrainment, indicating the limited effectiveness of increasing RP alone. Analysis of boundary layer characteristics and coolant trajectories reveals three distinct flow-response modes: attached plate-like jets under mild adverse or favorable pressure gradients, forked distributions caused by separation and reattachment under moderate adverse pressure gradients, and reverse entrainment under SAPG conditions. Based on these mechanisms, two modified hole geometries—a racetrack-shaped (RS) hole and a forward-inclined fan-shaped hole—are proposed. Both geometries stabilize the coolant trajectory and mitigate SAPG-induced recirculation, with the RS hole providing the most robust near-wall attachment under SAPG conditions.

papers.title: Laser-induced vapor bubbles in subcooled water: From nucleation to collapse and jet formation
papers.abstract: The collective dynamics of an ensemble of vapor bubbles during laser-induced boiling of a subcooled liquid was studied using high-speed visualization. The re-formation of vapor bubbles was initiated by prolonged exposure to continuous laser radiation transmitted through an optical fiber. This boiling is characterized not only by the nucleation, growth, and subsequent collapse of numerous bubbles but also by the formation of high-speed submerged jets. We found that the most powerful and fastest jets, penetrating farthest from the end of the fiber, are initiated by the collapse of bubbles, the radius of which is several times the radius of the fiber. The frequency of formation of these large bubbles strongly depends on the laser power. The results of the analysis showed that the formation of the conditions necessary for the appearance of bubbles is a highly nonlinear process, in which previously formed vapor bubbles play important role by directly impacting the thermal and hydrodynamic conditions. Thus, models based only on the dynamics of individual bubbles are insufficient to fully describe the boiling process under prolonged exposure to a laser. The results obtained are important for the development and optimization of applications such as minimally invasive laser surgery and precision microprocessor processing.

papers.title: Linking aneurysmal geometry and hemodynamics using computational fluid dynamics
papers.abstract: The development of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA) is related to complex flow patterns and wall-shear–driven mechanobiological stimuli, yet the quantitative relationship between aneurysmal geometry and hemodynamics remains poorly defined. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive hemodynamic analysis of 74 patient-specific abdominal aortas. A multiscale framework coupling zero-dimensional to one-dimensional (0D–1D) systemic circulation models with three-dimensional (3D) stabilized finite-element simulations is used to generate physiologically consistent boundary conditions and high-fidelity flow fields.
