The model was validated against the analytical solution of infinite-acting radial flow. The effects of reservoir heterogeneity, CO2 mole fraction, injection rate, formation permeability, and well pattern on CO2 storage, deposition rate, and porosity–permeability damage were systematically analyzed. Results show that increasing the CO2 mole fraction from 0.2 to 0.8 increases the deposition rate by 19.56%, accompanied by porosity and permeability damage increments of 29.69% and 46.91%, respectively. Increasing the injection rate from 2 × 104 to 8 × 104 m3/day reduces the deposition rate by 16.83% and significantly mitigates formation damage. Higher formation permeability also suppresses deposition and associated impairment. The inverted nine-spot well pattern provides the highest CO2 storage and the lowest damage. Gray relational analysis indicates that formation permeability most strongly controls deposition rate, whereas well pattern dominates storage efficiency and formation impairment. These results clarify the coupled mechanisms of CO2 storage and asphaltene-induced damage in deep reservoirs.

papers.title: Impact of blade tip clearance on vortex dynamics and energy loss in submersible slurry pumps
papers.abstract: Blade tip clearance is a key feature of open-impeller centrifugal pumps, influencing tip leakage flow, vortex evolution, and energy dissipation. In submersible slurry pumps with non-uniform inflow, tip clearance-induced vortices interact with the main flow, leading to complex momentum exchange and hydraulic losses. Existing studies focus mainly on traditional pumps, with limited insight into open-impeller slurry pumps under practical inflow conditions. This study develops a numerical model to simulate non-uniform inlet conditions in a submersible slurry pump, conducting experiments five double-sided blade tip clearance configurations. The impact of blade tip clearance on hydraulic performance, vortex evolution, and energy dissipation was analyzed under different flow rates. Results show that increased blade tip clearance strengthens tip leakage vortices, expands the vortex-dominated region, and shifts vortex formation downstream. These enhanced vortices amplify turbulent momentum exchange and turbulence kinetic energy, a major contributor to energy loss. While energy loss sensitivity is limited at partial load, a positive correlation is found at design flow. This study provides a theoretical foundation for optimizing blade tip clearance, vortex control, and energy-efficient designs in submersible slurry pumps.

papers.title: Crosstalk mechanism and design guidelines of extractor-electrode electrohydrodynamic nozzle array chip for high-uniformity printing
papers.abstract: Dot array deposition through multi-nozzle electrohydrodynamic (EHD) printing is widely used for high efficiency. However, the conventional study mainly focuses on the plain capillary array. The research on the mechanisms and design principles for extractor–electrode EHD nozzle array chip remains scarce. The extractor-electrode EHD chip is beneficial for improving the printhead's coaxial accuracy and integration level. In this work, the crosstalk mechanism and design principles of the extractor-electrode EHD nozzle array chip are revealed and proposed. A model is established by combining the Navier–Stokes equation, charge transportation equation, and phase field equation. The nozzle's conductivity is considered by introducing a charge transportation equation in the nozzle chip. The effect of the electric field on the liquid supply is analyzed. The mechanism of the generated droplet deflection is revealed. The droplet deflection is determined by the electric field of the nozzle chip and the charge ejected with the fluid. The most lateral droplets deflect to the middle of the nozzle chip, which is different from the plain capillary arrays. The effect of high potential electrode, nozzle conductivity, and nozzle structure on the printing feasibility and consistency is investigated. The large high-potential electrode, low nozzle conductivity, large nozzle spacing, and proper size/position of the extractor electrode are preferred for better printing consistency. The design guidelines of the extractor electrode and a new dumb nozzle design are finally proposed to enhance the printing feasibility and consistency. This work could be beneficial for understanding and designing the extractor-electrode EHD nozzle array with high uniformity.

papers.title: Grain-size heterogeneity controls non-equilibrium aeolian transport across large spatial scales
papers.abstract: In natural sandy environments, such as gobi deserts, inland dune fields, and coastal zones, surface sediments typically consist of mixed grain-size compositions. While extensive research has addressed aeolian transport over uniform sand beds, the spatiotemporal dynamics of sediment transport under large-scale, mixed-grain conditions remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to surface sorting and its feedbacks on transport efficiency. Here, we introduce a two-grain-size simulation framework, based on the Aeolis model, to quantify how wind velocity, sediment supply, grain-size combinations, and relative abundance influence sand flux and bed surface sorting. Results show that non-equilibrium transport is strongly modulated by the evolving accessibility of mobilizable grains, with threshold contrasts between fine and coarse particles producing pronounced shifts in relative flux contributions. These threshold differences not only reshape the spatial distribution of surface grains but also feed back into the pattern of surface shear stress, further amplifying the sorting effect. The results advance the physics of non-equilibrium, multi-grain aeolian transport, and provide a quantitative foundation for predicting landscape evolution on Earth and other planetary surfaces.

papers.title: Dynamical characteristics of the body-caudal fin joint of a carangiform swimmer and its influence on hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Hydrodynamics of fish swimming depends on the interaction between undulation of the body and the flapping of the caudal fin. This study develops a computational framework of a Jackfish-inspired swimmer with an independently mounted caudal fin that pitches passively under the action of fluid forces. The body-fin joint is modeled through linear and nonlinear torsional springs and damping. The fin synchronizes with the body when damping and stiffness parameters are tuned adequately, producing passive pitching that closely resembles to the displacement of an actively pitching counterpart. At Re = 3000, synchronized passive pitching generates coherent hairpin and ring vortices that reinforce streamwise momentum and contribute to thrust, whereas larger phase differences between active heaving and passive pitching motion of the caudal fin lead to wake spread in lateral direction and drag-dominated behavior. These results reveal that nonlinear mechanics of the body-caudal fin joint regulates amplitude, phase, and recoil, offering a biologically inspired pathway toward underwater robotic design using partially passive kinematics of the caudal fin.

papers.title: Two-dimensional magneto-hydro-dynamic simulation of breaking arc characteristics in medium-voltage switchgear
papers.abstract: Medium-voltage (MV) switchgear plays an important role in both control and protection within power systems. When a circuit is interrupted, an electric arc is inevitably produced. The performance of arc extinction directly influences the stability and reliability of the entire power supply system. This study focuses on the characteristics of arc extinguishing in MV switchgear by means of numerical simulation methods. A two-dimensional magneto-hydro-dynamic model is established to describe the gas arc behavior in a load switch during the interruption process. Based on the simulation results, the influences of transverse magnetic field, contact separation speed, arc current, gas pressure, and dielectric medium on arc dynamic characteristics are analyzed in detail. It is found that the transverse magnetic field drives the arc to deflect under the Lorentz force. With the increase in magnetic field intensity, the Lorentz force becomes stronger, which helps accelerate the arc extinguishing process. Faster contact separation contributes to a higher arc voltage and voltage peak during the breaking process, thus improving the interruption capability. In the case of hexafluoride–nitrogen (SF6–N2) mixtures, a higher proportion of SF6 leads to higher arc voltage peaks and breakdown voltages, which is favorable for arc quenching. The simulation results obtained in this work can provide theoretical support for the structural optimization and performance improvement of MV switchgears.

papers.title: Excess entropy scaling of the transverse sound speed in simple fluids
papers.abstract: A calculation of the transverse sound velocity as a function of excess entropy is presented for several simple fluids, including the Lennard-Jones, Yukawa, one-component plasma, inverse-power law (soft sphere), and hard-sphere models. A quasi-universal character of this dependence is established, extending Rosenfeld's excess-entropy scaling of transport coefficients to the transverse sound velocity. The results are discussed in terms of the soft- to hard-sphere crossover and the Frenkel crossover between gas-like and liquid-like dynamics.

papers.title: Coupled thermal and interfacial effects on the motion of a compound droplet near a planar surface
papers.abstract: In this study, we present a semi-analytical investigation of the thermocapillary motion of a concentric compound droplet suspended in an unbounded immiscible fluid near a hydrophobic planar wall. The droplet consists of an inner core encapsulated by an outer liquid shell, with both interfaces assumed spherical under low capillary number conditions. The compound droplet and its core translate along the axis normal to the wall with distinct migration velocities. The analysis is performed in the creeping-flow regime and accounts for coupled thermal and hydrodynamic interactions among the inner and outer interfaces and the nearby wall. Imposed temperature gradients generate Marangoni stresses at both interfaces, driving thermocapillary motion. This motion is strongly influenced by wall-induced distortion of the temperature and velocity fields. Semi-analytical solutions of the Stokes and energy equations are obtained using a collocation technique. These solutions yield accurate and well-converged migration velocities over a wide range of droplet–wall separations. The results demonstrate that the wall significantly modifies the magnitude of thermocapillary migration. This modification occurs through enhanced viscous dissipation and asymmetric interfacial stresses. The coupled effects of thermal conductivity ratios, viscosity contrasts, interfacial tension gradients, and geometric confinement are systematically elucidated. This work extends existing theories by incorporating multi-interface coupling and wall effects within a unified semi-analytical framework. It is directly relevant to the controlled manipulation of encapsulated droplets in microfluidics, targeted drug delivery, microscale thermal management, and cell-mimicking transport near solid boundaries.

papers.title: Flow control in tandem cascades using steady and unsteady end wall boundary layer suction
papers.abstract: Tandem cascades have attracted attention in the design of highly loaded compressors owing to their potential to increase load capacity and improve aerodynamic performance. However, under off-design conditions such as positive incidence angles, flow separation within the cascade, particularly corner separation near the end wall, significantly increases flow losses and degrades aerodynamic performance. This study numerically evaluates end wall boundary layer suction (EBLS) for flow control, comparing a baseline cascade with steady suction and unsteady end wall boundary layer oscillatory suction. The results show EBLS effectively suppresses separation and improves performance, with suction on the front-row cascade being most effective. A well-configured EBLS strategy, particularly on the front row, enhances performance under positive incidence and achieves extra loss reduction compared to steady suction. End wall boundary layer oscillation suction (EBLOS) adds unsteady excitation, reducing flow losses by an additional 10.5% beyond EBLS. However, its influence along the blade span is limited, constraining its control over the full three-dimensional corner separation. Vortex evolution and spectral analysis indicate that EBLOS induces vortex reorganization, transforming the originally disordered and separated flow state into an ordered vortex street with periodic shedding characteristics. Simultaneously, EBLOS locks the dominant frequency of vortex shedding with the frequency of oscillatory suction excitation, achieving forced resonance. This process effectively removes low-energy fluid within the boundary layer while enhancing energy exchange between the mainstream and end wall regions, thereby reducing flow energy loss.

papers.title: Two-dimensional topography estimation from noisy free surface synthetic data
papers.abstract: The inverse topography problem involves estimating the bottom topography from knowledge of a free surface. In this paper, we present a weakly nonlinear approach to address this problem using the forced Korteweg–de Vries equation for steady two-dimensional free surface flow of an inviscid incompressible fluid corrupted by measurement noise. Owing to the presence of noise, there is a compounding inverse solution error as the grid resolution is refined due to numerical differentiation and so a linear least squares regression method is proposed as a way to mitigate noise on the surface. A closed-form expression for the mean and variance of the inverse solutions is derived to examine the uncertainty of our topographic predictions. We demonstrate the adaptability of our contributions to six classical flow types, providing a systematic method for quantifying the uncertainty in topographic estimates that is insightful and interpretable.

papers.title: Physics constrained neural collision operators for hard sphere surrogates and ab initio angle prediction in direct simulation Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: The direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method is the gold standard for non-equilibrium rarefied gas dynamics, yet its computational cost can be prohibitive, especially for near-continuum regimes and high-fidelity ab initio potentials. This work develops a unified, physics-constrained neural-operator framework that accelerates DSMC while preserving physical invariants and stochasticity required for long-time kinetic simulations. First, we introduce a local neural collision kernel replacing the phenomenological hard sphere (HS) model. To overcome the variance suppression and artificial cooling inherent to purely deterministic regression surrogates, we augment inference with a physics-constrained stochastic layer. Controlled latent-noise injection restores thermal fluctuations, while cell-wise moment-matching is introduced as a numerical stabilization device to suppress long-time energy drift. Remarkably, the proposed operator can be deployed without retraining in a two-dimensional lid-driven cavity after being trained on collision samples harvested from a one-dimensional Couette flow. Since the underlying HS collision law is geometry-independent, this test is intended to assess robustness across flow configurations and collision-state distributions rather than the transfer of a geometry-specific law. The surrogate accurately reproduces the primary fields and higher-order non-equilibrium moments in the cavity case. Second, to bypass the extreme cost of trajectory-based classical scattering, we develop a dedicated ab initio neural operator for the Jäger interaction potential. Trained via a physics harvesting strategy on large-scale collision pairs, it efficiently captures the high-energy scattering dynamics dominating hypersonic regimes. Validated on a Mach 10 rarefied argon flow over a cylinder, the framework reproduces transport behaviors and shock features with high fidelity, achieving an approximate 20% cost reduction relative to direct numerical integration. Collectively, this work establishes physics-constrained neural operators as accurate, stable, and efficient drop-in surrogates for DSMC collision dynamics across both engineering HS setups and ab initio hypersonic simulations.

papers.title: The effect of an offloading ship on the hydrodynamics of a floating platform moored in an ice polynya
papers.abstract: Offloading operations alongside floating platforms are becoming increasingly important in Arctic offshore engineering. Although the hydrodynamics of multiple bodies in open water have been widely studied, research on multi-body interactions in an ice polynya remains limited. In this study, a hybrid numerical method combining the boundary element method and the matched eigenfunction expansion method is employed to investigate the influence of an offloading ship on the hydrodynamics of a floating platform in an ice polynya. The effects of ice thickness, the distance between the ship and the platform, the offloading ship configuration, and the polynya size on the hydrodynamics of the floating platform are analyzed. The results show that at high wave frequencies, the presence of the ice sheet causes the hydrodynamics to differ from those in open water. Increasing ice thickness enhances the effective flexural rigidity of the ice sheet and leads to more pronounced oscillatory characteristics in the hydrodynamics. When the offloading ship is located on the wave-facing side, the incident wave energy transmitted to the platform is reduced, leading to smaller load amplitudes despite the appearance of more resonance points. In contrast, positioning the ship on the lee side enhances wave reflection and increases load amplitudes. Increasing the separation distance produces more resonance points but reduces peak amplitudes, while a larger polynya size weakens reflected wave energy and results in more pronounced peaks and troughs in the hydrodynamics.

papers.title: Hemodynamic consequences of post-stenting geometry at the vertebral artery origin: A patient-specific fluid–structure interaction study
papers.abstract: This study employs a bidirectional fluid–structure interaction (FSI) numerical simulation method to investigate the hemodynamic consequences of stent-induced geometrical changes at the origin of the vertebral artery. The stent itself is not explicitly modeled; instead, postoperative and virtually modified lumen geometries are used to represent the morphological outcomes of stenting. Preoperative and postoperative computed tomography imaging data from a patient provided by the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine were utilized to construct personalized vertebral artery geometric models. Based on the postoperative model, virtual surgical scenarios were simulated by expanding the stented segment inward and outward by 0.2 mm, generating virtual postoperative vertebral artery geometric models. Hemodynamic parameters of four vertebral artery geometries were obtained and analyzed through bidirectional FSI numerical simulations, providing an in-depth exploration of the specific hemodynamic impacts of stent implantation at the vertebral artery origin. Although preliminary and based on a single patient, this study provides initial insights that may inform future research on optimizing vascular stent treatment strategies, particularly regarding the regulation of stent expansion rates.

papers.title: Global pressure fluctuations in numerical simulation of spatially developing jets
papers.abstract: This paper addresses some issues related to the numerical simulation of the spatial evolution of perturbations in highly unstable submerged jets. It is confirmed that artificial conditions at the outflow boundary lead to the generation of spurious global pressure fluctuations that transfer perturbations to the inflow region and initiate the occurrence of global instability. Estimates and interpretations explaining the mechanism of this phenomenon are presented. It is shown that the qualitative behavior of the solution depends not only on the length of the computational domain, but also on its transverse size. In the course of nonlinear simulations, it was found that global pressure fluctuations are emitted from regions of nonlinearity into the surrounding space, where the nonlinear terms have a negligibly small amplitude. This effect makes it possible to predict the position of the nonlinearity boundary depending on the amplitude of inflow disturbances and the width of the computational domain. The results obtained in this work can be extended to other highly unstable spatially evolving flows.

papers.title: Cavitation bubble dynamics near free surface with a half-submerged particle
papers.abstract: In this study, a theoretical model is developed and validated experimentally to describe cavitation bubble collapse and jet formation near a half-submerged spherical particle at a free surface. By introducing an anisotropy parameter, the collapse-induced jet, centroid migration, and collapse period of the bubble are quantitatively evaluated as functions of the particle radius and the bubble–particle distance. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: (1) A theoretical criterion for collapse jet modes is established based on the zero-anisotropy parameter, enabling effective identification of jets directed toward the free surface, jets directed away from the free surface, and neutral collapse modes. (2) A scaling law for the bubble centroid migration velocity is further derived, revealing the influence mechanisms of the particle, the free surface, and their coupled effects. (3) A functional relationship among the bubble collapse period, the particle radius, and the bubble–particle distance is established. The prediction function provides a theoretical foundation for controlling cavitation durations by adjusting local boundary geometries.

papers.title: Droplet digital polymerase chain reaction: Microfluidic advances and biomedical applications
papers.abstract: Droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) offers low sample consumption, high sensitivity, absolute quantification, and convenient parallel experimentation, making it a powerful tool for disease diagnosis, cell biology, and genetic engineering. A typical ddPCR workflow comprises three critical steps: droplet generation, thermal cycling, and output monitoring, each of which directly impacts detection efficiency and accuracy. In this review, we critically discuss and evaluate the recent technological and material advancements in ddPCR. The review begins by introducing the various types of ddPCR methods, categorized according to their thermal cycling techniques, droplet states, and the number of genes tested. Subsequently, the droplet types, generation techniques, materials, thermal stability, and heating methods are discussed in detail. This is followed by a discussion of output monitoring for ddPCR detection. Furthermore, we analyze and discuss the application of ddPCR in single-cell analysis, disease diagnosis, and pathogen detection. Finally, the review discusses the faced challenges of ddPCR and offers future perspectives on possible improvements and developments. We hope that this review can contribute to the ongoing advancement of ddPCR technology and its applications.

papers.title: Low-Reynolds-number turbulence with active vortex stretching in three-dimensional cryogenic sloshing
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional simulations of liquid sloshing underpredict damping by two orders of magnitude. This long-standing discrepancy is traced here to the structure of the energy cascade. Using three-dimensional volume-of-fluid simulations of liquefied natural gas (LNG) sloshing (in a Basilisk framework, up to 5123 effective resolution), we show that the flow occupies a previously uncharacterized regime: an active vortex stretching (ratio 2.67) at a Taylor-scale Reynolds number Reλ∼50–80 (measured directly via multi-scale variance decomposition separating turbulent fluctuations from organized sloshing), below the inertial-range threshold. We prove that both vortex stretching and strain-rate self-amplification (SSA) are the two mechanisms driving the forward energy cascade. The mechanisms vanish identically in two dimensions, establishing a fundamental, not merely quantitative, origin for the simulation failure. Direct measurement of the SSA-to-stretching ratio (3.24±1.22, consistent with the Betchov identity and the Carbone–Bragg prediction of ∼3) confirms that cascade physics operates at these low Reynolds numbers. Second-order velocity structure functions computed from the adaptive mesh refinement data show no inertial plateau, providing direct real-space spectral evidence for the sub-inertial classification. Free-decay analysis reveals anisotropic damping spanning three orders of magnitude with irreducible three-dimensional coupling (R=0.14–0.18,dynamic forces). Under Froude scaling, boundary-layer damping vanishes at the prototype scale (ζBL∼λ−3/4) while cascade damping remains scale-independent (ζ3D∼λ0), with direct implications for full-scale LNG damping prediction.

papers.title: Study on the evolution mechanism of gas–liquid two-phase flow in multistage centrifugal pumps
papers.abstract: Although gas–liquid two-phase flow in centrifugal pumps has been extensively investigated, the inter-stage evolution dynamics of bubbles in multistage pumps remain inadequately understood. This study numerically investigates the unsteady characteristics of a multistage centrifugal pump under varying inlet gas volume fractions (IGVF) at rated conditions. By resolving the pressure distributions, velocity fields, and transient gas-phase distributions, the underlying dynamics of pressure pulsations are explored through integrated time-frequency analysis. Furthermore, the power spectral density method is employed to elucidate the spatiotemporal evolution of pressure fluctuations at the outlets of successive impeller stages. The results indicate that the dynamic balance of inter-stage “coalescence–breakup–redistribution” drives the spectral evolution of pressure fluctuations. As IGVF increases, gas accumulation intensifies within the secondary impellers and first-stage diffusers, whereas the distribution remains relatively dispersed in the initial stage. The flow regime transition from dispersed bubbly flow to segregated flow induces a pronounced energy migration: the formation of large gas slugs suppresses low-frequency disturbances, while localized pressure waves from frequent bubble fragmentation markedly intensify medium-frequency pulsation energy. This study reveals a strong correlation between the spatial topological structure of the gas phase and the spectral energy distribution, offering new insights into the multiphase instability mechanisms in rotating centrifugal fields.

papers.title: Evolution and mechanisms of particle focusing patterns in straight and helical microchannels with viscoelastic fluids
papers.abstract: Viscoelastic-aided microfluidic focusing has attracted growing attention for its potential in high-throughput particle focusing and separation. However, the limited understanding of cross-sectional patterns and the underlying mechanics of particle migration in curved channels hinder further development. In this work, particle distributions in straight and helical microchannels are investigated using polyethylene oxide solutions as the working fluid over a wide parameter space (Re=0.2–140, particle confinement apd=0.06–0.27, and channel curvature D/d=80–320). Comparing to three typical focusing patterns identified in straight channels, six typical focusing patterns are identified in helical channels, and their transitions with changes in flow condition, particle confinement, and channel curvature are elucidated. Force analysis shows that particle focusing is associated with low-magnitude regions of the net lateral force, which arise from the shifting dominance among inertial lift, elastic, and Dean drag forces. A mechanistically informed pattern map is established using the characteristic inertial-force ratio γ, which characterizes the relative importance of inertial lift and Dean drag forces, together with an elastic scaling Re2(ap/d)3. The map captures the transition trends and organizes the observed focusing patterns across the explored parameter space. These findings reveal the order and complexity of particle distributions in non-Newtonian flows and offer useful guidance for particle focusing and separation in viscoelastic microfluidic systems.

papers.title: Application of a non-equilibrium wall model with convective term modeling in complex separated flows
papers.abstract: Algebraic wall models based on the stress-balance hypothesis and conventional EqODE (equilibrium ordinary differential equation model) models often lead to computational distortions when handling complex flow separation at high Reynolds numbers due to the neglect of non-equilibrium effects. To address this issue, a wall model that simultaneously considers the effects of convection terms and pressure gradients while avoiding the calculation of wall-parallel derivatives is developed by modeling the convective terms. Numerical simulations are performed on the periodic hill and the generic ship simplified frigate ship (SFS2) models using this model, EqODE, algebraic wall models, and WRLES (wall-resolved large-eddy simulation). Detailed comparisons between simulation results and experimental data indicate that traditional equilibrium models fail to effectively predict near-wall shear stress within the range of y+ between 10 and 50, resulting in the smoothing of skin friction distributions in the separation and reattachment regions. Furthermore, in cross-sectional flow separation, traditional equilibrium models cannot resolve the bistable structures of three-dimensional backward-facing step flows. In contrast, the Non-EqODE model accurately captures wall shear stress, pressure, Reynolds stress, and velocity distributions even under conditions of higher y+ and lower grid resolution, and successfully captures the turbulent asymmetric bistable characteristics in the wake field. This method significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring the numerical conservation of the equations, providing a new approach for the efficient simulation of complex flow fields at high Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Effects of a downstream detached splitter on the aerodynamics and wake flow patterns of a 5:1 rectangular cylinder
papers.abstract: The interaction between a 5:1 rectangular cylinder and a downstream detached splitter is investigated through wind tunnel experiments at the Reynolds number equal to 47 905. The gap ratio g/D is varied from 0 to 10.0, where g denotes the distance from the cylinder trailing edge to the splitter leading-edge tip and D is the cylinder height. The bare cylinder is also examined as the baseline case. Surface pressure measurements and aerodynamic force statistics are combined with power spectral densities (PSD) analysis to quantify the gap-dependent aerodynamic responses. Flow-field characteristics are further resolved using two-dimensional particle image velocimetry, together with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and phase-averaged wake reconstruction. Based on the evolution of wake dynamics and aerodynamic signatures, four distinct regimes are identified: the pre-von Kármán vortex (KV) formation regime (0≤g/D<1.0), the interaction regime (1.0≤g/D<7.0), the buffer regime (7.0≤g/D<9.0), and the decoupled regime (g/D≥9.0). Distinct regime-dependent features are consistently observed in the fluctuating pressure field, fluctuating lift, PSD peaks, and dominant POD modes, supporting the proposed flow classification. The underlying mechanism is attributed to a feedback interaction between the KV street and the detached splitter, which governs wake development and aerodynamic modulation across gap ratios.

papers.title: Enhanced mixing inside microdroplets due to interfacial-tension-induced flows of miscible components: A lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Mixing of miscible fluids with distinct interfacial tensions within microdroplets is a ubiquitous yet fundamentally important phenomenon in natural systems and microfluidic applications; however, the processes with mixing-induced dynamic interfacial tension have remained largely unexplored. Here, we used a ternary color-gradient lattice Boltzmann model to investigate the mixing of binary miscible phases with equal molecular mass inside microdroplet under the effect of concentration-dependent dynamic interfacial tension, demonstrating the coupled evolution of mixing, dynamic interfacial tension, interfacial energy, and flows. Simulations show that, in a static droplet, interfacial tension asymmetry generates tangential flows, driving the higher-interfacial-tension component rapidly toward the droplet interior, to reduce the total interfacial energy to its minimum, and enhancing mixing efficiency with a cashew-like concentration pattern. Extending the analysis to the formation and subsequent flow of binary-miscible-component droplet in microchannels, the influence of interfacial tension contrasts of two miscible dispersed phases against the continuous phase on internal mixing and droplet sizes was systematically examined over various diffusion coefficients. The interfacial-tension-driven flows are found to break the symmetric internal circulation inside droplet and that markedly enhance mixing, while increasing the interfacial tension contrast leads to a slight reduction in the droplet size. For rapid binary diffusion, the interfacial tension asymmetry is quickly relaxed, rendering its impact on flow and mixing insignificant.

papers.title: Erratum: “Effect of non-equilibrium aggregation of nanoparticles on heat and mass transport and sensitivity in nanofluid flow during blood circulation” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 122004 (2025)]
Numerical analysis of hydrodynamics in conical spouted bed reactors
papers.abstract: High-resolution numerical simulations were employed to quantify the effects of key operating and design parameters on the hydrodynamics of conical spouted beds (CSBs). The simulation model is validated against experimental pressure-loss measurements, showing good agreement. The simulated flow structures accurately reproduce characteristic behaviors reported in the literature. Parametric analysis reveals that increasing bed inventory significantly raises bed height and pressure drop, while reducing global specific kinetic energy (defined as the total kinetic energy of all particles divided by the total bed mass). In contrast, increasing gas velocity substantially elevates specific kinetic energy with negligible impact on bed height. Furthermore, enlarging the entrainment area, whether by increasing entrainment height or utilizing an open-sided draft tube, enhances solid influx from the annulus, thereby intensifying gas–solid momentum exchange and boosting specific kinetic energy. A spectral analysis of the gas-phase turbulent kinetic energy and static pressure identifies the dominant frequencies that dictate the hydrodynamic behavior of the CSB. A comparative assessment with bubbling fluidized beds (BFBs) under identical inventory and gas flow conditions demonstrates that while BFBs exhibit greater bed expansion and pressure drop, CSBs achieve higher specific particle kinetic energy, albeit at the cost of increased total energy input. These findings elucidate the governing hydrodynamic mechanisms and provide practical guidance for the rational design of CSB-based reactors and dryers.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of reactive solute transport in viscoelastic media under combined electroosmotic and pressure-driven flow
papers.abstract: This study investigates reactive solute transport in a viscoelastic solvent flowing through a rectangular microchannel subjected to combined electro-osmotic and pressure-driven forcing. The governing advection–diffusion–reaction equation is solved using two complementary approaches: an analytical multiscale homogenization technique and a fully implicit second-order finite-volume formulation with adaptive time stepping. A systematic stability analysis demonstrates that the numerical method is unconditionally stable and provides accurate long-time predictions with significantly reduced computational effort. The results reveal that the effective dispersion coefficient varies non-monotonically with the pressure-to-electro-osmotic drive ratio parameter ω, exhibiting a distinct minimum at a critical value ωc. This minimum occurs only under adverse pressure gradients and shifts to lower ω with increasing Debye–Hückel parameter K, reflecting the influence of electrostatic screening. Viscoelasticity shifts the critical parameter ωc to higher values relative to Newtonian fluids. Detailed concentration contour analysis shows strong coupling between ω, viscoelasticity, and electro-osmotic strength: favorable pressure gradients confine the solute band, whereas adverse gradients induce upstream stretching, with the transition dependent on K. Boundary absorption further modulates transport by creating asymmetric solute depletion near the plates and reducing overall bulk concentrations, highlighting the interplay between advection, diffusion, and wall reaction kinetics. Overall, the combined analytical–numerical framework provides comprehensive insight into how viscoelasticity, electrokinetic effects, and boundary reactions jointly control reactive solute dispersion in microfluidic systems, offering a reliable basis for the design and optimization of electrokinetically driven microchannel processes.

papers.title: Defects, corrugation, and temperature govern rarefied-air drag on graphene coatings
papers.abstract: In rarefied atmospheric environments, where continuum fluid dynamics breaks down, aerodynamic drag is governed by gas–surface momentum exchange, making surface structure and chemistry key design knobs. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we show that coating the α-Al2O3(0001) surface with graphene markedly reduces the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient (TMAC) of N2, shifting scattering toward more specular reflection and thereby lowering drag; we further benchmark this response against graphite. The reduction strengthens up to 900 K. While structural defects can increase TMAC via defect-induced corrugation and local atomic and electronic rearrangements, graphene retains its performance at experimentally relevant defect densities.

papers.title: Three-dimensional wake dynamics and vortex-induced vibrations of circular and hexagonal cylinders
papers.abstract: In the present work we conducted a deep investigation on identifying geometry and orientation-dependent effects on three-dimensional wake dynamics and fluid–structure interaction. The study employs a coupled Lattice Boltzmann method and Immersed Boundary Method to investigate the flow past hexagonal cross-section cylinders under two different orientations with respect to the free stream: one with a flat face perpendicular to the freestream and one with a corner aligned in the direction of the flow. The analysis spans different flow regimes, with Reynolds numbers ranging from 20 to 103. The framework adopts a Large Eddy Simulation approach based on the Smagorinsky subgrid-scale model for the highest Reynolds numbers investigated (Re=500 and Re=1000). Validation of the numerical method involved comparing simulated drag and lift coefficients, as well as surface pressure distributions with benchmark data obtained from traditional Navier–Stokes solvers. The aerodynamic behavior of the hexagonal cross-section cylinder was then compared to the circular cylinder case to highlight the influence of cross-sectional geometry on wake dynamics, showing that the orientation of the hexagonal cylinder significantly alters the wake topology and promotes the early transition to a three-dimensional wake structure. The study further focuses on the Vortex Induced Vibration problem at Re=200. In this context, the solid-to-fluid density ratio is kept constant among the different test cases at 10, while the ratio among the pulse of the lift fluid force and the natural frequency of the system is set at two different values 0.5 and 0.9 to investigate how the wake dynamics is affected by the displacement of the obstacle.

papers.title: Entropy consistent modeling of compressible two-phase flow in wide concentration range
papers.abstract: The two-phase flows containing dispersed phase usually display distinct flow patterns in dense and dilute concentration regimes. The typical case is the high-speed droplet-laden gas flow, in which permanent contact between droplets exists only in the dense concentration regime. For such two-phase flows, various models have been proposed adopting the two-fluids approach. Among them, some are well acceptable for a single flow pattern; however, few are considered suitable for both. This work presents a new model for such mixture flows, applying to a wide concentration range. In the dilute regime, it corresponds to a conditionally hyperbolic model that has been extensively studied in the literatures, while in the dense regime, it corresponds to a symmetric extension of the well-known Baer–Nunziato model. The entire model is fully entropy consistent, total momentum, and energy conserving, while enabling a smooth transition from dilute to dense regime. Analysis is provided for its characteristic as well as asymptotic limits in stiff mechanical relations. Finite volume-type method for numerical solution is designed consistently by combining sharp interface resolving solvers for the dense and dilute flow patterns. A series of numerical tests are carried out to illustrate the capability and advantage of the new model and its solution method.

papers.title: Nonlinear vortex-induced force model identification by combination of growth- and decay-to-resonance vibrations and applications
papers.abstract: This study addresses a key limitation in motion-described vortex-induced force (VIF) modeling connect to vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of bridge decks: parameter identification has traditionally based on incomplete response histories. Wind tunnel tests in this study are conducted on a sectional model with synchronized measurements of displacement, aeroelastic force, motion frequency, and phase angles. After quantifying the non-wind-induced aerodynamic damping and stiffness in still air, a nonlinear VIF model was identified by jointly using the growth-to-resonance (GR) and decay-to-resonance (DR) processes. The identified parameters are expressed in a motion-amplitude-dependent form according to the extracted energy-trapping characteristics. The combined GR–DR procedure improves the completeness of model parameters, extends their applicability to both higher and lower mechanical damping conditions, and avoids the parameter-range insufficiency reported in earlier three-dimensional applications. These results establish a more robust basis for nonlinear VIF identification and three-dimensional VIV analysis.

papers.title: Volume conservation endows soap bubbles distinctive roll-off characteristics
papers.abstract: We investigate the thinning and breakup of stretched soap bubbles and compare them with open soap films. We focus on the roll-off regime, the early nonequilibrium stage after the onset of spontaneous collapse, where volume conservation makes bubble dynamics qualitatively different from those of films. In this regime, rescaled bubble profiles exhibit approximate shape collapse over time, and the global profile is governed primarily by the dimensionless parameter V/R3, where V is the bubble volume, and R is the ring radius. At fixed V/R3, profiles for different R collapse onto a common curve. Within the experimentally accessible roll-off window, the minimum neck radius deviates from the film prediction hmin∼τ2/3 and is qualitatively closer to a τ1/2 trend.

papers.title: Mechanism of enhanced energy dissipation and flow blockage in free-form labyrinth seals via hierarchical Bayesian optimization
papers.abstract: The sealing effectiveness of labyrinth seals is fundamentally dictated by the complex interplay between wall curvature, localized boundary layer separation, and multi-scale vortex dynamics within the clearance. While traditional geometric designs have reached a performance plateau, this study explores the physical limits of flow control through free-form boundary evolution. Addressing the limitations of traditional configurations, this study proposes a free-form parameterization method based on decoupled mean-line and thickness distributions via B-splines. A hierarchical Bayesian optimization framework is established to navigate a 24-dimensional design space through a collaborative “macro-layout sizing and local micro-profiling” approach. The results demonstrate that, while maintaining a constant physical clearance, the hierarchical optimization achieves a significant sealing gain of 22.1%. Crucially, the free-form profiling stage uncovers a unique mechanism where the optimized wall curvature evolves into a strategic “tip-dimple” structure. This micro-geometry triggers a localized boundary layer separation, inducing an intensified aerodynamic blockage effect that effectively constricts the main leakage path without reducing the physical clearance. Quantitative identification using symbolic regression reveals that the mean-line feature points near the tooth tips contribute over 90% to the leakage characteristics (R2 = 0.9209). Flow mechanism analysis confirms that the optimized configuration reshapes energy loss pathways by strengthening viscous shear dissipation through vortex core compression induced by the tooth-tip dimple. The optimized seal also exhibits superior off-design robustness across a wide range of pressure ratios and Reynolds numbers, providing a novel theoretical perspective and technical route for high-performance seal design.

papers.title: Implicit large eddy simulation of nearly incompressible flows with a discontinuous Galerkin–Boltzmann formulation
papers.abstract: We present a high-order implicit large eddy simulation (ILES) approach for simulating flows at the nearly incompressible regime. Our methodology is based on the utilization of a nodal discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretization of the Boltzmann equations. The compactness and low-dissipative nature of the discontinuous Galerkin method are leveraged to mimic traditional large eddy simulations with subgrid-scale models. One of the key requirements of ILES is to provide dissipation only within a narrow band of high wavenumbers. This is validated through numerical experiments on the Taylor–Green vortex problem in detail at a Reynolds number where varying scales of coherent turbulent structures are present. Furthermore, the approach is validated for external aerodynamic configurations by simulating the flow over a sphere at a Reynolds number of Re=3700, capturing the laminar–turbulent transition and the complex multiscale vortex dynamics characteristic of this regime. The results demonstrate the capability of the high-order DG-Boltzmann formulation to accurately capture transitional and turbulent flow features without the use of explicit subgrid scale modeling, highlighting its potential as a robust and physically consistent framework for ILES of nearly incompressible turbulent flows.

papers.title: Research on the coupling of separation flow and tip leakage flow in low-solidity blade tip-turbine cascades
papers.abstract: The double-layer blade configuration, consisting of upper and lower blade with an intermediate connecting section, is extensively adopted in reversible gas turbines and variable cycle engines. For upper turbine (blade tip-turbine) of this blade configuration, the coupled flow loss induced by separation flow and tip leakage flow (TLF), which arises from low-solidity and a large diameter-height ratio, constitutes a critical bottleneck restricting the improvement of turbine performance, and relevant research remains scarce. The TLF migrates over a wider range and couples with suction-side separation flow, intensifying flow blockage and turbulent mixing. In this research, combining experiments and numerical simulations, a transonic low-solidity turbine rotor linear cascade is investigated. The regulatory effects of tip clearance (0–2.5%H), solidity (1.0–1.4), Mach number (0.4–0.8), and incidence angles (−20°–20°) on the vortex coupling strength are systematically examined. High-precision measurement devices including five-hole probe and pressure-scanning valves were utilized in the experiments to acquire comprehensive flow field data, such as the total pressure, static pressure, and flow angle at the cascade inlet and outlet, as well as the static pressure distribution on the blade surface. The research results show that as the solidity increases from 1.0 to 1.2, the separation point gradually shifts from 50% axial chord to 65% on the suction surface, and separation flow disappears completely when the solidity rises to 1.4. The slowdown in the rising rate of the absolute total pressure loss coefficient when tip clearance exceeds 2%, and the mixing of TLF and separation flow is the major factor for the increase in flow loss. The total pressure loss of low-solidity cascade is more sensitive to positive incidence angles. This research reveals the coupling flow mechanism of TLF and separation flow in low-solidity blade tip-turbines, and provides experimental and theoretical support for performance improvement.

papers.title: Dynamic mode decomposition and mechanism analysis of unsteady wind turbine wake evolution in complex terrain
papers.abstract: As wind energy shifts to complex terrains, the unsteady evolution of turbine wakes—marked by three-dimensional inhomogeneity and low-frequency unsteadiness—poses challenges for power optimization and structural integrity. This study develops a robust reduced-order model integrating large eddy simulation and dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to decode wake-topography interactions. Findings show the I-criterion offers superior interpretability over the traditional α-criterion. By accounting for spatiotemporal persistence, it captures critical low-frequency instability modes governing far-field meandering while filtering high-frequency transients. The research elucidates key “topography-wake” coupling mechanisms: favorable pressure gradients on windward slopes elongate wake structures, while adverse gradients at hilltops trigger multiscale structural nesting and accelerated energy cascades. Downstream, intense turbulence exerts a “decoupling effect,” fragmenting coherent topologies. For the idealized two-dimensional Gaussian-hill and neutral-atmospheric boundary layer cases considered here, retaining 30% of the dominant modes keeps the reconstruction error below 10% while preserving the main wake topology and meandering phase information. These results demonstrate the feasibility of DMD-based reduced-order analysis for idealized terrain-modulated wakes and provide a basis for future extension to more realistic three-dimensional terrains and atmospheric conditions.

papers.title: A machine learning-enhanced Eulerian framework for prediction of near-free-surface underwater explosion bubble dynamics
papers.abstract: Predicting bubble dynamics in near-free-surface underwater explosions (NFS-UNDEX) with high fidelity is crucial for engineering design and safety assessment, yet it remains a formidable challenge due to the dominant influence of free-surface effects, which invalidate conventional free-field theories. To bridge this gap, this study develops a novel data-driven framework that synergistically combines Eulerian simulation and a Back Propagation (BP) neural network. The framework is rigorously grounded in experimental validation. A dedicated small-scale underwater explosion test was conducted, providing data that not only verified the fidelity of our three-dimensional Eulerian model but also quantitatively exposed the significant inaccuracy (errors > 10%) of a classic free-field empirical formula (the Geers–Hunter model) under NFS-UNDEX conditions. Leveraging the validated model, a comprehensive dataset of 150 simulations was generated, covering charge masses from 10 to 100 kg and explosion depths from 0.6 to 7.2 m. The dataset encapsulates key parameters: maximum radius (Rmax), pulsation period (PP), time to reach Rmax (Tm), and the height (Hw) and width (Ww) of the accompanying spray dome. A BP neural network trained on this dataset achieves exceptional predictive accuracy. Its errors for Rmax and PP are below 5%, markedly outperforming the empirical formula. The model also reliably predicts spray dome morphology, with median absolute percentage errors below 2% for both height and width, and 95th percentile errors under 5.5%. This work establishes an efficient hybrid framework, validated by experiment, for the high-fidelity prediction of complex NFS-UNDEX bubble dynamics.

papers.title: The excitation patterns and surface pressure characteristics of torsional vortex-induced vibration for typical bluff-body sections
papers.abstract: As a commonly used bridge section, the 10:1 rectangular section shows strong sensitivity of vortex-induced vibration (VIV) to parameters such as angle of attack (AoA) and sectional geometry. To identify the excitation patterns of torsional VIV for a typical bluff-body section, wind tunnel tests and numerical simulations were employed to systematically investigate the surface load distribution characteristics and evolutionary patterns of flow fields during the torsional VIV process. During the research process, the vibration responses of four types of sections were first analyzed. Then, based on the flow field characteristics, the vorticity ratio was innovatively defined. The relationship between the average vorticity ratio and the amplitude was clarified, and the excitation patterns of torsional VIV at high AoA were summarized. The research results show that the lower leading-edge corner can effectively suppress the torsional VIV, and the presence of the leading-edge corner can significantly change the spatial distribution characteristics of the local mean pressure. However, the lower trailing-edge corner will exacerbate the torsional VIV. The unilateral asymmetric fluctuation of the surface pressure is the key factor inducing the torsional VIV. Additionally, the surface pressure in the key vibration-inducing region shows significant non-Gaussian characteristics during torsional VIV. The relationship between the mean vorticity ratio and torsional amplitude can be well fitted by an exponential function. Moreover, the amplitude of the torsional VIV at high AoA mainly depends on the leading-edge vortex and the impinging leading-edge vortex.

papers.title: Energy budget of flow over spanwise thermal heterogeneity with a stable stratification
papers.abstract: Energy dissipation in a stably stratified thermally heterogeneous channel at a constant friction Reynolds number Reτ=395 and a molecular Prandtl number of Pr=0.71 is studied through a series of large-eddy simulations. The heterogeneity is varied by altering the aspect ratio (λ), while variation in the stratification level is achieved by altering the temperature ratio (ϕ) of the hot strip to the cold strip. The channel is homogeneous along the streamwise direction, and the thermal heterogeneity is incorporated along the spanwise direction. The effect of ϕ and λ on the turbulent kinetic energy distribution, temperature variance, and heat transfer mechanisms is analyzed at three regions of the channel, viz., near-wall (0<y+<62), intermediate (62<y+<190), and outer-layer region (190<y+<395), where y+ is the non-dimensionalized wall-normal distance. Component-level analysis is performed for the turbulent kinetic energy balance, temperature variance, and heat flux balance under varying ϕ and λ conditions to critically analyze the contribution of these mechanisms to the redistribution of total energy. The stratification and heterogeneity cease to influence fluctuation velocity components very close to the wall (y+<20), while their implications are evident in the region y+≥20, extending to the center of the channel. Dissipation and viscous diffusion are stronger closer to the wall, with production countered by dissipation in the buffer layer region, which receives a substantial contribution from turbulent diffusion. A stronger stratification and heterogeneity have a greater depth of influence, extending to the intermediate region (62<y+≤190) with an adverse effect on the temperature–pressure gradient correlation.

papers.title: Free-surface vortex suppression and air-entrainment mitigation using multi-intake flow redistribution
papers.abstract: Free-surface vortices and air entrainment reduce the efficiency and operational stability of suction-driven hydraulic systems, particularly under low submergence and high discharge conditions where localized suction intensifies momentum non-uniformity. The present experimental study investigates vortex suppression through the redistribution of inflow using a multi-intake configuration combined with air separation and autonomous feedback regulation. Experiments are conducted in a transparent intake facility over submergence ratios 0.44≤H*≤3.0, and Reynolds numbers 2.5×103−7.7×104, employing one to five intake branches while maintaining constant total discharge. High-speed visualization, branch-wise pressure measurements, flow rate analysis, and direct quantification of air entrainment are used to characterize the vortex evolution. Partitioning the total discharge among multiple branches reduces local suction intensity and pressure non-uniformity, thereby weakening the concentrated rotational momentum responsible for vortex growth. Air-core vortices observed in single-intake operation transition to weaker surface disturbances and are fully suppressed under multi-intake configurations, even at low submergence. Measured reductions in vortex core volume, air-core penetration rate, penetration depth, pressure fluctuations, and entrained air demonstrate the effectiveness of momentum redistribution. Complete stabilization at high throughput is achieved through integration of closed-loop control and air separation, providing a practical and scalable strategy for mitigating vortex-induced air ingestion in hydraulic and industrial fluid systems.

papers.title: Control of tip leakage flow in a high subsonic compressor cascade under upstream wakes
papers.abstract: Tip leakage flow (TLF) is a dominant source of aerodynamic loss in high-subsonic compressors. In this study, delayed detached eddy simulation is employed to investigate the control of TLF using end wall distributed pulsed suction in a NACA65-K48 compressor cascade subject to upstream wake disturbances, providing an improved numerical basis for resolving vortex cores and unsteady flow features. Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is further applied to decouple the multi-frequency interference and elucidate the underlying control mechanisms. The results indicate that upstream wakes significantly enlarge the circumferential and spanwise extent of TLF, while their unsteady characteristics can be leveraged to enhance control effectiveness. Crucially, the analysis reveals that the spatial placement of the suction holes dictates the primary control authority, whereas the pulsed frequency serves as a secondary fine-tuning mechanism. Spatially, suction holes arranged along the tip leakage vortex (TLV) trajectory prove significantly more effective than those placed along the camber line, particularly near the vortex roll-up region. Temporally, for single-hole suction, a resonance effect is observed at the dominant frequency of the TLV (1F+). In distributed configurations, applying a sub-harmonic frequency at the downstream hole aligns with the evolved vortex timescale, with the 1 F++0.5 F+ scheme reducing the total pressure loss coefficient by approximately 6.65%. DMD analysis confirms that distributed suction effectively suppresses TLF energy fluctuations across the fundamental frequency and its higher harmonics (1 F+, 2 F+, and 3 F+), weakens the vortex cores, and mitigates breakdown-induced losses. These findings provide new insight into the interaction mechanisms of distributed pulsed suction and offer guidance for its application in advanced compressors under realistic inflow conditions.

papers.title: Physics-constrained spatiotemporal transformer network: A hybrid paradigm for meteorologically consistent wind speed prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate wind speed prediction plays a pivotal role in optimizing wind energy utilization and ensuring stable power grid operations. Despite advancements in data-driven techniques, many existing models generate predictions that deviate from established physical laws, limiting their real-world applicability. To bridge this gap, our study introduces a dual-methodological framework grounded in physics-aware machine learning. To address this, our work introduces two innovations: (a) A physics-informed hybrid architecture combining ConvNeXt-based spatiotemporal attention with a pyramidal transformer, designed to extract features while adhering to fundamental principles such as energy conservation, thermodynamic equations, and buoyancy effects. (b) A constrained optimization framework that enhances predictive accuracy while enforcing meteorological consistency. Evaluations across four seasonal datasets show superior performance over existing methods, with notable gains in both single and multi-step forecasts. For example, in dataset 1, our model attains a mean absolute percentage error of 0.204 (14.3% lower than the next-best approach) and a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.913 (3.6% higher). Physical constraints further bolster reliability, reducing errors by up to 19.6% (dataset 3) and ensuring compliance with atmospheric physics. Interpretability studies reveal that the model prioritizes physically meaningful variables: 80 m/10 m wind speed ratios dominate predictions, while temperature and humidity contributions vary seasonally.

papers.title: Large-scale circulation associated with an isolated oblique turbulent band in channel flow
papers.abstract: The large-scale circulation around an isolated oblique turbulent band in plane Poiseuille flow is investigated using direct numerical simulations in tilted narrow and large domains, combined with linear stability analysis. In the far downstream region, the disturbance field is found to be dominated by the least stable symmetric mode, which is oriented along the band at an angle θ to the streamwise direction. Upstream, however, the antisymmetric mode persists farther from the turbulent region and coexists with the symmetric mode. The obliquity of the large-scale circulation is shown to arise from the streamwise localization of turbulent fluctuations. Especially, it is found that at moderate Reynolds numbers (Re), both the symmetric and antisymmetric velocity components in the far fields exhibit spatial decay rates scaling as (Re sin θ)−1, a scaling derived analytically from the balance between momentum convection and diffusion. This work provides a theoretical explanation for the structure and scaling of the large-scale circulation associated with the isolated oblique turbulent bands in transitional channel flows.

papers.title: Aeroacoustic mechanisms and control of high-lift configuration via wall-modeled lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: The leading-edge slat in high-lift systems represents a dominant aeroacoustic source, driven by unsteady dynamics in the slat cove. Resolving turbulent structures on Cartesian grids presents a fundamental conflict between near-wall resolution and computational efficiency. To address this, we propose LBAcoustics, a framework based on the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM). It incorporates a near-wall modeling strategy that couples an interpolation bounce-back (IBB) scheme with wall function. This approach is validated against the 30P30N airfoil, effectively eliminating non-physical flow separation at an acceptable computational cost. The coupling of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and vortex sound theory facilitates the separation of hydrodynamic and acoustic fluctuations. Furthermore, the coherent superposition model reveals that large-scale coherent structures in the slat cove dominate noise generation because of their constructive interference, as validated by high magnitude-squared coherence. In addition, we establish a frequency-dependent physical map: low-frequency noise arises from global shear-layer flapping; mode fa stems from periodic vortex impingement at the reattachment point; fb is driven by two-/three-dimensional transition of Kelvin–Helmholtz (K–H) vortices; and fc results from trailing-edge scattering. Based on these insights, a steady-jet active flow control (AFC) strategy is implemented. The actuation creates a fluidic barrier that topologically restructures the shear layer, achieving a global noise reduction of 5.5 dB. Notably, the strategy virtual eliminates narrowband peaks (NBPs), with a maximum reduction peaking at 32 dB at fb.

papers.title: Mechanisms of flow-induced runner forces in a giant Francis turbine under wide load
papers.abstract: With the rapid increase in the penetration of wind and solar power in new-type power system, hydropower units are frequently required to serve as grid-regulation machines. Consequently, Francis turbines are compelled to operate over a much wider load range, which poses significant challenges to unit's safety and stability. However, the runner forces and flow characteristics that govern turbine stability remain insufficiently understood. In this study, three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations were performed to investigate wide operating conditions ranging from 5% to 110% of the rated power Pr. The flow patterns, vortex structures, pressure distributions, and runner forces were systematically analyzed. The results show that the loads lower than 40%Pr and higher than 100%Pr have degraded characteristics. The blade-channel vortices and the central backflow in the straight cone are the dominant factors responsible for the increase in radial and axial runner forces, respectively. The main regions contributing to radial and axial forces are located near the short blade inlet and the long blade outlet, respectively. The maximum radial and axial forces occur at 40%Pr and 5%Pr, respectively, while large-scale cavitation is developed at 5%Pr and 110%Pr. These findings provide reference for the safe and stable operation of giant Francis turbines under wide-load operating conditions.

papers.title: Slip-controlled crossover in pressure-driven viscoelastic channel flow
papers.abstract: Pressure-driven flows of viscoelastic fluids frequently exhibit wall slip, yet the combined influence of slip and elastic stress generation on macroscopic transport remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate fully developed creeping flow of polymer solutions in a planar channel with explicit wall slip, focusing on how slip interacts with bulk viscoelasticity across different constitutive models. We consider Oldroyd-B and three finitely extensible nonlinear elastic (FENE) models, including the FENE-P model, its conformation-dependent-drag variant (FENE-P-CD), and the Phan-Thien–Manero–Leal variant (FENE-PTML); and impose a Navier-type slip law in which the slip velocity is proportional to the total wall shear stress. By introducing slip-corrected and uncorrected excess flow rate measures, we separate boundary contributions from bulk elastic effects. The slip-corrected flow rate collapses onto model-specific master curves independent of slip strength, recovering known asymptotic scalings, while the uncorrected flow rate exhibits pronounced non-monotonic behavior. This behavior is characterized by a slip-controlled crossover Deborah number, marking a transition between elasticity-dominated and boundary-dominated transport. The location and scaling of this crossover depend sensitively on the constitutive model and slip strength, revealing qualitative differences between FENE-type models that are absent in no-slip theories. These results demonstrate that wall slip does not merely offset classical viscoelastic flow rate predictions but introduces new transport regimes governed by the competition between bulk elastic resistance and boundary slip.

papers.title: Flow mechanism of the underwater supersonic gas jet formed by the beveled nozzle
papers.abstract: The internal flow of underwater supersonic gas jets formed by beveled nozzles is highly complex. Such jets exhibit unstable characteristics, including deflection and swinging, which severely restrict the propulsion performance of underwater vehicles. In this paper, optical and Schlieren techniques are adopted to capture the flow field structures of underwater jets from quasi-two-dimensional beveled nozzles. The jet deflection characteristics and internal flow mechanism at different developmental stages are studied under various bevel angles and nozzle pressure ratios (NPRs). Results show that the development of underwater jets produced by beveled nozzles includes an initial bubble stage and a relatively stable conical stage, with continuous expansion and contraction of the jet interface. A quantitative correlation exists between the jet deflection angle, bevel angle, and NPR. An empirical formula is established in this paper, which can effectively predict the jet deflection angle. Significant swinging occurs in the jet during the initial bubble stage, and this phenomenon becomes more pronounced with a smaller bevel angle and a larger NPR. Swinging also exists in the jet during the conical stage. However, unlike the initial bubble stage, an increase in NPR gives rise to more obvious deflection but a weaker swing effect. In addition, during the conical stage, the variation of the upstream jet interface is mainly governed by the internal pressure of the jet, besides the influence of Kelvin–Helmholtz and Rayleigh–Taylor instabilities.

papers.title: Hydroelastic wave behavior of submerged elastic plates over a thick porous bed
papers.abstract: The hydroelastic interaction between surface gravity waves and submerged elastic plates is significantly influenced by both porous bed and plate parameters. Hence, in this study, the physical scenario is considered within the framework of linear water wave theory. Accordingly, the plates are described by thin elastic plate theory with in-plane compressive force, and the porous bed is represented through a frictional coefficient and a porosity parameter, allowing both impermeable and permeable bed conditions to be examined. Dispersion relations are derived and analyzed for real and complex values of the porous bed frictional coefficient, considering only propagating wave modes. The analysis focuses on the porosity and resistance parameter of the porous bed, as well as the plate compression and examines how they modify the hydroelastic wave behavior. The limiting case of a single-submerged plate configuration is analyzed, where the effects of porosity, resistance parameter, and plate compression on dispersion behavior, phase velocity, and group velocity are investigated. The results show that due to the porosity of the porous bed, the frequency branches become complex-valued over finite wavenumber ranges. In these ranges, the real parts of the frequency branches overlap, while their imaginary parts separate. This reflects the effects of porous bed dissipation. For the dual-submerged plate, the selective compression of both plates is shown, with different dispersion branches showing different effects on the interactions with the plate and porous bed. Time-domain simulations also demonstrate the particular characteristics of wave propagation of free surface modes and plate modes, along with the influence of compression on the plate response.

papers.title: Data-driven creation of compressor design charts for aeronautical applications
papers.abstract: The preliminary design of compressors depends upon a large number of parameters. Initially, the main characteristics and velocity triangles are defined by specifying the flow topology, i.e., whether the compressor is axial, mixed-flow, or centrifugal, the flow coefficient, and the loading coefficient, among other parameters. This paper presents a data-driven approach toward the creation of Smith charts for axial, mixed-flow, and centrifugal compressors on the basis of targeted three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics. The influence of the inlet hub-to-tip ratio, Mach number, the inlet Reynolds number, and the inlet boundary layer thickness on the Smith charts are analyzed. The results are applicable to the design of both single-stage and multi-stage compressors, such as the Mach number, Reynolds number, hub-to-tip ratio, and blockage vary from stage to stage. The compressors designed are then compared to the Cordier diagram. It is shown that the Mach number, Reynolds number, and hub-to-tip ratio significantly influence the Smith charts of compressors and limit the available design space in the Cordier diagram. In addition, changes in the suitable range of specific speeds of the topologies depending on the inlet conditions are shown. The diagrams presented in this paper serve as a guideline for the topology selection based on the flow coefficient and loading coefficient, considering the upstream flow conditions.

papers.title: Applications of physics-informed deep-learning in polymer rheology: Prediction and optimization for rheological molding process through integrated physical and data-driven learning
papers.abstract: The review explores the application of Physics-Informed Deep Learning (PIDL) in polymer rheology, highlighting its potential to address limitations of traditional rheological models. By integrating physical prior knowledge with data-driven methods, PIDL enhances the accuracy and reliability of fluid behavior predictions, fostering a more refined, intelligent, and interdisciplinary development in rheological research. The article outlines the fundamental principles, common architectures, and evaluation methods of PIDL, and presents practical examples of its applications in polymer rheology, including constitutive relationship modeling, fluid behavior prediction, experimental data analysis, multiscale simulation and optimization, and process parameter optimization. Challenges faced by PIDL in polymer rheology, such as data quality, model generalization capabilities, and multiscale problem-solving, are also discussed, along with current solutions.

papers.title: Liquid falling behavior in vertical partial annular pipes under gas–liquid countercurrent flow
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid two-phase flow in annular pipes is fundamental to heat and mass transfer processes in petroleum, chemical, and related engineering fields. This study experimentally and numerically investigates liquid falling dynamics in vertical partially annular pipes under top-injection conditions. The numerically predicted falling ratio agrees well with experimental data, and the average error is 6.93%. Based on visual observations, five typical flow morphologies are qualitatively classified, and key governing parameters, including gas velocity, liquid velocity, rheological properties, viscosity, and surface tension, are identified. The evolution of the liquid falling ratio is quantitatively examined, and its nonlinear variation from 0 to 1 is illustrated for Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. The results show that at low gas velocities, the critical gas velocity for complete falling and the falling ratio both increase with liquid viscosity, density, and surface tension, while they decrease with superficial liquid velocity. Furthermore, these quantities exhibit a non-monotonic trend with increasing liquid yield stress, initially rising and then declining. At high gas velocities, thinning of the liquid film weakens interphase momentum transfer and greatly reduces the sensitivity of the falling ratio to these parameters. Compared with shear-thinning fluids, shear-thickening fluids are more prone to complete falling at low liquid velocities, whereas the opposite occurs at high liquid velocities. This behavior originates primarily from the reversal of the effective viscosity gradient due to differences in shear rate. The findings of this study can provide an important theoretical foundation for blowout control and gas-lift optimization in petroleum engineering.

papers.title: Wave attenuation mechanism and geometry optimization of a π-shaped porous floating breakwater: A numerical study
papers.abstract: The expansion of offshore industries into deep-water environments necessitates a fundamental understanding of the fluid-structure interaction between surface gravity waves and permeable structures. This study investigates the wave attenuation mechanisms and energy dissipation characteristics of a π-shaped porous floating breakwater (PFB) through a macroscopic numerical framework based on the volume-averaged Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations. By modeling the porous matrix as a distributed body force within the momentum equations, this work demonstrates the utility of the macroscopic approach for the practical investigation of internal flow physics and geometric optimization of PFB. Our analysis reveals that wave energy dissipation is spatially non-uniform and is predominantly governed by frictional drag concentrated at the seaward part of PFB, where the relative velocity between the fluid and the pile-restrained skeleton is maximized. A distinct cyclic pattern of instantaneous dissipation is observed, synchronized with wave phases, where peak energy losses occur during the impingement of the wave crest and the strong reverse flow of the trough. The transition from a rectangular to a π-shaped cross section significantly modulates the internal energy dissipation rate. The deeper effective draft and the induction of wave overtopping enhance the dissipation efficiency of the upper regions. Notably, while the excavation of the lower cavity reduces the structural mass and the buoyancy-driven heave force, the π-shaped configuration maintains a heave response amplitude comparable to the rectangular baseline. This investigation elucidates the role of structural asymmetry in governing wave energy transport and highlights the effectiveness of macroscopic modeling in uncovering the underlying viscous-inertial mechanisms of porous floating systems.

papers.title: Lift enhancement of an airfoil using covert-inspired dual-side flexible flaps
