This disparity triggers a positive feedback loop involving trajectory deviation and tail slamming. Steeper water-exit angles increase fluid inertia, suppressing this feedback and enabling the vehicle to stably skim the cavity lip. Ultimately, nose shape and exit angle collectively dictate the free-surface effect's intensity. This study elucidates the fundamental mechanisms governing shallow-angle trans-media exits, providing insights into cavity asymmetry, motion characteristics, and hydrodynamic loading.

papers.title: Optimization techniques in self-similar compressible flow
papers.abstract: We investigate the one-dimensional (1D) inviscid compressible flow equations for an ideal gas through the lens of optimization techniques. It is the case that, to our knowledge, optimization analysis applied to the so-called “linear velocity” solutions of the Euler compressible flow equations has not been previously conducted. Through both gradient-based and variational techniques, new variants of well-studied flow scenarios, i.e., self-similar, 1D, linear velocity solution class to idealized inviscid compressible flow equations, are determined, as encoded in both the kinematic and thermodynamic properties of this self-similar solution class. With the kinematics of the said solutions being driven by a self-similar “scale radius” and the thermodynamics being driven separately through the appearance of an arbitrary function, a myriad of new solution classes is possible. Acting as a guide to more realistic physical circumstances as well as discovery, it is the hope that the presented cases serve as the framework for future investigations into the intersection of self-similarity and optimization techniques. Fields of study that may find this work to be of interest include aerodynamic design, flow control, inertial confinement fusion, physics-informed neural networks, and other related areas of interest.

papers.title: Nonmodal instabilities along the leeward side of a high-speed yawed circular cone
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed exceptionally low transition N-factors (below 2) based on modal instabilities for the leeward ray of yawed cones in the wind tunnels, suggesting that nonmodal growth mechanisms could potentially play a significant role. In light of these findings, the present work employs optimal growth theory to examine linear evolution of optimal disturbances on the leeward side of cones at 2° and 4° angles of attack in high-speed flows. Three distinct types of optimal disturbances are identified: low-frequency disturbance, Mack-mode-like disturbance, and entropy-layer disturbance. Among these, low-frequency disturbances exhibit the highest N-factors of approximately 5.5 near experimentally observed transition locations. Aside from the entropy-layer disturbance which relies solely on the Orr mechanism, the other optimal disturbances initially leverage the lift-up or Orr mechanism and progressively transition to growth driven by the modal instability mechanism downstream. The dominant energy production for all three types of disturbances mainly comes from the wall-normal shear of the base flow. Specifically, the low-frequency and Mack-mode-like disturbances gain energy inside the boundary layer, whereas the entropy-layer disturbance obtains its energy within the entropy layer region outside the boundary layer.

papers.title: Vortex shedding characteristics in air-assisted sprays: A phenomenological and quantitative study
papers.abstract: Vortex shedding at the edge of twin-fluid spray was systematically identified and analyzed. High-speed photography was used to capture air-assisted spray under varying fuel injection durations (Tf) and gas injection pressures (Pa), revealing vortex shedding at the spray edge. Image processing techniques enabled quantitative analysis of the spray edge near the outlet of the air-assisted injector. The dimensionless timing of vortex shedding demonstrated a linear relationship with the ratio of dimensionless fuel injection durations (T*) to dimensionless gas injection pressures (P*). The shedding location shifted further from the injector as Pa increased, regardless of Tf. Power spectral density analysis combined with sliding-window sampling techniques enabled detailed examination of spray edge evolution and provided both full time and time-resolved characteristic frequencies of vortex shedding under various conditions. The inherent instability of air-assisted sprays resulted in multiple characteristic peaks in the full time vortex shedding frequency. The time-resolved characteristic frequency initially increased and then stabilized. Across all conditions, the vortex shedding frequency decreased with longer Tf and increased with higher Pa. The dimensionless maximum vortex shedding characteristics frequency for each condition demonstrated a linear relationship with T*·1−ln P*. The autocorrelation function was employed to calculate the wave propagation delay, thereby determining wave propagation velocity and, subsequently, the minimum wavelength. Wave velocity increased exclusively with rising Pa, highlighting the dominant influence of the gas phase in wave propagation. A nearly linear relationship was observed between wave velocity and maximum vortex shedding frequency. The minimum wavelength increases exponentially, primarily with Tf.

papers.title: Longitudinal combustion oscillation suppression by quarter-wave resonators in bluff-body diffusion flames
papers.abstract: A longitudinal self-sustained combustion oscillation in a bluff-body-stabilized propane diffusion flame was experimentally suppressed using quarter-wave resonators. The baseline combustor exhibited a limit-cycle oscillation at 207.28 Hz, with a pressure amplitude of approximately 972.56 Pa and nearly in-phase pressure and heat release rate fluctuations. A nonlinear acoustic-impedance model of the QW was developed and validated by impedance-tube measurements; within the frequency range most relevant to the resonator function, most amplitude and phase errors remained within 5%. The experiments show that a single QW provides narrowband control and may either suppress or amplify the oscillation depending on its resonance frequency relative to the preexisting combustion oscillations frequency. To quantify this behavior, three nondimensional parameters were introduced: the normalized QW resonance frequency, normalized oscillation pressure amplitude, and normalized oscillation frequency. The optimal suppression cases were mainly located within −0.15 < ηfa < −0.07, whereas amplification became more likely when ηfa > −0.07. The strongest amplification occurred in case 3, where the oscillation pressure amplitude increased by 17.7%. Under the optimal 12-QW configuration, the pressure amplitude was reduced by 77.8% (13.1 dB), and the original single-mode limit cycle collapsed into weaker low-frequency components around 140 and 155 Hz. CH* dynamic mode decomposition further showed that the suppressed state was accompanied by an asymmetric projected flame-pulsation structure, which was qualitatively consistent with the simulated redistribution of transverse acoustic velocity near the resonator sidewall. These results indicate that QW suppression is governed primarily by resonator-induced acoustic-pressure-response redistribution and the associated modification of the flame–acoustic feedback loop, rather than by the sound absorption coefficient alone.

papers.title: Study of vortex motions over an inclined plate with periodic oscillating microstructures
papers.abstract: The surfaces of many animals and plants in nature are covered with deformable microstructures that engage in complex fluid–structure interactions and thereby control the flow. However, our understanding of the physical mechanisms by which these deformable microstructures regulate the flow remains limited. In this work, a bioinspired surface with periodically oscillating microstructures is designed to investigate how microstructures influence the flow over an inclined plate. The study employs a simplified model inspired by the dermal denticles of shark skin, and a method combining the immersed boundary method and the lattice Boltzmann flux solver is conducted for two-dimensional numerical simulations. The Reynolds number based on the plate chord and the incoming flow velocity is 2.0×104. The results show that changing the oscillation amplitude and frequency of the microstructures can effectively control the drag. With increasing frequency and amplitude, the drag reduction rate increases and reaches a maximum of 47.5%. The flow over different cases can be classified into two regimes, which are the coherent vortex shedding regime and the isolated vortex shedding regime. With large microstructure frequency and amplitude, the isolated vortex shedding regime appears and a substantial drag reduction is reached. In this regime, the microstructures periodically modulate the flow field near the leading edge, causing the characteristic frequency of the flow to become locked to the structural oscillation frequency. A parameter combining the microstructure frequency and amplitude is analyzed to predict the flow regime for different cases.

papers.title: Thermal transport and lift-drag dynamics in magneto-micropolar flow past over a bluff body within a lid-driven channel under localized magnetic field influence
papers.abstract: The thermal transport and lift-drag behavior of an unsteady magneto-micropolar fluid past a circular bluff body under a localized magnetic field are investigated numerically. The governing equations, formulated in a dimensionless framework consistent with the principles of magnetohydrodynamics and ferrohydrodynamics, are solved using the finite element method. The effects of micropolar parameter (K), Reynolds number (Re), Stuart number (N), and magnetic number (M) on flow stability, microrotation, and heat transfer are analyzed. Increasing M suppresses vortex shedding and stabilizes the flow, reducing oscillation in lift, drag, and wall heat flux. In contrast, higher K intensifies microrotation and enhances drag and thermal mixing, while increasing Re strengthen flow unsteadiness and convective transport. The results provide new insight into magnetically controlled micropolar flows relevant to cooling, biomedical and microfluidic systems.

papers.title: Acoustic field inconsistency in thermoacoustic oscillations of a swirling non-premixed flame: Forced vs self-sustained regimes
papers.abstract: Using a laboratory-scale, swirling non-premixed flame, we combine experiments, large eddy simulation-acoustic simulations, and phase-closure analysis to compare forced and self-sustained regimes. The results show that although the velocity fields upstream and immediately downstream of the swirler remain similar, significant discrepancies emerge within the combustor: in the forced system, velocity perturbations originate from upstream acoustic forcing, whereas in the self-sustained system, the flame itself acts as a volumetric expansion source. In addition, considering the oscillatory fuel jet induced by back-pressure oscillations in the self-sustained regime, acoustic simulations indicate that the jet-velocity pulsation at the porous fuel nozzle reaches about 30% of the mean velocity. Even at this level, simulations show the resulting flame response is relatively modest. The differing combustor acoustic fields, together with the periodic fuel pulsation, lead to pronounced differences between forced and self-sustained oscillations. Consequently, the phase transfer between oscillating velocity, pressure, and heat release rate fluctuations differs markedly between the two regimes. Under weak oscillations and short combustor lengths, the flame responses obtained from forced oscillations reasonably approximate those in self-sustained oscillations. However, at higher oscillation amplitudes or longer combustor lengths, strong velocity fluctuations within the chamber significantly distort flame pulsations, where phase closure error was found to exceed π/2 radian. Even with careful selection of the velocity reference plane in forced oscillation tests, the pronounced differences in the acoustic field and fuel pulsation introduce new challenges for flame transfer function/flame describing function studies.

papers.title: Transport and mixing of combustion-assisting agent in coal rock reservoirs for in situ methane explosive fracturing
papers.abstract: Targeting the high water consumption and easy fracture closure of conventional hydraulic fracturing for ultralow-permeability coal seams, in situ methane explosive fracturing requires no external water, with detonation-generated complex fractures featuring high, durable flow conductivity, making it an emerging solution to boost low-permeability coal rock gas recovery. The core lies in achieving efficient mixing of a combustion-assisting agent (CAA) with methane inside the reservoir. To reveal this mixing process, a three-dimensional wellbore-reservoir flow numerical model integrating the Realizable k–ε turbulence model and porous media model was established. The migration patterns and mixing characteristics of the CAA under open-hole and perforated completion conditions were comparatively analyzed. The results show that perforated completion can significantly enhance both the maximum injection distance and the sweep efficiency of the system by constructing a “perforation-dominated radial expansion” composite diffusion pattern. The volume proportion of the explosive zone reaches 24.50%, representing a 41.60% increase (relative) compared to open-hole completion (17.30%), while the extension distance of the explosive zone increases from 1.80 to 2.30 m. Parameter sensitivity analysis reveals that reservoir permeability, which governs the matrix seepage capacity, is the most fundamental parameter determining injection effectiveness. Increasing permeability from 0.01 to 0.2 mD enhances CAA sweep efficiency by 35.90% (absolute). Perforation depth and delivery pressure are the most sensitive engineering parameters for regulating the extent of the explosive zone, whereas the influence of perforation diameter (10–18 mm) is negligible. Based on the Peclet number, completion structure factor, and permeability factor, a quantitative evaluation model for CAA mixing efficiency is established. Validated against ten operating conditions, the model yields prediction errors below 2%. This study provides a theoretical basis for coal rock gas reservoir explosive fracturing.

papers.title: Wall-modeled large eddy simulation of high-speed high-enthalpy turbulent boundary layers with catalytic effects
papers.abstract: The catalytic effects intensify near-wall chemical reactions in high-enthalpy turbulent boundary layers and strongly influence the heat fluxes, posing significant difficulties for the wall-modeled large eddy simulation. To tackle these issues, this study proposes a multi-species ordinary differential equation (ODE) based wall model to describe the near-wall catalytic effects. A computationally robust and efficient framework is established based on the pseudo-time implicit iteration in conjunction with reaction-flow splitting. To incorporate turbulence–chemistry interactions (TCIs), the assumed probability-density-function method is considered by solving an ODE-based transport equation of temperature variance, thereby enhancing the prediction accuracy of near-wall species mass fractions. The model's performance is evaluated through systematic a priori and a posteriori validation. A priori tests confirm that TCI effects must be accounted for in high-enthalpy catalytic wall flows. A posteriori results demonstrate that the proposed model accurately captures the characteristics of high-enthalpy turbulent boundary layers with catalytic walls. Importantly, the errors in predicted skin friction and wall heat flux are less than 10%, meeting practical engineering requirements while balancing accuracy and computational cost.

papers.title: Forebody boundary layer diverting feature of submerged bleed array and its effects on submerged inlet
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic performance degradation at the Aerodynamic Interface Plane (AIP) caused by boundary layer ingestion from the fuselage presents a critical challenge for submerged inlets. A submerged bleed array is proposed as a flow control method to address this issue. The effects of the bleed array on the flowfield structure and aerodynamic performance of the inlet are numerically and experimentally investigated at freestream Mach numbers Ma0 = 0.50, 0.70, and 0.80. Results demonstrate that the bleed array effectively captures and redistributes low-energy fluid originating from the fuselage, significantly reducing the low-total-pressure region near the lower wall of the inlet. At the three investigated Mach numbers, implementation of the bleed array yields maximum increases in the AIP total pressure recovery coefficient of 2.0%, 3.1%, and 4.0%, respectively, along with maximum reductions in the total pressure distortion index of 51.4%, 55.0%, and 54.9%, respectively. Further analysis of the flowfield at Ma0 = 0.70 reveals that the enhanced total pressure recovery coefficient at the AIP primarily stems from reduced low-energy flow near the lower wall, while variations in the total pressure distortion index result from the coupled effects of side-edge vortices and near-wall low-energy flow. At higher AIP Mach numbers (MaAIP), the side-edge vortices exhibit smaller scales, and the bleed array effectively diminishes the low-total-pressure area near the lower wall, thereby reducing the distortion index. Conversely, at lower MaAIP, the side-edge vortices enlarge, and the low-total-pressure region becomes concentrated near the sidewalls after control, leading to an increased total pressure distortion index.

papers.title: Coupling mechanism of suction port position and intensity on aerodynamic performance of a suction-type turbosail
papers.abstract: The key to improving ship wind energy utilization efficiency lies in optimizing the aerodynamic performance of suction-type turbosails, yet the coupling mechanism of suction port position (α) and suction intensity (γ) remains unrevealed. Focusing on the attack angle of β = −15°, this study established a two-dimensional numerical simulation using the renormalization group k–ε turbulence model and semi-implicit method for pressure-linked equations algorithm to explore the coupling effect of α (5°–85°) and γ (0.2–2.0). Results show a significant synergistic regulation with three distinct regimes of aerodynamic performance. The optimal parameter range was identified as α = 35°–55° coupled with γ = 1.2–2.0, achieving high lift coefficient (CL = 5.168–6.217), low drag coefficient (CD = 0.290–0.556), and high lift-drag ratio (R = 10.652–21.241). Flow field analysis confirms favorable pressure gradient, over 85% airflow attachment rate, and a uniform and well-organized time-averaged wake structure. A three-level parameter zoning system was proposed. This study quantifies the α–γ coupling regulation law, fills the theoretical gap of multi-parameter collaborative optimization for turbosails, and provides directly applicable design criteria for full-scale ships, contributing to shipping decarbonization.

papers.title: A numerical investigation of three-dimensional flow dynamics in a density-driven channel confluence
papers.abstract: River confluences are critical nodes within fluvial networks, where hydrodynamic structures are inherently complex. Density contrasts between tributaries, stemming from differences in temperature, salinity, or sediment concentration, are increasingly recognized as a key factor regulating confluence hydrodynamics and mixing. However, a systematic understanding of how such density differences govern the three-dimensional flow structure and the critically important secondary circulation remains limited. This study employs a Reynolds stress model to numerically investigate the effects of both the magnitude and direction of density differences on the flow field, secondary flows, and turbulent kinetics in an open-channel confluence. The results demonstrate that density contrasts induce a fundamental shift from an inertia-dominated to a buoyancy-influenced regime. This shift manifests as a compression of the separation zone, a downstream extension of the recovery region, and—most critically—a buoyancy-dominated control over the secondary flow. The direction of the helical motion is dictated by the sign of the density difference: it aligns with the density-neutral rotation when the mainstream is denser but reverses when the tributary is denser. The influence on turbulence is non-monotonic; moderate contrasts enhance turbulent kinetic energy and secondary flow intensity, while strong contrasts suppress them through stable stratification. Notably, within the studied range (Richardson number Ri = 0.16–0.32), buoyancy transitions from initiating near-bed intrusion to dominating the secondary flow pattern. These findings quantify the coupling mechanism between buoyancy and inertia and provide a refined conceptual model for predicting flow structure and mixing efficiency in confluences affected by environmental gradients.

papers.title: Experimental study of turbulent thermal diffusion of inertial particles in a convective turbulence forced by oscillating grids
papers.abstract: We investigate the phenomenon of turbulent thermal diffusion of inertial solid particles in laboratory experiments with convective turbulence forced by one or two oscillating grids in the air. Turbulent thermal diffusion causes a non-diffusive contribution to the turbulent flux of particles described in terms of an effective drift velocity directed opposite to the gradient of the mean fluid temperature. For inertial particles, this effective drift velocity depends on the Stokes and Reynolds numbers. In the experiments, fluid velocity and spatial distribution of inertial particles are measured using a particle image velocimetry system, and the temperature field is measured in many locations by a temperature probe equipped with 12 thermocouples. Measurements of temperature and particle number density spatial distributions have demonstrated the formation of large-scale clusters of inertial particles in the vicinity of the mean temperature minimum due to turbulent thermal diffusion. In the experiments, the effective drift velocity caused by turbulent thermal diffusion which results in the formation of large-scale clusters of inertial particles (having a diameter 10 μm), is in 1.5–2.5 times larger than that for noninertial particles (having the diameter 0.7 μm) depending on the level of turbulence. This is in agreement with the theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Cavitation characteristics and induced runner erosion of a Francis turbine in Southern Xinjiang
papers.abstract: Hydraulic cavitation is the primary cause of cavitation erosion in Francis turbine runners. Under the special hydrological conditions prevalent in the desert margin areas of southern Xinjiang, cavitation erosion damage to the runner is particularly severe. Taking the HLJF2062-LJ-200 Francis turbine as the research object, this study employs unsteady numerical simulations of the full flow passage, incorporating the shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model, the volume of fluid multiphase flow model, and the Zwart–Gerber–Belamri cavitation model. It investigates the cavitation characteristics and erosion patterns of the runner under three guide vane openings (14° for low-load, 21° for rated-load, and 28° for high-load conditions) and within a cavitation coefficient range of 0.06–0.20. The results show that cavitation is concentrated on the suction side of the blades near the band side, which constitutes the core cavitation erosion zone. The critical cavitation coefficient increases as the guide vane opening decreases, with values of (σ = 0.06–0.08, 0.08–0.10, and 0.10–0.12) for large, design, and small openings, respectively. The simulation results are consistent with the field measurements of cavitation erosion of the prototype turbine under high-load conditions, providing a theoretical and engineering reference for the operational regulation and anti-cavitation protection of hydraulic turbines in high sediment-laden water regions.

papers.title: Flow distortion effects on the aerodynamics and performance of a low-pressure ratio fan in a boundary layer ingestion aft-fuselage propulsor
papers.abstract: Turbomachinery operating in boundary layer ingestion propulsion systems can experience substantial performance degradation due to elevated levels of inlet distortion. This paper presents a numerical investigation of the aerodynamics and performance of a low-pressure ratio fan designed for a tail-cone thruster integrated within a hydrogen-electric powertrain. The rotor is assessed in three flight conditions along the climb trajectory using unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations to examine the aerodynamic behavior, the energy exchange mechanisms, and the sensitivity to inflow distortion. The spoiled inflow induces significant excursions of the blade operating point, driven by axial and tangential momentum redistribution at the inlet plane. As a consequence, some azimuthal sectors operate under high blade loading and reduced mass flux, while others exhibit increased mass flow and relative velocity. The continuous migration of the working point toward both stall and choking conditions leads to an overall efficiency penalty of 2.5% in cruise. Earlier in the climb, the less severe distortion progressively attenuates performance degradation, but the operating point excursion is amplified by the reduction in compression characteristic. Under near-stall conditions, the rotor experiences loading levels locally beyond the clean inlet condition, but the blades are able to recover toward higher flow rates without incurring leading edge spillage.

papers.title: Radial bubble crossflow to reduce drag in vertical circular Couette flow
papers.abstract: This Letter studies the effect of radial bubble crossflow on drag reduction of the vertical Couette flow between an upward moving cylinder and a fixed outer coaxial cylinder. A simple formula is given for the reduced drag under the condition that the lift force coefficient equates to the added mass coefficient, which predicts that the effect of radial bubble crossflow on drag reduction increases with decreasing bubble size but decreases with increasing speed of the moving cylinder, in qualitative agreement with some known results. The practical applicability of the derived formula is illustrated with specific numerical examples.

papers.title: Separation control and lift enhancement of a conformal-slot co-flow-jet wing
papers.abstract: To mitigate the aerodynamic penalty of conventional co-flow-jet (CFJ) wings when the jet is off due to slot discontinuity, a conformal-slot CFJ wing (S809-based) was designed and evaluated in a wind tunnel using static force measurements and particle image velocimetry. With the jet off, the conformal-slot CFJ wing achieves near-baseline performance, with only a 1.82% average decrease in lift coefficient and a 0.25% average increase in drag coefficient. With the jet on, aerodynamic performance improves markedly as the jet momentum coefficient Cμ increases: the maximum lift coefficient rises by 40.01%, the maximum lift-to-drag ratio by 132.59%, and stall is delayed from 16° to 18°. Time-averaged velocity fields show a reduced separation region and a downstream shift of the separation point; at α = 16° and Cμ = 0.1, the low-speed separated region vanishes and the flow remains attached. Mean and phase-resolved vorticity indicate that continuous momentum injection accelerates shear-layer transition and suppresses separation–vortex growth, leading to a shift from separation-dominated to attachment-dominated flow.

papers.title: Computational fluid dynamics-population balance model and experimental investigation of gas–liquid mass transfer enhancement in a horizontal stirred tank agitated by a porous medium impeller
papers.abstract: This study investigates the enhancement characteristics of gas–liquid mass transfer in a horizontal stirred tank driven by a porous medium impeller. A coupled simulation approach combining computational fluid dynamics and population balance model, integrated with high-speed imaging experiments, was employed to analyze bubble behavior and gas–liquid interactions under varying stirring speeds. The results indicate that the porous medium impeller results in the smallest average bubble diameter in the system at 50 rpm, with the highest proportion of small bubbles among all stirring speeds. The optimal applicability of the Laakkonen breakage model for horizontal porous medium impeller aeration systems is systematically verified for the first time. The conclusion that bubble size distribution prediction in the impeller region is critical to full-reactor simulation is confirmed to be applicable to horizontal structures. An eddy cell mass transfer model suitable for the reactor is established via quantitative fitting, with a maximum error of 1.95%. Stirring speed significantly regulates flow field patterns: At 50 rpm, flow is confined near the impeller blades; at 100 rpm, a single large circulation loop forms; while at 200 rpm, double circulation loops develop, enhancing bubble breakage and strengthening gas–liquid mass transfer. This research establishes the regulatory mechanism of “flow field–bubble behavior–mass transfer efficiency,” offering theoretical support for industrial design of such reactors.

papers.title: Upscaled modeling of convective CO2 dissolution in water using an effective diffusivity approach
papers.abstract: Subsurface storage of carbon dioxide can be complicated by the convective mixing of CO2 with water. The convection cells can be just a few meters wide, whereas the storage reservoir can span over several kilometers. This difference in space scales is difficult to resolve in the numerical modeling of subsurface flows, which requires the development of effective approaches similar to those employed in the effective turbulence modeling. In the manuscript, we present an approach for the numerical modeling of the convective mixing using coarse simulation grids. We consider a sector of a water-saturated porous medium right beneath a CO2 plume. The approach utilizes an artificial amplification of the molecular diffusivity of CO2 in water. We develop the relations describing the amplification changes with time by adjusting the approach to the results of two-dimensional (2D) modeling of the mixing at different Rayleigh–Darcy numbers. Herewith, the diffusive mixing stage and the early and late convective stages are specifically addressed. We thereby construct an effective model that regards the mixing as a submesh process. The approach is validated by comparing the results of the effective model for a thin porous column with those of 2D modeling. We thus evaluate the range of the Rayleigh–Darcy number at which the approach is most accurate. The presented results may be of interest for researchers working in the field of subsurface CO2 storage.

papers.title: Flow mechanisms driving left atrial hemodynamics under mechanical circulatory support in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
papers.abstract: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) alters cardiac flow dynamics and can contribute to thrombosis. Although commonly used for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, its application in patients with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), nearly half of all heart failure cases, remains limited. Left atrial (LA) inflow cannulation may be advantageous for HFpEF patients due to their reduced ventricular volume, but the resulting LA flow disturbances are not well understood. This study evaluates how MCS affects LA blood flow dynamics in a HFpEF patient to clarify mechanisms influencing thrombosis risk. The effects of cannula length and drainage flow rate on thrombosis-related flow characteristics were quantified. To assess the importance of atrial mechanics, simulations incorporating LA contraction were compared with rigid-wall models, addressing the common simplification of rigid geometries. Predictions were validated against two-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging measurements obtained using a soft-robotic LA model. MCS increased washout by 50% under rigid-wall conditions and 27% with wall contraction compared with unassisted flow. However, thrombus risk increased with cannula advancement, driven by up to 151% higher shear stress. LA wall contraction reduced stasis by 68% and improved washout but also elevated predicted wall shear stress. Cannula advancement and its proximity to pulmonary veins and the mitral valve altered local flow structures and shear stress distributions, demonstrating the benefit of patient-specific positioning. Overall, MCS can enhance LA flow, but lower insertion depth and reduced pump flow may mitigate cannula-related thrombus risk. Even minimal atrial contraction notably affected washout, residence time, and shear stress patterns, highlighting its importance in thrombosis assessment.

papers.title: Investigation of local scour predictions beneath a submerged cylinder using Fourier neural operator variants
papers.abstract: Scour beneath submerged cylinders impacts the stability and lifetime of submarine pipelines, motivating fast surrogate models that can forecast scour evolution in real time. This study develops a Fourier neural operator (FNO)-based surrogate for predicting local scour beneath a submerged cylinder under steady inflow conditions. This problem is strongly nonlinear and contains a sharp interface between the deforming sediment bed and the water column, as well as multiscale interactions between the solid and fluid phases. These characteristics create formidable challenges for the accuracy and stability of conventional FNOs that aim to encode the flow using a limited number of Fourier modes. This study addresses these challenges with a novel U-Net enhanced FNO (U-FNO) architecture that augments global spectral convolutions with a U-Net path for local feature extraction. By using the data generated by a high-fidelity Eulerian–Eulerian two-phase flow model, the proposed U-FNO framework yields stable autoregressive rollouts with low relative errors across all predicted fields and achieves orders-of-magnitude faster inference than the baseline two-phase flow model. The results demonstrate that hybrid operator-learning architectures can extend FNOs' applicability to problems containing local sharp gradients, such as multiphase scour dynamics, while preserving computational efficiency.

papers.title: Displacement patterns in granular packs under gravitational and viscous instabilities: A three-dimensional visualization study
papers.abstract: Two-phase flow driven by coupled gravitational and viscous instabilities is widely encountered in many natural systems and engineering applications. The interfacial dynamics involved in such processes are highly complex and remain insufficiently explored experimentally in three dimensions (3D). In this study, a 3D visualization platform based on planar laser-induced fluorescence is developed to investigate the effects of injection rate and pore structure on immiscible displacement behavior in a non-wetting phase displacing a wetting phase under coupled gravitational–viscous instability conditions. We identify four distinct unstable displacement morphologies, namely, discrete buoyant droplet, slug, straight continuous fingering, and dendritic fingering cluster. We establish an experimental phase diagram of the displacement pattern in the space of capillary number and the Bond number. We also introduce a set of geometric descriptors to quantify morphological evolution and phase connectivity. This work reveals how the competition and coupling among capillary, viscous, and buoyancy forces govern fluid fragmentation, coalescence, and fingering development in 3D porous media. The findings provide mechanistic insights into multiphase flow instabilities and have direct implications for a number of subsurface applications.

papers.title: Reducing tip-vortex cavitation noise in marine propellers: Insights from a multi-fidelity optimization framework
papers.abstract: The increasing concern over anthropogenic underwater noise and its environmental impact has motivated the search for effective strategies to mitigate tip-vortex cavitation in marine propellers. This work investigates the physical mechanisms governing its formation and identifies pressure-side-oriented, smoothly tip-raked geometries as a promising mitigation approach. Medium-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations are employed to build a surrogate model, with tip rake and its radial evolution as design variables and hydrodynamic efficiency and the Lamb vector divergence as metrics of cavitation intensity and hydro-acoustic performance. Low-fidelity optimization loops serve as an efficient tool to rapidly explore the design space and identify physically meaningful geometries while reducing computational cost by over 98% relative to conventional fluid dynamics simulations. High-fidelity, scale-resolving simulations with dynamic mesh adaptation validate the physical findings, showing that pressure-side tip bending suppresses the primary tip vortex, attenuates secondary vortical structures, and preserves the quasi-steady sheet cavity. These modifications achieve broadband sound pressure level reductions of up to 20 dB in the 200 Hz–8 kHz range without compromising hydrodynamic efficiency. Overall, the study highlights the critical role of tip-vortex physics in underwater noise generation and demonstrates that multi-fidelity frameworks provide an efficient means to derive acoustically optimized propeller geometries, contributing to the reduction of environmental noise impact.

papers.title: On the trailing coherent structures of a Delta wing in ground effect
papers.abstract: Near-ground coherent structures are occasionally generated at the aircraft's trailing during takeoff, causing high risk to following aircraft because of hazardous rolling moments. This study numerically characterizes for the first time these three-dimensional vortex structures of the near-ground delta wing at Re=6000 (based on c-delta wing chord) using the lattice Boltzmann method with a block refinement framework. The simulation quantifies how the angle of attack (α) modulates vortex dynamics across four spatial regimes: pre-attachment, attachment, aloft, and post-attachment. In the pre-attachment regime, increasing α from 15° to 25° intensifies circulation and shifts the primary vortex ground-collision point upstream from 14c to 8c. Upon collision in the attachment regime, the primary vortices induce a strong adverse pressure gradient on the ground. This adverse pressure gradient generates secondary vortices that subsequently wraparound the primary vortex cores. This helical wrapping mechanism directly forces the primary pair into the aloft regime, where the vortices rebound vertically to a height of 0.45c and diverge transversely to spanwise length larger than c. Furthermore, the angle of attack dictates the structural breakdown in the farfield wake. At α=20° and 25°, the increased circulation accelerates mutual induction, which triggers the long-wavelength Crow instability and breaks the vortex pair into descending rings. In contrast to these high angles, α=15° reduces the circulation and completely suppresses the Crow instability.

papers.title: The operational calculus mild-slope equation
papers.abstract: This study presents the development and analysis of a new mild-slope wave equation derived using an operational-calculus framework. The derivation systematically incorporates both linear and nonlinear bottom variations through the introduction of a detuning-from-resonance operator, which enables a structured expansion of the governing equations. Although the formulation ultimately leads to a system of coupled second-order equations, retaining terms up to second order in this operator initially yields coupled fourth-order partial differential equations with bottom derivatives up to the fourth order. These equations are then reduced to a second-order form without compromising accuracy. This reduction retains the accuracy of the original model but subtly alters its mathematical structure, replacing the original elliptic formulation with a coupled second-order system. The proposed model is validated through numerical simulations of three benchmark cases: normally incident wave propagation over a sloping planar bathymetry, Roseau's non-planar bathymetry, and the quasi-three-dimensional case of oblique incidence, all of which have analytical solutions. The results demonstrate that the operational calculus-based equation improves accuracy relative to the complementary mild-slope equation, particularly for steeper bathymetric variations, making it a valuable tool for modeling wave behavior over varying topographies.

papers.title: Collective locomotion of two unconstrained self-propelled plates with temporally asymmetric anti-phase flapping
papers.abstract: Flow-mediated interactions can yield collective performance gains in animal groups without explicit communication, yet the role of temporal stroke asymmetry in formation selection and propulsive performance of fully unconstrained propulsors remains unclear. In the present study, numerical simulations are performed on two side-by-side self-propelled plates executing temporally asymmetric anti-phase flapping while remaining free to translate in both the horizontal and lateral directions. A regime map spanning stroke amplitude and temporal asymmetry over several actuation frequencies identifies four distinct modes: straight propulsion with a stable lateral spacing, deflected propulsion with persistent lateral drift, collision, and separation. Within the stable schooling regimes (straight and deflected propulsion), increasing asymmetry generally improves propulsive performance while reducing the equilibrium lateral gap distance. Propulsive performance within the stable modes is maximized when the trailing-edge outward stroke of the two plates is faster than the inward motion. Despite the slow inward motion, vortex-mediated interactions generated during the preceding rapid outward stroke strengthen a gap-directed flow that suppresses instroke-driven gap outflow, thereby sustaining a strong shared positive-pressure region. During the rapid outward motion, the plates further establish an intensified shared negative-pressure region. As a result, the combined enhancement of these pressures amplifies the pressure-driven normal forces, leading to improved propulsive performance. These results clarify how temporal asymmetry reorganizes wake-mediated interactions and formation selection in unconstrained side-by-side locomotion, and provide design guidelines for using asymmetric actuation to stabilize formations and enhance collective performance.

papers.title: Investigation of vortex flow fields around a circular cylinder using particle image velocimetry. II: Influence of strake cross-sectional geometry
papers.abstract: Building on Paper I, which demonstrates that three-start semi-elliptical (D-type) helical strakes fundamentally suppress the Kármán vortex street and reduce near-wake turbulence by approximately 30%–40% at high Reynolds numbers (Re), the present study extends the analysis to compare wake modification and turbulence-suppression performance among semi-elliptical (D-), square (S-), and triangular (T-type) strakes at Re ≈ 1.32 × 105. All strake configurations fragment the dominant counter-rotating vortex system and restore wake symmetry without periodic vortex shedding. Geometry-specific effects are evident: sharper-edged S- and T-type strakes induce earlier separation and stronger streamwise vorticity, producing more aggressive wake disruption than the smoother D-type configuration. Therefore, triangular strakes yield the most diffuse wakes, with square strakes performing comparably effectively, whereas semi-elliptical strakes leave slightly more organized residual structures. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measurements confirm these trends, showing that peak Reynolds shear stress decreases by 40%–60%, while the dominant in-plane turbulent kinetic energy (TKEip) in the principal wake region is reduced by approximately 50%–70%, with the local reduction varying depending on measurement location; the Q-criterion analysis further indicates that the organized rotational wake structures are weakened and redistributed by the strakes. At specific planes, triangular strakes reduce peak TKEip to one-third of the bare-cylinder value, with square strakes producing nearly equivalent results and semi-elliptical strakes exhibiting slightly higher but still markedly reduced residuals. Proper orthogonal decomposition of the PIV velocity fields is performed to gain a deeper understanding of the wake dynamics. This reveals the evolution of dominant energetic modes with varying strake geometries and illustrates how coherent structures are progressively fragmented along the span. The decisive mechanism, early three-dimensional and spanwise-decorrelated separation driven by the helical strakes, is common to all cases, breaking coherent rollers into smaller eddies and redistributing turbulence away from the centerline. Although sharper strake geometries accelerate wake breakdown (T ≳ S > D), the dominant mechanism for vortex-induced vibration suppression resides in the helical strake-induced, three-dimensional wake disruption, providing clear physical insight and practical guidance for optimizing passive flow-induced vibration control.

papers.title: Investigation on energy loss mechanism of hydrofoil cavitating flow based on velocity gradient tensor decomposition
papers.abstract: The presence of tip clearance can generate a leakage vortex, which complicates the cavitating flow characteristics and significantly affects the energy loss. This study numerically investigates the cavitating flow around a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0009 hydrofoil with a tip clearance. Based on velocity gradient tensor (VGT) decomposition and entropy production (EP) theory, the fluid motion patterns and the sources of vortices in hydrofoil cavitating flow are investigated; furthermore, the energy losses and their underlying mechanisms are revealed. The results show that pure shear (PS) is the predominant deformation in hydrofoil cavitating flow, while rigid rotation accounts for a relatively small proportion. The vortices can be divided into three categories based on their causes, including cavity growth induced vortex, cavity shedding induced vortex, and cavity collapse induced vortex. The detached cavity moves downstream with internal rotation rather than a simple translation. With increasing tip clearance, the energy loss presents a declining trend. The turbulence dissipation EP serves as the primary contributor, constituting over 90% of the total. The changes in cavity volume and EP exhibit opposite trends during one cycle. The distributions of EP rates exhibit a strong correlation with those of VGT components. The energy loss predominantly arises from the PS and compression/stretching (CS) deformation. Among them, direct dissipation EP mainly comes from CS, and turbulent dissipation EP is mainly caused by PS.

papers.title: Impact of mineralogical heterogeneity on pore-scale dissolution patterns in binary mineral systems
papers.abstract: Mineralogical heterogeneity is widely recognized as a key factor controlling reactive transport in porous media, affecting processes such as hydrocarbon recovery and geological CO2 storage. In this study, we used a pore-scale reactive transport model based on the Darcy–Brinkman–Stokes framework to examine how different mineral distributions control dissolution patterns. In single-mineral systems, classical dissolution patterns were reproduced in complex porous media, including compact, wormhole, and uniform dissolutions. In binary-mineral systems, composed of reactive and inert phases arranged either uniformly or patchily, heterogeneity exerted limited influence on compact and uniform dissolution patterns, but significantly affected wormhole development. Specifically, uniformly distributed inert minerals suppressed wormhole formation by increasing flow resistance and disrupting localized flow concentration, thereby weakening the wormhole-like dissolution front. Under wormhole-dominated conditions, the permeability of media with uniformly distributed inert minerals was considerably lower, about two orders of magnitude lower than that of single-mineral systems. A particle-tracking analysis then revealed that local reaction rates at wormhole tips in single-mineral systems could reach up to nine times the overall reaction rate, confirming the positive feedback mechanism that drives wormhole growth. In contrast, local reaction rates in uniformly distributed binary systems were more homogeneous. As a result, the overall effective reaction rate in such media is even higher than that of single-mineral systems after wormhole formation. Overall, the findings highlight the effect of mineral distribution on pore-scale flow and reaction patterns, providing a basis for understanding the evolution of dissolution under heterogeneous conditions.

papers.title: Vortex suppression and sedimentation reduction in generalized contraction–expansion flows
papers.abstract: The sudden contraction and expansion of the Yellow River section can induce flow separation and strong vortical structures due to abrupt changes in cross-sectional geometry, leading to low-velocity stagnation zones and enhanced sediment retention. To elucidate the mechanisms of vortex control and sedimentation reduction, a generalized three-dimensional water–sediment numerical model based on the Mixture two-phase flow approach was developed and validated using the field data. A total of 36 simulation cases were designed to systematically analyze vortex evolution, flow structure adjustment, and sediment transport responses. The results show that significant mainstream deflection and large-scale coherent vortices develop under contraction–expansion conditions, forming extensive stagnation zones that promote sedimentation and flow instability. Remediation measures can effectively weaken backflow intensity and improve sediment transport pathways by modifying local flow acceleration and shear characteristics. Compared with single measures, the combined strategy, through the synergistic effects of flow diversion and vortex control, reconfigures the mainstream structure, breaks down large-scale vortices, and enhances flow stability and sediment transport capacity. The optimal scheme improves flow velocity uniformity by 32.6%, reduces the deviation angle by 31.73°, and decreases sedimentation by 35.45%. This study clarifies the vortex dynamics mechanisms in contraction–expansion river sections and provides a theoretical basis for vortex control and sedimentation reduction in complex transitional reaches.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigation of the dynamic response of reinforced concrete piles under underwater explosion-induced wave loading
papers.abstract: A series of underwater explosion experiments were conducted, where the morphological characteristics of explosion-induced water mounds were recorded, and the relationships between underwater explosion-induced wave loading (UEWL) and key explosion test parameters were analyzed. This study aimed to examine the damage characteristics of reinforced concrete (RC) piles subjected to underwater explosion-induced waves (UEIWs). First, a numerical model of UEIWs was developed using the Structured Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian algorithm in LS-DYNA finite element software and validated by experimental data. Additionally, numerical models of underwater explosions were developed for both rigid cylindrical piles and RC cylindrical piles to analyze the distribution of UEWL around these structures. This study further investigates the dynamic response and failure characteristics of RC piles subjected to UEWL. The results indicate that wave impact on cylindrical piles is most significant at a dimensionless distance of 0.77. Compared with displacements induced by shock waves and bubble pulsation, those caused by UEWL accounted for only 5% and 1.8% at the mid-span, and 10.8% and 5.3% at the air–water interface, respectively. These results demonstrate that UEWL can still inflict noticeable secondary damage on RC piles, which is critical for the structural safety of high-pile wharves.

papers.title: Effects of impeller whirling vibration on the rotor–stator interaction in a centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: This study employs the dynamic sliding multi-region and the Reynolds averaged Navier–Stokes to conduct computational fluid dynamics numerical simulations on the centrifugal pump flow characteristics under four forms of impeller whirling vibrations. The influence mechanisms of different whirling forms on the unsteady flow characteristics and rotor–stator interaction are analyzed. Because of assembly errors and non-uniform support stiffness, the centrifugal pump impeller does not undergo simple eccentric rotation. Instead, it exhibits the complex whirling vibration with multiple kinematic characteristics, which has been neglected in previous studies. First, the numerical models of different whirling vibration forms are established to simulate the unsteady flow characteristics. The accuracy is verified using the test bench. Second, the study investigates the influence mechanisms of different whirling vibration forms on the flow characteristics and rotor–stator interaction. The results demonstrate that the rotor–stator interaction can be categorized into small-scale interaction from the single blade and large-scale interaction from the overall impeller under whirling conditions. The additional fluctuations caused by whirling vibration result from periodic variations in the magnitude and direction of the impeller outflow velocity. Under backward whirling, the modulation frequency amplitude of the flow characteristics is greater. This is because the high tangential speed region of the impeller is opposite to the whirling direction, thereby intensifying the unsteady flow characteristics caused by rotor–stator interaction. This study serves as a foundation for vibration and noise control and fault diagnosis of centrifugal pumps.

papers.title: Turbulent cylinder wake stabilization with intelligent distributed plasma actuators powered by deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates experimental deep reinforcement learning (DRL) control of a turbulent cylinder wake at a Reynolds number of 28 000. Two dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuators operated independently to seed disturbances to the cylinder boundary layer, and two hot-wire sensors submerged within the wake provide real-time feedback. Following the Deep Q-Network framework, the closed-loop control law is parameterized by a fully connected neural network and executed at 1 kHz on a field-programmable gate array. Results show that the DRL agent is able to identify an effective control policy in a single training run without prior knowledge, achieving the same-order drag reduction magnitude as the steady open-loop control by utilizing only 40% actuator power consumption of the latter. The learning process, however, is sensitive to the setting of hyperparameters, and poor reward configurations can lead to an unstable learning process. Diagnostics via a high-speed particle image velocimetry and a dimensionality reduction approach reveal that the agent learns a conditional actuation strategy. Namely, when the wake has a tendency to deflect significantly toward one side, intense plasma actuation should be applied on the opposite side to suppress this lateral oscillation, stabilizing the flow to high-reward states and thereby reducing drag reduction. These results underscore the potential of DRL for adaptive, energy-efficient control in turbulent flows.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation of instability in counter-rotating vortex pair–wall interaction
papers.abstract: This study investigates the three-dimensional interaction between a counter-rotating vortex pair subject to Crow instability and a flat wall in ReΓ=2500, 4000, and 6000 at h/r0=5.0, 10.0 (where h denotes the distance from the vortex center to the wall and r0 is the separation between the two vortex cores). The analysis combines quantitative measures, including total kinetic energy and enstrophy, with three-dimensional vortex-structure visualization based on the Q-criterion and helicity distribution, in order to elucidate the physical mechanisms governing vortex decay, reorganization, and breakdown. The results show that h/r0 determines the morphological evolution pathway of the vortex system as it approaches the wall. For h/r0=5.0, early interaction with the wall substantially alters the vortex dynamics compared with the unbounded case, leading to the formation of characteristic vortex tongues. In contrast, for h/r0=10.0, the Crow instability has sufficient time to fully develop and complete the reconnection process, forming a sequence of reconnected vortex rings prior to wall interaction. In addition, the effect of ReΓ manifests itself through a clear transition between different dynamical regimes. At ReΓ=2500, vortex decay is dominated by viscous diffusion. At ReΓ=4000, vortex stretching and three-dimensional (3D) twisting become significant, promoting the breakdown of the vortex system into hairpin vortices. At ReΓ=6000, the system undergoes a strong breakdown process, characterized by a sharp increase in enstrophy and the formation of a dense network of small-scale vortex structures, reflecting an intense transfer of energy from large to small scales. The helicity distribution is identified as an effective indicator of local 3D twisting intensity and the onset of coherent-structure breakdown. In particular, in ReΓ=4000–6000, a resonant twisting mechanism between the primary and secondary vortices is recognized as the main driver of scaly shaped structures and the collapse of vortex cores. Moreover, at ReΓ=6000, a figure-eight-shaped structure emerges in the trough region and undergoes a severing process at its neck, resulting in complete detachment from the original vortex system. These findings provide new insights into the decay dynamics of near-ground vortex wakes and are relevant to vortex-wake management problems in aviation.

papers.title: Comparison of the potential energy for different equilibrium configurations of symmetric and asymmetric floating drops
papers.abstract: We provide a numerical method for computing solutions to a free boundary problem arising from the equilibrium state of a floating drop. This numerical method is based on a Newton's method for the underlying nonlinear boundary value problems, and at each iterative step, a Chebyshev spectral collocation method is employed. The problems considered here are those that can be described by using generating curves and include problems in R2 and R3. The resulting nine-dimensional space of physical parameters is explored, and examples are given that highlight the potential energy of centrally located drops, wall-bound drops, and asymmetrical configurations in R2. Non-uniqueness of solutions to the corresponding Euler–Lagrange equations is displayed, and strong evidence of non-uniqueness of energy minimizers is given.

papers.title: Aerodynamic response of flapping wings to brief gust perturbations
papers.abstract: Natural fliers frequently encounter various perturbed flows during their daily flapping flights. To address the flight stability issue of the flapping micro aerial vehicles under additional aerodynamic loads induced by gust disturbances, inspired by natural flyers, this study numerically solves the unsteady Navier–Stokes equations to investigate the influence of brief gusts on the aerodynamic characteristics of rigid flapping wings. A comprehensive analysis is performed on the effects of gust amplitude, frequency, phase, and waveform on the aerodynamic forces and vortex shedding of the flapping wing. The results show that the lift response is stronger than the thrust response, and the variance of the net aerodynamic force increment is concentrated in the region where the gust amplitude is 1–1.5 times the maximum flapping speed and the gust duration is 0.5–1 times the flapping period. A phase difference between the gust input and the flapping stroke leads to a substantial increase in aerodynamic loads. The overall aerodynamic response of the flapping wing varies only slightly across different gust waveforms. The flapping wing performs better in resisting square-wave gusts but has greater difficulty maintaining balance under sawtooth-wave gusts. The present findings are valuable for developing robust flight control strategies and providing design guidance for micro aerial vehicles.

papers.title: Investigation of thermal-hydro characteristics in seepage channels of stratified porous media: A mesoscopic approach
papers.abstract: A hybrid thermal lattice Boltzmann model based on the immersed boundary method was proposed to address pore-scale thermal-flow coupling. The model incorporates the multiple-relaxation-time collision operator to enhance numerical stability. A fourth-order Runge–Kutta algorithm was introduced to solve the energy equation. The framework enabled precise capture of transient microscopic temperature gradients. Gravity-driven seepage in stratified porous media with lateral porosity variations was systematically investigated. The results revealed a flow-thermal separation mechanism induced by structural heterogeneity. Preferential flow channels in high-porosity zones accelerated fluid penetration. However, the shortened residence time hindered local thermal equilibrium. Consequently, steady-state temperatures in high-porosity zones remained lower than those in low-porosity zones. The temperature-flow coupling was clarified. High temperatures reduced surface tension and viscosity. These reductions weakened capillary effects in narrow pores and triggered a transition from fingering flow to piston-like displacement. Particle gradation analysis demonstrated that introducing coarse aggregates reduced fluid tortuosity and eliminated stagnant zones. These effects effectively enhanced thermal penetration efficiency. The study validates the hybrid framework for heat transfer and provides mesoscopic insights into transport within heterogeneous geological structures.

papers.title: Mechanisms of droplet departure on mixed wettability surfaces: Effects of length-scale separation
papers.abstract: Mixed wettability surfaces strongly influence droplet departure in surface engineering applications. Although homogeneous superhydrophobic surfaces provide optimal removal performance, real surfaces typically exhibit heterogeneous wettability. Here, we investigate droplet departure mechanisms on smooth surfaces with alternating wettability patches using a multicomponent pseudopotential lattice-Boltzmann method. Gravity-driven pendant detachment and gravity-assisted coalescence-induced departure are examined over a wide range of heterogeneity length scales relative to droplet wetted base length (a/w) and size (a/Req). Results show that homogeneous surfaces generally exhibit lower critical Eötvös numbers (Eocrit) than heterogeneous surfaces, with heterogeneity increasing the detachment threshold by approximately 5% and 16% for pendant and coalescence-induced departure, respectively. For pendant droplets, increasing a/w shifts detachment from continuous contact-line recession to pinch-off at a/w≈1; in this regime, Eocrit increases monotonically up to 15% on net hydrophobic surfaces (θeff=141°) but decreases by approximately 8% at larger patch length scales under near-neutral wetting (θeff=105°). For coalescence-induced departure, a competition between droplet coalescence and contact line jumping governs detachment behavior when a/Req≈0.06. In this regime, frequent stick–slip dynamics promote premature contact line jumping, which increases Eocrit by 20%. Under the Cassie framework of chemically inhomogeneous surfaces, strong heterogeneity can instead enhance droplet removal through controlled contact-line pinning, increasing droplet detachment performance up to 28%. A hysteresis analysis accounts for these effects of patch wettability contrasts, while a new proposed viscous-dissipation-based framework offers a preliminary mechanistic explanation for the influence of relative patch length on droplet departure.

papers.title: Unified convergent series solutions of Stokes waves of arbitrary height in arbitrary depth with machine-learning acceleration
papers.abstract: Stokes waves are a fundamental model for nonlinear wave dynamics and play a crucial role in understanding complex ocean phenomena. However, owing to their inherent nonlinearity, accurately and efficiently solving Stokes waves of arbitrary height in arbitrary depth has long remained a challenging problem. In this work, we propose a unified framework combining the homotopy analysis method (HAM) with machine learning to rapidly compute convergent series of Stokes waves across the entire physical parameter space. We introduce an accelerated HAM strategy, utilizing first-order iteration and precomputation, to solve Stokes waves for arbitrary prescribed depth and wave height conditions. Based on this, we develop a multi-stage, multi-scale neural network that maps wave parameters directly to the convergent series coefficients. This architecture effectively manages strong coefficient scale separation and preserves the high-order modes critical for resolving limiting crests, computing a Stokes wave in ∼0.01 s. Additionally, a Fourier neural operator (FNO) is employed to approximate the inverse conformal mapping, enabling the rapid reconstruction of physical quantities, such as velocity fields, in the physical plane. Therefore, the present model provides an end-to-end solution, allowing for rapid computation of convergent series for Stokes waves with arbitrary height in arbitrary depth, thus facilitating applications in ocean engineering. In this way, we propose a continuous semi-analytical series description of the Stokes wave family, which shows that periodic waves in deep and intermediate water, cnoidal waves in shallow water, and solitary waves in extremely shallow water can be interpreted within a unified solution framework.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence reconstruction of wall-pressure dynamics from sparse data in extreme flows
papers.abstract: Hypersonic environments constrain pressure instrumentation and make high-fidelity simulation datasets costly, leaving many applications with sparse wall-pressure measurements. This work develops and evaluates a hybrid reconstruction framework that recovers high-resolution hypersonic wall-pressure from strongly downsampled signals. The method first produces an initial estimate using cubic-spline interpolation, then refines it with a Transformer model that learns non-local spatial structure. Performance is assessed on datasets representative of Mach 5.3 wind tunnel conditions, spanning data-reduction factors from 2× to 64× and multiple turbulence-intensity regimes associated with shock–boundary-layer interaction. The hybrid approach delivers accurate reconstructions at low-to-moderate sparsity, with mean absolute percentage errors typically below 1% at low sparsity and generally below 4% at moderate sparsity, whereas degradation is primarily observed in the most extreme sparsity settings. A key finding is that reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on turbulence characteristics and input sequence length: a longer spatial context improves performance when the mean wall-pressure distribution exhibits longer correlation length scales, whereas a shorter context is preferable when the mean pressure exhibits more localized spatial variation (shorter correlation length scales). These results position Transformers as practical surrogates for reconstructing hypersonic pressure and provide actionable guidance on sensor sampling and sequence design in extreme-flow environments.

papers.title: Aeroelastic coupling effects on multiphase flow dynamics and vortex topology of floating offshore wind turbines
papers.abstract: The upscaling of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) introduces pronounced fluid–structure interaction effects, challenging the applicability of rigid-rotor assumptions in aerodynamic and wake predictions. This study develops a partitioned computational fluid dynamics–finite element method (CFD–FEM) framework integrated with Dynamic Fluid Body Interaction to investigate the aero-hydro-elastic response of a 15 MW FOWT under combined wind–wave excitation. By comparing rigid- and flexible-blade configurations, the effects of blade compliance on aerodynamic loading, platform kinematics, local inflow modulation, free-surface response, and wake evolution are examined. Under the H8 condition, blade flexibility attenuates the wave-frequency thrust fluctuation by 22.1% and reduces the peak-to-peak platform pitch response by 12.2%. Sectional kinematic reconstruction shows that the flapwise deformation velocity modifies the local relative inflow and moderates the reconstructed effective angle of attack, thereby reducing the suction-side pressure loading at the analyzed blade section. The free-surface analysis further suggests that this aeroelastic load-alleviation response reduces the body-relative transient run-up around the upwind column. In the wake, the flexible-blade case exhibits an earlier loss of coherent helical-vortex organization and a faster recovery of the mean velocity deficit at the intermediate-wake measurement plane. These observations are consistent with enhanced macroscopic momentum exchange between the ambient flow and the wake core. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating blade flexibility in blade-resolved coupled CFD–FEM simulations of ultra-large FOWTs, particularly for predicting unsteady aerodynamic loading, platform response, local free-surface elevation, and downstream wake evolution.

papers.title: On the dynamics of coherent structures near straight and T-head spur dikes
papers.abstract: This study employs improved delayed detached eddy simulation to investigate coherent flow structures and bed shear stresses around unsubmerged straight and T-head spur dikes. Vortex topology identified using the λ2 criterion reveals a strong horseshoe-like vortex (HSV) for the straight spur dike, whereas the T-head spur dike produces a weakened HSV and a dominant upstream circulation that suppresses downflow and near-bed vorticity production. Probability density function (PDF) and joint PDFs of velocity fluctuations reveal three distinct instantaneous flow states for the HSV: back-flow, zero-flow, and intermediate-flow, for both configurations. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) shows that for the straight dike, the first mode captures the mean-flow upwash and downwash induced by the HSV, while higher modes represent oscillations between the three flow states. In contrast, for the T-head dike, all dominant POD modes are associated with HSV oscillations. Analysis of the POD temporal coefficients shows that the zero-flow condition is more prevalent for the straight dike, whereas the back-flow condition dominates for the T-head dike. In the wake, both configurations generate shear-layer vortices that shed, merge, and form rib-like multiscale structures. Reduced vortex arching in the T-head dike keeps shear layer vortices more vertically oriented, suppressing near-bed horizontal vorticity and sediment entrainment. The bed shear stress distribution shows that the straight dike produces an order-of-magnitude greater probability of exceeding a critical sediment-mobility threshold than the T-head dike.

papers.title: Comparisons of direct simulation Monte Carlo modeling of nitric oxide emissions with electric arc shock tube measurements
papers.abstract: Emission measurements taken at the NASA Ames Electric Arc Shock Tube facility as part of Test Series 66 [Cruden and Tibère-Inglesse, “Radiative emission in incident air shocks from 3–7 km/s,” AIAA Paper No. 2024-3653, 2024] included air shocks in the range of 3–5 km/s. In this work, we use the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method to model unsteady one-dimensional shocks and replicate flow conditions observed for Shots 26 and 27 from this test series. The DSMC solutions are used along with a radiation solver, Nonequilibrium and Equilibrium Radiative Transport and Spectra Program, to compute nitric oxide (NO) emission in the infrared (IR) and ultraviolet (UV) spectral regions in the shock layer. The numerically generated estimates of NO emission provide good agreement with emission measurements in the IR spectral region in terms of absolute spectral radiance as well as relative spectral intensity providing validation of the thermochemical models used to model the NO ground electronic state. This was also observed from comparisons of NO ground electronic state populations and temperatures predicted by DSMC calculations and values derived from IR emission and tunable diode laser absorption measurements. However, numerical predictions of NO emission in the UV spectral region over-predict the spectral intensity in comparison with emission measurements while providing partial agreement for the relative spectral intensity highlighting a need for improvement in the modeling of mechanisms critical to the excitation and de-excitation of NO electronic state populations. This was further supported by comparisons of numerical predictions of NO excited electronic state populations and electronic temperatures with those inferred from UV emission measurements. The possible effect of the boundary layer, which is colder than the core flow, on NO IR and UV emission signals in the shock layer was also explored.

papers.title: Ultrasound propagation in multiphase porous media: A continuum-mechanical model for coupled effects of bubble dynamics and oil viscoelasticity
papers.abstract: Ultrasonic wave propagation in multiphase fluid-saturated porous media involves complex interactions among fluid rheology, interfacial dynamics, and dispersed gas phases, particularly in the ultrasonic frequency range, where relaxation processes become significant. Although these phenomena are relevant to a range of engineering applications, including ultrasonic-assisted enhanced oil recovery, a consistent theoretical framework for fundamentally understanding and integrating these coupled mechanisms remains limited. In this study, we develop a continuum-mechanical framework for ultrasonic wave propagation in multiphase porous media by extending multiphase poroelastic wave theory. The proposed model incorporates heavy-oil viscoelasticity, dynamic capillary pressure effects, and the oscillatory response of dispersed gas bubbles within a unified linearized formulation. Based on the derived dispersion relations, three longitudinal wave modes are identified and analyzed in terms of their phase velocities, attenuation characteristics, and underlying physical mechanisms. The results reveal that propagation behavior is strongly frequency-dependent and controlled by coupled processes involving viscous dissipation, viscoelastic relaxation, interfacial dynamics, and bubble oscillations, with distinct modal responses governed by different physical mechanisms.

papers.title: Experimental characterization and flow laws of graded coal fines under rheological modulation in coalbed methane horizontal wellbores
papers.abstract: Initial drainage in coalbed methane (CBM) horizontal wells is critical, as adhesive micron-sized coal fines mix with water to form slurry, altering flow and bed formation. These effects impose long-term constraints on drainage strategy regulation during subsequent production. Existing studies overlook rheology changes in the mixed slurry caused by micron-sized coal fines. This limits guidance on bed evolution during the initial drainage phase. To this end, we experimentally determined the viscosity of the mixed slurry with 0%–6% micron-sized coal fines by mass. We then established a fitted relationship between viscosity and micron-sized coal fines mass fraction. On this basis, we used the Hertz Mindlin–Johnson Kendall Roberts contact model to describe the coal particles adhesion behavior. A Computational Fluid Dynamics-Discrete Element Method coupled model was developed, integrating slurry rheological characteristics with particle adhesion. This framework links experimental characterization to the flow patterns of graded coal fines in horizontal CBM wellbores. The results show that the viscosity of the mixed slurry is one of the key factors controlling the evolution of bed thickness and morphology. Its influence becomes more pronounced at higher drainage velocities. At a drainage velocity of 0.3 m/s, increasing the viscosity from 1.03 to 2.00 mPa s reduces the bed thickness by approximately 21.6%. The proposed model provides theoretical support for regulating drainage strategies during the initial drainage stage of CBM horizontal wells.

papers.title: Optimization of a cell squeezing microfluidic chip using a non-Newtonian power-law model and gray relational analysis
papers.abstract: Constrained cell squeezing has demonstrated significant potential in applications such as intracellular drug delivery and in vitro immune cell activation, in which the constriction design critically determines squeezing efficiency and cell damage. Based on a validated two-phase flow and non-Newtonian power-law numerical model, this study systematically investigates the effects of the constriction geometry (including height, width, and shape) and the hydrodynamic boundary condition (inlet velocity) on the deformation dynamics of cells. Using the cell deformation index, deformation time, and interfacial shear stress as evaluation metrics, an orthogonal array design combined with gray relational analysis is employed to perform a multi-parameter and multi-objective optimization to identify the optimal combination of boundary conditions and geometric parameters. The results demonstrate that the constriction height and inlet velocity have the most significant impact on chip performance, while the effects of constriction shape and width are comparatively less pronounced. In addition, representative operating conditions are selected for the analysis of the underlying fluid dynamic mechanisms. This study elucidates the deformation behavior and mechanical characteristics of cell squeezing, providing theoretical and quantitative guidance for the structural design and operating condition optimization of high-performance squeezing-based microfluidic chips.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms of dissolved CO2 in electrohydrodynamic cone-jets: A comparative study with electric field and ionic effects
