papers.abstract: While electric fields and ionic additives are traditionally considered the primary governing factors of electrohydrodynamic (EHD) cone-jets, this work demonstrates that dissolved CO2 acts as an effective molecular-scale regulator of jet formation and fragmentation. Through systematic molecular dynamics simulations, the EHD cone-jet process of ethanol is investigated under varying electric field strengths, NaCl concentrations, and dissolved CO2 conditions, which have been insufficiently explored at the molecular scale. The results show that increasing electric field strength accelerates Taylor cone formation and jet emission by enhancing electrostatic stresses. The addition of NaCl facilitates jet formation by improving charge transport and weakening hydrogen-bond interactions, thereby affecting jet stability and droplet dispersion. In contrast, dissolved CO2 plays a distinct role compared with electric field and ionic effects. Increasing CO2 concentration accelerates the onset of cone-jet formation and produces thinner jets with more frequent nanoscale fragmentation. Molecular-scale analyses reveal that dissolved CO2 reduces liquid structural compactness and disrupts hydrogen-bond interactions by altering local molecular arrangement and intermolecular spacing. These changes make the liquid interface more susceptible to deformation under an applied electric field, leading to earlier jet formation and enhanced droplet breakup. The coupled evolution of hydrogen-bond number, solvent accessible surface area, cluster number, and interaction energies consistently supports these mechanisms. These findings provide new molecular-level insights into how dissolved CO2 modifies the liquid structure and regulates EHD cone-jet dynamics, offering guidance for EHD cone-jet-based technologies.

papers.title: A symmetry-consistent energy method for the stability of fluid motions: Beyond kinematic admissibility
papers.abstract: In the case of nonlinear stability of shear flows between parallel planes, the classical results of Reynolds, Sharpe, Orr, Serrin, and Joseph are reviewed. We demonstrate that the absolute-value modification in Joseph's function departs from the physical Reynolds–Orr energy identity, leading to overly conservative stability thresholds. We define a new subspace of kinematically admissible fields that preserves the fundamental symmetries and the invariance of the stationary linear perturbations and of the energy production term. By restricting the variational problem to this subspace, we reconcile the energy method with the underlying physics, effectively excluding purely “topological” but non-physical perturbations. We suggest that if the dynamical equations of linear perturbations of a basic motion possess a symmetry such that inverting a field variable leaves the system's behavior unchanged, then functions that break this symmetry in the energy functional are not dynamically representative. That is, we propose a symmetry invariance constraint that acts as a dynamical filter. Our proposal shifts the problem from topology (is there a function that maximizes the functional ratio?) to dynamics (is this function consistent with the symmetries of the Navier–Stokes equations?). For this, we need to restrict the space S of kinematically admissible test functions to a subspace Si of S consisting of invariant fields to make the energy method closer to real physics and obtain larger critical threshold values. The framework is extended to magneto-hydrodynamics and Rayleigh–Bénard convection with shear, offering a general method to obtain physically meaningful stability conditions.

papers.title: Multi-stage dynamics of horseshoe vortex around a bed-mounted cylinder: From laminar to fully turbulent flow
papers.abstract: The horseshoe vortex (HV) generated around a bed-mounted cylinder is the dominant flow structure responsible for initiating local scour at pile foundations of bridges, offshore platforms, port terminals, and other coastal and hydraulic engineering structures. Despite existing knowledge on HV characteristics and their influencing factors, several key knowledge gaps remain. First, the Reynolds number can vary over a wide range from laminar to fully turbulent conditions, yet systematic investigations covering the entire spectrum are lacking. Second, existing studies have primarily focused on velocity and vortex strength, while other critical dynamic parameters—such as bed shear stress and pressure gradient—remain underexplored. Third, a universal mesh size criterion for high-fidelity simulations of the HV is lacking. To address these issues, this study employs the detached-eddy simulation method to perform high-resolution three-dimensional numerical simulations over Reynolds numbers (ReD) ranging from 100 to 106. The results reveal the multi-stage dynamics of the HV, characterized by four distinct regimes: laminar, transitional, weakly turbulent, and fully turbulent. The mechanical characteristics of the HV in each regime—including morphology, velocity and pressure fields, vortex strength, and bed shear stress—are identified, and engineering-oriented dimensionless empirical correlations are proposed to describe the variations of key HV parameters within the investigated Reynolds-number range. In addition, a mesh criterion is proposed based on grid independence tests.

papers.title: Shock wave propagation characteristics and material hydrodynamic response under non-uniform converging loading
papers.abstract: The application of converging shock waves to compress solid materials can generate high-temperature and high-pressure environments, achieving a high compression ratio and high-density state, which is of significant importance for industrial applications. However, due to loading methods and material defects, converging shock waves often exhibit spatiotemporal non-uniform characteristics, leading to complex wave structures that reduce the compression performance of the converging shock waves. Therefore, it is crucial to study the propagation and evolution characteristics of non-uniform converging shock waves in solid media for achieving high-density and high-compression states in materials. Based on magnetically driven loading device, this study uses uniform cylindrical flyers to impact preabricated cylindrical targets with different amplitudes, generating non-uniform converging shock waves propagating inward. By employing 24-channel integrated laser velocimeter probes arranged in an offset pattern, the free-surface jump time and velocity are measured. Combined with numerical simulations, the study investigates the propagation characteristics of non-uniform converging shock waves and reveals the dynamic response characteristics of the interaction between non-uniform converging shock waves and materials. The research findings indicate that the intersection region of non-uniform converging shock waves exhibits an intersection enhancement effect, leading to a reverse growth characteristic of the free-surface spike amplitude. Unlike converging shock waves in gas, under the action of non-uniform converging shock waves and their derivative wave systems (free-surface reflection waves), the free surface exhibits spallation. Additionally, under the combined effects of convergence and shock wave intersection, the spallation and ejection of the working layer are more dispersed, the velocity of ejection are higher. Furthermore, shock wave intersections cause the free surface to accelerate, resulting in high-velocity points. Under the action of the derivative wave system of non-uniform converging shock waves, the free surface also exhibits secondary loading phenomena. These findings provide a certain foundation for the dynamic propagation study of non-uniform converging shock waves and hold theoretical significance for the development of compression science.

papers.title: Energy landscape and disorder-induced slow relaxation of droplets on heterogeneous wetting surfaces
papers.abstract: We develop an energy landscape framework for droplet equilibrium and relaxation dynamics on heterogeneous wetting surfaces. For a two-dimensional cylindrical droplet straddling a sharp wettability boundary, energy minimization of the Gibbs free energy functional ΔG(L1,L2) yields the spreading condition L2/|L1|=S(θ1)/S(θ2), where S(θ)=sin θ tan θ, showing that contact line partitioning depends exclusively on interfacial energy ratios and is independent of the Bond number. Two disorder models are examined. For a random contact angle field with amplitude σ and correlation length ξ, Monte Carlo simulations reveal that increasing disorder broadens the energy barrier distribution and drives a transition from exponential (β=1) to stretched exponential relaxation (β≈0.67–0.71), with the stretching exponent related to the mean barrier height by β≈Teff/E¯. For a contact angle hysteresis model with window Δθhyst, a metastable band forms whose width grows linearly with Δθhyst; the relaxation timescale shifts asymmetrically between advancing and receding scenarios while the stretching exponent remains invariant (β≈0.51). These results establish quantitative connections between disordered wetting and the statistical physics of glassy systems, and provide design criteria for functional surfaces requiring either droplet mobility or strong pinning.

papers.title: Time-evolving neural operator reconstruction and prediction of complex flows from sparse measurements
papers.abstract: Accurate reconstruction and prediction of complex flow fields from sparse measurements remain a critical challenge in chemical engineering, particularly for nonlinear and multiphase systems. Classical linear reduced-order models, such as dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), often fail to capture strongly unsteady and nonlinear flow dynamics, while high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are computationally prohibitive for real-time analysis and large-scale parametric studies. In this work, we evaluate a time-evolving neural operator (TENO) framework that learns the continuous spatiotemporal evolution of flow fields directly from practically limited and irregularly distributed observations. The performance of TENO is systematically evaluated on benchmark problems, from single-phase flows to an industrially relevant bubble column, where it consistently outperforms DMD in reconstruction and prediction accuracy. Compared with CFD simulations, TENO achieves relative errors on the order of 10−1 in a challenging three-dimensional bubble column benchmark, while significantly reducing computational cost and maintaining robustness under sparse/fixed-plane and noisy measurements.

papers.title: Pore-throat structure evolution governs multiphase flow in sustainable subsurface carbon and energy engineering
papers.abstract: Pore-throat structure evolution plays a critical role in controlling immiscible multiphase flow in subsurface systems relevant to carbon sequestration, hydrogen storage, hydraulic fracturing, acidizing, and microbially induced mineralization. However, how such structural changes reshape flow regimes and displacement efficiency remains insufficiently understood. This work integrates multiscale experiments and pore-scale simulations to elucidate the governing mechanisms. Two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance measurements on shale samples exposed to slickwater demonstrate that different pore-size classes respond unevenly to chemical perturbation: clay-scale pores contract slightly, mesopores expand, and macropores remain largely unchanged. These alterations collectively modify pore occupancy and transport properties. To isolate the intrinsic effect of pore-throat geometry, pore-scale numerical simulations were performed by uniformly scaling grain sizes using a geometric factor α. Smaller pore throats (α = 1.0) produce highly unstable capillary fingering dominated by recurring snap-off and coalescence, generating extensive cluster populations. Moderate enlargement (α = 0.9) reduces these interfacial instabilities, while further enlargement (α = 0.8) yields more compact invasion with no snap-off events. The combined experimental and numerical results demonstrate that pore-throat evolution governs multiphase flow by modulating capillary thresholds, interface stability, and cluster dynamics. This framework enhances mechanistic understanding of displacement behavior in evolving porous media and informs the sustainable design of subsurface carbon and energy engineering processes.

papers.title: Airflow characteristics induced by obstacle-generated backwater in partially filled circular pipes
papers.abstract: Obstacles at the bottom of sewer pipes can generate pronounced backwater effects and substantially modify airflow in partially filled conduits. This study experimentally investigates the airflow characteristics induced by obstacle-generated backwater in circular pipes under horizontal (S0 = 0) and sloping (S0 = 0.015) conditions. Laboratory experiments were conducted with different obstacle geometries and inflow discharges. Airflow rate, air pressure gradient, and water surface profile were measured, and representative flow observations were used qualitatively to support the analysis. Within the tested hydraulic ranges, the relative air demand decreases with increasing inflow Froude number in horizontal pipes, whereas the opposite trend was observed in sloping pipes. In horizontal pipes, the smaller head loss and smoother free surface weakened air–water interaction. In sloping pipes, larger head loss and stronger free-surface fluctuations enhanced interfacial drag and increased airflow in the pipe headspace. Pressure measurements further indicated pronounced air-pressure gradients within the backwater region. Force analysis showed that the airflow was governed mainly by the balance between air-pressure gradient and interfacial drag, whereas air inertia was negligible under the present conditions. These results clarify distinct airflow regimes associated with obstacle-induced backwater and provide a hydraulic basis for understanding ventilation and gas transport in partially filled pipes with internal obstacles.

papers.title: Anti-/deicing performance of hydrophilic–superhydrophobic wetting stripe surfaces and heat transfer mechanism analysis
papers.abstract: Ice accretion on solid surfaces poses severe and widespread threats to critical infrastructure including power transmission lines, aircraft wings, and various industrial facilities. Superhydrophobic surfaces (SHBS) are widely recognized as a promising passive anti-icing strategy with zero additional energy input during service. However, the air cushion that endows SHBS with anti-icing advantages simultaneously introduces extremely high interfacial thermal resistance, which severely hinders thermal deicing and creates an inherent contradiction between anti-icing and deicing performance. Here, we fabricated hydrophilic–superhydrophobic wetting stripe surfaces (WSS) via a facile mask spray method and systematically investigated the anti-icing and deicing performance of pure hydrophilic surface (HLS), SHBS, and WSS. The results show that WSS maintains a relatively long icing delay time close to that of pure SHBS, while achieving a much shorter melting time comparable to that of HLS, realizing a synergistic balance between anti-icing and deicing performance. Based on the experimental results, we established a unified one-dimensional thermal resistance superposition heat transfer model to correlate the anti-icing/deicing performance with the interfacial heat transfer behavior of the surfaces. This work provides theoretical guidance and technical support for the rational design, performance optimization, and engineering selection of anti-icing/deicing materials for practical service.

papers.title: Erosion wear in helical coiled tubing for multi-branch fracturing sandblasting tools
papers.abstract: The multi-branch zone fracturing sandblaster accommodates regional fracturing requirements, enabling fracturing across larger blocks and extended zones. To investigate erosion-wear characteristics of the coiled tubing (helical tube) in the tool's helical section and elucidate key influencing factors and mechanisms, numerical simulations were conducted based on erosion models and solid–liquid two-phase flow theory using computational fluid dynamics. This study analyzes the effects of flow field characteristics, sand-carrying fluid properties, pipe diameter, pitch, and spiral diameter on helical tube erosion wear. Based on the structural configuration and model parameters, results indicate that helical pipe erosion wear decreases with increasing pipe diameter, pitch, and helical diameter. In contrast, it intensifies with rising particle mass flow rate and inlet velocity of sand-carrying fluid. Additionally, erosion first increases and then decreases as particle size grows. Particle size significantly affects helical tubing erosion wear; as particle size increases, the maximum erosion rate rises first and then declines. From the coupling effects of fluid properties and structural features, large particle sizes make the inlet velocity a dominant factor for the erosion rate. Higher inlet velocity and mass flow rate lead to more severe erosion. With increased pipe and spiral diameters of helical tubing, the influence of particle size variation on erosion rate gradually weakens.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics of leakage-induced pressure waves in an evacuated tube transportation system
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigated the aerodynamic characteristics of pressure waves induced by sudden air leakage in a vacuum tube by simulating an evacuated tube transportation system failure. Using a scaled-down test section, leakage scenarios with various orifice diameters and initial pressures were analyzed. The flow field was classified into two distinct regimes based on the interaction between the underexpanded jet and the tube wall: supersonic core impingement (SCI) and decayed jet impingement (DJI). A dimensionless geometric criterion, 0.62<yM/dt<0.77, was identified as the transition threshold between these two regimes. The SCI regime generated severe localized impact pressures, whereas the DJI regime exhibited turbulent fluctuations. Despite the complex near-field structures, the flow rapidly reorganized into a one-dimensional planar shock wave within a short axial distance (x/dt≈3.23). In the far field, the shock wave demonstrated linear attenuation driven by turbulent boundary layer growth, governed by the Reynolds analogy. Furthermore, empirical power-law correlations for shock intensity and decay rate were derived to predict the local shock wave intensity. These findings provide fundamental insights into transient compressible flows in confined geometries and offer essential design criteria for the safety of vacuum-tube transportation systems.

papers.title: Mechanisms of spike-induced cavity dynamics and drag reduction in submerged high-speed flows
papers.abstract: High-speed underwater vehicles experience significant hydrodynamic drag, which limits their performance and operational efficiency. Spike devices have been proposed as an effective drag-reduction technique by inducing cavity formation in front of the vehicle. This present study focuses on the drag reduction mechanism induced by a spike under fully submerged high-speed conditions. Using the three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes approach based on the interPhaseChangeFoam solver in OpenFOAM®, high-speed underwater numerical simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the effects of flow parameters and structural parameters on the flowfield characteristics and force acting on the vehicle. The results reveal that the vehicle's drag is strongly dependent on the aerodisk diameter (d), inflow velocity (v), and angle of attack (α), whereas the length-to-diameter ratio (L/D) has a comparatively minor effect. An optimal d exists, namely an excessively small d fails to achieve a stable cavity, while an excessively large d causes the drag force on the spike to increase sharply. For the hemispherical aerodisk, critical values of d and L/D exist for the occurrence of cavitation instability. In contrast, the flat-faced aerodisk can generate a stable cavity at a smaller d and exhibit weak sensitivity to L/D. Higher v promote the cavity to fully wrap the vehicle. Increasing the α disrupts flowfield symmetry, leading to a rapid drag increase beyond 6°. Selecting an appropriate d, controlling the α, and optimizing L/D are therefore key strategies to enhance drag-reduction performance of trans-media vehicles.

papers.title: Flow cutoff characteristics of gas–liquid two-phase flow in the pipeline–riser system: Experimental studies and transient calculations
papers.abstract: Periodic flow cutoff in offshore oil and gas transportation systems, often triggered at slug catchers, causes severe pressure and flow fluctuations that may damage downstream equipment and threaten industrial operations and energy security. This study experimentally investigates gas–liquid two-phase flows in a pipeline–riser system under steady-state, choking, and start-up conditions. The coupling relationship between flow cutoff at the riser top and blockage at the riser base under different working conditions is explored, together with the impact of flow cutoff on system hydrodynamics. Based on the experimental findings, a transient model using ordinary differential equations is developed to describe two-phase flows in pipeline–riser systems. The analysis of the results demonstrates that, for steady-state conditions, the model described in this article is able to predict flow cutoff time and liquid slug length in the riser with less than 20% relative error for almost all configurations. The prediction regarding flow period shows even relative errors below 10%. Additionally, the model systematically captures all qualitative trends regarding pressure, slug length, and flow velocity, offering a robust numerical tool for pipeline design and safe operation. The predictions can be obtained within minutes on a standard portable computer. These insights enhance the reliability of offshore energy systems and mitigate potential risks to critical infrastructure.

papers.title: Aspect-ratio-driven pattern selection and heat/mass transfer in liquid metal double-diffusive convection under uniform magnetic fields
papers.abstract: Double-diffusive convection of low-Prandtl-number liquid metals under magnetic fields is numerically investigated in a laterally heated rectangular cavity, with particular emphasis on the coupled effects of aspect ratio and magnetic-field orientation (β=0°,90°). High-order numerical schemes are employed to resolve flow topology and transport characteristics over a wide range of aspect ratios (A∈[1,12]) at Ra=104 and 105. At the moderate Rayleigh number (Ra=104), the flow remains in steady or periodically oscillatory states for all aspect ratios considered, and the heat and mass transfer rates exhibit pronounced non-monotonic dependence on aspect ratio. These extrema are shown to be closely associated with transitions in the number of convection rolls, highlighting the role of flow structural reorganization in transport enhancement. At the higher Rayleigh number (Ra=105), the flow dynamics become significantly more complex, with increasing aspect ratio leading to successive transitions from steady convection to periodic oscillations and eventually chaotic behavior. The onset of chaos is attributed to the combined effects of intensified buoyancy forcing and geometric stretching of the flow domain, which promote nonlinear interactions that cannot be fully suppressed by magnetic damping. The magnetic field orientation is found to play a crucial role in modulating flow stability and transport efficiency, with vertical magnetic fields sustaining more coherent convective motion and yielding higher heat and mass transfer rates than horizontal fields due to the anisotropic action of the Lorentz force.

papers.title: A stable immersed boundary method for suppressing interface penetration into immersed solids in two-phase flows
papers.abstract: Conventional immersed boundary (IB) method, when coupled with interface-capturing schemes for multiphase flows, often suffers from unphysical penetration of the gas–liquid interface into immersed solids. This failure mode originates from velocity errors at fluid–solid interface nodes induced by strong temporal pressure gradients, which become particularly severe when the interior of the immersed body is initially filled with a light phase. Increasing the density of the virtual fluid inside the solid region can reduce this velocity error and suppress interface penetration. However, this strategy simultaneously amplifies the spurious pressure oscillations when the IB moves across the grid. These oscillations arise from geometric non-conservation of the inertial and body-force integrals associated with fresh and dead cells generated by immersed-boundary motion. To resolve this issue, a conservative cut-cell-based momentum forcing formulation is developed to restore discrete geometric conservation near the IB. The resulting framework naturally leads to a density-weighted hybrid velocity reconstruction and a modified velocity corrector. The performance and accuracy of the methodology are assessed using three test cases involving fluid–structure interaction in surface-piercing configurations, which demonstrate its capability to eliminate free-surface penetration into the structure and accurately predict hydrodynamic forces. Finally, the proposed method is applied to simulate the propulsion of a manta ray swimmer.

papers.title: Coalescence–rupture threshold in head-on collisions between micron-sized droplets and dust in suspension
papers.abstract: Collisions between droplets and solid particles may result in rebounding, coalescence, or droplet rupture. In spray-based dust suppression, coalescence is the most desirable outcome because it promotes particle mass increase and gravitational settling. Therefore, identifying the governing factors and critical conditions for coalescence is essential for improving spray dust mitigation efficiency. Although previous studies have made significant progress in establishing transition criteria between rebounding and coalescence, quantitative predictive models distinguishing coalescence from rupture remain limited, particularly for suspended particle–droplet interactions at the micro-scale. In this study, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model employing a dynamic mesh technique and the coupled level-set/volume of fluid (VOF) method is used to investigate the collision dynamics between suspended particles and droplets. The results demonstrate that the collision outcome is jointly governed by the solid–liquid density ratio, contact angle, relative impact velocity, particle-to-droplet size ratio, droplet viscosity, and surface tension. Based on momentum and energy conservation principles, a predictive criterion model for the transition between coalescence and rupture is proposed, revealing the underlying dynamic mechanisms controlling collision behavior. Based on the proposed model, the influence of key parameters on the coalescence regime is quantified, providing guidance for optimizing spray operating parameters and additive formulations. The present findings not only promote the development of spray dust suppression technology but also provide theoretical support for related fields, including particle surface modification, fire smoke scrubbing, and pharmaceutical engineering.

papers.title: Air–water dynamics and wave forcing mechanisms in a pneumatic long-wave tsunami generator
papers.abstract: The pneumatic tsunami generator enables the generation of Froude-scaled long waves in laboratory flumes through controlled air-pressure variation within a sealed tank. The internal water height responds to pressure evolution above the free surface, which in turn initiates wave formation at the connected flume interface. This configuration represents a canonical pressure-driven free-surface problem in which compressible gas dynamics are coupled to an incompressible liquid through a moving interface within a sealed volume. A reduced-order model for the air–water dynamics is developed in two asymptotic regimes: a quasi-static hydrostatic formulation with incompressible air and a dynamic non-hydrostatic formulation that accounts for air compressibility and water-column inertia. The model incorporates mass conservation, pressure–volume relations, and valve-pump inflow and outflow dynamics to describe the nonlinear response of the tank and the resulting near-field wave signal. Experimental data from a pneumatic tsunami generator system are used to examine the water-height evolution and associated near-field response. Model predictions show strong agreement with experimental observations, validating the underlying physical mechanisms. The model captures key dynamical features, including amplitude modulation, phase lag between air pressure and free-surface motion, and the approach to equilibrium between pump extraction and valve inflow. More broadly, the results clarify the dynamical role of air compressibility in pressure-driven free-surface systems and provide insight into transient compressible–incompressible coupling in sealed fluid configurations. These findings establish a mechanistic foundation for understanding crest- and trough-led long-wave formation and for future integration with full wave-propagation models.

papers.title: A Favre-averaging shallow water framework for aerated flows with friction factor decomposition
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of flow resistance in high-Froude-number aerated flows remains challenging due to air entrainment, which causes strong spatial variability in mixture density. Here, we introduce for the first time a density-weighted (Favre) averaging approach within a shallow water equation framework specifically tailored to account for this strong mixture density variability. Within this framework, we present a novel Darcy–Weisbach friction factor formulation that decomposes contributions associated with uniform flow, spatially varying flow, and temporally evolving flow and incorporates momentum and pressure correction factors reflecting the vertical structure of the mixture. Application to experimental data demonstrates that spatial flow development systematically reduces the effective friction factor relative to the uniform-flow estimate, and that momentum-based and energy-based formulations yield nearly identical results. The framework recovers classical uniform-flow predictions in the quasi-uniform downstream region and reduces to standard single-phase formulations in the absence of aeration. Overall, it provides a physically consistent tool for resistance prediction in high-Froude-number spillways, chutes, and open-channel systems, with a structure compatible with depth-averaged numerical solvers.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of normal micro-blowing in a turbulent boundary layer for wall shear stress reduction
papers.abstract: High-resolution particle image velocimetry is employed to investigate the interaction between the micro-blowing technique and a zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layer (TBL). In quiescent air, the micro-blowing jet exhibits a stable near-wall low velocity region combined with a main region accelerating with increasing blowing ratio. In TBL, the micro-blowing produces evident velocity decrease in a range from the wall to the logarithmic region of the time-averaged velocity profile, which intensifies with increasing blowing ratio. At the same time, a velocity fluctuation enhancement also exists due to the mixing between the micro-blowing jet and TBL. A maximum reduction in the local wall shear stress coefficient of 50% is achieved at high blowing ratios, which decays rapidly downstream. In contrast, low blowing ratios yield a moderate wall shear stress reduction but are more sustainable in space. Downstream of the blowing region, a low-speed wake is produced, which shrinks in the spanwise direction when propagating downstream. The wake swings obviously at low blowing ratios and is more stable at high blowing ratios. Quadrant analysis reveals that an important mechanism of wall shear stress reduction by micro-blowing is the suppression of turbulent sweep events. However, at high blowing ratios, an overshoot of ejection events exists downstream, which compromises the wall shear stress reduction performance downstream of the blowing region. These results provide an overall understanding of the TBL affected by the micro-blowing with a large blowing ratio range of 0%–20%.

papers.title: Shear-regulated platelet translocation and aggregation in heterogeneous arterial microflows: A three-dimensional transport–reaction model
papers.abstract: Arterial thrombosis is driven by shear-dependent platelet adhesion in which fast, transient glycoprotein Ibα (GPIbα)–von Willebrand factor (VWF) bonds initiate capture and rolling, followed by slower αIIbβ3-mediated stabilization via VWF and/or fibrinogen. Because these pathways co-occur with strong spatial shear heterogeneity, their combined contribution to aggregate morphology and growth dynamics remains difficult to quantify. Here, we present a three-dimensional continuum, transport–reaction model that resolves coupled hemodynamics, platelet advection–diffusion, and mechanosensitive surface kinetics for free-flowing, translocating (rolling), and irreversibly incorporated platelets. The evolving aggregate is represented as a permeable volume, enabling two-way feedback between growth-induced flow disturbance and platelet transport. Model parameters are calibrated and validated against microfluidic measurements at arterial wall shear rates (WSRs) of 800 and 4000 s−1, reproducing distinct shear-regulated growth regimes and morphologies. Using the finite-element method, the resulting computational model is then applied to two pathologic flow configurations: a stenotic microchannel that produces occlusive, high-shear aggregation and a block-post geometry representative of blood-contacting devices with sharp shear gradients. Simulations show that early platelet translocation, combined with co-acting, in vitro-calibrated binding kinetics, captures experimentally observed growth dynamics and three-dimensional morphology in both geometries. The porous aggregate representation is critical for accurate prediction of near-surface platelet fluxes and downstream transport. Finally, the model indicates that the translocating platelet layer acts as a transport corridor that enhances distal platelet availability, promotes lateral spreading, and facilitates coalescence of neighboring aggregates. Together, this study establishes a computational model for the investigation of the early stages of arterial thrombus formation under heterogeneous arterial microflows.

papers.title: Dynamic coupling evolution mechanism of shock waves and boundary layers in transonic compressor stall inception and its numerical study
papers.abstract: Spike-type stall inception remains a critical challenge for the stable operation of high-speed transonic compressors due to its abrupt emergence and rapid nonlinear evolution. The primary objective of this study is to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms driving the rapid growth of spike-type disturbances by establishing a quantitative theoretical model based on a positive feedback loop. This model focuses on the intricate coupling between passage flow blockage, shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction (SWBLI), and the resulting shock-front instability at the blade tip. By analyzing the trajectory of the disturbance evolution, we identify a distinct “rapid amplification stage” that serves as the core of the stall inception process. The results demonstrate a significant demarcation in timescales: while the global evolution from the first localized velocity deficit to a fully developed stall cell typically spans three to five rotor revolutions, the most critical phase of rapid growth, defined between the onset of blockage surge at Point C and the peak growth rate at Point D, is completed within approximately 1.3 revolutions. During this concentrated window, the positive feedback mechanism triggers an exponential-like increase in blockage, providing a rigorous physical explanation for the sudden “jump” observed in experimental stall precursors. These findings not only clarify the temporal dynamics of spike-type stall but also provide a theoretical framework for improving the precision of stall warning systems and the effectiveness of active stability control in advanced compression systems.

papers.title: 1-Methylnaphthalene tracer planar laser-induced fluorescence thermometry study of thermal mixing and scalar statistics of jet in swirling crossflow under ambient and elevated pressure
papers.abstract: The thermal mixing between jet and swirling crossflow is widely used in modern aero-engine and gas turbine combustors to achieve a favorable temperature distribution in the combustor outlet plane. Although practical combustors are usually operated under elevated pressure conditions, the pressure effect on thermal mixing has not been widely investigated. The present study utilized 1-methylnaphthalene single-shot dual-imaging planar laser-induced fluorescence thermometry to quantitatively measure the temperature distribution under normal (0.1 MPa, Rej = 30 866) and elevated (0.3 MPa, Rej = 92 070) pressure conditions within a three-dome optically accessible model combustor. A deeper penetration, a shorter deflection, and a quicker temperature evolution (indicating accelerated scalar dissipation) were observed for the 0.3 MPa condition. Through the analysis of statistical parameters including standard deviation, skewness, and excess kurtosis, a more efficient mixing region located on the windward side of the jet in swirling crossflow (JISCF) was discovered. Moreover, the regressed linear correlation between the measured skewness and the excess kurtosis achieved good agreement with literature values. In addition, the distribution of the temperature probability density function (PDF) for the current jet in swirling crossflow can be well described by the exact selection of the function form (Gaussian-based kernel density estimation or beta function), keeping the relative error of f2-property within 2%. The above analysis of statistical parameters and PDF can provide deeper insights into JISCF in aero-engine combustors, as well as a valuable reference for the combustor-relevant numerical models.

papers.title: Temporal nonlinear dynamics control of atmospheric pressure dielectric barrier discharge based on data-driven methods
papers.abstract: The temporal nonlinear dynamics of atmospheric pressure dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) poses a critical challenge in stabilizing the discharge mode. While ppm-level impurities can modulate the discharge, conventional numerical simulations struggle to efficiently determine doping content for mode transitions. Here, we combine a one-dimensional plasma fluid model with a data-driven framework that integrates feature dimensionality reduction and interpolation prediction to reveal the regulation mechanism of nitrogen content on the discharge mode in helium DBD. These results show that regardless of whether the initial discharge is chaotic, period-multiplying, or asymmetric single-period, the discharge behavior follows a common evolution with increasing nitrogen content: first entering or maintaining a chaotic state, then undergoing inverse period-doubling bifurcation, and finally stabilizing into a single-period mode. Moreover, the proposed quantitative criterion based on the discharge mode number M successfully determines the nitrogen content boundaries for mode transitions under different initial conditions. The predicted modes agree well with those calculated through the plasma model. Overall, this work provides both theoretical insight into the stability control of weakly ionized plasma fluids and a practical predictive tool for achieving stable, uniform atmospheric pressure DBDs through ppm-level impurity content.

papers.title: Concentration-polarization electroosmosis: Full numerical simulation and comparison with the thin double layer model
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive numerical study of concentration-polarization electroosmosis (CPEO) around a charged spherical particle subjected to an alternating current electric field. The analysis is based on the full solution of the coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck and Stokes equations, allowing us to assess the validity of commonly used theoretical approximations. In particular, we compare the full numerical results with the macroscale electrokinetic model of Schnitzer and Yariv (SY), which relies on the thin electrical double layer (EDL) assumption and is widely used to describe nonlinear electrokinetic phenomena. Our simulations are first validated against classical results for electrophoretic mobility, showing excellent agreement. We then investigate CPEO flows over a wide range of parameters, including electric field strength, frequency, zeta potential, and EDL thickness. For thin EDLs and sufficiently large zeta potentials, the SY model provides accurate predictions of both the flow structure and magnitude. However, significant deviations arise as the zeta potential decreases or as the EDL thickness increases. In the regime of thick EDLs, we observe qualitative changes in the flow, including a reversal of the quadrupolar pattern. Finally, we compare our numerical predictions with available experimental data, finding overall good agreement but also highlighting discrepancies at high electric field strengths, where the experimentally observed saturation of the flow is not captured by current models.

papers.title: Bubble-driven flow transitions in evaporating active droplets on structured surfaces
papers.abstract: The evaporation of particle-laden droplets on engineered surfaces is important in printing, sensing, and interfacial assembly. While the influence of substrate topography on passive particle deposition is well established, the combined effects of active particle dynamics, catalytic gas generation, and surface structuring remain unexplored. Here, we investigate the drying of aqueous droplets containing Janus particles (polystyrene–platinum, PS-Pt) on topographically patterned substrates in the presence of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) fuel. The catalytic decomposition of H2O2 at the Pt cap produces oxygen bubbles within the droplet, introducing strong, transient hydrodynamic perturbations that compete with evaporation-driven capillary flows and contact line interactions, thereby disrupting classical coffee-ring flow. We demonstrate that the final deposit morphology can be systematically tuned by controlling the topography and wettability of the substrate. Hydrophobic micropatterned substrates with feature sizes commensurate with particle diameter promote asymmetric deposits driven by bubble-induced vortices, whereas hydrophilizing the same surface suppresses bubble nucleation and yields uniformly distributed particle deposits. On nanopatterned substrates, bubble pinning within substrate grooves generates highly irregular deposits with chain-like particle assemblies. These results demonstrate how the coupling of catalytic activity, bubble dynamics, and substrate topography efficiently steer particle transport at the nanometer and micrometer scales. Such control of particle deposition during active droplet evaporation provides a new route for reaction-driven directed assembly.

papers.title: Two-way fluid–structure interaction in elastohydrodynamic lubrication of the piston/cylinder interface in deep-sea axial piston pumps
papers.abstract: Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) of the piston/cylinder interface critically affects the lubrication performance of axial piston pumps, yet its role under deep-sea conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study proposes an elastohydrodynamic (EHD) lubrication model for the piston/cylinder interface under deep-sea conditions, in which two-way FSI is realized through dynamic nodal data exchange. The proposed model integrates finite volume discretization of the Reynolds equation with finite element analysis of bushing deformation, and resolves the interdependence among film geometry, pressure distribution, and structural deformation by coupling piston dynamics with oil film lubrication equations within an iterative framework. The evolution of interfacial lubrication fields is characterized, and the effects of structural and operating parameters on energy consumption are quantified by comparing the EHD and hydrodynamic (HD) lubrication models. The results show that elastic deformation of the bushing under deep-sea conditions increases the leakage flow rate while reducing the viscous friction power loss. More importantly, although the leakage flow rate increases substantially with clearance, the EHD model reveals a non-monotonic dependence of viscous friction power loss on clearance, in contrast to the monotonic trend observed in the HD model. These findings provide useful guidance for the design and optimization of deep-sea axial piston pumps.

papers.title: Shock wave reflection near the seabed: Theory and high-resolution simulation
papers.abstract: Shock wave reflection from the seabed governs the loading on underwater structures, yet existing theories derived for gases are inapplicable due to water's high density and low compressibility. To address this gap, we establish an integrated framework that combines analytical theory, high-resolution simulation, and experiments to unravel the physics of near-seabed shock reflections. Theoretically, we derive explicit formulas for the reflection coefficients and, for the first time, the critical angle for Mach reflection in water. These predictions are validated against both high-fidelity simulations using a Runge–Kutta discontinuous Galerkin (RKDG) multiphase model and small-scale experiments, showing excellent agreement (errors < 8%). The simulations reveal the detailed dynamics of the regular-to-Mach transition and the non-uniform pressure distribution along the Mach stem. Crucially, by extending the analysis to deformable seabeds, we demonstrate that seabed stiffness is the primary factor controlling both the reflection mode and overpressure amplification—Mach reflection and high pressures occur only on stiff boundaries, while soft sediments suppress it entirely. These results provide a physically grounded, validated framework for predicting shock loads on the seabed, with direct implications for the design of resilient marine infrastructure.

papers.title: Effects of geometric parameters and arrangement of three-dimensional secondary recirculation jets on shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction in a supersonic isolator
papers.abstract: Shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction (SWBLI) in supersonic internal flows can induce large-scale flow separation, strong pressure rise, and localized thermal loading, thereby degrading inlet performance and operability. Building on passive flow control concepts, this study numerically investigates a three-dimensional secondary recirculation jet (SRJ) as a control strategy for SWBLI in a supersonic isolator. Through steady simulations, the effects of key geometric parameters, the number of SRJ units, and their spanwise arrangement are systematically examined to clarify the mean-flow control behavior and identify more effective configurations. The results show that the SRJ suppresses the separated low-momentum region by extracting fluid from the separation bubble and re-injecting it into the near-wall flow, thereby modifying the time-averaged shock structure and promoting boundary layer recovery. Among the single-SRJ configurations, the best-performing case reduces the separation-bubble volume by 37.70% relative to the uncontrolled baseline. Increasing the number of SRJ units further enhances the control effectiveness, and the optimized five-unit arrangement yields a maximum reduction of 83.75% relative to the single-unit reference. The SRJ also significantly alters the three-dimensional skin-friction topology and weakens the broad high-pressure footprint associated with SWBLI. However, the modified near-wall topology may still concentrate wall heat transfer near separation and reattachment, with the dominant Stanton-number peak appearing downstream of reattachment. These results indicate that the SRJ is a promising passive method for mitigating SWBLI at the mean-flow level in supersonic isolators, although further unsteady investigations are still needed to assess its influence on intrinsic low-frequency dynamics and thermal-load evolution.

papers.title: State classification and near-threshold dynamics of droplet detachment and stable levitation induced by an ultrasonic phased array on surfaces of different wettability
papers.abstract: Wall-borne droplet levitation under ultrasound is a fundamental process in contactless droplet transport, yet it is still commonly described using a single detachment threshold. Here, a 40 kHz, 16×16 ultrasonic phased-array platform is used to examine how surface wettability affects droplet detachment and the experimentally observed stable-levitation window, including its lower and upper state boundaries. Three reproducible states—Attached, Stable levitation, and Breakup—are identified, and the finite stable-levitation window is defined by the levitation and breakup thresholds. Under the present wall-attached initialization and ground-condition actuation, stable noncontact levitation is sustained over a droplet-volume range of 1–25 μl. To compare different droplet sizes and wettability conditions on a common basis, we introduce the Bond number, Bo=ρgR2/σ, and a dimensionless acoustic–gravity index, I*=(U/Uref)2(Rref/R), where U is the applied driving voltage and Uref is the levitation-threshold voltage under the reference condition of CA = 170° and V=25 μl. Decreasing contact angle markedly shifts the levitation threshold upward and progressively narrows the stable-levitation window; the window disappears near Bo≈0.44, 0.38, and 0.19 for CA=170°, 164°, and 157°, respectively, and is absent over the tested range for CA=122° and 110°. Near-threshold dynamics further show that increasing relative overdrive raises the levitation height but also amplifies residual oscillations. These results demonstrate that acoustically induced levitation of wall-borne droplets is governed by a wettability-controlled operating window rather than by a single detachment threshold.

papers.title: Shock transmission and its interactions with exhaust gases from an open detonation tube
papers.abstract: When a detonation exits a confined tube into open air, the transmitted shock weakens rapidly as the flow expands, interacts with the ground, and couples to the hot exhaust plume. We simulate this process using two-dimensional reactive Navier–Stokes calculations with a chemical–diffusive model, resolving the internal detonation dynamics and the external field in a coupled tube–atmosphere domain with a ground surface. At the tube exit, an acoustic-impedance mismatch generates a transmitted shock and an upstream-propagating rarefaction train that reduce the driving pressure and promote separation of the shock from the expanding product jet. Outside the tube, baroclinic torque deposits vorticity along the curved shock–plume interface, followed by shear-layer roll-up as Kelvin–Helmholtz instability becomes dominant. Ground impingement produces a reflected shock that reshocks the lower flow, further distorting the transmitted wave and enhancing mixing. Centerline pressure histories exhibit a blast-like signature—an initial overpressure peak, exponential decay, and a negative phase—before relaxing to an acoustic disturbance. A parametric study shows that tube diameter and ground clearance primarily control the transmitted overpressure, whereas the reactive mixture (hydrogen–air vs ethylene–air) has only a modest influence once diffraction into the far field occurs.

papers.title: Mapping mesoscale heterogeneity reveals the effect of structure and preparation protocol on the rheology of microgel suspensions
papers.abstract: The bulk rheology of microgel suspensions and other soft materials can be severely affected by the size and degree of clustering of their building blocks, which often span multiple length scales and can sensitively depend on preparation protocols. To evaluate these effects, microrheology techniques based on optical microscopy can provide critical information. However, they typically require a resolution which limits the field of view and thus hampers the access to large-scale heterogeneities. Here, we propose a simple and efficient approach to map rheological properties up to the millimeter scales, based on low-magnification microscopy and tracking of the motion of dispersed tracers under weak pressure gradients generated by capillarity effects in confined samples. The time scaling of the mean square displacement of particles allows us to identify the prevailing regime—arrested, diffusive, or ballistic—in each sample region, generating for the first time heterogeneity maps over a large field of view and providing insights into the mesoscopic structure. We apply this method to various types of microgel suspensions, undergoing different preparation protocols and displaying different bulk rheological properties. Our analysis allows to extract a spatial map of clusters in the samples and their size distribution, which result from the overall applied shear during preparation and in turn determine bulk microgel viscosity.

papers.title: Damping dynamics of bubble-driven oscillatory flows
papers.abstract: Oscillatory flows in confined geometries are susceptible to instability, presenting challenges in microfluidics, acoustics, and biomedical systems. Trapped air volumes passively damp these flows due to gas compressibility, yet a first-principles model capturing the full spatiotemporal response has been lacking. Here, we derive a unified theoretical framework that characterizes the damping of oscillatory liquid flows by a trapped air volume. The model reveals a dimensionless product (τω) as the governing scaling parameter, linking air compliance and fluidic resistance to amplitude reduction, phase shift, and a transient mean drift of the liquid front. This framework, analogous to a resistance–capacitance circuit in fluidic form, provides a complete analytical solution tested experimentally across a broad range of frequencies, resistances, and air volumes. By unifying amplitude, phase, and transient dynamics under a single scaling law, this work transforms trapped air from an unpredictable artifact into a quantifiable design element, offering fundamental insight into damping mechanisms in two-phase oscillatory flows.

papers.title: Large-scale separation-induced secondary turbulence amplification in shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction
papers.abstract: Turbulence amplification in shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interactions critically affects flow unsteadiness and wall loading in supersonic aerodynamic configurations. Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are performed at shock generator angles of β=8°, 10°, and 12°. At the two smaller angles, turbulence amplification is confined to the vicinity of the separation point. As β increases to 12°, however, a pronounced secondary amplification emerges near the reattachment point, giving rise to a bimodal streamwise distribution of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). Spectral analysis of the TKE production terms reveals that this secondary amplification is predominantly driven by shear production associated with large-scale vortical structures. Global stability analysis (GSA) of the mean flow further demonstrates that all unstable eigenmodes are intrinsically tied to the separation bubble, and the most unstable spanwise wavenumber predicted by GSA agrees closely with the dominant scale observed in the DNS. Reduced-order variational mode decomposition identifies an energetically dominant, low-frequency three-dimensional mode in the reattachment region for the β=12° case, characterized by coherent Görtler-like vortices whose spanwise wavelength is consistent with both the DNS and GSA results. These results suggest that the secondary turbulence amplification originates from the modal instability of the mean flow associated with the large-scale separation bubble and the coherent structures it induces.

papers.title: Staggered quantum Kármán vortex street in a two-component dipolar Bose–Einstein condensate
papers.abstract: The dynamics of a two-component dipolar Bose–Einstein condensate, which consists of two different dipolar bosonic atoms, through a moving obstacle potential is numerically studied. The numerical results show that the parametric regions of the staggered quantum Kármán vortex street and related vortex shedding patterns depend strongly on the obstacle width d, moving velocity υ, and dipole–dipole interaction strength addjk and reveal a spatially staggered half-quantum vortex street with anti-phase ordering between the two components. Moreover, the phase diagrams of various vortex shedding patterns under different obstacle potential widths and moving velocities are obtained. By analyzing the instantaneous drag force acting on the obstacle potential, the contribution of various vortex shedding to the drag force is obtained. As the dipolar interaction strength increases, the parameter range of vortex street decreases, and the shedding order of the vortex patterns also changes. The special two-component system considered here opens up another way to explore the vortex dynamics of dipolar quantum gases.

papers.title: Internally heated cellular convection cells: Temperature difference metrics, Rayleigh and Prandtl numbers
papers.abstract: Temperature and velocity in two-dimensional convection cells driven by internal heating and cooling are numerically calculated using three distributions of internal heating/cooling over depth, with dimensionless heating up to 1010, and for the two Prandtl numbers 1 or ∞. In all cases, hot and cold plumes form between cells. Three candidates for the metric to define the temperature difference, and hence to define the Rayleigh number, are considered. The first is the difference between the average top and the average bottom boundary temperatures. The second is the temperature difference at the mid-level of a single cell. The third is the root mean square of temperature. In a chamber eight times longer than its depth, the three Nusselt numbers vs Rayleigh number using the first, second, and third metrics follow power laws with exponents of 1/2, 0.87, and greater than 1. These motivate numerical results for a single cell that follow a power law with an exponent of 0.99 for the third metric for all three heating distributions and both Prandtl numbers. The other two metrics obey smaller power laws. This suggests that the root mean square metric is best. In addition, a simplified theory for a single cell is developed that is valid for both Prandtl numbers and asymptotically valid for large Peclet numbers. It follows a power law with an exponent of 1, in agreement with an exact solution by Miquel et al. [“Convection driven by internal heat sources and sinks: Heat transport beyond the mixing-length or ‘ultimate’ scaling regime,” Phys. Rev. Fluids 4, 121501 (2019)] that is valid for large heating rates.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of wake dynamics of a rotating cylinder undergoing vortex-induced vibration in turbulent flow
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the wake dynamics and flow physics of vortex-induced vibration of a rotating circular cylinder at a Reynolds number of 10 000. A direct forcing immersed boundary method coupled with a large eddy simulation is employed to resolve the interaction between the rotating vibrating cylinder and the surrounding turbulent flow. The effects of rotation rate, Reynolds number, and three dimensional wake structures on vibration amplitude and vortex shedding modes are systematically analyzed. The results confirmed that cylinder rotation causes flow separation and wakes to become more asymmetric and strength alternating lift forces, thereby enhancing the vibration response. The evolution of unsteady lift and drag forces governs the onset, growth, and suppression of vortex-induced vibration of a rotating cylinder. As the rotation rate increases, the vibration response transitions from a strongly coupled vibration regime at a rotation rate 0 to a weakened, partially decoupled state at a rotation rate 2 and ultimately to a regime, where vortex shedding is largely suppressed and the fluid–structure interaction vanishes at a rotation rate 2.5. The phase relationship between transverse displacement and lift force is in phase at low reduced velocities but becomes out of phase at the onset of the upper branch for the rotation rate between 0 and 1.5. However, higher rotation rates of 2 and 2.5 maintain an in-phase response over a wider range of reduced velocities. Additionally, the mechanical energy transfer from the fluid to the vibrating rotating cylinder increases as the rotation rate increases from 0 to 2, while the rotation rate of 2.5 nearly suppresses the energy transfer. In general, the findings show that cylinder rotation is an effective mechanism of controlling vortex-induced vibration through wake modification and energy transfer, providing much insight into the enhancement and suppression of vibration in rotating bluff body configurations.

papers.title: Electrophoresis of a rigid particle in a weakly non-Newtonian Carreau fluid with ion steric interactions
papers.abstract: The electrophoresis of a rigid particle in a weakly non-Newtonian viscoelastic fluid accounting the ion steric interactions of finite-sized ions is studied. Under the weakly non-Newtonian fluid consideration, which assumes a small deviation of the shear rate-dependent viscosity from the baseline Newtonian viscosity, the mobility can be expressed as a linear superposition of the Newtonian part and a non-Newtonian correction. We consider a modified form of the standard point-charge based Nernst–Planck–Poisson (PNP) model to incorporate the ion steric interactions arises due to the finite-sized ion consideration. The ion steric interactions is accounted through the excess electrochemical potential, which is modeled based on the Boublik–Mansoori–Carnahan–Starling–Leland equation of state. This modification of the PNP-model is relevant for a higher surface charge. The modified Nernst–Planck–Poisson model is solved numerically supplemented by a theoretical analysis under a thin Debye layer consideration. Under the thin Debye layer consideration with arbitrary ζ-potential the non-Newtonian correction of the mobility is expressed in terms of relaxation time and flow behavior index as well as the electrokinetic parameters, such as Debye length and ζ-potential. Ion steric interaction enhances the non-Newtonian part of the mobility in a similar manner as the Newtonian part. This makes the non-Newtonian part more significant in the particle motion at a higher ionic concentration or surface charge density. The nonlinear dependence of mobility on particle surface charge density at high charge levels arises from enhanced surface conduction. This effect is quantified by the Dukhin number, which measures the relative importance of surface to bulk conduction and thereby assesses the nonlinear dependence of mobility on the ζ-potential. Ion steric interactions decreases the Dukhin number by suppressing counterion accumulation near the surface, indicating counterion saturation.

papers.title: Analysis of the influence of contact rotational motion on the characteristics of vacuum arc plasma
papers.abstract: The characteristics of vacuum arc plasma determine the energy dissipation process of the arc during the breaking of vacuum switches. To explore the influence mechanism of the contact rotation motion on the energy transformation of vacuum arcs, a multi-scale coupled vacuum arc model integrating microscopic and macroscopic aspects is established. Based on the thermal-field emission characteristics of the contacts, the physical parameters, such as the density and dynamic viscosity of the high-energy particle flow in the vacuum arc, are analyzed by combining the microscopic particle reactions in the vacuum gap. Based on the physical parameters of the microscopic particles, a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model (the MHD equation separates the electron temperature from the ion/heavy particle temperature for solution. Due to the significant differences in the thermal motion speeds and collision frequencies between electrons and heavy particles, insufficient energy exchange results in a significant temperature difference) with rotational characteristics are established to study the effect of contact rotation motion on the more uniform spatial distribution of high-energy particles in the gap. This paper conducts vacuum breaking experiments with contact rotation motion at different arc initiation points. The results show that the contact rotation drives the vacuum arc to move in the gap. The farther the arc initiation point is from the center, the easier the arc enters the diffusion state and the faster the arc energy dissipates, further verifying the validity of the simulation model. This provides a research basis for exploring new technologies to develop high-breaking capacity vacuum switches.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of hypersonic boundary layer transition on the hypersonic transition research vehicle model lifting body at high angles of attack
papers.abstract: Large eddy simulations are performed to investigate transition of the hypersonic boundary layer over the Hypersonic Transition Research Vehicle lifting body at angles of attack of 7°, 9°, 11°, and 13°. The freestream Mach number is 6 with a unit Reynolds number of 1.0×107 m−1. Increasing the angle of attack drives a pronounced reorganization of the leeward flow topology, partitioning transition into a top region governed by a merged vortex converging near the centerline, and an outer shoulder region of persistent separation and crossflow. Transition in both regions shifts upstream with an increasing angle of attack. Simultaneously, the band of high friction in the top region contracts toward the centerline, while the footprint in the shoulder region splits from a single band into two, demonstrating a tendency toward multiple branches at the highest angle of attack. Spectra of the wall pressure and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition reveal that the earlier convergence and upward lifting of the top vortex core shift its dominant instability to lower frequencies. Concurrently, the shoulder region evolves into a compound system of two branches, featuring structures of high energy that are spatially separated yet spectrally coupled within the frequency band of the crossflow.

papers.title: Centrifugal creaming dynamics in dense shear-thinning emulsions
papers.abstract: Centrifugal creaming of non-Newtonian continuous-phase dense emulsions results from a complex interplay between droplet-scale hydrodynamics, shear-dependent viscosity, and concentration-driven hindrance. Despite extensive work on Newtonian systems, physically consistent modeling frameworks for shear-thinning continuous-phase emulsions remain limited. In the present study, we combine space- and time-resolved analytical centrifugation, a one-dimensional convection–diffusion model, and Euler–Euler computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to examine the effects of droplet size, dispersed-phase fraction, and polymer-induced rheology of the continuous phase on creaming dynamics. As expected, experiments using carboxymethylcellulose- and xanthan-thickened emulsions show that creaming velocity decreases with increasing the continuous-phase viscosity, shear-thinning intensity, and dispersed-phase fraction, while larger droplets migrate faster. The extended convection–diffusion model incorporates power-law rheology, polydispersity in the drop size, and hydrodynamic hindrance due to higher dispersed-phase fractions. Among the velocity formulations tested, the Kumar–Hartland model consistently provides the closest agreement with the experimental trends under the different tested conditions. CFD simulations provided local velocity and revealed stress gradients, the formation of compacted layers, and viscosity heterogeneities that corroborate the one-dimensional model predictions. Overall, the combined experimental and modeling approach provides a physically consistent and calibrated framework for analyzing phase separation dynamics in shear-thinning dense emulsions under centrifugal or gravitational fields.

papers.title: Magnetically modulated breakup pathways of multi-core compound droplets in simple shear flow
papers.abstract: This study examines the deformation and breakup of a three-core compound droplet in a simple shear flow under a uniform magnetic field for two material architectures: ferro-core and ferro-shell. Sharp-interface front-tracking direct numerical simulations are used to clarify how viscous shear, capillary resistance, and magnetic stress interact to drive distinct evolutionary pathways when the magnetic phase is placed in the cores or in the shell. The responses are classified into four outer-shell topological families: F0 (intact), F1 (connected filamentary non-breakup), F2 (compound-only breakup), and F3 (simple-droplet breakup). The results indicate that the Capillary number, Ca, acts as the primary breakup gate, determining whether the system remains on a non-breakup branch or enters a breakup-accessible window. Beyond this threshold, the magnetic-field orientation angle, α, acts mainly as a local post-threshold pathway selector, whereas the magnetic Bond number, Bom, can bias, reroute, or locally restabilize the response depending on the parameter window. Even under identical external controls, ferro-core and ferro-shell may evolve toward different terminal families. This suggests that the location of the magnetic phase affects how magnetic stress is transmitted through the core–shell structure and, in turn, modulates the terminal breakup topology. Breakup in the present system can therefore be interpreted through a consistent control hierarchy comprising Ca-gated access to breakup, α-dependent pathway selection, Bom-induced local bias or rerouting, and architecture-dependent divergence of the terminal topology.

papers.title: Vortex-induced vibrations of lazy-wave cables under platform surge excitation
papers.abstract: Surge motions of floating offshore platforms generate oscillatory fluid–structure interactions (FSIs) that can trigger vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) in attached lazy-wave cables. Due to their segmented geometry, the resulting vibration response is inherently non-uniform and remains poorly understood. A fully coupled three-dimensional FSI model is developed to investigate the VIV response of a lazy-wave cable subjected to platform surge excitation under representative operating conditions. The results demonstrate that surge-induced VIV is characterized by pronounced multi-modal behavior with strong spatial heterogeneity. Under moderate excitation, the response is dominated by lower-order modes with localized higher-mode contributions, whereas intense excitation simultaneously activates multiple higher-order modes, giving rise to modal competition. Position–frequency energy analysis further reveals strong spatial heterogeneity of vibration energy in the frequency–space domain, with distinct modal responses governing different cable segments. Fatigue damage is governed not only by vibration amplitude but also by modal redistribution along the cable; damage hotspots are concentrated near geometric transition regions and migrate upward with increasing surge intensity. Despite their short duration, extreme conditions contribute disproportionately to cumulative fatigue owing to concurrent increases in both vibration amplitude and modal frequency. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for understanding surge-induced VIV in lazy-wave cables and its implications for fatigue assessment in floating offshore wind systems.

papers.title: Effects of acoustic forcing on jet instability and droplet dynamics in micronozzles
papers.abstract: Controlled droplet formation is essential in many industrial processes, where flow instabilities govern droplet size and uniformity. In this study, the effects of acoustic forcing on jets and droplets formed from micronozzles were investigated to quantify how external acoustic perturbations interact with the Rayleigh–Plateau instability. Acoustic forcing was applied using a lead zirconate titanate (PZT) ring actuator coupled to a nozzle assembly with interchangeable nozzles with diameters of 16, 32, and 64 μm. High-speed, high-spatial-resolution imaging was employed to characterize breakup length and frequency, as well as the downstream evolution of droplet size, velocity, and aspect ratio up to 200 nozzle diameters from the orifice. An open cylindrical cavity acting as a Helmholtz resonator enabled efficient acoustic coupling between the actuator and the jets. Experiments were conducted at fixed Reynolds (Re) and Weber (We) numbers to decouple viscous-inertial and inertial-capillary effects. Local probability density functions (PDFs) were evaluated to characterize the downstream evolution of droplet diameter, velocity, and aspect ratio. Acoustic forcing was found to shorten the breakup length and increase the breakup frequency while reducing the mean droplet size and aspect ratio across all nozzle geometries. Depending on nozzle diameter and operating condition, the response ranged from off-resonant enhancement of breakup to subharmonic synchronization and near 1:1 lock-in, with the clearest frequency matching observed for the 64 μm nozzle under the constant We condition. These results indicate strong coupling between the acoustic field and the liquid jet, leading to the formation of more uniform droplets across all nozzle geometries.

papers.title: Boundary-layer receptivity to oblique freestream vorticity waves for a high-enthalpy hypersonic flow
papers.abstract: The receptivity of a Mach 15 straight-cone boundary layer to oblique freestream vorticity waves is investigated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) alongside linear stability theory and the linear parabolized stability equations. A thermochemical nonequilibrium gas model is used. Oblique freestream vorticity waves at frequencies of 400, 800, and 1200 kHz are considered, with incident angles ranging from 0° to 29.4° at 400 kHz, 0° to 15.7° at 800 kHz, and 0° to 20.6° at 1200 kHz. The 400 kHz case is of primary interest due to the strong second-mode amplification at this frequency. Although the underlying base flow is axisymmetric, the oblique vorticity waves lead to a fully three-dimensional boundary-layer disturbance whose characteristics vary depending on the azimuthal ray relative to the freestream wave. Moving downstream within the second-mode instability region, some clear trends emerge in terms of the boundary-layer disturbance amplitudes; that is, disturbance amplitudes are highest at the leeward ray (relative to the freestream wave), but weakest about halfway between the windward and leeward rays. Increasing the incident angle causes the amplitudes to increase on the leeward ray and decrease on the windward ray. Moreover, the boundary-layer disturbance throughout contains a wide spectrum of azimuthal wavenumbers in which the disturbance energy falls off at higher wavenumbers. Increasing the incident angle causes the azimuthal spectrum of the boundary-layer disturbance to broaden overall. Qualitatively similar results are found for the two higher frequencies leading up to the peak-amplitude locations corresponding to the second-mode instability.

papers.title: Effects of mask leakage characteristics on aerosol inhalability and deposition in the human nasal cavity
papers.abstract: Frequent emergence of infectious respiratory diseases has highlighted the importance of effective respiratory protection against airborne particle exposure. However, imperfect mask fitting often leads to leakage at the mask–face interface, which significantly influence aerosol inhalability and deposition in the human airway. In this study, a coupled numerical model including the breathing zone, face mask, facial interface, and nasal cavity was developed. The model was used to investigate airflow leakage and the subsequent transport and deposition behavior of inhalable aerosols. Representative leakage scenarios were simulated to evaluate effects of leakage location, breathing intensity, and leakage area on particle transport behavior. Results show that leakage location strongly affects airflow organization and particle transport. Midline leakage produced symmetric flow and deposition in the nasal cavities, while cheek leakage induced pronounced asymmetric deposition. Even with leakage, mask wearing still reduces particle penetration into the deeper respiratory tract. Compared with the no-mask condition, particle penetration decreases by an average of 7.36%, with the largest reduction (13.8%) observed under chin leakage. Increasing breathing intensity enhanced particle inertia and promoted inertial impaction in the upstream nasal regions. As the inhalation rate increased to 60 l/min, the overall nasal deposition efficiency reached 90.6%. In contrast, leakage area mainly redistributed particle deposition locations within the nasal cavity while exerting a limited influence on overall deposition–penetration balance. The findings provided insights into aerosol inhalation exposure under mask leakage conditions. It aimed to improving respirator design and respiratory protection strategies.

papers.title: Real-time visualization of cross-media transport of microplastics from water to porous media
papers.abstract: The environmental persistence and ecological impacts of microplastics have attracted considerable global attention. After entering aquatic environments, microplastics can settle and become trapped by subaqueous sediments, yet the cross-media hydrodynamics of microplastics remain unresolved. This study presents a laboratory-scale experimental investigation of the transport of continuously released microplastics from water to porous media, aiming to examine microplastic plume formation, interfacial impact, radial propagation, and infiltration within porous media as a coupled sequence. The refractive index matching technique combined with high-speed shadowgraph imaging was employed to enable real-time visualization of microplastic cross-media transport. Following impact, microplastics radially propagate along the porous media surface and exhibit two stages with distinct temporal variations of propagation distance, which are dominated, respectively, by impact momentum and by gravity current and vortex entrainment.
