A dimensionless scaling relationship was established to describe the radial propagation distance of microplastics varying with time across different stages, with the stage transition occurring at a dimensionless time of 0.7 based on a viscous timescale. A transition between sustained microplastic infiltration into the porous media and predominant accumulation on the porous media surface was observed when the microplastic-to-pore size ratio was approximately 1/8. An increased frontal infiltration velocity is obtained for microplastics with a more spherical shape and higher density under a smaller microplastic-to-pore size ratio and a larger mass injection rate. This study elucidates the previously unresolved dominant physical mechanisms and hydrodynamic characteristics governing the cross-media transport of microplastics, thereby advancing the fluid-mechanical understanding and predictive description of microplastic transport.

papers.title: Scaling analysis of capillary channel flow
papers.abstract: Capillary channel flow (CCF) is important in microgravity and microscale open-channel systems, where operation is limited by a critical flow rate above which the free surface collapses and gas is ingested, causing choking. Although one-dimensional models and three-dimensional computations can determine this limit numerically, a compact explicit scaling expression for different geometries remains desirable. In this work, steady CCF is analyzed using a balance among capillary pressure, convective acceleration, and viscous pressure loss. The resulting formulation predicts the critical flow rate from the critical velocity scale and channel cross-sectional area. Comparison with International Space Station experimental data shows that the model captures the measured length dependence for parallel-plate (PP), groove (GR), and wedge (WE) channels. The fitted coefficient is s=0.71 for both the PP and groove channels and s=0.45 for the wedge channel, indicating that neglected geometric and numerical factors remain of order unity. A parametric analysis based on the Ohnesorge number and visco-geometric parameter quantifies the transition between convection-dominated and viscous-loss-dominated regimes. In the convection-dominated and viscous-loss-dominated limits, the dimensionless critical velocity approaches V=s(1+2/Ω)1/2 and V=2s/(Kfl̃), respectively. These asymptotic expressions clarify how inertia, viscous loss, channel length, and free-surface curvature control choking onset. The fitted coefficient is further interpreted using a cross section-based Weber number as an a posteriori measure of the inertial–capillary balance. Once calibrated by one representative experiment or high-fidelity computation, the scaling analysis can estimate critical flow rate trends for geometrically similar open capillary channels under comparable boundary conditions.

papers.title: A temporal-spatial nonlinear dynamics approach for the thermo-vortical-acoustic coupling mechanism in a liquid rocket engine
papers.abstract: Combustion instability in liquid rocket engines is a prominent issue that seriously threatens their reliability and operating performance. To address the insufficient understanding of thermoacoustic instability, this paper takes the Continuously Variable Resonance Combustor (CVRC) as the research object and proposes a temporal-spatial nonlinear dynamics analysis framework that integrates nonlinear time series analysis and Lagrangian coherent structures, aiming to reveal the thermo-vortical-acoustic coupling mechanism in the CVRC. Recurrence plots and joint recurrence plots are adopted to characterize the temporal coupling among acoustics, vortex motion, and heat release. Lagrangian coherent structures are utilized to extract the spatial dynamic features of the flow field, including species transport and jet structures. Results demonstrate that combustion instability in CVRC originates from the thermo-vortical-acoustic coupling, where the interaction among acoustic waves, expanding points (describing vortex dynamics), and triple points (describing flame dynamics) governs the system state transitions. The expanding flow induced by acoustic oscillations modulates the transport and mixing of species, thus altering the triple flame structures. The phase portraits show that the expanding points and the triple points coincide under the stable state, yielding a fixed point in the vortical-thermal coupling phase trajectory. Conversely, they separate periodically under acoustic oscillations, forming a limit cycle. Furthermore, two novel indices, the disturbance index and mixing index, are proposed to quantify the acoustic-vortical and vortical-thermal coupling, respectively. The results indicate that acoustic disturbance exerts a predominantly positive excitation on vortex motion as well as the vortex motion to combustion.

papers.title: Comment on “Posterior comparison of model dynamics in several hybrid turbulence model forms” [Phys. Fluids 36 , 105148 (2024)]
Slamming loads and interaction behaviors on variable-curvature twin wedges during synchronous water entry
papers.abstract: This paper numerically investigates the synchronous water entry of two-dimensional, variable-curvature twin wedges, representative of marine engineering catamaran structures. It aims to extend conventional flat-wedge studies to water entry behavior of complex curved geometries. A Cartesian grid multiphase flow framework is employed, integrating the radial basis function ghost cell method and the gradient augmented level set method for accurate treatment of moving boundaries and violent free-surface deformations. A systematic parametric study is conducted, encompassing five local curvature configurations (C1–C5), five inter-body spacings (G0 = 0.2–2.0), and two water entry velocities (2.77 and 13.85 m/s). Results reveal that geometric curvature is a dominant parameter influencing pressure distribution. For wedges with higher curvature (i.e., blunter configurations), the peak slamming pressure increases significantly due to stronger fluid accumulation and reduced flow separation. In contrast, wedges with sharper profiles tend to promote earlier flow separation, leading to lower, pressure peaks. Moreover, the spacing between the twin hulls modulates the hydrodynamic interaction. At small spacing, the interference between the two wedges leads to pronounced pressure amplification and increased load fluctuations, whereas larger spacing tends to decouple the flow fields, making the water entry process resemble that of single-wedge cases. The present model also captures transient phenomena such as spray jets, splash formation, and free-surface fragmentation. These conclusions provide a basis for the design and optimization of curved twin bodies, such as high-speed ship bows/bottoms and seaplane floats.

papers.title: Numerical investigations of the effects of hub-mounted herringbone riblets on corner separation in a linear compressor cascade
papers.abstract: Corner separation can degrade the aerodynamic performance of a compressor, and even lead to stall or surge conditions, while the vortex details for lightly loaded compressor cascade at low-Reynold-number condition are not clear. In the present study, the relationship between the vortex structures and losses for the lightly loaded baseline cascade at a Reynolds number of 150 000 was investigated. Then, herringbone riblets are placed on the hub, upstream of the blade leading edge to mitigate the adverse effects of corner separation and reduce the overall pressure losses of the cascade. Based on experimental results, numerical simulations were carried out to gain an insight into their effect on the characteristics of the flow field. Our results show that introducing herringbone riblets in front of the blade leading edge can reduce total pressure loss by up to approximately 5.5%, depending on the angle of attack and the distance between the blade and the riblet strip. The results indicate that the vortices induced by the riblets enhance momentum transfer near the blade leading edge, while the riblet channels guide the fluid in the designed direction, thereby suppressing crossflow on the hub. In the baseline cascade, the interaction among the hub separation vortex, trailing edge vortex, and concentrated shedding vortex develops a distinct n-shaped vortex structure within the corner region, which causes a total pressure drop. In contrast, the hub-mounted herringbone riblets can redirect the suction part of the horseshoe vortex away from the blade, delaying and constraining the development of the hub separation vortex, and ultimately suppressing corner separation.

papers.title: From capillary to elastic timescales: Temporal memory in Newtonian and viscoelastic microfluidic jet breakup
papers.abstract: Liquid jets formed during microfluidic displacement exhibit markedly different breakup dynamics depending on dispersed phase rheology. Newtonian liquids frequently fragment into droplets, whereas polymer solutions form elongated filaments persisting over several milliseconds. We study this contrast using high-speed imaging of 35 experiments (Newtonian and viscoelastic fluids, 49 000 frames at 10 000 fps). Jet geometries are extracted automatically using a convolutional neural network, enabling systematic analysis. Autocorrelation analysis reveals that Newtonian jets decorrelate rapidly (characteristic timescale 0.54 ms), whereas viscoelastic jets retain temporal correlations for 4.40 ms. The viscoelastic memory timescale (τV=4.40±0.03 ms) falls quantitatively within the range of polymer relaxation times determined independently by shear rheology (λ=1.0−13.7 ms), directly attributing the observed temporal memory to elastic stress storage in stretched polymer chains. This agreement establishes autocorrelation analysis of high-speed imaging data as a noninvasive tool for extracting rheological relaxation timescales from interfacial dynamics in microfluidic complex-fluid flows.

papers.title: Non-Newtonian fluid–structure interaction in three-dimensional collapsible tubes: An immersed boundary-lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: The effects of non-Newtonian rheology on the dynamics of three-dimensional collapsible tube systems are investigated numerically using an immersed boundary-lattice Boltzmann method coupled with a finite element structural solver. A power-law constitutive model is employed to characterize shear-dependent viscosity effects across a wide range of power-law indices (n=0.7–2.0). The results reveal that fluid rheology significantly modifies the system's dynamic response and apparent stability: shear-thickening fluids (n>1) stabilize the collapsible tube and suppress flow-induced oscillations, while shear-thinning fluids (n<1) promote instability and trigger self-excited oscillations. Mechanistically, shear-thinning effects amplify local velocity gradients in collapsed regions, enhancing fluid–structure coupling and destabilizing the system. In contrast, shear-thickening effects increase effective viscosity in the high-shear areas, providing mechanical damping that suppresses oscillations. The rheological properties significantly affect both structural deformation patterns and the pressure drop—flow rate relationship, with these effects demonstrating the critical importance of accounting for non-Newtonian behavior in physiologically and technologically relevant applications.

papers.title: Flow control of a square cylinder at the most unfavorable angle of attack via bionic shark scales
papers.abstract: An experimental study was conducted to investigate the aerodynamic performance and wake flow of a square cylinder at varying wind angles of attack (AoAs). The efficacy of the bionic shark scale has been assessed for suppressing flow separation at the most unfavorable AoA. The Reynolds number was fixed to be 17 100. The root mean square (RMS) values of the pressure coefficient fluctuations on the upper and lower walls for the AoA = 0° were approximately twice those for the non-zero AoAs. To analyze the underlying mechanism, a high-speed particle image velocimetry system was employed to accurately capture the characteristics of the wake flow. The results indicate that the maximum turbulent kinetic energy, the saddle point closest to the surface, the largest fluctuations of the proper orthogonal decomposition mode coefficients, and the vortex-shedding position nearest to the cylinder all occur at AoA set to be 0°. Because of the strong unsteady pressure at 0°, the different spacing of the shark-scale texture and square cylinder was applied for flow stabilization and controlling unsteady pressure. The results show that the mean and RMS of the pressure coefficient are reduced by 17% and 53%, respectively, under the optimal control condition, and that the unsteady flow structure behind the cylinder is alleviated.

papers.title: The effect of a composite buffer chamber structure on the interior ballistic performance of a gas-driven launch system
papers.abstract: Gas-driven launch stands as a core enabling technology for realizing rapid space response and precise attitude adjustment of spacecraft, thereby exhibiting substantial application potential in the field of aerospace engineering. To address the dual requirements of high-pressure stable combustion and low-overload launch during propulsion, this study proposes and investigates a gas-driven system with a composite structure: a stable combustion environment is constructed via the synergistic design of a high-pressure chamber and a buffer chamber, while the low-overload launch target is accomplished relying on a multi-stage drive architecture. To verify the rationality of the system, a ground experiment prototype was developed, and a multi-parameter synchronous testing system was established, by which key performance indicators, including pressure, thrust, and launch velocity, were measured. Meanwhile, a numerical simulation method for two-phase flow in multi-stage series interior ballistics was constructed to finely describe the spatiotemporal distribution characteristics of the chamber flow field. Experimental and simulation results demonstrate that: the peak pressure of the high-pressure chamber reaches 77.46 MPa, whereas the peak pressures of the low-pressure chambers are all constrained within 7.1 MPa, successfully fulfilling the design objective of high-pressure combustion with low-pressure propulsion, the maximum error of key parameters between numerical calculations and experimental tests is merely 6.49%, and the theoretically calculated pressure curves are in good agreement with the measured ones in terms of variation trend, which validates the reliability and accuracy of the established numerical model. Based on the validated numerical model, parametric performance prediction was conducted to systematically investigate the effects of buffer chamber orifice size and the number of holes in the high-pressure chamber partition board on launch performance. The results indicate that the system achieves optimal launch performance when adopting the structural parameter combination of a double-hole high-pressure chamber outlet and a 5 mm buffer chamber outlet. This finding provides a theoretical basis and technical reference for the structural optimization design of similar gas-driven systems.

papers.title: Drag reduction via separation control using plasma actuators on a truck cabin side
papers.abstract: We investigate the drag reduction on a heavy-duty vehicle using dielectric-barrier discharge plasma actuators located on the A-pillars. An experimental campaign is carried out on a generalized truck model, the Ground Transportation System (GTS), which is known for its lateral separation bubbles on both sides of the truck's cabin. Measurements are performed for several yaw angles up to 7.5°. Actuation is applied individually on the leeward and windward sides as well as simultaneously. Load cell measurements show that the plasma actuators effectively reduce the axial force on the GTS, with symmetric actuation achieving the highest reduction. Leeward actuation demonstrates greater control authority than the windward one; at large yaw angles the latter has a negligible effect on the axial force. Regarding side force, the leeward actuation produces a drop in its magnitude while windward actuation produces an increase. Interestingly, actuating symmetrically also augments the side force. Particle image velocimetry reveals that the plasma actuator causes a reduction in the length and width of the separation bubble on the cabin side, reducing the apparent frontal area of the truck and thus its drag. Under crosswind conditions, the stronger authority of the leeward actuator is explained by the larger separation bubble. The side force variation is driven by the net lateral suction force, which correlates with the size of the lateral recirculation regions controlled by the actuators.

papers.title: Analysis of turning dynamics and aerodynamic performance in butterfly free flight
papers.abstract: This research investigates the effects of body motions on the turning flight trajectories and aerodynamics of butterflies across varying turning radii. In the butterfly free-turning flight motion capture experiment, 15 flapping cycles were recorded to classify the butterfly's turning radii, from sharp to slight turns. Eleven body and wing kinematic parameters were extracted to characterize turning motions. Based on these measurements, three-dimensional numerical simulations were performed to reproduce the observed flight postures and to systematically analyze the resulting aerodynamic forces and flow field structures during turning maneuvers. The study results revealed that body posture was the primary factor influencing the turning radius, specifically the pitch and roll angles. When butterflies adopted high and low pitch angles, the turning radius of the fitted flight path decreased by 36.9% and increased by 26.3%, respectively, compared to the moderate turning mode. These changes were attributed to variations in the wing flapping plane angle. Additionally, notable differences were observed between flapping-wing and fixed-wing turning behavior. During a roll angle of approximately 44°, the left wing of the butterfly generates a normal force during the downward stroke, while the right wing maintains a vertical force, thereby sustaining flight altitude. In contrast, fixed-wing aircraft at the same roll angle must additionally adjust the pitch attitude and increase the flight angle of attack to maintain lift. This study provides theoretical and experimental insights that offer qualitative guidance for the design and development of turning mechanisms in flapping-wing aerial vehicles.

papers.title: Entropy production analysis of interfacial hydrodynamic instability and gas-pocket evolution in a centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid two-phase flows in centrifugal pumps exhibit severe performance degradation driven by complex interactions among centrifugal forces, adverse pressure gradients, and dynamically evolving interfacial instabilities. This study establishes a generalized entropy production (EP) framework within the Eulerian–Eulerian paradigm to systematically quantify the irreversible energy dissipation mechanisms in a multistage centrifugal pump operating under both single-phase and gas–liquid two-phase conditions. Baseline single-phase analysis reveals that turbulent dissipation (TD), driven by intense shear-layer interactions, dominates EP in the diffuser, whereas viscous dissipation (VD) governs the loss within the impeller. For gas–liquid flows, a generalized theoretical expression for EP that explicitly accounts for interphase momentum exchange, interfacial viscous drag, and turbulent fluctuations of the continuous phase is formulated. The analysis uncovers a critical, previously overlooked loss mechanism: the interfacial VD is strongly coupled with gas-pocket instability at the impeller shroud. Furthermore, as the inlet gas volume fraction increases from 2% to 15%, the dominant dissipative regions undergo a spatial migration from the shroud-side outlet toward the hub-side inlet. Despite the significance of interfacial effects, the TD of the continuous liquid phase remains the paramount contributor to overall EP. These insights advance the thermodynamic understanding of energy degradation in multiphase rotating machinery, providing a theoretical baseline for the hydrodynamic optimization of gas-handling centrifugal pumps.

papers.title: Response to Comment on “Posterior comparison of model dynamics in several hybrid turbulence model forms” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 069101 (2026)]
Shock surface evolution in the interaction between a planar shock wave and turbulence
papers.abstract: The present study investigates the deformation process of a planar shock wave propagating through turbulence using direct numerical simulation. The shock wave is identified as a pressure isosurface, and its area change is examined using the surface evolution equation. The area evolution is governed by two mechanisms: the fluid-deformation term associated with velocity gradients and the propagation-deflection term associated with curved-shock propagation. The shock surface area increases because of fluid deformation after the shock wave enters the turbulent region and then gradually decreases in a quasi-steady state, where the propagation-deflection term suppresses the area increase. Although these terms nearly balance on average, the local area change is dominated by the propagation-deflection term, which contributes to both increases and decreases in surface area. Mean-curvature analysis shows that concave regions tend to decrease the surface area, whereas convex regions tend to increase it. Curved-shock propagation acts to flatten and stabilize the shock surface, as observed after the shock wave exits the turbulent region. Analysis of vortex tubes and vortex sheets further shows that the fluid-deformation term is closely related to the mean flow topologies around vortical structures. The surface area tends to decrease when the vorticity direction is nearly aligned with the shock-normal direction and to increase when it is nearly parallel to the shock surface. These results clarify the physical processes governing shock surface deformation and provide a physical basis for understanding how turbulence modulates shock waves.

papers.title: Supercavitation mechanics of rotating projectile: Insights from potential flow and computational fluid dynamics
papers.abstract: Supercavitation projectiles rely on a cavity enveloping the projectile to reduce drag and achieve high-speed motion. Meanwhile, projectile rotation can enhance its anti-interference capability and trajectory stability. However, when the attack angle and rotation act in synergy, the cavity evolution process is disturbed, thereby altering the projectile's motion behavior. This paper addresses the issue of asymmetric cavity deflection of rotating supercavitation projectiles at attack angle by combining numerical simulation with theoretical analysis. Numerical simulations were conducted on the cavity evolution characteristics of rotating supercavitation projectiles at different attack angles using the volume of fluid multiphase flow model and overset mesh technology. Furthermore, a theoretical prediction model for cavity center offset was established based on potential flow theory. The results indicate that the theoretical model can accurately predict the cavity deflection behavior. Compared with numerical simulation results, under un-wetted conditions, the maximum prediction error of the theoretical model does not exceed 2.78%. Within the wetted region under un-wetted conditions, the prediction error remains below 4.62%. The degree of cavity deflection exhibits a significant positive correlation with attack angles. Moreover, a pronounced twisting phenomenon is observed during the cavity development process, with the deflection distance accumulating as the axial distance increases. This study provides a theoretical basis and numerical reference for understanding the cavity evolution mechanism under the synergistic action of attack angle and rotation.

papers.title: Investigating the influence of water depth and expansion state on the pressure oscillation characteristics of solid rocket motors: An experimental study
papers.abstract: Solid rocket motors play an important role in underwater propulsion systems and trans-media vehicles. In this paper, the experimental study has been conducted on the ignition and operation process of a solid rocket motor under deep-water conditions. A variable-water-depth test system and a multi-point pressure measurement scheme for the nozzle is established to simulate the ignition start-up and operating characteristics of the motor at different water depths. Two experimental solid rocket motors are designed under different expansion states and the pressure oscillation characteristics of the motor and the separation flow in the divergent section are measured. The results show that the intensity of pressure oscillations increases with water depth, reaching a maximum at a depth of 330 m. Intermittent unchoked flow in a large expansion ratio nozzle under deep-water conditions is experimentally observed for the first time. This phenomenon causes the combustion chamber pressure to deviate from its sea-level value and exhibit sawtooth-shaped oscillations. There exists a critical depth for the occurrence of intermittent unchoked flow at the throat, which determines whether the combustion chamber pressure is affected by unstable jet behavior downstream of the nozzle throat. As the water depth increases, the flow separation line shifts closer to the throat. A lower equilibrium pressure in the combustion chamber results in a separation line position closer to the throat. At the depth of 330 m, the separation line moved upstream by 50.54 mm in high-pressure motor and 54.96 mm in low-pressure motor.

papers.title: Dispersion of solute under electro-magneto-hydrodynamically assisted flow through tube with spatially varying magnetic field
papers.abstract: The present study investigates solute concentration distribution of passive solute particles in an electro-magneto-hydrodynamically (EMHD) assisted flow of a Newtonian fluid. The flow is driven by pressure gradient, axial and radial electric fields, and spatially varying magnetic fields. Unlike conventional studies that assume low zeta potential ζ≤1 and uniform magnetic fields, the present work considers high zeta potential ζ>1, that realistically represent biomedical applications, together with a non-uniform magnetic field. Mei's multiscale homogenization technique is employed, and analytical approximate solution up to third-order of the advection–diffusion equation with first-order bulk reaction and convective damping effects due to inter-particle collisions are obtained. Comparative analysis with numerical solutions and stochastic Brownian dynamics simulations shows good agreement. Velocity results indicate that in the absence of the transverse electric field (S=0), flow exhibits significant velocity suppression accompanied by a pronounced dip phenomenon across the tube radius. The lateral electric forcing dominates over the constant viscous Lorentz force up to a critical Hartmann number Ha∗, beyond which the net volumetric flow rate decreases. The threshold of Ha∗ shifts with the magnetic non-uniformity parameter (A), yielding a Ha∗−S spectrum. Solute distribution under a uniform magnetic field dominates axial spreading and produces a downstream tail, whereas a non-uniform magnetic field suppresses the tail and promotes a near-Gaussian longitudinal profile with enhanced peak concentration. Parametric effects on dispersion coefficient, skewness, and kurtosis are also quantified. A high-dimensional regression model of dispersion coefficient demonstrates satisfactory results. Overall, it provides a framework for solute dispersion in EMHD-based systems.

papers.title: Investigation on topology optimization of flow and heat transfer in liquid-cooling channels for a blade-type battery with non-uniform heat generation
papers.abstract: Blade-type lithium-ion batteries are widely used due to their high structural integration and superior volumetric energy density. However, the high aspect ratio and meter-scale spacing between electrode tabs lead to pronounced non-uniform heat generation during charging, resulting in localized thermal accumulation and imposing stringent requirements on coolant transport. To address this issue, the present study proposes a topology-optimized (TO) liquid-cooling plate with irregular flow channels tailored to the non-uniform thermal characteristics of blade batteries. An electrochemical–thermal coupled model is established to capture spatial heat generation under charging conditions, revealing that the heat generation near the tab regions exceeds that in the central region by approximately 30kWm−3. A density-based TO framework is then integrated with a conjugate heat-transfer model to generate adaptive channel structures. The effects of inlet–outlet configuration and channel volume fraction on thermo-hydraulic performance are systematically investigated. The optimized structure forms a distributed branching flow network that enhances coolant redistribution toward high-heat regions and suppresses local stagnation zones. Compared with conventional designs, the temperature difference decreases by up to 68%, the maximum battery surface temperature decreases by up to 3.3 K, and the pressure drop decreases from approximately 44 Pa to about 18 Pa, corresponding to a reduction of nearly 59%. Overall, integrating realistic, non-uniform heat sources into TO significantly alters flow patterns, enabling coolant to be directed toward high-heat regions and thereby enhancing thermal management. The proposed framework provides a physics-based and energy-efficient design methodology for liquid-cooled blade batteries.

papers.title: Numerical and experimental hydrodynamic assessment of internally partitioned thin porous breakwaters under regular and irregular sea states
papers.abstract: Porous breakwaters play an important role in coastal protection by attenuating wave energy while allowing partial water permeation, thereby reducing wave reflection and structural loading. This study investigates the hydrodynamic performance of internally partitioned thin porous breakwater configurations using the dual boundary element method within the framework of linear wave theory. The quadratic pressure drop boundary condition is incorporated to better capture the effect of wave heights on energy dissipation and to represent pressure and velocity across the porous barriers. A series of structural configurations is numerically examined, revealing that for the triple-chambered configuration, the reflection coefficient (KR) is limited between 0.32 and 0.43, while the transmission coefficient (KT) is reduced by about 36%, and energy dissipation (KD) increases by about 20% compared with the base configuration over the tested range of k0h. Subsequently, it is chosen for experimental validation and parametric analysis due to its most balanced wave scattering behavior among the tested arrangements, with additional internal barriers adversely affecting energy dissipation. A porosity of ε=0.20 yields the highest energy dissipation (KD≈0.80) while maintaining controlled transmission (KT≈0.50) over the tested range. Further, the moderate chamber spacing and smaller barrier submergences provide the favorable hydrodynamic performance while maintaining material efficacy. Irregular-wave analysis shows that the proposed configuration maintains transmission (KT¯) below 0.50 and energy dissipation (KD¯) exceeding 60%, demonstrating its suitability for practical coastal protection and harbor applications.

papers.title: Flow control optimization of a circular cylinder with control rods using deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Control rods are a classical passive strategy for suppressing vortex shedding in circular-cylinder wakes, but their effectiveness is highly sensitive to rod position and diameter. In the present study, deep reinforcement learning is coupled with direct numerical simulation based on the high-order spectral/hp element method to optimize the control-rod position and diameter according to the hydrodynamic response of the main cylinder at Reynolds numbers of 80 and 150. The results show that the control responses exhibit a clear regionalized pattern in parameter space, with four representative functional regions identified as regions I–IV. In the variable-diameter case, the learned distribution of control-rod diameters is concentrated around 0.22D, where D is the main-cylinder diameter. Region I achieves drag reduction primarily by reducing the pressure drag through incoming-flow redistribution. Region II amplifies lift fluctuations by enhancing the instantaneous imbalance between the upper and lower shear layers and strengthening wake flapping. Region III produces the largest drag because strong direct interference with the separated shear layers simultaneously enhances local blockage and deepens the rear-side pressure deficit. Region IV most effectively suppresses lift fluctuations by inhibiting shear-layer development, delaying vortex formation, and weakening vortex shedding. These results indicate that the four representative regions correspond to distinct mechanisms of shear-layer evolution, recirculation-zone reorganization, and wake dynamics. This study provides a new perspective for the parameter design and physical understanding of passive wake control of circular cylinders.

papers.title: Stage-dependent modal energy partitioning for physics-guided sparse pressure reconstruction in ventilated cavitating flows
papers.abstract: This study investigates the sparse reconstruction of unsteady surface pressure fields in ventilated cavitating flows using an experimentally validated numerical framework and a data-driven strategy. A systematic numerical investigation is conducted to characterize the transient flow evolution and provide the ground truth for method development and evaluation. Based on this database, an integrated framework combining Gappy proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) with a clustering-guided unsupervised learning strategy is developed to identify dynamically similar regions and determine representative virtual sensor locations for sparse reconstruction. POD analysis reveals pronounced low-dimensional characteristics of the pressure dynamics, indicating that the dominant flow evolution can be represented by a limited number of coherent modes. During the re-entrant-jet-dominated stage, the first POD mode contains approximately 85% of the modal energy, indicating coherent low-order dominance. In contrast, during cavity break-off and shedding, the first-mode contribution decreases to approximately 65%, accompanied by a redistribution of modal energy toward higher-order modes and enhanced multi-scale pressure fluctuations. These flow-physics characteristics explain the variation in reconstruction difficulty across flow stages and provide a physical rationale for sparse pressure-field reconstruction. The reconstructed pressure fields agree well with the numerical ground truth, with eight virtual sampling points providing an effective compromise between reconstruction accuracy and measurement cost. The proposed framework also exhibits promising in-regime transferability under intermittent and transitional cavity conditions, together with satisfactory robustness to clustering initialization and measurement noise. Overall, the proposed framework offers physical guidance for future sensor placement under limited-measurement conditions.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation of helium–xenon binary mixture in a turbulent channel flow with significant heat transfer
papers.abstract: This study employs wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) with real thermophysical property models to investigate the turbulent flow and heat transfer characteristics of helium–xenon (He–Xe) binary mixtures in a channel with significant heat transfer while neglecting buoyancy effects. The simulations capture the effects of temperature-dependent density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, and He–Xe stratification. Despite the strong property variations across the channel, the nondimensionalized Favre-averaged velocity and temperature profiles can be largely collapsed into incompressible results through appropriate semi-local, wall-property, or Van Driest transformations, demonstrating the quasi-similarity of near-wall momentum transport. The distributions of Reynolds stress and turbulent heat flux deviate from incompressible behavior, with higher near-wall viscous and turbulent contributions, yet the strong correlation between stress and heat flux implies that the Reynolds analogy remains approximately valid. Although the different thermal diffusion coefficients of the He–Xe mixture lead to helium enrichment in the high-temperature near-wall region, this species stratification exerts a limited impact on the turbulent transport and can be eliminated by the semi-local scaling. The resulting property variations are effectively accounted for by the semi-local scaling, which preserves the collapse of the normalized profiles. Based on the LES data, new semi-local correlations for near-wall root-mean-square velocity, temperature fluctuations, and a modified turbulent Prandtl number (Prt) model for y+ < 20 are proposed. The integrated Prt model significantly improves the agreement with experimental data, bridging the gap between He–Xe mixture physics and Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes modeling for advanced gas-cooled and space reactor applications.

papers.title: Impact of bed slope on a supercritical flow overpassing a forward-facing step non-orthogonal to the flow direction
papers.abstract: This study investigates the behavior of a supercritical flow passing over a forward-facing step that is non-orthogonal to the flow direction. We first identify specific flow configurations that may develop across the step. Then, we explore the effects of bed slope, which is neglected in the theoretical analyses, through numerical simulations performed for varying values of step height, a, channel width, B, and bed slope, s. These parameters are demonstrated to critically influence the flow regimes in sloping channels. Specifically, simulations performed at constant sB/a exhibit the same nonlinear effects on flow acceleration, shock wave behavior, and flow field stability. The parameter sB/a emerges as a fundamental dimensionless parameter governing the interplay between vertical and horizontal length scales, the flow configurations, and the transition thresholds. In particular, it strongly influences the transition to choked flow, whose mechanisms are systematically analyzed, while the possible scenarios are identified and their governing conditions discussed.

papers.title: Triggering of extreme events and coherent-structure modulation in wall-turbulence under cyclostationary forces
papers.abstract: Atmospheric gusts expose wall-bounded turbulence to severe unsteady forcing, triggering complex non-equilibrium dynamics and extreme aerodynamic loads. In this study, direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate the spatiotemporal modulation of turbulent structures and the triggering mechanisms of near-wall extreme events under Gaussian-type transient forcing. The results reveal that high-amplitude gusts inject energy primarily into the streamwise velocity component, inducing a pronounced non-equilibrium phase lag during turbulent energy redistribution. This process produces hysteresis in wall friction and extends the relaxation time. Spectral and continuous wavelet analyses demonstrate that intense gust forcing suppresses high-frequency random fluctuations and reorganizes turbulent kinetic energy into low-frequency coherent structures. The characteristic frequency of these energetic structures locks onto the gust driving frequency, with a relative deviation of only 2.4%. Furthermore, the occurrence probability of extreme near-wall events, including extreme positive (EP) wall-shear-stress events and rare backflow (BF) events, increases by up to an order of magnitude under severe forcing. Using a two-step conditional averaging technique, we demonstrate that BF events are actively driven by intense, localized adverse pressure gradients and energetic ejections, which promote spanwise vortex roll-up in the buffer layer. By contrast, EP events are governed by energetic sweeps of high-speed fluid that compress intense spanwise vorticity into the immediate vicinity of the wall. These findings provide physical insights into non-equilibrium energy transfer and offer theoretical guidance for load alleviation and robust flow control of unmanned aerial vehicles operating in unsteady atmospheric environments.

papers.title: Analytical frequency response of pulsatile viscoelastic channel flow
papers.abstract: Flows in many biological and engineering applications are viscoelastic and subject to pulsatile disturbances. In this work, we analyze a pulsatile viscoelastic channel flow with the Oldroyd-B model. Using a Fourier framework, we obtain closed-form expressions for the velocity, polymer shear stress, pressure gradient, and wall shear stress for retained modes of a general periodic forcing. The polymer normal stress is evaluated through a spectral convolution that captures coupling between frequency modes. The frequency response is organized by a complex transfer function that relates the imposed flow rate waveform to the required pressure-gradient response. At low frequency, Oldroyd-B fluids require a smaller pressure-gradient pulsation than Newtonian fluids to deliver the same flow rate modulation, which defines a dynamic flow enhancement regime dominated by elasticity. A low frequency expansion yields an explicit critical elasticity for the onset of enhancement and its dependence on polymer concentration through the solvent viscosity ratio, β. As the forcing frequency and fluid elasticity increase, oscillations of the polymer shear stress weaken, and the dynamics approach a Newtonian limit. In this regime, the Oldroyd-B and Newtonian momentum equations become asymptotically equivalent under an effective Womersley number based on the solvent viscosity. Numerical evaluations confirm that this mapping accurately predicts the velocity distribution, critical pulsation amplitude, and reversal regions near the wall. These findings suggest a simplified way to account for pulsatile viscoelastic flows at high frequency, with potential implications that can guide the design and optimization of related biological and industrial applications.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of vortex structure evolution, flow, and heat transfer characteristics in hydrocarbon fuel boundary layer combustion
papers.abstract: Hypersonic flight increases the aerodynamic-thermal loads on propulsion systems, representing a principal bottleneck to performance advancement. Film-boundary-layer combustion using large-molecule hydrocarbon fuels, which simultaneously provides film cooling and combustion-induced drag reduction, is a promising technology to overcome this limitation. This study employs large-eddy simulation to examine C10H22 film-boundary-layer combustion at a mainstream (Ma = 1.75) and coolant (Ma = 1.22). Drag-reduction performance, vortex-structure evolution, and heat-transfer characteristics are contrasted between cases with and without film combustion, and the effects of dynamic pressure ratios of 0.11, 0.15, and 0.17 on these metrics are evaluated. Results show that boundary-layer combustion reduces turbulent kinetic energy in the mixing layer and decreases the wall skin-friction coefficient by roughly 20% relative to the non-reacting case. Vortex structures are zonally organized: near-wall regions are dominated by quasi-streamwise vortices, the outer layer by Ω-shaped vortices, and a transitional mid-layer exhibits multiscale vortex coexistence. Oxidative-cracking chemistry produces zonal wall-temperature responses: an initial region with negligible change, a cracking-dominated endothermic cooling region, and an oxidation-dominated region with slight warming but overall enhanced cooling. Within a certain range, increasing the dynamic pressure ratio aids drag reduction but weakens film cooling; a ratio of 0.15 achieves the best trade-off.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of two-stage acoustofluidic separation based on acoustic contrast factor differences
papers.abstract: In the field of micro-particle separation, acoustic separation technology is widely applied in areas such as fluid detection and biomedicine due to its non-contact and nondestructive nature. Existing methods predominantly rely on size differences, making it difficult to effectively separate particles with diverse acoustic properties and similar sizes, particularly due to the lack of systematic utilization of both the sign and magnitude of the acoustic contrast factor. To address this, we propose a two-stage sorting chip based on surface acoustic waves (SAW) and investigate its performance through numerical simulations using the finite element method. By integrating a standing surface acoustic wave (SSAW) field in a rectangular microchannel and tilted-angle standing surface acoustic wave (TaSSAW) field in a tapered microchannel, and by combining the sign and magnitude information of the acoustic contrast factor, the chip design achieves efficient and continuous separation of polycaprolactone (PCL), polystyrene (PS), and polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) on a single device. Theoretically, the trajectory slope is derived from particle force balance as a key parameter, which successfully characterizes the longitudinal displacement and reveals its quantitative relationships: non-monotonic dependence on the tilt angle, negative correlation with flow velocity, and positive correlation with the acoustic radiation force. The simulation results show that the scheme enables pre-separation of PCL and achieves optimal separation of PS and PMMA at a tilt angle of 10°. Furthermore, the study clarifies the coordinated regulation between flow velocity and acoustic pressure (e.g., 6 mm/s corresponds to 168 kPa). Under these optimized conditions, a maximum separation distance of approximately 600 μm is predicted. This computational study provides a new approach for multi-target sorting of same-sized particles in acoustofluidics and offers theoretical guidance for future experimental implementations.

papers.title: Displacement and deposition of cliff-bottom rocks using smoothed particle hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: Coastal and cliff-top boulder deposits have been of scientific interest for the last few decades. Recent scientific focus has been on boulder deposits already on top of cliffs that may move during storm events. Here, we focus on the boulder deposition process from the bottom to the top of the cliff. More specifically, a Computational Fluid Dynamics method, namely, the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method, was used to investigate the process under which a cliff-bottom boulder can be transported and deposited onto a cliff. The effects of the boulder's location, impact bore, and boulder submergence were studied. Although extremely rare, deposition was observed only under the most energetic conditions and with non-submerged boulders. Submerged boulders experience significantly lower horizontal and vertical displacements.

papers.title: Flow field in confined impinging jets of Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids
papers.abstract: A three-dimensional numerical investigation is conducted to characterize laminar confined impinging jets of Newtonian and shear-thinning fluids issuing from a rectangular duct. The jet impinges normally on a flat plate and subsequently divides into two streams confined by inclined plane walls, forming a diverging channel representative of compact fluid-handling devices. Shear-thinning fluids are modeled as purely viscous power-law liquids, enabling systematic variation of rheological properties while isolating viscous effects. The governing equations are solved using a finite-volume method with second-order accurate discretization schemes on non-orthogonal collocated grids. Numerical predictions are validated against detailed experimental velocity measurements for both Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids over Reynolds numbers between 10 and 800. The validated simulations are used to examine pressure losses, recirculation dynamics, and the three-dimensional flow structures that arise within the confined cell. The results show that total pressure losses are dominated by irreversible contributions associated with wall friction and flow separation, while reversible pressure recovery becomes significant only at the highest Reynolds numbers. Recirculation length increases with the Reynolds number for all fluids but exhibits a Reynolds-number-dependent and non-monotonic variation with shear-thinning intensity. Owing to the finite spanwise extent of the rectangular geometry, pronounced three-dimensional effects develop, including spanwise variations of recirculation length and secondary vortical motions characterized by helical trajectories within the separated regions. These secondary motions redistribute momentum across the span and significantly influence both separation dynamics and dissipation mechanisms. By resolving the full three-dimensional flow field, the present study clarifies the role of spanwise confinement in governing pressure-loss mechanisms and recirculation behavior in confined impinging jets, providing new insight into complex laminar flows involving geometric confinement and nonlinear rheology.

papers.title: Velocity resetting of inertial run-and-tumble particles in non-Newtonian media: Velocity distribution, diffusion, and first-passage time
papers.abstract: We study the dynamics of an athermal inertial run-and-tumble particle moving through a non-Newtonian medium in d=1, where the particle's velocity v is reset to zero at a constant rate r. The drag force from the non-Newtonian medium is represented by a nonlinear velocity-dependent function g(v). The run-and-tumble dynamics is modeled by a symmetric dichotomous noise with strength Σ and flipping rate λ. We begin with the Fokker–Planck (FP) equation for the velocity distribution P(v,t) of the particle. In the presence of resetting, however, the FP equation does not yield a closed-form solution even in the steady state. We, therefore, compute the steady-state velocity distribution Ps(v) directly from particle trajectories and compare it with the numerical solution of the FP equation, finding good agreement between the two approaches. For sufficiently large r, Ps(v) shows cusp-like singularity at v=0 and the particles display diffusive motion at long times. The effective diffusion coefficient Deff decays as r−2 in the large-r regime. These results hold irrespective of the specific form of g(v), and the values of λ and Σ. However, the mean first-passage time exhibits a strong dependence on the nature of the medium as the resetting rate r is varied. In shear-thickening media, there exists an optimal resetting rate that minimizes the time required to reach the target velocity vt. In contrast, no such optimal resetting rate is observed in shear-thinning media.

papers.title: Investigation of the air film around an axisymmetric projectile with a pressure-equalizing exhaust system
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates air film flow around a projectile with a pressure-equalizing exhaust system. Dimensional analysis is employed to identify the key dimensionless parameters governing flow regime transitions. The air film evolution is categorized into three distinct stages: rapid growth, periodic pulsation, and quasi-steady. The characteristics of the air film and the associated development of the flow field are analyzed. Analysis reveals that the reentrant jet strength and gas injection rate are the primary factors driving transitions in the flow pattern. The velocity vector field reveals that the upstream-propagating reentrant jet dominates interfacial instability and periodic air film shedding, governing the flow regime transition of the air film. During the rapid growth stage, the pressure gradient exhibits minor fluctuations. However, it intensifies markedly upon transition into the periodic pulsation stage. Wavelet analysis reveals that frictional drag is linked to air film geometry, while tail cavity pulsations dominate pressure drag. Pressure drag constitutes ∼95% of the total drag, driven by high-pressure pulsation from the tail cavity, which is affected by the shedding of air film convected downstream. This study provides valuable insights for the engineering design and active flow control of projectiles.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical study on hydrodynamic-driven erosion mechanisms of ice and sand particles in seawater pipeline elbows
papers.abstract: Particle erosion in liquid–solid two-phase flow presents a critical threat to the integrity of marine cryogenic pipelines, especially in elbow regions where turbulence and secondary flows induced by bend orientation dominate particle impact dynamics. This work combines paint-removal visualization experiments and computational fluid dynamics-discrete phase model two-way coupled simulations to investigate the hydrodynamically driven erosion mechanisms of ice and sand particles in 90° pipe elbows under three typical orientations: horizontal–horizontal (H–H), vertical–horizontal downward (V–H down), and horizontal–vertical upward (H–V up). Erosion hotspots, particle trajectories, and near-wall flow structures are analyzed using the Q-criterion, Reynolds number, particle Reynolds number, Stokes number, and buoyancy ratio to establish a physics-based interpretation framework. Results show that sand particles produce a maximum erosion rate four times higher than ice particles in H–H elbows. Sand erosion concentrates in stable high-velocity regions near the extrados, whereas ice erosion is more pronounced in vortex-dominated recirculation zones, leading to a wider and more uniform erosion distribution. For both particle types, the 45° axial position emerges as a critical transition region regarding erosion intensity within the investigated configurations. Hydrodynamic forces—including turbulent drag, centrifugal effects, and vortex-induced secondary flows—dominate particle inertia and impact kinematics, while buoyancy differentiates the erosion patterns between positively buoyant ice and negatively buoyant sand. These findings clarify the intrinsic fluid–particle–wall interaction mechanisms in curved liquid–solid flows and provide physical insights into erosion prediction and mitigation.

papers.title: Performance assessment of mixers in two-phase aeration tanks using computational fluid dynamics and field measurements. II. Assessment of alternative mixing scenarios for performance enhancement
papers.abstract: Ensuring efficient hydraulic performance in aeration tanks is a critical challenge for modern wastewater treatment facilities, as ungoverned flow distribution and weak axial mixing can compromise the overall process's stability. To address this, the present study employs an integrated approach that combines extensive multi-point field measurements with validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling, enabling a robust evaluation of flow behavior under real operating conditions. Unlike most previous studies, the entirety of the mixer setup installed in the treatment plant was directly embedded into the CFD model, ensuring an accurate representation of in situ hydraulic effects. The baseline analysis (case 0) revealed that the circulation generated was insufficient to sustain target velocities across the channel, leading to localized recirculation and weak axial momentum. Therefore, several operational scenarios were simulated to enhance flow distribution and mixing uniformity while maintaining practical feasibility. Additionally, a species transport model was incorporated as a qualitative diagnostic tool to evaluate outlet tracer concentration and mixing performance across different cases. The results showed that increasing the mixer speed by approximately 24% expanded the target-velocity zone by 16%. Applying counter-rotation between mixer pairs (case II) further increased this zone by 24% and promoted more balanced axial circulation. The combined configuration (case III) yielded the greatest enhancement, enlarging the target-velocity region by 32% and reducing outlet tracer concentration by 68%, effectively mitigating short-circuiting. Overall, the findings demonstrate that CFD-based scenario evaluation, reinforced by tracer diagnostics and field validation, provides a practical framework for optimizing hydraulic performance in full-scale aeration systems.

papers.title: Mixer performance in two-phase aeration tanks. I. Full-scale flow and validation
papers.abstract: Characterizing hydrodynamics in full-scale aeration tanks remains challenging due to limited in situ measurements under real operating conditions. As a result, most existing studies are restricted to laboratory-scale systems, which limits the direct applicability of their findings to actual treatment facilities. In this study, an integrated field-measurement and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) based investigation was conducted to analyze the hydrodynamic structure of a full-scale aeration tank operated with all mixers and diffusers active. Velocity measurements were collected at 120 spatial locations distributed over multiple depths and two symmetrical regions of the tank using an acoustic doppler current profiler (ADCP). The measured three-component velocity data (u, v, and w) were employed for rigorous component-wise validation of a three-dimensional two-phase CFD model. To improve model fidelity, the actual mixers installed in the plant were reverse-engineered through high-resolution three-dimensional scanning and explicitly incorporated into the CFD model using a sliding-mesh approach. The validated model revealed pronounced hydraulic deficiencies in the existing tank configuration. Only 13.2% of the total tank volume exceeded the critical velocity threshold of 0.30 m/s, while extensive stagnant regions dominated the central core of the reactor, indicating insufficient internal circulation and an increased risk of sludge deposition. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the current mixer-induced axial mixing is inadequate to ensure uniform circulation, highlighting the need for alternative operational scenarios to enhance the hydraulic efficiency of the system.

papers.title: From microscale transport to data-driven intelligence: The convergence of microfluidics and machine learning
papers.abstract: Microfluidics at its core is a multidisciplinary field that combines fluid mechanics, transport phenomena, and precision microfabrication to control fluid flows at the micrometer scale. Advances in design and fabrication, including soft lithography, photolithography, and advanced manufacturing techniques, have enabled highly integrated platforms for manipulating droplets, particles, and cells with remarkable precision, enabling quantitative characterization of microscale hydrodynamics, interfacial physics, and multiphase transport phenomena. In parallel, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a computational paradigm capable of extracting patterns, optimizing nonlinear systems, and performing predictive modeling on complex datasets. ML efficiently navigates the high-dimensional, multiphysics parameter spaces inherent to microfluidics, capturing couplings between flow and transport processes. This review highlights the fundamental convergence of microfluidics and ML, including physics-informed approaches that enable optimization grounded in physical principles, and presents recent advances connecting microscale transport phenomena with practical applications. ML-driven microfluidics enhances control across diverse systems, enabling systematic optimization of processes such as droplet generation, sorting, and mixing, while supporting diagnostic and therapeutic platforms. Predictive models further enable optimization of device operation and performance through the integration of mechanistic understanding with data-driven learning. We critically synthesize these advances, highlight emerging trends, and provide insights into future directions. While significant challenges remain, the convergence of microfluidics and ML is poised to enable self-optimizing devices, integrated closed-loop control, and adaptive operational strategies, transforming microfluidics into an intelligent, adaptive technology that bridges fundamental fluid mechanics and microscale transport phenomena with biomedical and engineering applications.

papers.title: Equatorial transport driven by periodically rotating wind stress
papers.abstract: The wind-driven transport on the equator is studied, analytically and numerically, in the case where the wind stress vector rotates periodically. The analysis of the Lagrangian model is enabled by substituting the pseudo angular momentum for the zonal velocity in the nonlinear, time-dependent, governing equations. For small-amplitude wind forcing, our results predict first-order oscillatory motions in the meridional and zonal directions at the inertial and forcing frequencies and their harmonics. These first-order oscillations are accompanied by second-order drift in the zonal direction, directed eastward or westward depending on the forcing frequency. There exist resonant frequencies at which the long-term averaged zonal speed is very fast, reaching 0.5 ms−1, while the oscillatory motion is greatly reduced and the water column moves mainly eastward, even though the wind forcing has no dominant direction.

papers.title: The effect of slip and inertia on the instability of bounded films: Linear instability and arbitrary-order lubrication theory
papers.abstract: Higher-order lubrication equations are derived for the van der Waals force driven dynamics of liquid films on slip substrates. Linear stability analysis is performed to evaluate the accuracy of the higher-order lubrication models and the classical lubrication models. By providing a more accurate asymptotic representation of the velocity field, the higher-order models overcome limitations of the classical lubrication equations, whose validity is typically restricted to specific slip regimes. The analysis further shows that, in the viscosity-dominated regime, increasing slip length accelerates film rupture and promotes larger-scale dewetting patterns. In the inertia-dominated regime, by contrast, the influence of slip is reduced because stronger inertia leads to a thinner boundary layer. Furthermore, the 3rd-order lubrication equations are solved numerically. Compared with the Navier–Stokes equations, the lubrication models significantly improve computational efficiency without sacrificing the essential information on interface evolution and velocity field structure.

papers.title: Interfacial designing of firefighting foams: Unveiling the molecular synergy for enhanced fluid stability and corrosion mitigation
papers.abstract: The prolonged contact of firefighting foams (e.g., Fluoroprotein foam, FP) with metallic components in fire suppression systems can cause severe corrosion, leading to equipment degradation, increased maintenance costs, and potential operational failure. To mitigate this problem, a low-corrosion FP formulation is developed via molecular synergistic design. The combination of nonionic surfactant alkyl polyglucoside with short-chain fluorocarbon surfactant, along with an optimized ternary corrosion inhibitor system (sodium gluconate-potassium sorbate-benzotriazole), enabled simultaneous enhancement of surface activity and corrosion inhibition. These results show that the developed system significantly reduces surface tension (∼7.32 mN/m lower than commercial FP) while decreasing the corrosion rates of Q235 galvanized steel and 1060 aluminum alloy by 62% and 48%, respectively, along with a notable reduction in corrosion current density. In terms of foam performance, the system exhibits improved foaming ability, foam stability, and retarded drainage. Extinguishing tests further demonstrate a reduction in extinction time by about 4 s compared to commercial FP. This study indicates that rational surfactant-inhibitor synergy design can significantly enhance the metal compatibility of FP while maintaining fire extinguishing performance, offering a feasible strategy for developing low-corrosion FP extinguishing agents.

papers.title: Wind tunnel investigation of pressure distribution and unsteady aerodynamics for a 3:2 rectangular prism in accelerating flow
papers.abstract: Accelerating flow is one of the typical characteristics of non-synoptic winds and acts as a key factor leading to sudden increases in wind velocity and pronounced unsteady aerodynamic responses that may cause severe structural damage and property loss. However, the underlying unsteady aerodynamic mechanisms governing these flow-structure interactions remain insufficiently understood. In this study, aerodynamic pressures on a sectional model with a 3:2 rectangular cross section were directly measured under various accelerating flow conditions. Surface pressures were compared with quasi-steady predictions based on steady coefficients at representative wind attack angles of α = 0°, 10°, and 50°. These results reveal that at α = 0°, acceleration suppresses shear-layer instability and vortex shedding, causing near-in-phase pressure variations on both side faces and a reduced lift amplitude relative to quasi-steady estimates. At α = 10°, acceleration amplifies the steady-flow asymmetry between the upper and lower side faces, producing a transient positive mean lift deviation due to vortex reattachment and intensified shedding. At α = 50°, enhanced suction fluctuations on leeward faces significantly increase lift variance while the mean value remains quasi-steady. These findings clarify the mechanisms of unsteady aerodynamic responses under accelerating flows and provide insights for transient wind-load modeling.

papers.title: Thermal elastohydrodynamic lubrication and subsurface stress in multilayer-coated angular contact ball bearings
papers.abstract: Multilayer coatings are widely used in modern mechanical equipment to prevent the tribopairs from surface wear and improve the fatigue life. This study develops a mixed thermal elastohydrodynamic lubrication model for a coated angular contact ball bearing, incorporating multilayer coatings on the raceway surface. The influence coefficients associated with elastic deformation and stress components in the multilayer contact problem are determined through frequency response functions. The correctness of the model is verified by comparing its results with available numerical results from the literature. Based on the dynamic characteristics analysis of bearings, the influences of multilayered gradient structure, gradient thickness, and gradient layer number on the lubrication characteristics of the bearing are investigated. Results show that the non-uniformly decreasing gradient structure provides the best surface lubrication performance at low speed, whereas the uniformly increasing gradient structure gives better comprehensive performance at high speed when both lubrication behavior and subsurface maximum shear stress are considered. The change rule of lubrication performance with the gradient thickness of different gradient structures is basically the same, and the greater the gradient thickness, the greater the difference between them. An increase in the number of gradient layers leads to a smoother and more homogeneous subsurface stress distribution, while exerting only a minor influence on the film thickness, pressure, temperature, and the magnitude of the maximum subsurface shear stress.

papers.title: Floquet stability analysis of a circular cylinder on a viscoelastic support
papers.abstract: A numerical stability analysis of the wake of a circular cylinder undergoing vortex-induced vibration (VIV) subject to viscoelastic support is presented. For this structural setup, the arrangement of the springs and damper is similar to that for the standard linear solid (SLS) model used to model a viscoelastic material. The SLS system is governed by two parameters: (a) the ratio of the linear spring constants, R, and (b) the damping ratio, ζ. All simulations are done for R=1, but covering ζ=0,0.001,1, and 10. Stability is investigated for the reduced velocity range over which there is a strong resonant response: Ur=[4.5,8], and for a mass ratio of m*=2.546. The dominant instability modes present are analogous to modes A, B, and QP (quasi-periodic) observed for a stationary circular cylinder wake, except at Ur=4.5, which shows modes B, QP, and a subharmonic mode, SH. The critical Reynolds number for two- to three-dimensional transition is observed to decrease with an increase of Ur. In this resonant range, for both the standard spring–damper system and the SLS-based VIV model, the critical Reynolds number below which two-dimensional simulations remain valid is Recr≈212, with transition first occurring at Ur=8 for a critical spanwise wavelength λcr≈4.0D. The results can be employed for setting Reynolds-number/reduced-velocity limits on two-dimensional numerical investigations of VIV under viscoelastic support.

papers.title: Numerical study on choking onset of Hyperloop systems: Effect of blockage ratio
papers.abstract: This study performs a numerical investigation into the choking onset of Hyperloop systems. As a pod travels through a near-vacuum tube, the bypass flow between the pod and tube walls accelerates, eventually reaching a choked state at the minimum bypass area (throat). Using a two-dimensional axisymmetric model, the choking onset—defined by the first occurrence of sonic flow at the throat—is analyzed across a blockage ratio (BR) range of 0.16–0.64. The numerical results indicate that the idealized isentropic limit underestimates the critical pod Mach number at the choking onset, with the discrepancy intensifying as BR increases. To account for this discrepancy, two effects are systematically analyzed: the upstream state change induced by the leading shock wave (LSW) ahead of the pod and the reduction in bypass area caused by boundary layer displacement on the pod and tube walls. At sufficiently low BR, the modified correlation incorporating only the LSW-induced upstream state change aligns reasonably well with the numerical results. However, the discrepancy between this LSW-only correlation and the numerical results intensifies as BR increases. Specifically, at the highest BR, the maximum deviation of −38% for the isentropic limit is reduced to +14.4% by accounting for the LSW effect and is ultimately reduced to +3.8% when the reduction in bypass area is additionally incorporated. These findings demonstrate that both effects must be considered to accurately predict the choking onset across a broad range of BR in Hyperloop systems.

papers.title: Spectral modal operator learning framework with decoupled spatial and temporal representations for unsteady flows
papers.abstract: Unsteady physical phenomena are governed by time-dependent partial differential equations, for which repeated numerical simulations under varying parameters remain computationally expensive. Although reduced-basis methods and operator learning frameworks, such as Proper Orthogonal Decomposition DeepONet (POD-DeepONet), have shown promise for time-dependent problems, they often struggle to capture high-frequency dynamics and nonlinear modal interactions due to the coupling between spatial and temporal representations inherent in modal decomposition-based approaches. To overcome these limitations, we propose Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition DeepONet (SPOD-DeepONet), a novel operator learning framework that incorporates frequency-resolved modal representations into the DeepONet architecture. The proposed method extracts spectrally coherent spatial bases across varying parameter conditions and embeds them into the trunk network, while the branch network, composed of separate temporal and parameter sub-networks, predicts the corresponding time- and parameter-dependent coefficients. This architectural design explicitly decouples spatial representations from temporal and parametric variations, thereby mitigating spatiotemporal entanglement and spectral bias. Comparative evaluations on two benchmark unsteady-flow problems indicate that SPOD-DeepONet accurately captures both large- and fine-scale dynamics over all time intervals. In comparison with Naïve-DeepONet, Fourier Neural Operator, and POD-DeepONet, the proposed model converged more rapidly, improved reconstruction of high-frequency vortical structures, and produced physically consistent power spectral density distributions. This work presents a generalized operator learning framework that combines spectral-domain decomposition with neural operator architecture, enabling efficient and interpretable modeling for complex unsteady systems.

papers.title: Simulation study on the atomization characteristics of a novel high mass ratio propellant
papers.abstract: High-test hydrogen peroxide offers the advantages of nontoxicity, storability, hypergolic ignition, and high density-specific impulse, making it a key focus in the research of green propellants. Leveraging the strong oxidizing characteristics of hydrogen peroxide paired with a reducing fuel, NASA Chemical Equilibrium with Applications software evaluations indicate that this propellant combination achieves the highest specific impulse at an oxidizer-to-fuel mass ratio of 4. A triple-jet impinging injector is employed, in which two high-velocity hydrogen peroxide jets and one fuel jet impinge to achieve intensive mixing and rapid ignition of the oxidizer and fuel. To investigate the atomization characteristics of this injection scheme, numerical simulations of the triple-jet impinging atomization process are conducted based on the Volume of Fluid method, with a focus on the effects of impingement angle and orifice-diameter ratio on atomization performance. The results show that the triple-jet injector configuration achieves favorable atomization and mixing under high mass ratio conditions. The symmetrically designed injector unit facilitates early shear-induced breakup at the edges of the liquid sheet. In this study, the spray angle gradually increases with increasing impingement angle. When the impingement angle exceeds 55°, the spray angle approaches 180°, and a further increase in impingement angle leads to droplet accumulation near the nozzle orifices. As the impingement angle increases, the Weber number of the liquid sheet, governed by the combined effects of liquid sheet velocity and thickness, first increases and then decreases. At impingement angles below 35°, the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability waves induced are relatively weak, and no observable breakup length is detected. At an orifice-diameter ratio of 1.1, the shear stress at the edges of the liquid sheet and the liquid sheet Weber number reach their peak values, resulting in the shortest breakup length and the minimum Sauter mean diameter of the spray field. Increasing the orifice-diameter ratio significantly broadens the droplet size distribution, exhibiting polydisperse characteristics. Compared to variations in the impingement angle, the droplet size distribution is more sensitive to changes in the orifice-diameter ratio. Based on this injection scheme, successful hypergolic ignition and stable combustion in an open environment have been achieved, with ignition delay times comparable to those obtained from drop combustion experiments.

papers.title: Interaction between a laser-induced cavitation bubble and a curved gas–liquid interface
papers.abstract: The geometric curvature of a gas–liquid interface plays a crucial role in regulating both the evolution of nearby cavitation bubbles and the resulting interfacial responses. To quantify these effects, we combine dual-frame-rate high-speed photography with an analytical framework based on Weiss theorem and the Kelvin impulse theory. An anisotropy parameter (ζ) is constructed, incorporating the dimensionless interface curvature (к*) and bubble–interface distance (d*) to characterize the patterns and intensity of the interfacial splash, the migration velocity of the bubble centroid, and the duration of the bubble collapse period. Specifically, three interfacial splash patterns are identified: splash with spike, splash with mound, and no splash. A critical splash initiation criterion is established as We = 1400 × (Frζ)2.7, along with a predictive scaling law for the maximum splash height (hm*) given by hm* = 1.29(Frζ)2. Regarding the bubble dynamics, the migration velocity of the bubble centroid is found to depend linearly on ζ. As к* increases, the interface-induced Kelvin impulse is attenuated, which directly suppresses the bubble migration. Furthermore, the bubble collapse period increases non-linearly with к*. A larger curvature provides stronger geometric constraints, thereby prolonging the oscillation, especially when d* is small. This study provides a unified theoretical and experimental basis for predicting the interactions between cavitation bubbles and curved boundaries.

papers.title: Water surface with nanometer thickness probed by oblique-incidence reflectivity difference
papers.abstract: The water surface thickness has been expected to reach the nanometer level for the bulk aqueous phase. To verify this prediction, in this work, the oblique-incidence reflectivity difference (OIRD) measurement was applied to characterize the water film thickness on a dynamically fluctuating water surface. By extracting wave parameters such as period, wavelength, and attenuation coefficient from the recorded optical signals, a physical model describing the surface wave dynamics was established and then integrated with the high-temporal-resolution OIRD data to reconstruct the temporal and spatial variation of the water film thickness during wave propagation. Our experiments reveal that the interfacial water film is only ∼1 nm thick and exhibits spatial heterogeneity that varies with position during fluctuations. As the oscillation amplitude gradually attenuates under the surface tension, the variation range of the water film thickness decreases accordingly and finally approaches a constant. This study combines OIRD with interfacial fluid dynamics, which provides a reference for further interdisciplinary research.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on the control of multi-mode thermoacoustic instabilities by utilizing an embedded-necked Helmholtz resonator in a premixed swirl combustor
papers.abstract: Lean premixed combustion is key to low-emission gas turbines and aero-engines, but its strong coupling between heat release and acoustics makes the system susceptible to self-excited thermoacoustic instabilities across various operating conditions.
