The collective sedimentation results further indicate that drafting–kissing–tumbling-like overtaking can occur beyond isolated particle pairs under the considered rheological conditions, while in yield-stress fluids the evolution of yielded and weakly sheared regions delays particle approach and weakens this overtaking behavior. These results demonstrate the capability of the proposed resolved framework to capture rheology-dependent particle-scale dynamics in non-Newtonian fluid–solid interaction.

papers.title: Scale effects on auto-ignition dynamics in scramjet combustors
papers.abstract: This study elucidates the scale effect on auto-ignition characteristics in cavity-stabilized scramjet combustors. Both experimental and numerical investigations are conducted on ethylene-fueled combustors at different geometric scales. Experimental observations indicate that the flame kernel consistently first emerges near the cavity rear wall across all scaled combustors. However, under the present experimental conditions, a scale-related delay in kernel formation is observed with increasing combustor scale, with an averaged apparent delay of approximately 80 ms in the √2-scale combustor compared with the reference-scale combustor. Cold-flow simulations are then performed to interpret this behavior. The results reveal that scaling does not alter the potential auto-ignition locations or the primary flow structures. Instead, the time delay is attributed to prolonged processes of fuel enrichment and heat accumulation. In 2-scale combustors, the fuel transportation path is extended, which reduces the efficiency of forming fuel-rich pockets. Concurrently, effective heat feedback within the recirculation zone is attenuated. As a result, more time is required for local fuel/oxidizer mixing to reach critical auto-ignition conditions. It is indicated that the scale effect during the auto-ignition stage manifests as a time delay in mixing and energy accumulation, rather than a fundamental change in the auto-ignition mechanism.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal gas dynamics in proton exchange membrane water electrolyzer via operando x-ray radiography
papers.abstract: In proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), optimizing the porous transport layer (PTL) thickness requires a delicate balance between minimizing the ohmic resistance and ensuring efficient two-phase mass transport. Although thinner PTLs are conventionally preferred to reduce charge transport distances, they can unexpectedly trigger severe performance degradation. To decouple the underlying mechanisms of this performance reversal, we combined electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, pore network modeling (PNM), and operando synchrotron x-ray radiography. Performance initially improved as PTL thickness decreased from 0.50 to 0.25 mm, but it unexpectedly deteriorated at 0.16 mm. PNM revealed uniform in-plane (IP) hydraulic conductivity for the 0.25 mm PTL, whereas the 0.16 mm PTL exhibited severe spatial non-uniformity. Operando radiography confirmed that the 0.25 mm PTL possessed highly efficient gas discharge dynamics. Conversely, the 0.16 mm PTL suffered severe gas accumulation under the ribs owing to restricted IP gas transport. Crucially, this trapped oxygen gas stagnates beneath the ribs, forming an insulating blanket that severely limits local water supply to the catalyst (elevating activation losses) and diminishes the effective electrical contact area (increasing ohmic losses). Ultimately, these findings highlight that designing PTLs for high-current density operation requires the prioritization of IP fluidic connectivity over mere thickness reduction, offering vital guidelines for next-generation PEMWE architectures.

papers.title: Triggering mechanism and passive control of reverse flow in multi-branch parallel ducts
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic stability of parallel multi-branch pipes within dividing manifold systems is importance to the internal fluid distribution network. However, under elevated Reynolds number conditions, severe flow field non-uniformity is frequently exhibited by these systems, manifesting as anomalous reverse flow in the upstream branches. Utilizing a combination of dimensional analysis, computational fluid dynamics, and particle image velocimetry, the triggering mechanisms of branch reverse flow and associated passive control methods within radiator pipe networks are investigated in this study. The results indicate that elevated inlet momentum results in a deflection of the streamlines toward the outer wall at the T-junction, thereby inducing a localized flow starvation zone that blocks the upstream branch, even inducing reverse flow. To alleviate this instability, a passive flow control strategy utilizing a customized micro-structure is proposed. Through the modulation of local streamline curvature, localized flow starvation is effectively alleviated by this micro-structure, and the fluid is redirected toward the radial branches, thereby suppressing reverse flow. Furthermore, the flow-regulating performance is contingent upon the geometric proportions of the micro-structure. It is demonstrated that optimal global hydrodynamic efficiency is achieved when the length-to-thickness ratio approaches η = 3, while branch reverse flow is simultaneously suppressed. Under this optimal configuration, the volumetric flow rate in the target branch is enhanced by a factor of 12.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation study of cavitating flow dynamics on a small-amplitude oscillating blade
papers.abstract: Unsteady cavitating flow dynamics over oscillating blades have attracted increasing attention in recent years. To elucidate cavitation instabilities induced by small-amplitude blade oscillations, this study employs large eddy simulation to investigate cavitation behavior over both stationary and oscillating blades. For the stationary configuration, the numerical results reasonably reproduce the experimentally observed transition from non-cavitating flow to attached cavitation and unsteady cloud cavitation with increasing angle of attack. For the oscillating configuration, the largest cavitation cloud appears during the transition from the maximum angle toward the mean angle due to hysteresis effects. Cavity destabilization is associated with the upstream propagation of a condensation shock inside the attached cavity. The oscillatory motion also modifies the distribution of total resolved fluctuation energy and the directional organization of the resolved fluctuation covariance within the investigated mid-span region. These results indicate that small-amplitude blade oscillations can substantially affect unsteady cavitation dynamics and resolved unsteady-flow organization.

papers.title: Richtmyer–Meshkov mixing induced by spike–spike collision for a shock-accelerated light fluid layer
papers.abstract: Richtmyer–Meshkov mixing induced by spike–spike collision in a light fluid layer is numerically studied. Eight SF6/air/SF6 fluid layers with different combinations of initial perturbation amplitudes and wavelengths are examined to assess the dependence of mixing on initial conditions. The spike–spike collision significantly suppresses the mixing-width growth, whereas it has almost no influence on the mixedness evolution, indicating that molecular-level mixing is insensitive to large-scale finger interactions. When the interacting interfaces are in the early stage of their evolution, the collision significantly affects the scalar dissipation rate of the SF6 mass fraction, leading to a non-monotonic evolution prior to the eventual decay. Moreover, the collision fails to establish an effective energy cascade, resulting in a slow decay of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). The TKE decay exponent |α| ranges from 0.14 to 0.42, while the mixing-width growth exponent θ falls below 0.15, both significantly smaller than the corresponding values (|α|≈1.4, θ≈0.2–0.6) reported for shock-driven mixing of random multimode interfaces. The suppression of mixing-width growth due to spike–spike collision is further strengthened by increasing the upstream-interface amplitude and the wavelengths of both interfaces, suggesting a potential pathway for controlling shock-driven interfacial mixing.

papers.title: A quasi-universal scaling law for transport properties in supercritical fluids via a dimensionless calorimetric parameter projection
papers.abstract: Supercritical fluids exhibit complex transport behaviors that are critical for applications in energy and chemical engineering, yet their prediction across the supercritical domain remains challenging. Here, we introduce a dimensionless calorimetric parameter (DCP), which is derived from measurable speed of sound and heat capacity ratios. When combined with the reduced density (ρr), the DCP establishes a quasi-universal link between equilibrium thermodynamics and non-equilibrium transport properties. We demonstrate a dimensionality reduction for supercritical CO2, its viscosity and self-diffusion coefficients, traditionally complex functions of temperature and pressure along various isobaric lines, collapse onto a single-variable curve when projected onto a newly constructed parameter X. This parameter X is a simple combination of the DCP and ρr, optimized by a rotation angle (θ = 4/7π) to capture the essential features governing transport. Crucially, this scaling extends to other simple supercritical fluids (CO2, N2, Ar, and CH4), revealing a quasi-universal monotonic relationship between their dimensionless transport properties and X. This implies that the dynamic behavior of diverse simple supercritical fluids follows a common, underlying physical principle across the entire supercritical regime. We further delineate the boundaries of this universality: while minor, systematic deviations are observed among the simple fluids, reflecting nuances in their molecular interactions, this scaling breaks down for highly associating fluids like water, highlighting the specific limitations imposed by strong hydrogen bonding. Ultimately, this calorimetric scaling provides an experimentally accessible, macroscopic approach to evaluate and predict supercritical fluid transport phenomena, thereby bypassing the computational limitations of complex micro-simulations.

papers.title: Oscillations of a vapor film on the surface of a hot sphere in a subcooled liquid
papers.abstract: We analyze the stability of a vapor film surrounding a hot spherical body immersed in a subcooled liquid under microgravity conditions. By modifying the Rayleigh–Plesset equation within a phenomenological approach, we derive the natural frequency and decay rate for radial (monopole) oscillations, identifying phase transition as a primary destabilizing mechanism. Direct numerical simulations complement the quasi-steady analysis, showing that advective heat transfer expands the oscillatory instability region, while unsteady thermal diffusion and liquid viscosity counteract it. Furthermore, coupling surface tension with pressure-dependent saturation temperature triggers a distinct monotonic instability at low temperature differences. For water–water vapor systems, we propose an approximate expression for the oscillatory instability threshold, demonstrating that substantial subcooling induces film breakdown only for small particles or low overheating, a result that contrasts sharply with predictions from the Newton–Richman heat transfer model.

papers.title: Fluid mechanics of mixing in dense liquid spray under elevated ambient pressure
papers.abstract: This study investigates global entrainment and spatially resolved liquid-phase mixture fraction distribution in dense non-evaporative liquid sprays. The measurements are done using two techniques: diffused back illumination to study macroscopic spray development and global gas entrainment, and one-phase structured illumination planar imaging with laser-induced fluorescence to suppress multiple scattering and obtain a corrected spatial distribution of mixture fraction. Diesel and naphtha are selected as liquids to enable the study of liquid property effects. The effects of injection pressure (500–1000 bars) and ambient pressure (10–40 bars) were also studied. Penetration length and spray cone angle are modeled using existing semi-empirical models. Global entrainment scaled linearly with a non-dimensional axial distance incorporating liquid and ambient density. The centerline mixture fraction profiles collapse across all operating conditions, following an inverse-power-law relation with the non-dimensional axial distance. The radial mixture fraction distribution consistently followed a Gaussian distribution across all operating conditions. These results provide experimentally grounded reduced-order correlations linking spray morphology, operating conditions, liquid properties, and the local mixture fraction distribution, suitable for the validation and development of dense spray models.

papers.title: A study of underwater high-speed gas jets through experimental flow visualization
papers.abstract: This study explores the unsteady flow physics of underwater supersonic gas jets. A controlled experimental facility has been constructed for direct flow visualization of the jet followed by an advanced image processing technique to derive both qualitative and quantitative insight into the flow evolution. The experiments are conducted for two different nozzle Mach numbers and several expansion conditions. It is found that the temporal evolution of the jet has broadly been divided into two major stages. In the first stage, the jet emerges from the collapse of a gaseous cavity. Here, the growth and collapse of the cavity have been investigated and tested through a parametric study over different Mach numbers for various expansion conditions. Afterward, several well-known flow phenomena observed during the continuous jet flow are investigated from the perspective of the two major modes of jet interface instabilities, which resemble the well-known Kelvin–Helmholtz and Rayleigh–Taylor instabilities. The instabilities are quantified from a time varying image processing analysis of the flow images. The effects of the operational parameters on the growth and control of those instability modes are examined. It is found that of the two instability modes, the second mode can aggravate the overall unsteadiness of the jet flow field, and it can be controlled by operating the jet at higher pressure. As the detrimental effect of back-attack during the initial stages of jet propagation can be critical to the propulsion performance of an underwater vehicle, the parametric dependence of the onset of first back-attack is also studied here.

papers.title: Coalescence-induced droplet detachment: Achieving restitution coefficients exceeding unity
papers.abstract: Viscous dissipation and contact-line friction generally constrain the restitution coefficient (ε) to values below unity. Here, we investigate a coalescence-induced super-kinematic rebound regime (ε>1) arising from the conversion of released surface energy into translational kinetic energy during head-on coalescence of droplets on hydrophobic surfaces. A reduced-order energetic scaling model is developed by incorporating coalescence-driven surface energy release, contact-line dissipation associated with contact angle hysteresis, and wave-induced oscillatory damping governed by the Rayleigh time scale. Parametric analysis shows that the restitution coefficient reaches a maximum (ε>1) at an intermediate droplet size ratio, while increasing Weber number enhances inertia-capillary oscillation and suppresses rebound efficiency through wave-induced dissipation. Numerical simulations further reveal two distinct detachment modes following coalescence: an efficient engulfment departure with high energy-conversion efficiency and a primary rebound departure involving substantial spreading and recoil on the substrate. The predicted super-kinematic regime and restitution peak remain robust under moderate parameter variation, indicating that the observed behaviors primarily originate from the underlying energetic scaling rather than parameter fine tuning. These findings provide physical insight into coalescence-assisted liquid removal on hydrophobic surfaces.

papers.title: Effects of discharge velocity and release height on the evolution of deep-sea mining tailwater plumes
papers.abstract: Tailwater discharge from deep-sea mining generates suspended sediment plumes that threaten benthic ecosystems, yet the hydrodynamic mechanisms governing their post-impingement evolution remain poorly understood. This study develops an improved numerical framework combining the mixture multiphase model with turbulence-modified drag correction, granular kinetic theory, and large eddy simulation, validated against experimental data with good agreement. We systematically investigate the coupled effects of discharge Reynolds number (Re = 3309–16 545) and dimensionless release height above the seabed (hn = 5.9–17.6). Results show that plume morphology and field distribution are dominated by Re and hn. Dimensionless concentration curves along the nozzle axis coincide initially, then diverge, with the divergence point shifting downward from −0.42 to −0.84 as hn decreases. Increasing Re from 3309 to 16 545 reduces near-bed vertical transport flux by 73.1%, while reducing hn from 17.6 to 5.9 increases near-bed horizontal transport flux by 371.4%. Mechanistically, turbulent entrainment driven by Kelvin–Helmholtz instability controls plume development. Local Richardson number analysis reveals a momentum-dominated core and buoyancy-dominated periphery. Dynamic mode decomposition confirms that higher Re amplifies turbulent modes, while lower hn truncates their development. These mechanisms are fully applicable within the Reynolds number range investigated in this study (Re = 3309–16 545). Since the laminar–turbulent transition lies close to this range, the influence of Re may weaken at much higher Re when the jet becomes fully turbulent. From a mechanistic perspective, however, these insights may extend to a broader spectrum of Reynolds numbers, thereby covering more deep-sea mining tailwater discharge scenarios. These findings elucidate the hydrodynamic controls on deep-sea mining plumes, providing a critical basis for optimizing pollution control strategies.

papers.title: Prediction formula for wind speed reduction by windscreens in three-dimensional flow conditions
papers.abstract: Windscreens play a vital role in engineering applications such as building insulation, ventilation, or dust suppression in open-pit stockyards. They not only reduce wind loads on structures and regulate indoor–outdoor air exchange rates but also contribute to improving local air quality and mitigating dust dispersion. Their protective performance is typically evaluated through wind tunnel experiments or numerical simulations; however, a reliable formula for accurately predicting the actual wind reduction effectiveness of windscreens remains lacking. In this study, Computational Fluid Dynamics simulations were employed to quantitatively investigate the effects and underlying mechanisms of six physical parameters—windscreen height, width, model scale, turbulence intensity, wind speed, and wind speed profile—on the overall protective performance of windscreens. The results indicate that aspect ratio, turbulence intensity, and wind speed profile exert dominant influences on wind reduction effectiveness. Using these three parameters as independent variables, a prediction formula for wind reduction performance under three-dimensional flow conditions was developed. Validation against wind tunnel experimental data shows that the formula yields prediction errors below 15% for ∼85% of the sheltered zone. In regions characterized by high turbulence intensity (e.g., near the ground surface and in the far-screen zone), prediction errors increase but remain within 25%. This formula can serve as a practical tool for rapid assessment of the protective performance of windscreens in engineering practice.

papers.title: Mechanism of dynamic stall delay via leading edge vortex control by steady and pulsed plasma actuation
papers.abstract: Bioinspired flapping-wing propulsion for micro air vehicles exploits flow unsteadiness to enhance lift at lower flight speeds and Reynolds numbers. However, it poses challenges, including leading edge vortex (LEV) detachment and, eventually, dynamic stall. The present study investigates the LEV detachment mechanism and its control using an alternating current dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator on a two-dimensional pure plunging airfoil. The volumetric plasma body force generated by the plasma actuator is modeled through an indirect method based on the Navier–Stokes equations and the experimental velocity database. The starting vortex induced by the actuator and the wall-jet velocities are well captured, validating the plasma force distribution. We employ counter-flow plasma, which requires significantly less power than co-flow plasma. High-fidelity simulations of a pure plunging airfoil at a Reynolds number (Re) of 104 are carried out to assess the efficacy of steady and pulsed plasma actuation. The findings from this study confirm that, when plasma actuation is employed, the LEV remains attached to the leading edge shear layer for a longer duration. This results in prolonged circulation accumulation and enhanced lift. For example, the steady plasma actuation increased the lift coefficient by ≈8%−12% and delayed the onset of stall by Δ t/T≈6%−31%, where T is the plunging duration. In contrast, pulsed actuation with a Strouhal number (St) of 2 and a duty cycle (DC) of 0.75 achieves maximum benefits, as a 25% reduction in DC implies a proportionate decrease in power consumption.

papers.title: Unifying formalism and closures for coarse-grained approaches to turbulence
papers.abstract: We propose the use of a unifying paradigm for the assessment and development of closed forms of the coarse-grained Navier–Stokes equations across approaches ranging from the statistical to the scale-resolving ones. It consists in the exact formalism provided by the temporally filtered Navier–Stokes equations. The fundamental idea is that the smoothing action of turbulent stresses can be described as a temporal filtering operator implicitly applied to the solution. Contrary to the average and spatial filtering operators, the temporal filter is a unifying operator that smoothly varyies within the statistical and scale-resolving realms. The potential of the temporal filtering paradigm is highlighted here by unveiling relevant algebraic properties and by deriving a new class of turbulence closures. A dynamic procedure is derived and shown to provide a unifying closure for both scale-resolving and statistical approaches. Results show that an improved physics is captured. Challenging phenomena such as the laminar to turbulence transition and the dependence of separation and reattachment on free-stream turbulence applied through boundary conditions are captured.

papers.title: Settling and drafting of spheres in quiescent fluids in microplastic-relevant regimes
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic settling of microplastic particles is yet to be explored in-depth, particularly in multiple-particle systems where wake interactions may affect settling dynamics. Here, we present an experimental study investigating the settling of spherical particles (∼1.92 mm, 1300 kg m−3) across a transitional particle Reynolds number range (Rep=6–185), relevant to microplastic transport. Using a dual-camera back-lit shadow-imaging system and Particle Tracking Velocimetry, we quantify single-particle terminal velocities and analyze pairwise interactions. Our findings reveal that trailing particles accelerate when entering the wake of a leading particle, with peak enhancements up to 68% above the single-particle terminal velocity. Interaction cases are characterized based on vertical and lateral spacing. In the key observed interaction pattern, drafting begins at a vertical distance of approximately two particle diameters and is accompanied by coupled lateral motion, indicating two-way interaction. These results demonstrate that particle–particle coupling during the drafting stage is stronger and more complex than predicted by classical models, and suggest that even weakly inertial microplastics can experience enhanced settling due to interparticle proximity. This work provides a foundation for improved predictive modeling of microplastic transport in aquatic environments.

papers.title: Low-frequency spectral and energetic imprints of the separation shock in unstarted nozzles
papers.abstract: Unstarted nozzles experience unsteady shock trains that exhibit low-frequency forced oscillations that can affect nozzle performance and structural integrity. Therefore, it is important to better understand the nature of these oscillations. In this paper, the spectral and energetic characteristics of the separation shock, leading the shock train, are investigated by conducting Schlieren imaging on a planar asymmetric de Laval nozzle operating in an unstarted condition. A shock detection scheme across time-resolved Schlieren successfully tracks the separating shock. The shock seems to exhibit low-frequency spectral activity, with the shock location on the wall showcasing an approximately normal distribution. Furthermore, energetic flow events are extracted using spectral and snapshot proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). Leading POD modes show large-scale flow structures associated with low-frequency peaks for snapshot POD and low- and high-frequency peaks for spectral POD. Comparison between shock detection and POD reveals a close link between the detected shock and high-energy flow events captured by snapshot POD mode 1. The strong synchronization between the shock motion and the leading snapshot POD coefficient suggests that the dominant low-frequency energetic content of the unstarted flow is fundamentally organized by the global translation of the separation shock.

papers.title: Dynamic Evolution of Ablation Steps and Flow–Surface Coupling in Composite Nozzles
papers.abstract: Differences in ablation behavior among constituent materials in composite nozzles lead to ablation steps during solid rocket motor operation, compromising the integrity of the thermal protection structure. To address limitations of existing studies in simultaneously capturing continuous wall recession and dynamic evolution of ablation steps, a two-way coupled recession model is developed by incorporating particle erosion under two-phase flow conditions, multicomponent gas flow, heterogeneous surface reactions, and conjugate heat transfer. The model is validated against the measured ablation morphology of a test nozzle, with a mean prediction error of 2.02%. Numerical results show that the convergent–throat step is governed jointly by high-speed condensed phase particle impingement and differences in thermophysical properties between dissimilar materials, whereas the throat–divergent step is controlled mainly by differences in thermochemical ablation rate between dissimilar materials. In the divergent section, particle erosion exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on mass flow rate, owing to the competition between secondary particle impingement and the gradual development of a particle-free zone. Continued step growth progressively reorganizes the local flow and heat transfer fields. Once the throat–divergent step becomes sufficiently large, it causes the flow to separate, form a recirculation zone, and reattach further downstream, thereby further intensifying local ablation. Specific impulse exhibits dynamic evolution during nozzle ablation, governed by the competition between wall thermal effects and ablation profile evolution. Mass flow rate changes the relative strength of these two effects and the point at which dominance shifts from wall thermal effects to ablation profile evolution.

papers.title: Effects of opening aerodynamic measures on vortex-induced vibration
papers.abstract: Opening aerodynamic measures, as an effective control measure for bridge vortex-induced vibration (VIV), allow fluid penetration and interfere with the development of separated shear layers. However, the effects of local boundary layers and the principles underlying equivalent design remain unclear. Therefore, perforated structures are selected as the research object, and wind tunnel tests and numerical simulations are combined to systematically investigate the influences of Reynolds number (Re = 0.2 × 104–1.4 × 104) and boundary layer effects on the drag coefficients and flow field characteristics. Subsequently, opening aerodynamic measures are designed based on the perspective of the boundary layer. The effectiveness in suppressing VIV is systematically investigated, and the principle of equivalent opening ratio design is clarified. The results indicate that, as the Re increased from 8166 to 13 611, the low-velocity region within the openings contracts, while the acceleration region intensifies. The drag coefficient exhibits a negative correlation with the area proportion. The simplified design based on the equivalent opening ratio is strongly dependent on the layout position of the railings. When the opening size is small, the aerodynamic effect of the railings is comparable to that of fully enclosed railings. Furthermore, based on the characteristics of the mean pressure coefficient, guide plates with the same opening ratios, but different opening sizes cannot be treated as aerodynamically equivalent.

papers.title: A computational fluid dynamics approach for predicting the transportation of subway tunnel particles to platform in train movement-induced unsteady fluid flow
papers.abstract: Air quality at subway platforms has raised increasing concerns nowadays. Tunnel particulate matter (PM) can be carried into platforms by piston wind and worsen the air quality at platforms. The national standards in China specify the maximum acceptable PM10 (with a diameter of less than 10 μm) concentration at the platform. In this paper, a computational fluid dynamics model with a discrete phase model was developed and validated through experiments. The model was used to study the dynamic distribution of airflow and PM10 during the train passage through a station. The influence of five key factors on the PM10 concentration at the platform was evaluated through gray correlation analysis. The results showed that train deceleration had the largest impact on PM10 concentration at the platform with a maximum gray correlation degree of 0.85, followed by the blockage ratio, train top speed, tunnel length, and train length. The maximum PM10 concentration increased by 254.74% when the train deceleration increased from 0.5 to 2.5 m/s2 after excluding the background concentration. A case study was conducted to observe PM10 concentrations during the entire operation hours. The two peaks of PM10 concentration were 188 and 180 μg/m3, which occurred during the morning and evening rush hours, respectively. PM10 concentrations during the morning and evening rush hours exceeded the specified concentration limit for 2.1 and 2.6 h, respectively. Based on the above results, four relevant suggestions for ventilation and dust removal were proposed for improving the air quality at platforms.

papers.title: The Wooding problem revisited
papers.abstract: The threshold conditions to convective instability in a semi-infinite porous layer saturated by a fluid are determined. The classical setup for this problem in geothermal fluid dynamics was originally modeled by Wooding in 1960. Its formulation is here reconsidered to allow for a finite heat transfer coefficient across the boundary, parametrized through the Biot number. The temperature boundary condition considered by Wooding is here recovered as the limit of an infinite Biot number. The linear stability analysis of the stationary boundary layer, which establishes in the porous medium, when a boundary steady suction occurs is carried out. Two different versions of the Rayleigh number are considered, namely, a temperature-difference-based version and a heat-flux-based version. While the former is the classical Rayleigh number for flow in porous media, the latter is a variant definition, which displays a finite limit at neutral stability in both the opposite limiting cases of an infinite or a zero Biot number.

papers.title: The role of wake merging in the hydrodynamic sensing performance of tandem seal whiskers
papers.abstract: Harbor seal whiskers possess exceptional wake-sensing capabilities, optimized by their unique undulating morphology. While significant progress has been made in understanding the hydrodynamics and sensing properties of isolated whiskers, the interaction mechanisms of tandem whiskers within biologically generated fin wakes remain poorly understood. In this paper, direct numerical simulations are employed to investigate wake–structure coupling and the resulting sensing performance for two tandem harbor seal whiskers placed in the wake of a flapping caudal fin. Three streamwise spacings, defined as the ratio of center-to-center spacing (T) to equivalent whisker diameter (D) (T/D = 4, 6, and 8), are considered. At T/D = 4, fin vortex rings (FVRs) concurrently load both whiskers, with the shear layers from the upstream whisker merging with those of the downstream whisker, resulting in localized spanwise vorticity intensification and the strongest downstream fin-locked response among the tested spacings. Consequently, both downstream signal power and wake correlation reach their highest values. Conversely, at T/D = 6–8, FVRs load the whiskers sequentially, and the upstream wake undergoes spanwise stretching and redistribution within the gap, yielding spatially diffuse forcing and reduced downstream coherence, despite persistent wake-induced vibration. Quantitative evidence demonstrates that wake merging induces a significant enhancement of hydrodynamic signals in tandem configurations, providing a physics-based explanation for the enhanced sensing performance of compact spacing within the tested whisker arrangement.

papers.title: Network structure evolution and rheological physics of clay–additives complex fluids under ultralow temperature
papers.abstract: The ultralow temperature environment in Antarctica poses a fundamental fluid physics challenge. The network evolution in clay suspensions at ultralow temperature controls the yield behavior, viscoelasticity, and thixotropy, but its underlying mechanisms have yet to be studied. This work investigated the complex rheological behavior of clay–additive (HRX) complex fluids and revealed the mechanism of internal structural changes in fluids under ultralow temperature conditions. The additive (HRX) significantly improved the viscoelasticity, thixotropy, shear-thinning, and gel strength by promoting the formation of a dense, continuous crosslinked network. Significantly, it increased G′ of the fluid by approximately 3.31 times, corresponding to a critical stress increase of approximately 8.70 times. The 10-min gel strength also increased from 1.5 to 3.5 Pa. Notably, the plastic viscosity remained only 31.0 mPa s. Meanwhile, the non-Newtonian characteristic of the fluid was significantly enhanced, as evidenced by the increase in yield stress (τy) and viscosity coefficient (K). Temperature-dependent analysis distinguished thermally activated structural relaxation at low temperatures from cold-induced gelation below −45 °C, revealing a network transition. Additionally, at −65 °C, 2% HRX maintained the colloid rate at 93.6% and increased the yield point by 125%. It also exhibited excellent filtration performance, with a 2% addition decreasing the filtration loss to 16 ml, ensuring wellbore stability. This study provides fundamental insights into the complex fluid physics in cold regions.

papers.title: Nonlinear forced response of a self-excited conical lean-premixed flame
papers.abstract: We employ a hybrid computational fluid dynamics (CFD)/low-order framework to investigate the forced response of a self-excited conical flame. The framework resolves flame dynamics using CFD while describing the acoustic field with a low-order model, concentrating computational effort on the dominant source of thermoacoustic nonlinearity. When the flame is self-excited and unforced, heat release rate fluctuations, Q′, are governed by flame pinch-off: Q′ reaches a maximum near pinch-off and a minimum when detached flame pockets disappear. When the self-excited flame is forced, the hybrid framework reproduces the suppression region and attenuation levels of acoustic pressure fluctuations, p′, satisfactorily, as reported experimentally before. Oscillation suppression arises from weakened thermoacoustic coupling, as the phase relationship between p′ and Q′ shifts from in-phase to out-of-phase, reducing acoustic energy production. Rayleigh-index analysis shows that forcing primarily affects the upper flame region, where pinch-off dominates, whereas the wavepacket-like structure in the lower half of the flame remains largely unchanged. These results identify flame pinch-off as the key mechanism linking open-loop forcing to thermoacoustic suppression and demonstrate the importance of resolving flame dynamics when predicting the forced response of self-excited flames. The proposed framework provides an efficient tool for studying thermoacoustic instability.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical studies on the impacts of skin effect on the groundwater flow velocity in a wellbore
papers.abstract: Groundwater flow velocity (GFV) in the monitoring well can be reliably measured using the Aqua Vision Colloidal Borescope. However, the presence of a wellbore screen (wellbore skin) induces a perturbation in the groundwater flow, thereby leading to significant GFV discrepancy between the wellbore and aquifer. Although the empirical equation effectively improves parameter estimation accuracy, its applicability is limited by the lack of precise GFV discrepancy data and the difficulty in determining the hydraulic conductivity of the wellbore skin (HCWS). To address these gaps, multiple experiments were conducted to analyze the GFV discrepancy between the wellbore and aquifer with different hydraulic gradients and wellbore radii. Additionally, a numerical model considering wellbore skin was established using the COMSOL Multiphysics program, and the experimental data were utilized for the calibration of the model and to estimate the HCWS. Several important results were obtained. First, a pronounced GFV discrepancy exists between the wellbore and the aquifer across all tested hydraulic gradients, with the ratio of wellbore GFV to aquifer GFV stabilizing at approximately 0.3. Second, the ratio of GFV between the wellbore and the aquifer increases with the wellbore radius, with a range between 0.236 and 0.400. Third, the HCWS estimated via the numerical model calibrated using experimental data is 7.3, 7.3, and 7.2 m/d for wellbore radii of 0.055, 0.045, and 0.0315 m, respectively. Finally, the empirical equation can reliably estimate aquifer GFV, with the estimation error ranging from 0.07% to 12.6%. These findings provide valuable insights for elucidating the mechanisms driving the GFV discrepancy between wellbores and aquifers.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic mechanisms governing millimeter-scale compound droplet formation in a gravity-constrained co-flowing device
papers.abstract: A gravity-constrained co-flowing device with a vertically upward configuration is developed to generate millimeter-scale water-in-oil-in-water (W1/O/W2) compound droplets with high monodispersity. Systematic experiments are performed to examine the effects of the dispersed-phase tube diameter ratio, chamber size, and gravity on droplet size, generation frequency, and formation dynamics. Three distinct flow regimes—namely, the transition regime, stable compound droplet regime, and multicore droplet regime—are identified. As the dispersed-phase tube diameter ratio increases, the stability window progressively narrows. Within the stable regime, the coefficient of variation of droplet size remains below 1%, indicating excellent monodispersity. The droplet size initially increases with the dispersed-phase flow rate due to enhanced inertial effects, and subsequently approaches a plateau as geometrical confinement and shear-dominated breakup become dominant. In contrast, the generation frequency exhibits a linear dependence on flow rate within the saturation regime. Chamber size plays a secondary role, primarily enhancing flow stability rather than directly determining droplet size. A comparative analysis of vertically upward and downward configurations elucidates the role of gravity. For larger droplets, gravitational effects become more pronounced, resulting in prolonged formation periods and increased droplet size under upward flow conditions. Combined experimental and numerical analyses elucidate the role of gravity in regulating droplet growth and neck evolution, thereby providing physical insight into the stable and continuous generation of large compound droplets. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of millimeter-scale compound droplet formation in gravity-constrained co-flowing systems and offer practical guidelines for the high-throughput, continuous generation of large, highly uniform compound droplets.

papers.title: Coupled effects of thermochemical nonequilibrium and roughness-induced flow structures on wall heat flux in hypersonic flow
papers.abstract: Local roughness structures on hypersonic vehicle surfaces are commonly induced by ablation, manufacturing imperfections, or in-service damage. Numerical simulations are performed for two representative roughness types, namely, isolated and distributed configurations, to investigate the coupled effects of high-temperature real-gas phenomena and roughness geometry on wall heat flux. The results show that for an isolated roughness element, the recirculating vortex within the windward-side separation region promotes chemical dissociation, leading to an increased degree of molecular dissociation and a reduction in the local wall heat flux. As the freestream Mach number and roughness height increase, the windward-side separation region expands and secondary vortical structures emerge. As a result, the local heat-flux distribution changes from a single-peak pattern to a multi-peak pattern, and the endothermic effect associated with chemical reactions induced by the recirculating flow becomes increasingly pronounced. In contrast, the expansion in the leeward-side separation region suppresses high-temperature dissociation reactions. For distributed roughness, the local wall heat flux exhibits periodic peak distributions corresponding to the periodic roughness pattern. The variation in these peaks is only weakly affected by thermochemical nonequilibrium but is mainly governed by the successive expansion and compression waves in the flow field.

papers.title: Flow field mechanism and performance optimization of adaptive bleed shingles for hypersonic inlet
papers.abstract: The hypersonic inlet is prone to the formation of large-scale separation regions during operation due to shock-wave boundary-layer interactions, which can lead to inlet unstart. Bleed technology can remove these separation regions, and therefore, improves inlet performance. Conventional bleed structures tend to leak the supersonic mainstream during vehicle cruise conditions, making it difficult to meet the flow control requirements of the inlet under both unstart and cruise states. To solve this problem, this paper proposes an adaptive bleed shingle structure. Numerical simulations are employed to investigate the flow field structure within the bleed cavity of the adaptive bleed shingle, and to analyze its bleed performance in both the inlet separation region and the supersonic mainstream, as well as its impact on the mainstream. The study shows that the adaptive capability of the shingled structure originates from the scale competition among the recirculation, transition, and supersonic regions within the bleed cavity, governed by the Reynolds number per unit structural scale. The scales of the recirculation and transition regions vary exponentially with this Reynolds number, with an inflection point at ReH=2×106. Compared to conventional bleed structures, the shingled structure suppresses supersonic mainstream leakage and improves inlet starting performance.

papers.title: Bed-load transport in flow with submerged vegetation: From vegetation-mediated energy cascade to its effect on sediment movement
papers.abstract: Bed-load transport capacity in vegetated open-channel flow is critical for ecological river management. However, accurate prediction of bed-load transport under submerged vegetation conditions remains challenging due to difficulties in determining bed shear stress. Drawing on the phenomenological theory of turbulence, this study derived an equation for bed shear stress for flows with submerged vegetation and integrated it with the bed-load transport formula originally developed for unvegetated flows to establish a predictive model applicable to both rigid and flexible submerged vegetation. The model involves the deflection height of flexible vegetation, which has conventionally been calculated via iteration and thus impairs model practicality. This study innovatively employs genetic programing to develop an explicit predictor for deflected height, whose integration into the bed-load transport framework markedly enhances the model's applicability. The proposed bed-load transport model elucidates distinct response regimes. Under a constant energy slope, the bed-load transport rate increases with submergence ratio but decreases with vegetation density, whereas these trends are reversed under constant flow velocity. Additionally, under identical hydraulic conditions, bed-load transport rate is lower in flexible vegetation than in rigid vegetation, indicating that flexible vegetation features better performance in controlling bed erosion. The model thus provides a robust tool for sediment management in river restoration projects.

papers.title: Effect of compression corners on Mack mode instability in high-speed boundary layers
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the Mack mode instability in high-speed (Mach number is 5.92) flat-plate compression corner flows. The harmonic linearized Navier–Stokes equations approach is employed to systematically calculate the evolution of Mack mode waves with different frequencies and spanwise wavenumbers in compression corner flows with various slope angles (SAs), obtaining the evolution characteristics of disturbance amplitudes and local growth rates. The flow features induced by different SAs, including pressure gradients, flow separation, and separation/reattachment shocks, are analyzed in detail. The mechanisms and rules by which these flow features modulate Mack mode evolution are revealed. Small SAs induce adverse pressure gradients and compression waves, whereas large SAs lead to flow separation accompanied by separation and reattachment shock waves. Mack mode waves are not only promoted by adverse pressure gradients but also significantly affected by flow separation and shock wave compression effects. Within the separation zone, the boundary-layer thickness increases rapidly and then decreases sharply, creating conditions for synchronization between fast and slow modes and for mode switching between different-order Mack modes. The dominant Mack second mode is suppressed by continuous mode switching within the separation zone, whereas it is significantly promoted in the downstream reattached boundary layer by the high unit Reynolds number and low wall temperature ratio induced by shock waves. The dominant three-dimensional Mack first mode waves are significantly amplified both within the separation zone and in the downstream reattachment region, with the evolution trend of local growth rates consistent with the wall-normal shear of the streamwise velocity in the shear layer.

papers.title: The lattice Boltzmann method for multicomponent flows with high viscosity ratios: A comprehensive review
papers.abstract: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has become a versatile computational framework for simulating multicomponent flows with high viscosity contrasts. This review provides a comprehensive examination of the theoretical foundations, model formulations, and numerical strategies that have enabled stable and accurate simulations across a wide range of viscosity ratios. We discuss the evolution of collision operators, from single-relaxation-time schemes to multiple-relaxation-time and central-moment formulations, highlighting their role in enhancing stability and reducing spurious currents. The review also analyzes multicomponent models, including pseudopotential, free energy, phase-field, and color-gradient approaches, and their adaptations for extreme viscosity contrasts, alongside developments in force implementation schemes, boundary treatments, and surface interactions that collectively improve numerical robustness. Representative benchmark cases and practical applications demonstrate how these methodological advancements have progressively extended the achievable viscosity ratio from modest values in early models to several orders of magnitude in recent implementations. This synthesis provides a clear perspective on the current capabilities and limitations of multicomponent LBM and identifies key directions for future research in simulating complex flows with extreme property differences.

papers.title: A multiphase constant volume depletion simulation considering critical flow saturation
papers.abstract: The constant volume depletion (CVD) test is widely regarded as a key pressure–volume–temperature experiment for capturing changes in fluid composition during depletion. However, this view is challenged by multiphase systems, as conventional oil–gas systems neglect the aqueous phase and its interactions with hydrocarbons and CO2. This work proposes a novel CVD simulation method that employs the Cubic-Plus-Association equation of state to perform multiphase flash calculations. During the depressurization process, the expelled phase and the corresponding volume are determined and allocated based on the phase's saturation and the proportion of its real-time mobility, which allows the model to reflect multiphase flow characteristics more realistically. The process is divided into three sequential stages based on the bubble point pressure (Ppb) and the gas phase critical flow pressure (Pcf) of the system: the elastic energy stage, the solution gas drive stage, and the gas convergence stage. For each stage, the differences in mobile phases, drive mechanisms, and recovery are analyzed in detail. Comparative analysis shows that the new model exhibits higher application potential and prediction accuracy in terms of production performance while also revealing the significant influence of the aqueous phase. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis is performed to evaluate the effects of water saturation (movable/irreducible water), injected CO2 mole fraction, and rock type (distinguished by pore size) on component recovery.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on the effect of fluid rheology in natural convection heat transfer around finite inclined plates
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the laminar natural convective flow and heat transfer of non-Newtonian power-law fluids over isothermally heated inclined plates of finite length. Such flows adjacent to inclined plates, which are commonly encountered in polymer processing, electronics cooling and solar collector design, present a case of interplay between the vertical and horizontal mechanisms of natural convection. Shear-thinning fluids (pseudoplastics) create a low-viscosity fluid layer near the wall that increases convective flow strength and improves heat transfer. Conversely, shear-thickening fluids (dilatants) generate regions of greater viscous effects in regions of high shear near the wall, consequently reducing convective motion and heat transfer. As the inclination approaches the horizontal, the streamwise buoyancy component vanishes, turning the flow into a purely normal-plume regime in which classical boundary-layer approximations fail. The lift-off point shifts from the trailing edge toward the center as the power-law index increases, indicating earlier plume detachment in shear-thickening fluids. This is attributed to the greater viscous resistance to the upward moving stream, and hence a greater tendency of the plume to detach from the plate. On the other hand, shear-thinning fluids show delayed plume detachment due to stronger buoyant forces near the plate. The Nusselt number is found to be greater in pseudoplastics as compared to dilatants for all inclinations, highlighting how increased viscous effects suppress buoyancy-induced natural convective flow. The existence of a minimum point in the variation of Nusselt number with inclination is observed for non-Newtonian fluids, and the location of this point shifts to higher values of inclination angle as the power-law index increases from 0.6 to 1.4. This may be attributed to the dominance of the horizontal mechanism over a greater range of inclinations in shear-thickening fluids.

papers.title: Gust-induced aerodynamic performance in insects' forward flapping flight
papers.abstract: Flapping-wing flight is inherently unsteady, where atmospheric gusts can substantially degrade the aerodynamic performance when their characteristic time scales are comparable to the wingbeat period. This study presents a numerical investigation and time–frequency characterization of gust-induced aerodynamic response of flapping wings of varying size, inspired by the flight of a longhorn beetle, Batocera rufomaculata. Geometrically similar wings spanning the biological range were simulated in forward flight under identical prescribed kinematics and a transient frontal gust with a smoothly ramped profile. Three-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations using the shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model were performed to resolve the instantaneous pressure field and three-dimensional vortex structures. The Q-criterion, pressure coefficient, and turbulent kinetic energy were analyzed to relate coherent vortices, turbulence production, and load fluctuations. Aerodynamic response was quantified using lift, pitching moment, and lift-to-drag ratio, while gust sensitivity and recovery were assessed through transient deviations and post-gust settling behavior. Time–frequency analysis of the non-stationary lift signal was used to track how gust forcing redistributed spectral content across the fundamental flapping frequency, its harmonics, and broadband components associated with vortex breakdown and flow reorganization. The results showed that gusts did not simply scale aerodynamic loads; rather, they transiently modified effective angle of attack and vortex topology, producing size-dependent differences in load amplification, turbulence redistribution, and recovery. Larger wings exhibited greater susceptibility to gust-induced loading and returned more slowly to pre-gust aerodynamic performance.

papers.title: Flow redistribution and convective heat transfer enhancement in confined air flows induced by triangular vortex generators
papers.abstract: Passive flow manipulation offers an effective route to enhance convective transport in confined air flows where weak mixing and flow maldistribution limit thermal performance. In this study, the effect of triangular vortex generators on flow redistribution and heat transfer is numerically investigated in a confined channel with distributed heat sources. Simulations are performed over a range of inlet velocities (0.5–2.0 m/s) and heat generation rates representative of practical operating conditions. The introduction of vortex generators induces localized flow separation, wake interaction, and enhanced cross-stream mixing, leading to improved penetration of cooling air into otherwise stagnant regions. These flow modifications disrupt thermal boundary layers and promote more uniform temperature fields within the domain. An optimal configuration is identified, yielding a maximum reduction of 7.2 K in peak temperature relative to the baseline case without vortex generators. The results further reveal that excessive blockage deteriorates thermal performance due to restricted flow pathways, highlighting a trade-off between mixing enhancement and flow resistance. Overall, the study demonstrates that strategically placed triangular vortex generators can effectively modulate flow structures and enhance convective heat transfer in confined air cooling systems.

papers.title: Long-distance piezoelectric drop-on-demand inkjet printing based on multi-waveform superposition
papers.abstract: Piezoelectric drop-on-demand inkjet printing technology is widely applied in the field of additive manufacturing due to its non-contact deposition, high-precision formation, and excellent compatibility with diverse functional inks. As application requirements gradually extend from planar substrates to complex curved and undulating surfaces, increasing the printing distance has become a key factor in enabling conformal printing. However, under long-distance printing conditions, the existing process is prone to droplet landing deviation and fluctuations in formation quality, thereby limiting the attainable stable working distance. In this paper, the superposition characteristics of flow field oscillations inside the piezoelectric printhead system were analyzed through experiments and simulations, and a method for increasing the printing distance was proposed. A multi-waveform superposition strategy was employed to achieve secondary regulation of the liquid-column formation process during the jetting stage. The results demonstrated that, under the newly designed waveform conditions, the printhead used in this study, with a nominal printing distance of less than 2 mm, could achieve controllable and stable single-droplet jetting even at a printing distance of up to 11 mm. This represented an increase in the printing distance by more than fivefold. In addition, various micro-patterns can be successfully fabricated by controlling the spacing between deposited droplets. This work provides a new strategy for achieving stable long-distance inkjet printing.

papers.title: Flow structures and thrust characteristics during deep-water propulsion
papers.abstract: To study the thrust characteristics of the solid rocket engine and flow structures of the gas jet in deep water, an experiment of underwater ignition was carried out in a pressure water tank. The morphological evolution process of the underwater gas jet was observed by a high-speed camera system. The combustion chamber pressure of the solid rocket engine and wake field pressure were measured, the stability of the rocket engine operating in atmosphere and deep water was compared, and the pressure pulsation characteristics of wake field in deep water were obtained. The results show that the overall trend of the pressure curve in combustor is similar to the ground test when the engine works underwater, and the engine has a slightly negative thrust phenomenon due to the inertia of the gas bubble flow during the early stages of ignition. Meanwhile, the pressure pulsation amplitude of the monitoring point is large in the initial stage of ignition, and the pressure pulsation amplitude decreases sharply after tens of milliseconds and then maintains a minimal pressure pulsation; furthermore, there are obviously expansion–contraction processes at low frequency of approximately 50 Hz, while the gas jet oscillates slightly at high-frequency range of approximately 800–1000 Hz in the core region of the jet.

papers.title: Experimental study of low-frequency instabilities in rotating detonation combustors
papers.abstract: This study investigates the propagation characteristics and stability of rotating detonation waves (RDWs) in a kerosene/air rotating detonation combustor (RDC), with a particular focus on low-frequency instabilities (LFIs). Pronounced low-frequency pressure oscillations are observed under certain operating conditions, exhibiting periodic temporal variations. Time–frequency analysis based on peak signal processing is employed to characterize the RDW dynamics. The fluctuation frequency is estimated based on simplified flow characteristics and further refined through comparison with experimental results. The results show that LFIs arise from the coupled effects of inlet conditions and combustor operation. Increasing the RDC pressure enhances LFI frequency and intensifies RDW instability, whereas increasing the inlet pressure ratio reduces LFI frequency, thereby mitigating pressure fluctuations and suppressing instability development. In addition, tri-axial vibration measurements indicate a strong coupling between RDW propagation and axial structural response. LFIs are found to simultaneously influence axial and radial vibration behaviors, suggesting a multi-physics coupling mechanism governing RDC stability.

papers.title: Friction–pressure drag competition over turbulent flows with adaptive surface structures
papers.abstract: Surface geometry can significantly modify turbulence characteristics and thereby influence drag in turbulent boundary-layer flows. While compliant surfaces have shown promise for drag reduction, the hydrodynamic role of the deformation-induced surface geometry itself remains insufficiently understood. In the present study, a deformation-inspired surface profile previously obtained from a single flexible-wall unit is adopted as a prescribed geometry for rigid surface arrays, and the resulting turbulent flow is investigated using improved Delayed Detached-Eddy Simulation (IDDES) based on the shear stress transport k–ω model. A series of array configurations with systematically varied unit width and spacing are examined to clarify their influence on drag characteristics and flow-modulation behavior. The results reveal a strong competition between friction-drag reduction and pressure-drag generation. Net drag reduction is achieved only when these competing mechanisms are balanced. The findings highlight the importance of geometric parameter tuning in arrayed surface designs and provide qualitative insight into the comparative flow-modulation behavior induced by deformation-inspired surface structures. The present IDDES framework partially resolves the turbulence structures while modeling part of the near-wall flow. Therefore, the turbulence analyses presented here are primarily intended to reveal comparative trends among different configurations rather than fully resolved near-wall turbulence mechanisms.

papers.title: Aerodynamic and aeroelastic effects of vertical greening on high-rise buildings
papers.abstract: In response to increasing demands for low-carbon development and sustainable urban infrastructure, fourth-generation high-rise buildings, characterized by integrated vertical greening systems on façades and balconies, have gained widespread attention. The presence of vegetation on building façades significantly alters the external flow field and aerodynamic excitation characteristics, posing challenges to conventional wind load evaluation methods. In this study, the aerodynamic and aeroelastic responses of vertically greened high-rise buildings are investigated through wind tunnel experiments using a 1:200 scaled model of a 200 m tall building. Four vegetation coverage ratios (0%, 3.4%, 4.5%, and 6.7%) are examined under two vegetation configurations: uniform distribution and corner-concentrated arrangement. The results show that uniformly distributed vegetation consistently reduces mean wind pressures on windward, side, and leeward surfaces, whereas sparse corner-concentrated vegetation may induce localized amplification of peak pressures. Spectral analysis of fluctuating pressures reveals a redistribution of energy from low to high frequencies, indicating suppression of large-scale coherent structures and enhancement of small-scale turbulence. Furthermore, vegetation significantly mitigates vortex-induced vibration. Corner-concentrated configurations exhibit monotonic suppression with increasing coverage, while uniform distributions show optimal mitigation at moderate vegetation coverage ratios due to competing effects between vortex disruption and turbulence enhancement. These findings provide new physical insight into vegetation–flow–structure interactions and offer guidance for the aerodynamic design of sustainable high-rise buildings.

papers.title: Impingement atomization behavior of supramolecular materials: A direct numerical simulation study
papers.abstract: Supramolecular materials have broad potential applications in aeroengines; however, their unique rheological properties introduce additional challenges to atomization performance. In this study, the impingement atomization dynamics of shear-thinning supramolecular gels are investigated using adaptive mesh refinement direct numerical simulation, resolving the entire evolution of the liquid phase from sheet to ligament and ultimately to droplets. The influence of rheological properties on the atomization process is analyzed through the spatial evolution of the local Ohnesorge number. Based on its distribution characteristics, the atomization flow is divided into a sheet breakup region and a ligament breakup region. In the sheet breakup region, the local Ohnesorge number is found to exhibit a distinct power-law dependence on the dimensionless streamwise distance, whereas it remains approximately constant in the ligament breakup region. Our results show that, compared with supramolecular gels of low apparent viscosity and excessively high apparent viscosity, the moderate apparent viscosity gels produce the largest number of dispersed droplets and a more uniform droplet size distribution, leading to the highest energy conversion efficiency. In addition, a contracted circular nozzle is found to enhance the atomization performance of excessively high apparent viscosity supramolecular gel, producing flow structures similar to those of the optimal viscosity cases and significantly increasing the atomized surface energy. This study provides fluid dynamic insights into the design of atomization systems for supramolecular materials in aeroengines.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic mechanism and quantitative model of surface gas transfer in open channel flows with floating vegetation
papers.abstract: Floating vegetation significantly alters the hydrodynamic structure of rivers and wetlands, yet its influence on air–water surface gas transfer remains poorly understood. Conventional prediction models focus on flow without vegetation and rely predominantly on bulk flow velocity and largely neglect additional turbulence caused by aquatic vegetation, leading to limited use in ecological water bodies. This study investigates surface gas transfer rates in open channel flows with floating vegetation through flume experiments conducted under varying cross-sectional averaged velocities, vegetation densities, and vegetation heights, and provides several new fluid physics insights. First, velocity shear at the vegetation–gap interface induces Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, generating large-scale coherent vortices, and constitutes the primary mechanism driving surface element renewal. Second, the surface gas transfer rate does not change regularly with any individual factor among vegetation density, vegetation height, and bulk flow velocity. Instead, variations in flow and vegetation conditions primarily modulate the turbulent velocity scale within the mixing layer, which exhibits a strong positive correlation with the surface gas transfer rate. Based on these findings, a modified surface renewal model is developed for flow with floating vegetation by incorporating the turbulent diffusion coefficient and characteristic scale of vortices in the mixing layer in place of the molecular diffusion coefficient and cross-sectional averaged velocity. The proposed model achieves a coefficient of determination of R2 = 0.94 across all experimental cases, demonstrating high accuracy. These findings provide mechanistic insights into evaluating greenhouse gas emissions and reaeration processes in natural aquatic systems and wetlands dominated by floating vegetation worldwide.

papers.title: Study on the non-Gaussian properties of fluctuating pressure and generation mechanism on long-span cylindrical latticed shell structures
papers.abstract: To investigate the non-Gaussian characteristics of fluctuating wind pressures on large-span cylindrical latticed shells and its underlying formation mechanisms, rigid-model pressure-measurement wind tunnel tests were conducted on a shell with a rise-to-span ratio of 1:2 and a length-to-span ratio of 2:1 under multiple wind directions. The statistical properties of the mean and fluctuating wind pressure coefficients, skewness, and kurtosis were examined. Results reveal that surface fluctuating wind pressures strongly deviate from Gaussian statistics: roughly 75% of measurement taps display negative skewness and kurtosis exceeding 3, with pronounced “negative-skewness and heavy-tail” characteristics in the windward-side transition regions and near the leeward structural edges. Based on an improved Hermite model, the maximum non-Gaussian peak factor reaches 8.8, far exceeding the Gaussian assumption and the code-specified value of 2.5. Adopting the code-specified fixed peak factor of 2.5 underestimates extreme wind pressures by 26%–78%, whereas the Gaussian assumption yields underestimations of 11%–66%. Numerical simulations confirm that intense non-Gaussian behavior in these zones arises mainly from flow separation and vortex shedding, which locally enhance turbulent kinetic energy and flow fluctuations.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning-enhanced aerodynamic characteristic analysis of bluff bodies under interference effects
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic interference has a critical impact on wind-resistant design. This study presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based explainable machine learning framework to predict and interpret the aerodynamic characteristics of bluff bodies under interference effects. A large-scale two-dimensional CFD dataset comprising 3360 three-bluff-body interference case configurations was established, covering 140 layouts and 24 wind angles. Detailed aerodynamic analysis shows that the observed behavior does not arise from a single interference mechanism like shielding effects, channeling effects, or wake interference, but rather from their coupled action. Their interactions reshape pressure distributions and global aerodynamic forces across different interference layouts. Based on this dataset, eight machine learning (ML) models were benchmarked for predicting aerodynamic force coefficients, among which the random forest (RF) model achieved the highest accuracy, yielding an R2 of 0.962. To enhance interpretability, global, conditional, and local SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses were conducted to quantify the contributions of wind angle of attack and interference location features to the aerodynamic loads, thereby linking dominant features to the underlying flow mechanisms. In addition, the RF model was further applied to predict surface pressure distributions with an R2 of up to 0.974, and SHAP analysis was performed to quantify the influence of interference location parameters on representative pressure points. Furthermore, uncertainty quantification was conducted to evaluate prediction reliability, providing confidence estimates alongside aerodynamic predictions for individual interference configurations. The proposed framework enables rapid and interpretable assessment for large numbers of interference scenarios, facilitating aerodynamic evaluation during early-stage design.

papers.title: The effect of branch angle on the wake of a wall-mounted cruciform
papers.abstract: We compare the flow field of a wall-mounted cruciform with three different branch angles at a Reynolds number of 15 000. A wall-mounted cruciform is a generic representation of structures of interest, such as piers, coral reefs, and oil rigs. These geometries alter the local ocean current and sediment transport, such as scouring of surrounding sediment. We show that modifying the branching cylinder angle modifies the shape and size of the wake. Incorporating an angle to the branching cylinder causes a shift in the location of the minimum streamwise velocity. In the wake of the cruciform, we find that the vorticity component wj is redistributed into wk contributions. When the branch is angled, the spanwise vortical structures become tilted along the vertical direction. Finally, we provide isosurfaces of the Q-criterion to show that the coherent vortex structures are tilted and vary in their downstream behavior.

papers.title: Curved jets
papers.abstract: This study explores the stability and nonlinear evolution of annular stratified jets in the presence of weak planetary rotation. The analysis is motivated by interest in the dynamics of finescale structures in the ocean, exemplified by turbulent wakes generated by propagating bluff objects. A conventional paradigm for the analysis of such systems is based on non-rotating, rectilinear basic flow models, in which planetary rotation and jet curvature are a priori neglected. However, the present investigation reveals that the impact of the Coriolis force and curvature can be profound even when the jet makes a wide turn and planetary rotation is weak. This sensitivity is reflected in both linear stability analyses and nonlinear simulations. Particularly intriguing are the effects that arise when the model simultaneously accounts for the Earth's rotation and the jet's curvature. For instance, weak planetary rotation leads to major differences in the evolution of commensurate cyclonic and anticyclonic jets. These results underscore potential pitfalls of overreliance on rectilinear models of finescale flows. In a similar vein, we question the use of the large Rossby number criterion as a sole justification for ignoring the effects of planetary rotation.

papers.title: Particle transport and resuspension mechanisms in rotating annular flows for enhanced wellbore cleaning
papers.abstract: During drilling in extended-reach and highly inclined wells, cuttings migrate toward the lower side of the annulus and form stable beds, increasing drillpipe torque and reducing the rate of penetration (ROP). This behavior is governed by flow asymmetry, rotational shear, particle inertia, and drilling fluid rheology. In this study, particle transport and wellbore cleaning in rotating annular flows are investigated using a three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework. A V-shaped helical-blade cuttings bed remover is introduced to enhance particle resuspension and axial transport by modifying near-wall flow structures. The effects of tool geometry, flow rate, drillpipe rotation, eccentricity, ROP, wellbore size, and fluid rheology are systematically analyzed. Results show that cleaning performance is controlled by the competition among gravitational settling, shear-induced resuspension, rotational mixing, and axial transport. Higher flow rate, drillpipe rotation, moderate eccentricity, and stronger low-shear rheology improve particle suspension and cuttings removal, whereas higher ROP and larger wellbore diameter promote cuttings accumulation by increasing solid loading or reducing effective transport capacity. Based on these mechanisms, a unified cleaning factor (UCF) is developed through dimensional analysis and multivariate nonlinear regression to quantify coupled hydraulic, rheological, operational, and structural effects. The UCF correlation agrees well with CFD results and provides a physically interpretable tool for predicting wellbore cleaning performance, identifying feasible operating windows, and guiding wellbore cleaning design in complex well geometries.

papers.title: Steady-state active flow inside a thin capillary: Coupled velocity field and active particle concentration distribution
papers.abstract: In this paper, we discuss the coupled problem of steady-state activity-gradient-driven flow of active liquids inside a thin circular capillary, with the active liquid being characterized by the presence of active particles demonstrating vortex defects. In this coupled problem, we solve for the flow field that is driven by the activity gradient, while the concentration distribution of the active particles (which provides this activity gradient) is shown to be dependent on the flow field. We identify an equivalent Peclet number governing the problem: an increase in the capillary radius increases this Peclet number, enforcing a deviation of the active particle axial concentration distribution from a simple linear profile. This concentration, which is a radially averaged one, shows a steeper profile at locations near the exit of the capillary. On the other hand, the radial dependence of this concentration is insignificant. Hence, the axial velocity, which varies with the axial gradient of concentration, shows a significant increase as one moves to locations near the end of the capillary, particularly for larger capillary radii. On the other hand, the radial dependence of the velocity field is similar to that previously reported. Thus, via the consideration of the presence of an activity gradient that is not constant, we are able to propose a new type of activity-driven fluid microscale flow, where the flow field is two-dimensional. We anticipate that obtaining such closed-form analytical results for velocity and concentration profiles for active capillary flows will be a useful contribution in the field of active flows.

papers.title: Physical mechanisms of compressor flow instability driven by transient state
papers.abstract: The new generation of aircraft engines integrate numerous adjustable mechanisms that induce large-scale transient variations in aerothermal cycles, which significantly affect compressor flow stability. This study focuses on the fluid dynamic mechanisms underlying compressor flow instability during transient operation, using asymmetric inlet guide vane (IGV) settings to generate a transient flow environment. Four cases were compared during the analysis process, including uniform IGVs with 0° (case 1), −2° (case 2), −4° (case 3), and asymmetric IGV with −4° to 0° (case 4). For the compressor characteristic, the instability boundary of case 4 shifted significantly to the right to compare with that of case 3, reducing the stall margin by 5.3%. The instability evolution process exhibited a spike-type instability inception in case 4. However, in the region where the rotor passed through the IGVs with gradually increasing pre-rotation angles, initial stall disturbance was induced, ultimately leading to compressor stall.
