To further analyze the occurrence mechanism of rotating stall, the numerical simulation was performed under the asymmetric IGVs. The unsteady full-annulus simulation is conducted by the computational fluid dynamics software (ANSYS CFX), which solves the compressible Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equation with the second-order upwind, implicit, and time-marching scheme. The Reynolds stress term is calculated with the shear stress transport k-omega turbulence model. The numerical simulations reveal that the blades can reach the maximum attack critical value at certain circumferential position under transient state, which further leads to the premature onset of compressor instability.

papers.title: Effects of reflux-hole position on gas–liquid separation and self-priming performance in a vortex self-priming pump
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of reflux-hole height on self-priming performance in a vortex self-priming pump. Three-dimensional transient simulations were performed using an Eulerian volume-of-fluid model, and Liutex-based vortex identification and local entropy production analysis were employed to reveal the coupling between vortex structures and irreversible energy loss. The baseline pump without a reflux hole serves as the reference case. Results show a distinctly non-monotonic effect of reflux-hole height: a low-position hole (58 mm) increases the inlet gas mass flow rate by 41% relative to baseline and reduces the self-priming time from 2.35 to 1.65 min, whereas intermediate heights (88–99 mm) degrade performance due to back-pressure accumulation, liquid-ring discontinuity, and blockage vortices. The optimal high-position hole (114 mm) achieves a 62% increase in gas mass flow and shortens self-priming time to 1.45 min. Entropy production analysis indicates that turbulent dissipation dominates energy loss, with severe irreversible loss arising mainly from shear-dominated deformation around vortex boundaries rather than rigid-body rotation. Within the tested pump geometry and operating conditions, intermediate reflux-hole heights should be avoided, while a high-position reflux hole near the gas-discharge side maximizes gas evacuation and minimizes nonproductive energy dissipation.

papers.title: Evaluating the curvature dependence of surface tension in nanoscale capillary filling via molecular dynamics
papers.abstract: Theoretical models of capillary flow typically rely on macroscopic governing parameters, such as the dynamic contact angle and effective viscosity. However, as pore dimensions approach the nanoscale, the curvature dependence of surface tension may become relevant, affecting theoretical predictions of capillary flow. The length scales and magnitude of this effect remain unresolved. In this work, we employ all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate spontaneous water imbibition in parallel-plate silica nanochannels with heights ranging from 4.5 to 10.5 nm. The simulation data are used to extract dynamic contact angles, velocity profiles, inertial regimes, and the mean curvature of the menisci, enabling a direct evaluation of the Lucas–Washburn–Bosanquet (LWB) equation. For the 10.5 nm channel, incorporating the dynamic contact angle model into the LWB equation yields excellent agreement with the capillary filling simulation. However, as the channel height decreases, a systematic departure between the theoretical model and the simulation results is observed. To address this, the curvature dependence of surface tension is incorporated using an upper-bound value for the Tolman length. This correction introduces an increase in the effective surface tension, partially compensating for the discrepancies observed in narrower channels. The resulting surface tension enhancement ranges from 11% at 4.5 nm to 4% at 10.5 nm, suggesting that curvature effects become negligible at larger nanoscale confinements. These results indicate that the curvature dependence of surface tension contributes to deviations from classical capillary models at the nanoscale, but does not fully account for them.

papers.title: Particle-laden flow diversion at a fracture junction: Mechanisms and controls
papers.abstract: Proppant diversion in branched fractures is a confined particle-laden flow process that governs effective support in complex fracture networks; however, the particle-scale mechanisms controlling diversion across branch geometries remain insufficiently understood. In this study, coupled computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method simulations were performed to investigate proppant diversion from a primary fracture (PF) into vertical and horizontal secondary fractures (SFs). The diversion process was quantified using sand-dune geometry, particle trajectories, velocity responses, and statistical comparisons between captured and bypassed particles. The results reveal a junction-scale capture–bypass mechanism in which diversion is controlled by the competition between branch-directed drag induced by flow deflection and the streamwise inertial persistence of particles approaching the junction. In the vertical SF, diversion evolves from a drag–gravity-coupled regime to a shear-enhanced, drag-dominated regime. By contrast, diversion into the horizontal SF is mainly drag-driven; gravity promotes particle settling in the PF but contributes little to lateral entry. Within the investigated ranges, the proppant diversion ratio increases with injection velocity, decreases with proppant concentration and proppant size, and varies non-monotonically with fluid viscosity. Parametric response identifies injection velocity and proppant concentration as the primary controls on diversion, whereas fluid viscosity and proppant size play secondary roles. These findings clarify the mechanisms governing capture and bypass in confined particle-laden branching flows and provide a physical basis for interpreting proppant partitioning in complex fracture networks.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of electro-osmotic flow in porous media and the induced film deformation
papers.abstract: A multiphysics numerical framework is established using COMSOL Multiphysics to systematically investigate electro-osmotic flow (EOF) in porous media and the induced film deformation. Our study reveals the intrinsic correlation between electro-osmotic driving pressure and film deformation. Specifically, the applied electric field induces a bottom-up EOF within the porous layer, driving fluid accumulation in the upper chamber and resulting in a parabolic deformation profile of the flexible film. While the electric field force and hydraulic pressure scale linearly with voltage, the film deformation exhibits a power-law growth. We demonstrate that the electrode channel configuration serves as a key tool to modulate hydraulic impedance and accelerate the temporal response without compromising the steady equilibrium. Porosity governs the trade-off between driving force and hydraulic resistance. Raising the porosity from 0.5 to 0.7 reduces the maximum deformation from 0.25 to 0.21 μm but curtails the response time from 2 to 0.33 s. This work is intended to provide a foundational reference for the design of high-performance, compact flexible sensing devices.

papers.title: A multiresolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics–peridynamics coupling framework for fluid–structure interaction
papers.abstract: Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) involving free-surface flows remains challenging due to complex free-surface evolution, transient hydrodynamic pressure transfer, and structural deformation. This study develops a direct coupling framework between smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) and non-ordinary state-based peridynamics (NOSBPD) to improve the accuracy, stability, and efficiency of free-surface FSI simulations. In the proposed framework, structural particles are directly treated as SPH boundary particles, and the FSI force is obtained through pressure interpolation and Newton's third law, avoiding additional virtual-particle generation. Flexible and independent spatial discretizations are allowed for the fluid and solid domains, so that their resolutions can be adjusted separately without simultaneous refinement of both domains. NOSBPD is used to describe structural deformation and directly calculate stress and strain fields. A condition-number-assisted particle shifting technique is introduced to improve the efficiency and stability of free-surface particle identification and particle distribution correction, reducing local pressure oscillations near the free surface and fluid–structure interface. The solver is accelerated using Taichi-based graphics processing unit computing with an optimized linked-list neighbor search, achieving more than 3 orders of magnitude speedup over single-core central processing unit computation. Benchmark tests show normalized root mean square error within 1% for structural deformation and below 3.5% for free-surface flow quantities. Compared with representative particle-based FSI results, the proposed model produces smoother pressure fields and more accurate structural displacement predictions. The last application simulation further demonstrates its capability to stably capture strong free-surface loading, large deformation of complex free-surface FSI simulations.

papers.title: Nonlinear effects on wave predictability in finite water depth
papers.abstract: The predictable zone helps assess the reliability of deterministic sea wave prediction results. In this study, a theoretical method that includes the effects of third-order wave nonlinearity is introduced to compute the predictable zone based on measurements from stationary or moving buoys. By comparing with linear results, nonlinear effects on the predictable zone are investigated over a range of wave steepness, directional spreading angle, and water depth. The impact of buoy speed on the predictable zone is also studied in both long-crested and short-crested wave fields. The analysis shows that the predictable zone is increased due to third-order nonlinearity, and the nonlinear effects are more significant as the wave steepness increases or the directional spreading angle decreases. The area of the predictable zone changes non-monotonically with the water depth, and the increase in the predictable zone induced by nonlinear effects is suppressed as the water depth decreases. In addition, as the buoy speed increases, the predictable zone becomes larger in head wave conditions, but becomes smaller in following wave conditions. The predictable zone disappears when the buoy speed reaches the minimum wave group velocity in the following wave conditions.

papers.title: Interfacial properties and drainage dynamics of high-temperature methane foams stabilized by SnS2 quantum dot-decorated MgO nanosheets
papers.abstract: The destabilization of gas–liquid foams at elevated temperatures is a critical problem in multiphase flow. This study investigates the underlying physical mechanisms by using novel SnS2 quantum dots anchored on MgO nanosheets (SnS2 QDs/MgO)—modifies the interfacial properties and bulk fluid properties to arrest these processes in methane foams under high-temperature conditions (80–120 °C). Through systematic variation of nanocomposite concentration (10–100 ppm), an optimal loading of 75 ppm was identified as maximizing foam half-life. High-resolution morphological analysis reveals that the nanocomposite refines the foam's microstructure by producing a finer texture with a reduced average bubble size (≈83.21 μm compared to ≈172.58 μm for the base foam) and a significantly increased lamella thickness (≈29.94 μm compared to ≈19.08 μm for the base foam). Interfacial measurements demonstrate that the SnS2 QDs/MgO reduces gas–liquid interfacial tension and modifies the disjoining pressure within the lamella by forming an interfacial layer whose characteristics are consistent with particle jamming, as quantitatively described in recent literature for nanoparticle-stabilized foams. Furthermore, it alters the rock wettability, shifting capillary forces to favor oil mobilization. Core flooding experiments at 120 °C validate the macroscopic efficacy of these microscale physical mechanisms, with the nanocomposite-stabilized foam achieving a final oil recovery of 42.43%—a 14.00 percentage-point increase over foam flooding. This work provides a multiscale physical understanding of foam stabilization, demonstrating a robust strategy for controlling complex fluid interfaces in high-temperature subsurface flows.

papers.title: Critical gel formation as a mechanical performance indicator for composite films of epoxy resin and ionic liquid
papers.abstract: This work systematically investigates the role of ionic liquids (ILs) to the curing of epoxy resin in the presence of a conventional amine-based hardener to establish their influence on the mechanical performance of the cured composite films. Our primary objective is to gain the deeper understanding of how these ILs might contribute in curing process along with its plasticizing effect in the epoxy-hardener system using in situ gelation rheology. Accordingly, the gelation behavior of epoxy resin blended with a conventional aliphatic amine-based hardener and IL was rheologically investigated over a temperature range of 25–70 °C. Particular emphasis was given to capturing the critical gel-state characteristics and correlating them with the mechanical properties of the cured films. To achieve this, three different ILs were examined to understand their influence on the overall mechanical performance of the final cured composite films in relation to the onset time and fractal dimension of the critical gel state. The present study reveals that the incorporation of ILs gives rise to a distinct critical gel state, which is otherwise absent when curing is carried out solely with the hardener at mild curing temperatures. Importantly, the critical gel-state characteristics (critical gel time and the fractal dimension) were found to be closely correlated with the final mechanical properties of the cured epoxy products. These findings suggest that understanding the IL-induced critical gel state can provide a useful criterion for selecting suitable ILs to tailor the mechanical behavior of epoxy-based composite materials.

papers.title: Multiscale flow dynamics and irreversible energy dissipation in a variable-speed pump-turbine during pumping transients
papers.abstract: Variable-speed pump-turbines are central to grid flexibility and accommodating the intermittency of renewable energy sources. Yet the transient flow physics and irreversible energy dissipation during pumping transients remain insufficiently understood. Here, the hydrodynamic instability and dissipation behavior of a variable-speed pump-turbine in pump mode are investigated using multiresolution dynamic mode decomposition and entropy production theory. Across five flow rates from 0.9Qd to 1.1Qd, the results reveal pronounced spectral asymmetry in the runner passages. Low-frequency pulsations of 36.7–62.3 Hz (≈2.0–3.4fn) on the blade suction side are mainly associated with rotational-frequency-related excitation and fluid–blade interaction, whereas the pressure side exhibits broader medium- and high-frequency components up to 293.3 Hz (≈16fn), suggesting stronger flow-separation- and stall-vortex-related hydraulic excitation. Variable-speed regulation modifies entropy production in a flow-dependent manner. Under partial-load conditions, entropy production is reduced to 0.64–0.99 times that of the fixed-speed case because separation-related losses are suppressed. Under overload conditions, it increases to 1.16–1.32 times the fixed-speed level, suggesting enhanced friction-related dissipation. Within the idealized synchronous-regulation framework, acceleration and deceleration exhibit distinct transient flow, force-response, and dissipation characteristics, indicating a hysteresis-like dependence on the regulation path. These findings clarify the coupling among multiscale unsteady flow structures, hydraulic-force response, and irreversible energy dissipation during variable-speed pumping, while noting that practical trajectories may be further affected by hydraulic inertia, guide-vane dynamics, and control delays.

papers.title: Multiple acoustic scattering characteristics of an underwater two-dimensional Taylor vortex pair
papers.abstract: Acoustic scattering by vortices is a fundamental problem in studies of wake scattering from underwater moving targets. To investigate dual-vortex scattering in low-Mach-number underwater wakes, this study constructs a two-dimensional equal-strength Taylor vortex-pair model and employs the convected wave equation to examine acoustic-wave scattering in an idealized dual-vortex flow field. The rotational configuration, incidence angle, and dimensionless parameter kL are taken as key control variables. The results show that, under low-kL conditions, the co-rotating vortex pair exhibits stronger overall equivalent-scatterer characteristics, with higher scattering energy and weaker sensitivity to the incidence angle. In contrast, the counter-rotating vortex pair is more sensitive to the incidence angle, and its scattering cross section varies in an approximately U-shaped manner, reflecting more pronounced interference characteristics. As kL increases, the mean scattering cross section follows an approximate (kL)4 power-law growth, and the scattered energy gradually concentrates in the forward direction. The mean scattering cross sections of the co-rotating and counter-rotating vortex pairs gradually converge, although differences remain in the mainlobe position, interference structure, and directional distribution. Interference-field analysis indicates that vortex-pair scattering is not a simple linear superposition of two single-vortex scattered fields. Instead, inter-vortex coupling modifies the local scattered field through rescattering and phase interactions, and this modification varies with the incidence angle and vortex spacing. These results reveal scattering-field interactions within the smallest multi-vortex unit and are of significant importance for analyzing multi-vortex acoustic scattering in the wake fields of underwater targets, as well as for vortex detection and identification.

papers.title: Three-dimensional numerical investigation of flow characteristics in meandering compound channels with interlaced vegetation on floodplains
papers.abstract: The coexistence of emergent and submerged vegetation, a crucial biological component of river systems, profoundly modifies the inherent turbulence structure and sediment transport processes in meandering compound channels, which critically influences both river morphological evolution and ecosystem sustainability. To elucidate the interaction mechanisms between vegetated floodplain flow and meandering main channel flow, large eddy simulation was applied. The mean flow field, secondary flow structures, turbulence characteristics, and mass and momentum transport were investigated under three relative flow depths (Dr). The results indicated that the secondary flow cell at the bend apex cross section of the main channel was always located on the concave bank side, and its rotation direction was related to the curvature of the main channel. The flow was influenced by centrifugal forces and vegetation drag, leading to a pronounced velocity difference between the main channel and vegetated floodplain, which in turn generates a concave bank vortex and horizontal vortices. The convex bank of the main channel in the bend section is prone to erosion due to higher turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), whereas the concave bank with lower TKE is more susceptible to sedimentation. Furthermore, mass exchange of the inbank flow of the main channel at the bend apex cross section is mainly from the convex bank to the concave bank, while the lateral momentum at the interface between the main channel and floodplain is mainly transferred from the floodplain to the main channel. These results provide a theoretical basis for channel management and flood control design in meandering compound channels with vegetation.

papers.title: Evolution of secondary shock wave system in a hollow rotating detonation afterburner with two-dimensional nozzle
papers.abstract: A three-dimensional numerical investigation was conducted to study the propagation characteristics and operational performance of a C2H4–air hollow rotating detonation afterburner (RDA) with a two-dimensional nozzle. Two sets of numerical cases were studied: the first examined the operational modes under different turbine inlet temperatures (1500, 1700, 1900 K) at a cruise condition (Mach 1.5, 10 km altitude), while the second evaluated the engine performance across a wide range of flight conditions (Mach 0.5–2.5). The results demonstrate the formation of a complex secondary shock wave system, originating from the reflection of detonation-induced oblique shock waves at the contoured walls of the circular-to-rectangular transition section. This secondary shock wave system, comprising reflected shock waves and doubled-reflected shock waves, propagates upstream, disrupts the fresh mixture injection layer, and induces pre-burning phenomena. This interaction significantly destabilizes the detonation wave, leading to unstable propagation, mode transitions, such as quenching and re-initiation (including the emergence of a counter-rotating detonation wave). Furthermore, the two-dimensional nozzle effectively reduces the flow non-uniformity at the exit. Both the detonation wave speed and peak pressure were found to increase with higher inlet pressure. The thrust coefficient increases with the flight Mach number, exceeding 0.8 under optimal conditions. This study provides insights into the combustion dynamics and performance of a hollow RDA with a two-dimensional nozzle, revealing the process of wave interaction in the circular-to-rectangular transition section.

papers.title: Acoustic perception of bio-inspired unmanned aerial vehicle propellers
papers.abstract: While bio-inspired blade modifications have been extensively investigated for aerodynamic performance enhancement, their influence on the flow mechanisms governing noise generation and perceived acoustic comfort remains insufficiently understood. This study integrates aeroacoustic and psychoacoustic analyses to evaluate the effects of leading-edge (LE), trailing-edge serrations (TE), and boundary-layer (BL) modifications on a small unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) propeller in hover. The flow field was resolved using a sliding-mesh delayed detached eddy Simulation framework based on the shear stress transport k–ω model, while far-field acoustics were predicted using the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings analogy. The results indicate that individual bio-inspired modifications introduce acoustic tradeoffs, whereby reductions in tonal noise may be accompanied by increased broadband emissions within the 1–5 kHz frequency range most relevant to human hearing. Specifically, LE modification promotes broadband amplification through increased radial-flow-induced unsteadiness, whereas the BL treatment increases high-frequency content through enhanced turbulent activity near the blade surface. In contrast, the combined TE+BL configuration shows the best acoustic performance. The interaction between trailing-edge serrations and boundary-layer trips reduces the persistence of large-scale coherent wake structures, leading to lower broadband noise levels and improved spectral characteristics. Quantitatively, the TE+BL configuration achieves an approximately 10 dB reduction at the fundamental blade-passing frequency relative to the baseline propeller. Psychoacoustic analysis further demonstrates concurrent reductions in loudness and sharpness, resulting in improved acoustic comfort. The findings highlight that effective UAV propeller noise mitigation requires controlling spectral distribution and high-frequency broadband content beyond reducing overall sound pressure level, demonstrating the value of integrating psychoacoustic considerations into propeller assessment.

papers.title: Study on the dynamic characteristics of underwater explosion bubbles in a finite domain
papers.abstract: To investigate internal underwater explosion bubble dynamics, load transmission, and structural response in finite open and closed domains, a transparent cylindrical tank was used as an oil-tank-like structure. High-voltage spark discharge, high-speed imaging, and acceleration measurements were combined with a boundary element method. Results show that bubbles exhibit multi-cycle “expansion–collapse–re-expansion” behavior. As water depth increases from 100 to 200 mm, bubble radius first rises from 17.37 to 22.76 mm, then drops to 20.3 mm. Under open conditions, shallower depths promote bubble penetration through the free surface and water jet formation, prolonging pulsation; greater depths enhance bubble expansion and collapse, increasing structural impact. Under closed conditions, the upper gas layer provides additional pressure feedback, leading to larger maximum bubble expansion (e.g., from 20.50 to 24.32 mm at H = 175 mm) but faster decay in subsequent cycles and easier formation of mixed clouds. Closed boundaries enhance positive pressure peaks mainly at shallower depths, while at larger depths they tend to induce persistent intensified negative pressure and cavitation. Notably, the absolute negative-pressure peak in closed cases increases continuously with depth, from 0.003 (H = 100 mm) to 0.107 MPa (H = 200 mm). These findings offer guidance for designing confined liquid-containing structures.

papers.title: Exploiting temporal coherence for self-supervised denoising of turbulent flows
papers.abstract: Denoising plays a crucial role in experimental fluid mechanics, where measurement noise can significantly contaminate flow structures and distort statistical quantities. A self-supervised denoising framework, incorporating a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) attention module and a convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) unit, referred to as SE–ConvLSTM, is developed by exploiting the temporal coherence of flows. The model reconstructs the target flow field from a sequence of preceding noisy snapshots, with performance primarily governed by the temporal correlation of the input data, determined by the input time span and the temporal interval between snapshots. The denoising capability of SE–ConvLSTM is systematically evaluated for two-dimensional flow fields under a wide range of noise intensities, noise types, and flow configurations, with comparisons against both classical and deep-learning methods. The results demonstrate that SE–ConvLSTM achieves superior performance for temporally uncorrelated noise, enabling more accurate noise removal while preserving fine-scale flow structures, spatial continuity, and turbulent statistics, particularly under severe noise contamination. The denoising performance is closely related to the ratio of the integral time scales of the noisy and reference flows, with improved accuracy obtained when temporal coherence is better preserved in the noisy field. Extension to three-dimensional flow fields further confirms the robustness of the framework in reconstructing volumetric structures. Overall, the SE–ConvLSTM provides an effective and generalizable approach for denoising noisy flow measurements.

papers.title: Interactional aerodynamics and flow characteristics of a quadrotor with ground effect
papers.abstract: This study investigates the near ground aerodynamic characteristics and flow mechanisms of a small-spacing quadrotor in ground effect through experimental measurements and transient numerical simulations. The global aerodynamic response is quantitatively characterized and related to the local fountain flow, axial through flow, and blade loading variations. The results show that the quadrotor exhibits a non-monotonic variation in thrust with ground clearance: positive ground effect dominates at very small clearance, while a negative ground effect region appears near h/R ≈ 1.5. Numerical results quantify the center fountain flow intensity and local through flow acceleration, and the 0.75R blade-section loading shows a corresponding reduction, confirming that the thrust deficit is caused by the coupled effect of enhanced fountain flow, accelerated local through flow, and weakened blade loading. At larger clearances, the flow structures weaken, and the aerodynamic response approaches the out of ground effect condition. Normalized ground effect trends remain consistent across the tested rotational speed range, indicating that the characteristic thrust deficit mechanism is mainly governed by clearance dependent wake ground and rotor–rotor interactions. These findings provide a quantitative physical link between global thrust variations and local flow mechanisms, offering guidance for performance evaluation and control design of quadrotors operating near the ground.

papers.title: A molecular perspective on the formation mechanism of supercritical heterogeneous structures based on energy competition
papers.abstract: The formation of heterogeneous structures in supercritical fluids (SF) is important for understanding their density fluctuations and anomalous properties. In this paper, we classify liquid-like (LL) and gas-like (GL) molecules in SF using the Stillinger method based on the local structure. From the perspective of the competition between kinetic energy and potential energy, the evolution of heterogeneous structures and energy distribution characteristics in LL, GL, and two-phase-like (TPL) fluids are revealed. When kinetic energy and potential energy are comparable, the ratio of LL and GL molecules is nearly equal, and the energy barrier for their conversion is minimal. This paper proposes an energy-based definition of the Widom line, where the total energy is zero. Furthermore, the potential energy part dominates as SF crosses the TPL region, indicating that more energy is used to increase intermolecular distance than to raise the temperature. These results provide a molecular-level understanding of the formation of supercritical heterogeneous structures.

papers.title: Absolute instability of annular power law liquid jets
papers.abstract: Annular liquid jets have wide ranging applications from gas combustion devices to pharmaceutical capsule production. With advances in polymer sciences, the use of non-Newtonian fluids is increasingly common in many industrial and engineering settings. Understanding the regimes of breakup associated with a non-Newtonian annular liquid jet is of paramount importance in such fields. In this paper, we investigate the convective and absolute instability of an annular liquid jet, modeled as a power law fluid with an inner inviscid core, falling under gravity surrounded by an inviscid medium. We explore how the critical Weber number, Wec, which demarcates convective and absolute instability, changes in relation to varying the inner-to-outer jet radius, the gas-to-liquid density ratio, the Reynolds number, as well as the flow index number of the annular layer. We identify a number of features of relevance, including the importance of the effect of gravity in determining the competing effects of fluid rheology on instability and growth rate of disturbances, the increased range of absolute instability for shear-thinning fluids and the impact of inner-to-outer velocity difference on critical Weber numbers.

papers.title: Thermal jet interaction and thermal impact under non-uniform outlet conditions
papers.abstract: Non-uniform outlet conditions are common in multiport diffuser systems but remain insufficiently understood in terms of their influence on thermal jet interaction and thermal impact. This study presents a combined experimental and numerical investigation of thermal jets under strongly non-uniform discharge conditions. Results show that non-uniform outlet conditions generate asymmetric jets and reorganize jet interaction and entrainment behavior. A transition between momentum- and buoyancy-dominated regimes is identified and governed by the Richardson number. The thermal impact volume exhibits a robust scaling governed by temperature rise and Richardson number. An amplification effect is further identified, whereby moderate adjustments in discharge velocity and temperature rise under a fixed heat load, revealing a nonlinear sensitivity of thermal accumulation to source-condition perturbations. These results offer a quantitative and controllable framework for optimizing multiport diffuser design and mitigating thermal impacts in coastal environments.

papers.title: Erratum: “Assessing morphology of Jhelum River and prediction of centerline shifting using autoregressive integrated moving average model” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 075141 (2025)]
Experimental investigation on flow characteristics of tail cavities attached to vehicles launched in viscous solution
papers.abstract: The motion and morphological evolution of cavities in viscous fluids exhibit strong coupling effects, which are particularly pronounced in the tail cavities attached to vehicles formed during the underwater launch. The flow behavior of tail cavities in viscous fluids was systematically examined in this study using solutions of various viscosities as the experimental medium. The evolution mechanisms, flow characteristics, and internal pressure dynamics of the tail cavity were analyzed. The impact of ventilation factors on tail cavity characteristics was investigated, and the fundamental explanations of morphological pulsations during cavity motion were clarified. The research results indicate that the pulsation cycle of the tail cavity is governed by the synergistic effects of cavity stretching induced by vehicle motion and pinching action from the surrounding flow. The pulsation phenomenon of the tail cavity is particularly noticeable in high-viscosity solutions, with increased internal pressure oscillation frequency and enhanced cavity stability. The increase in ventilation pressure leads to a significant increase in the length of the tail cavity, while the increase in ventilation duration has a weaker impact on the morphology of the tail cavity. These results demonstrate that different ventilation factors exert distinct and significant influences on the behavior of the tail cavities.

papers.title: Flame-pressure response of NH3/H2/air premixed combustion in a variable cross-section pipe
papers.abstract: The flame-pressure response of NH3/H2/air premixed combustion in a variable cross-section pipe is investigated using high-speed visualization, pressure measurements, and Chemkin-based kinetic calculations for hydrogen volume fractions (γ) of 40%–70% and equivalence ratios (Φ) of 0.8–1.2. The results show that hydrogen enrichment and increasing Φ accelerated flame propagation and strengthened the closed-end pressure response. Under lean or low-hydrogen conditions, the flame propagates more slowly and exhibits delayed wrinkling, weaker pressure fluctuations, and a thicker reaction zone. Under highly reactive conditions, the flame reaches the sudden expansion–contraction chamber earlier and develops stronger flame-front deformation and faster chamber filling. The strongest response occurs at Φ = 1.2 and γ = 70%, where the Vmax reaches approximately 145–150 m/s and Pmax reaches about 70–75 kPa. Chemkin calculations show increasing γ substantially increased SL, whereas Tad changes only modestly. Sensitivity, radical-profile, and reaction-pathway analyses indicate that the increase in intrinsic reactivity is mainly associated with enhanced H/O/N radical chemistry. These results show that the variable cross-section chamber mainly reshaped the flame under low-reactivity conditions but promoted stronger deformation, faster acceleration, and higher closed-end pressure buildup under hydrogen-enriched and fuel-rich conditions.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann model for generalized Navier–Stokes equations with source terms applied to shale gas transport
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose an improved lattice Boltzmann (LB) model for the generalized Navier–Stokes equations with a mass source term, based on the Guo–Zhao forcing scheme. The present model is capable of capturing fluid dynamics in porous media with mass sources, e.g., due to desorption or injection processes. The Chapman–Enskog expansion confirms that the generalized Navier–Stokes equations with a mass source term are exactly recovered from the present LB formulation. To evaluate the model's accuracy and confirm its second-order spatial convergence, two benchmark numerical tests are performed and validated against exact analytical solutions. In comparison with previous LB models, the present LB model achieves higher accuracy in solving the generalized Navier–Stokes equations without a mass source term. Furthermore, the proposed LB model is applied to simulate shale gas transport under desorption effects, considering both depletion-driven and constant-pressure-driven gas flows in porous media. The transport characteristics influenced by desorption are investigated in detail. This work not only presents a novel numerical tool for simulating fluid flows in porous media with mass sources but also provides a comprehensive analysis of shale gas transport incorporating desorption effects, thereby promoting the application of the generalized Navier–Stokes equations in scientific and engineering fields.

papers.title: Polyelectrolyte adsorption at the solid–liquid interface favors receding contact line instability
papers.abstract: Controlling the motion of non-Newtonian drops on surfaces is crucial for applications ranging from inkjet printing to biomedical devices and food processing. While the macroscopic behavior of viscoelastic drops sliding on tilted hydrophobic surfaces has been characterized—showing reduced velocities and elongation compared to Newtonian fluids—the underlying microscopic mechanisms remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we developed a high-speed, high-resolution reflection microscope that enables direct visualization of the contact line of sliding drops. We used water-soluble polyelectrolyte solutions based on polyacrylamide and allowed drops to slide on hydrophobic substrates composed of Teflon amorphous fluoropolymer and polydimethylsiloxane-coated glass slides. The substrate tilting angle was varied between 20° and 45°. We reveal how viscoelasticity influences the dynamics of the receding contact line and drop motion. Our experiments demonstrate that viscoelasticity can destabilize the receding contact line, triggering filament formation. This instability previously observed in the coating of thin viscoelastic films is reported here for sliding drops, for the first time on smooth surfaces. We further highlight the critical role of polymer charge in this process: while cationic and nonionic polymers promote filament formation, anionic polymers do not, a difference we attribute to the distinct wetting properties of the solutions. In conclusion, we clarify the interplay between rheology, surface interactions, and drop dynamics.

papers.title: Dimensional mapping and self-similar distribution statistics of the turbulent/non-turbulent interface in a turbulent jet
papers.abstract: This study investigates the three-dimensional (3D) interface and self-similar distribution statistics of the turbulent/non-turbulent interface (TNTI) in a temporally evolving turbulent plane jet by using high-resolution direct numerical simulation data. Particular emphasis is placed on quantifying the relation between two-dimensional (2D) planar measurements and the 3D interface. In the self-similar state, both the 3D surface area of the outer edge of the TNTI and the 2D line length within the measurement plane remain approximately constant. The ratio of the 3D wrinkling factor to the 2D wrinkling factor reaches a constant of 1.23, close to the value 4/π derived from the isotropic assumption. When normalized by the jet half-width, the surface area density and the line length density exhibit good collapse with a Gaussian shape. This collapse, together with the self-similarity analysis, confirms that the 3D and 2D wrinkling factors remain approximately constant during the self-similar period. This numerical study contributes to a better understanding of how planar diagnostics can be used to characterize the 3D TNTI geometry.

papers.title: Preparation of basalt fiber-reinforced dual-crosslinked self-healing hydrogel and mechanical property and plugging prediction
papers.abstract: Polyacrylamide (PAM)-based gels are frequently applied for plugging in low-permeability sandstone reservoirs. However, the relationship between self-healing gel strength and plugging performance in low-permeability sandstone reservoirs is unclear. This study reported a basalt fiber (BF)-reinforced dual-crosslinked plugging hydrogel (DCBF-NK-1) designed by AM, lauryl methacrylate, and BF. DCBF-NK-1 and BF-free single-crosslinked hydrogel (SC) were compared in mechanical, self-healing, and salt-temperature resistance properties. The mechanical and self-healing properties of BF modified gel were substantially enhanced. DCBF-NK-1 exhibited enhanced mechanical and self-healing properties, with fracture and healed stresses of 20.16 (3.2 × SC) and 11.92 kPa (1.91 × SC), respectively, along with excellent thermal-saline tolerance (swelling ratio: 15.88 g g−1 in 1% NaCl, 135 °C). This resulted from synergistic H-bonding and hydrophobic interactions increasing cross-linking density, combined with BF rigidity. Incorporating the relationship between gel strength and critical pore-throat pressure, a variable-mass flow model predicted that the migration and plugging of gel particles would achieve an 89.0% plugging efficiency and an 8% improvement over SC (81.3%). This enhancement was attributed to the healed gel's higher residual strength, which increased the critical pressure gradient, thereby improving particle retention and reducing permeability. Consequently, the BF-modified gel outperformed BF-free PAM gel mechanically pre- and post-self-healing, ensuring sustained deep plugging potential in sandstone reservoirs.

papers.title: Broadly applicable two-phase electrohydrodynamic model: Application to complex flows and cavitation
papers.abstract: This paper presents a broadly applicable two-phase electrohydrodynamic (EHD) model designed for enhanced applicability and extensibility. The model was implemented into computational fluid dynamics software, OpenFOAM®, with the implementation optimized through a comparative analysis of alternative expressions. The model's versatility is demonstrated across a range of simulations, including both low and moderate conductivity fluids. We evaluate the model using a one-dimensional case, simulations of stationary and settling drops, the electrospinning process, and cavitation phenomena. The results from the drop and the electrospinning simulations show good agreement with analytical predictions. Importantly, the electrospinning of a moderate conductivity liquid was simulated using an EHD model including the Navier–Stokes equations for the first time; however, the observed discrepancy in this case suggests that a revised theoretical framework is required for such fluids. Furthermore, to our knowledge, this work presents the first simulation of cavitating flow, specifically around a wire electrode, that incorporates the influence of an electric field, which led to a significant reduction in both the vapor area and the drag coefficient. Due to the complex nature of the coupled electric field effects and cavitation framework in confined geometries, the quantitative findings are presented as a pioneering, exploratory numerical study that establishes a baseline for future experimental investigations. We conclude that implementations of EHD models can be applicable to a wide range of flow scenarios.

papers.title: Study of thermal stratification effects on wind fields over a three-dimensional hill using an improved inflow turbulence generation method for large eddy simulation
papers.abstract: The influence of thermal stratification variations on the wind fields over hills poses greater challenges for the design of wind-sensitive structures in mountainous areas. In this study, large eddy simulation (LES) was performed to study such influence. The thermally stratified turbulent inflow for LES was generated using an enhanced narrowband synthesis random flow generation method, which integrates equilibrium boundary conditions with empirical stability functions and incorporates refinements to the spatial tuning, timescale, and spectral energy correction factors. Its effectiveness was validated through comparison with wind tunnel test data. The simulated wind flow fields around the hill were then compared across three thermal stratification conditions, including neutral, stable, and unstable stratification. Relative to neutral stratification, temperature variations under stable stratification enlarge both the standing vortex on the windward side and the separated vortex on the leeward side. Conversely, under unstable stratification, the area of the standing vortex increases while that of the separated vortex decreases. These changes in the above vortex position and area significantly alter the wind field distribution around the hill. In the wake region, vortex structures under stable stratification are larger in scale with more concentrated turbulence intensity, whereas under unstable stratification, vortex shedding is more pronounced and accompanied by more extensive turbulence dissipation. Furthermore, a wind field prediction model for hilly terrain, developed using the atmospheric stability data and wind field data under neutral stratification, was proposed and demonstrated satisfactory performance under both stable and unstable stratification conditions.

papers.title: Turbulence characteristics in the near-field of polyethylene terephthalate net panels
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigated the characteristics of near-field turbulence generated by polyethylene terephthalate net panels using particle image velocimetry measurements across varying twine diameters and net solidities. Within close proximity of the wake (x/L<2), jet-like acceleration was induced by the meshes with U/U0>1, whereas pronounced velocity deficits formed behind the twines (U/U0<1). These two regimes progressively converged downstream as shear-layer entrainment and turbulent mixing enhanced wake interactions, yielding a unified global wake. Increasing net solidity was associated with stronger blockage, higher peak jet velocity through the meshes, deeper velocity deficit behind the twines, and an upstream shift of the resolved turbulence-intensity peak. In the decay region downstream from the twines, turbulence intensity followed a power-law decay with fitted exponents generally increasing with net solidity, but remaining below unity, indicating slower decay than canonical high-solidity grids. The near field (x/L<10) was markedly inhomogeneous and anisotropic, and higher-order statistics revealed non-Gaussian behavior. In particular, streamwise skewness responded differently in mesh and twine regions, consistent with a transition from jet-driven acceleration at low net solidity to shear-layer separation and vortex shedding at higher net solidity. Vorticity analysis showed that reducing the twine diameter weakened the vorticity magnitude and shortened the vortex development length because of a weaker bluff-body effect. Consistent trends were observed in the velocity spectra. Transport through the mesh was dominated by rapid downstream advection, while the twine wakes enhanced mixing and increased the particle residence times.

papers.title: Effect of sampling methods on size dependency of hydraulic properties in rough-walled rock fractures
papers.abstract: Determining scale-dependent variability in hydraulic behavior of rough-walled rock fractures is essential for evaluating fluid flow in heterogeneous, field-scale fractured rocks. However, reported hydraulic representative elementary size (RES) values show significant variability originating partially from statistical deviations introduced by spatial sub-sampling methods rather than intrinsic fracture properties. To separate intrinsic hydraulic scale effects from sampling-induced variations, flow simulations were conducted on 10 × 10 m2 synthetic rough fractures under varying geometries. Four spatial sampling methods, including random window sampling method (RWSM), progressive window enlargement sampling method, disjoint block sampling method, and overlapping moving window sampling method (OMWSM), were evaluated. The results indicate that the determined RES strongly depends on how a sampling method handles spatial autocorrelation. The RWSM uses disjointed samples, which removes the spatial correlation between local flow fields, resulting in a faster statistical convergence and a smaller RES (e.g., 2.0 m). In contrast, the OMWSM utilizes overlapping samples that maintain spatial continuity. This introduces inter-sample covariance, requiring a larger domain size (≥3.0 m) to achieve a stable mean permeability. Furthermore, increasing surface roughness and shear displacement amplify flow localization by expanding these contact barrier clusters, thereby extending the correlation length of the resulting flow field and magnifying discrepancies between sampling estimates. To characterize this scale dependence, an empirical scaling law (K = a × bCr × lβ) is proposed, which captures the intrinsic hydraulic properties of the fractures with complex geometries. The findings provide a general framework for predicting hydraulic properties of heterogeneous fractured media encountered in diverse subsurface engineering.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic performance of three-dimensional active chordwise deformable oscillating hydrofoils under different spatial arrangements
papers.abstract: Oscillating hydrofoils inspired by fish caudal fin kinematics and schooling behavior exhibit great potential for ship drag reduction and autonomous underwater vehicle auxiliary propulsion. Their hydrodynamic performance remains a key research topic for designing high-performance biomimetic thrusters. This study establishes a kinematic model coupling chordwise deformation with pitch and heave motions and conducts numerical simulations to explore the hydrodynamic characteristics of three-dimensional deformable oscillating hydrofoils under different spatial arrangements. Results indicate that, under kinematic parameters (f0 = 2 Hz, k0 = 0.20L, n = 3) and flow conditions (Re = 500 000, U = 0.5L/s), single deformable hydrofoils increase the average thrust coefficient by 8.7% and propulsion efficiency by 11.4%, while reducing the cost of transport by 2.5% compared with single non-deformable ones. Deformable hydrofoils generate stronger trailing-edge vortex shedding and produce larger surface pressure differences. For parallel arrangements, thrust and efficiency decrease and stabilize with increasing spacing; a narrow spacing of 0.5L boosts the thrust coefficient by 5.08% via vortex bridging and merged jet formation. For tandem arrangements, performance first declines then rises, with 3.0L spacing yielding the highest efficiency and lowest transport cost due to weakened adverse vortex interference and strengthened co-rotating vortices. This work clarifies the propulsion mechanisms of deformable oscillating hydrofoils across different spatial configurations, offering a theoretical basis for optimizing marine vehicles.

papers.title: High-fidelity aerodynamic modeling and simulation of rapid transition maneuvers of a tiltrotor
papers.abstract: The rapid transition phase from the helicopter mode to the fixed-wing mode entails complex, highly unsteady aerodynamic phenomena induced by rotor tilting. Most prior studies adopt steady or quasi-steady assumptions, which fail to capture the transient aerodynamic characteristics throughout the continuous tilting process. To address these critical bottlenecks, this work investigates high-fidelity aerodynamic modeling and simulation for tiltrotor rapid transition maneuvers. A fully transient high-fidelity aerodynamic simulation framework is developed based on moving-embedded grids and computational fluid dynamics technology, and its validity is verified using the quasi-steady aerodynamic test data of the XV-15 tiltrotor and the transient aerodynamic test data of an experimental rotor. Leveraging the proposed framework, high-fidelity numerical simulations are performed to systematically analyze the evolution of aerodynamic characteristics and multi-scale vortex systems during the continuous dynamic tilting transition, and to examine the transient unsteady aerodynamic evolution of the rotor under coordinated control of tilt and collective pitch. The research results indicate that with the increase in the tilt angle, the rotor thrust decreases gradually, and the amplitude of transient thrust oscillation increases progressively. When the rotor tilts to the axial flow state, the periodic blade motion and high-intensity vortex clusters trigger self-excited oscillations, resulting in sustained and substantial oscillations of aerodynamic forces. Increasing the rotor collective pitch to compensate for the reduction in rotor effective angle of attack caused by tilting can alleviate the rotor thrust loss and effectively suppress the transient oscillation amplitude of rotor thrust simultaneously.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of vertical mixing effects on internal tide energy in the South China Sea
papers.abstract: This study investigates the modulation of internal tide energetics by vertical mixing in the South China Sea (SCS) and the Luzon Strait (LS) using a high-resolution numerical model. A series of experiments with varying vertical diffusivity distributions were conducted to assess the effects of mixing intensity, horizontal gradients, and vertical structure on internal tide generation, propagation, and dissipation. The analysis of the baroclinic energy budget reveals two opposing mechanisms: on one hand, weak mixing promotes local internal tide generation by modifying stratification in a localized area near topography; on the other hand, overly strong mixing alters stratification over a broader area, inducing a phase difference between stratification and the flow field, thereby suppressing internal tide generation. When mixing is relatively weak, its intensification promotes local internal tide generation by modifying stratification in a small area near the topography. In contrast, when mixing is already strong, further enhancement leads to widespread changes in stratification, disrupting the phase relationship between stratification and the flow field, thereby suppressing internal tide generation. In the SCS basin, mixing indirectly modulates internal tide energy through changes in westward-propagating energy from the LS. The latitudinally varying distribution has a significant impact on energy generation, while the vertical structure exerts a simultaneous influence on energy generation, propagation, and dissipation.

papers.title: Unraveling the coupled heat and water transport mechanism in metal-foam based gas diffusion layers at the pore scale: A lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Metal foams offer superior mechanical and thermal properties compared to conventional carbon-based gas diffusion layers (GDLs). However, the complex pore-scale coupling between liquid water distribution and thermal transport is still unclear for metal-foam based GDLs. This study establishes an integrated numerical framework combining Voronoi tessellation reconstruction with the lattice Boltzmann method to investigate the microscale heat and mass transfer in metal foams across varying porosities (0.69–0.88) and pores per inch (PPI = 60–120). Structural analysis reveals that metal foams are isotropic with a high coordination number of around 11–12 and a normal pore size distribution. Yet, its permeability is exponentially sensitive to pore density, leading to a drastic increase in hydraulic resistance for the more constricted pore-throat structures. Two-phase flow simulations identify a fundamental transition in flow regimes governed by pore topology: high-porosity structures facilitate a stable displacement via cooperative filling mechanisms, resulting in rapid breakthrough and high water saturation. Conversely, high-PPI structures trigger capillary fingering, where the enhanced capillary pinning effect in narrow throats delays breakthrough and leads to significant liquid retention. Thermally, the liquid phase acts as a “thermal bridge” to reduce fluid-domain thermal resistance and enhance local heat transfer, leading to a counter-intuitive conductivity “crossover,” where high-PPI foams surpass low-PPI counterparts at high saturation. Moreover, high-porosity structures demonstrate superior thermal uniformity, attributed to the liquid-phase compensation mechanism, where retained water eliminates insulating gas pockets and minimizes local thermal resistance discontinuities. Overall, low-PPI/low-porosity designs maximize gas transport pathways, while high-PPI/high-porosity architectures are essential for enhancing thermal homogeneity.

papers.title: Influence mechanisms and control of complex clearance flow on hydraulic instability in a pump turbine using optimization
papers.abstract: Pumped storage is vital for low-carbon energy systems. The crown labyrinth seal of a pump–turbine affects leakage, efficiency, and stability. Traditional seal designs rely on empirical rules and cannot balance multiple objectives. The physical role of clearance flow in hydraulic instability remains unclear. This study optimizes the crown seal of a 300–MW pump–turbine using multi–objective optimization. It combines computational fluid dynamics, a genetic–algorithm surrogate model, and entropy production analysis. The study shows that optimized seal reduces leakage by 17.10% and axial thrust by 7.20%. The S–shaped curve shifts only slightly. In contrast, the hump characteristic improves markedly: the hump margin rises from 2.66% to 3.21%. The study reveals the underlying flow physics. Reducing the clearance inlet size and labyrinth throttling lowers the jet momentum. The weaker jet enters the vaneless space with less lateral shear. This reduces circumferential velocity distortion, delays guide–vane separation, and alleviates blockage. The loss reduction is a spatial redistribution, not a uniform drop. The seal acts as a primary control for the hump but only a secondary modulator for the S–shape. A general design principle emerges: suppressing clearance jet momentum reduces vaneless–space shear, delays separation, and enhances stability. This principle is transferable to other high–head reversible machines.

papers.title: Effect of Mach number on shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction over a hypersonic compression corner
papers.abstract: This paper adopts direct numerical simulation to investigate the effect of Mach number on shock wave/turbulent boundary layer interaction over a hypersonic compression corner with inflow Mach numbers Ma∞=3,5,7. It systematically characterizes the flow phenomena in the interaction region at different inflow Mach numbers, including the flow structure and the evolution of the turbulent boundary layer. The mean skin friction decomposition method is employed to investigate the impact of Mach number on skin friction generation in the interaction region. Additionally, bidimensional empirical mode decomposition (BEMD) is used to quantify how turbulent structures with different spanwise scales contribute to wall friction. The results indicate that an increase in the inflow Mach number shrinks the size of the separation zone, causes the main shock wave closer to the wall, and suppresses the development of the downstream turbulent boundary layer. Furthermore, increasing the Mach number suppresses the turbulence amplification caused by the interaction. To explain these observations, the transport equation of the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) is analyzed. It is found that the turbulence production term primarily contributes to the TKE generation in the separation zone, and both the turbulence production term and the TKE gradually decrease as the inflow Mach number increases. Additionally, friction decomposition research conducted under varying flow conditions indicates that the turbulence-related term is a dominant contributor to skin friction. BEMD is utilized to decompose the turbulence-related term into four modes with specific spanwise scales. The results indicate that wall friction upstream of the corner is primarily influenced by small-scale structures near the wall. In contrast, wall friction in the interaction and reattachment region is dominated by large-scale structures in the outer region.

papers.title: Rarefaction effects on hypersonic boundary-layer transition over straight cone
papers.abstract: To investigate the potential influence of rarefaction effects on hypersonic boundary-layer transition, this paper develops a unified numerical simulation framework capable of encompassing the entire process from weakly rarefied flows, laminar boundary layers, transition, to fully turbulent flows. The nonlinear coupled constitutive relation model with slip boundary conditions is used to capture the additional nonlinear stress and heat flux due to rarefaction effects, and the modified γ-model is combined into the method for the ability of the all-speed compressible turbulent transition predictions. With the new computational strategy, we investigate the hypersonic laminar–turbulent transition on a straight cone under conditions reported by experiments. Results show that the rarefaction effects play a noticeable role in these cases even when the free stream Knudsen number is at a level considered as a definitely continuum flow regime. By considering the possible rarefaction effects, the transition position can be noticeably delayed, and the heat flux distributions especially in the fully turbulent regions fit with experimental data much better than the classical Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes solutions. These findings emphasize the necessity of unified physical models and numerical methods considering rarefaction effects and turbulent transition in the classical turbulence research field dealing with hypersonic flows.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation of wave overtopping flow kinematics and turbulence characteristics
papers.abstract: Wave overtopping over coastal structures involves highly transient shallow flows characterized by strong free-surface deformation and intense turbulence generation. Although considerable research has focused on overtopping discharge and volume, the detailed kinematics and turbulence characteristics of overtopping flows remain insufficiently understood. In the present study, a two-phase wall-modeled large-eddy simulation approach implemented in OpenFOAM is applied to investigate wave overtopping flow over a seawall under regular wave conditions. The numerical model is rigorously validated against laboratory measurements, including overtopping layer thickness and high-speed particle image velocimetry velocity fields, demonstrating good agreement in terms of free-surface evolution and overtopping flow kinematics. The results reveal that the overtopping flow is strongly phase-dependent and dominated by the streamwise velocity component, with pronounced turbulent fluctuations concentrated near the free surface and the bed. The overtopping flow remains supercritical (Fr>1.5) near the leading edge of the seawall crest, while the Froude number gradually decreases downstream due to bed friction and turbulent energy dissipation. The bed shear stress is highly transient, with instantaneous peak values exceeding the time-averaged values by a factor of 3–7. The subgrid-scale turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) accounts for only 6.05% of the total TKE within the resolved flow domain, confirming that the dominant turbulent structures are well captured by the present mesh resolution. The TKE budget further reveals that production and turbulent transport are the dominant terms during the active overtopping phase, with peak production concentrated near the leading edge and within the bottom boundary layer.

papers.title: Wake interference of multiple projectiles successively launched underwater at low angles of attack
papers.abstract: Vertically launched projectiles with a small transport velocity move at low angles of attack, generating complex wake vortices that can significantly interfere with the hydrodynamics of following projectiles in successive launches. To address the largely unexplored vortex dynamics at low angles of attack and the associated interference mechanisms among two or more projectiles, experiments and numerical simulations on successive launches of multiple projectiles initially arranged in a side-by-side configuration are conducted in this work. These results show that the wake is dominated by ladder-shaped vortex packets characterized by co-rotation and tail-to-tail connections between neighboring hairpin vortices, each consisting of vortex tubes and a vortex ring that serve as the legs and head, respectively. The interference exerted by these vortices on the nearby but non-immersed following projectile is identified, with the windward vortices weakening the crossflow over the body and reducing the pressure asymmetry between the windward and leeward sides. The interference increases with decreasing launch interval under the same launch sequence and is stronger under a downwind launch sequence than under an upwind launch sequence at the same launch interval due to the larger lateral vortex–body spacing. Vortex interference among three successively launched projectiles in aligned and triangular configurations is investigated. In the aligned configuration, vortex merging is observed and strengthens the original vortical structures. In contrast, the laterally offset vortices in the triangular configuration exert a weaker influence on the subsequent projectiles, resulting in a smaller reduction in pitch motion and the introduction of an additional yaw motion.

papers.title: The effects of cavitation number on multiphase flow characteristics and trans-media motion behaviors of a bionic manta-ray vehicle
papers.abstract: To investigate the trans-media motion dynamics of a bionic manta-ray, this study integrates the improved delayed detached eddy simulation model, energy equation, volume of fluid method, Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model, and overlapping grid technique. In addition, validations of the numerical approach are conducted, and the results are satisfactory. Load and motion characteristics during water–air transition under varying cavitation numbers are systematically examined. The cavitation number dominates cavity morphology and stability: low values facilitate large-scale, well-adhered cavities continuous with the tail surface, while high values suppress cavitation, inducing cavity shedding, fragmentation, and discrete low-water-volume-fraction zones. At cavitation number 0.694, the effective cavity volume fraction drops below 5% of that at cavitation number, with the downstream low-volume-fraction area shrinking over 80%. Vortex evolution is tightly coupled with cavity dynamics: high cavitation numbers disrupt shear-driven vortex generation, reducing high-magnitude vorticity volume by about 60% and weakening vortex coherence by about 70% relative to cavitation number 0.394. Moreover, cavity dynamics govern load characteristics and trans-media motion stability. High cavitation numbers trigger abrupt pressure changes, causing sharp force jumps and moment oscillations. This work provides a theoretical basis for optimizing bionic trans-media vehicles.

papers.title: Effects of electronic excitation on hypersonic ablation
papers.abstract: The high temperatures present in hypersonic flows produce a non-negligible amount of electronically excited states in NO, N2, CN, and C2, where the carbon-containing species are produced from ablation of a carbon vehicle's surface. The inclusion of electronically excited states in a chemical kinetics scheme will change the properties of the gas, for which the scheme is being modeled. In this work, we developed Ablative Solver for High Eenthalpy Nonequilibrium, a finite-rate chemical kinetics library for gas–material reactions and electronic excitation within two-temperature computational fluid dynamics solver Hy2Foam, to calculate the changes to the population distributions and surface properties of the hypersonic flow. The model considers chemical and thermal non-equilibrium, ablative material response to surface heating and reactions, and electronic excitation of gas-phase species of a reentry flow for the first time. We show in a number of different hypersonic cases that when these excited states exist in the gas phase, population distributions of both carbon-containing, air, and charged species, as well as mass blowing rates, change significantly. For a case at Mach 24 using an augmented air–carbon-ablation model of gas–material interaction, the mass blowing rate changes by up to 5%, and for Mach 8, the mass blowing rate changes by up to 10%.

papers.title: A finite volume-based Eulerian–Lagrangian framework for single quantized vortex dynamics in superfluid helium
papers.abstract: Simulating individual quantized vortices in superfluid helium in the presence of localized boundaries presents significant computational challenges. This paper develops a finite-volume method (FVM) implementation based on Open-source Field Operation And Manipulation for existing mesoscopic vortex-filament coupling formulations in spatially non-uniform fields. The solver incorporates the one-way vortex filament method, the traditional two-way (2W) coupling model, and the fully self-consistent two-way formulation within a unified Eulerian–Lagrangian workflow. Leveraging the geometric versatility of the FVM, the implementation accommodates complex non-conformal boundaries and synthesizes mass-conserving background potential flows. To improve the numerical robustness of the Lagrangian filament evolution without artificial geometric shrinkage, we integrate a Taubin λ−μ smoothing algorithm for spatial regularization. After benchmarking algorithmic fidelity against the intrinsic decay of bare and particle-decorated vortex rings, we investigate the symmetry-breaking kinematics of a single vortex traversing a localized thermal counterflow. Numerical results reveal that macroscopic spatial shear imposes an asymmetric mutual friction distribution on the vortex. This differential drag induces unequal descent velocities across the filament, tilting the orbital plane of the ring. The resulting reorientation of the self-induced velocity overcomes the local background superfluid advection, driving a continuous lateral drift that achieves a transverse displacement of 0.186 mm within 0.5 s. A mutual-friction dissipation analysis shows that this non-uniform trajectory reduces the length-normalized dissipation rate by 55.1% and the accumulated mutual-friction work by 30.4% relative to the uniform-counterflow case.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics and surrogate-based load prediction of a high-speed maglev vehicle-guideway system under varying inflow directions
papers.abstract: Crosswind-induced aerodynamic effects are a key factor governing the operational stability of high-speed maglev trains. When crosswinds interact with high-speed train motion, the resulting relative inflow can substantially modify the flow field around the train and the associated aerodynamic loads. In this study, a three-section high-speed maglev train is investigated using computational fluid dynamics to examine its flow structures and aerodynamic characteristics under a wide range of inflow conditions. The influence of yaw angle on surface pressure distributions, streamline patterns, and velocity fields is analyzed based on the numerical results. The evolution of the dominant vortex structures under crosswind conditions is then examined using the Q-criterion, highlighting the role of yaw angle in controlling the overall flow topology and wake development. In addition, a Kriging-based surrogate model is developed in the attack-yaw-angle parameter space to describe the aerodynamic responses of the train. Using this model, the combined effects of yaw angle and angle of attack on the aerodynamic force coefficients of the leading, middle, and tailing cars are quantified, and the differences in aerodynamic behavior among vehicle positions are systematically compared. The results show that the aerodynamic coefficients exhibit pronounced nonlinear variations with increasing yaw angle. For example, the lateral force coefficient of the middle car body decreases from 0 to −2.312, while its vertical force coefficient decreases from −0.578 to −3.975. Moreover, the pitching moment coefficient of the tail car body increases from 0.246 to 9.864, and the yawing moment coefficient of the leading car body decreases from 0.004 to −10.543. These findings improve the understanding of the aerodynamic behavior of high-speed maglev trains under crosswind conditions and provide a useful basis for related engineering analyses. Crosswind-induced aerodynamic effects are critical to the operational stability of high-speed maglev trains. When crosswinds interact with train motion, the resulting relative inflow significantly alters the surrounding flow field and aerodynamic loads. In this study, a three-section high-speed maglev train is investigated using computational fluid dynamics to analyze its flow structures and aerodynamic characteristics under various inflow conditions. The effects of yaw angle on surface pressure distributions, streamline patterns, and velocity fields are examined. Dominant vortex structures are further identified using the Q-criterion to reveal how yaw angle governs flow topology and wake development. A Kriging-based surrogate model is constructed in the attack–yaw-angle parameter space to predict the aerodynamic responses of the train. Based on this model, the combined effects of yaw angle and angle of attack on the aerodynamic force coefficients of the leading, middle, and tail cars are quantified and compared. The results show pronounced nonlinear variations in the aerodynamic coefficients with increasing yaw angle. Quantitatively, the lateral force coefficient of the middle car decreases from 0 to −2.312, while its vertical force coefficient decreases from −0.578 to −3.975. Meanwhile, the pitching moment coefficient of the tail car increases from 0.246 to 9.864, and the yawing moment coefficient of the leading car decreases from 0.004 to −10.543. These findings improve the understanding of crosswind-induced aerodynamic behavior and provide a useful basis for the engineering assessment of high-speed maglev trains.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation of high-pressure turbulent boundary layers across sub-, super-, and transcritical temperature regimes
papers.abstract: This study investigates zero-pressure-gradient flat-plate turbulent boundary layers at a supercritical pressure across subcritical, transcritical, and supercritical temperature conditions using direct numerical simulation. A body-force trip method is verified to effectively generate high-pressure equilibrium turbulence. In the transcritical regime, crossing the pseudo-critical temperature induces intense thermophysical property fluctuations and significant turbulent mass fluxes. The Trettel–Larsson transformation ensures a robust velocity profile collapse even under intense density fluctuations (ρ′ρ′¯/ρ¯) of up to 15%, demonstrating that Morkovin's hypothesis remains fundamentally valid. Turbulent-kinetic-energy analysis identifies a unique mass flux term and its dissipation mechanism enhanced by fluctuating viscosity. Furthermore, the transcritical case exhibits distinct structural coarsening, characterized by increased spanwise streak spacing and larger coherence lengths. These results clarify how transcritical real-fluid effects modulate momentum transport and near-wall coherent structures.

papers.title: A symbolic-regression-based turbulence modeling method with structural consistency constraints
papers.abstract: A novel explicit turbulence modeling framework is developed for high-Reynolds-number airfoil stall flows dominated by adverse pressure gradients (APG). The proposed framework integrates weighted proper orthogonal decomposition (wPOD) with a cross-condition structural consistency constraint. High-fidelity turbulence model correction fields are first obtained under multiple flow conditions through a field inversion procedure. An APG-wPOD is then applied to extract dominant low-dimensional structures shared across different conditions, effectively suppressing data noise in the inversion results. Within the resulting reduced modal space, an adaptive sampling strategy driven by the energy distribution of the dominant modes is employed to identify representative samples associated with stall onset and flow separation dynamics. Based on these samples, an explicit analytic correction model is constructed using symbolic regression. In addition, a cross-condition structural consistency constraint is imposed to ensure that the derived model preserves a stable and physically meaningful functional form across different flow conditions. Numerical results obtained for multiple operating conditions and different airfoil geometries demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves prediction accuracy for high-Reynolds-number airfoil stall flows, while maintaining the predictive capability of the baseline turbulence model for attached-flow regimes. The framework also exhibits favorable numerical stability and strong cross-condition generalization performance.

papers.title: Erratum: “Studies on the onset of carbon dioxide condensation undergoing rapid expansion through a converging–diverging nozzle” [Phys. Fluids 38 (5), 056115 (2026)]
Relation between the Nusselt and Bejan numbers in internal natural convection
papers.abstract: This Letter proposes a scaling relation between the Nusselt number Nu and Bejan number Be in internal natural convection. Entropy generation analysis and boundary-layer scaling show that Be−1 − 1 = a Nub emerges when heat transfer and entropy generation are governed by a common control parameter. The coefficients are not universal constants but depend on geometry, boundary conditions, Prandtl number, the irreversibility distribution ratio, nondimensionalization, and so on. Numerical results for side-heated cavities, Rayleigh–Bénard convection, and concentric cylinders support the proposed relation, suggesting a robust link between heat-transfer enhancement and thermodynamic irreversibility.

papers.title: Derivative neural operators with physics-guided diffusion refinement for predicting two-phase flow dynamics
papers.abstract: Time-dependent partial differential equations play a central role in modeling two-phase flow systems, but high-resolution long-term simulations remain computationally demanding.
