Although data-driven surrogate models provide efficient alternatives, they often suffer from temporal error accumulation and the loss of fine-scale physical structures. In this work, we propose a framework based on derivative neural operators with physics-guided diffusion refinement for fast high-resolution prediction of two-phase flow dynamics. A derivative neural operator is trained on coarse grids to learn the instantaneous temporal dynamics of the physical fields, and the predicted derivatives are advanced using a fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme for stable and efficient time integration. During the refinement process, the gradient of the governing-equation residual is incorporated as conditional physical guidance, encouraging the refined fields to satisfy the underlying two-phase flow dynamics. In this framework, the coarse-grid derivative operator captures the dominant temporal dynamics, whereas the diffusion refinement recovers interfacial morphology and vortical details that are lost during coarse-grid prediction. Numerical results on several representative systems demonstrate that the proposed framework improves predictive accuracy and spatial resolution.

papers.title: Scale decomposition of energy transfer in laser-driven magnetic turbulent dynamo
papers.abstract: The turbulent dynamo is the most plausible mechanism for generating strong magnetic fields in space. Recent laser-driven plasma experiments now reproduce relevant astrophysical conditions in the laboratory, enabling direct studies of this process. Using the FLASH code, we perform magnetohydrodynamic simulations of a turbulent dynamo in both two dimensions (2D) and three dimensions (3D) and conduct a scale decomposition analysis. While 2D simulations reproduce most basic plasma parameters, they exhibit an upscale energy transfer due to the vorticity conservation, absent in 3D, that renders 2D results unreliable at later evolutionary stages. Among energy transfer terms, the magnetic field line stretching term ⟨T2,l⟩ most efficiently converts kinetic to magnetic energy. Its solenoidal component T2s dominates the dilatational part T2d. The joint probability density function of R and Q, the second and third invariants of the velocity gradient tensor, shows that large T2s values occur where both Q and R are low, while small T2s appears where Q and R are large. The (R,Q) plane is divided into six regions corresponding to distinct topological structures and turbulent dynamo efficiencies. The most efficient region corresponds to (Q<0 and R<0) region or (D<0) region, where D is the discriminant of the velocity gradient tensor's eigenpolynomial. These numerical findings are supported by a simple analytical derivation. Our analysis identifies the most efficient turbulent dynamo topology in the (R,Q) plane, offering new insights into the underlying mechanism.

papers.title: Qualitative and quantitative analysis of wake dynamics in slotted elliptical cylinders for non-Newtonian fluids
papers.abstract: This study examines two-dimensional unsteady flow past slotted elliptical cylinders in power-law fluids at Reynolds numbers, Re, of 100 and 150. The objective is to investigate the combined influence of the aspect ratio (AR), longitudinal slotting, and shear-dependent viscosity on wake development and hydrodynamic forces. Two ARs (1 and 2) are considered, with the slot aligned along the major axis and a fixed slot-to-minor-axis ratio of 0.1. The non-Newtonian behavior of the fluid is represented using a power-law model in this study. The results show that AR establishes the baseline wake structure: the circular configuration (AR=1) exhibits stronger and more coherent vortex shedding, while the elongated case (AR=2) produces a comparatively smoother and more diffuse wake with reduced force fluctuations. Shear-thinning behavior weakens vortex coherence and increases wake enstrophy relative to the Newtonian case, although periodic shedding persists at Re = 150. The influence of the slotting depends on both Re and the rheology. For the circular configuration, the slot generally disrupts near-wake coherence and slightly reduces drag, with more noticeable effects at higher Re. For the elongated configuration, the impact of slotting varies with the power-law index, reflecting the interaction between shear layer development and slit-induced momentum redistribution. Consistent trends are observed in drag coefficients, enstrophy, centerline velocity recovery, and vortex identification λ2. Overall, the results demonstrate that wake characteristics arise from a coupled interaction between geometry, slot-induced modification of the shear layers, and shear-dependent viscosity, rather than from any single parameter in isolation.

papers.title: Data-driven modeling of three-dimensional wind velocity fields in building clusters
papers.abstract: Accurate characterization of urban wind fields is essential for reliable prediction of debris flight and impact on building envelopes. In this study, an efficient data-driven prediction model of wind fields around building clusters is proposed using conditional generative adversarial networks. The input of the prediction model is composed of the building cluster configuration and the inflow wind profile, and the output is the three-dimensional (3D) wind velocity field over the target domain. The training data for this prediction model are generated through computational fluid dynamic simulations and validated through a comprehensive database of wind tunnel measurements. To reduce the computational cost while retaining predictive performance, a sensitivity analysis of input parameters is conducted to inform efficient sampling for data generation. In the proposed framework, the 3D wind field is constructed using the predicted two-dimensional wind field at multiple heights, and the prediction models for the three wind velocity components are trained separately. Windborne debris impact on building envelopes is examined as an illustrative example to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed wind field prediction model.

papers.title: Effects of solvent viscosity and nozzle diameter on extensional properties of dilute polymer solutions using piezo-driven extensional rheometry
papers.abstract: Inkjet (IJ) printing is increasingly used not only for graphic applications but also for fabricating functional films and devices. However, the rheological behavior governing printing quality, particularly the extensional properties that enable stable jetting and precise droplet placement, remains insufficiently understood. In this study, the extensional rheological properties of dilute polyethylene oxide solutions containing glycerol were investigated using piezo-driven extensional rheometry. The glycerol content was varied to adjust the solvent viscosity, and the effect of the nozzle diameter on the material properties was examined under experimental conditions representative of IJ printing. The results show that the extensional relaxation time λE depends not only on the polymer concentration and molecular weight but also on the solvent viscosity and nozzle diameter, indicating that the characteristic length scale strongly influences the material response. Three characteristic times, namely the onset and termination of the elasto-capillary regime and the time of satellite droplet formation, were systematically organized using λE as the governing timescale of jet-breakup dynamics. The developed unified framework links the extensional relaxation time to jet-breakup dynamics while explicitly accounting for the solvent viscosity as an intrinsic material property and nozzle diameter as a characteristic length scale. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the extensional relaxation time λE serves as a key design parameter for predicting the filament lifetime and satellite droplet formation in IJ printing.

papers.title: On weak compressibility effects in low-Mach-number aeroacoustic simulations of small-scale rotors
papers.abstract: In low-Mach-number flow simulations, the incompressible approximation is commonly adopted to balance efficiency and accuracy, whereas acoustic waves in such flows exhibit weak compressibility and follow an isentropic relation. For aeroacoustic simulations of small-scale rotors, while far-field noise can be predicted using incompressible solvers coupled with acoustic analogy, it is crucial to assess weak compressibility effects to clarify the validity of both incompressible and weakly compressible models. In this study, we systematically evaluate two modeling approaches: the incompressible Navier–Stokes (INS) equations and an acoustic-wave-preserved artificial compressibility (APAC) method that introduces weak compressibility via an isentropic relation. Improved delayed detached-eddy simulations are performed for a two-bladed rotor in hover, covering tip Mach numbers from 0.12 to 0.24. Numerical settings are validated against anechoic chamber measurements, showing good agreement. Results suggest that both methods yield comparable and reliable predictions when an impermeable Ffowcs Williams and Hawkings (FW-H) integral surface is employed. However, when a permeable FW-H surface is used, the INS method significantly underpredicts high-frequency broadband noise because it cannot resolve sound-wave propagation, whereas the APAC method maintains good agreement with experiments. Near-field flow analysis confirms both methods produce comparable surface-pressure fluctuations and wall-pressure spectra near the trailing edge, indicating that weak compressibility marginally affects resolved turbulence statistics in current simulations. Additionally, the APAC method achieves an average speed-up factor of 1.93 over the INS method, demonstrating computational efficiency. The findings highlight that accounting for weak compressibility is essential for accurate aeroacoustic predictions of small-scale rotors, particularly with permeable FW-H formulations.

papers.title: Generation and posterior inference of spatiotemporal turbulent flows using latent neural fields
papers.abstract: Fast generation, reconstruction, and prediction of spatiotemporal turbulent flows from sparse, noisy observations are important for flow monitoring, control, and digital twins. These tasks are particularly challenging because turbulent states are high-dimensional, stochastic, and often defined on irregular geometries, which limits deterministic or grid-based deep-learning surrogates. Latent neural-field generative models offer a natural representation for such unstructured flows. However, they still face a tension between high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream generative learning. We show that latent recoverability during noising–denoising depends on how the learned representation organizes spatiotemporal flow evolution. Here, we introduce latent neural-field generation with confidence-region guidance (LaNF-CRG), a unified framework for representation, generation, and posterior inference of unstructured turbulent flows. The method first learns a generation-friendly multi-resolution conditional neural-field latent representation, regularized by a global flow-statistical anchor. A Flow Matching prior is then trained in this latent space and used for confidence-region-guided posterior inference from incomplete and noisy observations. Across four spatiotemporal flow benchmarks, LaNF-CRG supports unconditional generation, super-resolution, data restoration, sparse-sensor reconstruction, and temporal prediction without task-specific retraining. In three-dimensional turbulent-flow cases, it reduces statistical errors by 10–50-fold and accelerates inference by 17-fold relative to a latent diffusion baseline. These results indicate that LaNF-CRG provides an efficient framework for reconstructing and predicting complex unstructured turbulent flows from incomplete observations. Code is available at https://github.com/luzy2aa/LaNF-CRG.

papers.title: Structural mitigation of tsunami-like surge impact: Experimental and numerical assessment
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interaction between tsunami-like surge waves and structural mitigation measures using a combination of laboratory experiments and numerical simulations. The main focus is on the transient fluid–structure interaction processes governing surge transformation, momentum redistribution, and the mitigation of impact loads. Experiments were conducted in a horizontal rectangular flume (10 × 0.309 × 0.45 m3) under dry bed downstream conditions with varying initial reservoir water levels to simulate highly unsteady surge propagation caused by a dam-break mechanism. The flow depths were obtained using an image-processing technique, and the horizontal impact forces on the downstream structures were measured using a load cell system. The performance of the mitigation structures was evaluated with multiple hydrodynamic and loading parameters, including impact time, maximum water depth, maximum horizontal force, force concentration, and impulse. Rather than a single performance metric based on peak force reduction, this work shows that mitigation structures fundamentally alter the time-dependent nature of surge loading by redistributing the momentum transfer and increasing the duration of the impact. The results also indicate that the structural geometry, size, and orientation have a significant effect on the deformation of the surge front, the generation of localized turbulence, and the flow deceleration processes and, consequently, the instantaneous and cumulative loading characteristics experienced by the downstream structures.

papers.title: Wave–current interactions over a partially deformable seabed
papers.abstract: This manuscript is concerned with the propagation of nonlinear surface waves and uniform current over a seafloor consisting of combined rigid and deformable muddy sections. In the mathematical model, the deformable seafloor is represented by a thin elastic plate placed on a viscoelastic foundation consisting of viscous dampers and springs. The fluid flow is governed by the Level I Green–Naghdi equations, coupled with the equations of thin plate theory and the viscoelastic foundation to model seabed deformations. The results include interactions between cnoidal waves, uniform currents, and deformable seafloor with varying properties and length. Bottom deformations and the subsequent effects on the wave field are analyzed over a range of wave–current–seabed conditions. The results demonstrate the nonlinear effect of a rigid-deformable seafloor on the wave–current field and the presence of effective coupling between water waves and elastic waves on the deformable seafloor. Modal analysis reveals that the deformable bottom surface oscillates in multiple bending modes, the relative amplitudes of which depend on the length of the deformable seafloor, and the characteristics of the plate and the viscoelastic foundation. It is shown that a partially deformable seabed leads to combined energy attenuation and dissipation, and that wave reflection depends on the ratio of the wavelength to the length of the deformable seafloor region. The presence of current further introduces complexity to the dynamics, and its effect on the seabed response depends not only on the direction and magnitude of the current but also on the wave and bottom conditions.

papers.title: The pressureless limit of the Riemann solutions for the improved Aw–Rascle–Zhang traffic flow model with speed-density collaborative perception
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the pressureless limiting behaviors of the Riemann solutions for the improved Aw–Rascle–Zhang model with a logarithmic equation of state, which describes driver behavior with speed-density collaborative perception. We construct the Riemann solutions containing composite waves by using the “Liu-entropy” condition. Then we investigate the limiting dynamics of the Riemann solutions and demonstrate the formation of δ-shock waves and vacuum states as the pressure vanishes. Moreover, we quantitatively compare logarithmic gas, polytropic gas, and Chaplygin gas with respect to the singularity rates of density in their respective Riemann solutions. Finally, numerical simulations are performed to validate the theoretical results. Two highlights are noteworthy. First, composite waves do not persist as the pressure vanishes. Second, we find a new mechanism in cavitation formation that, as the pressure vanishes, the vacuum is formed only by the rarefaction wave dispersion, and is completely independent of the intermediate state of the Riemann solutions.

papers.title: Two settling spheres in a tube at intermediate fluid inertia
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional lattice Boltzmann simulations were performed to study the gravity-driven settling and interaction of two heavy spheres (density ratio 1.5) in a square tube (the width of the tube is five times the sphere diameter) at 140 ≤ Ga (Galileo number) ≤ 240, approximately corresponding to 160 < ReT (terminal Reynolds number) <310. Three distinct motion regimes are identified: steady motion (Ga ≤ 160), irregular helical motion (175 ≤ Ga ≤ 195), and regular helical motion (200 ≤ Ga ≤ 240). The onset of unsteadiness occurs at 160 < Ga < 165, slightly higher than for a single sphere, indicating that sphere–sphere interaction enhances effective confinement and suppresses wake instability. Irregular helical motion is marked by frequent circling direction reversals, strong inter-sphere separation fluctuations, and synchronized double-threaded vortex shedding. At Ga ≈ 225, a sharp wake transition from double-threaded to loop-like hairpin vortices coincides with a sudden increase in helical frequency and horizontal hydrodynamic force. Symmetric initial conditions yield consistent steady or regular helical motion, while irregular helical motion shows initial-position path dependence. Drag coefficients follow the order: two spheres > single sphere > unconfined sphere. These results reveal the strong coupling between sphere–sphere interaction, wall confinement, and wake topology in determining unsteady particle dynamics at intermediate fluid inertia.

papers.title: A single rising bubble under transverse ultrasonic standing waves
papers.abstract: An experimental study on the ascent dynamics of individual gas bubbles in quiescent water subjected to a transverse ultrasonic standing wave was conducted. The acoustic field distribution was quantified via high-speed Schlieren, confirming a stable, modulated standing wave pattern. High-speed imaging revealed that bubbles in the presence of ultrasound (BPU) were laterally attracted to and subsequently rose along pressure node corridors. Their vertical motion was substantially retarded compared to bubbles in the absence of ultrasound (BAU). While most BPU exhibited a steady speed reduction of approximately 30% (termed BPU-de), a distinct subset (BPU-dw) exhibited temporary dwelling at certain elevations. Two coupled mechanisms were identified to account for these observations. (i) A vertical component of the primary Bjerknes force periodically counteracted buoyancy. (ii) The acoustic carrier (20 kHz) was amplitude-modulated at 100 Hz, as evidenced by Schlieren; this low-frequency envelope periodically perturbed the bubble's boundary layer, intensifying vortex shedding and elongating the wake. Consequently, the local flow intensity rose by a factor of 2.8 relative to BAU, significantly increasing the effective drag. These findings elucidate the hydro-acoustic coupling governing bubble translation in transverse ultrasound fields and provided guidance for process intensification, flotation, and biomedical applications requiring non-contact bubble manipulation.

papers.title: Reflection and refraction of plane waves at the interface of multilayered media
papers.abstract: This research article explores the phenomena of the reflection and refraction of plane waves at two interfaces, one of which is the interface between the micropolar elastic solid half-space and viscous liquid layer and another interface between the inviscid liquid half-space and viscous liquid layer. The basic equations of micropolar elastic solids and viscous and inviscid liquids are converted into the xy-plane and solved with the plane harmonic solution method. On the plane interfaces, the primary wave (P-wave) or vertical shear wave (SV-wave) is considered to be an incident wave. The sliding contact parameter-influenced reflected waves in a micropolar elastic solid half-space, and the refracted waves in a viscous liquid layer are derived analytically. In micropolar elastic solids, there are three different kinds of waves named P-wave, SV-wave, and microrotational wave (MR-wave), each with different speeds. P-waves and SV waves are present in viscous liquids, while SV waves are present in inviscid liquid half-spaces. Thickness-influenced amplitude ratios are obtained at the interface boundary between the viscous liquid layer and the inviscid liquid half-space, whereas sliding contact parameter-influenced amplitude ratios are obtained at the interface boundary between the micropolar elastic solid half-space and the viscous liquid layer. The detailed study on the impacts of the sliding contact parameter and the thickness of the viscous liquid layer is presented graphically for a particular model.

papers.title: Flow and mixing of stirred tank reactors under continuous feeding
papers.abstract: The stirred tank reactor is widely used across various industries. Its primary function is to ensure uniform mixing of materials through mechanical agitation, with mixing efficiency influenced by multiple factors. This study focused on a 2000-liter industrial stirred tank reactor using computational fluid dynamics to simulate fluid flow during continuous feeding. This study primarily investigates the effects of impeller geometry and rotational speed on mixing efficiency and power consumption as well as the influences of feed flow rate, feed position, and the number of feed inlets on mixing efficiency. Mixing efficiency under different conditions was quantitatively evaluated using a mixing index, Mi, which provides a precise measure and serves as a reference for mixing performance. The results indicate that widening the impeller blades enhances mixing, with an optimal blade angle observed. Higher rotational speeds enhance mixing; lower feed flow rates are more favorable; feeding at half the tank radius improves performance; and increasing the number of feed inlets is beneficial. Wider blades, larger blade angles, and higher rotational speeds all increase power consumption.

papers.title: Mechanisms of flow transition and associated thermal transport for compressible fluids in liquid pistons
papers.abstract: This study investigates the unsteady gas–liquid two-phase flow evolution and associated thermal transport mechanisms driven by a moving interface within confined spaces. Utilizing Large Eddy Simulation coupled with the Volume of Fluid method, we characterize the complete dynamical pathway—transitioning from initial axisymmetric ordered convection to localized symmetry breaking, and ultimately to global chaotic turbulence. Particular emphasis is placed on the regulatory role of geometric constraints (aspect ratio λ) on flow topology and instability modes. Physical analysis reveals that high-aspect-ratio configurations suppress the nonlinear growth of radial perturbations by enhancing the coupling between sidewall confinement and viscous dissipation, thereby effectively retarding the spatiotemporal diffusion of turbulence. Regarding thermal transport, the breakdown of ordered convective structures is closely associated with the onset of nonlinear growth in gas temperature. Based on dimensionless analysis, we clarify the competitive mechanism among the timescales of perturbation growth, thermal diffusion, and characteristic compression. The results demonstrate that strong geometric constraints establish a near-isothermal physical limit by maintaining macroscopic ordered flow organization. This work provides new physical insights into the coupled “flow regime-thermal transport” laws in confined unsteady flows, offering a theoretical foundation for understanding complex interfacial dynamics.

papers.title: Transient radial flow in porous media: Competing viscous and inertial dissipation in a finite-thickness high-permeability zone
papers.abstract: Transient radial flow in porous media, under the combined influence of strong excitations and near-source high-permeability structures, can readily deviate from the linear Darcy regime and exhibit nonlinear dissipation characterized by the coexistence of viscous and inertial resistance. Existing models commonly approximate near-well heterogeneity as a zero-thickness boundary, making it difficult to capture the spatial accumulation of inertial resistance along radial flow paths and its impact on transient responses. To address this limitation, this study develops a dual-zone transient radial flow model in which the near-source high-permeability structure is explicitly represented as a finite-thickness region: the inner zone is formulated by combining radial diffusion with a Forchheimer-type flux-gradient relationship, whereas the outer zone follows Darcy's law, thereby establishing a dual-zone radial flow framework with near-source nonlinear resistance. Based on the Brady method and Laplace transform techniques, the transient response of the system is obtained, and the proposed theoretical model is validated through parametric analysis and laboratory radial experiments. The results show that the finite-thickness high-permeability zone exerts a dual control on transient radial flow: on the one hand, it reduces linear viscous resistance and enhances the effective transmissivity of the system; on the other hand, it sustains and extends the near-source high-velocity flow region, allowing inertial dissipation to accumulate continuously within a finite spatial domain. The competition between these two effects leads to a macroscopic head response characterized by early-time retardation followed by accelerated decay at intermediate to late times. Furthermore, by introducing the ratio of inertial resistance to viscous resistance as a local resistance-partitioning index, this study analyzes the spatiotemporal migration of non-Darcy effects in the radial system, where the inertial-dominated region is initially concentrated near the wellbore, subsequently expands within the finite-thickness high-permeability zone, and gradually contracts as the flow velocity decreases. This indicates that near-source non-Darcian effects are not merely localized boundary losses, but rather finite-scale spatial dissipation processes controlled by the thickness of the high-permeability zone.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of streamline inclination control in a deterministic lateral displacement array using lateral injection and suction
papers.abstract: Deterministic lateral displacement (DLD) enables size-based particle separation, but in conventional devices, the critical diameter is fixed by the geometry of the pillar array. Here, we experimentally investigate a flow-controlled DLD configuration in which the streamline inclination is adjusted by externally imposed transverse flow generated by lateral injection and suction. Particle image velocimetry measurements show that single-sided forcing produces a transversely non-uniform inclination field, implying spatial variation of the effective critical diameter and limiting control of sorting conditions. In contrast, simultaneous injection and suction provide a more uniform inclination of streamlines across the array. Using the integral control parameter α, we demonstrate continuous tuning of the streamline inclination and the corresponding effective critical diameter over a wide range. Particle sorting experiments confirm predictable transitions between zigzag and displacement modes. The results show that externally imposed transverse flow provides an experimentally validated means for tuning the critical diameter in DLD systems without modifying device geometry.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal unsteady dynamics of wall-bounded jet induced by a wide-sector dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator
papers.abstract: This study experimentally characterizes the unsteady induced-flow response of a wide-sector dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator (WS-DBD-PA) designed to extend the flow-control capability of conventional geometric DBD actuators, which predominantly impart streamwise momentum. Planar two-dimensional particle image velocimetry is employed to characterize the evolution of the near-wall jet under unsteady actuation. Owing to the coupling between a streamwise near-wall jet and a wall-normal vortex response, the WS-DBD-PA produces a broad near-wall induced flow within the sector region. The transient evolution of this induced flow can be classified into four stages: vortex-core formation, vortex growth, jet expansion, and stabilized jet development. Vorticity–velocity correlation analysis indicates that duty cycle and pulse frequency jointly regulate near-wall momentum injection and downstream diffusion. Reduced-order analyses based on proper orthogonal decomposition and dynamic mode decomposition further show that the duty cycle mainly affects the energy envelope, whereas the pulse frequency modulates the discreteness of momentum input, together influencing the transition between jet- and vortex-dominated flow responses. Under the tested unsteady-actuation conditions, the nondimensionalized velocity profiles collapse onto a self-similar trend, which can be empirically described by a quadruple-Gaussian correlation with good agreement (R2 ≈ 0.95). Overall, the results provide experimental evidence, within the present planar measurement framework, for interpreting the coupled streamwise-jet and wall-normal vortex response of the WS-DBD-PA under unsteady actuation.

papers.title: Numerical study on the hydrodynamic characteristics of an unmanned underwater vehicle with twin side-by-side pump-jet propulsors
papers.abstract: The development of unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), particularly those equipped with side-by-side twin-pump jet propulsion systems, is of great significance for enhancing comprehensive maritime capabilities. This paper employs a sliding mesh method to numerically investigate the hydrodynamic characteristics of a side-by-side twin-pump jet-propelled UUV, focusing specifically on flow field characteristics at two speeds: 4 and 6 kn. The study yields the flow field characteristics, unsteady thrust characteristics, and unsteady surface force characteristics of the side-by-side twin-pump jet-propelled UUV. The results indicate that there is no significant mutual interference between the twin propellers at the stern of this UUV, and the flow velocity and pressure conditions within the flow field are favorable. Under the influence of non-uniform inflow, the dominant frequency of the unsteady thrust pulsations generated by the propellers at the stern is the blade frequency, and the pulsation amplitude increases with increasing speed. Specifically, as the speed increases, both the time-domain and frequency-domain amplitudes of the thrust pulsations increase significantly; the thrust spectral amplitudes in the X and Z directions are approximately 50% of the axial (Y-direction) thrust frequency-domain amplitude. Regarding the transient surface force characteristics, the pressure pulsations on the propeller blades and fairing surfaces exhibit seven peaks and troughs within a single rotation cycle. This study provides effective numerical analysis methods and data references for the propeller design and hydrodynamic performance prediction and evaluation of UUVs with side-by-side propulsion systems.

papers.title: Investigation of collapse dynamics in multi-hole liquid carbon dioxide flash boiling jets
papers.abstract: Liquid CO2 (LCO2) flash boiling jets have been proposed for coalbed methane development and coal-rock drilling, with Martian in situ resource utilization as a potential application. Under low ambient pressure, rapid phase transition can induce strong jet interaction, and the consequent jet collapse critically determines the efficiency of rock breaking operations. Nevertheless, the underlying collapse mechanisms of multi-hole LCO2 flash boiling jets remain largely unexplored. In this study, optical imaging combined with the intensity-gradient method was employed to extract quantitative jet width data, while proper orthogonal decomposition and an image-based analysis method were applied to elucidate the collapse mechanisms of the jets. The findings reveal that jet collapse behaviors exhibit marked differences under varying nozzle angles and injection pressures. Specifically, small-angle nozzles demonstrate heightened complexity in collapse dynamics due to the competition between jet expansion and jet interactions, whereas high injection pressures dominate collapse mechanisms through vapor condensation effects. Based on the aforementioned investigation, this study advances LCO2 flash boiling jet collapse mechanisms in order to provide a theoretical reference for the precise modulation of LCO2 flash boiling jets.

papers.title: Amplitude-phase metasurface for the manipulation of diffraction-free spoof surface acoustic waves
papers.abstract: The integration of Airy beams with spoof surface acoustic waves (SSAWs) establishes Airy beams as an interfacial “information carrier” or “acoustic tweezer,” offering exceptional potential for advanced surface wave control. However, current SSAW-based Airy beams are excited purely through phase modulation (PM), and the lack of amplitude adjustability severely compromises their flexibility in precise wavefront control. Here, we design an amplitude-phase modulated acoustic metasurface composed of multi-cavity structure and slotted baffle, which, in combination, constitute “0” and “1” structural units. We realize independent control over transmittance from 0 to 1 of SSAWs under 0/π binary phases by separately tuning the cavity depth and slot width. Programable control of amplitude-phase distribution has been demonstrated by several examples. First, we validate the feasibility of generating high-quality Airy beams and Airy-Talbot beams, observing the self-imaging of nonperiodic signals along the curved trajectory. In addition, by symmetrically focusing two Airy beams, we realize acoustic focusing with a large focal depth, exhibiting outstanding self-healing performance. Our design overcomes the limitations of pure PM in exciting Airy beams, which is expected to provide a compact integrated platform for on-chip acoustic communication or microfluidics.

papers.title: Flow field and load characteristics of a trans-media unmanned aerial vehicle in the water-exit process
papers.abstract: When a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle crosses the water–air interface, it encounters strongly unsteady multiphase interactions that induce abrupt and irregular load variations. To resolve this process, a numerical framework integrating the overset grid method with a volume-of-fluid approach was developed, allowing detailed capture of the water-exit dynamics. The model was validated against classical sphere water-exit experiments, where the predicted free-surface peak differed by less than 6%, supporting its reliability. The flow evolution exhibits distinct stages, including initial surface disturbance, liquid film attachment, and subsequent fragmentation and shedding, rather than following a continuous progression. The influence of key control parameters on both aerodynamic loading and vehicle stability was systematically examined. Increasing rotational speed not only enhances thrust and exit velocity but also intensifies flow-induced fluctuations, which may lead to noticeable attitude instability. This trade-off is particularly sensitive to the timing of speed transition. A switching height of approximately 0.05 m yields a more balanced response, whereas earlier switching introduces torque asymmetry due to persistent fluid coupling. Vehicle attitude further affects the dynamics. Even slight deviations from vertical alignment produce asymmetric near-surface interactions, altering thrust distribution among rotors. As the inclination increases, this imbalance grows rapidly; for example, an initial tilt of 15° can result in pitch deviations exceeding 30°, indicating loss of control. These findings highlight the nonlinear nature of cross-medium transitions and emphasize the need for coordinated structural and control design.

papers.title: Radial oscillations of a lipid-shelled microbubble in shear-thinning blood inside a cylindrical elastic microvessel
papers.abstract: Ultrasound contrast agents, encapsulated gas microbubbles, are widely used in diagnostic imaging and show promise for targeted drug delivery. Their dynamics inside blood vessels are governed by gas compressibility, shell viscoelasticity, blood rheology, and vessel confinement. Existing models typically treat blood as Newtonian, neglecting its shear-thinning character, which is significant in microvessels where the shear rate varies by orders of magnitude. We present a modified Rayleigh–Plesset model for an encapsulated microbubble on the axis of a cylindrical elastic microvessel, with blood modeled as a power-law fluid. The Marmottant model captures lipid-shell buckling and rupture, and a lumped-parameter membrane captures vessel-wall deformation. We derive the non-Newtonian stress integral in closed form, showing how the confinement ratio ϵ=R0/a and power-law index n enter the viscous damping. Non-dimensionalization yields seven dimensionless groups; an asymptotic analysis in ϵ gives explicit resonance-frequency and damping expressions, and a Lindstedt–Poincaré expansion yields an amplitude-dependent frequency shift explaining the nonlinear amplification. A numerical study spans both acoustic forcing and free Rayleigh collapse. Comparison with the Carreau–Yasuda model confirms that the power-law approximation is accurate in the high-shear inertial-cavitation regime, with peak-amplitude differences below ∼1% across Pa∈[50,400] kPa. Both non-Newtonian models depart from the Newtonian baseline as Pa grows. Shear-thinning amplifies bubble oscillations, sharpens resonance curves, and increases the stress on the vessel wall; the peak transmural wall pressure rises by ∼4% at 50 kPa and ∼21% at 400 kPa, most pronounced during inertial collapse. These findings bear on contrast-enhanced imaging and bubble-mediated therapy.

papers.title: Modal decomposition and surrogate modelling of non-Newtonian flow in corrugated channels with linearly varying entrance amplitude
papers.abstract: This study presents a thermo-hydraulic performance and entropy generation analysis of non-Newtonian power-law fluid flow through wavy channels with linearly varying entrance amplitude. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) surrogate reduced order model are coupled to link flow dimensionality with thermodynamic irreversibility. Finite element simulations span Reynolds number, Re 10–400, power-law index, n = 0.5–1.5, and dimensionless entrance length (EL) = 0, 5.5, 11.5, and 22.5. A regime-dependent reversal in hydraulic penalty is identified and explained: shear-thinning fluids (n < 1) exhibit the lowest pressure ratio at low Re but the highest at Re = 400, where intense recirculation vortices form. At low Re, thermal irreversibility dominates (volume-averaged Be > 0.999). At Re = 400, the local Bejan number falls below 0.5 in the shear layers of shear-thinning fluids. EL = 22.5 yields the highest performance factor (PF ≈ 0.92 at Re = 25). POD of 40 velocity and temperature snapshots reveals the flow is intrinsically low-dimensional: six modes reconstruct the velocity field within 0.8% L2 error. Mode 2, carrying only 0.63% of total energy, encodes spatially concentrated recirculation zones whose modal coefficient quantifies rheology-dependent recirculation intensity and is associated with the hydraulic penalty reversal. The GPR surrogate, trained on 100 computational fluid dynamics cases and validated at two withheld Re of 150 and 300, achieves test-set Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) below 2.3% for all seven outputs. The low R2 (0.18) for PF at EL = 5.5 reflects near-flat test-set topology (MAPE = 0.55%), not surrogate failure. The surrogate identifies EL = 22.5 as globally optimal when both EL and n are simultaneously optimized, across the full Re range, establishing a PF envelope from 0.92 at Re = 25 to 0.72 at Re = 400. These results establish a quantitative design envelope for managing pressure drop and heat transfer in compact thermal systems handling rheologically complex fluids.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of the dynamics of continuous bubble chains in uniform flow and boundary-layer flow
papers.abstract: This study systematically investigated the kinematic response and dynamic mechanisms of vertically rising continuous bubble chains in unconfined countercurrent flow and wall-bounded laminar flow fields through dual-camera orthogonal shadowgraphy. The research focused on the coupled effects of bubbling frequency (fb), equivalent bubble diameter (deq), and dimensionless wall distance (S*) on the evolutionary patterns of the bubble chains. As fb increases, the wake of leading bubbles reduces the drag experienced by trailing bubbles, thereby increasing their rising velocity. In the low fb regime, as fb increases, the dimensionless amplitude increases, while the dimensionless wavelength decreases. However, as fb increases to approximately 8 Hz, the effect of frequency on the bubbles' spatial motion parameters tends to saturate. The deq has both a promoting and an inhibiting effect on bubble velocity and spatial trajectory parameters. Meanwhile, deq significantly affects the aspect ratio of the bubble. As deq increases, the bubble aspect ratio increases, indicating a progressively greater deviation from a spherical shape. S* significantly influences trajectory stability. The near-wall region facilitates the lateral oscillation of bubbles, and the bubble velocity increases slightly. Predictive models for the lift coefficient (CL) and drag coefficient (CD) were established. CL decreases with increasing S* but increases with St, whereas CD decreases with St and slightly increases with S* and Eo. The ratio CL/CD was introduced so that the relative importance of lateral lift effects compared to the axial drag resistance could be qualitatively evaluated. Under near-wall and high-frequency conditions, a larger CL/CD indicates a stronger tendency for lateral trajectory deflection.

papers.title: Flexural-gravity waves induced by uniform flow past a cylinder beneath a finite elastic plate
papers.abstract: This study investigates the two-way coupling between flexural-gravity waves (FGWs) and bluff-body wake dynamics for uniform flow past a circular cylinder beneath a finite elastic plate. A remeshing-enabled arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian finite-volume fluid–structure interaction framework resolves the viscous wake, plate deformation, and hydrodynamic loading in the deforming cylinder–plate gap. Unlike prescribed-load or potential-flow-based hydroelastic models, the simulations reveal a closed feedback loop: the cylinder-induced pressure field and vortex shedding deform the plate, while the evolving plate shape modifies the gap, pressure asymmetry, vortex shedding, and forces. The response shows that the submerged cylinder can generate a localized upstream flexural-wave-like deformation and a downstream gravity-wave-like depression, reflecting the combined effects of wake-induced pressure redistribution, hydroelastic restoring forces, and wave propagation. Relative to the rigid-wall counterpart, the elastic plate modifies the cylinder forces by reducing the mean drag, suppressing lift fluctuations and shifting the mean lift through deformation-induced gap variation and pressure redistribution. The parametric results further show that plate extent and cylinder submergence depth control different aspects of the coupled feedback: the downstream plate extent governs the gravity-wave-like branch and the cylinder forces, whereas the submergence depth mainly modulates the effective gap, wall-side vortex shedding, and lift response. These findings demonstrate that submerged-body-induced FGWs beneath a finite elastic cover are governed not only by hydroelastic dispersion but also by viscous wake dynamics, pressure recovery, and deformation-induced gap variation. These results clarify how wake dynamics and hydroelastic deformation jointly govern hydrodynamic loads and wave-induced deformation relevant to under-ice navigation and non-contact icebreaking.

papers.title: Synergistic effects of the free surface and flat wall on the bubble dynamics within confined spaces
papers.abstract: The present paper systematically investigates the evolution of the cavitation bubbles under the synergistic effects of the free surface and flat wall within confined spaces. The influences of free surface and flat wall on the flow field and the Kelvin impulse are investigated, and the jet enhancement phenomenon induced by the combination boundary is analyzed and is also compared with the case of the single boundary. Quantitative investigations are conducted to elucidate the impacts of the free surface-flat wall distance and the bubble-free surface distance on the collapse jet formation, bubble interface motions, and liquid velocity. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: (1) The free surface exhibits a more dominant contribution to the high-velocity region, while the flat wall contributes more markedly to the low-velocity region. (2) The opening angle of the bubble jet near the flat wall is smaller than that near the free surface, but the jet velocity is similar. (3) The jet morphology transitions from an arcuate jet to an angular jet as the bubble-free surface distance increases.

papers.title: Thermodynamically consistent phase-field modeling for mass transport with interfacial reaction
papers.abstract: A thermodynamically consistent phase-field model is proposed to describe the mass transport and reaction processes of multiple species in a two-phase flow. A key feature of this model is that the nonlinear reactions between different species occur only at the interface, and the reaction products accumulated on the interface subsequently modify the local interfacial tension. For the governing equations derived based on the energy variation method, we propose a structure-preserving numerical scheme that satisfies molar quantity conservation and energy dissipation laws at the discrete level. A series of numerical experiments is conducted to validate the effectiveness of the model as well as the accuracy and stability of the scheme. In particular, we simulate microvessels with bifurcated geometries to demonstrate the potential risk of microaneurysm formation.

papers.title: Suppressing acoustic error amplification in phase-field lattice Boltzmann methods with a high-order bulk viscosity damping term
papers.abstract: This study proposes a high-order bulk viscosity damping term to suppress acoustic error amplification in phase-field lattice Boltzmann methods for multiphase flows with high density ratios and Reynolds numbers. Although bulk viscosity is commonly introduced to improve numerical stability near diffuse interfaces, the discrete lattice Boltzmann framework inherently generates higher-order truncation errors that can amplify nonphysical acoustic errors and trigger instability. To address this issue, a Fourier stability analysis is conducted to identify the mechanism of acoustic error growth, and a new damping term is developed to selectively attenuate the unstable high-order acoustic error without altering the recovered Navier–Stokes equations. In addition, since the proposed term affects only the higher-order moments of the acoustic mode, it does not modify the hydrodynamic moments associated with the non-acoustic modes. The proposed term is incorporated into a lattice-kinetic-scheme-based phase-field lattice Boltzmann model and validated through four benchmark tests: a static droplet, Rayleigh–Taylor instability, droplet impact on a dry surface, and droplet impact on a wetted surface. The results show that the proposed term effectively suppresses acoustic noise amplification and significantly improves numerical stability under high density ratio and high Reynolds number conditions. These results demonstrate that the proposed damping approach provides a simple and effective way to enhance the robustness of phase-field lattice Boltzmann simulations while maintaining physical fidelity in complex multiphase flow problems.

papers.title: Toward accurate wave height prediction by developing an encoder–decoder long short-term memory network with variational mode decomposition
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of ocean waves is of great significance for both scientific and engineering applications, but no numerical approach can fulfill the task due to the complexity of physics behind. The advent of high-performance computing (HPC) technology with machine learning models has enhanced the possibility in relatively low sea conditions, although existing work often exhibits noticeable delays and error accumulation with severe sea conditions such as typhoons and storms. To address this issue, this paper proposes a robust multi-step wave forecasting model by integrating variational mode decomposition (VMD) with a long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network. An encoder–decoder framework is incorporated into the proposed model to enhance prediction accuracy. To validate the newly developed model, we conducted a 36-month field measurement campaign in the Kau Yi Chau and West Lamma Channel regions of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), China. We found that this area is significantly influenced by extreme meteorological events, such as typhoons, which lead to pronounced occurrences of extreme waves. Furthermore, the proposed model was compared with traditional machine learning approaches, including the LSTM neural network and the Random Forest model. The results showed that the model developed in this study provides accurate forecasts of sea states, even under complex conditions. This study demonstrates that the VMD-based LSTM model with the encoder–decoder framework exhibits superior performance, robustness, and generalization ability for short-term wave estimation.

papers.title: Cavitation dynamics of a yawed T-foil: Multistage shedding and asymmetric evolution
papers.abstract: The cavitation dynamics of a yawed T-shaped hydrofoil (T-foil) comprising a surface-piercing strut and a submerged hydrofoil significantly undermine the high-speed maneuverability of the hydrofoil craft. In this study, the unsteady cavitating flows over a T-foil at various yaw angles (β) are systematically investigated by coupling constrained launching experiments and large eddy simulations. It is found that, at β = 0°, a symmetric cavity multistage shedding observed from the T-foil is elucidated. As β ≥ 5°, the cross-flow effect drives a symmetry-breaking cavity evolution. Cavitation on the windward side progressively regresses to sheet cavitation and is ultimately suppressed, while violent unsteady cloud cavitation persists on the leeward side. Consequently, the excitation mechanism for lateral force fluctuations sequentially transitions from bilateral symmetric to unilateral dominant, and ultimately to strut–hydrofoil coupled. Furthermore, a flow regime map of the yawed T-foil is established, revealing asymmetric divergence of the cavitation inception boundaries between the leeward and windward submerged hydrofoils, primarily driven by the strut-induced vortex velocity modulation effect. The drag coefficient continuously increases with decreasing cavitation number, whereas the lateral force coefficient and lift coefficient first increase slightly and then decrease significantly in cavitating flow, and undergo abrupt transitions under the fully ventilated regime. These findings provide preliminary insights into the hydrodynamic design and stability control of similar T-foil configurations.

papers.title: Computational study of crossing shock-induced separation in laminar boundary layers
papers.abstract: A numerical investigation is conducted to examine symmetric crossing shockwave–laminar boundary-layer interactions generated by opposed sharp, unswept fins on a flat plate at M∞=4, for fin leading-edge angles αf=7°,9°,11°, and 13°. The interaction of crossing oblique shockwaves produces a strong adverse pressure gradient that consistently induces open separation, resulting in a complex but highly organized three-dimensional flowfield. Despite variations in shock strength, the global topology remains robust and is characterized by primary separation and attachment lines, a distinct centerplane separated region, secondary separation, and counter-rotating centerline vortices originating near the fin apexes. Surface flow visualization, limiting streamlines, and singularity analysis reveal a coherent structure governed by nodal and saddle points, while the presence of a virtual conical origin indicates partial quasiconical behavior. However, deviations from classical single-fin similarity are observed, particularly in the lack of full pressure collapse in the upstream influence region, reflecting the breakdown of self-similarity due to shock–shock interactions. Spanwise pressure distributions further confirm systematic evolution of the flowfield, including upstream migration of singular points, strengthening of centerplane separation, and earlier consolidation of vortex structures with increasing αf. Overall, the results demonstrate that laminar crossing shockwave/boundary-layer interactions exhibit a stable yet highly sensitive topology governed by shock strength and geometry, providing new physical insight into separation mechanisms and vortex formation in laminar crossing shock interactions.

papers.title: Quantifying CO2 huff-n-puff enhanced oil recovery in shale reservoirs via nuclear magnetic resonance experiments and compositional simulation
papers.abstract: Shale oil reservoirs possess abundant resources yet face low primary recovery (<10%). CO2 huff-n-puff has attracted significant attention as a promising enhanced oil recovery (EOR) method for these reservoirs. However, based solely on experimental investigations, the underlying EOR mechanisms remain poorly understood. To address these challenges, we propose an integrated method combining experiment and numerical modeling to distinguish and quantify the mechanisms during CO2 huff-n-puff. Experimentally, we employed nuclear magnetic resonance to monitor real-time fluid migration within shale cores. Analysis of dynamic T2 spectra and one-dimensional frequency-encoded signals enabled calculation of real-time recovery rates and effective distances. Numerically, a core-scale compositional simulation model was built and calibrated to match experimental data. Experimental results show that CO2 effective distance is primarily governed by diffusion and limited to the centimeter scale, resulting in low oil recovery. The effective distance increases significantly with soaking time but is unaffected by injection pressure, indicating that pressure alone is insufficient to mobilize deeper oil. The calibrated model quantified the contributions of four mechanisms: oil swelling, diffusion, dissolved gas drive, and elastic energy release. Dissolved gas drive was identified as dominant, accounting for over 40% of total oil recovery. Parameter variations showed that higher injection pressure enhances diffusion of oil molecules into the CO2 phase, improving recovery via oil-molecule diffusion, while prolonged soaking time facilitates CO2 diffusion into the matrix, boosting recovery through oil swelling and dissolved gas drive. These findings provide mechanistic insights for optimizing CO2 huff-n-puff strategies and improving shale oil recovery efficiency.

papers.title: Wake-induced load redistribution and suppression of shear-layer reattachment in a hybrid vertical-axis wind turbine–trough condenser array
papers.abstract: This study investigates the active modulation mechanism of an upstream vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) wake on the aerodynamic loads of a downstream trough condenser array. By performing proper orthogonal decomposition and frequency-domain correlation analysis on the pressure fields at elevation angles of 30°, 60°, and 90°, the physical essence of load suppression in the hybrid system is revealed. The results show that the rotating wake of the VAWT acts as a dynamic shearer, inducing significant energy cascade and spectral flattening, which forces the energy to transfer from large-scale coherent structures to higher-order dissipative scales. Spatial coherence analysis quantitatively confirms the release of phase-locking at characteristic frequencies, particularly with a significant coherence drop in the 90° case. For the investigated array configuration, this wake-induced spatial decoherence is associated with an approximately 40% reduction in the global extreme-suction envelope and a 10% narrowing of the pressure-fluctuation range under favorable wake-interference conditions. Three-dimensional physical mode reconstruction visually demonstrates the topological transformation of dominant structures from coherent bands to fragmented patches. The findings indicate that the hybrid system effectively suppresses transient extreme pressures by physically disrupting spatial coherence, offering a novel perspective on dynamic modulation for the aerodynamic protection of solar arrays.

papers.title: Porosity-controlled aqueous humor dynamics in pupillary block: A porous iris–lens channel model
papers.abstract: Pupillary block in PACG impedes aqueous humor (AH) flow through the iris–lens channel (ILC), while existing models that simplify the ILC geometry fail to accurately capture this flow and its role in PACG pathophysiology. A computational model is developed to investigate AH flow in the anterior segment of the human eye, in which the ILC is represented as a porous medium with variable porosity to account for different ILC conditions. The ILC is modeled as an equivalent porous medium to represent effective flow resistance rather than a physiological porous structure. The governing flow and solid mechanics equations are solved to systematically examine the effects of pupillary block severity on AH flow, pressure distribution, iris deformation, and energy dissipation. The results demonstrate that ILC porosity plays a critical role in determining the severity of pupillary block and the extent of anterior chamber angle (ACA) closure. When the porosity decreases below 0.35, the posterior–anterior pressure difference increases sharply to 419.14 Pa, driving anterior iris displacement and subsequent contact with the trabecular meshwork, thereby inducing ACA closure and increasing flow resistance and energy dissipation. In contrast, for porosities above 0.35, iris deformation is reduced by up to 67%, the ACA remains open, and AH flows smoothly, indicating a significantly alleviated pupillary block condition. This study provides new insight into the role of the ILC in pupillary block and suggests a novel therapeutic strategy based on modulation of ILC porosity to improve AH dynamics in PACG.

papers.title: Turbulent flow through and around an array with different arrangements of rigid solid cylinder-idealized real-world configurations
papers.abstract: Flow through arrays of obstacles in both natural and engineering systems commonly involve a large number of elements whose spatial distribution, particularly in natural settings, is often random. Moreover, such flows span a wide range of Reynolds numbers. However, previous studies have primarily focused on the near field of such flows in laminar conditions. In this work, we investigated turbulent flows in both near and far fields (at Red = 4000 and ReD = 160 000) of four different arrangements (containing 61 solid cylinders), i.e., evenly (scenario 1) and randomly (scenario 2) distributed as well as randomly distributed with high central density (scenario 3) and with peripheral clustering (scenario 4). Using the highly accurate three-dimensional large eddy simulation approach, we found that non-linear effects are more pronounced downstream of the array in all scenarios considered. Furthermore, comparison of the results related to different scenarios revealed that the largest array wake's momentum deficit occurs in scenario 3, while the smallest one is observed in scenario 1. Taking the evenly distributed arrangement (scenario 1) as a reference, such momentum deficit is reduced by approximately 44.2% in scenario 2, 95.1% in scenario 3, and 46.5% in scenario 4. On the other hand, drag coefficient reaches its maximum in scenario 4 and its minimum in scenario 3, corresponding to a 5.5% increase and a 14.3% decrease, respectively. These findings show that the spatial location of dense obstacle regions, not necessarily the presence of randomness, plays the key role in controlling drag production and wake characteristics in obstacle-array flows.

papers.title: Double-stage cavity formation during water entry of partially melted ice particles
papers.abstract: A unique double-stage cavity phenomenon has been discovered through water-entry experiments involving partially melted ice particles—a behavior absents in the entry of solid particles or liquid droplets. The water entry of a partially melted ice particle comprises two consecutive yet distinct stages. The first stage, dominated by the surrounding liquid layer, generates a crater-shaped upper cavity. The second stage, governed by the remaining solid core, produces a cylindrical lower cavity. During the secondary water entry, variations in the solid core's velocity relative to the deformed liquid surface, as well as changes in the core's diameter associated with different melting degrees, lead to fluctuations in the corrected Weber number. These fluctuations, in turn, determine whether gas entrainment occurs. The present study provides new insights into the water-entry dynamics of mixed-phase particles and contributes to a deeper understanding of the pore formation mechanism in the field of additive manufacturing.

papers.title: Investigation on mode transition of rotating detonation waves and flow field stability under spatial fluctuation of inlet total pressure
papers.abstract: To investigate the underlying mechanism of rotating detonation wave (RDW) mode transition and flow field stability under inlet total pressure spatial fluctuation, numerical simulations of premixed C2H4/air rotating detonation are performed using OpenFOAM. A sinusoidal spatial fluctuation is imposed on the inlet total pressure, and the spatial amplitude and spatial frequency are varied in a coupled manner while the mean inlet total pressure is kept constant. The results show that the final stable mode of RDWs is governed by the coupled effect of spatial amplitude and spatial frequency, rather than by either parameter alone. The underlying mechanism is associated with the formation and evolution of contact discontinuities between the fresh C2H4/air mixture and high-temperature combustion products. As the spatial frequency increases, the distribution density of contact discontinuities increases, which enhances the interactions among counter-rotating shock waves, RDWs, and oblique shock waves and promotes the transition of the high-temperature reaction zone from a discrete distribution to a more continuous distribution. The flow field stability, in terms of pressure signals, RDW velocity, heat release rate, and outlet thrust, demonstrates strong parametric coupling. Within the present parameter range, high spatial frequency combined with an appropriate medium to high spatial amplitude enhances the overall stability of the flow field.

papers.title: Physical similarity and scaling laws for ground shear stress in circular twin-jet impingement flow
papers.abstract: Twin impinging jets are utilized in various engineering fields such as electronics cooling and aerospace vehicles. The fundamental physics of nonlinear load transitions remains unclear despite the wide use of these jets. High-resolution steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations are performed using the k−ω shear stress transport model. A macro-scale diameter of 1.2 m is selected to ensure high numerical resolution. The numerical model is validated through a comparison with standard experimental data. Nozzle spacing and altitude are found to be the primary parameters of nonlinear load transitions. The localized decrease in ground load at specific geometric conditions is defined as the low-wall shear stress (WSS) valley. This transition is caused by a flow regime shift from individual jet dominance to an upwash fountain structure. A viscous scaling relation is identified where WSS is proportional to velocity raised to the power of 1.82 within the investigated low-Mach conditions. Critical load regions are identified through geometric parameters on a 2D regime map. The results provide practical guidance for interpreting load trends within the investigated range.

papers.title: Fluid–structure coupled vibro-acoustic modeling of steel-string guitars with coated strings
papers.abstract: A steel-string acoustic guitar is modeled as a coupled vibro-acoustic system consisting of six strings, a bridge-coupled modal representation of the soundboard, and the surrounding acoustic domain. The strings are modeled with steel cores coated with a Ni–P/IF-WS2 nanocomposite layer. The soundboard is modeled as an orthotropic plate, and the surrounding air is described using the linearized Euler equations. Energy transfer is represented through bridge coupling and fluid–structure interaction at the soundboard–air interface. Manufacturing and material uncertainties are propagated by Monte Carlo simulation, and their effects are evaluated using sound-pressure level (SPL), decay behavior, spectral centroid, fundamental frequency, and band-energy distribution. The model is validated against experimental bridge-admittance data, showing good quantitative agreement. Results show that coating thickness and bridge stiffness are the most influential parameters in the uncertainty analysis; however, the coating-induced acoustic changes remain extremely small. The maximum predicted SPL shift is approximately 0.011 dB, far below established loudness just-noticeable-difference thresholds, while the fundamental frequency remains unchanged and spectral-centroid variations are negligible. Thus, the main practical outcome is acoustic neutrality: the Ni–P/IF-WS2 coating preserves the guitar's radiated sound while offering potential durability-related benefits.

papers.title: Efficient and physically consistent transient modeling of gas flows in pipelines
papers.abstract: Transient simulation of compressible gas flows (e.g., CO2, H2, and CH4) in pipelines plays a critical role in system monitoring and operational decision-making in industrial applications, yet large-scale and real-time applications require modeling frameworks that are both efficient and physically reliable. Distributed-parameter models provide high physical fidelity, but their computational cost limits their applicability in such scenarios. In contrast, lumped-parameter models (LPMs) offer high computational efficiency, yet they may exhibit spurious transient modes, manifested as observable nonphysical oscillations, particularly in long-distance pipeline simulations. In this study, a physically consistent transient simulation framework is developed to investigate and suppress such behaviors. These spurious modes are shown to be closely associated with a mismatch between the finite disturbance time and its lumped numerical representation. The proposed framework combines a refined spatial integration scheme based on the Euler–Maclaurin expansion, an adaptive time-delay correction to account for finite disturbance propagation, and an equivalent inertia factor treatment to mitigate phase-leading phenomena associated with inertia bias. The proposed framework is evaluated through a series of numerical experiments, including comparisons with finite-difference method under different operating pressures, gas compositions, and transient boundary profiles. Within the tested cases, the proposed framework improves simulation accuracy and reduces the computational cost relative to the finite-difference benchmark while retaining a low-dimensional formulation. These findings provide practical guidance for improving the representation of finite disturbance propagation and inertia-related effects in LPM of compressible gas flows.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic characteristics of end-plate collaborative spoiled rudder accounting for propeller-rudder interaction
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic characteristics of the end-plate collaborative spoiled rudder (EPCSR), a novel marine rudder integrating end plates and a spoiler, are investigated with full consideration of propeller-rudder interaction through numerical simulations. A grid convergence analysis strategy for the hydrodynamic numerical simulations of propeller-rudder systems is proposed, and the numerical method is validated based on experimental data. Then, numerical simulations on four rudder configurations: conventional rudder (CR), end plate rudder, collaborative spoiled rudder, and the EPCSR are conducted to reveal the influence mechanism of end plates and spoiler on the hydrodynamic performance of the propeller-rudder system. The results show that the end plates effectively suppress the rudder's end effect, increasing propeller thrust and rudder lift while minimizing drag increase, and the spoiler significantly enhances rudder effectiveness but causes notable drag increments. The combined action of end plates and spoiler in EPCSR achieves a synergistic effect: it further boosts rudder lift, mitigates the efficiency reduction caused by the standalone spoiler, and only leads to a negligible decrease in propeller efficiency. The optimal matching point of the EPCSR is obtained through equal lift analysis for the target lift. The EPCSR is found to generate the target lift at a much smaller rudder deflection angle with a 24.12% hydrodynamic efficiency improvement over the CR. Additionally, the EPCSR optimizes the propeller-rudder flow field, moderates the unsteady hydrodynamic fluctuations of propeller blades to some extent for a constant lift. These features demonstrate superior comprehensive hydrodynamic performance compared with other rudder configurations.

papers.title: Seasonal freeze–thaw induces fluctuations of submarine groundwater discharge in coastal aquifers
papers.abstract: We reveal that freeze–thaw processes induce an asymmetric response of submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) to ground surface temperature under seasonally frozen ground conditions. In our simulations, this response is characterized by an advanced minimum and a delayed maximum. Cryosuction during freezing drives freshwater upward to the unsaturated frozen zone, retaining it within the frozen layer. The release of this retained freshwater during thawing increases seaward freshwater flow. The freeze-induced freshwater retention and its subsequent release produce pronounced temporal variations in SGD, particularly in fresh groundwater discharge. Higher mean ground surface temperatures amplify the magnitudes of SGD variations.

papers.title: Spontaneous transport and orientation locking of Janus particles with anisotropic anchoring in confined active nematic fluids
papers.abstract: Surface anchoring plays a pivotal role in governing colloidal dynamics in active nematic fluids. This study numerically investigates the transport mechanisms of Janus particles with heterogeneous surface anchoring in a two-dimensional confined microchannel. The results demonstrate that in a pure active bath, +1/2 topological defects tend to pin at the anchoring junctions of the Janus particle, inducing topological polarization. This symmetry breaking effectively rectifies microscopic active stresses into macroscopic active driving forces and torques, achieving efficient spontaneous directional transport of the particle. In a Poiseuille flow, the particle transport is governed by the active-to-shear stress ratio. In the active-dominated regime, the synergy between chaotic vortices and asymmetric anchoring drives significant transverse near-wall migration of the particles. Simultaneously, constrained by the minimization of nematic elastic free energy and the dynamic balance of fluid-solid interfacial torques, the Janus particles exhibit an “orientational locking” tendency in the near-wall region. This effect prevents the particles from releasing local stresses through free continuous rotation, which exacerbates interfacial momentum dissipation and results in severe slip retardation and an anomalous dynamical feature of “high kinetic energy but low transport efficiency.” This study unravels the physical mechanisms underlying the use of surface topological asymmetry to induce active propulsion, shedding light on potential applications in regulating the transport of active matter.

papers.title: Atmospheric stability effects on farm-to-farm wake interactions: A large-eddy simulation study
papers.abstract: This study uses large-eddy simulations to examine how atmospheric stability and inter-farm spacing jointly influence wind–farm interactions. The results demonstrate that farm-to-farm interactions are governed by the coupled action of turbulence-mediated wake recovery and gravity-wave-mediated large-scale atmospheric adjustment, whose relative importance varies with stability. Under stable conditions, reduced ambient mixing promotes highly persistent farm wakes, with velocity deficits extending beyond 15 km and first-row power losses of up to 40% in the downstream farm. In contrast, convective conditions accelerate wake recovery, although inter-farm influence remains measurable due to stratification in the free atmosphere. In all cases, the turbulence generated by the upstream farm accelerates the recovery of the wake from the downstream farm, with the strongest relative impact under stable, low-turbulence conditions. Despite large inflow velocity deficits, the turbulence intensity within the downstream farm rapidly adjusts to levels comparable to those within the upstream farm, suggesting that turbine-generated mixing largely governs in-farm turbulence. In strongly stratified cases, this turbulence-driven interaction is further coupled with gravity-wave-like vertical flow adjustments that modulate blockage and wake evolution. As a result, power output reflects the combined effects of turbulence history, stratification, and wave-induced pressure adjustment, with blockage effects ranging from ∼18% in stable conditions to ∼4% in conventionally neutral cases. The cumulative presence of two wind farms also alters the boundary-layer structure, promoting internal boundary-layer-like adjustments, Coriolis-induced asymmetries, and stability-dependent changes in turbulent momentum transport.

papers.title: Motion behaviors of active particles in a contraction and expansion microchannel flow
papers.abstract: The motion of self-propelled particles in microchannels with variable cross sections is important for particle sorting, targeted drug delivery, and microrobot navigation. In this work, the lattice Boltzmann method coupled with the squirmer model is used to investigate the locomotion dynamics of a single self-propelled particle in a contraction–expansion microchannel. By varying the geometric confinement ratio K, channel Reynolds number Re, inclination angle of the contraction segment θ, and self-propelled type parameter β, four distinct locomotion modes are identified: vortex trapping, corner trapping, upstream sliding, and downstream transport. Through the construction of Re–β phase diagrams and K–Re–β three-dimensional phase diagrams, the critical transition conditions governing the effects of each parameter were systematically revealed. The results show that fluid inertia has a dual effect on pusher-type particles (β < 0). At moderate Reynolds numbers, pushers with small |β| such as β = −1 are entrained by downstream separation vortices and exhibit periodic orbital motion. In contrast, pushers with β ≤ −7 can resist inertial flushing even at Re = 300 and maintain upstream wall-sliding motion. Increasing the confinement ratio K effectively alleviates wall-normal confinement, promoting the transition of particles from corner trapping to vortex trapping or downstream transport, thereby enhancing the efficiency of particle passage through the constriction. In contrast, adjusting the inclination angle of the contraction segment (30°–90°) only modifies the passage probability of particles at low Re without systematically facilitating escape. Mechanistic analysis shows that stable vortex trapping is consistent with a near-cancellation between the propulsion-related tendency and the pressure-gradient-induced hydrodynamic tendency. Corner trapping, by contrast, results from geometric confinement, wall attraction, and localized low-pressure stagnation points. This study contributes to the understanding of transport mechanisms of self-propelled particles in complex confined geometries and provides theoretical guidance for optimizing microchannel structures.

papers.title: Computational fluid dynamics investigation of hydrodynamic instabilities and turbulence modulation in a sediment-laden centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: This study presents a computational fluid dynamics investigation of hydrodynamic instabilities induced by inertial particles (Cw=14%) in a centrifugal pump under Southern Xinjiang irrigation conditions. Using high-fidelity Eulerian–Eulerian simulations with four-way coupling via the kinetic theory of granular flow, we identify a critical Stokes number (Stcrit≈0.45) that marks the transition from stable, stratified particle-laden flow to unstable regimes. Below this threshold (St≪1), fine particles follow fluid streamlines with negligible vorticity distortion, preserving the base flow stability. At the critical threshold, vorticity amplification occurs in the impeller core, characterized by the formation of coherent vortical structures, pressure distortion, and vortex-induced backflow. For coarse particles (St>1), the system enters a developed inertial instability regime featuring significant turbulence modulation and a nonlinear energy cascade from mean flow kinetic energy into particle fluctuation energy (quantified by granular temperature). Experimental validation via scanning electron microscopy confirms that simulated instability zones and high-impact regions correlate with observed material wear patterns. These findings identify a critical Stokes number threshold for instability onset under the investigated conditions, providing a reference for flow regime prediction in sediment-laden centrifugal pumps.

papers.title: Flow characteristics around the low-drag Ahmed body under crosswind condition
