papers.abstract: The aerodynamic behavior of a low-drag Ahmed body under yaw conditions was investigated using wind tunnel experiments and numerical simulations. The investigation focused on the evolution of flow structures across various yaw angles. The flow characteristics were systematically analyzed, with particular attention to front separation, lateral pressure distribution, spanwise vortex dynamics, the development of longitudinal vortices, and variations in vertical vortex structures. The displacement of the front saddle point led to the recovery of surface pressure on the front body when the yaw angle exceeded 20°, which was identified as the main contributor to drag reduction under high yaw conditions. Asymmetric front-end separation caused notable disparities in the side-surface flow and wake structures. Despite intensified pressure fluctuations on the windward side, the pressure differential between the two sides serves as a reliable indicator for estimating lateral force or yaw angle. A transition in the near-wake structure from a low-drag to a high-drag mode was observed from the windward to the leeward side. At a yaw angle of 16°, the near-wake fully transformed into a high-drag configuration. These findings enhance the understanding of crosswind aerodynamics in bluff vehicle bodies.

papers.title: Stability, complex mode motion, and displacement response of spinning pipes conveying solid–liquid two-phase flow
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the vibration and stability of simply supported spinning pipes conveying solid–liquid two-phase flow. The governing equations are derived via Hamilton's principle and solved using the Galerkin method and state-space eigenvalue approach. Model validation against single-phase flow results from the literature confirms the reliability of the present formulation. For the two-phase flow model, the first divergence velocity and the first flutter velocity are reduced compared to the single-phase flow model, while the sequence of dynamical instability (stable → divergence → stable → flutter → mode combined flutter) remains unchanged. Increasing the slip factor (β) reduces both the divergence flow velocity and the divergence spinning velocity; similarly, raising the solid-phase mass ratio (γ) lowers the divergence flow velocity and makes the system more prone to vibration divergence. Conversely, a higher liquid-phase mass ratio (α) increases the divergence velocities, but its effect saturates beyond a “sensitive zone,” where stability can be effectively enhanced. In complex mode motion, both β and γ accelerate the traveling wave propagation velocity without altering the whirling direction. The displacement response shows that the vibration amplitude grows significantly with γ, whereas β mainly lengthens the vibration period. Thus, the solid-phase mass ratio is identified as a key parameter that induces divergence instability, while the liquid-phase mass ratio offers a tuning knob for stability enhancement within the sensitive range.

papers.title: Effects of incomplete surface accommodation on rarefied hypersonic nozzle flows
papers.abstract: A comprehensive numerical analysis is performed to investigate rarefied hypersonic gas flows in a nozzle using the direct simulation Monte Carlo method and Cercignani–Lampis–Lord model. Various accommodation coefficient (AC) combinations are considered to acquire detailed knowledge of effects of incomplete accommodation in the normal and tangential directions on flow features, surface properties, and aerodynamic drags. Three free-stream Knudsen numbers, i.e., Kn∞ = 0.1, 1, and 10, are considered to cover the entire rarefied transition regime. At the relatively low Kn∞ of 0.1, uninterrupted inter-molecule collisions make them play an overwhelmingly dominant role over molecule-surface collisions (MSCs) in gas flows, so flow patterns, mass flux contours, thermodynamic nonequilibrium behavior, surface quantities, and aerodynamic drags, together with their pressure and friction components, are almost independent of ACs. As Kn∞ grows, MSCs and the consequent ACs play an increasingly important role, so the discrepancies in flow features, surface properties, and drag components between various AC cases become larger, and they vary dramatically with ACs. Incomplete accommodation in the normal direction intensifies the backflow and consequently produces or enlarges the recirculation zone, causing a significant drop in mass flux. In contrast, incomplete accommodation in the tangential direction facilitates the passing of gas through the nozzle and consequently shrinks or eliminates the recirculation zone, thus achieving a considerable increase in mass flux. Surface shear stress contributes more to aerodynamic drag with the increase in Kn∞. Friction drag accounts for less than 6% of the total drag at Kn∞ = 0.1, but this percentage grows to about 50% at Kn∞ = 10. Incomplete accommodations in both directions enhance temperature jump, while velocity slip is mainly affected by incomplete accommodation in the tangential direction, which also intensifies thermodynamic nonequilibrium slightly. There is a strongly positive correlation between local flow separation and the abnormally small velocity slip.

papers.title: Flow regime transitions and vortex dynamics in response-modulated triply periodic minimal surface lattice structures
papers.abstract: To address the severe heat dissipation challenges in aerospace thermal management systems, this study proposes a response-modulated diamond lattice based on the implicit function of the triply periodic minimal surface. By incorporating a spatial perturbation coefficient a and a thickness fluctuation amplitude b, the channel tortuosity and local throttling effects are independently decoupled under a constant porosity. The intrinsic vortex dynamics and energy dissipation mechanisms are investigated through combined numerical simulations and experimental testing. Furthermore, response surface methodology is employed to analyze the nonlinear coupling between geometric variables and operating conditions. The results reveal a distinct flow regime boundary where the internal flow transitions from a secondary flow enhancement mode to an aerodynamic blockage mode. Specifically, excessive geometric distortion shifts the dominant drag mechanism from viscous friction to form drag. However, moderate topological modulation effectively thins the thermal boundary layer while suppressing disordered turbulent dissipation in the mainstream. Quantitatively, the optimal mildly modulated configuration achieves a 7.04% increase in the Nusselt number at Re = 1040 compared to the baseline diamond model, while strictly limiting the friction factor penalty to 9.93%, resulting in a peak performance evaluation criterion of 1.055. This work provides clear theoretical boundaries for designing compact heat exchangers with favorable flow-thermal equilibrium.

papers.title: A probabilistic reconstruction method for discrete bubble distribution from Euler–Euler model simulations
papers.abstract: In industrial systems, such as nuclear reactors and chemical bubble columns, the precise predictions of bubble size, morphology, and spatial distribution in gas–liquid two-phase flows are crucial. Although the conventional Euler–Euler model (Two-Fluid Model) is widely adopted due to its computational efficiency, it inherently provides only time-averaged or transient continuous gas volume fraction fields, failing to resolve geometric information of discrete bubbles. This study proposes a novel post-processing technique based on a probabilistic reconstruction method combined with prior assumption for bubble size distribution (BSD) to reconstruct high-resolution discrete bubble distributions from the gas volume fraction fields computed using the Euler–Euler model. The approach was validated using a classic two-dimensional bubble column case of a transient air–water flow characterized by a meandering bubble plume. The numerical robustness of the Euler–Euler input field was first established through a systematic mesh and time-step sensitivity study. The results indicate that the reconstructed discrete bubble fields are not only macroscopically consistent with original plume morphologies but also faithfully preserve the prescribed BSD. Furthermore, the method enables the direct extraction of the interfacial area concentration (IAC), effectively capturing local heterogeneity and bubble-clustering “hotspots” that are typically smoothed out in Euler–Euler frameworks. The framework is robust to the choice of unimodal BSD prior (cross-prior coefficient of variation of mean IAC < 0.5%) and to input-field perturbations (IAC error within 3% under a 10% perturbation), while requiring only 5.17%–5.52% of the Euler–Euler simulation time. When driven by an independently measured gas holdup profile, the reconstructed IAC agrees with four-point optical-probe data to within 10.7%. The proposed method functions as a meso-scale structure recovery operator rather than a stand-alone bubble-dynamics model: it bridges the informational gap between Euler–Euler averaged fields and discrete bubble fields, augmenting routine simulations with directly computable physical observables that are otherwise inaccessible. Consequently, by combining the Euler–Euler method with the reconstruction algorithm presented here, microscopic flow details, such as bubble-scale distributions, can be obtained at a relatively low computational cost, offering a new pathway for industrial two-phase flow analysis.

papers.title: A new automatic vortex (Liutex) core line identification method in boundary-layer transition
papers.abstract: Conventional isosurface-based vortex visualization depends strongly on user-specified vortex-strength thresholds, which may hide weak vortices. Liutex core lines provide a line-based representation of vortex structure that is not dependent on a single global vortex-strength threshold and can display local vortex-strength variation along the vortex skeleton. However, an automatic extraction of Liutex core lines remains challenging in complex three-dimensional flows because real core lines usually pass through sub-grid locations, and redundant seed points may cause repeated or incorrect line generation. In this work, an automatic Liutex core line identification method is developed by combining a Liutex-based predictor–corrector procedure, two criteria for identifying Liutex core points, and a grouping algorithm for assembling these points into continuous core lines. The method is applied to both a micro-vortex-generator wake flow and a flat-plate boundary-layer transition flow. The results show that the method correctly captures the vortex structures in these two cases. Compared with conventional isosurface visualization, Liutex core lines can reveal weak structures that may be lost at a prescribed threshold while maintaining a clear representation of strong vortices. The method also reveals dual-core structures within hairpin vortex ring isosurfaces, providing new insight that the formation of hairpin vortices may be related to Kelvin–Helmholtz instability.

papers.title: Particle image velocimetry network embedded with Kolmogorov–Arnold networks for near-wall shear flow measurement
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) is a nonintrusive flow visualization technique that extracts dense flow fields directly from raw particle images. However, due to the dominant viscous actions of fluids, tracer particles are inherently sparse within the immediate near-wall region. This localized information void severely hinders the reliable identification of fluid–solid boundaries. Simultaneously, the near-wall shear layer generates severe, nonlinear velocity gradients, which collectively exacerbate the measurement difficulties in these boundary-adjacent zones. Consequently, conventional PIV methods face severe challenges in accurately resolving near-wall shear flows. To overcome these boundary identification deficits, this study introduces a fusion-informed deep learning model named the all-feature adaptive fusion and Kolmogorov–Arnold network for particle image velocimetry (AFKAN-PIV). This neural network framework incorporates an all-feature adaptive fusion (AAF) module and a U-shaped Kolmogorov–Arnold network (U-KAN). The AAF module fuses static particle and dynamic flow features via spatial and channel weighting to optimize fluid–solid boundary segmentation. Building directly upon these geometric boundary constraints, the U-KAN architecture leverages learnable nonlinear spline functions to precisely fit the steep, high-gradient velocity variations, thereby achieving high-fidelity measurements. Evaluated on synthetic datasets, AFKAN-PIV demonstrates superior accuracy over existing methods, achieving an average reduction of approximately 21.73% in mean squared error. Furthermore, extensive evaluations confirm that AFKAN-PIV offers an excellent balance between structural complexity, computational efficiency, measurement performance, and generalization capability, providing a more reliable solution for near-wall shear flows compared to current measurement methods.

papers.title: A dual-channel feature modulation network for simultaneous prediction of pressure and velocity field in thoracic aortic models
papers.abstract: Hemodynamic analysis of the thoracic aorta is fundamental to the diagnosis and prognostic assessment of cardiovascular diseases. Although traditional computational fluid dynamics provides high-fidelity results, the requirements for complex mesh generation and significant computational overhead currently preclude its integration into real-time clinical workflows. To address these limitations, this study presents the dual-channel feature modulation network (DCFM-Net), a lightweight point cloud-based deep learning framework designed for the simultaneous prediction of aortic pressure and velocity fields. The architecture incorporates a distance field (DF) and positional encoding to refine geometric boundary characterization and enhance the representation of high-frequency spatial features, respectively. Furthermore, a feature-wise linear modulation mechanism is utilized during the feature fusion stage to adaptively modulate local features based on global geometric context, while a dual-branch decoder facilitates joint physical field prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that DCFM-Net reconstructs three-dimensional flow fields within milliseconds, achieving average errors of 4.50% ± 0.90% for velocity and 3.49% ± 1.66% for pressure. This approach outperforms several baseline neural networks and significantly improves computational efficiency. To enhance model transparency, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method is employed for interpretability analysis. SHAP quantifies the contributions of spatial coordinates and DF features to reveal the network's feature-utilization patterns. These importance trends are consistent with the spatial characteristics of the predicted flow fields. Overall, the proposed method offers a substantial improvement in computational efficiency without compromising accuracy, representing a promising data-driven surrogate modeling technique for the rapid assessment of hemodynamics within controlled computational environments.

papers.title: Discontinuity-aware autoencoder for dimensionality reduction of shock-dominated supersonic flows
papers.abstract: Supersonic flows are characterized by strong non-stationarity and discontinuity arising from the coexistence of turbulent fluctuations and shock waves. Classical dimensionality reduction approaches exhibit inherent limitations in this regime. Linear methods such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) are constrained by the Kolmogorov barrier, while nonlinear autoencoder (AEs)-based manifolds (e.g., multilayer perceptron, MLP, and Kolmogorov–Arnold networks, KAN) rely on inherently smooth representations and, therefore, struggle to accurately resolve discontinuities. To address these challenges, a discontinuity-aware autoencoder (DAE) is proposed to better extract low-dimensional representations of shock-dominated flows. The method extends the KAN-based AE by incorporating learnable non-smooth basis functions into the spline-based activation functions, enabling the unified representation of both smooth and discontinuous flow features. The proposed approach is evaluated on the shock-dominated Burgers' equation, a supersonic square cylinder wake, and flow past cylinder arrays involving strong shock–shock and shock–vortex interactions. The results demonstrate that the DAE consistently outperforms POD, MLP-based, and KAN-based AEs in reconstruction accuracy while requiring fewer modes and parameters. This improvement is attributed to the ability of DAE to explicitly capture discontinuous features and preserve sharp gradients without Gibbs-type oscillations. These findings suggest that incorporating discontinuity-aware representations is essential for efficient dimensionality reduction and reduced-order modeling of shock-dominated systems and provide a physically consistent framework for data-driven modeling of compressible flows.

papers.title: Aerodynamic noise suppression of finite-length three cylinders in equilateral triangular arrangement via internal flow ventilation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms behind aerodynamic noise and control strategy in a configuration of finite-length three circular cylinders arranged in an equilateral triangle. Experiments were conducted in an acoustic wind tunnel at Reynolds numbers of (2.7–6.7) × 104, based on the diameter D of a single cylinder. The study first examines the effects of the spacing ratio L/D (=1.2–5.5) and the angle of incidence α (=0°–60°), where L is the cylinder center-to-center spacing. Results indicate that at α = 0°, the system exhibits high sensitivity to the spacing ratio, where a smaller spacing (L/D ≤ 2.0) generates strong mutual interference, a deflected gap flow, and a significantly increased Strouhal number (0.4–0.6). Furthermore, for each spacing ratio tested, maximum noise occurs when the incoming flow aligns with the three-cylinder axis of symmetry (α = 0°), and an angular deviation of 0°–60° effectively suppresses the overall noise level. To mitigate the intense tonal noise at α = 0°, a passive control method known as the internal flow ventilation (IFV) was applied. This approach achieves higher control efficiency at small spacing ratios (L/D ≤ 2.0). Further analyses using flow visualization and proper orthogonal decomposition reveal the underlying noise mechanism. An angular deviation of the three-cylinder arrangement disrupts the periodic alternating shedding of large-scale coherent structures, thereby weakening the dipole sound sources. Meanwhile, the IFV stabilizes the separating shear layers and delays their roll-up, inducing energy degradation and spatial fragmentation in the high-energy alternating vortex structures, which ultimately results in significant noise reduction.

papers.title: Memory effects in wave-induced microplastic transport
papers.abstract: Microplastics are transported by ocean surface waves in ways that cannot always be described by the Stokes drift of fluid parcels, and accurate modeling of this transport requires accounting for forces beyond linear drag. Existing models of microplastic transport often neglect the Basset–Boussinesq history force, effectively limiting their use to the smallest particle sizes. Here, we extend the applicability of models under the classical Maxey–Riley framework by implementing the history term with a multi-step integration scheme, allowing us to capture the transport of larger microplastics in linear surface waves of arbitrary depth. We quantify when the Basset–Boussinesq history force significantly affects microplastic transport by surface gravity waves, with both relative and absolute metrics, under the classical Maxey–Riley framework. We show that, under this framework, memory effects become the leading-order horizontal drag once S=St̂/γ exceeds S≈0.25, where St̂ is the density-independent Stokes number, and γ is the density ratio of the particle and the fluid. The corresponding critical St number is found to be a factor of about three smaller than that given by classical inertial estimates that neglect history effects. These results help provide regime maps that can be used as guidance for when history effects can be safely neglected. Our simulations also reveal that history effects significantly increase horizontal transport distances and alter orbit deformation of particle ensembles.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of performance enhancement in a vertical-axis wind turbine using genetic algorithm
papers.abstract: This study aims to improve the performance of a vertical-axis wind turbine (VAWT) by optimizing the airfoil shape using two-dimensional numerical simulations with a genetic algorithm (GA). We define the airfoil geometry using the parametric section method with 11 design variables. The optimization results show that two- and three-bladed wind turbines with optimized airfoils exhibit significantly higher torque coefficients than those with the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) 0021 airfoil, resulting in improvements of 14.1% and 28% in the power coefficient, respectively. A flow analysis of a two-bladed wind turbine reveals that the enhanced turbine performance at θ=90° in the optimized case is due to a notably lower pressure near the leading edge of the blade. It also suggests that this pressure reduction can be attributed to an increase in the velocity near the leading edge that is caused by a shift in the location of the stagnation point on the outer surface of the optimized blade, compared to the NACA 0021 blade. These findings demonstrate that airfoil optimization using a GA is an effective approach for improving the performance of straight-bladed VAWTs.

papers.title: Fractional Navier–Stokes equations from a hierarchical cascade: Derivation, exact analytical solutions, and comparison with turbulent pair-dispersion data
papers.abstract: Fractional Navier–Stokes equations have been postulated phenomenologically for decades to model anomalous transport, with the fractional order α fitted to data. We derive these equations as the formal continuum limit of a discrete hierarchical fluid parcel system with Riemann–Liouville dynamics, and prove that the piecewise-constant parcel field converges strongly in L2(0,T;L2(Ω)) to a weak solution of the fractional Navier–Stokes system. The temporal order is fixed by the cascade branching number through αk=2−2/(Nk+1), so that Nk=1, 2, and ∞ recover the classical Navier–Stokes limit (α=1), the Richardson regime (α=4/3), and wave transport (α→2). We obtain closed-form solutions for the fractional Stokes first problem, channel start-up, and Couette flow, verified against the classical limits at machine epsilon. An analytic mapping connects the parametric N-body velocity vk(θ)=2 sin 2θ to the channel Fourier amplitudes, presented as a mathematical construction rather than a physical mechanism. The binary-cascade exponent α=4/3 reproduces the direct numerical simulation (DNS)-confirmed ⟨r2⟩∝εt3 pair-dispersion law through the Richardson closure, with constant g=0.607 inside the DNS range [0.50, 0.70]; g enters through the Kolmogorov–Obukhov constant C2 and is not a free parameter. Nine independent superdiffusive measurements from DNS, spacecraft, and laboratory plasmas match the cascade-to-α map within uncertainties under a pre-specified χ2 test, presented as a comparison with the broader fractional transport class rather than direct validation of the momentum equation.

papers.title: Mineralogy impact on pore accessibility of shale nanopores and its implications on gas injection enhanced oil recovery: A molecular perspective
papers.abstract: In this work, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to explain the distinct behaviors of hydrocarbon retention and transport during gas injection enhanced oil recovery in clay-rich and carbonate-rich shales, as observed in small-angle neutron scattering and ultra-small-angle neutron scattering experiments. A series of MD simulations have been conducted to investigate the adsorption behaviors as well as transport mechanisms of methane and carbon dioxide (CO2) based cyclic injection in Permian shales. The simulations reveal that clay-rich shale rock tends to retain greater amount of heavy hydrocarbons due to the water blockage of pore throats caused by the presence of irreducible water adsorbed on clay surfaces. In contrast, carbonate-rich shale facilitates more efficient decane recovery during methane huff-n-puff. In general, CO2 demonstrates a higher sweeping efficiency than methane. The findings highlight the critical roles of pore size distribution, surface properties, and the impact of irreducible water in influencing hydrocarbon accessibility and removability. These insights advance the mechanistic understanding of gas injection processes in heterogeneous shale formations, guiding the development of optimal injection strategies and reservoir screening criteria for unconventional reservoirs.

papers.title: A study on shrinkage dynamics of a toroidal bubble rising in a surrounding fluid
papers.abstract: Dynamics of toroidal bubble shrinkage during its rise in a surrounding fluid enclosed in a vertical pipe is studied. Surrounding fluid entrapment and bubble breakup during its shrinkage are reported. The fluid entrapment and bubble breakup are influenced by Eötvös number (Eo), Galilei number (Ga), initial circulation (Γ), initial ring radius (R0), and viscosity ratio (μr). Regime maps of bubble shrinkage behavior on Ga–Eo, Γ−Eo, Γ−Ga, Eo−R0, and μr−Eo planes are presented. The entrapment and breakup are associated with low Eo and high Ga values. Necking of bubble and joining of inner entrapped fluid with the outer fluid by filling the necking region is found to be the mechanism behind the bubble breakup. For strong surface tension, entrapped fluid volume is almost the same for Ga greater than a critical value. The invariant bubble dynamics during the phase of bubble shrinkage for high Ga values makes the entrapped fluid volume independent of Ga. For a given bubble volume, a bubble with higher initial ring radius entraps larger fluid volume. The entrapped fluid volume decreases with an increase in initial toroid circulation. A lower bubble to surrounding fluid viscosity ratio promotes the breakup.

papers.title: Rheological and impedance analysis for in-line evaluation of the internal structure of carbon suspension
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal structure of conductive suspensions is crucial for controlling their rheological and electrochemical properties during the manufacturing process. However, conventional off-line measurements cannot fully capture the internal structural changes that occur within continuous processing lines. In this study, we propose an in-line evaluation method that combines rheological analysis and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to investigate the internal structure of graphite suspension in a pipe flow. The internal structural changes of the graphite suspension under flow conditions were evaluated through rheological and morphological analyses and numerical simulation. As the flow rate increased, the particles in the pipe were oriented along the flow direction. The EIS analysis showed that these internal structural changes altered conduction pathways, leading to distinct impedance responses at different electrode positions.

papers.title: The multi-region conservation-enhanced physics-informed neural network for solving shock waves
papers.abstract: Supersonic flow is characterized by strong nonlinear and multi-scale physical phenomena, such as shock waves. Despite their success in low-speed simulations, traditional physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) struggle with strong discontinuities in high-speed flows. Lacking effective constraints for local steep gradients, they suffer from reduced accuracy, numerical instability, and a heavy reliance on costly observational data. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a multi-region conservation-enhanced physics-informed neural network (MRCE-PINN), integrated with a pressure-based adaptive gradient guidance (APGG) strategy. This approach obviates the requirement for additional observational data by partitioning the computational domain into discrete sub-regions and embedding local integral conservation constraints of mass, momentum, and energy, thereby providing rigorous physical feedback for network optimization. Concurrently, the APGG strategy is employed to dynamically track high-gradient regions within the flow field to apply targeted constraints. The proposed method is validated under supersonic conditions through three benchmark cases: two-dimensional oblique shock waves, expansion waves, and conical models. Numerical results demonstrate that by strengthening local physical conservation, the method effectively compresses the thickness of the shock wave transition layer and suppresses numerical diffusion near wave fronts and geometric singularities. Comparative evaluations confirm that MRCE-PINN outperforms traditional PINN, conservative physics-informed neural networks, and physical information neural network embedded with multi-scale Fourier features in terms of shock-capturing sharpness, resolution of local flow features, and global prediction stability.

papers.title: Particle dynamics in Faraday wave-driven flow
papers.abstract: Resonant acoustic mixing (RAM) excites Faraday waves to mix complex, particle-laden flows. These surface waves are known to be coupled to the subsurface flow. However, no previous studies have investigated how the Faraday wave surface structure affects subsurface particle dynamics at particle–surface distances much larger than the viscous length scale. This study investigates particle dynamics during oscillatory flow with Faraday wave instability. Holography was used to track particle motion and compared to solutions of the Maxey–Riley equation for particle motion using both rigid and Womersley models for fluid motion. The Womersley model incorporated a characteristic wavenumber to quantify the influence of surface waves on the fluid motion. Measured particle settling velocity was shown to decrease as acceleration increased because higher amplitude oscillation particles travel greater distances through their own wake, thus increasing the Basset force contributions. The particle displacement amplitude normalized by the container displacement amplitude was shown to increase with acceleration. Analysis indicated that the increase in particle displacement amplitude was due to an increase in the work done by the surface on a particle for an unstable surface. The changing surface curvature creates a pressure perturbation from the capillary pressure. The coupling between surface deformation and multiscale energy redistribution is extended here to include work on particles. This study quantitatively links subsurface particle dynamics with surface waves' behavior and addresses the relative force contributions for surface waves on a particle.

papers.title: Field-effect control of ionic transport in power-law fluids in soft nanochannels
papers.abstract: Soft nanochannels have attracted considerable attention in micro-/nanofluidic applications due to their unique capability for regulating ion transport. However, the coupling mechanism between the rheological behavior of non-Newtonian fluids and electrokinetic transport, particularly under active field-effect transistor regulation, remains insufficiently understood. In this study, a coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck and Navier–Stokes numerical model was developed for polyelectrolyte layer (PEL)-functionalized soft nanochannels to systematically investigate the electrokinetic transport characteristics of power-law fluids under field-effect control. The results demonstrate that negative gate voltages significantly enhance electro-osmotic flow (EOF), ionic current, and cation selectivity compared with positive gate voltages. As the PEL charge density increases, cation selectivity is continuously strengthened, while both EOF velocity and ionic current under negative gate voltage significantly increase. For instance, at a power-law index of 0.8, a PEL thickness of 5 nm, and a gate voltage of −50 V, increasing the PEL charge density from 10 to 100 mol/m3 enhances the EOF velocity by approximately 476%, the ionic current by 144%, and the cation selectivity coefficient by 10%. In contrast, the influence of PEL thickness exhibits a more complex behavior. Increasing the PEL thickness generally promotes ionic current while simultaneously reducing ion selectivity, whereas the EOF velocity displays a non-monotonic dependence on PEL thickness. These findings reveal that the interplay between gate-induced charge regulation and fluid rheology governs ion transport in soft nanochannels, providing fundamental insights for the precise and tunable manipulation of electrokinetic transport in nanofluidic systems.

papers.title: Waveform shaping controls residual energy and satellite breakup in drop-on-demand jetting
papers.abstract: Satellite droplets in drop-on-demand (DOD) jetting typically originate from excessive ligament stretching followed by capillary-driven necking and secondary breakup, and can be further promoted by post-actuation meniscus rebound. Here, we show that introducing a short pull-back-induced pressure recovery (pull-back) segment into the driving waveform provides an effective route to control ligament dynamics and suppress satellite formation for a high-viscosity ink (μ = 0.0198 Pa s) ejected from a 20 μm nozzle. High-speed imaging reveals that the pull-back waveform shortens the trailing ligament and attenuates post-ejection meniscus recoil, thereby reducing secondary pinch-off and satellite droplets. Quantitatively, across N=20 steady jetting events, the satellite-free fraction increases from 0% (0/20) for the baseline waveform to 95% (19/20) with pull-back-induced pressure recovery, corresponding to a decrease in satellite occurrence probability from 100% to 5%. Meanwhile, jetting repeatability improves, with the relative velocity fluctuation decreasing from 1.97% to 1.27%. A dimensionless interpretation indicates that the optimized waveform shifts the dynamics away from an inertia-dominated stretching regime (reduced Re and We) while keeping the actuation short compared with the inertio-capillary relaxation time, tp<tσ. These results support a mechanistic picture in which pull-back-induced pressure recovery damps meniscus recoil and limits ligament extension, and they provide a physics-based basis for waveform design to mitigate secondary breakup and satellite formation in viscous, low-Z DOD jetting.

papers.title: Light-field-aware physics-informed learning for super-resolved volumetric flow reconstruction from sparse light field particle image velocimetry measurements
papers.abstract: Light field particle image velocimetry (LF-PIV) enables single-camera volumetric flow measurement, but its performance is limited by low spatial resolution and large depth-wise velocity uncertainty. This study proposes a LF-aware physics-informed neural network (LF-PINN) for super-resolved flow reconstructions from sparse LF-PIV measurements. Building on standard PINNs, which enforce governing equations during learning, the proposed method further incorporates LF imaging characteristics into the physics-informed framework to improve the reconstruction accuracy. This is achieved by introducing a degradation model and a reliability-weighted learning strategy that account for the spatial averaging effect and the anisotropic velocity uncertainty inherent in LF-PIV measurements. Numerical tests on forced isotropic turbulence demonstrate that LF-PINN effectively corrects depth-wise velocity errors, reducing the relative error of the depth-wise velocity component to below 10% when initial measurement errors reach 20%. Incorporating pressure information further enhances flow reconstruction accuracy, reducing the root mean square divergence of the flow field by 22%. Compared with standard PINN formulations and a proper orthogonal decomposition-based interpolation method, LF-PINN achieves superior performance in both spatial and temporal super-resolution reconstruction from sparse measurements. Fine-scale vortical structures and turbulence statistics are recovered with higher fidelity. Experimental measurements of the wake behind a circular cylinder further show that LF-PINN produces clearer wake structures and velocity profiles that are in better consistence with planar-PIV references. These results demonstrate that embedding LF imaging characteristics into physics-informed learning provides an effective route toward super-resolved and physically consistent volumetric flow reconstruction.

papers.title: Unsteady modulation mechanism of bogie fairing on aerodynamic loads and flow field of high-speed trains under multiple yaw angles
papers.abstract: The bogie fairing is a key component governing the aerodynamic performance and flow-field stability of high-speed trains, with its influence pronounced under crosswind conditions. However, its unsteady modulation of aerodynamic loads and flow-field evolution across multiple yaw angles remains insufficiently clarified. In this study, the improved delayed detached-eddy simulation is employed to investigate how bogie fairing configurations affect the unsteady aerodynamic response and flow-field evolution of a high-speed train. Hilbert–Huang transform results show that, with increasing yaw angle, the band energy of the lateral force rises overall as the dominant frequency range broadens and the dominant frequency components vary more frequently over time. At 15°, an instantaneous-frequency standard deviation of 10.49 and a mid-frequency dwell ratio of 0.47 indicate that the dominant response remains concentrated in a narrow mid-frequency band, corresponding to an organized separated-shear-layer oscillation before strongly wake-dominated unsteadiness develops. The bogie fairing significantly reduces the bottom pressure fluctuation on the head car, with the root mean square pressure fluctuation decreasing by 67.66%, and shifts the local pressure excitation toward a lower dominant frequency. Meanwhile, the fairing modifies wake recirculation and leeward-side velocity non-uniformity, with the maximum increase in velocity standard deviation in the upper car-body region reaching 56.30%. The bogie fairing shortens the dominant periods of velocity and vorticity, reflecting shorter-period fluctuations and less persistent vortical structures. Overall, this study clarifies how bogie fairings modulate unsteady aerodynamic loads and flow fields over multiple yaw angles, providing quantitative guidance for fairing design and aerodynamic safety evaluation under crosswinds.

papers.title: Visualizations and fluctuation measurements of the spanwise unsteady motions over a backward-facing step under periodic perturbations
papers.abstract: The spanwise unsteady characteristics induced by the development of large-scale vortex structures along the shear layer over a backward-facing step with Re=9630 was investigated. The flow was perturbed periodically using a synthetic jet at separation. Structures were visualized from top and side views using a smoke-wire, while the induced velocity fluctuations were measured with a movable spanwise hot-wire sensor array. Comparisons were made for perturbation frequency varying from StA=fAH/Uo=0.04 to 0.39, and StA=0.22 was found to be the optimal frequency, as forming spanwise heterogeneous three-dimensional shedding structures with the maximum turbulent kinetic energy. In optimal cases, structures were paired in a staggered span-wise order, causing a doubling period. Structures became smaller and showed weaker interactions under superoptimal perturbation, while a large-scale two-dimensional low-speed bubble was observed at suboptimal perturbation, StA=0.04.

papers.title: Mechanisms of wettability-controlled multiphase flow in nanoporous media: A coupled molecular dynamics and lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Flow mechanisms in nanoporous media are crucial for improving shale and tight oil recovery. Fluid transport in nanoporous media cannot be accurately described using conventional continuum-based models because strong fluid–solid interactions induce interfacial slip and noncontinuum effects. In this study, to address this challenge, a multiscale coupling framework integrating molecular dynamics (MD) and the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) was developed to investigate oil–water two-phase flow in nanoscale pores. MD simulations were employed to quantify slip behavior at solid–fluid interfaces under different wettability conditions. The resulting slip lengths were incorporated into LBM as wettability-dependent boundary conditions, enabling accurate representation of nanoscale interfacial effects. Comparisons between conventional LBM and the coupled MD-LBM model demonstrated that the proposed framework captures noncontinuum flow behavior more effectively. A complex nanoporous medium was then constructed to analyze phase distribution, saturation evolution, and recovery performance under various wettability configurations. Results show that wettability significantly influences both microscopic phase arrangement and macroscopic transport efficiency. Water-wet conditions favor continuous water pathways, whereas oil-wet surfaces enhance oil mobility. Among three mixed wettability patterns: water-wet to oil-wet transition, oil-wet to water-wet transition, and random distribution—the random configuration yields the highest recovery factor. This improvement results from spatial wettability heterogeneity, which promotes multipath flow networks and optimizes the interplay among capillary forces, viscous forces, and interfacial effects. The proposed multiscale framework provides new insights into wettability-controlled transport under nanoscale confinement and offers guidance for enhanced recovery and subsurface fluid management in unconventional reservoirs.

papers.title: Influence of different wake flow patterns behind a square cylinder on the evolution of turbulent structures in a developing boundary layer
papers.abstract: This work presents a direct numerical simulation study of turbulent boundary-layer disturbance and reorganization induced by a square cylinder at gap ratios G/D = 0.0 and 2.0. The cylinder substantially modifies both upstream flow organization and downstream development, with the strength of these effects strongly dependent on the gap ratio. Upstream of the cylinder, disturbance intensity increases as the flow approaches the cylinder and the wall, and its streamwise influence extends further in near-wall regions. The downstream recovery of the boundary layer is characterized by pronounced oscillatory dynamics. This oscillatory behavior represents the dominant mechanism governing flow reorganization and is closely coupled with coherent-structure evolution, including hairpin vortex breakdown, secondary vortex regeneration, and vortex merging. As the flow evolves, velocity differences develop multiple secondary peaks that merge and migrate toward higher wall-normal positions with increasing amplitude. Fluctuation intensity exhibits cyclic attenuation and amplification, while structural length scales undergo significant modulation, accompanied by multiple near-wall energy peaks within the inner layer. At the larger gap ratio, enhanced three-dimensional interactions intensify vortex fragmentation and structural complexity. Throughout the oscillatory recovery process, the boundary-layer thickness increases continuously, with a stronger thickening effect at G/D = 2.0, and energetic structures shift toward higher wall-normal regions.

papers.title: A stabilized two-fluid non-equilibrium method for collocated grids using momentum interpolation and flux reconstruction
papers.abstract: Collocated grids can induce pressure–velocity decoupling due to non-compact discretization stencils. The interpretation of non-equilibrium two-phase dynamics on collocated grids depends critically on how the modeled momentum is transferred between cell centers and conservative face fluxes. This study proposes a methodology for the two-fluid non-equilibrium model based on center-to-face momentum interpolation and face-to-center full-flux reconstruction. The pseudo-momentum formulation relates the complete modeled momentum balance between cell centers and conservative face fluxes and thereby reduces checkerboard pressure modes and spurious cell-centered velocity oscillations. The benchmark sequence relates the mechanism to conservative phase-boundary transport, transient inertia-gravity exchange, gravity-driven front propagation, mechanical non-equilibrium, and boiling phenomena. The results indicate that the proposed complete formulation improves the consistency of the pressure field, phasic velocities, void fraction, and interfacial momentum response in resolved non-equilibrium dynamics, while the boiling and drag behaviors remain governed by the underlying constitutive models. This work provides a stable, accurate, and extensible approach for simulating two-phase flows with non-equilibrium and phase change.

papers.title: Buoyant plume interaction with ceiling smoke layer and thermal feedback mechanisms of spill fires in confined space
papers.abstract: Confined spill fires are governed by the coupled evolution of liquid fuel spreading, buoyant plume development, ceiling smoke layer formation, and thermal feedback redistribution. This study experimentally investigated n-heptane spill fires in a 3 × 3 × 4 m3 confined space at fuel discharge rates of 5.8–12.6 g/s, focusing on the scaling of the maximum centerline temperature rise and the interaction between the buoyant plume and the ceiling smoke layer. The maximum flame temperature rise followed a piecewise relationship with hHQ̇*. When hHQ̇*<1.2, the temperature rise decreases with height following a negative power law, corresponding to a flame and plume-controlled region. When hHQ̇*≥1.2, the temperature rise approaches a plateau, indicating the transition to a ceiling smoke layer-controlled region. This transition arises from confinement-modified plume entrainment, vertical flame stretching, hot gas accumulation, and thermal stratification beneath the ceiling. Heat transfer analysis further shows that the dominant feedback mode shifts from convection-influenced feedback in the early stage to radiation-dominated feedback once the flame, smoke layer, and heated walls all contribute to radiative exchange. At peak burning, radiative feedback accounts for approximately 72% of the total feedback, while the fuel absorbs only about 18%. These findings provide a fluid physics interpretation of the regime transition and thermal feedback redistribution in confined spill fires.

papers.title: Propagation characteristics of detonation waves in a semi-confined straight channel with transverse concentration gradients
papers.abstract: This study uses the OpenFOAM platform to simulate detonation wave propagation in semi-confined straight channels with transverse concentration gradients. The effects of gradient magnitude and gradient direction on lateral expansion, wave system evolution, cellular structure, and propagation distance are examined. The results show that a small concentration gradient favors stable propagation, because reflected waves can detach from the inert gas interface and regenerate transverse waves on the detonation front. As the gradient increases, incomplete reaction behind the wave becomes more severe, local decoupling is more likely to occur, and the detonation wave quenches over a shorter distance. The direction of the concentration gradient plays a decisive role. For a negative concentration gradient, reflected waves tend to move downward and interact with the wall or transverse waves, which helps recover the cellular structure and extend the propagation distance. For a positive concentration gradient, reflected wave development near the inert gas interface is weakened, and the propagation distance is generally shorter. However, when the positive gradient is large, the wavefront inclines strongly toward the bottom wall. This promotes local convergence of transverse waves and reflected waves, forming high-temperature and high-pressure regions that reinforce the detonation structure. As a result, the propagation distance under a large positive gradient can exceed that under the corresponding negative gradient. These findings clarify how transverse concentration gradient direction controls detonation lateral expansion and provide guidance for rotating detonation combustor design and explosion safety in non-uniform leakage environments.

papers.title: Shear-triggered coalescence forecasts mixing-induced destabilization of particle-stabilized emulsions
papers.abstract: In the present study, we demonstrate that measurements of coalescence time between two droplets using a cantilevered-capillary force apparatus (CCFA) can forecast the rate of phase separation in emulsions. In our previous study with a CCFA, we revealed that individual droplets stabilized by cellulose nanocrystals in a 10 mM NaCl solution can exhibit a nearly tenfold increase in the probability of coalescence under shearing collisions as compared to head-on collisions. Here, we employed the same materials to prepare emulsions and compare the rate of phase separation under two conditions: at rest or under gentle mixing. We observed that emulsions stabilized by cellulose nanocrystals also show an approximately 30-fold increase in the rate of phase separation under gentle mixing, as compared to when stored at rest. Furthermore, we found that the enhanced phase separation only occurred at the intermediate concentration of 10 mM NaCl (and not at 2.5 mM or ≥16 mM), just as seen in the previous study with a CCFA. We were able to conclude that the enhanced rate of phase separation only occurs at intermediate mixing speeds and is not attributable to simple differences in average coalescence time, and is unlikely to be caused by the non-Newtonian rheology of the suspending phase. This work represents an important step forward in our ability to bridge mechanistic studies of emulsions at the microscale to the macroscopic phenomena in emulsions.

papers.title: Erratum: “Aerodynamic response of flapping wings to brief gust perturbations” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 061909 (2026)]
Effect of isolator configuration on shock train motion characteristics under dynamic backpressure conditions
papers.abstract: This study systematically investigates the impact of geometric configuration on shock train dynamics within supersonic isolators under dynamic backpressure conditions. Numerical simulations elucidate the governing roles of cavity-induced background waves and recirculation zones in modulating these unsteady flow structures. Key findings indicate that the cavity configuration exhibits a distinct “residence-jump” motion, characterized by alternating phases of shock stabilization (“residence”) and rapid upstream propagation (“jump”). During the backpressure reduction phase, a hysteresis mechanism is identified: the leading shock forms a Mach disk with bistable behavior where the flow field prioritizes adaptive morphological adjustments over global displacement to respond to pressure variations. Furthermore, the results clarify that while the final shock equilibrium position depends solely on backpressure magnitude and isolator geometry, a higher backpressure change rate (rp) significantly amplifies flow reconstruction time and enhances the hysteresis effect, particularly in cavity-configured isolators. These findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for the design and flow control of hypersonic engine isolators under high-speed dynamic conditions.

papers.title: Disturbance penetration in Poiseuille flow over sinusoidal and triangular wavy walls
papers.abstract: Disturbance penetration in pressure-driven channel flow over corrugated walls has been studied extensively for smooth sinusoidal geometries, whereas corresponding analyses for piecewise-linear triangular profiles remain limited. In the present study, linear perturbation analysis and finite-volume simulations are used to examine the wall-normal disturbance structure and to quantify the penetration depth Pv under identical amplitude and wavelength conditions. For sinusoidal walls, the perturbation results agree well with earlier theoretical and experimental studies, as well as with the present finite-volume simulations. The results show that disturbance penetration is governed by both the viscous length scale θ and the geometric parameter α. Under otherwise identical conditions, triangular walls generally produce weaker penetration than sinusoidal walls, with the difference becoming more pronounced in deeper channels. Over the parameter range considered here, the penetration-depth data follow an approximate relation of the form Pv∼C θ1/3 within selected intermediate ranges of θ. This behavior is most evident for deep-channel configurations, while the prefactor C depends on wall shape and channel confinement.

papers.title: Roughness-sublayer flows over building arrays with uniform and non-uniform heights: A wind tunnel study
papers.abstract: Elucidating the dynamics in the roughness sublayer (RSL) of a city is crucial for assessing street-level turbulence, ventilation, and heat removal over heterogeneous urban morphology. Although building-height variability has been examined in urban-canopy studies, its role in regulating RSL turbulence and ventilation under controlled uniform- and non-uniform-height configurations still needs further quantification. In this paper, we conduct a wind tunnel investigation using LEGO® bricks to fabricate building arrays of both uniform (h, 2h, 3h, 4h) and non-uniform (3h + 2h, 4h + 2h) heights. Here, h is the height of a LEGO brick. Hot-wire anemometry is employed to measure mean wind speed, turbulence statistics, boundary-layer parameters, turbulent length scale, and ventilation efficiency. Results show that height heterogeneity amplifies turbulence and vertical momentum flux, thereby enhancing the mixing within RSLs. The RSLs over non-uniform-height configurations are higher than their uniform-height counterparts, underscoring the critical role of building height variability. Across all the configurations tested, RSL turbulent length scales deviate significantly from classical predictions, reflecting local building-induced disturbance and distinct turbulence generation mechanisms. A tight correlation between the square root of the drag coefficient Cd 1/2 and ventilation efficiency is found that offers a reliable estimate for RSL ventilation in urban environments. These findings demonstrate the important role of building heterogeneity in RSL dynamics and reveal deviations from classical scaling in response to heterogeneous urban surfaces. This improved understanding advances the parameterization of RSL dynamics as well as sheds light on the transport mechanism, effectuating ventilation strategies in complex, heterogeneous built environments.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation of turbulent flow and coherent structures over rotated random-height building arrays
papers.abstract: Urban canopy flows exhibit complex interactions between geometric heterogeneity and turbulent organization, posing challenges for air-quality, ventilation, and low-altitude urban-flow prediction. While canonical studies have characterized idealized building arrays, realistic urban morphologies often involve building-height variability (H/3≤h≤H) and variable orientations relative to prevailing winds, whose combined effects remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigates turbulent flow over rotated building arrays with randomly sampled heights at 0°, 15°, 30°, and 45° using large-eddy simulations, with single-cube validation and array-level grid-refinement checks. A balanced rotation–height matrix retains the same sampled height layouts across orientations, allowing trends associated with the rotation-induced projected-blockage change to be distinguished from realization-dependent variability. Mean velocity and wake-deficit fields show that local height contrast influences passage acceleration and channeling flows between buildings, whereas array rotation induces wake deflection, skewness, and wake-deficit organization. Across the 16 rotation–height cases, array rotation increases projected frontal blockage, domain-averaged turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), and low-to-intermediate spanwise spectral energy. The transition from θ = 30° to 45° separates wake-deficit and turbulence responses: wake-deficit metrics decrease or saturate in several realizations, whereas TKE and transport-related quantities continue to increase. A projected-blockage-adjusted comparison relates the remaining TKE response to the spanwise gradient of turbulent streamwise-momentum transport. Local analyses show that height realization modulates wake asymmetry and turbulence redistribution. These results support a multiscale interpretation in which the rotation-induced projected-blockage response is associated with canopy-scale wake organization and turbulence response, whereas height arrangement and spanwise exchange remain important for local recovery.

papers.title: Bundle size selection in dynamic elastocapillary aggregation of elastic fins
papers.abstract: Elastocapillary aggregation is studied under quasi-static conditions, yet many applications involve dynamic withdrawal from a liquid bath. Here, we show that withdrawal speed governs bundle formation in parallel elastic fin arrays. At low speeds, bundle size is independent of withdrawal speed. At higher speeds, a dynamic meniscus amplifies capillary forces and promotes larger bundles. At the highest speeds, the bundle size saturates at an upper limit set by the sample design. We introduce the dry length of formed bundles as a proxy for the dynamic meniscus height and develop a theoretical model predicting the equilibrium bundle size through an energy balance. The resulting scaling collapses all experimental data, establishing withdrawal speed as a tunable parameter for elastocapillary aggregation.

papers.title: A second-order two-step chemical reaction model for detonation numerical simulation
papers.abstract: A second-order two-step chemical reaction model is presented, whose ignition delay time is of pressure-dependence. This model is well validated by the ignition delay time, one-dimensional detonation, and two-dimensional cellular detonation. This model can be used in detonation numerical simulations, especially in the cases of detonation interaction with expansion waves and detonation diffraction in open space.

papers.title: Destabilizing effects of oxidation-driven mass injection on the second mode of high-speed flows under conjugate heat transfer
papers.abstract: Flow stability in high-speed boundary layers is critically influenced by high-temperature gas effects and surface reactions occurring on thermal protection materials. In this study, linear stability theory has been employed to investigate the effects of wall catalysis and ablation on flow stability during unsteady flow-solid conjugate heat transfer over a blunt cone with a Mach number of 15.99. The key physical insight is that oxidation-driven mass injection is the primary mechanism destabilizing the second-mode disturbance. Specifically, the oxidation reaction injects mass at the wall, thickening the boundary layer and shifting the second mode to a lower frequency with an enhanced growth rate, which expands the unstable region upstream. In contrast, a temporal increase in wall temperature, regardless of whether catalysis or ablation occurs, gradually stabilizes the second mode by lowering its frequency and reducing its growth rate. Boundary conditions for mass fraction and velocity perturbations are found to have negligible influence on the linear stability theory results.

papers.title: A primary breakup model for pressure-swirl nozzles based on linear stability analysis
papers.abstract: This study investigates the primary breakup of a rotating annular liquid film issuing from a pressure-swirl nozzle. A dispersion relation is derived within the framework of linear stability theory by simultaneously accounting for liquid-film rotation and liquid viscosity. Based on the resulting instability characteristics, a Primary Fluctuation Breakup Model (PFBM) is developed to predict the breakup length and the Sauter mean diameter (SMD) during primary breakup. The proposed model is evaluated against a water/pressure-swirl-nozzle experimental dataset covering five injection-pressure conditions and shows improved predictive performance compared with the classical Linearized Instability Sheet Atomization model under the investigated conditions. Formulated in terms of dimensionless parameters, the PFBM provides a general physics-based framework for describing dynamically similar primary-breakup processes of rotating annular liquid films. A parametric study is then performed to examine the effects of swirl intensity, liquid Weber number, liquid Reynolds number, and gas-to-liquid velocity ratio on the instability characteristics and breakup behavior. The results show that increasing swirl intensity and Weber number enhances disturbance growth, shortens the breakup length, and increases the SMD during primary breakup. The Reynolds number mainly influences breakup through viscous damping, especially in the low-Reynolds-number regime, whereas the gas-to-liquid velocity ratio has a non-monotonic effect through interfacial aerodynamic shear. These results establish a clear physical link between operating conditions, dominant instability characteristics, and primary-breakup outcomes and provide a theoretical basis for improving the design and performance of pressure-swirl atomizers.

papers.title: Viscous folding of non-Newtonian micro-threads in diverging microchannels
papers.abstract: Viscous folding offers significant application value across fields such as materials science, biomedicine, and chemical synthesis. While viscous folding has been extensively characterized for Newtonian fluids, systematic investigations on the folding of non-Newtonian fluids remain limited. In this work, we experimentally studied the viscous folding dynamics of non-Newtonian threads in diverging microchannels. We investigated the effects of non-Newtonian fluid flow rate Q1 and viscosity ratio χ, as well as diverging channel angle α and width Wd, on thread morphology and geometric characteristics. The results reveal that the shear-thinning behavior of non-Newtonian fluids results in six distinct morphologies. The folding frequency f scales linearly with characteristic shear rate γ for Newtonian fluids but follows a power-law relationship f=0.581γ0.551 for 1 wt. % polyethylene oxide aqueous solution (PEO) and f=0.265γ0.512 for 2 wt. % PEO. The dimensionless thread diameter ε increases with both flow rate ratios φ and χ, obeying ε=(φ/2)0.32 for 1 wt. % PEO, ε=(φ/2)0.28 for 2 wt. % PEO, and ε=(φ/2)0.19 for 3 wt. % PEO. The envelope width for 2 wt. % PEO is approximately twice that for 1 wt. % PEO. The folding initiation distance for 2 wt. % PEO is 80.96% larger than that for 1 wt. % PEO at Q1 = 10 μl/h and φ = 1/12. Expanding α or Wd destabilizes the flow and hinders the formation of stable viscous folding. The quantitative findings of this study provide comprehensive guidance for non-Newtonian viscous folding.

papers.title: Accurate particle three-dimensional diagnostic in noisy combustion environments through holographic similarity analysis
papers.abstract: In situ particle characterization is crucial for experimentally evaluating multiphase flow systems, where digital holography offers unique three-dimensional diagnostics. However, reliable particle localization remains challenging under strong optical noise encountered in practical environments. This study introduces a similarity-driven autofocusing framework that reformulates depth sensing by leveraging inter-particle holographic similarity, quantified by mutual information (MI), as a robust, collective focus criterion. Through systematic benchmarking against seven conventional algorithms, MI demonstrates superior localization accuracy under diverse noise conditions (Gaussian, Speckle, and Salt and Pepper noise at signal-to-noise ratio ∼ 10 dB). The core innovation lies in the first application of MI to establish a noise-immune focus signature from correlated particle-pair propagation. Experimental validation on noisy holograms of combusting metal particles confirms the method's efficacy. This work bridges information theory and computational optics, establishing a new approach for reliable particle tracking in combustion diagnostics, aerospace propulsion, and industrial spray characterization.

papers.title: Robust numerical calculation of Lyapunov exponents for chaotic bubble dynamics
papers.abstract: Bubble dynamics is highly nonlinear and can exhibit complex behaviors, including transitions to chaos. Lyapunov exponents provide a standard way to characterize such dynamics by quantifying sensitivity to initial conditions. It can also be used as a practical metric for classifying chaotic and non-chaotic dynamical regimes. In acoustic cavitation, Lyapunov exponents are typically computed numerically from simulated radius–time traces or acoustic emissions. However, numerical algorithms commonly used for this purpose become numerically unstable in the strongly nonlinear, high-amplitude regime, limiting their reliability for identifying chaotic states. To address this limitation, we present a robust algorithm based on the Benettin–QR method, which combines tangent-space propagation with QR re-orthonormalization and incorporates analytical Jacobians derived for canonical bubble models, including the Rayleigh–Plesset, Keller–Miksis, and Gilmore equations. Benchmarking against established numerical approaches, together with verification on the Lorenz system, shows that the proposed method is numerically stable and can estimate exponent estimates across broad parameter ranges and complex bubble dynamics regimes. These results establish the approach as a reliable tool for quantifying and classifying chaotic behavior in nonlinear bubble dynamics.

papers.title: Performance characterization and kinetic analysis of intake for an atmosphere-breathing electric propulsion system with the direct simulation Monte Carlo method
papers.abstract: Atmosphere-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) systems utilize rarefied atmospheric particles as propellant for long-duration ultra-low Earth orbit (ULEO) missions. The internal flow within an ABEP intake operates in the free molecular to transitional regime, where gas–surface interactions govern particle transport and compression, yet the coupled effects of flow misalignment and wall accommodation on the underlying kinetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study presents a direct simulation Monte Carlo investigation into the rarefied gas dynamics of a three-stage ducted parabolic intake, focusing on the physical mechanisms by which the freestream incidence angle and the wall accommodation coefficient (σ) control particle collection and compression. A key finding is the discovery of an accommodation coefficient reversal: in contrast to simple chamber-only configurations where increasing σ enhances compression, the presence of an inlet duct causes both collection efficiency and compression ratio to decrease monotonically with σ. This reversal is shown to arise from cumulative energy dissipation through multiple diffuse reflections within the inlet duct, which randomizes particle momentum and disrupts the specular reflection-based parabolic focusing mechanism. The analysis further reveals that at lower altitudes (∼150 km), where the outlet-tube Knudsen number approaches the transitional regime, Knudsen layer formation adjacent to the tube wall introduces an additional kinetic mechanism that amplifies the σ-sensitivity through near-wall backflow of thermalized particles. These findings establish that intake performance in the ULEO altitude band is governed by the interplay between geometric focusing, gas–surface accommodation, and Knudsen layer-modified transport—phenomena that are fundamentally characteristic of confined rarefied gas flows. Although the intake performance decreases with increasing altitude, a feasibility analysis for thrust–drag balance indicates a viable operational window between 150 and 250 km altitude, where the ABEP system can theoretically achieve a positive thrust-to-drag ratio. The study provides insights into the critical design factors for successful ABEP system operation and identifies key areas for future research.

papers.title: Linear stability of plane Couette–Poiseuille flow with slip boundary conditions
papers.abstract: We present a linear stability analysis of plane Couette–Poiseuille flow bounded by walls coated with superhydrophobic materials. The classical slip boundary conditions based on the Navier model are applied to the wall surfaces. We investigate flow stability under symmetric (both walls slipping) and asymmetric (one wall slipping) configurations and introduce a generalized boundary condition to continuously map the transition between these two cases. For symmetric configurations, increasing slip length strongly stabilizes the flow, leading to higher critical Reynolds numbers and larger cutoff angles. In contrast, asymmetric configurations exhibit reduced critical Reynolds numbers and distinct cutoff behavior, indicating that slip may promote instability rather than suppress it. The generalized condition further clarifies how stability properties evolve as the degree of asymmetry increases. Overall, the results conclusively show that slip length does not universally stabilize shear flows, emphasizing the critical role of boundary configuration.

papers.title: Experimental study on vortex-induced vibration suppression of straight-fin helical strakes and traditional continuous helical strakes
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) critically accelerates cumulative fatigue failure in marine risers. Traditional helical strakes effectively suppress VIV but induce substantial drag penalties and pose manufacturing challenges due to their complex three-dimensional structure. To address these limitations, a new type of straight-fin helical strake was proposed in this study to balance VIV suppression, drag penalty, and ease of manufacturing. Experimental investigations compared the VIV response of a cylinder with both strake types and without strakes. Hydrodynamic coefficients were calculated using the least squares method based on the energy competition model, and a linear drag prediction model was proposed to quantitatively correlate the drag coefficient with vibration amplitude. The experimental results showed that both strake types provide effective VIV suppression, reducing the excitation coefficient CEY to near-zero under most conditions and narrowing the variation of the added mass coefficient Cmey. Notably, the proposed straight-fin helical strake with a pitch of 17.5D (D is the cylinder diameter) matches the VIV suppression performance of conventional designs. Crucially, it exhibits a better hydrodynamic efficiency, characterized by a lower drag coefficient CD and baseline drag coefficient CD0 within the proposed drag model. The suppression performance of the straight-fin configuration exhibits a sensitivity to the pitch, with the frequency lock-in phenomenon eliminated exclusively at higher pitch. This study validates the 17.5D-pitch straight-fin helical strake as a promising alternative for deep-sea riser applications, offering comparable VIV suppression efficiency alongside a reduced drag penalty.

papers.title: Co-flow jet control for separation-induced noise reduction of an airfoil at high angles of attack
papers.abstract: Large eddy simulation coupled with the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings acoustic analogy is employed to investigate the effects of a co-flow jet (CFJ) on the separation-induced noise of a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 airfoil at high angles of attack (12°–16°) and a chord-based Reynolds number of 4×105. Aerodynamically, the CFJ effectively suppresses massive flow separation, significantly elevating the equivalent lift-to-drag ratio from approximately 3 to 44. Acoustically, an angle-of-attack-dependent optimal CFJ actuation mitigates separation-induced noise across the entire frequency spectrum, achieving a maximum overall sound pressure level reduction of up to 15.39 dB. Spectral and coherence analyses demonstrate that optimal actuation globally curtails both the wall-to-far-field pressure coherence and the spanwise coherence length; conversely, under-actuation anomalously amplifies these coherences, leading to an enhancement in high-frequency noise (St ≈ 4–36). Flow-field and modal analyses further elucidate the underlying mechanisms: optimal control physically fragments highly coherent two-dimensional vortices into decorrelated three-dimensional small-scale vortical structures, forcing the turbulent energy to transition into a multi-mode cascade, thereby degrading the radiation efficiency of the dipoles. Furthermore, dynamic mode decomposition results reveal that over-actuation generates intense local shear, re-amplifying Kelvin–Helmholtz instability wave packets and triggering new highly coherent structures, ultimately resulting in the degradation of noise-reduction efficacy.

papers.title: Fluid–structure interaction and scaling laws for deterministic encapsulation of hyperelastic cells in microfluidic droplets
papers.abstract: The precise encapsulation of deformable particles in multiphase flows involves complex transient fluid–structure interactions and topological interfacial changes. In the context of single-cell analysis, a numerical framework that couples the Cahn–Hilliard phase-field model with the arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian method is employed to investigate the dynamics of deformable cell encapsulation in flow-focusing microchannels. By resolving the coupling between the hyperelastic cell, carrier fluid, and evolving interface, we propose a dimensionless scaling law to quantitatively predict the operational spatial window for deterministic encapsulation. Furthermore, the physical presence of cells modulates the droplet generation flow regime via a “geometric blockage effect,” shifting the transition boundary from the squeezing to the dripping regime toward lower flow rate ratios. The droplet generation period demonstrates a non-monotonic dependence on the cell blockage ratio Γ, which induces a competitive mechanism between shear enhancement and hydraulic resistance and consequently leads to a hydrodynamic balance at Γ≈0.32 under the parameters we simulated. Finally, we find that while droplet periodicity is robust to variations in cell stiffness, the transient stress field within the cell is highly sensitive, particularly during the capillary pinch-off singularity. This work clarifies the fundamental interaction between hyperelastic cells and multiphase flows and provides helpful guidelines for optimizing cell encapsulation systems.

papers.title: Non-Newtonian diffusion and seepage channel evolution of graphene oxide-modified cement grout in freeze–thaw fractured rock masses
papers.abstract: Grouting reinforcement of rock strata is a key technical measure for groundwater control and safe mining operations in cold-region mines. To elucidate the intrinsic relationship among grout rheology, fracture propagation, and seepage behavior of the consolidated body under freeze–thaw (F–T) conditions, true triaxial grouting experiments were conducted on rock masses subjected to different degrees of F–T damage. Acoustic emission monitoring, computed tomography-based three-dimensional reconstruction, seepage simulation, and microstructural characterization were further employed to compare the diffusion and sealing behaviors of ordinary cement grout (OC) and graphene oxide-modified cement grout (GO). The results indicate that freeze–thaw cycling progressively transforms rock pores and fractures from isolated damage zones into interconnected networks, causing the grouting mechanism to evolve from high-pressure fracture initiation dominance to preferential-channel leakage dominance. The incorporation of GO enhances the viscosity and dispersion stability of the grout, thereby suppressing rapid leakage through macrofractures while maintaining a relatively high local pressure gradient at fracture tips. This process promotes lateral microcrack diversion and multistage grout vein branching. After 45 freeze–thaw cycles, the permeability of the GO-consolidated body reached 1.68 × 10−3 μm2, representing a 21.1% improvement compared with the OC-consolidated body. The addition of GO enables cross-scale coupling from grout rheological regulation to seepage channel reconstruction by altering the flow regime during the grouting stage and the pore connectivity during the consolidation stage. This study provides a theoretical basis for the hydrodynamic design of cement-based grouting materials in cold-region rock masses.

papers.title: Evaluation of the MIX- μ t turbulent viscosity correction method for Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes predictions on trailing edge cutback film cooling
papers.abstract: Trailing-edge cutback cooling is widely used in turbine blades because of its favorable aerodynamic performance. However, conventional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) models often fail to accurately predict cutback cooling effectiveness, mainly because they cannot resolve the unsteady mixing process dominated by lip-shedding vortices. The applicability of the MIX-μt turbulent viscosity correction method, originally proposed for film hole cooling, to trailing-edge cutback cooling is evaluated. By adjusting the turbulent Schmidt number and empirical correction parameters, the influence of this method on RANS prediction accuracy is assessed. The results show that turbulent viscosity correction can significantly improve the prediction of trailing-edge film cooling effectiveness. Without correcting the turbulent viscosity, adjusting only the turbulent Schmidt number cannot provide a consistent improvement under different blowing ratios. When the empirical parameter is set to 1.5, the model moderately enhances turbulent viscosity in the mainstream–coolant mixing region, thereby compensating for the underprediction of unsteady mixing caused by lip-shedding vortices and shear layer entrainment in steady RANS simulations. This parameter is calibrated using pressure-sensitive-paint data for a smooth trailing edge at blowing ratios of 0.25 and 0.50 with a density ratio of 1.0, yielding maximum deviations of 5.5% and 3.5%, respectively, in terms of the spanwise-averaged film cooling effectiveness.
