Further verification is obtained for the straight-ribbed trailing edge with a blowing ratio of 0.50 and the literature trailing-edge configurations with blowing ratios of 0.40 and 1.0–1.5. Nevertheless, the physical mechanisms and universality of the optimized parameters require further investigation.

papers.title: Higher-order separations in laminar fin-induced shockwave/boundary-layer interactions
papers.abstract: The surface flowfield in a fin-induced laminar swept shockwave/boundary-layer interaction was numerically investigated at freestream Mach numbers of 2.64, 2.95, 3.44, and 3.93. The leading edge angle of the sharp unswept fin mounted perpendicularly on a flat plate was varied from 10° to 19° with increments of 3°. All configurations produced sufficiently strong adverse pressure gradients to induce boundary layer separation. The resulting surface topology, capturing key features of fin-induced interactions, was visualized and analyzed. A detailed examination of the primary separated region revealed multiple embedded separated regions. Detailed analysis of limiting streamlines, cross plane flowfields, and surface pressure distributions shows the emergence of secondary and a previously undocumented tertiary separation and attachment lines whose size and prominence increase with Mach number and fin angle. Despite these higher-order separations, the overall flowfield retains quasi conical symmetry, with all major topological features collapsing to a virtual conical origin. The results demonstrate that laminar swept interactions develop a hierarchical separation topology, with multiple nested recirculation regions driven by strong, spatially varying adverse pressure gradients. Cross-plane analysis reveals that tertiary separation corresponds to localized low-momentum regions embedded within the primary vortex, while surface-pressure distributions exhibit distinct additional plateaus and localized pressure peaks associated with secondary jet-like impingement. The emergence of these higher-order separations is interpreted through an impinging supersonic jet mechanism analogous to an Edney type IV interaction, providing a physically consistent explanation for the observed pressure amplification and asymmetric separation structure.

papers.title: Flow pattern transition of oil–air two-phase flow in inclined scavenge pipes based on a one-dimensional two-fluid model
papers.abstract: The flow pattern of oil–air two-phase flow in aero-engine scavenge pipes significantly affects the stability and reliability of the oil scavenging process. However, most existing flow pattern transition criteria are established based on air–water or refrigerant media, making them difficult to apply directly to aero-engine scavenge pipes with high-viscosity oil, small diameters, and inclined configurations. In this paper, an experimental setup with multiple inclination angles is built for inclined scavenge pipes (ID 14 mm). Within the operating ranges of oil viscosity 0.579 Pa s, liquid flow rate 0.16–9.29 l/min, and air flow rate 0.02–6.35 g/s, inclined angles 30°and 45° are observed using a high-speed camera system. Typical flow patterns, including stratified flow (SS and SW), intermittent flow (I), and annular flow (AN), are identified, and flow pattern maps are constructed. By applying the one-dimensional two-fluid model, the mechanical balances for stratified and AN patterns are constructed, leading to the derivation of the non-dimensional liquid height and film thickness control equations. It shows that the proposed transition criteria can effectively distinguish stratified, annular, and intermittent flow regions at different inclination angles. The theoretical boundaries agree well with the inclined scavenge experimental data and can be well applied to flow pattern prediction. It provides a theoretical basis for the pipeline design of aero-engine scavenge systems.

papers.title: An experimental particle swarm optimization-driven real-time control of Tollmien–Schlichting waves on a flat plate
papers.abstract: This experimental study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating particle swarm optimization (PSO) within a hardware-in-the-loop framework for real-time active flow control. The objective is the attenuation of Tollmien–Schlichting (TS) waves developing in an incompressible, two-dimensional laminar boundary layer, using dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuators. Single- and multi-frequency TS waves are artificially excited and amplify before reaching the control region. Control actions are optimized online using PSO, which iteratively updates a population of candidate solutions based on a pressure-based performance metric. In single-frequency scenarios, candidate solutions are parametrized as finite impulse response filters, convolved with an upstream pressure signal to generate the control voltage. In multi-frequency scenarios, the controller constructs a linear superposition of sinusoids at the triggered TS frequencies, identified online. The effectiveness of control is quantified by the attenuation of pressure fluctuations measured by wall-mounted microphones downstream of the actuator. Upon convergence, the best-performing control actions are re-tested in independent experiments, using two-component particle image velocimetry (PIV) to assess the effect of the controller on the velocity field inside the boundary layer. The results show that PSO consistently achieves appreciable TS waves suppression, as evidenced by pressure fluctuation levels reduced by 30%–40% relative to the uncontrolled case and by weakened phase-coherent velocity disturbances. Furthermore, phase-free PIV measurements demonstrate a downstream delay in the growth of velocity fluctuations of up to 15 δ0*, where δ0* is the displacement thickness at the control location. These findings confirm the feasibility of PSO-driven optimization for real-time flow control in transitional boundary layers.

papers.title: Undulatory micro-organisms swimming in finitely extensible nonlinear elastic-Peterlin model: Effects of finite polymer extensibility
papers.abstract: We numerically investigate the undulatory locomotion of a finite-length swimmer in an FENE-P (finitely extensible nonlinear elastic-Peterlin) viscoelastic fluid using the immersed boundary method. The FENE-P model allows us to examine how finite polymer extensibility affects swimming behaviors. For soft swimmers, the swimming speed and efficiency exhibit a non-monotonic dependence on Weissenberg number Wi. This behavior arises from the competition between elastic hindrance and the variation in effective swimming amplitude: the soft swimmer does not reach the prescribed swimming amplitude, but its effective amplitude increases with Wi, allowing it to swim faster than in the Newtonian fluid when Wi≳1. Stiff swimmers generally maintain the prescribed amplitude and are hindered by fluid elasticity, but they achieve faster swimming speeds and higher efficiencies in FENE-P fluids than in Oldroyd-B fluids. By varying the extensibility parameter L2, we reveal that the finite extensibility of the polymer enhances swimming speed and efficiency by suppressing excessive polymer stretching and reducing elastic resistance.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on non-spherical effects in immersed granular collapse
papers.abstract: The collapse of immersed granular columns serves as a proxy for submarine landslides, yet natural sediments are rarely the ideal spheres typically assumed in models. To elucidate the poorly understood influence of particle geometry on immersed granular collapse dynamics, this study employs a coupled computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method framework explicitly accounting for non-spherical characteristics. Using the aspect ratio to parameterize particle shape, we analyze the collapse and transport processes of granular columns composed of particles with varying aspect ratios in a fluid environment by digging into the evolution of collapse morphology, particle contact characteristics, energy budgets, and excess pore-fluid pressure responses. This study reveals that increasing particle aspect ratio (i.e., more elongated particles) enhances geometric interlocking effects among particles. This enhanced interlocking constrains both translational and rotational movements, thereby reducing the kinetic energy and energy dissipation of the immersed granular column. Consequently, a greater proportion of energy is retained as potential energy within the deposit, ultimately manifesting as decreased front propagation velocity and reduced final runout distance. Furthermore, variations in the particle aspect ratio influence the dilatancy–contractancy behavior of the granular column, resulting in diminished excess pore-fluid pressure fluctuations with increasing particle aspect ratio. The study also demonstrates that the final runout distance is proportionally correlated with the front kinetic energy, and this relationship remains independent of the particle aspect ratio. These findings advance our understanding of submarine landslide dynamics and provide a theoretical foundation for risk assessment and mitigation of marine geohazards.

papers.title: A posteriori cross-case parametric learning of the Spalart–Allmaras model for separated flows
papers.abstract: The paper presents a computational fluid dynamics driven parametric learning approach for the Spalart–Allmaras Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes model, focused on the class of separated flows. A key feature of the approach is a two-stage learning procedure: training on a physically representative problem that encapsulates the key flow mechanisms of the target class (separation at a sharp edge, shear mixing, recirculation, and reattachment), followed by strict cross-validation on independent flows, each isolating specific mechanisms to test the model's generalization ability. Closure coefficients were learned using gradient-free algorithms via an OpenFOAM–Python coupling. The obtained set of coefficients eliminates the qualitative discrepancies of the standard model on the training case (a square cylinder on a wall). Cross-validation on benchmark cases from the turbulence modeling resource database confirms that the learned model preserves the log-law of the wall, correctly reproduces the mixing layer development and the recirculation zone length behind a backward-facing step, and qualitatively captures the stall onset on an airfoil with increasing angle of attack. Physical analysis shows that the identified parameters restore the balance between the turbulent shear layer and the recirculation zone. The obtained parameter values lie within the “family of acceptable solutions” originally defined by Spalart and Allmaras during calibration on free shear flows, confirming the physical consistency of the results. The developed approach can be extended to other closure models and flow classes.

papers.title: Linear onset of reactive solutal convection with reaction-modified stratification and mixed wall regularization
papers.abstract: We study the linear onset of reactive solutal convection in a horizontal fluid layer when momentum and solute transport are regularized by hyperviscosity and hyperdiffusion, and the wall-normal velocity satisfies a mixed higher-derivative wall law. A key feature of the model is that reaction and solute hyperdiffusion modify the conductive concentration profile itself, so the buoyancy-production term in the perturbation problem is governed by a depth-dependent base-state gradient rather than by a constant imposed stratification. The resulting onset problem is a coupled higher-order normal-mode eigenvalue system for the critical solutal Rayleigh number and the preferred horizontal wavenumber. It is solved by shifted Chebyshev spectral collocation, including a boundary-fitted implementation that satisfies the mixed wall conditions exactly. The computations show that increasing reaction, hyperviscosity, and hyperdiffusion all delay the onset, but through distinct mechanisms: reaction weakens and redistributes the available buoyancy source through the layer, whereas the higher-gradient terms suppress strongly curved velocity and concentration structure. The wall regularization exerts its strongest influence in the small-δ regime, where it acts as a pronounced mode-selection mechanism. A supplementary weighted-energy analysis places the linear threshold against a sufficient finite-amplitude decay level within the same normalization. Overall, the study shows how reaction-modified stratification, scale-selective bulk regularization, and mixed wall control jointly determine the first transition from diffusion-dominated transport to buoyancy-driven recirculation.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of vortex-induced vibration of a 5:1 rectangular cylinder: Nonlinear aerodynamic damping and flow modal analysis
papers.abstract: Amplitude is a critical parameter influencing vortex-induced vibration (VIV), and accurately obtaining nonlinear aerodynamic damping is essential for predicting VIV amplitude. This study investigates a 5:1 rectangular cylinder using large eddy simulation. Through various numerical methods, including free vibration, constant-amplitude forced vibration, and variable-amplitude forced vibration, the effects of vertical amplitude on flow characteristics and aerodynamic damping are systematically studied. Furthermore, the flow field evolution is analyzed using dynamic mode decomposition. The results indicate that increasing amplitude leads to a reduction in the streamwise size of the primary vortex and a forward shift of the vortex center, which significantly alters the surface pressure distribution. When the amplitude reaches A/D = 4%, the dominant flow mode shifts from the static vortex shedding frequency to the structural vibration frequency and its harmonics, indicating that structural vibration governs the flow evolution. While the free vibration method can capture aerodynamic damping trends, it suffers from high computational costs. Forced vibration methods effectively overcome this limitation: the constant-amplitude method reveals the nonlinear transition of aerodynamic damping from negative to positive as amplitude increases; the variable-amplitude method extracts the continuous distribution of aerodynamic damping through a single simulation, significantly enhancing efficiency by reducing the required fluid–structure interaction cycles from approximately 140–50, thereby cutting the total central processing unit time by roughly 64%. This method also captures the stabilization of aerodynamic damping at large amplitudes, suggesting an upper limit to vibration suppression. The variable-amplitude forced vibration method provides an efficient and reliable numerical approach for extracting nonlinear aerodynamic damping and predicting VIV amplitude at a lower computational cost.

papers.title: Investigation on multi-objective optimization and flow control mechanism of a bird-inspired bionic geometry for compressor cascades
papers.abstract: Inspired by the wing structure of the Grey Heron, this paper proposes a bird-inspired bionic geometry. A multi-objective optimization is performed with the total pressure loss coefficients at design (0°) and near-stall (10°) incidences as objective functions. The optimal geometry reduces the mass-flow-average total pressure loss by 6.19% at the design incidence and by 10.22% at near-stall incidence. The optimal bionic geometry reduces aerodynamic losses mainly by suppressing dissipation in the trailing-edge and wake regions. The suction-side groove reshapes the suction-surface pressure gradient, balancing blade loading and weakening the concentrated shedding vortex in the separation region. Meanwhile, the wavy trailing edge structure creates a localized low-pressure gradient zone near the trailing edge, which inhibits the trailing edge wrapping flow. Shapley additive explanations analysis reveals that increasing groove depth and moving its starting point toward the leading edge reduce aerodynamic losses and improve the flow field. However, the optimal period of the wavy trailing edge varies with incidence: a larger period is favorable for loss reduction at the design incidence, whereas a smaller period yields better performance at the near-stall incidence condition. Compared with the design incidence, a larger amplitude A of the wavy trailing edge is preferred at the high-incidence condition.

papers.title: Empirical scaling laws for predicting in-vacuum operated gas-focused sheet jet emergence, width, and length
papers.abstract: The formation, dimensions, and stability of in-vacuum, gas-focused liquid sheets were investigated experimentally, with a focus on sheet width, sheet length, and the emergence of the liquid chain regime. The study varied gas and liquid flow rates, nozzle height, nozzle capillary cross section, and liquid properties, including surface tension and viscosity, using water and isopropanol. Increasing the gas mass flow rate enhanced both sheet width and length, while increasing the liquid flow rate primarily increased sheet length and had only a weak influence on sheet width due to competing axial and transverse momentum effects. Increasing the nozzle height reduced both sheet dimensions by constraining the sheet within the nozzle. Surface tension was identified as the dominant liquid property governing sheet dimensions. The governing parameters were reformulated using the Weber number (We) and the gas-to-liquid momentum ratio (MR), which are determined by nozzle geometry and gas and liquid flow rates. Empirical power-law scaling relations were derived for the nondimensional sheet width and length, revealing sensitivities to inertia, surface tension, and gas–liquid momentum coupling. The transition between open sheet and liquid chain regimes was described using a logistic regression model, yielding a condition of the form We/MR0.7 for regime occurrence. These results provide experimentally based scaling relations and regime criteria for predicting liquid sheet dimensions and stability under vacuum conditions, which should be interpreted as approximate tools for rapid, initial guidance in the design and optimization of liquid sheets as sample delivery systems in spectroscopy and scattering experiments.

papers.title: Shear and nonlinear density effects in double-diffusive finger convection: Numerical investigations
papers.abstract: Double-diffusive convection in the form of salt-finger instability plays a fundamental role in scalar transport and mixing in stratified fluids. Extending previous investigations of shear-induced finger dynamics [Ouzani et al., “Numerical study of salt fingers dynamics and mixing in laminar shear flow,” Phys. Fluids 37, 123613 (2025)], the present study examines the combined effects of laminar shear flow, equation of state (EOS) nonlinearity, and buoyancy intensity on salt-finger convection. The governing two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations are solved using a high-order finite volume method employing a fifth-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory scheme for nonlinear advection, a fourth-order central discretization for viscous terms, and a third-order total variation diminishing Runge–Kutta scheme for time integration. Simulations are performed for Reynolds numbers in the range 0–700 and thermal Rayleigh numbers varied from 7 × 104 to 7 × 108, considering both linear and nonlinear EOS, with density varying quadratically with temperature and linearly with salinity. The results reveal that the coupled effects of EOS nonlinearity, shear intensity, and thermal Rayleigh number strongly influence the morphology, dynamics, and transport properties of salt fingers. At low Rayleigh number 7 × 104, weak buoyancy forces render the flow highly susceptible to shear-induced deformation, leading to fewer and less coherent finger structures. The moderate Rayleigh number regime RaT = 7 × 106 is characterized by a more balanced competition between buoyancy-driven convection and shear advection, resulting in well-developed salt fingers and enhanced scalar transport. In contrast, at high Rayleigh number 7 × 108, intensified buoyancy-driven transport promotes the formation of more numerous and finer-scale finger structures, accompanied by enhanced interfacial activity and mixing. Under nonlinear conditions, the flow exhibits a marked asymmetry with respect to the mid-plane of the domain, characterized by accelerated and narrowed descending fingers due to enhanced buoyancy forces, while ascending fingers are damped and increasingly tilted under shear. Furthermore, probability density function analysis show that the mixing characteristics are strongly dependent on the combined effects of Rayleigh number, shear intensity, and EOS nonlinearity, significantly modifying scalar distributions, transport efficiency, and interfacial mixing.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation of the hydrogen/air ignition process in a model combustor with linearly arranged swirling burners
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate the ignition process of lean hydrogen/air mixtures in a model combustor with three linearly arranged swirling burners. Ignition is initiated in the internal recirculation zone of the central burner and evolves through three characteristic stages: an initial flame-growth stage following kernel establishment, a flame-reorganization stage, and a near-stabilized stage. The flame propagation is strongly flow controlled and markedly asymmetric, leading to earlier ignition of the right neighboring burner. The results show that the ignition dynamics are governed by a change in the local flame-surface balance. At the early stage, the flame stretch is positive and dominated by tangential strain, which promotes flame-surface production and rapid flame growth. As ignition proceeds, the curvature-stretch contribution becomes increasingly negative and is controlled mainly by the curvature-diffusion term, leading to flame reorganization and a reduction in the overall flame area. Principal curvature analysis further shows that the flame-surface topology evolves from a state dominated by leading-edge-type geometries to one increasingly dominated by trailing-edge-type geometries. However, fuel consumption analysis reveals that geometrically dominant regions and regions contributing most strongly to fuel consumption do not fully coincide, since leading-edge-type structures remain major contributors to fuel consumption until the near-stabilized stage.

papers.title: Reorientations of a turbulent large-scale convective flow in a cylindrical cell
papers.abstract: Long-term numerical simulations of turbulent Rayleigh–Bénard convection of an incompressible fluid with Pr=0.7 in a cylindrical cell of unit aspect ratio and moderate Rayleigh number Ra=108 are performed to analyze the dynamics of reorientations in large-scale circulation (LSC). Special attention is paid to the comparative analysis of the vertical component of the integral angular momentum (mean azimuthal flow) and the characteristics of the LSC, including its intensity, orientation, and angular velocity. Observed rotations of the LSC plane occur either without a significant decrease in LSC intensity, or with cessation of LSC followed by LSC regeneration in a random direction. A pattern common to all reorientations has been revealed—the lower the intensity of the circulation, the higher the angular velocities of the LSC plane rotation. It is shown that the rotation of the LSC plane does not correlate with the mean azimuthal rotation of the fluid, the magnitude of which fluctuates randomly, changing sign. Moreover, unlike the cubic cell, the reorientation is not accompanied by a noticeable increase in the angular momentum. Thus, the reorientation of the LSC in a cylindrical cell is not associated with the azimuthal rotation of the fluid. Furthermore, the characteristics of the LSC follow those of the buoyancy force moment with a short time delay.

papers.title: Mode transition and combustion characteristics of a dual-mode scramjet engine using flamelet modeling
papers.abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of mode transition and combustion characteristics in a dual-mode scramjet engine, employing a compressible flamelet/progress variable (CFPV) model coupled with a self-adaptive turbulence eddy simulation (SATES) approach. The flamelet tables were generated for a methane/ethylene/air mixture using the Gas Research Institute 3.0 chemical mechanism. A mixture-fraction-dependent lookup table was incorporated to rescale the source term of progress variable, thereby accounting for the pressure effects. Steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations against experimental measurement from a strut and a cavity model combustor confirm that the present CFPV model yields more accurate predictions of wall pressure, flame topology, and heat release distribution than the conventional uncorrected flamelet/progress variable model. Detailed SATES simulations were performed at flight Mach numbers of 5.8 and 6.5 to resolve the inherent mode transition characteristics. The transition process from the ramjet to scramjet mode was well captured as the inflow Mach number and overall equivalence ratio increase, which was accompanied by a shift in the flame stabilization mechanism from a jet-wake stabilized to a cavity-assisted jet-wake flame mode. Further statistical analyses distinguish variations in turbulent combustion regimes and premixed/diffusion flame proportions under different operating conditions, and transient shock-induced auto-ignition events inside the jet-wake region are reasonably reproduced by the proposed numerical approach.

papers.title: Active chiral rotors: Hydrodynamics and chemotaxis
papers.abstract: The active rotor studied here is a spherical particle that can self-rotate and generate a chiral flow pattern through active-surface slip velocity rather than through external fields. For instance, if the flow around the upper hemisphere of the rotor is in a clockwise direction, then the flow in the lower hemisphere is in the anti-clockwise direction, and vice versa. In this paper, we aim to study the combined behavior of hydrodynamically interacting active rotors in the presence of an external chemical gradient. While a single isolated rotor is stationary in a fluid, a pair of rotors can move in linear or closed orbital paths as they hydrodynamically interact with each other. It is observed that the emergent linear or closed orbital trajectories depend on the type of rotors and the orientation of their rotation axes. The dynamics of the rotors are altered in a more complex environment, such as in an external chemical gradient. Interestingly, we observe two types of motion: chemotaxis and anti-chemotaxis. In the anti-chemotaxis case, both rotors are driven away from the target; in the chemotaxis case, only one rotor reaches the chemical target, as the other loses its propulsion and cannot continue toward it. This behavior reflects cooperative rather than competitive chemotaxis. The study provides insights into the collective behavior of self-propelled microorganisms and artificial swimmers.

papers.title: Effects of wave-front angle on the transformation of a mode-2 internal solitary wave over a slope–shelf
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of front-slope steepness on the transformation of very large-amplitude mode-2 internal solitary waves (ISWs) propagating over a submerged slope–shelf system using three-dimensional numerical simulations. The Navier–Stokes equations are solved with a finite-volume method, while turbulence is represented using the improved delayed detached eddy simulation model. Unlike previous studies that mainly focused on two-dimensional wave evolution, the present work reveals the three-dimensional dynamics associated with wave–topography interaction. The results show that vortex shedding and density overturning are generated immediately after wave formation, producing complex three-dimensional flow structures behind the leading crest. These vortical motions gradually dissipate during propagation, allowing the wave to recover a coherent mode-2 structure before reaching the obstacle. Upon interacting with the slope–shelf topography, strong wave reflection induces counter-rotating vorticity systems and enhances turbulent mixing. The intensity of these processes is strongly controlled by the front-slope angle. Mild slopes promote prolonged wave–topography interaction and greater attenuation of transmitted wave amplitude and energy, whereas steep slopes generate more localized but stronger vortical motions, resulting in pronounced flow asymmetry and substantial energy loss. The results demonstrate that front-slope steepness plays a critical role in regulating vortex evolution, density mixing, and energy transformation during mode-2 ISW propagation. These findings provide new physical insight into three-dimensional wave–topography interactions and contribute to a better understanding of internal-wave dynamics in complex coastal and shelf environments.

papers.title: Minimal flow units of turbulent channel flow under spanwise wall oscillation
papers.abstract: The minimal flow unit (MFU) provides an efficient framework for probing the self-sustaining dynamics of wall-bounded turbulence. In this study, the MFU concept is applied, for the first time, to turbulent channel flow subjected to spanwise wall oscillation control. Large ensembles of realizations with randomized initial conditions are generated through direct numerical simulations to statistically assess the ability of MFUs to sustain turbulence. The turbulence sustainment probability is introduced to identify the minimal domain dimensions required under different oscillation parameters. The results show that spanwise wall oscillation significantly increases the minimal spanwise and streamwise dimensions required to sustain turbulence, and that the required MFU size grows with increasing oscillation period and amplitude. A distinction is further made between MFUs that merely sustain turbulence and larger flow units capable of producing statistically “healthy” turbulence. The predictive capability of such MFUs is validated by comparisons of wall-shear statistics, mean velocity profiles, turbulence intensities, Reynolds shear stresses, and energy spectra against full-size channel simulations. Finally, MFUs are employed to quantitatively analyze the phase-dependent response of near-wall quasi-streamwise vortices under wall oscillation. The results demonstrate that appropriately sized MFUs can accurately reproduce both statistical properties and coherent-structure dynamics of controlled channel turbulence, offering a powerful and economical tool for fundamental studies of turbulence control.

papers.title: Experimental characterization of spherically forced flows of Carbopol solutions
papers.abstract: Spherical forcing by means of propellers has proven to be a convenient method for generating homogeneous isotropic turbulence with a reduced mean flow. Being a relatively recent approach, it has been exclusively used with Newtonian fluids. The present work consists of a first experimental characterization of the flow properties of aqueous solutions of Carbopol, a well-known test fluid possessing shear thinning and yield stress properties, under spherical forcing. Experimental conditions generated from two Carbopol concentrations, together with pure water, and five propeller speeds are evaluated by means of stereo particle image velocimetry. We assess the suitability of this forcing method for fundamental studies by quantifying the degree of homogeneity, isotropy, and mean flow magnitude and by obtaining fundamental flow properties, namely integral length and velocity scales, Taylor microscales, and dissipation rates. In addition, to assess the influence of viscosity variability on the flow dynamics, we combine rheometric measurements with velocimetry data to estimate viscosity statistics. For the Carbopol solutions, the velocity fields present levels of homogeneity and isotropy comparable to water flows, as well as excellent homogeneity for viscosity statistics. Although the mean flow magnitude increases in the non-Newtonian cases, it remains within acceptable limits. Among the modifications to turbulent properties introduced by Carbopol, viscosity fluctuations generate new mechanisms of energy dissipation, which present a significant impact. These findings provide valuable insights into the flow response of Carbopol solutions to mechanical forcing and highlight the critical importance of a proper understanding of the impact of shear-dependent viscosity on flow dynamics.

papers.title: Chaotic mixing in a microfluidic confinement via a rotating magnetic microsphere chain
papers.abstract: Droplet-based microfluidics enables the manipulation of discrete fluid quanta in the form of microdroplets that provide numerous benefits for analyzing biological and chemical assays. However, because of the extremely low Reynolds numbers in such systems, mixing is limited by molecular diffusion only, which is often insufficient for many lab-on-a-chip applications. Therefore, dedicated strategies to enhance mixing within microdroplets are essential. Magnetic bead-based mixing leverages self-assembled, rotating chains of magnetic micro-particles, suspended in a droplet, behaving as a stirrer for mixing. Herein, we present a numerical investigation of mixing dynamics in a two-dimensional cylindrical micro-well stirred by a rotating magnetic bead-chain. The simulations solve the conservation equations for mass, momentum, and species transport in a boundary-fitted coordinate system. The effect of rotational speed and rotational direction on mixing efficiency is analyzed through observing massless tracer-species contour plots and a quantitative mixing index based on its concentration profile. Results show that chain-rotation significantly enhances mixing via chaotic advection compared to the diffusive mixing. Higher rotational speeds accelerate mixing in early stages, although long-term mixing plateaus at higher speeds. Importantly, alternating the rotation direction at regular, short intervals produces stronger vortex shedding and leads to faster mixing as compared to that in unidirectional rotation. These findings demonstrate that chain-rotation, specifically with directional flipping, can be tuned to optimize droplet-scale mixing, offering practical guidelines for the design of efficient micromixers in lab-on-chip applications.

papers.title: An influence mechanism of the tributary morphology on the hydrodynamic characteristics at the confluence
papers.abstract: Confluent channels are ubiquitous in nature, with tributary morphology exhibiting diverse forms. To explore the influence mechanism of tributary morphology in a confluent channel on the hydrodynamic characteristics of the main channel, the validated renormalization group k–ε turbulence model is employed in this work to investigate the effect of tributary morphology of the upstream bend (UB), straight channel (SC), and downstream bend (DB) with varying flow ratio (q*) on the hydrodynamic characteristics of a 90° equal-width confluent channel. Results reveal that the tributary morphology has a significant impact on the flow structure, separation zone, and secondary flow of the main channel. Mean vortex structures form within the tributary before it flows into the main channel when the tributary morphology is UB, resulting in a larger area of horizontal vortices near the water surface in the downstream of the confluence zone. Compared with SC and DB, the dimensionless length of the separation zone and secondary flow intensity are the largest when the tributary morphology is UB. In addition, the variation range of dimensionless length and width as well as secondary flow intensity with various tributary morphologies decreases with increasing q*. The findings of this study will contribute to a better understanding of the hydrodynamic characteristics of the 90° equal-width confluence, providing valuable insights for river management and ecological restoration.

papers.title: Receptivity to decayed turbulent stage of two-dimensional Taylor–Green vortex problem investigated by quadruple precision simulation
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) Taylor–Green vortex (TGV) dynamics is investigated here by performing a direct numerical simulation (DNS) from the receptivity to decayed turbulence stage, with the specific intention of finding the explicit role played by round-off error. The governing Navier–Stokes equations are solved using the stream function–vorticity formulation by removing errors caused by spatial discretization, adopting the Fourier spectral method, while controlling temporal discretization error with different time steps used for the four stage, fourth order Runge–Kutta method. The resultant error dynamics are predominantly governed by the round-off error for which we have reported here results comparing double and quadruple precision computations. To our knowledge, such a study of performing quadruple precision DNS has not been reported before. The effects of round-off errors on receptivity to turbulence of fluid flows have been demonstrated by performing extremely high-accuracy simulations of the benchmark 2D TGV problem by controlling all other forms of numerical errors, barring the round-off error. The choice of the 2D TGV problem is explained by highlighting the effects of round-off error. The quadruple precision results demonstrate the qualitatively different route from the receptivity to the decayed turbulence stages compared to double precision computations—specifically the identification of the receptivity stage, which is a novel feature. The presented research is relevant for physical instabilities, emphasizing the effects of precision accurately.

papers.title: Study on wind field characteristics in mountainous gully terrain
papers.abstract: This study investigates wind field characteristics in complex terrain (5 km diameter and 580 m elevation difference) using a 1:1000 scale model in wind tunnel experiments and large eddy simulation. Key parameters—acceleration coefficients, wind yaw angles, turbulence intensity, power spectral density (PSD), and integral turbulence scale—are analyzed along the river channel line, ridge line, and their intersections under gully terrain conditions. The influence of different incoming wind profiles on the wind environment is compared. Major findings are as follows. (1) Uniform flow fields are more suitable for analyzing mountain bridge wind environments than other inflow conditions. (2) For river channel winds, the inlet geometry strongly affects the internal wind field. Narrow entrances enhance wind speed and turbulence intensity due to funnel effects, causing sharp spatial variations and notable fluctuations in integral turbulence scale. Downwind of wide entrances, wind speed and direction change smoothly, while turbulence intensity increases near the exit due to terrain-induced disturbances. (3) Vertical wind contribution to resultant wind speed varies notably under different inflow conditions. On slopes, the vertical component can contribute up to 30%. (4) At intersection points, the wind speed profile along the ridge line is lower than that of Class D terrain, while the river channel profile falls between Class B and Class D. Turbulence intensity is higher along the ridge line than along the river channel, with the lowest value observed at the riverbed entrance. Upwind PSD exceeds that in other directions, and low-frequency PSD at the narrow river entrance is higher than at the wide entrance.

papers.title: Bayesian calibration and bootstrap-based multifractal characterization of turbulence in sand-laden atmospheric surface layers under variable stratification stability
papers.abstract: To address the breakdown of classical turbulence scaling under particle-laden and unstable conditions, this study develops an integrated hierarchical Bayesian and multifractal framework to quantify the coupled effects of stratification stability (z/L) and saltation flux (Q). Using field measurements from a near-surface saltation layer, we calibrate a robust empirical stability function, ϕTi(z/L), for the streamwise turbulence intensity. Bayesian posterior inference, validated via Gibbs sampling and posterior predictive checks, confirms a statistically significant non-linear damping effect of Q on Ti, isolating physical structural variance from observational noise. Furthermore, bootstrap-based multifractal analysis uncovers a “shift-vs-width” paradox in the intermittency dynamics. While enhanced unstable stratification drives a pronounced rightward shift of the singularity spectrum f(α)—consistent with classical convective energy cascading to lower frequencies—the spectral width Δα remains constrained under fixed particle loading. We articulate that the aerodynamic drag exerted by heavy saltating particles acts as an effective low-pass “scale filter,” preferentially damping high-frequency vortical fluctuations via apparent viscosity effects. This inertial suppression rigorously caps the boundaries of extreme velocity gradients, rendering the intermittent strength highly insensitive to thermal instability. By bridging macroscopic statistical parameterizations with microscale multi-phase fluid dynamics, this study provides rigorous uncertainty quantification for boundary-layer modeling in arid environments.

papers.title: Theoretical and experimental calibration of hot-sphere anemometers under low-pressure and simulated microgravity conditions
papers.abstract: Hot-sphere anemometers exhibit significant measurement deviations in microgravity-related and low-pressure environments, creating a need for recalibration. In this study, a compact low-pressure and low-velocity wind tunnel calibration system is developed by combining heat transfer theory with ground-based experiments. Based on the Gr/Re2 criterion and Kn number analysis, it is verified that the flow remains in the continuum regime at 40 kPa. In addition, buoyancy-induced natural convection is sufficiently suppressed when the wind velocity exceeds 0.097 m/s, demonstrating the feasibility of extrapolating ground-based calibration results to microgravity-related forced-convection conditions. The results show that the initial measurement error of the probe under atmospheric pressure reaches 19.84%. After recalibration, the correlation coefficient (R2) increases to 0.9993, with an expanded uncertainty ranging from 0.036 to 0.039 m/s. At low-pressures (90–40 kPa), the measured wind velocity exhibits an attenuation trend, with a maximum attenuation rate of 66.02% relative to standard atmospheric pressure. Although thermal radiation accounts for only 4.5% of the total heat dissipation under the reference condition, its relative contribution increases under low-pressure and low-velocity conditions; therefore, it is treated as a secondary heat-loss pathway. With conductive heat loss through the wire neglected, the energy conservation equation is modified, and a forced-convection-dominated empirical calibration correlation is established, with residual heat-loss effects incorporated into the fitted coefficients. This correlation enables low-pressure wind velocities to be estimated from atmospheric-pressure baseline calibration data within the calibrated range, with a prediction error of less than 10%. This study provides a reliable calibration method for hot-sphere anemometers under microgravity-related low-pressure conditions.

papers.title: Transport–reaction coupling under hydrodynamic mixing in batch systems
papers.abstract: Mixing plays an important role in microalgae cultivation as it directly affects nutrient transport, light exposure, and overall reactor performance. However, the extent to which improvements in hydrodynamic mixing enhance biomass productivity remains unclear, particularly under batch conditions where nutrients are limited. This study investigates that question through numerical simulations of a coupled fluid–microalgae model, in which biomass and substrate are transported as scalar fields within an incompressible flow and interact through Monod growth kinetics. Four jet-driven flow configurations are examined alongside a no-flow reference and three complementary limiting regimes: a diffusion-limited case, an intermediate spatially uniform substrate model, and a fully mixed limit. Simulations are initialized from highly segregated conditions to isolate the role of transport processes. The central finding is that, despite marked differences in mixing efficiency across configurations, domain-averaged biomass trajectories converge to within 0.5%, with peak biomass gains confined to a narrow 2–3% range. In the absence of advection, substrate remains inaccessible to biomass, causing net biomass loss driven by endogenous respiration. When flow is introduced, substrate and biomass rapidly come into contact within O(200 s), activating growth. This convergence is explained by a transport–reaction decoupling argument: once advection overcomes the initial segregation and the system enters the reaction-limited regime (Da≪1), integrated yield becomes insensitive to the details of the flow field. Biomass production is then governed primarily by substrate inventory rather than mixing intensity, a result explained by the clear separation between hydrodynamic and biological timescales.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on off-center pursuit collision dynamics of molten glass microbeads
papers.abstract: Off-center pursuit collisions of high-viscosity molten glass microbeads are ubiquitous in industrial manufacturing, playing a critical role in determining product sphericity and ultimate performance. We developed a three-dimensional numerical framework using the open-source solver Basilisk, integrating the volume of fluid method with adaptive mesh refinement, and investigated the effects of Weber number (We) and impact parameter (B) on morphological evolution, internal flow topology, and energy conversion during off-center pursuit collisions. Six distinct collision regimes are identified: (I) bouncing, (II) coalescence, (III) reflexive separation with satellite droplets, (IV) reflexive separation without satellites, (V) stretching separation with a single satellite, and (VI) stretching separation with multiple satellites. The results indicate that in head-on collisions (B = 0), the reflexive separation observed at high We is driven primarily by end-pinching mechanism. For off-center collisions (B > 0), impact-induced angular momentum significantly alters the flow topology, triggering non-axisymmetric shear flows. As B increases to 0.5, the regime transitions to stretching separation, governed by the interplay of shear forces and centrifugal effects, accompanied by multiple satellite formation. A coupled analysis of velocity and pressure fields reveals that vortical motion induced by moderate B mitigates violent collision focusing at the geometric center, thereby promoting coalescence. Furthermore, energy budget analysis demonstrates that rotational kinetic energy sustains high surface energy during the elongation phase, facilitating stretching separation. Through comparison with the results of other researchers, we observe that the critical We required for separation increases with increasing Oh. This study provides theoretical guidelines for optimizing spheroidization parameters to suppress agglomeration and splashing defects while enhancing product sphericity.

papers.title: Field-induced rheology of surfactant-stabilized aqueous magnetorheological fluids
papers.abstract: The flow behavior of aqueous magnetorheological (MR) suspensions is strongly governed by the competition between hydrodynamic stresses and magnetic dipolar interactions, while their practical use is often limited by poor colloidal stability. In this work, we investigate the field-induced rheology of surfactant-stabilized aqueous MR suspensions, where Triton X-100 is employed to modify interparticle and interfacial interactions in carbonyl iron particle dispersions. Steady shear measurements reveal a transition from viscous to yield stress-dominated behavior with increasing magnetic field strength, consistent with field-induced chain formation. The flow curves are well described by a Herschel–Bulkley framework, with the yield stress exhibiting a nonlinear power-law dependence on magnetic field strength, indicating dipolar interaction-controlled structuring. The viscosity and magnetoviscous response exhibit saturation at high magnetic fields, indicating limited microstructural growth. Analysis of viscosity-field, viscosity increment (Δη), and shear-rate behavior reveals strong shear-thinning governed by the competition between hydrodynamic and magnetic forces, with surfactant-mediated interactions modifying the scaling of the response. Mason number analysis further reveals a clear Bingham-type scaling relationship between hydrodynamic and magnetic forces governing the suspension microstructure. Oscillatory rheology shows dominant elastic behavior, indicating mechanically robust particle networks, with a slight reduction in modulus attributed to interfacial separation induced by the surfactant layer. These results establish a direct link between interfacial modification, field-driven microstructure evolution, and macroscopic flow behavior, providing a physics-based framework for designing stable, field-responsive MR suspensions.

papers.title: Investigation of spontaneous imbibition characteristics in mixed-wettability capillary channel for tight oil reservoir
papers.abstract: Spontaneous imbibition is a key mechanism for oil recovery in tight reservoirs, where pore walls often exhibit mixed wettability, with both oil-wetting and water-wetting patches. In such systems, the competition between water-wetting and oil-wetting surfaces produces complex interfacial behavior that cannot be captured by traditional homogeneous-wettability models. This study establishes a phase-field numerical model for spontaneous imbibition in mixed-wettability capillary channels, considering the effective viscosity effect, wall slip effect, and dynamic contact angle effect. To validate the model, a mixed-wettability capillary channel is fabricated using a local surface modification method. The simulated and measured imbibition front position agree within 2.5%, confirming the reliability of the model. Using the validated model, we examine how interfacial morphology, capillary pressure, wetting fraction, wetting strength, and capillary radius jointly govern imbibition behavior. Numerical simulations reveal that wettability heterogeneity induces non-uniform curvature at the advancing meniscus, generating a heterogeneous capillary pressure field that promotes preferential water-phase flow along water-wetting walls and enhances sweep efficiency. Three distinct spontaneous imbibition patterns are identified as a complete-stripping high-efficiency pattern, an oil-wetting-dominance low-efficiency pattern, and an inlet-constraint ineffective pattern. These patterns are governed primarily by wetting fraction and wetting strength but remain independent of capillary radius. A simple criterion, fwcosθw + focosθo > 0, is proposed to predict when high-efficiency imbibition can occur, offering practical guidance for recovery enhancement in mixed-wettability tight reservoirs.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic characteristics of a coupled system of forced-oscillating cylinder and undulating foil
papers.abstract: The interaction mechanism between fish and unsteady flow fields is a crucial topic that warrants further investigation. This study numerically examines the interaction between a forced-oscillating cylinder and a downstream undulating foil using the immersed boundary method. Results show that the foil achieves a hydrodynamic advantage in the cylinder wake compared with uniform inflow. Vortex shedding from an oscillating cylinder exhibits distinct patterns, including the 2S (two single vortices per cycle) and P + S (one vortex pair plus a single vortex per cycle) modes, determined by the cylinder oscillation parameters. For the 2S wake, the flow is classified into three distinct domains according to the foil's influence on cylinder vortex shedding with varying downstream placement of the foil: the suction-extension, beating, and weak-influence domains. Compared with the suction-extension and weak-influence domains, the beating domain exhibits more distinctive coupled flow characteristics between the foil and cylinder. In this domain, the pre-established lock-in state of the cylinder vortex shedding is disrupted, and the foil thrust coefficient exhibits relaxation oscillations when the undulating motion of the foil is in-phase or anti-phase with the cylinder vortex shedding. Furthermore, proper phase synchronization between the two motions yields consistently higher thrust and generally favorable propulsive efficiency of the foil across all wake domains. For the P + S wake, reducing the foil–cylinder gap suppresses secondary vortex shedding of the cylinder, and the foil exhibits inferior overall hydrodynamic performance in the P + S mode compared with the 2S mode.

papers.title: Near-wall structures of topographic hill flow: Skin friction, surface pressure, and derived quantities
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the near-wall structures of the viscous flows over isolated axisymmetric topographic hill models embedded inside the incoming turbulent boundary layer (simply called the hill flows) with different relative heights for different Reynolds numbers. The relative skin friction fields are obtained in global luminescent oil-film measurements in a wind tunnel, and then the relative surface pressure fields are extracted from the skin friction fields. The skin friction topology of the hill flows is characterized by isolated critical points (saddles and nodes) connected by separation and attachment lines. The topology remains qualitatively unchanged in a limited range of the Reynolds numbers based on the base diameter of the hill model, and the normalized skin friction magnitude fields enjoy certain similarity. The normalized surface pressure fields are characterized by the high-pressure region on the front and the low-pressure region on the leeside, which directly correspond to the skin-friction topological features. As the relative hill height to the incoming boundary-layer thickness increases, the topological evolution of the normalized skin friction fields is revealed along with the corresponding normalized surface pressure fields. The relevant surface quantities are calculated from the skin friction and surface pressure fields, including the boundary enstrophy flux (BEF), surface vorticity, skin friction divergence, surface pressure gradient, surface pressure Laplacian, and curvature-vorticity quadratic form. These quantities, particularly the BEF and skin friction divergence, determine the near-wall flow structures.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic study of a four-module rectangular configuration undulating fin robot for underwater self-propulsion
papers.abstract: To provide a hydrodynamic basis for improving the adaptability and maneuverability of underwater robots in complex environments, a modular underwater robot driven by biomimetic undulating fins is proposed. A four-module rectangular configuration composed of front, rear, left, and right propulsion units is considered, and its self-propulsion hydrodynamic characteristics are systematically investigated using computational fluid dynamics simulations. The effects of uniform fin actuation on propulsion performance are analyzed by varying fin undulation frequency and amplitude. The results show that, under different parameter combinations, the rear fins consistently generate stronger propulsion contributions than the front fins, indicating pronounced asymmetry in multi-fin hydrodynamic interactions. Motivated by this phenomenon, differential front–rear fin actuation cases with different fin frequencies and amplitudes are further investigated. The results indicate that frequency differences exert a stronger influence on propulsion stability and transient force fluctuations, whereas amplitude differences mainly affect thrust magnitude with relatively weaker influence on dynamic stability. Furthermore, exchanging the front–rear fin parameters demonstrates that configurations with smaller front fin parameters and larger rear fin parameters achieve superior propulsion performance. The present study reveals how both uniform and front–rear differential fin actuation influence vortex interaction, momentum redistribution, and coupled wake dynamics in multi-fin propulsion systems. These findings provide theoretical guidance for the hydrodynamic design and control of modular self-reconfigurable underwater robots, while also contributing to the understanding of unsteady propulsion physics in undulating fin systems.

papers.title: Source modeling for the assessment of the effects of finite computational domains and wind tunnel working sections
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes linear and planar source lattices to model two- and three-dimensional bodies in finite computational domains and wind tunnel working sections. Tunnel walls and most boundary conditions used in numerical simulations of fluid flow prevent the outward flux of mass required by the Lagally–Filon equation. This equation shows the body drag is associated with a source of irrotational fluid much like the lift is associated with a vortex bound to the body through the Kutta–Joukowsky equation. The source distribution, however, can extend many body-lengths downstream. Source lattices provide the lateral constraint due to walls and boundary conditions. Thus, the velocity upstream of the body is less than the velocity at infinity which the velocity outside the wake. Corrections are given for these effects on numerical simulations and measurements of the drag of airfoils, normal flat plates, and circular cylinders. In two-dimensions, the velocity induced by a linear lattice has a simple closed form solution but the best result for the planar, three-dimensional lattice is the short-distance series solution for the streamwise velocity along the centerline using the “Chowla-Selberg” formula and the large distance solution from the extended Chowla–Selberg formula. These contain series whose terms are exponentially convergent as opposed to algebraically convergent terms in the original sums. To facilitate the further development of corrections and analysis of the wake, the formulas are used to generate tables of the velocity induced by a source lattice accurate to six figures.

papers.title: Gas-driven arc transport and pressure buildup in a polyamide 66-assisted direct current breaker chamber
papers.abstract: Polyamide 66 (PA66) gassing materials are widely used in direct current molded case circuit breakers, yet the fluid-dynamic mechanism by which their decomposition gases regulate arc transport, pressure buildup, and enclosure loading remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the effects of PA66 position and volume on arc dynamics, chamber pressure, enclosure stress, and shell damage. The results show that PA66 decomposition gases, mainly H2, CO, and H2O, do not merely act as an arc-cooling medium. Instead, they modify local thermophysical properties and generate pressure-driven flow, forming a fluid-dynamic feedback mechanism that couples gas generation, species transport, energy redistribution, arc motion, and structural loading in a confined chamber. Among the investigated configurations, placing PA66 near the corner of the anode arc runner provides the most favorable alignment between gas expansion and magnetically driven arc motion, thereby promoting arc transport toward the splitter plates and reducing enclosure loading. Increasing PA66 volume enhances gas-assisted arc acceleration, but excessive gas generation intensifies pressure accumulation, arc-root stagnation, structural loading, and shell damage. These findings suggest that the PA66 layout should be designed by balancing arc-transport enhancement with enclosure reliability.

papers.title: Capillary-wave-driven droplet spreading on particles: Curvature-induced pseudo-hydrophobicity at low Weber numbers
papers.abstract: We investigate droplet–particle interactions in the low Weber number regime, which play dominant roles in many engineering applications, such as bioprinting and cell spray processes, but have been less explored compared to impacts in the moderate-to-high Weber number regimes. We demonstrate curvature-induced pseudo-hydrophobicity, which can be understood as a hydrophobic-like dynamic response that emerges on intrinsically hydrophilic curved targets without any change in the intrinsic equilibrium contact angle. More specifically, on a highly curved surface, the difference between the apparent and equilibrium contact angles during the initial spreading stage decreases, resulting in a reduced capillary force. This effect is analogous to that induced by increased hydrophobicity. Three major parameters that typically characterize spreading dynamics in the low Weber number regime –namely, (i) the spreading extent, (ii) the propagation of capillary waves, and (iii) the film thickness– are quantitatively examined in detail. These characteristic features on a highly curved hydrophilic surface mimic those typically observed on a hydrophobic substrate, including reduced spreading extents, weakened capillary waves, recovery of the film thickness, thicker coatings, and reduced energy dissipation. This previously overlooked curvature-induced effect provides new insights into the low-Weber-number droplet spreading dynamics and suggests a geometric route for manipulating droplet–particle interactions.

papers.title: Heat release characteristics of rotating detonation in an afterburner under high-temperature low-oxygen inflow conditions
papers.abstract: Rotating detonation afterburner (RDA) is a promising approach for thrust augmentation in turbofan engines, yet its heat release characteristics under high-temperature, low-oxygen inflow remain poorly understood. This study employs a two-dimensional Eulerian–Lagrangian method to simulate kerosene/air rotating detonation under typical afterburner inlet conditions (total temperature 795–1329 K and oxygen mass fraction 13.4%–18.9%). Under a baseline condition (1061 K and 16.4% O2), the RDA sustains stable single-wave propagation with a “lean-rich-lean” fuel vapor stratification driven by droplet evaporation lag. Decreasing oxygen content thickens the detonation wave front, reducing peak heat release rate while preserving total detonation heat release through wave broadening. Increasing total temperature triggers single-to-multi-wave transitions, sharply intensifying parasitic combustion and degrading evaporation at excessive temperatures due to reduced droplet residence time. Under coupled parameter variation within the present two-dimensional model, the velocity deficit exhibits a non-monotonic trend and reaches a minimum of 6.8% at 1061 K and 16.4% O2. Conventional threshold-based detonation/deflagration classification fails under these conditions, necessitating more refined identification approaches. These findings clarify the governing mechanisms of RDA heat release and support future afterburner design.

papers.title: Heterogeneous condensation mechanism of carbon dioxide: A molecular simulation study
papers.abstract: Investigating the condensation of carbon dioxide (CO2) is crucial for optimizing natural gas decarbonization processes and refining condensation theories. However, there is a lack of microscopic understanding of the CO2 condensation process involving heavy hydrocarbon impurities. In this study, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to systematically investigate the CO2 condensation mechanisms. Compared with other models, the flexible transferable potentials for phase equilibria model provides the best predictions of CO2 properties, with average relative errors of 7% and 3% for density and self-diffusion coefficient, respectively. As the temperature decreases from 250 to 220 K, the first main peak in the radial distribution function of CO2 surged from 7.1 to 28.8, indicating that lower temperature can drastically shorten the nucleation lag time and cause a more compact molecular arrangement. The nucleation rates predicted by classical models were 1–3 orders of magnitude lower than those of MD simulations. In the initial condensation stage, the first main peak between n-hexane and CO2 molecules is higher than that of CO2 molecules. Trace n-hexane preferentially undergoes spontaneous aggregation to form condensation sites, upon which CO2 subsequently attaches and grows, significantly reducing the nucleation barrier of CO2. In addition, the potential energy of the CO2–n-hexane system declines earlier and more drastically. As the concentration of n-hexane increases, the increasing attachment sites contribute to a further enhancement in the CO2 nucleation rate. Furthermore, the n-hexane–CO2 system forms a well-mixed cluster structure, and the mole fraction of n-hexane across all layers of the droplet remains constant.

papers.title: Spanwise structure of the “monami” phenomenon in an open-channel with submerged flexible vegetation
papers.abstract: This study aims to reveal the spanwise structure of the monami phenomenon and the phase difference between two vegetation tip motions at different spanwise positions in fully developed, submerged flexible vegetation flows by flume experiments. Effects of the submergence depth ratio on temporal and spatial scales of the fluid-vegetation interactions are investigated by comparing the measurement results for seven cases with different flow depths. First, we capture the high- and low-speed streaks over the flexible vegetation canopy by particle image velocimetry (PIV) and evaluate their spanwise length-scale. Then, the instantaneous flow velocity field and vegetation tip positions are simultaneously measured by PIV and particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) to clarify how the high- and low-speed streaks cause the monami phenomenon. Moreover, correlation analysis is conducted for the tip motion data of multiple vegetation elements at a fixed streamwise position obtained by PTV to evaluate the spanwise length-scale of the monami phenomenon. The velocity measurements capture a characteristic flow structure called the “subchannel” structure, where the high- and low-speed streaks exist alternately in the spanwise direction. The two-point velocity correlation suggests the spanwise width of each subchannel can be scaled by the mixing layer thickness and that the subchannel width increases with the flow depth. Moreover, a group of vegetation elements located below the high-speed streak are deflected simultaneously, meanwhile those below the neighboring low-speed streaks are erect oppositely, demonstrating that the spanwise extent of the monami phenomenon is equivalent to the subchannel width.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics of a rotor near a wavy surface
papers.abstract: When helicopters hover near the water surface, the rotor thrust increases due to the water surface influence, which is similar to the ground effect and is known as the near water effect. While the rotor near calm water effect has been studied by some scholars, there are relatively few studies on the aerodynamic characteristics of rotors under the wave surface effect. This paper investigates the aerodynamic characteristics of the rotor near water/wave surface effect by combining the model test and computational fluid dynamics method. The analysis focuses on the influence of the wave surface effect on rotor thrust, and a wave surface effect theoretical model for thrust prediction is developed. The results show that the rotor thrust increases as the relative height of the rotor above the water decreases, especially when the height is less than 0.6 times the rotor diameter. The rotor thrust under the wave surface effect is related not only to the instantaneous height above the wave surface but also to the vertical induced velocity at the rotor disk due to the wave motion. However, the rotor thrust is primarily affected by the instantaneous height, with the vertical induced velocity having a relatively minor influence.

papers.title: Cavitation instabilities and control strategies: A physics-based unified review
papers.abstract: Cavitation—the nucleation, growth, and collapse of vapor cavities in liquids—remains one of the most complex and impactful phenomena in fluid engineering. Its consequences, including erosion, vibration, noise, and efficiency loss, generate significant economic and operational challenges across applications such as hydropower, marine propulsion, turbomachinery, fuel injection, and biomedical devices. Despite more than a century of research since Lord Rayleigh's pioneering work, cavitation continues to pose fundamental challenges due to its multiscale, multiphase, and highly unsteady nature. Existing studies are extensive but fragmented across fluid physics, experimentation, numerical modeling, and control, lacking a unified framework linking physical mechanisms to effective mitigation strategies. This review addresses this gap by proposing a physics-based framework that connects dominant cavitation instability mechanisms—including reentrant jet dynamics, cloud shedding, interfacial instabilities, bubble collapse, and vortex-core cavitation—to targeted control approaches. Instabilities are classified according to their driving physics, enabling identification of key control variables. The review synthesizes advances in cavitation fundamentals, bubble dynamics, instability scaling, and both passive (geometric optimization, coatings, flow control) and active (gas injection, acoustic forcing, adaptive control) mitigation techniques. In addition, critical challenges in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling are assessed through comparison of cavitation and turbulence models, alongside evaluation metrics and scalability considerations. Emerging directions, including hybrid CFD–machine learning approaches and real-time control strategies, are also discussed. By integrating theoretical, experimental, and computational insights, this work provides a structured, mechanism-based foundation for understanding cavitation and guiding the design of effective, application-specific mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Nonlinear lift behavior in medium-aspect-ratio wings at low Reynolds numbers: An extension of the Polhamus–Lamar model
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic behavior of low- and medium-aspect-ratio (LAR/MAR) slender wings operating at low Reynolds numbers is critical for the design of modern unmanned aerial vehicles. The widely used Polhamus–Lamar model (PLM) effectively captures the lift characteristics of LAR wings by representing vortex and potential lift components. However, the existing PLM approaches may lose accuracy at higher angles of attack (AoA) and increasing ARs. This study introduces a simple modification to the PLM that (1) reduces model nonlinearities, (2) preserves the vortex and potential lift components, and (3) extends its applicability to MAR wings and higher AoA. The proposed model is assessed through computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, wind tunnel experiments, and comparison with published experimental data. The CFD visualizations qualitatively illustrate the evolution of vortical and separated-flow structures as AoA increases. Experimental and numerical results show that the proposed parameterization improves the representation of nonlinear lift attenuation relative to classical PLM-based predictions within the studied conditions. The proposed methodology extends the useful range of the PLM structure while preserving its fundamental decomposition into potential and vortex-related lift terms.

papers.title: Effects of inclined obstacles on flame acceleration and deflagration-to-detonation transition in curvature-controlled micro-spiral channels
papers.abstract: Efficient flame acceleration and deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT) in curved geometries are critical for micro-propulsion and explosion safety. However, curvature introduces flow asymmetries that fundamentally alter obstacle-induced combustion enhancement compared to straight channels. This study performs high-fidelity quasi-direct numerical simulations to investigate the effects of inner-wall inclined obstacles (−75° to +75°) in micro-spiral channels. The results show that curvature-induced centrifugal effects shift the high-momentum region toward the inner wall, leading to a strongly asymmetric flow field. Backward-inclined obstacles (θ < 0°) promote flame acceleration by increasing flow blockage, which intensifies flame–vortex and flame–shock interactions. In contrast, forward-inclined obstacles (θ > 0°) exhibit a flow-guiding effect that enhances energy accumulation and preheating within curved pockets via reflected shocks. Detonation consistently initiates in these pockets near the outer wall through three distinct mechanisms: (i) delayed pressure amplification via shock–wall interactions; (ii) quasi-isochoric ignition from shock focusing; and (iii) flame compression–expansion ignition. While the DDT time increases monotonically with inclination angle, the DDT distance follows an asymmetric V-shaped trend with a minimum at θ = 0°. A segmented optimization strategy is also proposed: upstream obstacles are arranged in a backward-inclined orientation, while downstream obstacles are configured vertically or with a small forward inclination, which can significantly enhance ignition performance.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance and vortex-induced vibration of a completed triple-box girder: The role of gap ratio
papers.abstract: Triple-box girders have recently emerged as an attractive cross-sectional form for long-span bridges, with their aerodynamic performance and vortex-induced vibration (VIV) strongly affected by slot gap spacing. However, for completed (as-built) triple-box configurations, a systematic understanding of how gap ratio governs aerodynamic performance, VIV, and the associated flow mechanisms remains limited. In this study, wind tunnel tests were performed to measure surface pressures and vibrations for five gap ratios, i.e., GW/H = 0.81, 1.62, 2.43, 3.24, and 4.05. Complementary computational fluid dynamics simulations were conducted to examine the vorticity evolution and clarify the underlying excitation mechanisms. The results indicate that gap ratio influences the mean pressure coefficient, force coefficients, fluctuating pressure coefficient, mean square amplitude spectra of fluctuating pressures, Strouhal number (St), VIV, and flow characteristics to different extents. In particular, the effects of gap ratio are more evident for the midstream and downstream girders than for the upstream girder. Further examination of St values derived from different dominant frequencies reveals a clear transition in the frequency domain response at GW/H = 2.43, whereas the maximum VIV amplitude is observed at GW/H = 3.24. Flow field visualization reveals that vortex shedding from the upstream girder interacting with slot gap recirculation amplifies unsteadiness around the midstream and downstream girders, while inter-girder interference weakens as the gap ratio increases. These findings improve understanding of how flow evolution governs aerodynamic interference and VIV in completed triple-box girders.

papers.title: Characteristics of multiphase detonations and phase transitions in solid-particle fueled continuous rotating detonation ramjet engines
papers.abstract: Solid fuels possess great potential for hypersonic flight due to their high energy density and resistance to high-temperature dissociation. However, traditional idealized chemical reaction assumptions fail to accurately describe the complex multiphase detonation and phase transition mechanisms in reactive flows. To address this, a multiphase chemical equilibrium framework is established to systematically investigate the thermodynamic evolution of boron or aluminum fuels within a continuous rotating detonation ramjet engine (CRDRE) physical testbed. Results indicate that the irreversible complete reaction assumption fails completely across Mach 3–7, as it neglects the dissociation effects at high temperatures and pressures. On the other hand, because the gaseous chemical equilibrium assumption fails to capture the condensation phase transitions when products cross their saturated vapor pressures, the assumption is partially invalid for boron at high equivalence ratios, while it exhibits a global failure for aluminum. Consequently, a condition of Mach 7 and 26 km altitude, presenting the most severe dissociation, is selected as the test condition. Using the irreversible complete reaction assumption for boron leads to an overestimation. Conversely, for aluminum, this assumption does not always overestimate engine performance, which is the result of a balance among the combustor heat release, and the heat release/phase transition losses within the nozzle. Furthermore, results indicate that aluminum yields a higher specific thrust compared to boron, whereas boron exhibits a superior specific impulse. This study enables the rapid calculation of solid-particle fueled detonation parameters and solid-particle fueled CRDRE performance, providing reference for multiphase detonation and phase transitions of solid fuels.

papers.title: Vortex initiation detection and evolution analysis on a pitching airfoil under reverse flow conditions
papers.abstract: Dynamic stall under reverse flow conditions exhibits distinct aerodynamic behaviors compared to conventional stall, yet the timing of critical vortex events remains poorly understood. This study establishes a pressure-based method for detecting the initiation of the dynamic stall vortex (DSV) and trailing-edge vortex (TEV) for an airfoil under reverse flow conditions. Due to the dominance of the DSV and TEV structures on the surface pressure distributions, the proposed method provides a simple yet robust means of identifying key vortex events using single-port pressure measurements at the leading and trailing edges, thereby eliminating the need for information on the full surface pressure. Validation against the proper orthogonal decomposition method confirms the accuracy of the approach: the proposed method detects DSV and TEV initiation times with averaged relative deviations of 2.4% and 1.0% of the cycle period, respectively. While existing methods, such as the spatial distribution coefficient of pressure (SDCP) and the modulated location of peak pressure, face limitations in the reverse flow regime, the proposed method offers a robust alternative to the modified SDCP and high-order central moment of pressure methods, which require full surface instrumentation.
