The application of the proposed method reveals that the reduced frequency k is a crucial parameter governing DSV evolution, which proceeds through two distinct phases: an initial separation phase dominated by boundary layer separation and a major convection phase strongly influenced by reduced frequency. In the first phase, increasing k results in a milder evolution rate specifically for cases with DSV-dominated flow. In the second phase, however, the evolution rate decreases significantly with increasing k across all cases, leading to stronger vortices due to prolonged vorticity accumulation. For a low pitching amplitude of 5°, the evolution rate remains low for both phases regardless of k. In contrast, the mean angle of attack acts primarily as a phase-shift parameter, advancing or delaying the DSV life cycle without altering its intrinsic evolution dynamics.

papers.title: Flow mechanism control of aerosol deposition in a standardized and a real model of the human airway under transient inhalation
papers.abstract: This study investigates aerosol transport and deposition in nasal airways during transient inhalation using computational fluid dynamics coupled with a Lagrangian discrete phase model. Unsteady airflow and particle transport were simulated in a standardized nasal airway and a realistic human nasal airway reconstructed from computed tomography data at inhalation flow rates of 15 and 30 l/min. The unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations were solved using the shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model. The results reveal that particle deposition is governed by the combined effects of inertial impaction, secondary flow induced transport, and localized flow separation. In the standardized airway, smoother and more direct flow pathways enhance inertial impaction in the anterior vestibule, leading to greater particle deposition near the nasal valve. In contrast, the realistic airway generates stronger secondary flows and recirculation zones within the turbinate region, which redistribute particles and reduce direct impaction. Consequently, during the inhalation phase, the standardized airway predicts substantially higher total deposition efficiencies than the realistic airway, reaching 8.3% and 15.1%, compared with 3.6% and 9.0% in the realistic airway at 15 and 30 l/min, respectively, despite exhibiting lower pressure drop and wall shear stress. These findings indicate that aerosol transport in nasal airways is controlled by the interaction between airway geometry, secondary flow structures, particle inertia, and recirculation zones. Furthermore, this study highlights the need for the future improvements in standardized nasal airway geometry to more accurately represent realistic nasal airway and aerosol transport processes.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulations of streamwise-aligned riblets: Investigations of the blockage ratio
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulation is employed to investigate turbulent flows over streamwise-aligned rectangular riblets in a half-channel at a friction Reynolds number of (Reτ) of 180. The effects of the blockage ratio BR = w/s (the ratio of riblet width to spacing) are examined for BR = 0.05–0.8 at three viscous-scaled spacings s+ = 20, 30, and 40, with a fixed height-to-spacing ratio h/s = 0.335. The results show that s+ is the primary parameter determining whether the surface reduces or increases drag, while BR plays a secondary modulating role. The mean velocity profiles confirm that the riblet influence is confined to the near-wall region and that outer-layer similarity persists for all geometries. Using the Fukagata–Iwamoto–Kasagi (FIK) identity, the total drag is decomposed into laminar, turbulent, and dispersive contributions. The dispersive term, arising from secondary flows (SFs), remains below 4% of the total drag for all cases. Pearson correlation analysis reveals that the turbulent contribution correlates strongly with s+, whereas the dispersive contribution exhibits a strong negative correlation with BR at each fixed s+. SF vortices induced by spanwise heterogeneity are an order of magnitude weaker than the background turbulence and diminish with increasing BR and decreasing s+. The spatial redistribution of turbulent kinetic energy production demonstrates a strong link between the geometric parameters (s+, BR) and vortex organization. Overall, the primary drag-modification mechanism is the direct interaction between riblet geometry and near-wall turbulence, with s+ governing the drag regime and BR controlling the spanwise flow heterogeneity.

papers.title: Initial dynamic behavior of droplet impact considering the tangential force effect
papers.abstract: The dynamics of droplet impact on a rotating surface is a fundamental but complex problem. In this study, the impact of droplets on a rotating surface was experimentally investigated. The effects of tangential velocity, impact velocity, and liquid viscosity on the initial dynamic behaviors of the droplet were analyzed. The experimental results show that increasing the tangential velocity causes the droplet to change from symmetric spreading to asymmetric deformation and eventually to film breakup. During droplet spreading, the wetting length first increases rapidly and then gradually enters a stable state. As the liquid viscosity increases, the viscous effect dominates droplet spreading, resulting in a significant reduction in the maximum wetting length and causing the liquid film to enter the stable retraction stage earlier. In addition, the mechanism of droplet breakup induced by the tangential force was analyzed. The results show that the enhanced tangential inertia promotes the instability of the liquid film interface and plays a dominant role in the transition between droplet spreading, secondary droplets, and splashing. It is also found that the boundary distinguishing different droplet dynamic behaviors changes with variations in the tangential Weber number and normal Reynolds number when the effect of the tangential force is considered. A breakup threshold model was proposed to distinguish droplet spreading and breakup. A breakup classification model was proposed to distinguish droplet splashing and secondary droplets. These findings may provide useful guidance for quantitative investigations of droplet impacts on rotating surfaces.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of the wake-control mechanisms and pre-duct parameter sensitivity in a ship propulsor with propeller boss cap fins
papers.abstract: The wake behind a single-screw ship contains both non-uniform axial momentum and near-hub swirl-related kinetic-energy loss. This study investigates a combined pre-duct and propeller boss cap fins (PBCF) configuration using unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations coupled with the volume-of-fluid method and a sliding-mesh approach. A local wake-energy diagnostic framework is established by coupling axial momentum utilization, circumferential kinetic-energy proportion, non-axial kinetic-energy density, and positive-contribution statistics. Based on this framework, the complementary interaction between the duct-induced axial momentum enhancement and PBCF-induced near-hub swirl attenuation is clarified, and the sensitivity of the duct outlet diameter, chord length, axial position, and duct angle of attack is quantitatively ranked. The Duct-PBCF configuration increases the near-hub axial momentum utilization by approximately 9.1% and 5.0% at sections S2 and S3, respectively, compared with the bare propeller. It also reduces the circumferential kinetic-energy proportion by about 14.96% at S2 compared with the duct-only configuration. Among the duct parameters, the overall sensitivity follows A > D > X > L, with normalized weights of 0.36, 0.28, 0.21, and 0.14, respectively. Within the tested range, Dd/Dd,0 = 0.9 yields the largest efficiency improvement of approximately 3.2%, whereas a moderately positive duct angle of attack improves the thrust–torque balance. These results indicate that the Duct-PBCF design should be formulated as a multi-objective matching problem rather than as the optimization of a single performance index, involving propulsive performance, axial momentum enhancement, and vortex-energy reduction.

papers.title: Bifurcation and scaling laws of momentum shunting and Darcy shielding in double-layer porous media: A unified analytical and numerical study
papers.abstract: This study investigates the momentum transport physics of pressure-driven, steady, and laminar flow within a composite double-layer domain through a unified analytical and numerical framework. The domain comprises a Darcy–Forchheimer–Brinkman (DFB) porous medium overlying a clear Navier–Stokes (NS) fluid, a linear Darcy–Lapwood–Brinkman zone, or a secondary non-linear DFB layer. By coupling closed-form analytical solutions with a custom finite-volume solver in OpenFOAM, the results identify two distinct physical regimes: momentum shunting and Darcy shielding. In the momentum shunting regime, increasing the resistance of the overlying medium paradoxically amplifies flow within the underlying channel, revealing a bifurcation in interfacial velocity trends for various configurations. In contrast, the unified DFB/DFB system characterizes a transition from inertial compression to Darcy shielding. Inertial compression dominates high-permeability media where the momentum boundary layer (MBL) thins under the Forchheimer inertial resistance (A), with the thickness scaling as O(1/A). Conversely, Darcy shielding occurs in low-permeability media where flow becomes invariant to inertial fluctuations and is governed by the Darcy viscous resistance (B), following a derived O(1/B) scaling law. Furthermore, the DFB/DFB configuration exhibits a unique, non-monotonic interfacial strain rate, reaching a minimum within the resistance-dominated regime before rising as the MBL approaches an asymptotic floor. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for optimizing transport in industrial filtration, thermal management, and subsurface hydrology.

papers.title: Mixing enhancement mechanism and flow characteristics of a micromixer with lune-shaped spoiler
papers.abstract: Efficient mixing remains a fundamental challenge in microfluidic systems due to the dominance of laminar flow at low Reynolds numbers. In this work, we propose a novel micromixer integrated with lune-shaped spoiler array units. Combining experimental flow visualization and numerical simulation, we systematically investigate the influence of concave–concave, concave–convex, convex–convex, and convex–concave lune-shaped spoiler micromixer (VC-LSM) arrangements on internal flow patterns and mixing performance over the Reynolds number range of 1–100. The results show that lune-shaped spoilers effectively enhance mixing by inducing secondary flows and complex vortex structures that disrupt the stratified fluid interface. Among all designs, the VC-LSM configuration exhibits the optimal comprehensive performance. It achieves a maximum mixing index of 0.9996, while maintaining a pressure drop of 46.40 kPa at Re = 100. From the perspective of vortex topology evolution, the potential mechanism of the VC-LSM mixing enhancement was revealed. It is found that horseshoe vortices, hairpin vortices, and ivory vortices were generated in mixing channel of VC-LSM, and their combined effect enhanced the fluid shear and disturbance. Particularly, the newly formed ivory vortex induces the generation of additional shear layers, which continuously act on the fluid interface. The mutual entrainment of the fluids is enhanced, resulting in an increase in the contact area, which is a key factor for the excellent mixing performance of VC-LSM. These findings provide a practical structural design strategy for high-performance passive micromixers, with promising applications in lab-on-a-chip systems, biochemical analysis, and microreactors.

papers.title: Scale-conditioned structure-based closure for homogeneous turbulence: Ray–Column Interacting Particle Representation Model
papers.abstract: The particle representation model (PRM) and the interacting particle representation model (IPRM) represent homogeneous turbulence through an ensemble of orientation-conditioned structural states. In the classical cluster-averaged form, the conditional state is organized by the unit spectral direction, while the radial spectral coordinate has already been integrated out. This paper introduces a scale-conditioned extension in which the spectral vector is decomposed into orientation and radial wavenumber, and the conditional structure state is projected onto finite radial bands. We refer to the resulting finite-band formulation as Ray–Column IPRM, or RC-IPRM. The formulation is developed first at the level of the continuum spectral tensor and is then reduced to the ray–packet ensemble sums used in the numerical implementation. The finite bands are interpreted as projections of an orientation–wavenumber spectral density. Their role is to retain scale-conditioned structural populations for closure evaluation, while cascade modeling is left outside the present reference closure. The rapid dynamics remain ray–packet resolved. The nonlinear slow and terminal closure coefficients are evaluated from band-aggregate structure tensors, obtained by integrating over orientation and wavenumber within each retained band before the final one-point reconstruction is formed. A reference scale-conditioned closure is obtained by combining PRM rapid kinematics, band-local effective-gradient response, and slow rotational randomization based on band-aggregate structure tensors, together with an active large-scale-enstrophy (LSE) terminal-drain map. The original IPRM used a modified ε equation for the second scale; in the present active-LSE closure, the continuous complementarity invariant Ψfd regularizes the active LSE structure-to-dissipation map of Structure and Scales in Turbulence Modeling. The Ray–Column formulation then evaluates this active map on band-aggregate structural populations. The model is assessed in irrotational strain, homogeneous shear, elliptic-streamline, and rotating-shear configurations. The results show that the retained bands provide more than internal resolution: they reveal how scale-conditioned structure affects spectral migration, terminal-drain assignment, and filtered observables before one-point averaging removes radial scale information.

papers.title: Decorated caves preservation: Double-diffusive natural convection in a semi-circular cavity with inhomogeneous temperature
papers.abstract: This work presents a numerical investigation of double-diffusive natural convection in a two-dimensional semi-circular cavity, representing a simplified cross section of decorated caves. The lower wall is maintained at a high temperature and humidity, while the arch is subjected to linearly decreasing temperature and concentration profiles. The governing equations were solved using the finite volume method. The analysis was conducted for total Rayleigh numbers upto 2.1×106. At low Rayleigh numbers, heat and mass transfer occur purely by conduction. The onset of convection is observed at Ra=3350 adopting an asymmetric structure characterized by three recirculation cells. The flow becomes symmetric with two counter-rotating recirculation cells at Ra=5500. As the Rayleigh number increases beyond 9×104, boundary layer separation at the arch induces a loss of symmetry and the emergence of a third recirculation cell. This transition significantly alters the distribution of heat and mass transfer, as reflected in the local Nusselt and Sherwood numbers. For Rayleigh numbers above 6×105, the two main recirculation cells reach a critical size, while the third cell continues to grow in intensity. These results provide new insights into flow bifurcation mechanisms and transfer processes in semi-circular geometries relevant to cave microclimate studies.

papers.title: Nanosuspension droplet impact and deposition pattern on micro-patterned polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) surface
papers.abstract: The impact dynamics and the subsequent drying of nanosuspension droplets on micro-structured surfaces are governed by the coupled effects of inertia, surface tension, viscous dissipation, contact-line pinning, and particle transport. While nanofluid wetting, droplet impact, and evaporation on textured surfaces have been extensively investigated independently, their coupled interaction on compliant micro-structured substrates throughout the complete droplet lifetime has not been systematically investigated. Understanding this coupling is essential because the impact-induced initial hydrodynamic and wetting states govern subsequent evaporation dynamics, particle transport, and ultimately the final deposition morphology. Addition of nano-sized particles modifies the wetting dynamics and enhances the spreading of the droplets. Compared to plain surfaces, micro-structured surfaces restrict lamella expansion and suppress retraction due to contact-line pinning on surface features, leading to altered oscillation damping characteristics. These impact-induced variations strongly influence the subsequent evaporation-driven particle redistribution, resulting in distinct dried deposition morphologies on plain and micro-structured surfaces.

papers.title: Coupling interactions between wave resonance in the narrow gap and heave motion responses of two moored boxes
papers.abstract: This study investigates the coupling between the heave motion responses of two heaving boxes and the free surface oscillation in a narrow gap, and proposes a semi-analytical method to determine the resonant frequencies of the coupled system. The underlying mechanism of two in-phase and one out-of-phase resonant frequencies is identified, where in-phase and out-of-phase describe the phase relationship between the two heaving boxes. At the first and second in-phase resonant frequencies, the free surface oscillation and heave motion responses are phase-synchronized and phase-opposed, respectively. The free surface oscillation in the narrow gap plays an important role in the occurrence of these three resonant frequencies, particularly the two in-phase resonant frequencies. The effects of radiation damping and dissipation damping are characterized by the damping ratio and the Keulegan–Carpenter number, respectively. A conceptual model consisting of two main spring–mass oscillators with an attached spring–mass oscillator is established to qualitatively interpret the multi-peak variation in heave motion responses and free surface oscillations. The results indicate that the coupled system can be approximated as a three-degree-of-freedom system.

papers.title: Enrichment mechanism of oil-borne particles driven by acoustic radiation force in an orthogonal acoustic streaming field
papers.abstract: Acoustic radiation force-driven particle manipulation in viscous microfluidic environments is governed by the interplay between the spatial structure of the acoustic pressure field and viscous dissipation. In this study, a three-dimensional fully coupled electro-solid–acoustic-fluid model is developed to investigate the formation mechanism of standing wave fields and the resulting particle migration dynamics in oil-based suspensions. The system is driven by piezoelectric transducers operating under single, in-phase dual, and quadrature-phase dual excitation conditions, enabling systematic analysis of the transition from one-dimensional to two-dimensional acoustic pressure node configurations. Results show that the acoustic radiation force distribution is strongly determined by the topology of the pressure field, and quadrature-phase excitation generates a stable point-like pressure node at the channel center, leading to symmetric two-dimensional force convergence and significantly enhanced particle trapping efficiency. Parametric analysis further reveals that the particle migration behavior is governed by the competition between acoustic radiation force magnitude, viscous drag, and residence time, while voltage and flow rate primarily modulate the effective strength and duration of acoustic interaction rather than altering the fundamental force topology. These findings elucidate the acoustofluidic mechanism underlying particle manipulation and provide a theoretical foundation for parameter optimization of particle enrichment systems in oil.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigation of high-load compressor with large turning angle tandem cascade blades
papers.abstract: A combined experimental and numerical methodology was utilized to investigate the angle-of-attack features of a three-row tandem cascade, offering a comprehensive description of the separated flow evolution process within the cascade at different angles of attack (AoAs). The results demonstrate that the tandem cascade substantially decreases total pressure loss at negative angles of attack, attaining a 27.6% reduction at −12° AoA. Nevertheless, at positive angles of attack, a sudden deterioration occurs, with the total pressure loss exceeding that of the prototype cascade. Subsequent investigation reveals that at positive angles of attack, the substantial separation vortex responsible for corner stall originates at the leading edge of the first row of blades and develops toward the inter-row region and the subsequent blade-row passages as the angle of attack increases, thereby inducing the accumulation of low-momentum fluid and large-scale asymmetric separation. This result reveals the relationship between the positive-angle-of-attack performance deterioration of the three-row tandem cascade and the transport of separation vortices, wake mixing, and boundary-layer development among multiple blade rows. It indicates that its aerodynamic performance is not only determined by geometric-parameter variations, but also controlled by the separated-flow evolution mechanism during the multi-stage deflection process. Effective regulation of the first row of blades and the inter-row flow is essential for further improving the performance of the three-row tandem cascade and can also provide a physical basis for subsequent load distribution and inter-row matching optimization.

papers.title: Wind pressure analysis on a flat-roof building under the local acceleration wind profiles
papers.abstract: This study examines wind pressure distributions on a flat-roof building subjected to a locally accelerated wind profile. Two sets of wind profiles are considered: (1) profiles defined by the height of the peak wind speed at 40%, 60%, and 80% of the building height (H), all under a constant acceleration factor of 1.1, and (2) profiles defined by a higher acceleration factor (1.3) at fixed peak heights of 0.4H and 0.8H. Relative to the traditional atmospheric boundary layer profile, the locally accelerated profile significantly amplifies windward surface pressures, particularly at elevations aligned with the acceleration zone. A higher acceleration region (Hacc) combined with a larger acceleration factor (β) results in increased wind pressures on the roof. For an acceleration factor of 1.3 with a fixed peak height of 0.8H, the area-averaged time-mean corner-region pressure coefficient rises by approximately 25.37% compared with the category A wind profile. The spectral proper orthogonal decomposition method is employed to analyze roof-surface vortical structures and successfully isolates energetically dominant coherent vortices exhibiting periodic behavior. Overall, these findings offer important guidance for the wind-resistant design of flat-roof buildings in complex flow environments, highlighting the coupled effects of accelerated flow and resulting pressure loads.

papers.title: Critical velocity and fluid–structure responses during the launch of tethered balloon systems at high Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: The launch of tethered balloon systems under strong wind conditions involves highly unsteady fluid–structure coupling, yet the mechanism responsible for launch failure remains insufficiently understood. In this study, three-dimensional simulations of a teardrop-shaped tethered balloon are performed at Reynolds numbers of Re=O(106)–O(107), corresponding to free-stream velocities of U∞=6–12 m/s, by coupling the shear stress transport–based improved delayed detached eddy simulation method with six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body dynamics and a catenary tether model. The results show that launch stability is governed not only by the static buoyancy but also by an unsteady negative-lift effect, which arises from pressure-field redistribution associated with the geometric asymmetry of the balloon, pitch-induced changes in separation, and wake deflection. To characterize the launch dynamics, two dimensionless quantities ΠF and ΠV are introduced, whose sign combinations classify the process into three fluid–structure response modes: dynamic ascent mode (DAM), competition mode (CM), and descent mode (DM). For the present configuration, the launch process is dominated by DAM at U∞=6 and 8 m/s, exhibits repeated transitions among DAM, CM, and DM near U∞=10 m/s, and becomes descent-dominated at U∞=12 m/s. Based on the zero crossings of the two dimensionless criteria, the critical launch wind speed is estimated to be approximately 9.45 m/s under the present idealized inflow and release conditions. These findings show that negative lift plays a major role in launch instability and provide a response mode-based criterion for assessing the safe launch range of tethered balloon systems.

papers.title: Non-equilibrium polyatomic gas flows: Nonlinear coupled constitutive relations and topological study of three-temperature relaxation
papers.abstract: Non-equilibrium gaseous phenomena at high temperatures may activate additional degrees of freedom that remain dormant at lower temperatures, such as vibrational modes. An accurate prediction of the forces and heat flux acting on a body in such an environment requires detailed information on the energy distribution among rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom. The present study aims to analyze non-equilibrium flows by carefully accounting for the relaxation processes among various degrees of freedom. As higher-order constitutive equations, the nonlinear coupled constitutive relations (NCCR) were employed to obtain more accurate approximations of the stress and heat flux terms by extending the two-temperature formulation proposed by Srivastava et al. [Phys. Fluids 37, 036154 (2025)] to a three-temperature relaxation case. The present study further examined various relaxation models for internal energy to evaluate their effectiveness and accuracy. In addition to the standard energy exchange that considers only translational and other modes, the energy exchange between rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom was investigated. A topological study was further incorporated to observe the changes in the solution space within the second-order NCCR formulation relative to the first-order constitutive relations, i.e., the Navier–Stokes–Fourier formulation. Finally, the new set of equations derived from the three-temperature relaxation model was used to investigate shock wave structures in polyatomic gases.

papers.title: Orientation and rotation of spheroidal inertial particles in compressible turbulent channel flows
papers.abstract: This study investigates the dynamics of spheroidal particles in compressible turbulent channel flows using point-particle direct numerical simulations. We examine particles covering Stokes numbers from 1 to 100 and aspect ratios spanning 1/50 to 50, suspended in compressible turbulent channel flows with bulk Mach numbers from 0.3 to 3.0. Our results show that the increased flow compressibility, which introduces non-uniform mean fluid density and viscosity, significantly alters particle rotational motion and orientation. In the near-wall region, prolate particles with small inertia (St+=1,5) exhibit spinning motion about the streamwise direction, which is enhanced with increasing aspect ratio and bulk Mach number. In contrast, oblate particles with small inertia primarily spin about the spanwise direction, and as Mb increases or particles become more flattened, they tend to align with the wall-normal direction while maintaining spinning. Prolate particles with large inertia (St+=30,100) tend to tumble at a nearly constant angular speed in the x–y plane, and this tumbling motion weakens as Mb increases, especially for more elongated particles. Meanwhile, oblate particles with large inertia exhibit a strong tendency to spin about the spanwise axis. This tendency strengthens with increasing Mb, but weakens as particles become more flattened. In the turbulent core region, non-spherical particles preferentially rotate about the axis corresponding to their lower rotational Stokes number (prolate particles spin, while oblate particles tumble), while maintaining their long axis in the x–z plane. This tendency is enhanced with increasing bulk Mach number, but weakens with increasing particle Stokes number.

papers.title: Bifurcation phenomena in rotating lid-driven square cavity flow: Hydrodynamic balance and vorticity-dynamical analyses
papers.abstract: This study presents the first lattice Boltzmann simulation of two-dimensional incompressible viscous flow in a rotating lid-driven square cavity. A consistent forcing scheme is implemented to accurately account for centrifugal and Coriolis forces within both the numerical model and the modified boundary conditions. We consider the clockwise and counterclockwise rotating systems at two Reynolds numbers (Re=500,1000) over a wide range of Rossby numbers (Ro=0.025−∞). A hydrodynamic balance analysis confirms that the continuum flow physics is faithfully captured across all simulations. For each Re, the Navier–Stokes solutions reveal bifurcation phenomena in velocity and vorticity fields with respect to Ro, from which two primary bifurcation branches (attractors) are clearly identified. Within each branch, the steady flow fields exhibit little sensitivity to Ro and are essentially governed solely by Re. The rotation direction of the cavity remains indistinguishable in the first primary branch but becomes discernible in the second. Vortex structures are investigated using a recently proposed streamline-based, direction-dependent vorticity decomposition (ω=R+s), revealing that axial vortices are dominated by the orbital-rotation mode R, while shear layers are governed by the spin mode s. The vorticity-mode distributions reveal coexisting Klein–Kaden–Betz (KKB, same-sign) and anti-KKB (opposite-sign) patterns, where KKB regions correspond to shear-layer roll-up strengthening axial vortices, while anti-KKB regions indicate competitive modal interactions that limit excessive vorticity intensification. The physical roles of the Coriolis force are highlighted in advection and redistribution of the wall-generated spin mode. First, during the unsteady evolution stage, it induces circulatory currents and creates new axial vortices, promoting the conversion of s into R. Second, irrespective of the cavity rotation direction, the enhanced Coriolis force at a smaller Ro facilitates the conversion of s to R stored within the corner vortices, naturally leading to a reduction in the swirling strength of the primary axial vortex. A self-sustaining physical feedback loop is proposed within the framework of boundary vorticity dynamics, linking the boundary generation of the spin mode by surface pressure gradient and centrifugal force to its spatiotemporal evolution modulated by Coriolis force. These findings offer a novel perspective for understanding the nonlinear vortical-flow phenomena in wall-bounded confined rotating systems.

papers.title: Nonisothermal global-pressure exactness in fractured multiphase flow with aperture feedback
papers.abstract: Global-pressure formulations recast multiphase Darcy flow in terms of a single pressure driving the total flux. Their exact equivalence to phase-pressure formulations holds only when the constitutive data satisfy the compatibility conditions required for a total-differential structure and its generalized nonisothermal extension. Here, we derive the exactness criterion for temperature-dependent mobilities and capillary pressures. We show that equivalence depends on whether the mobility-weighted capillary contribution is path independent in the saturation–temperature domain, so that it can be absorbed into a scalar global pressure. This yields the classical compatibility conditions within the saturation sector and a distinct mixed saturation–temperature condition that arises only in nonisothermal settings. We then incorporate this structure into a reduced matrix–fracture model with heat transport, matrix–fracture thermal exchange, and evolving aperture. Numerical benchmarks recover the three regimes predicted by the theory: globally exact, exact on each fixed-temperature slice but not on the full saturation–temperature domain, and fully nonexact. In fractured systems, thermal forcing alone can drive transitions between these regimes, while aperture evolution changes the path through state space. When saturation-sector exactness is lost, a least squares projection on fixed-temperature slices extracts the nearest gradient component of the mobility-weighted capillary field. This yields a conservative slice-wise scalar-pressure surrogate and a quantitative projection residual. The residual separates saturation-sector nonintegrability from the mixed saturation–temperature incompatibility that controls genuinely nonisothermal loss of exactness. The framework links nonisothermal exactness theory, fractured-flow dynamics, and conservative reduced closure in a global-pressure formulation.

papers.title: Three-dimensional analytical solution for immiscible displacement flow in a rectangular duct
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional confinement plays a critical role in shaping the structure and transport characteristics of displacement flows, yet its influence remains insufficiently understood beyond two-dimensional approximations. In this study, the physical effects of transverse confinement on viscous-dominated displacement flow are investigated in a straight, near-horizontal rectangular channel with low density contrasts between fluids. An analytical solution of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations, under the assumptions of parallel-flow and zero streamwise momentum diffusion, is derived for two immiscible, Newtonian, iso-viscous fluids, providing full access to the velocity field and interfacial structure. The results reveal that lateral confinement induces a non-uniform redistribution of momentum across the channel cross section, leading to significant modifications of velocity profiles, volumetric flow partitioning, and maximum velocity compared to two-dimensional predictions. In particular, the interplay between buoyancy-driven motion and viscous resistance is shown to depend sensitively on channel aspect ratio, with sidewall effects introducing distinct three-dimensional flow structures that govern the displacement process. These findings provide clear insight into how confinement controls the dynamics of gravity-driven exchange flows and establish a physically consistent framework for analyzing displacement processes in inclined, confined geometries.

papers.title: Mass-flux-controlled diffuse stationary jumps in dense granular flows upstream of a finite-width obstacle
papers.abstract: Granular flows impacting obstacles may develop jump-like structures whose height, upstream extent, and deposit morphology depend sensitively on the incoming flow state and obstacle geometry. For finite-width obstacles, however, part of the incoming material can bypass the obstacle laterally, so that the stationary jump is governed not only by a local front condition but also by system-scale mass redistribution. Here, we develop a depth-averaged control-volume model for diffuse stationary jumps (DSJ) formed upstream of a finite-width obstacle in dense granular flows down an incline. The model is derived from mass and momentum balances across the reverse-propagating jump front and retains the effects of gravity, effective friction, finite jump length, and weak compressibility. We show that, once a statistically stationary DSJ is reached, the normalized mass flux at the jump front is in one-to-one correspondence with the local Froude number under the dense-flow approximation. This relation allows the conventional Froude-based jump relation to be reformulated in terms of a mass-flux variable that is directly linked to the imposed inflow and lateral redistribution in the finite-width-obstacle configuration. Comparisons with discrete element method simulations and available experimental data show that the model captures the jump-height ratio in the dense DSJ regime. By coupling the jump relation with geometric closures for the post-jump deposit, the model further predicts the deposit length and height within the range of configurations considered here. The results provide a compact framework for connecting inflow supply, jump-front adjustment, lateral bypass, and stationary deposit morphology in dense granular flows interacting with finite-width obstacles.

papers.title: Three-dimensional effects and turbulence characteristics in heated urban canyons
papers.abstract: Ground heating in urban environments generates buoyancy that interacts with wind-driven shear and modifies street-canyon ventilation and heat removal. Although thermally affected flows in two-dimensional (2D) canyons have been widely investigated, the response of three-dimensional (3D) canyons remains unclear as lateral exchange, tip-corner eddies, and buoyant uplift occur simultaneously. This study presents a wind tunnel comparison of 2D and 3D street canyons under similar oncoming flow conditions and controlled floor heating, at floor temperatures from ambient to 150 °C for the 2D canyon and to 190 °C for the 3D canyon. Time-resolved and scanning stereo particle image velocimetry and thermocouple measurements quantify mean flow structures, turbulence statistics, turbulent momentum-transfer events, and thermal stratification. Results show that lateral channel flow and tip-corner vortices weaken the mid-span primary recirculation in the 3D canyon compared to the 2D canyon. Ground heating strengthens the buoyancy-assisted updraft along the leeward wall and enhances roof-level exchange. In the 2D canyon, increasing thermal forcing can reorganize the flow toward a more coherent buoyancy-driven regime. In the 3D canyon, lateral exchange persists and maintains stronger spatial variability and event intermittency. Reynolds-stress and quadrant analyses show that moderate thermal forcing amplifies ejection and sweep events near the canyon top, whereas stronger forcing can reduce the intermittency of shear-driven motions in the 2D canyon. Temperature and gradient Richardson number profiles indicate that 3D lateral mixing smoothens local stability gradients while allowing buoyancy-driven vertical heat removal. These findings clarify how three-dimensionality modulates the balance between shear-driven exchange, buoyant uplift, and lateral redistribution in heated urban canyons.

papers.title: Assessment of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes modeling of jet interaction in fan-array wind generator flows
papers.abstract: Fan-array wind generators (FAWGs) provide controlled turbulent inflow conditions that cannot be reproduced in conventional wind tunnels. Despite their increasing use in experimental studies, numerical modeling of FAWG-generated flows remains largely unexplored. The present study assesses the capability of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) modeling to predict jet interaction in a 10×10 FAWG. Numerical predictions are compared against experimental measurements of axial velocity and turbulence intensity from a reference configuration. Individual fan units are represented using a pressure-jump boundary condition based on a reconstructed performance curve derived from manufacturer data. Grid convergence is verified, and the influence of fan representation, swirl strength, operating point, and inflow turbulence conditions is examined. The results show that RANS modeling captures the global jet interaction topology and downstream velocity decay with reasonable accuracy. However, systematic magnitude discrepancies are observed in the near-field injection region and peripheral shear layers. Turbulence intensity predictions exhibit larger deviations, reflecting limitations of the eddy-viscosity closure in highly mixing-dominated flows. A low-aspect-ratio flat plate is included as a demonstrative application to illustrate the aerodynamic impact of FAWG-generated inflow. A parametric assessment further confirms that prescribed fan swirl exerts a substantial effect on the downstream flow field. Overall, the study shows that RANS modeling, combined with a pressure-jump fan representation, provides a computationally efficient framework for predicting the mean-flow structure of FAWG systems, while exhibiting clear limitations in resolving localized turbulence characteristics.

papers.title: Parameter estimation for subgrid-scale models using Markov chain Monte Carlo approximate Bayesian computation
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the use of approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) combined with an “improved” Markov chain Monte Carlo (IMCMC) method to estimate posterior distributions of model parameters in subgrid-scale (SGS) closures for large eddy simulations (LES) of turbulent flows. The ABC–IMCMC approach avoids the need to directly compute a likelihood function during parameter estimation, enabling greater flexibility compared to full Bayesian inversion methods. The method also naturally provides uncertainties in parameter estimates, avoiding the artificial certainty implied by many optimization methods for determining model parameters. In this study, we outline the salient features of the present ABC–IMCMC algorithm, including the use of an adaptive proposal and calibration step to accelerate the parameter estimation process. We demonstrate the approach by estimating parameters in two nonlinear SGS closure forms using three different types of reference data from direct numerical simulations of homogeneous isotropic turbulence. We show that the resulting parameter distributions give excellent agreement with reference probability density functions of the SGS stress and kinetic energy production rate in a priori tests, while also providing stable solutions in forward LES (i.e., a posteriori tests). The ABC–IMCMC method is thus shown to be an effective and efficient approach as compared to traditional ABC for estimating unknown parameters, including their uncertainties, in SGS closure models for LES of turbulent flows, and can be straightforwardly applied to other model forms and reference data.

papers.title: Optimization and characterization parameters of microgroove drag reduction based on genetic algorithm
papers.abstract: Surface drag reduction is of crucial importance in enhancing fluid mechanical efficiency and reducing energy consumption. Microgroove structures inspired by shark skin have shown promising potential for reducing turbulence drag. However, further investigation is required into their systematic parameter optimization and universal characterization parameters. The present study selects five typical microgroove configurations: isosceles triangle (V), ellipse (U), rectangle (I), trapezoid (T), and right triangle (R). Employing computational fluid dynamics simulations in combination with genetic algorithms, the study optimizes geometric parameters with drag reduction rate as the objective. It is proposed that three new dimensionless parameters for characterizing drag reduction be introduced: hydraulic diameter (HD+), periodic hydraulic diameter (PHD+), and modified periodic hydraulic diameter (MPHD+). Compared with the commonly used dimensionless cross-sectional scale (L+), these novel parameters achieve a maximum reduction of approximately 27% in the coefficient of variation within the optimal drag reduction range, thereby demonstrating superior consistency in characterization. The study further generates cloud maps of drag reduction performance for the five grooves and validates the optimization results through circulating-water-tunnel experiments. The simulation captures the same trend of drag reduction as the experiments. The microgroove structures effectively suppress near-wall turbulence pulsations, optimize the wall shear stress distribution, alter near-wall vortex patterns, and reduce turbulent dissipation, thereby achieving drag reduction. The present research provides theoretical foundations and engineering references for the design and performance prediction of microgroove drag reduction surfaces.

papers.title: Inter-well interference between non-condensable gas-assisted and conventional cyclic steam stimulation: Dynamic evolution mechanism and predictive model
papers.abstract: Non-condensable gas-assisted cyclic steam stimulation (NCG-CSS) elevates reservoir pressure during heavy oil recovery; however, the resultant thermal front expansion triggers complex multiphase inter-well interference with adjacent cyclic steam stimulation (CSS) patterns. The fluid mechanics and thermodynamic mechanisms governing this interference remain poorly understood. Integrating multi-stage experiments, this study elucidates the spatiotemporal evolution of temperature profiles and multiphase flow behavior during NCG-CSS and CSS interaction. We formulate a zonal characterization model for NCG and steam flow that, coupled with a stepwise quasi-steady-state approach, enables precise prediction of interference onset and fluid recovery. Results reveal interference evolves through two distinct thermodynamic phases: the X–Y and Y stages. Initially (X–Y stage), the thermal front expands along the inter-well axis, confined near preexisting heated zones. Subsequently (Y stage), longitudinal deflection of the temperature distribution penetrates orthogonally into cold oil zones. While aggregate cumulative production is enhanced by 6.3% and 16.1% during these respective stages, energy efficiency degrades, with the oil–steam ratio dropping by 15.3% and 30%. The interference is governed by thermal front expansion: steam supplies the dominant heat input, whereas NCG redistributes pressure and promotes steam and hot water flow. Excessive injection enlarges the radius disparity between adjacent thermal fronts, weakening interference-area expansion. Thermal redistribution between wells affects production performance, a mechanism that becomes increasingly pronounced as interference intensity rises. By extending wellbore-constrained flow theory from the vertical (X–Z) to the horizontal (X–Y) plane, this study provides a holistic multiphase framework for multi-well interaction in porous media.

papers.title: Fluid–structure interaction response of a buried submarine pipeline under near-field underwater explosion
papers.abstract: Buried submarine pipelines are widely used in offshore infrastructure, yet their response to near-field underwater explosions remains poorly understood because seabed confinement fundamentally alters bubble collapse and structural deformation. Here, a compressible fluid–structure interaction model is employed to investigate the coupled dynamics between explosion bubbles and buried pipelines. The results show that burial depth governs a transition in the interaction regime. Under shallow burial conditions, structural compliance dissipates part of the explosion energy and leads to global cross-sectional crushing of the pipeline. In contrast, deeper burial suppresses global motion and confines the damage to localized denting. Parametric analyses further reveal that the effects of detonation azimuthal angle, hydrostatic pressure, and explosion intensity are non-monotonic, and that peak damage is governed by the competition between load concentration and structural stiffness. These findings elucidate the underlying mechanisms in explosion-induced pipeline failure and offer guidance for blast-resistant design of submarine pipelines.

papers.title: Effects of fuel Lewis number on Reynolds stress distribution and its transport during oblique flame–wall interaction
papers.abstract: The influence of the fuel Lewis number LeF on Reynolds stresses and their transport during flame–wall interaction (FWI) is studied using a direct numerical simulation database of oblique wall-quenching of V-shaped premixed flames in a turbulent channel flow. Simulations are conducted for LeF=0.6,1.0, and 1.4. Results indicate that LeF significantly affects the magnitude and anisotropy of the Reynolds stresses. In these cases, the location of the FWI is affected by LeF, with the flame at LeF=0.6 interacting closest to the flame holder, while the flame with LeF=1.4 interacts farthest from the flame holder. The wall-normal distributions of the Reynolds stress components deviate significantly from those recorded in the non-reacting turbulent channel flows, with deviations strongly influenced by LeF. The production of the streamwise Reynolds stress component by the mean velocity gradient exceeds sink contributions from other terms, especially downstream of the FWI region. The pressure–strain term plays a dominant role in Reynolds stress transport in the spanwise direction, facilitating Reynolds stress redistribution. In particular, local equilibrium between the generation and dissipation of Reynolds stresses is not achieved, particularly as LeF decreases, leading to anisotropy of Reynolds stresses. These findings highlight the impact of LeF on near-wall flow dynamics and the production, redistribution, and dissipation of Reynolds stresses. The study provides valuable information for improving turbulence models for Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations of FWIs under varying LeF conditions, advancing the understanding of turbulent boundary layer flows with premixed flames.

papers.title: A multi-frame analysis of flow reversal in tidal bore
papers.abstract: A tidal bore is a nonlinear step like surge propagating on the top of a river countercurrent. The scientific literature reports that the passage of the tidal front may induce local flow reversals and, in some cases, a global reversal of the river current. Here, combining particle image velocimetry measurements and two-dimensional numerical simulations based on a weakly compressible smoothed particle hydrodynamics method, we show that the flow classification of tidal bores must explicitly take into account the frame of reference. When the river flow does not reverse after the bore passing, this is a consequence of the perspective imposed by the background current (itself resulting from the previous tide and the natural river discharge toward the sea). Depending on the relative magnitudes of the river current and the velocity field induced by the bore, one may observe a global reversal, a local reversal (or both), or no reversal at all. When the tide is spatially inhomogeneous, with a tidal range that varies along the estuary rather than a simple step in water depth, transitions between bore types may occur during the bore passing.

papers.title: Unsteady drag force model coupled with non-hydrostatic quasi-three-dimensional model for vegetated dam break flows
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of dam break flows (DBFs) through vegetated channels and floodplains is crucial for assessing flood hazards and designing nature-based flood mitigation measures. This study systematically evaluates three drag force formulations: conventional, nonuniform, and unsteady drag force models, for simulating DBFs through rigid emergent vegetation with depth integrated models including two-dimensional calculation and quasi-three-dimensional models of the specialized bottom velocity calculation and the general bottom velocity calculation (GBVC) method. To validate the models, experimental results covering three flow regimes characterized by different initial Froude numbers (high, middle, and low Fri) and six vegetation configurations with varying densities and coverage lengths are compared with the simulation results. The comparisons show that the conventional and nonuniform drag models exhibit systematic shortcomings to accurately represent DBFs propagations. On the other hand, the proposed unsteady drag force model achieves substantial improvements across all numerical frameworks and vegetation configurations, reproducing accurately wave height, celerity, and bore transformations, and eliminating systematic errors of the other drag formulations. Notably, the GBVC formulations deliver the best performance, especially for low Fri conditions with pure undular bores where nonhydrostatic effects are prominent. The successful integration of the unsteady drag model into the advanced numerical frameworks marks a significant step forward in simulating DBFs through vegetation. These findings are expected to contribute to more reliable flood hazard assessment and support the development of robust mitigation strategies in vegetated floodplains.

papers.title: Nonlinear magneto-vortex dynamo in an obliquely rotating ternary hybrid nanofluid driven by a small-scale non-helical force
papers.abstract: We develop a nonlinear theory of magneto-vortex dynamo in an obliquely rotating ternary hybrid nanofluid (Galinstan/Ag (silver)/CNT (carbon nanotubes)/graphene) driven by a small-scale non-helical force. Using multiscale asymptotic expansions in the small Reynolds number R≪1, we derive closed nonlinear equations for the large-scale vortex and magnetic fields. The effective dimensionless parameters, such as the rotation parameter D, Chandrasekhar number Q, magnetic Prandtl number Pm, solutal Rayleigh number RC, and Lewis number Le, are expressed analytically through the nanoparticle volume fractions and morphology-dependent mixture ratios A, B, and S. Linear analysis identifies two coupled instabilities: a hydrodynamic α-effect and a magnetohydrodynamic αH-effect, whose competition produces two distinct dynamo regimes controlled by nanoparticle composition. In the nonlinear stationary limit, the magnetic subsystem supports two types of structures: spatially localized kinks and nonlinear periodic waves, whose existence and spatial scales are predicted within the present effective-medium model.

papers.title: Effects of trimethyl phosphate spray duration on hydrogen mixing natural gas explosions
papers.abstract: Hydrogen mixing into natural gas is a near-term route to decarbonize end-use energy while using existing infrastructure for storage and distribution. Yet, the higher reactivity of hydrogen mixing natural gas increases explosion hazards in confined corridors. This study systematically investigated the explosion suppression efficacy of the organic phosphorus inhibitor trimethyl phosphate under different spray durations and different hydrogen mixing ratios. The experiments showed that the spray-induced disturbance temporarily outweighed the developing physicochemical inhibition at hydrogen mixing ratios of 10% with a 500 ms spray, leading to an increase in peak overpressure and an evident explosion-promoting response. Prolonging the spray duration significantly reduced flame acceleration and explosion overpressure. Coupled chemical-kinetic and density-functional calculations indicated that some initial trimethyl phosphate activation reactions are exothermic and can generate reactive C1 fragments, which may contribute to the early pressure rise under short-spray conditions. With longer sprays, continuous formation of phosphorus radicals enhances key free radicals scavenging and sustains chain-termination cycling, leading to slower flames and lower peak pressures. The disturbance, chemical, and physical model integrating disturbance, chemical inhibition, and thermodynamic cooling rationalizes the transition from disturbance-driven promotion to suppression dominated by cooling and phosphorus-mediated termination. These results provide mechanistic guidance and quantitative benchmarks for active explosion-suppression design in complex confined infrastructures.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent pulsating flow through an aortic arch analog
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations of pulsating flow were performed using an aortic arch model, which was represented as a curved pipe. The overarching objective was to investigate the potential implications of pulsation characteristics on the development and progression of vascular diseases. In particular, the study explores flows with varying pulsation frequencies, curvature ratios, and amplitude ratios, focusing on the effects of steady and unsteady inflow boundary conditions. For all cases, the centrifugal force shifts the peak velocity toward the outer wall of the curved section and leads to the formation of Dean vortices, while transition is induced on the outer side of the arch. The breakdown of Dean vortices in the mean is significantly altered by the amplitude ratio and the curvature ratio. Although the low-amplitude and low-frequency cases show similar breakdown characteristics to the steady case, the flow breaks down more rapidly for the high amplitude and large curvature cases. However, the unsteady behavior of the vortices with pulsating inflow was found to be quite different from that of the mean flow. The effects on the transitional flow and the generation of turbulence also affect the topology of the coherent and stochastic turbulent fluctuations in terms of the Reynolds stress tensor. The outer downstream region, representing the descending aorta, exhibits notably high time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), whereas the mean pressure is maximized toward the inlet of the bend along the outer wall of the pipe. The magnitude of the fluctuating WSS and pressure was found to be the same order of magnitude as the mean values, with distributions that were much more sensitive to the inflow parameters. The results highlight how the details of the inflow conditions and aortic geometry can influence the unsteady behavior of the flow field and thereby have important implications for the onset and progression of vascular diseases.

papers.title: Beyond the mean-flow: A spectral-dynamic approach to unraveling the physics of droplet capture in fog harvesting meshes
papers.abstract: Fog harvesting efficiency with mesh collectors is governed by complex interactions between droplet inertia and geometry-induced flow structures. Although previous studies have primarily relied on mean-flow metrics, the present work introduces a spectral-dynamic framework to examine an important but often overlooked control on droplet capture. A two-way coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian model is used to simulate droplet–laden flow (2–40 μm) across five representative mesh geometries. The results show that capture efficiency correlates not only with the magnitude of velocity fluctuations, but also with their spectral distribution and persistence. Frequency-domain analysis indicates that mesh geometry redistributes fluctuation energy across pore and obstruction regions, thereby defining a characteristic flow timescale. By comparing this flow timescale with the droplet response time, a dynamic matching parameter, Π=droplet response time/flow time scale, is introduced. The highest capture efficiency occurs when Π is order unity, corresponding to sustained droplet-flow interaction in the near-mesh region. Geometries that generate broadband, moderately amplified spectral content (e.g., triangular mesh) increase droplet residence time and interception probability, whereas geometries with either weak or highly localized fluctuations reduce performance through insufficient forcing or premature bypass. A physics-inspired correlation for capture efficiency is proposed based on this condition. The study therefore provides mechanistic design guidance, rather than a definitive optimum, for geometry optimization in fog-harvesting meshes.

papers.title: Critical flow parameters and detachment criterion for bubble-particle aggregate under shear flows with different orientations
papers.abstract: Fluid shear is a primary factor governing the detachment of bubble-particle aggregates in flotation systems. Identifying the critical hydrodynamic conditions that trigger detachment is essential for controlling aggregate stability. In this study, a customized multi-configuration turbulent experimental system was developed. High-speed imaging, coupled with particle image velocimetry, was employed to systematically investigate the detachment dynamics of bubble-particle aggregates under shear flows with different orientations, namely normal, vortex, and tangential shear. The critical flow parameters and the interfacial evolution during detachment were quantitatively characterized, and the influence of flow structure on the detachment mechanism was elucidated. Furthermore, based on macroscopic inertial-capillary scaling and dimensional analysis, a dimensionless shear detachment criterion (De) was proposed using the macroscopically measurable physical parameters. The results show that shear orientation strongly influences aggregate stability, which decreases in the following order: normal shear, vortex shear, and tangential shear. In the normal shear flow, detachment is dominated by tensile stretching along the normal direction. In the tangential shear flow, lateral shear destabilizes the aggregate through sliding of the three-phase contact line. The vortex shear field exhibits a combined mechanism involving both tensile and shear effects. A fitted relationship between the shear detachment number and the detachment probability was established, providing an empirical macroscopic classification of the measured detachment behavior for the three flow configurations investigated in this study. The results provide a measurable representation of fixed bubble-particle detachment under the present experimental conditions.

papers.title: Graph neural networks vs transformers for predicting critical properties of hydrocarbons
papers.abstract: We present and compare two state-of-the-art machine learning frameworks, a Message Passing Graph Isomorphism Network with Edges (GINE) and a Simplified Molecular Line Entry System (SMILES)-based Bidirectional Encoder Representation Transformer (BERT), for predicting four critical properties required in real-fluid equations of state: critical pressure (Pc), temperature (Tc), volume (Vc), and acentric factor (ω). SMILES-BERT is trained using 2581 randomized SMILES entries curated from 157 validated molecules utilizing string-based representations, while GINE is trained directly on the corresponding unique molecular graphs (atoms as nodes and bonds as edges) to avoid representation-level leakage. Both models are evaluated on an out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset of hydrocarbon species from CoolProp. A minimum R2-based hyperparameter optimization is conducted on 8–16 NVIDIA H200 Graphics Processing Units to enable fair comparison in accuracy, efficiency, and generalization. GINE achieves performance comparable to or better than SMILES-BERT across most targets on the test and OOD datasets, while using 59× fewer parameters and achieving 37× faster training; inference speeds are comparable under matched evaluation sizes. Additional evaluation based on synthetic aviation fuel-relevant molecular families shows that GINE performs consistently better for structurally regular compounds, such as n-alkanes, alkylbenzenes, and polyaromatics, while results are mixed for cycloalkanes. An additional study on large fuel radicals and peroxy intermediates produced during combustion reveals differing extrapolation behavior, with GINE preserving smooth, fuel-like prediction trends more reliably. Overall, this work highlights the role of molecular representation and chemical regime in model performance.

papers.title: Data-driven modeling of nonlinear dynamics in a rotating detonation combustor via finite dimensional approximations of the Koopman operator
papers.abstract: A rotating detonation combustor (RDC) is a promising technology for increasing efficiency in propulsion and power generation applications. The dynamics of the RDC are governed by continuously propagating detonation waves within an annular combustion chamber. Multiple operating modes can be observed, including nonlinear interactions between counter-rotating waves and the emergence of standing wave patterns. Koopman operator theory provides a framework to globally linearize nonlinear dynamical systems by representing their evolution in the space of observables rather than states. In this work, finite-dimensional approximations of the Koopman operator are constructed using variants of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) applied to high-speed video data capturing the natural flame luminosity of the detonation waves in the RDC at the Technical University Berlin. By introducing time-delay embeddings as a dictionary of observables, this approach overcomes the limitations of standard DMD methods, particularly for accurate reconstruction of standing wave patterns and for capturing nonlinear interactions. In addition, a technique is presented to mitigate the influence of sensor noise in the luminosity measurements. Finally, it is shown that the DMD-based models provide insight into the dynamics of different operating modes by decomposing the reconstructed signal into its characteristic features.

papers.title: Weakly nonlinear pressure waves in bubbly liquids based on a two-fluid model: Importance of liquid compressibility
papers.abstract: Pressure waves in bubbly liquids are dispersive, with two branches commonly called the slow and fast modes [Egashira et al., Fluid Dyn. Res., 34, 317–334 (2004)]. This study develops a two-fluid-model theory for weakly nonlinear modulation of one-dimensional quasi-monochromatic pressure waves in a compressible bubbly liquid, neglecting thermal and dissipative effects. Starting from a two-phase formulation with spherical bubble dynamics and compressible equations of state, we apply a multiple-scale expansion in a strongly dispersive high-frequency, short-wavelength regime and derive nonlinear Schrödinger equations for the slow and fast modes. To discuss the role of liquid-phase compressibility, we also derive an analogous envelope equation under the incompressible-liquid approximation (incompressible mode). The dispersion and nonlinear coefficients are evaluated as functions of wavenumber and void fraction. The incompressible approximation reproduces the slow mode only in a limited parameter range; as the void fraction decreases, it can predict nonphysical behavior, including group velocities exceeding the sound speed of the pure liquid, and it yields large errors in both dispersion and nonlinearity. The fast mode is fundamentally different: the dispersion coefficient has the opposite sign, and the nonlinear coefficient depends more strongly on void fraction and may change sign. By comparing dispersion relations, we show that a previously reported “slow-mode” envelope equation corresponds to incompressible-mode behavior [Kanagawa et al., J. Fluid Sci. Technol., 5, 351–369 (2010)], and we delineate when the incompressible approximation can serve as a proxy for the physical slow mode.

papers.title: On the primary instability in the wake of polygonal cylinders
papers.abstract: A numerical study was undertaken to investigate the primary instability of the flow past polygonal cylinders, with the side number N∈Z[5,16], and at non-dimensional incidence angles (α*) from corner to face orientation. The primary instability is invariably the result of a Hopf bifurcation, with the bifurcation point determined using the linearized Landau equation. The critical Reynolds number, Recr, shows a nonlinear dependence on N and α*. Analysis of sensitivity to base flow modifications with respect to the circular cylinder revealed that the variation in Recr is related to the direction of backflow modifications, from which a negative correlation is established between Recr and the variation of eigenvalues calculated based on the direct and the adjoint eigenmodes of the perturbed fields. Endogeneity analysis was applied to identify the contribution of the local mechanism to the global growth of the leading mode. The contribution from the production mechanism is shown to be insensitive to N and α*, whereas that from the convection mechanism shows a negative relation to Recr.

papers.title: Collaborative active control of the wake of an Ahmed body using multiple sweeping jets
papers.abstract: Sweeping jet (SWJ) collaborative actuation offers a promising approach for manipulating the wake of a slanted Ahmed body, yet its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently explored. In the present study, numerical simulations are performed at a Reynolds number of Re=1.97×105 to investigate the mean wake response under SWJs deployed at different locations. The results show that single-point actuation primarily induces localized modifications to the wake, such as altering the upper and lower recirculation bubbles or the corner vortices. Owing to the strong coupling between these structures, the overall drag reduction remains limited. In contrast, collaborative actuation produces a more global modification of the mean wake, characterized by an elongated and more symmetric recirculation region, resulting in a significant drag reduction at low momentum coefficients. The flow response can be interpreted in terms of a mass-dominated regime, in which the balance between entrainment and recirculating flux promotes the expansion of the recirculation region and enhances pressure recovery. As the momentum coefficient increases, the flow transitions to a momentum-dominated regime, where the increased jet momentum is associated with stronger rear-body entrainment, leading to a contraction of the recirculation region and a deterioration of drag performance. Compared with the steady-blowing cases considered here, the SWJ actuation achieves higher drag-reduction efficiency ηD at low momentum input, indicating improved momentum-input efficiency. These findings clarify the link between actuation configuration, mean wake topology, and drag response for the present low-drag Ahmed-body configuration and demonstrate the potential of collaborative SWJ actuation for efficient wake control.

papers.title: Modeling the critical conditions for puffing and microexplosion of unstable emulsified fuel droplets
papers.abstract: Intense heating of emulsified fuel droplets injected into combustion chambers of aviation engines leads to their puffing and microexplosions. In this study, we develop a new heat and mass transfer model, accounting for phase separation in emulsified fuel droplets and the formation of a core–film structure, to predict critical puffing/microexplosion conditions. The dynamics of phase separation in emulsion droplets containing various surfactants is investigated using a transient phase-field model. The problem considers coupled heating, evaporation, and phase separation of an emulsified fuel droplet in a gas–air environment. Numerical simulations are performed in software COMSOL Multiphysics using the heat transfer in solids and fluids, laminar flow, deformed geometry, and phase field modules, supplemented by user-defined functions. The behavior of unstable emulsion droplets is compared with that of two-liquid droplets up to critical puffing/microexplosion conditions. Parametric calculations cover droplet sizes from 0.01 to 1 mm, ambient gas temperatures from 500 to 1100 K, dispersed phase (water) concentrations up to 10 vol. %, and mean dispersed-phase sizes ranging from 1 to 100 μm. The results show that phase separation accounts for no more than 50% of the total puffing/microexplosion delay time. Additionally, the rate of temperature rise in emulsion droplets is found to be much lower than in immiscible two-liquid droplets. The influence of phase separation dynamics on critical droplet breakup conditions is analyzed for a wide range of initial and threshold parameters.

papers.title: Pressure reconstruction for airfoil gust response based on sparse measurement points
papers.abstract: To address the complex unsteady flow phenomena encountered by aircraft in gust, traditional gust sensing methods, such as wingtip acceleration and root bending moment measurements, are limited by installation space, resulting in the acquisition of only localized and discrete flow information. It is impossible to sense the complete information of the flow field around the aircraft. Thus, the real-time gust pressure reconstruction models are developed in this study using compressed sensing based on proper orthogonal decomposition (CS-POD) and Gappy POD (G-POD), respectively. First, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) modes are extracted based on computational fluid dynamics simulations under multi-frequency sinusoidal gust conditions, and reconstruction of the airfoil surface pressure under various gust scenarios is achieved through the solution of the temporal coefficients. The effects of the number and distribution of measurement points, as well as noise, on reconstruction accuracy, generalization capability, and robustness were systematically analyzed. Finally, wind tunnel tests were carried out to validate the engineering applicability of the proposed model. In contrast to G-POD, which requires five measurement points, comparable accuracy and robustness are achieved by the CS-POD with only three measurement points. In addition, wind tunnel tests validate the applicability of the CS-POD in real engineering environments. Despite the presence of factors such as model vibration and three-dimensional effects, the real-time gust pressure reconstruction model constructed using the CS-POD can still accurately reconstruct the surface pressure distribution of the airfoil.

papers.title: Physics-informed multi-scale spatiotemporal learning for transient incompressible flow prediction
papers.abstract: Data-driven learning provides a promising route for accelerating computational fluid dynamics, yet transient flow prediction remains challenging because models must simultaneously capture evolving temporal dynamics and cross-scale spatial structures while generalizing across geometries and operating conditions. In this work, we study one-step-ahead prediction of two-dimensional incompressible transient flows from historical snapshots and propose Multi-Scale Spatiotemporal Flow (MuST-Flow), a physics-informed multi-scale spatiotemporal network for recurrent forecasting of velocity and pressure fields. The central idea of MuST-Flow is to couple cross-scale feature extraction with physical regularization, enabling the model to better resolve localized high-gradient flow structures while maintaining physically consistent evolution. Specifically, MuST-Flow adopts a multi-scale spatiotemporal convolutional design with dilated receptive fields to learn hierarchical flow representations and incorporates a hybrid loss derived from the residuals of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations to encourage mass and momentum consistency during training. To evaluate generalization beyond fixed configurations, the proposed method is assessed on transient hydrofoil flow data under cross-geometry testing with varied operating conditions. Experimental results show that MuST-Flow achieves the lowest mean absolute error, highest structural similarity, and lowest speed and velocity-direction errors among both generic spatiotemporal prediction baselines and flow-oriented neural-operator baselines, while maintaining competitive divergence and Navier–Stokes residuals. These results demonstrate its effectiveness as an efficient surrogate modeling framework for two-dimensional incompressible transient flow prediction.

papers.title: Spatial distribution of bipolar functional groups modulates water and ion transport in carbon nanotube
papers.abstract: Functional group modification in carbon nanotubes alters charge distribution and steric hindrance, which strongly influence the transport of water molecules and ions. Molecular dynamics simulations are used to examine how the number and spatial arrangement of carboxyl and amino groups in carbon nanotubes influence transport behavior in the channel. As the number of functional groups increases, water transport efficiency decreases, whereas ion rejection increases. Bipolar functionalization enhances ion selectivity while improving the continuity of water migration. Further comparison of double-ring, linear, helical, and coupled distributions shows that the linear and semi-helical coupled distribution constructs continuous low-resistance channels and optimizes the local charge regulation network, thereby reducing the energy barrier for water migration and enhancing ion selectivity, which leads to the best overall transport performance. This study reveals the intrinsic mechanisms by which the spatial distribution of bipolar functional groups regulates transport behavior in nanochannels, providing a theoretical basis for the design of functionalized nanochannels.

papers.title: Secondary-flow-controlled hydrocarbon fuel coking in curved regenerative cooling channels with evolving coke layers
papers.abstract: Reactive wall deposition in curved internal flows involves coupled secondary motion, heat transfer, chemical conversion, and moving-boundary evolution. In hydrocarbon-fuel regenerative cooling channels, curvature-induced secondary flow can enhance local heat transfer and suppress coke deposition, whereas the growing coke layer reshapes the flow passage, thermal resistance, and reaction. This study investigates the fluid-physical mechanisms governing coke deposition in a three-dimensional curved cooling channel. A novel critical vector method within a dynamic mesh framework is developed to directly track the evolving coke layer without prescribing its geometry. The results show that coke deposition is governed not only by wall temperature, but also by the redistribution of momentum, heat, and species. Buoyancy-driven cross-stream transport produces distinct deposition levels under different gravity orientations, with a total coke difference of approximately 26%. In the corner section, centrifugal-force-induced secondary motion increases the local heat transfer coefficient by 50%–65% and suppresses coke accumulation. As deposition proceeds, however, flow-area reduction and increased near-wall thermal resistance lead to overall thermal and hydraulic deterioration. Damköhler-number analysis reveals a streamwise transition from reaction-dominated to transport-controlled regimes. When the minimum flow area decreases to about 87% of its initial value, the maximum wall temperature increases by about 30 K and the pressure drop rises by approximately 20%. These findings identify a nonlinear feedback mechanism among secondary motion, reactive deposition, and evolving transport in curved channels.

papers.title: Investigation of the collapse characteristics of the cavitation bubble near the convex wall
papers.abstract: The present paper investigates the collapse dynamics of a cavitation bubble near a convex wall.
