To address this issue, an integrated framework combining theoretical development, experimental emulation, and numerical modeling is established to investigate phase behavior and transport in shale 15 nanopores. A gas–liquid–adsorbed three-phase equilibrium algorithm is developed based on thermodynamic principles and coupled with a simplified local density functional theory to characterize adsorption under confinement. Meanwhile, a customized nano-microfluidic platform is constructed, including single-scale nanopores of 150, 80, and 10 nm and dual-scale nanopores with orthogonal staggered channels of 150 and 10 nm depth, enabling direct visualization and validation of nanoconfined phase transitions and flow behavior. Results show that decreasing pore size markedly contracts the gas–liquid two-phase envelope, lowers bubble point pressure, raises dew point pressure, and suppresses critical condensation pressure and temperature. Stronger confinement also promotes preferential adsorption of heavier components on pore walls while retaining lighter components in the bulk phase. In dual-scale nanopores, gas bubbles nucleate first in larger pores, and transition pathways are strongly controlled by gas–oil ratio. Finally, a nanoconfinement-enabled multiphase multiscale flow model is implemented in MATLAB Reservoir Simulation Toolbox, incorporating phase equilibrium and interphase mass transfer to predict CO2–hydrocarbon phase behavior and transport in shale nanopores.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic behavior of bubbles in a vertical liquid jet flow field
papers.abstract: The breakup behavior of bubbles in complex flow fields is key to understanding multiphase flow dynamics and controlling mass transfer processes. In this paper, an experimental study is conducted on the hydrodynamic behavior of bubbles in a vertical liquid jet field, with a focus on the breakup modes and evolution characteristics under different jet conditions and bubble sizes. Using high-speed photography combined with bubble image velocimetry, the instantaneous motion, deformation, and breakup processes of bubbles in the vertical jet field are systematically observed. Quantitative analyses are performed to evaluate the effects of jet velocity and initial bubble diameter on breakup mode, breakup region, breakup frequency, and daughter bubble size distribution. The experimental results reveal two typical breakup modes of bubbles in the vertical liquid jet field: jet breakup and jet–vortex breakup. As the jet velocity increases, the occurrence probability of jet–vortex breakup rises significantly, while that of jet breakup decreases correspondingly. The bubble breakup region is mainly concentrated within approximately 8 mm on both sides of the axis below the jet outlet, with both its width and height expanding as the jet velocity increases. The breakup frequency and the number of daughter bubbles generated both increase with increasing jet velocity and initial bubble size. This study reveals the dynamic mechanisms underlying bubble breakup in a vertical liquid jet field, clarifies the coupled effects of jet velocity and bubble size, and provides experimental data and insights that are applicable to bubble breakup in vertical liquid jet configurations under the tested conditions (Vj = 0.928–2.122 m/s, DN = 2–6 mm, and ambient-temperature water) and may serve as a reference for the design and optimization of related gas–liquid contactors and aeration systems operating within similar parameter ranges.

papers.title: Transient reconstruction of urban wind field via physics-constrained reduced-order data assimilation
papers.abstract: Ensuring the operational safety of urban air mobility (UAM) in high-density environments relies on real-time, high-resolution sensing of the low-altitude wind field. Traditional computational fluid dynamics is constrained by the trade-off between computational efficiency and transient accuracy, while sparse sensor observations fail to capture full three-dimensional spatial flow fields. This study introduces a reduced-order data assimilation framework that integrates scale-adaptive simulation with a three-dimensional variational algorithm accelerated via proper orthogonal decomposition subspaces. Real-time, sparse LiDAR observations are dynamically mapped into a low-dimensional physical subspace, preserving macroscopic transport constraints while eliminating iterative loops. The framework is validated against the urban canopy flow around the Shenzhen Electronics Group Plaza. Statistical cross-validation suggests that the framework rectifies numerical background biases, reducing the root mean square error of three-dimensional velocity components by 77.8%–86.9% within the observation envelope. Furthermore, local spatial generalization analysis indicates that the framework replicates high-altitude turbulence intensity profiles across downstream blind zones, while restricting an online solution latency to 0.0414 ms per step. This framework provides a low-latency, physically constrained foundation for online UAM trajectory planning and risk forecasting.

papers.title: Investigation of thermal and flow characteristics of Casson fluid in porous medium under magnetohydrodynamic influences
papers.abstract: The influence of an inclined magnetic field on the flow characteristics and thermal behavior of Casson fluid between two parallel rectangular porous channels is being investigated in this mathematical model. The investigation focuses on the determination of velocity profile, temperature distribution, and flow rate by applying analytical derivations, graphical interpretations, and numerical simulations. A comparative assessment between Casson and Newtonian fluid models is also presented, wherein graphical representations show the fundamental differences in velocity profile, thermal distribution, and flow rate with the variation of the Casson parameter, permeability parameter, porosity, Hartmann number, inclination angle, Brinkman number, and Reynolds number. The numerical findings validate the analytical outcomes and emphasize the non-Newtonian features of Casson fluids under magnetohydrodynamic circumstances.

papers.title: A computational investigation of microjet focusing with secondary fluid and compressible gas
papers.abstract: Double-flow focusing nozzles (DFFNs) are used to produce liquid microjets for sample delivery in serial femtosecond crystallography (SFX), where crystallized samples are dispersed in a primary liquid jet and delivered into the x-ray beam path. Such jets are generated by focusing a primary liquid jet with a coaxial secondary liquid and outer gas. Precise control of microjet stability and morphology is crucial for efficient sample delivery. This study presents a comprehensive numerical model of double-flow focused liquid jets from a DFFN, where the liquid phase consists of water and ethanol, and the focusing gas is helium. An axisymmetric, Newtonian, compressible, two-phase gas–liquid and two-component water–ethanol model is formulated and solved using the finite-volume method and volume-of-fluid framework. The water–ethanol mixing and resulting changes in density, viscosity, and surface tension as a function of ethanol concentration and temperature are simulated using the Jouyban–Acree model. The jet characteristics as a function of material mixture properties, focusing-gas compressibility, and temperature are investigated numerically. A parametric analysis is performed over the typical SFX operating range, varying the water and ethanol flow rates from 0 to 20 μl/min and the helium gas flow rate from 0 to 20 mg/min. Jet stability, diameter, length, and velocity are analyzed. The influence of local mixture properties, mapped onto the Ca–We plane, reveals transitions between viscous-dominated and inertia-driven jetting regimes. The predicted jet diameters are consistent with the Young–Laplace equation and scaling expression. The findings provide a physical insight required for the virtual design of DFFNs.

papers.title: Effect of magnetic field on the entrainment of magnetic fluid by a moving boundary of a plane slot
papers.abstract: The effect of constant magnetic field on the outgoing flow of a magnetic fluid (MF) from a fluid “plug” (bridge) that it forms in a thin horizontal slot is studied. The flow is driven by the motion of the lower slot boundary (substrate) with constant velocity. The system is treated in the general framework of the Landau–Levich approximation. Namely, the solutions are, first, obtained for two distinct zones: the steady meniscus near the slot edge and the film flow along the moving substrate. The dynamics problem in the outgoing film, being singular on both its boundaries, is highly nontrivial and needs sophisticated handling. The overall flow regime is derived by splicing the “near” and “far” zone solutions. Involvement of magnetic field changes the situation drastically in comparison with the classical case as the field creates a body force inside the MF and an additional pressure jump at its surface. The resulting solution evidences that in the presence of magnetic field, the MF drain saturates and allows for large slot thicknesses, the regime that is totally impossible for any ordinary fluid. The built-up description may serve as a model prototype for an MF acoustic contact, an inherent element in any ultrasonic nondestructive testing technique. Such a contact can reduce the drain and stabilize the fluid bridge, for example, at rough scanned surfaces. The developed theory may also be applied to the coating problems, making ferromagnetic doping of the deposited compound a technologically advantageous feature.

papers.title: Bacterial residence time near a plane for smooth swimmers
papers.abstract: Bacterial dynamics near a boundary surface are biologically important. It has been demonstrated that bacteria can stay near the boundary surface for a prolonged time as if they are trapped. When the eventual escape of bacteria out of such entrapment is modeled as a classical one-dimensional Kramers problem concerning only the orientational degree of freedom, a simple but elegant formula can be obtained, but if/how the formula applies is unclear since the model totally neglects the contribution from the equally important translational degree of freedom characterized by the surface distance between the entrapped bacterium and the boundary surface. In this work, we systematically study the dynamics of smooth-swimming Escherichia coli near a planar boundary through numerical simulations, from which we can extract the bacterial residence time to compare with the analytical solution of the corresponding Kramers problem. It is demonstrated that two parameters, a characteristic pitch angle and a characteristic surface distance, are both needed for the correct parameterization of the analytical solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the characteristic pitch angle and surface distance can be modulated by bacterial dimensions, i.e., the characteristic sizes of bacteria, leading to diverse residence times (almost a factor of two orders of magnitude) for bacteria with small variations in dimensions.

papers.title: Two-dimensional numerical simulation of R245fa flow boiling heat transfer in a horizontal microchannel
papers.abstract: A two-dimensional numerical simulation is conducted based on the volume of fluid model to investigate the bubble dynamics, flow pattern evolution, and heat transfer characteristics of dispersed bubbly/slug flow during flow boiling in a horizontal microchannel. The results indicate that the heat transfer coefficient (HTC) increases monotonically with flow velocity due to the thinning of the thermal boundary layer, whereas a higher saturation temperature reduces the HTC because of reduced latent heat and weaker bubble-induced turbulence. A significant non-monotonic gravity effect is revealed in microchannel flow boiling, with a pronounced risk of dry-out under high gravity conditions, which is closely related to bubble departure frequency, flow disturbance characteristics, and flow pattern transition. Furthermore, as the gravity level increases, both the fluctuation frequency and amplitude of the void fraction decrease, accompanied by the formation of a stable wavy vapor film along the top wall of the microchannel. These findings provide theoretical support for the design of thermal management systems for high heat flux electronic devices and aerospace applications.

papers.title: Flow characteristics past a normal flat plate at Re = 5–10 000
papers.abstract: A normal flat plate with infinite span is one of the representative two-dimensional bluff bodies. Most studies on the flow past a normal flat plate have been conducted for Re=Uh/ν≤1000 by numerical simulations and for Re≥10 000 by experiments, where U is the free-stream velocity, and h is the plate height. We perform two-dimensional and three-dimensional numerical simulations of flow past a normal flat plate with b/h=0.05 (b is the plate thickness) at 5≤Re≤200 and 145≤Re≤10 000 (large eddy simulations are conducted for Re≥1000), respectively, to provide the flow statistics at these Reynolds numbers and to fill the gap in our knowledge of the flow characteristics in the range of Re=1000–10 000. Various flow regimes are identified according to the Reynolds number, such as the transition from steady to unsteady flow at Re=34, two-dimensional to three-dimensional flow at Re≈145 for the present b/h, appearance of strong streamwise vortex ribs at Re≈200, and transition to turbulent flow in the wake at Re=1000. At 2000≤Re≤10 000, the mean flow quantities such as the mean drag and base pressure coefficients, mean recirculation length, and Strouhal number are nearly independent of the Reynolds number. The shear-layer instability arises at Re=1000, and the power law of the shear-layer frequency follows fSL/fK=0.1066Re0.67, where fSL and fK are the shear-layer and vortex-shedding frequencies, respectively. This is analogous to the power laws for the flows over the circular [Prasad and Williamson, “The instability of the shear layer separating from a bluff body,” J. Fluid Mech. 333, 375–402 (1997)] and square [Lander et al.,“Scaling of square-prism shear layers,” J. Fluid Mech. 849, 1096–1119 (2018)] cylinders.

papers.title: Modeling the compressible flow field of an impulsively started circular cylinder with refined potential flow theory
papers.abstract: Understanding compressible flows over bluff bodies, such as circular cylinders, is critical for applications in aerospace engineering, space exploration, and astrophysics. However, the complexity of viscous and unsteady flows, compounded by compressibility effects, remains a challenge for experimental and computational methods. This study explores the compressible flow field of an impulsively started circular cylinder using Refined Potential Flow Theory (RPT), an analytical model that extends classical potential flow theory to include compressibility effects. The governing equations, boundary conditions, and refined stream function are developed to capture the density, velocity, and pressure fields in subsonic and transonic regimes. The results demonstrate that compressibility marginally increases vortex enstrophy at low Reynolds numbers, while its influence on wake flow stability diminishes at higher values. The study reveals that compressibility suppresses shear layer instability, reduces wake velocity deficits, and introduces smaller-scale structures that disrupt the inertial range of turbulence in the low subsonic regime. At higher Mach numbers (M∞≥0.6), local supersonic pockets and shock waves emerge, forming complex λ-shock systems and bow shocks. The predictions of the Strouhal number from RPT show marginal changes for 0.2≤M∞≤0.5, consistent with experimental and computational trends. Although RPT aligns with existing methods to capture key flow features, discrepancies in wake stability and recirculation zone dimensions highlight areas for further refinement. This research underscores the potential of RPT in developing optimization tools that complement experimental and numerical studies, offering valuable insights into compressible flow physics for engineering applications in high-altitude flight and space exploration.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of immiscible drop formation and transport in collapsible tubes at intermediate Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Immiscible drop transport in compliant, thin-walled vessels is relevant to a range of cardiovascular and biomedical applications, yet the behavior of drops at moderate Reynolds numbers within collapsible geometries remains poorly understood. This study experimentally investigates the formation and transport of neutrally buoyant immiscible drops in both undeformed and deformed elastic tubes across Reynolds numbers spanning 101–103. High-speed imaging and particle image velocimetry were employed to visualize flow regimes, drop trajectories, and velocity fields. In undeformed tubes, the Weber number (Wei) governs the dripping-to-jetting transition while the Capillary number (Cao) controls drop size, which follows a reciprocal decay relationship with the flow rate of the continuous phase. Drop velocity exhibits a nonlinear dependence on Cao and cannot be directly inferred from the mean velocity of the continuous-phase flow. At low Wei and high Cao, unsteady helical drop trajectories emerge as smaller drops sample higher-velocity regions of the parabolic velocity profile. Vessel deformation fundamentally alters drop dynamics: the collapsed geometry enables dual-channel drop transport in the dripping regime, enhances Rayleigh–Plateau instability and accelerates drop pinch-off in the jetting regime, and promotes wall adhesion and channel clogging at low Cao where surface tension dominates. A distinct plug flow regime is identified at high Wei and low Cao in the collapsed vessel, where the initial liquid plug occludes one channel and diverts the jet toward the remaining open channel. These findings provide physical insight into drop transport in flexible vascular conduits, with implications for venous thrombosis, microgravity physiology, and liquid embolization procedures.

papers.title: Effects of turbulent inflow parameters on aerodynamic admittance of a road vehicle on a streamlined bridge girder
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic admittance is an important transfer function between turbulent inflow and vehicle buffeting forces. Its accurate determination is important for calculating unsteady aerodynamic forces on vehicles and evaluating driving comfort. For road vehicles on bridge decks, this transfer process is affected by the interaction between incoming turbulence, vehicle geometry, and the local flow field modified by the bridge girder. However, the dependence of vehicle aerodynamic admittance on turbulence intensity and integral length scale remains insufficiently quantified, particularly for road vehicles exposed to bridge deck flow environments. To study the effects of turbulence parameters on vehicle aerodynamic admittance, several representative turbulent wind fields were generated in a wind tunnel using different grids. Wind tunnel tests of a scaled coach model were then carried out. Based on the measured wind speed histories and unsteady aerodynamic force histories, the aerodynamic admittance functions of side force, lift, rolling moment, and pitching moment were identified. The results show that both turbulence integral scale and turbulence intensity affect vehicle aerodynamic admittance. In general, aerodynamic admittance increases with increasing turbulence integral scale. The effect of turbulence intensity is relatively more complex. A function model of aerodynamic admittance was established by considering the turbulence integral scale, turbulence intensity, and vehicle characteristic dimensions. The fitted results agree well with the experimental data. This indicates that the proposed model can reasonably describe vehicle aerodynamic admittance under different turbulent flow conditions and can provide a reference for predicting vehicle buffeting forces.

papers.title: Pattern formation in nonlinear dynamics of nematic liquid crystals above the flexoelectric instability threshold
papers.abstract: For many decades, researchers have been studying various types of electrohydrodynamic instabilities in liquid crystals. A significant amount of experimental data has been collected; however, the theoretical interpretations of the results typically rely on linear analysis. In response to this limitation, we investigate the nonlinear stage of the flexoelectric instability in nematics, focusing on liquid crystals with negative dielectric permittivity and electrical conductivity anisotropies. We base our analysis on a comprehensive set of nonlinear electrohydrodynamic equations for nematics subjected to an external alternating electric field. The equations predict an instability that is driven by the flexoelectric effect. To examine the specific features of this phenomenon, we use a model that was proposed in our previous publications {Pikina et al., “Nonlinear electrohydrodynamics of liquid crystals,” Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. 164, 129 (2023) [JETP 137, 114 (2023)] and Pikina et al., “Dynamic exoelectric instabilities in nematic liquid crystals,” Phys. Rev. E 110, 024701 (2024)}, which allows us to perform numerical simulations of the nonlinear dynamics. We examine patterns that are formed above the instability threshold. Through numerical simulations, we identify static and dynamic patterns that occur on time scales much longer than the period of the external electric field. The static patterns are one-dimensional structures, whereas the dynamic patterns are standing or traveling one-dimensional waves. The type of realized pattern depends on the material and experimentally controlled parameters. We found that the standing waves are stable with respect to small transverse perturbations, whereas the propagating waves are unstable. We present a Ginzburg–Landau-like phenomenology that applies near the instability threshold. This approach allows us to rationalize our numerical findings with a few parameters.

papers.title: Differential effects of geometric dimension intervals on supercavitating vehicle ranges
papers.abstract: This article presents a new discovery: different geometric dimension intervals yield distinctly different variation characteristics of the ranges of supercavitating vehicles. To clarify the influence of geometric dimensions on the different variation in the range of supercavitating vehicles, this work presents a systematic investigation combining underwater motion experiments of supercavitating vehicles and numerical simulations. Experimental observations reveal that during the tail-slapping motion of high-speed supercavitating vehicles, inappropriate geometric parameters may puncture the supercavity wall and trigger local fragmentation of the cavity. As the fragmented region expands, severe atomization occurs upon supercavity collapse. Building upon these experimental findings, a coupled numerical model integrating unsteady rigid-body dynamics with unsteady cavitating flow was established to further investigate the influence of geometric dimensions on the ranges of supercavitating vehicles. Quantitative analysis reveals a differential relationship between geometric dimensions and ranges. Specifically, when ηL>0.6, the ranges ηS of the vehicle can be approximately predicted by ηS=17.2ηD−1.725. The optimal combination of ηD and ηL that maximizes the ranges of the supercavitating vehicles satisfies ηL=0.0782ηD−1.236.

papers.title: Dynamics and acoustics of orifice-detached bubbles: The role of contact angle and modeling correlations
papers.abstract: Bubble size, a pivotal parameter governing the efficiency of heat and mass transfer in gas–liquid two-phase flows, possesses a distinct signature. While influenced by various exhaust system parameters, the wettability of the nozzle material, specifically the contact angle, exerts a critical role in determining bubble dimensions. This study utilizes seven nozzles fabricated from distinct materials to systematically investigate the coupled dynamics of bubble formation and acoustic emission. A predictive correlation model for bubble size is established, incorporating the specific influence of the contact angle. The results demonstrate that both the equivalent bubble diameter and peak sound pressure attain minimum values when the nozzle contact angle approximates 90°. These findings provide a theoretical basis for the active modulation and control of bubble size in relevant engineering applications.

papers.title: Propagation and evolution of inlet acoustic disturbances in a supersonic wind tunnel nozzle
papers.abstract: In quiet wind tunnels, the inlet acoustic disturbances induce test section pressure fluctuations through propagation within the nozzle's flow field. However, the propagation of acoustic disturbances in subsonic–transonic–supersonic flows remains poorly understood. This study developed a novel supersonic acoustic disturbance propagation test facility, enabling precise control of inlet acoustic pressure amplitude and frequency. Single-frequency plane acoustic waves covering a Helmholtz number range of ka = 0.015–0.77 were introduced at the nozzle inlet. High-frequency dynamic pressures were measured at ten axial stations along the nozzle. Amplitude evolution and spectral coherence were investigated. Results show that, in the time domain, pressure fluctuation amplitudes induced by acoustic disturbances peak downstream of the throat across all frequencies. The relative disturbance amplitudes are amplified from the inlet to the exit. In the frequency domain, low-frequency disturbances with ka≤0.1 lose coherence rapidly, whereas mid-frequency disturbances with 0.1<ka≤1 remain coherent. This study offers experimental insights into the frequency-dependent propagation of acoustic disturbances in supersonic nozzles, providing guidance for disturbance control and noise reduction in high-speed aerodynamic systems.

papers.title: Nozzle-lip effects on co-flow self-excited cavitating waterjets for cavitation peening
papers.abstract: Cavitation peening offers a promising non-contact surface treatment alternative to conventional shot peening, but its application is often limited by the requirement of submerged operation. Co-flow cavitating waterjets overcome this constraint by using an annular liquid curtain to sustain cavitation in air. However, the role of nozzle geometry remains poorly understood. Here, we examine how the nozzle-lip geometry governs this process by comparing two distinct configurations—a horn lip and a cylindrical lip—in a co-flow self-excited cavitating waterjet equipped with an organ-pipe resonator. Through erosion tests on pure aluminum, high-speed imaging, proper orthogonal decomposition, acoustic and pressure spectral analysis, and complementary large-eddy simulations, we establish a mechanistic link between lip-induced near-field hydrodynamics and the resulting erosion intensity. The horn lip produces a markedly stronger cavitation response: it increases the mean mass loss by approximately 31% and expands the erosion-ring area by about 26% relative to the cylindrical lip. This enhanced performance is traced to a fundamental reorganization of the near-nozzle flow field—the horn geometry generates a stronger low-pressure region near the exit, induces localized backflow, intensifies the shear layer, and promotes vortex coalescence, leading to larger, more coherent cavitation clouds and a lower shedding frequency. Crucially, this reorganization strengthens the acoustic–hydrodynamic coupling with the organ-pipe resonator, amplifying the internal pressure response from 538 to 1565 Pa. These results demonstrate that nozzle-lip geometry is not merely a passive boundary condition, but an active control parameter that governs vapor-cloud organization, resonant feedback, and erosion intensity in co-flow self-excited cavitating jets, offering a design pathway for more efficient cavitation-peening nozzles.

papers.title: Linear stability analysis of buoyancy-affected non-equidiffusive premixed flame in an inclined Hele–Shaw cell in the presence of wall heat loss
papers.abstract: This study presents a quasi-two-dimensional theoretical framework for the linear stability analysis of buoyancy-affected premixed flame propagating in inclined Hele–Shaw cells with wall heat loss. The model incorporates finite-rate Arrhenius chemistry, non-equidiffusive transport, buoyancy, and non-adiabatic wall heat losses while fully resolving the internal flame structure. The stationary flame solutions and the associated eigenvalue problem are solved numerically to determine the dispersion relation and stability boundaries. Wall heat loss reduces the burning velocity and flame temperature, giving rise to multi-branch stationary solutions and significant changes in the dispersion relation. Buoyancy exhibits a strong directional effect: positive gravity destabilizes downward-propagating flames, whereas negative gravity stabilizes upward-propagating flames and can completely suppress perturbation growth. Furthermore, wall heat loss significantly modifies the critical gravitational acceleration required for complete stabilization. The present framework provides physical insight into the coupled effects of buoyancy, heat loss, and differential diffusion on flame stability in confined combustion systems.

papers.title: Time-resolved three-dimensional morphology and velocity field measurement in the initial stage of a developing wobbly bubble
papers.abstract: When a bubble detaches from a nozzle and ascends through a quiescent fluid, it undergoes rapid morphological transformations during its initial transient phase before developing a steady spiral or zigzag trajectory, depending on its size. To elucidate the coupled morphology-flow dynamics during the initial phase, this study experimentally quantifies the time-resolved three-dimensional (3D) morphology and the surrounding velocity, acceleration, and pressure fields for a representative ellipsoidal air bubble with a mean equivalent diameter of 4.88 mm. Our findings reveal that immediately upon detachment, the bubble initially follows an approximately rectilinear vertical trajectory undergoing an initial morphological cycle characterized by severe vertical contraction and subsequent expansion. Subsequently, the bubble transitions into an asymmetric ellipsoidal shape, which coincides with the onset of lateral migration and the development of zigzag motion. The vorticity distribution during the initial transient phase is characterized by localized vortex pairs generated directly at the bubble interface closely associated with rapid interfacial deformation before a fully developed downstream wake is established. The reconstructed hydrostatic-subtracted hydrodynamic pressure field further shows that localized low-pressure regions develop near the rapidly deforming interface and become asymmetric at the onset of lateral migration. These pressure features coexist with the asymmetric high-speed and vortical structures indicating morphology-dependent pressure redistribution during the transition from rectilinear ascent to wobbling motion.

papers.title: Flapping strategies for high-maneuverability pitching in the cownose ray
papers.abstract: Most previous studies on ray swimming focus on hydrodynamic characteristics of separate single fins while neglecting multi-fin vortex coupling, and few studies quantify the combined pitching control effects of coordinated asymmetric pectoral flapping and caudal fin deflection. To fill this research gap, this paper uses three-degree-of-freedom (3-DoF) self-propelled simulations relying on an in-house fluid solver to investigate the high-maneuver pitching hydrodynamics of cownose rays. Results show that increasing the caudal fin deflection angle (α) improves pitching agility with a thrust penalty. At α = ±40°, caudal vortex shedding displaces pectoral trailing-edge vortices, and the synergistic vortex interaction produces large pitching moments for rapid attitude adjustment. Due to the asymmetric body morphology of rays, α = 20° contributes to stable swimming, and downward deflection achieves better pitching performance than upward deflection. The heave amplitude ratio (HAR) also determines the vertical pitching direction of rays. HAR = 3.00 generates upward pitching with large-scale leading-edge vortices (LEVs), whereas lower HAR leads to downward pitching with suppressed LEVs. The coordination of dual-fin kinematics realizes somersault locomotion, with forward somersaults possessing superior agility and faster response than backward somersaults. These findings reveal that synergistic fin kinematics and multi-fin coupling strategies allow rays to achieve rapid, highly maneuverable pitching and somersaulting and provide reliable theoretical support for the design of high-agility bionic underwater vehicles.

papers.title: Slurry conveying characteristics of coarse particles in vertical hydraulic slag discharge system
papers.abstract: This study investigates the transport mechanisms of coarse particles within vertical solid–liquid two-phase flows, focusing on the influence of fluid rheological properties on particle dynamics. A series of experiments were conducted to evaluate the kinematic behavior of large-scale particles across a wide range of fluid viscosities. To achieve high-precision kinematic measurements, an unsupervised learning algorithm integrated with simple linear iterative clustering superpixel segmentation was developed for robust particle identification and velocity tracking. The experimental results reveal a distinct three-stage evolution of the particle absolute velocity—defined as the particle acceleration stage, the efficient transport stage, and the transport suppression (TS) stage—as the fluid viscosity increases. This trend is fundamentally governed by the balance between enhanced slurry-carrying capacity and increased hydraulic resistance. Concurrently, the slip velocity between the solid and liquid phases undergoes a significant reduction with increasing viscosity, indicating enhanced interphase synchronization and fluid carrying capacity. By synthesizing the tradeoffs between absolute transport velocity and phase slip, a critical viscosity regime for optimal transport efficiency was identified. Furthermore, the transition between different transport regimes was further corroborated by acoustic emission measurements in practical vertical flow environments. The field data successfully captured the peak particle flux within the predicted ET stage, demonstrating the scalability of the proposed fluid–particle interaction models. This work provides a theoretical framework for optimizing vertical hydraulic slag discharge systems and offers a mechanistic basis for enhancing energy efficiency in complex viscous multiphase flows.

papers.title: Volume effects on landslide-generated impulse waves and dam run-up in a canyon reservoir
papers.abstract: Landslide-generated impulse waves pose a major threat to dam safety in high mountain canyon reservoirs, where narrow valleys, steep banks, and irregular boundaries strongly affect wave evolution. In this study, a 1:150 large-scale three-dimensional integrated landslide–reservoir–dam physical model was constructed based on the Gushui Reservoir, China, truly reproducing the authentic complex boundary topography of the 8-km gorge reach. Distinct from previous simplified configurations or fixed-volume investigations, a series of physical experiments with eight sequential landslide volumes was conducted as the sole control parameter to systematically quantify the isolated volume effects on the full-process hydrodynamic chain. The results show that granular landslide entry generated non-stationary initial wave trains. The dimensionless initial wave amplitude increased approximately linearly with dimensionless landslide volume, demonstrating that landslide volume strongly influences the wave-generation process and subsequent hydrodynamic responses. During propagation, channel curvature and bank reflections induced non-monotonic wave fluctuations and localized amplifications. A power-law relationship was established for near-field primary wave attenuation, and the attenuation exponent decreased with increasing landslide volume. An empirical formula for maximum dam run-up was further developed using landslide velocity, landslide volume, and incident wave amplitude. These findings elucidate the nonlinear full-process mechanism of volume-driven impulse waves and support rapid quantitative hazard assessments in complex canyon reservoirs.

papers.title: Novel forcing method to generate quasi-stationary and homogeneous stratified turbulence
papers.abstract: This study extends our previous work [Iida, “Turbulent structure of stably stratified inhomogeneous flow,” Phys. Fluids 30, 045101 (2018)], in which direct numerical simulations using a spectral method were performed for a stably stratified inhomogeneous flow. In that study, a fringe region with an artificial body force was introduced to locally disturb the flow, and the resulting disturbances were horizontally diffused into an otherwise laminar region in the form of jet-like structures. In the present study, we propose a novel forcing strategy in which jets emitted from opposite edges of the fringe region interact in the center of the computational domain. This interaction produces quasi-stationary and homogeneous turbulence under stable density stratification. The turbulent statistics of the dissipation rate obtained with this forcing method are in quantitative agreement with those of conventionally forced homogeneous stratified turbulence. This result demonstrates that approximately homogeneous and stationary stratified turbulence can be generated without artificially forcing the entire computational domain.

papers.title: Microjet in nonspherical bubble collapsing under modulated water-hammer shocks
papers.abstract: Bubble collapse is a high-energy process in fluid dynamics with broad relevance to industrial, medical, and environmental applications. While shock-induced bubble collapse has been extensively studied, most existing work is restricted to planar shock–bubble interactions, leaving the role of shock characteristics in governing jet dynamics insufficiently explored. In this study, a simple topology based on collision to generate modulated shock waves is presented, where the considered collision velocities are ranging from 20 to 100 m/s. The high-resolution numerical simulations are conducted to investigate four distinct shock types—planar, converging, planar–planar, and planar-converging, and their interactions with bubbles. The collapse behavior is quantitatively examined in terms of collapse time, maximum jet velocity, and jet morphology. Results show that converging shocks significantly intensify microjets through focused pressure amplification, whereas sequential dual-shock interactions modulate jet structure and prolong collapse duration, enabling regulation of energy accumulation. By integrating the Rayleigh collapse framework with pressure distributions along the axis of symmetry, a semi-empirical models are further established to capture the evolution of jet velocity and collapse dynamics, demonstrating good agreement with numerical predictions. These findings elucidate the mechanisms of asymmetric bubble collapse under different shock characteristics and advance the theoretical understanding of shock–bubble interactions. The outcomes also offer guidance for the controlled exploitation of microjets in precision material processing, ultrasonic medicine, and environmental remediation.

papers.title: Macroscopic and microscopic insights into CO2-responsive viscoelastic foam for conformance control and enhanced oil recovery
papers.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO2) flooding is an effective enhanced oil recovery (EOR) method, yet its application is often restricted by gas channeling due to reservoir heterogeneity. To overcome the insufficient stability of conventional CO2 foams, a highly stable viscoelastic CO2-responsive foam system (DETA/SDS) was adopted. Its EOR and channeling control performance were evaluated through macroscopic physical simulations (single long and parallel sand-packed tubes) and microscopic glass-etched models. In single long sand-packed tubes, the DETA/SDS CO2 foam increased oil recovery by 37.66% relative to pure CO2 flooding, with a maximum resistance factor of 96 and a residual resistance factor of 36, outperforming N2 foam and confirming CO2 responsiveness. In parallel sand-packed tubes, the foam enhanced recovery by 35.94% and 53.16% for high- and low-permeability layers, respectively, effectively blocking the high-permeability layer while displacing oil from the low-permeability one. Microscopic visualization indicated that foam generation in porous media was dominated by rock cutting and necking separation, attributed to the high elastic modulus of the gas–liquid interface (high Wi). Notably, the foam system not only plugged dominant seepage channels via the superimposed Jamin effect but also emulsified crude oil into O/W emulsions, which further increased flow resistance and mobilized residual oil. The synergistic interplay of the Jamin effect (expanding sweep volume) and emulsification (facilitating oil detachment and transport) was identified as the core EOR mechanism, enabling effective utilization of residual oil in both mainstream lines and corner areas. This study offers a new strategy for mitigating CO2 channeling in heterogeneous reservoirs.

papers.title: A physics-informed relaxation-decomposed neural collision model for discrete Boltzmann dynamics
papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of collision operators is essential for reliable mesoscopic simulation of complex multiphase flows, where interfacial dynamics and long-time evolution are highly sensitive to the relaxation process. In this work, we propose a relaxation-decomposed network (RDN) for learning collision operators in discrete Boltzmann equations. The proposed model takes the discrete distribution function as the modeling variable and represents the collision term through two coupled components: an equilibrium-target correction and a relaxation-time model. These two components are parameterized by the E-net and the τ-net, respectively, leading to a structured equilibrium–relaxation formulation of the neural collision operator. Physical consistency is treated at different levels: the positivity of the constructed target equilibrium and relaxation time is enforced by the relaxation-decomposed parameterization, conservation is promoted through a soft moment-regularization term, and entropy-related behavior is assessed through theoretical estimates and numerical diagnostics. The proposed framework is instantiated within a pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann framework for multiphase flows and evaluated on representative benchmark problems, including phase separation, a static bubble, and droplet impact on a solid wall. Compared with standard neural networks and residual neural networks, numerical results show that the RDN achieves better interface preservation, smaller deviations in macroscopic quantities, and improved long-time stability during multiphase-flow evolution. The entropy-related analysis further indicates that the relaxation-decomposed structure helps maintain more stable thermodynamic behavior during long-time prediction. These results demonstrate that incorporating an explicit equilibrium–relaxation decomposition into neural collision learning provides a promising route toward robust and physically consistent mesoscopic modeling of complex multiphase flows.

papers.title: Dynamic evolution of steam channeling in porous media and response mechanism of two plugging systems
papers.abstract: In this paper, the loose sandstone is used as the porous medium model, and the formation and evolution of steam channeling channels and the response mechanism of two different plugging systems to channeling are systematically studied. First, the effects of steam injection rate, steam temperature, and pore pressure on the evolution characteristics of core permeability, porosity, and pore structure were quantitatively characterized by a high-temperature and high-pressure dynamic reactor and nuclear magnetic resonance T2 spectrum, respectively. The mechanical mechanism of permeability contrast as the core control variable of steam channeling instability was revealed. Second, the visualization experiment of steam channeling was carried out by using the high-temperature and high-pressure visual physical simulation device. The two-way flow phenomenon of the top steam overlapping upward and the bottom condensate water migrating downward was observed. This behavior was interpreted as a two-way fingering (steam-water double channeling) mode driven by a density difference. Finally, the mechanical response of the two plugging systems to channeling was quantified by nitrogen foam (Jiamin effect plugging high-permeability channels) and thermosetting plugging agent (mobility control) experiments: the vertical/plane recovery degree increased by 45.31/17.10 percentage points, respectively.

papers.title: Evolution of counter-rotating vortex pairs and their impact on eccentric jets and cavitation in a high-pressure angle valve
papers.abstract: High-pressure angle valves, while essential for industrial flow control, frequently suffer from premature failure due to harsh operating conditions. Large pressure drops and asymmetric geometries provoke severe fluid instabilities, notably eccentric jets and localized cavitation. This flow-induced erosive wear drastically curtails valve service life and poses critical safety risks. In response to the existing challenges, this study investigates the influence of cavity vortex structures on the eccentric jet and cavitation intensity by modifying the valve stem geometry. Initially, the presence of the stem induces a counter-rotating vortex pair (CVP) within the valve cavity. Constrained by the solid walls, the CVP, characterized by high normalized helicity and positive vortex-stretching characteristics, is prevented from breaking down into smaller-scale coherent structures. The persistence of this CVP induces a momentum deficit in the wake region behind the stem, aggravating the flow non-uniformity and subsequently intensifying both the eccentric jet and localized cavitation erosion. Specifically, a cylindrical stem triggers secondary separation, generating a CVP that occupies a substantial volume of the cavity and resulting in severe eccentric jets and asymmetric cavitation distributions. Conversely, a streamlined stem effectively mitigates the separation intensity and weakens the upstream vorticity generation and stretching-maintenance mechanism of the confined-cavity CVP, yielding a 13.48% reduction in CVP volume and significantly suppressing the eccentric jet and local cavitation damage. Furthermore, quantitative analyses based on the defined regional velocity deviation index and velocity centroid eccentricity (EZ) demonstrate that the streamlined stem decreases the non-uniform velocity distribution by 15.27% and shifts the velocity centroid of the high-speed jet 5.57% closer to the centerline. The distribution of the impact force (Fγ) further corroborates the effectiveness of the streamlined stem in alleviating local erosive wear. Ultimately, these findings reveal how valve stem geometry regulates downstream eccentric jets and asymmetric cavitation through the confined-cavity CVP mechanism, offering theoretical guidance for designing valves with low wear, high reliability, and an extended service life.

papers.title: Dynamics of laminar diffusion flames at sub-atmospheric pressure under axial acoustic forcing
papers.abstract: Acoustic forcing substantially alters the dynamics of laminar diffusion flames. Previous studies at atmospheric pressure have shown that acoustically forced laminar diffusion flames exhibit amplitude-dependent transitions from forcing-locked oscillations to nonlinear flame responses. However, the dynamics of laminar diffusion flames under axial acoustic forcing at sub-atmospheric pressures remain unclear, particularly the effects of reduced pressure on transition pathways between flame behaviors. This experimental study investigated the combustion dynamics of coaxial methane–air laminar diffusion flames at atmospheric and sub-atmospheric pressures under axial acoustic forcing. The flame-acoustic coupling processes were examined at ambient pressures (100, 40, and 30 kPa) over forcing amplitudes (A=û/u¯=0.05–0.5) and forcing frequencies (30, 60, and 90 Hz). The observed flame responses can be classified into several flame-acoustic coupling behaviors, including sustained oscillatory combustion (SOC), periodic liftoff and reattachment (PLOR), periodic pinch-off (PPO), and permanent flame liftoff (PFLO). Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of high-speed flame images and OH* chemiluminescence analysis were used to characterize the dynamical signatures of different flame behaviors and identify their pressure-dependent transition pathways. The transitions were identified from changes in POD modal energy distribution, variations in phase portrait smearing, and the appearance of additional peaks in the spectrograms. The results show that reduced pressure weakens flame-base anchoring, thereby promoting liftoff-related responses, including PLOR and PFLO. These findings provide insight into the dynamics of flame-acoustic coupling and flame stability in acoustically forced laminar diffusion flames at sub-atmospheric pressures.

papers.title: Willis coupling and asymmetric reflection of water waves over a periodically stepped bottom
papers.abstract: Periodic depth modulation offers a potentially useful route for controlling linear water waves. In this work, we investigate Willis coupling in a one-dimensional water-wave system with an asymmetric periodic depth profile. Using linear water-wave theory and transfer-matrix homogenization, we derive effective constitutive relations in terms of the free-surface hydrostatic pressure and the depth-integrated horizontal volume flux. We show that broken spatial inversion symmetry induces Willis-type cross coupling between these variables. Although this coupling cancels from the bulk dispersion relation, it modifies the pressure–flux matching condition at the boundaries of a finite depth-modulated structure. As a result, the reflection coefficients for forward and backward incidence acquire direction-dependent phases, while their magnitudes remain identical in the passive, lossless, and reciprocal system considered here. Two-dimensional numerical simulations and a mode-matching correction quantify the influence of localized evanescent modes near abrupt depth steps. Wave-flume experiments verify the predicted Willis-type asymmetric reflection, showing nearly symmetric reflection magnitudes and a clear direction-dependent reflection phase shift. These results extend Willis-medium concepts to linear water waves and provide a framework for tailoring water-wave reflection through depth modulation.

papers.title: Flow physics-informed learning of relative permeability in porous media
papers.abstract: Predicting relative permeability (kr) curves directly from three-dimensional (3D) digital rock images remains a significant challenge in digital rock physics (DRP). Existing methods either rely on computationally expensive pore network modeling (PNM) or direct numerical simulation (DNS) during inference, or use purely data-driven networks that lack physical consistency. This study introduces a permeability-field physics-informed neural network (PF-PINN), a coupled deep learning surrogate that maps a 3D binary rock image, through its local thickness transform, to drainage kr curves for both wetting and non-wetting phases. This approach embeds two-phase Darcy flow physics into the training loss, ensuring physically admissible predictions without requiring a simulation during inference. The model architecture integrates a 3D U-Net encoder to extract a spatially varying permeability field and a global morphological feature vector, a pressure multilayer perceptron (MLP) that satisfies Darcy boundary conditions, and a relative permeability MLP conditioned on pore geometry. Ground truth data were generated using a PNM workflow applied to 350 sub-volumes from seven rock types, with voxel resolutions ranging from 4.94 to 17.17 μm/voxel. Two evaluation protocols were employed, namely a stratified random split with a 20% holdout per rock and 70 test samples, and a rock-type holdout in which Bentheimer and Monte Gambier were fully withheld, resulting in 100 test samples. Under the stratified protocol, the PF-PINN achieved Rmean2 = 0.952 (Rw2 = 0.963, Rnw2 = 0.941). Under the rock-type holdout, the model achieved Rmean2 = 0.927 on unseen geological classes, demonstrating physics-informed cross-lithology generalization. The wetting-phase R2 difference between the two protocols was only 0.013, suggesting that embedding Darcy mass conservation enables an effective transfer of flow behavior across the geological families.

papers.title: Parametric modeling and optimization of hypersonic glide vehicles under stringent loading constraints
papers.abstract: In the aerodynamic design process of hypersonic glide vehicles (HGVs), multiple constraints must be considered. Based on B-spline theory, this work proposes a parametric modeling method for HGV surfaces under stringent loading constraints. Through a surface deformation approach involving “projection, construction, control, and superimposition,” precise control over the HGV's aerodynamic shape is achieved, effectively overcoming the limitations of traditional parametric methods in handling local deformations under stringent loading constraints. Building on this parametric modeling method, an aerodynamic optimization platform for HGV is established, enabling comprehensive optimization studies and result analyses. The results show that under the premise of strictly satisfying geometric and loading constraints, the optimized one exhibits inward-concave upper and lower surfaces compared with the baseline configuration. This structure significantly enhances the pressure differential at the side edges, resulting in a 10.7% lift increase, while the drag only rises by 5.6%. Consequently, the lift-to-drag ratio of the HGV is improved by 4.9%. Flow field analysis indicates that the inward contraction of the lower surface can reduce side edge spillover, while the inward contraction of the upper surface can alter the position of expansion waves on the upper surface.

papers.title: Horizontal seam lowers the inverse Magnus threshold of a spinning cricket ball
papers.abstract: Near-field wake pressure distributions were characterized for a new, unworn, transversely spinning cricket ball with the seam held horizontal at Re≈1.25×105 over 0≤Γ≤0.84 using a pressure-rake traversal technique. With increasing spin ratio Γ, the downstream low-pressure core migrated toward the advancing side, accompanied by wake contraction and lateral drift. At Γ=0.21, the wake approached lateral symmetry, and the net wake-pressure imbalance reversed sign, indicating an inverse Magnus state with retreating-side pressure deficit and reversed inferred transverse force. A within-study smooth-sphere control confirms that this transition threshold lies below the smooth-sphere value at comparable Re, demonstrating that a horizontal seam lowers the inverse Magnus onset. Results apply to a new ball at the tested Re and are most relevant to horizontal-arm bowling deliveries achieving elevated spin ratios.

papers.title: Tuning rheological behavior of functionalized liquid polybutadiene: Hydrogen bonding and metal–ligand interactions
papers.abstract: Unentangled liquid polybutadiene is functionalized via hydroaminoalkylation to introduce one and five N-methylaniline (NMA) groups to create associative polymers, and subsequently coordinated with various transition-metal ions to form metallo-supramolecular polymer networks. The hydrogen-bonding and metal–ligand coordination control the thermal behavior, the chain relaxation dynamics, and the microstructure of the functionalized unentangled liquid polybutadiene. Amination and subsequent metal coordination increase the glass-to-rubber transition temperature (Tg), consistent with reduced segmental mobility. Coordination of mono-functionalized polybutadiene blocks by various metal ions produces a metallo-supramolecular polymer with a distinct rheological response due to the differences in the metal–ligand bond strength: labile Ni2+–ligand interactions caused only minor changes; Zn2+ coordination forms stronger supramolecular junctions with a slower relaxation process and higher viscosity. However, Cu2+ coordination leads to thermorheological complexity (failure in time-temperature superposition), gel-like behavior, and formation of phase-separated-copper-rich aggregates, as confirmed by wide- and small-angle x-ray scattering. Increasing the NMA content and Zn2+ loading further increased the Tg and broadened the transition region due to the enhanced dynamic heterogeneity in the polymer network. Higher Zn2+ ion concentration promoted highly connected transient networks and physical aggregations, leading to a slower relaxation process. This work provides design rules for recyclable and reprocessable supramolecular materials by combining different associations.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of particle-laden plumes in density-stratified fluid with a computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method coupling model
papers.abstract: This study presents a compressible computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method (DEM) coupling model for simulating particle-laden plumes in density-stratified fluids. The model integrates a volume-averaged Navier–Stokes framework with salinity-dependent density stratification, a buoyancy-modified k–ϵ turbulence closure, individual particle tracking via DEM, and a specially formulated pressure Poisson equation for large density variations. Validated against Barnard's experimental data (N=0.3 s−1), systematic simulations for N=0.3–0.9 s−1 reveal that (i) the simulated maximum plume height agrees closely with the experimental measurement, with a relative error of only 2.9%; (ii) flow transitions from momentum-dominated to buoyancy-dominated regimes as the dimensionless source momentum-to-buoyancy parameter σ=M0N/B0 decreases, where M0 is the source momentum flux and B0 is the total source buoyancy flux; (iii) recirculation structures govern entrainment and mixing dynamics; and (iv) particle residence times range from approximately 14 to 22 s, exhibiting an overall decrease with increasing stratification, while pair correlation analysis reveals significant short-range particle clustering. These findings establish a validated framework for predicting multiphase buoyant flows in oceanic and industrial applications.

papers.title: Increasing cooling efficiency with electric field and feedback
papers.abstract: In this article, we present mesoscopic simulations of the fluid flow and heat transfer in a model of a heat pipe with the action of a non-uniform electric field on the fluid, based on the lattice Boltzmann method. We demonstrate in numerical experiments the possibility to realize the controlled quasiperiodic flow of a film of dielectric liquid in the vicinity of a non-conductive inset using the cyclic change of the electric field and the regularly switching flow of liquid condensed in the cold section back to the cooled hot surface. We model the process of the pulse action of a non-uniform electric field on the liquid film with a feedback based on the thickness of the liquid films at the cooling region and at the vapor condenser. Such combined action ensures the increased average value of the heat flux from the heater. In our experiments, the value of the heat flux was 1.7 times higher than the heat flux without the electric field for the same geometry of the region, the same temperatures, and the same amount of the cooling fluid.

papers.title: Transient hydrodynamics of high-speed craft in waves during impulsive missile firing
papers.abstract: High-speed craft advancing in waves experiences strongly transient hydrodynamics when localized firing loads are imposed over a timescale much shorter than the wave period. This study examines the associated unsteady free-surface physics using a three-dimensional time-domain potential-flow formulation based on the translating-pulsating source Green function. The frequency-to-time-domain transformation retains the forward-speed free-surface condition and velocity-dependent convective terms. The results show that firing does not excite a quiescent body-fluid system. Instead, the impulse interrupts a preexisting wave-body-radiation state, in which hull motion, incident waves, and outgoing radiation are already phase-coupled. The transient response is therefore controlled by the partition of impulse energy among rigid-body motion, near-body pressure redistribution, and free-surface radiation. Firing phase plays a decisive role in this process, and the most unfavorable phases for heave and pitch are different, reflecting distinct translational and rotational pathways for impulse-energy transfer. Firing near the motion trough promotes a slower radiation-memory pathway, reducing the critical pitch deviation by more than 90% while delaying the peak response over multiple wave cycles. Load-history effects further show that equal total impulse does not produce dynamically equivalent responses. A high-amplitude short-duration load injects stronger high-frequency content into the free surface and excites a more persistent radiated-wave field. In contrast, a lower-amplitude longer-duration load distributes the same momentum over a longer timescale, reducing the additional displacement deviation and shortening the settling time by nearly two wave cycles. These findings suggest that firing-phase selection and load-duration control can be used to mitigate firing-induced transient responses in waves.

papers.title: Automatic design of an efficient forward-curved centrifugal blower using gradient-free approaches
papers.abstract: This study presents the design of a high-efficiency forward-curved centrifugal blower (FCCB) using a fully automated optimization framework based on gradient-free methods. The framework integrates three open-source tools, including Salome for computer-aided design and mesh generation, OpenFOAM 8 for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and Dakota for optimization, coupled through several Python scripts. Several gradient-free approaches, such as artificial neural network, efficient global optimization, Gaussian process (GP), and multivariate adaptive regression spline, are employed for the FCCB design. Eleven design variables related to both the impeller and the housing are selected to design the FCCB for maximum total efficiency ϵtot. In addition to the design process, a quadratic response surface is constructed to evaluate the influence of individual design variables and their interactions on the objective function, providing further insight into the FCCB design space. Turbulent flow within the FCCB is modeled using the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, closed with the k–ω shear stress transport model. In addition, unsteady simulations are performed for the optimized configuration to investigate the transient flow structures and provide further physical insight into the aerodynamic behavior of the FCCB. Based on the results, the GP model identified the most efficient FCCB design with ϵtot=59.1%, showing a negligible difference of 0.2% compared to CFD validation and a difference of 3.13% in the pressure rise compared to the experimental results at the design point. The flow field analysis demonstrates that the improved aerodynamic performance is primarily associated with a more uniform impeller discharge flow, a smoother circumferential pressure distribution, and a more organized flow field within the impeller–volute region.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic mechanism of planar motion in cycloidal-propelled underwater vehicles: Configuration transition from H to X
papers.abstract: As a novel propulsion device, the cycloidal propeller offers superior maneuverability and controllability. However, there is still insufficient understanding of how cycloidal propellers should be arranged on a vehicle so that their advantages can be fully exploited, enabling more rational thrust distribution and improved control of the pressure and vorticity fields, and thereby optimizing hydrodynamic performance. To clarify the fluid-dynamic principles underlying this problem, this study takes a four-cycloidal-propelled underwater vehicle as the research object and systematically investigates the planar motion performance of two propulsor layouts, namely the H-configuration and the X-configuration, using computational fluid dynamics. First, the two vehicle configurations and their corresponding planar motion modes are established. Then, the hydrodynamic parameters, pressure distributions, and three-dimensional vortex structures of the two configurations during planar motion are comparatively analyzed. Finally, the performance differences caused by the configuration change are interpreted from the perspectives of thrust distribution, wake interaction, and flow-field reconstruction. The results show that the H-configuration provides a higher degree of thrust organization along the motion direction, thereby producing more coherent wakes, reducing inter-propulsor interference, and achieving higher steady cruising speed and propulsion efficiency. In contrast, in the X-configuration, part of the propulsive effort generates lateral force components and is canceled during force synthesis; meanwhile, stronger wake interaction and broader vortex spreading further weaken the effective propulsion, resulting in lower planar-motion speed and efficiency. However, by utilizing the lateral force components generated by the propulsors, the X-configuration can achieve omnidirectional planar motion without changing the body orientation. This study explains, from a fluid-dynamics perspective, the intrinsic mechanism by which propulsor layout determines the planar motion performance of cycloidal-propelled underwater vehicles and can provide a reference for future research on propulsion layout design.

papers.title: Transverse wave-controlled near-limit reinitiation of hydrogen detonations over semi-cylindrical obstacles
papers.abstract: In this study, two-dimensional simulations are performed to investigate hydrogen–air detonation interactions with a semi-cylindrical obstacle. A comprehensive regime map covering propagation, reinitiation, and quenching behaviors is established by varying the blockage ratio (BR) and channel height (H). The results show that while the classical gap-size to cell-size ratio (d/λ) criterion provides a useful first-order classification of detonation regimes, but it fails to capture the highly sensitive and non-monotonic behavior observed near critical conditions. Near the propagation/reinitiation boundary, boundary-induced shock attenuation is shown to weaken the leading shock. Given the Arrhenius dependence of the reaction rate on post-shock temperature and pressure, this increases the local induction length and produces transient shock–flame decoupling. Subsequent transverse wave interactions recompress the mixture and recouple the shock and reaction front, enabling anomalous detonation survival. Near the reinitiation/quenching boundary, an anomalous quenching “dead zone” is identified, where neither bottom-boundary nor top-boundary reflection mechanisms provide sufficient compression to sustain reinitiation, resulting in expansion-dominated attenuation and global failure. The channel height is further shown to alter the near-limit dynamics. For identical gap sizes, larger channels can reduce curvature-induced expansion and enhance upstream pre-compression, thereby suppressing shock and reaction zone decoupling and broadening the reinitiation regime. Thus, the present results demonstrate that near-limit detonation behavior is governed by a delicate interplay between local geometric effects and multidimensional transverse wave dynamics, and cannot be fully characterized using a single global scaling parameter.

papers.title: Tornadic aerodynamic loads on tall building: Effects of swirl ratio
papers.abstract: The effects of the swirl ratio of tornadoes on the tornadic aerodynamic loads of tall buildings were investigated through multi-point synchronous pressure measurements on a CAARC (Commonwealth Advisory Aeronautical Research Council) standard tall building model. The experiments were conducted in a newly developed large-scale Ward-type tornado simulator, which is the largest of its kind in the world. The simulator generated stationary tornado-like vortices with five swirl ratios ranging from 0.18 to 0.87. At the lowest swirl ratio (0.18), the narrow one-celled vortex core with strong near-ground velocity gradients and strong updrafts results in the most intense suction at the bottom corners and on the roof, as well as highly non-uniform building surface pressure distributions. As the swirl ratio increases from 0.18 to 0.87, the vortex core expands and evolves from a narrow one-celled structure to a broad two-celled structure with downdrafts reaching the ground, leading to a significant reduction in building surface suction and yielding more uniform building surface pressure distributions. All mean pressure and force coefficients decrease monotonically with increasing swirl ratio, whereas the fluctuating coefficients first decrease sharply (reaching a minimum at a swirl ratio of 0.60) and then rebound at the highest swirl ratio of 0.87, exhibiting a non-monotonic variation. The swirl ratio also significantly modulates the proper orthogonal decomposition modes of surface fluctuating pressure fields, power spectral densities, and spatial correlations of the wind forces. These findings provide information to advance understanding of tornado effects on tall buildings and to improve tornado-resistant structural design codes.

papers.title: Supercooled droplet impact-freezing on cold multi-pillar and multi-hole superhydrophobic surfaces with conjugate heat transfer
papers.abstract: The impact-freezing dynamics of supercooled droplets on cold surfaces are important for anti-icing applications. In this study, direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate the impact of supercooled water droplets on −30 °C multi-pillar surfaces (MPSs) and multi-hole surfaces (MHSs). The coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid method is adopted to capture the droplet interface, while the enthalpy-porosity solidification/melting model is used to reproduce freezing. Fluid–solid conjugate heat transfer is also considered to examine the influence of substrate thermal conductivity. The numerical framework is first validated against several experimental datasets. The results show that, on MPSs, the droplet penetrates into pillar gaps, causing freezing on the pillar sidewalls and strong contact-line pinning. In contrast, MHSs can maintain a more stable non-wetting state by trapping air inside the holes, which suppresses droplet penetration and confines ice formation near the upper solid structures. When the hole width reaches or exceeds the critical value, MHSs produce less ice and lower heat transfer than all MPS cases, indicating the effectiveness of MHSs in suppressing ice formation. In addition, off-set impact on MHSs weakens local pinning and further reduces ice formation compared with head-on impact. Furthermore, low-thermal-conductivity substrates such as Teflon significantly reduce heat transfer and ice formation, enabling full rebound, whereas only partial rebound occurs on copper. These findings provide physical insights for designing structured anti-icing surfaces.

papers.title: Evolution of the wetted zone and splash characteristics of droplet impacting on high-speed rotating hydrophobic surface
papers.abstract: This study conducted experiments on the changes in the wetted zone and the splash characteristics during the impact of droplets on a rapidly rotating hydrophobic surface. Based on the experimental setup, the study systematically analyzed the effects of rotational linear velocity (vr) and the impact Weber number (We) on the morphology of the wetted zone, the separation modes of the tail liquid, and the growth patterns of the liquid finger. The study found that droplet impact on rotating hydrophobic surfaces exhibits four typical tail separation modes: “edge retraction,” “tearing,” and “fragmentation,” among which “edge retraction” forms a closed wetted zone and accounts for the largest proportion. In the variation of wetted zones, the circumferential wetted length Lc* is primarily driven by centrifugal force, whilst the radial length Lr* is significantly influenced by We; the two exhibit a certain degree of competition. Furthermore, the number of liquid fingers increases in direct proportion to vr and We, and is significantly stimulated by the synergistic effect of centrifugal force and initial kinetic energy. These findings reveal the underlying mechanisms governing the motion of wetted zones and the splashing of tail liquid on rotating hydrophobic surfaces, providing a theoretical basis for the design of anti-icing and anti-wear systems in relevant equipment.

papers.title: Physics-guided discrete cosine transform neural network for fast prediction of cavitation and pressure fluctuations in micro axial piston pumps
papers.abstract: Evaluating the coupled evolution of internal cavitation and pressure fluctuation in micro axial piston pumps (MAPPs) across diverse operating conditions remains computationally expensive for conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD). To reduce this cost within a defined operating envelope, a deep-learning-based surrogate model that combines discrete cosine transform-based frequency-domain representation with time-domain physical regularization is introduced for rapid prediction of key transient responses. Driven by CFD reference data, nonlinear mappings between operating parameters and key physical quantities, including cavitation volume, piston chamber pressure, and outlet pressure, are established by the proposed model. The results show that the principal dynamic features of the target variables can be reconstructed with good agreement with CFD reference results under the tested operating conditions. A conventional CFD simulation requires approximately 3 h for a single operating condition, whereas the proposed model requires 35 s for training and 0.7 s for a single inference, yielding an inference speedup of about 15 429×. These results indicate that the proposed method can substantially reduce computational cost for CFD-based multi-condition assessment of MAPPs under the fixed geometry, fluid-property, gas-content, temperature, and outlet-boundary conditions considered in this study.

papers.title: Active and passive flow stabilization of Mach-4 free jets: A numerical study
papers.abstract: Free-jet wind tunnels (FJWT) are widely used for supersonic aerodynamic testing; however, their effectiveness is primarily limited by the formation of conical or diamond-shaped jet cores downstream of the nozzle exit. These flow structures arise from complex interactions between expansion waves, shock reflections, and shear-layer growth, resulting in reduced flow uniformity and a shorter effective test-section length. Although numerous mitigation strategies have been proposed, including pressure matching, geometric modification, and active flow control, their relative effectiveness and underlying physical limitations have not been fully characterized. In this work, a comprehensive numerical investigation is conducted to elucidate the dominant mechanisms governing conical free-jet formation under Mach-4 operating conditions and to assess selected passive, active, and hybrid flow-conditioning strategies within a unified computational framework. Quantitative uniformity metrics are used to enable direct comparison across control approaches under identical operating conditions. The results show that pressure-based and active control strategies can locally alter the shock structure but are highly sensitive to tuning and facility-specific constraints, thereby limiting their robustness and scalability. By contrast, passive geometric modification at the nozzle exit is shown to provide a reliable and energy-neutral means of flow stabilization. Straight cylindrical nozzle-exit extensions delay shock formation, suppress jet contraction, and displace shock–shock interactions downstream of the test section, resulting in a marked increase in the usable uniform-flow region while maintaining Mach number variations within accepted experimental tolerances. These findings provide new physical insight into the limitations of conventional free-jet control strategies and offer practical guidance for improving flow quality in supersonic FJWT.

papers.title: Effects of grid refinement strategies on propeller tip vortex cavitation patterns and induced pressure fluctuations
papers.abstract: The evolution of propeller tip vortex cavitation (TVC) is an important source of near-wake hydrodynamic pressure fluctuations in marine propulsor wakes. To mitigate numerical dissipation in scale-resolving simulations, this study evaluates three wake mesh refinement schemes with axial helical-refinement lengths of 0D, 0.25D, and 0.5D, denoted as 0T, 0.5T, and 1T, respectively, where D is the propeller diameter and T = 0.5D is the characteristic axial projection length of the helical refinement zone. The simulations are performed using the improved delayed detached eddy simulation method coupled with the volume of fluid approach. The 1T strategy, in which the helical refinement zone extends to 0.5D downstream of the propeller disk and connects smoothly with the downstream wake-refinement region, mitigates numerical dissipation among the three mesh-refinement strategies examined in this study and better preserves a relatively high negative-pressure extremum (−Cp,min ≈ 2.3) at x/D = 0.5. The improved wake resolution reveals how gas–liquid phase-change dynamics and local cavity collapses modulate near-wake hydrodynamic pressure fluctuations. The second time derivative of cavity volume, d2Vc/dt2, is used as a monopole-type indicator of cavity-volume acceleration associated with near-wake hydrodynamic pressure fluctuations. At σ = 3, the 1T mesh resolves a 1928 Pa near-wake first-order blade passing frequency amplitude, whereas 0T gives 631 Pa, 67.3% lower, demonstrating 0T under-resolution and the importance of axial wake-mesh continuity in reducing numerical dissipation and resolving TVC structures and pressure fluctuations.

papers.title: A hybrid dual-medium discrete fracture model for horizontal wells with complex fracture systems and waterflooding interference
