papers.abstract: A piezoelectric cantilever-driven pneumatic servo pilot valve involves confined slit throttling, compressible jet expansion, shear layer instability, and pressure-induced structural deformation. These coupled mechanisms remain insufficiently understood, especially under different outlet back pressures. In this study, a three-dimensional fluid–structure interaction model was developed to investigate the flow regime, flow losses, and passive structural response of a nozzle–flapper pneumatic pilot valve under six operating conditions, combining three opening conditions and two outlet back pressures. The results show that outlet back pressure governs the flow regime. Under low back pressure, the pressure ratio far exceeds the critical pressure ratio of air, the slit chokes, and supersonic expansion develops with a maximum Mach number of 2.68, whereas under high back pressure the flow remains subsonic and incompressible. A key finding is the supersonic jet-induced negative pressure attraction effect under low back pressure. The choked slit flow forms a high-speed wall-attached jet along the lower surface of the piezoelectric cantilever. The combined effect of local supersonic expansion and wall-jet acceleration reduces the lower surface pressure below the upper surface pressure, causing the free end to bend toward the nozzle. Under high back pressure, this attraction mechanism disappears, and the distributed high pressure on the lower surface pushes the cantilever away from the nozzle. The energy loss analysis shows that the total flow loss under low back pressure is more than 300 times that under high back pressure, with the dominant loss region localized in the wall jet and downstream shear layer. These results reveal the pressure ratio controlled flow regime transition, supersonic jet-induced attraction mechanism, and localized irreversible loss structure in piezoelectric pneumatic pilot valves.

papers.title: Amphiphilic polymer control of rheology and filtration in high-temperature saline drilling fluids
papers.abstract: During deep and ultra-deep drilling, water-based drilling fluids (WBDFs) are frequently exposed to high-temperature and high-salinity environments, which can exert adverse impacts on the aggregation state of clay particles, rheological response, and filtration performance. In this work, a salt- and temperature-resistant amphiphilic polymeric filtrate reducer (poly-IADS) was synthesized by using itaconic acid (IA), 2-acrylamido-2-methylpropanesulfonic acid (AMPS), dimethyl diallyl ammonium chloride (DMDAAC), and sodium p-styrene sulfonate (SSS) to regulate the microstructure, rheology, and filtration behavior of bentonite-based drilling fluids. The chemical structure, molecular weight distribution, and thermal stability of poly-IADS were characterized, and its influences on the operational American Petroleum Institute (API) rheological parameters and API filtration loss (FLAPI) of bentonite-based drilling fluids under saline and high-temperature conditions were systematically evaluated. Over the investigated NaCl concentration range of 0–30 wt. %, the FLAPI of WBDF + poly-IADS increased from 6.04 to 14.98 ml, whereas that of WBDF + polyanionic cellulose (PAC) increased from 9.24 to 35.18 ml. After aging at 180 °C for 16 h, the FLAPI of polymer-based slurry (PBS) + poly-IADS was 9.20 ml, which was lower than those of PBS + PAC and the PBS blank under the same conditions. Zeta potential and particle size measurements indicated changes in the electrokinetic environment and particle size distribution of the suspensions. Adsorption measurements directly demonstrated the adsorption of poly-IADS onto bentonite particles. Taken together, the results are consistent with a filtration control mechanism involving polymer adsorption, clay particle aggregation, and filter cake formation.

papers.title: Study on cavity evolution characteristics during the water entry of two parallel cylinders under reduced-pressure conditions
papers.abstract: Multi-body cross-medium deployment is common in marine equipment deployment, underwater vehicle launching, and cluster deployment, where cavity interaction and motion response strongly affect water-entry stability. This study investigates the parallel water entry of two cylinders under reduced-pressure conditions. The independent effects of the Froude number and cavitation number are identified through independent parametric control, and single-cylinder water entry is compared with two-cylinder parallel water entry under identical Froude and cavitation numbers. Numerical simulations, validated by experiments, are used to analyze cavity evolution and motion response. The results show that, at a fixed cavitation number, the cavity closure mode changes from deep closure to surface closure as the Froude number increases. Under high-Froude-number conditions, splash rollback near the free surface is intensified, cavity closure occurs earlier, and post-closure fluctuations become more pronounced. Compared with single-cylinder water entry, the global cavity morphology in parallel water entry remains mirror-symmetric, whereas each cylinder exhibits clear inner–outer cavity asymmetry, accompanied by deflection and lateral migration. At a fixed Froude number, increasing the cavitation number suppresses cavity expansion, advances necking and closure, and enhances the attitude response. Overall, the Froude number mainly governs cavity expansion and closure mode, whereas the cavitation number primarily affects cavity contraction and motion-response intensity.

papers.title: Spontaneous translation of charged droplets during evaporation on dry surfaces
papers.abstract: Evaporating sessile droplets are usually treated as capillary objects, but droplets generated by routine handling can carry tens to hundreds of picocoulombs of electric charge. Here, we combine Faraday-cup charge measurements with optical imaging to determine how such charge evolves as water droplets evaporate on dry polymer substrates. A zero-time protocol shows that a reproducible initial charge is preserved on poly(methylpentene) (PMP), whereas polydimethylsiloxane, slippery omniphobic covalently attached liquid surfaces, and polystyrene yield substrate-dependent recovered-charge responses, including heterogeneous exchange, rapid net charge relaxation, and interfacial charging. On PMP, ensemble-resolved measurements reveal two regimes: the charge remains nearly constant during early evaporation and then decreases abruptly once the droplet reaches a small-volume state. This charge collapse coincides with spontaneous lateral translation rather than jetting or breakup. A Rayleigh-normalized analysis, including a spherical-cap stress correction and an effective contact-line retention scale, shows that motion occurs only after evaporation drives the droplet into a high electro-pinning state. High-speed imaging and kinematic analysis support a picture in which the subsequent motion is governed by repeated contact-line depinning and re-pinning: the total distance traveled is strongly affected by dry-surface pinning, whereas the peak translational velocity serves as a more robust indicator of the discharge strength. Footprint-shape statistics further show that visible pre-depinning elongation relaxes as translation accelerates but that its major axis does not predict the rapid-burst direction. Complementary side-view measurements reveal a transient left–right apparent-angle asymmetry during slip. These results identify a dry-substrate mode of evaporation-driven electrostatic relaxation, distinct from Coulomb fission on lubricated surfaces, in which substrate electrostatic passivity enables charge retention, droplet geometry selects the instability onset, and whole-droplet translation provides the charge-release pathway.

papers.title: Foam-induced mobility control and pore-scale residual-oil mobilization by nanoparticle-enhanced nitrogen foam in heterogeneous porous media
papers.abstract: This study examines the ability of nanoparticle-enhanced N2 foam (NENF) to redistribute flow resistance and mobilize residual oil in heterogeneous porous media. Cross-scale experiments, including high-temperature and high-pressure static foam evaluation, single- and parallel-sandpack flooding, and micromodel visualization in computed tomography-derived irregular pore networks, were conducted at 80 °C and 5 MPa. Static foam tests identified a NENF formulation consisting of 0.3 wt. % sodium fatty acid methyl ester sulfonate and 0.1 wt. % Y-1 nanoparticles, which yielded a maximum foam volume of 480 ml and a half-life of 512 min. Single-sandpack experiments identified a gas–liquid ratio of 1:1 for the subsequent parallel-sandpack tests. In parallel sandpacks, NENF treatment preferentially increased the flow resistance of the high-permeability pathway and redirected the subsequent displacement fluid toward the low-permeability region. The most pronounced flow-profile redistribution among the tested conditions occurred at a measured permeability contrast of 4.43 (nominal value of 4) and an injection timing of 98% water cut. Following NENF injection and subsequent waterflooding, the observed total post-treatment oil recovery increments reached 25.56 percentage points in the low-permeability sandpack and 22.77 percentage points in the overall system. Micromodel experiments further provided qualitative evidence that residual-oil mobilization was morphology dependent. Clustered and columnar residual oils were associated with foam-induced squeezing, Jamin-effect-related pressure buildup, and snap-off fragmentation; film-like residual oil was associated with interfacial stripping and local emulsification; and dead-end residual oil was mobilized by localized squeezing of the deformable foam front. Collectively, these findings support a cross-scale interpretation in which NENF treatment was associated with preferential-flow regulation at the sandpack scale and morphology-dependent residual-oil mobilization at the pore scale.

papers.title: Entropy generation analysis using a meshless local radial basis function method for natural convection in an inclined U-shaped porous cavity
papers.abstract: Natural convection and entropy generation in an inclined porous U-shaped cavity with a cold square dip at the top wall and a uniformly heated bottom wall are investigated numerically, with a comparison to parabolic dip configurations of equal area. Steady, incompressible flow through an isotropic porous medium is modeled via the Brinkman–Forchheimer–Darcy formulation with the Boussinesq approximation and solved using a meshless local radial basis function method providing geometric flexibility and stable discretization for the chosen complex cavity configuration. The effects of inclination angle (0°≤γ≤90°), aspect ratio (AR=0.2–0.6), Rayleigh number (105≤Ra≤106), Darcy number (10−4≤Da≤10−3), and Prandtl number (Pr=0.71 and 6.2) are examined. The average Nusselt number (Nu¯) increases monotonically with AR for all parameter combinations, while exhibiting a non-monotonic dependence on γ. Low-Ra and Da cases show heat transfer peaking at intermediate angles, whereas high Ra and Da yield complex behavior due to competing buoyancy and geometry effects. The total entropy generation (Stotal) increases monotonically with AR. Its variation with inclination angle (γ) is non-monotonic and dependent on Ra and Da. At lower Ra and Da, Stotal rises to a peak before falling with increasing γ; conversely, at higher Ra and Da, it exhibits a complex decrease–increase–decrease trend. The Bejan number (Be) increases with γ at high Ra and Da, decreases mildly at intermediate angles for low Da, and remains uniformly high for low Ra. For the vertical configuration (γ=0°), comparison with equal-area parabolic dip results reported in prior studies shows that the parabolic geometry enhances heat transfer by up to ∼29%, while increasing entropy generation (up to ∼36% at low permeability), indicating a trade-off with thermodynamic irreversibility.

papers.title: Analytical model for incipient sediment motion in ice-covered channels: Integrating multi-motion modes of saltation, rolling, and sliding
papers.abstract: Natural rivers in high-latitude northern regions develop a stable ice cover under extremely low-temperature conditions. The formation of ice cover during this phase influences flow characteristics of the river channel and thereby modifies sediment transport processes in cold-region rivers. As the key juncture of sediment transport, the incipient sediment motion serves as a critical threshold governing subsequent sediment transport behavior and channel morphological evolution. Given this, the threshold velocity formula for incipient sediment motion in ice-covered channels is derived under the saltation, rolling, and sliding modes by modeling forces acting on the sediment particles and accounting for the degree of sediment exposure. The calculation results of the incipient motion velocity demonstrate a high degree of agreement with the measured values, validating the effectiveness of the analytical solution. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis of the three modes indicates that the incipient motion velocity exhibits a nonlinear positive correlation with particle diameter, bed roughness, sediment density, and relative exposure degree, while it shows a nonlinear negative correlation with ice cover roughness and bed slope. This study provides a theoretical basis for elucidating sediment incipient motion mechanisms in ice-covered channels and contributes to a better understanding of sediment transport processes in cold-region rivers.

papers.title: Settling dynamics of intruders in confined particulate suspensions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the settling behavior of intruders in neutrally buoyant particulate suspensions with varying particle volume fractions confined by walls using a coupled lattice-Boltzmann method and the discrete element method, in which all solid particles are fully resolved. The simulation models are rigorously evaluated and validated. We employed a homogenized, viscosity-matched Newtonian effective fluid as a surrogate for particle-resolved suspensions to examine the mechanisms governing intruder settling. The results indicate that while the effective fluid effectively captures the fundamental motion of the single intruder and the overall damping effects associated with varying particle volume fractions, it breaks down when dealing with complex paired-intruder sedimentation, especially in suspensions with high particle concentrations. Specifically, the suspended particles in the suspension act as discrete obstructions, leading to the premature separation of tumbling intruders and the reduced critical separation angle compared to their behavior in a uniform effective fluid. Following separation, suspensions facilitate the intruder pair to drift significantly further apart horizontally, a kinematic divergence primarily driven by the Magnus effect. These findings highlight the necessity of accounting for discrete particle effects when modeling multi-intruder dynamics in dense particulate suspensions.

papers.title: Local-equilibrium assumptions of turbulent kinetic energy estimation models in inhomogeneous flows
papers.abstract: In homogeneous isotropic turbulence with high Reynolds number, the normalized dissipation rate Cε is often regarded as asymptotically constant. However, in spatially inhomogeneous turbulence, Cε exhibits non-equilibrium departures from the constant behavior. To obtain an analytical expression for Cε and exploit it to improve turbulence modeling, a key step is to estimate the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE). Building on a perturbation approach, [Bos and Araki, “Equilibrium and nonequilibrium statistics in inhomogeneous and unsteady turbulence,” Phys. Rev. Fluids 10, 044603 (2025)] derived two TKE estimation models based on two distinct local-equilibrium assumptions, leading to two different explicit expressions for Cε and consequently to ambiguity in their practical use. To remove this practical ambiguity, the present study does not aim at introducing a new TKE model; instead, we assess the applicability of the two TKE estimation models and establish a criterion for selecting the appropriate local-equilibrium assumption on the basis of their performance. The criterion is assessed using direct numerical simulations (DNS) of a two-scale wake flow with pronounced non-equilibrium characteristics. With the criterion, the discrepancy between the estimated TKE and DNS statistics is markedly reduced relative to the DNS statistics, and statistically consistent agreement is obtained. In addition, in this spatially inhomogeneous two-scale wake, the equilibrium spectrum and its nonequilibrium correction still exhibit the predicted scaling behaviors over finite ranges of wavenumber, indicating that the corresponding theoretical scaling laws remain valid in this class of spatially inhomogeneous flows.

papers.title: Propagation dynamics of shockwave via intense laser–solid interaction in ambient air: Strong-to-weak shock transition
papers.abstract: In the present study, we investigate the characteristics of the laser-induced shockwave generated on a solid nickel target propagating in ambient air. The shock evolution is examined in high-fluence regimes (30 and 66 J/mm2) using two optical diagnostics: pump–probe transmission and shadowgraphy. The propagation characteristics of the shockwave spanning ≈ 0.1–2 cm are independently established by both techniques, showing mutual agreement. Comparison of the shockwave propagation with contemporary blast wave models, namely the Sedov–Taylor and Jones' model, alludes to a transitional nature of the shock, indicating a progressive decay from a strong to a weak shock regime. This transition is preliminarily evident from the shock front velocity profile, which exhibits an initial rapid decay followed by a nearly constant propagation phase. Analogously, quantitative analysis of the probe transmission, such as variation in the signal attenuation, identifies the corresponding transition point. Moreover, the transition point exhibits a dependence on fluence, occurring at ∼4 mm for 66 J/mm2 and ∼3 mm for 30 J/mm2. In parallel, the key parameters of shockwave propagation, such as the Mach number and compression ratio, are observed to approach nearly similar thermodynamic conditions at the respective transition points. This study provides an explicit experimental identification of the strong-to-weak shock transition during the propagation of a nanosecond laser-induced shockwave generated through laser–solid interaction in ambient air.

papers.title: Vortex interaction and wake instability of a propeller under oblique inflow
papers.abstract: Oblique inflow modifies propeller wake transition by breaking the symmetry of the helical tip-vortex system and altering vortex interaction. A high-fidelity numerical investigation of the wake dynamics of a propeller under oblique inflow is conducted using the lattice Boltzmann method–large eddy simulation. Simulations are performed at four representative advance coefficients (J = 0.394, 0.591, 0.787, and 0.984) and four inflow angles, including an axial inflow case (β = 0°) and three oblique inflow conditions (β = 15°, 20°, and 25°), to examine the coupled effects of loading condition and inflow angle on wake evolution. The results show that oblique inflow breaks the symmetry of the wake and induces lateral deflection, leading to spatially asymmetric evolution of tip vortices. As the inflow angle increases, vortex trajectories are distorted and brought into closer proximity, which enhances vortex interaction and promotes earlier onset of pairing, merging, and breakdown. Consequently, the unstable wake region shifts upstream and expands in spatial extent. Quantitative analyses of tip-vortex characteristics show that the advance coefficient primarily controls the strength of vortex interaction, whereas the inflow angle governs the asymmetry and instability development. Increasing J weakens vortex interaction and delays vortex breakdown, while increasing β intensifies asymmetric vortex evolution and accelerates the transition toward instability. The unsteady flow characteristics are further quantified in the near-, intermediate-, and far-field wake regions. Velocity fluctuation intensity and power spectral density analyses show that strong vortex interaction leads to amplified fluctuations and rapid spectral redistribution, whereas weaker interaction results in a more gradual transition toward broadband unsteadiness. The results establish that the transition from coherent tip-vortex structures to disordered wake flow is governed by vortex interaction strength controlled by loading, while the inflow angle determines the asymmetric evolution pathway.

papers.title: Physics-informed graph Laplacian-augmented Kolmogorov–Arnold networks
papers.abstract: Physics-informed approximation of solutions to forward problems governed by partial differential equation on geometrically irregular domains become challenging when geometric representation, residual evaluation, and neural approximation are not consistently integrated. This study proposes a physics-informed graph Laplacian-augmented Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PI-GLaK) for approximating solutions to the steady incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in two-dimensional vascular geometries. The proposed framework establishes a coefficient-based neural parameterization of the velocity and pressure fields within a common mixed finite-element formulation. Mesh-induced graph connectivity, Laplacian-augmented Kolmogorov–Arnold network layers, and Galerkin residual evaluation are defined using the same Taylor–Hood finite-element representation. The proposed PI-GLaK was evaluated on aneurysm–bend, bifurcation, and stenosis–aneurysm configurations, and its performance was compared with that of a conventional physics-informed neural network (PINN) and a physics-informed graph Galerkin network (PI-GGN). The proposed PI-GLaK achieved total relative L2 errors of 0.048–0.069, compared with 0.017–8.98 for the conventional PINN and 1.03–3.24 for PI-GGN. The proposed PI-GLaK exhibited more consistent accuracy across the three configurations than the PINN baseline and substantially lower errors than the graph-based Galerkin baseline. A gradient-based analysis of the residual loss components characterized geometry-dependent interactions during training and their relationship to the optimization behavior of the proposed formulation. These results demonstrate that graph connectivity, neural coefficient parameterization, and Galerkin residual evaluation can be integrated within a common mixed finite-element representation for physics-informed approximation on geometrically irregular domains.

papers.title: Influence of contact angle hysteresis on bubble interactions in flow boiling
papers.abstract: In flow boiling, surface contact angle hysteresis influences bubble interaction and heat transfer performance. In this work, an improved contact angle hysteresis model is incorporated into the lattice Boltzmann method to investigate bubble coalescence behaviors and boiling heat transfer characteristics in flow boiling. The results indicate that bubble coalescence gives rise to elevated heat flux in the bubble contact region. A larger contact angle hysteresis window reduces the peak heat flux while expanding the spatial range of flow disturbance induced by bubble coalescence. Moreover, the effects of solid thermal conductivity and cavity spacing are examined. A greater hysteresis window enhances wall heat flux under high solid thermal conductivity, whereas the opposite trend is observed under low solid thermal conductivity.

papers.title: Interfacial fluid characteristics of amphiphilic carbon dot dispersion and multifunctional performance as foam stabilizer and oil displacement agent
papers.abstract: Unconventional oil reservoirs have issues, such as high temperatures, high salinity, and complex reservoir structures. Traditional oil displacement agents do not handle heat and salt well and are not great at emulsifying, so their use is limited. This article uses acetaldehyde as the raw material to prepare amphiphilic carbon dots (ACDs) and optimizes the dispersible solution formula, determining the best preparation conditions as a mass ratio of ACDs to anhydrous ethanol of 1:8, 30 mg of 10 wt. % NaOH solution, and a standing time of 40 min. Tests show that the critical micelle concentration of ACDs is 400 mg l−1, corresponding to a surface tension of 34.2 mN m−1. They can maintain stable interfacial activity across 20–100 °C, a wide pH range, and high-salt environments. They effectively reduce oil–water interfacial tension and can switch oil-wet surfaces to hydrophilic ones, while also having excellent emulsifying and foaming stability. The microfluidic oil displacement experiment results show that the oil displacement efficiency of the ACDs solution can reach 83.32%, which is 12.76% higher than using pure water. Capillary number calculations indicate that ACDs flooding increases the capillary number by approximately 12.8 times compared with water flooding, directly correlating with the improvement in microscopic displacement efficiency. This study elucidates the behavior of ACDs at gas–liquid and oil–water interfaces, and establishes a physical model for wettability reversal, emulsification, and foam synergistic flow, providing theoretical and technical support for the application of ACDs in chemical flooding.

papers.title: Effect of porosity on the threshold pressure gradient of oil–water two-phase flow in low- to ultra-low-permeability porous media
papers.abstract: Threshold pressure gradient (TPG) is an important parameter for characterizing low-velocity non-Darcy flow in low- to ultra-low-permeability reservoirs. Existing TPG prediction models mostly use permeability as the core parameter, while the regulatory effect of porosity under nearly identical permeability conditions remains insufficiently understood. Therefore, in this study, low- to ultra-low-permeability clastic reservoir cores from the H, Z, and Y blocks were selected as research objects. Overburden porosity–permeability measurements, constant-rate mercury injection (MICP), and oil–water two-phase TPG experiments under irreducible-water conditions were conducted to analyze the effects of permeability, porosity, and pore–throat structure on TPG, and a dual-parameter prediction model was established. The MICP results show that pore–throat radius has a stronger correlation with permeability than with porosity. The coefficients of determination between median pore–throat radius and permeability and porosity are R2 = 0.5427 and R2 = 0.413, respectively. After introducing the dual parameters of permeability and porosity, the coefficient of determination of the median pore–throat radius prediction model increases to R2 = 0.775. TPG experiments on 36 cores show that TPG exhibits a significant negative power-law relationship with permeability, with a fitted coefficient of determination of R2 = 0.7997. Under nearly identical permeability conditions, the TPG values of low-porosity cores are generally higher than those of high-porosity cores, indicating that porosity has a measurable effect on the fluid initiation process. Based on the MICP data and paired-core experimental results, an interpretive concept of “pore-body pressure storage–throat pressure release” is proposed to explain the observed experimental trend. This concept suggests that high-porosity cores may provide more developed pore space for pressure buffering and redistribution, thereby contributing to lower fluid initiation resistance. Constrained by capillary flow theory and the Kozeny–Carman relationship, a dual-parameter TPG prediction model was established as λ = 0.1188 K−0.5083φ−0.2061. The model achieved a fitting R2 of 0.9862 and an RMSE of 0.017 MPa/m. Overall validation using 79 experimental and literature data points yielded R2 = 0.855. Validation using 43 external literature data points gave R2 = 0.829, while fivefold cross-validation gave R2 = 0.9734. These results indicate that the model has good prediction accuracy and stability within the low- to ultra-low-permeability range. This model can provide a reference for oil–water two-phase TPG prediction and refined development of low- to ultra-low-permeability clastic reservoirs.

papers.title: Energy-based amplitude characterization of large-amplitude viscous droplet oscillation
papers.abstract: This work investigates the large-amplitude oscillation of viscous droplets with initially spheroidal and axisymmetric shapes by direct numerical simulations with Free Surface 3D (FS3D). A normalized surface energy excess is introduced as a unified measure of oscillation amplitude. Within the present parameter range, the temporal asymmetry, as one characteristic feature of nonlinear oscillation, is found to depend only weakly on viscosity. The frequency deviation from the dominant oscillation frequency of the second mode decreases approximately linearly with the surface energy excess. For a given viscosity, the results collapse approximately onto a nearly unique relation between frequency deviation and surface energy excess, independent of the initial amplitude. The slope of this relation is interpreted as reflecting primarily nonlinear effects, whereas the main viscous contribution appears as a viscosity-induced effective-inertia contribution and affects mainly the fitted offset. By analyzing the vorticity field, two distinct regimes are identified. In the low-viscosity regime, the near-interface vorticity profiles are only weakly affected by viscosity and can be approximately scaled by the droplet radius. In the high-viscosity regime, the vorticity profiles collapse when scaled by the viscous length scale. The fitted offset follows an approximate square-root dependence on the Ohnesorge number in this regime, consistent with the leading-order argument. This vorticity analysis supports the interpretation that the offset behavior is associated with viscosity-induced effective inertia. The analytical reference model, based on the potential-flow assumption, is used to support the proposed decomposition of the frequency deviation into a nonlinear contribution and a viscosity-induced effective-inertia contribution.

papers.title: Effects of aspect ratio, sidewall thermal condition, and layer depth on two-layer Rayleigh–Bénard–Marangoni convection
papers.abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of two-layer Rayleigh–Bénard–Marangoni convection for a water–2cSt silicone oil fluid combination using an indigenously developed finite-difference-based flow solver. A comprehensive parametric analysis is conducted in a two-dimensional rectangular domain, examining the effects of domain height (3, 6, 9, and 12 mm), aspect ratio (1, 2, 3, and 4), and sidewall thermal conditions (adiabatic and isothermal) on flow transitions and pattern formation. For adiabatic sidewalls, a flow-pattern map is constructed correlating domain height and temperature difference to delineate distinct flow regimes. For isothermal sidewalls, the interplay between interfacial tension and buoyancy forces induced by sidewall temperature gradients is systematically analyzed. The extensive parametric study presented here addresses a significant gap in the literature, where such detailed parameter sweeps are notably absent. The findings provide critical insights into the complex dynamics of two-layer thermocapillary–buoyant convection, with implications for applications involving liquid–liquid systems under thermal gradients.

papers.title: Flow-guiding and confinement mechanisms of pressure concentration in trimaran section water-entry slamming
papers.abstract: Cross-deck slamming during high-speed trimaran navigation poses a serious threat to structural integrity, yet the mechanism by which different sectional configurations affect slamming characteristics remains to be further clarified. An improved moving particle semi-implicit method is therefore developed by incorporating the slightly compressible adaptive mixed source term and the free-surface with conceptual particles treatment. The improved method reproduces the measured slamming-pressure peak with an error of less than 8%. The improved model is then applied to perform numerical simulations of wedge- and T-shaped trimaran sections under different water-entry velocities, and the pressure response, global vertical force, and flow-field evolution are analyzed. The effect of section mass on the slamming response of the wedge-shaped section is also examined. The results indicate that, owing to abrupt geometric transitions, the T-shaped section is prone to local flow confinement, thereby leading to pressure concentration. In contrast, the wedge-shaped section is more effective in mitigating slamming loads owing to the flow-guiding effect of its inclined surfaces. Moreover, the local loads exhibit pronounced region-dependent characteristics, with transient high pressures and sustained pressure impulses occurring across different hull regions. Increasing the section mass leads to deeper penetration and increases the global vertical force coefficient and pressure impulse, whereas the local peak pressure at the main-hull bottom is comparatively less sensitive to mass.

papers.title: Effects of submerged sills on debris flow resistance and hydraulic characteristics under erodible bed condition
papers.abstract: Submerged sills, as a fully submerged bed-stabilizing measure for debris flow regulation, have poorly understood mechanisms governing their impact on flow motion resistance. In this study, a series of flume experiments were conducted to investigate the flow and resistance characteristics of debris flows under varying channel slopes, unit weights, solid volume concentrations, and longitudinal submerged sills spacings. The results show that debris flows and submerged sills interaction follows a staged evolutionary process, with upstream scour and run-up as the core resistance enhancement and energy dissipation mechanisms. Scour progression gradually exposes the sills, inducing flow run-up and continuous kinetic energy dissipation via particle collisions and turbulence, resulting in a resistance increment of 11.18%–88.37%. Submerged sills convert local energy loss into cumulative along-flow dissipation through continuous multi-structure action, an effect significantly controlled by sill spacing, with total energy dissipation rates of 44.88%–70.20%. Notably, submerged sills exhibit the optimal regulation effect in high-erosion environments with low unit weight and steep channel slopes. The resistance coefficient increases with decreasing spacing, decreases with rising channel slope and debris flow magnitude, and exhibits a nonlinear trend of rapid initial increase followed by a plateau with increasing solid volume concentration. Based on these findings, a resistance calculation model within the Darcy–Weisbach framework was established by partitioning total resistance into fluid properties, channel bed conditions, and submerged sill-induced additional structural drag, which accurately reflects resistance variations across different working conditions. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for optimized submerged sills layout and debris flow resistance prediction.

papers.title: How sparse and how noisy? Systematic benchmarking of inverse physics-informed neural networks for Manning friction estimation in shallow water equations
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a promising framework for inverse hydrodynamic modeling because they can combine sparse observations with governing physical constraints. However, their reliability for estimating hydraulic parameters under realistic data limitations remains insufficiently characterized. This study systematically benchmarks inverse PINN recovery of the Manning friction coefficient in the shallow water equations under controlled variations in observation sparsity, observation noise, and observed variable type. Two benchmark cases are considered: a one-dimensional MacDonald subcritical channel with an analytical steady reference solution and a two-dimensional sloped channel with a parabolic transverse bed generated using a balanced finite-volume solver. The Manning coefficient is treated as a trainable positive scalar and recovered jointly with the flow field using a two-phase optimization strategy that first fits the available observations and then incorporates the physics residual. Results show that the two-dimensional benchmark achieves stable friction recovery, with errors below 5% for as few as five observations of depth and velocity and noise levels up to 20% of the field standard deviation. Recovery remains stable up to 20% noise when 50 observations are used, and the residual error level coincides with the discretization error of the finite-volume reference solution itself, which bounds the accuracy attainable on that benchmark. In contrast, the one-dimensional benchmark exhibits an error that decreases systematically with observation count, from approximately 11% with five observations to 0.2% with fifty, indicating a data-density limitation. Observation-type ablation further shows that friction recovery degrades substantially when only depth or only velocity is observed, demonstrating that joint depth–velocity information is essential for reliable inverse identification. Overall, the results provide a reproducible benchmark for assessing when inverse PINNs can and cannot reliably estimate Manning friction from sparse and noisy shallow water observations.

papers.title: Deposition–resuspension dynamics of unmelted particles on a film-cooled wall in a rotating frame
papers.abstract: Unlike molten or semi-molten ash particles in conventional gas turbines, unmelted solid particles may rebound from the wall, adhere temporarily, or be resuspended after impact. The rotation of turbine rotor blades further affects these processes and adds complexity to particle deposition–resuspension. In this study, a numerical framework in a rotating reference frame was developed to describe film-cooling flow, particle transport, and particle–wall interaction in a representative rotating blade passage. Particle trajectories were calculated using a Lagrangian approach, and the effects of rotating-frame intensity, particle size, and blowing ratio on collision, rebound, and deposition were investigated. The results show that rotation modifies the film-cooling distribution through centrifugal and Coriolis forces, shifting both the cooling flow and the particle-collision region toward the side farther from the rotation axis. Rotation also changes the force balance of adhered particles: aerodynamic and centrifugal effects promote resuspension and suppress stable deposition. For the 3000 rpm-rated helium turbine investigated here, centrifugal-dominated particle resuspension occurs only at speeds substantially above the rated condition. For some higher-speed helium turbines, however, centrifugal force may become the dominant resuspension mechanism. Larger particles collide with the wall more readily but are less likely to remain deposited after impact, so stable deposition may approach zero under centrifugal-dominated high-speed conditions. The effect of blowing ratio is pronounced at low rotation but weakens when rotation-induced resuspension dominates.

papers.title: Suppression of segregation in ternary granular mixtures with large density differences through mixer geometric optimization: A discrete element method–smoothed particle hydrodynamics coupling study
papers.abstract: Significant differences in particle density frequently induce severe segregation during mixing processes. Although the addition of liquid can mitigate this issue, the underlying interaction mechanisms between the liquid phase and mixer geometry remain inadequately understood. In this study, a bidirectional coupled discrete element method–smoothed particle hydrodynamics approach is employed to simulate both dry and wet mixing of particles with three distinct densities in a blade-type mixer. A full-factorial numerical experimental design is implemented to systematically assess the influence of the blade length-to-shell radius ratio (L/R) and the number of blades on mixing performance. Results reveal that at a low L/R ratio (L/R = 0.6), insufficient moment transfer to the fluid phase fails to counteract sedimentation, thereby exacerbating the settling of high-density particles. At higher L/R ratios (L/R = 0.8 and 0.9), the liquid phase effectively suppresses density-driven segregation during the sedimentation stage by suspending particles, thereby maintaining a well-mixed state with comparatively stable performance. This work elucidates the intricate coupling among mixer geometry, fluid dynamics, and granular flow, offering mechanistic insights and practical guidance for the rational design of anti-segregation mixing equipment.

papers.title: Competing energetics govern gas permeation in polymer of intrinsic microporosity (PIM) membranes
papers.abstract: Polymer membranes, particularly polymers of intrinsic microporosity (PIMs), hold great promise for gas separation applications. However, the long-dominant solution-diffusion model, which treats the membrane as a nonporous homogeneous medium, does not resolve how gas–solid atomic interactions govern molecular transport in intrinsic micropores, limiting the rational bottom-up membrane design. In this work, we employ non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the permeation of various gases (He, H2, CH4, N2, O2, and CO2) through PIM-1 as a representative PIM membrane across a range of temperatures. By analyzing the scaling of gas permeability with molecular mass, we identify a temperature-induced transition in the dominant transport mechanism. We demonstrate that this transition is governed by the competition between gas–wall interaction potential energy and thermal kinetic energy: weak interactions or elevated temperatures facilitate Knudsen-type ballistic transport, whereas strong interactions and lower temperatures favor adsorption-mediated surface diffusion. Furthermore, molecular trajectory analysis at the membrane interface reveals two distinct entry pathways: direct entry through pore openings and surface-diffusion-assisted entry. The surface-diffusion-assisted pathway greatly promotes the entry of strongly interacting gases into the membrane, contributing to higher overall permeability, albeit this enhancement diminishes with increasing temperature. These findings offer a mechanistic picture of gas permeation in PIM-1 and explain the dependence of gas permeation on both gas type and temperature. More broadly, they highlight the importance of adopting a pore-mediated flow perspective to understand gas transport in microporous polymer membranes.

papers.title: Patient-specific computational evaluation of blood rheology models for identifying thrombosis-prone regions in portal venous flow
papers.abstract: Portal vein thrombosis is a major cause of portal hypertension and hepatic dysfunction. Although blood is often modeled as a Newtonian fluid in computational fluid dynamics studies, the low flow velocity and elevated viscosity in the venous system suggest that non-Newtonian rheology may affect thrombosis-related hemodynamics. In this study, three patient-specific portal vein geometries before and after thrombosis were reconstructed from computed tomography images. Hemodynamic simulations were performed using a Newtonian model and five representative non-Newtonian models (Power Law, Casson, Carreau, Herschel–Bulkley, and Quemada). Velocity, viscosity, and wall shear stress (WSS) were quantified and retrospectively compared with observed thrombus-related regions. Across all patients, all models consistently identified low-velocity and low-WSS regions that spatially corresponded to thrombus locations, indicating that vascular geometry strongly influences the location of thrombosis-related hemodynamic regions. Non-Newtonian models revealed stronger spatial heterogeneity in viscosity, particularly near low-shear regions adjacent to thrombi, but had limited impact on global flow structure. Quantitative differences were mainly associated with the strong increase in viscosity predicted by the Casson model at very low shear rates and the Quemada model's hematocrit-dependent viscosity formulation. Overall, the Newtonian model provides a practical approximation for first-order assessment of geometry-associated hemodynamic patterns at the portal vein scale, whereas yield-stress or hematocrit-dependent models may provide additional information for refined local analysis under low-shear conditions or when hematocrit-dependent effects are of specific interest.

papers.title: Helicity dynamics in turbulent premixed swirl-stabilized combustion
papers.abstract: Helicity is a fundamental quantity characterizing the three-dimensional kinematics of turbulent flows, yet its dynamic characteristics in reacting flows, particularly in turbulent combustion, remain largely unexplored. In this study, we derive the transport equation for the resolved helicity density and investigate the dynamics of the helicity in a turbulent confined swirling premixed flame using large eddy simulation. A comparative analysis between reacting and non-reacting flows reveals that vortex breakdown consistently induces a sign reversal of the mean helicity density; by contrast, combustion enhances its magnitude in the annular jet region while attenuating it within the central recirculation zone. Based on a budget analysis of the helicity transport, the helicity evolution within the flame brush is shown to be predominantly governed by convection, pressure-gradient, and baroclinic terms. The baroclinic term, together with the pressure-gradient term, counteracts convective transport of helicity, and this competition differs from the helicity dynamics previously observed in laminar knotted flames. Furthermore, the baroclinic effect on helicity dynamics is driven both by small-scale local pressure gradients induced by turbulence and by large-scale global pressure gradients originating from the mean swirling flow, as indicated by a doubly conditional averaging analysis. A scaling analysis suggests that the relative contribution of the swirl-induced global pressure gradient increases with the swirl number and decreases with the Reynolds number, consistent with the scaling behavior observed in enstrophy dynamics.

papers.title: Effects of chordwise flexibility and joint layout on the propulsive performance of a torsional-spring-based two-joint oscillating panel
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the propulsive performance of a torsional-spring-based two-joint oscillating panel, which focuses on the effects of chordwise flexibility and joint layout. A three-dimensional fluid–structure interaction model is established using a strongly coupled computational fluid dynamics method, with the leading edge undergoing prescribed horizontal oscillation, while the rigid panels pitch passively through the connection by flexible joints. The study first compares the performance of single-joint and two-joint panels, then examines the influence of the stiffness distribution between the two joints and the chordwise position of the second joint. Results show that, compared to the single-joint configuration, the two-joint panel achieves higher hydrodynamic efficiency, albeit with a moderate reduction in thrust. Decreasing the torsional stiffness of the second joint further improves efficiency but reduces thrust. The chordwise layout of the second joint plays a critical role: positioning the joint at one-third of the chord length leads to higher efficiency than at two-thirds of the chord length, as it promotes a more favorable pressure distribution, which assists thrust generation and reduces lateral velocity losses that enhance hydrodynamic efficiency. The findings provide insights into the propulsion mechanisms and may advance the design of high-performance bio-inspired oscillating propulsors.

papers.title: Capturing unsteady nonlinear fluid dynamics using physics-informed convolutional leaky-integrator recurrent network
papers.abstract: Accurately capturing unsteady flow dynamics remains challenging for physics-informed neural networks because nonlinear convection, multiscale structures, boundary effects, and accumulated temporal errors can degrade long-time prediction accuracy. This work proposes a physics-informed convolutional leaky-integrator recurrent network for capturing time-dependent flow fields. By combining local convolutions with learnable leaky memory, the proposed method provides a compact recurrent time-marching model with fewer parameters than multi-gate recurrent architectures. To support long-time prediction, the temporal domain is decomposed into overlapping windows coupled by consistency constraints, governing-equation residuals are evaluated using finite-difference differentiation matrices, and prescribed boundary conditions are enforced through hard constraints. The framework is evaluated on incompressible Navier–Stokes flows, including forced two-dimensional flow and the pre-merger interaction of two co-rotating vortices in a no-slip square cavity. Numerical results show that the proposed method reconstructs velocity and vorticity fields with low errors and provides temporally consistent solutions over the tested intervals. For the co-rotating-vortex case, vortex-core kinematics, vorticity statistics, circulation, restricted enstrophy, and the second moment of vorticity are evaluated. The proposed method captures the mutual rotation and gradual approach of the vortex cores and reproduces the principal trends in vorticity redistribution and restricted-enstrophy decay. Compared with the Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory variant, the proposed method achieves errors of the same order of magnitude while using fewer trainable parameters and requiring shorter runtimes in the main recurrent comparisons. Additional tests in Appendix B illustrate its applicability to selected nonlinear evolutionary partial differential equations.

papers.title: Effects of Reynolds number on boundary layer and wake development of embedded turbine vane stages
papers.abstract: To address the aerodynamic challenges associated with low-Reynolds-number operation typical of high-altitude cruise conditions in aero-engines, this paper presents an experimental investigation—conducted on a large-scale, low-speed, multi-stage axial turbine facility—in which both the velocity triangles and the reduced wake-passing frequency were held constant. Synchronized hot-film measurements were conducted on the blade surface, and the dynamic flow field at the second-stage stator (S2) exit plane was acquired using a triple- and hot-wire probe. The study examines the effects of Reynolds number (Re = 7.4 × 104 and Re = 8.5 × 104) on the attached-flow transition and wake mixing characteristics of the S2 suction surface. The results indicate that at the lower Reynolds number, the thickened boundary layer and enhanced viscous effects lead to shear sheltering of external disturbances, resulting in a delayed transition onset and attenuated wall shear stress fluctuations. Consequently, the merging and evolution of turbulent spots are restricted, causing the calmed regions at the trailing edge to exhibit stronger intermittency. This process leads to wake broadening, an elevation of global turbulence levels, and a significant increase in velocity deficit magnitude (>1.5%), ultimately resulting in a significantly deeper and wider exit wake profile, indicative of increased aerodynamic loss.

papers.title: Mechanisms of enhanced hydraulic fracture complexity through carbon dioxide pre-injection induced permeability evolution
papers.abstract: Sequential injection of fluids with contrasting mobility in porous media causes the leading fluid's pressure history to reshape the permeability field, which then governs the seepage and fracture propagation of the following fluid. Using a cross-scale model that couples seepage and discrete element fracturing and distinguishes the flow behaviors of CO2 and water, this study investigates CO2 pre-injection enhanced hydraulic fracturing in coal, capturing permeability evolution driven by CO2 pressure diffusion and subsequent hydraulic fracture propagation. The CO2 pressurization rate controls the time for pressure diffusion, thereby determining permeability uniformity; an intermediate rate creates a moderately heterogeneous field, maximizing fracture length, area, and fractal dimension, while lower and higher rates, respectively, over-homogenize and over-localize the field, reducing complexity. CO2 pre-injection pressure governs the magnitude and heterogeneity of permeability enhancement, transitioning fracture propagation from length-dominated to complexity-dominated. Constant pressure duration regulates the spatial extent of CO2 diffusion, longer durations homogenizing the field and favoring primary fracture extension over complexity. Water injection pressure governs the driving pressure gradient and the shift from branching networks to localized channel flow. Below this threshold, the gradient cannot fully penetrate the CO2-treated zone, limiting fracture complexity; above it, faster flow suppresses branching, widens fractures, and reduces the fractal dimension. Orthogonal analysis reveals a hierarchical control: water pressure has the greatest influence, followed by CO2 pressure, water pressurization rate, constant pressure duration, and CO2 pressurization rate. These findings link pore pressure diffusion and permeability evolution to fracture complexity, providing a theoretical basis for the optimization of process parameters.

papers.title: Particle size and concentration as primary controls on sediment deposition under meandering flow
papers.abstract: During flood seasons, gently sloping meandering rivers are prone to developing high-concentration, fine-grained sediment-laden flows with non-Newtonian behavior, which existing discrete-phase numerical models struggle to reproduce accurately in terms of sediment deposition patterns. Based on field-measured sediment parameters, this study employed an Eulerian multiphase mixture model coupled with the Krieger–Dougherty viscosity equation to represent the non-Newtonian properties of the mixture. A three-dimensional geometrically scaled numerical model of the river channel was constructed, followed by mesh-independence testing and validation against field observations. Nine scenarios combining three particle sizes and three inlet sediment concentrations were considered, and a sediment deposition intensity index was introduced to quantitatively analyze the mechanisms underlying spatial differentiation of sediment deposition. The results show that coarse sediment rapidly deposits in upstream bends, whereas fine sediment is transported downstream before settling. Increasing sediment concentration expands the spatial extent of deposition, and under high-concentration conditions, deposition becomes nearly uniform across the riverbed. Channel-widening bends act as sediment deposition hotspots. These findings provide numerical support for sediment management and reservoir operation in high-sediment meandering reaches of inland rivers.

papers.title: A generalized entropic velocity profile for open-channel flow
papers.abstract: In recent years, entropy-based models have proved useful for estimating velocity distribution and flow discharge in open-channel flows. In the literature, Shannon and Tsallis entropies have been widely used for this purpose. In this work, we investigate Kaniadakis entropy to derive generalized analytical expressions for the vertical and transverse distributions of the time-averaged streamwise velocity component in open channels. The normalized velocity is treated as a spatial random variable, and its probability density function is obtained through the principle of maximum entropy subject to physically meaningful integral constraints. The first-order moment constraint represents mean velocity and discharge, while the second-order moment constraint is related to momentum transport through the momentum distribution coefficient. The proposed formulation recovers the Shannon entropy-based velocity profile in the exact limiting case and connects asymptotically with the Tsallis entropy-based model through the power-law behavior of the associated probability density functions. Both fixed- and varying κ formulations are developed. For the fixed case κ=1/2, an explicit analytical velocity profile is obtained, whereas the general varying κ case yields an implicit analytical solution. The model is validated using several laboratory and field datasets covering wide and narrow channels, including dip-phenomenon case. Its performance is also compared with Shannon, Tsallis, and Rényi entropy-based velocity models, as well as with available numerical simulation results. Quantitative error analysis shows that the proposed Kaniadakis entropy-based model provides improved agreement with measured velocity profiles. The results further indicate weak sensitivity to κ and the momentum distribution coefficient β for the datasets considered, supporting practical use without extensive parameter tuning. It is concluded that the deformation parameter κ can be interpreted as a statistical measure of deviation from the classical Shannon entropy-based velocity distribution, indirectly reflecting the degree of cross-sectional velocity nonuniformity caused by sidewall effects. The proposed model is therefore a physically constrained, information-theoretic velocity profile formulation that can complement the classical hydrodynamic solvers in data-limited hydraulic applications.

papers.title: Identification of orthogonal sensor locations for flow determination using Biot–Savart inspired spatial modes
papers.abstract: The external flow around a submerged body produces pressure and shear stress distributions on its surface, and the full flow field is often of great interest. While sensors fixed to the body can easily measure the pressure and shear stress, they cannot measure the external flow field. However, those surface distributions can be considered an encoding of the full field, and the goal of the problem investigated here is to establish a physics-based framework for identifying optimal sensor locations on the body surface that enable independent and non-redundant decoding of the surrounding flow field, providing a systematic foundation for reduced-order flow reconstruction from surface measurements. To address this challenge, we develop a physics-based framework that integrates the Biot–Savart law with the modal structure of Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD). By expressing the Biot–Savart relation in a matrix-based form, the velocity field induced by vorticity is interpreted as a set of spatial kernels analogous to POD modes. This formulation establishes explicit relationships between body geometry, sensor locations, and the corresponding spatial modes in a simplified two-dimensional configuration. Using this representation, we identify sensor locations whose induced kernels are orthogonal over the computational domain, enabling the construction of POD-like modes directly from sensor geometry. Numerical results show that for a circular body, a fixed reference sensor admits two orthogonal partner locations, whereas geometric deformation increases the number of admissible orthogonal locations. In particular, peanut-shaped geometries yield up to six candidate orthogonal sensor positions relative to the reference. These findings demonstrate that body geometry directly shapes the orthogonality structure of the resulting kernels and therefore plays a critical role in sensor placement for reduced-order flow reconstruction.

papers.title: Lateral dynamics of ellipsoidal drop impact on wettability-controlled surfaces
papers.abstract: Achieving enhanced lateral transport through wettability-engineered surfaces has emerged as an effective strategy for directional liquid manipulation, yet the role of initial drop anisotropy in regulating liquid redistribution and momentum generation remains largely unexplored. Numerical simulations and theoretical modeling reveal the effects of drop ellipticity, wettability contrast, Weber number, impact offset, and surface inclination on impact dynamics. Positive-ellipticity drops transport substantially more liquid across the wettability boundary during spreading than spherical and negative-ellipticity drops, resulting in markedly enhanced lateral momentum generation. The rebound mode on inclined surfaces is governed by the competition between wettability-induced lateral momentum and downslope tangential momentum, leading to transitions among downslope rebound, vertical rebound, upslope rebound, and upslope rolling. A theoretical model based on the overlap area between the spreading footprint and the wettability pattern predicts the lateral momentum for different drop ellipticities and wettability contrasts. These findings demonstrate that the initial drop geometry provides an effective strategy for maximizing lateral transport and achieving controllable liquid motion on inclined surfaces.

papers.title: Axial propagation and radial spreading characteristics of pulsed underexpanded helium jets in low vacuum
papers.abstract: Pulsed underexpanded jets in low vacuum environments are relevant to vacuum gas injection, propulsion plumes, and transient gas transport, but their axial and radial diffusion characteristics remain difficult to quantify because the reduced ambient density weakens Schlieren contrast. In this study, high speed Schlieren imaging is used to investigate pulsed underexpanded helium jets in a low vacuum chamber. Two image based descriptors are extracted from boundary layer features: the propagation velocity of vortex ring structures, Vvr, and the radial spreading width at a fixed axial location, Wrs. The experiments show that decreasing the ambient pressure increases Vvr and substantially enlarges Wrs, with the radial enhancement being especially pronounced in the low pressure range. Semi-empirical models based on a global expansion velocity scale, the Mach disk location, and the relative measurement position capture the main pressure dependent trends of both quantities. A comparison of two nozzle pressure ratio (NPR) pathways further shows that increasing the upstream pressure at fixed ambient pressure and decreasing the ambient pressure at fixed upstream pressure produce similar axial velocity responses, but markedly different radial spreading responses. These results indicate that NPR is an effective descriptor for the axial propagation of boundary layer vortex structures, whereas radial spreading is additionally controlled by the normalized ambient density and the associated weakening of transverse confinement in low vacuum environments.

papers.title: Analysis of the initiation and transient dynamics of n -heptane oblique detonation waves using a robust three-step chemical kinetics model
papers.abstract: The complex chemical behavior of large-molecule hydrocarbon fuels presents a severe computational bottleneck in simulations of hypersonic propulsion wave dynamics. To balance numerical efficiency with physical fidelity in such simulations, this study develops a robust three-step global chemical-kinetics mechanism for n-heptane oblique detonation waves (ODWs). Calibrated against shock-tube ignition-delay data and validated against equilibrium combustion temperatures and theoretical detonation velocities, the mechanism accurately resolves the key thermomechanical coupling. High-fidelity two-dimensional simulations indicate that this framework reliably reproduces steady-state ODW topologies and unsteady transient evolution. The numerical results also capture the pronounced sensitivity of the wave structure to flight altitude and mixture composition: lower altitudes induce abrupt structural bifurcations and geometric kinks owing to intense localized heat release, whereas high altitudes yield spatially dispersed exothermicity and smooth transitions. Furthermore, the simplified model reliably captures highly complex, unsteady flow–chemistry interactions, including thermal-choking-induced bow-shock detachment. Moreover, it achieves an ∼125-fold reduction in computational cost compared to a 42-species skeletal mechanism while preserving macroscopic wave dynamics and thermodynamic accuracy, thereby serving as a practical framework for engineering-scale parametric optimization.

papers.title: Entropy-production-based mapping of irreversible energy loss mechanisms in a centrifugal blood pump
papers.abstract: Energy loss in centrifugal blood pumps affects hydraulic efficiency, heat generation, and hemocompatibility. Conventional pressure-drop and efficiency analyses primarily characterize global hydraulic performance but provide limited insight into the spatial origins and underlying mechanisms of local energy loss. In this study, an entropy-production-based framework was established to map irreversible energy-loss mechanisms in a centrifugal blood pump. The numerical model was validated by grid-independence testing and by comparison with experimental data. The results show that, unlike many industrial centrifugal pumps, energy loss in this blood pump is governed mainly by internal velocity gradients and shear-driven dissipation. Viscous entropy production accounts for 63.6%–85.4% of the total entropy production, whereas turbulent and wall entropy production contribute 9.77%–32.6% and 3.85%–4.82%, respectively. Regionally, the impeller is the dominant loss source, contributing 58.9%–74.2%, followed by the volute (24.3%–38.0%) and the inlet (0.53%–3.12%). Different pump subdomains possess distinct irreversible-loss mechanisms. In the inlet, secondary-passage backflow induces inlet recirculation and enhances turbulent entropy production under low-flow conditions. In the impeller, loss is governed by inlet-jet deflection, blade-surface separation, and rotor–stator shear. In the volute, the dominant loss mechanism evolves from near-tongue viscous shear to high-flow turbulent dissipation associated with Dean-type vortices and outlet-pipe recirculation. The narrow secondary flow path acts as a shear-dominated rotor–stator clearance, resulting in substantially higher viscous entropy production than in other regions. These findings reveal the mechanistic link between local flow structures and high entropy production, providing a foundation for hydraulic-loss reduction and local flow optimization in centrifugal blood pumps.

papers.title: Local helicity distribution distinguishes controlled incompressible vortex-tube states
papers.abstract: Distinguishing vortex states with identical visible geometry but different internal twist, or with identical total helicity but different spatial organization, is a basic diagnostic challenge in helical fluid dynamics. This study shows that the spatial distribution of local helicity density resolves both ambiguities in controlled periodic incompressible vortex-tube benchmarks. In both counterfactual families, conventional diagnostics based on core geometry or total helicity remain at baseline accuracy, while local-helicity-distribution diagnostics identify the hidden state information across the tested noise levels. Held-out-separation tests, top-tail threshold scans, direct grid checks, and short projected Navier–Stokes evolution confirm that the signal is not confined to one separation, one threshold, one grid, or the initial field. These results show that the spatial organization of helicity, not only its volume integral, carries distinct vortex-state information that is lost when only global measures are used. The benchmarks are idealized two-tube fields, not direct simulations of laboratory turbulence.

papers.title: Particle collision-induced surface charge accumulation on wind turbine blades in sand–laden flows: Implications for lightning attachment
papers.abstract: Wind turbines operating in wind-blown sand environments are subjected to severe particle adhesion driven by electrostatic effects, which significantly degrades aerodynamic performance and increases operational risks. However, the mechanisms of particle–blade collision charging and the resulting spatial distribution of surface charge remain poorly understood. To address this gap, the present study develops a numerical modeling framework that integrates the discrete phase model with a custom user-defined collision–charging model. Key parameters, including impact velocity and rebound probability coefficient, are incorporated to quantify energy transfer, particle rebound, and charge generation during collisions. These results show that particle collision and deposition are predominantly concentrated near the blade leading edge. Wind speed governs the transition from gravity-dominated, dispersed deposition at low speeds to flow-dominated impact patterns at higher speeds. Particle deposition exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on wind speed due to the competing effects of increased collision frequency and enhanced rebound. In addition, larger particle sizes and higher wind speeds lead to markedly increased charge accumulation and broader high-charge-accumulation regions on the blade surface. Simulated high-charge-accumulation regions are shown to coincide with actual lightning strike locations on in-service blades, demonstrating that enhanced charge accumulation may increase the likelihood of electrostatic discharge and lightning attachment. Scaled to a 24 h sandstorm, the accumulated surface charge can produce electric fields approaching corona inception thresholds. The proposed framework provides practical guidance for the design of anti-static coatings and lightning protection strategies for wind turbines operating in arid environments.

papers.title: Investigation of the flow phenomena through a pump impeller in stall conditions with high-fidelity simulations
papers.abstract: Centrifugal pumps account for a significant share of global industrial energy consumption. Optimizing the shape of all components is the main goal in the design process to improve operating efficiency and reduce environmental impact. However, centrifugal pumps often operate under off-design conditions, where the flow is characterized by large separations. The stall process of the impeller of a centrifugal pump is investigated in this work with high-fidelity simulations, considering all channels of the impeller instead of the reduced domain used in the literature under the assumption of a periodic flow behavior, in order to assess whether this assumption holds throughout the evolution of the stall process and whether the non-periodic behavior reported in the literature is phenomenological or related to the numerical setup. In particular, the goal is the description of the flow phenomena with different inlet flow rates, with a focus on the configuration of the vortices and the non-periodic behavior of the flow between the channels of the impeller. The setup of the simulations—e.g., the spatial accuracy of the meshes, the numerical schemes, and the formulation of the turbulence models—is assessed to avoid numerical errors that lead to poor accuracy and a deviation from the periodic behavior of the results. A large number of simulations are carried out, and the results are compared with experiments and other high-fidelity simulations available in the literature. The flow phenomena in the evolution of the stall process are progressive, where the increase in the dimensions of vortices is proportional to the decrease in the inlet flow rate. The stall is steady at each inlet flow rate, and the configuration of the vortices is periodic between all channels at the design and pre-stall conditions, and periodic between alternate stall and non-stall channels at the off-design conditions, confirming the periodic behavior assumed in most of the literature at the deep off-design conditions. All the non-periodic behavior of the flow can be ascribed to the spatial accuracy and turbulence model and decreases with high spatial accuracy, suggesting that it is more related to the numerical setup than to the flow phenomena. The proposed formulation of the turbulence model for high-fidelity simulations demonstrates the best compromise between accuracy and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Self-consistent model of arc discharge in liquid incorporating arc–bubble energy coupling
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a self-consistent model to numerically investigate the discharge evolution at different pulse time scales (ranging from several to hundreds of milliseconds) and experimentally validates the simulation via a combined high-speed optical and electrical diagnostic approach. Results indicate that the arc transfers energy to the bubble mainly via light radiation and influences bubble pulsation, while pressure variations during bubble pulsation conversely regulate arc evolution. In the short-period oscillation stage, when the bubble radius is much larger than the arc radius, the arc–bubble system is in a weak coupling state; the net deposited power of the bubble is negative, and heat conduction loss to the electrodes dominates the energy dissipation of both (40%–70% for the arc and 90% for the bubble). When the bubble contracts to collapse and the radii of the bubble and arc are comparable, the system transitions to a strong coupling state; the net deposited power of the bubble becomes positive, and light radiation dominates the energy dissipation of the arc (60%–80%) and the energy deposition into the bubble (95%). In the quasi-steady-state stage, the net deposited power of both approaches zero, with energy deposition and dissipation maintaining dynamic equilibrium. Interface instability induced by bubble collapse is the key trigger for the transition from short-period oscillation to the quasi-steady state, while the self-stabilizing characteristic of the arc further strengthens the system's dynamic equilibrium. This work quantitatively elucidates the arc–bubble energy coupling mechanism, providing a new theoretical analysis tool for arc discharge in liquid.

papers.title: Aerodynamic mechanisms of flutter control for a π -shaped section with a central stabilizer and a spoiler
papers.abstract: The π-shaped section, as a typical blunt section, exhibits significant airflow separation around its section, making it susceptible to wind-induced vibrations. To investigate the flutter mechanism and control measures of a π-shaped section, the Ebtehaj cable-stayed bridge is taken as a case study. Wind tunnel tests and numerical simulations are combined to examine the effects of an upper central stabilizer and a spoiler. The differences in the flutter control performance are clarified through analyses of the spatiotemporal evolution of vortices and the characteristics of zonal aerodynamic work. The results show that an upper central stabilizer with a height of two-thirds of rib height can completely eliminate divergent vibration, while, within the tested parameter range, 60° is identified as the optimal aerodynamic angle for the spoiler. The upper central stabilizer suppresses flutter by modifying the vortex distribution over the upper surface, interrupting the vortex correlation between the upstream and downstream regions of the stabilizer and enhancing vortex interactions in the wake region. However, the spoiler primarily regulates the flow by suppressing vortex generation on the upper surface and altering the vortex distribution on the lower surface. From an energy perspective, the central stabilizer enhances the negative aerodynamic work at the leading edge while altering the aerodynamic work characteristics at the trailing edge. The spoiler, on the other hand, significantly strengthens the negative aerodynamic work at the leading edge and changes the aerodynamic work in the mid-leading-edge region from negative to positive.

papers.title: Effects of microstructure resolved numerical homogenization of unit cell on the breakthrough curve prediction using the volume averaging model in water filtration
papers.abstract: Breakthrough curve (BTC) is a significant result for the estimation of contaminant adsorption period on the porous surface in water filtration techniques. In water filtration, the process of trace amounts of contaminants being transported and adsorbed by the walls of porous medium is governed by the advection-dispersion equation. The upscaling technique, using the volume averaging method (VAM), highlights the presence of total dispersion tensor (Dβ) and adsorption induced vector (Uβ) in macroscopic equation derived from the advection-dispersion equation at micro scale. Such a macro-micro coupling model using VAM is considered for modeling and simulating the contaminant transport and adsorption process in a unit cell for the creeping flow. However, different particle shapes such as circle, rectangle, orientation, and particle count inside a unit square cell that resemble the representative elementary volume have been considered here to study the effects of microstructure resolved numerical homogenization on effective transfer coefficients and BTC. Initially, average velocity of fluid for such geometries of adsorbent particles is solved using the Stokes flow equation. The coefficients Uβ and Dβ are calculated using the closure formulation equations. The average velocity and coefficients obtained with each geometry along with effective transfer coefficients are then used to obtain the BTCs using VAM. Also, such numerical exercise is performed for validating with three available experimental BTCs.

papers.title: Boundary-layer separation and vortex evolution in a centrifugal pump: Large-eddy simulation and particle image velocimetry
papers.abstract: To elucidate the evolution of unsteady internal flow structures in a low-specific-speed centrifugal pump under different flow rate conditions, large-eddy simulation (LES) was employed to systematically investigate the flow within the impeller. Particle image velocimetry) measurements were conducted to validate the reliability of the numerical method in predicting the planar velocity field and the dominant vortical structures. On this basis, particular attention was paid to boundary-layer separation on the blade surfaces and its coupling with the vortical structures within the blade passages. The results show that, under the high-flow rate condition, boundary-layer separation on the blade pressure side is primarily governed by the adverse static-pressure gradient. The maximum separation length exhibits a phase lag of approximately 37° relative to the peak adverse pressure gradient. Localized vortical structures are also evident near the blade suction side, where they enhance local momentum exchange and, to some extent, constrain the development of boundary-layer separation. As the flow rate decreases, the low-velocity and separated-flow regions on the blade suction side progressively expand, further promoting the formation of large-scale vortical structures within the blade passages.
