At 0.6Qd, the suction-side separation region increases markedly, and the vortex volume identified using a fixed Liutex threshold is approximately 69% greater than that at 1.3Qd. These large-scale separated-flow structures substantially reduce the effective flow area at the entrances of several blade passages, thereby leading to the formation of stalled passages. Furthermore, the three-dimensional LES results reveal that the large-scale vortical structures exhibit an alternating circumferential distribution in the six-bladed impeller and show no evident rotational propagation within the present statistical sampling period. Through hydraulic blockage and momentum redistribution within the blade passages, the large-scale separation vortices on the blade suction side delay or suppress, to some extent, the development of boundary-layer separation on the pressure side.

papers.title: Electrohydrodynamic wall jets from surface dielectric barrier discharge in confined air and nitrogen flows
papers.abstract: We examined the effects of gas composition on ionic wind generation by surface dielectric barrier discharge (SDBD) in a confined rectangular channel. Air and nitrogen cases were compared under 2 kHz sinusoidal excitation while varying the applied voltage using the same channel and bulk flow rate. To characterize the coupled discharge-flow response, electrical measurements, optical imaging, and particle image velocimetry (PIV) were performed in the same configuration. Electrical measurements show that nitrogen discharges produce greater charge transfer and higher input power than air, accompanied by stronger optical emission and longer streamer propagation under comparable voltage conditions. From the PIV measurements, air produces higher near-electrode wall-jet velocities, whereas nitrogen sustains near-wall momentum farther downstream. The zero-dimensional ZDPlasKin kinetic calculation indicates different charge-carrier evolution in the two gases, with oxygen-based negative-ion formation and post-field persistence being more pronounced in air. The kinetic result is used to support the gas-dependent charge-carrier interpretation, while the wall-jet response is interpreted together with the measured discharge footprint and the phase-dependent nature of electrohydrodynamic forcing. These findings show that the electrical/optical discharge response and the wall-jet response do not necessarily scale together in confined SDBD actuation.

papers.title: Physics-enhanced neural operator for predicting hydrodynamic lubrication in slipper pairs
papers.abstract: The transient dynamics of the micrometer-scale slipper-pair oil film in axial piston pumps are governed by multi-factor coupling effects, rendering traditional numerical methods inadequate for real-time simulation and rapid design optimization. This paper proposes a physics-enhanced neural operator (PENO) to predict transient lubrication characteristics. PENO combines a motion module that predicts the film thickness at three feature points with a hard-constrained Fourier neural operator for pressure reconstruction. The pressure field is decomposed into a logarithmic, boundary-compatible background field and a masked residual field that analytically enforces the radial Dirichlet pressure boundary conditions. Reynolds-equation residuals and force/moment equilibrium residuals are incorporated into the loss function to improve physical consistency. Evaluations across various operating conditions show that PENO can accurately predict the lubrication characteristics of the slipper-pair oil film. Across the evaluated operating conditions, the full-cycle relative L2 errors of the predicted pressure fields range in order of magnitude from 10−4 to 10−2, while the full-cycle oil-film thickness root mean square errors (RMSEs) range from 10−3 to 10−1 μm. The prediction results meet the physical consistency requirements, with the largest full-cycle RMSEs for the axial supporting force and supporting moments being 7.4 N and 3.8 × 10−3 N m, respectively. Compared to traditional numerical methods, PENO reduces the average full-cycle prediction time from 3.32 × 103 to 6.96 × 10−2 s, representing a speedup of 4.76 × 104. When the mesh size increases from 31 × 121 to 98 × 382, the inference time remains at 7.64 × 10−1 s, indicating favorable inference-time scaling over the tested mesh resolutions.

papers.title: Magnetically induced flow redistribution and reverse perfusion in pulsatile non-Newtonian blood flow through a bifurcated artery with a localized porous obstruction: An inductionless lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Pulsatile non-Newtonian blood flow in an idealized bifurcated artery is investigated under an externally imposed magnetic field in the presence of a localized porous obstruction. The flow is solved using a Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook lattice Boltzmann formulation, while electromagnetic effects are introduced through an explicit inductionless coupling under a uniform applied field, Bapp=B0ẑ. Blood rheology is described by the Carreau–Yasuda law, and the obstructed region is modeled as a localized Darcy–Forchheimer resistance in one daughter branch. Before analyzing the coupled response, the numerical framework is assessed through six complementary steps: exact recovery of the hydrodynamic baseline at Ha=0, a manufactured-solution test for the electric-potential Poisson solver (relative L2 error 0.09%), monitoring of the discrete current-conservation defect, an in situ electromagnetic diagnostic, a quantitative Hartmann-channel benchmark, and a Brinkman–Forchheimer porous-channel benchmark of the localized-resistance treatment. The retained moderate-obstruction case exhibits a threshold-controlled redistribution of branch perfusion. On the refined meshes, the obstructed branch remains forward perfused at HaR=4 and HaR=5, becomes hydraulically marginal near HaR=6, and is negatively perfused in the cycle-averaged sense by HaR=6.5, where the reversed flow is an order of magnitude larger than the solver's cycle-averaged mass-conservation residual. The precise zero-crossing of the small residual branch flow is mesh- and geometry-sensitive and is not resolved to a tight interval by the present resolutions; we therefore report a robust mean reverse-perfusion regime above HaR≈6 rather than a single universal critical value. The reversal is shown to be independent of the outlet boundary treatment (seven outlet formulations in the reversed-flow regime) and robust to obstruction severity, bifurcation angle, and obstruction position. The central physical finding is preserved: electromagnetic forcing can overcome the residual hydraulic support of a moderately obstructed branch and induce mean reverse perfusion when the branch is close to hydraulic marginality, through an asymmetric, global redistribution of the Lorentz force rather than through the magnitude of the local porous resistance.

papers.title: Unsteady aerodynamic force on an ice-covered conductor in turbulent flow: Turbulence–motion coupling and spectral correction of aerodynamic derivatives
papers.abstract: Unsteady aerodynamic forces on ice-covered conductors in turbulent flow involve the coupled effects of incoming turbulence, structural motion, and separated-flow memory, which are not fully captured by conventional quasi-steady aerodynamic models. This work develops an unsteady aerodynamic lift model for an oscillating ice-covered conductor section under turbulent inflow. By analyzing the effective angle of attack, the streamwise turbulent fluctuation is shown to modify the motion-induced lift through both dynamic-pressure variation and effective-angle modulation, producing a first-order Uu-type turbulence–motion coupling term. This mechanism is incorporated into a double-convolution time-domain formulation and then simplified in the frequency domain by introducing a turbulence autospectrum-based correction to the aerodynamic derivatives. The formulation indicates that the streamwise turbulent energy near the structural oscillation frequency is the main contributor to the additional unsteady lift. Forced-vibration wind tunnel tests on an elliptically ice-covered conductor section in grid-generated turbulence validate the model. Compared with the original aerodynamic derivative formulation without spectral correction, the corrected model predicts the measured lift histories more accurately. Parametric results show that turbulence intensity strongly amplifies the unsteady lift, whereas the integral length scale has a weaker and gradually saturating influence. The proposed framework clarifies how turbulent inflow modifies motion-induced lift on ice-covered bluff conductors and provides a compact model for wind-induced response analysis.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of single microscale droplet impact on a heated wall under vertical overload
papers.abstract: Droplet impact on heated walls is important in aerospace thermal management and other high-heat-flux applications, yet the effects of overload on the dynamics and heat transfer of microscale droplets have not been systematically quantified. In this work, a volume-of-fluid model coupled with a phase-change evaporation model is developed to simulate the impact of water microdroplets on a heated wall under altered effective gravity, with a dynamic contact-angle model incorporated to capture nonequilibrium moving-contact-line behavior. The dynamic contact-angle treatment has little influence on the initial inertia-dominated spreading, but markedly improves the description of recoil, oscillation damping, and heat-flux evolution at later stages. For 60 μm droplets in both the 5 m/s and free fall cases, the droplet dynamics and global thermal response are insensitive to vertical overload from 1g to 20g; under free fall, overload mainly advances the impact and heat-transfer processes in time while barely altering the spreading amplitude and final thermal state. For a larger 300 μm droplet, at which the Bond number rises to the order of 0.1, overload still leaves the spreading amplitude and wall heat transfer essentially unchanged and induces only a weak phase shift of the post-spreading oscillation. Instead, these characteristics are governed primarily by the Weber number and the droplet length scale. For normal overload aligned with the impact direction, 1g design data for the spreading amplitude and peak heat flux therefore remain applicable without an overload correction.

papers.title: Experiment and modeling on the morphological response and dynamic evolution of water droplet induced by rising CO2 bubble in oil phase
papers.abstract: During CO2 enhanced oil recovery, bubble migration in the oil phase may disturb the interfacial stability of water-in-oil droplets, thereby affecting their deformation, motion, and destabilization. To clarify the two-dimensional disturbance mechanism induced by rising CO2 bubbles, a visualization platform was established. High-speed imaging and image processing algorithms were used to investigate the effects of oil phase viscosity, particle size ratio, and initial horizontal distance on droplet dynamic responses. A dynamic model coupling the Oseen spherical flow field with the Maxey–Riley (MR) equation was further introduced to predict the droplet motion under non-contact conditions. The results show that droplet deformation and motion exhibit distinct staged characteristics in the bubble-induced flow field. Increasing continuous-phase viscosity delays the peak response and suppresses the transient disturbance, causing the peak deformation in high-viscosity oil to drop to 33% of that in low-viscosity oil. A smaller particle size ratio enhances droplet inertia and weakens its response to external disturbances. In contrast, reducing the dimensionless initial horizontal distance from 1.15 to 0.43 triggers a nonlinear near-field enhancement, increasing the maximum deformation ratio by approximately 49.0%. The MR–Oseen model reasonably captures the overall evolution of droplet velocity and displacement, achieving a mean displacement error of 9.5% in high-viscosity oil, whereas larger deviations reaching 51.9% occur under low-viscosity conditions. This study provides insight into bubble-induced droplet deformation and migration, which may act as precursor hydrodynamic processes of emulsion destabilization during CO2 flooding.

papers.title: Analytical solution for the abrupt cessation of pulsatile flow through a circular pipe
papers.abstract: We develop a mathematical model to characterize the abrupt cessation of one-dimensional, incompressible, laminar pulsatile flow at an arbitrary time tc and describe the resulting transient flow in a circular pipe. The initial pulsatile flow velocity is expressed as Ui=Umi+Uoi sin(ωt), where Umi and Uoi are the mean and oscillatory components, ω is the angular frequency, and t is the time. Analytical solutions, derived through Laplace transforms, provide expressions for velocity, velocity gradient, pressure gradient, wall shear stress, and skin-friction factor as functions of radius r and t. By using Umi, Uoi, tc, and the Womersley number α as parameters, we demonstrate that our generalized solution encompasses known results for steady and non-periodic unsteady flows as subsets. We also derive a novel special-case solution describing the decaying flow following the abrupt cessation of oscillatory flow. Using these solutions, we characterize decaying flow behavior in steady, oscillatory, and pulsatile regimes. The parametric study concerns cessation from a periodically developed pulsatile flow. Key findings show that the maximum skin-friction factor depends strongly on λom=UoiUmi (ranging between 1−100), α (ranging between 1−100), and ωtc (ranging between 0°−360°): its absolute peak decreases with increasing α, and the cessation phase at which it is largest shifts from 90° toward 141° as α increases, independently of λom. Under the fixed-mean-velocity comparison adopted here, the peak is largest for pulsatile flow, but since the solution is linear in the mean and oscillatory amplitudes, this reflects the superposition of a non-zero oscillation on a fixed mean rather than an intrinsic ranking of the flow classes. For applications requiring higher wall friction forces, cessation should occur at a phase angle between 90° and 141°, whereas for lower friction forces, cessation should occur at a phase angle outside this range.

papers.title: Physical and modeling investigation of hydrodynamic impacts of submerged breakwater on wave transformation at complex fringing reef
papers.abstract: Coral reefs possess unique geomorphological features that strongly influence wave transformation processes and reduce the amount of wave energy reaching coastal regions. In recent years, reef degradation and changing environmental conditions have altered hydrodynamic processes within reef systems. The installation of submerged breakwater (SBW) on coral reefs may further modify wave propagation, wave breaking, and flow-field evolution. However, the hydrodynamic responses associated with wave interactions with intermittently arranged submerged breakwaters in reef environments remain insufficiently understood. Therefore, physical model experiments and numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the effects of submerged breakwaters on wave transformation over a fringing reef. The results show that the presence of SBW modifies wave-breaking characteristics, wave transformation processes, and flow-field structures over the reef. Under most tested conditions, the SBW reduce the wave energy, wave setup, and wave runup propagating onto the reef flat. Furthermore, the SBW modifies the spatial distributions of turbulent kinetic energy, vorticity, and coherent vortex structures. The numerical results suggest that regions of elevated turbulence activity tend to shift from the reef edge toward the breakwater crest and gap regions, indicating a redistribution of hydrodynamic processes within the coral reef system.

papers.title: Experimental investigation on the effect of leading-edge geometry on the roughness sensitivity of compressor aerodynamic performance
papers.abstract: Surface roughness exerts a significant influence on the aerodynamic performance of compressor blade airfoils. To investigate the influence of leading-edge geometry on the sensitivity of airfoil aerodynamic performance to roughness, this study conducted planar cascade experiments with variable surface roughness to comprehensively measure the total pressure loss characteristics and blade surface pressure distributions of controlled diffusion airfoils with circular and spikeless leading edges. The laws of aerodynamic performance degradation under variations in roughness size and location within the sensitive regions of the blade were obtained. Results indicate that increasing roughness in geometrically sensitive regions induces a linear reduction in the available incidence range. In contrast, the minimum total pressure loss rises sharply once the roughness exceeds a certain value. The spikeless leading-edge airfoil exhibited significantly lower performance degradation in both minimum loss and available incidence range, indicating superior aerodynamic robustness against surface roughness. Increased surface roughness causes laminar separation bubbles (LSBs) to migrate rapidly upstream and collapse prematurely at smaller inlet flow angles. The LSBs on the suction surface of the circular leading-edge airfoil are consistently more susceptible to the disturbance of surface roughness, and turbulent separation is more likely to occur near the trailing edge.

papers.title: Acoustofluidic suppression of Rayleigh–Taylor instability and fluid mixing: Stabilization of stratified fluids in a minichannel
papers.abstract: Rayleigh–Taylor Instability (RTI) typically arises when a dense fluid is superimposed on a lighter fluid, where the destabilizing gravitational force acting on miscible fluids drives chaotic mixing. We theoretically present an acoustofluidic method utilizing standing bulk acoustic waves to counteract RTI and suppress the mixing of fluids. To successfully achieve this suppression, we demonstrate that two concurrent conditions are to be satisfied: the acoustic energy density (Eac) of the standing waves must exceed its critical threshold (Ecr), and the orientation of the acoustic waves must be perpendicular to the fluid–fluid interface. This acoustofluidic mechanism reduces the mixing index by up to an order of magnitude compared to the mixing induced solely by gravity. By analyzing the interplay between acoustic and gravitational forces, this study elucidates the acoustically modulated mixing dynamics in minichannels.

papers.title: Transient heat flux evolution in pool boiling on inhomogeneous surfaces: A data-driven lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Capturing the highly nonlinear, transient temporal dynamics of nucleate boiling heat flux imposes severe computational burdens, particularly when involving complex inhomogeneous surfaces where intense liquid–vapor interactions induce chaotic thermal fluctuations. To deeply reveal these underlying phase-change mechanisms, this study establishes a coupled framework integrating the hybrid pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann method with deep learning architectures. Systematic analysis reveals that the transient surface heat flux exhibits pronounced high-frequency oscillations, which are fundamentally driven by the periodic physical cycles of vapor blanketing, bubble departure, and rapid surface rewetting. While conventional neural networks (such as multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks) structurally disrupt the temporal continuity of this thermal history, the recurrent neural network (RNN) uniquely aligns with the physical periodicity of the boiling cycle. The internal memory cells of the RNN function analogously to the thermal inertia of the heating wall, successfully capturing the cyclic destruction and reconstruction of the thermal boundary layer and yielding superior predictive accuracy. Furthermore, on inhomogeneous surfaces with isosceles trapezoidal microstructures, the fundamental periodicity of boiling is physically disrupted. Intense contact line pinning and premature lateral bubble coalescence drastically prolong localized vapor blanketing, shifting the multiphase heat transfer from a stable cyclic process to a highly chaotic, nonlinear dynamic regime. The proposed framework effectively tracks these complex transitions, proving that structural micro-confinement profoundly modulates the localized thermal fluctuations.

papers.title: Curvature-controlled three-dimensional flow structures in a natural sharp-bend confluence with tributary inflow: The Baima reach of the Wujiang River
papers.abstract: Natural sharp-bend confluences involve simultaneous tributary momentum injection and curvature-induced pressure adjustment, but their coupled control on three-dimensional flow organization remains poorly understood. Here, a validated three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-based model was applied to the Baima Reach of the Wujiang River to examine flow responses to different tributary-to-mainstream discharge ratios (RQ) at a tributary confluence near a 90° bend. The results show that the free-surface response was primarily organized by bend curvature. The longitudinal rise–fall pattern in water level persisted even without tributary inflow, whereas increasing RQ mainly changed its amplitude. The transverse water-surface gradient strengthened near the upstream bend apex, weakened immediately downstream of the confluence, and recovered in the middle–lower bend reach; its dependence on RQ was spatially variable, decreasing with RQ immediately downstream of the confluence but increasing farther downstream. Velocity distributions showed a curvature-controlled migration of the high-velocity zone from the upstream convex-bank side to the downstream concave-bank side, with vertically asynchronous adjustment over depth. Tributary inflow modified local velocity magnitude, lateral contrast, and positions of the circulation cells, but did not replace the curvature-controlled migration pathway. Under high tributary discharge, turbulence intensity increased markedly in the inflow-side surface layer and was redistributed toward the downstream near-bed region. These findings demonstrate that tributary momentum acts mainly as a local modulation imposed on preexisting curvature-controlled pressure and secondary-flow fields, providing a physical basis for understanding three-dimensional flow structures in natural sharp-bend confluences.

papers.title: Vortex dynamics and phase transformation of flow past an isolated sphere in power-law fluids
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate the wake evolution of power-law fluid flow past an isolated sphere over the parameter ranges of 100≤Re≤600 and 0.4≤n≤1.6. The results show that, as the power-law index decreases, the wake successively undergoes four regimes: steady axisymmetric, steady planar-symmetric, unsteady planar-symmetric, and unsteady asymmetric states. For cases exhibiting periodic vortex shedding, the hairpin-vortex head is associated with stronger vorticity and enstrophy, whereas the vortex legs maintain a more ordered streamwise evolution. As the power-law index decreases, periodic hairpin-vortex shedding becomes increasingly irregular, while large-scale hairpin vortices lose their coherence and breakup earlier, causing the wake to transition toward a more complex unsteady state dominated by interactions among multiscale vortical structures. The boundary-vorticity-flux analysis, based on a formulation that includes the apparent-viscosity-gradient contribution and accounts for the spherical-wall geometry, shows that the tangential wall-vorticity flux is closely related to the formation of the hairpin-vortex head. Decreasing the power-law index weakens and localizes this flux, thereby suppressing the formation of a complete vortex head. The invariants of the second moments of velocity fluctuations indicate that the fluctuation energy becomes more evenly distributed among the three directions as the power-law index decreases. The force analysis shows that the reduction in mean drag mainly results from the decrease in streamwise friction force, whereas the pressure drag changes only slightly. Meanwhile, the force fluctuations are significantly enhanced in the unsteady asymmetric wake.

papers.title: Flow past a long, tilted cylinder near a plane wall
papers.abstract: The flow past a tilted cylinder at a Reynolds number of 500 is investigated using direct numerical simulation. Two tilt angles, φ = 1.5° and 2.5°, defined relative to the bottom wall, are examined, with wall-parallel cylinders at different gap ratios serving as reference cases. The primary distinction between the tilted and wall-parallel configurations lies in the emergence of a tilt-induced spanwise flow in the near wake, reaching a maximum magnitude of approximately 0.32 times the free-stream velocity. This spanwise flow substantially modifies the wake dynamics, hydrodynamic forces, and time-averaged flow characteristics. It elongates the recirculation zone and delays the onset of periodic vortex shedding, increasing the critical gap ratio (Gcr) for shedding to Gcr/D = 0.4, where D is the cylinder diameter, compared with Gcr/D = 0.3 observed for a wall-parallel cylinder. Along the tilted cylinder sections with vortex shedding, two distinct vortex-shedding regions are identified: an oblique and a regular vortex shedding region. A reduction in lift-force fluctuations is observed in the oblique vortex-shedding region, attributed to the elongation of the recirculation zone and frequent vortex dislocations. These findings demonstrate that spanwise variations in gap ratio can fundamentally modify near-wall wake dynamics and provide a basis for understanding more complex flows around tilted cylindrical structures in engineering applications.

papers.title: An aerodynamic and aeroacoustic study of a badminton shuttlecock
papers.abstract: This study investigates the aerodynamic and aeroacoustic characteristics of a badminton shuttlecock using an open-jet anechoic wind tunnel at 10–60 m/s. The work provides a combined experimental dataset of force and moment measurements under controlled and natural rotation, particle image velocimetry-resolved wake fields, and acoustic source and correlation analyses for the same shuttlecock configuration. A sting system with a proportional–integral–derivative-controlled motor enabled axial rotation of the shuttlecock and variation of angles of attack (α) from 0° to 90°. Aerodynamic loading measurements revealed that the drag coefficient stabilizes at higher Reynolds numbers. Lift, drag, and moment coefficients peaked at α = 40°, 65°, and 40°, respectively, with a maximum lift-to-drag ratio of 1.1 at α = 30°. Axial rotation affects rotational moment, drag at low α, and side force at nonzero α. Flow analysis indicates that higher rotational speeds increase wake turbulence and aerodynamic drag at low to moderate α, though this effect becomes negligible at α = 45°. Additionally, increasing α transforms the vortex shedding at α = 0° into a shear layer, whereas rotational speed exerts no significant impact on overall wake vorticity. Aeroacoustic analysis identified tonal noise at 20 m/s from rachis and thread vortex shedding, transitioning to broadband noise at 40 m/s. Temporal acoustic correlations confirmed coherent structures at 20 m/s, which diminish at 40 m/s. These findings enhance understanding of shuttlecock flight and provide data for future aerodynamic and aeroacoustic validation.

papers.title: Supersonic combustion induced by shock waves and streamwise vortices
papers.abstract: This study investigates supersonic combustion features induced by the interaction between two streamwise vortices and shock waves at a Mach number of 3.5 using a hypermixer fuel-injector strut mounted at the center of a combustor. Hydrogen fuel is injected from the rear of the strut into the combustor at a jet Mach number of 1.5 with an equivalence ratio of 0.6. To further enhance combustion performance, this study numerically investigates the effects of fuel injection position on supersonic combustion, based on a combustion-enhancement indicator proposed previously. The results show that complex vorticity fields generated by the streamwise vortices, fuel jets, and the first and second shock interactions play a major role in expanding the combustion zone. After interacting with the shock waves, the hydrogen distributions in the cross-flow planes are asymmetrical and consistent with previously reported experimental results. Although vortex breakdown induced by shock waves and combustion does not occur in this study, the second shock interaction has a significant influence on combustion, and the flame spreads throughout the flow channel due to the complex flow field. Moreover, the flame structure can be roughly estimated using Da=2 contour lines. Since the combustion efficiency increases rapidly downstream, further improvements are expected. Therefore, the proposed injection position significantly influences combustion driven by counter-rotating streamwise vortices generated by the strut.

papers.title: Optimization and data-mining analysis of variable geometry turbine blades for wide operating conditions
papers.abstract: The adjustable guide vanes in variable geometry turbines (VGTs) subject the rotor blades to a highly variable flow environment, imposing stringent requirements for maintaining high aerodynamic efficiency across a broad operating range. Consequently, conventional single-point design methods struggle to meet practical engineering demands. To address this issue, this study proposes a multi-condition optimization framework that integrates a high-degree-of-freedom direct free-form deformation parameterization with the loss-aware dynamic weight average update strategy. Furthermore, data-mining techniques are employed to elucidate performance synergies and conflicts and to identify the most influential variables. With the dynamically updated weighted total pressure loss (TPL) as the objective and outlet mass flow rate as the constraint, a comprehensive wide-range optimization and sensitivity analysis are conducted. Results reveal that the sensitivity of TPL to design variables is highly consistent at incidences of −20° and 0°, but diverges significantly at 20°, confirming the necessity of multi-condition optimization. Compared to conventional fixed-weight strategies, the proposed dynamic weight mechanism markedly improves optimization efficiency. Notably, the optimized design effectively reduces TPL across the entire −20° to +20° incidence range, achieving a maximum relative reduction of 10.58%. Flow-field analysis demonstrates that these performance gains stem from improved blade loading distributions and the suppression of adverse flow structures. This research offers novel insights and a robust methodological framework for the wide-operating-range design of VGT rotor blades.

papers.title: Digital twin architectures for industrial pumps: Integrating data perception, reduced-order modeling, and implementation paradigms
papers.abstract: As the core energy-driven general machinery, pumps play an irreplaceable role in safeguarding national economic development and national defense security. However, the structural contradiction between the high energy consumption of traditional pump systems and the global “Dual Carbon” goals has become increasingly prominent. With the evolution of digital transformation and the continuous elevation of industrial internet security standards, the pump maintenance paradigm has undergone a profound shift from reactive responses to proactive, forward-looking interventions. To facilitate this transition, Digital Twin (DT) technology provides a system-level informatics solution by constructing virtual mirrors of physical entities. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of the lifecycle operation and maintenance of pumps, focusing specifically on how cutting-edge data perception and twin model frameworks serve as imperative elements to overcome bottlenecks in industrial deployment. Comprehensive analysis indicates that the interdisciplinary integration of multisource data fusion and non-intrusive reduced-order modeling synergistically improves real-time responsiveness while preserving the physical fidelity of fluid-dynamics knowledge. Furthermore, by leveraging the latest data mining and physical mechanism fusion technologies, this paper constructs a diversified paradigm for the “Four-Pre” functions, including pre-forecasting, pre-warning, pre-simulation, and pre-planning, which provides a critical reference framework for the architectural design and engineering application of subsequent industrial-grade pump DT. To further advance this paradigm, the deep coupling of real-time perception with reduced-order models and the construction of system-level dynamic architectures should be identified as future directions to empower the real-time, system-wide coordination of on-site industrial operations.

papers.title: Optimizing rheology and suppressing powder–binder separation in highly filled suspension flows: Role of interfacial compatibility and solid loading
papers.abstract: Powder injection molding (PIM) enables the mass production of complex-shaped components, yet powder-binder separation in dense suspension flow feedstock poses a major challenge to manufacturing reliability. This study revealed the dominant trends of flow stability and particle migration in concentrated non-Newtonian suspensions (solid loading >50 vol. %) by tailoring interfacial compatibility and particle packing. Rheological characterization revealed a distinct critical solid loading, marking a transition point where the power-law index and flow activation energy reached minima, and viscoelastic behavior stabilizes. Although epoxy resin modification increased shear viscosity, it promoted a continuous binder network at the particle–fluid interface, which significantly enhanced resistance to shear-induced particle migration. A hybrid model combining power-law and Krieger–Dougherty equations accurately captured the viscosity divergence below critical solid loading. Through numerical simulation and experimental validation using a designed mold, powder segregation was consistently predicted and observed in low-flow-velocity regions (e.g., corners, thin-wall sections), accompanied by flow-induced particle size classification. Both approaching the critical loading and enhancing interfacial compatibility were confirmed to suppress flow instabilities. These findings provided a generalized framework for predicting and mitigating segregation in the processing of dense particulate suspensions.

papers.title: On the trajectory scaling and counter-rotating vortex pairs of tandem transverse jets in a crossflow
papers.abstract: Steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equation-based simulations of single and tandem jet-in-crossflow (SJICF and TJICF) were performed to examine universal trajectory scaling. For SJICF, the velocity ratio, momentum ratio, and Reynolds number, Rej=ρjUjd/μj, were varied from r=2−8, MR=4−64, and Rej=1100−4400 respectively. In TJICF, two equal jets were separated by s/d=2, with the same total momentum as that of single jet for each momentum ratio. Results show that “rd”-scaling performs better than “d”- and “r2d”-scalings for trajectory collapsing, suggesting that a universal scaling law for SJICF and TJICF can be attained by introducing an effective velocity ratio, reff=Cr, where C accounts for the effects associated with the tandem-jet configuration and interactions. For the fixed separation distance of s/d=2 considered here, C values from present results range at C=1.5−1.8, as compared to C=1.5−1.6 reported earlier, and tends to approach 1.8 at higher momentum ratios, based on the MR=36 and 64 cases, suggesting a possible trend toward approximately 1.8 at higher momentum ratios within the present parameter range. To interpret this scaling behavior, the mean pressure and vortical fields are further examined. Analyses along the symmetry plane and normal to jet trajectories clarify the momentum-ratio-dependent interaction and merging of fore and aft jets counter-rotating vortex-pairs (CVPs). Pressure coefficient distributions further show that fore jet shielding consistently delays CVP development aft, ultimately leading to its merging with the stronger fore CVP.

papers.title: Analytical and experimental investigation on the capillary rise of heterogeneous porous-grooved AlN–Cu ceramic wick structures
papers.abstract: The ceramic vapor chamber has garnered significant attention for high-heat-flux dissipation in high-power chips, owing to its thermal expansion coefficient matching that of semiconductor materials. However, its relatively low heat transfer performance limits its widespread application. This study proposes a heterogeneous porous-grooved aluminum nitride–copper (AlN–Cu) ceramic wick structure fabricated via high-temperature solid-state sintering and laser layer-by-layer processing. This morphology aims to significantly enhance the fluid transport capabilities of ceramic vapor chambers. The composite wick architecture comprises macro-scale primary grooves integrated with a micro-scale porous matrix that features sintering necks and multi-scale pore networks. The effects of AlN/Cu particle sizes, copper powder content, and structural parameters on the surface morphology and capillary performance of the wicks were systematically investigated. The results indicate that the copper content significantly influences the surface morphology of the wick. Because copper inherently resists laser ablation, higher concentrations yield micro-pillar structures that disrupt the hydrodynamic uniformity of the grooves, thereby severely degrading the capillary performance. The optimal configuration (100–150 μm particle size, 25% Cu, and 500 μm groove width) establishes a more open liquid transport space, achieving a superior hydrodynamic balance between capillary driving pressure and flow resistance. This optimization establishes a superior hydrodynamic balance between the capillary driving pressure and flow resistance, rendering this configuration the top performer among all tested combinations. As a result, the maximum capillary rise height reaches 40.17 mm, representing a 77% improvement over resistance-dominated small-particle-size groups. Concurrently, the calculated capillary performance parameter (Ka/Reff) exhibits an average increase of 251%.

papers.title: Dynamic mechanism of pressure fluctuations characterized by lamb-vector divergence in a mixed-flow nuclear coolant pump
papers.abstract: The dynamic coupling mechanism between transient flow structures and pressure pulsation in nuclear coolant pumps remains insufficiently understood. In this study, a mixed-flow nuclear coolant pump is investigated through high-fidelity transient simulations based on the stress-blended eddy simulation model. Lamb-vector divergence is introduced as a diagnostic parameter to characterize flow-field dynamics, and to elucidate the dynamic coupling characteristics among flow structure evolution, momentum transport, and pressure pulsation. Results show that Lamb-vector divergence within guide vane exhibits significant spanwise non-uniformity. Multiple bands of negative divergence convergence emerge in the mid-span region, forming a non-uniform spatial structure dominated by momentum exchange. The vortex stretching term spatially coincides with negative divergence regions, and relative helicity quantifies vortex axis deflection, revealing the cascading evolution process of angular momentum transport, vortex stretching energy accumulation, and momentum flux convergence. Along the flow path, the dominant excitation sources gradually shift from high-frequency pulsations induced by rotor–stator interaction to low-frequency components governed by local vortex shedding. Spatiotemporal correlation analysis reveals a significant negative correlation (correlation coefficient = −0.77) between pressure and positive divergence in the runner passages, whereas a strong positive correlation (correlation coefficient = 0.862) at guide vane trailing edges. The phase of Lamb-vector divergence variations generally precedes the pressure response, indicating that negative divergence convergence plays a critical role in pressure pulsation generation. These findings provide theoretical insights for understanding pressure pulsation mechanisms and for optimizing active and passive flow control strategies in nuclear coolant pumps.

papers.title: Charge distribution and electric field characteristics in dust storms
papers.abstract: Sandstorms are a typical representation of high-Reynolds-number wall-bounded turbulence, accompanied by particle charging and strong wind-blown sand electric fields. Existing numerical simulations, mostly based on Reynolds-averaged flow fields, single particle sizes, and point-charge Coulomb electric field models, fail to reproduce the observed fluctuations in flow and electric fields, their spatial structures, and the layering phenomenon of the vertical mean electric field. To address this, the present study employs large-eddy simulation, a Lagrangian point-particle model, and the particle–particle–particle–mesh method for electric field solving to numerically simulate a wind–sand–electricity multi-field coupled saltating sand flow with a mixed particle size distribution and charge-to-mass ratio. The simulation results reveal that, in the turbulent flow field resolved by large-eddy simulation, the mean particle size first increases and then decreases with height, leading to vertical layering of the mean charge-to-mass ratio and mean charge density; simultaneously, the electric field exhibits a similar layered structure. Furthermore, we propose a theoretical model linking charge layering to electric field layering, which successfully explains the observed electric field layering in the simulations. This model can be extended to real sandstorms to explain the experimentally observed “non-unipolar” phenomenon, where the vertical mean electric field exhibits up to six layers.

papers.title: Stochastic modeling of Fourier modes in two-dimensional turbulence via filtered white noise
papers.abstract: Modeling turbulent flows by a random Fourier decomposition is a classical procedure in order to use simplified models of turbulence in heat transport and other applications. We investigate the Fourier time series of two-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations with friction and damping, forced at intermediate scales, and identify significant statistical structures. In particular, we find the existence of a typical time correlation length and propose a stochastic model for the Fourier components. Finally, we compute the transport of a passive scalar under advection–diffusion dynamics by means of direct numerical simulation of the stochastic damped Navier–Stokes equation and compare it with analytical predictions of the effective diffusion produced by the stochastic model.

papers.title: Data-driven unsteady entire flow field estimation using time-series multiple-field-of-view particle image velocimetry data
papers.abstract: High-resolution flow field measurements often face a trade-off between spatial resolution and field of view (FOV) size, particularly in particle image velocimetry (PIV). To address this issue, we propose a data-driven method for reconstructing temporally consistent entire flow fields from time-series multi-FOV data acquired independently using a single camera. The method uses reduced-order modeling and sparse sensing to estimate time-varying coefficients of the proper orthogonal decomposition modes by minimizing discrepancies in overlapping regions between adjacent FOVs. The sparse sensor placement is optimized using a greedy algorithm, and the reconstruction problem is solved as a linear regression problem. The proposed method was validated using both simulated benchmark data and experimental PIV data obtained around a flat-plate airfoil. Results demonstrate that the proposed method accurately reconstructs unsteady flow structures, including vortex shedding and separation phenomena, with a normalized estimation error of approximately 0.17 when sufficient sensors are deployed. Moreover, the sensor distributions, which are concentrated in highly varying regions, indicate effective feature capture. This proposed method enables high-resolution observation of unsteady aerodynamic phenomena with minimal hardware.

papers.title: Isolator flow characteristics with fuel injection upstream and downstream of the shock-train separation region
papers.abstract: This study experimentally and numerically investigates transverse sonic injection in a Mach 2.5 rectangular isolator, focusing on the effect of injector location relative to the shock-train-induced separation region. Two injection configurations were studied: an upstream injector (positioned upstream of the separation shock) and a downstream injector (placed in the separation zone induced by the shock train). Results show that upstream injection, which significantly changes the internal flow structure of the isolator, anchors the shock train to the bowshock reflection from the top wall, which creates a higher pressure rise and a higher upstream displacement (ΔX/L = 0.036 higher) of the leading separation shock compared to the downstream injection under similar operating conditions. On the other hand, the underexpansion and the upstream shock movement are relatively weaker for downstream injection due to interaction with an already decelerated flow field. The upstream injection configuration results in a larger separation region and stronger core flow upward deflection than the downstream injection case. Downstream injection causes a significantly enhanced jet penetration in the near field, i.e., by 30.6%, primarily because the jet is introduced into the separated flow region and also due to the locally reduced crossflow momentum. Upstream injection leads to a more pronounced barrel shock structure and a stronger flow asymmetry with higher sidewall separation. Moving the downstream injector closer to the initial separation shock increases upstream shock displacement, resulting in a stronger underexpanded jet and reducing jet penetration.

papers.title: Non-monotonic flow resistance of bidisperse high-internal-phase emulsions in microchannels
papers.abstract: High-internal-phase emulsions (HIPEs) exhibit distinctive rheological behavior in microchannels that remains insufficiently clarified. To better understand the influence of polydispersity, the microchannel flow of bidisperse HIPEs, with varying droplet size ratio (RL/RS), large droplet fraction (ϕL), and interfacial tension (γwo), is investigated using dissipative particle dynamics simulations. Compared with monodisperse counterparts, a bidisperse HIPE shows less pronounced steplike features in the velocity profile and flows more slowly. Its flow velocity rises with decreasing RL/RS or increasing γwo but varies non-monotonically with ϕL. In addition, all flow curves are well described by the Herschel–Bulkley model, with identical yield stress and flow index under narrow confinement. Microstructural analyses reveal that bidisperse HIPEs in the microchannel display limited droplet deformation and hinder the formation of a layered structure observed in monodisperse HIPEs. When large droplets are added to a small-droplet-dominated system, greater disorder emerges than in the reverse scenario. Moreover, the degree of droplet ordering correlates with flow velocity: layered structures reduce flow resistance, whereas disordered arrangements cause more frequent droplet collisions, increasing flow resistance.

papers.title: Sessile surface-active droplets: Evaporative thermo-fluidics and deposition
papers.abstract: We investigate thermo-solutal transport phenomena and the resulting deposition patterns during the evaporation of surfactant-laden droplets, via experiments and theoretical scaling analysis. Experiments on surfactant-laden sessile aqueous droplets were conducted on both hydrophilic substrates (HPS) and superhydrophobic substrates (SHS). Infrared thermography and particle image velocimetry (PIV) were conducted to deduce the temperature and internal flow velocity distributions, respectively. The constant contact radius, constant contact angle, and mixed evaporation regimes were studied using dimensionless geometrical parameters. Experiments demonstrated that surfactant molecules modulated evaporation rates, with the surfactant concentration and the wetting state playing decisive roles. The surfactant molecules enhanced the evaporation rate with an increase in concentration for the SHS. In contrast, the evaporation rate increased up to a normalized surfactant concentration of 0.5 critical micelle concentration and then decreased on the HPS. We show that the morphed evaporation kinetics are explained by considering internal advection, rather than by diffusive transport alone. The evaporation rates were explained using the advection velocities obtained from the PIV analysis, the advection being strongly dependent on surfactant concentration and wettability. The theoretically obtained velocities were in close agreement with the experimental values, and solutal Marangoni advection was noted to dominate over thermal Marangoni advection and buoyancy-driven flows. However, surfactant crowding and viscous effects at higher concentration may dampen the strength of solutal advection. The role of thermo-fluid dynamics on the morphology of deposition patterns was explored via microscopy, and the instabilities therein were discussed. The contact line velocities showed sudden and rapid fluctuations, illustrating stick–slip behavior at certain stages, which complement microscopic visual observations of the deposited patterns.

papers.title: Joint reconstruction and temporal prediction of three-dimensional wind turbine wakes using Fourier neural operators
papers.abstract: A reconstructive channel-UNet-assisted Fourier neural operator (ReCUFNO) is proposed for joint three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction and temporal prediction of wind-turbine wakes from limited two-dimensional (2D) observations. The model reconstructs and forecasts the three-dimensional scalar field of streamwise velocity, u, on a 3D grid from two orthogonal planar u-velocity slices conditioned on yaw angle. The approach combines a reconstructive channel-assisted layer with Fourier neural-operator forecasting and UNet-based spatial refinement to improve multi-scale wake representation and autoregressive stability. To address the mismatch between 2D inputs and 3D outputs, a reconstruction-consistent rollout maps each predicted volume back into planar inputs through slice extraction and roll-and-update feedback. Evaluated on yawed large-eddy simulation (LES) datasets, ReCUFNO achieves a single-step wind turbine error of approximately 5% and a single-step structural similarity index of 0.66, while maintaining bounded error growth over 30-step rollouts. Additional wake-focused diagnostics, including wake deflection, wake angle, centerline correlation, and rotor-disk power-deficit estimates, show improved agreement with LES relative to a UNet baseline. These results indicate that ReCUFNO provides a stable surrogate for observation-limited reconstruction and short-horizon prediction of yawed wind-turbine wake velocity fields.

papers.title: Synchronized molecular dynamics method for thin-layer flows of complex fluids
papers.abstract: We propose a multiscale computational method for thin-layer flows of complex fluids, termed the synchronized molecular dynamics (SMD) method, which directly couples local molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with a macroscopic lubrication description. In thin layers, the flow can be decomposed into cross-sectional dynamics that is strongly influenced by interfacial effects and streamwise transport along the channel. The SMD method exploits this separation of scales by sparsely distributing local MD cells along the channel and synchronizing them through macroscopic conservation laws. In this framework, the macroscopic continuity equation is enforced by iteratively updating the numerical driving forces applied to each MD cell, thereby allowing the cross-sectional velocity profiles and the streamwise pressure distribution to be obtained without prescribing constitutive relations or boundary conditions. The method is validated for pressure-driven and wall-driven flows of Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluids in a wedge-shaped channel, demonstrating excellent agreement with a modified Reynolds equation that accounts for boundary slip. The SMD method is further applied to polymeric lubrication flows modeled by the Kremer–Grest chain model. At large pressure differences, the present approach naturally captures pronounced shear-thinning behavior coupled with microscopic polymer conformation dynamics. The results demonstrate that the SMD method provides an efficient and physically consistent framework for the multiscale simulation of complex fluid thin-layer flows.

papers.title: Decoupling geometric confinement and surface roughness in nanoporous media: A molecular study of gas adsorption and diffusion
papers.abstract: Fluid transport in nanoporous media is governed by confinement-induced modifications to intermolecular interactions and interfacial energy landscapes, leading to behavior that deviates fundamentally from macroscopic systems. While the independent roles of pore structure and surface roughness are critical to nanoconfined gas dynamics, experimental limitations make them difficult to decouple. This study overcomes this limitation by constructing molecular models of representative nanopores (cylindrical and ink-bottle-shaped) and introducing surface roughness while strictly maintaining pore geometry. The impacts of pore structure and interfacial heterogeneity on gas adsorption and diffusion were investigated. Key findings reveal a clear functional divergence: pore geometry primarily controls both adsorption capacity and thermodynamic stability, but in opposite directions. Ink-bottle-shaped pores suppress total adsorption capacity (reducing amount from 3.24 to 2.53 mmol/g) due to restricted access, yet they enhance confinement stability, as evidenced by higher isosteric heats (16.64–16.51 kJ/mol at high pressure) under equal loading conditions. This decoupling demonstrates that a single pore geometry can simultaneously reduce uptake and strengthen molecular retention. Crucially, although the ink-bottle-shaped structure restricts gas transport, at equal amount, surface roughness does not hinder diffusion. Instead, by reducing the influence of surface polar sites and creating a heterogeneous distribution of potential energy surfaces, it lowers the energy barrier for surface migration. This results in an increase in diffusion coefficients of 5% and 16% in rough cylindrical pores, and by 16% and 25% in rough ink-bottle-shaped pores, respectively. These findings demonstrate that nanoconfined gas transport is controlled by the interplay between geometric confinement and energy landscape heterogeneity, providing a fundamental physical framework for understanding transport in complex nanoporous systems.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of the influence of free ends on vortex-induced vibrations of circular cylinders
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of finite-length circular cylinders is strongly influenced by free-end effects. However, the mechanism by which free ends affect the flow structures and vibration responses under different aspect ratios remains unclear. In this study, three-dimensional numerical simulations are performed using the shear stress transport-based delayed detached eddy simulation method in OpenFOAM to investigate the VIV characteristics of elastically mounted circular cylinders with finite lengths. The study first compares a nominally infinite cylinder and a finite-length cylinder with the same aspect ratio of L/D=3.14. The results show that the finite-length cylinder requires a higher reduced velocity to fully develop the four typical vibration branches, indicating a delayed onset and evolution of the VIV response. In addition, larger vibration amplitudes are observed within the same response branch. Flow-field analysis shows that free ends enhance spanwise flow and lift fluctuations, thereby altering the vibration response. The influence of aspect ratio is further examined by considering cylinders with L/D= 1, 2, 3.14, and 6. For short cylinders with L/D= 1 and 2, the lower branch and desynchronization stage are absent. This behavior results from dominant free-end effects that suppress coherent vortex shedding and lock-in. As the aspect ratio increases, the mid-span flow gradually recovers features similar to those of an infinite cylinder. These findings clarify the role of free ends in regulating vortex shedding and vibration responses of finite-length cylinders and provide useful guidance for the prediction, suppression, and potential energy-harvesting application of VIV in offshore and ocean engineering structures.

papers.title: Quantifying assessment of the effects of fracture complexity on the behavior of CO2 water-alternating-gas fracturing flooding in low-permeability oil reservoirs
papers.abstract: Fracturing flooding with CO2 water-alternating-gas (WAG) is a novel approach for the efficient exploitation of low-permeability oil reservoirs. The key lies in creating fractures during field construction while maintaining fracture morphology stability. However, the mechanism by which fracture complexity after fracturing flooding affects CO2 WAG efficiency appears to be ambiguous. A series of tree-shaped fracture models with varying complexity, characterized by fractal dimension (Df) over a range of 1.13–1.65, was constructed, and their effects were systematically analyzed. The results revealed an optimal fracture complexity at Df = 1.56 (∼60 MPa), where waterflooding recovery reached 54.9% and total recovery peaked at 88.4%. As Df increased from 1.13 to 1.56, waterflooding sweep efficiency rose from 54.3% to 69.1%, while CO2 sweep efficiency increased further to 79.8%. Cluster oil decreased to 15.7% after waterflooding and was further reduced to 1.2% by CO2, partially converting into columnar oil, which peaked at 6.2%. Fracture contribution increased from 32.4% to 45.7% during the waterflooding and peaked at 55.5% during the CO2 flooding, while matrix contribution declined correspondingly. Conversely, as Df increased from 1.56 to 1.65, waterflooding recovery decreased to 44.2%, fracture contribution rose to 49.3%, and cluster oil rebounded to 26.4%. In the CO2 flooding, recovery fell to 62.6%, fracture contribution dropped to 45.1%, and columnar oil declined to 2.9%, indicating that excessive fracture complexity led to the entrapment of residual oil. This research provides a theoretical basis for optimizing CO2 WAG fracturing flooding schemes in low-permeability oil reservoirs.

papers.title: Spray-flame dynamics of liquid oxygen/methane swirl coaxial injectors with varying lip thickness ratios
papers.abstract: Based on the experimental method, the gas–liquid interactions governed by the lip thickness ratio of the liquid oxygen/methane swirl coaxial injectors were studied to evaluate its influence on spray-flame dynamics and combustion stability. With the help of dual-camera laser background imaging technology and a visual rectangular combustor, the combustion parameters are captured, including spray and flame structure, static/dynamic characteristics of combustor pressure, and so on. The results indicate that for the injector with a small lip thickness ratio, approximately 26.2% of the annular gas passage's cross-sectional area is occupied by the conical liquid sheet, thereby increasing the methane injection pressure drop by 30.2%. Furthermore, the spray and flame exhibit dual oscillations at 312 and 3544 Hz simultaneously. As the lip thickness ratio increases, the medium-frequency oscillations of the spray and flame are suppressed, and the high-frequency oscillation frequency gradually decreases. There is a critical lip thickness ratio, identified between 0.08 and 0.20, at which high-frequency combustion instability will be induced. The gas–liquid interaction in the near-field of the small lip thickness ratio injector is most intense, leading to the widest radial flame distribution and the highest heat release rate, with the position of maximum heat release rate located closest to the injection panel. Increasing the lip thickness ratio reduces the spray cone angle and flame spreading angle, thereby weakening the gas–liquid interaction and causing the position of maximum heat release rate to move progressively further from the injection panel.

papers.title: Transient growth and streak instabilities of high-speed flows over a blunt wedge
papers.abstract: Laminar–turbulent transition in boundary layers is of fundamental significance in the design of high-speed vehicles. Subcritical transition occurring upstream of the linear instability region is frequently observed in high-speed blunt wedge flows. To identify the nonmodal perturbations which may lead to subcritical transition, the boundary layer instability of a 500 mm-length blunt-nose wedge with Mach 7.0 is investigated by the nonmodal stability method, the BiGlobal stability analysis method, and direct numerical simulation. The nonmodal stability method is developed by solving the harmonic linearized Navier–Stokes equations and the corresponding adjoint system. This method is capable of finding the most dangerous nonmodal perturbations (optimal perturbations). The optimal perturbations are shown to be temporally steady (with zero frequency), streamwise growth, and spanwise periodic. These perturbations can evolve into streamwise streaks, which are prone to secondary instabilities. The BiGlobal results indicate that the most unstable secondary instability mode exhibits a high growth rate, with the N factor exceeding more than 14, which is sufficient to trigger the boundary layer transition. Mode transformation from subcritical sinuous modes into most unstable sinuous modes is verified. During the nonlinear evolution, higher-frequency harmonic modes are excited. The nonlinear evolution of the secondary unstable modes exhibits a relatively uniform saturation amplitude, which is subjected to the mean flow distortion (MFD). The MFD plays a major role during the nonlinear process. This study provides the physical mechanisms behind nonlinear secondary instability modes in high-speed boundary layers.

papers.title: Wave-induced extreme surface effects on a near-surface airfoil unit under wind–wave coupling
papers.abstract: Ground effect plays a critical role in shaping aerodynamic performance and is widely utilized in both biological and engineering applications. However, the unsteady aerodynamic response of near-surface airfoils over wind waves remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding wave-modulated loading and coherent wake structures. In this study, direct numerical simulation (DNS) is employed to investigate the wave-induced extreme surface effects on a near-surface airfoil unit under wind–wave coupling. The effects of geometric angle of attack (α) and mean relative clearance (H*) are examined through lift response, surface pressure distribution, airfoil–wave passage flow, and wake structures. An auxiliary Reynolds-number scaling method based on an open-source airfoil analysis and design program is used to estimate the amplitude level of the DNS lift response at the target Reynolds number. The results show that the lift response is strongly modulated by the wave surface at small clearance. At H*=0.5, the lift coefficient exhibits pronounced wave-locked oscillations and is highly sensitive to the instantaneous geometry of the airfoil–wave passage. To quantify this passage-flow effect, an empirical model is proposed using a wave-influence coefficient (γ) and a channel-shape parameter (β), which captures the main lift variation under extreme-clearance conditions. Flow–structure and proper orthogonal decomposition analyses further show that as the clearance increases, the direct influence of the wave surface weakens, and the dominant coherent structures evolve from near-surface, wave-coupled patterns to wake-dominated structures extending farther downstream. These findings provide a physical basis for understanding extreme surface effects in maritime environments.

papers.title: Passive fish-like body dynamics in bluff-body wakes
papers.abstract: Fish swimming in the wake of bluff bodies can exploit ambient vortices to reduce energy expenditure. In this work, a two-dimensional fluid–structure interaction study of a fish in the wake of an upstream circular cylinder shedding a von Kármán vortex street is performed for Re=100–300, using an arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian framework. The fish head is fixed while the tail remains flexible. The effects of streamwise spacing length/diameter (L/D=2–24), cylinder diameter (D=0.1–0.3 m), and Cauchy number (Ca=2×10−4, Ca=5×10−5, and 5×10−6) on the hydrodynamic forces are examined. The results show that negative drag (thrust) is generated over a finite range of L/D, extending up to L/D≈6 at Re=300. This thrust is associated with the presence of a vorticity extremum within approximately 1.5 diameters upstream of the fish head, which induces a pressure deficit and reduces the net drag. As the distance from the cylinder increases, vortex strength decays, leading to a transition from thrust to drag. The root-mean-square lift coefficient exhibits a peak at intermediate L/D, corresponding to maximum vortex strength, followed by a downstream decay. While the mean drag is largely insensitive to Ca, lower Ca results in larger fluctuations in drag and lift. Force decomposition shows that the vortical contribution, which is predominantly negative in the streamwise direction, constitutes the thrust component and governs the reduction in net drag. These findings provide a mechanistic understanding of vortex–body interactions and their role in thrust generation in unsteady wake environments, with implications for the design of bio-inspired propulsion systems.

papers.title: Restoring pressure consistency in condensation under body forces
papers.abstract: Condensation is widespread in nature and in various industrial heat-transfer devices, and many condensation phenomena occur in open systems or spaces with continuous mass exchange. Therefore, open-boundary conditions are commonly used in pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann method simulations involving liquid–vapor phase change. However, it is found that, under the action of a body force, open boundaries may generate spurious mass flux under isothermal conditions, leading to nonideal condensation or evaporation. Consequently, the phase change induced by pressure mismatch can contaminate the condensation mechanism that should be primarily governed by wall subcooling, and this effect is gradually intensified with increasing gravity strength and interfacial width. To address this issue, a body force-conforming boundary improvement method is proposed in this study. In this method, the boundary density is determined by considering the dynamic pressure–equilibrium relation between the body force and the vapor–liquid distribution during condensation. The proposed method maintains good effectiveness under different body forces and interfacial widths, reducing the spurious mass flux by nearly three orders of magnitude, and the obtained pressure and density distributions agree well with the theoretical solutions. In addition, this study considers the consistency of energy input in the actual condensation process and proposes a temperature boundary condition matched with the pressure boundary. The dropwise condensation simulation results show that the proposed boundary method can reduce the interference of spurious mass flux with the nucleation time, condensate mass, and transient heat-flux response, allowing the wall-subcooling-driven condensation process to be predicted and interpreted more reliably.

papers.title: Closed-form Péclet-regime framework for chloride exclusion in marine concrete covers under engineered counter-advective flow
papers.abstract: Chloride-induced corrosion in marine concrete covers is the controlling durability threat for seawalls, piers, and offshore foundations, and premature service-life loss dominates coastal-infrastructure renewal cost. Resistance-based design, which lowers the diffusion coefficient D or thickens the cover, postpones chloride arrival but cannot suppress the steady-state ceiling at the reinforcement, and existing closed-form solutions for semi-infinite or constant-boundary problems cannot resolve whether an opposing hydraulic head difference Δh delivers permanent exclusion or only delayed breakthrough. A closed-form solution for the finite-domain advection–diffusion equation with two independently time-dependent Dirichlet boundaries was derived, the inner boundary closed through flux continuity to capture coupling with the imposed flow field. Coupling the classical Péclet number with Darcy's law gave a head-based Péclet number Peh=−Δh/(D/K), where Δh is the imposed head difference, D is the effective chloride diffusion coefficient, and K is the saturated hydraulic conductivity, in which the controllable head and the material ratio D/K appear as two independent design variables. The solution was verified against finite-element simulations across Peh = −10 to +10 and was validated against laboratory measurements over Peh = −0.86 to −2.52. Under opposing flow, a negative-feedback closure emerged in which rising concentration amplified outward advective flux until the net inward flux vanished, yielding a predicted critical threshold Peh,cr of 3.1–7.9 across the examined chloride ingress potential range; this prediction presumes the opposing head is sustained, lies beyond the experimentally validated range (Peh=−0.86 to −2.52), and awaits field verification. The ratio D/K, rather than D alone, set the balance scale, and the steady-state ceiling at the reinforcement dropped by 82% between Peh = 0 and Peh = −5. The framework recasts durability assessment from transient service-life prediction into regime classification, hydraulic-feasibility check, and steady-state certification for actively protected marine concrete covers.

papers.title: The role of viscous normal stresses in Saffman–Taylor fingering
papers.abstract: This article presents a novel approach to the Saffman–Taylor fingering problem by introducing a fundamentally different stabilization mechanism: viscous normal stresses at the interface. Using a conformal mapping technique and perturbative analysis, we derive the modified governing equation. We demonstrate that, similar to the classical surface tension case, the first-order perturbation is regular on the physical interface and primarily modifies the finger shape by elongating the tip. However, because the new dynamic boundary condition increases the order of the differential equation, the perturbation is inherently singular. This implies that the strict selection of a unique finger width is not captured at the fundamental first-order level and likely relies on exponentially small, beyond-all-orders effects. The proposed physical mechanism is universally applicable and highly relevant to partially miscible or weakly miscible fluids where surface tension is negligible small or completely absent, thereby opening a new class of selection problems in interfacial dynamics.

papers.title: Entropy dissipation and transient pulsation suppression via coordinated dual-vortex source regulation in wide-range rotating machinery with parametric composite profiles
papers.abstract: Conventional aero-fuel centrifugal pumps with cylindrical blades and annular volutes suffer from inherent drawbacks, including limited geometric adjustability, severe impeller-volute flow field mismatch, and narrow high-efficiency operating ranges. This study proposes a parametric composite profile design (PCPD) strategy based on physics-informed neural networks. Combined with very large eddy simulation-shear stress transport k–ω turbulence simulations and experiments, the wide-range internal flow regulation mechanism is revealed from vortex dynamics, irreversible entropy generation, and transient time-frequency pulsation characteristics. The PCPD strategy effectively homogenizes internal velocity gradients and suppresses flow separation and wake disorder. The mean radius Rm and initial angle of spiral α0 are identified as the core geometric parameters dominating the overall flow field uniformity. Pump internal flow instability is jointly governed by two distinct vortex sources. The vortex stretching term induces large-scale periodic vortices and low-frequency pulsations near the wake and volute tongue, whereas the Coriolis term continuously generates microscale vortex clusters that dominate high-band energy dissipation. The PCPD strategy weakens the intensity of dual vortex sources, suppresses the development of coherent vortices, and mitigates irreversible entropy generation losses. The coordinated dual-vortex regulation attenuates full-band pressure pulsations and diminishes high-energy pulsation regions. Experimental results verify the reliability of the flow homogenization and dual-vortex coordinated suppression mechanism. The PCPD prototype improves hydraulic efficiency by 3.22% at 1.0Qd and reaches a maximum increment of 5.94% at 1.6Qd. This study elucidates the coupled dynamic relationship between multi-scale vortex evolution and energy dissipation, laying fundamental fluid dynamic foundations for wide-range high-efficiency pump design.

papers.title: Kriging-based multi-objective optimization of bubble path complexity under non-uniform electric fields in vertical channel
papers.abstract: This article presents a multi-objective surrogate-based optimization study of electrohydrodynamically (EHD) controlled bubble trajectories in a vertical channel under a non-uniform electric field. This is achieved by coupling a Kriging surrogate model with a genetic algorithm search, building on our previous work. Optimization aims to make a trade-off between the complexity of the bubble trajectory, quantified by the relative path complexity, and the electrical energy input represented by the electric capillary number (CaE). Two parametric frameworks are evaluated: a four-parameter model (electrode length L, inter-electrode gap G, electric capillary number CaE, channel width w) and an extended five-parameter model that additionally includes bubble diameter Db as a design variable. Latin hypercube sampling generates an initial design space, and OpenFOAM-based volume of fluid simulations supply high-fidelity evaluations. The Kriging surrogate is adaptively updated via expected hypervolume improvement, producing a well-resolved Pareto front that spans CaE = 1.0–4.47 in the four-parameter study and CaE = 1.0–3.19 in the five-parameter study. The key findings reframe the design problem, highlighting Db as the most influential parameter in the system. The results confirm that surrogate-assisted optimization serves as a practical and efficient design framework for EHD systems.

papers.title: Fine-scale urban wind field prediction via small-scale generator and spectral loss with rolling-out transfer learning
papers.abstract: Fine-scale urban wind field prediction at 12 s temporal resolution is investigated by extending the 3DSwinUrbanNet framework in two directions. First, a variational bottleneck (a β-weighted variational autoencoder) inserted into the Swin Transformer backbone invariably leads to either posterior collapse or Kullback–Leibler divergence explosion across more than fifteen configurations, rendering the variational approach ineffective. Second, SSRollingUrbanNet appends a small-scale generator after the Perceiver decoder, which is trained with a combined mean squared error and spectral loss. The small-scale generator trained with mean-squared-error loss alone increases prediction error, whereas adding the spectral loss reduces the mean squared error by 48.1% relative to the 3DSwinUrbanNet baseline at the first prediction step (12 s), demonstrating that spectral supervision is essential for physically consistent fine-scale generation. For extended prediction over a 20-min horizon, a two-stage transfer-learning strategy—single-step pre-training followed by three-step rollout fine-tuning—achieves the lowest mean squared error throughout, outperforming both single-step and direct three-step training. Comprehensive evaluation through probability density functions, energy spectra, spatial correlations, mean flow, Reynolds shear stress, turbulence intensity, and Q-criterion isosurfaces confirms that this three-step-rollout, fine-tuned model most faithfully sustains the filtered large-eddy-simulation turbulent characteristics, with richer instantaneous vortical structures than the 3DSwinUrbanNet baseline despite multi-step autoregressive rollout.

papers.title: Multi-scale analysis of drag reduction mechanisms for a diving submersible with hair-strand appendages
papers.abstract: This study investigates the drag reduction mechanism of a submersible equipped with hair-strand appendages. After confirming Reynolds number independence, hair-strand appendages with varying length ratios (Lh/Li = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, and 2.5) and number ratios (Nh/N0 = 1/11, 3/11, 7/11, 1, and 14/11) were applied to the submersible at a Reynolds number of 19 572 for passive flow control, and drag force was measured using torque sensors. Experimental results demonstrate that hair-strand appendages achieve a maximum drag reduction of 4.7% at Lh/Li = 1 and Nh/N0 = 1; moreover, the drag coefficient is more sensitive to changes in the length ratio of hair-strand appendages, and the number ratio governs the overall rigidity of the hair-strand appendage array. Particle image velocimetry experiments reveal that as the number of hair-strand appendages increases, the recirculation zone, turbulent kinetic energy, and Reynolds shear stress all decrease. The oscillation of hair-strand appendages dissipates turbulent kinetic energy while reducing Reynolds shear stress. Spectral analyses, including continuous wavelet transform, discrete wavelet transform, and multi-resolution dynamic mode decomposition (mrDMD), reveal that the hair-strand appendages enhance momentum exchange. To further resolve the multi-scale vortical behavior in the wake, Liutex-based vorticity fields were analyzed using mrDMD. These results confirm that hair-strand appendages accelerate turbulent energy transfer by converting large-scale coherent kinetic energy into high-frequency, microscale turbulence.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of multi-mechanism coupled nanoparticle coagulation in Taylor–Green vortex flow
papers.abstract: Most existing models of nanoparticle coagulation assume a single dominant process, yet unsteady vortical flows involve the concurrent action of multiple physical mechanisms.
