This study numerically investigates multi-mechanism coupled nanoparticle coagulation in a decaying two-dimensional Taylor–Green vortex flow using the average kernel-iterative direct numerical simulation framework. A hierarchical coupling strategy is developed: intra-Brownian coupling (continuum-free-molecular) via harmonic mean, and inter-mechanism coupling (Brownian-shear) via root mean square (RMS) synthesis. The moment method tracks the first three moments (number concentration, M0; volume concentration, M1; and polydispersity, M2), with high-order compact schemes and fourth-order Runge–Kutta for discretization. Nine cases cover Reynolds numbers 6.29×102–6.29×104 and initial particle diameters 0.1–1 μm. The asymptotic moment ratio MC=M0M2/M12 universally approaches self-similar limit of 2 at long times (t→∞) for all cases considered. Results reveal that lower initial flow velocity accelerates the decay of the domain-averaged number concentration (due to physical time stretching and increased Damköhler number), whereas larger initial particle diameter slows decay (transport limitation by high Schmidt numbers). RMS synthesis provides the most physically balanced inter-mechanism coupling, with negligible early-staged but significant long-term effects. Unlike pure shear-induced coagulation, inclusion of Brownian motion prevents a frozen non-equilibrium state, driving the system toward the classical self-similar limit. This work establishes a physically consistent multi-mechanism framework extendable to realistic environmental and industrial flows.

papers.title: Effects of dissociation–recombination kinetics on electric current and flow structure in electrohydrodynamic systems with dielectric liquids
papers.abstract: Mathematical models of electrohydrodynamic (EHD) flows usually assume Langevin ion recombination and no limitation on the concentration of species available for dissociation. However, for weakly conducting liquids with surfactant additives, these assumptions may be insufficient for a consistent description of electric current and fluid-flow characteristics. Here, this issue is analyzed for two EHD systems using the same working liquid, dodecane with 10% Span 85: a plane–six wires–plane cell and an EHD pump based on metal-coated dielectric barriers with aligned holes. The conventional model overpredicts the measured current–voltage (I–V) response in both systems; for the pump, the flow rate–pressure head (Q–P) characteristics are also overpredicted. Three possible reasons for this discrepancy are examined: uncertainty in ion mobility, a reduced effective recombination coefficient, and an effective limitation of field-enhanced dissociation. In addition to the integral I–V and Q–P characteristics, the corresponding space charge and velocity distributions are analyzed to clarify how these assumptions modify the EHD flow structure. The results show that mobility variation cannot explain the discrepancy. A reduced recombination coefficient provides the most consistent improvement, decreasing the charge retained in high-field regions, reducing the mechanical power transferred from the electric field to the liquid, and improving the predicted pump performance. A limitation of field-enhanced dissociation, although physically plausible, does not provide an equally consistent description in its present simplified form.

papers.title: Abnormal frequency shifting of unmanned underwater vehicle roll motion in a moonpool: Role of confined wave–flow coupling
papers.abstract: A computational fluid dynamics-based numerical framework is developed to investigate the abnormal frequency shifting behavior of unmanned underwater vehicles (UUV) roll motion during moonpool recovery under wave conditions. The roll response exhibits dominant frequencies that deviate from the incident wave frequency, including both single-frequency shifts and dual-frequency (bimodal) patterns. A systematic analysis considering variations in mass, center-of-gravity position, moonpool geometry, degrees of freedom, and wave direction demonstrates that conventional mechanisms—such as resonance, heave–roll coupling, or wave directionality—cannot explain the observed behavior. Parametric studies reveal that the UUV mass suppresses frequency deviation, whereas the vertical position of the center of gravity governs the magnitude of the frequency shift. The integrity of the moonpool boundaries is identified as the key factor: partial confinement produces a dual-frequency response, while complete removal eliminates frequency shifting entirely. These results indicate that the phenomenon originates from a nonlinear coupled mode driven by confined wave–flow interactions within the moonpool. The findings provide new insight into fluid–structure interactions in confined marine environments and have implications for the design and operation of moonpool-based UUV recovery systems.

papers.title: Effects of Reynolds number on flow structures and broadband forces of a pump-jet propulsor under non-uniform inflow
papers.abstract: Under non-uniform wake conditions, the effects of Reynolds-number variation on the broadband-force response of a pump-jet propulsor remain unclear. In this study, an experimentally validated large-eddy simulation method is used to systematically examine Reynolds-number effects on the upstream wake structure, internal flow-field evolution, and spectral characteristics of rotor broadband forces. These results show that increasing Reynolds number leads to a marked contraction of the aft-body boundary layer and the low-speed wake upstream of the propulsor. At the higher Reynolds number, flow separation and wake diffusion in the stator region are suppressed, while rotor–stator shear interaction and local turbulence intensity near the rotor inlet are enhanced. Meanwhile, velocity fluctuations upstream of the rotor are attenuated, reducing the amplitudes of blade lift fluctuations. Flow separation over the rotor blade surface is weakened, and the regions of elevated skin-friction coefficient and pressure fluctuations from the aft half-chord to the trailing edge shrink substantially. These changes significantly reduce broadband fluctuations in the rotor thrust coefficient. The findings provide a physical basis for model-scale testing, numerical prediction, and design optimization of pump-jet propulsors.

papers.title: Effect of wetting-step line geometry on bubble growth and detachment
papers.abstract: Bubble growth and detachment under circular and regular polygonal wetting-step line (WSL) constraints, where a WSL denotes the boundary between superhydrophilic and superhydrophobic regions, were investigated experimentally at identical contact-line perimeters and circularities from 0.60 to 1.00. Synchronized dual-view imaging showed that decreasing circularity progressively increased the discrepancy between the two characteristic bubble profiles and strengthened the spatial anisotropy of the apparent contact angle. During quasi-static growth, non-circular WSLs produced a faster reduction in the Laplace pressure ratio between the bubble base and apex, leading to earlier necking and detachment. The plateau-averaged apparent contact-angle difference increased approximately linearly as circularity decreased. An effective capillary-retention coefficient calculated from the measured apparent contact angles increased from approximately 0.86 for the triangular WSL to 0.94 for the circular WSL, and was empirically correlated with circularity. A quasi-static force-balance model linked this coefficient to the normalized detachment volume. The measured normalized detachment volume increased from approximately 0.62 at a circularity of 0.60 to approximately 0.90 at a circularity of 1.00, with a linear regression coefficient of determination of 0.991. The circular result was close to previously reported axisymmetric WSL data. These results show that reduced circularity redistributes interfacial curvature and apparent contact angle, reduces the net vertical capillary-retention force, and causes bubble detachment at a smaller volume under equal-perimeter constraints.

papers.title: A heat-flux discontinuity principle for thermal immersed boundary methods
papers.abstract: In immersed boundary methods (IBMs) for heat transfer, the volumetric heat source used to enforce thermal boundary conditions is equivalent to the heat-flux discontinuity across the boundary. This observation provides a new physical interpretation of the volumetric heat source in thermal IBMs. Building on this physical interpretation, we develop a thermal IBM based on the heat-flux discontinuity principle within the lattice Boltzmann framework. The proposed method is validated through typical benchmark problems involving two- and three-dimensional stationary- and moving-boundary flows with heat transfer. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to previously reported methods. More importantly, the heat-flux discontinuity principle provides a unified physical basis for future IBMs for conjugate heat transfer and melting/solidification.

papers.title: Recursive shock-interaction mechanism governing pressure amplification in multiple-shock converging system
papers.abstract: This study investigates the recursive shock-interaction mechanism responsible for the focal-pressure amplification during the convergence of multiple shock waves in the predominantly regular reflection regime. Rather than attributing pressure amplification to isolated shock reflections, the present work suggests that converging shock systems primarily evolve through a recursive shock-interaction chain. Motivated by this physical picture, an idealized recursive shock-interaction convergence (RSIC) framework is developed. This framework isolates the recursive shock-interaction mechanism using shock-polar theory, a recursively linked family of moving reference frames, and an equivalent focal shock (EFS) closure designed to regularize the geometric singularity at the convergence center by imposing the stagnation condition. The framework is validated using Cartesian-grid simulations with a high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory-based method. Within the RSIC framework, the local flow states associated with successive oblique shock interactions are analyzed, including pressure evolution, flow deflection, and particle-velocity variation. This recursive shock-interaction chain is further confirmed by an established experimental case in air and its numerical reproduction, providing qualitative support for the proposed RSIC framework. By incorporating an equivalent reflected shock, the EFS closure effectively predicts the focal pressure of converging shocks, particularly for relatively weak incident shocks and configurations involving fewer interacting shocks. Although the deviation becomes more pronounced beyond this range, the predicted focal pressure for configurations involving more than two shocks still exceeds that from conventional two-shock oblique-reflection theory and agrees well with numerical simulations, with a maximum deviation below 11.23%. The results further demonstrate that focal-pressure amplification is governed primarily by the cumulative effect of recursive shock-interactions rather than by the amplification associated with any individual reflection. The proposed framework provides new physical insights into the pressure-amplification mechanism in multiple-shock converging systems, although it does not fully replicate real multiple underwater explosion dynamics.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of diffusion effect of non-condensable gas on cavitating flows around isolated hydrofoil based on mass transfer model with its advection
papers.abstract: It is known that non-condensable gas (NCG) sometimes plays a non-negligible role in cavitating flows. In general, NCG can be present in a liquid in the following two forms, either dissolved in a liquid or trapped in free nuclei. Currently, the effect of the dissolved NCG on a cavitation process, especially for the diffusion effect, has usually been neglected in most numerical cavitation models because the diffusion is generally slow compared to the flow convection. Nevertheless, the diffusion effect should be paid attention to in some special cases such as the cavitating performance of pumps operated at off-design conditions, especially in the case of low flow rates. To achieve a breakthrough in predicting cavitating flows, our group have proposed a simple mass transfer model across liquid-gas interface based on a well-known homogeneous cavitation model by Sauer and Schnerr (SS model), called as SS-NCG model, and also coupled an additional advection-diffusion equation of the NCG concentration for a two-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulation around a hydrofoil. In the present study, a three-dimensional delayed detached eddy simulation coupled with the cavitation model has been employed to investigate the detailed influence of NCG on cavitation. By comparing three typical cases, i.e., no dissolved oxygen (SS model), low and high amounts of dissolved oxygen cases (SS-NCG model), the unsteady and statistical features of the NCG influences are indicated. The results show that the presence of NCG will enhance the cavitation degree and may lead to the occurrence of gaseous cavitation. From the perspective of unsteady characteristics, the cavitation process is stabilized and damped by NCG. The NCG concentration in cavitating regions is statistically lower than that in the bulk liquids, and the concentration difference is increasing in the case with a higher value of NCG content. In addition, it is found that the mechanism of the cavitation process considering NCG and not considering it is quite different. With the presence of NCG, cavitation can be regarded as an interaction between the varying pressures inside and outside the bubbles, where the NCG mainly affects the cavitation dynamics through its modulation of the local compressibility inside the bubbles. In contrast, the cavitation process without NCG is only dominated by the local static pressure.

papers.title: Gerstner gravity–capillary waves and their collapse mode
papers.abstract: The propagation regimes of nonlinear gravity–capillary waves in deep water are studied. The fluid motion is described by exact solutions of the 2D equations of an ideal incompressible fluid in Lagrangian variables. The trajectories of fluid particles are circles whose radius decreases exponentially with depth (as in the Gerstner wave). The pressure on the free surface is non-uniform and depends harmonically on time, which correlates with the wind effect on the fluid in the near-surface layer. For a steady (Gerstner) profile, the existence of a limiting wave steepness determined by the magnitude of the external pressure is demonstrated. For unsteady Gerstner waves, examples of a gravity–capillary rogue wave and a breaking wave, which appears as a single elevation (soliton) on a uniform background wave, are constructed.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic force and vortex dynamics around an inclined cylinder in oscillatory flow
papers.abstract: Large eddy simulation is performed to investigate oscillatory flow around a circular cylinder at a Reynolds number of Re = 3900 under Keulegan–Carpenter numbers of KC = 15, 30, and 60 and inclination angles of α = 0°, 30°, 45°, and 60°. The validity of the independence principle (IP) is analyzed, and the contributions to drag and lift are quantified using the force partitioning method (FPM). The results indicate that the validity of IP expands significantly with increasing KC. At KC = 15, the inline drag coefficient is comparable only for α ≤ 30°, whereas at KC = 60, it remains nearly invariant up to α = 60°. This is because the longer stroke length at high KC allows vortices to fully develop within each half-cycle, producing more coherent primary wake structures and helping preserve quasi-two-dimensional flow characteristics even at large inclination angles. FPM reveals that the forces in both the x and y directions are highly correlated with the vortex-induced forces. Decomposition of the vortex force shows that the spanwise–vortex contribution dominates the drag and lift force. Moreover, as the inclination angle increases, the reduced normal velocity and enhanced axial velocity weaken near-cylinder vortex formation and promote axial stretching of vortices, thereby reducing vortex coherence and lowering the peak magnitudes of the vortex-induced forces.

papers.title: Study on hydrodynamic interaction of a disk-shaped autonomous underwater vehicle near the wavy seabed
papers.abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of the hydrodynamic characteristics of a novel disk-shaped autonomous underwater vehicle—the autonomous underwater helicopter operating near a wavy seabed. A prescribed-motion method is employed to simulate the straight-line cruising over the wavy terrain. The effects of cruising speed and altitude are investigated. Compared with a flat bottom terrain, the wavy terrain induces significantly more intense hydrodynamic responses, characterized by an increase in drag force with cruising speed, while the lift force exhibits non-monotonic behavior. Furthermore, two distinct effects associated with the bottom terrain are proposed: a blockage effect that induces a positive lift force and an acceleration effect that cause a negative lift force. The relative contributions of these two effects vary with the position with respect to the terrain, the altitude, and the cruising speed, leading to regular oscillatory patterns in the hydrodynamic interactions. A critical altitude accounting for the transition of lift from negative to positive is identified, and its value varies non-monotonically with cruising speed. This study provides insights into the motion control and maneuvering of underwater vehicles operating in close proximity to complex seabed terrain.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of substrate melting and resolidification during ceramic splat formation under plasma-spray-like conditions
papers.abstract: Several manufacturing processes, such as spray deposition and splat cooling, are strongly affected by how a droplet of molten metal or ceramic impinges, spreads, and solidifies on a substrate. In this study, two-dimensional axisymmetric and three-dimensional computations are performed to investigate the deformation and solidification of a ceramic droplet after impact on a substrate under plasma spraying conditions. This investigation also considers the melting of the substrate and its subsequent re-solidification during the splat formation. The transient flow upon the droplet impact, as well as its subsequent spreading, cooling, and solidification, are modeled using the Navier–Stokes and energy equations, including the effects of thermal contact resistance, wettability, and surface tension forces. These equations are solved using the finite element method with a rectangular mesh. The level-set approach was selected to delineate the interface and interactions among phases accurately. The equations governing solidification in the substrate are also resolved to predict the evolution of the melting front within the substrate. Along with the simulation of droplet spreading and solidification, the results also provide some insight into the melting and re-solidification of the substrate, which enhances comprehension of the bonding between the substrate and the formed splats, and consequently, the coating material. It is observed that the melting and re-solidification of the preheated substrate occur when larger superheated droplets with a low impact velocity impact it. Furthermore, it was observed that the splat rapidly solidified while the substrate was still melted, which would allow better coating-substrate adhesion.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal evolution and internal kinematics of three-dimensional granular convection driven by a laterally oscillating cylindrical boundary
papers.abstract: Granular convection driven by a laterally oscillating boundary governs internal mass transport and the macroscopic evolution of the surrounding granular bed. Previous studies have mainly relied on two-dimensional visualization or post-test excavation. However, former research cannot detect interior convective structure and continuous particle trajectories, and the three-dimensional development and internal particle kinematics of this phenomenon remain poorly resolved. This study develops a three-dimensional granular flow visualization framework utilizing a semi-cylindrical oscillating boundary. Particle image velocimetry together with the layered sectioning method of colored tracer sand is used to reconstruct the three-dimensional convective cells and track internal particle migration. The convective cells exhibit a bilaterally symmetric ear-shaped morphology with nonlinear depth-wise contraction and geometric similarity of normalized boundaries. Their growth follows an evolution pattern, and an empirical spatiotemporal model is proposed. From a kinematic perspective, granular transport is governed by a coupled downward and horizontal migration along the driving boundary, which feeds into an internal recirculation region, followed by radially outward and upward diffusion. Compared with two-dimensional results, the three-dimensional condition produces stronger depth-wise boundary contraction and faster lateral velocity decay. Increasing vibration amplitude significantly enlarges both the convection extent and intensity, whereas frequency and saturation have weaker effects. These findings clarify the internal kinematics of three-dimensional granular flows driven by an oscillating cylindrical boundary.

papers.title: Assessment of the barotropic one-velocity, one-pressure two-phase flow model to cavitating water-hammer
papers.abstract: This paper presents a numerical and experimental assessment of a barotropic one-velocity, one-pressure two-phase flow model for the simulation of cavitating two-phase water-hammer phenomena. The model is formulated as a hyperbolic system of three conservation laws, consisting of two phasic mass conservation equations and one mixture momentum equation. This reduced formulation describes the transient interaction between the liquid and gas phases under mechanical equilibrium, assuming a common pressure and velocity, while also accounting for pipe hoop elasticity. The novelty of this work lies in the systematic evaluation of this reduced two-phase formulation, coupled with an exact Riemann-solver-based Godunov finite-volume method, for experimentally validated cavitating water-hammer configurations. A series of Riemann problems is first considered to assess the first-order Godunov-type solver in cases where analytical solutions are available. The model is then evaluated using experimental gas–liquid water-hammer configurations in which the dispersed gas phase significantly affects the effective wave speed, pressure amplitude, and damping behavior. Numerical predictions are validated against experimental measurements and compared with reference numerical results available in the literature. The results show good agreement with the available data, demonstrating the capability of the barotropic one-velocity, one-pressure model to reproduce the main features of cavitating two-phase water-hammer flows, including pressure-wave attenuation, wave-speed reduction, and the influence of gas content and pipe elasticity on the transient hydraulic response.

papers.title: Equilibrium positioning of buoyant, deformable drops in a channel
papers.abstract: We investigate the motion and positioning of density-mismatched, deformable drops in pressure-driven flow through horizontal rectangular microchannels using three-dimensional boundary-integral simulations and complementary experiments. For neutrally buoyant drops at a moderate undeformed drop diameter to channel height ratio (D/H≲0.5), we observe off-center equilibrium positions in addition to positioning at the channel centerline over intermediate viscosity ratio ranges, with the range of viscosity ratio narrowing with increasing D/H. When a buoyant drop is released from the channel centerline (or elsewhere), it migrates laterally under gravity until reaching an equilibrium position determined by the balance between buoyancy and deformation-induced hydrodynamic lift forces, independent of initial position. Through systematic parametric studies spanning Bond numbers Bo=0–3, capillary numbers Ca=0.1–0.7, drop-to-medium viscosity ratios λ=0.05–10, and confinement ratios D/H=0.15–1.2, we demonstrate that drops can be predictably positioned at various heights between the wall and centerline by tuning the flow conditions. Larger drops migrate closer to the centerline due to stronger deformation-induced lift forces and thus have higher steady-state velocity, while increasing the Bond number drives drops toward the wall and promotes deformation. We identify critical combinations of Bo, Ca, and D/H, beyond which drops undergo breakup rather than reaching steady states. Higher-viscosity drops settle farther from the centerline due to suppressed internal circulation and weaker deformation-induced lift. Quantitative comparison with experiments shows reasonable agreement, with discrepancies potentially due to surfactant contamination that suppresses interfacial mobility and weakens centering mechanisms.

papers.title: Instantaneous aerodynamic heat characteristics and mitigation strategies for the evacuated tube maglev transportation
papers.abstract: The evacuated tube maglev transportation (ETMT) system offers advantages in terms of high speed, efficiency, and safety and has emerged as a crucial development trend in the future transportation sector. Nevertheless, the special enclosed environment renders the thermal environment within the ETMT System highly complex and even endangers the security of the operation. Thus, investigating the formation mechanisms of aerodynamic heat and the mitigation strategies discussed herein provides technical support for engineering applications. The subject of this paper is to analyze the aerodynamic heat, that is, as presented by the waves and temperature changes within the tube, using the shear stress transport k–ω model, in conjunction with the dynamic mesh technique. The cardinal result is that the distance between the train and the normal shock waves increases linearly as the train's operating time extends. Besides, an increase in the train's speed led to a reduction in the velocity difference between the train and the air within the tube. Thereby improving the kinetic energy transfer efficiency and amplifies the temperature gradient variations in the choked flow ahead of the train. In addition, the mitigation strategies can reduce 21.5 °C in the choked flow region and shorten the shock wavelength at the rear of the train.

papers.title: Influence of splitter plate thickness on flow structure, turbulence, and mixing in high-aspect-ratio plane parallel jets
papers.abstract: The influence of the middle plate thickness (t) on the flow structure of a free, parallel-jet rectangular nozzle was experimentally investigated. In this work, four middle plate thicknesses were employed, with the remaining geometry unchanged, to assess their effect on the flow structure. Mean and turbulent characteristics of the jet were measured along the streamwise and lateral directions using a two-dimensional Constant Temperature Hot-Wire Anemometry. Also, Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) were employed to investigate the flow characteristics. The findings indicated that increasing the middle plate thickness fundamentally changes the near-field flow structure and the interaction of the inner shear layers. A linear bending trend in the lateral velocity toward the symmetry line was observed as plate thickness increased; however, its magnitude showed a nonlinear trend. Furthermore, changing the plate thickness results in a different flow structure: from a stream of small vortices to a flapping motion to a separated flow. The most effective middle plate thickness (among the four tested) enhances velocity fluctuations and increases turbulent transport of normal and shear stresses via lateral velocity fluctuations, thereby improving mixing and increasing lateral spreading. PIV and POD demonstrated vortex interaction in the inner and outer shear layers, vortex behavior within the recirculation zone, and a coherent structure with significant variation. The Strouhal number (Sth) was found to increase as the middle plate thickness decreased. This experiment demonstrates that altering a single parameter can influence flow control, with implications for a broad range of industrial free-turbulent-jet applications.

papers.title: Temperature effects on flow and aeroacoustic characteristics of supersonic rectangular jets
papers.abstract: Rectangular nozzles are a favorable afterbody design for high-speed aircraft, while the temperature exhausted from supersonic rectangular jets may significantly impact noise levels, oscillation patterns, and fluid-acoustic feedback mechanisms. In this study, implicit large-eddy simulations of a rectangular nozzle are performed to analyze the temperature effects on flow and aeroacoustic characteristics of supersonic rectangular jets, operating at three nozzle pressure ratios (NPR = 2.3, 3.0, and 5.0) and three nozzle temperature ratios (TR = 1.0, 3.0, and 7.0). Results show that, as the jets are heated and the Reynolds number decreases correspondingly, the jet potential cores are shortened, and the number of shock cells is reduced, regardless of the NPRs. The noise levels of Mach waves are amplified with increasing jet temperature, due to the acceleration of shear-layer convection. The thermal heating decreases the non-dimensional frequencies of the screech tones. The oscillation modes and the fluid-acoustic resonance mechanism associated with the screech tones are investigated by using Fourier transformation, dynamic mode decomposition, and wavenumber spectra analysis.

papers.title: Drag reduction of hydrofoils for high-performance sailing: A review
papers.abstract: Hydrofoil technology has transformed high-performance sailing by dramatically reducing wetted surface area and enabling vessel speeds that were previously unattainable for wind-powered craft. As hull-borne resistance is largely eliminated during foiling operation, hydrofoil drag becomes the dominant limitation to further performance gains. This review synthesizes findings from 136 peer-reviewed studies published between 2006 and 2026 and examines drag-reduction strategies spanning biomimetic surface modifications, cavitation management, free-surface interaction control, advanced materials and manufacturing, machine-learning-assisted optimization, air lubrication, and practical sailing applications. A unifying framework is proposed in which hydrofoil drag-reduction technologies are classified according to the dominant physical mechanisms they address: viscous drag, pressure drag, cavitation-related losses, and free-surface-induced drag. Reported drag reductions range from approximately 4%–8% for riblet surfaces and up to 80% for air-lubrication systems under favorable conditions, although performance varies substantially with Reynolds number, cavitation number, angle of attack, submergence depth, and implementation strategy. The review reveals a significant imbalance between computational investigations and full-scale validation, with most technologies remaining at intermediate stages of technological maturity despite promising laboratory-scale results. Key challenges include Reynolds-number scaling, turbulence–cavitation interactions, long-term durability, multiphysics coupling, and the lack of standardized validation methodologies. Overall, the literature indicates that future advances will depend less on isolated improvements within individual technologies and more on the integration of complementary drag-reduction mechanisms within adaptive hydrofoil systems capable of maintaining performance across diverse operating conditions.

papers.title: Weakly nonlinear instability and bifurcation in rotating phototactic bioconvection
papers.abstract: In this work, we report a weakly nonlinear analysis of rotating bioconvection in a suspension of phototactic microorganisms bounded below by a rigid horizontal boundary and above by a stress-free/rigid horizontal boundary, which is uniformly illuminated from above by a light source. This work aims to explore the effect of rotation on the post-critical evolution of instability by inspecting the bifurcation phenomena and the convective flow structures that govern the observable dynamics of the system. Such analysis is important for understanding pattern formation and biomass transport in photobioreactors used for advanced biofuel production. Linear stability theory is employed to determine the critical conditions for convection, after which the corresponding eigenvalue and adjoint problems, along with the first harmonic and the modification of the conductive cell concentration profile, are solved numerically to derive the Stuart–Landau amplitude equation. A systematic analysis was conducted to examine the influence of the Taylor number across different values of the cell swimming speed, optical depth, critical light intensity, and boundary surface combinations. The sign of the Landau constant is used to identify the nature of the bifurcation and to distinguish between supercritical and subcritical transitions. Depending on the parameter regime, both stationary and oscillatory instabilities are found. Stationary convection undergoes a pitchfork bifurcation, while oscillatory convection experiences a Hopf bifurcation. The results also indicate that the rotation suppresses the equilibrium convective amplitude and significantly modifies the weakly nonlinear saturation dynamics.

papers.title: Blockage-driven turbulent vortex dynamics and modal evolution in high-Reynolds-number cavity flows
papers.abstract: This study presents two-dimensional particle image velocimetry measurements acquired at the mid-plane of the cavity, together with higher-order dynamic mode decomposition (HODMD) analysis, for lid-driven square-cavity flows containing cubical obstacles at high Reynolds numbers (Re = 1.161 × 105–3.483 × 105). Obstacle sizes of 3, 6, and 9 cm, corresponding to h/D = 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30, were systematically examined to clarify blockage-driven variations in vortex dynamics, velocity distribution, planar turbulent kinetic energy (TKE2D), and modal characteristics on the cavity middle plane. The results show that increasing Reynolds number drives the primary vortex toward the cavity center and promotes a transition from relatively fragmented, high-rotation structures to smoother large-scale recirculation. Meanwhile, increasing obstacle size strengthens geometric confinement, shifts the primary vortex toward the left wall, and induces vortex splitting at the largest blockage ratio. The low-velocity region expands markedly, reaching 43.29% for h/D = 0.30, while the high-velocity region is reduced to 0.8% at the highest Reynolds number. At Re = 2.322 × 105, increasing h/D from 0.10 to 0.30 increases the area proportion of the high normalized-TKE region from 0.83% to 4.74%, while decreasing that of the low normalized-TKE region from 50.72% to 36.52%, indicating a blockage-induced redistribution of the resolved in-plane fluctuation energy. HODMD further identifies a dominant zero-frequency mean-flow mode and higher-order modes with clear harmonic relations, corresponding to the multi-scale evolution of the cavity flow. The reconstructed flow fields show a root mean square error as low as 2.08%, substantially lower than that of standard DMD in strongly nonlinear conditions. These results provide experimental evidence for blockage-controlled turbulent vortex dynamics in high-Reynolds-number cavity flows and offer reference data for the validation of numerical simulations in confined flow systems.

papers.title: An efficient hydrodynamic-structure unified state-space model for the coupled dynamics during floating wind turbine wet-towing construction
papers.abstract: Wet-towing is a critical installation stage for a large floating offshore wind turbine (FOWT), yet the tower is still commonly treated as a rigid component in all existing towing simulations. This simplification may compromise the prediction of hydroelastic load transfer as turbine capacity and tower height continue to increase. To address this limitation, this study develops an efficient hydrodynamic-structural coupled time-domain model for the wet-towing of the International Energy Agency 15 MW FOWT for the first time. A static condensation method is introduced to incorporate tower elasticity into the global six degrees of freedom floating body formulation, while a state-space model is established to replace the radiation memory convolution in the Cummins equation. The further derived hydrodynamic-structural unified state-space model enables rapid time-domain simulation of the towing system under forward speed effects. The proposed model is first validated against Newman's classical double-barge benchmark and free decay simulations. Frequency-domain results reveal that forward speed mainly governs the evolution of surge, heave, and pitch response amplitude operators, while tower elasticity significantly reshapes the hydroelastic resonance characteristics. The tower base loads are concentrated mainly in the frequency ranges of 0.8–1.0 and 1.2–1.5 rad/s, whereas the most critical tower top stress is controlled by a low-frequency surge-pitch coupled regime near 0.19–0.22 rad/s rather than by heave resonance. Time-domain comparisons with a validated OpenFAST and AQWA coupled framework show that the proposed model accurately reproduces the dominant pitch motion, nacelle acceleration, tower shear force, and stress evolution under both regular and irregular wave conditions. The results further indicate that stronger turbulent wind, longer wave periods, and higher towing speed intensify fore-aft bending. Additionally, the proposed model reduces computational time by approximately 80% in regular waves and more than 54% in irregular waves, which demonstrates strong potential for efficient engineering assessment of FOWT towing safety.

papers.title: Balanced investigation of impeller geometric effects on energy conversion and hydraulic loss in a pump as turbine under pump and turbine modes
papers.abstract: Pump as turbine (PAT) is a key technology for industrial residual pressure-energy recovery. However, achieving satisfactory hydraulic performance under both pump and turbine operating modes remains challenging, primarily because the internal flow structure and energy conversion mechanism are altered during reverse operation, and the influence of geometric parameters on dual-mode performance remains unclear. In this study, the entropy production theory and vorticity transport analysis were combined to investigate the effects of geometric parameters on dual-mode hydraulic performance and flow mechanisms, elucidating the intrinsic relationship between vorticity generation and energy dissipation. The results indicate that the influence of blade geometric parameters on dual-mode performance is markedly asymmetric, which can be attributed to the reversal of the flow direction leading to changes in the velocity triangles. The blade wrap angle exhibits a strong positive correlation with efficiency in pump mode, whereas a negative correlation is observed in turbine mode. In pump mode, turbulent entropy production dominates, whereas wall entropy production increases in turbine mode. Vorticity transport analysis reveals that the Coriolis force term and the relative vorticity stretching term are the dominant mechanisms of vorticity generation, and their spatial distribution is consistent with that of the regions of high entropy production, indicating a strong correlation between vortex dynamics and irreversible energy dissipation. Velocity triangle analysis further demonstrates that the attack angle is the key parameter determining impact losses and separation losses. The parameter coordination design strategy proposed in this study provides a theoretical basis and quantitative reference for achieving efficient dual-mode operation of PAT.

papers.title: Vortical structures of twin annular swirling jets with a fixed inner jet
papers.abstract: High-speed stereoscopic particle image velocimetry is employed to investigate the flow characteristics of swirling jets in twin annular configurations with a fixed inner geometry. The inner-stage jet is set at a pre-vortex-breakdown state with an inner swirl number of 0.5, while the outer swirl number ranges from 0.35 to 0.77, covering both co-rotating and counter-rotating configurations. In the dual-stage cases, as the outer swirl number increases, the spectral characteristics exhibit two distinct peaks corresponding to two precessing vortex cores (PVCs). The upstream PVC is located near the nozzle outlet and is primarily influenced by the inner swirling flow, whereas the downstream PVC is located at the flow merging region and is mainly governed by the merged flow. The presence of two PVCs reveals a zoned characteristic within the central recirculation zone, even though the recirculation zone appears as a single entity. With increasing swirl number, the amplitude of the downstream PVC first increases and then decreases, while its frequency decreases monotonically; the upstream PVC amplitude follows a similar trend. Owing to the bidirectional effect of the swirl number, the upstream PVC exhibits a substantially higher amplitude at lower swirl numbers. The decrease in amplitude of both PVCs is associated with the increasing expansion angle of the inner swirling flow. Counter-rotating cases reveal competition between the staged jets, resulting in the formation of a gourd-shaped recirculation zone and a transition in the dominant frequency from high-frequency dominance to a broadband (spectrally diffuse) state and subsequently to low-frequency dominance.

papers.title: Fluid compatibility, interfacial stability, and buoyancy-driven multi-fluid displacement in primary well cementing: A review
papers.abstract: Primary well cementing involves sequential displacement of drilling mud, chemical washes, spacers, and cement slurry in the annular space between casing and formation. Although widely used in energy applications, the underlying fluid-mechanical process is not fully understood. This review synthesizes current knowledge on fluid compatibility and buoyancy-driven multi-fluid displacement from a fluid-mechanics perspective. Fluid compatibility governs the chemical and rheological stability of interacting fluids and depends on formulation variables, contamination, temperature and pressure, mixing history, and additive chemistry. Incompatible interactions may induce viscosification, flocculation, or phase separation, which destabilize interfaces and degrade displacement efficiency. Beyond compatibility, cement placement is controlled by the hydrodynamics of buoyant displacement between fluids with contrasting density and non-Newtonian rheology. Experimental and theoretical studies show that displacement regimes range from stable plug-like propagation to unstable modes such as slumping, fingering, separation, and intense mixing. These transitions depend on the competition between buoyancy, viscous stresses, yield-stress resistance, and imposed flow, as well as geometric factors such as inclination and annular eccentricity. Dimensionless groups including Reynolds, Froude, Atwood, Bingham, and Capillary numbers provide a framework for interpreting regime transitions across laboratory and field conditions. The review highlights how density–rheology hierarchies and interface-control fluids stabilize displacement fronts, and identifies open challenges including turbulent regimes, multi-interface systems, particle-laden suspensions, realistic annular geometries, and data-driven modeling approaches.

papers.title: Experimental study of subsonic projectile deceleration in aqueous foams
papers.abstract: The detonation of explosive devices generates high-velocity metallic fragments that constitute one of the primary lethality mechanisms of improvised explosive devices. Aqueous foams are promising protective barriers owing to their ease of deployment and high-energy-dissipation capacity. This study investigates the deceleration of a subsonic spherical projectile in aqueous foam under controlled physicochemical conditions. A magnetized neodymium projectile was tracked inside an opaque foam-filled test section using electromagnetic induction coils, combined with high-speed imaging upstream and downstream, providing a continuous velocity profile over 750 mm at two liquid fractions (Φf=2% and 8%) and two initial velocities (vp,0=55 and 110 ms−1). The normalized deceleration profile is found to be largely independent of the initial velocity, with velocity losses reaching 24% at Φf=2% and 65% at Φf=8%. Three modeling approaches are successively evaluated: a Kelvin–Voigt cell model, a component-based two-phase model, and an effective medium drag model. Only the effective medium approach reproduces both the magnitude and the velocity-independence of the measured deceleration, demonstrating that aqueous foam dissipates kinetic energy more effectively than the sum of contributions from its individual components.

papers.title: Flow control mechanisms of partially porous blade tip on tip leakage vortex in pump-jet propulsor
papers.abstract: Large eddy simulation coupled with a porous medium model and a sliding mesh technique was employed to investigate the flow control mechanism of partially porous blade tips in a pump-jet propulsor (PJP). Two porous tip configurations with 1/3 and 2/3 coverage were examined, and the numerical methodology was validated against published reference data with errors below 5%. The results show that the porous medium suppresses the tip leakage jet by introducing viscous and inertial resistance, thereby weakening the development of the tip leakage vortex (TLV). Compared with the conventional rotor, the TLV core strength is reduced by more than 30%, while the pressure fluctuation amplitudes decrease by 5.07%–12.93% and 27.53%–33.02% for the 1/3 and 2/3 porous tip configurations, respectively. Increasing the porous coverage enhances vortex suppression but also increases thrust loss from approximately 6%–9% to 16%–22%. Under oblique inflow conditions, the 1/3 porous tip configuration achieves the best balance between vortex control and propulsion performance. At θ = 10°, pressure fluctuation amplitudes are reduced by more than 10%. These findings demonstrate the potential of partially porous blade tips as an effective passive flow control strategy for mitigating TLV-induced flow instability in PJPs.

papers.title: Thermo-bioconvective instabilities in Rivlin–Ericksen nanofluids with micro-organisms: Implications for bioreactors in biomedical systems
papers.abstract: This study presents a linear stability analysis of thermo-bioconvective instability in a horizontal Rivlin–Ericksen viscoelastic nanofluid layer containing gyrotactic micro-organisms confined between free-free boundaries under no-flux conditions for both nanoparticles and micro-organisms. The model incorporates higher-order viscoelastic stresses, Buongiorno-type nanoparticle transport, and gyrotactic micro-organism redistribution within a unified framework. Normal mode analysis yields closed-form expressions for the critical thermal Rayleigh number governing stationary and oscillatory convection. For stationary convection, nanoparticle buoyancy (Rn) and modified diffusivity ratio (NA) are the primary destabilizing factors, while micro-organism induced buoyancy (Rab) remains secondary unless strongly coupled through concentration transport. The Lewis number (Le) exhibits a density-regime-dependent dual role, destabilizing for heavier nanoparticles (Rn>0) and stabilizing for lighter nanoparticles (ρp<ρf, Rn<0). Oscillatory convection is gated exclusively to the lighter nanoparticle regime (Rn<0), where viscoelastic phase lag, restoring nanoparticle stratification, and micro-organism-induced buoyancy constitute mutually necessary conditions for overstability, a three-way coupling mechanism absent in Newtonian and Maxwell-type formulations. Unlike Maxwell fluids, where elasticity lowers the oscillatory threshold, Rivlin–Ericksen viscoelasticity raises it, indicating a distinct stabilization effect. Sensitivity analysis shows that bioconvection parameters (Rab, Qb) remain weakly sensitive (|S|<1) across all configurations, ensuring proportional and structurally bounded stability responses, whereas nanofluid parameters (Rn, Le, NA) exert the dominant control over the stationary convection but become subdued in oscillatory convection. The study extends classical thermo-bioconvection theory to Rivlin–Ericksen fluids and offers useful guidance for viscoelastic bio-nanofluid systems in bioreactors, biomedical microchambers, and microfluidic devices.

papers.title: Experimental study of airlift transport and pressure response of cylindrical cores regulated by gas–liquid flow structures
papers.abstract: Airlift reverse-circulation coring transports cylindrical cores by injecting gas into a riser. Near-pipe-diameter cores are wall-confined, making their motion sensitive to gas–liquid structures. A visualized airlift core-transport system was used to examine the coupling among gas–liquid structures, pressure response, and core motion through high-speed imaging, multi-point pressure measurements, and an instrumented core. Increasing gas injection drove the flow from bubbly flow to large-scale intermittent structures. Correspondingly, the pressure response shifted from high-frequency, low-amplitude disturbances to low-frequency, high-amplitude pulsations. Core introduction increased near-field pressure-fluctuation amplitude, with limited changes in characteristic pressure frequency. Instrumented-core measurements showed larger attitude and axial-acceleration fluctuations during airlift transport than during hydraulic single-phase transport, consistent with intermittent core support. The pressure-inferred recurrence length mapped the pressure-fluctuation timescale to a spatial recurrence scale based on gas-phase convection. Mean core transport velocity was positively associated with the in situ gas velocity estimated using two drift-flux correlations, giving through-origin slopes of 0.3185 and 0.3368. Model selection changed the fitted coefficient but did not alter the observed velocity association. The cycle-scale ratio of core displacement to recurrence length was approximately one third and is interpreted as a kinematic transport scaling rather than an independent causal correlation. These results show that intermittent gas–liquid structure dynamics are essential for characterizing airlift core transport beyond the mean liquid velocity alone. Within the tested air–water laboratory conditions, the results provide local-scale guidance for interpreting pressure response and core transport in airlift reverse-circulation systems.

papers.title: Pancake-shaped turbulence with strong near-wall compression in separation-induced transition
papers.abstract: This study identifies pancake-shaped turbulence in the near-wall region within a laminar separation bubble over the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) 0012 airfoil at low Reynolds numbers, which occurs only in moderate-to-high subsonic regimes and a limited low-Reynolds-number range. This turbulence is dominated by wall-normal limiting compression within the viscous sublayer and part of the buffer layer. It exhibits a limiting symmetric, pancake-shaped structure with strong compressive characteristics, distinct from the conventional separation-induced transition and the near-wall quasi-two-component turbulence. As the separated flow approaches the wall, the wall-normal Reynolds stress is compressed, and the spanwise and streamwise Reynolds stresses reach nearly equal magnitudes, thereby forming the near-wall pancake-shaped turbulence. This phenomenon causes a pronounced intensification of spanwise turbulence within the viscous sublayer and part of the buffer layer (n+ < 15). It is also observed in the flow field of a low-Reynolds-number compressor blade, suggesting its potential universality across different physical scenarios and indicating that it may be a common feature in high-speed subsonic flows within a limited low-Reynolds-number regime. Investigating its characteristics and underlying physical mechanisms provides new insights into the transition processes of laminar separation bubbles.

papers.title: Experimental study and scaling analysis on hydraulic jump formed by a circular liquid jet impacting a wall
papers.abstract: The liquid film cooling formed by jet-wall impingement plays a crucial role in thermal protection of thrust chamber walls in rocket engines. Accurate prediction of hydraulic jump formation is essential for enhancing cooling reliability. This study systematically investigates the effects of fluid properties, wall wettability, and downstream obstacle parameters on jump patterns and sizes. Visualization results reveal that jump patterns are predominantly governed by flow conditions. Reduced volume flow rate or increased obstacle height induces instability in low-viscosity fluid jump structures. Quantitative analysis demonstrates a strong linear correlation between jump radius and volume flow rate, with the slope and intercept governed by different combinations of key parameters including dynamic viscosity, gravitational acceleration, surface tension coefficient, downstream obstacle parameters, and other factors. A novel empirical correlation is established through scaling analysis and coefficient of variation optimization, utilizing two characteristic lengths and two constants to precisely predict jump radius. The proposed empirical correlation demonstrates improved predictive accuracy compared to existing models, with 95.90% of predictions for 244 experimental cases falling within engineering-acceptable error margins.

papers.title: Ligament pinch-off mechanism of stable satellite droplets stream generation in continuous jet breakup
papers.abstract: Regarding satellite droplets as utilizable droplets can address the engineering challenges resulting from the growing need for small droplets in industrial manufacturing. In this paper, we investigate the generation process from ligament to stable satellite droplet, as a prerequisite for utilizing satellite droplets. Following our previous experimental work, we found that stable satellite droplets are generated from downstream pinch-off instead of being conventionally recognized as symmetric pinch-off. A two-dimensional axisymmetric model with periodic flow is applied to describe the liquid dynamics, and the changes in volume and momentum throughout the process are considered. The entire jet breakup process can be divided into three stages: growing, flattening, and necking/pinch-off. Perturbation parameters significantly affect the ligament pinch-off modes. The analysis of field variables at the ligament pinch-off instants for various perturbation amplitudes reveals that the jet velocity decays as the perturbation grows. Based on ligament flattening and necking, we show that perturbation amplitude governs necking-point positions and thus controls the volume evolution from ligament to satellite droplet, providing the basis for analyzing satellite merging modes. A deviation in the downstream necking dynamics of the entire flattening and necking process relative to the self-similar theory alters the conventional correspondence between satellite merging and ligament pinch-off modes. The momentum per volume for the ligament evolution process should be analyzed using the specific capillary impulses in the upstream and downstream necking regions during the flattening stage. This work provides guidance for understanding and modulating ligament pinch-off modes to achieve stable satellite droplet generation.

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of stencil configuration, forcing scheme, and resolution effects in the stratified Taylor–Green vortex: A lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: The rigorous simulation of stratified turbulence remains challenging due to pronounced flow anisotropy, suppressed vertical transport, and high sensitivity to numerical dissipation. This study systematically evaluates the predictive capability of the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) for a three-dimensional stratified Taylor–Green vortex. Within a double-distribution-function framework under the Boussinesq approximation, we examine the influence of stencil configurations, forcing formulations, and spatial resolutions up to 2563, with validation against spectral direct numerical simulation benchmarks. The results demonstrate that the D3Q27×19 configuration achieves an optimal balance between numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, accurately reproducing the temporal evolution of kinetic and potential energies as well as the characteristic double-peak dissipation structure. Grid-sensitivity analysis further reveals that potential energy and fine-scale turbulent structures are significantly more resolution-dependent than kinetic energy, requiring a minimum resolution of 2563 for quantitative convergence. Moreover, under strongly stratified conditions, the velocity-shift forcing schemes outperform discrete source-term approaches, reducing the overall error by approximately 45.33%. Finally, a symmetry-breaking velocity-error diagnostic shows that the previously used D3Q27×7 configuration, despite reasonable global energy predictions, accumulates substantially larger hidden symmetry errors than D3Q27×19 under strong stratification. Overall, this work provides practical guidelines for high-fidelity LBM simulations of stratified turbulence and highlights that the coordinated selection of stencil isotropy, spatial resolution, force discretization, and symmetry preservation is essential for accurately capturing energy cascade and mixing dynamics.

papers.title: Analysis of hypersonic plasma flow field evolution and wake particle distribution characteristics under thermochemical–mechanical ablation
papers.abstract: To investigate the effects of carbon–carbon (C–C) material ablation on the plasma-flow characteristics of hypersonic vehicles under high-enthalpy conditions, this study combines multiphysics numerical simulations with plasma-wind tunnel experiments. First, a coupled thermochemical–mechanical ablation model was established to describe the transport of carbon-based gaseous products and solid particles in the near-wall region, wake region, and downstream diffuser region. The numerical results indicate that ablation products affect the local flow-field parameters through mass blowing, near-wall blockage, and chemical deionization effects. Second, based on the Experimental research apparatus for electromagnetic science of hypersonic vehicle plasma in nearspace, electron-density measurements were conducted using electrostatic probes under the plasma wind tunnel (PWTs) ablation condition with the C–C ablating model. The results show that C–C ablation reduces the peak electron density near the stagnation region. Owing to the downstream transport of ablation products, the electron-density distribution exhibits a characteristic trend of reduced peak value and expanded affected range. The difference between the electron-density measurements and numerical predictions under the same wind tunnel operating condition is within 10%. Finally, the spatiotemporal distribution of mechanically eroded particles in the wake and diffuser regions was analyzed. The numerical results reveal a spatial correlation between geometry-induced recirculation and near-wall particle enrichment in the diffuser. By combining the blockage-ratio evolution with the Kantrowitz-based theoretical reference, an assumption-dependent equivalent blockage ratio was introduced for a preliminary engineering assessment of potential diffuser blockage risk. This provides a numerical and experimental reference for evaluating particle accumulation risks during high-power PWT operation.

papers.title: An overall iterative method for fluid–structure interaction analysis of high-speed maglev train-guideway systems
papers.abstract: As the operating speed of high-speed maglev trains increases, the two-way interaction between unsteady aerodynamic loads and vehicle motion becomes increasingly important. An overall iterative coupling framework integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and multibody dynamics is developed to investigate the vertical fluid–structure interaction of a high-speed maglev train-guideway system. In each overall iteration, the unsteady aerodynamic load histories obtained from the flow-field simulation are applied to the train-guideway dynamic model, and the resulting vertical and pitching motions are subsequently prescribed in the CFD model to update the surrounding flow field and aerodynamic loads. For a three-car train operating at 430 km/h, the responses converge after three overall iterations. At 500 km/h, the middle car satisfies the residual criterion after three iterations, whereas the head and tail cars require a fourth iteration; the final global residuals of all response quantities are below 0.04. At 600 km/h, the self-excited lift and pitching moment increase progressively and the vehicle responses fail to converge within five overall iterations, indicating negative-aerodynamic-damping-type feedback. The 500 km/h case therefore represents a transitional but still stable coupled state between the rapidly convergent 430 km/h response and the non-convergent amplification at 600 km/h. The results demonstrate that vehicle-motion feedback modifies the integrated unsteady aerodynamic loads and coupled responses; neglecting this feedback may lead to an incomplete assessment of coupled aerodynamic and dynamic behavior.

papers.title: Aerodynamic anti-overturning optimization of high-speed trains with airbag structures under crosswind
papers.abstract: Under crosswind conditions, multiple flow separations occur in the leeward side (LWS) region of the trains, leading to the formation of large-scale vortical structures that reduce surface pressure and generate significant lateral aerodynamic loads. Disrupting these large-scale vortices and increasing the LWS pressure therefore represents a promising approach to improving the anti-overturning performance of high-speed trains. In this study, numerical simulations were performed to investigate the flow-field characteristics around the train equipped with airbag structures (ASs) installed on the LWS. The improved delayed detached eddy simulation turbulence model was employed to evaluate the flow-control effectiveness of the ASs and its influence on aerodynamic performance under crosswind conditions. The results show that the ASs effectively reduce both the lateral force and overturning moment by modifying the dominant leeward vortices, shifting them away from the train body, and splitting the near-body vortex into two smaller vortices. These flow-field alterations improve the pressure distribution on the LWS, thereby mitigating adverse aerodynamic loads. Compared with the baseline configuration, the lateral force and overturning moment coefficients decrease by 3.84% and 6.49%, respectively, with the AS configuration. In addition, the installation of the ASs influences lift characteristics, increasing the lift coefficient of the middle car by 41.58% and that of the entire train by 10.94%. The present study proposes a novel passive flow-control strategy for enhancing the operational safety of high-speed trains subjected to crosswinds.

papers.title: On the transient dynamics of shock wave–bubble interaction near a solid boundary: Influence of the pressure waveform and standoff distance
papers.abstract: Shock wave–bubble interaction (SBI) involves the formation of high-speed liquid jets and the emission of strong shock waves, which attracts the interest of researchers in various fields, such as underwater explosion, marine propeller, and shock wave lithotripsy. In this study, we performed a comprehensive numerical study on the transient dynamics of SBI near a solid boundary. Two types of incident shock waves are explored, including a lithotripter shock wave (LSW) and a blast wave (BW), with their pulse duration (tFWHM) and pressure amplitude (ps) varying. Several unique features are observed. First, the maximum jet speed (ujetmax) for the SBI with an incident LSW exhibits a non-monotonic trend as dimensionless standoff distance (γ) increases, while for cases with an incident BW, the SBI induces higher jet speeds under the same γ due to its longer pulse duration, and ujetmax increases monotonically with increasing γ, following a scaling law ujetmax∼C(psρ)0.5γ0.41. Second, the maximum wall pressure (pwallmax) is highly relevant to the pressure waveform of the incident shock wave other than γ. As the pulse duration (tFWHM) of the BW increases, pwallmax increases nonlinearly, and the water pressure could reach 1.5 GPa, far exceeding the yield strength limit of conventional materials. Finally, it is found that a higher pressure amplitude or longer pulse duration of the incident shock wave lead to a shorter collapse time compared to those without an incident shock wave.

papers.title: Erratum: “Assessment of Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes modeling of jet interaction in fan-array wind generator flows” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 075188 (2026)]
Nonlinear resonance mechanisms and cross-order harmonic coupling of deep-water waves excited by a moving pressure field
papers.abstract: Within the framework of the homotopy analysis method, the method of directly defining inverse mapping is applied to investigate the strongly nonlinear resonance and cross-order harmonic coupling of deep-water waves excited by a moving pressure field. By directly defining new inverse operators, this analytical framework offers a practical way to handle the small-divisor difficulty encountered in traditional perturbation theories. It does not require the weak-nonlinearity assumption or the scale-separation procedure used in methods such as multiple scales. In the primary resonance region, the nonlinear dispersion of deep-water waves causes the forced-response branches to bend rightward and develop fold bifurcations. An empirical relation is obtained for the moderate-to-strong nonlinear regime to characterize cross-order coupling in the discrete spectrum. It suggests that the higher-order harmonics of the deviation velocity potential are strongly influenced by adjacent lower-order background-wave components, which act as an important source of parametric excitation through nonlinear steepening. This study elucidates the regularities of discrete spectra and the cross-order evolution mechanisms of deep-water forced waves under resonance modes.

papers.title: Nonequilibrium dissipation scaling in fan-array-generated uniform and uniform-shear turbulence
papers.abstract: We investigate dissipation scaling in fan-array-generated turbulence under controlled mean-flow conditions. Experiments are performed using a wind generator driven by an 8×8 array of 64 counter-rotating fans with row-wise pulse width modulation control, which enables repeatable realization of two canonical configurations: nominally uniform mean flow and nominally uniform shear flow. Hot-wire anemometry is used to obtain turbulence statistics, including the Taylor-scale Reynolds number Reλ and the nondimensional dissipation rate Cε. To go beyond global long-time-averaged measures, we apply a short-time local analysis to the velocity records and evaluate Cε within local subensembles. When the streamwise root mean square velocity fluctuation is used as the velocity scale, the global and local results in both configurations exhibit decreasing trends of Cε with increasing Reλ that are broadly consistent with an inverse-Reynolds-number dependence. In the nominally uniform-flow configuration, this local tendency is more apparent upstream and weakens downstream, whereas in the nominally uniform shear-flow configuration it shows weaker streamwise variation. For the shear flow, however, an additional normalization based on the approximate turbulent kinetic energy produces a similar decreasing global trend but a substantially weaker local dependence on Reλ. These results show that fan-array forcing enables systematic comparison of dissipation behavior across mean-flow configurations, while also demonstrating that local conditional scaling in anisotropic shear turbulence can be sensitive to the velocity scale used for normalization.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of wave elevation and velocity evolution for a solitary wave passing a submerged spherical-cap topography
papers.abstract: This study investigates the free-surface elevation and underlying velocity fields of a tsunami-like solitary wave propagating over a submerged spherical-cap topography, aiming to explore the physical connection between wave amplification and three-dimensional flow reorganization. An array of wave gauges is deployed to capture the spatiotemporal evolution of the free-surface elevation over a wide range of incident wave heights and submergence depths. A three-dimensional breaking criterion is established, indicating that the classical two-dimensional breaking condition cannot be directly applied because lateral energy redistribution alters the local wave-energy accumulation. The topography further induces pronounced lee-side wave focusing through the combined effects of shoaling, refraction, and diffraction. The maximum wave elevation at key measurement points is further described by an empirical power-law relationship involving the relative submergence depth and the wave-height-to-depth ratio, providing a quantitative characterization of topography-induced wave focusing. To resolve the flow mechanism beneath the free surface, a self-developed underwater two-dimensional three-component particle image velocimetry system is employed to measure the velocity fields at several characteristic cross sections. The measured velocity fields reveal the transition from front-side diffraction to lee-side spanwise convergence, together with vertical velocity reorganization near the topography. These results demonstrate that lee-side wave amplification is not governed by shoaling alone, but by the combined effects of shoaling, diffraction-induced convergence, vertical flow reorganization, and breaking-induced dissipation. The present measurements therefore provide direct experimental evidence linking free-surface amplification to three-dimensional flow structures over submerged topography, offering benchmark data and physical insight for modeling nonlinear wave-topography interactions.

papers.title: Droplet impact-solidification behavior on cold surfaces: Role of wettability, undercooling, and impact inertia
papers.abstract: Droplet impact on cold substrates involves coupled inertial spreading, capillary recoil, and solidification, yet the combined influence of these processes remains unclear. In this work, we experimentally investigate the impact dynamics of succinonitrile droplets on substrates with varying wettability and thermal properties over a range of Weber numbers (5–100) and undercooling ΔT = 23–43 °C. The results show that the early-stage spreading is inertia-dominated and largely independent of thermal conditions, whereas the post-impact evolution is governed by the competition between recoil and solidification. High-wettability and thermally conductive surfaces promote rapid heat removal, leading to early contact-line arrest and suppressed recoil, while low-wettability and thermally insulating surfaces allow significant retraction and oscillations. A unified framework based on the ratio of the characteristic freezing and spreading timescales, Π=tfreeze/tspread, captures the transition between impact regimes. When Π<1, the droplet reaches its maximum spreading before significant solidification, resulting in hydrodynamically dominated spreading. For Π∼1, solidification and spreading occur over comparable timescales, leading to partial retraction and damped oscillations. When Π>1, rapid solidification during the advancing stage arrests the contact line and reduces the maximum spreading factor. These findings demonstrate that droplet impact with phase change is governed by a coupled hydrodynamic-thermal balance and provide a physically based framework for predicting impact outcomes on cold surfaces, supporting applications involving controlled deposition and solidification.

papers.title: Nanoparticle transport and plugging in non-Newtonian drilling-fluid flow through three-dimensional porous media
papers.abstract: Transport and retention of nanoparticles in non-Newtonian drilling fluids through porous media are critical for evaluating the sealing potential of micrometer-scale leakage channels in low-permeability reservoirs. A three-dimensional pore-scale model (43 × 25 × 8 μm3) was developed to investigate nanoparticle transport and flow restriction in a shear-thinning drilling fluid. The fluid rheology was described by the Meter model, and nanoparticles were tracked using a two-way-coupled dense discrete phase model. A user-defined concentration–viscosity relation allowed the local particle volume fraction to dynamically modify the effective viscosity. Nanoparticles preferentially accumulated near the inlet, on upstream-facing matrix surfaces, and in constricted throats, forming bridge-like particle-rich regions across the thickness direction. Approximately 80% and 91% of the final retained-particle number were reached by 30 and 40 s, respectively. At 80 s, the lower-Péclet-number case (Pe = 9.4 × 103) retained ∼1.52 × 104 particles, over four times the ∼3.6 × 103 retained at Pe = 4.8 × 104. Because the particle injection rate was fixed while the inlet velocity varied, this difference arose from the combined effects of convection, residence time, and inlet particle concentration. Increasing the matrix-sphere diameter from 2.5 to 3.5 μm reduced the final retained-particle number from ∼1.82 × 104 to 1.53 × 104, while increasing the domain-volume-averaged static pressure from ∼41 to 163 Pa. The heterogeneous structure retained more particles during rapid filling but fewer during intermediate bridge-like accumulation.

papers.title: Effect of circumferential grooving on the performance and flow mechanism of an axial flow fan with a large tip-clearance ratio
papers.abstract: This study investigates an industrial axial flow fan with a large tip-clearance ratio of 1%. We use numerical simulations and experimental validation to examine how the number, axial location, and distribution of circumferential casing grooves affect aerodynamic performance under near-stall conditions. The results indicate that a single circumferential groove enlarges the low-velocity separation region within the tip clearance, intensifies turbulence, and aggravates flow blockage, thereby deteriorating fan performance. In contrast, a properly arranged multigroove configuration effectively suppresses tip leakage. The configuration involving a continuous circumferential groove structure significantly reduces blockage of the passage, which is associated with reverse-flow regions. Under near-stall conditions, this configuration increases static pressure by up to 15.7%, improves static pressure efficiency by 12%, and enhances the stall margin by 8.3%. These findings further reveal a zonal control mechanism of casing treatments in industrial axial flow fans with large tip-clearance ratios. Finally, grooves near the leading edge expand the radial clearance and promote the interaction and dissipation between reverse leakage flow and primary leakage flow. Conversely, grooves positioned near the trailing edge generate stable vortex structures that suppress the accumulation of reverse flow.

papers.title: Asymmetric collapse of double cavitation bubbles at oil–water interface and associated coupling effect
papers.abstract: In multiphase flow applications such as pipeline transportation, the presence of oil–water interfaces and interactions between cavities jointly affect the collapse behavior of double bubbles. This study employs high-speed cameras to conduct an investigation into the pulsation characteristics of double cavitation bubbles near oil–water interfaces, focusing on the effects of the distance from the interface (γ), the distance between bubbles (λ), and the size ratio S. This study reveals that the enhancement effect of the interface on bubble re-expansion intensifies as the bubble approaches the oil–water interface. The primary Bjerknes forces acting on double bubbles are relatively weak; the resulting nonspherical deformation only becomes apparent after the bubble collapses, whereas the nonspherical deformation caused by the secondary Bjerknes forces becomes apparent during the bubble's first oscillation cycle. For equal size bubbles far from an interface, collapse occurs at the midpoint; near the interface, they migrate away from the interface. Unequal size double bubbles collapse asymmetrically, migrating toward the smaller one. At the end of the first oscillation cycle of the larger cavitation bubble, the ratio of the centroid migration displacements of each bubble pair exhibits an approximate inverse-square dependence on the initial size ratio S.

papers.title: Interference of dynamical arrest, thermodynamic instabilities and energy-scale competition in symmetric binary mixtures
papers.abstract: While energy scale competition dictates equilibrium phase behavior, kinetic barriers often drive soft-matter mixtures into dynamically arrested states, rendering conventional phase diagrams incomplete. We extend the classification of binary systems into regions of thermodynamic instability to explore the interplay between phase separation and dynamical arrest. Strong cross-attractions kinetically suppress demixing, whereas competitive energy scales yield either condensation- or demixing-driven amorphous states. We show that this morphological crossover is parameterized by a structural order parameter, χ, providing a unified non-equilibrium framework that reconciles theoretical predictions with experimentally observed arrested mixtures.

papers.title: Publisher's Note: “Shape and size effects on incipient motion regimes of irregular particles in confined non-Newtonian annular shear flow” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 083106 (2026)]
Many-body dissipative particle dynamics study of mesoscale liquid film dewetting: Formation of heteromorphic droplets
papers.abstract: The dewetting behavior of nano-liquid films, strongly influenced by film thickness and substrate wettability, plays a key role in micro- and nano-device performance but remains inadequately described by traditional continuum models.
