In this study, a many-body dissipative particle dynamics (MDPD) framework is employed to construct a mesoscale liquid film dewetting model that bridges nanoscopic interactions and macroscopic statistical behavior. Dewetting kinetics are systematically investigated under varying film thicknesses and interfacial conditions, and five representative dewetting modes are identified: spinodal dewetting, nucleation dewetting, stable dewetting, heteromorphic-droplet dewetting, and stable films. Through energy and molecular force analysis, droplet pattern formation is found to comprise three stages: accelerated contraction, decelerated contraction, and droplet dissipation. In ultrathin films, the initial instability is mainly governed by thickness-dependent interfacial forces, whereas the later-stage retraction and droplet relaxation are influenced by curvature-dependent capillary effects. To rationalize multiple dewetting morphologies, the classical disjoining-pressure model is extended within the MDPD framework by introducing an exponential structural-force term, and the zero-crossings of the first derivative of the disjoining pressure are used as a semi-quantitative indicator for distinguishing dewetting regimes. Overall, nano-liquid film dewetting originates from the balance between internal molecular forces and substrate-induced interfacial forces. Based on this mechanism, a mesoscopic dewetting phase diagram is established, linking substrate wettability and film thickness to distinct dewetting morphologies. These findings provide insight into nano-film dewetting and guidance for wetting control and surface engineering in micro- and nano-device applications.

papers.title: Capillary waves on a liquid metal surface: Classical dispersion and effective surface tension under an oxide skin
papers.abstract: This study investigates capillary waves excited by droplet impact on a deep pool of Ga–In–Sn liquid metal, which spontaneously forms a nanometric oxide skin. High-speed specular reflection imaging is employed to capture the concentric wave rings, from which the wavelength and phase speed are extracted. The results demonstrate that the waves obey the classical dispersion relation ω2 = σk3/ρ despite the presence of the oxide layer. The effective surface tension retrieved from the dispersion law averages 0.313 N/m, which is close to the reported value for gallium oxide (∼0.35 N/m) but substantially lower than that of the pristine metal (0.614 N/m). This indicates that the oxide skin renormalizes the surface tension without altering the functional form of the dispersion. These findings establish droplet-impact capillary waves as a simple, contact-free probe for determining the effective surface tension of reactive liquid surfaces.

papers.title: Thermal effects on coupled density-driven solute transport in a layered heterogeneous coastal aquifer
papers.abstract: Variable-density flow and solute transport in porous media are fundamentally governed by groundwater–seawater thermal gradients and permeability heterogeneity. However, the coupled influence of temperature-induced variations in viscosity and density, together with stratification, on solute transport remains poorly understood. This study integrates laboratory experiments with numerical simulations to investigate solute transport dynamics under non-isothermal conditions in a stratified coastal aquifer containing a subsurface dam. Spatiotemporal variation, migration pathways, spreading characteristics, and solute mass fluxes are systematically evaluated under varying aquifer–ocean temperature contrasts and layered permeability configurations. Results reveal that cooling freshwater causes the saltwater wedge to contract while the upper saline plume expands. This phenomenon is driven by thermally induced changes in fluid density, viscosity, and hydraulic conductivity. Warmer freshwater reduces viscosity, enhancing localized hydraulic conductivity and accelerating flow within the freshwater zone. However, it simultaneously suppresses particle movement within the saltwater wedge through enhanced vertical density stratification. Conversely, colder freshwater markedly decelerates solute transport and reduces maximum mass discharge nearly threefold. Solutes released from the lower layer are more susceptible to mixing with residual saltwater upstream of the subsurface dam, with the average residence time prolonged by 1.8 times. The total efflux of upper-released solutes exhibits a distinct double-peak pattern due to post-discharge retention caused by the low-permeability layer. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that thermal forcing and permeability exert substantial impacts on plume spreading and mass discharge. Collectively, these findings provide fundamental physical insights into the coupled thermo-hydrodynamic mechanisms governing density-dependent solute transport in heterogeneous porous media.

papers.title: Data-driven short-crested wave prediction with improved generalization via hybrid feature standardization and training strategy
papers.abstract: Accurate phase-resolved prediction of multidirectional short-crested waves is essential for offshore engineering applications, yet the performance of data-driven models often deteriorates when encountering unseen sea states because of the distribution shift between training and testing conditions. To improve cross-sea-state generalization, this study proposes a hybrid optimization strategy that combines feature standardization based on significant wave height and mean wave period with multi-sea-state data fusion. The proposed strategy is validated using wave-basin experiments covering four short-crested sea states generated under a Joint North Sea Wave Project spectrum. Four representative neural-network models, including long short-term memory (LSTM), temporal convolutional network (TCN), convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM), and patch time series transformer (PatchTST), are employed to evaluate the model-independence of the proposed optimization strategy. The results demonstrate that the proposed strategy consistently improves the prediction accuracy of all evaluated models. Under the present experimental conditions, maximum root mean square error reductions of 37.2%, 19.0%, 43.7%, and 67.7% are achieved for the LSTM, TCN, ConvLSTM, and PatchTST models, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed optimization strategy effectively enhances the cross-sea-state generalization capability of the evaluated neural-network models under controlled laboratory conditions, providing a practical foundation for future validation under more diverse environmental conditions and field observations.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal asymmetric cavity dynamics during oblique water entry
papers.abstract: Cavity dynamics during water entry dictate the energy transfer and fluid–structure interactions that govern projectile stability. While oblique water entry induces pronounced spatiotemporal asymmetry in cavity expansion and contraction—differentiating it from vertical entry—the quantitative scaling laws and underlying physical mechanisms of this asymmetric behavior remain elusive. In this study, the asymmetric cavity evolution during oblique water entry is systematically investigated based on a coupled theoretical and numerical framework. A revised analytical model integrating velocity decay effects into the traditional constant-velocity framework is proposed, which substantially enhances the prediction accuracy of actual cavity boundaries. Validated multiphase flow simulations subsequently reveal substantial spatiotemporal asymmetries: the maximum radius and expansion duration of the upper cavity boundary exceed those of the lower boundary by up to 99% and 163%, respectively. Flow-field analysis demonstrates that this asymmetry is driven by a highly non-uniform pressure distribution. Specifically, the upper cavity boundary experiences a weaker adverse pressure gradient compared to the lower boundary, thereby demanding less work for expansion. This dynamic pressure imbalance enables greater radial growth and prolonged expansion on the upper side, dictating the asymmetric morphology. These findings provide a crucial theoretical foundation for evaluating hydrodynamic loads and trajectory stability in complex water-entry scenarios.

papers.title: Effect of vortex generator types on flow over a baseline and tubercle wing sections
papers.abstract: Passive flow control through leading-edge tubercles and vortex generators delays stall and enhances lift. The combined effects of these devices on the flow field and aerodynamic performance lack in-depth analysis. This study investigates the influence of three vortex generator (VG) geometries—rectangular, triangular, and a novel hybrid configuration—on baseline and tubercle-modified wing sections through Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes simulations with the k–ω shear stress transport turbulence model and complementary wind tunnel experiments at a Reynolds number of 2.74 × 105. VGs were placed at three chordwise positions (20%, 40%, and 50% chord) to assess their performance. Flow-field analysis of spanwise and chordwise vorticity distributions, along with turbulent kinetic energy contours, revealed the mechanisms by which VG-generated streamwise vortices energize the boundary layer and suppress separation. The results demonstrated that all VG types extend the stall angle by ∼3° and enhance the lift in both pre-stall and post-stall regimes. On the baseline wing, the hybrid VG at the 0.2C position delivers the maximum lift and aerodynamic efficiency across most angles of attack. In contrast, the triangular VG proves most effective in synergizing with tubercle-induced vortices to maximize lift on the tubercle wing. The hybrid configuration, however, demonstrates superior post-stall efficiency on both baseline and tubercled wing sections. These findings offer design guidance in unmanned aerial vehicles, wind turbines, and other low-speed applications where stall delay and lift enhancement are highly essential.

papers.title: Tip leakage effects on near-tip power transfer and energy dissipation in an axial pump-as-turbine
papers.abstract: To quantify the near-tip power-distribution reconfiguration and energy-dissipation characteristics induced by tip leakage in an axial pump-as-turbine (PAT) operating in pump mode, experimentally validated numerical simulations were performed on an axial PAT model. Tip leakage flow, mechanical energy transport, power distribution, and entropy production were analyzed under different flow coefficients and clearance ratios. The results show that pronounced tip leakage vortices and recirculation occur under low-flow rate conditions, whereas local reverse flow develops near the blade leading edge under high-flow rate conditions. Increasing the tip clearance expands the spatial extent of the leakage flow and tip leakage vortex and significantly enhances the forward mechanical energy input within the clearance. However, the specific energy carried by the leakage flow gradually decreases and subsequently exhibits reduced sensitivity to further clearance enlargement, indicating that the increased mechanical energy input is mainly driven by leakage-magnitude expansion. Power decomposition shows that near-tip energy input remains dominated by pressure power, whereas viscous shear power is more sensitive to clearance variation; the outermost 2% of the blade span is the most affected region. Within the investigated clearance range, the modeled local entropy production rate becomes less sensitive to further clearance enlargement beyond the intermediate-clearance range, indicating a gradual saturation tendency rather than a universal threshold. An additional open-tip mixed-flow PAT operating in pump mode exhibits consistent clearance-dependent trends. These results demonstrate the coupled responses of leakage-flow expansion, cross-clearance mechanical energy transport, near-tip wall-power reconfiguration, and associated local irreversible loss.

papers.title: Transient diffusion-controlled droplet growth beyond self-similarity: Insights from physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Droplet growth and evaporation are ubiquitous in nature and technology. In this work, we focus on diffusion-controlled condensational droplet growth under isothermal conditions. Obtaining a closed-form solution to this problem is challenging because of the moving-boundary condition at the droplet surface (the Stefan condition). However, in the limiting case of a vanishing initial radius and a constant diffusion coefficient, a self-similar solution exists, predicting that the droplet radius grows as the square root of time. The Stefan condition also complicates numerical solution using conventional methods. Here, we employ a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework to solve the governing diffusion equation coupled with the interfacial mass balance, treating the droplet radius as an additional trainable function of time. The PINN accurately reproduces the analytical self-similar solution, including both the droplet growth law and the concentration profiles. We then apply the framework to transient diffusion problems for which self-similar solutions are unavailable by considering droplet growth from a finite initial radius and introducing a concentration-dependent diffusion coefficient. In both cases, the numerical solutions converge toward the classical self-similar growth regime. These results demonstrate that the PINN framework provides an effective tool for solving moving-boundary diffusion problems beyond the reach of analytical methods, while also supporting the robustness of the classical self-similar solution.

papers.title: Electrohydrodynamic jet stability of ionic liquid–hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) mixtures under thermochemical propulsion constraints
papers.abstract: Hybrid propulsion systems combining electric and chemical propulsion have attracted considerable attention because they can provide both high specific impulse and high thrust within a single propulsion architecture. This study investigates the feasibility of ionic liquid–hydroxylammonium nitrate (HAN) mixtures as a single propellant for hybrid electro-chemical propulsion systems through electrospray experiments and thermodynamic performance analysis. Electrospray experiments were conducted under atmospheric conditions using a downward-oriented annular slit emitter to examine the effects of HAN concentration, applied voltage, and flow rate on jet morphology, droplet formation, and pulsation behavior. Increasing HAN concentration significantly altered electrospray characteristics by reducing viscosity and increasing electrical conductivity. Higher applied voltages promoted finer atomization and increased pulsating frequency, whereas higher flow rates generated larger droplets due to enhanced inertial effects. Among the tested compositions, mixtures containing 50%–75% HAN exhibited stable jet emission, favorable atomization characteristics, and enhanced pulsation response. To evaluate chemical propulsion performance, NASA chemical equilibrium with applications calculations were performed at a chamber pressure of 300 psia and a nozzle expansion ratio of 50. HAN-rich mixtures showed higher adiabatic flame temperatures, increased specific impulse, and lower molecular-weight combustion products. Overall, the results demonstrate that mixtures containing 50%–75% HAN provide the most favorable balance between electrospray stability and combustion performance. This study identifies an optimal propellant composition range (50%–75% HAN) that simultaneously satisfies the competing demands of electrohydrodynamic emission stability and chemical propulsion performance, providing a key design guideline for future single-propellant hybrid propulsion systems.

papers.title: Sweep-angle-regulated aerodynamic interference mechanisms in dragonfly tandem wings
papers.abstract: Dragonflies achieve remarkable flight performance through their unique tandem-wing configuration; however, the aerodynamic interference mechanisms regulated by wing morphological parameters remain insufficiently understood. In this study, numerical simulations based on prescribed flapping kinematics were conducted to investigate the effects of sweep angle on the aerodynamic interactions between the forewing and hindwing of dragonfly-inspired tandem wings. Variations in aerodynamic forces, vortex structures, and aerodynamic efficiency were analyzed. The results indicate that the sweep angle is a key parameter governing the coupling between the forewing wake and the hindwing leading-edge vortex (LEV). When the sweep angle remains small (δ ≤ 10°), strong aerodynamic interactions exist between the two wings. As the sweep angle increases, the relative spatial relationship between the hindwing and the forewing wake changes, thereby weakening the inter-wing interaction. More importantly, the dominant interference mechanism exhibits a pronounced dependence on the forewing–hindwing phase difference. Under in-phase flapping, the forewing trailing-edge vortex and the hindwing LEV form an inter-wing dipole vortex structure that suppresses the development of the hindwing LEV. For 45° ≤ ψ ≤ 135°, the aerodynamic response of the hindwing is governed by the pronounced strip-shaped disturbance region generated as the forewing root vortex sweeps across the hindwing surface. When the phase difference increases to 180°, the dominant interference shifts to the wrapping interaction of the forewing tip vortex with the hindwing, which modifies the vortex structures and pressure distribution. Overall, sweep angle regulates tandem-wing aerodynamic performance by controlling the phase-dependent interaction pathways between distinct forewing wake structures and the hindwing.

papers.title: Characteristics of combustion instability mode transition under transient switching operations in a coaxial staged combustor
papers.abstract: To address the unclear mechanisms underlying the mode transition of combustion instability induced by variations in fuel staging ratios, transient numerical simulations of the dynamic fuel switching process in a natural gas coaxial staged combustor were conducted using Wall-Modeled Large Eddy Simulation coupled with the partially premixed Flamelet Generated Manifold approach. Combining the Synchrosqueezing Wavelet Transform and delay-coordinate phase-space reconstruction, the temporal evolution and trajectory morphology of the combustion response were analyzed. The time-frequency evolution characteristics of the heat release rate (HRR) alongside temperature and velocity flow fields were comprehensively tracked. The results demonstrate that the combustion response depends strongly on the initial operating condition and switching path. Identical target fuel-staging ratios may exhibit distinct combustion responses owing to different switching histories, demonstrating path dependence. The variation in HRR induced by changing the fuel staging ratio was closely associated with the mode transition. Specifically, during the S4 → U1 switch, a transient decrease followed by an increase in HRR was observed during the early switching stage. This variation was associated with changes in the shear-layer dynamics and vortex evolution, which contributed to the subsequent transition of the combustion mode. Spectral and correlation analyses showed coincident dominant pressure and global-HRR frequencies of 300–450 Hz with high magnitude-squared coherence in seven cases, whereas S5 → U2 exhibited frequency mismatch and a substantially lower zero-lag Pearson correlation coefficient. Moreover, delay-coordinate phase portraits further revealed distinct trajectory morphologies among the switching paths, supporting the path dependence identified from the time-domain analysis.

papers.title: Lamella evolution of glycerol–water droplets on a rotating surface
papers.abstract: The study presents an experimental investigation of droplet impact on a rotating smooth stainless-steel surface. High-speed imaging was used to quantify the time-resolved lamella area for water and glycerol–water solutions over rotational speeds from 0 to 10 000 rpm and impact velocities from 1.2 to 1.8 m s−1. The results show that for water droplets, a four-stage lamella evolution is identified at intermediate rotational speeds, consisting of inertia-driven spreading, capillary-driven receding, rotation-induced secondary spreading, and a capillary–centrifugal annular expansion stage. At sufficiently high rotational speeds, capillary-driven receding is fully suppressed, and the lamella expands continuously under rotation-dominated conditions. Increasing viscosity reduces the maximum lamella area and slows capillary-driven recession, while also stabilizing the lamella against rapid thinning. A distinct transition time τtr is identified from the reversal of viscosity ordering in the lamella area: before τtr, more viscous liquids spread less, whereas after τtr, they retain a larger lamella. This reversal is enhanced by rotation but originates from late-time viscous–capillary dynamics rather than from the regime-map transition itself. The normalized transition time remains of order unity relative to the inertial-capillary time, confirming that inertial-capillary relaxation controls the timing of the reversal, while rotation primarily governs the strength of the post-transition reorganization. A regime map and rotational Bond number analysis further distinguish between temporal control of the transition and centrifugal dominance after transition.

papers.title: Wax esters solubility in triacylglycerols: Molecular dynamics study of liquid state interactions and conformations
papers.abstract: The dissolution of wax esters (WEs) in liquid oils plays a central role in the bulk solution thermodynamic characteristics, yet the molecular origins of their solubility remain poorly understood. In the current study, the fluid organization of WEs in medium-chain triacylglycerol (TAG) was explored using molecular dynamics simulations. Three WEs differing in their total carbon number, and having equal asymmetry between the lengths of their alkyl chains, were examined as pure systems and at 10 mol. % mixed in a model TAG. Excess volumes and excess enthalpies were calculated to evaluate deviations from ideal mixing, while molecular conformations, radial distribution functions, Kirkwood–Buff integrals, and aggregate statistics were evaluated. The simulations revealed ideal mixing for CN30ΔCN2 and CN34ΔCN2, whereas CN46ΔCN2 exhibited significant positive excess volume and excess enthalpy, indicating reduced compatibility with the TAG. Analysis of molecular conformations showed that shorter WEs possess alkyl chain end-to-end distance distributions closer to those of the TAG fatty acids, resulting in greater conformational compatibility. Structural analysis demonstrated that local organizations in these fluids are primarily governed by interactions between the central polar ester moieties rather than by alkyl-chain packing. The longest WE exhibited reduced local density fluctuations, explaining its larger deviation from ideality. Aggregate analysis showed that shorter WEs form fewer but larger and more interconnected transient clusters, whereas longer WEs form smaller organizations. These findings provide a molecular-level framework linking molecular conformations, local fluid structure, and non-ideal mixing in WE–TAG mixtures, offering fundamental insight into the structure–thermodynamics relation of complex organic fluids.

papers.title: Adjoint-based swirling flow injection control in a model combustion chamber: A numerical study
papers.abstract: In the present work, an adjoint-based flow control strategy to suppress the precessing vortex core (PVC) in a swirl-stabilized model combustion chamber was studied. A global linear stability analysis of the mean flow yielded a marginally stable mode with azimuthal wavenumber m=1, accounting for the PVC oscillations. The structural sensitivity map, constructed from the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions, identified the wavemaker region near the flow separation point, which was parametrically tested for the PVC suppression. In the main-flow simulations, a constant airflow of 2%–8% of the total flow rate was injected at different positions inside the area of the highest sensitivity. Pressure probe spectra indicated that injection at the wavemaker achieved around 50% attenuation with a modest 4% flow rate, while off-wavemaker positions yielded stronger suppression (70%–80%) at higher injection rates. However, a more detailed analysis using spectral proper orthogonal decomposition revealed the following: injection at the wavemaker x0 and at the downstream position x1 both suppressed the PVC by approximately 70% at 8% flow rate, with shifting the PVC frequency. In contrast, injection at the upstream position x2 led to an increase in the PVC energy, which was not captured by the pressure probe spectra. The results demonstrated that the sensitivity map reliably guides actuator placement, achieving effective PVC mitigation.

papers.title: Wake phase interference for passive self-damping of pressure fluctuations in a negative curvature valve
papers.abstract: Passive control of pressure fluctuations in internal flows is of fundamental interest in stability-sensitive hydraulic and transport systems. This study develops a phase-based concept for understanding passive filtering effects arising from wake-forcing interaction. Specifically, the analysis demonstrates that downstream pressure modulation is governed by amplitude-phase coupling within the wake, rather than by vortex intensity alone. On this basis, a theoretical criterion is derived to distinguish regimes of attenuation and amplification, thereby identifying vortex strength, phase separation, and modal coherence as the key controlling parameters. To validate the proposed criterion, a spherical check valve and several concave modifications are examined as a representative configuration. The finite-element simulations show that attenuation can be achieved either by strengthening a dominant vortex or by increasing vortex multiplicity. Under an optimal concave geometry, the peak pressure fluctuation amplitude is reduced by up to 58.4% relative to the spherical valve. Conversely, excessive vortex fragmentation degrades coherence and shifts the system into amplification. Furthermore, tests under triangular forcing and varying amplitudes reveal that the mechanism persists under broader spectral conditions, although its efficiency is ultimately governed by timescale competition between vortex formation and external forcing.

papers.title: Study on mechanism and microstructural characteristics of mineral dissolution and pore evolution driven by high-temperature steam flow
papers.abstract: High-temperature steam flow in unconsolidated sandstone triggers complex coupling among hydrodynamic motion, interfacial mass transfer, and mineral dissolution, which further reshapes pore networks and alters fluid transport properties. However, the reactive–seepage coupling mechanism governing mineral dissolution-induced pore network evolution under high-temperature steam flow remains poorly understood. This work conducts sand-packed flow simulation experiments under formation compaction conditions with varied particle geometric features and steam parameters. Scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy were used to characterize microscale grain and pore variations. The results show that grain evolution is jointly controlled by hydrodynamic shear and thermal stress. The overall dissolution rate depends on both particle and flow conditions, while the maximum dimensionless dissolution amount is governed solely by particle geometry, reaching a peak of 4.10% at a grain size of 0.10 mm. A predictive model combining boundary-layer mass transfer theory and Noyes–Whitney kinetics is established, with a high fitting accuracy of R2≥0.97. This work reveals the fundamental coupling rules of flow, mass transfer, and solid reaction in granular porous media and provides theoretical support for evaluating pore evolution during high-temperature fluid displacement.

papers.title: Representing submerged flexible vegetation with buoyancy-dominated, non-uniform surrogates
papers.abstract: Submerged flexible vegetation significantly influences aquatic flow dynamics, as well as mass and energy transport. While simplified plant surrogates have facilitated theoretical, numerical, and experimental studies, many existing models rely on uniform blades, beams, cylinders, or other simplified flexible structures, and therefore, only partly represent the distributed leafy clusters and thin tensile stems of many submerged plants. In this study, we introduce a buoyancy-dominated, non-uniform plant surrogate composed of pellets connected by a thin flexible filament to represent a class of aquatic plants with compliant stems and distributed leaf clusters, such as Cabomba caroliniana and Ceratophyllum demersum. We develop a mechanistic model that links hydrodynamic forces to plant posture, where posture denotes the time-averaged inclination and bending shape of the surrogate in the streamwise–vertical plane. The analysis yields non-dimensional parameters that predict surrogate behavior and clarify how drag coefficient CD, density ratio ρ*, pellet Froude number Fr*, and submergence ratio H* affect the force balance. Virtual stiffness is introduced as an equivalent, flow-condition-dependent measure of bending produced by spatially varying pellet properties. Laboratory experiments with an isolated physical surrogate test the theoretical model for the surrogate itself; they do not by themselves establish full biological equivalence to natural vegetation. The comparisons show that most posture predictions fall within a ±15% visual error band under the tested moderate-flow conditions, while larger deviations occur when pellet interaction, filament drag and unsteady motion become more important. The results provide an efficient framework for three-dimensional physical and mathematical modeling of fluid–vegetation coupling.

papers.title: Effect and correction of turbulence coefficient on performance calculation of aerostatic thrust bearing lubricated by supercritical CO2
papers.abstract: In this article, the flow field and bearing performance of aerostatic thrust bearing (ATB) lubricated by supercritical CO2 (ATB-SCO2) are analyzed by solving the Reynolds equation with the laminar model and four turbulence models (Hirs model, Ng–Pan model, Constantinescu model, and Elrod–Ng model) through the finite difference method. The calculation accuracy and efficiency of ATB-SCO2 performance under different flow and CO2 models are discussed. Furthermore, the turbulence coefficient is corrected by analyzing the influences of empirical coefficient and empirical exponent on the calculation results of ATB-SCO2 performance. The turbulence models with turbulence coefficients increase the pressure and Reynolds number but decrease the velocity in the lubricating film. The ideal gas assumption shows the same effect (i.e., an increase) on pressure but opposite effects (i.e., an increase) on Reynolds number and velocity. Moreover, both turbulence models with turbulence coefficients and ideal gas assumption increase the bearing load capacity and stiffness but reduce the mass flow rate. Compared to Elrod–Ng model, the calculation adopting laminar model, Hirs model, Ng–Pan model, and Constantinescu model are less accurate but more efficient. The accuracy using the model with corrected turbulence coefficient improves by 86.02%, 82.03%, and 79.56% compared to Hirs model, Ng–Pan model, and Constantinescu model, respectively, and the calculation time reduces by 92.56% compared to Elrod–Ng model. The corrected turbulence coefficient is further verified by the performance calculation of ATB-SCO2 at eight working conditions.

papers.title: Slag crust solidification in copper–steel composite cooling staves for blast furnaces
papers.abstract: Intensified blast furnace ironmaking has aggravated refractory erosion and cooling component failure, making the formation of a stable slag crust increasingly important for long campaign life. In this study, a three-dimensional transient model coupling molten slag flow, heat transfer, and phase change was developed to quantify slag crust formation on a copper–steel composite cooling stave. The enthalpy–porosity method and temperature-dependent thermophysical properties were employed to describe the evolution of the liquid fraction, mushy zone, and effective slag crust thickness. The model was validated using in-plant thermocouple measurements from the furnace belly. The results show that a continuous solidified band forms within 10–15 s, and complete coverage of the hot face is achieved after approximately 60 s. The effective slag crust thickness increases from approximately 5–6 to 23 mm during 30–600 s and reaches approximately 43 mm at 2400 s. The safety threshold of 30 mm is first reached at approximately 1170 s. In addition, the predicted peak thermocouple temperature of approximately 228 °C and recovery time of approximately 32 min agree well with the measured response during severe spalling events. These results demonstrate that the proposed model can quantitatively describe the transient formation and re-formation of the slag crust and the corresponding thermal response of the cooling stave, providing a basis for slag crust evaluation and cooling strategy optimization.

papers.title: Numerical investigation on the early-stage high-speed water entry of trans-media vehicle with spike
papers.abstract: Compared with low-speed water entry, high-speed water entry involves stronger impact loads and more complex multiphase flow phenomena. Accurate prediction of flowfield evolution and impact load is therefore essential for the development of trans-media vehicles. In this study, a solver enhancement based on overInterPhaseChangeDyMFoam is proposed by combining the volume of fluid method with the Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model and incorporating air effects into a two-phase cavitation framework. This solver enables simulations of cavitation during high-speed water entry and is validated against published experimental and theoretical results. The validated solver is then used to investigate the early-stage water-entry process of a spiked trans-media vehicle, with emphasis on flowfield development and hydrodynamic response. These results show that the spike effectively induces flow separation and establishes a stable low-pressure region near the vehicle nose, thereby promoting rapid supercavity formation. The cavity maintains a slender geometry and exhibits quasi-self-similar evolution, whereas radial expansion follows a nonlinear growth trend. As the cavity gradually envelops the vehicle body, the wetted area decreases markedly. Consequently, the drag coefficient rapidly approaches a low quasi-steady level, vehicle deceleration is suppressed, and penetration depth increases approximately linearly with time.

papers.title: Pressure loss in confluence flow with small branch angles and variable mainline geometry
papers.abstract: This work identifies a special confluence flow emerging at the confluence sections between the mainline and the on-ramp of bifurcated tunnels, which is characterized by small branch angles and variable mainline cross sections and hence is distinct from conventional confluence flow in T-shaped pipes in terms of its flow pattern and pressure loss mechanism. A numerical model was constructed and validated against experiments and then utilized to investigate the pressure loss characteristics. Results showed that because of the small branch angle of bifurcated tunnels (usually no more than 30°), flow separation at the junction of conventional T-shaped pipes no longer occurs. Instead, airflow from the branch with a larger velocity (either the mainline or the on-ramp) enters the confluence section as a jet, and the turbulence dissipation on the jet boundaries contributes a large part (sometimes over 80%) to the pressure loss. Subsequently, effects of the variation of cross section under different lane configurations and also the velocity difference between the mainline and the ramp were discussed quantitatively. Finally, a novel semi-theoretical model embracing the turbulence dissipation under different lane configurations was developed accordingly to predict the confluence loss coefficient of both the mainline and the ramp, and then validated against experimental data in the literature to demonstrate its applicability.

papers.title: Effects of the Atwood number on three-dimensional azimuthal instability of a shock-accelerated spherical bubble
papers.abstract: The shock-driven evolution of a three-dimensional (3D) spherical gas bubble occurs frequently in natural phenomena and engineering applications. In the present study, the interaction between a planar shock wave and a spherical interface is investigated numerically by solving the 3D, compressible Euler equations using a fifth-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory scheme. A series of numerical cases spanning a wide range of Atwood (At) numbers is performed to examine the shock–bubble interaction (SBI), with emphasis on azimuthal instability. The results indicate that a primary vortex ring is consistently formed following shock acceleration of the spherical interface, whereas a leading vortex ring appears only in the case of heavy bubbles (At>0). As the distorted interface evolves, a pronounced At-dependent azimuthal instability emerges, exhibiting a clear modal distribution dominated by the m=4 mode: for heavy bubbles, the growth of azimuthal instability increases with increasing At number. Larger At numbers lead to stronger vortex ring formation; the accompanying shock wave reflections further reinforce the azimuthal disturbances, resulting in the growth of azimuthal modes over a broad range of scales. As the At number decreases, the azimuthal instability shifts toward the gradual amplification of small-scale perturbations. In contrast, for light bubbles (At<0), strong convective transport promotes a more pronounced development of azimuthal modes. These findings highlight the critical role of azimuthal instability in SBI beyond traditional streamwise analyses, with the dominant modal behavior consistently observed but its quantitative characteristics dependent on the adopted computational configuration.

papers.title: Mean field responses in disordered systems: An example from rotating nonlinear magnetohydrodynamic
papers.abstract: This study extends mean-field magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) theory by incorporating rotational effects, represented by the Coriolis term fk×u (where f is the Coriolis parameter, k is the unit vector along the rotation axis, and u the velocity fluctuation). The four principal mean-field tensors α(1), α(2), Γ(1), and Γ(2) are reformulated to account for rotation. Key findings show that rotation breaks symmetry, generating a nonzero Γ(1) tensor that couples mean flow and magnetic fields. The α(1) dynamo effect is modulated along the rotation axis, depending on helicity distribution. Rotation generally suppresses certain instabilities while promoting hybrid rotation magnetic field instabilities. Under weak to moderate rotation, the system exhibits a broader linear response range, indicating that rotation mitigates chaotic turbulence and stabilizes mean-field quantities (i.e., it reduces the growth rate of large-scale perturbations and broadens the range of mean-field amplitudes over which the electromotive force responds linearly). This work extends mean-field MHD to rotating systems, offering a more comprehensive framework for analyzing large-scale dynamo processes and instabilities in astrophysical and laboratory settings.

papers.title: Mechanisms of stripe-like heat transfer and shock-induced thermal loads on transonic turbine blade tips with varying clearances
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of turbine blade tip clearance on thermal characteristics and flow structures through combined experimental and numerical methods. Three different tip clearance sizes (t = 0.50%, 0.83%, and 1.33% of the blade height) are analyzed in detail to reveal the underlying physical mechanisms of over-tip leakage (OTL) flow. The results demonstrate that enlarging the tip gap considerably increases the leakage mass flux, leading to a corresponding rise in the area-averaged heat transfer coefficient (HTC) on the tip by 8.2%. A distinctive stripe-like HTC pattern is observed in the midchord region of the tip, which is fundamentally attributed to the mixing of high-energy main leakage flow and low-energy near-wall fluid. As the clearance size increases, the scale of the leakage vortex expands, resulting in larger-scale heat transfer stripes. Furthermore, the study reveals that the heat transfer performance of transonic OTL flow is strongly influenced by complex shock wave structures. Flow separation and reattachment, induced by shock reflection and shock–boundary layer interaction, create alternating regions of high and low thermal load. In larger clearance cases, the emergence of normal shocks downstream further intensifies the heat load near the pressure side. The interaction between shock waves and the boundary layer, together with flow reattachment, increases heat load nonuniformity, and the high heat transfer region moves toward the midchord of the tip.

papers.title: Investigation of convection velocities of three velocity components and scalars in the atmospheric boundary layer
papers.abstract: In this study, a dataset of synchronously measured wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity acquired by an unmanned aerial vehicle array at multiple streamwise locations is employed to investigate the convection velocities of three velocity components, temperature, and relative humidity in the atmospheric boundary layer at heights up to 150 m. Results show that the global convection velocities of the streamwise (Ucu), spanwise (Ucv), and vertical (Ucw) wind speed components, as well as temperature (Uct) and relative humidity (Uch), are statistically slightly larger than the local mean velocity (U). Statistical analysis of the ratios between each convection velocity and the U reveals that the convection velocities of three velocity components and scalars are roughly 10% higher than U. Scale-dependent convection velocities of streamwise velocity, temperature, and relative humidity show that these values decrease with increasing frequency within the range 0.01 Hz ≤ f ≤ 0.1 Hz, and the convection velocities of large-scale (or low-frequency) flow structures at f = 0.01 Hz are approximately three times larger than U. In contrast to laboratory turbulent boundary layer flows, atmospheric boundary layer flow can receive energy input at its upper boundary, which may drive high-speed flow structures toward the ground. This is consistent with the hypothesis that the enhanced convection velocities may be associated with large-scale turbulent structures and the possible downward transport of high-speed flow structures in the atmospheric boundary layer.

papers.title: Drop deformation in planar extensional flows: Numerical study on viscoplastic drops and viscoplastic surrounding media
papers.abstract: The deformation of a drop in an extensional flow of a second immiscible fluid has importance in various industrial processes. In most of the industrial applications, fluids exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. Despite their importance, the mechanism governing the deformation of non-Newtonian drops subjected to an extensional flow remains poorly understood. The same assertion applies to Newtonian drops immersed in non-Newtonian fluids. This work numerically investigates the effects of plasticity on the deformation of a drop immersed in a second fluid undergoing planar extensional flow. We start our analysis with both fluids being Newtonian. The deformation of a viscoplastic drop in a planar extensional flow of a Newtonian fluid is analyzed and qualitatively compared with a work that explored axisymmetric extensional motions. Next, the deformation of a Newtonian drop immersed in a viscoplastic material under planar extensional flow is analyzed. When both liquids are Newtonian, the deformation increases with capillary number for a fixed viscosity ratio. Similarly, the deformation is higher at higher viscosity ratios when the capillary number is kept fixed. For a viscoplastic droplet immersed in a Newtonian fluid, we find that increasing the droplet's plasticity increases its deformation. If the suspending medium is a viscoplastic material and the drop is Newtonian, our results show that stronger plastic effects reduce droplet deformation and increase the critical capillary number. To interpret the results, we recall that the Newtonian–Newtonian system was shown to exhibit an Oldroyd-B-like behavior with the elasticity coming from the interface. Hence, the viscoplastic-Newtonian system can be considered elasto-viscoplastic. We also compared some tendencies obtained in this work with the problem of long drops immersed in a second fluid in a tube under a pressure gradient.

papers.title: Morphological evolution patterns of intrinsically curved flexible fibers in a simple linear shear flow
papers.abstract: The dynamics of flexible fibers remains complex in a linear shear flow. Although this problem has been extensively investigated, the effect of intrinsic curvature has received comparatively little attention. Actually, the fiber often possesses a finite intrinsic curvature, making the commonly assumed straight configuration an idealization that may not accurately represent realistic behavior. In this study, the effect of intrinsic curvature is incorporated into the analysis. Using a simplified bead-chain model, we simulate the motion of flexible fibers in a linear shear flow and identify several distinct morphological evolution patterns. Based on the dynamical characteristics of patterns, we propose a procedure to efficiently distinguish between these patterns. Furthermore, phase diagrams are obtained in the parameter space of intrinsic curvature angle and the bending-to-hydrodynamic ratio. The results show that fiber dynamics is highly sensitive to intrinsic curvature when it is small, but once the curvature angle exceeds a critical threshold, i.e., θ≈0.4π, the morphological evolution of fibers depends primarily on the bending-to-hydrodynamic ratio. Additionally, transitions between different patterns are mainly controlled by the competition between intrinsic curvature and hydrodynamically induced bending.

papers.title: Synergistic drag reduction of cross-medium propellers using biomimetic leading-edge tubercles and superhydrophobic surfaces
papers.abstract: To mitigate efficiency loss and excessive drag of cross-medium propellers operating in air and water, we evaluate a synergistic drag-reduction concept combining biomimetic leading-edge tubercles with a superhydrophobic surface (SHS). Three propellers were fabricated: a smooth baseline (A0), a 2.5%-chord tubercled propeller (A2.5), and a tubercled SHS propeller (AS2.5). Thrust coefficient (KT), torque coefficient (KQ), and efficiency (η) were measured in towing-tank and open-air tests, and surface pressure and skin-friction distributions were analyzed in STAR-CCM+ using multiple reference frame–Reynolds-average Navier–Stokes with the shear stress transport k–ω model. In water at J = 1.0, A2.5 increased KT by 13.5% and η by 1.4% vs A0, while AS2.5 increased KT by 18.6% and η by 3.6%, with a 12.47% higher peak η. In air, AS2.5 improved η by 6.5% at J = 1.0 and raised peak η by 17.1%. Numerical simulations and mechanistic analyses indicate that the biomimetic leading-edge tubercles generate streamwise vortices, redistribute and segment the low-pressure region near the leading edge, and delay local flow separation, whereas the superhydrophobic interface reduces near-wall friction through effective slip. Their integration on the same blade surface couples geometric flow control with interfacial friction reduction, causing the increase in propeller thrust to exceed the accompanying increase in torque and thereby achieving drag reduction and enhanced propulsive efficiency.

papers.title: Field measurements of the effects of tunnel parameters on aerodynamic pressure and longitudinal airflow velocity inside a metro express train
papers.abstract: Increasing the design speed of metro express lines leads to intensified airflow velocity and pressure fluctuations within carriages, thereby compromising passenger ride comfort. In this study, field measurements were conducted on an express metro line with a design speed of 120 km/h. The formation mechanisms and spatiotemporal characteristics of longitudinal airflow velocity and transient pressure variations within the carriage were investigated, and the effects of tunnel length and blockage ratio on these aerodynamic parameters were evaluated. The results show that aerodynamic effects are the dominant mechanism governing the formation of longitudinal airflow during train operation in tunnels. Under these conditions, the longitudinal airflow velocity exhibits a positive correlation with the exterior–interior pressure difference. During the stable flow stage, the maximum average longitudinal airflow velocity reaches 4.27 m/s. For short tunnels, the relatively low energy dissipation of pressure waves during propagation results in larger pressure amplitudes on train surfaces. In contrast, their effect on the average longitudinal airflow velocity remains insignificant. Furthermore, reducing the blockage ratio can substantially alleviate aerodynamic effects. Specifically, when the blockage ratio drops from 0.438 to 0.365, the maximum reductions in pressure amplitude and average longitudinal airflow velocity reach 33.57% and 59.69%, respectively. When the train operates at the maximum speed of 120 km/h in a tunnel with a blockage ratio of 0.438, only the airflow velocity in the head car remains within the acceptable range for passengers. These findings provide essential data to support the design of tunnel parameters for metro express lines.

papers.title: Confinement-induced transitions in the dynamics of self-diffusiophoretic microswimmer under Poiseuille flow
papers.abstract: The dynamics of artificial microswimmers in confined flows remain poorly understood despite their relevance to microfluidics, drug delivery, and the navigation of active particles through physiological pathways. Here, we investigate the self-diffusiophoretic motion of spherical Janus particles in pressure-driven Poiseuille flow within microchannels, systematically spanning the weak to strong confinement regime. Using bispherical eigenfunction expansions for the solute and flow fields, we analyze swimmer-boundary interactions in weak to moderate confinement, while complementary finite-element simulations are employed to examine the strongly confined regime without invoking artificial steric potentials. Our analysis reveals that confinement fundamentally reshapes swimmer trajectories: near-wall equilibria characteristic of weak confinement is destroyed, giving rise to centerline attractors, oscillatory states with confinement-dependent wavelengths. Furthermore, the non-trivial coupling between diffusiophoretic slip, hydrodynamic interactions with opposing walls, and the curvature of Poiseuille flow yields striking modifications of trajectories, including confinement-induced transitions from centerline to wall-bound states. These results demonstrate that strongly confined environments cannot be captured by far-field or weak-confinement theories, and they emphasize the essential role of geometric confinement in dictating active particle transport. Beyond providing physical insight into the interplay between chemical activity, hydrodynamics, and flow curvature, our findings further establish design principles for the controlled deployment of microswimmers in narrow fluidic passages of technological and biomedical significance.

papers.title: Thermal flows with moving boundaries via adaptive Cartesian grid discrete unified gas kinetic scheme
papers.abstract: In recent years, the discrete unified gas kinetic scheme (DUGKS) has attracted considerable attention and demonstrated remarkable potential in the simulation of a wide range of challenging multi-scale flow problems. Nevertheless, the majority of existing studies remain confined to uniform rectangular grids. Although certain recent works have explored static non-uniform grid configurations, their capacity to efficiently handle unsteady problems is still limited. To overcome this limitation, the present work proposes an adaptive Cartesian grid (ACG) strategy within the DUGKS framework. A refinement criterion based on local vortex intensity is employed. The mesh is refined in regions where the local vortex indicator exceeds a prescribed upper threshold, and coarsened in regions where it falls below a prescribed lower threshold. Information transfer between the old and new grids is accomplished through second-order linear or bilinear interpolation, while conservation properties are rigorously maintained throughout the adaptation process. The proposed ACG-DUGKS method is validated through a series of benchmark simulations, including lid-driven cavity flow, natural convection in a square enclosure, mixed convection in a cavity with an eccentrically placed cylinder, non-isothermal flow past a circular cylinder, and the settling of two hot particles in an enclosure. The numerical results demonstrate that the ACG-DUGKS method achieves excellent accuracy, computational efficiency, and geometric flexibility. Furthermore, the simulation of unequal-density dual-particle settling reveals that placing a lighter particle beneath a heavier one promotes faster particle approach and earlier collision, thereby enhancing inter-particle mixing.

papers.title: Wind-tunnel study of the effect of autorotation on feather and nylon badminton shuttlecock
papers.abstract: An experimental investigation of the aerodynamics of popular models of synthetic nylon and duck/goose-feather shuttlecocks used in badminton, with and without autorotation, is conducted in a low-speed wind tunnel over a speed range of 20–70 m/s. The coupled influence of autorotation and structural deformation on their aerodynamic performance is examined. Synthetic shuttlecocks exhibit significantly larger structural deformation due to their more flexible skirt and, unlike the feather shuttlecock, buckle beyond a critical speed. Non-rotating shuttlecocks show a reduction in the cross-sectional area of skirt with increasing speed, accompanied by a corresponding decrease in drag coefficient. In contrast, rotating shuttlecocks demonstrate an initial decrease in drag at lower speeds, followed by an increase in both drag coefficient and cross-sectional area of the skirt at higher free-stream speeds. Rotation results in an increase in drag and eliminates buckling of skirt or delays it to higher speed. The autorotation speed increases approximately linearly with an increase in free-stream speed up to speeds where the change in the cross-sectional area of the skirt is small. Expansion of skirt increases autorotation speed while its contraction reduces it. Of the two models of nylon shuttlecock tested, one of them experiences very large autorotation speed and expansion of the skirt beyond a certain speed resulting in much larger drag coefficient compared to that for a feather shuttlecock.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic interactions and rotational dynamics of tandem cylindrical particles in shear-thinning fluids
papers.abstract: In this study, the torque, rotational dynamics, and steady-state orientation characteristics of tandem cylindrical particles in the linear shear flow of shear-thinning fluids are investigated using particle-resolved direct numerical simulation. The coupling mechanisms among fluid inertia, shear-thinning properties, shear strength, and particle spacing are revealed. The results indicate that the interaction between two particles significantly affects the torque coefficient, rotational velocity, and equilibrium orientation angle of the trailing particle, while having a smaller effect on the leading particle. Stronger shear-thinning reduces the torque coefficients of the two particles, while weakening the effect of particle–particle interactions on torque and rotational dynamics. The rotational behavior of the particles exhibits single directional rotation and damped oscillatory rotation. The rotational oscillation amplitude of the trailing particle is significantly larger than that of the leading particle, and it requires a longer time to reach a steady state. The steady-state orientations of the two cylindrical particles show the same orientation at low Reynolds numbers and opposite orientations at high Reynolds numbers. Multiplicative scaling-law relations are established to quantify the effects of the governing parameters on the torque coefficient and equilibrium orientation angle of the two particles. Finally, support vector regression models are established to predict the torque coefficient and equilibrium orientation angle of the two particles based on the governing variables. These findings enrich the dynamic theory of the interaction between multiple cylindrical particles and non-Newtonian fluids.

papers.title: Mechanism of unsteady flow and fluid–structure coupled vibration during rapid startup of a large Francis turbine
papers.abstract: Rapid startup of large Francis turbines involves strongly coupled guide-vane motion, runner acceleration, water-hammer propagation, cavitation evolution, and structural vibration. However, the fluid–physical pathway through which these transient flow processes generate runner dynamic stress remains insufficiently clarified. In this study, a one-dimensional–three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics–finite-element method coupled model is developed for a prototype large Francis turbine to investigate the complete startup process. The results reveal that rapid guide-vane opening produces a high-speed annular swirling jet in the vaneless space because the guide-vane opening rate is not synchronized with runner acceleration. This jet impinges on the runner inlet and drives the early-stage vortex formation, flow separation, and impact cavitation. As the runner accelerates, the vortical structures migrate downstream along the blade passages, and the cavitation pattern evolves from impact cavitation to vortex cavitation and cloud cavitation near the blade trailing edge. The dominant pressure-pulsation components also shift from low-frequency water-hammer-related fluctuations to rotor–stator interaction frequencies. The resulting hydraulic excitation is transmitted to the runner structure, producing pronounced dynamic stress near the blade trailing edge and the crown/band junctions. The suction-side trailing edge shows the strongest stress response, indicating that vortex-cavitation evolution is a primary source of local flow-induced vibration during rapid startup. These findings clarify the transient coupling chain from guide-vane motion to swirling flow, cavitation, pressure pulsation, and runner stress response, providing physical guidance for startup regulation and vibration-resistant runner design.

papers.title: Effect of superimposed steady and oscillatory shear flows on rheology of dilute bubble suspensions
papers.abstract: We theoretically investigated the rheological properties of dilute bubble suspensions under parallel combined shear deformation consisting of both non-zero mean and superimposed oscillatory shear. The viscoelastic behavior is governed by three dimensionless parameters: two capillary numbers representing the magnitudes of the mean and oscillatory shear components, and a dynamic capillary number characterizing the unsteadiness of bubble deformation. The rheology is essentially classified into four regimes. We propose a strategy for evaluating viscoelasticity under parallel combined shear deformation and demonstrate its usefulness.

papers.title: Adsorption-induced wettability alteration in chemical enhanced oil recovery: Interfacial mechanisms, characterization methods, and flow-regulation effects
papers.abstract: Wettability alteration is a key mechanism in chemical enhanced oil recovery (C-EOR) because it controls capillary pressure, fluid distribution, residual-oil mobilization, and multiphase flow pathways in porous media. In most chemical-flooding designs, adsorption on reservoir rocks is treated as an unfavorable loss because it reduces the effective concentration of injected agents. However, increasing evidence shows that when adsorption occurs at appropriate interfacial locations and remains stable during flow, it can modify surface energy, adjust oil–water–rock contacts, and change how fluids occupy and transport through pore networks. This review explores adsorption-induced wettability alteration as an interfacial process that links chemical retention with displacement response. It begins with the initial wetting state of reservoir rocks, which is controlled by mineral surface chemistry, adsorbed polar crude-oil components, organic matter, brine ions, and water-film stability. It then compares how different chemical agents alter oil–water–rock interfaces through distinct adsorption modes and evaluates characterization and modeling methods according to whether they quantify adsorption, locate interfacial reconstruction, and connect wettability alteration with dynamic flow behavior. Two EOR pathways are emphasized: microscopic oil mobilization, where adsorption-induced changes in interfacial energy, capillary pressure, and oil–rock adhesion promote oil-film detachment, capillary desaturation, and residual-oil mobilization; and sweep improvement, where adsorption layers, hydration layers, particle deposition, structural disjoining pressure, or disproportionate permeability reduction modify local flow resistance and redistribute injected fluids. Finally, the review distinguishes functional adsorption from excessive adsorption according to adsorption location, persistence under flow, measurable interfacial or flow-regulation benefits, and low-damage performance.

papers.title: Settling of finite-size slightly negatively particles under plunging breaking waves
papers.abstract: Vertical transport of microplastics is strongly influenced by highly transient, energetic surface breaking waves. In this study, we experimentally investigate the settling dynamics of millimeter-scale slightly negatively buoyant spherical particles entrained by a laboratory plunging breaker. Particle image velocimetry is used to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the breaker-generated turbulence, while particle tracking velocimetry resolves the particle trajectories and settling response. The measurements reveal a strongly non-stationary post-breaking environment: the turbulent dissipation rate decreases from 2.60 to 6.91 × 10−4 m2/s3, while the particle diameter-to-Kolmogorov length-scale ratio remains between 3.28 and 54.6 and the settling number spans 0.18–1.45. This parameter range indicates a transient finite-size regime in which gravitational settling competes with rapidly decaying turbulent fluctuations and coherent wave-induced sloshing. Under these conditions, the mean settling response remains strongly suppressed, with measured settling velocities only ∼28%–42% of the corresponding quiescent values. The suppression is particle size-dependent: smaller particles exhibit broader and more non-Gaussian velocity distributions, stronger early-time retardation, and a more persistent response to the combined action of turbulent fluctuations and coherent sloshing. Concentration measurements further show that the cloud evolves from an initially well-mixed intrusion to a progressively weakened, broadened, and downward-shifted structure. Comparison with a recent finite-size settling model developed for homogeneous isotropic turbulence reproduces the qualitative recovery trend as turbulence decays, but generally overpredicts the settling response. These results show that turbulence-based parameterization alone is insufficient for breaking-wave flows and that coherent sloshing introduces an additional suppression of net downward transport. The measurements provide a physically grounded basis for incorporating breaking-induced settling retardation into predictive models of microplastic transport.

papers.title: On the droplet size effect on propagation speed of a mist flame
papers.abstract: The flame propagation speed is a fundamental quantity for the theory of premixed combustion, as it links chemical kinetics and molecular transport for a specific mixture. Injecting a portion of the fuel as liquid droplets can significantly alter this property. We report on the droplet size effect on the flame propagation speed in an example of an ethanol/air mist flame in a Bunsen burner configuration. Based on parametric numerical investigations, a general correlation is suggested between the mean flame propagation speed and the droplet size for monodisperse fuel mist, using a Damköhler number for the evaporation time.

papers.title: Wake dynamics and transition of the flow around a square cylinder sliding along a wall
papers.abstract: The dynamics and transitions of the flow past a square cylinder sliding along a wall are investigated numerically for Reynolds numbers (Re) between 20 and 300, and gap distances (G) between 0.05 and 1.0 side length of the square (D). The presence of the wall is found to fundamentally alter the wake dynamics and three-dimensional transitions of the wake. The two-dimensional computations show that, for G/D≥0.2, the onset of vortex shedding is delayed to higher Reynolds number with decreasing gap ratio. A period-doubling shedding regime is identified for G/D≥0.8 at higher Re, driven by a feedback mechanism where the vortex formed by the shear layer from the top of the cylinder modulates subsequent shedding. The transition from two-dimensional to three-dimensional flow using linear stability analysis is studied. Results show that the wake initially undergoes a regular bifurcation from a steady two-dimensional flow to a steady three-dimensional wake for G/D≤0.35. In this regime, Floquet stability analysis of the periodic base flow reveals the complex behavior of three-dimensional instabilities. For G/D≥0.36, five separate instability modes (two subharmonic modes, two synchronous modes, and one periodic mode) bifurcating from the unsteady base flow are identified. Curves of marginal stability for all of the modes are presented in a parameter space map, and the associated characteristics of each mode are analyzed in detail.

papers.title: Optimization and backpressure mechanisms of a ramjet flowpath in an over/under turbine-based combined cycle inlet
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional variable-geometry inlets are key to wide-envelope operation of over/under turbine-based combined-cycle engines, but their ramjet flowpaths must balance aerodynamic compression, installation constraints, and flow regulation during mode transition. For a single fixed ramjet-flowpath geometry operating over Ma∞=3.5–7.0, an aerodynamic-prior-guided gated deep neural network (AP-GDN) is coupled with differential evolution to perform weighted multi-condition optimization, followed by a low-Mach-number backpressure analysis. AP-GDN combines freestream-condition gating with a total-pressure-recovery-to-throat-Mach-number cascade to capture cross-condition nonlinearities; R2 is at least 0.985 for all five test-set outputs. With the adjustment-preference coefficient α=0.10, the selected configuration increases the multi-condition aerodynamic-performance component and the composite objective by 5.0% and 11.7%, respectively, relative to the baseline. At Ma∞=7.0, it achieves φ=0.939, raises PRth by 10%, and increases δ2 from 5.39° to 7.60°. Quasi-steady backpressure loading shows that upstream motion is controlled jointly by an asymmetric X-type shock train and separation-induced blockage along the lower wall; the critical backpressure ratios are ∼18 and 24 at Ma∞=3.5 and 4.0, respectively. The framework quantitatively reconciles wide-range aerodynamic performance, second-ramp adjustment requirements, and low-Mach-number backpressure tolerance under a prescribed mission preference.

papers.title: Under-expanded hollow-cone hydrogen jets in low-pressure direct injection: Shock-vortex dynamics, thermodynamics, and pressure-dependent mixing
papers.abstract: Low-pressure direct injection of hydrogen through outward-opening hollow-cone injectors is attractive for maximizing usable tank content, yet even at nominal injection pressures near 20 bars, the annular flow chokes and discharges as an under-expanded jet whose shock-induced expansion, vortex dynamics, and mixing govern in-cylinder performance. Here, a computed-tomography-informed, experimentally constrained compressible computational fluid dynamics framework is developed to resolve the transient dynamics, thermodynamics, and mixing of such jets from a production-representative Bosch hollow-cone injector. A time-resolved inlet mass-flow rate boundary condition derived from measured needle-lift and injected-mass data drives the simulations, which are validated against high-speed schlieren over ambient pressures of 1–5 bar (penetration, projected area, morphology) and against local one-dimensional Raman measurements of hydrogen concentration and temperature. Validation against Raman measurements showed that the predicted hydrogen concentration field was largely unaffected by the selected energy formulation, while noticeable differences were observed in the predicted temperature distribution. The jets are governed by upstream and downstream recirculation and coherent vortex rings whose scale and intensity depend on ambient pressure. Crucially, lower ambient pressure increases penetration and projected area but does not improve mixture homogenization, as large coherent vortical structures promote axial convection, allowing locally rich pockets to persist over longer downstream distances. In contrast, higher ambient pressure produces a more confined jet with a shorter characteristic mixing length, promoting more rapid dilution of the rich hydrogen core and faster homogenization toward lean and near-stoichiometric conditions despite the reduced jet penetration.

papers.title: Capillary assistance in falling film redistribution over horizontal tube bundles with bottom fin arrays
papers.abstract: Liquid films on horizontal tube bundles tend to converge along preferential paths during repeated detachment, free fall, impingement, and rewetting, producing wetting attenuation that intensifies row by row. This study combines conductivity-probe measurements, high-speed visualization, and image-derived apparent interfacial-activity proxies to compare isothermal water-film flow on smooth and bottom-fin-array tube bundles over Re=184–959. The fin array is placed at the tube-bottom detachment region, where the inter-row liquid path is selected, and intercepts near-detachment liquid for redistribution through multiple capillary-assisted channels. In the column-to-sheet transition regime, the smooth bundle exhibits progressive amplification of wetting loss, with the per-step loss from rows 3 to 5 markedly exceeding that from rows 1 to 3. The fin array suppresses this row-by-row contraction over the entire tested range, raising the row-5 wetting ratio by up to about 105%; it also stabilizes the inter-row transfer sites and converts concentrated, burst-dominated apparent interfacial renewal into a weaker and more spatially uniform form. Geometric analysis shows that wetting retention is governed primarily by inter-row inertial transport capacity and saturates beyond a threshold, while capillary guidance provides the necessary conditions for stable redistribution through liquid interception, liquid-bridge connectivity, and channel drainage. Under the present conditions, the effective geometric window is h=5–6 mm, w=1–2 mm, and p=3–4 mm. These conclusions apply to the present isothermal water-film experiments only; heat- and mass-transfer performance has not been directly verified.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of surface wave transition thresholds for sessile droplets under vertical vibration: Roles of dimensionless parameters
papers.abstract: Surface-wave transitions in vertically vibrated sessile droplets are important to ultrasonic atomization, vibration-assisted deicing, and interfacial transport phenomena. Although several droplet oscillation modes have been identified, the critical transition from directly forced zonal waves to azimuthally non-uniform meridional waves remains difficult to quantify using two-dimensional axisymmetric models. In this study, single-droplet vibration experiments and three-dimensional numerical simulations are combined to investigate the surface-wave characteristics and transition thresholds of hemispherical sessile droplets. The effects of dimensionless displacement amplitude ΔD, Weber number (We), and Reynolds number (Re) are systematically examined. The results show that ΔD mainly controls disturbance growth. Once ΔD exceeds a finite critical value, the droplet transitions from an axisymmetric zonal-wave state to a non-axisymmetric meridional-wave state, while the selected wavelength remains nearly unchanged. Increasing We shortens the selected wavelength in agreement with the capillary-inertial scaling λ/D0∝We−1/3 and lowers the meridional-wave threshold. Increasing Re reduces viscous dissipation, shortens the meridional wave instability time and drives ΔD,c toward a finite, We-dependent high-Re plateau, which represents the effective inviscid-limit threshold under the corresponding operating conditions. A critical-threshold map over Re = 300–1 × 106 and We = 50–5000 further shows that meridional instability is governed jointly by disturbance persistence and capillary smoothing. These results provide a consistent physical framework for interpreting zonal-to-meridional wave transitions in vertically vibrated sessile droplets under the conditions considered here.

papers.title: A thermo-rheological model for predicting extrusion force in fused filament fabrication
papers.abstract: We present a thermo-rheological model to predict the extrusion force required for polymer flow in fused filament fabrication hot ends. To capture the complex rheology of polymers, the model accounts for their yield-stress-dominated, solid-like behavior below the glass transition temperature and their shear-thinning behavior above it, using a hybrid rheological formulation to smoothly describe the transition. Thermal boundary conditions of the problem are derived from energy balance principles, eliminating the need for empirical calibration. This approach allows for the dynamic evolution of these conditions, similar to the wall boundary condition, which changes from free-slip to no-slip depending on the local thermal state. For a prescribed volumetric flow rate, the axial pressure gradient is obtained sequentially through a scalar root-finding procedure assuming a quasi-steady, locally fully developed velocity. This axial-marching formulation reduces the computational cost of solving the coupled flow and temperature fields by two orders of magnitude compared to conventional computational methods. Validation against measured extrusion forces for three amorphous and crystalline polymers across a wide range of wall temperatures demonstrates that the model accurately captures the nonlinear increase in force with print speed. Parametric sensitivity analysis reveals a clear hierarchy: thermal properties govern the temperature field, melt rheology influences the force magnitude due to sensitivity to temperature, and solid-state rheological parameters have negligible direct impact on force predictions, while influencing the solid-to-melt transition. The framework provides quantitative guidance for designing 3D printers and identifies progressive thermal under-development at high Péclet numbers as the physical origin of the observed force–velocity transition.

papers.title: A front-tracking method for the flow of a capsule in a Newtonian fluid
papers.abstract: This study examines the deformation dynamics of elastic capsules in viscous flows through a fully coupled fluid–structure interaction framework. Skalak (Sk) and Neo-Hookean (NH) membrane models are employed to describe thin elastic shells subjected to planar simple shear and hyperbolic flows. The incompressible Navier–Stokes equations are solved using the front-tracking method for a capsule with a specific constitutive law. The membrane is represented by a Lagrangian grid enabling accurate modeling of large deformations. The influence of the capillary number on capsule deformation, normal load distribution, and equilibrium shape is systematically analyzed. In planar hyperbolic flow, distinct differences are observed between the Sk and NH models in both capsule shape and normal load distribution. With increasing capillary number, the Sk model predicts elongated shapes with sharp edges, whereas the NH model exhibits concave regions near the capsule ends. These contrasting responses arise from their different sensitivities to surface area variation: the Sk model resists area dilation, producing non-uniform stresses and sharp features, while the NH model allows larger area changes and smoother deformations. The results emphasize the key role of membrane constitutive behavior in stress and normal load localization, providing insights relevant to microfluidic design, cell mechanophenotyping, and biomedical encapsulation.

papers.title: Mixed lubrication characteristics of water-lubricated stern bearings considering coupled shaft deflection and wear evolution
papers.abstract: Water-lubricated stern bearings commonly operate in mixed lubrication because the low viscosity of water limits film formation and propeller-induced shaft deflection creates a nonuniform axial clearance, leading to asperity contact and wear. However, the feedback between shaft deflection and wear-induced clearance evolution remains unclear. A time-marching model combines the averaged Reynolds equation with formulations for asperity contact, bearing elastic deformation, shaft deflection, and wear. At each wear increment, shaft deflection is determined from load equilibrium, and local clearance is updated using the accumulated wear profile. Results show that shaft deflection reduces film thickness near the trailing end and concentrates hydrodynamic and asperity-contact loads, thereby accelerating wear. As wear progresses, clearance growth reduces asperity-contact pressure and shifts the hydrodynamic pressure peak toward the leading end. The resulting redistribution of the fluid-film support alters the force balance on the shaft and further increases deflection. Higher bearing-specific pressure and larger radial clearance strengthen this interaction, whereas the effect of journal speed is governed by competition between hydrodynamic film formation and accumulated sliding distance.
