This is because on hydrophobic surfaces, the head-on part bounces off spheres with significant rotational motion, followed by the occurrence of separation. For this situation, the bouncing kinetic energy drives the separation process, instead of the off-center kinetic energy. Based on different mechanisms of separation, two boundary equations are proposed by using distinct driving kinetic energy, which show good agreement with our simulation results.

papers.title: Cavitation dynamics in Venturi-type microchannels: Experimental observations and numerical modeling
papers.abstract: Cavitation in fluids can severely hinder the efficiency of the associated flows. This undesired phenomenon is strongly influenced by local flow conditions, flow orientation, proximity to boundaries, and liquid/gas properties at saturation. When liquid flow is severely constricted and cavitation occurs, diverging microchannels can suppress vapor formation through effective pressure recovery; however, the behavior of such microchannels under different geometric and operating conditions remains unclear. This work combines experimental data and computational modeling to elucidate the intricate flow dynamics of cavitation-induced phase change of refrigerant (R134a) flow in a Venturi-type microchannel. Full-field numerical simulations are carried out using the interPhaseChangeFoam solver in OpenFOAM®, with the model coefficients being validated against experimental data obtained with an identical system. The effects of flow rate, channel opening angle, and inlet cross-sectional geometry are explored with a focus on pressure drop, velocity distribution, and cavitation characteristics, including vapor fraction. The results highlight the roles of flow velocity, orifice-to-channel width ratio, orifice size, and channel divergence angle on overall pressure drop. A channel opening angle of 12° minimizes pressure drop, in contrast with conventional single-phase Venturi geometries where the optimal opening angle typically lies between 5° and 7°. The study underscores that the cavitation number, including its sign, serves as a critical quantitative indicator of cavitation severity—where increasingly negative values correspond to intensified vapor generation in microscale constrictions. By identifying the relationships between operating conditions and cavitation phenomena, this work provides a framework for understanding and optimizing microchannel designs under conditions prone to cavitation.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics and gas dispersion characteristics of a self-aerating flotation cell
papers.abstract: This study used an intrusive in situ telecentric vision probe (TVP) method to measure and analyze the bubble size distribution (BSD) and the Sauter mean bubble diameter d32 in the lower circulation zone and the quiescent rising zone of a self-aerating flotation cell. A population balance model was coupled with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to predict BSD in the cell, and the predicted d32 was validated against the TVP measurements to assess the accuracy of the numerical simulations. The population balance equation was solved using the homogeneous multiple size group model (MUSIG) approach, and the model accounted for bubble breakup and coalescence through the Martínez-Bazán breakup kernel [Martínez-Bazán et al., “On the breakup of an air bubble injected into a fully developed turbulent flow. Part 1. Breakup frequency,” J. Fluid Mech. 401, 157–182 (1999)] and the Prince and Blanch coalescence kernel [Prince and Blanch, “Bubble coalescence and break-up in air-sparged bubble columns,” AIChE J. 36(10), 1485–1499 (1990)]. The BSD exhibited a right-skewed shape, and the effects of impeller speed on the flow field, turbulence intensity, vorticity, the Kolmogorov length scale, and the BSD were systematically analyzed to elucidate bubble breakup behavior in the flotation cell. BSD, bubble Reynolds number, and axial interfacial area flux were further integrated into a unified framework for gas dispersion evaluation. These results provide a basis for developing multiphase CFD-based predictive models for flotation kinetics.

papers.title: Coupling response and thermal–fluid–structure interaction characteristics of a circular cylinder subjected to lead–bismuth eutectic flow
papers.abstract: This paper reports the vibration and thermal–fluid–structure interaction characteristics of a circular cylinder subjected to lead–bismuth eutectic flow with temperature-dependent properties. The numerical simulations were conducted at inlet Reynolds numbers of 100 and 200 with inlet-to-wall temperature ratio Tin/Tw ranging from 2.0 to 3.3 and reduced velocity Ur varying from 3 to 12. Two near-wake patterns and four wake evolution regimes are identified, depending on Ur and Tin/Tw. The high-amplitude vibration is associated with the transition of the near-wake pattern. The velocity boundary layer of the vibrating cylinder is significantly thinner than that of a stationary cylinder, whereas the thermal boundary layer is much thicker than that of the latter. Nevertheless, both the velocity and thermal boundary layer thicknesses increase with Tin/Tw. The initial and lower branches occur at Ur = 3–4 and Ur > 4, respectively. The critical condition of Ur = 4 presents the largest vibration amplitudes and fluid force coefficients, which is consistent with the transition of the near-wake pattern.

papers.title: Transport by turbulent subsurface cores in internal solitary waves
papers.abstract: Internal solitary waves (ISWs) are known to induce material transport through various mechanisms, with important implications for physical and ecological processes. We report direct numerical simulations of an ISW under conditions favorable for the development of a subsurface core, a situation particularly suitable for significant horizontal transport. The results show that the core is dynamically active and strongly three-dimensional, characterized by persistent turbulence. Analysis based on passive tracers reveals that the core exhibits continuous entrainment of ambient fluid, followed by turbulent mixing, temporary retention, and eventual leakage. Entrainment occurs primarily across the upstream–upper core boundary and is closely associated with shear and convective instabilities that persist throughout the wave evolution. Once entrained, fluid is redistributed by turbulence within the core and remains trapped for a finite duration before being released downstream. Increasing the background shear strength by a factor of four increases the entrainment by approximately 67.4%, and reducing the wave amplitude by 9.1% decreased the entrainment by approximately 10.4%. Our simulations reveal that subsurface cores in ISWs under shear currents should not be considered as closed-streamline trapped cores but rather as turbulent, leaky transport systems.

papers.title: Influence of head shape on cavity flow characteristics during vertical ice-breaking water entry of projectiles
papers.abstract: Investigating the flow field evolution during high-speed water entry of projectiles is crucial for developing advanced trans-medium weapons for ice-covered seas. Using the coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian method, a numerical model for vertical high-speed ice-breaking water entry is established. The cavity evolution, impact loads, structural response, and motion characteristics are compared for projectiles with different head shapes, and the mechanisms governing ice layer crack propagation are elucidated. Results show that the influence of head shape on both cavity size and ice hole size follows the order: flat > conical > hemispherical. The retardation effect of the ice layer on cavity closure intensifies as ice hole size decreases. The flat head produces the largest annular crack area, while the conical head generates no annular cracks and fewer radial cracks. The peak loads in ice-free conditions are approximately 70% of those during ice-breaking entry at the same velocity. In ice-covered environments, the conical head exhibits plastic strain but achieves the best stability, whereas the hemispherical head shows the worst stability. These findings provide theoretical guidance for the design of trans-medium weapons for ice-covered seas.

papers.title: Identification of chaotic cavitation structures by periodically extended preprocessing for dynamic mode decomposition
papers.abstract: Experimental cavitation flows are highly non-stationary and nonlinear, which can degrade the performance of the linear dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). This study proposes a preprocessing method based on temporal image periodic extension (DMD-PE), which mitigates non-stationarity effects to improve mode extraction. For bubble, cloud, and supercavitation, the reconstruction errors after periodic extension are 1.91%, 4.55%, and 2.45%, respectively. These errors are less than half of those without extension. DMD modal analysis suggests that bubble cavitation is dominated by low-frequency modes, and its spectral characteristics are consistent with quasi-periodic evolution. Cloud cavitation has dominant modes concentrated in high decay-rate regions, suggesting strong transient chaotic perturbations. Supercavitation exhibits relatively high modal energy concentration, and its evolution appears to be governed by quasi-periodic large-scale cavity motion, indicating strong coherence and dynamic stability. This study proposes an effective DMD data preprocessing method for experimental cavitation flows, reveals the modal characteristics of dynamic structures in three typical cavitation regimes, and provides a modal-based dynamic interpretation for cavitation evolution mechanisms.

papers.title: Rising behavior of a two-dimensional single bubble in a viscoelastic fluid
papers.abstract: The rising behavior of gas bubbles in two-phase flow systems is a fundamental phenomenon; however, the impact of non-Newtonian fluid properties on bubble path stability remains complex and not fully understood. In this study, we conducted two-dimensional numerical simulations of a single bubble rising in Oldroyd-B viscoelastic fluids, using the volume of fluid method with adaptive mesh refinement within the BASILISK framework. By systematically varying the Galileo number (Ga) and Eötvös number (Eo), we constructed a Ga–Eo phase diagram to elucidate bubble behavior across different fluid regimes. The results indicate that fluid viscoelasticity exerts a complex and non-monotonic influence on bubble dynamics. Two factors contribute to bubble path instability: oscillations in viscoelastic stress disrupt bubble symmetry, leading to instability, while high stress concentrations around the bubble suppress flow separation, thereby inhibiting instability. Regarding bubble breakup mechanisms, we demonstrate that weak elasticity facilitates central breakup, accompanied by the formation of micro-bubbles due to the interaction between the elastic memory effect and necking extensional flow. Conversely, strong elasticity suppresses central breakup, resulting in a “contracting-zigzag” trajectory driven by an “elastic stress plug zone” and subsequent symmetry breaking. Peripheral breakup is monotonically suppressed by attenuated wake vortices, but at intermediate Wi, stress-oscillation asymmetry produces a one-sided skirt breakup not reported previously.

papers.title: Mode transition dynamics and stability criteria of a dual-inlet integrated solid rocket ramjet under combustor residual effects
papers.abstract: The transition process of a dual-inlet integrated solid rocket ramjet (ISRR) remains insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the role of combustor residues. To address this issue, a combined approach integrating free-jet experiments and three-dimensional unsteady full-flowpath simulations was employed. The effects of residual-induced gas release on transition dynamics and stability were systematically investigated. The results indicate that the transition can be categorized into four stages: post-boost exhaust, cavity oscillation, inlet startup with combustor filling, and combustion establishment. During the outlet-closed phase, a self-sustained oscillation at ∼59.8 Hz was observed, which was associated with shock reflection–incoming flow coupling. Once combustor residues were introduced, the system response shifted from a rapid monotonic establishment to a delayed process accompanied by pronounced unsteadiness. The peak combustor exit pressure increased by ∼89%, while a low-frequency oscillation (∼2 Hz) emerged near the throat, triggering inlet unstart–restart behavior. Moreover, the presence of residues markedly altered local equivalence ratio distribution and intensified heat-release non-uniformity, thereby promoting transition delay and low-frequency instability. Based on comparative analysis, a transition stability criterion incorporating residue effects was proposed, revealing the coupled influence of equivalence ratio distribution, heat-release fluctuation, and pressurization rate on system stability. These findings provide theoretical guidance for transition sequencing, residue management, and engineering design of hypersonic propulsion systems and extend current understanding of dual-inlet ISRR transition mechanisms.

papers.title: Slope effects on hydraulic characteristics and energy dissipation of stepped spillways with trapezoidal piers
papers.abstract: Stepped spillways provide excellent energy dissipation, which can considerably reduce the size of downstream stilling basins. Previous research has confirmed that installing roughness elements on stepped surfaces can further improve energy dissipation efficiency, which is highly sensitive to the chute slope and the geometry of the added elements. Aiming to clarify the unclear slope sensitivity of stepped spillways with trapezoidal piers, this work intends to systematically reveal how slope variation affects the hydraulic characteristics, pressure-aeration distribution, and energy dissipation mechanism of the spillway. Five slope cases were designed, and numerical simulations were carried out using the renormalization group k–ε turbulence model to compare flow patterns, velocity, pressure, air-concentration characteristics, and energy dissipation performance. Results show that a gentler slope increases the critical Reynolds number required for the development of fully skimming flow and reduces the velocity difference between the bottom and surface layers, resulting in a more uniform velocity distribution. Negative pressure mainly occurs at the convex corners of the steps, where relatively high air concentrations develop, effectively mitigating the risk of potential cavitation damage. The energy dissipation rate of all cases exceeds 65% and increases gradually as the slope decreases. Under steep-slope conditions, the energy dissipation rate responds strongly to slope variation; however, this sensitivity weakens noticeably as the slope becomes gentler. This study provides a theoretical basis and technical reference for the optimal design and performance enhancement of stepped spillways with trapezoidal piers, particularly for projects with stringent requirements for high energy dissipation and cavitation protection.

papers.title: A convergence-guided molecular modeling framework for CO2/N2/CH4 competitive adsorption in coal during hot flue gas enhanced methane recovery
papers.abstract: Hot flue gas injection for enhanced coalbed methane recovery holds potential to enhance methane recovery and enable geological CO2 sequestration. Predictions of CO2/N2/CH4 competitive adsorption and transport in molecular simulations are sensitive to coal molecular model size, coal rank representation, and temperature and pressure conditions. Quantitative criteria for representative molecular models remain lacking. This work treats coal macromolecule number selection as a finite-size convergence issue and establishes a convergence scoring framework accounting for density, pore structure, adsorption capacity, isosteric heat of adsorption, and competitive adsorption selectivity. Integrating PoreBlazer, grand canonical Monte Carlo, and molecular dynamics simulations, this work investigates adsorption, diffusion, and intermolecular interactions of CO2/N2/CH4 in lignite, bituminous coal, and anthracite. Results show minimum representative model sizes of 50, 40, and 30 macromolecules for lignite, bituminous coal, and anthracite, respectively. Larger models reduce isolated free-volume artifacts and improve statistical representation of adsorption sites and diffusion pathways. In the ternary pore gas mixture, pressure drives a transition from high-affinity site occupation to progressive pore filling. CO2 enriches at favorable sites to displace CH4, while N2 shows weaker interaction and higher mobility. The competitive adsorption is governed by synergistic site occupation and pore filling, and an increase in temperature shortens the residence times of molecules at the adsorption sites, thereby suppressing adsorption. Nonlinear mean squared displacement indicates transport via intermittent trapping in connected free volume rather than unrestricted diffusion. This work provides a quantitative convergence criterion to replace empirical model-size selection in coal molecular simulations.

papers.title: Species-resolved non-equilibrium condensation of light hydrocarbons in a rotating compressible natural-gas flow
papers.abstract: Light-hydrocarbon condensation in rapidly expanding natural-gas flows couples finite-rate multicomponent phase change with species-dependent supersaturation and latent-heat feedback. Its response in rotating compressible passages remains insufficiently resolved. A species-resolved non-equilibrium condensation model is formulated for a lean CH4/C2H6/C3H8/N2 mixture undergoing low-temperature expansion. The formulation combines a partial-pressure-based supersaturation criterion, real-gas equilibrium correction, species-resolved source terms, and latent-heat feedback in a three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged compressible-flow framework for a radial-inflow passage. Under the investigated conditions, propane dominates homogeneous nucleation and establishes the primary droplet population, whereas ethane condenses mainly through growth on existing droplets; at the lowest inlet temperatures, downstream ethane growth can provide the larger liquid-mass contribution. For the baseline composition, condensation is pronounced below ∼ 210 K and weakens as the inlet total temperature increases from 180 to 220 K. At 180 K, the non-condensing calculation overpredicts the isentropic and polytropic efficiencies by 2.84 and 2.74 percentage points, respectively; the differences become negligible as condensation weakens. At 220 K, increasing the propane mole fraction from 0.69 to 2.07 mol. % raises the outlet liquid mass fraction from nearly zero to about 4.31%. The condensation front is controlled by the coupled evolution of species partial pressure, saturation pressure, phase relaxation, and passage-scale aerodynamics.

papers.title: Dynamics of cantilevered piping system conveying two-phase flow
papers.abstract: This work explores the dynamics of two-phase flow in cantilevered pipes, emphasizing the role of flow pattern transitions in system stability. A unified model that couples flow parameters with the vibration equation is established, grounded in a precise slug flow model and regime transition conditions. The equations are discretized via the Galerkin method, and the 4th-order Runge–Kutta serves to solve for the nonlinear dynamic responses. Validation of the model is conducted using experimental data and published results and compared with the improved drift flux model (DFM). Theoretical analysis indicates that the critical flutter velocity predicted by DFM is lower than that of the slug dynamics model. When superficial gas velocity increases and flow pattern transitions to annular flow, DFM fails to predict the restabilization caused by redistribution of flow velocity and liquid holdup. Under DFM, with superficial liquid velocity as the variable, an instability–restabilization–instability pattern is observed. Thus, DFM reliability is questionable under flow patterns with weak interfacial interaction. Nonlinear analysis shows that both models exhibit flutter instability with periodic motion. The effect of dissipation on stability is mass-dependent: to a certain extent, dissipation enhances stability, but when the dimensionless mass exceeds a critical value, it causes negative effects.

papers.title: Effects of blowing/suction slot distribution on the transient tunnel aerodynamics of high-speed maglev trains
papers.abstract: High-speed maglev trains operating at 600 km/h are subjected to severe transient aerodynamic disturbances when traversing tunnels, which may compromise operational safety and passenger comfort. Active blowing/suction flow control has emerged as a promising approach for mitigating tunnel-induced aerodynamic effects, whereas the influence of slot distribution topology on control performance remains insufficiently understood. To address this issue, four onboard blowing/suction configurations with identical total opening area, namely, rectangular, slit, 3-slot, and 6-slot layouts, are proposed and systematically evaluated. Three-dimensional compressible unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations coupled with the Re-Normalization Group k–ε turbulence model are solved using the sliding-mesh approach to capture the transient train–tunnel aerodynamic interactions. The results demonstrate that all configurations effectively suppress pressure-wave propagation, reduce aerodynamic loads, and weaken slipstream velocities. The overall control performance follows the order: rectangular > 3-slot ≈ 6-slot > slit. Among the examined layouts, the rectangular configuration achieves the highest mitigation efficiency by concentrating jet momentum near the nose stagnation region and tail wake core, thereby enhancing pressure wave attenuation and wake pressure recovery. In contrast, the slit and decentralized multi-slot configurations exhibit reduced effectiveness due to momentum dispersion and weakened flow-control authority. Compared with the baseline, the rectangular layout reduces the peak pressure at the train nose and mid tunnel by 16.4% and 16.0%, respectively, decreases the lateral force amplitude of the head car by 19.3%, and lowers the maximum slipstream velocity by 31.0%. This study further elucidates that local jet momentum flux density, rather than total flow rate or opening area, dominates pressure wave attenuation efficiency under different slot distribution configurations. It also figures out the relationship between slot topology and aerodynamic control effectiveness, which complements the existing research framework of topology design for active flow control in high-speed maglev tunnel aerodynamics.

papers.title: Post-earthquake groundwater hydraulic behavior in tunnels subjected to water inrush
papers.abstract: In the post-earthquake engineering setting, tunnel water inrush is controlled not only by water sources, but also by how fault and fracture pathways, excavation boundaries, and operation conditions reshape groundwater pressure. Here, we proposed a source-pathway constrained framework integrating an Almon-type distributed lag model, hydrochemical and isotopic constraints, mineral saturation screening, and three-dimensional groundwater simulations to characterize post-earthquake groundwater hydraulic behavior in the Mozi–Chayuan Tunnel, Southwest China. The event-adjusted distributed-lag model identified a primary significant rainfall-drainage response window of 35–76 d in tunnel 1/tunnel 1', whereas tunnel 2 showed no significant delayed response, confirming that rainfall acted mainly as delayed recharge rather than an immediate trigger. Hydrochemical facies, isotope-derived recharge elevations, and saturation-index patterns indicate the inrush water was predominantly meteoric-derived water supplied by adjacent catchments and shallow fractured aquifers, without evidence for a dominant deep saline or hydrothermal contribution. The simulations reveal a clear fluid-mechanical transition: excavation converted the tunnel into a near-zero-pressure drainage boundary, whereas lining and 8 m full-section grouting established a pressure-bearing boundary with pressure heads of approximately 70–110 m in the route-change section during operation. The fault-related damage zone and route-change section remained the main zones of pressure-head redistribution across all simulated conditions. Local piezometer validation at 4100 m yielded relative errors of 2.09% and 5.45%, supporting the reliability of the framework for post-seismic tunnel groundwater response assessment. This framework supports the safe operation and pressure-control design of the Mozi–Chayuan Tunnel and provides a transferable reference for assessing tunnel groundwater responses in earthquake-prone regions.

papers.title: Turbulence modeling using physics-informed neural networks: The importance of training points distribution and hyper parameters
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are employed to solve the Navier–Stokes equations with a standard k–ω turbulence model for flow over a period, focusing on how the spatial placement of training points and hyperparameters affect accuracy. Wall-bounded turbulence modeling includes challenges because variables like the specific dissipation rate (ω) exhibit high near-wall gradients. To address this, the research was conducted in three phases. First, learning rate (LR) and optimizer iterations were studied, and analysis revealed that increasing iterations does not necessarily improve prediction accuracy, and specific LR scheduling is required for improved accuracy. Second, various network capacities and sampling methodologies of random, shear-aligned, and convective were analyzed simultaneously, and revealed that random and convective sampling fail to capture near-wall turbulence characteristics, causing considerable predictive errors in ω. While shear-aligned point selection achieves lower ω error, it requires prior knowledge of the flow field. Third, a novel multi-objective Monte Carlo active learning (MOMCAL) algorithm was developed to address this issue. It evaluates spatial gradients, partial differential equation residuals, and current errors to semi-stochastically select new training points. By applying MOMCAL, the neural network easily learned the highly sensitive ω field. It reduced the ω prediction error considerably. The generalizability of MOMCAL is confirmed on two additional geometries, achieving similar reductions in ω error, and comparisons with existing adaptive refinement methods demonstrate its superior performance. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that intelligent LR scheduling combined with physics-aware point selection is essential for building reliable, high-precision PINNs turbulence models.

papers.title: Erratum: “Analytical criteria for bristle spacing on microinsect wings to maintain high aerodynamic force” Phys. Fluids 37 , 101707 (2025)
Elastohydrodynamic instability in an inertia-less Taylor–Couette flow past a deformable cylinder
papers.abstract: The present study investigates the stability of a Taylor–Couette flow (TCF) past a cylinder coated with an elastic medium using linear stability theory. The flow arises from the rotation of a rigid inner cylinder, whereas the stationary outer cylinder is coated with a deformable solid medium described as a neo-Hookean elastic solid. The fluid–structure interaction renders the inertia-less TCF past a deformable solid layer unstable when the rotational speed of the inner cylinder exceeds a critical value. The comparison of two-dimensional and three-dimensional disturbances suggests that the two-dimensional non-axisymmetric disturbances in the (r,θ)-plane are the most unstable (or least stable) modes. The instability is attributed to the work done by the mean flow at the fluid–solid interface, resulting in energy transfer from the mean flow to the traveling disturbances. In the thin fluid gap limit, the stability behavior of the plane Couette flow (PCF) past a deformable solid is recovered. Increasing the fluid gap has a stabilizing effect on the flow, leading to an increase in the critical rotational speed for the onset of instability. In addition to the fluid gap, the critical speed is influenced by the solid-layer thickness and the interfacial tension. For a fixed fluid gap, increasing the solid-layer thickness reduces the critical rotational speed of the inner cylinder. The instability is excited by the finite-wave mode as well as the short-wave mode of disturbances, driven by the fluid shear rate and the first normal-stress difference in the solid in the base flow, respectively. In the absence of interfacial tension, a transition from finite-wave to short-wave instability occurs for a thinner solid layer with respect to the fluid-layer thickness. The presence of interfacial tension tends to attenuate the short-wave instability. Compared to PCF, the Taylor–Couette configuration with curved streamlines delays the onset of instability due to the reduced interfacial shear rate and the associated shear work necessary to trigger the elastohydrodynamic instability.

papers.title: Combining symbolic regression and turbulence physics to develop a compact inner-layer production–dissipation closure
papers.abstract: We combine symbolic regression with a closure-based analysis of the turbulent-kinetic-energy budget to develop a compact four-constant expression for the inner-layer production-to-dissipation ratio P/ε(y+). Symbolic regression on channel-flow direct numerical simulation (DNS) at Reτ=180–5200 identifies a linear-tanh ratio. Van Driest eddy-diffusivity and Kolmogorov dissipation closures motivate a squared-numerator M16 variant that enforces the kinematic (y+)3 wall exponent, but this construction uses empirical closures and DNS-calibrated constants rather than constituting a first-principles derivation. An exact paired audit on identical points and masks shows that the original PySR (Python Symbolic Regression) expression outperforms printed M16 on 18 of 19 intended-domain external profiles; the source-balanced M16 changes are ΔR2=−0.004 38 and +17.8% in root mean square error (RMSE). We, therefore, recommend the original PySR expression for finite-domain prediction and retain M16 as an asymptotic benchmark. Without refitting, the recommended expression gives R2≥0.978 on all 19 external zero-pressure-gradient profiles from four DNS codes distinct from the training code. Accuracy deteriorates for strong adverse pressure gradients; the closure is not an outer-wake model, and it fails out of domain on plane Couette flow. An optional ln(Reτ) extension of the M16 benchmark gives α5=0.0436 with a profile-bootstrap 95% interval [0.0132, 0.0678] over Reτ=180–5200, but is not validated beyond that range. In an a priori diagnostic using DNS-resolved production and dissipation budgets, replacing ε=P with ε=P/F(y+) reduces inner-layer dissipation–prediction RMSE by 88–95%; performance when production is supplied by imperfect Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-predicted mean shear and Reynolds stress remains untested.

papers.title: Droplet clustering and collective gasification in reacting and non-reacting swirling fuel sprays
papers.abstract: The influence of annular air swirl on droplet clustering and collective gasification is investigated in a model spray burner. Experiments are conducted with an acetone spray under non-reacting and reacting conditions, with and without imposed swirl (S = 0 and 0.77), at a constant fuel mass flow rate. Droplet clusters are identified using Voronoi analysis of Mie-scattering images, and cluster statistics are combined with droplet size measurements to evaluate the group number (G) and associated gasification rates. Air swirl markedly alters spray topology and reaction-zone structure. Droplet clustering spans a broad range of spatial scales, confirming its multiscale nature, while the wide distribution of group numbers (G≈ 0.1–10) indicates the coexistence of multiple gasification regimes. In non-reacting sprays, air swirl generates smaller, denser clusters with reduced inter-droplet spacing, leading to only weak changes in gasification rates. In reacting sprays, clustering is intensified; however, air swirl suppresses large-scale clusters, narrows the G distribution, and reduces the prevalence of the external-group mode. As a result, the reacting swirling case exhibits a lower weighted-average group number and an enhanced mean gasification rate.

papers.title: Axisymmetric phase-field lattice Boltzmann simulation of droplet retraction and bubble entrapment with contact-line pinning
papers.abstract: Droplet retraction on hydrophobic surfaces is strongly influenced by contact-line pinning and hysteresis, which can suppress radial recoil and induce interfacial phenomena such as Worthington jets and central bubble entrapment. In this study, high-speed impact experiments are combined with a conservative axisymmetric phase-field lattice Boltzmann method to examine droplet retraction over the range of Re≈500–1400 and We≈2.7–16.3. The numerical framework couples a radius-weighted symmetric axisymmetric formulation with an effective soft-pinning treatment, in which unresolved surface-induced pinning is represented by a contact-angle hysteresis window and a near-wall kinetic depinning threshold. The simulations capture the main experimentally observed stages, including spreading, recoil, cavity collapse, Worthington jet formation, and bubble pinch-off. Quantitative comparisons of the contact evolution, pinch-off time, and entrapped bubble size show reasonable agreement with the experimental measurements. The internal-flow and energy analyses suggest that stronger contact-line pinning suppresses contact-line recession, promotes axial pressure focusing during cavity collapse, and is associated with jet-induced bubble entrapment near the symmetry axis. These results indicate that the proposed axisymmetric phase-field LBM provides a useful framework for studying hysteretic droplet retraction and related topological transitions within the examined parameter range.

papers.title: Coupled effects of particle morphology and confinement on irregular particle regime and drag coefficient
papers.abstract: The settling behavior of irregular particles in a confined space is critical to chemical engineering applications but remains incompletely understood due to the coupled effects of particle morphology and wall confinement. A two-dimensional coupled particle dynamics-lattice Boltzmann model for the gas–liquid–solid flow with an irregular particle represented by a multi-sphere algorithm is employed to simulate three-phase flows. Using a clover particle, we examine settling dynamics under different confinement widths, particle major axis and roundness, solid-to-liquid density ratios, and physical properties of the upper and lower fluids. Three distinct flow regimes are identified: stable rectilinear settling (Regime I), sustained lateral oscillation (Regime II), and wall collision settling (Regime III). A regime map clearly delineates the zones for the three regimes. The confinement width modulates the settling velocity more strongly than the particle major axis, and both effects are non-additive, their relative roles dictated by the change pathway. In Regime II, particle rotation is coupled with lateral oscillation, while increasing the density ratio drives the transition to Regime III. A new empirical drag coefficient correlation incorporating both particle roundness and confinement parameters is proposed. These findings offer a unified framework for predicting sedimentation behavior of irregular particles in a confined space.

papers.title: Predictive modelling of the dominant axisymmetric pressure mode of a high-speed turbulent jet flow using spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and machine learning
papers.abstract: Analysis of dominant features associated with coherent structures in turbulent flows is essential for the development of Reduced-Order Models (ROMs) in many fluid dynamics problems. As the first step in this direction, the axisymmetric pressure mode is extracted from the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) of a high-speed round jet flow, analyzed, and reconstructed using flow decomposition and Machine Learning (ML) techniques. The motivation of these data-driven analyses is to ultimately develop robust methods for modeling turbulent flows using only a fraction of the LES time series for training purposes, thus minimizing computing costs. The considered LES solution is based on the high-resolution Compact Accurately Boundary Adjusting high-REsolution Technique accelerated on Graphics Processing Unit cards for conditions of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Small Hot Jet Acoustic Rig experiment with a round jet at acoustic Mach number 0.9. A frequency-domain Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD) of the LES data is performed to extract the time-varying coefficients. The SPOD coefficients condense important unsteady features of the turbulent jet flow, while preserving its spatiotemporal coherence. The coefficients are reconstructed using four machine-learning approaches. The predictive ROMs developed here based on ML are specifically focused on reconstructing the leading SPOD time coefficient of the axisymmetric (m=0) pressure mode at St=0.1 that corresponds to the dominant hydrodynamic mode that is known to strongly contribute to the peak-noise radiation of high-speed round jets at small angles to the jet axis. The first ROM approach employs Feedforward Neural Networks, a technique previously recommended for modeling turbulent flows over a plunging airfoil [Lui and Wolf, “Construction of reduced-order models for fluid flows using deep feedforward neural networks,” J. Fluid Mech. 872, 963–994 (2019)]. The second ROM uses Genetic Programing, a symbolic regression method widely recognized in the optimization literature, though it has not yet been applied to unsteady fluid dynamics problems. The third approach adopts Echo State Networks, a time-series prediction and reconstruction technique originating from the field of Reservoir Computing. Finally, the fourth approach leverages Transformer, one of the most advanced architectures within the family of Artificial Neural Networks. Although transformers have demonstrated efficiency in long-term reconstruction of turbulent wake flows, their application to high-speed jet modeling remains unexplored. The stability and accuracy of the considered ML methods for turbulent signal reconstruction are evaluated in terms of capturing its essential properties, such as the amplitude distribution and convection phase.

papers.title: Understanding flow and heat transfer characteristics of liquid sodium metal under confined nanochannels of metallic iron: Insights from molecular dynamics simulation and density functional theory
papers.abstract: Liquid sodium plays a vital role in advanced thermal systems and nuclear reactor applications, necessitating a detailed understanding of its flow and heat transfer behavior in both bulk and confined states. In this study, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to evaluate the thermophysical properties of sodium metal over a wide range of temperatures. Density functional theory and the Boltzmann transport equation were used to evaluate the electronic thermal conductivity, and MD was used to calculate the phonon thermal conductivity of the sodium metal. Non-equilibrium MD simulations were further performed to investigate flow and heat transfer characteristics of sodium metal under nanoscale confinement of iron walls. The results revealed pronounced interfacial layering of sodium atoms, contributing to increased thermal resistance quantified via Kapitza length. With an increasing temperature gradient, interfacial structuring weakened, resulting in ∼15% reduction in thermal slip length and a 22% increase in heat transfer coefficient (HTC). Under Poiseuille flow, velocity slip increased by 335% with increasing driving force from 1 × 10−4 to 7 × 10−4 eV/Å. The enhanced convective transport and reduced thermal resistance of interfacial sodium atoms lead to a 74.17% increase in HTC for an increase in the sodium Reynolds number from 0.26 to 1.3. Similarly, in Couette flow, increasing wall velocity significantly enhanced HTC owing to distortion of interfacial sodium structure. The multiscale findings demonstrate that interfacial effects dominate heat transfer under nanoscale confinement, yielding HTC values on the order of ∼108 W m−2 K−1, nearly four orders of magnitude higher than macroscale systems.

papers.title: Observation-guided diagnostics of one-dimensional inertial confinement fusion implosion dynamics with diffusion modeling
papers.abstract: Inertial confinement fusion (ICF) experiments require precise control over high-dimensional capsule-design and pulse-drive parameter spaces to achieve thermonuclear ignition. Sparse experimental diagnostics and partial observations limit the resolution of complex implosion dynamics and make high-precision inverse inference difficult. In this work, we adopt a conditional diffusion model framework as an advanced physics-diagnostic tool to model one-dimensional laser/radiation-driven ICF implosions and to quantify forward diagnostic recovery and inverse parameter design under partial observations. An Euler forward-gradient-corrected sampling method is introduced, and actual observational guidance is incorporated to ensure that the predicted results remain consistent with both sparse diagnostic information and the radiation-hydrodynamic state manifold represented by the simulation data. Using this framework, we perform global sensitivity analysis with accumulated local effects and vector projection-based sensitivity indices to identify the dominant drivers of systematic variations across 35 physical output variables, including neutron yield and hot-spot pressure. In addition, ensemble sampling is used to reveal how stochastic uncertainty propagates into the design space and to identify specific parameters that are prone to structural instability. These results provide an efficient diagnostic route for optimizing target-capsule performance and pulse-shape architecture.

papers.title: Mechanistic investigation of particle separation in standing-wave acoustofluidic microchannels
papers.abstract: Microparticle separation has become a powerful label-free detection technique. This study presents a microfluidic particle separation method based on acoustic standing waves. A multiphysics coupled model integrating acoustic fields, laminar flow, and particle tracing was developed to characterize particle migration and separation behaviors under the combined action of acoustic and hydrodynamic fields. We systematically investigate the effects of acoustic field parameters, hydrodynamic conditions, and particle material properties on particle separation. The results reveal that particle migration is governed by acoustic radiation forces and hydrodynamic transport. Under the optimized operating conditions, the numerical model achieved complete size-selective separation of 1, 5, and 10 μm particles, corresponding to 100% separation efficiency and 100% separation purity. Enhanced acoustic excitation promotes transverse displacement, whereas flow regulation alters streamline distributions and outlet collection regions, thereby influencing particle redistribution. Distinct separation behaviors are observed under different acoustofluidic conditions, resulting in under-migration, stable separation, or excessive lateral displacement. In addition, particle material properties significantly affect separation trajectories and outlet distributions because of differences in the acoustic contrast factor. Particles with moderate acoustic contrast achieve optimal confinement, while weak or strong responses compromise separation performance. This study demonstrates that effective separation can be achieved through coordinated control of acoustic and hydrodynamic effects. These findings provide mechanistic insights into standing-wave acoustofluidic separation and offer guidance for the design and optimization of acoustofluidic devices.

papers.title: Regulation mechanism of underbody flow field and aerodynamic drag reduction for high-speed trains via mixed-gas jets
papers.abstract: The bogie region is the primary source of aerodynamic resistance for high-speed trains, making it a key target for flow control strategies aimed at drag reduction. Numerical simulations were performed to explore the flow regulation mechanism and associated drag reduction effect of underbody mixed-gas jets with varying helium mass fractions (HMF) and velocities (Vjet). Results indicate that applying air jet in front of the leading bogie with increasing velocities leads to an intensified downward deflection of the underbody flow, which suppresses the initial flow separation at the front lower edge of cavity and the re-separation at the leading edge of bogie wheels. The entrainment effect induced by the descending free shear flow weakens flow reattachment on the cavity rear end and suppresses the formation of vortex structures. Since the effect of velocity on jet momentum is more pronounced than that of gas density, an increase in HMF exerts varying degrees of influence on the regulation of the underbody flow field across different velocity levels. Under a high jet velocity, the momentum reduction induced by an increased HMF imposes only a marginal degradation on the jet's ability to regulate flow separation and vortices, while concurrently inhibiting the cavity rear-face flow reattachment that is typically observed in low-velocity jets with high HMF. The pure helium jet at Vjet/U = 0.5 achieves a maximum drag reduction rate of 10.3% along with optimal net energy-saving performance. This study provides fundamental physical insights for underbody aerodynamic control of high-speed trains.

papers.title: A general phenomenological theory for asymptotic inclined jet-driven scour in cohesive soils
papers.abstract: The erosion mechanism of silts and clays significantly differs from that of granular materials, because cohesive counterparts exhibit a variety of erosion modes and stochastic kinetics. While gravity is the dominant force opposing the flow erosive action in granular beds, the physicochemical properties (e.g., plasticity, percentage of clay, water content, etc.) significantly alter the resistance of both pure cohesive materials and mixtures, making the prediction of scour geometry particularly difficult. The first two authors of this paper have recently presented a first-principles-based framework, illuminated by the Phenomenological Theory of Turbulence, to estimate the equilibrium scour depth caused by a water jet impinging onto a granular bed across the entire spectrum of flow conditions. The framework in its current form needs to be supplemented to incorporate the effects of cohesion. More generally, a theory capable of translating the complex behavior of scour in cohesive soils into a predictive equation is still missing. To narrow this gap, in this study: (1) we extend the above-mentioned framework by incorporating the cohesive properties of the bed material; (2) we validate the numerical solutions of the obtained equations against an extensive database which includes laboratory tests from various authors; (3) we analyze the mechanisms governing the scour induced by inclined jets, highlighting the differences and similitudes due to the soil characteristics. Notably, in so doing, we preserve the analytical structure of the framework, thus adding another piece to the path outlined by the first two authors toward the development of a universal theory.

papers.title: Quantifying uncertainty in propeller cavitation flow using an implicit large eddy simulation-based verification and validation framework
papers.abstract: To address the adverse effects of unsteady vortices and cavitation on propeller efficiency and navigational safety at high operating speeds, this study performed numerical simulations of cavitating flow around the marine propeller PC456 using an implicit large eddy simulation (LES) approach coupled with the boundary data immersion method and a local mesh refinement strategy, with five systematically refined meshes. The flow-field characteristics were systematically analyzed. Sheet cavitation developed along the blade leading edges, while tip-vortex cavitation originated near the blade tips and evolved into helical structures in the near wake. Their interaction generated strong local fluctuations in pressure and velocity fields. The wake-vortex system was primarily composed of tip vortices and a hub vortex, with tip vortices dominating the wake dynamics. A verification and validation framework based on implicit LES was established by combining the five-equation method with the safety factor method to quantitatively evaluate numerical and modeling uncertainties in key flow parameters. To address the limitations of the conventional five-equation method, specifically its sensitivity to initial guesses and susceptibility to convergence to local optima in strongly nonlinear cavitating flows, an improved optimization strategy incorporating multiple randomized initial guesses and penalty-term constraints was introduced and applied to the cavitating flow field. The results showed close agreement with experimental measurements in terms of thrust and torque coefficients, while velocity and pressure uncertainties remained within reasonable bounds. The proposed framework provides a quantitative methodology for evaluating cavitating-flow predictions and guiding future engineering applications.

papers.title: Optimization of hydrogen buffer gas on tin transport for extreme ultraviolet lithography
papers.abstract: A hydrodynamic model is developed in this study for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) nanolithography to investigate the tin transport in a hydrogen buffering environment, where hydrogen is often adopted to avoid tin contamination of the optical reflective mirror from high-energy tin plasma and debris. The combined diffusion coefficient method is first employed in an EUV lithography chamber to describe the tin-hydrogen diffusion under the concentration, temperature, and pressure gradients. The results show that injecting bulk hydrogen gas can effectively control the tin mass fraction near the mirror down to 10−3–10−5. Two or more vortices are generated within the flow field by the interactions between multiple hydrogen streams and their interactions with the walls, which on an excessively large scale, can alter the transport processes of tin, exacerbating tin contamination on the mirror. Concentration diffusion dominates the diffusion processes of the tin majority near the central axis, while pressure diffusion is the key for tin deposition on the mirror and outer walls, and temperature diffusion has a relatively small influence near the vane wall. By optimizing the three hydrogen inlet fluxes, the tin-hydrogen flow field transitions from three vortices to two vortices far from the center with reduced vortex scale, thus reducing the tin mass fraction on the mirror significantly below 5 × 10−6. Our work provides a deeper flow-diffusion mechanism of tin under buffering hydrogen, contributing to strategies for reducing tin contamination in EUV lithography.

papers.title: Flame properties of auto-ignition assisted supersonic shear layer hydrogen flames
papers.abstract: Shear layer flames play a critical role in flame stabilization and combustor design in hypersonic air-breathing engines, whereas the development of shear layers is sensitive to inlet conditions that vary significantly with operating conditions. This study uses large eddy simulations to investigate the supersonic shear-layer flames subject to variations in static air temperature, simulating the afterburner combustion with an inflow air stream of Mach number 2.1 and an inflow fuel injection at Mach number 1.1. With the static temperature of the vitiated air stream increasing from 1050 to 1600 K, the liftoff length of the shear layer flame decreases, while the flame initiation location moves progressively toward leaner fuel/air mixtures with lower mixture fraction Z. The shear layer flame exhibits a bimodal structure, in which the distributions of HO2 radical show peaks on both the fuel-lean and fuel-rich sides. The flame liftoff length, correlated with the local mixture properties, is closely influenced by the incoming air temperature. Further sensitivity analysis reveals that radical H has the most pronounced effect on promoting the auto-ignition assisted flame stabilization processes, within the present O. Conaire mechanism and LES-PaSR modeling framework. Additionally, quantitative analysis of shear layer development summarizes the coupling of flow and combustion processes on shear layer thickness and mass entrainment, as combustion reduces the entrainment rate and development of the shear layer.

papers.title: Unsteady dynamics of logarithmic wall laws under periodic mass injection: Nonlinear response and scaling behaviors
papers.abstract: The unsteady dynamics of logarithmic wall laws in turbulent boundary layers subjected to periodic mass injection are investigated. Using the boundary-layer approximation, the velocity and total enthalpy profiles are obtained by implicitly solving the time-dependent one-dimensional Partial Differential Equations of momentum and energy conservation. The dynamic log-law responses are analyzed by the transfer functions across a broad parametric space of blowing ratio, pulsation frequencies, and amplitudes. Periodic wall mass injection induces a generalized Stokes resonance when the Stokes penetration depth aligns with the buffer layer, yielding the maximum phase delay. The momentum and thermal transport exhibit different resonance frequencies: the momentum shows stronger nonlinear temporal persistence, with a bandpass resonance governed by the inner-scaled frequency ωres+≈6×10−3 (a band ≈(4–8)×10−3; dimensionally f≈15–30 Hz, condition-dependent), whereas the thermal field has greater temporal inertia. The velocity log-law achieves a near-universal collapse under the inner-scaled frequency (ω+); this collapse breaks down for the thermal field, which requires a (Reτ/Reref)γh correction with an empirical sign-and-order exponent [γh∼−O(1)] accounting for outer-layer thermal relaxation. The thermal relaxation disparity drives transient intra-cycle oscillations in the effective turbulent Prandtl number (Prt,eff=Ah/Au), invalidating the steady Reynolds analogy. An analytic transfer function is proposed to accurately fit the log-law dynamics, capturing the high-frequency rebound and plateau resulting from the competition between convection and diffusion. The time-averaged deviations under unsteady mass injection follow a quadratic scaling in amplitude in the weakly nonlinear regime and require a fourth-order correction at large amplitudes.

papers.title: Level-set lattice Boltzmann method for dynamic three-phase contact lines on arbitrarily curved solid surfaces
papers.abstract: A level-set lattice Boltzmann method (LS-LBM) is developed and coupled with a geometric contact angle scheme to simulate dynamic three-phase contact lines on arbitrarily curved surfaces in this study. This unified framework reduces numerical dissipation and can simulate gas–liquid interfaces wetting solid boundaries. Static droplet contact angle validations show that the LS-LBM model predicts contact angles with maximum absolute errors of 1.63° on flat surfaces and generally within 2.5° on cylindrical geometries, effectively mitigating staircase approximation errors. In dynamic micro-droplet impact tests at the Weber number (We=12.8) and the Reynolds number (Re=238), the model accurately captures transient spreading and retraction phases on both hydrophilic (θ=31°) and hydrophobic surfaces (θ=107°). In simulations of supercritical carbon dioxide (scCO2) displacing brine in porous media under an unfavorable viscosity ratio (M=μscCO2/μbrine) of 0.0396, shifting the surface wettability from a hydrophilic angle of θ=45° to a hydrophobic angle of θ=120° significantly suppresses capillary fingering and reduces trapped dead zones. Additionally, increasing the capillary number (Ca) from Ca=2.465×10−5 to Ca=9.242×10−5 shifts the flow regime from capillary-dominated to viscous-dominated fingering, accelerating breakthrough. These results demonstrate the model's accuracy and robustness in handling multiphase flows with complex solid boundaries.

papers.title: Squire instability in wavy bag during secondary breakup
papers.abstract: The formation and evolution of surface waviness on inflated liquid bags during secondary drop breakup remain poorly understood. This study investigates their spatiotemporal development through shock-tube experiments on low-Ohnesorge-number isopropyl alcohol drops in the bag and bag-stamen breakup regimes. High-speed imaging reveals an initial stage of exponential bag elongation followed by nonlinear growth as the bag approaches its metastable configuration. This evolution is accompanied by pronounced thickness localization, with liquid accumulating in the trough regions while the crest regions remain comparatively thin. Fourier analysis quantifies the progressive growth of higher-order surface modes, while tracking the crest and trough positions provides their temporal growth rates and characteristic wavelengths. Comparison with the classical Kelvin–Helmholtz prediction shows that the measured crest and trough growth rates are substantially higher than those obtained using the semi-infinite-interface approximation. The corresponding measured-to-predicted growth-rate ratios range from approximately 18 to 38 over the investigated Weber-number range. The experimentally evaluated nondimensional thickness parameter, kβ/2, remains below unity, indicating the increasing importance of the finite thickness of the evolving bag sheet. The measured growth rates and wavelength selection show reasonable agreement in magnitude and trend with the predictions of Squire's finite-thickness liquid-film instability, particularly at low Weber numbers. The thickness non-uniformity becomes more pronounced with increasing Weber number, while deviations from the linear-film prediction at higher Weber numbers indicate the growing influence of nonlinear deformation and spatially varying sheet properties. These findings suggest that a Squire-type finite-thickness instability provides a physically consistent local interpretation of the late-stage bag waviness.

papers.title: Phase transition kinetics and heat transfer characteristics of nanoscale liquid film induced by vibration of zirconium-based substrate
papers.abstract: During the reflooding phase of a loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA), an ultra-thin nanoscale liquid film forms on the fuel cladding surface, which simultaneously undergoes high-frequency, low-amplitude vibrations induced by flow instabilities, jet impingement, and thermal stress fluctuations. While viscous heating effects induced by vibrations are significantly important at micrometer and nanometer scales, the experimental investigation faces numerous challenges. The influence of viscous heating on the phase transition in the liquid film and its mechanism is not yet well-defined. This study focuses on micro-nanoscale phase transition heat transfer during LOCA in nuclear reactors. The influence of zirconium substrate vibration on the phase transition behavior of surface nanoscale liquid films is investigated using molecular dynamics simulations. The results indicate that vibration induces three distinct phase transition modes: diffusive evaporation, nucleate boiling, and film boiling, which are jointly governed by the substrate temperature and vibration parameters. Notably, amplitude regulates heat transfer more significantly than frequency. A dimensionless acoustic-thermal atomization parameter is proposed to quantify the intensity of viscous heating, confirming it as the primary driver of the phase transition. Further analysis shows that vibration energy reduces the energy barrier of the system through viscous dissipation, accelerating bubble nucleation and altering interfacial thermal resistance. This study provides a theoretical basis for understanding micro-nanoscale boiling heat transfer under extreme vibration conditions and offers insights for reactor safety analysis.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of cough-induced droplet generation and transport in the upper airway
papers.abstract: A physics-based computational model is used to investigate mucus film instability, droplet generation, and transport during cough in a human upper airway. Mucus film dynamics and droplet transport are simulated using a coupled Eulerian wall film–discrete phase model framework. Droplet detachment is modeled using a Weber-number-based stripping criterion, linking mucus film stripping to the inertial-surface tension balance. The results show that droplet generation occurs in anatomically constricted regions during the peak expiratory phase, where rapid airflow acceleration produces local film Weber numbers exceeding the critical threshold, resulting in localized film stripping. The predicted exhaled droplet size distribution is unimodal, peaking in the intermediate range (50–75 μm), consistent with experimental measurements. Droplet transport exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on Stokes number, with maximum escape occurring in an intermediate escape-favorable regime (Steff ≈ 5–20), indicating that droplet fate is governed by size-dependent transport within the airway. Only a small fraction of generated droplets are exhaled, while the majority deposit on airway surfaces through inertial impaction and flow-geometry interactions. Residence-time analysis shows that escaped and deposited droplets experience distinct transport times, with droplet fate influenced by the relative timescales of particle relaxation and the finite time available for transport through the airway. Parametric analysis shows that variations in mucus surface tension and critical Weber number affect droplet generation by modifying the extent of mucus-film stripping, while the subsequent transport mechanism remains governed by particle inertia. These findings support a coupled physical mechanism, in which the Weber-number-based stripping criterion governs droplet generation, while droplet fate is primarily determined by Stokes-number-dependent transport.

papers.title: Dynamics of droplet splitting upon impact on surfaces with contact angle hysteresis
papers.abstract: Droplet splitting upon impact is an intricate interfacial process governed by contact-line motion, contact-line dissipation, pinning, and capillary oscillations. Although dynamic contact angle (DCA) models are widely used in moving contact-line simulations, they often fail to describe the evolution of the apparent DCA (θd) during advancing, receding, and pinned regimes as the contact-line velocity (UCL) approaches zero. This limitation becomes critical when subtle variations in contact angle hysteresis (CAH) alter the droplet post-impact dynamics. Here, we report droplet splitting on a nanoporous surface, where a slight spatial variation in CAH, with nearly unchanged static contact angle (θs), produces two distinct modes: single and double split. High-speed imaging experiments at Weber number We ≈ 7.1 show that these modes involve different evolutions of the contact line and θd. To capture this phenomenon, we develop an improved DCA model that describes a monotonic–nonmonotonic variation in θd as UCL approaches zero. Direct numerical simulations coupled with this model reproduce the observed splitting dynamics and show that CAH governs the balance between contact-line dissipation, pinning, and oscillatory dynamics. For θs=135°, the model identifies a cutoff at CAH ≈ 85°, separating single and double splitting modes.

papers.title: An asymptotic analysis and an integral equation method approach for erosion in porous media
papers.abstract: In nature, erosion caused by water or air flow is one of the most prevalent geological and mechanical processes. This phenomenon occurs at the fluid–solid interface when the total shear stress induced by the flow exceeds a specific critical threshold that depends on the properties of the solid material. This research project focuses on the mathematical modeling and simulation of the erosion process in a porous medium characterized by axisymmetric channels. We employ an integral equation method (IEM), which enables an efficient and accurate analysis of the erosion process within the porous medium. In addition, we present a detailed comparison between the numerical solutions from our model and a reduced mathematical model using asymptotic analysis. This comparison provides critical insights into erosion patterns and validates the proposed computational approach for sufficiently small pore geometries. Our results demonstrate that while the asymptotic model provides a highly efficient approximation for slender channels, the IEM is favorable for comparably wider pores.

papers.title: Electrochemomechanical coupling and electrowetting deformation of nanoconfined droplets on active electrodes: Implications for electrochemical analytics
papers.abstract: The electrochemical response of confined droplets in scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) is not only electrochemical but also electromechanical. Here, we show that strong electric fields within the compact region of the electrical double layer (EDL), composed of the Inner Helmholtz Plane and the Outer Helmholtz Plane, can store electrostatic energy capable of deforming the droplet via electrowetting under hydrostatic equilibrium conditions, thereby dynamically coupling interfacial electrolyte electrostatics to droplet geometry. This coupling reduces the electrode contact angle, enlarges the liquid–solid (electrode) area, and increases the measured current. Systematic simulations reveal that, under hydrostatic equilibrium conditions, increasing the micropipette–electrode confinement height significantly enhances both the wetted electrode area and the limiting current, whereas increasing the micropipette–electrolyte contact angle reduces the droplet volume and the active electrode area, thereby weakening the current response. Although the shape of the polarization curve remains unchanged, the current magnitude depends heavily on the electromechanical feedback between EDL energy and droplet geometry. These findings indicate that electrowetting can contribute significantly to the SECCM signal under the quasi-static conditions and modeling assumptions considered here and should therefore be considered when interpreting experimental data.

papers.title: Drag reduction regimes of multi-fin coupling in manta ray gliding
papers.abstract: The morphological changes of the manta ray's cephalic and pectoral fins can jointly regulate its gliding performance, but the hydrodynamic mechanism underlying their coupling remains unclear. In this paper, three-dimensional manta ray models with four cephalic fin postures: embracing, spreading, outwardly turned, and curling, are constructed using a parametric modeling method. Numerical simulations based on the immersed boundary sphere function-based gas kinetic scheme are then conducted to investigate the gliding flow fields and hydrodynamic characteristics under different angles of attack and bowed angles. The results show that the cephalic pectoral fin coupling exhibits three typical drag reduction modes depending on the angle of attack. At large negative angles, a “cephalic pectoral fin synergy mode” is observed, wherein curling cephalic fins suppress wake vortex shedding and mitigate the rearward shift of the low-pressure region, while pectoral fin bowing further reduces the trailing edge low-pressure zone. At near zero angles, a “cephalic fin dominant mode” is identified, in which curling cephalic fins achieve a more stable drag reduction by optimizing the ventral body-attached vortex and local pressure distribution. At large positive angles, a “pectoral fin dominant mode” is found, wherein bowed pectoral fins deflect wake vortex propagation toward the streamwise direction, serving as the primary drag reduction source. This study elucidates the flow control mechanism of static cephalic pectoral fin coupling in manta rays, providing new physical insights into multi-fin coupling, as well as design references for biomimetic underwater vehicles and guidance for cephalic fin-inspired actuators.

papers.title: Numerical model parameters optimization of ventilated cavitating flow around an axisymmetric body by ensemble Kalman filter data assimilation
papers.abstract: To improve the predictive accuracy of numerical simulations for ventilated cavitating flows, this study presents a data assimilation framework based on the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) to calibrate four key parameters in a large eddy simulation model for an axisymmetric body: the Smagorinsky constant, the number of smoothing iterations for interface curvature calculation, the characteristic velocity, and the characteristic length. Thirty parameter sets generated via Latin hypercube sampling are utilized to establish the initial flow field ensemble. Using time-series cavity lengths from water tunnel high-speed photography as observational data, an iterative EnKF algorithm derives the optimal parameter combination (CS = 0.0773, MM = 4, U = 0.7873U0, and L = 3.646D). Results demonstrate that the optimized model reduces the relative error of time-averaged cavity length from 7.8% (baseline) to 1.37% against experimental data. Furthermore, while activating subgrid dissipation and interfacial smoothing successfully filters out unphysical grid-scale numerical currents and regularizes macroscopic phase-boundary stability, the single-scalar length observation primarily constrains global geometric scales, leaving fine-scale transient shedding frequencies and localized gas leakage dynamics loosely constrained. Cross-condition validations across varying ventilation rates and freestream velocities confirm the strong multi-condition generalizability of the calibrated parameter matrix for macroscopic cavity predictions.

papers.title: Numerical analysis of film cooling with microporous walls for rotating detonation engines
papers.abstract: Thermal protection of the combustor wall under extreme pulsating heat flux is a critical bottleneck for the engineering application of rotating detonation engines (RDEs). Ordinary film-cooling schemes face severe challenges in the strongly unsteady environment of rotating detonation waves (RDWs), including periodic coolant blockage, flow reversal, and cooling film coverage failure. To address these issues, this study proposes an innovative film-cooling scheme based on a microporous wall configuration. Using numerical simulations, the coolant transport mechanisms, reverse-penetration resistance, and overall cooling performance of the micropore configuration under periodic RDW sweeping are systematically investigated. The results indicate that the microporous configuration, by generating a large number of fine, dense jets, significantly enhances the lateral spreading and merging of the coolant along the wall, forming a more continuous, uniform, and wall-attached low-temperature cooling film compared to ordinary round-hole designs. In the critical region where the RDW interacts with oblique shock waves, the microporous configuration demonstrates outstanding resistance to hot-gas reverse penetration, with a significantly lower reverse-flow time fraction than that of conventional round holes. Increasing the coolant mass flow ratio further improves the continuity and integrity of the film coverage, thereby effectively reducing the time-averaged wall temperature and heat flux, though with a slight increase in the peak combustion pressure. Comparative analysis with ordinary round-hole configurations confirms that the microporous design provides clear advantages in reducing the instantaneous peak wall heat flux and improving cooling efficiency uniformity, albeit at the expense of higher instantaneous pressure fluctuations. By refining the flow field and regulating the vortex system, the microporous configuration establishes a more stable and reliable cooling foundation in the vulnerable upstream region, offering an efficient, robust, and less intrusive thermal protection strategy for RDEs.

papers.title: Enhancement of biodiesel droplet interface deformation and breakup under an electric field
papers.abstract: Biodiesel suffers from inherently high surface tension and viscosity that impede droplet atomization and subsequent air–fuel mixing upon injection. In this study, biodiesel droplet generation under a direct current electric field (BoE < 6.03) at flow rates of 5–20 ml/h was examined via high-speed photography, focusing on the effect of the electric field on the interface deformation and subsequent droplet breakup. The findings indicate that the imposed electric field markedly enhances interface evolution. Specifically, the outward normal Maxwell stress overcomes the restoring effect of surface tension, driving morphological transitions from dripping mode (BoE < 1.58) to a cone-jet mode (1.58 < BoE < 3.2), and ultimately to a multi-jet mode (BoE > 3.2). The high relaxation time ratio Cτ=6.17 leads to capillary-gravity instability breakup at low electric fields, whereas high fields enable dynamic coupling of charge migration and interface deformation, producing droplet breakup at frequencies above 104 Hz. In the cone-jet regime, the droplet diameter D32 is reduced by approximately 33 times compared to the field-free condition. The size distribution evolves from a broad bimodal profile into a sharp monodisperse peak, with the relative span factor converging to a stable range of 0.3–0.5 for BoE > 1.8. Further validation is conducted by comparing the experimental results with the prediction of the scaling laws. It is found that the droplet size distribution fits better with the scaling laws. Overall, electrospray technology shows significant promise for improving biodiesel atomization and provides a viable pathway toward cleaner combustion in engines.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann study of bubble escape and entrapment in a solidifying molten droplet
papers.abstract: Molten droplet solidification is encountered in additive manufacturing, laser cladding, and related droplet-based thermal processes. In these systems, bubbles retained inside the droplet may be captured by the advancing solidification front and eventually form pores, which degrade the quality of the final deposit. To clarify this mechanism, a three-dimensional multiphase, multicomponent lattice Boltzmann method coupled with a liquid–solid phase-change model is employed to study the rise of a single bubble inside a cooling molten droplet. The model is validated against the evolution of the solid–liquid interface, the total solidification time, and the rise velocity of a single bubble. The effects of substrate undercooling, initial bubble height, and bubble radius are then examined systematically. The results show that the final fate of the bubble is governed by the competition between upward bubble motion and the advancing solidification front. Lower substrate undercooling, a higher initial bubble position, and a larger bubble size all promote bubble escape. The simulations further show that thermal conditions and initial bubble geometry jointly affect the final pore position and shape, with larger bubbles tending to produce more asymmetric pores. These results clarify the physical mechanisms of pore formation in solidifying droplets and may inform defect-control strategies in droplet-based manufacturing and related solidification processes.

papers.title: Modeling the vertical structure of turbulence characteristics in the atmospheric boundary layer: A physics-informed neural operator and symbolic regression method
papers.abstract: Accurately modeling turbulence intensity (TI) and gust factor (GU) is crucial for ensuring the structural integrity and operational efficiency of wind turbines. This study develops a physics-informed model for turbulence characteristics in the complex atmospheric boundary layer, leveraging 1 year of Doppler wind lidar observations and Weather Research and Forecasting numerical simulations for both stationary and non-stationary models. A combined analysis of observations and simulations reveals a distinct vertical structure of turbulence. Based on this, we further develop an explicit symbolic regression physical model and a physics-informed neural operator deep learning model. The results show that both TI and GU exhibit a C-shaped vertical profile below 200 m under various atmospheric stability conditions, decreasing with height up to an inflection point at approximately 120 m, then increasing. A genetic algorithm-driven symbolic regression method yields a physically interpretable analytical model (coefficient of determination R2 ≥ 0.953) that accurately captures this structure, significantly outperforming traditional empirical formulas. Furthermore, a hybrid model integrating bidirectional long short-term temporal modeling, neural operator architecture, and embedded physical constraints is developed. It achieves maximum R2 values of 0.960 for TI and 0.962 for GU, while maintaining superior consistency in representing vertical profiles. This work demonstrates that embedding explicit physical knowledge into neural operator learning frameworks effectively improves the fidelity and physical consistency of turbulence vertical-structure representation in the present dataset. It offers a potentially useful, physically consistent pathway for wind resource assessment and load-related turbulence-risk evaluation in complex terrain.

papers.title: Coupling between kerogen structural evolution and CO2–shale oil competitive adsorption in water-bearing shale composite nanopores: A molecular dynamics study
papers.abstract: Interactions among water, CO2, and multicomponent shale oil in nanopores significantly affect fluid distribution and nanopore structural response. However, the coupling mechanism between kerogen structural evolution and CO2–shale oil competitive adsorption in water-bearing shale composite nanopores remains unclear. In this study, a hydroxylated quartz–type-I kerogen organic–inorganic composite slit pore model was constructed for the Yanchang Formation shale reservoir of Ordos Basin. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate fluid-induced kerogen swelling and CO2–shale oil competitive adsorption at different water contents. The results show that water molecules preferentially accumulate at hydroxylated quartz–kerogen interface. Among the water contents investigated, the outward migration of the kerogen boundary is most pronounced at 10.4%. Interfacial hydrogen bonding promotes this migration. As the water content increases, water clusters form within the kerogen matrix and suppress further boundary migration through steric hindrance.
