Fluid invasion induces kerogen swelling and pore structure reorganization, whereas occupation of the pore free volume reduces the effective porosity. Under water-bearing conditions, competitive adsorption occurs mainly on the kerogen side of the composite substrate, where supercritical CO2 exhibits stronger adsorption affinity than shale oil. Light saturated hydrocarbons can penetrate kerogen micropores and directly compete with CO2, whereas medium saturated hydrocarbons mainly compete on the kerogen surface and in larger pores. Among the water contents investigated, CO2 accumulation and its competitive adsorption against saturated hydrocarbons are most pronounced at 10.4%. Further increases in water content inhibit CO2 penetration and diffusion. These results provide molecular insights into water-dependent CO2–shale oil competitive adsorption in shale nanopores.

papers.title: Electron beam zone-irradiated wettability-step surfaces: Synergistic pinning of underwater bubbles from instability to robustness
papers.abstract: The bubble drag reduction method based on the gas–liquid interfacial slip effect is recognized as having its environmental friendliness and controllable cost. However, in dynamic flow fields, issues, such as gas film instability, bubble rupture, and detachment, are encountered, leading to a sharp decline in drag reduction performance. In this work, a strategy using wettability-step surfaces was proposed to enhance bubble stability. Wettability-step surfaces with different wettability contrasts (40°–140°) and spacings (2–6 mm) are fabricated by a self-developed electron-beam zone irradiation technique. The attachment, deformation, and detachment behaviors of bubbles are systematically investigated by combining underwater bubble dynamic monitoring experiments with multiphase numerical simulations. The results indicate that bubbles are trapped by superhydrophobic regions, while additional pinning forces are generated by hydrophilic regions through the contact angle hysteresis effect. The critical bubble detachment velocity increased to 3.0 l/min by the synergistic action of these two regions. At this flow velocity, a reduction in wall frictional drag of 17.5% is obtained compared with a smooth surface. As the wettability contrast increases, the pinning force is increased from 26 to 104 mN, the receding contact angle is raised from 30° to 122°, and the contact angle hysteresis reaches 100°. The hydrophobic regions form a continuous gas film within the micrometer-sized pits through capillary action, while the hydrophilic regions generate an additional pinning force through the contact angle hysteresis effect at the wettability-step boundary. The synergistic action of these two effects further increases the critical bubble detachment velocity.

papers.title: Lagrangian ellipsoid diagnostics in rough two-dimensional synthetic flows: Aspect-ratio saturation and reduced modeling
papers.abstract: We develop and test a Lagrangian methodology for extracting finite-cloud geometry and reduced dynamics from particle trajectories. A volume-filled cloud in a rough, incompressible, two-dimensional synthetic flow is represented simultaneously by a mass/gyration ellipse, which describes the particle-weighted bulk, and by a minimum-area enclosing ellipse, which describes the outer envelope and its boundary-supporting particles. The homogeneous Gaussian–Hölder velocity has finite Ornstein–Uhlenbeck temporal memory, and the moving cloud centroid is followed explicitly. The principal empirical finding is unexpected: although the cloud is continually deformed by a non-smooth velocity field, the normalized aspect ratios of both ellipses reach broad, order-one distributions that are approximately stationary when conditioned on cloud scale. The mass ellipse is more elongated, whereas the enclosing ellipse covers a substantially larger radial envelope and has the more scale-stable conditional shape distribution. To understand this saturation, we compare two finite-cloud descriptions of the velocity gradient. A gradient averaged spatially over the enclosing ellipse predicts more aligned stretching than the particles actually experience. The corresponding finite-cloud gradient correction provides most of the negative contribution that offsets aligned stretching; a smaller correction remains specific to representing the evolving outer cloud by an enclosing ellipse. Finally, we demonstrate a data-to-model workflow. The measured time series is transformed to regular intrinsic variables, a constrained hierarchy of finite-lag stochastic models is fitted, and the models are compared on independent held-out realizations. The fitted coefficients and detailed stochastic equations are specific to this synthetic experiment. The intended transferable contribution is the methodology: paired cloud geometries, finite-cloud coarse graining, intrinsic variables, a transparent correction decomposition, and held-out validation for future direct numerical simulations and experiments.

papers.title: Surrogate-assisted aerodynamic shape optimization of low-rise buildings with large-eddy simulation validation and flow-mechanism analysis
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic shape optimization of low-rise buildings requires repeated evaluation of wind-induced forces over many geometric parameters and wind directions, making direct wind tunnel testing or high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics impractical for broad design-space exploration. This study develops a data-efficient surrogate-assisted framework for reducing peak aerodynamic force coefficients of isolated low-rise buildings and investigates the flow mechanisms responsible for the optimized performance. A Kolmogorov–Arnold network is trained using the experiment database to predict the peak drag, cross-wind, and lift-related coefficients as functions of height-to-breadth ratio, depth-to-breadth ratio, roof pitch, and wind direction. The model is compared with backpropagation and radial basis function neural networks and achieves improved accuracy and generalization with substantially fewer trainable parameters. The trained surrogate is coupled with a multi-objective genetic algorithm to identify Pareto-optimal building geometries that simultaneously reduce the three target aerodynamic coefficients over the considered wind-direction range. Representative optimized configurations are then examined using large eddy simulation (LES). The LES results show close agreement with surrogate predictions and reveal that load reduction is associated with modified roof separation, weakened suction zones, and altered wake development around the optimized geometries. The proposed approach links data-driven optimization with flow-physics verification and provides a computationally efficient route for the aerodynamic shape design of isolated low-rise buildings under wind loading.

papers.title: On the scaling of cavitation inception in tip-leakage vortex flows
papers.abstract: The scaling of cavitation inception in tip-leakage vortex flows remains a fundamental challenge in fluid mechanics, primarily due to the complex coupling between macroscopic flow structures and microscopic bubble dynamics. In this study, an Euler–Lagrange framework coupling large eddy simulation with discrete bubble tracking is employed to investigate these scale effects. After validating the model against experimental results, three distinct scale effects are systematically analyzed: velocity scale effect, size scale effect, and the scale effect at the same Reynolds number (Re). The results reveal that the inception cavitation number (σi) exhibits a strong positive correlation with both incoming velocity and size ratio. Even at identical Re, σi increases with the physical size of the hydrofoil, indicating that Reynolds number alone is insufficient to characterize inception scaling. Mechanistically, increasing incoming velocity or size ratio reduces both the time-averaged and fluctuating pressures within the vortex core, while simultaneously increasing the number density of entrained gas nuclei. Crucially, while the macroscopic pressure field maintains spatiotemporal similarity at the same Re, the microscopic gas nuclei distribution varies distinctly with physical scale. Consequently, the conventional velocity and size scale effects are jointly governed by macroscopic pressure variations and microscopic nuclei dynamics, whereas the scale effect at identical Re is fundamentally dictated by the microscopic nuclei transport. These findings provide new insights into the multi-scale physics governing vortex cavitation inception.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for two-way fluid–particle interaction: Data-free forward and motion-only inverse problems
papers.abstract: Free rigid-particle motion in a viscous fluid couples the incompressible Navier–Stokes and Newton–Euler equations through the traction on a moving interface; this same coupling underlies falling-body viscometry when the observed motion is used to infer fluid properties. We present a physics-informed neural-network framework with a single field-load-motion formulation comprising neural velocity and pressure fields on the moving space–time domain, surface-traction integration, and enforcement of the rigid-body momentum balance. In the data-free forward mode, the balance acts as the equation of motion: force and torque integrated from the network's own stress determine free translation and rotation through an under-relaxed fixed-point iteration, with no labeled flow or trajectory data. In the motion-only inverse mode, a single particle-centroid velocity record prescribes the moving-boundary kinematics, and its time derivative provides the acceleration that, together with the momentum balance, supplies an integral-force target. Following manufactured-solution verification, seven benchmarks against arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian reference solutions yield trajectory and velocity errors below 5% and flow-field errors within 9.0%; transfer learning reduces coupled wall-clock cost by a factor of 9.8. From one transient velocity record and without interior flow observations, the inverse mode identifies viscosity with 1.13% relative error and reconstructs the withheld fields to 6.8%–8.2% mean error, degrading gradually under up to 5% record noise. Accuracy is retained at Re ≈ 32; at Re ≈ 118, the formulation underpredicts instability-driven wake growth, delineating the present scope. The framework thus provides a label-free neural closure of the two-way fluid–particle coupling in forward mode and a controlled proof of concept for extending falling-body viscometry to joint recovery of viscosity and the unobserved flow.

papers.title: Reynolds number and solid volume fraction effects on turbulence–particle interaction in large-eddy simulation–discrete element method simulations of vertical solid–liquid pipe flow
papers.abstract: The transport of coarse heavy particles in turbulent vertical pipe flow underlies hydraulic systems such as deep-sea mining risers, yet how finite-size particles modulate the carrier-phase turbulence remains poorly understood. We perform large-eddy simulations coupled with the discrete element method of solid–liquid upflow with spherical particles (diameter 7.6% of pipe diameter, density ratio 2.45) at bulk Reynolds numbers of 52 944, 71 254, and 90 271 and solid volume fractions of 2.41%, 5.0%, and 7.5%. In inner scaling, the near-wall and streamwise-component statistics depend only weakly on Reynolds number, while the mid-radius transverse and shear stresses scale faster than the friction velocity squared, and the energy partition is essentially Reynolds-independent. Loading produces the dominant effect. Near the wall, the Reynolds shear stress and the normal stresses are suppressed at broadly similar rates at the highest loading (by about 20% and by 10%–21%). The decisive decoupling occurs instead in the particle-dense core, where collective streamwise wakes raise the streamwise normal stress roughly threefold and drive the local Reynolds shear stress to near zero, producing a near one-component state distinct from, and to our knowledge rarely observed in, single-phase wall-bounded turbulence. The ejection-to-sweep balance reverses in the innermost dense core, where the streamwise velocity skewness also changes sign. Voronoi tessellation shows that the global nonrandomness of the particle arrangement weakens monotonically with Reynolds number and is nearly unchanged by loading, while a radial decomposition shows that local clustering in the dilute near-wall layer strengthens with loading.

papers.title: Flow around a circular cylinder inside a hybrid channel
papers.abstract: Motivated by the substantial contribution of the wheel region to ground-vehicle aerodynamic drag, the present study examines flow around a circular cylinder inside a straight-curved hybrid channel as a reduced-order representation of the coupled wheel-ground-housing system. Large-eddy simulations are employed to quantify the aerodynamic forces and Reynolds-number-dependent evolution of the associated flow structures. The Reynolds number based on the cylinder diameter spans ReD = 3.6 × 103 to 3.6 × 106, and that based on the half-channel height covers Reδ = 4.0 × 102 to 4.0 × 105. The results show that increasing ReD significantly reduces the mean drag coefficient C¯D from 8.0 to 1.1 while increasing the mean lift coefficient C¯L from 3.9 to 5.9. The root mean square drag and lift coefficients rise rapidly from a regime in which the separated shear layers remain relatively stable, and wake fluctuations are of limited amplitude, attaining a maximum at ReD = 3.6 × 104. Combined examination of the surface pressure gradient and wall shear stress identifies flow separation occurring near 277°–287°, with its extent strongly influenced by both Reynolds number and curvature-induced acceleration. Upstream of the curved section, the velocity-deficit profiles depart from the canonical parabolic form, with stronger near-wall deficits at lower Reδ. Downstream of the cylinder, the peak streamwise velocity fluctuation moves progressively toward the cylinder as Reδ increases, while its magnitude first increases and then decreases, consistent with the trends of force fluctuations. These results demonstrate that the aerodynamic loading, separation behavior, and wake dynamics are controlled by the coupled action of non-uniform confinement, wall curvature, and streamwise flow acceleration.

papers.title: Wall shear stress in coronary arteries and grafts using computational fluid dynamics and physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) were used to quantify wall shear stress (WSS) in 12 patient-specific coronary geometries, including four healthy cases, five coronary artery bypass graft cases with saphenous vein grafts, and three coronary artery disease cases without bypass grafts, under both Newtonian and Carreau–Yasuda blood viscosity models. The analysis focused on area-weighted average WSS, average WSS at bifurcations, the area fraction where WSS exceeds 40 dynes/cm2 normalized by the total vessel area, area-weighted average WSS above 40 dynes/cm2, and the interquartile range (IQR) of WSS. Diseased coronary arteries and diseased grafts (DGs) exhibited elevated WSS compared with healthy arteries and healthy grafts. The area-weighted average WSS above 40 dynes/cm2 in DGs reached up to ∼148 dynes/cm2, while healthy vessels showed lower values in the present cohort. IQR values were also higher in diseased vessels, indicating increased spatial heterogeneity of WSS. An exploratory elevated WSS threshold of 40 dynes/cm2 effectively differentiated healthy and diseased regions. Compared with the Newtonian model, the Carreau–Yasuda formulation captured shear-rate-dependent viscosity effects in stenotic and bifurcation regions. Furthermore, physics-informed neural network surrogate models incorporating random Fourier feature encoding were trained to reconstruct the CFD fields for the 12 patient-specific cases. Under a dense 20% within-geometry holdout of CFD target values, the Newtonian surrogate achieved a mean normalized root mean square error of 0.93% with a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.98, while the Carreau–Yasuda surrogate achieved 0.97% with a coefficient of determination of 0.98, with both rheologies evaluated on a common per-patient vessel subset so that the comparison is strictly like-for-like. Both models showed strong agreement with CFD results within their respective training geometries, with holdout Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.99 and 0.99, respectively.

papers.title: Propagation characteristics of ultra-low-frequency surface-trapped acoustic-gravity waves excited by an underwater point source
papers.abstract: At ultra-low frequencies, underwater pressure fields may be influenced by dynamic free-surface motion as well as conventional water-column acoustics. This study investigates whether gravity-restored free-surface coupling creates a surface-trapped acoustic–gravity-wave pathway that is absent from a pressure-release model. A pressure-based finite-difference time-domain model is verified against Gaussian pressure-disturbance and Pekeris-waveguide benchmarks and then applied to paired simulations in a penetrable water–sediment waveguide. For a 0.1 Hz point source, both models produce nearly identical early compressional arrivals, whereas only the gravity-restored model generates a delayed, long-lived response concentrated beneath the free surface. Under continuous forcing, this response develops into a coherent, comparatively low-loss, radially propagating wave train. Wavenumber–frequency spectra, phase- and group-velocity estimates, and mechanical energy-flux calculations identify the response as belonging to the finite-depth surface-gravity branch. Singular value decomposition (SVD) further shows that the surface-localized SVD mode weakens as source frequency and source depth increase; deeper sources increase the second-mode fraction and broaden the vertical pressure distribution. These results demonstrate that gravity-restored free-surface coupling enables a distinct pathway for ultra-low-frequency energy redistribution and near-surface transport in underwater waveguides.

papers.title: Performance variation and loss mechanism of a radial inflow turbine under off-design conditions
papers.abstract: Radial inflow turbines (RITs) are key expansion devices in organic Rankine cycle (ORC) systems for low-grade waste heat recovery. Under practical operation, variations in heat source conditions and system loads cause deviations in inlet temperature, pressure ratio, and rotational speed, affecting turbine performance and irreversible losses. This study investigates a pentane-based ORC RIT using three-dimensional numerical simulations and entropy generation analysis. The effects of inlet temperature, pressure ratio, and rotational speed on performance, flow characteristics, and loss distributions are systematically evaluated. The results show that turbine power increases while isentropic efficiency decreases with increasing inlet temperature and pressure ratio. Both efficiency and power exhibit an inverted “U-shaped” trend with rotational speed. Extreme rotational speeds induce different incidence mismatch patterns, leading to changes in flow separation and high-entropy-generation regions. Entropy generation analysis identifies the rotor as the dominant loss source, with turbulent dissipation contributing the largest proportion. The intermediate passage accounts for approximately 67.7%–74.5% of the rotor local entropy generation, indicating that inlet mismatch triggers loss development, while irreversible losses mainly accumulate during downstream evolution of separation vortices, shear layers, and secondary flows. This study provides a region-resolved, entropy-based quantitative characterization of loss evolution and redistribution in the investigated pentane ORC RIT under off-design conditions.

papers.title: γ-Ray-based void fraction analysis in aero-engine lubrication scavenge lines
papers.abstract: The void fraction, as a critical parameter for characterizing the composition of oil and gas mixtures, indicates the volumetric distribution of oil and gas phases within the scavenge pipe. It has a substantial influence on the performance of the scavenge pump, oil radiator, and oil–gas separator. This study refers to the scavenge pipe diameter and flow parameters of an aeronautical turboshaft engine. It focuses on the horizontal scavenge pipe with a two-phase flow of lubricating oil and air as the test subject. Research on testing methods for the void fraction in the scavenge pipe is conducted using the gamma-ray method. First, based on the continuous attenuation characteristics of radioactive sources, the basic theory of measuring gas holdup of oil–gas two-phase flow using the gamma-ray method was analyzed and the mathematical relationship for the void fraction measurement was derived. Then, the structural design of the oil–gas ratio testing device was completed. Second, a test system was established to generate the mixture and measure the void fraction. Then, the absorption coefficient a key parameter in the oil–gas two-phase test was calibrated, and a compensation model for the density influence of lubricating oil and air was established. Finally, the void fraction test was carried out in the horizontal pipe with a diameter of 12 mm, and the void fraction of the test ranges from 7% to 99%. Based on existing void fraction models, the experimental data were validated, and a back propagation neural network model was established to predict the void fraction.

papers.title: Energy conversion mechanisms and flow boundaries of gas–liquid multiphase flow in a mixed-flow electrical submersible pump for offshore oilfields
papers.abstract: Gas entrainment threatens the hydraulic stability and energy conversion efficiency of electrical submersible pumps (ESPs). To elucidate multiphase performance variations and underlying energy dissipation mechanisms, a mixed-flow ESP widely applied in offshore oilfields was investigated. A robust Euler–Euler inhomogeneous multiphase numerical method was experimentally validated to quantitatively evaluate the spatial distributions of input power, effective power, and power losses within the impeller. Furthermore, critical flow pattern transition boundaries were systematically extracted across varying liquid flow rates and inlet pressures. Results show that gas accumulation and flow blockage near the suction side severely obstruct flow passages and induce intense wake vortices; specifically, at a 15% inlet gas volume fraction (GVF), global power loss surges by 280%, causing a 44.5% plunge in effective power. Macroscopically, pressurization exhibits a three-stage degradation. Elevating inlet pressure effectively shrinks the deteriorated gas pocket region, substantially broadening the stable operational envelope. Additionally, critical gas tolerance boundaries demonstrate a distinct nonlinear “hump” morphology, achieving optimal gas handling capacity near the design flow rate due to minimized incidence-induced separation and maximized interphase sweeping momentum. Ultimately, by incorporating a flow-deviation-based Gaussian decay term alongside phase density and pressure ratios, a critical GVF prediction model is proposed. This model dynamically evaluates the pump's gas handling capability, providing a reliable theoretical guideline for the operation of offshore oilfield ESP systems.

papers.title: Cavity-dynamic modulation of pressure and hydroacoustic spectra in a cavitating axial-flow pump
papers.abstract: Cavitation-induced hydroacoustic variation in axial-flow pumps cannot be characterized solely by vapor volume or overall sound pressure level, but also depends on how evolving vapor structures reorganize rotor–stator pressure excitation. A box-culvert axial-flow pump is investigated using model-test validation, transient very-large-eddy simulation of cavitating flow, and a one-way surface-pressure-driven computational fluid dynamics–finite element method hydroacoustic calculation. Cavitation stages are identified from hydraulic degradation, vapor-volume statistics, and cavity morphology. Cavity-volume oscillation, section-resolved pressure and hydroacoustic spectra, blade passing-frequency (BPF)-centered energy ratios, and acoustic spectral entropy are then analyzed. Pressure-hydroacoustic spectral reorganization already appears during developing cavitation, when the head-drop ratio is only 1.91%, below the conventional 3% head-drop criterion. With decreasing cavitation number, vapor structures evolve from attached cavities with blade-passage-related modulation to longer-period vapor accumulation, blockage-like vapor structures, and blade-exit shedding. This transition weakens harmonic pressure organization, particularly in the impeller outlet–guide-vane inlet interaction region. The hydroacoustic response is therefore not uniformly amplified: the BPF remains dominant, whereas its energy contribution decreases and low-frequency components, fragmented fine spectral features, and non-BPF components become more pronounced under severe cavitation. The accompanying decrease in BPF-centered acoustic energy and increase in spectral entropy quantify the redistribution of acoustic energy over a broader frequency range. These results identify cavity-dynamic modulation of rotor–stator pressure excitation as the mechanism underlying cavitation-induced pressure-hydroacoustic spectral reorganization.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal distribution and statistical kinematics of saltation load over a movable bed
papers.abstract: Observations of bedload saltation over movable beds are crucial for understanding fluvial sediment transport. However, unlike fixed-bed studies, capturing microscale saltation dynamics over movable beds is severely hindered by the highly dynamic granular background and dense particle occlusion. To overcome this measurement challenge, we combined particle tracking velocimetry with a Kalman filter algorithm to obtain continuous particle trajectories from flume experiments. Based on these new high-resolution data, we investigated the spatiotemporal evolution and statistical kinematics of saltating particles across varying flow intensities, with particular emphasis on differences in particle-bed collisions between movable-bed and fixed-bed conditions. Our results suggest a gradual transition from predominantly stochastic particle entrainment toward increasingly spatially correlated collective transport as flow discharge increases, accompanied by velocity fluctuations dominated by low-frequency surging (≤20 Hz, accounting for 70%–85% of total fluctuation energy). Saltation kinematics are jointly governed by fluid forcing and particle–bed collisions. While stronger flows compress the distributions of saltation height and step length, rendering macroscopic trajectories more uniform, bed collisions impose a persistent geometric constraint that stabilizes rebound angles despite highly dispersed impact conditions. Compared with fixed-bed conditions, the movable bed acts as an energy buffer, dissipating nearly 47% of the incident kinetic energy to mobilize resting particles and reducing the restitution coefficient by approximately 27%. These findings provide insight into improving macroscopic sediment transport rate formulations and microscopic computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method models.

papers.title: Sparse-sensor flow reconstruction and motion prediction during water exit of an underwater-launched vehicle
papers.abstract: Real-time monitoring of the complex hydrodynamic states of underwater-launched vehicles during water-exit processes remains challenging due to highly nonlinear multiphase evolution, wake instability, and strong fluid–structure coupling. In this study, a physics-guided sparse sensing framework is developed to establish the relationship between limited wall-pressure measurements, global flow structures, and vehicle motion responses. The framework employs a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and Transformer-based multi-task learning strategy, where POD provides a physically interpretable latent representation of flow dynamics, while Transformer-based feature learning captures global correlations among modal features and sensor locations. By incorporating operating-condition information through feature modulation and attention-based fusion, the proposed framework simultaneously reconstructs pressure, velocity, and vorticity fields and predicts vehicle motion states. The results demonstrate that sparse wall-pressure measurements contain sufficient information to recover the dominant coherent structures and dynamic responses during the water-exit process. Under varying Froude number conditions, reconstruction errors are mainly concentrated in wake shear layers and vortex-dominated regions associated with highly unsteady flow structures, whereas the large-scale flow characteristics governing overall evolution remain accurately captured. Furthermore, sensor configuration analysis reveals that for the investigated vehicle geometry and flow conditions, a 12-sensor layout provides an effective balance between measurement sparsity and reconstruction accuracy, indicating the existence of an effective sensing threshold for capturing essential flow information. These findings provide new insights into the observability of complex water-exit flows, the encoding mechanism between sparse wall measurements and global flow dynamics, and the coupling between hydrodynamic evolution and vehicle motion responses.

papers.title: Control of corner-induced disturbances in confined rotating airflow within a spin-coating chamber using rectifying plates
papers.abstract: A square rotating boundary imposes non-axisymmetric forcing on the confined airflow in a spin-coating chamber, where the periodic passage of the substrate corners induces flow separation and vortical structures. These disturbances disrupt circumferential momentum transport and produce non-uniform velocity gradients and aerodynamic shear above the substrate. In this study, rectifying plates are introduced to regulate the confined rotating flow, and their effects are investigated through gas-phase numerical simulations and spin-coating experiments. The numerical results show that the square-substrate corners generate pronounced non-axisymmetric flow structures and local rotational enhancement. The rectifying plates constrain the corner-induced vortical structures and guide the airflow along a more continuous circumferential path, thereby stabilizing circumferential momentum transport and the near-substrate shear distribution. Compared with the conventional chamber, the fluctuations in airflow velocity, rotation rate, and shear rate are reduced by 12.3%, 90.5%, and 89.6%, respectively. An orthogonal analysis identifies a plate length of 330 mm, a height of 7 mm, and eight plates as the optimal configuration within the investigated parameter range, with plate length being the dominant factor. Spin-coating experiments further show that this configuration reduces the film-thickness non-uniformity from ±5.24% to ±2.07% for photoresist films and from ±8.79% to ±5.82% for silica sol–gel films. These findings clarify how corner-induced disturbances disrupt the circumferential organization of confined rotating flow and demonstrate that rectifying plates can stabilize circumferential momentum transport and aerodynamic shear in rotating systems with non-circular boundaries.

papers.title: Flow-mode transition induced by anchoring orientation asymmetry in nematic liquid crystals
papers.abstract: The backflow effect in nematic liquid crystals provides a basis for non-contact microfluidic manipulation, yet how the initial director configuration governs the cooperative mode and net transport of backflow remains poorly understood. This study investigates the backflow mode transition induced by anchoring orientation asymmetry in twisted nematic cells. We show that the initial anchoring configuration presets the backflow cooperative mode by dictating the symmetry of the elastic energy landscape. A mirror-symmetric anchoring orientation drives constructive superposition of backflow, resulting in a net directional flow, whereas a reverse orientation asymmetry causes exact cancellation, yielding zero net flux and a localized oscillatory flow. This flow-mode transition is accompanied by a systematic shift in the observed dissipation pattern: under symmetric anchoring orientation, the viscous dissipation is distributed and temporally asymmetric, correlating with sustained directional transport; under reverse orientation asymmetry, the dissipation becomes localized and temporally symmetric, consistent with the reciprocal oscillatory flow that yields zero net flux. We further introduce the director rotation intensity and rotation–flow coupling index to provide quantitative criteria for this transition. These findings establish a three-dimensional physical framework, encompassing the elastic, viscous, and electric dimensions, for programing flow modes in liquid-crystal microfluidic devices via interfacial anchoring.

papers.title: Similarities between the speed limit in relativity and the sound barrier in inviscid fluid flows
papers.abstract: The Prandtl–Glauert–Lorentz transformation establishes a deep mathematical correspondence between compressible potential flow theory and special relativity. Despite being implicit in the aerodynamic literature since the early twentieth century, this analogy remains largely unrecognized across the two communities and has never been surveyed in a unified manner. This review presents, in a self-contained and pedagogical framework accessible to both communities, the historical, mathematical, and applied dimensions of this correspondence. After tracing the parallel developments that gave rise to compressible aerodynamic theory and special relativity, we establish the formal equivalence between the Lorentz transformation and the Prandtl–Glauert coordinate change, and reinterpret relativistic concepts such as time dilation, the Doppler effect, and the Lorentz factor within the acoustic framework. Thanks to the added mass concept, we finally extend this analogy and show that the whole mathematical framework of special relativity is exactly mirrored by the linearized compressible potential flow theory.

papers.title: The gravity-driven flow of Herschel-Bulkley fluids in a syringe and the transition to dripping
papers.abstract: Many food, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical products exhibit yield stress, which conditions their flow. In this study, experiments and simulations were combined to provide a quantitative understanding of the effect of the rheological properties of Herschel-Bulkley fluids on the gravity-driven flow in a syringe. Such a flow is key for drip feeding and intravenous drug administration. It is also used worldwide to assess the “consistency” of drinks and their safety for people with swallowing disorders, according to IDDSI (International Dysphagia Diet Standardization Initiative). The transition between jetting and dripping regimes is discussed, and an expression is proposed for the critical Weber number below which dripping occurs, considering its dependence on the Bond, Ohnesorge numbers and on the flow index. Rheological maps are proposed to quantitatively describe the interplay between rheological properties on the flow and the volume left after 10 s, which conditions the IDDSI consistency classification. The analysis shows the dominant role of viscous dissipation for fluids classified as IDDSI levels 2 and 3, in contrast to the more pronounced influence of the Herschel-Bulkley yield stress on the flow for less viscous fluids (level 1 consistency). Finally, a dimensionless hydrostatic-yield time is proposed, which allows explaining all experimental and simulation flow results using a single master curve. These findings provide new insights into gravity-driven flow in a syringe, and into the jetting-to-dripping transition. They could contribute to improving the formulation and safety of beverages for people with swallowing disorders, as well as improving popular protorheology methods, such as the syringe flow test.

papers.title: Multi-scale graph neural network modeling of near-wall turbulence with robust flow generalizability
papers.abstract: A new graph neural network (GNN) subgrid-scale (SGS) stress modeling framework based on multi-scale self-similarity input features is investigated as an improvement in generalizability over a previous GNN model developed by the authors' group. Training and a priori testing are conducted with an incompressible direct numerical simulation (DNS) database comprising homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT), turbulent mixing layer, and turbulent channel flow (CH) cases, each across five Reynolds numbers. DNS fields are filtered at two different scales using both Gaussian and box kernels to create a diverse large eddy simulation training dataset. The multi-scale Leonard stress tensor and spatial velocity fluctuations are used as inputs to capture scale interactions from a broader portion of the turbulent energy spectrum. Galilean invariance and scale equivariance are ensured by input definition and nondimensionalization, respectively. Randomized data augmentation is used to improve model robustness to changes in orientation. Spline-based graph-convolution layers enable non-local feature extraction while maintaining model compatibility with unstructured grids. A priori analysis of four GNN SGS models shows that graph convolution and multi-scale input features provide significant improvement in accuracy for incompressible flows at Reynolds numbers below, within and above the training range, with particular impact in the near-wall region. Model generalizability to compressible reactive flows is high except in a wall-bounded case. In a posteriori testing with incompressible turbulent CH, one multi-scale GNN was found to better match reference DNS profiles than conventional eddy-viscosity models, with computational overhead comparable to that of a dynamic k-equation model.

papers.title: Deep learning semantic segmentation for cloud cavitation image analysis
papers.abstract: Cavitation—and, in particular, cloud cavitation—plays a critical role in the operation of fluid systems due to its strong influence on hydrodynamic performance and material erosion. In this study, we present a novel image-processing framework based on a modified U-Net architecture for the detection of cavitation structures from high-speed photography. The model performs pixel-level segmentation of cavitating regions, followed by a post-processing step employing a heuristic algorithm to distinguish between the cavity sheet and the shed cloud. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework specifically designed to systematically identify and differentiate sheet and cloud cavitation, a distinction that is essential for many studies in cavitation research. The method is applied to cloud cavitation developing about the benchmark NACA 0015 hydrofoil at a fixed Reynolds number and incidence, while varying the cavitation number. The proposed approach enables the extraction of characteristic length scales, including the unsteady sheet length, cloud size, and their spatial distribution. These measurements provide the basis for a statistical analysis of cavitation dynamics. The framework offers a fast, robust, and versatile tool for detecting cavitation phenomena, providing detailed information on the location, extent, and evolution of cavitation structures. As such, it constitutes a practical tool for the systematic investigation of cavitation phenomena in fundamental research.

papers.title: Characterization of partially filled mixing in a baffled twin-screw channel via the implicit incompressible smoothed particle hydrodynamics method
papers.abstract: To improve the flow characteristics in the weak-mixing regions of conventional symmetric twin-screw extruders (TSEs), this study proposes asymmetric baffle twin-screw (BTS) elements with different screw baffle heights. The flow and mixing behavior in BTS and conventional twin-screw (TS) configurations under partially filled conditions are simulated using the Implicit Incompressible Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics method, which provides improved solution accuracy and numerical stability. Visualization experiments confirm good agreement between the simulation results and experimental observations. The BTS elements induce an alternating pattern of fluid splitting and merging in the intermeshing zones, as opposed to the isolated helical flow pattern and symmetric conveying characteristics in conventional TSE elements. This mechanism enabled by the novel BTS configurations significantly improves distributive mixing, with greater geometric asymmetry further amplifying chaotic mixing, across a broad range of fluid viscosities.

papers.title: Principal-direction-frame diagnostics of near-wall vorticity transport over a stationary and deforming Gaussian bump in duct flow
papers.abstract: Boundary vorticity flux (BVF) and boundary enstrophy flux (BEF) characterize the transport of vorticity and enstrophy at solid walls. For curved and deformable boundaries, interpreting these fluxes in relation to local surface geometry requires a direction-resolved representation that is independent of surface parametrization. Existing formulations in the principal-direction non-holonomic frame provide such a theoretical description, but their application to numerical flow fields requires consistent transformations of both physical components and the spatial derivatives involved in BEF and BVF. Building on this theoretical basis, the present study develops a computational procedure that connects numerical flow fields represented in general curvilinear coordinates with principal-direction analyses. Explicit transformation relations are derived for the required velocity and vorticity components and their first- and second-order derivatives, with the spatial variations of the transformation coefficients and local basis vectors retained. The geometrical consistency of the transformed quantities is assessed through the Gauss–Codazzi relations, and the resulting formulation enables term-by-term evaluation of the BEF and BVF decompositions from discrete flow data. The procedure is demonstrated for laminar flow at Re=200 through a square duct with a stationary or periodically deforming Gaussian bump. In the stationary-wall case, the decomposition distinguishes the dominant effect of near-wall shear gradients from the local curvature-weighted modulation of the BEF. Sign changes in the curvature-weighted contribution occur near surface-type boundaries identified by KG=0, illustrating the coupled influence of surface curvature and near-wall vorticity. The BVF analysis further identifies strong competing contributions whose cancelation is obscured in the total flux. At the deformation extrema, the results distinguish the effects associated with instantaneous surface geometry from the unsteady near-wall response retained from the preceding wall motion. The developed procedure thereby makes geometry-resolved BEF and BVF analyses accessible to numerical investigations of curved and deformable wall flows under different configurations and flow conditions.

papers.title: Hydrogen combustion effects on turbine vane aerodynamics and heat transfer
papers.abstract: Hydrogen-fueled gas turbines experience changes not only in the combustion chamber but also in turbine aerodynamics and heat transfer, owing to differences in combustion products. Variations in the thermophysical properties of the combustion gases, which serve as the working gas in the turbine section, can modify the aerodynamic and thermal response of turbine components. In this study, a coupled combustion and computational fluid dynamics framework was employed to investigate the effects of hydrogen combustion on turbine-side aerodynamics and heat transfer under fixed energy input and turbine inlet temperature constraints. Combustion gas properties corresponding to varying hydrogen blending ratios were obtained from combustion simulations, revealing reduced density and increased specific heat and thermal conductivity, along with a decrease in the mass flow rate entering the turbine section. Based on these working gas conditions, the aerodynamics and heat transfer characteristics of the NASA C3X turbine vane were analyzed. The hydrogen combustion gases exhibited weaker expansion through the vane passage, resulting in higher downstream pressure and reduced pressure loading, which were accompanied by decreases in lift and drag coefficients and in total pressure loss. Dynamic pressure normalization effectively distinguished density-driven aerodynamic scaling, while the normalized aerodynamic characteristics remained largely unchanged. Meanwhile, the heat transfer coefficient increased because of altered thermal properties, with a localized enhancement near the suction peak associated with thermal boundary layer compression. These results show that hydrogen combustion moderately modifies turbine aerodynamics and heat transfer, highlighting the importance of turbine-side investigations of hydrogen gas turbines.

papers.title: A non-uniform local reference frame method for the simulation of rotating geometries with non-conformal grids on the hybrid recursive regularized lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Turbomachinery simulations with rotating components require accurate computational fluid dynamics methods. Lattice Boltzmann methods are attractive for such applications as they have low numerical dissipation, low dispersion, and mesh complex geometries easily using Cartesian grids. The Local Reference Frame (LRF) approach handles rotation by maintaining separate reference frames for static and rotating domains. However, current LRF implementations require uniform grid resolution across the overlap region where the two grids communicate. This prevents local refinement near walls or in wakes, which is problematic for industrial cases. We present a non-uniform LRF method that progressively removes this constraint, allowing mesh refinements of ratio 1:2 to cross the overlap region. The key contribution is the proper rescaling of the non-equilibrium stress tensor when interpolating between different grid levels. This rescaling accounts for both molecular viscosity and subgrid-scale (SGS) contributions in Large Eddy Simulations. We derive the rescaling from acoustic scaling principles and Kolmogorov turbulence theory and use temporal interpolation to synchronize fine and coarse grids. The proposed method is validated on three test cases: Taylor–Couette flow, two-dimensional rotating cylinders (Re=200,0.5≤α≤3.0), and three-dimensional turbulent flow past a rotating cylinder (Re=5000,α=1.0). Aerodynamic coefficients agree with uniform LRF within 4%. It is shown that proper SGS rescaling reduces spurious noise significantly. The method aims to enable the simulation of configurations that were previously problematic: installed propellers, shrouded turbines, or any case where rotating geometries operate near static surfaces and require local grid refinement.

papers.title: Coupled aerodynamic characteristics of suction port position and angle of attack for suction-type turbosail
papers.abstract: To address the high carbon emissions of the shipping industry and help achieve the emission reduction targets set by the International Maritime Organization (IMO), this study investigates a suction-type turbosail for wind-assisted propulsion. Using Fluent with the Renormalization Group (RNG) k–ε turbulence model, the paper systematically explores the influencing mechanisms of the circumferential position of suction ports, sail angle, incoming flow angle of attack, and momentum coefficient on aerodynamic performance and flow field structures, with a focus on revealing the laws of boundary layer separation suppression and vortex shedding regulation. The results show that active suction effectively suppresses boundary layer separation, weakens trailing-edge vortex shedding, and substantially improves the aerodynamic performance of turbosail. The optimal operating range of the angle of attack is from −30° to −20°, where the thrust coefficient maintains a desirable level. More importantly, this work quantitatively establishes for the first time that the optimal circumferential layout of the suction port lies ∼10° downstream of the boundary layer separation point under the unsucked baseline condition. The inherent physical mechanism of synergistic effects among boundary layer momentum replenishment, adverse pressure gradient regulation, and wake vortex breakdown at this characteristic position is elaborated, enabling simultaneous optimization of turbosail thrust and aerodynamic efficiency. These findings provide theoretical guidance and engineering references for parameter optimization, structural design, and full-scale ship application of suction-type turbosails.

papers.title: Bifurcation of viscoelastic flow in two- and four-sided lid-driven cavities at an extremely low Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Purely elastic instabilities can drive flow transitions even when inertial effects are negligible. The present study investigates whether these purely elastic instabilities can also lead to flow bifurcations and determines the corresponding bifurcation behavior. The evolution of the flow from steady to unsteady and complex regimes is also examined. The analysis is performed at Re=10−4 using an Oldroyd-B fluid in two canonical square lid-driven cavity configurations: (a) the two-sided lid-driven cavity (TSLDC) and (b) the four-sided lid-driven cavity (FSLDC). The primary analysis considers the classical unregularized lid-velocity profile, R0:u(x)=U, while additional simulations with a regularized lid-velocity profile (R1) examine the influence of the imposed wall-velocity distribution on the bifurcation behavior. For the R0 profile, increasing Wi produces distinct bifurcation behaviors in the two configurations. The TSLDC undergoes a Hopf bifurcation at Wicr=0.8, whereas the FSLDC undergoes a pitchfork bifurcation at Wicr=0.4. At the pitchfork bifurcation, the stable symmetric solution branch splits into two stable asymmetric branches and one unstable symmetric branch, resulting in multiple coexisting flow states. With increasing Wi, the TSLDC transitions from a steady flow to an unsteady quasi-periodic regime, whereas the FSLDC evolves from a steady flow to an unsteady quasi-periodic state and subsequently develops a complex transitional regime preceding fully developed elastic turbulence. The R1 profile smoothly reduces both the wall velocity and its spatial gradient to zero at the lid–sidewall junctions, thereby mitigating the corner singularities. Although R1 retains the same maximum lid velocity as R0, its spatial distribution produces lower effective wall forcing. A comparison of the R0 and R1 cases shows that R1 shifts the bifurcation onset to higher Wi in both cavity configurations. This shift results from the combined effects of corner-singularity mitigation and reduced effective wall forcing associated with the R1 profile. These results demonstrate that purely elastic instabilities can produce flow bifurcations at negligible inertia, while the imposed wall-velocity distribution influences their onset.

papers.title: Active jet control for wake uniformity improvement in submarine stern flows
papers.abstract: The circumferential non-uniformity of the submarine stern wake field significantly affects propulsion performance and acoustic stealth capability. An active flow control method using jet holes near the stern rudders is proposed in this study. Stereo particle image velocimetry experiments and improved delayed detached eddy simulation numerical simulations are combined to systematically investigate the effects of jet parameters on wake non-uniformity. Results indicate that jets parallel to the inflow exhibit limited intervention in the horseshoe vortex region. Conversely, transverse jets perpendicular to the hull wall effectively suppress the horseshoe vortex, with the hole positioned upstream of the stern rudder achieving the most significant effect. Quantitative evaluation using newly introduced wake non-uniformity and momentum-based efficiency metrics reveals a critical cost-benefit: a moderate jet velocity ratio of 1.5 yields a maximum wake uniformity improvement of 47.4% experimentally and 55.4% numerically. However, a lower velocity ratio of 0.8 provides a substantially higher momentum-based efficiency, identifying it as a more cost-effective control strategy. Excessively high jet velocity shifts energy toward the outer radius, producing adverse interference. Sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition reveals that at optimal ratios, jet-induced shear layers break down low-frequency large-scale coherent structures, redistributing vortex energy toward a more uniform circumferential distribution.

papers.title: Physics-informed super-resolution of dual-cylinder wake flow fields from coarse-grid data
papers.abstract: High-resolution flow fields are essential for resolving wake interaction and pressure-coupled unsteady features in bluff-body flows, yet their acquisition from experiments or high-fidelity simulations remains expensive. In dual-cylinder configurations, the interaction between the cylinders can substantially alter the near-wake topology, pressure evolution, and dominant vortex-shedding characteristics, making physically reliable reconstruction from coarse data particularly challenging. In this study, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are employed for super-resolution reconstruction of dual-cylinder flow fields at Reynolds number 200 using direct numerical simulation data. To address the non-uniqueness of pressure reconstruction in standard PINNs, a pressure-constrained PINNs (PC-PINNs) framework is proposed by introducing sparse pressure supervision at specific locations to anchor the absolute pressure field. Furthermore, a transfer-learning-enhanced framework (TL-PINNs) is developed to accelerate convergence across related cylinder arrangements. Rather than focusing only on reconstruction accuracy, the present study examines whether the reconstructed fields preserve physically meaningful observables, including near-wake structures, pressure distributions, pressure-fluctuation histories, and dominant spectral signatures. The results show that standard PINNs can recover the major velocity structures but suffer from pressure drift, whereas PC-PINNs markedly improve pressure reconstruction and enable more reliable recovery of pressure-related wake features. TL-PINNs further reduce the training cost while maintaining predictive fidelity and physical interpretability. These findings demonstrate the potential of pressure-constrained physics-informed reconstruction for mechanism-oriented analysis of interference-induced bluff-body flows from coarse-resolution data.

papers.title: Cavitation flow characteristics of liquid ammonia in a multi-orifice injector
papers.abstract: Cavitation in throttling devices involves complex phase transition and flow-energy interactions that influence injector stability. For thermosensitive fluids, cavitation is governed by both hydrodynamic effects and thermodynamic feedback. Liquid ammonia, featuring high saturated vapor pressure, large latent heat of vaporization, and strong temperature dependence, exhibits distinct cavitation behavior compared with conventional fuels. This study investigates thermo-hydrodynamic cavitation in a multi-orifice ammonia injector through high-speed visualization and three-dimensional simulations. The effects of inlet pressure, back pressure, needle lift, and fuel temperature are systematically examined. Results show that ammonia cavitation is controlled by the competition between inertial enhancement and thermodynamic suppression. Increasing inlet pressure initially promotes vapor formation, whereas excessive pressure strengthens vaporization-induced thermal suppression, producing a peak cavitation intensity at ∼50 MPa. Increasing back pressure and needle lift reduces vapor accumulation and improves flow transport; the average vapor volume fraction decreases by 7.82% and 19.57%, respectively. The multi-orifice structure generates spatially heterogeneous cavitation: gap-region orifices exhibit wall-attached vortex cavitation induced by throttling and flow separation, while pressure-chamber orifices develop string-like cavitation in high-speed regions. Temperature affects cavitation through coupled variations in vapor pressure, viscosity, and vaporization cooling, resulting in different thermal responses among injector regions. These findings clarify the thermo-hydrodynamic mechanism of ammonia cavitation and provide guidance for injector optimization.

papers.title: Frequency-structured cross-fidelity errors in multiscale flow reconstruction
papers.abstract: Coarse-grid, filtered, and downsampled flow fields often retain the dominant large-scale organization of a high-fidelity (HF) solution while losing localized gradients, interfaces, shear layers, corner vortices, and curved-wall details. We, therefore, examine cross-fidelity errors from a fluid-mechanics perspective and formulate HF recovery as a frequency-decoupled, multi-fidelity, physics-constrained reconstruction task. Fourier-enhanced multi-fidelity neural networks (FE-MFNN) combine a shared low-frequency backbone, a Fourier-enhanced cross-fidelity residual branch, adaptive Fourier-basis screening, and progressive physics-constrained training based on low-fidelity (LF) data, boundary information, and residuals of the governing partial differential equation (PDE). Direct LF–HF spectral diagnostics show that the Burgers and Allen–Cahn residuals contain substantially larger high-band energy fractions than their corresponding HF fields under the same 75% cumulative-energy cutoff. Computational fluid dynamics diagnostics reveal weak co-location between cavity velocity-residual energy and HF vorticity but a stronger association between cylinder pressure-residual energy and HF pressure-gradient structures. Across scalar PDE benchmarks, lid-driven cavity flow, and subsonic compressible flow around a cylinder, FE-MFNN improves high-frequency reconstruction in shock-like, interface-dominated, and shear-layer-dominated cases and remains competitive for curved-boundary compressible flow. These results support frequency-decoupled reconstruction as a physically interpretable strategy in the tested multiscale-flow settings. The reported frequency structure is an empirical diagnostic of the archived coarse-resolution and separately exported LF datasets, not a universal physical law.

papers.title: Predicting jet direction and jet suppression in cavitation bubble pairs and triplets
papers.abstract: Jetting during cavitation–bubble collapse is driven by pressure asymmetries and redirects collapse energy into liquid motion, thereby reducing spherical focusing and limiting attainable gas compression, which can degrade the performance of applications such as sonochemistry. Here, we propose a computationally efficient predictor for multi-bubble jetting based on a coupled spherical-bubble framework: the bubble dynamics are obtained from the Gilmore equation, and the surrounding pressure field is reconstructed using the Kirkwood–Bethe hypothesis with Lagrangian wave tracking. From the angular non-uniformity of the reconstructed pressure around each bubble, we define a dimensionless, time-integrated jet vector whose direction predicts the jet orientation and whose magnitude indicates the propensity for jet formation. The model is validated against experiments for bubble pairs and triplets. Jet-regime maps for bubble pairs are compared with direct numerical simulations. For bubble pairs, jet suppression is found to occur for low jet vector magnitudes (|J|<0.04), while the criterion remains reliable only for moderate collapse intensities (γ≲10). For stronger collapses, additional simulations reveal clear limits of this criterion, including delayed, two-sided, and irregular jets despite a vanishing time-integrated asymmetry. For axially aligned bubble triplets, simultaneous near-zero-jet vectors do not generally guarantee jet suppression, but they still provide useful guidance for identifying configurations that improve gas compression.

papers.title: Curvature-induced margination and adhesion of circulating tumor cells in microvessels
papers.abstract: The selective retention and adhesion of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in microvessels are key biophysical events during early hematogenous metastasis. Although experiments have reported preferential CTC adhesion at vascular bends, the underlying mechanical mechanism remains unclear. Here, an immersed boundary–lattice Boltzmann method coupled with a probabilistic receptor–ligand adhesion model is used to simulate CTC migration and adhesion in three-dimensional curved microvessels. The effects of arch height, hematocrit, CTC membrane bending stiffness, and initial CTC position are systematically examined. Vessel curvature displaces the local velocity peak toward the wall facing the local center of curvature and reorganizes the red blood cell (RBC) distribution. The resulting lateral exclusion promotes CTC margination and spatially selective wall contact. Increasing arch height modifies the local flow structure and wall-contact probability, thus regulating adhesion strength and adhesion-enriched regions. Hematocrit alters the near-wall cell-free layer and the intraluminal shear-rate distribution, while membrane bending stiffness controls deformation-dependent wall contact and bond accumulation. The initial lateral position sets the distance from the near-wall low-velocity layer and consequently determines the onset of margination and the final adhesion site. Overall, CTC adhesion in curved microvessels is governed by the coupled effects of shear flow, RBC redistribution, cell margination, and near-wall residence time. These findings clarify the biomechanical origin of curvature-induced CTC adhesion and provide a hemodynamic basis for assessing metastasis-prone microvascular regions.

papers.title: Capillary-regulated flow boiling of R245fa in hierarchical micro–nano-structured sintered mesh tubes
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates the flow boiling performance of R245fa in hierarchical micro–nano-structured sintered mesh tubes. A hierarchical sintered mesh tube (HSMT) was fabricated by electrochemical deposition of nanostructures onto a conventional sintered mesh tube (SMT). Flow boiling experiments were conducted over mass fluxes ranging from 200 to 700 kg/(m2 s) and heat fluxes up to 75 kW/m2. Compared with the SMT, the HSMT exhibited enhanced boiling-heat transfer performance, with a maximum heat transfer coefficient of 15.18 kW/(m2 K). The hierarchical micro–nano structures promoted nucleation activity and improved liquid replenishment within the porous mesh layer, particularly under high vapor-quality conditions. In addition, the hierarchical surface delayed local dryout and maintained more stable boiling behavior during two-phase flow. Performance evaluation based on the enhancement factor (EF) and performance evaluation criterion (PEC) showed that the HSMT achieved a maximum EF of 2.23 and a maximum PEC of 1.87 at x = 0.3, corresponding to 1.27 times and 1.40 times increases compared with the SMT, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of hierarchical porous mesh structures for enhancing flow boiling-heat transfer in compact thermal management systems.

papers.title: Effects of tributary confluence location on flow structure in a curved confluence flow
papers.abstract: Curved confluent channels are widely distributed in natural river networks, where tributaries enter the main channel at different confluence locations. To investigate the effects of the tributary confluence location on the flow structure in the confluence, a numerical model based on the validated renormalization group k–ε turbulence model is established. The effects of tributary confluence locations (θ) and flow ratios (q*) on the water surface elevation (WSE), longitudinal velocity distribution (u), separation zone, and secondary flow were systematically examined. The results show that the WSE increases with increasing q* in the upstream of the confluence, while it decreases in the downstream. Regarding the velocity distribution, θ alters the direction of the transverse velocity (v) in the confluence and the position of the maximum velocity zone. In contrast, increasing q* enhances the longitudinal velocity (u) and enlarges the maximum velocity zone. In addition, the scale of the separation zone increases with increasing q*. As θ increases, the separation zone scale initially increases and then decreases, reaching relatively large values near θ = 90°–120°. The secondary flow primarily consists of the inner bank circulation and the outer bank circulation. The mean secondary flow intensity (Sw¯) reaches its peak value downstream of the confluence, and the peak value increases with increasing q*. The dimensionless flow recovery distance (Xr*) exhibits a unimodal variation with q* and θ. These findings advance the understanding of momentum redistribution, the three-dimensional structure of the separation zone, and secondary flow evolution in curved confluent channels.

papers.title: Vertical transformation of mesoscale eddies crossing the Kuroshio Extension: Evidence from cyclonic and anticyclonic rings
papers.abstract: The Kuroshio Extension is one of the most energetic frontal systems in the World Ocean, separating subtropical and subarctic water masses. Mesoscale eddies regularly cross this front, enabling cross-jet transport of heat, salt, and hydrographic properties despite the barrier nature of the jet. Previous studies have mainly focused on the horizontal component of this transport, while the vertical evolution of eddies remains poorly understood. Here, we present a quantitative investigation of mesoscale eddy transformation during Kuroshio Extension crossing using two representative events: a cyclonic ring (2002) and an anticyclonic ring (2024). Three-dimensional eddy structure was examined before, during, and after frontal crossing. Results show that crossing a density front causes not only horizontal transport but also substantial vertical adjustment of eddy cores driven by buoyancy changes relative to surrounding waters. The cyclonic ring, transporting dense subarctic waters into the subtropical region, exhibits a 320 m deepening of the σθ = 26.50 kg m−3 isopycnal, a 400 m deepening of the 5 °C isotherm, and a 200–500 m downward displacement of S = 34.0 Practical Salinity Unit isohaline boundaries. In contrast, the anticyclonic ring undergoes a maximum transient uplift of 150 m of the σθ = 26.50 kg m−3 isopycnal during frontal crossing, followed by partial relaxation to a net uplift of 100 m. Similar behavior is observed for the upper saline-core boundary and the 5 °C isotherm. Simultaneously, the warm saline lens transforms into a dome-shaped structure. This restructuring involves changes in eddy geometry and the distributions of temperature, salinity, and velocity. We propose a buoyancy-controlled mechanism of vertical eddy adjustment after frontal crossing, applicable to mesoscale eddies interacting with major density fronts throughout the World Ocean.

papers.title: The generation and movement of large water droplets in a converging airflow
papers.abstract: In this study, the generation, breakup, size evolution, and movement of large water droplets in a converging airflow were experimentally investigated. This work not only showed the general formation and acceleration processes of large water droplets but also revealed the underlying mechanism of these processes. A detailed parameter study on the flow rate (Qwater = 350–550 ml/h) and the airflow velocity (Uair = 14.18–22.87 m/s) was carefully performed. The phenomena of droplet formation, droplet collision, droplet coalescence, and droplet movement were observed. The results showed that the breakup length fluctuated within a certain range under the influence of the airflow, and the increasing airflow velocity directly amplified this unstable state. In addition, the breakup length, breakup diameter, and the disturbance length first increased and then decreased as the flow rate increased when the airflow velocity was the same. The average and minimum droplet diameters both decreased with the increasing flow rate. Furthermore, the generation velocity of droplets increased gradually with the rising liquid flow rate, while the movement velocity of droplets increased significantly as the airflow velocity increased. In addition, new correlations for the droplet average diameter and movement velocity were proposed in this study.

papers.title: Experimental imaging and computational shape optimization of an airfoil with a roughened leading edge
papers.abstract: In the field, aging wind turbine blades have been observed to accumulate significant levels of roughness. This aerodynamic performance issue is consistently cited by the wind energy industry as a major concern for turbine efficiency, installation longevity, and energy forecasting. This work aims to characterize the aerodynamic effects of leading-edge roughness accumulation and assess the potential of computational shape optimization to partially recover aerodynamic performance losses associated with leading-edge roughness. To this end, both the blade suction surface and the leading-edge region were studied in experiments using particle image velocimetry. These experimental conditions were modeled, and both parameterized and gradient-based geometry optimization studies were conducted with the aim of improving the performance of blades, which have become rough at the leading edge. The control effect of the airfoil on the freestream flow at the leading edge was observed to be weakened by roughness, reducing the incident flow angle, consistent with a reduction in the apparent circulation around the airfoil. Parameterized and adjoint optimization studies found leading-edge thickness reduction and camber increase to compensate somewhat for performance losses due to leading-edge roughness accumulation.

papers.title: Murray's law and local junction dissipation at vascular bifurcations
papers.abstract: Murray's law predicts a cubic relation between vessel radius and flow rate by balancing distributed Poiseuille dissipation against material cost. We extend this local variational framework for a single vascular bifurcation by adding a positive-definite junction-dissipation term associated with velocity mismatch and irreversible mixing. For prescribed parent flow and daughter-flow partition, minimization determines the stationary daughter-to-parent radius ratios. In the equal-length Poiseuille baseline, the reduced problem is governed by one dimensionless parameter η, measuring the relative strength of localized junction dissipation and distributed viscous dissipation. As η→0, the classical cubic Murray allocation is recovered; when junction dissipation dominates, the optimum approaches velocity matching, for which the total daughter area equals the parent area. Intermediate values produce a continuous crossover between these limits. Symmetric bifurcations are described by a single η-dependent effective exponent, whereas asymmetric bifurcations generally require distinct branchwise exponents depending on both η and the imposed flow partition. Analytical approximations and direct numerical minimization characterize this local correction to Murray's law. Retaining the complete pairwise closure, including daughter–daughter velocity mismatch, preserves the limiting solutions while shifting the finite-crossover asymmetric radius allocation. The resulting framework provides a local steady-flow variational extension of the Poiseuille–Murray model, in which junction dissipation shifts the optimal radius allocation continuously away from cubic scaling.

papers.title: Development and validation of semi-empirical models for liquid-film spreading induced by an oblique jet impinging on a wall
papers.abstract: Liquid-film spreading induced by an oblique jet impinging on a wall is a representative free-surface flow relevant to liquid-film cooling and wall protection. However, a unified predictive framework for the characteristic spreading dimensions and film thicknesses has not yet been well established. In this study, an experimentally validated semi-empirical framework is developed to predict the spreading and thickness characteristics of liquid films generated by an oblique water jet impinging on a vertical flat wall. High-speed visualization is employed to determine the maximum spreading width and maximum spreading length, while light-emitting diode-induced fluorescence is used to reconstruct the film-thickness field and extract the characteristic thicknesses of the thin-layer zone and rise zone. Three-dimensional volume-of-fluid simulations are introduced as a complementary tool for interpreting flow mechanisms and extending the analysis under controlled wettability conditions. Based on scaling analysis and regression of the experimental and numerical data, the proposed model describes four representative characteristic quantities: the maximum spreading width, the maximum spreading length, the thin-layer zone thickness, and the rise zone thickness. The results indicate that the spreading-scale quantities and thickness-related quantities exhibit distinct response regularities and should not be expected to possess the same level of predictability. In particular, the macroscopic spreading dimensions mainly reflect momentum redistribution after impingement, whereas the rise zone thickness is more strongly affected by local accumulation, recirculation, and free-surface unsteadiness. The predictive performance of the proposed model shows clear differences among the characteristic quantities. The maximum spreading width exhibits the highest predictive consistency (R2 = 0.9889), whereas the maximum spreading length captures the overall trend (R2 = 0.9695) but shows greater scatter. For thickness prediction, the thin-layer zone thickness remains reasonably predictable (R2 = 0.910). In contrast, the rise zone thickness, even after refinement of the fitted dataset, remains less consistent (R2 = 0.777) owing to the stronger influence of local thickening dynamics. These results indicate that different liquid-film characteristics possess inherently different levels of predictability. The present study therefore provides an experimentally supported predictive model for rapid estimation of liquid-film spreading and thickness characteristics, while clarifying the applicability and limitations of different characteristic quantities within the investigated water–air system and operating range.

papers.title: Droplet detachment time and droplet volume in co-flow microfluidics
papers.abstract: We investigate droplet detachment times and droplet volumes for water-in-oil in glass capillary co-flow microfluidic devices. While detachment time scales with flow rate in single-parameter systems, its role in multi-parameter fluidics remains unclear. By systematically varying inner and outer flow rates, we show that identical detachment times can produce completely opposite trends in droplet size. This decoupling occurs because droplet volume is governed by competing inertial and shear forces. Thus, detachment time is not a predictor of droplet volume. By introducing two dimensionless parameters scaled by the orifice diameter, we successfully collapse all data onto a single curve. The slope of this curve matches the predicted slope from the volume-mass conservation within 11%.

papers.title: Elastic versus viscoelastic physics-informed neural networks for transient flow modeling in high-density polyethylene pipes
papers.abstract: This paper highlights a crucial aspect of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): their success hinges on accurately capturing the dominant physical mechanisms. This principle is illustrated for fluid-borne transient waves within high-density polyethylene (HDPE) pipelines by comparing two PINN formulations across negligible- and dominant-viscoelastic regimes. Utilizing numerical and experimental test rigs, an elastic PINN, based on the classical wave equation, was contrasted with a viscoelastic PINN incorporating a generalized Kelvin–Voigt representation of HDPE wall rheology. The analysis reveals a critical threshold dictated by the Deborah number (De=τ/Ts), which compares the HDPE pipe wall's viscoelastic retardation time (τ) with the excitation timescale (Ts) associated with the fluid-borne wave. In numerical simulations, viscoelastic retardation is negligible when De≫1, and both formulations achieve comparable accuracy with nearly identical convergence rates. For De∼O(1), the elastic PINN can partially compensate for the neglected viscoelastic effects through data-driven learning, but requires substantially more training iterations. Under these conditions, the viscoelastic PINN converges more than 50% faster while achieving comparable accuracy. In laboratory experiments under realistic noise and measurement uncertainty, the viscoelastic PINN achieves markedly higher accuracy than the elastic PINN, with correlation coefficients of 0.93 and 0.78, respectively, while converging an order of magnitude faster. These findings confirm that embedding the dominant physics improves the efficiency, consistency, and accuracy of PINN-based transient modeling.

papers.title: Investigation of the oblique-flow-induced flow mechanism and acoustic characteristics of the submarine
papers.abstract: To study oblique-flow-induced hydrodynamic mechanisms and acoustic characteristics, this study employs a combination of Large Eddy Simulation and the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings equation to analyze the flow field and flow noise of an underwater vehicle at a sailing velocity of 6 kn, under oblique flow angles of 0°, 2°, 4°, 6°, 8°, and 10°. The pulsating pressure on the sail surface was measured in the towing tank at Northwestern Polytechnical University to validate the numerical method, and the method performed favorably. The results reveal that the hull lateral force is the most sensitive to the orientation of the oblique flow. Even a minor oblique flow angle of only 2° generates a lateral force reaching 76.12 N. As the oblique flow angle increases from 0° to 10°, the overall resultant force rises by 460.85%, accompanied by lateral migration of the stagnation point along the sail leading edge. Such flow field evolution primarily modulates the amplitude of surface pressure fluctuations while exerting a marginal influence on flow-governed natural frequencies. Meanwhile, oblique flow reshapes the directional features of submarine flow noise. In the horizontal plane, the acoustic radiation footprint on the leeward side expands with increasing noise levels, whereas the windward radiation region contracts, driving the flow noise directivity to transition from symmetric to asymmetric.
