papers.title: Effect of shock waves on evolution of tip leakage vortex in axial compressors
papers.abstract: This study investigates the tip leakage flow in both low-speed and transonic rotors using hybrid Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-large eddy simulation methods to explore the unified mechanism governing the evolution of the tip leakage vortex (TLV), with a particular focus on the effect of shock waves on TLV breakdown. Vortex structures are identified using the local trace criterion, while the unsteady characteristics and breakdown patterns of the TLV are analyzed using particle-tracing techniques. The results demonstrate that the TLV exhibits a similar evolutionary process in both rotors prior to shock wave interaction, whereas the presence of the shock wave significantly alters the trajectory and breakdown patterns of the TLV. Specifically, the TLV undergoes solely spiral-type breakdown in the low-speed rotor, whereas both spiral- and bubble-type breakdowns occur in the transonic rotor. For both rotors, the instability of the TLV is significantly influenced by the secondary leakage flow from the adjacent blade passage; furthermore, the shock wave primarily amplifies the inherent unsteadiness of the TLV rather than directly triggering its instability. These findings provide deeper insight into the mechanisms underlying TLV breakdown and the influence of shock waves on rotor stability, offering valuable guidance for the aerodynamic design and optimization of axial compressors.

papers.title: Gas–liquid interaction and annular-pressure evolution under multi-mode production-tubing leakage in ultra-deep gas wells
papers.abstract: Under the extreme depth, temperature, and pressure conditions in ultra-deep gas wells (UDGWs), thermally induced trapped annular pressure (TAP) and leakage-induced sustained annular pressure (SAP) may coexist and dynamically interact, giving rise to complex pressure-driven gas–liquid migration and annular-pressure evolution. A transient coupled SAP model is developed by integrating annular-fluid thermal expansion, real-gas thermophysical properties, and multi-mode production-tubing leakage encompassing scenarios such as perforation and thread leakage. The model extends single-mode descriptions and captures bidirectional gas–liquid migration between the production tubing and annulus under the coupled TAP–SAP pressure field. Comparisons with published field annular-pressure data and component-level gas- and liquid-leakage experiments show good agreement. The model is used to investigate temperature–pressure evolution and gas–liquid exchange under single-point and multi-point leakage conditions. Results show that TAP governs the initial leakage direction by creating an initial iso-pressure point in the middle-to-deep wellbore. Above this point, fluid within the production tubing leaks into the annulus, whereas submerged leak points below it promote reverse inflow of annular liquid into the production tubing. Perforation leakage produces faster pressure buildup and higher quasi-steady SAP, whereas thread leakage exhibits a slower pressure increase and a longer buildup period. Among the multi-point configurations investigated, the larger-upper/smaller-lower perforation case generates the strongest gas–liquid exchange and the highest annular-pressure risk. Increasing the production rate suppresses the SAP peak induced by shallow leakage but intensifies annular liquid-level loss. These results provide a physical basis for annular-pressure assessment, leakage diagnosis, and wellbore-integrity management in UDGWs.

papers.title: Large-scale experimental investigation of freshwater–brine buoyant jets relevant to horizontal salt cavern leaching
papers.abstract: Large-scale experiments and integral-model analysis were performed to examine horizontal freshwater–brine buoyant jets relevant to salt cavern leaching. Freshwater was discharged into initially quiescent saturated brine in a cylindrical tank with a diameter of 13 m and a height of 8 m, using nozzle diameters of 0.10–0.26 m and inlet velocities of 1.0–4.0 m/s. The tests covered nozzle Reynolds numbers of 1.57×105–6.27×105 and initial densimetric Froude numbers of Fr0=1.78–7.14. Increasing Fr0 enhanced horizontal penetration and delayed buoyant rise. The classical momentum–buoyancy length scale LM helped organize the measured centerline trajectories, whereas the measured characteristic half-width was better organized by the source length scale LQ, indicating that the two morphology measures are more effectively represented by different scales within the tested range. A steady centerline-marching integral model captured the mean centerline trend but showed stronger sensitivity in half-width prediction; model comparisons indicate an effective entrainment-coefficient range of α=0.075–0.090. Empirical correlations are fitted for the trajectory and half-width within the tested parameter range. Together, these results provide a large-scale dataset and a quantitative assessment of classical scaling and entrainment-based integral modeling for freshwater–brine jets with a strong density contrast relevant to horizontal salt cavern leaching.

papers.title: Aerodynamic role of rapid wing pitch-up at mid-stroke in hovering mosquitoes
papers.abstract: Mosquito wings execute rapid pitch-up during mid-stroke, markedly differing from the nearly constant-angle-of-attack flapping observed in many other insects. However, the aerodynamic role of this motion in mosquito hovering remains incompletely understood. Here, we numerically compare the aerodynamic performance using real measured wing kinematics with that under an artificially constructed trapezoidal pitch profile. The results show that both cases generate sufficient cycle-averaged vertical force to balance body weight, with nearly identical cycle-averaged energy expenditure. Nevertheless, the temporal distributions of force and aerodynamic power differ significantly: the real case produces large force peaks during the middle of the stroke, which are absent in the trapezoidal case, where large force peaks instead occur at stroke reversals. Further flow field analysis reveals that rapid pitch-up not only facilitates the rapid generation of vortices but also enhances force generation during mid-stroke by keeping the leading-edge vortex continuously and closely attached to the wing leeward surface, thereby enabling the delayed stall mechanism to function effectively. This rapid pitch-up can also prevent abrupt force fluctuations at stroke reversals, alleviating the potential risk of damage to the slender mosquito wing. These findings deepen our understanding of mosquito hovering aerodynamics and provide guidance for designing small-stroke-amplitude flapping-wing micro air vehicles.

papers.title: A three-dimensional tomographic particle image velocimetry approach for cross-interface imaging in confined space based on reverse ray-tracing
papers.abstract: Tomographic particle image velocimetry (Tomo-PIV) is a powerful technique for measuring three-dimensional, three-component velocity fields in complex flows. However, in confined spaces with refractive interfaces (e.g., optical engines), traditional Tomo-PIV faces challenges due to light path deviations. This study proposes a cross-interface tomographic PIV (CI Tomo-PIV) framework to address this. The core innovation is the integration of a physically accurate reverse ray-tracing model with spherical voxels into the reconstruction kernel. Unlike traditional Tomo-PIV models that assume straight-line projection, this method enforces Snell's law at the voxel level, correcting geometric distortions during projection. Benchmarking against polynomial models shows that CI reduces point spread function computation time by ∼70% while maintaining comparable accuracy. Numerical validation with synthetic toroidal vortices and Johns Hopkins turbulence databases turbulent flows demonstrates its accuracy advantages over the uncorrected model. CI Tomo-PIV consistently yields high-fidelity displacement fields with cross correlation coefficients stably within 0.85–0.9, surpassing the uncorrected model (∼0.5). Quantitative error analysis shows that under ideal conditions, the root mean square (RMS) error is below 10%, with bias within 2.5% and random uncertainty ∼9.7%. Even with realistic noise and calibration residuals, RMS error remains 13%–17%. A proof-of-concept experiment in an optical engine cylinder shows that the reconstructed fields resolve the evolution of swirling structures, capturing plausible topological features such as linear velocity decay toward the vortex core. This confirms the need to integrate CI models into reconstruction, extending high-precision PIV beyond the uncorrected model to confined flows with curved refractive boundaries.

papers.title: Particle-resolved computational fluid dynamics modeling of coupled heat and mass transfer in fixed-bed adsorbers
papers.abstract: Fixed-bed adsorbers are simulated at full particle-scale resolution to predict the coupled evolution of gas-mixture flow dynamics, mass transfer, adsorption kinetics, and heat effects during CO2 capture. A porous-based, direct-forcing immersed boundary method is developed and implemented in the open-source Computational Fluid Dynamics platform OpenFOAM to resolve interstitial flow and transport within a realistically packed bed while avoiding body-fitted meshing around individual pellets. The model is applied to a cylindrical adsorbing bed containing roughly 5000 spherical Zeolite-13X beads of diameter dp=1.5 mm. This representation reflects a realistic adsorber segment under industrially relevant operating conditions. The model is applied to adsorption from a binary CO2/He mixture (50%/50%) at atmospheric pressure with an initial temperature of 295 K and a maximum temperature rise up to around 350 K due to adsorption-induced thermal effects, and it is validated by comparing predicted breakthrough behavior and thermally coupled front dynamics against experimental data from the literature. In addition to reproducing outlet composition histories, the particle-resolved framework provides space- and time-resolved fields of velocity, concentration, and temperature, enabling mechanistic quantification of channeling, wall effects, and the synchronization between mass and thermal fronts. The proposed approach offers a validated high-fidelity reference for developing improved closures and reduced-order models for pressure and temperature swing adsorption cycles design and energy-efficient adsorber/heat-management optimization.

papers.title: Interjet vortex coupling and mixing in spanwise transverse jet arrays of supercritical hydrocarbon fuel
papers.abstract: Fuel injection and mixing play a critical role in supersonic combustion of air-breathing engines, such as scramjet, rocket-based combined-cycle, and turbine-based combined-cycle engines. Supercritical hydrocarbon fuel is usually transversely injected into combustors, where the jet evolution and mixing efficiency are jointly governed by real-gas effects, compressibility, shock structures, and vortex-driven transport. In this work, a three-dimensional numerical model incorporating real-gas thermophysical properties is developed to examine the coupling of multiple transverse jets. Under the investigated non-reacting conditions, finite spacing redistributes the streamwise vortices across the array: neighboring plumes restrict the inner counter-rotating vortex pairs (CVP) and interjet entrainment, whereas the exterior vortices develop with less lateral confinement and become the principal large-scale entrainment structures downstream. The resulting effect of spacing is not universal, but varies with injection pressure and the coupled crossflow condition. At M∞ = 1.89 and Pr = 1.47, larger spacing preserves independent shear layers and improves mixing over most downstream locations. Increasing Pr to 1.96 promotes plume penetration and early merger, thereby weakening the spacing effect. At the lower freestream Mach number M∞ = 0.71, the combined effects of reduced dynamic-pressure confinement and increased J allow stronger CVP development and yield higher mixing efficiency. Results obtained in this paper provide a solid foundation for fuel-injection configuration design and mixing-performance optimization in air-breathing engines.

papers.title: Physics-constrained deep learning for prediction of three-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional turbulence is inherently chaotic and multiscale, posing significant computational challenges for traditional simulation methods, such as direct numerical simulation (DNS), large eddy simulation, and Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models. Although deep learning (DL) offers a promising data-driven alternative, most existing studies have focused on two-dimensional flows, limiting the physical fidelity and applicability to realistic turbulent processes. This article presents a physically constrained DL framework for predicting three-dimensional homogeneous isotropic turbulence. A neural network was augmented with a Fourier projection to enforce incompressibility and was trained using a two-term loss function that accounted for both the velocity and vorticity fields. The model was trained on DNS data at Reλ = 58, and its generalizability was evaluated on higher-Reynolds-number datasets at Reλ = 92, 160, and 433, where the larger domain was divided into subvolumes matching the training size, the flow fields of which were predicted separately, and then concatenated to reconstruct the full domain. Temporal sampling over several finite lead times enabled the forecasting capability of the model to be evaluated. The proposed approach accurately reproduces key turbulence statistics, resolves three-dimensional vortex structures, and maintains divergence-free velocity fields across prediction horizons up to a lead time of 0.3 Eulerian integral timescale. The results demonstrate that combining data-driven DL with physics-based constraints enables the efficient and reliable prediction of three-dimensional turbulence, balancing computational efficiency and physical fidelity.

papers.title: Wave generation by initial impulsive disturbances in finite-depth water with an inertial surface
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the two-dimensional Cauchy–Poisson problem in a finite-depth ocean covered by an inertial surface, involving impulsive initial disturbances. Three different types of impulsive disturbances, such as rectangular, Gaussian, and exponential profiles, are considered. Within the framework of linear water wave theory, the problem is formulated as an initial-value problem for the velocity potential describing the fluid motion. Laplace and Fourier transform techniques are employed to obtain the inertial surface elevation in an integral form. The resulting integral expression is analyzed asymptotically using the method of stationary phase for long time and large distance from the source of disturbance. The asymptotic behavior of the inertial surface is illustrated graphically for different values of the inertial parameter. The analysis of the three impulsive disturbance profiles reveals that increasing the inertial parameter reduces the wave amplitude, while waves associated with a higher inertial parameter persist for a longer duration and propagate over greater distances. Furthermore, the initial disturbance profile influences both the amplitude and phase of the waves generated by the different profiles. The rectangular and exponential profiles retain appreciable amplitudes over extended periods, whereas those generated by the Gaussian profile decay more rapidly and become negligible after a certain time. The results enhance our understanding of blast-induced wave generation and may aid in assessing their impact on ships, submarines, and coastal structures for naval defense and maritime safety.

papers.title: Jet dynamics of the restricted cavitation bubble near a reflex angle wall based on Kelvin impulse theory
papers.abstract: The present paper investigates the jet dynamics of a restricted cavitation bubble near a reflex angle wall. Typical jet phenomena during the bubble collapse are analyzed through high-speed photography, and a quantitative regime map of the jet patterns is established based on the bubble–wall distance and the reflex angle. The Kelvin impulse theory is employed to analyze the dynamics of cavitation bubbles. Furthermore, the variations in Kelvin impulse strength and its sensitivity under different parameters are investigated. The main conclusions are given as follows. (1) Three typical collapse jet patterns are observed: the acute jet, the obtuse jet, and the no jet. At smaller reflex angles and bubble–wall distances, the jet velocity is higher (exceeding 38 m/s), presenting as an acute angle jet, which reflects a strong wall effect. (2) The wall effect on the bubble collapse jet can be characterized by the extent of the locally high-velocity region in the surrounding liquid. (3) The Kelvin impulse exhibits the same decreasing trend as the bubble centroid displacement with increasing bubble–wall distance and reflex angle.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of free-field blast loads generated by end-initiated cylindrical charges with varying aspect ratios in arbitrary orientation
papers.abstract: The characterization of near-field blast loads in arbitrary orientation is critical for accurately evaluating damage effects. However, conventional equivalent spherical-blast correlations frequently overlook the flow-field anisotropy induced by the finite geometry and end-initiation mode of cylindrical charges. In this study, numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the shock-wave evolution generated by an end-initiated cylindrical charge using a multiphase Eulerian approach. The research findings demonstrate that the blast field undergoes a multistage evolution involving near-source high-pressure formation, wavefront coalescence, multistage shock interactions, and quasi-spherical attenuation. This wave structure produces pronounced directional nonuniformity in the near-field blast loads. When the scaled distance surpasses a certain critical threshold, the directionality of the pressure load decreases significantly. As the aspect ratio increases, the near-field disparity between axial and lateral loads becomes more pronounced, whereas the critical scaled distance shows an overall decreasing trend with local fluctuations. A semiempirical model grounded in Fourier expansion has been developed to delineate the coupled influences of aspect ratio, scaled distance, and azimuthal angle on peak overpressure and specific impulse. Good consistency with the simulation results was obtained. These results provide a basis for the rapid characterization of directional blast loads and damage assessment for end-initiated cylindrical charges.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of unsteady cooling characteristics in triply periodic minimal surface-based transpiration cooling
papers.abstract: Triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices provide a promising architecture for transpiration cooling by promoting uniform near-wall coolant coverage. Although their time-averaged cooling performance has been investigated, the unsteady organization of the wall thermal response and the associated flow structures remains insufficiently understood. In this study, wall-resolved large eddy simulations were performed for diamond and gyroid TPMS transpiration cooling at coolant injection ratios of 9.0% and 18.0%. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) was applied to the fluctuating wall cooling effectiveness and wall-normal velocity fields to quantify modal energy distributions and identify leading unsteady structures. Results show that, for both lattices, the coolant coverage extended farther downstream at F = 18.0% than at F = 9.0%, while the area-averaged standard deviation of cooling effectiveness differed only slightly between the two conditions. The diamond lattice produced around 20% higher area-averaged cooling effectiveness and a 5% lower relative fluctuation level than the gyroid lattice, indicating more effective and temporally stable wall protection under the present conditions. The POD energy spectra of both TPMS lattices were broadly distributed across multiple modes, with each leading mode accounting for only a limited fraction of the total fluctuation energy. The leading thermal modes were concentrated near the local jet exits of the TPMS lattices, reflecting unsteady coolant discharge and variations in near-wall coverage in the exit region. Their broadband spectra demonstrated that the leading wall thermal response spanned multiple time scales. The instantaneous fields and velocity POD modes further revealed multiscale flow disturbances with streamwise convective organization, and several velocity modes exhibited preferred-frequency peaks.

papers.title: Experimental study on aerodynamic characteristics of two inline rectangular cylinders under varying wind incidence angles
papers.abstract: To precisely characterize the aerodynamic performance of two inline rectangular cylinders with a width-thickness ratio of 2, wind tunnel pressure measurement tests based on rigid test models were implemented. The mean aerodynamic coefficients and Strouhal numbers were systematically measured and analyzed across a combined range of wind incidence angles (0°–90°) and spacing ratios (0.2–12.0). Meanwhile, the aerodynamic characteristics of the single cylinder are utilized for benchmark validation and contrast analysis. The experimental results indicate that the mean aerodynamic characteristics of the two rectangular cylinders can be classified into three categories based on wind incidence angle: small incidence angles (0° ≤ α < 10°), medium incidence angles (10° ≤ α ≤ 60°), and large incidence angles (60° < α ≤ 90°). Under small incidence angles, the mean aerodynamic coefficients exhibit relatively stable variation. Under medium incidence angles, the aerodynamic interference is strong at small spacing ratios, whereas the interference effect becomes weaker at large spacing ratios. Under large incidence angles, the aerodynamic coefficients evolve in a non-monotonic manner as the spacing ratio increases from 0.2 to 4.0. The vortex shedding characteristics can be classified into four categories according to wind incidence angle: extremely small incidence angles (0° ≤ α < 10°), small incidence angles (10° ≤ α ≤ 35°), medium incidence angles (35° < α < 70°), and large incidence angles (70° ≤ α ≤ 90°). The patterns and characteristics of vortex shedding vary across these categories, with dual Strouhal numbers observed under medium incidence angles.

papers.title: Particle transport regime transitions in fractured media under gas–liquid two-phase flow
papers.abstract: Particle transport in confined channel flows under gas–liquid two-phase conditions is governed by the interplay among fluid drag, particle inertia, wall shear stress, and turbulent fluctuations. This study investigates the transport regime transitions of particulate solids in planar fracture channels through combined transparent-fracture visualization experiments and Euler–Lagrange gas–liquid two-phase flow and particle-tracking numerical simulations. The experiments cover gas flow rates of 3–10 l/min, liquid flow rates of 10–100 l/h, and particle diameters of 50–200 μm. Two image-derived indicators are introduced: front migration distance Lm for along-channel travel capacity and suspension area fraction As/A0 for the extent of particle detachment from the deposited bed. Dimensionless power-law relationships are established (Lm/L∝ReG0.51ReL0.17; As/A0 ∝ ReG0.23ReL1.94), showing that gas-phase flow intensity primarily governs normalized streamwise migration, whereas liquid-phase flow intensity mainly controls the suspension extent. Four transport regimes are identified (I: bottom deposition and local disturbance; II: wall slip and along-channel migration; III: recirculation entrainment with local suspension; IV: large-scale suspended transport), with an additional III–IV transitional zone. Numerical simulations reveal the differentiated flow-structure control mechanisms: increasing the liquid flow rate primarily enhances wall shear stress, promoting near-wall particle mobilization; increasing the gas flow rate primarily elevates turbulent kinetic energy, strengthening entrainment and streamwise transport. Fine particles more readily enter the suspended regime due to weaker inertia, whereas coarse particles are dominated by gravity and tend to settle. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how wall shear stress and turbulent kinetic energy jointly control particle entrainment, migration, and suspension in confined multiphase channel flows.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of hydrodynamic interaction between adjacent submerged vehicles operating beneath ice cover
papers.abstract: In this study, hydrodynamic interactions between two under-ice vehicles operating side-by-side were investigated. A mathematical model is established for the intricately coupled dynamics of different submerged vehicles and ice by considering the ice cover as an elastic plate and describing the fluid field using potential flow theory. The corresponding numerical solution employed the panel method based on the Green function for a point source pulsating within the water beneath the ice cover. On this basis, a computer program was developed, and rigorous validations were performed for side-by-side arranged cylindrical and rectangular bodies floating on a free surface and a pair of widely spaced submerged spheres beneath an ice sheet. Systematic investigations of the hydrodynamic interaction effects on two adjacent under-ice vehicles, represented by a Newman slender body and a SUBOFF submarine, with varying ice thicknesses, separation distances, and relative sizes, were carried out. The results show that the disturbance from an adjacent body generates additional hydrodynamic interaction forces, which can lead to uncontrollable motion of the two vehicles. The presence of ice reduces the variation amplitude of the hydrodynamic coefficients. Beyond a critical ice thickness, the hydrodynamic forces become independent of the frequency and approach those under a rigid surface. The SUBOFF interacts more strongly with the Newman slender body when the separation distance is decreased, whereas it is expected to be negligible at a sufficiently large distance. In addition, by comparing different hydrodynamic coefficient components at various relative sizes, it was found that the hydrodynamic interaction between adjacent under-ice vehicles had a more pronounced influence on the smaller body.

papers.title: Investigation on splash and airflow evolution mechanism during water-entry of a hydrophobic sphere
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal and external flow field characteristics during the water entry is crucial for elucidating the evolution mechanisms of splash and cavity dynamics. This experiment investigates the gas–liquid flow phenomena during sphere water entry through synchronized flow field measurements, focusing on two distinct cavity closure types: deep seal and surface seal. Using flow visualization velocity measurement technology, we characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of internal/external flow fields and analyze vortex development mechanisms associated with two closure modes. Key findings demonstrate that cavity volume change rate directly governs airflow entrainment during expansion phases. Under surface seal formation, the volume change rate maintains a precise correlation with gas flow characteristics throughout the process, whereas this correspondence becomes invalid during deep seal retraction. The study identifies a mutually reinforcing coupling between splash closure kinematics and vortex ring development, demonstrating how this positive feedback mechanism influences closure processes. We further identify distinct vortex transition sequences: shear-to-separated-to-forced vortex transformation in deep seal mode vs shear-to-separation vortex evolution in surface seal mode, each exhibiting unique dissipation characteristics. These findings provide new insights into the aerodynamic control of splash dynamics, providing a reference for future investigations of Fr number effects on vorticity evolution and quantitative vortex ring dynamics.

papers.title: Statistical analysis of liquid detonation wave structure
papers.abstract: Liquid-fueled detonation has attracted considerable interest due to the high volumetric energy density of liquid fuels. In the present work, detonation wave propagation in n-dodecane droplets was investigated through two-dimensional simulations. The dispersed droplets were tracked based on the Lagrangian framework, while the continuous phase was solved in an Eulerian way. The Pilch–Erdman model was applied to account for droplet breakup. A detailed reaction mechanism was used for n-dodecane combustion. Three cases with different liquid equivalence ratios and oxygen mass fractions were considered. The simulation results of the detonation cell width were generally consistent with those of the experiment, with quantitative deviations of approximately 10%–40%. The droplet size distribution and breakup behavior were analyzed. It was shown that droplet breakup is the most pronounced behind the Mach stem. Three types of fuel droplets were identified behind the detonation front, i.e., droplets just shocked by the detonation front, shocked droplets progressively relaxing toward equilibrium with the surrounding gas, and small droplets associated with localized intense transverse detonations. Two distinct peaks were observed in the probability density functions of droplet diameter. In the case with low oxygen concentrations, a higher probability of smaller droplet diameters is identified. The liquid equivalence ratio has only a minor effect on the droplet diameter distribution. The statistical analysis of the leading front was conducted to characterize the detonation front dynamics. The leading front showed significant velocity deficits in all cases. It was found that the most probable velocities of the leading front decrease with increasing mass loading ratios. The joint probability density function of the detonation speed and the induction length was also examined, and a negative correlation between the two quantities was observed. Droplet breakup and evaporation significantly lengthen the induction zone to approximately 2–4 times that of the corresponding purely gaseous detonation.

papers.title: Investigation on internal flow characteristics and cavitation mechanism of a counter-rotating cavitation algae removal device
papers.abstract: To address the ambiguous cavitation mechanism and limited algae inactivation efficiency of conventional hydrodynamic cavitation devices, this work systematically investigates a counter-rotating hydrodynamic cavitation device. Combining high-speed flow visualization and numerical simulations, it comprehensively analyzes complex flow structures and cavitation evolution within the rotor interaction gap. Through detailed analysis of velocity, pressure, and vortex structures, the multi-physical coupling mechanism of cavitation is thoroughly revealed. The superposition of radial and tangential velocities between counter-rotating rotors generates strong shear and induces periodic pressure pulsations. These pulsations act as the dominant driving force for cavitation inception. High-vorticity regions align well with low-pressure zones in spatial distribution. Low-pressure vortex cores provide essential hydrodynamic conditions for cavitation bubble nucleation and growth. In turn, cavitation phase change intensifies flow shear and turbulent fluctuations. It promotes the stretching and fragmentation of vortex structures. A bidirectional dynamic coupling pattern of vortices inducing cavitation and cavitation strengthening vortices is, thus, formed, along with a multi-scale cavitation-vortex-turbulence synergistic mechanism. In addition, Chlorella inactivation experiments are conducted at a rotor speed of 3200 rpm to quantitatively evaluate the biological treatment performance. Results show that after 20 min of treatment, the maximum absorbance of Chlorella decreases by 88.2%. These findings confirm that micro-jets and strong oxidative radicals from cavitation bubble collapse can effectively damage algal cell structures and photosynthetic systems.

papers.title: Effects of combined localized wall cooling and porous surface on instability in hypersonic boundary layer transition
papers.abstract: The study in this paper investigates the effects of combined nose tip wall cooling and porous surfaces on boundary layer transition over a 7° half-angle sharp cone under Mach 6 flow conditions, using a combination of wind tunnel experiments and parabolized stability equations analysis. Experimental results indicate that nose tip cooling promotes the emergence of high-frequency instability modes and advances the onset of boundary layer transition compared to the uncooled wall condition. N-factor analysis further corroborates the destabilizing effect of nose tip cooling, showing good agreement with the experimental observations. To achieve more effective control of broadband instability disturbances, a combined control strategy is proposed, in which a porous surface is applied downstream of the cooled region to suppress the growth of high-frequency modes. The results demonstrate that, compared with wall cooling alone, the combined approach significantly reduces the growth rates of broadband disturbances and delays the onset of transition. Bispectral analysis further reveals that the integrated control strategy effectively suppresses nonlinear interactions within the hypersonic boundary layer, including both high-frequency harmonic interactions and low- and high-frequency coupling. In contrast, single control strategies mitigate only one type of nonlinear interaction, thereby underscoring the superior performance of the combined approach.

papers.title: Dust deposition on sand dune-mounted photovoltaic arrays and its impact on power output efficiency
papers.abstract: Desert areas possess abundant solar energy resources, making them prime sites for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power plants. However, as a typical desert landform, sand dunes create unique terrain conditions, under which dust deposition on PV arrays has not been sufficiently studied. This study uses three-dimensional numerical simulations to investigate dust deposition on sand dune PV arrays and the resulting decline in power generation efficiency. The results show that as the dune slope increases, the incoming flow climbs along the windward slope, and the deposition rate on the downstream PV modules increases significantly. The maximum average increase in the overall deposition rate of the PV array reaches 26.02%. The dust deposition rate varies non-monotonically with the tilt angle of the PV modules, and the overall deposition rate of the array reaches a maximum of 2.42% at a tilt angle of 30°. In addition, dust deposition on the PV array surface increases with particle size and decreases with increasing wind direction angle and incoming wind speed. The PV array's power generation efficiency declines continuously with exposure time and is strongly affected by terrain conditions. At a sand dune slope of 20°, the power generation efficiency loss increased by 35.48% compared with that under the 5° slope condition. Therefore, site selection for sand dune PV plants should avoid large-scale deployment in areas with large slopes as much as possible to reduce dust accumulation risk. This work provides a theoretical basis for siting and array layout of PV plants in dune areas.

papers.title: Head-on quenching of laminar premixed CO2-diluted oxy-methane flames under subcritical and supercritical conditions
papers.abstract: One-dimensional simulations of head-on quenching CO2-diluted oxy-methane flames were performed over a wide range of pressures and CO2 dilution levels, encompassing operating conditions of both subcritical combustion and supercritical combustion in direct-fired supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) power cycles. Flame/wall interaction characteristics were analyzed in terms of quenching distance and wall heat flux. The quenching distance was found to increase with increasing CO2 dilution and decreasing pressure, whereas wall heat flux exhibited the opposite trend. After normalization using flame characteristic parameters, the normalized quenching distance, i.e., the quenching Peclet number, ranges from 0.2 to 0.6, and the normalized maximum wall heat flux from 0.4 to 0.9. The near-wall heat release behavior was further examined. Near-wall heat release enhancement was observed under conditions of low pressure and low CO2 dilution, primarily due to the radical recombination reaction between H and CH3 and hydrogen chain propagation reactions. Increasing CO2 dilution hinders radical transport to the wall, suppressing near-wall reactions. Increasing pressure affects the competition among low-activation-energy H-consumption channels through reduced species diffusivity and enhanced three-body reactions. Specifically, the H and CH3 recombination reaction is increasingly suppressed with pressure, whereas hydrogen chain propagation reactions are enhanced at low pressures but inhibited at high pressures. The occurrence of near-wall heat release enhancement was found to correlate strongly with the quenching Peclet number. A radical diffusion length scale is introduced, and near-wall heat release enhancement occurs only when the quenching distance is smaller than this length scale. A predictive criterion based on the Damköhler number is further proposed.

papers.title: Unsteady aerodynamic response mechanism of double-delta wing under high angle of attack
papers.abstract: This study conducts a numerical investigation into the unsteady characteristics of a 80°/65° double-delta wing at high angle of attack using delayed detached-eddy simulation. By combining power spectral density analysis and dynamic mode decomposition, the characteristic frequencies and spatial patterns of the dominant vortex motions are identified, and their frequency-resolved relationships with the associated aerodynamic responses are revealed. Near the strake–main-wing junction, the strake-vortex system interacts with the main-wing leading-edge shear layer and develops into a dominant primary vortex downstream, while a weaker counter-rotating secondary vortex remains near the main-wing leading edge. As the primary vortex develops downstream, vortex breakdown occurs, accompanied by the formation of helical structures. The unsteady motions in the entire flow field can be categorized into three distinct frequency bands: low-frequency, medium-frequency, and high-frequency oscillations. The dominant unsteady motions are organized into a low-frequency harmonic family associated with vortex breakdown point oscillation (Stf≈0.0199, 2Stf≈0.0398), a medium-frequency mode associated with downstream helical structures(St≈0.619), and a high-frequency mode associated with primary vortex axis motion(St≈0.859). In terms of aerodynamic response, the unsteady fluctuation of normal force is dominated by low-frequency vortex breakdown point motion and medium-frequency helical structure motion, whereas the pitching moment is jointly affected by all three bands of oscillations.

papers.title: Hybrid flow control of airfoil dynamic stall using dielectric-barrier-discharge plasma actuator and Gurney flap
papers.abstract: To suppress dynamic stall-induced aerodynamic degradation of pitching National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 airfoils, this paper presents a hybrid active and passive flow control method using a leading-edge burst-mode dielectric-barrier-discharge (DBD) plasma actuator and a trailing-edge Gurney flap (GF, height = 0.02c). Two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations are performed at Re = 7.5×104 and reduced frequency k = 0.1 to compare vortex evolution, surface pressure/friction distributions, and aerodynamic hysteresis across baseline, standalone GF, standalone DBD, and hybrid control cases. Results show that a standalone GF not only increases the peak lift coefficient by 20.2% (from 1.997 to 2.401) by strengthening dynamic stall vortex (DSV) compared to the baseline but also leads to higher peak drag and a more negative pitching moment. In contrast, standalone DBD plasma actuation injects high-momentum wall jet near the leading edge to eliminate leading-edge laminar separation bubbles, fragments large-scale DSV, and reduces the lift hysteresis loop, drag, and alleviates the negative pitching moment. However, this approach inevitably leads to a lower peak lift coefficient of 1.881. The hybrid method synergistically integrates the lift-enhancing effect of the GF with the stall-delaying capability of the DBD actuator, achieving a peak lift coefficient of 2.186, which is 16.2% higher than the DBD-only case. Meanwhile, the hybrid control reduces the peak drag coefficient by 22.5% relative to the GF-only case and alleviates the nose-down pitching-moment peak, demonstrating a distinct synergistic effect.

papers.title: Flow-driven translocation of toroidal and worm-like micelles: Size-dependent dynamics in nanochannels
papers.abstract: We employ a hybrid simulation approach that combines the lattice-Boltzmann method for fluid flow with a molecular dynamics model for polymers to investigate the translocation of toroidal and worm-like micelles through confined nanochannels. For toroidal micelles, we observe both intact and fragmented translocation when the nanochannel diameter is slightly smaller than the micelle's outer diameter, with intact translocation being the predominant mode. However, under stronger confinement, only fragmented translocation occurs. In contrast, worm-like micelles can still undergo intact translocation even when the nanochannel diameter is slightly smaller than their axial diameter. Our findings indicate that the critical flow flux decreases as the nanochannel diameter increases for both types of micelles, and this relationship is much more pronounced under strong confinement compared to weak confinement. These results highlight that micellar topology, along with micelle size and nanochannel diameter, significantly influences the translocation behavior of confined micelles. This research provides valuable insights into the flow-driven transport of soft, self-assembled structures in confined environments.

papers.title: A semi-analytical study on diffusiophoresis of pH-responsive diffuse soft particles
papers.abstract: This study focuses on analyzing the diffusiophoresis of a diffuse soft particle comprising a hydrophobic rigid core coated with an inhomogeneous polyelectrolyte layer (PEL). Inhomogeneity in the diffuse PEL is incorporated by assuming that the polymer segment density varies spatially, resulting in a smooth transition in the electrohydrodynamic properties from the PEL to the bulk electrolyte. The PEL is further considered to contain zwitterionic functional groups, generating a pH-responsive volume charge density. A linear-perturbation technique is employed under the assumption of a weak concentration gradient, and the resulting coupled perturbed equations are solved using a finite-difference-based numerical method to determine the diffusiophoretic mobility. Moreover, an analytical mobility expression is derived for a weakly charged soft particle with a homogeneous PEL. The diffusiophoretic behavior of the soft particle is systematically analyzed by illustrating the mobility distribution as a function of pertinent electrokinetic parameters. Results show that inhomogeneity in the PEL can enhance or attenuate particle motion, depending on whether the Debye layer is thick or thin, when the flow is characterized by chemiphoresis, whereas it augments the diffusiophoretic mobility when chemiphoresis and electrophoresis act jointly. The influence of the decay length on the diffusiophoretic mobility is extensive as pH moves farther from the isoelectric point. An increasing decay length enhances particle mobility when the PEL is highly permeable, whereas it reduces particle mobility when the PEL is low-permeable. A rise in the core surface hydrophobicity amplifies the impact of the decay length on the diffusiophoretic mobility of the soft particle.

papers.title: Budget-controlled low-energy-fluid accumulation and secondary tip-leakage-vortex breakdown in a coupled-casing-treated axial compressor
papers.abstract: Coupled casing treatment (CCTF) extends the stable range of axial compressors by coupling downstream extraction with upstream injection, but the physical mechanism limiting its extended stability remains unclear. This study combines full-compressor measurements, full-annulus 3.5-stage simulations, and a local IGV-R1-S1 unsteady model to identify the final stall-limiting process in a 3.5-stage axial compressor. The results show that CCTF changes the instability mechanism rather than simply delaying stall: axial-slot injection maintains a coherent and transportable tip-leakage vortex, while rear-groove extraction redistributes low-energy fluid. With further throttling, rear suction-surface separation drives low-energy-fluid migration toward the casing, causing the supply rate to approach and exceed the effective removal capability. For the present compressor and CCTF geometry, the competition ratio Rc increases from 0.63 to 1.29, marking a transition from removal-dominated transport through a near-balance regime to supply-dominated accumulation. Meanwhile, the leakage-vortex trajectory angle increases from 23.7° to 44.1°, xBD/Cax shifts from 0.82 to 0.66, and λ2/Q statistics reveal a reduction in coherent vortex-core length from 0.948 to 0.566 and an increase in broken-volume fraction from 0.058 to 0.547. These mutually consistent trends identify a configuration-specific change from primary tip-leakage-vortex breakdown to budget-controlled secondary breakdown; Rc ≈ 1 is interpreted as a critical regime in this case rather than a universal threshold.

papers.title: Erratum: “Analytical solutions for oscillatory flows of two-layer immiscible viscoelastic fluids” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 053316 (2026)]
Study on regulation mechanism of separated vortex ring with umbrella-shaped macroporous structure
papers.abstract: The separated vortex ring (SVR) generated by dandelion pappus is a key aerodynamic mechanism for stable seed dispersal and provides inspiration for biomimetic micro-air vehicles. However, conventional simplified quasi-dandelion pappus models are mainly based on discrete geometric descriptions, which limit the quantitative characterization of radial material distribution and its coupling with wake-flow structures. In this study, a continuous parametric framework for umbrella-shaped macroporous pappus structures is proposed by introducing the circumferential linear porosity εcr and the filament occupation angle θr. Based on this framework, the model is divided into three functional regions: the central disk, the densified region, and the sparse region. Validated steady numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the effects of regional geometric parameters on SVR formation, vortex morphology, wake-pressure recovery, and aerodynamic performance. The results show that the densified region plays a dominant role in SVR formation, whereas the central disk mainly affects near-wall vortex structures and the sparse region continuously regulates the morphology of fully developed SVRs. A drag-locking phenomenon is identified: once the SVR is fully developed, the pressure drag remains nearly unchanged despite an increase in the windward projected area. This work provides a quantitative framework for understanding the SVR regulation in porous biomimetic structures and offers guidance for the aerodynamic design of dandelion-inspired micro-air vehicles. The steady parametric results characterize the mean-flow regulation of stable SVRs under steady inflow and rigid-model conditions.

papers.title: Jet-induced droplet breakup: Internal penetration and cascade channeling
papers.abstract: Localized gas-jet impingement produces droplet–deformation pathways that differ fundamentally from classical aerodynamic breakup under approximately uniform crossflow. Experiments and axisymmetric volume-of-fluid simulations are used to investigate millimetric water droplets exposed to gas jets whose diameters are smaller than or comparable with the droplet diameter. For sufficiently localized forcing, the jet produces an internal gas cavity or channel before large-scale disk-like deformation occurs. Three responses are distinguished within this localized-forcing range: nonpenetrating cavity formation, collapse-limited cascade channeling, and continuous single-shot piercing. Cascade channeling results from competition between axial channel-front advance and capillary–inertial closure of the windward opening. A pressure–capillary analysis provides a penetration criterion, while a curvature-induced momentum-turning correction leads to an effective axial Weber number that represents the reduction in penetration-driving momentum as the jet footprint extends over the curved droplet surface. The experimental and numerical results support an approximate crossover centered near Δ=Dj/Dd∼0.2, rather than a universal sharp threshold, above which internal channeling becomes progressively less dominant and the response approaches global, crossflow-like deformation. A two-mass Taylor analogy breakup-type model is developed to represent the relative motion of an effective channel-front mass and the bulk droplet. This reduced-order model captures the penetration threshold and principal trends for part of the localized-channeling range, but its velocity predictions are semi-quantitative and it does not describe three-dimensional fragmentation. The principal contribution is the identification and mechanistic interpretation of internal channeling, including its repeated collapse-and-reopening form, as a geometry-dependent response to localized aerodynamic forcing.

papers.title: Acoustic effects on flutter instability in supersonic cascades across different vibration mode shapes
papers.abstract: Acoustic propagation states, shock-wave structures, and vibration mode shapes are core factors governing the aeroelastic stability of compressor systems in aero-engines. Their combined effects directly dictate the flutter boundary. To elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms, this study focuses on the blade-tip-section cascade that dominates flutter behavior. The first bending mode, which is prone to instability, is adopted as the representative vibration mode shape. The flutter instability mechanisms of a supersonic cascade are systematically investigated. The results reveal that the twist component of the first bending mode is the key factor governing instability onset. The flutter mechanisms vary significantly across different acoustic modes. Further analysis demonstrates that the transition of the interaction between the decomposed motion components of the first bending mode constitutes the key cause of flutter in the supersonic cascade, as opposed to the stable subsonic cascade. Different acoustic modes exert a regulatory effect on the stability downstream of the shock wave. Regarding shock-wave effects, although the shock wave induces a highly stable aerodynamic damping region upstream on the blade surface, it indirectly undermines stability downstream of the shock and on the pressure surface through unsteady pressure disturbances. From a global perspective, the shock-free condition is more favorable for maintaining overall cascade stability. This study provides a physical foundation for understanding the coupled effects of acoustics, shock waves, and mode shapes on cascade flutter mechanisms.

papers.title: Mechanisms of quantized vortex-ring migration and ring-plane rotation in sheared thermal counterflow of superfluid helium
papers.abstract: Classical viscous rings can tilt and deform through vorticity redistribution within finite cores. A quantized ring in superfluid helium lacks this pathway, leaving its response to controlled shear under two-way coupling unclear. We simulate a ring in sheared thermal counterflow. Migration and ring-plane rotation reverse with the imposed gradient and vary approximately with its strength. At T=1.65 K and Lx=Ly=1.0 mm, the dissipative α term contributes most to migration, whereas background-superflow advection contributes most to rotation. Similar reorientation of classical and quantized rings therefore need not share the same physical origin.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical study on discharge characteristics in atmospheric pressure nanosecond pulsed CO2 plasmas
papers.abstract: Atmospheric pressure nanosecond pulsed CO2 discharges have attracted interest because of their importance in plasma-assisted CO2 conversion and the transient physics of streamer discharges. In this work, the characteristics of atmospheric pressure nanosecond pulsed CO2 pin-to-pin discharge were investigated by electrical measurements, time-resolved optical emission spectroscopy (OES), intensified charge coupled device (ICCD) imaging, and numerical simulation. The results show that the discharge current rises rapidly after breakdown and then decays. The ICCD images demonstrate that the discharge originates near the high-voltage needle electrode and then expands radially and axially, rapidly bridging the discharge gap. The streamer propagation exhibits a stochastic branching tendency, which is consistent with the limited seed-electron supply and weak photoionization characteristics reported for CO2 streamers. The maximum streamer-head axial propagation velocity reaches up to 1.78 × 105 m/s. The OES measurements show that the discharge spectrum is dominated by atomic and ionic radiation, while no clear molecular bands suitable for gas temperature diagnosis are observed. Therefore, a representative gas–temperature range was estimated from independent physical constraints, and its influence on the Stark broadening-based electron density diagnosis was evaluated. Within this temperature range, the inferred electron density is weakly sensitive to the assumed gas temperature. Based on the Stark broadening of the Hα and O I lines, the temporal evolution of electron density was obtained, and its normalized temporal evolution showed a similar general trend to that obtained from the simulation. These results provide insight into transient discharge development in atmospheric pressure nanosecond pulsed CO2 plasmas and demonstrate the value of combining experiment with simulation for plasma parameters difficult to access by experiment.

papers.title: Decoupling flow rate and phase fraction in gas–liquid two-phase flow through coupled target-force and cross-target differential pressure responses
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid two-phase flow measurement is complicated by the coupled dependence of flow rate and phase fraction on mixture momentum and local pressure loss. This study proposes a decoupling method based on the coupled target-force and cross-target differential-pressure responses generated by a cross-shaped pressure-sensing target. As the gas–liquid mixture passes through the target section, the incoming flow produces a target force governed mainly by mixture momentum flux. Meanwhile, the target induces local throttling and resistance losses, producing a differential pressure across the target. Because these two responses have different sensitivities to mixture velocity and phase fraction, they can provide coupled constraints for parameter decoupling. A theoretical model was established to relate target force, cross-target differential pressure, volumetric flow rate, and phase fraction. Numerical simulations were used to analyze the internal pressure field, velocity distribution, and force distribution on the target, thereby clarifying the fluid-mechanical origin of the coupled response. Air–water experiments under different flow rates and phase fractions were then conducted to validate the model and determine the dynamic pressure correction coefficient and local resistance coefficient. The results show that the target force and cross-target differential pressure vary consistently with the theoretical model and can reflect changes in the two-phase flow state. Within the tested operating range, the relative error of the volumetric flow rate was between −10% and +5%, and the absolute error of phase fraction was within ±8%. The results confirm the feasibility of the proposed decoupling method under bubbly-flow, dispersed-bubbly-flow, and weakly fluctuating transitional-flow conditions, although the flow coefficients still require experimental calibration. These findings provide a fluid-mechanical basis for the development of compact, online gas–liquid two-phase flow metering technologies.

papers.title: Unsteady separated-flow dynamics over a box-girder section under sinusoidal inflow: Effects of angle of attack and Keulegan–Carpenter number
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic behavior of bluff bridge-deck sections in unsteady inflow depends on both the angle of attack and the time scale of the imposed velocity fluctuation. Active-control wind tunnel measurements and two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations are used to examine surface pressure, aerodynamic forces, and time-averaged separated-flow topology of a streamlined box-girder section under sinusoidal streamwise inflow. The measurements validate the imposed velocity oscillation and pressure response at experimentally accessible frequencies, while the simulations span −15° ≤ α ≤ 15° and Keulegan–Carpenter numbers 0.5 ≤ KC ≤ 24.0. For |α| ≤ 8°, mean and root mean square pressure distributions vary comparatively smoothly, and the influence of KC on mean force coefficients is generally weaker than that of α. At |α| = 12° and 15°, chordwise pressure redistribution and upper-lower asymmetry become pronounced, while RMS pressure and force coefficients increase markedly, particularly at lower KC, which here represents shorter forcing periods. Pressure and force spectra remain dominated by the imposed frequency (F = f/fu = 1), with only weak second harmonics in some lift spectra. The parameter Πα,KC, incorporating KC and the angle-dependent projected dimension, approximately organizes fluctuating drag for both signs of α, whereas fluctuating lift remains strongly dependent on the sign of α. Time-averaged streamline and vorticity fields show that α and KC jointly reorganize mean recirculation regions and alter the mean-wake width, deflection, asymmetry, and streamwise organization. These findings distinguish excitation-frequency locking from amplitude modulation and clarify the coupled roles of α and KC within the present two-dimensional scope.

papers.title: Experimental investigation on the influence of herringbone riblets on the incident shock/turbulent boundary layer interactions
papers.abstract: Shock/turbulent boundary layer interactions (STBLIs) seriously affect the structural safety and aerodynamic performance of supersonic/hypersonic engine inlets. Herringbone riblet (HR) is a promising passive flow control device, yet its influence on the incident STBLI remains unclear. In this paper, the influences are experimentally investigated in a Mach 3.4 wind tunnel. The results indicate that under the incident shock-induced adverse pressure gradient, HRs disrupt the smooth separation structure, yielding spanwise-varying separation zones. At the convergence line, the separation zone enlarges and shifts upstream, accompanied by an intensified near-wall recirculation within it and enhanced downward flow above its rear half. At the divergence line, sunken HRs reduce the size of the separation zone, whereas the protruding HRs slightly expand it. These topological changes within and downstream of the separation zone impart spanwise variations to the local compression waves, which in turn yields the separation shock with both spanwise variations and heightened unsteadiness. Compared with the sunken configuration, protruding HRs induce stronger spanwise variations in the boundary layer and shock-induced separation zone, along with greater dispersion of the separation shock. Furthermore, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition results suggest that without shock incidence, both HR configurations shift the pulsating energy of the turbulent boundary layer from low to high frequencies. With shock incidence, protruding HRs sustain low-frequency pulsations, whereas sunken HRs lead to a more uniform energy distribution. In both cases, the HRs extract energy from the mean flow and channel it into specific modal ranges depending on the background flow conditions.

papers.title: Study on wake–tailplane interactions in transonic buffeting separated flow: Horizontal tail in pre-buffet states
papers.abstract: In transonic flight, the fluctuating loads imposed on the horizontal tail by wing shock-induced flow separation are critical factors affecting both flight safety and structural integrity. In this study, a delayed detached-eddy simulation approach based on the Spalart–Allmaras (S–A) turbulence model is employed to systematically investigate the evolution of the turbulent wake generated by the main wing and its unsteady interaction with the horizontal tail. The analysis focuses on the shock buffet flow over an OAT15A airfoil at a 5.0° angle of attack under transonic conditions. The accuracy of the numerical method in simulating the shock motion range, buffet frequency, and turbulent kinetic energy dissipation in the wake is validated. The results show that during the forward motion of the main wing shock toward the leading edge within one buffet cycle, a large-scale separation bubble is generated and shed, forming highly fluctuating alternating vortex structures accompanied by high-frequency pulsations of the shear layer at the shock foot. Turbulent kinetic energy analysis reveals that although the separated wake dissipates rapidly during downstream transport, it still retains about 30% of its peak energy intensity in the region where the horizontal tail is located. Using sliding-window proper orthogonal decomposition and flow field reconstruction, it is found that the large-scale separated vortices from the main wing undergo vortex breakup when interacting with the horizontal tail, with energy transferring to small-scale separation vortices on the tail surface and upstream-traveling wave modes. The aerodynamic forces on the horizontal tail exhibit unsteady fluctuations associated with the fundamental frequency of the main wing shock oscillation and its harmonics, and show distinct spectral response characteristics at different tail angles of attack. This study reveals the complex energy transfer mechanism of shock–vortex–tail coupling in the separated buffet flow, providing a flow-physics basis for the dynamic load analysis of horizontal tails on transonic aircraft.

papers.title: Hemodynamics and wall mechanics of cerebral aneurysms at different internal carotid artery locations: A fluid–structure interaction study
papers.abstract: Growth and rupture of cerebral aneurysms are strongly influenced by local hemodynamics and wall mechanics, which are dependent on aneurysm location and growth status. In this study, fluid–structure interaction is modeled for aneurysms at three internal carotid artery (ICA) locations—cavernous ICA, posterior communicating artery (PCoMA), and ICA terminus, for patient-specific growing and stable cases. Physiological pulsatile flow is prescribed at the inlet and a three-element Windkessel model is applied at the outlets to represent downstream vascular beds. Wall prestress is incorporated to approximate the in-vivo stressed configuration. The results show that the growing aneurysms exhibit larger intra-aneurysmal recirculatory flow regions, lower viscous dissipation ratio, and a greater dome area exposed to low wall shear stress (WSS) when compared with stable aneurysms. Slow-flow regions associated with daughter sacs are observed in growing aneurysms at all locations, accompanied by low WSS and relatively significant oscillatory shear index. Wall displacement and stress distributions are sensitive to flow impingement and local dome geometry, with growing aneurysms at the terminus and PCoMA locations exhibiting larger dome areas subjected to elevated displacement (up to 98% and 90%, respectively) and more concentrated tensile stress within the dome regions. These findings suggest that the combined hemodynamic and structural conditions may contribute to aneurysm wall degradation and progression, particularly at the ICA terminus and PCoMA locations, consistent with the higher instability risk reported clinically. However, these observations require validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Cavitation-induced evolution of unsteady flow structures and energy dissipation mechanisms in a multistage liquid-cooling pump
papers.abstract: Rising heat-flux densities in high-performance computing centers impose stringent requirements on the stability of liquid-cooling circulation systems, in which centrifugal pumps are susceptible to cavitation-induced flow instabilities. However, the physical mechanism by which cavitation disturbances are generated and attenuated in multistage liquid-cooling pumps remains unclear. In this study, unsteady cavitating flow in a three-stage liquid-cooling pump under the rated flow condition is numerically investigated using variational mode decomposition, rigid-vorticity identification, and entropy production analysis. The results reveal that cavitation does not uniformly amplify pressure pulsations; instead, it selectively enhances rotational-frequency disturbances. This amplification is strongest at the inlet of the first-stage impeller and gradually attenuates downstream, indicating a first-stage-dominated instability mode. The underlying mechanism is associated with the coupling among leading-edge cavitation evolution, suction-vortex-induced inlet flow distortion, and blade-sweeping effects. Periodic cavity growth, shedding, and collapse modify local pressure and velocity gradients, while suction vortices periodically vary the incoming flow angle during blade passage. This coupled process intensifies shear, recirculation, and flow separation near the first-stage impeller inlet, thereby increasing rotational-frequency disturbances. Entropy production analysis further shows that the hydrodynamic irreversible losses under cavitating conditions are mainly concentrated in the first-stage impeller and diffuser, with limited influence on subsequent stages. These findings identify the first-stage impeller inlet and suction-side leading edge as critical regions for suppressing cavitation-induced unsteady disturbances and energy loss in the investigated pump under the rated flow condition.

papers.title: Effects of reduced frequency on the unsteady aerodynamic and aeroacoustic characteristics of a pitching National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0018 airfoil
papers.abstract: Periodic pitching produces pronounced unsteady aerodynamic and acoustic responses in airfoils. Yet, the manner in which reduced frequency redistributes acoustic energy and reorganizes source-related flow structures remains unclear. Large-eddy simulation coupled with the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings analogy is used to investigate a pitching NACA 0018 airfoil over reduced frequencies from k = 0.004 19 to 0.084. As k increases, the response transitions from quasi-steady behavior to pronounced dynamic stall. The peak lift coefficient increases from approximately 1.05–1.66. In contrast, the peak overall sound pressure level rises from about 104–117 dB and exhibits an increasing phase lag relative to the aerodynamic loading. The acoustic response is strongly frequency-dependent rather than uniformly amplified. In the 0–0.5 kHz band, broadband energy and components at the pitching frequency and its low-order harmonics increase markedly with k. In the 1.5–2.3 kHz range, corresponding to Strouhal number based on the trailing-edge boundary-layer thickness (Stδ=0.10–0.15), localized narrowband peaks arise from instability waves in the boundary layer near the trailing edge or separated shear layer and their subsequent scattering at the trailing edge. Phase-averaged pressure–velocity coupling and enstrophy fields show that the region associated with the acoustic sources remains concentrated near the trailing edge, while increasing k extends rotational activity along the suction-side shear layer and near wake. Upstroke–downstroke spectral differences at identical instantaneous angles demonstrate a clear motion direction dependence, whereas smoother far-field directivity is consistent with coherence loss and phase cancelation during propagation.

papers.title: Flow and heat transfer predictions of supercritical pressure hydrocarbon fuel in three-dimensional Kagome lattice structures using physics-informed neural network
papers.abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics faces prohibitive computational costs due to complex cooling structures and variable operating conditions. This study developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) driven by Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes data to predict the flow and heat transfer of supercritical hydrocarbon fuel in three-dimensional Kagome lattice structures. By enforcing governing physical laws, the PINN effectively suppressed the numerical over-smoothing inherent in purely data-driven artificial neural networks (ANN), precisely preserving large velocity gradients within complex wake recirculation and boundary layer separation regions. Under local parametric extension conditions slightly outside the training bounds, the incorporated physical priors prevented non-physical numerical drift, significantly reducing the temperature prediction error from 2.18% (ANN) to 1.04% (PINN). Across the entire fluid domain, the average relative errors for temperature, velocity magnitude, and pressure predictions were strictly bounded to 2.17%, 2.58%, and 0.016%, respectively. Furthermore, utilizing the trained PINN as a rapid surrogate, this study explicitly quantified the diminishing cooling benefits with increased mass flux. Specifically, an equivalent increase in the coolant supply yields a substantial maximum wall temperature reduction, decreasing from 39.5 to 11 K under low flow rate conditions, whereas this temperature drop becomes gradually attenuated under high flow rate conditions. This framework captures how the convective heat transfer coefficient growth rate follows a decaying trend with increasing mass flux. Ultimately, this physics-driven approach establishes reliable quantitative baselines for performance evaluation, offering guidance for the prediction of flow and thermal fields under applied thermal boundary conditions.

papers.title: Finite-pulse rupture and release windows of compressible encapsulated microbubbles with interface-energy-induced residual stress
papers.abstract: Finite-thickness polymeric or composite microbubbles can experience residual prestress, compressible shell deformation, rupture, gas venting, and payload release under finite ultrasound bursts. We formulate a radial-dynamics model in which a compressible viscoelastic shell is resolved as a finite-thickness continuum and coupled to radius-dependent interface energies, a pre-acoustic equilibrium boundary-value problem, supra-threshold damage history, persistent opening, gas leakage, and mass-conserving shared-reservoir release. The radial-dynamics core is verified against tissue-confined and interface-energy reference limits. Rupture predictions are then assessed against two independent experimental settings. Using a single global rupture-strength scale fitted to the 10-cycle Chen et al. fragmentation threshold, the 2-, 5-, and 20-cycle predictions give a mean absolute relative error of 4.9% and a root mean square error of 12.7 kPa; these three points were not used to fit numerical parameters, although they informed model-form assessment. Without Chitnis-specific refitting, the model also captures the monotonic shell-thickness-to-radius trend measured by Chitnis et al., although it underpredicts the absolute quasi-static rupture pressures. The results show that stretch–curvature coupling primarily constrains static admissibility, whereas shell compressibility controls the deformation pathway and rupture threshold. Finite-pulse thresholds approach a long-duration plateau, and the shared-reservoir formulation separates permeability-mediated subrupture transport from opening-assisted release. The framework is intended for finite-thickness shells; the release variables remain uncalibrated reservoir fractions rather than quantitative drug-mass predictions.

papers.title: Intensification and annihilation of recirculating vortices in Taylor cones
papers.abstract: Vortical structures within the Taylor cone are key hydrodynamic features that govern internal recirculation and momentum redistribution in electrospinning and electrospraying. Despite their importance in sustaining the steady cone–jet configuration, their origin, organization, and persistence remain poorly understood. In this study, we employ electrohydrodynamic simulations to investigate recirculating flows across experimentally relevant ranges of flow rate, viscosity, and applied voltage. The internal flow topology is analyzed using a nonlinear dynamical-systems approach in which fixed points of the velocity field are identified as centers or saddle points. Quantitative descriptors, including eigenvalue magnitudes indicating vortical strength, a distortion parameter capturing vortex deformation, and the quadrilateral area formed by the four fixed points, are introduced to track the evolution, interaction, intensification, or annihilation of vortical structures. Increasing the Weber or Ohnesorge number progressively weakens and obliterates the counter-rotating vortex pair, consistent with enhanced axial momentum or viscous diffusion overwhelming the electrostatic shear layer responsible for recirculation. In contrast, increasing the electrical capillary number sustains and intensifies the vortices while driving the interface inward. These contrasting responses reflect competition between tangential Maxwell stress and the associated pressure adjustment that drives recirculation, and convective transport or viscous processes that suppress it. In all cases, the surface charge density is insensitive to the controlling parameter, consistent with a quasi-electrostatic regime where charge relaxation is faster than interfacial advection. Overall, our findings provide a mechanistic basis for selecting conditions that promote or suppress recirculation, with implications for jet stability and droplet monodispersity in electrohydrodynamic atomization and electrospinning.

papers.title: The influence of divergence angle on the diffraction characteristics of hydrogen–oxygen–argon detonation waves
papers.abstract: Detonation diffraction in expanding channels is important for hydrogen safety and rotating detonation engine applications, but quantitative criteria for distinguishing self-sustained propagation from failure remain uncertain. This study examines detonation diffraction, re-initiation, and quenching in a premixed H2:O2:Ar = 2:1:7 mixture in symmetric diverging two-dimensional channels using the in-house Density-based Compressible Reactive Flow Solver, an explicit fourth-order Runge–Kutta method, finite rate chemistry, and adaptive mesh refinement. The main simulations cover divergence angles from 7.5° to 45°, and additional near-critical cases at 25°, 27.5°, and 29° are used to resolve the transition interval. Increasing divergence angle strengthens rarefaction-induced front curvature, shock reaction front decoupling, and transverse wave attenuation, producing a transition from self-sustained propagation to quenching. A composite semi-empirical diagnostic index, Ω, combines transverse wave pressure amplification, velocity retention, and normalized decoupling distance. For the present mixture, pressure, and channel scale, Ω>3 indicates self-sustained propagation, with values sufficiently above 3 corresponding to robust self-sustained behavior; 1 < Ω ≤ 3 corresponds to near-critical or marginal propagation; and Ω≤1 indicates a tendency toward quenching. A semi-empirical Chester–Chisnell–Whitham-type attenuation correlation with a calibrated geometric-divergence correction and a phenomenological heat-release term is also assessed. Both relations are calibrated diagnostic descriptions for the present numerical configuration and are not independently validated predictive models.

papers.title: Flow physics of progressive-curvature Coanda surfaces in transonic circulation control
papers.abstract: Premature jet separation severely limits the control authority of transonic circulation control (CC) airfoils. This study investigates the flow physics governing Coanda jet attachment and develops a progressive-curvature Coanda surface at Ma=0.72 through shape optimization of the NASA-SC(2)-0714-CC supercritical airfoil. Relative to the constant-radius baseline, the optimized progressive-curvature surface achieves 37.0% lift enhancement and extends jet deflection from 79.4° to 125.0°. Flow-field analysis shows that the performance improvement is governed by two coordinated curvature effects. A locally smaller curvature radius near the slot exit lets the under-expanded jet expand more fully along the wall. A confined shock-induced separation bubble is then bridged and reattached, and shock-cell oscillations are damped. The subsequent progressive increase in the curvature radius reduces the required centripetal acceleration as the jet momentum decays, thereby sustaining the wall-normal pressure gradient and delaying separation. The optimized geometry also retains its effectiveness at Ma=0.3, yielding 23.2% higher lift-to-drag ratio than the baseline configuration. These results demonstrate that matching surface curvature to evolving jet momentum governs transonic CC effectiveness.

papers.title: Pressure-fluctuation feature characterization and flow-pattern identification in gas–water two-phase flow
papers.abstract: Wellbore inclination redistributes the gravitational components acting on gas–water two-phase flow, thereby altering phase distribution and the wall-pressure fluctuation response. Understanding this mechanism is essential for interpreting production-logging responses in gas–water flow. In this study, three-dimensional transient numerical models were developed for horizontal, 45° deviated, and vertical wells using the volume-of-fluid interface-capturing method coupled with the large-eddy simulation wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity turbulence model. Fourteen gas–water flow conditions were simulated, covering gas superficial velocities of 0.2–8.0 m/s and liquid superficial velocities of 0.1–3.8 m/s, and wall-pressure signals were collected using an 18-channel monitoring array distributed along the upper and lower wall surfaces.
