The results show that stratified flow in horizontal wells exhibits clear phase separation, whereas slug and bubbly flows in vertical wells remain approximately axisymmetric. In the 45° deviated wellbore, slug flow is marked by upward displacement of gas slugs and an inclined, asymmetric gas–liquid interface. Under identical inlet velocities, the peak pressure fluctuation in the 45° deviated wellbore reaches approximately 7500 Pa, about 1.53 times that observed in the vertical wellbore. The gas-slug propagation velocity captures the axial coherent motion, while the fluctuation intensity is additionally controlled by gas-slug offset, asymmetric liquid-film distribution, and liquid-slug momentum sweeping. Based on a seven-dimensional multiphysics feature set, the linear discriminant analysis classifier achieved a flow-pattern identification accuracy of 97.62%. These findings provide a physical basis for flow-pattern identification in complex wellbores and for the interpretation of distributed acoustic sensing monitoring data.

papers.title: Edge waves over general bathymetries: Invariant imbedding and singular-end point Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin analysis
papers.abstract: We develop an invariant imbedding formulation for edge waves propagating along a straight shoreline over a general one-dimensional bathymetry. The shallow water wave equation is transformed into a first-order Riccati equation, for which the regular shoreline asymptotics provide a natural initial condition. Matching to the exponentially decaying solution over a uniform offshore shelf yields a scalar eigenvalue condition. For higher-order modes, an equivalent first-order linear system avoids the poles of the Riccati variable at the nodes of the eigenfunctions. The formulation is validated against exact or analytical results for plane, concave exponential, and convex exponential beaches. Excellent agreement is obtained, with deviations near the shelf cutoff arising when the analytical reference problem has a different offshore continuation. We then investigate power-law beaches, h(x)∝xα, with 0<α<2. A self-similar large-K limit gives Ωn∼ηnK2−α, where ηn is the nth eigenvalue of the corresponding scaled half-line problem. A Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin analysis adapted to the singular shoreline yields the exponent-dependent end point phase correction 1/[2(2−α)] and provides analytical estimates of ηn that agree closely with the numerical large-K limits, with increasing accuracy for higher modes. The outer turning point scales as K−1, quantifying the stronger offshore localization of convex profiles and the broader modal structures supported by concave profiles. Finally, an S-shaped hyperbolic-tangent bathymetry illustrates a crossover from local shoreline control of the spectrum at large K to sensitivity to the full bathymetric profile at smaller K, demonstrating the applicability of the formulation beyond analytically tractable and self-similar beaches.

papers.title: Erratum to “Peristaltic transport of viscoelastic fluid in curved ducts with ciliated walls” [Phys. Fluids, 36 , 033619 (2024)]
Investigation on aerodynamic characteristics of horizontal-axis wind turbine with boundary-layer suction based on γ -Re θ transition model
papers.abstract: Boundary layer suction (BLS) mitigates flow separation and stall on horizontal-axis wind turbine (HAWT) blades by sucking low-momentum fluid from the suction surface, thereby enhancing aerodynamic performance. Three-dimensional numerical simulations of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory Phase VI wind turbine are performed using the γ-Reθ transition shear stress transport (SST) k–ω turbulence model to investigate the aerodynamic effects of BLS. The numerical results for the clean blade have been validated against the NREL Phase VI wind tunnel experimental data, and this work focuses on the regulatory roles of the momentum coefficient, tip speed ratio (TSR), and spanwise suction slot layout in regulating power output and flow fields. It is demonstrated that BLS effectively enlarges the attached flow area, increases the blade pressure difference, delays separation, and improves flow stability. Significant power gains are obtained at TSRs ranging from 2.5 to 3.8. At the optimal momentum coefficient, the net power output evaluated after deducting the theoretical suction pump power and accounting for additional power losses reaches 193% of that of the clean blade; the gain is observed to increase with decreasing TSR but to drop at an extremely low TSR. Spanwise tip-only control and combined middle-tip control achieve the best aerodynamic performance via the maximum attached flow coverage and suppression of local separation vortices. Numerical results of this work support HAWT active flow control research, and preliminarily prove the γ-Reθ transition SST k–ω turbulence model fits BLS optimization studies.

papers.title: Mechanism linking the space-time characteristics of wall pressure fluctuations to hypersonic inlet working states
papers.abstract: Wall pressure fluctuations generated by hypersonic inlets are an important factor that might cause great damage to the aircraft structure. To reveal the mechanism of wall pressure fluctuations, numerical computations using the delayed detached eddy simulation method are performed to calculate the unsteady flow structure in a hypersonic inlet. Different adverse pressure gradients are simulated by varying the throttling ratio at the exit of the intake duct. The investigation results show that both the static pressure and pressure fluctuations are determined by the working status of the inlet, and inlet unstart always causes a significant increase in the wall pressure fluctuation amplitude. The time-frequency characteristics indicate that the spectral energy of pressure fluctuations is mainly concentrated in the high-frequency range in the started inlet, whereas dominant low-frequency oscillations are observed in the unstarted inlet. The space-time correlation reveals that pressure fluctuations are convected downstream in the started inlet and upstream in the unstarted inlet. To further address the working mechanism of the inlet, modal analysis of wall pressure fluctuations is also conducted in this work. An interesting phenomenon is observed, whereby the dominant mode of pressure fluctuations shift from the hydrodynamic mode to the acoustic mode as the inlet transitions from the start to the unstart state.

papers.title: Two-way coupled transport and deposition of charged metal droplets with arc-driven gas flow during direct current arc interruption
papers.abstract: Splashed metal droplets from arc root erosion in a direct-current (DC) air circuit breaker interact with the arc plasma and form a multiphase plasma-flow system. In this study, a two-way coupled magnetohydrodynamic framework is extended to account for charged metal-droplet transport and feedback on arc-driven gas flow. Droplet motion is governed by drag force, electric force, gravity, and Lorentz force. Droplet-induced body-force source terms and electromagnetic feedback are incorporated into the governing equations. Droplet charge level determines the transport and spatial-distribution regimes. Flow-dominated dispersion is observed at low charge levels, clustered transport occurs at intermediate charge levels, and localized trajectories form at high charge levels under stronger electric-field influence. Drag force dominates momentum attenuation and transport distance. Electric force controls the migration direction and spatial concentration, while Lorentz force induces only weak trajectory deflection. These forces also alter droplet trajectories, spatial distribution, and residence positions. The relative motion and drag exchange between the droplets and gas are, therefore, changed, producing a charge-dependent momentum-feedback pathway distinct from that of neutral droplets. At 6.4 ms, charged droplets increase the local temperature by approximately 200 K and reduce the gas flow velocity by 15.07% relative to the case without droplet coupling. Convective transport is weakened, thermal retention is enhanced, and the decay of the conductive arc channel is suppressed. These results reveal a charge-dependent droplet-feedback mechanism in confined arc plasma and provide new insight into multiphase transport during DC interruption.

papers.title: Floquet-guided reinforcement learning for active flow control of a low-Reynolds-number three-dimensional wing
papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning (RL) control of three-dimensional separated flows is computationally demanding because the number of sensor inputs and independent actuator outputs increase rapidly with spanwise resolution. This study develops a Floquet-guided RL strategy for active flow control of a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 straight wing at a chord-based Reynolds number of Re=500. Floquet analysis of the two-dimensional time-periodic baseline flow identifies the most amplified spanwise wavelength, which is embedded in a harmonic actuation basis so that the agent optimizes only the time-dependent amplitude and phase of each blowing slot. The resulting four-dimensional action space replaces a much larger set of independently controlled spanwise actuators. The learned policy increases the period-averaged lift by approximately 7.29%. Flow-field analysis shows that the spanwise-modulated blowing generates streamwise vortices that transport higher-momentum fluid toward the separated upper-surface region, extend the low-pressure region downstream, and improve resistance to the adverse pressure gradient. These results demonstrate that linear stability information can provide a physically interpretable low-dimensional control basis for RL in a laminar/transitional wing flow.

papers.title: Flow reorganization of buoyant pool-fire plumes by a single-layer obstacle
papers.abstract: The interaction of a buoyancy-driven reacting plume with a partially permeable single-layer obstacle was investigated using n-heptane pool-fire experiments and large-eddy simulations. The obstacle interrupts the continuous axial transport of the plume and redistributes the flow, fuel vapor, and thermal energy between gap penetration and lateral bypass. At an obstacle height of 20 cm, the concentrated continuous-flame region penetrates predominantly through the gaps, whereas increasing the obstacle height to 30–50 cm allows greater plume spreading, ambient-air entrainment, and oscillation before impingement, leading to stronger lateral diversion, flow separation, recirculation, and locally restricted flame development. The resulting flame heights are substantially lower than the Heskestad free-flame predictions, and an H/D-based correlation quantifies the dependence of normalized flame height on the relative obstacle position. The obstacle also reorganizes the thermal plume into a heat-accumulation region below the obstacle, a rapid temperature-transition region near it, and an entrainment-cooled region above it. The temperature remains approximately 800–900 °C near the fire source but decreases abruptly after plume–obstacle interaction. A localized pressure-deficit region is spatially associated with flow reversal and vortical structures near the obstacle. A modified McCaffrey-based correlation describes the resulting zonal centerline temperature decay. These results identify the flow-partitioning and pressure-mediated recirculation mechanisms through which a partially permeable obstacle reorganizes a variable-density reacting plume.

papers.title: Gas–surface interaction effects on Rayleigh–Bénard convection in rarefied flows
papers.abstract: Non-continuum Rayleigh–Bénard convection of a monatomic gas is investigated using the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo method for Knudsen numbers in the range 0.01≤Kn≤0.04. The influence of gas–surface interaction (GSI) on flow stability and heat transfer is examined using fully diffuse, partially diffuse, and Cercignani–Lampis–Lord (CLL) kernels applied at isothermal hot and cold boundaries. The CLL formulation permits independent variation of the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient, σt, and the normal energy accommodation coefficient, αn, enabling their individual contributions to be assessed. The onset and development of convection exhibit pronounced sensitivity to the choice of GSI model and accommodation coefficients. Lower values of σt increase velocity slip and reduce viscous damping, thereby promoting instability, whereas larger values of αn reduce temperature jumps and enhance thermal coupling between the gas and the walls. The combined influence of these accommodation processes alters the predicted stability boundaries, with a low σt, high αn combination extending the admissible rarefaction limit for convection onset from Kn=0.029 for the fully diffuse kernel to Kn=0.037 for the CLL kernel. The results indicate that the critical Rayleigh number is a function of accommodation coefficients, Knudsen and Froude numbers. Since these parameters are functions of the gas species, surface properties, and thermodynamic conditions, a single critical Rayleigh number cannot adequately characterize convection in the non-continuum regime. Heat transfer analysis shows broadly similar trends across different GSI kernels, with enhanced transport observed for larger αn and smaller σt, highlighting the sensitivity of quantitative transport predictions to gas–surface interaction modeling in rarefied convection.

papers.title: Ill-posedness of uniform flows and formation of roll waves in the one-dimensional shallow water equations
papers.abstract: The one-dimensional shallow water equations (1D SWEs) represent the conservation laws of mass and momentum governing open channel flows. The 1D SWEs have significant non-trivial unsteady solutions known as roll waves, which are weak entropy solutions characterized by being continuously differentiable almost everywhere, while also containing discontinuities. Despite widespread use of the 1D SWEs in hydraulic engineering, their well-posedness issues have received comparatively limited attention. A well-posed problem implies existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on the given data, or stability, of its solution. This study critically examines Cauchy problems for the 1D SWEs with two aims: to demonstrate the existence of roll waves as weak entropy solutions and to investigate the conjecture that, when the trivial uniform flow is taken as the initial data, the Cauchy problem becomes ill-posed due to a loss of stability. Numerical experiments with periodic boundary conditions indicate that small perturbations of the trivial uniform flow at the initial time evolve into the emergence of roll wave solutions.

papers.title: Study on pressure pulsation induced by the draft tube vortex rope in a pump–turbine based on the Biot–Savart law theory
papers.abstract: The draft tube vortex rope critically affects pump–turbine stability. This study compared low load spiral vortices with high load columnar vortices, and combined Biot–Savart law to reveal the fluid dynamics laws governing draft tube vortex ropes in pump–turbines. Research has shown that the maximum sweeping radius of the spiral vortex core is 100.6% of the inlet of the draft, which is three times the maximum sweeping radius of the columnar vortex. The spiral vortex exhibits higher turbulent kinetic energy, chaotic near-wall low-pressure regions, and progressive vortex breakdown, whereas the columnar vortex maintains axially uniform pressure with a central low-pressure zone. Pressure pulsations follow a periodic trigonometric pattern, confirming Biot–Savart law predictions. Spectrally, near the inlet wall both vortices show a dominant frequency of 1.8 times the rotational frequency. Downstream, the spiral vortex introduces an additional 2.6 component, while the columnar vortex shifts its dominant frequency to 3.4. The spiral vortex induces peak-to-peak pressure pulsations of 0.61%–2.06% of the head, exceeding the 0.36%–1.86% induced by the columnar vortex. These contrasting kinematic and dynamic features highlight the more severe threat of the spiral vortex to unit stability. This study reveals the essential relationship between vortex-rope dynamics and pressure pulsation, providing a theoretical reference for prediction, suppression, and stability optimization.

papers.title: Rheological and interfacial characterization of menstrual fluid
papers.abstract: Menstrual fluid is a complex biological fluid composed of blood, endometrial tissue, vaginal epithelial cells, cervical mucus, and microbiota. Its physical properties remain largely unexplored, despite their relevance for applications such as the in vitro testing of absorbent products. Current industrial simulants are typically simplified water- or blood-like fluids that may not adequately reproduce the complex behavior of real menses during absorbency testing. Here, we present the first systematic characterization of the bulk and interfacial properties of menstrual fluid, including shear rheology, small-amplitude viscoelasticity, extensional dynamics, and surface tension. Measurements were performed on 228 samples collected during 20 menstrual periods from 12 healthy volunteers. Our results show that menstrual fluid viscosity is approximately fourfold higher than blood and forty-fold higher than water. Menstrual fluid behaves as a structured, non-Newtonian fluid exhibiting yield stress, shear-thinning, and extensional viscoelasticity, with a predominantly solid-like response in the linear viscoelastic regime. Surface tension is significantly lower than that of water and comparable to that of venous blood, although with a broader range. Rheological and interfacial properties systematically change with the menstrual flow rate, defined here as the mass of fluid discharge per unit time. Together, these findings provide a quantitative description of the rheological and interfacial properties of menstrual fluid, supporting future research in female hygiene and health care, as well as applications in menstrual product testing.

papers.title: Modeling surface tension in multi-species flows using a Roe solver with stiffened gas equation
papers.abstract: This paper presents a numerical method for simulating multi-species flows with surface tension, integrating a Roe-type Riemann solver, the gamma model, and the continuous surface force (CSF) model into a Navier–Stokes framework with a stiffened gas equation of state. In the present formulation, the fluids are treated as non-reacting species, and no phase change or mass transfer is considered. The approach resolves shock waves, contact discontinuities, and interfacial dynamics in conservative form. Validation encompasses a one-dimensional shock tube test, capturing discontinuities with errors below 2% using Van Leer and optimum symmetric polynomial-ratio expression limiters, and static droplet simulations in two dimensions and three dimensions, predicting pressure jumps within 10% of Young–Laplace theory. Parasitic currents, on the order of 10−2, persist as a numerical artifact despite mesh refinement, highlighting a limitation of the CSF implementation. Comparisons with analytical solutions and prior studies confirm robustness across diverse scenarios. This method achieves high accuracy and stability, offering potential for microfluidics, environmental flows, and industrial applications involving interfacial phenomena. Future work could mitigate parasitic currents through enhanced schemes and extend the model to dynamic multi-species flows.

papers.title: High-gradient-aware wavelet-aligned U-Net for airfoil Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes flow-field prediction
papers.abstract: Near-field flow prediction around airfoils is essential for aerodynamic analysis and design, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations remain computationally expensive. Although data-driven surrogate models can substantially accelerate flow-field evaluation, accurately reconstructing localized high-gradient structures around the airfoil surface, leading and trailing edges, and wake remains challenging. This study proposes the wavelet-aligned U-Net with coefficient-domain cross-attention (WAX-UNet) for predicting airfoil velocity, pressure, and density fields. WAX-UNet combines a U-Net backbone with selective wavelet-domain refinement. The wavelet-bottleneck cross-attention refinement module couples low-resolution global context with wavelet detail coefficients through linear cross-attention, while the hierarchical cross-attention refinement module introduces high-frequency encoder sub-bands into decoder-side feature fusion through sub-band-specific modulation. A dynamically weighted high-gradient-region-of-interest (HG-ROI)-aware root mean square error objective further emphasizes physically sensitive regions during training. Experiments on the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign airfoil dataset show that WAX-UNet achieves the lowest component-wise relative L2 errors and overall root mean square error among representative convolutional, neural-operator, and transformer-based baselines. It also achieves the lowest HG-ROI errors for streamwise velocity and pressure and the lowest errors in the near-wall, trailing-edge, and wake regions. Physical-consistency diagnostics indicate lower continuity-residual and wall-normal-velocity errors, while WAX-UNet achieves the lowest errors for all four variables on the geometry-extreme out-of-distribution test set. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of the proposed modules and training objective. Averaged over three independent runs on the geometry-balanced test set, WAX-UNet achieves relative L2 errors of 0.499%, 2.089%, 0.109%, and 0.008% for u, v, p, and ρ, respectively, with moderate computational cost.

papers.title: Competing effects of thermal and chemical nonequilibrium on shock train flow in a high-Mach-number scramjet isolator
papers.abstract: To investigate thermochemical nonequilibrium effects in high-Mach-number scramjet isolators, the flow characteristics of the isolator were studied using thermally perfect gas, chemical nonequilibrium gas, thermal nonequilibrium gas, and thermochemical nonequilibrium gas models. The results indicate that the thermochemical nonequilibrium model exhibits the shortest shock train and the highest total pressure recovery coefficient among the four gas models. Chemical nonequilibrium suppresses the development of the small separation region, whereas thermal nonequilibrium promotes it. With increasing inlet Mach number, the isolator shock train becomes shorter and exhibits a more pronounced asymmetric structure. The dominant governing mechanism in the small separation region transitions from thermal nonequilibrium to chemical nonequilibrium, with the influence of thermochemical nonequilibrium effects reaching a minimum under the Ma∞ = 10 condition. In contrast, the scale of the large separation region remains primarily controlled by chemical nonequilibrium effects, owing to its larger spatial extent and the tendency of chemical reactions to approach equilibrium. The enhancement of shock train asymmetry is attributed to the reduction in the peak adverse pressure gradient at the separation location and the decrease in the separation shock angle β with increasing inlet Mach number. In addition, nonequilibrium effects play a dominant role in determining the degree of shock train asymmetry. Chemical nonequilibrium enhances the asymmetry, whereas thermal nonequilibrium suppresses it. These findings may provide useful guidance for the flow control design of high-Mach-number scramjet isolators.

papers.title: Magnetohydrodynamics driven vortex and heat transfer enhancement by a rotational magnetic field in a circular channel
papers.abstract: This work numerically studies the effects of a rotating magnetic field with different lengths on electrically conductive fluid flow and convection of heat transfer within a channel with circular cross section, based on a magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) model. Simulations are performed for Hartmann numbers Ha=0.5 and Ha=5.0, and for several rotational velocities of the magnetic field. The primary analysis focuses on Re=10, with additional cases at Re=1000 and Re=5000. The results show that the rotating magnetic field induces an MHD-driven vortex, which generates secondary flows in the radial direction through the interaction of centrifugal forces and pressure gradients. These secondary flows significantly enhance convective heat transfer. The Nusselt number increases across a wide parameter range. The length influenced by the magnetic field that leads to heat transfer enhancement expands with increasing Reynolds number. A configuration involving multiple rotating magnetic fields separated by gaps is also explored, demonstrating further potential for enhancement. Pressure drop analysis reveals that, due to the absence of inserted objects, the associated penalties are relatively small; in some cases at low Hartmann numbers, the pressure drop even decreases. However, additional energy is required for the rotational magnetic field, including physical work and Joule heat dissipation, which are obtained for all cases and compared with baseline pump power. Overall, the study demonstrates that by tuning the field and flow parameters, vortex flows can be generated with different intensities throughout the channel without introducing internal physical obstructions, enabling controllable heat transfer enhancement in different sections of a certain channel.

papers.title: Experimental investigation and mechanistic modeling of porosity–permeability damage induced by dry-out and salt precipitation in underground gas storage reservoirs
papers.abstract: Dry-out and salt precipitation (DSP) near the wellbore is a frequently observed phenomenon in underground gas storage during injection–withdrawal cycles. It causes pore-space contraction and localized pore–throat clogging, thereby reducing reservoir porosity and permeability. However, existing clogging relations often fail to explicitly represent how clogging material occupies and evolves within the pore space, and they also struggle to capture the strongly nonlinear permeability response in a unified manner. To address these limitations, we conducted long-term gas-flooding experiments and measured key petrophysical properties and clogging-state variables before and after DSP. Mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) combined with fractal analysis was further used to characterize the evolution of salt-precipitation–induced microscale heterogeneity. Building on two classical conceptual frameworks—capillary bundles (CB) and equal-diameter sphere packings (EDSP)—we propose a clogging state-variable–driven strategy to construct porosity–permeability relations for occupancy-type clogging. By incorporating dual-fractal theory, we further establish a generalized porosity–permeability relation that simultaneously accounts for cumulative pore cross-sectional-area scaling (described by Ds) and volumetric space filling of the connected pore network (captured by the pore-volume fractal dimension Dv), together with a parameter-reduced form for data-limited applications. The CB and EDSP relations emerge as assumption-dependent, geometry-specific special cases of the proposed dual-fractal framework. Experiments show that DSP decreases both porosity and permeability, with permeability being markedly more sensitive. Permeability exhibits pronounced nonlinear decay with increasing solid-salt saturation and clogging factor. The MIP-derived Dv exhibits physically interpretable associations with petrophysical properties and clogging-state variables, whereas the corresponding Ds, inferred from Dv through the stated additive approximation, provides a model-consistent representation of pore-surface scaling rather than independent experimental evidence. Taken together, these results indicate that salt clogging is manifested not only by pore-volume reduction but also by changes in the effective scaling characteristics and flow-relevant heterogeneity of the connected pore system. Evaluations across relations and published DSP and other occupancy-type clogging datasets confirm that the generalized dual-fractal relation provides the best overall in-sample fit among the four proposed forms, while the CB/EDSP and simplified-fractal forms provide comparable descriptions of the dominant trend and remain useful lower-complexity alternatives in data-limited settings. This work provides a mechanism-informed and implementable framework for interpreting and predicting DSP-induced permeability impairment, and it supports embedding clogging relations into numerical simulators for performance assessment in occupancy-dominated clogging scenarios.

papers.title: Real-time visualization of shear-induced structures in turbulent flow of wormlike micellar solutions and physically interpretable machine-learning prediction of drag reduction
papers.abstract: The role of shear-induced structures (SIS) in surfactant drag reduction (DR) is difficult to verify directly in fully developed turbulent pipe flow. This study combines rheology, pressure-drop measurements, laser-sheet imaging, ultrasonic velocity profiling (UVP), and machine learning in excess-counterion surfactant solutions. Friction was measured in three pipe diameters at Reynolds numbers up to 165 000, high-speed imaging followed SIS formation, and UVP provided mean velocity and turbulence intensity profiles in the 40-mm pipe. A shear-thickening window of 50–3000 s−1 was identified, and the drag-reduction onset in all three diameters fell within it, consistent with near-wall shear triggering SIS nucleation. Sparse structures can appear slightly before measurable DR, whereas abundant SIS occur only within the drag-reducing regime and their growth parallels DR. Velocity profiles in this regime lie above the Newtonian turbulent profile, with enhanced near-wall streamwise fluctuation intensity, in line with the bilayer picture. Three machine-learning models were trained on Reynolds number, pipe diameter, and surfactant concentration, operational inputs independent of the pressure measurement that defines DR. Support vector regression generalized best, and Shapley Additive Explanations analysis ranked features consistently with the shear-controlled interpretation. Overall, the rheology, friction, imaging, and velocimetry results agree with a shear-controlled picture in which SIS formation accompanies drag reduction, and the machine-learning model provides a practical, physically consistent predictor within the tested operating domain. This combined evidence establishes a strong correlation; a causal demonstration would require simultaneous microstructural and turbulence diagnostics, which lie beyond the scope of this study.

papers.title: Unified shock and interface capturing in an adaptive high-order discontinuous Galerkin method for compressible two-phase flows
papers.abstract: To improve the robustness and efficiency of high-order discontinuous Galerkin (DG) simulations for compressible two-phase flows, this study develops an adaptive shock capture DG strategy that combines a sub-cell limiter with adaptive mesh refinement (AMR). This work extends the shock capture sub-cell limiter strategy from conventional shock-dominated flows to two-phase interface simulations by treating the material interface as a shock-type numerical discontinuity. In this framework, both shock waves and material interfaces are handled within a unified sub-cell limiter-based and AMR-based DG formulation, so that discontinuous thermodynamic states, steep density gradients, and localized interfacial structures can be resolved in a stable and efficient manner. The proposed method is first assessed using the Sod shock tube, two-dimensional Riemann and Mach 3 wind tunnel problems. These benchmark tests demonstrate that the method accurately captures shock waves, contact discontinuities, slip lines, and shock reflections while suppressing nonphysical oscillations near strong gradients. The method is then applied to compressible two-phase interface simulations, where the sub-cell limiter is activated in interfacial regions to stabilize numerical flux evaluation across discontinuous material states and to preserve sharp interface structures without introducing additional degrees of freedom into the governing equations. Meanwhile, AMR automatically concentrates resolution around shocks and material interfaces, enabling detailed reconstruction of localized flow features with reduced computational cost. The numerical results show that the proposed unified shock/interface treatment can robustly resolve interacting shocks, material interfaces, and complex discontinuity-dominated structures, providing an efficient, high-fidelity tool for compressible two-phase flow simulations.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic and turbulent wake characteristics in response to sacrificial piles
papers.abstract: Sacrificial piles are a potential scour mitigation measure, but their application to offshore wind turbine foundations remains limited. Their effects on tidal currents, the vorticity balance, and turbulent wake recovery under reversing flow remain unclear. This study investigates the hydrodynamic mechanisms through which sacrificial piles modify monopile wake structures, with a focus on the underlying dynamical forcing, vorticity budget, and turbulence evolution. Results show that sacrificial piles fundamentally reshape the tidal-current structure by modifying the balance of driving forces, in which barotropic pressure gradient (xba) dominates, combined with horizontal nonlinear advection (xadh) at the surface and vertical nonlinear advection (xadv) at the bottom. Analysis of the vorticity budget reveals that sacrificial piles also amplify the dominant vorticity-budget terms, including the advection of relative vorticity (varv) and the barotropic curl (vbac) by approximately 2.5–3 times compared with the monopile-only case. In terms of turbulence characteristics, sacrificial piles increase subsurface wake intensity while exerting limited influence on wake width. The transverse configuration amplifies relative excess turbulence by a factor of 2–5, whereas the triangular configuration produces stronger near-field turbulence enhancement, with peak values reaching five to seven times. At recovery thresholds of Δ = 1 and 0.1, the triangular configuration has the longest downstream recovery distance; at Δ = 0.01, the transverse configuration has the longest. These findings advance the understanding of the hydrodynamic effects of sacrificial piles and establish a framework for future investigations that incorporate sediment transport, morphological evolution, and field-scale validation.

papers.title: Eliminating artificial surfactant-mass drift in nonlinear weighted-residual models of soluble-surfactant-laden falling films
papers.abstract: A soluble surfactant may adsorb at a free surface and desorb into the liquid bulk, but in a closed periodic falling film the total amount of surfactant must remain constant. We use this invariant as a test of nonlinear weighted-residual models for soluble-surfactant-laden films. The models of Pascal et al. [“Stability of inclined flow of a liquid film with soluble surfactants and variable mass density,” Phys. Rev. Fluids 4, 054004 (2019)] and D'Alessio et al. [“Marangoni instabilities associated with heated surfactant-laden falling films,” J. Fluid Mech. 887, A20 (2020)] correctly include the bulk-surface exchange mechanism, but their nonlinear surface closure contains a coefficient that prevents exact conservation of the reduced total surfactant mass. The problematic contribution is proportional to (5/4)ΓΓxhx: it leaves a residual ΓΓxhx that is not a conservative streamwise flux and therefore behaves as an artificial source during nonlinear evolution. We return to Stone's [“A simple derivation of the time-dependent convective-diffusion equation for surfactant transport along a deforming interface,” Phys. Fluids A 2, 111–112 (1990)] material-surface balance, add the Langmuir adsorption–desorption flux, and then take the thin-film long-wave limit used in the weighted-residual reduction. The normal-motion/curvature area-dilation term in Stone's [“A simple derivation of the time-dependent convective-diffusion equation for surfactant transport along a deforming interface,” Phys. Fluids A 2, 111–112 (1990)] equation is shown explicitly to enter two orders higher in the nondimensional surface balance than the retained Marangoni correction. With the same velocity and concentration ansatz used in the earlier weighted-residual framework, the conservative reduction gives the coefficient 1/4. The nonlinear surface term then becomes (1/4)∂x(hΓΓx), the corresponding bulk Marangoni term is also a periodic flux, and the adsorption–desorption terms cancel between the bulk and surface equations. Nonlinear simulations for a comparable parameter set based on the earlier published studies confirm that the corrected model conserves the total reduced surfactant mass to numerical accuracy and removes the secular growth in the surface concentration range, while leaving the linear stability problem unchanged.

papers.title: Mechanisms of local flow separation in negative-pressure-driven converging flows during multi-borehole gas extraction
papers.abstract: Borehole gas extraction is a key measure for preventing and controlling gas hazards in underground coal mines. During negative-pressure-driven multi-borehole extraction, abrupt changes in flow direction and local adverse pressure gradients can induce flow separation within the boreholes and manifold, thereby increasing flow resistance and reducing extraction efficiency. However, current research has not yet clearly elucidated the formation mechanism of flow-separation zones during the multi-borehole converging-flow process. Therefore, based on actual underground borehole-layout parameters, this study established a three-dimensional numerical model of multi-borehole gas-extraction convergence and used Fluent to simulate the gas-flow characteristics under extraction negative pressures ranging from 10 to 30 kPa. The results show that, during multi-borehole gas extraction, the gas-flow direction changes at the convergence locations, where low-velocity separation zones form under the combined effects of boundary-layer separation and adverse pressure gradients. These separation zones exhibit strong spatial correspondence with low-pressure regions. As the extraction negative pressure increases from 10 to 30 kPa, the maximum gas velocity rises from 1.4208 to 1.9070 m/s, indicating enhanced axial gas-transport capacity. However, higher extraction negative pressure also intensifies the velocity gradient, pressure gradient, and turbulent effects. With increasing negative pressure, the separation-zone area ratio first increases and then decreases, reaching a peak of 0.1985 at 20 kPa, while its overall variation remains limited. Thus, negative pressure primarily regulates the local flow intensity within the separation zones rather than significantly altering their structure. These findings provide a theoretical basis for optimizing negative-pressure regulation and improving the transport efficiency of gas extraction.

papers.title: Analysis of the shear layer instability process of a laminar separation bubble by means of spatial dynamic mode decomposition technique
papers.abstract: In the present study, spatial dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is applied to experimental data of flat plate laminar separation bubbles, accounting for variations in Reynolds number, free-stream turbulence intensity, and streamwise adverse pressure gradient representative of low-pressure gas turbine blade operating conditions. Measurements are performed using particle image velocimetry (PIV). For each flow case, PIV snapshots are divided into temporal subsets, within which DMD is performed on fixed-size blocks shifted in the streamwise direction to span the entire domain. This approach enables the decomposition of the flow into modes characterized by streamwise wavenumbers and growth/decay rates, providing insight into the spatial evolution of shear layer disturbances as the flow parameters vary. By identifying the mode with the highest growth rate within each block, a statistical representation of growth rate and wavenumber distributions along the streamwise direction is obtained. The analysis shows that increasing the Reynolds number shifts the peak growth rate location upstream, in agreement with the upstream displacement of the maximum bubble thickness, and increases the streamwise wavenumber, corresponding to smaller characteristic length scales. Notably, the streamwise wavenumber exhibits a sudden change below a critical Reynolds number, reflecting the transition from short to long separation bubbles. While the peak growth rate location (linked to the transition position) can guide the design and placement of flow-control strategies on the blades, the streamwise-averaged wavenumber can provide a simple yet effective supplementary metric to distinguish bubble states and identify the onset of bursting.

papers.title: Fluid property engineering for regulating confined cavitation erosion of 1060 aluminum alloy
papers.abstract: This work establishes a two-way Euler–Lagrangian multiphase framework to simulate transient bubble cloud evolution, acoustic streaming, and wall impact loads under variable liquid properties. Furthermore, we employ sonochemical and multiscale surface characterizations to experimentally verify the fluid-induced damage on the 1060 aluminum alloy. Novel fluid physical insights are revealed from vapor fraction oscillation characteristics and flow field momentum transport: High viscosity (1.05–1.60 mPa s) introduces strong viscous dissipation, flattening quasi-steady vapor fraction curves and suppressing synchronized bubble implosion, which weakens microjet kinetic energy and restricts maximum erosion depth to 10 μm with only 14.9% methylene blue degradation efficiency. Moderately lowered surface tension (72–45 mN/m) breaks the nucleation energy barrier, generating dual vapor fraction peaks synchronized with the acoustic rarefaction and compression cycles, alongside dense synchronized bubble clusters that amplify vertical jet momentum, boosting degradation efficiency to 74.9% and peak pit depth to 20.9 μm. Excess surfactant triggers supersaturated bubble accumulation and acoustic impedance mismatch, forming a near-wall vapor shielding layer that converts violent bubble collapse into low-amplitude high-frequency elastic pulsations, leading to degraded cavitation performance. By correlating multiphase flow dynamics with cross-scale material removal metrics, this study proposes four fluid-dominated cavitation–wall interaction modes and quantitatively elaborates the bidirectional competitive modulation law of viscosity–surface tension on confined cavitation flow fields. The physical mechanism framework provides fundamental fluid guidance for targeted regulation of ultrasonic cavitation intensity.

papers.title: Water balloons as macroscopic droplets: Effective surface tension and impact dynamics
papers.abstract: Water balloons provide a simple model system for studying the dynamics of membrane-confined liquids, yet their quantitative relationship to classical liquid droplets remains unclear. In this work, we experimentally investigate the mechanical properties and impact dynamics of water balloons and compare them with those of classical liquid droplets impacting superhydrophobic surfaces. Inflation–deflation experiments reveal a broad stretch-independent regime (1.5<λ<2.7) in which the membrane tension remains nearly constant at T≈122.7 N/m despite the nonlinear hyperelastic response of the latex membrane. Independent measurements of the equilibrium shape of water-filled balloons demonstrate that the pressure–curvature relation obeys a generalized Young–Laplace equation within this regime, validating the analogy between the membrane tension and the liquid surface tension. The membrane tension is then defined as the effective surface tension of the water balloon. Based on this result, an effective Weber number is introduced for water balloons. Impact experiments show that water balloons and droplets exhibit similar impact-induced wave, spreading, retraction, and rebound dynamics over a wide range of Weber numbers. Using the effective Weber number, the maximum spreading factor and normalized contact time of the two systems show similar trends over the entire Weber number range investigated and exhibit closely comparable capillary–inertial scaling behavior within their respective scaling regimes. The maximum spreading factors follow power-law dependences in the high Weber number regime with exponents of 0.26 for water droplets and 0.22 for water balloons, both close to the classical inertial–capillary scaling βmax∝We1/4, while the normalized contact times exhibit a common scaling in the low Weber number regime. These results demonstrate that water balloons can behave as macroscopic droplets governed by a surface-tension-like restoring force when the global membrane deformation remains within the stretch-independent regime, although local non-equibiaxial deformation may fall outside this regime. The present work establishes a quantitative connection between membrane-confined liquids and classical capillary systems, providing a unified description of impact dynamics governed by either the membrane tension or the molecular surface tension.

papers.title: Uncertainty optimization of shaft texture for lip seal under working condition fluctuation
papers.abstract: Texturing the rotating shaft is an available approach for improving the performance of a lip seal. However, the sealing mechanism is always solved based on time-consuming numerical solution methods, such as finite differences, finite element methods, and so on. To address this problem, an uncertainty optimization framework for rotary lip seals under working conditions fluctuating is proposed based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN). Based on PINN, a surrogate model is developed for the sealing mechanism model to improve computational efficiency, which integrates the governing equations and experimental data. Then the surrogate model is used to predict friction torque, pumping rate, and wear rate when optimizing the shaft texture. Working condition variation is modeled as stochastic variables, whereas texture processing errors are represented as bounded interval variables. Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis and Pareto screening are combined with Analytic Hierarchy Process-based decision making to select texture designs, while Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to an Ideal Solution and weight-sensitivity analysis are used to examine the dependence of the ranking on the decision criterion and objective weights. The effectiveness of the surrogate model is validated by experimental data and numerical simulation. The results show that it is much faster than the finite difference-based method with similar prediction accuracy. The simulation duration has been reduced from minutes to seconds. As a result, we can optimize the shaft texture considering both processing errors and working condition fluctuation. The optimal texture given by our method is better than the other one neglecting the working condition fluctuation, focusing on the friction torque, pumping rate, and wear rate.

papers.title: Stern–Gerlach-type beam splitting of spherical Beltrami vortices in a background vorticity gradient
papers.abstract: We investigate localized spherical Beltrami vortices advected by an inviscid, incompressible background flow with an approximately uniform vorticity gradient. These compact, helicity-carrying vortex wavicles possess an orientation axis. For a vortex core small relative to the background length scale and vorticity strong relative to the background vorticity, an adiabatic description separates rapid precession, slower orientation selection, and orientation-dependent centroid drift. The unit vector s=(sx,sy,sz) represents orientation, with sx, sy, and sz its Cartesian components, and ẑ is the unit vector along the imposed vorticity-gradient direction. For the slab background, the locally frozen orientation equation is exactly solvable. The Stern–Gerlach regime has inverse-time alignment rate γ≡ω0k0/k<0, where ω0 is the reference background vorticity, k0 its inverse variation length, and k>0 the Beltrami wavenumber. Every initial orientation with sz(0)≠0 approaches s=sgn[sz(0)]ẑ; sz(0) is the initial component along ẑ and sgn is the sign function. The two attractors +ẑ and −ẑ define the hydrodynamic “spin-up” and “spin-down” states, while sz(0)=0 is their basin separatrix. The exact solution also supplies a finite-transit condition for a narrowly bimodal output. Although instantaneous drift varies continuously with s, orientation selection makes its asymptotic ẑ component approach one of two opposite values. Thus, an initially collimated beam can separate into two robust branches through a classical, purely hydrodynamic mechanism. A rotated vorticity-gradient region may renew the same selection-and-drift process.

papers.title: An adaptive direct-forcing immersed boundary method with subcycled time advancement for compressible flows over irregular solid boundaries
papers.abstract: An adaptive direct-forcing immersed boundary method (IBM) is developed for numerical simulation of compressible flows involving irregular solid boundaries. The method is constructed on block-structured adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) and achieves computational efficiency through the coupling of subcycled time advancement with the direct-forcing IBM workflow. In the proposed framework, the solid surface is represented by Lagrangian points on the finest AMR level, where immersed-boundary momentum and energy source terms are evaluated to approximately enforce the prescribed boundary conditions. For AMR time advancement, a subcycling strategy is introduced in which different levels of grids advance with different time steps. The effect of the immersed boundary is transferred to coarser levels through fine-to-coarse averaging operations at synchronization times. This treatment improves computational efficiency while preserving the coarse-fine consistency of the immersed boundary forcing. The method is applicable to representative compressible flows such as shock reflection and diffraction, subsonic and supersonic body flows, aerodynamic force evolution, and viscous boundary-layer effects. Numerical tests are conducted to validate the proposed method, and the results are in good agreement with reference data such as shock diffraction, surface pressure distributions, and aerodynamic force coefficients. Computational cost comparisons demonstrate the efficiency improvement obtained from AMR and the subcycling strategy. Finally, a downburst wind-field simulation over a conical hill is presented to illustrate the capability of the proposed approach for practical complex-flow applications.

papers.title: Aerodynamic pressure prediction and non-Gaussian characteristics of airborne floating objects under turbulent flows: A hybrid modeling strategy integrating proper orthogonal decomposition and deep learning
papers.abstract: Airborne floating objects (AFOs) pose a serious threat to the safe operation of civil aviation and low-altitude aircraft. Accurately determining the flight trajectories of AFOs is an urgent task, with the core component being the precise prediction of wind pressure. This study focuses on AFOs in the form of ellipsoidal balloons and proposes a hybrid model framework for predicting the surface wind pressure on these AFOs. The proposed approach combines proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), a convolutional neural network (CNN), and a long short-term memory (LSTM) module. First, the wind pressure characteristics of the balloons are investigated through wind tunnel tests under two different turbulence intensities. The wind pressure on the balloon surface exhibits non-Gaussian characteristics under both types of turbulence, being distributed along the leading edge in the windward region and toward the leeward zone. Typical measurement points are then selected for model training and wind pressure prediction. A comparison between the experimental and predicted results demonstrates that the POD–CNN–LSTM model proposed in this paper effectively captures the spatiotemporal characteristic structures underlying complex turbulent wind pressure fluctuations. Our research findings provide a reliable, data-driven method for predicting wind pressure on AFOs.

papers.title: Effects of tip water injection on near-stall flow structure and performance of a transonic compressor
papers.abstract: Near-stall operation of transonic compressors is critical for achieving high pressure ratio and efficiency, but it is accompanied by sensitive tip-region flow structures that strongly affect compressor performance. Discrete water injection near the blade tip is investigated as an active flow-control method to modify the near-tip flow field at a representative near-stall operating condition of a transonic axial compressor. Three-dimensional unsteady Euler–Lagrange multiphase simulations are performed for NASA Rotor 37. The carrier phase is solved using the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, while water droplets are tracked in a Lagrangian framework with two-way coupling of momentum, heat, and mass transfer. Representative spray conditions are used to examine the coupled compressor–spray response. The results show that tip water injection increases the compressor mass flow rate and adiabatic efficiency by approximately 3% and 5%, respectively, with only a minor change in total pressure ratio. Comparisons between evaporating and non-evaporating cases distinguish two concurrent mechanisms: axial momentum addition from the injected droplets and evaporative cooling of the near-tip flow. Together, these mechanisms induce a coupled reorganization of the near-tip flow through droplet momentum exchange and tip-region loading redistribution, which weakens leakage-jet penetration, moderates vortex roll-up and tip separation, and suppresses the near-tip recirculation zone, thereby reducing blockage and aerodynamic loss. Droplet-size analysis shows that breakup and evaporation govern downstream spray evolution and droplet–flow interaction. These findings clarify how discrete tip water injection modifies near-tip flow behavior and promotes a more robust compressor response at the investigated near-stall condition.

papers.title: Flow-induced alignment of rigid fiber suspensions in cylindrical channels with high confinement ratios
papers.abstract: A computational study utilizing fiber-resolved simulations is presented that examines the flow dynamics of rigid fiber suspensions within straight cylindrical channels. The fiber aspect ratio as well as the overall fiber volume fraction are systematically varied across the dilute, semi-dilute, and concentrated regimes. The confinement ratio (the ratio of the fiber length to the channel diameter) varies between 0.07 for the shortest fibers and 0.86 for the longest fibers. The results particularly focus on characterizing how the fiber orientation and local fiber volume fraction vary radially from the channel centerline to the outer wall. A high degree of heterogeneity is found to occur for both of these parameters, which deviate from the often-used continuum orientation models, e.g., the Folgar–Tucker model, due to the high confinement ratios considered herein. This study provides new insights into the degree and uniformity of hydrodynamic fiber alignment often utilized for additive manufacturing and other applications.

papers.title: Mixing enhancement characteristics and mechanism of supersonic Coandă jet
papers.abstract: The supersonic Coandă jet is a pivotal active flow control technique whose performance is closely tied to the evolution of shear layer mixing. Spanwise-distributed protrusions on the nozzle lip have been proven to significantly modulate mixing behavior, yet the influence mechanism of protrusion parameters (i.e., spacing and geometry) remains poorly understood. To address this research gap, the present study numerically investigates the effects of protrusion spacing (quantified as forcing wavelength λ) and geometry on the jet mixing characteristics, adopting the delayed detached-eddy simulation based on the two-equation shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model. The results reveal that protrusions induce initial streamwise vortices immediately downstream of the nozzle exit, which entrain ambient fluid and radially transport high-momentum core fluid, thus dominating the entire shear layer mixing process. The efficacy of this vortex-induced mixing enhancement depends strongly on vortex scale: larger vortices have longer persistence and a wider influence range, thus enabling more effective mixing. The vortex scale is directly determined by the imposed forcing wavelength. The effective wavelength initially coincides with the forcing wavelength, but evolves into three distinct development modes downstream: the self-sustaining mode occurs at longer forcing wavelengths (λ = 2h and 4h), while splitting or merging modes are observed at shorter forcing wavelengths (λ = 1h and 0.5h). Although vortex splitting and merging modify the effective wavelength, the eventual wavelength remains smaller than that of the unforced baseline case. Meanwhile, an excessively large forcing wavelength (λ = 4h) can induce unintended main flow deviation from the wall, which degrades overall mixing performance. Consequently, an optimal forcing wavelength exists (i.e., λ = 2h in the present study) that yields the maximum mixing efficiency. Furthermore, despite differences in vortex evolution at short forcing wavelengths, mixing characteristics are nearly identical for different protrusion geometries when the effective wavelength is the same. The only exception is triangular protrusions, which deliver inferior mixing performance due to the weaker initial flow perturbations they induce.

papers.title: Cavitation surge driven by backflow-vortex cavitation in an inducer under low-flow conditions
papers.abstract: Cavitation surge under low-flow conditions is a major form of flow instability in inducer-equipped high-speed pumps, yet its spatiotemporal coupling with inlet backflow-vortex cavitation remains insufficiently resolved. In this work, synchronized high-speed visualization and pressure-pulsation measurements were employed to investigate the flow physics of cavitation surge in an inducer operated under low-flow conditions. The results show that cavitation surge is accompanied by the periodic growth, elongation, and collapse of large-scale backflow-vortex cavitation clouds in the inlet duct upstream of the inducer. This cyclic cavity evolution is closely correlated with a pronounced low-frequency pressure oscillation, indicating that the surge is more strongly associated with the unsteady dynamics of the backflow-vortex cavitation structure than with blade-passing-frequency fluctuations. As the available suction head decreases within the surge regime, backflow-vortex cavitation generally intensifies, the pressure-pulsation level increases, and the flow stability deteriorates. Cavitation surge is observed only in the low-flow regime and is closely associated with the formation of a fully developed, coherent backflow-vortex cavitation cloud at the inducer inlet. These results provide experimental evidence supporting a close physical link between periodic cavitation-cloud dynamics and cavitation surge and suggest that backflow-vortex cavitation is closely associated with low-frequency instability in inducer flows.

papers.title: Retraction dynamics of droplets impacting on a vibrating superhydrophobic surface under low pressure
papers.abstract: The retraction dynamics of droplets impacting on solid surfaces show great potential for applications such as anti-icing and self-cleaning. However, most existing studies are based on stationary surfaces under atmospheric pressure, while practical applications involving general aviation aircraft and other equipment operating at medium and high altitudes often involve direct interactions of droplets with moderately low-pressure environments and vibrating surfaces. In this study, using high-speed imaging under natural moderately low-pressure conditions on a highland, we investigated the retraction dynamics of low-Weber-number (We < 30) droplets impacting on a vibrating superhydrophobic surface under low-pressure. The results show that as the ambient pressure decreases, gas-phase damping weakens, leading to significant increases in the maximum spreading radius, maximum retraction velocity, and maximum rebound height of the droplets, and the retraction process exhibits stronger inertial characteristics. Under vibration, the maximum retraction velocity exhibits a clear cosine-type variation with phase, and this phase-modulation effect becomes stronger with increasing vibration frequency and amplitude. In contrast, the occurrence time of the maximum retraction velocity remains concentrated within a stable time interval, indicating that the retraction timescale is primarily governed by the inertial–capillary balance. Based on an energy conservation framework, a scaling model for the maximum retraction velocity was developed by accounting for both pressure-dependent gas-phase dissipation and vibration-induced effective impact velocity variation. The experimental data collapse onto the proposed dimensionless energy-release scale, and the model predictions show generally good agreement with the measured maximum retraction velocities. This study provides new physical insights into droplet impact dynamics in complex environments and offers a theoretical basis for controlling droplet behavior under low-pressure and dynamic conditions.

papers.title: Time-evolving Brinkman flow around a porous spherical particle
papers.abstract: The unsteady motion of a porous spherical particle embedded in an unbounded porous medium is theoretically investigated under creeping-flow conditions. Both the particle interior and the surrounding medium are modeled as permeable continua, and the fluid motion in each region is governed by the unsteady Brinkman equation. The system is driven by the sudden application of a uniform external body force, generating time-dependent flow fields both inside and outside the porous particle. By employing the Laplace transform technique, analytical expressions for the velocity fields are derived, leading to a closed-form solution for the particle translational velocity in the Laplace-transform domain. The corresponding time-dependent velocity is then obtained numerically using the Stehfest inversion algorithm. The analysis demonstrates that the combined effects of the particle and surrounding-medium permeabilities strongly influence the hydrodynamic response and particle mobility. The particle velocity evolves monotonically from rest toward a steady-state value, while the rate of approach to equilibrium depends sensitively on the permeability ratio, porosity, and density contrast between the particle and the host medium. Increased particle permeability generally enhances particle mobility; however, the hydrodynamic resistance imposed by the surrounding porous matrix may either promote or hinder the motion depending on the relative permeability scales. The present study provides a theoretical framework for understanding particle transport in porous environments, with potential applications in filtration systems, subsurface transport, and biomedical processes involving motion through porous tissues and gels.

papers.title: Numerical study on enhancing propagation stability of semi-confined detonation waves by increasing inert gas temperature
papers.abstract: To sustain the propagation of rotating detonation waves, a method for suppressing triple-point escape in gas interfaces is proposed in this paper. The attached oblique shock (AOS) or detached oblique shock (DOS) configuration of shock–detonation complexes at gas interfaces is governed by the acoustic impedance ratio. The low impedance ratio between the high-temperature combustion products and the low-temperature injected explosive mixtures yields the DOS configuration, which enables the stable propagation of detonation waves. To determine the critical inert-gas temperature T* for the transition between AOS and DOS configurations, the flow field of detonation transmission is theoretically resolved. Polar analysis identifies the dimensionless threshold temperature T* = 1.51 for hydrogen–oxygen–nitrogen mixtures. The reactive Euler equations with a two-step Arrhenius chemistry model are adopted. Numerical results verify the temperature threshold and reveal the complex structure of the DOS configuration. Numerical simulations of multi-head detonation transmission are conducted to investigate the confinement effect of inert gas layers. Under the conditions of T* = 1.44, 2.25, and 4.44, the triple-point reflection ratios of detonation waves at the gas interfaces are 0%, 20.0%, and 66.76%, respectively. It was found that the DOS configuration continuously expands in scale. As the length of its branched transmitted wave (BTW) grows to approximately the induction length of detonation, two transverse waves and a high-pressure induction zone (HPIZ) form. The collision between the triple point and the two transverse waves compresses the HPIZ, triggers an explosion, induces the triple-point reflection, and constitutes the formation mechanism of detonation cellular patterns. A higher T* shortens the time required to form a BTW with a size comparable to the detonation transverse wave, thereby enhancing triple-point reflection. The findings of this study can provide a reference for the working condition design of rotating detonation waves.

papers.title: Bridging physics and data: A review of machine learning approaches for turbulence closure modeling
papers.abstract: Turbulence closure modeling remains one of the central challenges in computational fluid dynamics. Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising paradigm to augment and, in some cases, replace classical turbulence models by leveraging high-fidelity simulation data and advanced neural network architectures. We argue that a single obstacle recurs across the field—a mismatch between the pointwise, offline objective on which data-driven closures are trained and the solver-coupled, multi-scale, statistically stationary way they must perform—and we trace it to intrinsic physical properties of turbulence (extreme multi-scale chaos, non-locality, and the absence of scale separation). Through this lens, we survey three established pillars: (i) ML-enhanced Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) closures, (ii) ML-based subgrid-scale models for large-eddy simulation, and (iii) physics-informed approaches, notably physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Their characteristic failure modes—RANS ill-conditioning, the a priori/a posteriori gap, and PINN spectral bias—are local signatures of this common root. Emerging paradigms—neural operators, graph neural networks, transformers, diffusion models, and foundation models—are assessed by whether they change the objective or merely the architecture, and we propose concrete protocols for testing whether learned fields respect the Navier–Stokes dynamics statistically rather than pointwise. We critically examine generalizability across flow configurations, interpretability, numerical stability under solver coupling, and the scarcity of high-fidelity data, and conclude that aligning data-driven methods with physical constraints—and the training objective with deployment—is the path toward reliable, generalizable, and computationally efficient turbulence models for engineering applications.

papers.title: Transient characteristics of gas-assisted atomization under different injection strategies
papers.abstract: Gas-assisted liquid atomization facilitates fine droplet generation at reduced injection pressures. In this study, the transient microscopic characteristics of gas-assisted sprays under two injection strategies were investigated. A phase Doppler particle analyzer was employed to measure droplet diameters and velocities, while a time-binning method was used to characterize their transient behavior. Results indicate that, compared to the conventional fuel pilot injection (FPI) strategy, the gas leading injection (GLI) strategy, featuring a pre-established high-speed leading gas flow, results in up to 54% and 84% increases in droplet and gas-phase velocities, respectively. Unlike the continuous droplet deceleration observed in the FPI spray, the leading gas flow in the GLI spray induces early droplet acceleration before subsequent deceleration. Notably, as the gas pre-flow duration increased from 0 to 4 ms, the axial position at which the droplet slip velocity reached equilibrium shifted from 38 to 140 mm. Transient analysis reveals that the FPI strategy tends to discharge massive fuel early, resulting in larger initial Sauter mean diameters (SMDs). In contrast, the pre-established flow in the GLI strategy provides highly stable aerodynamic shear, maintaining the droplet SMD within a narrow fluctuation range. Spatial and temporal uniformity evaluations confirm the significant advantages of the GLI strategy. The shape parameter of the Rosin–Rammler distribution for the GLI spray stabilizes at around 3, compared with a value below 2.3 for the FPI spray, indicating a narrower size distribution for the GLI spray. Shannon entropy was employed to evaluate time-resolved spray uniformity, revealing that the FPI spray uniformity progressively deteriorates with increasing axial distance.

papers.title: Thermophysical-property-dependent fragmentation of liquid films during centrifugal granulation of metallurgical melts
papers.abstract: The recovery of high-temperature waste heat from metallurgical by-products motivates the development of dry centrifugal granulation. However, the relation between melt thermophysical properties and transient interfacial instability remains incompletely resolved. Here, a three-dimensional transient multiphase framework is used to compare the centrifugal granulation of molten magnesium chloride and copper slag. Under the investigated conditions, the lower-viscosity, lower-density, and lower-surface-tension magnesium chloride predominantly exhibits film-rupture fragmentation driven by perforation growth, whereas copper slag exhibits edge fingering followed by ligament-mediated breakup. Increasing the rotational speed from 600 to 1000 r/min decreases the Sauter mean diameter from 1.69 to 0.87 mm for magnesium chloride and from 1.74 to 1.16 mm for copper slag. The present simulations of real metallurgical melts with a 92-fold viscosity contrast reveal a counterintuitive regime in which low-viscosity melts demand higher critical mass flow rates for continuous film formation and validate Weber-number scaling laws (L/d ∼ We0.5, error ≤ 5.1%) governing ligament breakup.

papers.title: Baroclinic wave dynamics in the Ekman-free rotating rectangular annulus with localized forced plume
papers.abstract: We report numerical simulations of a rotating rectangular annulus that isolates the Ekman-free bulk of the cylindrical baroclinic annulus, subjected to bi-directional temperature gradients imposed by a uniformly cooled inner wall and a localized forced heated plume at the outer bottom. The finite-volume OpenFOAM solver is employed across combinations of source Richardson number Ri0=99,4,1 and Rossby number Ro=0.3,0.1,0.07. A non-dimensional scaling of the governing equations identifies geostrophic-hydrostatic balance as the leading-order bulk state, a result confirmed a posteriori by the x- and z− momentum budgets. Baroclinic waves of mode m=2 at Ro=0.3 transition to m=3 as Ro decreases, consistent with the contraction of the Eady deformation radius Lρ=NH/f; complex empirical orthogonal function analysis characterizes the wave regime and detects a Hopf-bifurcated vacillating state (quasi-periodic amplitude modulation) at Ri0=99, Ro=0.1. The plume morphology, classified through the Morton length scale and source flux-balance parameter, transitions from weak, laterally swept structures at Ri0=99 to sustained columnar plumes traversing the full baroclinic depth at Ri0≤4. The plume entrainment coefficient Γ(z) shows opposite rotational sensitivities at low and high Ri0, which we organize through a local plume Rossby number Rop=w/(2Ωb). A mixing-length argument predicts a bulk turbulent heat flux 〈u′T′〉∝Ri0−1/2, anticipating an order-of-magnitude enhancement from Ri0=99 to Ri0=1, in agreement with the simulations. A regime map in the (Ri0,Ro) plane reveals that, within the explored range, the plume-regime and wave-selection problems are approximately separable: Ri0 sets the plume regime while Ro selects the dominant baroclinic wave mode.

papers.title: Modeling disperse phase stresses in Eulerian simulations for bubbly and particulate flows based on kinetic theory
papers.abstract: The present work applies the kinetic theory approach initiated by Reeks (1991; 1992) to model disperse phase stresses in multiphase flows. This approach offers an alternative to the standard derivation of the Eulerian continuum equations that has not yet found wide application in multiphase flow simulations. A comprehensive exposition of the theory in its simplest form is given eliminating errors and inaccuracies found in the literature, and then extended to a two-way coupled model taking into account the back-action of the disperse phase on the continuous one. An additional insight provided beyond standard Euler–Euler modeling is that the disperse phase pressure and stress derive from those of the liquid rather than being imposed by additional constitutive relations. Moreover, the availability of a simplified solution of the disperse phase kinetic stress equation allows to include the velocity fluctuations of the disperse phase, which have been neglected in many works based on standard Euler–Euler modeling. The resulting disperse phase stress model is implemented in the Open Field Operation and Manipulation (OpenFOAM) Foundation software and validated by comparison to a database of experimental results collected from the literature comprising a variety of configurations.

papers.title: Role of water activity on the nucleation and growth of ice crystals in aqueous liquid of NaCl, glucose, and konjac glucomannan
papers.abstract: The microscopic mechanisms by which solutes influence ice crystal nucleation and growth in aqueous systems are fundamental to controlling freezing in various food and biological contexts. While the understanding of the initiation mechanism of pure water freezing is becoming increasingly clear, the mechanisms of ice nucleation and growth in hydrophilic colloids, such as polysaccharide dispersions, still rely on theoretical speculation and empirical assumptions. In this study, we experimentally demonstrated that polysaccharides regulated water freezing by affecting the water activity in the liquid phase. Konjac glucomannan (KGM) complicated the formation of critical ice nuclei, lowered the nucleation temperature, and shortened the ice crystal growth time by reducing water activity (aw) and altering the state of water within the system. The ice crystal growth for solution systems depended not only on freezing conditions but also on aw. Furthermore, by combining polarized light imaging with MATLAB data analysis, we conducted a comparative analysis of the differences in optical property changes during ice crystal growth between KGM dispersion and other solutions.

papers.title: Turbulent wake instability and bifurcation in high-fineness-ratio axisymmetric bodies: A Reynolds-stress dynamical-systems framework
papers.abstract: This paper investigates anisotropy-driven instability and bifurcation of the turbulent wake behind a high-fineness-ratio axisymmetric body, employing a Reynolds-stress dynamical-systems framework; a torpedo-shaped geometry provides the motivating physical configuration. The turbulent normal stresses R11 and R22, which govern streamwise and transverse wake anisotropy, are modeled through reduced-order Reynolds-stress transport equations retaining production, pressure–strain redistribution, and dissipation, while neglecting spatial diffusion as a first-order simplification. For the U.S. Navy Mk 1 geometry (length 7.7 m and diameter 533 mm), linearization of the three-dimensional ordinary differential equation system about its fixed point yields a Jacobian eigenvalue structure λ = [−0.0162, +0.0146, −0.0254], identifying the equilibrium as a saddle point. A model-derived critical bifurcation speed of approximately 5.23 m/s is identified, below which all eigenvalues are negative, and the wake attractor is asymptotically stable; above this threshold, one eigenvalue becomes positive, and the wake transitions to a saddle-type unstable equilibrium. The spectral abscissa ρ = 0.0146 indicates local instability, while the negative trace tr(J) = −0.027 indicates an overall dissipative tendency. Longitudinal hydrodynamic coefficients computed from the force-balance framework are compared against published towing-tank data for torpedo-class geometries; deviations remain within 8%, providing an indicative first-order check on the force model. This comparison does not constitute geometry-specific validation of the bifurcation point, for which dedicated high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulations or towing-tank experiments on the exact configuration are needed. The framework proposes an anisotropy-driven mechanism associated with wake instability in high-fineness-ratio streamlined bodies and motivates targeted follow-on campaigns.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of cavity fuel–air injection on flame dynamics and stability in a trapped-vortex combustor
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of injecting premixed fuel–air mixtures into the cavity of a trapped-vortex combustor on its thermoacoustic behavior and lean blowout characteristics. Two cavity injection conditions were examined: a lean mixture with an equivalence ratio of ϕc=0.8 and a rich mixture with ϕc=1.12. The analysis focuses on the influence of cavity injection on flame stabilization, combustion dynamics, and the extension of lean operating limits under different global equivalence ratios. Experiments were conducted over a wide range of cavity size ratios (L/D=0.75–2.4) while varying the equivalence ratio from stable operation to lean blowout. High-speed OH* chemiluminescence imaging was employed to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the flame and to examine the formation and stability of the cavity-anchored flame (trapped vortex) within the cavity. Statistical analysis based on the cavity-to-shear-layer intensity ratio and the normalized vertical flame centroid are employed to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the cavity-stabilized reaction zone, demonstrating how changes in the cavity equivalence ratio from lean to rich conditions shift the lean blowout limit.
