Understanding this coupling is relevant to the design of structured surfaces for controlled drop retention, spreading, and evaporation. Although edge pinning is well established, it remains unclear how the resulting macroscopic distortion propagates from the contact line into the bulk of a sessile drop. Water drops were deposited on circular, triangular, and square aluminum pillars and characterized using 360° rotational imaging. The azimuthal variation of the apparent contact angle was measured, three-dimensional drop geometry was reconstructed, and the height-dependent polygonal distortion was quantified using circularity and support-function Fourier modes. Polygonal pillars produced two repeatable wetting states: a maximum edge-effect state near the midpoints of the polygon sides and a lower-angle restrained-lamella state oriented toward the vertices. The angular contrast depended on pillar geometry and was largest for triangular pillars because their longer sides and larger side-to-vertex radial variation imposed the strongest azimuthal constraint. The reconstructed cross sections were non-circular near the solid surface and became more axisymmetric with height. The leading symmetry-compatible modes were (n = 3) for triangular pillars and (n = 4) for square pillars, while the first higher harmonics decayed more rapidly and remained concentrated closer to the surface. These trends were consistent with exponential relaxation predicted by a Young–Laplace-based perturbation framework. The circularity profiles indicated near-field curvature adjustment and global interface reshaping. The results provide three-dimensional quantification of how polygon-imposed contact-line distortions propagate into and relax through a sessile drop.

papers.title: Theoretical and numerical investigation on capillary wicking dynamics of liquid hydrogen on micro-structured surfaces
papers.abstract: Efficient management of cryogenic propellants in microgravity is critical for long-term on-orbit coasting and deep-space exploration. Surface tension-driven liquid acquisition devices (LADs) are promising solutions for ensuring gas-free delivery of cryogens. However, the pore-scale wicking dynamics on micro-structured surfaces, which dictate the performance of LADs, remain insufficiently understood. In this study, the capillary wicking of liquid hydrogen (LH2) on regular micropillar arrays is investigated using a three-dimensional central-moment pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann model coupled with a modified Benedict–Webb–Rubin (MBWR) equation of state (EOS). The central-moment formulation enables stable computation at the extremely low lattice kinematic viscosity of LH2 (νl = 0.005 035), while the MBWR EOS provides the accurate coexistence densities required to quantify the non-negligible inertial response arising from the extremely low viscosity of LH2. An inertia-inclusive pore-scale model is established by retaining capillary driving, cumulative viscous resistance, and the unsteady momentum of the moving liquid. Dimensionless-number analysis shows that the overall process remains capillary driven, whereas inertia becomes comparable to capillarity during rapid advancement between successive micropillar rows. Two dimensionless transport indices are introduced to distinguish the long-time wicking capability and the microscale local acceleration capability. Over the finite propagation interval considered in the present work, the front motion deviates from the classical Washburn scaling, L ∼ t1/2, because the inertial contribution remains dynamically relevant. A power-law empirical relation, L* = a(t*)b, is used to characterize the influence of inertia on the finite-range wicking behavior, where a represents the overall transport-rate magnitude and b reflects the departure from the viscous-dominated Washburn limit. These findings provide a quantitative pore-scale framework for the geometric design of liquid-hydrogen acquisition structures.

papers.title: Mechanism-resolved interface momentum transfer in immersed-boundary lattice Boltzmann simulations
papers.abstract: Immersed-boundary lattice Boltzmann method (IB-LBM) simulations of cylinder and particle flows are usually compared by ranking boundary-enforcement schemes, kernels, and collision models. Such comparisons can obscure the mechanism that controls each response. Here, canonical fixed-cylinder, oscillating-cylinder, and sedimenting-particle cases are used as controlled probes of Eulerian–Lagrangian interface momentum transfer. For prescribed bodies, differences among direct forcing, multi-direct forcing, and distribution-function correction (DFC) are most clearly discriminated by local no-slip fidelity rather than by a universal drag ranking. For DFC, the kernel-dependent drag-coefficient ranking reversal between the hat and Peskin 4-point kernels is associated with the spatial redistribution of the marker-resolved correction and the resulting near-boundary slip and pressure deviation, rather than the total correction magnitude alone. For sedimenting particles, single-particle settling provides a moving-body baseline, whereas two-particle differential-density wake-interaction sedimentation shows the wake-exposed light particle to be comparatively more sensitive to the explicit internal-mass correction in the force evaluation, a configuration-dependent, finite-window moving-boundary closure response. Targeted two-relaxation-time and central-moment multiple-relaxation-time collision controls remain secondary to the boundary and closure mechanisms within the tested regimes (prescribed-body comparisons at Re≤200, two-dimensional, and the reported moving-particle cases). The resulting picture replaces a universal scheme ranking with a mechanism-resolved interpretation of IB-LBM interface momentum transfer.

papers.title: Microstructural and vorticity analysis of micropolar nanofluid in pentagonal cavity for industrial thermal and mixing applications
papers.abstract: The industrial and technological processes of electronic cooling and micro-heat exchangers and polymer processing and solar thermal devices depend on efficient systems that manage heat and fluid mixing. This study numerically investigates natural convection of carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)–Al2O3 micropolar nanofluid in a pentagonal cavity using a vertex-centered control volume finite element method. The effects of the Rayleigh number (103≤Ra≤106), the Hartmann number (0≤Ha≤40), the micropolar coupling number (0≤Λ≤4), and nanoparticle volume fraction (0≤φ≤0.05) on flow behavior, heat transfer, entropy generation, and nonlinear dynamics are systematically examined. Performance is evaluated through the average Nusselt number, wall shear stress, couple stress, fluid temperature, entropy generation, and Bejan number. The results indicate that increasing the Rayleigh number strengthens buoyancy-driven convection, producing a transition from steady symmetric flow to asymmetric, periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic regimes, while enhancing the average Nusselt number by 172%. Conversely, the induced magnetic field suppresses convection, reducing the average Nusselt number and kinetic energy by 29.6% and 88.7%, respectively. A higher micropolar coupling number weakens microrotation and heat transfer, resulting in a 28.6% reduction in the average Nusselt number and lower entropy generation. Response surface methodology and artificial neural network models accurately predicted heat transfer performance (R2 = 0.9786), providing an efficient optimization framework. These findings provide quantitative insights for optimizing micropolar nanofluid-based thermal systems and offer practical guidance for the design of advanced heat transfer devices.

papers.title: Disturbance propagation and shock-front evolution in underwater shock diffraction around convex corners
papers.abstract: Underwater shock diffraction around structural corners can substantially alter shock-front geometry and redistribute pressure and impulse along nearby boundaries. Although geometrical shock dynamics (GSD) has been widely applied to air-shock diffraction, its applicability to relatively weak underwater shocks remains insufficiently established. In this study, underwater shock diffraction around a convex corner is investigated using high-resolution weighted essentially non-oscillatory simulations combined with GSD-based analysis. Three formulations are examined: the classical GSD model, the GSD model with transverse flow effects (GSDT), and the GSD model with distributed disturbance effects (GSDD). The simulations show a relatively simple flow topology, with diffraction-induced secondary structures absent or negligibly weak, such that the evolution is dominated by the curved shock front. The recalibrated GSDT model empirical coefficient kemp for underwater conditions shows a strong dependence on the post-shock flow Mach number, approaching approximately 0.76 for uI/cI ≥ 0.2. Comparison with the simulated shock-front evolution indicates that disturbance propagation characteristics vary spatially: distributed disturbance effects dominate near the triple-point (TP), the relative characteristic disturbance speed varies continuously through an intermediate transition region, and transverse flow effects dominate toward the downstream wall. Accordingly, GSDD model reliably predicts the TP motion, whereas the GSDT model satisfactorily captures the wall shock state. At sufficiently low incident pressures, the classical GSD and GSDD models predict a limiting wall angle below which the shock-front solution cannot reach the wall, whereas no such limit is obtained from the recalibrated GSDT model. The results further manifest that no single disturbance propagation mechanism can fully account for the spatial evolution of the entire curved shock front. In addition, the normalized impulse transmission coefficient is nearly independent of incident shock strength and decreases from approximately 1.0 to about 0.38 as the wall angle θw decreases from 0° to −90°.

papers.title: Liquid film evacuation and heat transfer characteristics in the rotating cavity with swept-wall geometry
papers.abstract: Efficient oil evacuation from aero-engine rotating cavities is essential for maintaining stable lubricant circulation. However, the physical coupling between liquid film transport and wall heat transfer under swept-wall guidance remains insufficiently clarified. This study investigates two-phase transport and thermal responses within the rotating cavity, identifying key influencing parameters and their interactions. The results demonstrate that the swept wall induces a trade-off between liquid film evacuation and wall heat transfer by reorganizing oil-film transport. Compared to a circular rotating cavity, the swept-wall cavity directs the oil film toward the sump and suppresses its redispersion into the main rotating flow, thereby increasing the scavenge ratio by 6.52%. However, this process also reduces oil-film coverage and near-wall shear, resulting in a 9.91% decrease in the wall Nusselt number. Further parametric analysis shows that increasing the rotational Reynolds number and air inflow Reynolds number reduces the scavenge ratio but increases the wall Nusselt number, whereas increasing the oil supply Reynolds number increases liquid input and improves both responses. Wall heat transfer also increases with the Prandtl number. Sensitivity analysis indicates that rotational speed is the dominant factor governing the scavenge ratio, while oil supply temperature primarily controls the wall Nusselt number. These findings deepen the understanding of geometry-induced coupling between flow and heat transfer in rotating two-phase flow systems.

papers.title: Characterization of wake behind a cylinder using spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and integral bispectrum
papers.abstract: Characterizing nonlinear interactions in unsteady flow fields is often challenging, particularly when multiple competing frequencies are present. In the present work, a combined methodology based on spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) and integral bispectral analysis is employed to investigate nonlinear flow field dynamics in the wake of a circular cylinder subjected to periodic forcing. Two types of perturbations are considered: asymmetric forcing produced by rotational oscillation of the cylinder and symmetric forcing produced by inline oscillation. Numerical simulations are performed for Reynolds numbers in the range of 100–200, and velocity field data are analyzed using SPOD to identify dominant coherent structures and their associated frequencies. The nonlinear interactions among coherent flow structures are quantified using the integral measure of the bispectrum, which enables the identification of triadic frequency coupling in the flow field. The analysis reveals distinct differences between lock-on and non-lock-on shedding regimes. In the non-lock-on regime, triadic interactions occur primarily between the excitation frequency and the natural vortex shedding frequency, whereas in the lock-on regime, higher harmonics arise primarily through nonlinear self-interaction of the excitation frequency. For rotational oscillation, the dominant flow frequency in the lock-on region coincides with the excitation frequency, whereas for inline oscillation, the dominant response occurs at sub-harmonic frequencies. The SPOD mode shapes effectively capture the transition between lock-on and non-lock-on regimes and provide physical insight into the governing flow mechanisms. Overall, the combined SPOD-bispectral framework proves to be a powerful tool for identifying coherent structures involved in nonlinear interactions and for understanding the underlying dynamics of forced bluff-body wakes.

papers.title: Sound-source-oriented Bayesian optimization for efficient airfoil tonal noise control
papers.abstract: This study optimizes tonal noise suppression for a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 airfoil. The airfoil operates at a Reynolds number of 5000 and an angle of attack of 5°. A sound-source-oriented Bayesian optimization framework integrated with multi-process acoustic theory is adopted. This framework optimizes the position and angle of steady wall blowing/suction under different amplitude conditions. It effectively overcomes the challenges of high-dimensional parameter space and time-delay effect in tonal noise control. Mode decompositions and continuous wavelet analysis are employed. The spatiotemporal features, energy sources, and instability origins of the acoustic modes are characterized in detail under varying control amplitudes. These analyses elucidate the underlying control mechanisms. The results indicate that the optimal suction locations are concentrated around the flow separation point of the uncontrolled baseline airfoil. The optimal suction angle is maintained near the wall-normal direction. As the control amplitude increases, the optimal suction position gradually shifts downstream. Concurrently, the dominant instability undergoes two distinct transition stages: from double-vortex shedding to single-vortex shedding and ultimately to suppression of the wake instability. Notably, the transition to single-vortex shedding yields the highest noise reduction efficiency. This shift in dominant mechanisms is accompanied by a migration of the instability mode's peak amplitude away from the wall. Energy analysis reveals that the instability modes are sustained by both the mean flow and nonlinear interactions. Both of these contributions are significantly attenuated under active control.

papers.title: Wavepacket dynamics and noise control pathways in supersonic impinging jets subject to passive nozzle exit modifications
papers.abstract: Supersonic impinging jets produce intense acoustic loading from interactions among coherent wavepackets, shock-cell structures, and the impingement plate, yet how passive nozzle exit geometry modifies wavepacket dynamics remains unclear. Compressible large-eddy simulation, hybrid computational aeroacoustics, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) are applied to four exit configurations: base, bevel, chevron, and tab at nozzle pressure ratio 5.0 impinging on a flat plate at H/D = 11. The SPOD spectral gap, wavepacket envelope, two-point coherence, and band-integrated coherent pressure energy reveal three distinct modification pathways. Chevrons reduce the spectral gap from 7–10 to 5–7 dB, shift wavepacket saturation upstream, and reduce plate-arrival amplitude to 18% of baseline, yielding a 2.6 dB reduction in the meridional acoustic-energy proxy. Tabs collapse the spectral gap to 2–4 dB, fragment the organized downstream wavepacket, and reduce plate-arrival amplitude to 4%, suppressing the impingement tone with a 3.9 dB proxy reduction and a 2–3 dB high-frequency penalty at upstream angles. Beveling retains plate-arrival amplitude at 55% while deflecting the wavepacket asymmetrically, redistributing directivity rather than globally attenuating sound, with a 1.1 dB proxy reduction. Within the four examined configurations, a lower spectral gap is associated with greater far-field reduction, and impingement-tone intensity scales with plate-arrival amplitude rather than total turbulent kinetic energy; no transferable correlation is claimed.

papers.title: Effect of liquid viscosity on the resonant oscillations of a gas bubble in an acoustic field
papers.abstract: We investigate parametrically excited shape perturbations of a spherical gas bubble oscillating in a sound wave field within a liquid. The parameters of the acoustic excitation are chosen such that the sound wavelength significantly exceeds the bubble size, allowing the pressure field far from the bubble to be considered uniform. Starting from first principles and employing the method of multiple scales together with a boundary-layer-resolving coordinate transformation, we investigate the effect of weak liquid viscosity on the parametric instability of shape modes driven by the forced monopole mode. In the first parametric resonance zone, the acoustic excitation frequency must be close to half the natural frequency of one of the capillary modes. The equations governing the evolution of the resonant mode near the threshold of parametric instability excitation are determined. The dependence of the threshold amplitude of the acoustic pressure on the problem parameters and the frequency detuning from the resonant value in the first resonant zone is found. For each mode number, the threshold is minimized at a specific bubble radius at which the resonance frequency considered here approaches the natural frequency of the bubble's monopole mode. Additionally, under the assumption of large surface shear viscosity, the effect of a surfactant layer adsorbed onto the bubble surface is analyzed. It is found that the surfactant effect is non-monotonic and size-dependent. Within the present model and parameter ranges examined, the surfactant layer can reduce the instability threshold for smaller bubble radii (R0≲1 mm), but tends to increase the threshold for larger bubbles. Furthermore, it is shown that the presence of a surfactant leads to a measurable decrease in the resonant frequency. In the clean-bubble case, the viscous damping decrement and the threshold scale linearly with the kinematic viscosity ν, whereas for the surfactant-laden bubble both the damping decrement and the threshold scale as ν, reflecting the transition from bulk viscous dissipation to boundary-layer-dominated dissipation.

papers.title: An efficient spectral element phase-field method for incompressible multiphase flow simulation
papers.abstract: This study develops a graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated spectral element phase-field method for efficient and accurate simulation of incompressible two-phase flows. The objective is to reduce the cost of the repeated elliptic subproblems that dominate Navier–Stokes–Cahn–Hilliard simulations while retaining high-order accuracy and robust interface resolution. The governing system is advanced with a decoupled time-integration strategy in which the phase-field, pressure, and velocity subproblems are solved sequentially. The dominant elliptic operators are reformulated as constant-coefficient Poisson and Helmholtz equations, so the corresponding spectral element operators can be assembled, diagonalized, and reused throughout the computation. A tensor-product GPU solver based on one-dimensional eigenvalue decompositions then performs multidimensional elliptic solves through separable transforms and pointwise operations rather than repeated construction of variable-coefficient matrices. The method is assessed through central processing unit (CPU)–GPU performance comparisons, manufactured-solution convergence tests, Laplace-law verification, bubble coalescence, rising-bubble benchmarks, and Rayleigh–Taylor instability. The results confirm high-order spatial accuracy and efficiency of the present method. The time cost for the two- and three-dimensional rising-bubble case are separately 2.9 and 43.0 min for 15 000 time steps. The GPU solver reaches a peak speedup of 7.30 times and remains 3.66 times faster than the CPU reference for the largest tested problem with 1.24×108 degrees of freedom, while the maximum CPU–GPU difference stays at the round-off level. These results indicate that the proposed method provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for large-scale phase-field simulations of incompressible multiphase flows.

papers.title: Coupled effects of fracture geometry and fluid properties on two-phase flow in rough fractures
papers.abstract: Two-phase flow in rough fractures is governed by the coupled effects of geometric heterogeneity and fluid properties, yet the physical mechanisms linking fracture complexity with phase transport remain insufficiently understood. In this study, a fractal-based analytical model is developed to describe two-phase flow in rough fractures by incorporating fracture roughness, aperture distribution, and flow tortuosity. Analytical expressions for permeability and relative permeability are derived. Comparison with multiple independent experimental datasets demonstrates that the model accurately reproduces the nonlinear relative permeability behavior observed in fractured media. The results reveal that fracture geometry regulates fluid transport by modifying the available flow space and resistance along flow pathways. Fracture roughness and aperture heterogeneity restrict effective transport regions and enhance energy dissipation, whereas tortuous pathways increase hydraulic resistance. In two-phase flow, relative permeability is controlled by phase distribution associated with saturation and interfacial momentum transfer induced by viscosity contrast. A lower viscosity ratio strengthens interfacial shear interaction and suppresses the mobility of the nonwetting phase, resulting in a pronounced reduction in its relative permeability. These findings elucidate the coupling between fracture geometry, interfacial dynamics, and phase transport, providing new insights into multiphase flow behavior in complex confined geometries.

papers.title: Unified dynamics of capillary-driven drainage and spontaneous imbibition in porous media
papers.abstract: Capillary-driven drainage and spontaneous imbibition govern fluid redistribution in porous media and are central to hydrocarbon recovery, geological carbon storage, groundwater remediation, and underground hydrogen storage. Predictive descriptions of capillary equilibration are often empirical and do not explicitly connect the observed relaxation time to measurable rock, fluid, and experimental properties. Here, capillary equilibration is represented as an incremental storage-transport process following a discrete change in the imposed phase-pressure difference. The resulting characteristic time depends on porosity, permeability, effective relative permeability, viscosity, transport length, the saturation increment, and the capillary-pressure increment. The formulation is extended to account for the equilibrium capillary-pressure–saturation curve, saturation-dependent relative permeability, wettability through the Brooks–Corey and Leverett relations, finite porous-plate resistance, incomplete equilibration between sequential pressure steps, dual-storage systems, and nonlinear resistivity-saturation behavior. Archie's law shows that the commonly used linear resistivity–volume relation is a local approximation about a reference saturation, whereas the hydraulic volume response remains first order under constant stepwise coefficients. Analytical expressions are given for water production, water saturation, true resistivity, and resistivity index for both drainage and spontaneous imbibition. Sequential-step calculations and parameter-sensitivity analyses illustrate the experimental regimes in which equilibration extends from days to months. The drainage formulation is assessed retrospectively against previously published sandstone and carbonate porous-plate capillary-pressure/resistivity-index measurements rather than through fully independent validation; the spontaneous-imbibition extension is presented as a theoretical prediction that requires future experimental assessment. The framework provides a compact, physically interpretable basis for designing and analyzing capillary-pressure equilibration experiments.

papers.title: Experimental correlation between tip vibration dynamics and aerosol generation in dentistry
papers.abstract: Dental ultrasonic scaling generates bioaerosols that can carry respiratory pathogens and contribute to airborne transmission risk, yet the physical parameters governing their generation remain poorly quantified. Here, we experimentally quantify the effects of ultrasonic scaler tip geometry, vibration amplitude, and contact angle on aerosol generation for cooling water and artificial saliva. Empirical correlations were developed for the aerosol generation rate, and a normalized Ohnesorge-number scaling captured the droplet-size dependence. Among the tested tips, the smallest diameter produced the highest aerosol generation rates and release velocities. Remarkably, once normalized, data from different tips collapsed onto a single Ohnesorge-based master curve, indicating that tip geometry primarily sets the absolute aerosol yield while leaving the relative size distribution nearly unchanged. Tip geometry and vibration amplitude were the dominant factors influencing aerosol generation, whereas contact angle played a comparatively minor role. These findings advance the quantitative understanding of aerosol generation during ultrasonic scaling and provide a physics-based basis for aerosol emission prediction and transmission risk assessment in dental settings.

papers.title: Stationary and moving simulations on the aerodynamic performance of high-speed maglev trains under different yaw angles
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the effects of yaw angle on the aerodynamic characteristics of an electromagnetic suspension high-speed maglev train by comparing moving and stationary simulation methods. The numerical simulations employ the delayed detached eddy simulation method based on the elliptic blending k–ε model and are conducted for a 1:10-scale train model at yaw angles of β = 0°, β = 5°, and β = 10°. The results show that as the yaw angle increases, the aerodynamic load differences between the two simulation methods widen, with the most pronounced discrepancies observed for the tail car. At β = 10°, the errors in the lift coefficient and rolling moment coefficient of the tail car reach 25.146% and 27.739%, respectively. In terms of the flow-field structure, the leeward-side longitudinal vortices develop more significantly in the moving simulation, and the wake region exhibits more abundant secondary vortex structures and higher turbulent kinetic energy levels, indicating stronger three-dimensional unsteady characteristics. Overall, significant differences exist in the aerodynamic loads and flow-field characteristics of the train obtained from stationary and moving simulations under crosswind conditions, and these differences become more pronounced with increasing yaw angle.

papers.title: Numerical simulation of water evaporation and evaporation-induced thermal convection in a bottom-heated cylindrical pool at low pressures
papers.abstract: This paper examines water evaporation and the resulting thermal convection pattern in a bottom-heated cylindrical liquid pool under low-pressure conditions using three-dimensional numerical simulations. The effects of pressure ratio, heating temperature, and liquid depth on evaporation, temperature and flow fields, and Bénard–Marangoni (BM) convection structures are analyzed. The results show that the evaporation rate decreases as the pressure ratio increases. At fixed pressure ratio and heating temperature, the increasing liquid depth weakens evaporation by extending the heat-transfer path. At low heating temperatures, conduction dominates and BM convection cells do not form. With raising heating temperature, buoyancy and thermocapillary forces strengthen, producing diverse BM patterns. Lower pressure ratios intensify evaporative cooling, which can either suppress bottom-heated plumes by forming a cold cap or promote unsteady convection by enhancing vertical and interfacial temperature gradients. Thermocapillary circulation is more prominent in shallow layers, whereas the relative contribution of buoyancy increases with liquid-layer depth. These findings offer guidance for low-pressure evaporative cooling, liquid-pool thermal management, and interfacial phase-change heat-transfer control.

papers.title: Nonlinear thermo-fluid–structure interactions of two interacting flexible cantilever plates in a differentially heated cavity
papers.abstract: This study investigates the thermo-fluid–structure interaction dynamics of two flexible cantilever plates in a two-dimensional differentially heated square cavity. A fully coupled fluid–structure interaction framework resolves the interplay between buoyancy-driven convection, vortex dynamics, and structural deformation. The effects of Rayleigh number (Ra), geometric confinement, structural asymmetry, and plate thermal boundary conditions on nonlinear bifurcation behavior are systematically examined. The results show that the coupled system remains in a stable steady state at low Ra, while increasing thermal forcing produces self-sustained periodic oscillations, followed by amplitude-modulated multi-frequency dynamics and, at high Ra, a chaotic response supported by a positive largest Lyapunov exponent. For symmetric fixed-cavity configurations, decreasing the inter-plate spacing narrows the flow passage and increases the plate length and structural compliance. Fixed-flexible-span control calculations reveal a non-monotonic dependence on tip-to-tip distance (Ds), showing that the earlier instability of smaller-gap configurations cannot be attributed to geometric confinement alone. Structural asymmetry redistributes hydrodynamic forcing between the plates and suppresses synchronized motion; however, its influence is non-monotonic, with the intermediate asymmetric configuration producing the strongest structural response. Plate thermal boundary conditions also strongly affect the route to unsteadiness. Adiabatic, cold-isothermal, strongly cooled, and heated plates exhibit distinct transitions between regular and chaotic responses, with representative chaotic states supported by positive largest Lyapunov exponents. The mean upper-wall Nusselt number increases with Ra, while its temporal fluctuations become pronounced in the irregular high-Ra regime. Overall, variations in plate geometry and thermal condition provide practical means of modifying the nonlinear response of confined natural convection systems.

papers.title: Vortex-induced vibrations of a diamond cylinder of different aspect ratios at a low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: This study uses a two-dimensional stabilized finite element formulation to examine undamped vortex-induced vibrations of rigid diamond cylinders in transverse-only or single-degree-of-freedom (1-DOF) and coupled streamwise-transverse or two-degrees-of-freedom (2-DOF) motion. Computations are performed for aspect ratios (AR) of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1 at mass ratio (m* = 10), Reynolds number 100, and reduced velocity, U* = 1–12. The cylinder height is kept constant while the width is varied to obtain different ARs. The results show that all configurations experience significant oscillation amplitudes. The overall trends in 1-DOF and 2-DOF responses are similar, although the 2-DOF motion of the AR = 0.25 case is noticeably weaker than its 1-DOF response. In the upper branch (UB), the phase between lift and displacement resembles that reported for circular cylinders at much higher Reynolds numbers, indicating a similar synchronization mechanism. The UB is also marked by a wake pattern consisting of two vortex pairs (2P) and one single vortex (S) shed during each cycle, a configuration known as 2P + S. These results demonstrate that low-aspect-ratio diamond cylinders exhibit distinct vibration and wake characteristics, strongly governed by geometry.

papers.title: Nonhydrostatic mixing and three-dimensionality of gravity currents under turbulent pulsating flow
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate the impact of flow instabilities, nonhydrostatic mixing, and phase-dependent flow behavior on gravity currents propagating against a pulsating flow in a lock-exchange configuration. Two regimes are considered: (i) laminar pulsating flow, with two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) DNS at Re=3000 using eight combinations of Froude numbers Frm and Fro, representing dimensionless velocity amplitudes of the opposing mean flow and the oscillatory component, respectively; and (ii) turbulent pulsating flow, with 3D DNS at Re=1.2×104, Frm=0.46, and Fro=0.5. Across both regimes, the gravity current evolution is strongly phase dependent and shaped by nonhydrostatic processes: Kelvin–Helmholtz instabilities, lobe-cleft structures, lifting of the gravity current, Rayleigh–Taylor-like instabilities, and their impact on 3D mixing. We show that long-term processes and large-scale phenomena can be captured with 2D DNS. Other properties, related to nonhydrostatic processes, such as instabilities and lifting, active on shorter time scales (smaller than the oscillation period) or small-scale flow phenomena, require full 3D DNS. Turbulent ambient flow conditions modulate these short-time and small-scale processes significantly, thus always requiring full 3D DNS (or large-eddy simulation) and having a clear impact over the full oscillation cycle. Together, the presented results clarify which aspects of evolving gravity currents under pulsating flow conditions can be captured with 2D models and identify the 3D mechanisms that must be represented when parameterizing mixing and entrainment in estuarine salt-intrusion applications.

papers.title: A hybrid data-driven explicit algebraic subgrid-scale closure for improved inter-scale energy transfer and turbulence structure prediction
papers.abstract: The explicit algebraic (EA) subgrid-scale (SGS) closure is shown to overpredict inter-scale energy transfer in turbulent channel flow, leading to excessive SGS dissipation, attenuation of turbulence fluctuations, and degradation of flow statistics. The SGS kinetic energy, KSGS, is identified as the key modeling variable in EA closure, as it determines the SGS timescale, controls SGS dissipation, and scales the nonlinear stress contributions. In this regard, the currently employed dynamic equilibrium KSGS model is identified as a key component of the coupled EA closure, whose limitations propagate through the SGS timescale and nonlinear stress coefficients, leading to less accurate prediction of the inter-scale energy transfer and turbulence statistics. To address this deficiency, a hybrid physics–machine-learning framework is developed in which a deep neural network, trained on filtered direct numerical simulation data at Reτ=381 and two filter scales, is proposed to predict KSGS, while the algebraic structure of the SGS model is fully retained. The proposed model is assessed through both a priori and a posteriori analyses at friction Reynolds numbers up to Reτ=2000. The improved prediction of KSGS improves the balance between turbulent kinetic energy production and dissipation, reduces the artificially diffused streamwise Reynolds stress, and improves the underprediction of the mean velocity in the buffer layer. Corresponding improvements in energy spectra, two-point velocity correlations, and integral length scales demonstrate an improved representation of turbulence structure. The results show that enhanced modeling of KSGS is fundamental to restoring inter-scale energy transfer and turbulence structure in EA SGS closures, providing an effective hybrid framework that remains robust across a wide range of Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of mass-flow-rate-based parameter compensation in multi-orifice opposing jets on a variable-bluntness leading edge
papers.abstract: To mitigate severe aerodynamic heating at the rudder/wing leading edges of high-speed vehicles, opposing-jet active thermal protection is investigated. Three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations at Mach 8 and 30 km altitude examine single-orifice, dual-orifice, and spanwise multi-orifice jets over variable-bluntness leading edges under a constant mass flow rate constraint. The results show that the restriction on radial jet expansion caused by a reduced orifice diameter can be compensated by the enhanced expansion associated with an increased jet total pressure ratio (PR). Consequently, macroscopic shock structures and wall thermal loads remain highly consistent for different combinations of orifice diameter and PR. This compensation behavior is maintained under both strong and weak dual-orifice interference. For spanwise multi-orifice arrays, the constant mass flow rate per orifice strategy provides more uniform thermal protection than the constant PR strategy and gradually establishes a downstream dynamic equilibrium region with stable flow structures. Under constant PR, the mass flow rate and jet strength decrease with orifice size, causing pronounced increases in downstream local pressure and heat flux peaks. The present study verifies the applicability of mass-flow rate-based parameter compensation predicted by classical jet scaling relations to complex flows involving three-dimensional sweep, multi-orifice interactions, and variable-bluntness leading edges, and provides a design basis for orifice parameter matching and mass flow distribution in multi-orifice opposing-jet thermal protection systems.

papers.title: Propagation characteristics of AlH3/air gas–solid two-phase rotating detonation wave
papers.abstract: Utilizing high-energy solid powder fuel is the key path to enhancing the performance of rotating detonation engines. However, traditional solid fuels have problems such as slow reaction kinetics or long ignition delay, which restrict their energy release efficiency in detonation environments. The thermal decomposition temperature of AlH3 is low, and its hydrogen storage density is high, which can provide a feasible path for gas–solid two-phase detonation. This paper employs the Eulerian–Lagrangian method to solve the gas–solid two-phase detonation problem, and the effects of different parameters on the flow field and detonation wave propagation characteristics are considered. The results show that the detonation wave exhibits two spatially separated heat release zones behind a single shock front. The forward reaction zone is dominated by the H2–O2 homogeneous reaction, while the rearward reaction zone is dominated by the Al(s)–O2 heterogeneous reaction. As the equivalence ratio increases, the wave velocity and pressure first increase and then decrease. The same non-monotonic trend is observed when the inlet total temperature is raised. Excessive equivalence ratio reduces the energy contribution of aluminum combustion, shifting the detonation toward hydrogen-dominated propagation, whereas excessive inlet temperature causes premature AlH3 decomposition ahead of the wave. The inlet mass flow rate monotonically increases the front pressure, but the wave velocity exhibits an optimal range. At excessively low flow rates, aluminum particles burn incompletely; at excessively high flow rates, particles tend to escape through the triple wave point, both of which degrade the effective fuel utilization.

papers.title: Dynamic behavior of the counter-flow jet for drag reduction in hypersonic laminar flow under short penetration mode
papers.abstract: Depending on the counter-flow jet (CFJ) injection characteristics, the flow field can be classified into the short penetration mode (SPM) and the long penetration mode. Although SPM is generally considered stable, the pressure drag coefficient exhibits significant fluctuations exceeding 10%, which cannot be explained by penetration length alone. Numerical simulations in a hypersonic laminar regime, combined with fast Fourier transform and multi-resolution dynamic mode decomposition (mrDMD) analyses, suggest that the dominant oscillatory behavior is closely associated with the dynamic evolution of the extended jet layer within a coupled system of shock, shear-layer, and recirculation dynamics. The mrDMD analysis further indicates that the interaction between the extended jet layer, unsteady shock structures, and surface pressure distribution forms a self-sustained feedback loop governing the oscillatory CFJ behavior. The motion of the extended jet layer enables the prediction of maximum and minimum drag states, demonstrating that the pressure drag coefficient undergoes a quasi-periodic, sine-like oscillation that can be decomposed into six characteristic steps. Furthermore, the mrDMD results show that this six-step feedback process is organized across multiple temporal scales, with slow background modes interacting with fast shock–jet oscillations. These findings provide new physical insight into the oscillatory mechanism of the SPM by identifying the coherent flow structures associated with drag fluctuations beyond the conventional interpretation based solely on penetration characteristics.

papers.title: The effect of localized friction on the disruption of self-similarity
papers.abstract: The present study demonstrates the absence of self-similarity formation in the distribution of mean concentration fields. An examination in both the physical and spectral spaces revealed that the convection−diffusion mechanism and the development of short- and long-range dispersion play a minimal role in influencing the nature of self-similarity. The friction concentration is considered as the key factor in determining the emergence of self-similarity. It is observed that as the rate of change of friction concentration fields tends to zero, the mean concentration fields stabilize into self-similar patterns more effectively.

papers.title: A rheological model for two-step yielding behavior of coastal mud under oscillatory shear loading
papers.abstract: Modeling the rheological response of coastal mud under oscillatory shear loading is essential for understanding wave-mud interactions and the dynamics of muddy seabeds. Recent studies have shown that mud exhibits a characteristic two-step yielding process. However, existing two-step yielding models have difficulty of capturing the evolution of viscoelastic behavior during the yielding process under oscillatory shear loading. Based on rheological experiments, this study developed a rheological model for the two-step yielding behavior of coastal mud using fundamental elements of viscoelastoplastic mechanics. The corresponding rheological response of the model under oscillatory shear loading is then derived analytically. In the solid state, the model reduces to a Kelvin–Voigt model; in the solid–fluid transition state, it reduces to two Kelvin–Voigt elements connected in series; and in the fluid-like state, it reduces to a Jeffreys model. Empirical relationships among the model parameters, the two yield stresses, and solid volume fraction were established for the tested mud. The model was further evaluated using published data. Results show that the proposed model captures the main features of the rheological response of coastal mud under oscillatory shear loading. This study provides scientific support for the mechanistic characterization of the oscillatory rheological behavior of coastal mud and for subsequent investigations of wave-mud interaction.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural network enhanced particle image velocimetry for granular flows with pressure-dependent rheology
papers.abstract: Accurate characterization of granular flows depends on the reliable identification of internal stress states and boundary slip behaviors, which remains challenging due to the limited observability of stress fields and near-wall dynamics in Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) measurements. To address these limitations, this study proposes a physics-informed computational framework to extend the capabilities of traditional PIV. By employing the μ(I) rheology to constitutively couple kinematic states with internal stresses and by embedding macroscopic momentum conservation equations as rigorous constraints within a Residual Neural Network, this approach enables the simultaneous enhancement of PIV velocity fields and the inversion of latent pressure fields directly from the kinematic data. The method is first validated against analytical solutions for unsteady granular chute flows corrupted with a controlled noise. The results demonstrate exceptional noise robustness; even when the input data is corrupted by up to 20% noise, the method accurately reconstructs both velocity and pressure fields. The framework is subsequently applied to complex granular flows using synthetic PIV data generated from discrete element method simulations. The results show that the proposed method achieves physics-consistent super-resolution reconstruction of PIV measurements, successfully inverts the internal pressure distributions, and overcomes near-wall optical blind spots through physics-informed extrapolation, enabling accurate prediction of wall slip velocities. Overall, the proposed framework significantly enhances the information extraction capability of PIV and provides a new pathway for investigating granular rheology and boundary mechanisms.

papers.title: Uniqueness of two-dimensional and three-dimensional flow solutions in a symmetric sudden expansion channel
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) flow models were established for the fluid flow in the symmetrical sudden expansion channel. Analysis revealed that the 3D model yielded a 2D solution akin to the 2D model. Numerical simulations provided the velocity distribution of the flow field in both models at varying Re. The nonlinear characteristics and variances in flow between the 2D and 3D models were scrutinized based on the numerical findings. The results demonstrated that under different Re, both models exhibited nonlinear phenomena, such as pitchfork bifurcation. In the absence of bifurcation, both model types exhibit a unique, symmetrical, and steady-state velocity field, with the 2D solution fully aligning with the 3D solution. In cases of weak bifurcation, the solutions for both models become non-unique, yielding a pair of antisymmetric steady-state asymmetric solutions. The 2D and 3D models maintain identical solutions, with no emergence of 3D flow characteristics. Conversely, in scenarios of strong bifurcation, 3D flow develops within the channel, rendering the 2D model's solutions inadequate to replace those of the 3D model. These findings delineate the conditions under which 3D problems can be simplified to 2D ones in experimental and numerical simulation. When the spanwise length remains constant, the flow corresponding to solid wall boundary conditions exhibits greater stability. Conversely, when the spanwise boundary conditions are uniform, an increase in spanwise length correlates with increased flow instability. This article further elucidates the physical mechanisms underlying the generation of spanwise flow.

papers.title: Cyclonic ring shedding as a mechanism of cross-jet transport in the Kuroshio Extension
papers.abstract: Using the 2002 Kuroshio cyclonic ring as a case study, we document that a cyclonic meander north of the Kuroshio Extension can evolve into a detached ring that crosses the jet and transports water masses across to the southern side of the current, and we use this event as a testbed for comparing different detection methodologies. We combine satellite altimetry with complementary Eulerian and Lagrangian diagnostics to resolve the formation, detachment, and post-detachment evolution of the ring, including its center trajectory, boundary evolution, and transport pathway across the jet. The results show that the ring develops from a cyclonic meander north of the main Kuroshio jet axis, then detaches and is advected to the southern side of the jet while maintaining a coherent core. These results illustrate that ring shedding provides a pathway for cross-jet transport, and highlight how the choice of Eulerian vs Lagrangian diagnostic strongly influences the quantitative characterization of the eddy's size, shape, and lifetime, even when the physical phenomenon itself is robustly identified.

papers.title: Passive control of aerodynamic noise from tandem airfoils using a micro-perforated leading-edge array on the downstream airfoil
papers.abstract: To address turbulence-interaction noise induced by strong wake–leading-edge interactions in tandem airfoils of turbomachinery, this study considers National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 6412 tandem airfoils and designs three micro-perforated array configurations with different chordwise coverages at the leading edge of the downstream airfoil. Acoustic wind tunnel noise measurements, transient particle image velocimetry flow-field measurements, and proper orthogonal decomposition analysis are combined to systematically investigate the acoustic characteristics and noise-reduction mechanism. The results show that pronounced discrete tonal noise peaks are generated when the downstream airfoil is located within the core region of the upstream wake. The micro-perforated array with a chordwise coverage of 12.4% achieves a maximum noise reduction of 15 dB in the dominant noise-frequency band of 400–2000 Hz, completely suppresses the discrete tonal noise peaks, and reduces the overall sound pressure level by approximately 5 dB across the measured polar range of 75°–120°, and no notable change in far-field noise directivity is observed within this angular coverage. The primary noise-reduction mechanism is that the leading-edge permeability effect weakens near-wall separation vortices and turbulent fluctuations, disrupts the large-scale periodic vortex street formed by wake-wall coupling near the downstream leading edge, and promotes the cascade and dissipation of unsteady energy into higher-order small-scale modes. These findings can be applied to reduce noise in rotating machinery, such as guide blade rows, fan blade rows, and turbine blade rows.

papers.title: Vortex-induced vibration characteristics and aerodynamic interference of tandem 5:1 rectangular cylinders
papers.abstract: Wind tunnel tests and numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the vortex-induced vibration (VIV) characteristics and aerodynamic interference of tandem 5:1 rectangular cylinders. Influences of spacing ratio (L/B = 0.2, 1.0, and 3.0), constraint conditions, and damping ratio on VIV were systematically examined. Results reveal that the upstream cylinder (UC) dominates the VIV behavior of the tandem system. A freely vibrating UC excites large-amplitude VIV in the downstream cylinder (DC), up to three times that of an isolated cylinder, whereas a fixed UC almost eliminates DC vibration. The amplitude of DC depends nonlinearly on UC vibration under varying damping ratios, while the phase difference between the two cylinders varies systematically with both wind speed and damping ratio, reflecting the synchronization between vortex convection and structural vibration. The influence of DC on UC is confined to small and intermediate spacings and arises primarily from flow disturbance induced by proximity effects rather than by DC vibration. Flow-field analyses reveal distinct spacing-dependent interference mechanisms: at small spacing, UC vibration strengthens the leading-edge vortices of DC via vortex merging and gap cross flow; at large spacing, the periodic wake synchronized with UC vibration promotes strong leading-edge vortex shedding on DC. When the UC is fixed, the suppression mechanism also depends on spacing: at small spacing, a shielding effect suppresses leading-edge flow separation and vortex formation on DC; at large spacing, the Strouhal-frequency wake from the stationary UC prevents synchronization between DC shedding and structural vibration.

papers.title: Capillary reorientation and interfacial transitions under geometric confinement in a bipropellant tank
papers.abstract: Capillary-driven redistribution in a closed, geometrically confined container involves coupled wetting, interface-curvature evolution, and gas-pocket topology changes. Here, a three-dimensional volume-of-fluid model is used to examine these mechanisms in a common-bulkhead container under 10−6 g0 for fill fractions of 20%–95%. The Bond and Ohnesorge numbers indicate that the global response is dominated by capillary-inertial dynamics, with residual gravity providing only a weak axial preference. The interface evolves from an initially open surface through wall-wetting spreading to a closed central gas pocket. Fill fraction produces a non-monotonic response: low-fill cases are limited by insufficient liquid inventory and high-fill cases are limited by restricted gas space, whereas intermediate fill fractions of 40%–60% permit the greatest interface deformation and axial mass redistribution. The upper and lower compartments exhibit different center-of-mass responses because their boundaries, initial interfaces, and fluid properties set different capillary pathways and inertial time scales. These results identify the physical mechanism by which finite gas volume and compartment geometry regulate capillary-driven interfacial transitions in closed containers, with implications for spacecraft propellant management.

papers.title: Bridge formation and contact-line dynamics of a sessile and a pendent drop coalescing over a superhydrophobic substrate
papers.abstract: Coalescence of two liquid drops in dropwise condensation enables a combined drop to jump off the substrate. In this context, we study the coalescence of vertically aligned water droplets placed over a superhydrophobic surface using numerical simulations validated against high-speed imaging experiments. Coalescence begins when the pendent drop touches the sessile drop. Large curvature differences between the newly formed bridge and the drop interface with air drive flow into the bridge. A capillary wave originating at the bridge travels along the sessile drop interface, approaches the droplet base, and triggers spreading and retraction of the contact line. Near-wall behavior for various initial conditions, substrate wettability, droplet size ratio, and viscosity ratio relative to the ambient fluid is examined. Simulations support experimental observations from the onset of coalescence to the evolution of contact-line motion. The coalescence dynamics depend on the shape of the pendent drop. For non-spherical drops, the bridge radius initially grows with time following a power-law exponent of 0.5, while the axial radius of curvature evolves with an exponent of 1.5, similar to the coalescence of two spherical drops. At later stages, however, deviations from these initial scaling exponents are observed. Simulations show that a thin air film is trapped between the liquid mass and the substrate once the capillary wave reaches the contact line. Capillary waves propagate over the water droplet, bending the interface and entraining air, thereby forming an air tongue, whereas in glycerol drops, viscous damping suppresses the passage of these waves.

papers.title: Unsteady carrier airwake under complex sea states flow characteristics and time-conditioned prediction
papers.abstract: Carrier motion under complex sea states continuously changes the relative inflow in the landing glide-path region and produces an unsteady airwake. High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can resolve this coupled wind–wave–carrier problem, but long-sequence and multi-condition calculations remain expensive. Here, a coupled CFD framework is used to examine the temporal and downstream evolution of the airwake. Wave-induced heave and pitch produce a clear phase-related modulation of the sectional velocity fields. The angled-deck landing region contains separated velocity-deficit branches that are transported, deformed, and redistributed downstream rather than forming a single uniform wake. A time-conditioned one-shot residual network (TCO-ResNet) is then developed for rapid flow-field prediction. The initial flow field and target time are mapped directly to the specified future state, avoiding recursive time marching. Wake region-of-interest weighting, physics-guided constraints, and texture loss are used to retain wake boundaries and velocity-transition regions. Compared with an autoregressive ResNet, TCO-ResNet avoids the error growth associated with recursive prediction. Tests on unseen longitudinal sections retain both the phase-related evolution and the main multi-branch wake pattern. Integral wake measures further show that the strong low-velocity cores contract downstream, while the total streamwise velocity deficit changes much less, indicating redistribution rather than uniform wake attenuation. After transfer from Sea State 6 to Sea State 4, the phase-related evolution is still recovered, whereas the weaker wind–wave forcing produces less downstream reorganization. The method therefore provides a rapid reconstruction of the main temporal and spatial characteristics of carrier airwakes across the two sea states considered.

papers.title: Separation feasibility for chiral particles with linear anisotropic susceptibility in rotating magnetic field: Theoretical study in low magnetic field
papers.abstract: We theoretically discuss the separation of chiral particles having anisotropic magnetic susceptibility in a rotating magnetic field. Particles with anisotropic magnetic susceptibility can be aligned in either the parallel or perpendicular direction to the magnetic field, depending on their anisotropic properties. When a rotating magnetic field is applied, the particles undergo rotation. In our previous study, we theoretically demonstrated that chiral particles having a dipole moment in a rotating field can be separated from a racemic mixture; such chiral particles move along the axis of the rotating field in a direction that depends on their chirality. In this study, we show that the migration velocity of particles characterized by a susceptibility tensor can be estimated by the Brownian dynamics theory for arbitrary-shaped particles at a low Péclet number. The result indicates that the migration velocity is proportional to the fourth power of the magnetic field. The direction of the migration parallel to the rotation axis of the magnetic field depends on both the chirality of the particle and the frequency of the magnetic field. Propeller-like particles, which are composed of two thin disks and a thin rod, are used as illustrative examples. The migration direction is expressed as a function of the twist angle, which determines the degree of chirality of the propeller-like particle.

papers.title: Conditional normalizing flow for gas–surface scattering from thermal to hypersonic velocities
papers.abstract: Accurate aerodynamic modeling of satellites in very low Earth orbit (VLEO) requires gas–surface interaction models that capture the full velocity spectrum from thermal to orbital speeds. Atmospheric particles initially strike spacecraft surfaces at hypersonic velocities of 6 000– 10 000 m/s. Due to surface roughness and complex geometries, especially within air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) intake systems, multiple collisions occur, progressively reducing the particle velocities. A recent machine learning framework for deriving scattering kernels from molecular dynamics simulations has shown promise but remains limited to high-velocity single impacts and possibly violates fundamental equilibrium principles such as detailed balance. This work extends this machine learning-based scattering kernel to cover the complete velocity range using conditional normalizing flows trained with physics-informed constraints, enabling accurate modeling of macroscopic multi-bounce scenarios in realistic VLEO applications. We train a conditional real-valued non-volume preserving model on expanded molecular dynamics simulations covering velocities from thermal to hypersonic speeds, incorporating a detailed balance loss term. The resulting model demonstrates improved accuracy compared to previous approaches even in the original high-velocity regime, while successfully capturing thermal-velocity scattering. Quantitative assessment shows that thermalization is approximated within acceptable tolerances. This framework provides essential capabilities for accurate ABEP intake optimization and VLEO mission planning while offering a general methodology applicable to broader rarefied gas dynamics problems requiring thermodynamic consistency.

papers.title: Geometric model complexity effects on aircraft wake vortex parameters and structures
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of initial aircraft wake vortex parameters provides a foundation for wake turbulence separation optimization and efficient simulation. To clarify the impact of aircraft model complexity on the wake vortex generation and the resulting parameters and structures, numerical simulations are performed using four models: an isolated wing, an equivalent wing retaining the fuselage width, a wing incorporating fuselage, and a wing incorporating fuselage and empennage. Aerodynamic forces, surface pressure, vorticity magnitude, Q criterion fields, primary wingtip vortex spacing, circulation, and peak vorticity are compared. Results demonstrate that retaining the fuselage-width contribution through an equivalent-wing representation alters forces, whereas the empennage has little influence on the main wing pressure and forces under the present fixed-incidence, untrimmed condition with relatively small tail loads. Fuselage-induced pressure differences are mainly concentrated near the wing-body junction and inner wing, and gradually decrease toward the outer wing. Wake vortex structure analysis indicates that effective wingspan is the dominant factor governing the lateral position and spacing of the primary vortices. Omitting the fuselage width underestimates the primary vortex spacing by ∼3.9 m at x = 20 m and 3.6 m at x = 80 m, and reduces the downstream contraction ratio to 2.78%, compared with 3.36%–3.66% for models retaining the fuselage width. Under the same effective wingspan, the realistic fuselage and empennage exert limited influence on primary vortex spacing but introduce fuselage wake, wing-body junction vortices, and empennage-induced vortices, producing a more complex multi-source central wake structure. These results clarify the effects of aircraft model complexity on wake vortex parameters, structures, and near-field downstream development, providing a physical basis for aircraft geometry simplification and model selection in wake vortex studies.

papers.title: Ejection and deposition of atomic clusters at a liquid copper–vapor interface under conditions of normal evaporation
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations of equilibrium liquid–vapor copper systems and non-equilibrium impacts of copper monomers and dimers on a liquid copper film are performed to reveal the mechanisms of ejection and deposition of clusters from liquid metals under conditions of normal evaporation. A lifetime-based retrospective cluster identification algorithm is developed to identify long-lived stable clusters in the vapor phase. It is found that clusters of multiple sizes are ejected directly from the surface, and the mass fraction of monomers in the evaporation flux can be as small as 65%. This result is explained by collective interaction of atoms in metals, when the ejection of a cluster can be energetically more favorable than the ejection of individual monomers. The velocity distributions of ejected clusters can be approximated by the Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions with the temperature parameter smaller than the system temperature. The rotational and vibrational energy distributions of evaporated clusters are close to equilibrium distributions at the system temperature, indicating the absence of energy equipartition during cluster detachment from the surface. The equilibrium condensation coefficient of monomers varies from 0.74 at 3500 K to 0.68 at 5000 K. In the non-equilibrium simulations, the condensation probability of monomers and dimers is determined for broad ranges of the impact speed, angle of incidence, and surface temperature and then used to calculate the non-equilibrium condensation coefficient. A model of cluster evaporation and condensation that can be used as boundary conditions in gas kinetic simulations is developed. The key findings of this work indicate that the direct ejection of clusters from a liquid surface can be an important source of dimers in metal vapor plumes and jets.

papers.title: Control of airfoil flow separation using internal acoustic excitation
papers.abstract: Internal acoustic excitation has shown considerable potential for suppressing airfoil flow separation. Recent force measurements by Kiley et al. [“Unsteady aerodynamic flow control at low Reynolds numbers via internal acoustic excitation,” Phys. Fluids 36, 094120 (2024)] have demonstrated that acoustic excitation can improve the lift coefficient, yet the associated transient flow evolution and control mechanism remain unclear. In this study, miniature loudspeakers are embedded inside the leading edge of a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 airfoil to control large-scale flow separation on the suction side at a Reynolds number of Re=1.5×105 and angle of attack α=20°. Three excitation frequencies, 50, 250, and 500 Hz, are selected for detailed investigation using time-resolved particle image velocimetry. The results show that acoustic excitation significantly suppresses the suction-side separation bubble and promotes a nearly attached mean flow. Reynolds-stress analysis shows that the applied excitations enhance momentum exchange in the separated shear layer. The enhanced momentum-exchange region for the 50 Hz case is located lower than those for the 250 and 500 Hz cases. Transient flow analysis indicates that, without excitation, the leading-edge vortex is relatively weak and dissipate rapidly, merging into the separated shear layer, whereas acoustic excitation strengthens the leading-edge vortex, enhances near-wall momentum exchange, and drives the separation point downstream. The spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) for the baseline case reveals no distinct peak, confirming that the natural separated flow lacks a dominant frequency. For the 50 Hz case, SPOD analysis reveals pronounced spectral peaks at the excitation frequency and its harmonics, together with alternating streak-like modal structures downstream of the separation point, indicating that the 50 Hz excitation modifies the dominant coherent structure, thereby suppressing flow separation.

papers.title: Comparative analysis of flow field characteristics and cavitation mechanisms in liquefied natural gas ball valves with two different valve core structures
papers.abstract: Cryogenic ball valves are widely used in transportation systems involving liquefied natural gas (LNG), liquid nitrogen, and other low-temperature media, where cavitation may occur during operation and significantly affects the flow structure, energy transfer, and valve performance. In this study, three-dimensional numerical simulations of O-type and V-type LNG ball valves are conducted based on the Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model to systematically investigate the flow resistance characteristics, cryogenic cavitation evolution, vortex structures, and entropy production at different valve openings. Within the valve opening range of 30%–90%, the flow coefficient (Kv) increases from 0.11 to 0.85 for the O-type valve and from 0.015 to 0.20 for the V-type valve. Cavitation reaches its maximum intensity at 70% valve opening for both valve configurations, with the V-type valve exhibiting more severe cavitation. Vortex analysis based on the Q-criterion reveals a strong coupling between cavitation regions and high-intensity vortex structures, where vortex entrainment accelerates bubble generation and transport. Entropy production analysis further demonstrates that the O-type ball valve exhibits a larger total entropy production area and a higher peak of direct dissipation, while the entropy generation of both valves is primarily concentrated near the valve core outlet. These results clarify the effects of valve core geometry on cryogenic cavitation dynamics, flow evolution, and irreversible energy loss, providing theoretical guidance for structural optimization, cavitation suppression, and reliable operation of cryogenic ball valves.

papers.title: Microwave-driven transport and breakthrough kinetics of coalbed methane through nanoconfined water barriers
papers.abstract: Capillary blocking by liquid films, commonly known as the water lock effect, severely restricts methane transport in coal nanopores. This study employs nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to systematically investigate the microwave-regulated migration of nanoconfined water and its impact on methane breakthrough dynamics across various pore sizes, hydration levels, and coal ranks based on realistic macromolecular structures. Results indicate that microwave irradiation markedly accelerates nanoconfined water diffusion and destabilizes the pore-throat liquid film. This enhancement is strongly governed by fluid–solid interfacial adsorption states; increasing hydration levels and coal rank promote the transition from strongly adsorbed to weakly adsorbed or free fluid phases, thereby intensifying the microwave response. Conversely, expanding the pore size under constant water content increases intrinsic diffusivity but diminishes the marginal microwave enhancement due to the weakened wall-confinement potential. Crucially, the improvement in fluid mobility arises from the synergistic contributions of thermal and non-thermal effects. At an initial temperature of 313 K, the non-thermal effect driven by high-frequency perturbations of the hydrogen-bond network contributes up to 59.4% of the total diffusion enhancement. In the tri-phase methane–water–coal system, microwave irradiation substantially shortens the methane breakthrough time by accelerating interfacial rearrangement. Within 319–349 K, the non-thermal microwave contribution accounts for 6.7% to 45.2% of the overall acceleration in overcoming the capillary barrier. These findings provide fundamental physical insights into the external-field manipulation of nanoconfined multiphase flows in coalbed methane reservoirs.

papers.title: Excitation force mechanisms in a composite pump-jet propulsor under stationary-structure variations
papers.abstract: Minimizing the excitation force of a composite pump-jet propulsor is critical for suppressing propulsion-system noise and enhancing the acoustic stealth of the platform. When the fluid–structure interaction (FSI) deformation of the composite rotor interacts with variations in structural parameters, the resulting excitation force becomes highly nonlinear. To address this issue, a steady-state FSI algorithm is employed for the pre-deformation design of the composite rotor, and a transient FSI algorithm is adopted to investigate the influence of three parameters—stator angle, duct length, and tip clearance—on the rotor excitation force. The results show that: (1) the stator angle directly affects the rotor excitation force by altering the inflow angle of attack. A larger stator angle increases the time-averaged rotor thrust, which in turn amplifies the excitation force amplitude at the stator blade-passing frequency. (2) The duct length indirectly influences the rotor excitation force by changing the internal flow rate and consequently the wake fraction of the inflow field. Variations in duct length introduce two competing mechanisms: increasing the duct length suppresses radial flow diffusion in the mid-to-low radius region, thereby raising the local flow rate; conversely, the accompanying increase in wall friction expands the turbulent wake region at higher radii, reducing the local flow rate. The interplay between these effects produces a synchronous V-shaped variation in flow rate, pressure distribution, wake fraction, and excitation force amplitude as the duct length changes. (3) The tip clearance affects the rotor excitation force by modifying the turbulence characteristics within the clearance. Changes in clearance height generate two competing mechanisms: a larger clearance intensifies turbulent mixing between the tip-leakage flow and the mainstream, which decreases the time-averaged thrust and thereby reduces the excitation force amplitude; however, it also enhances the phase coherence of excitation forces across different radial sections, which amplifies the overall excitation force amplitude. The net excitation-force response is determined by the competition between these two effects. (4) Replacing the metal rotor with a composite rotor while retaining the baseline geometry yields superior excitation-force characteristics without altering the stator angle, duct length, or tip clearance, and maintains comparable propulsive efficiency. For the specific pump-jet geometry and operating condition investigated in this work, the present study elucidates the mechanisms by which composite rotors suppress excitation forces and provides a theoretical foundation for the engineering design of low-noise composite pump-jet propulsors.

papers.title: Vortex modulation by a bionic impeller for erosion suppression in a double-suction centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: Sediment erosion driven by sand-laden water causes severe degradation of the hydraulic performance and service life of double-suction centrifugal pumps. In this study, experiments and numerical simulations are combined to evaluate the anti-erosion effectiveness of a bionic impeller featuring convex domes inspired by the surface textures of desert organisms, and the underlying mechanisms are elucidated. The results reveal that compared with the prototype, the bionic impeller greatly reduces erosion across all critical regions under identical operating conditions and remains substantially less eroded even after nearly twice the operating time. The numerical simulations reproduce the experimentally observed erosion patterns and can, therefore, be employed to examine coupled vortex–particle dynamics. The results of a comparative analysis indicate that the bionic design achieves its anti-erosion performance primarily through a substantial reduction in the number of particle impacts. The hydrodynamic mechanism originates from the restructuring of the internal vortex system by the convex domes. Notably, the domes modify passage vortex evolution to prevent the formation of concentrated particle impacts on the suction-side outlet and suppress particle accumulation on the pressure side. Simultaneously, they transform the concentrated outlet vortex core into a distributed hairpin-like vortex array, thus inhibiting local particle accumulation. These vortex modulations collectively reduce the number of particle impacts by redirecting particle trajectories, thereby suppressing localized erosion. These findings identify vortex-system reconstruction as a physics-based mechanism for designing surface-microstructured erosion-resistant impellers in sediment-laden flows.

papers.title: Dynamics of bubble-enhanced natural convection in a superheated water cavity
papers.abstract: In this paper, we report on direct numerical simulations of bubble-enhanced natural convection in a cavity filled with water. The bottom wall is superheated, resulting in the formation of bubbles, while the free surface remains subcooled. The governing equations of the liquid are solved in the Eulerian framework and those of the bubbles in the Lagrangian one, employing two-way coupling between the two phases. We consider cases at Rayleigh numbers Ra=3.3×105 and Ra=3.3×106. Our study focuses on the effect of superheat. At very low superheat, the bubbles condense rapidly without impacting the flow dynamics. However, when the superheat is sufficiently high for the bubbles to reach the bulk of the domain, they induce a reorganization of the large-scale circulation and increase the vertical velocity of the liquid. Furthermore, they tend to homogenize the temperature distribution in the bulk and shift it toward the saturation temperature. Our simulations further confirm that the hydrodynamic interactions between the bubbles and the liquid promote significantly thermal mixing and convective heat transport. More specifically, at high superheat levels, the Nusselt number can be up to three times greater than that computed in the corresponding single-phase flow.

papers.title: Effects of machined surfaces with different topographies on fluid flow performance in rough contact interfaces
papers.abstract: In mechanical engineering, components are manufactured using different surface processing techniques, and machining methods produce distinct texture characteristics on workpiece surfaces. To investigate fluid infiltration behavior at the contact interface of actual machined surfaces, this study examined the effects of surface roughness and machining method on fluid infiltration and spreading within rough contact interfaces using a self-built in situ observation system. The experimental results demonstrate that surfaces fabricated by planing, turning, and milling all form anisotropic microchannels under loading, and the feature length of these microchannels decreases with increasing load. For planed surfaces, the feature length of interfacial microchannels is positively correlated with the surface arithmetic mean height Sa, the fastest decay autocorrelation length Sal, and the valley void volume Vvv and is inversely correlated with the texture aspect ratio Str. For surfaces with identical Sa values but different machining methods, the feature length of microchannels is inversely correlated with Sal.
