In contrast, the protrusion generates a coupled low-pressure, low-velocity, and recirculating region downstream, which promotes the sustained accumulation of the initial gas cluster and the ventilated gas, thereby enabling the formation of a persistent attached cavity over the simulated interval. The ventilation-hole position strongly affected cavity development: the attached-cavity volume increased from 2.10 × 10−2 m3 at D = 0.3 m to a maximum of 2.36 × 10−2 m3 at D = 0.4 m (four times the protrusion height), and then decreased to 1.19 × 10−2 m3 at D = 0.7 m. These findings demonstrate that a properly placed protrusion and ventilation hole can reorganize the local wake to enhance gas entrainment, confinement, and replenishment, providing a practical route for cavitation control over curved leeward surfaces.

papers.title: Airfoil pitch control in the wake of a backward-facing step via spatiotemporal deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Closed-loop lift control for an airfoil in a strongly nonuniform inflow is challenging, especially when only partial surface-pressure observations are available. This study investigates pitch control of a NACA (National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics) 0012 airfoil descending through the wake of a backward-facing step. A spatiotemporal deep-reinforcement-learning-based control framework is developed, in which the controller adopts sparse surface pressure and airfoil kinematics as feedback. The proposed MSALSTM policy, trained with proximal policy optimization, combines multi-head self-attention for spatial pressure encoding with long short-term memory for temporal inference of hidden flow states. Among the learned architectures, MSALSTM provides the most stable lift tracking and the smallest pitch oscillation. It also outperforms the fixed-angle and gain-scheduled proportional–integral–derivative baselines under the same descent condition. When a drag penalty is added to the reward function, the learned policy further increases the mean lift-to-drag ratio by 46%. Further analysis reveals that the attention module adaptively redistributes sensor emphasis according to the evolving flow state, while the recurrent memory organizes pressure-history information into structured hidden-state trajectories. These results demonstrate that spatiotemporal learning can reconstruct effective flow-state information from sparse wall-pressure data for high-Reynolds-number aerodynamic control.

papers.title: Vibro-acoustic coupling and multi-path interference in shallow-water scattering of flexible shells via programmable Gaussian splatting reconstruction and isogeometric boundary element method
papers.abstract: This study presents an automated framework integrating Programable Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction (PGSR) with isogeometric boundary element method for simulating submerged flexible structures in shallow water. The framework generates watertight, analysis-ready surface meshes directly from multi-view imagery, achieving reconstruction accuracy with Hausdorff distance below λ/100(<2.47 cm at 600 Hz). A coupled formulation incorporating seabed and sea-surface reflections is established for realistic environments. Numerical validations on spherical, shark, and manta ray models show that the PGSR-reconstructed meshes maintain stable acoustic predictions across 50–600 Hz. Spectral peak density varies markedly with geometry—sparse for the sphere, isolated for the shark, and dense for the manta ray—suggesting that geometry-dependent vibro-acoustic coupling and multi-path interference cannot be fully captured by decoupled approaches.

papers.title: Rheotaxis of microswimmer in colloid-laden channel flow
papers.abstract: Microswimmers are often found in heterogeneous and crowded environments within narrow conduits under external flow conditions, exhibiting interesting translational and rotational motions, such as upstream swimming, wall-following, and oscillatory motion. To investigate the rheotactic behavior of microswimmers in a channel flow with the presence of hard, monodisperse spherical colloids, we use the spherical squirmer model coupled with a mesoscale simulation framework, multi-particle collision dynamics. We find that the presence of colloids significantly modifies the rheotactic behavior of the squirmer. At low flow strengths, pushers preferentially occupy the channel center with a dominant upstream orientation, whereas pullers move away from the center toward the walls. In contrast, in a colloid-free channel, pushers exhibit near-wall motion with a downstream orientation dominance, and pullers near the channel center with upstream orientation dominance. At sufficiently high flow strengths, the imposed flow dominates the squirmer-induced hydrodynamics, leading pushers, neutrals, and pullers to adopt a common upstream-oriented state. We also observe that, for a constant colloidal packing fraction, the streamwise velocity of the puller is less than that of the pusher.

papers.title: Linear stability of the rest state of viscoelastic liquid in the circular pipe under the effect of magnetic field
papers.abstract: We have studied the eigenvalue problem for the rest state of the viscoelastic liquid in an infinite cylinder with a uniform magnetic field directed along the centerline of the cylinder. It was shown for axisymmetric disturbances that the eigenspectrum has negative real parts regardless of the values of the parameters presented in the problem. For the simplified case of a perfectly conducting liquid, we obtained the eigenfunctions of the problem, while in the general case, we justified the stability of the state by the energy estimates.

papers.title: A time-accurate implicit simplified unified gas-kinetic scheme for unsteady multi-scale diatomic gas flows from continuum to free-molecular regimes
papers.abstract: The unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) solves multi-scale flows within a single framework, but its explicit formulation is inefficient for unsteady simulations due to severe Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) constraints arising from disparate mesh scales. We develop a time-accurate implicit UGKS with a simplified multi-scale flux for unsteady diatomic gas flows. The method employs a Crank–Nicolson scheme with a dual-time-stepping strategy, enabling CFL numbers hundreds of times larger than those of the explicit scheme and achieving an order-of-magnitude speedup. The simplified multi-scale flux recovers the Navier–Stokes limit in the continuum regime and accurately resolves non-equilibrium effects under rarefied conditions. Systematic calibration of four key numerical parameters (CFL number, weighting factor ε, point-relaxation symmetric Gauss–Seidel sweeps, and inner iterations) using Sod's shock tube establishes practical guidelines for balancing accuracy and efficiency. The method is validated on benchmark problems spanning from continuum to free-molecular regimes: laminar flow past circular and square cylinders, flow expansion between two connected cavities, and nozzle plume flow. Numerical results demonstrate that the method accurately captures the distinct vortex-shedding dynamics of square and circular cylinders, thermal non-equilibrium under rarefied conditions, and flow patterns of the nozzle plume under different degrees of ambient rarefaction.

papers.title: Yielding of bentonite suspensions under oscillatory shear considering boundary slip and shear inhomogeneity
papers.abstract: The rheology of bentonite suspensions under oscillatory shear flow was investigated using parallel-plate shearing geometries, considering both smooth and rough boundaries. With a smooth boundary, the oscillatory response consistently exhibited a two-step yielding phenomenon, which was identified as the onset of slip at the boundary followed by yielding in the bulk. With a rough boundary, a unique yielding transition was observed, accounting for the bulk yielding alone. Furthermore, considering the effect of shearing frequency, the yield stress for smooth boundary increased more remarkably with frequency compared to the condition using rough boundaries. The concentration dependence of the oscillatory characteristic stresses could be described by a Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek-based semi-empirical model adapted from the framework previously established for steady shear, indicating that interparticle interactions provide a physical basis for the observed concentration-dependent stress evolution, while empirical parameters account for the effects of particle arrangement and boundary conditions. These results provide a unified interpretation of slip-related and bulk-yield transitions in structured clay suspensions under oscillatory loading and clarify the coupled roles of boundary roughness, gap, and frequency.

papers.title: Effect of inflow velocity on cavitation state transition and flow mechanism in a pump-jet propulsor
papers.abstract: Cavitation state transition and the underlying flow mechanism are core issues in fluid physics, especially in the underwater propulsion systems. Inflow velocity variation alters local flow structure and pressure distribution, regulating cavitation inception and critical collapse in pump-jet propulsors (PJPs). This study focuses on the fluid physics of cavitation state transition, investigating the effects of inflow velocity on cavitation inception (cavitation number σn = 3.0) and critical collapse state (σn = 1.5) in a PJP using improved delayed detached eddy simulation coupled with the Schnerr–Sauer cavitation model. The results reveal a critical advance coefficient J = 0.8 at σn = 1.5, which serves as the boundary for cavitation state transition: for J ≤ 0.6, the flow field is dominated by strong backflow in the mid-chord region, leading to severe cavitation with chaotic vortex structures, characterized by cavitation volume Cv = 0.0106 and coverage area Cs = 93.41% at J = 0.2; for J ≥ 0.8, the flow transitions to a forward-flow dominated state, vortex structures recover to organized horseshoe and tip vortexes, and Cs = 48.69% at J = 0.8. At σn = 3.0, cavitation is strongly suppressed, with Cv at J = 0.2 only 0.93% of that at σn = 1.5, and the flow field remains stable despite occasional excitation force spikes. A key new finding is that inflow-driven flow pattern transition governs cavitation regime shift, where backflow-vortex-collapse coupling causes sudden hydrodynamic degradation. Furthermore, the interquartile range of rotor excitation force, which reflects flow unsteadiness, is approximately 2.4 times higher at J = 0.2–0.6 than at J = 0.8, confirming the close correlation between flow stability and cavitation state. This study provides theoretical guidance for cavitation suppression in underwater propulsion systems.

papers.title: Effects of scarfed jet configuration on the flow field and hydrodynamic characteristics of a supercavitating vehicle
papers.abstract: To enhance the tail-slap stability of the supercavitating vehicle during maneuvers, an active stabilization control method using aft scarfed gas jets is proposed. By establishing an unsteady gas–vapor–liquid multiphase coupled numerical model, the reconstruction mechanisms of the coupled flow field under varying nozzle scarfed angles θ and axial positions x0/L are analyzed. The results indicate that the scarfed jet enlarges the radial clearance between the vehicle tail and the cavity boundary, thereby providing a greater deflection margin for the longitudinal pitching. Regarding the total pitching moment coefficient and the center of pressure coefficient, as θ increases from 25° to 90°, both coefficients exhibit an initial decrease before flattening, which is attributed to the coupling of thrust vector attenuation and windward shoulder moment compensation. Furthermore, as x0/L shifts from 0.65 to 0.8, both coefficients increase monotonically, driven jointly by control moment arm extension and windward high-pressure region expansion. The jet-induced asymmetric surface pressure redistribution dominates the pitching moment variation, exerting a significantly stronger influence than the direct jet thrust. Overall, within the investigated parameter range, adopting a small scarfed angle and an appropriate rearward layout significantly enhances the longitudinal static stability characteristics of the vehicle under the operating conditions considered. Specifically, with θ = 25° and x0/L = 0.8, the pitching moment coefficient increases by 152.5% relative to the baseline, while the center of pressure coefficient shifts rearward by 15.8%.

papers.title: Unsteady hydrodynamics and energy loss during the water-exit process of a delta wing
papers.abstract: Delta-wing layout is a promising design in trans-medium vehicles. However, its water-exit process involves complex interactions among three-dimensional vortex evolution, free-surface deformation, and hydrodynamic loading, leading to flow and loading characteristics that differ from those commonly reported for canonical blunt bodies. In this study, high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulations are conducted to investigate the water-exit dynamics of a neutrally buoyant three-dimensional delta wing. The evolution of vortex structures, free-surface deformation, hydrodynamic loads, and moment characteristics is analyzed over a range of initial velocities. Unlike blunt bodies, for which flow separation may occur over an extended and geometry-dependent region, the sharp leading-edge corners of the delta wing promote concentrated flow separation and coherent tip vortices, resulting in a distinct wake topology and subsequent vortex evolution. As the wake develops, progressive deformation and asymmetric evolution of the vortex system lead to increasingly asymmetric three-dimensional vortex structures, producing an imbalance in hydrodynamic loading and resulting in pronounced roll and yaw moments even when the wing motion is constrained to a single vertical degree of freedom. The results suggest that, if rotational degrees of freedom are released, the vortex-induced moment imbalance may lead to wing deflection and trajectory instability. Meanwhile, the free surface undergoes strongly nonlinear deformation accompanied by pronounced wave radiation, with most of the wave energy propagating in the spanwise direction. The energy analysis reveals that hydrodynamic dissipation dominates the kinetic energy loss during the submerged stage, while free-surface effects become increasingly important during emergence. These findings provide new insight into the coupled evolution of vortex structures, free-surface deformation, and hydrodynamic loads during the water-exit process of finite-span lifting surfaces and highlight the potential importance of vortex-induced moment imbalance for the stability and control of trans-medium vehicles.

papers.title: Flow physics of Prandtl–rheology coupling in non-Newtonian natural convection and entropy generation within a cylindrical annulus
papers.abstract: Buoyancy-driven flow of non-Newtonian fluids in annular geometries is relevant to a range of thermal engineering applications. However, the jointly effects of fluid rheology and the Prandtl number on heat transfer and thermodynamic irreversibility in this geometry are still not well characterized. We address this gap through two-dimensional simulations of a power-law fluid undergoing steady laminar buoyancy-driven motion inside a concentric cylindrical annulus held at Ra=104, spanning three rheological states (n=0.6,1.0,1.4) crossed with three thermal-diffusivity regimes (Pr=0.0.026,0.7,10). Circulation patterns, heat transport, and entropy generation are analyzed using a comprehensive set of diagnostics, including stream-function, isotherm, and heat-function contours, along with wall-averaged Nusselt numbers, spatial entropy-generation maps, and the Bejan number. Numerical results show that the effect of Pr depends strongly on the fluid rheology. For the shear-thinning fluid, increasing Pr enhances buoyancy-driven circulation, reduces the thermal boundary-layer thickness, and increasingly confines heat transfer to the heated wall. This shift changes the dominant irreversibility from thermal to fluid-friction entropy generation. In contrast, shear-thickening fluids remain weakly convective, thermally dominated, and only weakly sensitive to the Prandtl number, while Newtonian fluids exhibit an intermediate response. A unified scaling framework is build to connect thermal boundary-layer thickness, the magnitude of heat-transfer enhancement, and irreversibility generation to Ra, Pr, and the power-law index acting together. These outcomes provide a unified physical framework for rationalizing heat transmission and thermodynamic performance for buoyancy-driven flow of shear-dependent fluids.

papers.title: Three-dimensional numerical investigation of the droplet detachment and retainment on a symmetric three-sphere cluster: The role of contact angle hysteresis
papers.abstract: How the advancing angle, receding angle, and contact angle hysteresis window independently modulate the droplet detachment, retainment, and wetting dynamics on an irregular particle has received little attention. The dynamic mechanisms of droplet impact on a symmetric three-sphere cluster are systematically investigated using a validated three-dimensional phase-field lattice Boltzmann model. By regulating the advancing angle, receding angle, surface tension, impact velocity, and gas–liquid viscosity ratio, particular attention is paid to the macroscopic deformation and mass retainment behavior of the droplet during impact. Three flow patterns are identified. The advancing angle plays a dominant role in determining flow pattern transition, whereas the receding angle acts as a fine regulator of morphological parameters such as contact area, bubble entrapment, and droplet position within a given pattern. Droplet dynamics on curved surfaces are governed by the competition among inertia, surface tension, and gravity. The initial velocity controls the impact strength, surface tension determines the dominant driving regime, and viscosity exerts only a threshold-dependent influence within specific Bond and Weber number ranges. Three flow patterns are clearly demarcated in the flow pattern map and appear sequentially. By adjusting the contact angle parameters and physical properties, the desired flow pattern can be tailored to meet specific requirements for wetted area and droplet retainment volume, enabling targeted control of droplet behavior on complex curved surfaces.

papers.title: A priori analysis of a presumed subfilter probability density function model for soot modeling in large eddy simulation
papers.abstract: This study proposes and evaluates a presumed subfilter probability density function (PDF) model for soot–turbulence–chemistry interactions in large eddy simulations (LES). Subfilter-scale variability of soot moments is modeled using an exponential distribution, whose peak near zero allows the main features of soot intermittency to be represented without introducing an explicit intermittency factor. Goodness-of-fit metrics show that the exponential form outperforms alternative distributions in most cases and closely matches soot statistics extracted from direct numerical simulation (DNS) data. The model is assessed through a series of a priori tests using filtered DNS data of turbulent flames, focusing on the reconstruction of filtered source terms, including coagulation and oxidation. For the coagulation source term, which involves nonlinear coupling among soot moments and thermochemical quantities, the exponential PDF performs better than traditional delta-function-based closures. For soot oxidation, the exponential PDF conditioned on the moment M0,1 provides the most accurate predictions. Incorporating a mixture-fraction-dependent conditional exponential PDF via a Heaviside function further improves agreement with DNS by suppressing unphysical oxidation in fuel-lean regions. Overall, the results establish the exponential distribution as a robust subfilter PDF model for soot, enabling the main effects of intermittency and soot–thermochemistry coupling to be represented in LES of turbulent combustion without additional intermittency parameters.

papers.title: Thermodynamic-force mixing activity and Darcy-scale flow-dissipation diagnostics in three-phase compositional flow through porous media
papers.abstract: Miscible and near-miscible porous-media displacement is commonly described by fronts, phase-behavior thresholds, and phase-occupancy maps. These descriptors locate compositional advance but not thermodynamic-force mixing activity or its relation to Darcy-scale pressure-work dissipation. We combine conservative three-phase compositional transport, equation-of-state fugacity, and Darcy fluxes to diagnose the compositional transition envelope ΩZ, high mixing-activity region ΩS, and high pressure-work core ΩF. The framework is evaluated in one-dimensional displacement and two-dimensional continuous-gas injection, water-alternating-gas (WAG), and concentration-controlled gas-mobility-reduction calculations. The one-dimensional case shows that the relative-fugacity-gradient indicator Imμ follows the component transition more closely than the gas-occupancy front. Within the tested covariance family, all five realizations at each nonzero permeability contrast have a broader pore-volume-averaged transition envelope than the homogeneous reference. The largest resolved increase occurs between the homogeneous and lowest-contrast cases; subsequent increments remain within realization variability, and the activity-weighted position has no monotonic trend. Chance-corrected, phase-resolved analyses show that WAG cycles reorganize contact between pressure-work pathways and hydrocarbon bands retaining relative-fugacity gradients. Water slugs redirect mechanical dissipation to water-connected pathways, while high mixing activity persists in incompletely homogenized oil-rich bands. Gas-mobility reduction requires a larger phase-potential gradient to sustain the imposed flux and restricts gas-rich compositional advance, increasing pressure work while reducing envelope area and integrated mixing activity. Carrier-phase switching, compositional relaxation, and permeability connectivity therefore jointly govern flow–mixing coupling.

papers.title: A geometry-based dynamically constrained sub-grid model for large-eddy simulation
papers.abstract: A new sub-grid scale (SGS) model for large-eddy simulation (LES), referred to as the cascade-admissible geometric SGS (CAGS) model, is proposed based on an invariant representation of the local velocity gradient. The model interprets SGS activity through the geometric structure of the resolved deformation field using invariant ratios that quantify the volumetric richness of the velocity-gradient tensor. The model naturally suppresses SGS activity in laminar or rank-deficient flow configurations while remaining invariant under coordinate transformations. Since geometric degeneracy of the deformation field does not necessarily imply absence of turbulence, a cascade-admissibility mechanism preserves SGS activity when the local flow remains capable of sustaining vortex stretching and turbulent energy transfer. Correct near-wall asymptotic behavior is derived directly from the progressive rank collapse of the velocity-gradient tensor, eliminating empirical damping functions. The closure relies solely on local tensor invariants and avoids eigenvalue or singular value evaluations, making it computationally efficient and numerically robust. Performance is assessed through homogeneous isotropic turbulence decay, periodic hill flow, and zero-pressure gradient flat plate boundary layer development. Additional validation is performed for the three-dimensional asymmetric diffuser flow of Cherry et al. [“Separated flow in a three-dimensional diffuser: Preliminary validation,” in Annual Research Briefs (Centre for Turbulence Research, Stanford University, 2006)], one of the most demanding wall-bounded LES benchmarks, characterized by corner separation, secondary flow, strong adverse pressure-gradients, and low-frequency large-scale dynamics. The results indicate that the CAGS model maintains stable laminar suppression, realistic near-wall behavior, and improved prediction of separation, reattachment, and secondary flow structures relative to several established SGS closures.

papers.title: Erratum: “Granular contact-line pinning and the collapse of macroscopic surface-energy barriers” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 083341 (2026)]
Drag-reduction mechanisms in autonomous underwater vehicle formations: Physical analysis and physics-guided surrogate optimization
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic interaction between closely spaced autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) in formation produces strongly nonlinear drag responses. In the present configuration space, two dominant pressure-related mechanisms are identified: stern pressure recovery at the leader and bow low-pressure immersion at the follower. To map these mechanisms over a wide formation parameter space, a physics-guided surrogate framework is constructed from 666 Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations of dual-AUV configurations. Total resistance is decomposed into pressure and viscous contributions and modeled separately. Guided by the effective-boundedness principle of Learning and Inference assisted by feature-space engineering, the feature space incorporates bounded geometric descriptors, a regularized turbulent-wake power-law decay, a Gaussian lateral wake profile, and pressure-interaction proxies. The resulting surrogate achieves pressure-drag R2≈0.974–0.986 and enables formation optimization over the prescribed feasible design space. At V=5.14 m/s (approximately 10 kn), the system-optimal arrangement yields a 5.9% total-drag reduction relative to two isolated AUVs, with computational fluid dynamics verification errors below 1%. The individual optima are associated with geometrically incompatible mechanism-favorable regions: the leader optimum is located on the centerline (b/D=0), whereas the follower optimum occurs at b/D=1.5, where D denotes the maximum hull diameter. This lateral separation of 1.5D places the two individual minima in different regions of the static formation space, so they are not attained simultaneously by a single feasible configuration. A nondominated leader–follower Pareto front quantifies the resulting tradeoff and locates the system optimum as a compromise between the two competing drag objectives.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic noise and noise source characteristics of an upstream hydrofoil and propeller system
papers.abstract: The upstream hydrofoil and propeller system (UHPS) is not only a major source of hydrodynamic noise in underwater vehicles but also a classic problem in fundamental fluid mechanics. This paper employs large eddy simulation and the Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings equation to study the influence of hydrofoil incidence angle on the hydrodynamic noise of the UHPS. The flow-field and acoustic prediction methods are validated. By identifying the noise sources in the system, the mechanisms linking the evolution of noise sources and far-field noise are revealed. As the hydrofoil incidence angle increases, the permeable surface noise of the UHPS increases significantly, mainly in the low-frequency range. The maximum increase reaches 6.40 dB, while the direction of maximum radiation shifts from 180° to 170°. The low-frequency energy of both the dipole and quadrupole noise is enhanced. This increase arises from two mechanisms. First, the increase in dipole noise sources is primarily caused by the amplification of near-wall pressure fluctuations on the propeller blade at shaft frequency (fs), blade passing frequency (fbp), and their harmonic frequencies. Second, the increase in wake noise sources is attributed to both the amplification of turbulent energy in the hydrofoil wake and the enhanced interference between the hydrofoil tip vortices and the propeller wake. Overall, this study reveals new physics mechanisms by which increasing the hydrofoil incidence angle strengthens the interaction of the hydrofoil and propeller, leading to enhanced pressure fluctuations on the blades and propeller wake distortion. These effects redistribute the dominant noise sources, intensifying far-field noise of the UHPS.

papers.title: Vortex instability induced by blade-attached vortex generators in a supersonic compressor cascade under downstream throttling
papers.abstract: The unsteady flow related to shockwave/boundary layer interaction is one of the key factors leading to compressor instability, so it is important to develop an effective flow control method. In this study, based on three-dimensional numerical simulation, the control mechanism of blade-attached vortex generator (BVG) on shockwave oscillation in a typical C-type supersonic cascade is systematically investigated. The results show that the BVG induced vortices (VGV) can suppress 50.8% of the separation and significantly weaken the oscillation of the shockwave; therefore, the maximum pressure ratio increases by 7.8% and reduces the total pressure loss by 8.1% at the limit stall condition. The VGV shape is closely coupled with the direction of shockwave motion. When the shockwave moves upstream, bubble-type breakdown becomes evident; when it moves downstream, the breakdown develops into spiral type. Further research shows that BVG array spacing is the key to determining the control effect: the smaller spacing scheme (BVG 1, d = 2.5x) remains primarily synchronized with the main shockwave and maintains the spanwise symmetry, while the larger spacing scheme (BVG 2, d = 2.75x) introduces a local spanwise-asymmetric response within a single periodic BVG unit. Mode analysis further indicates that mode 1f represents the fundamental shockwave motion, mode 2f characterizes the local shockwave structure and passage shockwave, and mode 0.4fBVG 2 and mode 0.6fBVG 2 are associated with the spanwise-asymmetric VGV breakdown in 0.6–0.8Cax downstream of the shockwave. The results indicate that BVG spacing affects not only the separation suppression but also the dynamic stability of shockwave–VGV coupling.

papers.title: Effects of blockage location in the impeller passages of a high-speed coolant pump on energy loss and unsteady flow characteristics
papers.abstract: High-speed coolant pumps are core components of thermal management systems in new energy vehicles and data centers. Their operational stability directly determines system heat transfer efficiency and safety. Investigating the impact of impeller blockage is crucial to enhancing equipment reliability. However, the influence of blockage location within flow passages on unsteady flow and energy loss remains unclear. Using combined numerical simulations and experiments, this study analyzes how blockages at different locations on the impeller pressure surface affect the energy characteristics, internal flow, and pressure fluctuations of a high-speed coolant pump. Results show that inlet blockage has the most significant impact on hydraulic performance. Under high flow rates, impeller entropy production accounts for over 50% of the total loss. Mid-section blockage causes local flow acceleration and static pressure drops, raising upstream pressure fluctuations at the shaft frequency. However, this disturbance weakens downstream due to passage constraints. Outlet blockage severely disrupts outflow uniformity, creating a high-kinetic-energy distorted jet. This jet strongly impinges on the tongue, inducing flow separation and mixing losses that cause a sharp efficiency drop under high flow rates. Additionally, pressure fluctuation characteristics and rotor radial force vector distributions can effectively locate the flow distortion source.

papers.title: Wake dynamics and flow mechanisms of narrow-gap flow beneath a slender rectangular cylinder under unsteady inflow
papers.abstract: Narrow-gap flow beneath a slender rectangular cylinder is relevant to small-opening discharge in hydraulic structures, yet the mechanisms governing wake dynamics and turbulence evolution remain unclear. A coupled volume of fluid-large eddy simulation framework is employed to investigate the flow characteristics and hydrodynamic responses under different opening ratios E and hydraulic head differences P*. The results show that E regulates narrow-gap flow through geometric confinement and downstream momentum transport. Smaller openings intensify gap-jet acceleration and extend transient shear-layer development, whereas larger openings promote wake expansion and turbulent transport. The downstream wake is divided into three regions: the narrow-gap-influenced region, approximate self-similarity region, and far-downstream confinement region. Furthermore, increasing E advances the onset of approximate self-similarity, which occurs at x/D ≈ 5 for E = 0.2. Meanwhile, the enhanced downstream turbulence is accompanied by reduced local shear production and subgrid-scale dissipation near the gap. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition reveals that the transient wake is governed by multiple energetic coherent structures rather than a single periodic vortex shedding process. These flow features modify surface pressure distribution, with upstream mean pressure decreasing by approximately 44% as E increases. In contrast, P* primarily controls transient hydraulic forcing. A larger P* enhances pressure-driven acceleration, strengthens shear-layer instability and vortex development, and increases pressure fluctuations and hydrodynamic loading. The maximum drag coefficient increases approximately threefold as P* rises from 0.1 to 0.3. These findings clarify the effects of geometric confinement and hydraulic forcing on transient narrow-gap flow and hydrodynamic response.

papers.title: Breakup, three-stage velocity and internal flow structures of low-Weber-number liquid-metal jets under transverse magnetic fields
papers.abstract: Using three-dimensional direct numerical simulations, this study investigates breakup and internal flows of liquid-metal jets in the dripping regime (We=1.695) under transverse magnetic fields (0≤Ha≤360). Increasing Ha enhances stability. Morphology turns from asymmetric at Ha=0 to uniform at Ha≥180. Breakup length remains stable at Ha=180 but grows with breakup events at Ha=288 and 360. Centerline velocity transitions from a two-stage to a three-stage pattern between 180<Ha<288: two-stage for Ha≤180, three-stage for Ha≥288. In Segment I, velocity decreases linearly with deceleration rising as Ha increases. For Ha≥288, Segment III shows linear velocity increase with expanding coverage but declining growth rate. For the two Ha≥288 cases, Segment I's deceleration zone uniformly extends to x*=0.65. Internal flow reveals progressive longitudinalization of the velocity core, with transverse gradients nearly vanishing at Ha=360. Lorentz-force momentum confinement homogenizes velocity and lengthens the jet. Since only discrete Ha values are simulated, the exact transition threshold is bracketed within 180<Ha<288. These results support magnetic regulation of liquid-metal jets for fusion devices. Future work will refine sampling between 180 and 288 and extend to higher Ha and varied We.

papers.title: Mesoscopic modeling and analysis of flow and heat transfer around a roughness-controlled string-grid wire
papers.abstract: String-grid wires are typical fine-scale heat-transfer and flow-disturbance elements in wet string grids, air-handling systems, and gas–liquid heat and moisture exchange devices. Their surface structures directly affect near-wall boundary-layer development, wake-vortex evolution, and the overall heat-transfer performance. To reveal the effect of regular roughness on flow and heat transfer around a string-grid wire, a two-dimensional model with circumferentially arranged roughness elements was developed. A double-distribution-function D2Q9 lattice Boltzmann model was established to solve the flow and temperature fields, while the rough fluid–solid boundary was treated using solid-region mask identification and a halfway bounce-back scheme. The effects of relative roughness e/D on the velocity field, vorticity field, drag coefficient, temperature field, and average Nusselt number were systematically analyzed. The results show that roughness elements significantly modify the near-wall flow and wake-vortex structures by inducing local acceleration, flow separation, and enhanced wake disturbance. As e/D increases, the time-averaged drag coefficient rises from 1.57 for the smooth wire to 2.48 at e/D = 0.16, indicating a substantial increase in flow resistance. The average Nusselt number first decreases slightly and then increases with increasing roughness. At e/D = 0.12 and 0.16, the average Nusselt numbers reach 6.55 and 6.68, respectively, both higher than that of the smooth wire, 6.22. The simulated fields suggest competition between local stagnant shielding and thermal-boundary-layer renewal; this is a qualitative physical interpretation rather than a directly quantified mechanism. At e/D = 0.16, the Nusselt-number gain is approximately 7.4%, whereas the drag-coefficient increase is approximately 58.0%. The findings provide a numerical basis for evaluating roughness structures on string-grid wire surfaces and designing fine-scale enhanced heat-transfer elements.

papers.title: Wind-load characteristics of photovoltaic arrays over dune terrain with windbreak barriers
papers.abstract: The construction of photovoltaic (PV) power stations on dune landforms represents an important pathway for coordinating ecological protection and energy development. However, PV arrays in dune regions are vulnerable to strong winds, making windbreak barriers an important protective measure for reducing wind loads. Previous studies have primarily investigated the wind-protection effects of windbreak barriers on PV systems over flat terrain, whereas the wind-load characteristics of PV arrays under the coupled effects of windbreak barriers and dune terrain remain underexplored. Therefore, numerical simulations were used to investigate the effects of windbreak barrier porosity, installation distance, barrier height, and PV panel tilt angle on the wind-load characteristics of PV arrays in dune terrain. The results show that, as barrier porosity increases, the absolute value of the overall resultant force coefficient of the PV array (∣CN∣) first decreases and then increases, reaching a minimum at a porosity of 0.4. Increasing the distance between the barrier and the PV array causes the leeward recirculation zone to shift forward and weakens the wind-protection effect. As barrier height increases, the CN initially decreases markedly and then tends to stabilize at a height of 2 m, where it is ∼54.12% lower than that under the no-barrier condition. With increasing PV panel tilt angle, the overall ∣CN∣ first decreases and then increases, reaching a minimum at a tilt angle of 30°. This study provides a theoretical reference for optimizing windbreak barrier parameters and improving the wind-resistant design of PV power stations in dune regions.

papers.title: Design and characterization of a Taylor–Couette device for studying factors affecting turbulence-induced hemolysis
papers.abstract: Blood-perfused medical devices operate predominantly under turbulent flow conditions, associated with increased flow-induced hemolysis. However, current hemolysis models are based on laminar flow experiments and do not account for turbulence. This study establishes an experimental setup to quantify turbulence-induced hemolysis and enables the development of hypotheses regarding interactions between turbulent flow and erythrocytes. A Taylor–Couette-device with counter-rotating cylinders was developed, operating with 20 ml fluid volume and capable of generating, visualizing, and measuring laminar and turbulent flow properties at identical mean shear rates. Flow regimes were characterized using an image-based, custom-trained neural network to ensure consistent classification across fluids. Experiments were performed with water and water–dextran solution as mono-phase blood-analogue fluids at physiologic mean shear rates of 256, 396, and 537 s−1, with one laminar and three turbulent measurement points. Laser Doppler anemometry (LDA) provided flow characterization, while torque measurements at the inner cylinder were used to estimate energy dissipation. The system reliably achieved laminar and turbulent flow regimes. LDA measurements provided velocity profiles, turbulence intensities, and Reynolds shear stresses in good agreement with literature. The intended increase in turbulence intensity across the turbulent points was realized at 396 and 537 s−1 but not at 256 s−1. Torque-, wall shear stress-, and LDA-based estimates of dissipation and Kolmogorov length scales agree in order of magnitude, with a near-constant offset attributable to bearing friction and motor losses. The Taylor–Couette-device is suitable for controlled study of turbulence-related hemolysis. Higher mean shear rates will require a reduced gap width, and two-phase blood-analogue fluids should be considered in future studies.

papers.title: A theoretical model on the critical pressure of one colloidal particle entering the constricted throat
papers.abstract: The migration, deformation, and plugging of colloidal particles in porous media are crucial in oil field operations such as profile control, water shutoff, and enhanced oil recovery. Traditional research constantly oversimplifies colloidal particles as rigid or linear bodies, hindering the accurate description of their nonlinear mechanical responses to significant deformations in a constricted throat. To address this issue, this paper observes the plugging behavior of colloidal particles within a constricted throat in the experiments, and subsequently employs the two-parameter Mooney–Rivlin hyperelastic constitutive model to establish a theoretical analysis framework and a finite element numerical simulation method for the passage of a colloidal particle through a constricted throat. The validity of the theoretical model is confirmed via the temporal variation of elastic strain energy in the simulation. The findings reveal that higher particle hardness, larger particle size, smaller pore throat diameter, and greater friction coefficient enhance the elastic recovery force, average normal contact pressure, and energy dissipation, thereby reinforcing the plugging tendency of colloidal particles. Additionally, higher external pressure improves the ability of colloidal particles to overcome energy barriers, enabling deeper migration. Importantly, dimensionless driving ratio and migration coefficient are introduced to establish criteria for distinguishing colloidal particle passage, critical migration, and plugging states. Moreover, an empirical correlation between critical pressure, matching ratio, and friction coefficient is proposed. This paper addresses the size design, optimization of the material parameter, and regulation of injection pressure for profile control and water plugging agents.

papers.title: Pressure characteristics of multiphase flow in an underwater pressure vessel subject to gas injection and water discharge
papers.abstract: This study investigates the multiphase coupling characteristics and evolution mechanisms of the flow field induced by high-pressure gas release in a confined space. The gas supply and drainage mechanisms that occur during the gas–liquid displacement are systematically clarified through a combined experimental–numerical methodology that accounts for the pressure decay and air compressibility effects of the air tank on the water drainage process. The results demonstrate that the transient pressure characteristics of the gas supply system play a dominant role in determining the drainage dynamics. On this basis, the ascent time of pressure-driven drainage in the water tank can be predicted with a maximum error of 1.4%. Furthermore, the concept of an effective pressure-driven drainage interval is proposed. Theoretical derivation and dimensional analysis reveal that this effective pressure-driven drainage interval is inversely correlated with the drainage duration. The results presented herein allow us to establish a framework for understanding pressure-driven ballast systems, and provide references for pressure-based surfacing design and strategy optimization.

papers.title: Interfacial oscillations and internal flow dynamics of a freely closed ventilated supercavity
papers.abstract: An experimental investigation was conducted to examine the interfacial oscillations and internal flow dynamics of freely closed ventilated supercavities. Within the present parameter range, five closure modes were observed: Foam cavity, hybrid foam cavity and transparent cavity, re-entrant jet (RJ), hybrid twin vortex and re-entrant jet, and twin vortex. The cavity closure mode exhibits path dependence, and a stable RJ mode cannot be obtained at fixed ventilation rates and incoming flow velocities. The interfacial oscillations of the cavity propagate downstream with time, and their propagation velocity is primarily governed by the incoming flow. The low-frequency pressure fluctuations inside the cavity (0–50 Hz) are influenced by the incoming flow, whereas the intermediate-frequency fluctuations (50–300 Hz) are self-excited by the cavity. In the high-frequency range (300–3000 Hz), equally spaced energy peaks induced by standing-wave effects are observed. For all test conditions, local energy peaks occur at f = 125 Hz in both the pressure spectra and the cavity interface oscillation spectra. The internal flow can be divided into a ventilation affected region, a shear layer region, and a recirculation region. The axial velocity inside the cavity increases with increasing ventilation rate but decreases with increasing Froude number. Limited and gas exchange between the shear layer and recirculation regions is observed within the measurement range, without abrupt or order-of-magnitude variations.

papers.title: GINTO: Geometry-informed transformer neural operator for fluid flows on arbitrary domains
papers.abstract: Generalizing neural operators across varying geometries remains a central challenge in scientific machine learning. While most operator-learning frameworks assume fixed geometries and parametric variability in boundary conditions or coefficients, many fluid-dynamics problems require prediction across distinct domains. In this work, we introduce the Geometry-informed transformer neural operator (GINTO), a physics-informed architecture that reformulates the physics-informed neural transformer operator (PINTO) paradigm for domain-geometry generalization. The proposed model uses a spatial representation of obstacle geometry encoded as point clouds and propagates geometric information to interior evaluation points through stacked linear cross-attention blocks. The approach is based on a point-wise collocation representation and does not require a structured or unstructured body-fitted mesh, geometric parameterization, or domain alignment. Training requires neither data nor reference solutions, physical consistency is enforced through residual minimization of the steady incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. To systematically study geometric generalization, we introduce a composite geometric distance metric and construct training subsets with controlled coverage of the geometric space. Numerical experiments demonstrate that extrapolation accuracy strongly depends on geometric diversity in the training set. Increasing coverage yields substantial improvements up to a saturation regime, beyond which gains become marginal. Compared with the original PINTO architecture, the proposed model achieves comparable accuracy while delivering a 7–10-fold reduction in training time on the benchmark problems considered in this study, thereby enabling large-scale experiments with diverse geometry sets. The results establish geometry-conditioned transformer operators as a scalable and physically consistent surrogate modeling framework for fluid flows on arbitrary domains, with relevance to shape optimization and geometry-driven simulation tasks. The code and experiments are available in the open-source framework MultiPINN at https://github.com/labadt/multipinn.

papers.title: Microfluidic experimental study on clay particle migration and pore-throat clogging: Implications for hydrate-bearing clayey-silty sediments
papers.abstract: Hydrate dissociation significantly changes pore water salinity and fluid flow conditions in clayey-silty sediments, triggering the migration of clay particles. However, previous studies have predominantly used spherical SiO2 particles as substitutes for clay minerals, leaving the migration and clogging behavior of actual clay particles, and its quantitative characterization, largely unresolved. In this study, microfluidic experiments were systematically conducted to investigate the migration and clogging behaviors of clay and SiO2 particles under various conditions, including different pore-particle diameter ratios, particle mass fractions, flow rates, gas–water ratios, and salinities. The results show that clay particles exhibit significantly lower critical clogging mass fractions (e.g., 0.2%–0.4% at a pore-throat diameter of 50 μm) than SiO2 particles (0.6%–1.0% under the same pore-throat diameter), indicating that SiO2-based proxies may systematically underestimate the risk of pore clogging. Moreover, clay-induced clogs demonstrate greater structural stability, whereas SiO2-induced clogs are prone to “clogging instability” under dynamic flow conditions. Mechanistic analysis reveals that clay migration is governed by electrostatic forces and salinity-dependent double-layer effects, whereas SiO2 migration is fluid-controlled. These quantitative findings provide a more accurate framework for predicting permeability damage in hydrate-bearing clayey-silty sediments.

papers.title: A condition-driven globally aware point cloud network for rapid surface field prediction of cross-domain flight vehicles
papers.abstract: Rapid prediction of aerodynamic and aerothermal surface fields is critical for the design and real-time monitoring of cross-domain flight vehicles, yet conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) remains prohibitively expensive. Here, a condition-driven globally aware point cloud network (CD-GPN) is presented, achieving millisecond-scale, near-CFD-accuracy predictions of surface pressure and heat flux. Based on PointNeXt, CD-GPN integrates three core components: geometrically enhanced inverted residual modules for local geometric perception; a condition feature modulation mechanism via feature-wise linear modulation to inject flight conditions into deep feature streams; and a global interaction module on condition-modulated latent modes to capture long-range flow-field correlations. Extensively tested across Mach 5–15, altitudes of 20–40 km, and angles of attack of 0°–10°, CD-GPN outperforms mainstream baselines. Specifically, it yields a mean normalized root mean square error of 1.77% for single-configuration pressure prediction, and 1.03% and 2.07% for multi-configuration pressure and heat flux predictions, respectively. Furthermore, it demonstrates good extrapolation robustness to unseen flight conditions and novel geometries, and transfer fine-tuning with only a small number of target-configuration samples can further reduce the cross-topology blind-prediction error. Meanwhile, in terms of efficiency, it reduces the single evaluation time from 45 min (CFD) to 134 ms. These results establish CD-GPN as an efficient, physics-aware surrogate bridging offline simulation and online monitoring for next-generation aerospace vehicle design.

papers.title: Low-density gas cavity-mediated underwater shaped charge jet penetration enhancement: Fluid shielding and shock-induced target pre-weakening
papers.abstract: To address the penetration performance degradation of underwater shaped charge jets due to severe kinetic energy attenuation and interfacial instability in water, this study proposes a coupled structure combining a linear shaped charge (LSC) and flexible detonating cord (FDC) and examines the interactions among the shock wave, gas cavity, and LSC jet. In this structure, the FDC is first detonated to create a gas cavity. At its maximum expansion, the LSC is initiated, allowing the jet to form and stretch within the low-resistance gas cavity. This reduces resistance and limits momentum exchange with the surrounding water. The study describes the “slow–fast–slow” three-stage stretching behavior of the jet as it travels across the water–gas interface, along with the interaction between the shock wave and the gas cavity. A criterion is proposed for selecting the coupling distance. The changes in jet velocity, effective stretch length, and penetration depth at the selected coupling distance are also discussed. Results show that, at a 5-cm coupling distance, jet length increased from 5.12 to 7.49 cm, compared with 4.76 to 6.31 cm for the single LSC; thus, net jet extension increased by 52.9%. Jet-tip velocity increased from 893 to 1160 m/s (+29.9%), while at 183 μs, penetration depth increased from 4.19 to 7.03 mm (+2.84 mm). The proposed criterion can be used to estimate the coupling distance for various water depths and charge parameters, providing a reference for structural design and parameter optimization in underwater shaped charge applications.

papers.title: Pulsatile non-Newtonian blood flow in arterial aneurysms: Parametric hemodynamic characterization using the finite volume incompressible lattice Boltzmann method
papers.abstract: Arterial aneurysms pose a significant public health challenge, with their rupture leading to life-threatening cardiovascular complications. The present study investigates the interplay between aneurysm size, pulsatile flow conditions (Reynolds and Womersley numbers), blood rheology (Carreau number), and key hemodynamic indices—time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS), oscillatory shear index (OSI), and reverse flow fraction (RFF)—to characterize the hemodynamic environment associated with aneurysm progression and rupture risk. Pulsatile non-Newtonian blood flow is simulated using the finite volume incompressible lattice Boltzmann method (FV-iLBM), which captures shear-rate-dependent viscosity through the Carreau model while recovering the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on unstructured meshes without an iterative pressure–velocity coupling. Increasing Reynolds number raises peak TAWSS and intraluminal pressure while reducing the wall area with OSI >0.20 from 64% to 2.65% (Re=50–200)—exposing competing inertial and oscillatory pathways whose dominance shifts with Re. Higher Womersley numbers amplify shear-layer oscillations and separation dynamics, whereas lower Carreau numbers sustain an elevated effective viscosity that suppresses vortical structures and lowers OSI. Aneurysm size critically modulates these effects: larger aneurysms generate a peak RFF roughly twice that of smaller lesions (∼16% vs ∼7.5%), a distal peak TAWSS about 16% higher, and an 18% collapse of centerline velocity, whereas smaller aneurysms exhibit higher local OSI peaks. By resolving these competing mechanisms, the study demonstrates that no single index captures aneurysm rupture risk and that geometric growth simultaneously escalates peak mechanical stress, expands the atheroprone wall footprint, and elevates the wall pressure loading.

papers.title: Valve flow–coupled temperature–pressure modeling for hydrate formation conditions prediction in underground gas storage wellbores
papers.abstract: Valve actuation during gas withdrawal from underground gas storage triggers coupled flow, pressure, and temperature transients that can rapidly push wellbore fluids into hydrate-stable conditions. Conventional models prescribe flow rate or decouple thermal and hydraulic fields, missing how valve dynamics reshape the thermodynamic path. We develop a transient framework that integrates a dynamic valve flow relation, a two-way coupled wellbore temperature–pressure model, and the Chen–Guo hydrate phase equilibrium model. The framework reproduces field flow rates within 10%, and temperature and pressure profiles within 2%, and matches independent hydrate equilibrium data within 0.5%. The simulations show that valve regulation introduces competing hydraulic and thermal response timescales in the evolving wellbore thermodynamic state. Rapid regulation generates strong pressure transients but allows little cooling, temporarily preserving the hydrate-free margin. Slow regulation permits substantial thermal relaxation, dropping the gas temperature by more than 3 °C under low flow and dramatically shrinking the safety margin. This competition determines whether pressure or temperature governs the approach to the hydrate stability boundary. Tubing diameter alters the coupling strength by modifying velocity, frictional pressure loss, and Joule–Thomson cooling; heavier hydrocarbons raise the hydrate equilibrium temperature and favor structure II hydrate formation. These results indicate that valve dynamics should be treated as a time-dependent operational boundary when evaluating the wellbore thermodynamic trajectory and hydrate risk during UGS withdrawal.

papers.title: Effects of tangential-orifice diameter on low-frequency combustion stability of a hypergolic dual-swirl liquid–liquid injector
papers.abstract: In a liquid–liquid coaxial dual-swirl injector, the tangential-orifice diameters affect the tangential-entry area, pressure drop, swirl strength, liquid-sheet momentum balance, and injector dynamic response, thereby influencing combustion stability. In this study, nine monomethyl hydrazine/nitrogen tetroxide (MMH/NTO) hot-fire conditions were tested in a model combustor using a baseline faceplate and two modified faceplates with separately reduced fuel-side and oxidizer-side tangential-orifice diameters. For the baseline configuration, self-sustained chamber-pressure oscillations were observed over the tested oxygen-to-fuel (O/F) ratio range, with peak-to-peak amplitudes exceeding the instability threshold. Reducing the fuel-side tangential-orifice diameter to 0.78d suppressed the dominant chamber–injector–feed coupling mode over the tested O/F range. Under the near-rated condition, the chamber-pressure peak-to-peak ratio decreased from 34.21% to 3.67%, and the combustion efficiency increased. Injector-response calculations indicate that the reduced fuel-side orifice decreases the dynamic gain near the sensitive frequency band, while the increased estimated fuel momentum–flux ratio may enhance inner/outer liquid-sheet interaction. These effects jointly weaken the feedback loop responsible for medium–low-frequency combustion instability. In contrast, reducing the oxidizer-side tangential-orifice diameter to 0.75D produces a strong operating-condition dependence. Stable combustion was obtained only under the fuel-rich condition, whereas near-rated and oxidizer-rich conditions remained unstable. The results show that the stability response to fuel-side and oxidizer-side tangential-orifice reduction is asymmetric, highlighting the dominant role of fuel-side injector dynamics in the present MMH/NTO dual-swirl combustor. The findings provide experimental support and physical guidance for optimizing injector elements in high-pressure liquid attitude and orbit control thrusters.

papers.title: Suppressing the instability of impinging two-phase flow by anisotropic wetting strips
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of anisotropic wetting strips in suppressing interfacial instability within a gas–water impinging system in a T-shaped microchannel. To accurately capture the high-speed interface dynamics, a modified dynamic contact angle model was implemented within the Open-source Field Operation and Manipulation framework. Numerical results indicate that the primary drivers of interfacial instability are intense pressure fluctuations and kinetic energy surges induced by the violent impinging of the gas and liquid phases. The findings demonstrate that introducing anisotropic strips with a pronounced wettability gradient is a highly effective method for enhancing interfacial stability. This wettability contrast generates a significant unbalanced Young's force at the strip boundaries, which serves as a robust anchoring mechanism to tightly pin the triple-phase contact line (TPCL). This pinning effect effectively suppresses the random oscillation and slippage of the TPCL, thereby stabilizing the global flow field. Furthermore, comparative analysis reveals that high-gradient anisotropic strips maintain a straight TPCL and a smooth, stable concave meniscus, whereas uniform surfaces or low-gradient strips result in chaotic interfacial deformations.

papers.title: Separation control, resistance reduction, and convective heat transfer enhancement in tube bundle using upstream splitter plates
papers.abstract: Enhancing thermal transport while reducing flow resistance remains a fundamental challenge in bluff body flows. Downstream splitter plates can alleviate leeward form drag but fail to reduce the windward form drag. To simultaneously minimize both the windward and leeward form drag while enhancing heat transfer, a novel heat transfer channel design with upstream splitter plates is proposed. The impact of the plate length ratios L/D of the upstream splitter plates on the flow and thermal fields is numerically studied. The results show that the upstream splitter plates notably reduce the adverse pressure gradient on the leeward side of the tube, which delays the boundary layer separation, thereby shrinking the wake size. Meanwhile, the upstream splitter plates reduce the favorable pressure gradient on the windward side of the tube, which reduces the windward form drag. These two mechanisms effectively reduce the total form drag of the cross-flow tube bundle. Furthermore, the combined effects of the delay of the separation point and the splitter plates lead to a significant improvement in heat transfer. Compared with the channel without splitter plates, f decreases by up to 23.49%, while Nu increases by up to 64.20%. Under identical flow conditions, the optimal overall performance η is 1.42 at L/D = 1.0, whereas under identical pump power, it is 1.31 at L/D = 1.5. These findings indicate that installing upstream splitter plates is an effective passive strategy for simultaneously reducing flow resistance and enhancing heat transfer in cross-flow tube bundle channels.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation of interference-induced aerodynamic characteristics and flow dynamics around a high-rise building
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic interference among high-rise buildings can substantially alter surface pressures and unsteady wind loads in urban environments. This study investigates the interference effects induced by an interfering building on a principal tall building using a validated large-eddy simulation framework benchmarked against wind tunnel measurements. Representative configurations involving lateral offset, rotation angle, and height ratio are examined through pressure interference factors, flow-field distribution, power spectral density (PSD), and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). Results show that mean pressure interference is mainly expressed as large-scale pressure redistribution, with the maximum absolute mean pressure interference factor reaching approximately 2.0. In contrast, root mean square (RMS) pressure interference is more localized near the windward-edge and adjacent side-face regions, with the maximum RMS pressure interference factor reaching approximately 3.0. Lateral offset configuration promotes asymmetric wake-edge exposure and enhances pressure fluctuations near the exposed region of the windward face and the adjacent lateral face. Building rotation redistributes the wake trajectory and pressure-interference pattern, while similar mean wake patterns may exhibit substantially different temporal coherence and pressure spectra. The height ratio of the interfering building governs the vertical transition from roof-level overflow impingement to wake-dominated shielding. POD analysis shows that the leading coherent mode contributes up to 42.2% of the fluctuation energy in the lateral-offset cases. Together with PSD results, this indicates that localized pressure amplification is governed primarily by low-frequency coherent wake motions rather than spatially uniform random turbulence amplification. These findings reveal the underlying mechanism by which geometric interference reorganizes coherent wake motions and induces localized aerodynamic amplification.

papers.title: Flow control and wake vortex dynamics induced by trailing edge serrations in cascade blade
papers.abstract: Trailing-edge (TE) serrations serve as an effective flow control strategy with the superior wake-flow adaptability. While existing studies are mainly focused on overall aerodynamic benefits of blade cascade, the underlying wake/vortex control mechanisms, particularly the effects of serration spanwise positions, remain to be further understood. Based on aerodynamic performance tests in a cascade wind tunnel, the accuracy of computational fluid dynamics numerical model is validated. Then considering the different incidences and Mach numbers, flow wake and vortex dynamics are analyzed in tip/middle/root spanwise positions. The results show that the serrated TE significantly reduces aerodynamic loss and improves flow characteristics of the blade cascade. Compared to the baseline, the average ω of serrated cascade decreases by 7.05% at 0.4Ma and 0° incidence. For the role of serration, the tip region exhibits the largest reduction of 16.2% in total pressure loss, the middle region significantly promotes momentum transport and turbulent mixing, and the root region achieves pressure fluctuation attenuation. This is mainly attributed to the serration-induced jet flow and wake-vortex breakdown. In addition, different incidences and Mach numbers have a sensitive effect on aerodynamic performance of serrated cascades. Relative to the baseline cascade, the moderate positive incidence can contribute to reducing unsteady pressure fluctuations and flow stability, and the middle region of serration at 0.7Ma exhibits a maximum local reduction of 35.9% in total pressure loss. These findings provide a theoretical basis and engineering guidance for the high-performance biomimetic blade design.

papers.title: Effect of the internal cooling structure on film outflow under rotating conditions. II. Hole position
papers.abstract: This paper experimentally investigates the effect of two hole positions (post-rib and pre-rib) on film outflow characteristics under different rotation numbers (Ro = 0, ±0.4, ±0.8) and blowing ratios (M = 0.5, 1.0) by time-resolved particle image velocimetry. The results indicate that at M = 1.0, both hole positions maintain normal film outflow. At M = 0.5, mainstream backflow into the internal cooling channel is observed for the first time under rotating conditions, which is alleviated with increasing Ro, especially under counterclockwise rotation. The post-rib configuration promotes coolant entry into the film hole, whereas the pre-rib configuration, located within the recirculation zone behind the rib, significantly hinders outflow and intensifies backward flow. At the same absolute Ro, counterclockwise rotation enhances film outflow more effectively than clockwise rotation, and this enhancement is more pronounced at the lower blowing ratio. Additionally, the coolant jet exhibits spanwise deflection under the combined action of centrifugal force and Coriolis force. Clockwise rotation causes a pronounced rightward deflection, while counterclockwise rotation results in minimal lateral shift due to force cancellation. The jet velocity and normal range are substantially larger for the post-rib than for the pre-rib.

papers.title: Fully coupled two-dimensional numerical simulation of wave interaction with an elastic wall in a narrow gap
papers.abstract: Narrow-gap resonance is commonly investigated under rigid-wall assumptions, although deformable boundaries occur in many confined-water systems. This study aims to clarify how elastic-wall deformation and the geometry of the bottom passage affect the coupled hydrodynamic and structural responses of an open-top confined-water system. A two-dimensional strongly coupled partitioned finite volume method–finite element method model, implemented using OpenFOAM, CalculiX, and preCICE, is validated against published hydroelastic results and wave-flume measurements. Wall stiffness and draft are varied to evaluate the local flow, confined free-surface motion, wave reflection and dissipation, hydrodynamic loading, wall displacement, and response phase. The results show that decreasing wall stiffness increases wall deformation and weakens the high-velocity region beneath the wall, thereby reducing the free-surface oscillation inside the confined region. The near-rigid and moderately elastic cases retain a low-reflection–high-dissipation response within a similar frequency range, whereas the most flexible case weakens this feature, with a higher reflection minimum and a lower dissipation maximum. The most flexible wall exhibits reduced load amplitudes at intermediate and higher frequencies, together with a more pronounced phase lag. Reducing the wall draft enlarges the bottom passage, shifts the reflection minimum and dissipation maximum toward higher frequencies, and decreases both load and displacement amplitudes. The results provide guidance for selecting wall stiffness and draft in flexible wave-energy devices and elastic coastal-protection components.

papers.title: Thermochemical non-equilibrium effect on the combustion signatures of rocket exhaust plumes
papers.abstract: Thermochemical non-equilibrium effects directly influence temperature and species distributions in rocket exhaust plumes. However, studies focusing on the thermochemical non-equilibrium effects in rocket plumes are limited. This study develops a two-temperature flow field model incorporating translational–rotational and vibrational–electronic temperatures through an additional internal energy equation coupled with the Navier–Stokes (NS) equations. Energy relaxation is computed using the Landau–Teller formula with Park's high-temperature correction. Transport properties are derived from Wilke's mixing rule combined with Blottner's viscosity curves and Lennard-Jones collision integrals. A nine-species, ten-reaction finite-rate chemistry model describes the chemical kinetics. Simulations of an aluminum-free double-base propellant rocket plume are conducted across altitudes of 20–80 km and free-stream velocities of 1500–2500 m/s. At 20 km, the translational and vibrational temperatures differ by less than 13% locally, indicating near-equilibrium conditions. At 80 km, the temperature separation reaches 300 K in shock regions, and species concentration predictions deviate by over 50% from equilibrium model results. The thermochemical non-equilibrium factor increases by three orders of magnitude from 20 km (10−4) to 80 km (0.3–0.4). The free-stream velocity effect exhibits altitude-dependent reversal: at altitudes below 50 km, higher velocities increase species factors by suppressing dilution, whereas above 60 km, enhanced shear-layer mixing causes species factors to decrease with velocity. For the investigated aluminum-free double-base propellant rocket plume configuration, these findings establish 60 km as the critical altitude above which two-temperature non-equilibrium models become necessary for accurate plume characterization.

papers.title: Electrohydrodynamic migration of charged non-spherical particles in non-Newtonian Poiseuille flows
papers.abstract: The precise active manipulation of complex suspensions plays a critical role in frontier applications such as microfluidic cell sorting, electrochemical crystallization, and polymer composite processing. Therefore, this study develops a mesoscopic computational framework based on the diffuse-interface lattice Boltzmann method to investigate the electrohydrodynamic migration of charged highly anisotropic particles in non-Newtonian Poiseuille flows. By coupling the leaky dielectric model with generalized power-law constitutive equations, the dynamic interplay among background shear-flow, localized rheological modifications, and external electrostatic driving forces is decoupled. Transient kinematic analyses reveal that external electric fields induce highly nonlinear trajectory bifurcations, forcing the particle to cross the channel centerline and reverse rotational direction upon exceeding a critical voltage threshold. Furthermore, the topological anisotropy of fourfold symmetric cross-shaped structures triggers periodic tumbling and wavy migration trajectories, driven by relentless competition between localized electrostatic alignment torque and continuous hydrodynamic shear torque. Extending this investigation into non-Newtonian regimes unveils complex macroscopic transport phenomena. While shear-thinning fluids accelerate cross-stream migration through a low-viscosity lubricating envelope, shear-thickening fluids similarly facilitate faster attainment of steady-state equilibrium. This accelerated migration is primarily attributed to generating low-viscosity stagnation zones at the poles of the migrating particle alongside an amplified upward shear-gradient lift. Finally, a multiphysics phase diagram is constructed to delineate terminal dynamic states, identifying three regimes: central oscillation, chaotic tumbling, and wall-constrained rocking. The established boundaries highlight rheological dependence, demonstrating that local viscosity modifications delay the onset of wall-constrained rocking. These findings provide theoretical insights for optimizing electrokinetic separation technologies involving multimorphic suspensions.

papers.title: Internal solitary wave attenuation, spectral evolution, and induced flow fields beneath rigid ice covers
papers.abstract: The interaction between internal solitary waves (ISWs) and ice cover is an important process governing wave deformation, energy dissipation, and mixing in polar oceans. In this study, laboratory experiments were conducted in a strongly stratified silicone oil–water two-layer system using a rigid, nondeformable ice-cover model to examine the combined effects of ice-cover position and incident-wave amplitude on ISW evolution. Five dimensionless ice-cover positions and four incident-wave amplitudes were considered. Image-based interface extraction, particle image velocimetry, and wavelet analysis were used to quantify waveform evolution, spatial amplitude attenuation, spectral redistribution, and flow-field responses. The results show that the vertical position of the ice cover strongly regulates the transition of ISWs from stable propagation to instability-dominated evolution. Four representative regimes were identified: wave flattening, wave reflection, interfacial instability, and wave breaking. Under upper-layer ice-cover conditions (hi/h1 = 0.4, 0.6), wave-height attenuation was relatively limited, with the downstream normalized amplitude remaining at approximately 0.85–0.95. In contrast, when the ice cover was located near or below the density interface (hi/h1 = 0, −0.4, and −0.6), the normalized amplitude decreased sharply to approximately 0.50–0.65, indicating substantially enhanced wave deformation, reflection, and localized energy dissipation. Increasing the incident-wave amplitude further intensified nonlinear wave–ice interaction, producing stronger waveform distortion, broader wavelet spectra, and more fragmented vortical structures. These findings demonstrate that ice-cover position mainly controls the attenuation pathway and dissipation mode of ISWs, while incident-wave amplitude regulates the strength of nonlinear instability and spectral energy redistribution beneath ice-covered waters.

papers.title: The compound mechanisms of plunging jet-induced sediment transport: The roles of turbulence-enhanced pressure (pressing), flow velocity gradient (scraping), and vortical structures
papers.abstract: Past research on plunging jet-induced sediment transport (PJST) acknowledged heterogeneous effects on scour evolution and semi-empirically associated the heterogeneous effects with flow velocity and turbulence based on the classical theories of sediment transport. The classical theories were mostly derived from sediment entrainment by channel flow induced bed shear action and metastable bursting cycles without jet impingement. Jet impingement, however, is inherently vital for PJST, and its phenomenological mechanisms causing the heterogeneous effects remain poorly documented. This research generates quantitative indices of dynamic pressure across the global-domain scour hole by numerically solving the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes or Navier–Stokes equations with particle image velocimetry data. An index, i.e., the ratio of pressure energy to averaged kinetic energy, quantitatively demonstrates the dominant role of dynamic pressure in PJST, which has always been ignored in the existing models of PJST. This research provides a detailed spatiotemporal analysis of the individual and compound effects of pressure, turbulence, flow velocity gradient, vorticity, and vortical structures on jet-induced sediment transport in the jet impingement region. Most importantly, this research phenomenologically unveils the compound mechanisms of PJST by explaining the heterogeneous effects of jet impingement on different parts of the scour slopes.

papers.title: Throat localized magnetohydrodynamic actuation for thrust enhancement in supersonic rocket nozzles
papers.abstract: Among other important considerations in rocket nozzle design, the geometry limitations remained a big challenge. The geometry constraint imposed by the throat section can greatly influence the effects of flow choking, pressure profiles, and overall thrust efficiency; thus, this research explores the idea of using the localized magnetic field in the throat area to control the flow. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flow control offers a non-mechanical approach to modifying high speed compressible flows by interacting with electrically conducting gases. In the present study, a two-dimensional computational fluid dynamics framework coupled with MHD model is developed to investigate the influence of localized magnetic fields on the flow dynamics and performance of a supersonic rocket nozzle. The governing Navier–Stokes equations are coupled with electromagnetic source terms to account for Lorentz force effects, and the numerical model is validated against baseline nozzle flow characteristics. A circular arc-contour nozzle is analyzed under four magnetic field intensities (0, 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 T) applied near the throat region. The study systematically examines the resulting changes in flow structure, pressure distribution, and thrust related performance metrics.
