The results demonstrate that localized magnetic fields alter the acceleration process and suppress adverse flow features, leading to enhanced exit flow characteristics and improved thrust performance. These findings establish the effectiveness of MHD-assisted flow control as a viable strategy for modulating supersonic nozzle behavior without mechanical actuation.

papers.title: Joint inference of nonlinear oscillation frequency and physical parameters of gas bubbles from sparse sub-period observations
papers.abstract: The oscillation frequency is a gas bubble's most important dynamical descriptor, yet every standard route to it—perturbation expansions, Fourier or zero-crossing analysis, and harmonic balance—either assumes weak nonlinearity or requires a complete oscillation cycle. We formulate the inverse problem of recovering the nonlinear frequency, together with unknown physical parameters, from sparse and noisy radius samples spanning less than one oscillation period, where spectral estimators are undefined by construction. The frequency is embedded in the governing Rayleigh–Plesset operator through the strained coordinate τ=ωt¯ and coupled to the data through the phase map τj=ωt¯j, so that frequency, trajectory, and parameters are constrained jointly. A central result is an exact energy-balance identity proving that envelope parameters such as viscous damping carry zero Fisher information under any strictly periodic representation, while restoring-force parameters remain identifiable—a model independent statement of what short records can determine. From twelve samples spanning 0.8 of a period at 3% noise, the method recovers the polytropic exponent to about 1.3% without bias, and a Fisher-information analysis shows that accurate recovery requires not merely a sub-period record but one containing the first turning point of the trajectory, where the frequency and parameter sensitivities decorrelate. The formulation extends to the compressible Keller–Miksis equation and, with surface tension, exposes a linear-order degeneracy that only finite-amplitude nonlinearity resolves.

papers.title: Gas–liquid atomization physics of fan-shaped nozzles: Pressure threshold and droplet penetration characteristics
papers.abstract: Spray cooling is a key secondary cooling technique for continuous casting. The water penetration ratio, a critical parameter for calculating the heat transfer coefficient between sprayed water and slab surfaces, is governed by nozzle water pressure, air pressure, and spray height. This study focuses on fan-shaped air–water nozzles and develops a three-dimensional flow-field simulation coupled with multiphase flow and discrete phase models. The numerical model is validated via a self-built test platform, with a maximum prediction error of 3.33%. We systematically investigate droplet size, velocity distribution, and water penetration ratio under various pressure conditions. The results show that higher water pressure intensifies primary and secondary atomization, moving the initial droplet breakup upstream and causing non-monotonic changes in droplet diameter and axial velocity. Within 0–98 mm spray height, rising air pressure makes droplet diameter increase first and then decrease, while axial velocity rises continuously. As the air–water ratio increases from 1.0 to 2.0, the penetration ratio declines steadily with growing spray height. Two critical pressure thresholds are identified: 0.20 MPa for water pressure and 0.15 MPa for air pressure, which explain asymmetric droplet dispersion from distorted flow fields of fan-shaped nozzles. For the first time, a linear correlation between penetration ratio and spray height is established. This work provides theoretical support and quantitative references for optimizing secondary cooling parameters in continuous casting.

papers.title: Effects of surface mass flux on the stability and receptivity of the rotor boundary layer in a rotor–stator system
papers.abstract: Rotor–stator configurations are common in turbomachinery, where rotating boundary layers may undergo instability and transition. A local linear framework is developed to determine how surface mass flux modifies the stability and receptivity of the rotor boundary layer in a rotor–stator cavity. The rotating core provides an outer flow condition that differs from that over an isolated rotating disk. The base flow, convective and absolute instabilities, and receptivity are analyzed under injection, zero surface mass flux, and suction. Injection thickens the rotor boundary layer, expands the unstable domain of the inviscid Type I mode, and increases its growth rate. At representative conditions, the growth rate of the viscous Type II mode is less sensitive to surface mass flux than that of the Type I mode. Contributions from the base flow and its gradients largely cancel for the Type II mode. The representative Type I adjoint mode is concentrated near the critical layer. The principal Type II peak occurs where the effective shear vanishes. A radially localized wall displacement with a specified azimuthal mode number represents stationary roughness or unsteady wall forcing. Combining local receptivity with spatial growth gives the downstream disturbance level. The radius of maximum local receptivity does not necessarily produce the largest downstream amplitude because the available growth interval also matters.

papers.title: A synergistic lubrication regime: Improving the anti-friction performance of water-lubricated systems via a trace auxiliary lubricant
papers.abstract: To reduce the asperity contact in water-lubricated friction pairs (such as stern bearings) under harsh conditions, a lubrication method using an auxiliary lubricant is proposed. Integrated experimental tests and numerical simulations are performed to systematically investigate the fluid physics governing the transport, interfacial diffusion, and friction-reducing mechanisms of the auxiliary lubricant under varying injection parameters. The results indicate that under elastohydrodynamic lubrication (EHL) condition, the left injection position is the most effective for promoting auxiliary lubricant diffusion, with the lubricant having the largest spreading area and the longest “residence time” in the contact zone. For the left injection position under mixed lubrication (ML) condition, however, the flow of lubricating water acts as a “porter” that continuously carries away the auxiliary lubricant near the contact zone, resulting in severe asperity contact and poor friction-reducing performance. Whether under ML state or EHL state, the auxiliary lubricant exhibits the optimal friction-reducing and lubrication performance at an injection angle of 90°. For vertical injection (90°), the auxiliary lubricant is carried by the “backflow effect” to form a vortex and then pushed back into the contact zone to participate in the lubrication again. Under the ML state, due to the balance of flow diffusion and adsorption film-forming performance, the medium-viscosity lubricant has the best anti-friction performance. For medium/high-viscosity auxiliary lubricants under EHL state, besides a portion entering the vortex, another portion adsorbs on the surface of the friction ring. This adsorbed lubricant is then carried by the rotating ring back into the contact zone to participate in the “second lubrication,” which indicates superior lubrication effect. This work provides theoretical and experimental foundations for novel water-lubrication auxiliary technologies and two-phase flow diffusion under extreme conditions.

papers.title: Flame height, stability, and transition characteristics of non-premixed jets under sub-atmospheric pressures: From laminar to turbulent flow
papers.abstract: Diffusion jet flames exist widely in industrial combustion devices and aerospace combustion at high altitude under sub-atmospheric pressure environments. Ambient pressure strongly alters gas density, molecular diffusion, and air entrainment, hence significantly changing flame height, laminar–turbulent transition, and instability characteristics. However, systematic experimental quantification and unified scaling laws for jet flame in sub-atmospheric pressures remain insufficient. In this work, a comprehensive experimental study covering 291 test cases was carried out in a large reduced pressure chamber (3 × 2 × 2 m3) with propane as a fuel. Three nozzle diameters (1, 2, and 3 mm) and ambient pressures ranging from 40 to 100 kPa were adopted to capture full flame evolution from laminar flow, laminar–turbulent transition to turbulent blowout. Non-dimensional similarity analysis was performed based on momentum–buoyancy characteristic length (Lm) and flow rate characteristic length (Lq). Results show that at fixed environmental pressure, flame height first increases and then decreases with jet exit velocity, and flame height decreases monotonically with reducing ambient pressure at same exit velocity due to weakened air entrainment strength. Small diameter (1 mm) flames may blow out under laminar conditions at pressures below 50 kPa, while blowout only occurs in turbulent regions for 2 and 3 mm diameter nozzles. A normalized correlation incorporating pressure-dependent air entrainment strength (αT) is introduced, which achieves asymptotic convergence of flame height for all nozzle diameters in turbulent near-blowout regions responding to Lm/Lq > 20. The present study provides a fluid physics interpretation of flame height and transition of non-premixed jet flame under sub-atmospheric pressures.

papers.title: A physics-oriented review of neural-network-based modeling for bluff-body flows
papers.abstract: Bluff-body flows combine early separation, coherent wake organization, vortex shedding, and strong sensitivity to geometry, Reynolds number, inflow condition, and three-dimensional transition. These features make them both canonical fluid-mechanics benchmarks and demanding targets for neural-network-based modeling. This review provides a representative, physics-oriented synthesis of neural-network approaches for bluff-body flows. Instead of organizing the field by architecture or prediction task, the review asks which wake mechanisms current models represent and which validation evidence makes those claims trustworthy. It examines how current models represent separation, wake topology, pressure-wake coupling, coherent shedding, turbulence statistics, closure behavior, and flow-control mechanisms. We discuss data sources, flow representations, model classes, validation practices, and practical uses in surrogate prediction, reconstruction, monitoring, control, and digital-twin-type workflows. The review emphasizes that low numerical error by itself does not establish physical learning, and argues for validation based on topology, spectra, force response, uncertainty, generalization, and interpretable mechanism evidence.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of shear-thinning and disturbance wave development characteristics in gelled impinging liquid sheets
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate the atomization characteristics of impinging-jet injectors under the influence of non-Newtonian mechanical properties. A three-dimensional volume of fluid to discrete particle model coupled with adaptive mesh refinement was employed. This approach resolves the coupled gas–liquid interaction, shear-thinning behavior, and sheet breakup dynamics during impinging-jet atomization of the gel. The simulation results indicate that the breakup of the gelled liquid sheet is driven by the development of disturbance waves. After jet impingement, initial disturbances on the liquid sheet are gradually amplified by aerodynamic shear. This amplification ultimately destabilizes the sheet, leading to breakup into discrete ligaments and droplets. However, the overall oscillation amplitude of the disturbance waves on the liquid sheet is constrained by the sheet's viscous forces and surface tension. The average amplitude initially increases after jet impingement and then gradually decays to a stable range. On the liquid sheet surface, the shear rate is significantly higher on the windward side of disturbance waves than on the leeward side. This disparity correlates positively with the surface wave amplitude. Increasing the impingement angle enhances jet impact force, yielding a thinner, more unstable sheet. This results in amplified disturbance waves, elevated peak shear rates, and consequently, earlier sheet breakup. Higher gelling agent concentrations suppress disturbance development on the sheet surface and accelerate the damping of amplitude oscillations.

papers.title: Modal and nonmodal stability analysis and subcritical transition in two-dimensional curved channel flow
papers.abstract: This study investigates the hydrodynamic stability of two-dimensional curved channel flows. Using spectral/hp element method, time-stepper eigenvalue algorithm, and direct numerical simulation, modal and non-modal stability analyses are performed for wall curvature radii ranging from R = 20 to R = 200 over Re = 500–5816. Curvature exerts a pronounced destabilizing effect, significantly reducing the critical Reynolds number. The strong curvature (R = 20) substantially enhances transient growth, yielding a maximum energy amplification far exceeding those of weak-curvature cases and plane Poiseuille flow (PPF). The dependence of global maximum energy growth Gmax on the Reynolds number Re is established for various curvature configurations. The results for the minimal-curvature of R = 200 asymptotically approach those of the PPF, demonstrating the continuity of the physical model. Furthermore, the linear optimal disturbances tilted against the mean shear in curved channels resemble those in the PPF. However, with strong curvatures, the optimal disturbances undergo severe distortion and exhibit asymmetric characteristics. The primary mechanism by which curvature promotes transient growth lies in the generation of localized high-shear regions near the upper and lower walls, thereby providing a more favorable environment for the perturbations to extract energy from the mean shear. Finally, using the linear optimal perturbations as initial conditions, subcritical transitions to turbulence are successfully triggered in the cases of R = 200, R = 100, and the PPF. Notably, the threshold Reynolds numbers for triggering subcritical transition in the curved cases are lower than the value for the PPF.

papers.title: Taylor-vortex onset and coefficient responses of friction and torque in finite-length narrow-gap helium Taylor–Couette–Poiseuille flow
papers.abstract: Taylor–Couette–Poiseuille flow couples inner-cylinder rotation with axial throughflow, leading to a competition between centrifugal instability and axial transport in annular gaps. Motivated by cooling and loss-control passages in high-speed rotating machinery, this study investigates the Taylor-vortex onset, wall-shear redistribution, and the integral resistance coefficient response in a finite-length, high-radius-ratio narrow annulus. Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations are performed over 20≤N≤200 and 1.698×107≤Ta≤9.916×109, where N measures the relative strength of inner-cylinder rotation to axial throughflow. An operational onset position, zonset, is introduced to identify the establishment of the first sustained Taylor-vortex cell. The results show that N primarily determines the establishment and onset location of the sustained Taylor-vortex train, yielding the fitted relation zonset/L=286N−1.8, whereas Ta mainly controls the intensity of the established vortical state. Downstream of the onset, Taylor vortices redistribute axial and angular momentum across the gap, producing sign-alternating axial wall shear and sign-preserving modulation of azimuthal wall shear. By decomposing the axial friction and torque coefficients into pre-onset and Taylor-vortex-region contributions and their effective full-length values, the analysis links local wall-shear redistribution to the friction and torque coefficient responses. These findings provide references for predicting and regulating wall friction and torque in finite-length narrow rotating annular passages.

papers.title: Flow physics and surrogate-assisted machine learning optimization of a stacked-blade shrouded Savonius rotor
papers.abstract: Small drag-driven Savonius rotors are suitable for low-wind-speed turbulent conditions found in urban and built environments. However, their aerodynamic efficiency is limited by the negative torque generated by the returning blade, which reduces the overall efficiency of the rotor. This study proposes a stacked-blade shrouded Savonius rotor (SB-SSR) in which a flanged shroud, a spanwise-stacked non-uniform blade, and a helical layer of blades, which act as a single internally augmented system, are compared with a conventional Savonius rotor whose bucket profile is parametrized by a cubic Bézier curve. Three-dimensional transient simulations are combined with Taguchi design of experiments and five machine learning surrogate models to determine the optimal blade curvature, shroud angle (α°), and helical angle (β°) parameters. It is observed that the optimal Bezier curve shape along with the optimal shroud and helical angle has resulted in more uniform localized inflow pressure distributions on the blade surface and higher azimuthal torque coefficients than the Bézier Savonius profile. The spanwise non-uniformity (σUU¯) decreases from 0.017 in Bézier Savonius to 0. 011 for the SB-SSR, suggesting strong three-dimensional turbulent mixing and flow redistribution. At x/D = 6, the kinetic energy flux factor (ØKE) of SB-SSR is 0.656, and for Bézier Savonius is 0.534, meaning greater wake recovery for the SB-SSR. The Q-criterion and pathline analysis have shown more compact shroud edge vortices and delayed flow separation for the SB-SSR, which reduces negative torque of the rotor.

papers.title: Unsteady aerodynamics and fluid–structure interaction of the variable-camber morphing wing driven by a dielectric elastomer
papers.abstract: The development of low-altitude intelligent morphing aircraft has created an urgent demand for adaptive aerodynamic configurations in strongly unsteady flow environments. Dielectric Elastomers (DEs) have become promising actuators for morphing wings owing to large deformation capacity, lightweight, and fast response. However, the underlying coupling mechanisms among electric actuation, structural deformation, and unsteady flow remain unclear. In this paper, a fluid–electro–structure framework is developed to investigate fluid–structure interaction (FSI) and unsteady aerodynamics of a DE-driven variable-camber wing. The coupled electromechanical and aerodynamic responses are simulated employing the Lattice Boltzmann-Finite Element Method. The results show that FSI significantly influences wing deformation and aerodynamic performance. With the increase in DE driving voltage, the camber of the trailing edge and the lift of the deformed wing increase, and the excessive deformation aggravates the wake instability and drag growth. Furthermore, the effectiveness of active camber control strongly depends on the angle of attack. It is revealed that the aerodynamic gains originate from deformation-induced wake reconstruction and vortex dynamics. Our findings will provide physical insights into the multi-physics coupling mechanisms of DE-driven morphing wings and offer guidance for the design of intelligent adaptive flight systems and active flow control strategies.

papers.title: An iteratively corrected inverse-distance-weighting immersed-boundary multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann method for fluid–structure interaction
papers.abstract: The accuracy of the immersed boundary-lattice Boltzmann method hinges on the boundary-force scheme, yet exact no-slip enforcement often incurs high computational cost, whereas existing low-cost simplifications are confined to low-Reynolds-number laminar flow by residual wall slip, hindering their extension to higher flow complexities. This work proposes an iteratively corrected inverse-distance-weighting (IDW) immersed boundary method (IC-IDW) that lifts this restriction. The diagonal step is retained not as the solution but as the preconditioner of an over-relaxed multi-direct-forcing iteration whose residual slip is measured through the full interpolation and spreading operators; the iteration therefore converges to the exact solution of the implicit no-slip system with linear work per correction sweep for bounded support sizes and without forming any matrix, and the relaxation factor can be selected from the spectrum of the geometry-dependent preconditioned operator. The IC-IDW correction is coupled to a multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann solver and closed by a wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity (WALE) model. The resulting solver is validated on the decaying Taylor–Green vortex, the lid-driven cavity, steady, unsteady, and in-line oscillating circular cylinders, and a flapping wing, with the results agreeing with the experimental and numerical reference data. Enabled by the WALE closure, the method further computes the turbulent cylinder wake at Re = 3900—well beyond the reach of the original simplified IDW method—where the mean and second-order wake statistics match the reference database, demonstrating that the framework extends the low-cost inverse-distance route to moderate-to-high-Reynolds-number turbulent flow.

papers.title: Reduction of wake turbulence by microfiber coating
papers.abstract: A wake downstream of a circular cylinder is governed by the separated shear-layer development, vortex formation, and turbulent momentum transport, which together determine the unsteady characteristics of bluff-body flows. This study experimentally investigates the modification of near-wake turbulence by a microfiber-coated strip applied to the rear surface of a circular cylinder. Planar particle image velocimetry measurements were performed at a Reynolds number of 6.1 × 104, corresponding to the subcritical flow regime, to quantify the mean-flow field and turbulence statistics downstream of uncoated and microfiber-coated cylinders. The microfiber coating substantially altered the post-separation wake development. Compared with the uncoated cylinder, the coated cylinder exhibited an elongated recirculation region, slower wake recovery, and a downstream shift in the spatial development of velocity fluctuations. The maximum streamwise turbulence intensity was reduced by up to 29%, while the peak transverse turbulence intensity along the wake centerline was reduced by approximately 25% and shifted farther downstream. The two-dimensional estimate of turbulent kinetic energy and Reynolds shear stress were also reduced in the separated shear-layer region, indicating weaker in-plane turbulent fluctuation energy and reduced cross-wake momentum transport. These results suggest that the microfiber coating does not simply suppress local shear but modifies the spatial development of the separated shear layers and shifts the amplification of wake fluctuations downstream. This study extends previous drag-focused investigations by providing a turbulence-statistical characterization of wake modification by microfiber coating.

papers.title: Gas–water two-phase transport after hydraulic fracturing in dual-porosity coal: A sequential discrete element method–finite element method study
papers.abstract: A sequential discrete element method–finite element method framework was developed to link hydraulic-fracture development with subsequent gas–water two-phase transport in a dual-porosity coal medium. Fracture traces generated using particle flow code were transferred to a continuum drainage model incorporating methane desorption and diffusion, saturation-dependent relative permeability, poroelastic evolution of porosity and permeability, and a prescribed constant gas–water pressure difference of 0.05 MPa. After 350 days, cumulative gas production in the water-free case was 109% higher than that in the water-bearing case. Incorporating the hydraulic-fracture network also shortened the time required to reach the same target fracture gas pressure by 16 days. The effects of water injection pressure and borehole diameter were evaluated using the original particle packing and three additional independent packings. Under the controlled numerical conditions with high imposed water injection pressures, the cumulative-production increment from 50 to 52 MPa was 90.59%–95.07% smaller than that from 48 to 50 MPa across the four realizations, although crack number and total crack length continued to increase. Increasing the borehole diameter from 90 to 100 mm raised cumulative production by 0.627%–0.720%, whereas the increase from 100 to 114 mm was 3.180%–3.860%. After normalization by the diameter increment, the latter response was 3.57–3.86 times the former. The repeated realizations consistently exhibited reduced marginal sensitivity to water injection pressure within the range of 48–52 MPa and enhanced diameter sensitivity within 100–114 mm. These intervals characterize model-dependent changes in transport response rather than exact or universally applicable thresholds.

papers.title: Nonlinear evolution of Rossby solitary waves under time-dependent shear: A variable-coefficient Gardner model solved by physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Constant-coefficient models inadequately capture how time-dependent shear flows alter the propagation of Rossby solitary waves, and traditional numerical methods face inherent difficulties with such variable-coefficient systems. We derive a variable-coefficient Gardner equation from quasi-geostrophic dynamics and solve it using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that integrate residual-adaptive refinement with a two-stage Adam and Limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno optimizer. For the constant-coefficient test case, the PINNs reproduce the exact two-soliton solution with a maximum absolute error of 5.53×10−3, a relative L2 error of 1.02×10−3, and a mean absolute error of 6.41×10−4. In the time-dependent regime where the quadratic nonlinearity coefficient m(t) periodically crosses zero, the PINNs reveal a complete steepening-and-recovery cycle. At the zero-crossing instant, quadratic nonlinearity is momentarily suppressed, triggering abrupt wave steepening together with a transient compression of the wave field in which the crest–trough separation narrows; as m(t) recovers, the waveform broadens again. This cyclic mechanism accounts for the intermittent amplitude fluctuations documented in the satellite altimetry. The amplitude-dependent phase speed c=c0+(m/3)A0+(n/6)A02, together with mean-flow Doppler shifting, quantitatively explains a 50% phase-speed increase from the eastern to western Pacific and the breaking of β-refracted fronts into isolated eddies. Our mesh-free PINN framework provides a robust solution strategy for variable-coefficient ocean wave problems, with clear potential for data assimilation and three-dimensional extensions.

papers.title: Bubble dynamics and insulation characteristics of C6F12O in the nonuniform electric field
papers.abstract: The nonuniform electric field regulates bubble motion through interfacial polarization, Maxwell stress, and electrohydrodynamic effects, while bubble migration redistributes the local electric field and alters dielectric breakdown characteristics. To clarify the relationship between these phenomena in two-phase C6F12O, bubble dynamics under nonuniform electric fields were experimentally investigated, and multiphysics simulations coupling the electric, thermal, flow, and phase fields were performed to analyze bubble deflection at different field strengths. Dielectric breakdown experiments further examined the effects of heat flux, electrode gap, and electric-field uniformity on the breakdown characteristics of the two-phase medium. The results show that, as the electric field strength increases, bubbles migrate toward lower-field regions, with the deflection ratio increasing from about 8% to over 30%, together with an increase in bubble velocity. At four normalized field levels, experimental and simulated deflection ratios exhibited a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.988 and a mean absolute difference of 2.13 percentage points, indicating good agreement. The breakdown voltage initially decreased and then approached a stable range with increasing heat flux, becoming less sensitive at higher heat fluxes. A similar trend was observed with variations in electrode gap, suggesting that bubbles within or near the critical high-field region degrade dielectric performance. Electric-field nonuniformity significantly affects liquid-phase breakdown voltage, whereas under two-phase conditions, increasing bubble presence in the electrode gap reduced the relative influence of the initial field distribution. These findings clarify the mechanisms of bubble transport and dielectric breakdown and provide guidance for optimizing C6F12O-based phase-change-cooled power equipment.

papers.title: Improving wind flow simulation over complex terrain for wind resource assessment through a hybrid data-driven and physics-informed generalized k– ω framework
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of wind speed and turbulence over complex terrain remains challenging because terrain-induced separation and atmospheric boundary layer turbulence are not fully represented by conventional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) closure models. This study develops Mod-GEKO-ML, a hybrid framework combining adjoint optimization and machine learning (ML) calibration of spatially varying generalized k–ω (GEKO) free coefficients with physics-informed modification of selected traditional closure constants. The GEKO-ML mapping is trained on the H42 bump, tested on H38 and H31 for in-family transfer, and applied without retraining to Askervein Hill and Bolund Island. The turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) objective best balances mean flow and turbulence improvement, while reducing the input from eight features to five preserves predictive capability. Field scale evaluations demonstrate partial- and region-dependent transferability, with improved wind speed prediction in terrain affected regions and consistent TKE error reduction. Component analysis shows that ML calibration mainly improves local terrain-induced mean flow responses, whereas closure modification improves upstream TKE preservation and contributes more strongly to TKE error reduction. Feature space analysis shows that H42 training support varies across terrain regions and does not directly determine ML improvement. At Askervein Hill, Mod-GEKO-ML reduces lee side root mean square error (RMSE) by 13.7% for wind speed and 44.8% for TKE relative to standard GEKO. At Bolund Island, TKE RMSE decreases in all three terrain regions under both inflow directions. This framework provides a practical RANS-based approach for wind flow and turbulence prediction over complex terrain.

papers.title: Physics informed surrogate-assisted optimization of embedded stack sine neck Helmholtz resonators for low-frequency fluid noise absorption
papers.abstract: Low frequency fluid-borne noise control in hydraulic piping and ducted acoustic systems remains challenging because effective acoustic attenuation is often limited by spatial constraints. This study proposes an embedded stack sine neck Helmholtz resonator (ESSHR) for low-frequency fluid noise absorption. The stack sine neck geometry is generated by zero-order-hold sampling of a continuous sine profile and evaluated using three-dimensional frequency domain finite element method simulations. Single-parameter parametric analyses demonstrate that the resonant frequency, absorption coefficient, and acoustic velocity distribution are collectively modulated by the effective neck inertance and the frequency-dependent acoustic impedance of the discretized neck-cavity system. To optimize the coupled geometric parameters, a physics informed adaptive surrogate (PIAS) model combining Gaussian process regression/Kriging, radial basis function, and support vector regression is developed and coupled with non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II and gray relational analysis. The optimized ESSHR achieves a resonance frequency of 57.5 Hz and a peak absorption coefficient of 0.8703, corresponding to a 55.77% reduction in resonance frequency compared with the initial design. Under the same envelope constraints, it outperforms the smooth-neck resonator, which exhibits a peak absorption coefficient of 0.64 at 62.5 Hz. The improved performance can be attributed to the modified acoustic inertance, the optimized impedance response, and the redistribution of oscillatory acoustic motion in the sinusoidal neck region of the stack. The proposed ESSHR and PIAS-assisted optimization framework provide a compact and physically interpretable strategy for low-frequency fluid noise absorption.

papers.title: Pressure amplification and water–air two-phase flow in rough cracks of high-speed railway tunnel linings
papers.abstract: To investigate the pressure amplification effect and water–air two-phase flow characteristics in rough cracks of high-speed railway tunnel linings, this study introduces a methodological innovation by coupling the successive random addition method for rough crack surface reconstruction with a two-phase Volume of Fluid model, which enables quantitative analysis of the interplay between multi-scale crack roughness and transient water–air flow dynamics under train-induced aerodynamic loads, revealing the spatial evolution of pressure amplification and the inertial overshoot mechanism of water movement. Crack position and orientation effects on pressure are examined. The main conclusions are as follows: The amplitude and rate of train-induced pressure waves are significantly enhanced in water-rich cracks while uniformity decreases; the positive and negative pressure peaks at the crack tip are 1.74 and 1.36 times those at the entrance; the standard deviation of the pressure peak approaches zero at the crack tip due to the geometric constraint. The positive peak of rate of pressure change is largest at the tip, and the negative peak is largest at the end section of the air area. The magnitude and rate of pressure change at the crack tip correlate positively with water displacement and velocity; owing to water inertia, the water movement overshoots the equilibrium position, resulting in larger displacement and consequently the pressure amplification effect. Positive pressure amplification is strongest in longitudinal and sidewall cracks; negative in crown; circumferential weakest due to gravity. The results provide a basis for the treatment of lining cracks in high-speed railway tunnels.

papers.title: Effective inflow velocity reconstruction in separated airfoil flows using an effective control body model
papers.abstract: Effective inflow velocity reconstruction recovers a reference velocity, representing the external inflow from a near-field velocity field affected by the airfoil. Under attached flow, the difference between local velocity and effective inflow is mainly associated with bound circulation. A circulation distribution on the airfoil profile can, therefore, provide a physically consistent induced velocity correction. Under separated flow, however, near-wall reverse flow and separated vortices distort the local velocity direction, making the airfoil surface inconsistent with the external effective flow. To address this limitation, an effective control body (ECB) model is proposed. It treats the airfoil and separated region as an integrated control body and relocates the circulation support boundary outside the separated region. Two variants define this boundary using a total pressure contour line or stagnation point streamlines. The method is evaluated using unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes flow fields around the Delft University 00-W2-350 airfoil. Under deep stall, the Shen2 model retains a pronounced directional deviation. Both ECB variants recover nearly parallel effective inflow streamlines, bring the inflow angle closer to the prescribed direction, and improve spatial uniformity. During unsteady separation, vortex evolution changes the induced velocity correction with phase, but both variants maintain small inflow angle deviations. Under the investigated two-dimensional separated flow conditions, relocating the circulation support boundary outside the separated region makes the induced velocity correction more consistent with the external flow. The ECB model, therefore, provides a physically motivated approach to effective inflow reconstruction for the examined cases.

papers.title: Investigation of flow-directed vortex on penetration characteristics of transverse injection of multiphase fuel
papers.abstract: This study investigates the regulatory mechanism of vortex generators (VGs) concerning the penetration and mixing characteristics of sub/supercritical kerosene transverse jets within a dual-variable combustor. Combining shadowgraph imaging experiments and numerical simulations under inflow conditions simulating combustor entry (Ta = 500 K, pa = 0.3 MPa, Va = 50 m/s), the effects of VG height (Hv = 5–10 mm) and expansion angle (β = 30°–60°) on the evolution of multiphase jet behavior (constant fuel flow rate ṁf = 1.6 g/s) were systematically studied. Experimental results demonstrate that the introduction of VGs universally enhances jet penetration depth. Supercritical jets (Tinj = 670 K) demonstrate enhanced mixing efficiency in comparison to liquid jets (Tinj = 425 K), necessitating approximately 70% less axial distance to attain equivalent mixing levels. Numerical simulation analysis reveals that the principal flow mechanisms for improving penetration involve the induction of streamwise vortices and the creation of low-speed wake regions by VGs. These phenomena modify the local momentum ratio and augment the transport of normal momentum. Furthermore, an optimal range exists for VG geometric parameters (Hv = 7.5 mm, β = 36°–45°), achieving a balance between flow control benefits and turbulent losses. This research provides a substantial theoretical basis and evidence-based optimal design guidelines for the development of high-efficiency fuel injection systems in dual-variable combustors.

papers.title: High-dimensional wind farm wake modeling and efficiency optimization using a hybrid modeling approach
papers.abstract: The performance optimization of wind turbines faces challenges due to wake interactions, leading to overall power losses in wind farms. Wake steering through the yaw control strategy has strong potential; however, conventional algorithms are hindered by high computational costs for large-scale real-time deployments. This study presents a fast and scalable approach for the performance optimization of wind farms under different environmental conditions through wake steering. The methodology integrates the Gauss–curled hybrid wake model with a serial refined to investigate how physically resolved wake mechanisms influence yaw control optimization while maintaining computational efficiency. The approach reduces high-dimensional optimization problems into sequential upstream to downstream turbine search for optimal yaw angles by reducing the computational cost and improving the physical accuracy. The framework was first applied to onshore wind farm turbines and then extended to an offshore wind farm comprising 96 wind turbines. The results indicate that wake interaction significantly affects the downstream performance owing to the wake overlap. The proposed method effectively models and mitigates wake effects through integrated wake modeling and an optimized yaw control strategy. The results demonstrate that dynamic wake interaction, yaw-induced wake deflection, and wake recovery enable physically consistent and scalable wake steering optimization under different environmental conditions. The agreement between the results obtained from the second wind farm and the monitoring data from supervisory control and data acquisition confirmed the reliability of the proposed framework for real-time applications. This wake steering technique verified by monitoring data provides an efficient tool for managing wake control across large-scale wind farm arrays.

papers.title: Influence of the convex or concave terrain topography on the free surface water flow through a finite patch of cylinders
papers.abstract: Vegetation plays a significant ecological role by interfering with flow fields and influencing the transport of nutrients. The hydrodynamic processes of vegetation water flow involve multi-scale and multi-physical mechanisms, and simplified models are often employed in research to reduce the complexity or concentrate research focus. Most studies often simplify the terrain as flat bottoms to remove the influence of the terrain topography. This paper primarily investigates vegetation water flow over uneven terrain topography. A rigid cylinder patch was used to mimic the emergent vegetation, and regular cosine functions were employed to mimic the convex or concave terrain. The hybrid Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes Equations and Large-Eddy Simulation numerical model were implemented to investigate the hydrodynamics focused on two key factors, i.e., the solid volume fraction (SVF) of the cylinder patch and the terrain maximum slope (Sm). The analysis of the eddy coherent structures and the hydrodynamic loads on cylinders reveals the transformation of the shedding vortex in patch scale and stem scale with variant SVF and Sm. Compared to the flat terrain, the convex or concave topography significantly dominants the spatial distribution of the forces on each individual cylinder within the patch. The hydrodynamic forces converge to the crest of the convex terrain or diverse from the trough of the concave terrain rather than approximately align in the main streamwise direction as in flat-terrain conditions. It is hypothesized that flexible vegetation stems may exhibit inclination deformation due to different terrain topography.

papers.title: Linear instability of nanofluid film flowing over heated or cooled inclined planes
papers.abstract: A comprehensive linear stability analysis is conducted for nanofluid films flowing down uniformly heated or cooled inclined planes. The governing equations are formulated within Buongiorno's two-component framework, which fully accounts for nanoparticle migration and the resultant stratification of viscosity, density, specific heat, and thermal conductivity. The analysis reveals that nanoparticles generally exert a stabilizing influence on the thermocapillary S-mode and P-mode; however, their impact on the H-mode is governed by a competition between stabilizing and destabilizing mechanisms, and strong thermophoretic effects under heated-wall conditions may further exacerbate the instability. Specifically, the thermal conductivity and viscosity stratification induced by nanoparticle thermophoresis effectively suppress the thermocapillary S-mode and P-mode, whereas the consequent density and viscosity stratification promote the instability of the H-mode. Increasing the Biot number, which corresponds to enhanced surface heat transfer, modulates flow instability independently of thermocapillary effects. This modulation is attributed to the coupled effects on the base-flow temperature and nanoparticle concentration fields. Additionally, comparing heated and cooled wall scenarios indicates that reversing the direction of thermophoretic migration alters stratification patterns and fundamentally modifies the characteristics of flow instability.

papers.title: Reduced-order contour modeling of liquid-ammonia flash-boiling sprays in transverse crossflow
papers.abstract: Liquid ammonia can undergo flare flash boiling after depressurization at room temperature, but injection into a transverse gas stream simultaneously expands and bends the spray. This coupled two-dimensional optical envelope is not described by conventional non-flashing liquid-jet-in-crossflow correlations or by quiescent flash-boiling spray models. Here, a reduced-order contour model is developed for projected spray boundaries extracted from high-speed diffused back-illumination images of liquid-ammonia sprays in subsonic crossflow. The model combines a finite-offset saturating term for near-nozzle flash expansion with a logarithmic-square term for far-field aerodynamic bending. Its closure is established from three complementary datasets: quiescent ammonia, non-flashing methanol in crossflow, and flash-boiling ammonia in crossflow. The quiescent ammonia fit gives R2=0.987, while the pure-crossflow model reproduces thirteen methanol contours with R2>0.990 and yields the bending-rate law Bcw*=0.079q−0.35 together with a derived effective column drag coefficient Cd(q)=0.22q0.36. For the coupled ammonia cases, each coefficient is inherited from a limiting regime: the bending amplitude stays within the pure-crossflow band, the bending rate decreases as Bc=0.15q−0.17 mm−1, and the windward flash amplitude equals the quiescent expansion attenuated to roughly 40% by the factor Φ(q)=0.13q0.22. The resulting model reproduces the measured contours with a median contour-wise R2=0.961. Increasing the liquid-to-gas momentum-flux ratio q weakens aerodynamic bending, preserves a larger windward flash-expansion amplitude, and raises both the windward transition height yt and the maximum penetration height ymax, whereas yt/ymax remains close to 0.51. The framework provides a compact envelope-level description of flare-flashing ammonia sprays within the tested, correlated momentum-flux and gas Weber number matrix.

papers.title: Fluid dynamics simulation on droplets formation process of cathode molten pool in vacuum arc
papers.abstract: In high-current vacuum arc, the droplets generated from the cathode molten pool can remain in the contact gap for a relatively long time and may affect post-arc dielectric recovery, whereas their possible formation pathways are still not fully understood. In this paper, a two-dimensional axisymmetric volume-of-fluid model was established to investigate the generation process of Type II droplets from a CuCr50 cathode molten pool under different operating conditions. The results show that a perturbation on the molten pool can gradually develop into a liquid–metal protrusion, which is further stretched into a liquid column. The liquid column subsequently undergoes pinch-off, resulting in the detachment of the primary droplet, while the remaining liquid column later breaks up into droplets. The current and initial protrusion size significantly influence the droplet formation process by changing the molten-metal shape, liquid column slenderness, and pinch-off behavior. The simulated droplet size and motion characteristics show consistent trends with experimental observations of cathode molten-pool droplets in high-current vacuum arc. This work provides insight into one possible formation pathway of Type II cathode molten-pool droplets and offers a reference for understanding metal droplet formation during vacuum interruption.

papers.title: A physics-based deep learning framework for super-resolution in fluid dynamics based on higher-order singular value decomposition
papers.abstract: In this work, a novel methodology combining higher-order singular value decomposition (HOSVD) with deep learning is presented for the super-resolution (SR) of computational fluid dynamics and sparse experimental datasets. This approach, referred to as HOSVD-SR (The software is available at https://modelflows.github.io/modelflowsapp/), integrates modal decomposition with machine-learning techniques to create a physics-based hybrid model that enhances spatial resolution while preserving the dominant flow structures. The proposed methodology leverages HOSVD, a higher-order extension of SVD that is well suited to high-dimensional data arranged in the tensor form. HOSVD independently extracts the mode matrices and singular values associated with each tensor dimension, including the spatial and temporal dimensions. This dimension-wise treatment is physically motivated: by decomposing the data independently along each spatial direction, HOSVD identifies the energetically dominant and spatially organized flow structures while filtering low-energy noise and spatial redundancies. This is particularly relevant to the accurate reconstruction of laminar, transitional, and turbulent flows. Each low-resolution spatial mode matrix, together with its corresponding singular values, is provided as input to an independent decoder/autoencoder-type neural network trained to increase the spatial dimensionality of that mode matrix. The enhanced spatial mode matrices are subsequently combined with the unchanged component and temporal mode matrices and the core tensor to reconstruct the high-resolution flow database. The method, therefore, enhances resolution from spatial patterns extracted from a sequence of physically consistent flow fields rather than treating individual snapshots as independent images. The HOSVD-SR methodology is evaluated using three databases of different complexity: two- and three-dimensional numerical simulations of flow past a circular cylinder and a numerical database of flow in two axisymmetric concentric jets. For the cylinder-flow cases, HOSVD-SR accurately reconstructs the wake topology, including the von Kármán vortex street, near-body structures, and, where applicable, asymmetric and three-dimensional flow features. For the concentric-jets case, the method recovers the oscillating structures developing along the jet shear layers, even after severe spatial downsampling. Across the investigated datasets and compression ratios (CRs), HOSVD-SR produces lower reconstruction errors than the previously proposed SVD-SR methodology. For the numerical test cases in which deterministic interpolation is also evaluated, HOSVD-SR substantially outperforms the interpolation baseline, particularly at high CRs for which important flow structures are absent from the retained spatial samples. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed physics-based framework as a new approach to the SR of fluid-dynamics data. Although additional developments concerning network optimization, computational efficiency, scalability, and validation for other flow configurations remain for future studies, the dimension-wise formulation makes the method potentially transferable to databases generated using other numerical and experimental approaches in fluid mechanics.

papers.title: Numerical study on nonlinear resonant responses inside moonpools with varying recess lengths under head waves
papers.abstract: Recessed moonpools have been adopted in certain drillship designs, and their hydrodynamic performance can be significantly affected by nonlinear effects under resonant conditions. The free-surface responses inside moonpools of a fixed drillship under head waves are simulated using computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Sensitivity analyses of grid resolution, time step size, and turbulence model are conducted. The CFD model is then validated against the experiments [Zhang et al., “The effect of a recess on the nonlinear free-surface responses of three-dimensional moonpools,” J. Fluid Mech. 1029, A41 (2026)]. The free-surface responses inside the recessed moonpool show that when an integer multiple of the excitation angular frequency ω approaches a sloshing natural frequency, the corresponding superharmonic component triggers the secondary resonance and locally amplifies the free-surface motion. The effects of wave steepness and recess length on the response amplitude, harmonic content, and spatial distribution of the free-surface motion are then investigated. Increasing wave steepness strengthens the nonlinear piston-mode response and enhances the higher-harmonic components, while increasing recess length leads to greater spatial asymmetry and more pronounced nonlinear amplification. The vorticity and volume-fraction fields further indicate that corner-generated vortices, local wave breaking, and jet-like free-surface deformation are closely associated with the enhanced nonlinear response in recessed moonpools.

papers.title: Pressure-dependent thermal response and localized transport pathways in the enclosed rotating chamber of a large hypergravity centrifuge
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics was used to investigate the pressure-dependent thermal response of an enclosed rotating chamber representative of a large hypergravity centrifuge. Windage heating generated by a large rotating arm was balanced by heat removal through an isothermal cooled wall. The torque-derived simulated windage-heating power reproduced the order of magnitude and operating-condition trends of the experimental system-level power reference, with relative deviations of 11.0%–19.7%. When pressure decreased from 101 to 10 kPa, the effective air-side heat-removal capability weakened markedly: the probe-temperature-based effective heat-transfer coefficient decreased from 280.43 to 46.45 W m−2 K−1 at 400 g and from 307.60 to 96.87 W m−2 K−1 at 1000 g. A coefficient based on the chamber volume-mean gas temperature exhibited the same pressure dependence, demonstrating that this conclusion is robust to the choice of gas–temperature reference. However, the chamber-mean gas-to-wall temperature difference also decreased because the reduction in windage-heating input exceeded the reduction in effective heat-removal capability. Wall heat-flux analysis showed that absolute heat-removal intensity decreased with pressure, whereas the normalized heat-flux distribution became more non-uniform. For the 600–1000 g cases, the coefficient of variation increased by 48%–62%, and the relative high-heat-flux area increased by 59%–82%. Velocity-gradient and thermal-gradient analyses identified an arm-tip and outer-annular transport pathway, with a local peak of the velocity-gradient indicator near r*=0.89. Q-criterion visualizations further revealed longer arm-induced wakes, wake-vortex packets, and wall-constrained vortex structures at low pressure. These results show that low pressure attenuates global heat generation and heat removal while enhancing the relative prominence of localized shear- and wake-controlled transport pathways.

papers.title: Synergistic suppression of droplet penetration through inclined prewetted meshes
papers.abstract: This study investigates the penetration of droplets of a Newtonian liquid through inclined, prewetted meshes experimentally and theoretically. Systematic experiments using high-speed shadowgraphy examine seven governing parameters: mesh inclination, pore size, prewetting height, impact velocity, liquid viscosity, surface tension, and diameter. The results show that increasing the mesh inclination, prewetting height, liquid viscosity, or surface tension each increases the critical impact velocity for secondary droplet formation, whereas larger pore sizes decrease it. On a dry mesh, the operational critical velocity exhibits a modest but statistically detectable decrease with increasing droplet diameter, whereas the pore-scale model predicts radius independence only at leading order, consistent with the theoretical prediction that the critical condition for secondary-droplet formation is governed by the local pore-scale pressure balance rather than by the macroscopic Weber number. Notably, mesh inclination shows threshold-level synergistic suppression with both prewetting and increased liquid viscosity: together, they suppress secondary-droplet formation when either factor alone is insufficient. We develop a semi-empirical critical-condition model based on the balance among dynamic pressure, capillary resistance, and viscous dissipation, combining previously separate models for prewetting, inclination, and viscosity within a common force-balance framework. By introducing the Ohnesorge number, the model yields an explicit formula for the critical impact velocity. The model predictions capture the overall transition trends in the present data and in previously reported results across the tested parameter ranges.

papers.title: Dipole polarization and Lewis acid–base asymmetry in electrowetting
papers.abstract: Electrowetting has emerged as a versatile technique for manipulating discrete liquid volumes. However, its practical utility is constrained by the saturation of the contact angle at elevated applied voltages, where further increases in voltage produce diminishing changes in wettability. In this work, we formulate a bounded statistical-mechanical description of the interfacial dipoles under an externally applied electric field. The resulting model recovers the classical quadratic voltage dependence in the low-field limit, while in the high-field limit the apparent contact angle saturates to a constant value. The probabilistic modulation also accounts for the asymmetry in electrowetting under positive and negative bias when the solid surface and the liquid possess unbalanced acid–base character. This work provides a self-consistent and experimentally falsifiable electrowetting framework, offering both a molecular-level interpretive tool for existing data and a predictive approach to rational design in digital microfluidic platforms.

papers.title: Generation of double emulsions in a gas phase in a microchannel
papers.abstract: Double emulsions are widely used in academic and industrial applications because their compartmentalized structures enable the encapsulation and isolation of materials. However, liquid/liquid/gas (L/L/G) double emulsions have received comparatively limited attention. Generating double emulsions in a gas phase can eliminate the need to remove a continuous liquid phase and reduce the risk of contamination, offering potential advantages for applications requiring clean and contamination-sensitive droplets. Here, we numerically investigate the generation of L/L/G double emulsions in a coaxial microchannel using the volume-of-fluid method. We systematically examine the effects of flow rates and fluid properties on the generation dynamics, with particular attention to droplet size, generation frequency, deformation, and eccentricity. The results provide mechanistic insights into the generation and control of L/L/G double emulsions in microchannels and establish a basis for their controllable generation.

papers.title: Streamer-to-spark transition in interacting multi-channel pulsed discharges with gasdynamic effects
papers.abstract: The development of a streamer-to-spark transition in atmospheric-pressure air driven by a capacitor discharge in a resistor–capacitor circuit is simulated. The radial gasdynamic expansion of interacting plasma channels, along with the current–voltage characteristics, translational temperatures, electron density, pressure, and current density, is analyzed. The simulation results demonstrate that when the plasma channels are closely spaced in a linear configuration, the gasdynamic expansion of the inner filaments is spatially constrained. Consequently, the reduced electric field inside these inner filaments becomes significantly lower than that in the peripheral channels, which carry the bulk of the electric current. A quantitative criterion is established to define the transition between the mutual interaction of plasma channels and their independent development. Furthermore, the gasdynamic study demonstrates that modeling a spark discharge in atmospheric-pressure air at temperatures up to 7000 K does not strictly require a variable molar mass approach. The standard equation of state with a constant molar mass, coupled with density evaluation from the mixture continuity equation, yields no significant errors, at least from a gasdynamic perspective.

papers.title: From cavitating flow to vibroacoustic response in a deflector jet servo valve pilot stage under wide temperature and back pressure conditions
papers.abstract: Deflector-jet servo valves are key hydraulic control elements in aerospace actuation, where wide temperature excursions and back-pressure variations can reorganize cavitating pilot-stage flows and generate pressure pulsations, noise, and vibration. How this flow reorganization is transmitted into acoustic radiation and mode-selective structural amplification remains insufficiently understood. Nine thermal–pressure conditions spanning 20–120 °C and 0.20–0.35 MPa were examined using large-eddy simulation, Lighthill volumetric-source acoustics, and independent dry-modal analysis. Lower back pressure weakens local pressure recovery and extends the low-pressure shear layer and vapor structures toward the receiver passages; temperature-dependent thermophysical changes intensify shear-layer roll-up, vapor fragmentation, and collapse, raising the characteristic pressure-fluctuation frequency by ∼4.3–4.6 times. This spatiotemporal reorganization redistributes the volumetric-source spectrum and changes the radiation topology. At 120 °C and 0.20 MPa, the 7.341 kHz branch produces the strongest internal acoustic response and an XOY radiation field dominated by the third circumferential order (95%). Structural amplification follows the modal-coupling condition: at 120 °C and 0.35 MPa, the 1.134 kHz excitation lies only 0.063% from the first dry mode at 1.134 72 kHz, concentrates 99.4% of the modal-energy measure in this mode, and yields a 1.39 mm linear frequency-domain deflector response. For the acoustically stronger 7.341 kHz state, detuning increases to 0.876%, the absolute modal-energy measure is 17.4 times lower, and the response is 0.236 mm. These results establish a continuous condition-dependent pathway from cavitation reorganization to volumetric-source radiation and mode-selective vibration, showing that pressure-field organization, frequency matching, and spatial pressure–mode coupling jointly control modal-energy transfer. The framework provides a mechanistic basis for jointly assessing acoustic severity and resonance susceptibility in wide-envelope servo-valve design.

papers.title: Force-spectrum-resolved micromechanics of macroscopic rheology in inertially sheared dense granular flows
papers.abstract: The macroscopic rheology of dense granular flows originates from heterogeneous and dynamically evolving contact networks. However, conventional binary strong–weak classifications obscure the differentiated mechanical roles of contacts across the continuous force spectrum. This study develops a force-spectrum-resolved micromechanical framework by combining two-dimensional discrete element simulations of inertial plane shear, a ten-subinterval decomposition based on the instantaneous mean normal contact force, and stress–force–fabric analysis. During shear startup, the contact network evolves from an approximately homogeneous state through localized differentiation and strong-force-chain percolation before recovering statistical spatial homogeneity. This reconstruction is accompanied by progressive force-spectrum polarization, manifested by depletion of intermediate-force contacts, accumulation near zero force, and extension of the ultra-strong tail. Increasing inertia intensifies shear dilation, network rarefaction, load concentration, and force heterogeneity, while the polarization trend remains robust under alternative partition schemes. The anisotropic response is governed jointly by force magnitude and principal-direction alignment. The lowest-force weak contacts mainly enhance contact-orientation anisotropy, whereas normal-force anisotropy arises from weak-contact reorientation and the nearly coaxial contribution of ultra-strong contacts. Tangential-force anisotropy and the increase in shear resistance are dominated by the ultra-strong tail. Stress partitioning further reveals that macroscopic rheological stability emerges from dynamic compensation between overloaded strong contacts and weak contacts possessing redundant internal shear strength. The proposed framework extends the conventional strong–weak description and provides a spectrum-resolved micromechanical basis for constitutive modeling of dense granular rheology.

papers.title: Learning cylinder wake dynamics across Hopf bifurcation via a regime-adaptive dual-branch physics-informed neural network
papers.abstract: The ability to represent fluid dynamics across regime transitions remains a fundamental challenge in physics-informed machine learning. In cylinder wake flows, the Hopf bifurcation at the critical Reynolds number Rec≈52 induces a transition from a steady, nearly symmetric base state to periodic von Kármán vortex shedding, accompanied by a qualitative reorganization of the underlying solution manifold. This raises a key question of whether nonlinear fluid systems admit a unified neural representation across bifurcation-induced reorganization of the solution manifold. Here, we propose a regime-adaptive dual-branch physics-informed neural network to investigate this question. The model explicitly decomposes the solution space into steady and unsteady dynamical components, which are coupled through a continuous Re-dependent gating mechanism centered at Rec≈52, thereby reducing cross-regime interference during optimization. To ensure stable learning under continuous parameterization, we combine continuous Reynolds-number feature embeddings with a multi-stage curriculum learning protocol that progressively restores the contributions of time-resolved observations and transient physical constraints while retaining the complete Reynolds-number range throughout training. Using supervised computational fluid dynamics data at 11 Reynolds numbers over 5≤Re≤120, the framework is evaluated on six held-out in-range Reynolds numbers and two extrapolation cases, Re=2 and 126. The model accurately reconstructs the principal wake structures and key flow statistics at unseen Reynolds numbers, with particularly strong performance across the held-out in-range cases. These results show that explicitly encoding regime separation in the neural architecture improves the representation of bifurcation-induced solution-manifold reorganization and enables continuous parametric surrogate modeling across steady and periodically shedding wake regimes.

papers.title: Energy dissipation mechanisms of hydrophilic–hydrophobic silica bidisperse shear-thickening fluids in Hele–Shaw flow
papers.abstract: The energy dissipation behavior of hydrophilic–hydrophobic silica bidisperse shear-thickening fluids in Hele–Shaw flow is investigated. An energy dissipation framework is developed based on a gap-averaged model to describe the displacement process. The velocity field at the fingering front is obtained using the optical-flow method, enabling quantitative evaluation of local energy dissipation. The results show that energy dissipation exhibits a spatially non-uniform distribution, with high-dissipation regions primarily concentrated at the viscous fingering front. As the viscous fingering evolves, the dissipation field evolves synchronously with the interfacial morphology. An equivalent dissipation coefficient, Cd, is introduced to characterize the macroscopic dissipation capacity of different systems. Scaling analysis is further conducted to establish the relationship between energy dissipation rate and flow rate. The empirical scaling exponent α is defined to characterize the relative contributions between viscous and frictional dissipation mechanisms. The work suggests that the dissipation behavior does not exhibit an abrupt transition, which may be associated with the interplay between solvation-layer structures and frictional contact networks. The dissipation mechanism gradually evolves from viscosity-dominated toward a greater contribution from frictional dissipation, accompanied by an increase in the empirical scaling exponent. For the investigated shear-thickening fluids, this increase in α is interpreted as an indication of increasingly nonlinear dissipation associated with frictional interactions. A phase diagram is proposed to capture the coupled evolution of macroscopic dissipation capacity, dissipation mechanism, and shear intensity. These results suggest a unified quantitative description of the coupling between viscous fingering evolution and macroscopic energy dissipation in non-Newtonian displacement flows.

papers.title: Dynamic erosion evolution and aerodynamic degradation of wind turbine airfoils
papers.abstract: Continuous sand particle impingement on wind turbine blades causes leading-edge erosion, resulting in surface morphology degradation and aerodynamic performance deterioration. Existing studies focus on predefined erosion morphologies, while the dynamic evolution of erosion damage and its influence on aerodynamic characteristics remain insufficiently understood. To address this issue, this study develops a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based dynamic erosion framework for the S809 wind turbine airfoil, incorporating Lagrangian particle tracking, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes, large eddy simulation, an erosion model, and a dynamic mesh. The effects of angle of attack and particle diameter on erosion morphology, particle impact behavior, and aerodynamic degradation are investigated. Results show that sand particles mainly impact the leading-edge region due to particle inertia and near-wall flow characteristics, causing morphology evolution from discrete pits to irregular roughened surfaces. The angle of attack affects particle impact distribution and maximum erosion regions, leading to different erosion patterns and degradation behaviors. At 8°, after 100 h of erosion, the lift coefficient decreases by 4.6%, the drag coefficient increases by 18.1%, and the lift-to-drag ratio decreases by 19.2%. Larger particles with stronger inertia generate more severe erosion damage, and the maximum erosion depth reaches 263 for 100 μm particles. Further analysis indicates that erosion-induced roughness modifies pressure distribution, promotes separation, and alters vortex structures. LES results further reveal the influence of erosion morphology evolution on three-dimensional unsteady vortex structures. This study clarifies how dynamic erosion evolution accelerates aerodynamic degradation and supports erosion-resistant design and service prediction of wind turbine blades.

papers.title: Investigation of effect on boundary layer due to insoluble surfactants on rising bubbles
papers.abstract: We report axisymmetric direct numerical simulations (DNS) of rising bubbles laden with insoluble surfactant, spanning 0.5≤Bo≤10, 5≤Ga≤140, 0≤Ma≤45, and 0.01≤Ψ0≤0.10, with a clean (Ma=0) series extending to Bo=50. A closed-form scaling law is derived for the Marangoni boundary-layer thickness, δBL/db=F(Ψ0)/(Ma Ψ0 Ga0.5 Bo0.25) with F(Ψ0)=1−2.5 Ψ0; the Galileo and Bond exponents are DNS-fitted rather than asymptotic and F is an empirical closure, each stated with its calibration basis. The law is calibrated and validated over the narrower window Bo=0.5–2, 0.3≲Ma≤15, 0.02≤Ψ0≤0.10, and 5≤Ga≤140. The resolution criterion it implies is verified by grid convergence, and the clean-bubble velocity correlation reproduces the DNS to 7.7% r.m.s. where boundary-layer theory applies (Re≥25). Measured separately, the momentum boundary layer at the contaminated interface follows δ/db=0.644 Re−1/2 to 7.0% r.m.s. over twenty-eight cases; twenty-three sit at a common Reynolds number, where the measured thickness is independent of both Ma and Ψ0, identifying it as the velocity-recovery scale rather than the Marangoni stress scale. At the highest loading, the campaign is bounded by interface failure rather than resolution: at Ψ0=0.10 the rear stagnation region draws into an axial cusp above Ma≈10 at Ga=100.

papers.title: Modulation of non-spherical particle orientation in turbulence by fluid-inertia torque and particle inertia
papers.abstract: The slip-induced fluid-inertia torque strongly affects the orientational dynamics of non-spherical particles settling in turbulence, yet the role of particle inertia in modulating this effect and the balance between the fluid-inertia and Jeffery torques remains insufficiently understood. Using a Lagrangian particle-tracking approach coupled with direct numerical simulations of the carrier flow, we investigate the dependence of particle orientation distributions on particle inertia. Here, we mainly concern the cases with and without the fluid-inertia torque over a range of Stokes numbers (0.1≤St≤2) and particle aspect ratios (0.01≤λ≤100) at a fixed settling number (Sv=2). The relative contributions of the Jeffery and fluid-inertia torques to the rotational dynamics are also quantified. Without the fluid-inertia torque, prolate and oblate particles exhibit only weak preferential orientation at low St, and their orientation distributions become nearly uniform as St increases. When the fluid-inertia torque is included, both particle shapes exhibit strong preferential orientation at low St, but the distributions broaden progressively with increasing St. Over the lower-St range, the orientation distributions also retain a dependence on particle shape. The root mean square fluctuations in particle orientation remain relatively small at low St but vary markedly with St. At larger St, their variation with St becomes weaker. The ratio of the magnitudes of the fluid-inertia and Jeffery torques further indicates that, at small St, the rotational dynamics of prolate particles are governed predominantly by the Jeffery torque, whereas the two torques are generally comparable for oblate particles. As St increases, the relative importance of the fluid-inertia torque generally increases for both particle shapes.

papers.title: Effects of boundary conditions and heating mode on the linear and nonlinear onset of convection with temperature-dependent viscosity
papers.abstract: We investigate the effects of boundary conditions on the extent of the subcritical region in a fluid layer heated either from below or internally, with exponential temperature-dependent viscosity and the infinite Prandtl number. The nonlinear stability threshold is estimated for localized convection at a viscosity contrast across the layer of 1010. We consider free-slip and no-slip mechanical boundary conditions as well as fixed temperature and fixed heat flux at the bottom boundary, while keeping the temperature at the top boundary fixed in all cases. The linear critical Rayleigh number is determined using standard linear stability analysis, and direct numerical simulations are used to determine both the linear and nonlinear stability thresholds. Among all cases considered, Rayleigh–Bénard convection with free-slip boundaries and fixed temperatures has the widest subcritical range, extending down to about half the linear critical Rayleigh number. Changing the bottom boundary condition from fixed temperature to fixed heat flux reduces the subcritical range by roughly a factor of 4, while internal heating reduces it by a factor of 4–7. Mechanical boundary conditions have a relatively minor effect. These results show that the subcritical localized convection proposed to occur at the margins of the convective region in the nitrogen-ice layer of Sputnik Planitia on Pluto can occur under a range of conditions. However, the strong sensitivity of the nonlinear convection threshold to thermal boundary conditions and heating mode suggests that better constraints on the nitrogen-ice layer and studies of convection under more realistic conditions are needed.

papers.title: A practical framework for time-resolved three-dimensional wake reconstruction of a circular cylinder undergoing vortex-induced vibration using sparse planar measurements
papers.abstract: Time-resolved volumetric measurements are essential for characterizing the three-dimensional wake dynamics of fluid–structure interaction (FSI) systems, yet their experimental acquisition remains costly and technically demanding. This study extends the snapshot optimization (SO) framework to reconstruct three-dimensional, time-resolved wake flow fields in vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of a circular cylinder using only two orthogonal planar measurements. The method leverages approximate spanwise statistical homogeneity to infer volumetric flow structures from sparse experimental data. An enhanced averaging snapshot optimization framework is implemented to reduce the discontinuities associated with discrete snapshot matching, producing smoother and more dynamically consistent volumetric reconstructions than the baseline SO method. Validation against time-resolved volumetric particle tracking velocimetry measurements demonstrates successful reconstruction of both 2S and 2P vortex shedding regimes across the VIV lock-in range. Quantitative validation using normalized root mean square error, correlation analysis, and proper orthogonal decomposition demonstrates good overall agreement with the reference measurements, with mean instantaneous spatial correlations of 0.89 and 0.94 for the 2S and 2P regimes, respectively. The reconstruction captures the dominant coherent wake structures and their temporal evolution, while spanwise velocity fluctuations and higher-order modal dynamics are less accurately recovered. The results demonstrate that sparse planar measurements can provide a practical alternative for obtaining dynamically meaningful three-dimensional wake information in FSI problems where fully volumetric diagnostics are impractical.

papers.title: On steady particle distribution in particulate microchannel pipe flows
papers.abstract: An analytical method is presented to study the steady particle distribution in an axisymmetric particulate microchannel pipe flow when the effect of gravity is ignored. It is assumed that the initially uniformly distributed particles are injected slowly into the pressure-driven pipe flow at the pipe entrance. Analytical predictions are given for the particle volume fraction based on the adopted shear-induced lift force model with a positive lift force coefficient, which show that the lift force-driven lateral particle migration toward the centerline leads to a parabolic-like steady particle distribution over the pipe cross section. An explicit asymptotic expression is obtained for the steady particle volume fraction for a large axial distance from the entrance where the lateral particle migration settles down. When the particle-to-fluid inlet velocity ratio is at least one order of magnitude smaller than unity, a specific radial location (at a distance of about 0.58 times the pipe radius from the centerline) is identified at which the steady particle volume fraction remains nearly equal to its migration-free value, regardless of the specific values of the lift force coefficient, the particle Stokes number, and the particle-to-fluid density ratio. An explicit formula is given for the critical particle Stokes number, which defines the limitation of the present analysis, and the present method and derived formulas break down when the particle Stokes number is greater than the critical particle Stokes number. The predicted results are compared with available known data, with some qualitative agreement.
