papers.title: Elasto-inertial particle focusing and separation in mechanically driven oscillatory flows
papers.abstract: Oscillatory flows create a virtual infinite channel that repeatedly exposes particles to elasto-inertial lift forces, enabling superior focusing and size-based separation compared with unidirectional flows. Existing pump-free oscillatory microfluidic platforms require manual operation or rotating magnets that introduce flow-field asymmetry and obscure the intrinsic competition between elastic and inertial lift forces. Here, we develop a pump-free, mechanically driven oscillatory microfluidic platform enabled by phase-change liquid metal (LM). By embedding LM that undergoes reversible solid–liquid phase transition within designated channel regions, we significantly reduce the local Young's modulus, allowing efficient and reversible channel deformation under mechanical pressing. This approach generates symmetric and tunable oscillatory flows without external pumps, valves, or magnets, while maintaining a simple single-layer architecture that is easy to fabricate and highly reproducible. We systematically investigated the effects of concentration of viscoelastic medium, oscillation time, channel aspect ratio, and driving frequency on particle migration. Leveraging this differential migration, we demonstrated the effective separation of cancer cells from blood cells under mechanical actuation. This LM phase change-assisted mechanically driven platform enables the investigation of elasto-inertial migration under symmetric oscillatory flows, offering a scalable route toward automated and handheld point-of-care diagnostics.

papers.title: Discrete Boltzmann model at Burnett level for compressible multicomponent flows under external forces
papers.abstract: A discrete Boltzmann model at the Burnett level is established to investigate compressible multicomponent flows with external forces. A set of 25 discrete velocities is designed to provide high isotropy and numerical stability. Both the equilibrium discrete function and the force term are constructed using a moment-matching approach, ensuring that 25 independent kinetic moments are accurately recovered. This formulation enables the model to describe interspecies mass diffusion and capture thermodynamic nonequilibrium behaviors in compressible multicomponent systems. A series of canonical numerical benchmarks, including multicomponent diffusion, Sod shock tube, thermal Couette flow, Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, and Rayleigh–Taylor instability, is adopted to verify the numerical precision and stability of the newly developed model.

papers.title: Droplet breakup in Y-shaped microchannels: Bypass-flow regimes and stage-dependent necking dynamics
papers.abstract: Confined droplet breakup in Y-shaped bifurcating microchannels involves the coupled effects of geometric confinement, pressure redistribution, continuous-phase bypass flow, branch-induced deformation, and interfacial tension. In this study, a two-dimensional transient two-phase numerical model was employed to investigate the effects of bifurcation angle, initial droplet length, and continuous-phase capillary number on droplet breakup. Nine bifurcation angles ranging from 30° to 150° were considered. Based on the droplet blockage state and the connectivity of the continuous-phase bypass flow, four characteristic regimes were identified: non-breakup, breakup with permanent obstruction, breakup with partial obstruction, and breakup without obstruction. The breakup process was further divided into squeezing, transition, and rapid pinch-off stages. During the transition stage, liquid-bridge thinning is governed by the competition among pressure-driven deformation, viscous and extensional forcing, bypass-flow-mediated pressure release, and capillary restoration, whereas the final pinch-off is increasingly dominated by localized capillary effects. The bifurcation angle exhibits a pronounced non-monotonic influence on breakup dynamics. Intermediate angles of approximately 75°–90° provide the highest transition-stage necking efficiency, while either smaller or larger angles lead to slower sustained contraction. Although the effective extensional rate near the liquid bridge generally increases with bifurcation angle, the necking rate does not vary monotonically, indicating that extensional-flow intensity alone cannot determine breakup behavior. Instead, the angle dependence arises from the coupled regulation of flow redirection, droplet blockage, pressure transmission, bypass-flow connectivity, and liquid-bridge stretching. These results provide physical insight into angle-controlled droplet breakup and guidance for the design of passive droplet-splitting microfluidic structures.

papers.title: Recent advances in viscous fingering: Control, numerical techniques and applications
papers.abstract: Viscous fingering (VF) remains a central instability in porous media or Hele–Shaw cell flows, critically impacting applications such as enhanced oil recovery, CO2 sequestration, and environmental remediation. This review synthesizes recent advances in the control, numerical techniques and applications of VF through physical, chemical, thermodynamic, and artificial intelligent strategies. Physical interventions, ranging from engineered heterogeneity to wettability manipulation, alter local flow fields to stabilize or destabilize displacement fronts. Chemical strategies such as reactive transport and in situ viscosity modulation expand control through feedback mechanisms, while multiphysics approaches incorporate non-isothermal and phase separation effects. Phase-field and lattice Boltzmann models are widely used for high-resolution simulations, and artificial intelligent methods, including machine learning and surrogate modeling, now support real-time control and sensitivity analysis. Across scales, benchmarking and reproducibility remain critical challenges. Discrepancies between numerical solvers, model setups, and experimental validation underscore the need for standardized benchmarks and hybrid experimental-numerical workflows. This review provides a comparative synthesis of control techniques and identifies future research directions to bridge multiscale modeling, experimental realism, and control efficacy.

papers.title: Physics-informed wavelet–Fourier representation for multiscale fluid dynamics
papers.abstract: Multiscale fluid flows often contain localized flow structures, such as viscous shock layers, wet–dry fronts, steady viscous wakes, decaying vortical structures, and vortex-shedding patterns, whose accurate prediction requires the simultaneous preservation of global conservation trends and small-scale gradients. This study examines these flow-physics requirements through a physics-informed wavelet–Fourier (PIWF) representation for multiscale fluid dynamics. Instead of relying on a monolithic neural approximator, the formulation separates two complementary components of the flow field within a physics-informed neural representation: long-range coherent modes through a Fourier-basis branch and localized steep-gradient or vortical features through a compactly supported wavelet branch. The outputs are fused with a residual multilayer perceptron using channel attention, and the governing equations, initial conditions, and boundary conditions are imposed directly through the physics-informed loss. The model is assessed on five canonical fluid-dynamics problems: Burgers' equation, the shallow water equations, Kovasznay flow, Taylor–Green vortex flow, and two-dimensional cylinder wake. The results show that PIWF improves the resolution of shock-like gradients, wet–dry interfaces, steady wake fields, decaying vortical structures, vorticity extrema, and broadband wake spectra relative to standard physics-informed neural networks and physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold networks. These findings indicate that a wavelet–Fourier physics-informed representation can provide a useful route for analyzing multiscale flow phenomena when high-fidelity interior reference data are limited or unavailable.

papers.title: Experimental validation of a particle finite element model for sloshing in a horizontal tank with circular cross-section
papers.abstract: This study investigates the sloshing in a horizontal tank with circular cross section. A frequency sweep is performed around the first natural frequency, combined with different filling levels. The free-surface elevation is measured using ultrasonic sensors at predefined control points. In addition, the experiments are recorded using a high-speed camera, which allows to determine by image post-processing the entire free surface during the time-periodic regime along the cross section of the tank. Ultrasonic measurements and image-tracked wave heights are compared to ensure the consistency of the experimental data. Some experimental cases are further numerically modeled using a particle finite element method approach. In the simulations, the response is evaluated at the same control points used in the experiments, enabling a direct comparison of the free-surface dynamics. In spite that the numerical analysis is restricted to two-dimensional configurations, a satisfactorily experimental validation of the computed results is obtained, confirming that the numerical method is able to accurately predict the transient free-surface behavior.

papers.title: Pulsation, translation, and deformation of dual cavitation bubbles in confined blood vessels under multi-frequency ultrasound
papers.abstract: Regulation of intravascular cavitation is important for improving the safety and efficacy of ultrasound-mediated vascular therapies. This study investigates the pulsation, translation, and deformation of dual cavitation bubbles in confined blood vessels under multi-frequency ultrasound excitation. A bidirectionally coupled bubble–blood–vessel model incorporating the Carreau–Yasuda constitutive relation was developed to account for shear-rate-dependent blood viscosity and the interactions among cavitation bubbles, blood, and the vessel wall. Under the present equal-time-averaged-intensity normalization, triple-frequency excitation produces the greatest translation and deformation; however, the multi-frequency waveforms can also generate larger instantaneous peak rarefactional pressures through constructive superposition. Increasing equal initial bubble radii enhances pulsation, translation, deformation, and the secondary Bjerknes force. For unequal bubble sizes, the larger bubble exhibits stronger pulsation, whereas the smaller bubble shows more pronounced translation-related and deformation responses. Bubble shape has a limited influence on radial pulsation but a clearer effect on translation, with laterally ellipsoidal bubbles exhibiting the greatest reduced-order translational response. During pulsed ultrasound irradiation, bubble pulsation and the secondary Bjerknes force rapidly weaken after the acoustic input ceases, whereas the translational response exhibits a delayed evolution within the reduced-order model. Vascular confinement primarily modifies inter-bubble separation and translational behavior. A direct comparison between the Carreau–Yasuda and Newtonian descriptions shows only minor differences in the principal bubble-dynamics quantities under the investigated high-shear conditions. These findings clarify the coupled effects of multi-frequency excitation, vascular confinement, and bubble characteristics on intravascular cavitation dynamics, while demonstrating that the blood constitutive description has only a limited influence on the principal bubble dynamics under the investigated conditions.

papers.title: Investigation of formation mechanism and flow pattern evolution of ventilated supercavity regulated by cavitator geometry with annular hydrofoil
papers.abstract: This paper experimentally and numerically investigates the transient evolution of ventilated supercavitation regulated by an annular hydrofoil, focusing on the effects of axial position, angle of attack, and diameter on cavity morphology, internal velocity, and pressure fields. The results reveal that the hydrofoil cavity consistently exhibits a dual-layer structure throughout its growth, comprising a continuous bubble-laden film at the trailing edge and an internal ventilated supercavity. When placed immediately behind the cavitator, strong stagnation and gas-entrapment effects produce a high-pressure region that elevates internal pressure. Shifting the hydrofoil downstream weakens these effects, reducing pressure and enlarging cavity diameter. Increasing the angle of attack from 0° to 10° transforms the flow from symmetric to strongly asymmetric, intensifying lower-side separation and recirculation, which shortens the cavity and disrupts the bubble-laden film. The hydrofoil diameter exhibits a threshold: only when exceeding the natural cavity diameter does it constrain the cavity, forming a bubble-laden film and expanding the high-pressure zone, thereby enhancing stability. Velocity-pressure coupling analysis demonstrates that the annular hydrofoil modulates impingement direction and flow separation, thereby controlling cavity shape and internal pressure distribution.

papers.title: Large eddy simulation of particle mixing and deposition risk characteristics in metal powder fuel water ramjets: Role of integrated hollow bluff-body and groove inclination
papers.abstract: This study proposes the vortex-enhanced bluff groove, an integrated hollow bluff-body-groove mixing configuration, and, through large-eddy simulations, shows how its inclination angle affects the relationship between particle mixing characteristics and near-wall accumulation (an indirect deposition-risk proxy) in a metal powder/water ramjet combustor. The groove generates alternating high-velocity low-pressure and low-velocity high-pressure zones in the main flow. Driven by drag, particles accumulate in the low-pressure regions. At 0°, stable annular separation vortices maximize the wake shedding frequency; particles exhibit a single-layer annular distribution concentrated in the central region, yielding the lowest area-averaged mixing degree and near-wall accumulation tendency. As the inclination angle increases, the area-averaged mixing degree peaks at 40° (Ω=0.297) and remains high at 60° (Ω=0.266), whereas the near-wall particle concentration (i.e., deposition risk) increases monotonically from 0° to 60° (0.236–0.834 kg/m3). At 60°, premature boundary-layer separation under the adverse pressure gradient transports particles outward; the double-ring distribution places an outer concentration band in the wall-adjacent region, yielding the highest deposition risk despite a high mixing degree. The 40° configuration, thus, combines the highest mixing degree with a moderate deposition risk and dominates the 60° configuration. The study characterizes the influence of groove inclination on particle mixing and concentration distribution, quantifies how groove inclination sets the mixing-deposition trade-off, and provides a design criterion informing ramjet combustor design: if mixing and combustion efficiency are prioritized, 40° is recommended; 0° when wall deposition risk is the primary concern; and 20° as an intermediate trade-off, whereas the dominated 60° configuration is not recommended.

papers.title: Role of the thermal Marangoni effect in droplet evolution during electroslag remelting: Interfacial flow redistribution and necking-detachment dynamics
papers.abstract: The thermal Marangoni effect, arising from temperature-induced surface-tension gradients, can affect droplet dynamics in high-temperature multiphase systems. However, its role in droplet evolution during electroslag remelting (ESR) remains poorly understood. This study extends an existing two-dimensional axisymmetric model by introducing temperature-dependent slag-metal interfacial tension into a coupled electromagnetic–flow–thermal framework, thereby accounting for the thermal Marangoni effect. The model is assessed against experimental data from a published laboratory-scale ESR study. Both the constant-interfacial-tension model and the thermal Marangoni model reasonably reproduce the experimentally observed droplet-displacement history, whereas the thermal Marangoni effect produces only limited changes in the global multiphysics fields. Its influence is concentrated near the slag-metal interface, where the interfacial temperature gradient generates a tangential thermal Marangoni stress and redistributes the local interfacial flow. During droplet formation, the model predicts enhanced interfacial flow near the region of maximum radial expansion and accelerated neck thinning, consistent with increased drainage from the connecting neck. During descent, a flatter morphology is predicted, although the contributions of smaller detached volume and interfacial-flow redistribution are not separated. These findings suggest a localized fluid-mechanical pathway through which the thermal Marangoni effect modifies near-interface momentum transport, necking dynamics, and droplet deformation during ESR. The interfacial coefficient and local velocity field are not independently validated; the interpretation is limited to the modeled laboratory-scale case.

papers.title: Finite-time scalar retention and slow mixing tails in uncertain passive-scalar transport
papers.abstract: Mixing of a passive scalar in a time-dependent flow is usually judged from the variance decay of a nominal flow. In many applications, though, stirring protocols and flow parameters are uncertain, and the more relevant question is whether the required level of homogenization is reached within a finite time. We study this reliability question for incompressible advection–diffusion with uncertain forcing parameters, using a time-periodic double-gyre flow as the main benchmark and a periodically stirred cavity as a secondary test. Direct numerical simulations show that delayed mixing is not a fluctuation around the mean variance decay curve. Instead, slow realizations retain coherent scalar remnants near weakly exchanging regions of the flow, which produces a persistent upper tail in the mixing time distribution. To identify these slow events without running a full simulation for every parameter sample, we build a parameter- and phase-dependent reduced transport operator by combining a proper orthogonal decomposition-based Koopman representation with a polynomial-chaos expansion in the uncertain parameters. From this operator, we compute a finite-time scalar-retention score based on the leading singular direction of the learned propagator in a scalar-energy metric. The diagnostic ranks parameter realizations by their tendency to retain scalar energy, identifies the realizations contributing to the upper tail of the mixing time distribution, and recovers the scalar structures responsible for delayed homogenization. Reliable mixing under uncertainty is therefore controlled not only by the mean variance decay, but also by the least-damped scalar directions of the uncertain transport operator, which suggests that designs targeting reliable mixing should act on these directions directly.

papers.title: Thermodynamics-informed input reparameterization for neural prediction of real-fluid thermodynamic properties in supercritical combustion
papers.abstract: Real-fluid thermodynamic property evaluation is a major computational cost in supercritical combustion simulations. In the enthalpy-based pressure-correction formulation considered here, the cell-local closure evaluates temperature T, density ρ, and the compressibility coefficient ψ from the solver-available state (h,p,Y) through enthalpy–temperature inversion and repeated real-fluid equation-of-state evaluations. Neural-network surrogates offer fixed-cost inference, but a direct mapping from (h,p,Y) to (T,ρ,ψ) must represent both the caloric relation between enthalpy and temperature and the non-ideal equation-of-state response, resulting in a complex regression problem. This work introduces a thermodynamics-informed input reparameterization strategy, termed target-aligned input reparameterization (TAIR). TAIR replaces the raw enthalpy coordinate of each property network with a target-matched thermodynamic coordinate: the temperature network uses a temperature estimate obtained by inverting a constant-cp ideal-gas mixture enthalpy approximation, whereas the density and compressibility networks use an ideal-gas density estimate. These explicit algebraic transformations use only solver-available variables and species constants, guiding the networks to learn real-fluid departures from ideal-gas-based baselines rather than reconstructing the full closure from raw enthalpy. The method is assessed using supercritical methane–oxygen counterflow flame data against a raw-input baseline and target-inconsistent cross-reparameterization controls. TAIR reduces held-out test-set root-mean-squared error by factors of approximately 1.5, 2.0, and 7.5 for T, ρ, and ψ, respectively. For an unseen-strain-rate flame within the augmented thermodynamic envelope, the corresponding factors are 3.6, 14.5, and 6.0. The target-inconsistent controls perform markedly worse, indicating that the gains arise from thermodynamically matched input design rather than generic preprocessing.

papers.title: Experimental investigation on friction characteristics and inlet/outlet flow parameter sensitivity of duct flow with transverse microgrooves on the inner wall
papers.abstract: In active cooling systems, increased wall friction in coolant transport ducts reduces the coolant mass flow rate and outlet Mach number under the same driving pressure, thereby impairing the cooling performance. Arranging transverse microgrooves on the duct wall offers a promising solution, but their drag reduction performance and quantitative effects on duct inlet/outlet flow parameters remain unclear. Experiments using a custom-built system investigate the effects of microgroove depth and coverage length on the mean friction coefficient in non-choked square duct flow, with the friction coefficient back-calculated from measured inlet total pressure and mass flow rate based on Fanno flow theory. Sensitivity expressions are derived to quantify how inlet/outlet parameters respond to changes in the mean friction coefficient under different inlet conditions. The results indicate that increasing the coverage length ratio and decreasing the depth-to-diameter ratio both delay the transition from drag reduction to drag increase. At the same inlet Reynolds number and coverage length ratio, the microgrooved model with a smaller depth-to-diameter ratio exhibits a drag reduction performance approximately 5%–10% higher than that of the model with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio. At constant inlet Reynolds number, pressure parameters, and Mach number at the inlet show increasing sensitivity with inlet Reynolds number, while outlet parameters and mass flow rate remain highly insensitive (order 10−3). Under constant inlet total pressure, however, inlet/outlet Mach numbers, mass flow rate, and inlet Reynolds number are highly sensitive to the mean friction coefficient (−0.32 to −0.46). These findings quantitatively inform microgrooved duct design and coolant flow regulation for enhanced thermal protection.

papers.title: Effects of local oxygen enrichment on thermal nonequilibrium supersonic combustion in a Mach 12 scramjet engine
papers.abstract: For scramjet engines operating at high Mach numbers (Ma>8), the classical ideal-gas and single-temperature assumptions become severely inaccurate. The physical understanding of high Mach number turbulent combustion must be reconstructed from the perspective of thermal nonequilibrium. In this study, the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulation with Park's two-temperature approach in combination with the chemistry–vibration coupling model was employed in the nonequilibrium simulations of turbulent combustion in the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency scramjet engine designated M12-02 under a Mach 12 flight condition. To address the severe oxygen depletion and incomplete combustion observed downstream of the fuel injection, a localized oxygen-enriched injection strategy is proposed. Three key parameters of the proposed strategy are systematically evaluated, namely the oxygen enrichment percentage (EP), the injection angle, and the injection location. The results indicate that a moderate oxygen enrichment percentage (EP=12.5%) provides the best balance between combustion enhancement and isolator stability, increasing the combustion efficiency at the nozzle exit by 21.6% relative to the EP=0% case. In contrast, excessive oxygen enrichment induces a stronger upstream pressure response and increases the risk of inlet unstart. Among the injection orientations considered, the 45° co-flow case has the smallest mean reverse-flow area and a smoother downstream development of mixing efficiency. Among the injection locations considered, the 30 mm transition-region case gives the highest nozzle-exit combustion efficiency and produces a more distributed reaction zone than the core-region case.

papers.title: Effects of forward-facing and backward-facing steps located upstream of the synchronization point on the hypersonic boundary-layer transition
papers.abstract: The forward-facing step (FFS) and backward-facing step (BFS) have been shown to significantly influence the growth of the second-mode wave in hypersonic boundary layers. However, the role of the step location relative to the synchronization point remains incompletely understood. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effects of a step placed upstream of the synchronization point on hypersonic boundary-layer instability. Experiments are conducted on a 5° flared cone at zero angle of attack in the Mach 6 quiet wind tunnel at Peking University. The step height is approximately equal to the local boundary-layer thickness. The evolution of instability waves is measured using both flush-mounted pressure fluctuation sensors and infrared thermography. For this specific configuration and flow condition, our results show that, both FFS and BFS located upstream of the synchronization point promote boundary-layer transition, with the BFS exhibiting a stronger promotion effect. Compared with the no-step case, the propagation velocity of the second-mode wave is significantly reduced behind both step types. In addition, the FFS decreases the local boundary-layer thickness, whereas the BFS increases it. However, cross-bicoherence analysis, which distinguishes between sum-frequency and difference-frequency nonlinear interactions, reveals that under the tested conditions, the dominant difference-frequency interaction between the second-mode wave and its first harmonic persists, although steps modify transition locations and wave properties. The difference-frequency interactions between the second-mode wave and its first harmonic play a dominant role throughout the transition process.

papers.title: Influence of density maximum on the route to chaos in double-diffusive Rayleigh–Bénard convection
papers.abstract: This study explores the effect of the maximum density property of a fluid in double diffusive Rayleigh–Bénard convection. A nonlinear density-temperature relation (DTR) approximated up to a cubic-order polynomial is considered. The lower and upper boundaries are assumed to be isothermal and isoconcentration and are subjected to combinations of stress-free and rigid velocity boundary conditions. The Maclaurin series method, followed by the multivariate Newton-Raphson method, is employed to perform linear stability analysis. The presence of solutal concentration gradients is observed to delay the onset of regular convective motion, thereby exerting a stabilizing influence on the system. The weakly nonlinear regime is analyzed using a modified five-dimensional autonomous generalized Lorenz model (GLM), determining the onset of chaos, Hopf bifurcation, and extended periodicity. The behavior of the GLM is analyzed by the bifurcation diagram, largest Lyapunov exponent plot, and phase portrait. Results from the study reveal that a decrease in solute concentration is found to advance the onset of chaos, followed by the Hopf bifurcation, while a non-monotonic behavior is observed as the surface temperature and Lewis number vary. A coexistence region is identified for systems with linear and cubic DTR, revealing that the Hopf bifurcation and the onset of chaos are distinct dynamical transitions. This study is subsequently extended to water, characterized by a density maximum at 3.98 °C, where increasing Le leads to a transition from stationary to oscillatory convection, with instability occurring at a thermal Rayleigh number significantly lower than that required for stationary convection.

papers.title: Hydraulic characteristics of side-by-side settling of centimeter-sized twin particles using smoothed particle hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: In this study, a numerical model for simulating the settling process of centimeter-sized twin particles released side by side in still water is developed by coupling the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method with the equations of solid motion and implemented using a Fortran 90 code. Particle shifting technology and tensile instability control algorithms are incorporated to improve the accuracy and robustness of the SPH method. The numerical model is validated through comparisons between the predicted settling trajectories and laboratory experimental results, demonstrating its capability to accurately simulate the settling process of centimeter-sized twin particles. Experimental observations show that, during side-by-side settling, the twin particles initially undergo an approximately vertical descent and subsequently exhibit an “away-approaching” motion phenomenon. Based on the validated numerical model, the underlying mechanisms governing this phenomenon are investigated. The results indicate that the force due to pressure difference between the inner and outer sides of each particle in the horizontal direction is the primary driver of lateral displacement. The evolution of the flow field and vorticity field, the variation in particle attitude, and the influence of particle density on settling behavior are also examined.

papers.title: Cavity dynamics and energy budget for composite-driven and jet-driven regimes in air-jet-assisted water entry
papers.abstract: This study investigates the air-jet-assisted water entry and provides a numerical analysis of the experimentally observed composite-driven and jet-driven cavities. We employed numerical simulations to elucidate the differences in cavity propulsion, closure dynamics, and energy distribution during water entry. The results reveal that the closure of composite-driven cavities exhibits pronounced forced characteristics, arising from the abrupt transition between jet-driven and carrier-driven propulsion modes. In contrast, jet-driven cavities maintain stable propulsion for a significantly longer duration and close at greater depths. A dimensionless supply–demand ratio, combined with power-law fitting and velocity-based scaling parameters, demonstrates that the macroscopic closure processes of both cavity types are predominantly governed by a gravity–inertia mechanism, while the fitted exponent for the jet-driven case reveals a secondary, non-gravitational modification to the local self-similar scaling. Energy statistics further indicate that, in air-jet-assisted water entry, the overall energy partition is characterized by dominant dissipation, followed by boundary transport, with relatively limited energy storage. Jet-driven cavities exhibit a more uniform energy distribution compared to composite-driven ones.

papers.title: Impact of through-flow and swirling magnetohydrodynamic flows of liquid metal in a cylindrical channel on the transport of temperature non-uniformities
papers.abstract: This article presents an experimental and numerical study of the generation of low-frequency temperature pulsations in liquid-metal pipelines and the possibility of suppressing pulsations that may cause thermal-cycling fatigue through the electromagnetic generation of counter-vortex mixing flows. Flows arising in a cylindrical channel under the influence of oppositely rotating magnetic fields (RMFs) are considered both with and without a through-flow. The source of the temperature fluctuations is a localized heater. It is shown that under the action of a solitary RMF, a rotational flow with secondary poloidal circulation occurs. The simultaneous action of two counter-rotating magnetic fields generates complex structures, such as regular quasi-harmonic jet-like streams, localized tornado-like vortices, and chaotic multi-vortex modes. It was found that the jet-like flow ensures efficient radial heat transfer and shifts the temperature-pulsation spectrum toward lower frequencies (less than 1 Hz). Maps of the hydrodynamic modes were obtained as a function of the electromagnetic forcing intensity. Characteristic temperature pulsation frequencies were determined for each mode. Characteristic temperature pulsation frequencies were determined for each mode.

papers.title: Hysteretic tip-leakage vortex dynamics in a variable-speed multiphase pump
papers.abstract: A pronounced hysteretic response is identified between imposed rotational-speed variation and rigid-vorticity evolution in a tip-leakage vortex (TLV). Identical rotational speeds during acceleration and deceleration correspond to different vortex intensities and spatial configurations, revealing a memory effect in the internal rotating flow. This behavior is investigated in a gas–liquid rotodynamic multiphase pump using transient numerical simulation, Liutex–Omega vortex identification, rigid-vorticity decomposition, and transport analysis. The hysteresis arises from a mismatch between the timescale of external speed forcing and the relaxation timescale of the vortical flow. After the rotational speed changes, the preexisting vortex system undergoes viscous attenuation and structural reorganization before establishing a configuration compatible with the new operating condition. During acceleration, inherited vortex structures initially weaken and then develop into a stronger, more concentrated vortex system. During deceleration, fluid inertia temporarily sustains the leakage-jet momentum and previously established vortices, delaying their attenuation and breakdown. The Coriolis-related rotational term and the rigid-vorticity viscous-diffusion term dominate this transient response, while the pseudo-Lamb term promotes rigid-vorticity quasi-generation during acceleration. Stretching and dilatation mainly regulate localized vortex-tube deformation and make smaller overall contributions. These results show that TLV evolution under transient forcing is controlled by relaxation, reorganization, and flow memory rather than responding instantaneously or monotonically to rotational speed, providing a generalizable description of hysteretic vortex dynamics in variable-speed rotating flows.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigation on dynamic flow separation during water-entry of an open cavity
papers.abstract: In this paper, the water-entry behavior of an open cylindrical cavity is investigated by laboratory experiments and numerical simulations. Laboratory experiments are conducted in a water flume, with high-speed imaging used to capture cavity bubble evolution across a range of entry velocities, corresponding to Froude numbers Fr from 0 to 2.433. Three distinct flow patterns have been identified: a turbulent pattern (Fr<0.75), a transitional pattern (0.75≤Fr≤1.75), and a wave-forming pattern (Fr>1.75). The process is characterized by periodic liquid inflow and outflow, leading to repeated compression and expansion of the trapped gas, which in turn induces significant wall oscillations and morphological instability. A computational fluid dynamics model is utilized to further study the effect of the open-end bottom on the velocity and acceleration of the cavity. The results show that the open configuration experiences slower penetration, sustained fluctuations in velocity and acceleration, and enhanced unsteady dynamics due to internal fluid exchange.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of oil–water interfacial flow dynamics in porous media: Effects of anisotropic pore structures on the critical pressure difference
papers.abstract: In this study, we numerically investigate the effects of anisotropic pore structures on oil–water interfacial penetration using direct numerical simulations based on the level contour reconstruction method. Building on our previous two-dimensional study, which identified penetration as a local path-finding problem and proposed a Young–Laplace-based theoretical model for the critical pressure difference, we extend the analysis to both two- and three-dimensional systems with particular attention to the effects of anisotropic pore structures. Two-dimensional simulations reveal that pore anisotropy, characterized by aspect ratio and inclination angle, significantly influences the critical pressure difference by altering local interfacial curvature and surface tension forces. A correction function is introduced to account for these effects, enabling accurate prediction of the critical pressure difference. Three-dimensional simulations further demonstrate the multiple curvature effects associated with structural topology on the interfacial penetration, which cannot be represented by two-dimensional systems. The effective characteristic length scale is introduced with a new structural coefficient, leading to a combined simple semi-empirical model. The proposed model shows good agreement with simulation results across a wide range of anisotropy, characteristic length scales, and structural variations. A validation example using three-dimensional randomized anisotropic pore structures confirms that our semi-empirical model reasonably reproduces critical pressure differences in three-dimensional anisotropic porous media.

papers.title: Swirl flow in microchannels: Patterned slip walls enhance heat transport
papers.abstract: Microchannel heat sinks are widely used for thermal management in high-power electronics due to their ability to dissipate large heat fluxes with minimal coolant consumption. While numerous strategies—such as geometric modifications, surface disruptions, and enhanced coolant formulations—have been explored to improve heat transfer, many of these approaches increase hydraulic resistance and pumping power requirements. Recent studies have shown that slip/no-slip wall patterns can enhance flow rates and convective heat removal without additional energy input, and that patterned microstructures can induce secondary swirling motions known to promote mixing and heat transfer. Motivated by these findings, we investigate a slip/no-slip pattern specifically designed to generate swirl flow inside a straight microchannel. Building upon prior work on passive chaotic advection and boundary-condition engineering, we assess the hydrodynamic and thermal performance of this patterned configuration under conditions relevant to laminar microchannel cooling. Our results demonstrate that appropriately arranged slip/no-slip regions can induce swirl without geometric perturbations or increased pumping power, ultimately improving heat transfer efficiency at fixed volumetric flow rate. This study highlights the potential of boundary-condition patterning as a simple, energy-neutral strategy for enhancing the performance of microfluidic heat-transfer devices.

papers.title: Frequency-selective response: A novel phenomenon of supersonic combustion in a cavity-stabilized combustor under unsteady perturbation
papers.abstract: We investigate the response of a direct-connect, dual-cavity scramjet combustor to controlled unsteady perturbation. The perturbation is imposed by a high-frequency fuel supply system at six frequencies (100–350, 50 Hz steps) and a fixed amplitude of approximately 15%. The response is characterized using wall-pressure and CH* (electronically excited CH radical) chemiluminescence statistics, time-averaged flame distributions, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) energy spectra and modal analysis. The combustor response is not monotonic in the perturbation frequency. The unforced baseline and the 100, 200, and 300 Hz cases form group I, whereas the 150, 250, and 350 Hz cases form group II. Group I exhibits higher upstream mean wall pressure and CH* chemiluminescence intensity, a more vertically extended mean luminous field, and a broader SPOD energy distribution. Group II exhibits lower upstream mean wall pressure together with a higher relative wall-pressure fluctuation intensity, lower CH* intensity, redistribution of the mean luminous field toward the near-wall region, stronger spectral concentration, higher mode 1 dominance, and more spatially localized mode 1 structures. These mutually consistent statistical, spectral, and spatial signatures establish the frequency-selective grouping as a robust response feature. Of the linear and nonlinear mechanisms considered, a Rayleigh–Crocco phase-delay interpretation is the one consistent with the observed alternation.

papers.title: Zonal evolution and prediction model of shock wave pressure field from near-seabed underwater explosions
papers.abstract: The propagation of shock waves from an underwater detonation near a seabed is governed by the nonlinear interplay among the rigid boundary, evolving gas bubble dynamics, and Mach reflection, producing a highly intricate spatial pressure field challenging to model. In this work, we establish a zonal framework that partitions the pressure field into three physically distinct regions: the reflection amplification region (RAR), the bubble attenuation region (BAR), and the Mach enhancement region (MER). Integrating high-fidelity discontinuous Galerkin simulations, small-scale experiments, and theoretical analysis, we develop predictive models for each region. For the RAR, we propose a dynamic equivalent source method that reconstructs the reflected wave field with an attenuation factor of 1.065. For the BAR, we identify the bubble-shadowing effect and establish an attenuation model with mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 6.48%. For the MER, we derive an analytical overpressure model for underwater Mach reflection, complemented by an exponential decay law, yielding a MAPE of 3.33%. The framework is further extended to realistic seabed compositions via material degradation coefficients. On rocky seabeds, Mach reflection occurs only when a dimensionless parameter exceeds 2.321, and the triple-point trajectory is predicted with MAPE of 6.65%. Overall, the framework enables quantitative prediction of the near-seabed pressure field and provides a physically grounded tool for understanding shock-boundary interactions in compressible multiphase flows, with implications for numerical validation and hydrodynamic loading assessment.

papers.title: Chemical regulation of displacement-front stability in porous media through viscosity ratio and miscibility control
papers.abstract: Multiphase displacement in porous media depends on viscous and capillary forces, molecular diffusion, and fluid phase behavior. An unfavorable viscosity ratio can promote/ viscous fingering and early breakthrough, reducing sweep efficiency. Here, we investigate how additive-induced changes in CO2-rich phase properties affect pore-scale displacement patterns and oil recovery. Molecular dynamics simulations evaluated additive effects on density, apparent shear viscosity, CO2 diffusion, and CO2–hydrocarbon miscibility. The resulting density and viscosity correlations were incorporated into pore-scale simulations to evaluate front evolution, swept area, residual-oil distribution, and recovery. The investigated additives decreased CO2 diffusion coefficients and increased the apparent shear viscosity of the CO2-rich phase. Anionic surfactant sodium bis(2-ethylhexyl) sulfosuccinate (AOT) produced the largest viscosity increase, 239.14%, at the highest investigated additive molecular count. With Span 20, the simulated minimum miscibility pressure decreased from 10.03 to 9.21 MPa. The latter value was 5.3% below the experimental reference of 9.726 MPa. Pore-scale simulations incorporating the density and viscosity changes showed less pronounced fingering and broader lateral spreading of CO2. At an injected volume of one pore volume, the swept area increased by approximately 15% for the Span-series additives and 26.27% for AOT relative to the additive-free case. Micromodel experiments further show delayed preferential-channel formation and enhanced residual-oil mobilization, with Span 20 increasing recovery by 4.69 percentage points under the investigated immiscible conditions. These results link additive-induced fluid-property changes to pore-scale displacement behavior and identify potential benefits for sweep and oil recovery under the investigated conditions.

papers.title: Three-dimensional delineation of the Lofoten Vortex using the R-tube method for the analysis of water exchange mechanisms based on the Regional Ocean Modeling System
papers.abstract: A new Lagrangian approach for the three-dimensional analysis of mesoscale eddies, the R-tube method, is presented as an extension of the Lagrangian Eddy Boundary Delineation Algorithm. The method is applied to the quasi-persistent Lofoten anticyclone in the Norwegian Sea using a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System simulation. A horizontal R-contour constructed at 400 m is vertically extrapolated over the 0–1000 m range to form a unified pseudo-three-dimensional eddy boundary. Three-dimensional trajectories of approximately 1 × 106 passive markers are computed over 40 days to investigate material exchange between the vortex and the surrounding flow. The results reveal a strongly coherent subsurface regime extending from 100 to 1000 m and a dynamically distinct surface layer. Within the subsurface vortex, rotational trapping strongly suppresses radial material transport, whereas exchange occurs intermittently through localized finite-time deformation, lobe formation, and lobe detachment. Thus, material export is organized into coherent pulses rather than continuous leakage, indicating that deformation at the vortex periphery provides the principal pathway for releasing water from the isolated core. The eddy core (150–900 m) retains most markers throughout the simulation, demonstrating strong Lagrangian coherence and long-term water-mass isolation. The R-tube method therefore provides a quantitative framework for linking three-dimensional vortex structure, coherent transport, and intermittent material exchange in geophysical flows.

papers.title: Nonlinear resonance dynamics of a floating body with a moonpool and heave plates
papers.abstract: Moonpool resonance and heave-plate-induced vortex shedding are both important features of offshore floating structures, but their coupled effects on gap free-surface oscillations and body motions remain insufficiently understood. In the present study, the nonlinear hydrodynamic coupling between a moonpool and bottom-mounted heave plates is investigated under fixed and free-heave conditions utilizing a two-way coupled potential-viscous-flow solver. The numerical method is validated against analytical solutions for regular-wave propagation and experimental measurements of gap resonance and wave-induced body motion. For the fixed-body cases, the heave plates substantially suppress the resonant gap elevation while producing only a negligible shift in the resonance frequency. Flow-field analysis shows that the heave plates dissipate energy through vortex shedding, thereby reducing the velocity flux and vorticity near the moonpool entrance. When heave motion is released, the coupled system develops a distinct two-peak coupled gap response. The low-frequency peak follows the heave resonance and shifts to lower frequencies as either wave amplitude or plate width increases, whereas the high-frequency peak remains close to the moonpool resonance in the fixed-body condition. The heave Response Amplitude Operator exhibits clear amplitude dependence. When incident-wave amplitude is increased, the peak response is reduced and shifted toward lower frequencies. This behavior is associated with amplitude-dependent increases in heave added mass and damping, which become more pronounced for the heave-plate configuration. These results demonstrate that heave plates not only attenuate moonpool oscillations but also alter the resonance frequencies and response characteristics of the coupled system, which should be considered in the hydrodynamic design of offshore floating structures incorporating both moonpools and heave plates.

papers.title: Effects of thermochemical nonequilibrium on shock interaction flow of V-shaped leading edge
papers.abstract: This paper numerically investigates the effects of thermochemical nonequilibrium on the shock interactions and aerodynamic heating over the V-shaped leading edge. The numerical methodology is validated against experimental data from the JF22 hypervelocity wind tunnel. A comparative study is performed using the calorically perfect gas (CPG) model, as well as the one-temperature and two-temperature five-species chemical reaction models of air. The results demonstrate that thermochemical nonequilibrium significantly modifies the post-shock thermodynamic state through internal energy excitation and chemical reactions, thereby altering the shock-layer structure and detached-shock standoff distance. The different relaxation processes predicted by the one-temperature and two-temperature models lead to distinct shock interaction patterns, with the one-temperature model inducing a transition from Mach reflection to regular reflection from the same family. Compared with the CPG model, thermochemical nonequilibrium models predict enhanced wall heat flux due to the coupled effects of modified shock-layer states, conductive heat transfer, and species enthalpy transport. In particular, under the fully catalytic wall condition, atomic recombination releases chemical formation enthalpy, contributing to the species enthalpy diffusion term and the enhanced wall heat flux predicted by the thermochemical nonequilibrium models. These findings demonstrate that accurate thermochemical nonequilibrium modelling is essential for the reliable design and performance assessment of high-enthalpy scramjet inlets.

papers.title: Shear-induced volumetric response and particle normal stress partitioning in proppant sand dunes within a single-wing fracture
papers.abstract: Fluid-induced shear acting on proppant particles affects their transport distribution. It also influences the morphological evolution of sand dunes. However, the role of shear-induced contraction/dilatancy responses in this evolution remains insufficiently understood. Therefore, an existing solid-phase dilatancy/contraction formulation is incorporated into an Eulerian two-phase flow framework to investigate the effects of injection velocity and particle size on proppant transport and sand dune morphological evolution, with particular emphasis on the relationship between shear-induced volumetric response and the partitioning of particle normal stress between the shear-induced and permanent-contact components. The results show that, with increasing injection velocity, sand dune morphological evolution is closely associated with an increasingly dilated packing state in the surface layer. As the injection velocity increases from 0.25 to 1.0 m/s, the surface layer packing state becomes increasingly dilated relative to the local critical packing condition, with the corresponding surface averaged response metric reaching approximately 11.1 times its value at 0.25 m/s, while the local permanent-contact stress in the surface layer decreases by approximately 18.9%. These results indicate that the intensified surface layer response, associated with this increasingly dilated packing state, is accompanied by a reduced permanent-contact contribution to the local particle normal stress and enhanced downstream particle redistribution. Under a fixed injection velocity, decreasing particle size shifts the depositional region farther downstream, while the locally averaged permanent-contact normal stress in the surface layer decreases by approximately 49.8%. Taken together, these results further elucidate the relationship between shear-induced volumetric response and continuum scale particle normal stress partitioning, as well as the association of stress partitioning with variations in sand dune morphology.

papers.title: Shock train reconfiguration under different suction strategies in a scramjet isolator
papers.abstract: This numerical study investigates boundary layer suction effects on shock train dynamics in an isolator using Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations with the shear stress transport k–ω model. Twenty-seven configurations explore suction port location and quantity under fixed backpressure, covering single-side, symmetric, and asymmetric strategies. Three distinct physical mechanisms are identified. Single-side suction triggers a momentum deficit redistribution. The boundary layer on the wall with suction is strengthened, whereas separation appears on the wall without suction due to mass conservation constraints, with the shock train leading edge (STLE) located further upstream. Symmetric suction results in stepwise STLE positioning. Each additional pair of suction holes corresponds to a downstream shift of the STLE, and the shock train appears more compact in structure as the number of holes increases. Asymmetric suction is associated with a downstream position of the STLE, while the total pressure recovery coefficient remains relatively high over a range of suction ratios. These observations are interpreted in terms of three constraints, namely separation zone size, mass conservation, and pressure matching. The findings establish the physical basis for adaptive suction control in scramjet isolators.

papers.title: Shared sparse sensing and DeepONet-enabled relative optical path difference prediction in a lithography slit flow
papers.abstract: Thermo-pressure disturbances in the confined slit of lithography metrology perturb the refractive index and accumulate along optical paths, producing optical path difference (OPD) errors. To clarify how coupled thermo-fluid disturbances are transported and converted into optical error, shared sparse sensing reconstructs the global thermo-pressure fields, while a deep operator network rapidly predicts the relative optical path difference (OPD′), representing the fluctuating component of OPD, for physical analysis. Using a transient computational fluid dynamics dataset spanning 27 conditions, 20 shared sensing locations support field reconstruction and end-to-end OPD′ prediction with coefficients of determination (R2) near 0.98 under unseen conditions. Controlled parameter scans reveal distinct response trends. Increasing purge velocity from 8 to 13 m/s reduces the temporal-fluctuation root-mean-square (RMS) amplitude by 27.67% while changing the mean spatial RMS by only −0.46%. Increasing purge temperature produces the strongest amplification of both measures, whereas increasing wall heat flux affects temporal variability more strongly than the mean spatial magnitude. Despite these changes, the normalized OPD′ spatial pattern remains nearly unchanged. The temperature-induced component accounts for 99.61%–99.87% of the mean spatial RMS and 98.88%–99.60% of the temporal-fluctuation RMS. Path-resolved analysis shows that higher purge velocity weakens the temperature fluctuations sampled along the coordinate-dependent optical paths without substantially shifting the main thermally affected path region. Within the dominant thermal contribution, OPD′ is governed not by local temperature-fluctuation amplitude alone, but by unequal path-integrated thermal contributions among the optical paths, while nearly common contributions are largely removed by spatial-mean subtraction. A low-order empirical relation predicts the condition-level differential thermal fluctuation with a mean absolute percentage error of approximately 1.40% for extrapolation cases, while the inferred thermal coefficient differs by only 0.54% from the local temperature sensitivity of the Edlén relation. These results reveal a flow-optical coupling process controlled by thermal loading, purge-flow transport and fluid renewal, and differential thermal accumulation among optical paths.

papers.title: Coupled bulk acoustic streaming and acoustothermal effects: A high-frequency focused beam example
papers.abstract: High-frequency focused acoustic beams are promising for selective trapping of cells in fluids, but the related acoustic absorption may generate large acoustothermal effect which could cause thermal heating on cells or microparticles and bring extra acoustic body force due to the thermal gradient. The theory of the bulk acoustic streaming and acoustic radiation force in a focused beam for the three-dimensional selective trapping of a cell has been developed [Li and Gong, “Competition between acoustic radiation force and streaming-induced drag force in focused beams for three-dimensional cell trapping,” Phys. Rev. Fluids 11, 054201 (2026)]; however, the acoustothermal effect and its feedback on the acoustic field at high frequency with strong absorption remain weakly understood. To solve this issue, we develop a theoretical and numerical model that couples acoustic propagation, bulk acoustic streaming, and the acoustothermal effect in water. The acoustic body force is decomposed into a viscous-attenuation-induced acoustic body force fE and a temperature-gradient-induced acoustic body force fT, while the temperature field is fed back to the frequency-domain acoustic calculation through the temperature-dependent material properties. Taking the single focused beam, for example, within the pressure range constrained by the mechanical index, fT remains weaker than fE, whereas streaming-induced convection can markedly reduce the temperature rise when the thermal Peclet number (PeT) exceeds unity. This work establishes a theoretical basis for predicting and controlling the intercoupling of bulk acoustic streaming and the acoustothermal effect of high-frequency focused beams, which will be helpful for the design of single-beam acoustical tweezers.

papers.title: Dominant geometric sensitivities and associated aerodynamic mechanisms of a co-flow jet airfoil
papers.abstract: Co-flow jet (CFJ) is an active flow-control technique with strong potential for lift enhancement, drag reduction, and separation suppression. However, the relative importance, influence directions, and aerodynamic mechanisms associated with CFJ geometric parameters remain insufficiently understood. In this study, Kriging surrogate models were constructed using Latin hypercube sampling. Sobol global sensitivity analysis and Spearman rank-correlation analysis were used to quantify the effects of geometric parameters on the maximum lift coefficient and maximum corrected aerodynamic efficiency at a jet momentum coefficient of 0.04. Controlled single-parameter computational fluid dynamics analyses were then conducted for representative parameter variations, followed by sensitivity-guided variable screening and multi-objective optimization. The results show that the injection-slot position dominates the maximum lift coefficient, whereas the suction-surface downward translation has the strongest influence on the maximum corrected aerodynamic efficiency. Moving the injection slot downstream improves near-wall momentum retention and delays suction-side separation. Although the suction-slot position has a weaker influence on maximum lift, it still affects separation onset and stall. Increasing the suction-surface downward translation reduces the power-consumption penalty at moderate angles of attack but weakens attachment near stall. The five-variable optimization retains performance close to that of the full six-variable model, while the four-variable model shows a more evident reduction in corrected aerodynamic efficiency. After optimization, the stall angle increases from 12° to 16°–17°, the maximum lift coefficient improves by more than 11%, and the maximum corrected aerodynamic efficiency increases by more than 44%.

papers.title: Large-scale modal depletion and strain-gradient amplification precede palinstrophy bursts in two-dimensional forced Kolmogorov flow
papers.abstract: Intermittent palinstrophy bursts in two-dimensional forced Kolmogorov flow are examined by connecting the established large-scale (1, 0) modal precursor to the local palinstrophy-production budget. Production is expressed through the exact identity ΠP=APGP, where GP=⟨σstr|∇ω|2⟩ measures strain-gradient magnitude and AP=ΠP/GP is a bounded signed alignment factor. Across 21 independently initialized trajectories, partitioned into disjoint fitting, selection, and held-out subsets, event-aligned profiles place modal depletion and GP growth in an earlier precursor regime, followed by increased ΠP near burst onset. Fixed-window lead-lag correlations support a finite modal lead for raw, detrended, and increment signals, whereas GP and ΠP correlate most strongly with palinstrophy at or near zero lag. The ordering of modal and GP threshold crossings depends on the burst definition. Exact finite-change attribution identifies the magnitude-associated term A0ΔGP as the dominant positive contribution to the production increase at four examined pre-onset and onset times, with trajectory-bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the alignment-associated term is not sign-resolved. The modal depletion score has the largest episode F1 among eight tested single-mode and spectral-shell definitions. Robustness checks include alternative burst definitions, held-out initial conditions, grid refinement, autoencoder parameter variations, and time step halving. The three-trajectory time step comparison retains positive near-onset magnitude contributions but does not establish invariant staging. A two-stage criterion represents the observed temporal staging but is not statistically superior to the modal precursor or the strongest multivariate scalar models. These results quantitatively connect large-scale modal reorganization with near-onset palinstrophy production within the examined flow regime.

papers.title: Jet-induced recirculation and non-monotonic particle transport in a full-scale train carriage enclosure
papers.abstract: Particle transport in elongated confined enclosures is strongly affected by the interaction between supply jets, geometric confinement, and recirculation, yet the mechanism by which increasing jet momentum alters particle residence and removal remains insufficiently resolved. This study investigates jet-induced recirculation and non-monotonic particle transport in a full-scale train carriage enclosure using controlled experiments and validated transient computational fluid dynamics and discrete phase model simulations. The results show that increasing supply-jet velocity enhances the overall carrier-flow intensity but does not eliminate persistent low-velocity regions near seating and lower-side zones. Moderate jet momentum promotes advective transport and confined turbulent mixing, thereby reducing peak particle concentrations and accelerating post-release decay. At higher velocity, however, stronger jet penetration induces larger recirculation cells and low-velocity retention zones, leading to renewed local particle accumulation and a non-monotonic particle-field response. Particle-source strength mainly scales the concentration magnitude without fundamentally changing the transport pattern. Both the coefficient of variation and peak response ratio (Rp) exhibited their lowest responses within the supply-jet velocity range of 0.75–0.80 m/s, identifying this interval as a favorable range with respect to the selected particle-dispersion metrics. These findings provide full-scale experimental insights into velocity-dependent particle transport under controlled carriage conditions and establish a basis for future investigations involving more complex scenarios.

papers.title: Dual-pump reverse series effect of an electric ducted fan-disk suction unit
papers.abstract: This study focuses on a suction unit in which an electric ducted fan (EDF) drives flow through a gap flow resistance, referred to as the electric ducted fan–disk suction unit (EDFD). First, comparative experiments on suction force demonstrate that the suction capability of the EDFD significantly outperforms that of a standalone EDF. Subsequently, smoke flow visualization experiments reveal an intriguing anomalous phenomenon: varying the gap height induces flow reversal within the EDFD, manifesting as distinct positive and negative flow states. Because it is challenging to directly measure this flow rate without disturbing the internal flow field of the EDFD, an indirect measurement approach based on the momentum theorem is formulated. Furthermore, given that the EDF blades simultaneously act as both an “axial flow pump” and a “centrifugal pump,” we postulate that the EDFD essentially constitutes a system characterized by a “dual-pump reverse series driving a gap flow resistance.” Alterations in the gap height shift the flow characteristic curve of the “centrifugal pump–gap flow resistance” subsystem. This shifted curve intersects the flow characteristic curve of the axial flow pump at either the positive or negative flow regions, thereby elucidating the underlying mechanism of the EDFD flow reversal. Finally, the EDFD is implemented on a wall-climbing robot, demonstrating exceptional suction performance and obstacle-negotiation capability.

papers.title: A pediatric-specific model for age-dependent intraocular biofluid dynamics and atropine transport
papers.abstract: Low-concentration atropine is used for myopia control in children, but existing intraocular drug delivery models based on adult ocular geometry and physiological parameters may not accurately predict age-dependent drug transport in pediatric eyes. In this study, three-dimensional pediatric ocular drug transport models for children aged 4–7 and 8–12 years are established, incorporating age-dependent ocular geometries and physiological parameters to investigate the effects of age and dosing timing on intraocular heat transfer, biofluid flow, and atropine transport following topical administration. The results show that pediatric eyes exhibit lower temperature gradients in the anterior segment and lower peak aqueous humor and vitreous humor velocities than adult eyes, with the 4–7-year-old group exhibiting 9.95% and 13.20% lower peak atropine concentrations in the retina and choroid, respectively, but a 9.10% higher iris concentration than adults. Compared with nighttime dosing, daytime dosing increases the peak atropine concentrations in the retina and choroid by 18.98% and 18.02%, respectively. Under nighttime dosing, administration approximately 2 h before bedtime achieves target tissue concentrations comparable to those obtained with daytime dosing. These findings demonstrate the value of pediatric-specific ocular models incorporating age-dependent biological fluid dynamics, combined with optimized dosing timing, for predicting intraocular drug transport and improving atropine treatment strategies.

papers.title: Stall inception analysis on axial compressor with swept rotor under inlet circumferential distortion
papers.abstract: To investigate how blade sweep modulates compressor stability under circumferential inlet distortion, this study integrates steady numerical simulations, a linear stability model, and experimental measurements on a low-speed axial compressor. Model predictions under uniform and 55° circumferential total-pressure distortion align closely with experimental data, with a maximum error of 4% in stall mass flow trends, validating the model's capability to capture sweep-induced aerodynamic effects. Supplementary experiments further cover a wider range of distortion extents. Results indicate that relative to the prototype rotor under uniform inflow, forward sweep enhances stability by reducing the stall mass flow by approximately 1.6%, whereas backward sweep increases it by 2.2%, significantly degrading stability. Under circumferential distortion, the stability advantage of forward sweep is completely eliminated, and the stall mass flow of the backward-swept rotor is further elevated. However, the stall mass flow becomes insensitive to further increases in distortion angle. Flow field analysis reveals that blade sweep primarily modulates stability by regulating rotor loading above 50% span. The forward-swept configuration effectively suppresses tip leakage vortex intensity and deflects its trajectory away from the adjacent blade pressure surface, while the backward-swept configuration intensifies vortex development and amplifies cross-passage interaction. Under severe 125° distortion, the backward-swept rotor generates intense broadband disturbances in the tip region, which mask coherent stall precursors and obscure the stall inception boundary.

papers.title: Aerodynamic investigation and experimental validation of fifth-order polynomial serpentine hypersonic inlets at Mach 5
papers.abstract: Scramjet engines are air-breathing propulsion systems capable of sustained flight at Mach 5 and above, with the inlet serving as a critical subsystem that compresses the freestream air while minimizing total pressure losses. Although serpentine S-duct inlets provide low-observable airframe integration, they introduce complex shock-wave/boundary-layer interactions and secondary flows that degrade total pressure recovery (TPR) at the aerodynamic interface plane (AIP). Experimental investigations of hypersonic serpentine inlets remain limited. This study investigates four novel fifth-order polynomial serpentine inlet configurations (C1, C2, C3.5, and C5), parameterized by a single curvature coefficient governing the inlet profile. Two-dimensional and three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations employing the shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model were performed under Mach 5 conditions. Using average TPR at the AIP as the primary performance metric, the C1 configuration achieved the highest average TPR of 0.2791, representing a 64.27% improvement over the rapid-exit baseline (0.1699), with a peak TPR of 0.6274. Increasing the curvature coefficient produced smoother internal shock structures and improved static-pressure uniformity but did not increase average TPR, highlighting the trade-off between pressure recovery and flow uniformity. The C1 configuration was subsequently validated experimentally in a Ludwig hypersonic shock tunnel using CO2 as the test gas through high-speed schlieren flow visualization and surface static pressure measurements. The experimental results confirmed inlet start under shock-on-lip conditions and showed strong agreement with the computational predictions, validating both the numerical methodology and the effectiveness of the proposed fifth-order polynomial serpentine inlet for Mach 5 scramjet applications.

papers.title: Method of viscous dipole domains (VDD) for simulation of three-dimensional flows of viscous incompressible fluid. Physical mechanism of instability
papers.abstract: The viscous dipole domains method is a kind of the Lagrangian impulse-particle method using the diffusion velocity method and the particle strength exchange. We prefer to call particles as domains because a particle is associated with a concrete volume of fluid and moves with its velocity. When using diffusion velocity, we track a reference point that moves relative to the fluid. We assign this point a volume equal to the inverse density of points near it. This paper presents a detailed description of the method. The physical mechanism underlying the onset and evolution of numerical instability, which reflect the underlying physics of turbulent cascades, is revealed. A numerical stability criterion consistent with Kolmogorov scaling is derived. A new model for the diffusive motion of particles is proposed, ensuring a more uniform spatial distribution. The application of the developed method is demonstrated through numerical simulations of the evolution of vortex rings.

papers.title: The effect of stratification ratio on combustion instability in a full-scale premixed arrayed micro-tube combustor
papers.abstract: Experiments were conducted on a full-scale premixed arrayed micro-tube hydrogen combustor to explore the effect of the stratification ratio (SR) on combustion instability. Four typical flame modes were observed. Attached main-stage flames were most frequently observed over SR = 0.8–1.5. At an air mass flow rate of 220 g/s and a total equivalence ratio of 0.300, the pressure amplitude exhibited a W-like local-extrema pattern for pilot equivalence ratios of 0.4 and 0.5. Under the same air mass flow rate and total equivalence ratio, the dominant frequency changed from approximately 480 Hz at SR < 0.8 to 420–450 Hz at SR > 0.8. These spectral changes are reported as observations rather than evidence of stage-wise acoustic-mode dominance. Further results indicate that high-amplitude oscillations concentrate in high-SR regions, and increasing pilot-stage equivalence ratio reduces pressure amplitude at SR > 1.6. The pressure amplitude rises significantly with global equivalence ratio, which lowers the critical SR for high-amplitude oscillations.

papers.title: Effects of anisotropic confinement on droplet rebound from superhydrophobic surfaces
papers.abstract: On flat superhydrophobic surfaces, droplet rebound is well described by a single inertio-capillary timescale, yielding a contact-time that is independent of impact energy [Richard et al., Contact time of a bouncing drop, Nature 417, 811 (2002); Bird et al., Reducing the contact time of a bouncing drop, Nature 503, 385–388 (2013)]. This single-mode response reflects the radial symmetry of flat-plate impacts. We demonstrate that an anisotropic geometric constraint, imposing a fixed spreading length along one axis, breaks this degeneracy and splits the rebound into a reciprocal pair of inertio-capillary modes. The fixed length also couples the contact time to the Weber-dependent maximum spread, introducing an impact-energy dependence absent on the flat plate. We realize this constraint with grooved substrates, simulated using a non-ideal, entropic, multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann method and validated against the experiments of Chantelot et al. [Water ring-bouncing on repellent singularities, Soft Matter 14, 2227–2233 (2018)]. Building on their blob model, which identifies an effective droplet sub-volume governing contact time, we show that anisotropic confinement introduces complementary transverse and axial modes whose time scales vary reciprocally. Both modes are organized by the same geometric blob number, which we further relate to the imposed Weber number and groove width. These modes are recovered directly in simulations of non-wetting grooves and are used to explain an observed two-branch structure in the contact time response on mildly wetting, superhydrophobic grooves. Predictions tied to global energy balance reproduce cleanly across all conditions, while those tied to the details of the droplet's spread morphology are approximate but directionally correct. These results show that anisotropic confinement turns contact-time reduction from a question of accelerating a single rebound mode into one of selecting between conjugate inertio-capillary modes.

papers.title: Bifurcation taxonomy of three-dimensional flexural-gravity waves beneath elastic covers
papers.abstract: Flexural-gravity waves beneath elastic covers are central to understanding ice-shelf dynamics and very large floating structures, yet their three-dimensional nonlinear wave states remain poorly classified. We derive a three-dimensional Boussinesq model with asymptotic scaling anchored to the plate-rigidity and transverse-coupling scales, supplemented by physically motivated effective parameterizations for mixed-derivative anisotropy and Landau-type polynomial restoring terms arising from material nonlinearity and fluid–structure interaction. Analyzing this model via a complementary dynamical-algebraic framework, we obtain seven exact traveling-wave solutions that form a bifurcation taxonomy organized by a single solution discriminant set by the combined model coefficients: symmetric cnoidal waves transition through a rational critical state to asymmetric periodic waves, with homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits acting as topological separatrices between physically realizable and mathematically singular regimes. The elliptic modulus of the cnoidal family provides an unbroken bridge from infinitesimal linear waves to the isolated soliton. Five representative parameter sets are used to illustrate the solution classes and their bifurcation topology; quantitative physical interpretation is restricted to parameter regimes consistent with the weakly nonlinear long-wave assumptions. The taxonomy provides a framework for interpreting how distinct dynamical regimes of the cover-fluid system produce qualitatively different flexural-gravity wave patterns.

papers.title: Mitigation effect of interfacial mixing on resonance between interfacial and surface waves
papers.abstract: We present laboratory measurements of the evolution of large sub-harmonic interfacial waves and the associated mixing in a miscible two-layer fluid when these waves are resonantly generated by a surface wave. A standard resonant wave interaction analysis to the third order of nonlinearity is carried out. The standard theory overpredicts the ultimate amplitudes of the observed interfacial waves by a factor of up to 1.8. When we incorporate the wave frequency shift caused by interfacial mixing into the theoretical model, the predictions agree with the measurements within a margin of 15%. The results indicate that the effect of mixing of the upper and lower fluids significantly affects the amplitude of the steady-state interfacial waves, although the thickness of the resulting diffuse layer is two orders of magnitude smaller than the layer depths. The modified theory supports the conclusion that the interfacial waves stop growing after the rate of energy transfer from the surface wave to the interface decreases due to mixing- as well as nonlinearity-induced frequency mismatches of the waves. The frequency mismatch because of interfacial mixing is as high as 2.5% while that due to nonlinearity is 0.7%.

papers.title: Local heat flux distribution at the solid–liquid interface during droplet impact and spreading at a hot substrate
papers.abstract: Local heat transfer during single droplet impact onto a heated substrate is critical for predictive spray-cooling models, yet direct access to fully space- and time-resolved wall heat flux distributions remains limited.
