This study employs three-dimensional (3D) direct numerical simulations with the multiphase solver Free Surface 3D to investigate the impact of a water droplet at a lower Weber number onto a heated substrate under non-boiling conditions. Conjugate heat transfer is resolved, and the local interfacial heat flux is reconstructed from the computed temperature field using stencils. The simulated spreading dynamics and maximum wetted diameter show very good agreement with published experimental data, while the area-averaged interfacial heat flux is compared with analytical solutions for validation. The simulations reveal a robust radial structure of the interfacial heat flux: a minimum at the impact center, a secondary maximum beneath the lamella, a sudden drop just upstream of the rim, and a global maximum near the contact line, with all magnitudes decaying in time as the substrate cools. Detailed analysis of the rim flow identifies a narrow throat, a flow-division region, and a stagnation zone that control local residence times and thereby produce the observed heat flux minima and maxima. Parametric variations of thermal diffusivity ratio, as well as surface wettability, demonstrate how the flow field influences the heat transfer mechanism, guiding the development and assessment of advanced spray-cooling technologies.

papers.title: Effects of aluminum particle additives on explosive performance; a small-scale study with hemispherical C-4 charges
papers.abstract: Aluminum particles in the micrometer range are frequently used to enhance the effects of high explosives. The present experimental study is focused on the shape, content, and size of the charges, studying laboratory-sized small hemispherical charges with homogeneous charge-particle mixtures. The percentage of particle-charge weight is given in the range of 0%–40%. Two different charge sizes and two different particle sizes are used in the experiments. The reactive particle experiments were further supplemented with an additional set of reference experiments performed with inert particles of comparable size and density. The experiments are performed on a specially designed instrumentation table and documented with pressure sensors mounted flush with the table top surface. A symmetry check of the radial pressure distribution is achieved by using pairs of sensors at corresponding radial distances. Additionally, the Edgerton retroreflective shadowgraph technique is used to document the initial phase of the detonation photographically. When the aluminum particle percentage is high, the results demonstrate a pronounced increase in the positive duration of the explosive event, also for the smallest charges. Although the primary shock is less affected by the particle content, an increase in the pressure level behind the incident shock is observed for the aluminum dense charges. The increased pressure and temperature in the gas behind the incident shock lead to an increase in the secondary peak pressure and secondary shock velocity. Both the secondary peak pressure and the secondary shock velocity are found to increase with increasing aluminum particle content. In this micro-sized particle range, the particle content percentage was found to be of greater importance than the particle size for parameters such as pressure impulse and positive duration.

papers.title: Eulerian–Lagrangian relations in decaying two-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes fluids across initial vorticity packing and Reynolds number
papers.abstract: A recent study [Phys. Fluids 38, 045159 (2026)] showed that, at a fixed high Reynolds number (Re), variations in the initial vorticity packing fraction (VPF) were associated with a general Eulerian–Lagrangian relationship during the inverse-cascade regime and a more direct correspondence between Eulerian statistical organization and Lagrangian transport in the late coherent-dipole regime. Here, we examine the robustness of these connections across a broader (VPF,Re) parameter space, together with random-phase, long-time, and alternative initial-vorticity geometry tests. During the inverse cascade, the broad VPF-associated organization of transport remains comparatively robust, although the quantitative transport exponents vary non-monotonically across Re. In the late coherent-dipole regime, however, Lagrangian transport varies strongly and non-monotonically across Re and exhibits considerably greater sensitivity to the initial random-phase realization and continued coherent-state evolution. High-VPF Eulerian states nevertheless remain consistently KMRS-like across the investigated Re range. Thus, similar Eulerian statistical organization can coexist with substantially different late-time Lagrangian transport, demonstrating that the direct Eulerian–Lagrangian correspondence identified at fixed Re is not universal under variations of Reynolds number, initial random-phase realization, coherent-state evolution, and initial-vorticity geometry.

papers.title: Flying through sandstorms: Aerodynamic performance of an airfoil in turbulent sand-laden flows
papers.abstract: Airfoil aerodynamic performance in turbulent sand-laden flows is important for wind turbines in desert environments and rotorcraft operating in dusty conditions, yet the underlying coupling mechanisms between air flow and sand particle dynamics remain poorly understood. This study experimentally investigates a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) 0018 airfoil in turbulent air–sand two-phase flow across a range of angles of attack and inflow particle concentrations. Aerodynamic load measurements, combined with phase-resolved particle image velocimetry, quantify the effects of sand particles on lift, drag, carrier-phase flow evolution, and dispersed phase dynamics. The results show that the presence of sand particles affects airfoil performance differently in pre-stall and stall regimes: they increase drag with an aerodynamic penalty before stall, but reduce drag under stall conditions. Phase-resolved measurements reveal that, owing to their large inertia, sand particles largely retain their incoming streamwise velocity and separate from the airfoil suction side. The resulting slip velocity produces an interphase momentum exchange that is consistent with the measured carrier-phase velocity changes over the suction side, including reduced wind velocity before stall and increased velocity at post-stall conditions, which contributes to the associated drag variation. In addition, the dispersed phase suppresses the carrier-phase Reynolds shear stress under the stall regime. A reduced-order advection–diffusion framework well captures the main trends in particle concentration and feedback load distributions between two phases. These findings provide new insight into turbulent particle-laden flow dynamics over airfoils and highlight the role of dispersed phase inertia in modulating aerodynamic response in sand-laden environments.

papers.title: Erosion behavior and material damage mechanism of fracturing pump valves: Successive particle impacts and kinetic energy transfer based on multi-scale simulation
papers.abstract: In hydraulic fracturing operations, solid particles entrained in the fracturing fluid readily cause erosive damage to the valves of fracturing pumps, significantly reducing equipment service life and operational efficiency. To reveal the cross-scale evolution mechanism from macroscopic erosion behavior to atomic-scale damage mechanisms, this paper proposes a hierarchical multi-scale correlative analysis method that combines computational fluid dynamics with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The results indicate that variations in the valve disk stroke and inlet flow velocity lead to erosion occurring at the junction surface of the valve chamber and the bottom of the valve disk. The erosive wear is fundamentally induced by the continuous impact of particles on the material surface, guided by vortices within the flow field. The microscopic MD simulations take impact frequency and impact velocity as input parameters to reveal the damage mechanism of the substrate material under successive particle impacts. It is found that under particle impact, the substrate exhibits a characteristic of local self-repair associated with plastic deformation; however, under higher kinetic energy impacts, dislocation explosion is induced, leading to irreversible spalling damage on the surface. Through multi-scale analysis, this paper provides a theoretical basis for erosion-resistant design, structural optimization, and operational parameter adjustment of fracturing pump valves.

papers.title: Unveiling combined thermal and magnetic field effects in ferrofluid marble evaporation: An experimental exploration
papers.abstract: Ferrofluid marbles, formed by encapsulating a ferrofluid core with a hydrophobic nanoparticle shell, offer high mobility and environmental isolation while enabling noncontact, remote manipulation through an external magnetic field. These characteristics make them a suitable model system for investigating the coupled effects of evaporation, magnetic forcing, and morphological deformation. This study systematically investigates the evaporation dynamics of ferrofluid marbles under steady vertical magnetic fields and varying substrate temperatures, with comparisons to de-ionized-water marbles. The hydrophobic nanoparticle shell significantly retards evaporation compared with bare ferrofluid droplets, while in the absence of a magnetic field, ferrofluid marbles evaporate slightly faster than water marbles, consistent with their higher thermal conductivity. Application of a steady magnetic field slows the evaporation rate, with the effect being more pronounced at lower substrate temperatures and increasing the total lifetime by up to 20.8%. The magnetic field induces vertical elongation of the marble, reducing the effective surface area for evaporation and altering the internal fluid dynamics. This manipulation also controls the final deposition pattern, transitioning from flat (without field) to peaked (with field). The findings provide new insights into the control of evaporation dynamics in ferrofluidic marbles, with implications for digital microfluidics, drug delivery, and surface patterning.

papers.title: Attenuation and modulation of weak shock waves by a porous wall layer in a shock tube
papers.abstract: Interactions between shock waves and porous materials can modulate wave behavior, as reflected in changes in the post-shock pressure. This study investigated the modulation of weak shock waves at incident shock Mach numbers of Ms,i = 1.03–1.21 using an open-cell porous layer installed on the bottom wall of a rectangular shock tube. Upon encountering the porous-wall section, the incident shock was partially diffracted toward the porous layer and reflected on the bottom wall, yielding a wave system comprising the leading shock wave (LSW), expansion waves, and reflected shock wave (RSW). These shock waves eventually coalesced to form a merged shock wave (MSW), with its post-shock pressure depended on Ms,i, the propagation distance, and the porous-layer thickness. The MSW exhibited a significantly reduced post-shock overpressure and a smeared pressure rise behind it. This attenuation was described by introducing the Chester–Chisnell–Whitham (CCW) model to account for shock-wave diffraction, thereby comparing it with the conventionally used Frolov mass-suction model. The proposed CCW-based model better reproduced the attenuation observed in closed-tube experiments. The LSW attenuation increased with shock strength. However, weaker shocks achieved greater overall MSW attenuation because both the LSW and RSW underwent greater attenuation before merging. At Ms,i=1.03, where the porous-layer thickness was 0.2 times the shock-tube height, the shock-induced overpressure was reduced by up to 90% over a propagation distance equivalent to 40.5 times this height. The study findings hold promise for attenuating weak shock waves in advanced applications, e.g., in tunnels for ultrahigh-speed trains powered by superconducting linear motors.

papers.title: Propagation of normal shock waves in chemically reactive non-ideal turbulent flows with nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Recent advances in hypersonic propulsion, high-enthalpy reacting flows, and plasma energy systems rely on normal shock waves in high-temperature compressible flows. Nanoparticles change flow characteristics and improve energy transport; turbulence modifies shock structure and stability; chemical heat release significantly affects shock strength; and non-ideal gas effects become important at high temperature and pressure. The novelty of the present work lies in the development of a modified Rankine–Hugoniot model that incorporates the combined effects of non-ideal gas behavior, chemical reactions, turbulence, and nanoparticles into a unified analytical framework. The study takes into account nanoparticles such as alumina (Al2O3), silica (SiO2) and carbon nanotubes, which have an impact on the pressure-density relationship. Lower-density nanoparticles result in stronger compression. The Levenberg–Marquardt backpropagation algorithm is employed to develop an Artificial Neural Network surrogate model that accurately predicts the analytical shock parameters while significantly reducing computational effort. Turbulence and non-ideal gas effects strengthen the shock, increasing pressure ratios, while a higher Arrhenius number further enhances intensity. For endothermic reactions, shock jumps also increase with Arrhenius number. Entropy generation and significant shock parameters, such as Mach number, velocity variation, and ultimate compression, are also assessed. The design and optimization of high-speed aerodynamic and energy systems can benefit from these findings.

papers.title: Influence of magnetic field deformation on the aerothermodynamic characteristics of a hypersonic reentry capsule
papers.abstract: The effects of magnetic field deformation on magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) control of a hypersonic reentry capsule were examined quantitatively. For the numerical analysis, a three-temperature thermochemical nonequilibrium model is coupled with induced electric and magnetic field models. Comparison of the coupled MHD model with the measured pressure, heat flux, and shock standoff distance (SSD) shows that changes in SSD are reproduced within the experimental uncertainty for most conditions. However, the model does not reproduce the increase in stagnation pressure and predicts the shell-averaged heat flux to be approximately 2.4 times the measured value at the highest magnetic field strength. The model is then applied to the Stardust capsule under 71.2 km flight conditions to evaluate the effects of magnetic field deformation on its aerothermodynamic characteristics. The secondary shock wave induced by the magnetic field increases the SSD and reduces the heating rate. This effect becomes more pronounced with increasing applied current. However, magnetic field deformation by induced currents partially counteracts the applied magnetic field. This deformation alters the interaction between the secondary shock wave and the bow shock, yielding higher surface heat flux and total drag than those predicted by models in which deformation is neglected. These findings suggest that the applicability of the low magnetic Reynolds number assumption should be assessed based on the parameters themselves as well as the secondary shock wave formation and its interaction with the bow shock. The analysis of magnetic field deformation can help determine the appropriate level of MHD modeling for reentry capsule environments.

papers.title: Interphase momentum transfer and transient spray development in an air-assisted aviation kerosene injector
papers.abstract: Air-assisted spray combustion of aviation kerosene surrogates involves complex interactions among transient interphase momentum transfer, vapor redistribution, and local thermochemical stratification. A full-geometry numerical model was developed using n-dodecane as a surrogate for rocket propellant-3 aviation kerosene. Needle-valve opening shifts the dominant momentum carrier from the confined liquid phase to the assist gas, promoting droplet acceleration, secondary breakup, and spray development. Increasing the assist-gas pressure from 2 to 4 bar increases spray penetration by 24% and reduces the final Sauter mean diameter (SMD) by 39%. Increasing the ambient back pressure from 1 to 3 bar decreases penetration by 13% and increases SMD by 71%, whereas increasing the fuel-injection pressure from 5 to 7 bar increases penetration by only 5% but increases SMD by 15% because increased liquid loading weakens gas-assisted atomization. The nozzle-orifice diameter (d0) affects combustion through recirculation-assisted transport and local temperature–equivalence-ratio (T–φ) stratification. An intermediate orifice (d0 = 0.75 mm) produces the highest heat-release rate, whereas a larger orifice (d0 = 1.00 mm) sustains late-stage combustion but increases carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons and shows a stronger relative soot-formation tendency. A smaller orifice (d0 = 0.50 mm) shows a lower relative soot-formation tendency but promotes nitrogen oxides (NOx) formation. These results demonstrate how transient interphase momentum transfer governs spray evolution and how injector geometry regulates combustion through local mixture stratification.

papers.title: Information transport and observability in compressible aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Pressure measurements provide sparse but direct observations of compressible aerodynamic flows, yet how information about hidden aerodynamic parameters is transported through the flow and encoded in these observations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate information transport and observability in compressible aerodynamics using a differentiable shock-capturing immersed-boundary solver. By propagating gradients through the full unsteady flow solution, an automatic-differentiation-based observability metric is formulated from parameter-to-measurement sensitivities to quantify the informativeness of sparse pressure measurements for inverse learning. Full-field pressure-sensitivity analysis shows that parameter-induced sensitivity structures evolve with the compressible-flow structures and propagate downstream, providing a quantitative description of the spatiotemporal transport of aerodynamic parameter information. The results reveal that aerodynamic information is distributed non-uniformly through the flow field, producing localized regions of high observability. Inverse-learning experiments further demonstrate that observability and learnability are related but distinct concepts: although highly observable probes generally facilitate parameter recovery, the highest-observability probe is not consistently the most effective for parameter inference. The observability distribution and sensor ranking also vary with aerodynamic operating condition and airfoil geometry, indicating that informative sensing locations are condition dependent. Coupled pitch–heave inference and sensitivity-conditioning analysis further show that successful single-parameter recovery does not necessarily imply favorable multi-parameter distinguishability. These findings establish a quantitative framework connecting parameter sensitivity, information transport, sparse-sensor observability, parameter distinguishability, and inverse learnability in compressible aerodynamics.

papers.title: Derivation of laminar-to-turbulent transition criteria and pressure decrease in curved pipe flow using simple and local physical relations
papers.abstract: The transition of secondary flow in a curved pipe was studied analytically and experimentally. Flow was visualized using ink injection, and pressure was measured in five curved pipes with different radii of curvature. When the Reynolds number was below 1300, the flow was laminar. As the Reynolds number increased, spiral flow appeared in place of puff flow. Disturbed fluid began to flow at a Reynolds number of ∼2200. A reduced-order analytical model of the secondary flow was constructed; an overall flow condition was constructed using simple and local physical relations, and equations for flow conditions were derived. The formalized secondary flow velocity ratio and development length were applied to the entropy model. The transitions were examined with the change in entropy in the curved pipe flow. The Reynolds number for the transition from plain laminar flow to spiral flow, calculated with the entropy model, agreed with the experimental results, and the delayed appearance of spiral flow was explained by the model. The calculated boundary Reynolds numbers for turbulent flow also agreed with the Reynolds numbers of experimental and past results. The present model successfully estimated changes and transitions in secondary flow conditions with the entropy model. The calculated friction factors agreed with the experimental results except during the transition from laminar to spiral flow. The large friction factor observed in laminar flow was discussed in terms of the acceleration of the fluid in the radial direction within the pipe.

papers.title: Non-Gaussian characteristics of wind pressure and extreme wind loads on large-span irregular curved roofs with multiple openings
papers.abstract: Large-span curved roofs with distributed openings create pressure-communication pathways that interact with separated shear layers and local reattachment, producing intermittent suction pulses and strongly non-Gaussian pressure fluctuations. Gaussian peak-factor formulations can, therefore, underrepresent local extreme suction. Rigid-model wind tunnel pressure tests are used to examine a large-span irregular curved roof with multiple openings. Opening and closed regions are compared over all tested wind directions using pressure time histories, skewness and kurtosis, the peak-over-threshold method, probability density functions (PDFs), and non-Gaussian peak-factor models. Opening-region records exhibit more frequent and longer negative-pressure pulses, predominantly negative skewness, and elevated kurtosis. These signatures are consistent with pressure communication through the openings interacting with intermittent separation and reattachment, thereby shifting probability toward strong suction states. The measured PDFs show heavier tails than a Gaussian model, particularly for negative net pressure. Relative to the Davenport Gaussian reference, the Hermite-polynomial method gives larger unfavorable minimum pressure coefficients; the maximum suction amplification reaches 36.38% in the opening zone, 30.14% in the closed-edge zone, and 44.13% in the closed-center zone. Zonal extreme wind-pressure coefficients are then combined with a least squares boosting gradient-boosted regression-tree model for supplementary interpolation. The results connect recurrent pressure-pulse events, heavy-tailed statistics, and extreme suction and provide a fluid-physics-based criterion for identifying locations where Gaussian peak assumptions become nonconservative.

papers.title: Analysis of near-surface spreading and fountain formation in bubble plumes and curtains
papers.abstract: The classical bubble-plume theory predicts linearly spreading and self-similar profiles, but its direct application becomes limited as the bubbly flow approaches a free surface, where redistribution of vertical momentum and surface deformation become important. This study presents an experimental investigation of single-source round bubble plumes and line-source bubble curtains as they approach a free surface. Using planar particle image velocimetry to capture the liquid-phase velocity field, we observe a gradual transfer of vertical momentum into lateral motion near the free surface, which forms the physical foundation for our model development. Based on these observations, we formulate a scaling model for the non-self-similar region that represents the exponential spreading profiles of both configurations over the tested range of dimensionless flow rates. This near-surface model is coupled with the classical linear model below a critical height to cover the entire flow domain. At the free surface, a local momentum-flux-density estimated from void-fraction distributions is used to model the fountain profiles, showing good agreement with the measurements. Together, these results provide a physics-based framework that relates subsurface spreading to free-surface deformation for both point-source and line-source configurations within the tested parameter range.

papers.title: Sustained jet direction control using a dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator combined with the Coanda effect
papers.abstract: A dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuator (PA) was installed in a Coanda nozzle with an inclined flap to control the jet direction by combining PA-induced flow with the Coanda effect. Conventional active flow control requires continuous energy input to maintain jet deflection, limiting practical applications. To address this issue, this study focused on the characteristics that induce the Coanda effect through the flow generated by the PA and, by examining their hysteresis, experimentally attempted to realize control in which the Coanda effect induced during PA actuation is maintained even after the PA is turned off. Experiments were conducted using a low-speed fan-driven jet at velocities of 2–7 m/s, corresponding to Reynolds numbers of 200–3400 (based on throat height), with applications to air-conditioning and ventilation systems. To clarify the effects of nozzle geometry, the nozzle throat height (2–7 mm), Coanda surface diameter (20–80 mm), and Coanda surface mounting angle (0°–45°) were systematically varied. Jet deflection angles were quantitatively evaluated using particle image velocimetry. Under conditions allowing the jet direction to be maintained, a deflection angle of 95° was continuously maintained after the PA was turned off, even at the maximum jet velocity of 7 m/s. Furthermore, dimensionless parameters describing the nozzle geometry were related to the Reynolds number to classify jet behavior into rectilinear, hysteresis, and deflected-flow regions based on the experimental results. The boundaries between these regions were expressed using empirical equations.

papers.title: A universal relation between intermittency and dissipation within and beyond homogeneous isotropic turbulence
papers.abstract: Fundamental quantities of turbulent flows, such as the dissipation parameter Cε and the intermittency parameter μ, are examined in relation to each other for a broad class of inhomogeneous turbulent flows. In the context of the energy cascade, it is known that Cε reflects its basic overall properties, while μ quantifies the intermittency of the cascade. Using an extensive hot-wire dataset of turbulent wakes, grid-generated turbulence, and an axisymmetric jet, we individually analyze these quantities as one-dimensional surrogates of the energy cascade, considering only data that exhibit consistent scaling behavior. We find that μ is inversely proportional to Cε, offering a new empirical principle that bridges the gap between large and small scales in arbitrary turbulent flows. The generalized framework presented here recovers the established values and trends reported for homogeneous isotropic turbulence and expands them to cover inhomogeneous situations.

papers.title: Flow-regime transitions and cross-sectional maximum resultant-velocity decay of propeller jets under near-bed boundary confinement
papers.abstract: Near-bed confinement alters the spreading, velocity distribution, and turbulence of ship propeller jets, resulting in development distinct from that of a free jet. Flume experiments were conducted under different clearance-height and rotational-speed conditions, and instantaneous three-component velocities were measured using an acoustic Doppler velocimeter at locations in the centerline longitudinal plane. Three successive flow regimes were identified: free-jet spreading, jet impingement, and wall-jet development. Reducing the relative clearance height restricted downward jet spreading, shifted the representative regime boundaries upstream, and nearly eliminated the free-jet spreading regime at the lowest clearance. Increasing rotational speed primarily increased the jet velocity and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), while exerting limited influence on the regime boundaries. Axial velocity dominated the downstream development, whereas decreasing clearance displaced the velocity and TKE peaks toward the bed. Within the resolvable 0.098–12.5 Hz frequency band, near-bed velocity-fluctuation energy and the relative energy contribution from the upper portion of the band decreased downstream, indicating progressive attenuation and redistribution of the resolved fluctuations. To quantify jet decay, the maximum resultant velocity extracted from the centerline longitudinal plane, Vp-max, was used as an approximation of the cross-sectional maximum under the approximately symmetric experimental conditions. At Zp/Dp = 1.00, normalized decay was gradual during free-jet spreading, rapid during impingement, and characterized by local recovery and slow adjustment during wall-jet development. Continuity-constrained linear, power-law, and quadratic functions described these regimes, respectively. These results provide a regime-based framework for characterizing near-bed propeller-jet development and velocity decay within the tested range.

papers.title: Hemline-shaped thread formation by coupling of inlet perturbations and core-annular folding
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamics of hemline-shaped thread formation in a co-flowing microchannel under periodic inlet perturbations are numerically investigated using the volume of fluid method. Two flow regimes, dome-shaped threads and hemline-shaped threads, are identified and mapped onto regime diagrams. The transition between these regimes is governed by a critical threshold of the waveform steepness, which captures the combined effects of perturbation frequency, amplitude, and flow rate ratio. The hemline formation process has protruding and folding stages. During the protruding stage, inertial momentum surplus at each velocity crest drives the protrusion formation. In the subsequent folding stage, differential advection arising from the core-annular axial velocity gradient progressively folds the protrusions into hemline structures. The generated hemline is stretched in the axial direction without significant radial deformation. Hemline length is governed by the waveform steepness. Increasing the frequency, amplitude, or flow rate ratio steepens the waveform, thereby enhancing folding dynamics and resulting in longer hemline length. Hemline pitch is primarily controlled by the generation frequency. Higher frequency compresses the temporal period of protrusion formation, generating more protrusions per unit time. Based on these mechanistic insights, predictive scaling laws are established and validated against numerical data. The dimensionless hemline pitch is inversely proportional to the dimensionless frequency, while the dimensionless hemline length follows a superlinear scaling with the amplitude and flow rate ratio. These scaling laws provide a quantitative basis for the design of hemline-shaped microfibers with tunable liquid-transport capabilities.

papers.title: Turbulent transport and inertial deposition in lead-bismuth eutectic wire-wrapped rod bundles
papers.abstract: Inertial particle transport and deposition in helically forced wall-bounded turbulence are controlled by turbulent diffusion, near-wall shear, secondary motion, and finite particle inertia. The wire-wrapped rod bundle is treated as a representative configuration in which spacer wires generate cross-flow, local acceleration, and narrow-gap transport pathways. A discrete-phase model with two-way momentum coupling was established to simulate Fe3O4 particle migration and deposition in a 19-pin wire-wrapped rod-bundle flow with lead-bismuth eutectic as the carrier fluid. The continuous phase was resolved using the shear stress transport k–ω model, and a particle–wall collision and deposition criterion was used to distinguish rebound from deposition. Particles of 1–100 μm were tracked to analyze axial migration, transverse redistribution, near-wall enrichment, and wall deposition. Results show that inlet velocity gradients and wire-induced cross-flow drive particles away from streamlines and toward near-wall low-speed regions. For 1–10 μm particles, 61.8% of the area-integrated wall deposition occurred within the first 0.5 wire pitch. Deposition hotspots occur mainly on upstream-facing wire surfaces, box-wall edges, and narrow gaps among the wire, cladding, and box wall. Increasing particle diameter raises relaxation time and Stokes number, enhancing trajectory deviation and collision probability while shifting concentration and deposition-flux peaks downstream. As the particle size increases, the dimensionless deposition rate increased and showed a sublinear dependence on the Stokes number, while the deposition rate remained far below unity, indicating that deposition is governed by coupled turbulent diffusion, near-wall shear, wire-induced transverse migration and finite inertia rather than inertia alone.

papers.title: Modulation of square-cylinder wake dynamics and coherent structures by large-amplitude, low-frequency sinusoidal inflow
papers.abstract: The wake dynamics of a square cylinder under a prescribed large-amplitude, low-frequency sinusoidal inflow, characterized by û/u¯=1 and fuD/u¯=0.01, are investigated experimentally over 6.0×103≤Re≤1.7×104. A posteriori harmonic decomposition was employed to separate the deterministic first-harmonic response from the residual wake fluctuations. The deterministic harmonic energy was concentrated mainly along the separated shear layers, whereas the residual energy developed farther downstream and remained substantially higher and more spatially extensive than the fluctuation energy under smooth inflow. Two-point correlation analysis showed that the alternating wake organization was retained under sinusoidal inflow, but its spatial coherence was weakened. The streamwise coherence length and correlation-based wake width decreased, while the vortex formation length increased over the investigated Reynolds-number range. Spectral analysis identified a statistically robust, spatially organized higher-frequency component in the sinusoidal residual wake at Re=6.0×103. Together, the residual-velocity evolution, broadened two-dimensional Fourier spectra, spectral entropy, and non-primary-band energy fraction show the development of multi-scale flow structures under sinusoidal inflow. Proper orthogonal decomposition further reveals a redistribution of residual wake energy from the leading coherent mode pair to additional modes. A four-component decomposition successfully separates the mean, deterministic harmonic, phase-averaged coherent residual, and remaining non-phase-locked motions. Under the present large-amplitude, low-frequency forcing condition, these results show that sinusoidal inflow reorganizes the separated shear layers and residual wake dynamics rather than merely superposing a low-frequency velocity oscillation.

papers.title: Effect of wake vortices on the solidification of tandem droplets in a crossflow
papers.abstract: Airflow can strongly modify droplet solidification by inducing deformation and altering the thermal transport around the droplet. Here, we investigate the solidification of two tandem droplets deposited on a substrate under transverse airflow, focusing on the effects of droplet spacing, Reynolds number (Re), and Prandtl number (Pr). We find that droplet spacing governs the strength of inter-droplet aerodynamic interactions and, consequently, the solidification dynamics. At small spacings, wake vortices shed by the upstream droplet interact strongly with the downstream droplet, limiting the streamwise shift of its liquid-phase centroid and resulting in a less deformed final solidified shape. With increasing spacing, this wake-mediated interaction progressively weakens, and the solidification behaviors of the two droplets converge. Increasing Re by increasing the inflow velocity enhances aerodynamic forcing, leading to stronger droplet deformation and faster contraction of the solidification front, while increasing the overall non-dimensional solidification time. In contrast, Pr has only a minor effect on both solidification morphology and non-dimensional solidification time. More importantly, the non-dimensional solidification time exhibits a systematic dependence on the inflow velocity. By incorporating a spacing-dependent coefficient, the non-dimensional solidification time data for the downstream droplet at different spacings collapse onto a unified empirical correlation. This correlation is applicable within the investigated two-dimensional configuration and parameter range.

papers.title: Non-monotonic effects of wettability on two-phase leakage in mechanical seals under rotational shear
papers.abstract: Leakage across contact mechanical seal faces develops within rough, confined microgaps under a driving pressure difference and rotating-ring tangential shear, making it a two-phase interfacial process governed by capillary invasion, interfacial pinning, and pore-scale connectivity with wettability acting as a primary control; however, how rotational shear reshapes this control remains unclear. Here, a two-dimensional pseudopotential multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann model with a Peng–Robinson equation of state and curved-boundary wettability calibration resolves interface migration, wall adhesion, breakthrough, and shear redistribution on the measured, contact-deformed topography of a real seal face, with rotating-ring traction imposed via a depth-averaged Couette–Poiseuille closure. Leakage exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on wettability: moderate hydrophobicity produces the longest breakthrough delay, whereas stronger hydrophobicity weakens wall adhesion and redirects the advancing front into better-connected pathways. Steady-state leakage follows a wettability-dependent transition from a shear-maintained film-spreading state sustaining no axial pressure difference to a channelized through-flow state. Larger pressure differences weaken the hydrophobic suppression of steady-state leakage by re-activating liquid-connected pathways, whereas higher viscosity primarily delays leakage initiation and makes the latest-breakthrough window less distinct at the maximum viscosity. Incorporating the out-of-plane capillary pinning between the seal faces as an equivalent source term preserves these mechanisms while strengthening the monotonic decrease in leakage with increasing hydrophobicity. These results demonstrate that the wettability regulation of two-phase seal leakage must be evaluated jointly with the driving pressure difference and medium viscosity.

papers.title: Influence of yield stress on electroosmotic flow mixing in a charged modulated microchannel
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates vortex-induced electroosmotic mixing of a Casson viscoplastic fluid in a wavy microchannel with sinusoidally heterogeneous surface charge. The coupled electrokinetic transport is described using the Navier–-Stokes–Poisson–Nernst–Planck formulation, while the flow, stress, and species-concentration fields are resolved using a finite volume method. The analysis reveals a coupled mechanism in which wall corrugation and spatially varying surface charge generate transverse recirculation and enlarge the interfacial contact area between the incoming streams, whereas the yield stress modifies the flow through the formation and growth of unyielded regions. Increasing the wave amplitude α and yield-stress parameter τ0 enhances mixing, although the latter simultaneously increases flow resistance and pressure loss. The electrical double-layer (EDL) thickness also plays a decisive role in the mixing process. A thicker EDL strengthens electrokinetic interactions with the bulk fluid and enhances mixing, whereas a thinner EDL weakens these effects. Consequently, for τ0=0.30 and α=0.10, the mixing efficiency decreases by approximately 23% as κH increases from 10 to 40. A maximum mixing efficiency 96.5% is obtained for α=0.25, κH=10, and τ0=0.30. These findings highlight the dual influence of viscoplasticity on mixing performance. Increasing the yield stress enhances fluid homogenization through changes in the yielded–unyielded flow structure but simultaneously increases hydraulic resistance and pressure loss. To capture this trade-off, a mixing performance factor is defined as the ratio of mixing efficiency to the average pressure drop. This metric identifies an operating regime in which enhanced electroosmotic mixing can be achieved without an excessive pressure-loss penalty, providing a physically based criterion for designing efficient micromixers for viscoplastic fluids.

papers.title: Shear jamming-induced intelligent tool passivation: A novel green and high-performance approach without external fields
papers.abstract: This study proposes a novel intelligent tool passivation technique utilizing shear jamming fluids. The shear jamming effect is an intelligent, self-organized response arising from the fluid's internal particle network, characterized by rapid response, high energy efficiency, and reduced environmental burden. The research begins by combining impact and tensile load experiments with computational fluid dynamics simulations to elucidate the influence of dispersed phase volume fraction on the intensity of the jamming effect. Results indicate that increasing the volume fraction from 38.13 to 48.03 vol. % enhances the peak impact force by 11.3 times and reduces displacement by 95.4%, demonstrating pronounced dynamic hardening behavior. Subsequently, a discrete phase model for tool passivation is established to systematically investigate the governing mechanisms of key parameters—including tool speed, container speed, abrasive concentration—and shear stress on the surface of the cutting tool. The study identifies container rotational speed as the predominant factor influencing passivation uniformity, with its increase raising the average shear stress on the tool surface by 82%. Through orthogonal experimental optimization, the optimal parameter set is determined: tool speed of 2400 rpm, container speed of 20 rpm, abrasive volume fraction of 9.00 vol. %, and abrasive size of 80 mesh. Under these conditions, material removal on both the rake and flank faces is maximized. Microscopic defects on the cutting edge are effectively eliminated, edge radius consistency is significantly improved, and material removal on the flank face is generally higher than on the rake face.

papers.title: Inertia-driven spatial organization of liquid water in metal foams for proton exchange membrane fuel cells based on a scalable dual-pressure pore network approach
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional metal foam flow fields represent a promising pathway toward high-power-density proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs); however, elucidating their internal water–gas dynamics remains constrained by the computational limits of conventional pore-scale models. Moreover, existing pore network models (PNMs) universally assume Darcy flow, neglecting the gas-phase inertial effects intrinsic to highly porous metallic structures. Herein, we develop a computationally scalable dual-pressure PNM incorporating a Forchheimer-type nonlinear gas-phase solver and an orthogonal two-phase boundary condition system—to the best of the authors' knowledge, the first such framework to resolve inertia-driven two-phase organization at the experimental active-area scale. Simulating a full experimental-scale domain (1 × 1 cm2), the results reveal that gas-phase inertia is the primary driver of spatially organized water distribution, with quantitative scaling laws linking the organization index and mean saturation to the Forchheimer and pore-scale Reynolds numbers. The nonlinear inertial pressure field generates localized low-pressure zones that divert liquid water from the catalyst layer, mitigating cathode flooding. An optimal inertial operating window and a dimensionless wettability criterion are identified, while a tailored forward through-plane wettability gradient further enhances water redistribution. Beyond providing transferable, physics-based guidelines for the surface engineering and flow field optimization of next-generation PEMFCs through these dimensionless scaling laws, the proposed highly efficient computational framework simultaneously paves the way for realizing full fuel cell active-area scale modeling in the future.

papers.title: Regime transition between external air supply and turbulent entrainment in ventilated cavity flows
papers.abstract: Aeration in high-speed free-surface flows is governed by the competition between externally supplied air and turbulence-induced air entrainment, yet the transition between these supply-limited and entrainment-limited states remains poorly understood. Systematic laboratory experiments were conducted by varying the relative ventilation area (Aa/Aw), where Aa denotes the total geometric ventilation area of the two ventilation shafts and Aw denotes the upstream flow area, thereby examining the competition between external air supply and turbulence-induced air entrainment. The results show a consistent nonlinear response of cavity pressure deficit, cavity length, and air discharge to increasing ventilation capacity, characterized by an initial rapid variation followed by a subsequent weaker response or saturation. A transition between the supply-limited and entrainment-limited regimes is inferred to occur at Aa/Aw ≈ 0.101, suggesting a shift in the dominant constraint from external air-supply capacity toward the entrainment capacity of the turbulent free surface. The dimensionless cavity pressure deficit (PN) is identified as an important hydraulic variable linking these two processes and provides an observable indicator of the imbalance between air-supply capacity and turbulence-induced air-entrainment demand. A combined scaling parameter, Π = (Aa/Aw)/Fr2.5, provides a reasonable empirical collapse of the cavity-pressure data in the supply-limited regime, supporting a unified empirical description of the effects of ventilation capacity and flow intensity on cavity pressure. The transition occurs near PN ≈ 0.02, suggesting that cavity pressure provides a measurable operational indicator of the governing flow regime under the present experimental conditions. These findings provide a pressure-based framework for interpreting the transition between supply-limited and entrainment-limited behavior, while the proposed criterion and scaling relationship remain configuration-dependent and require further validation under other flow and ventilation conditions.

papers.title: Contact-line depinning and transport of a droplet impacting a vertically vibrated inclined surface
papers.abstract: Droplet impact on inclined surfaces is encountered in spraying, coating, and anti-icing, yet the combined influence of oblique impact and substrate vibration remains poorly understood. We experimentally investigate water droplets impacting a dry plexiglass plate inclined at 45°, while the substrate undergoes vertical sinusoidal forcing. The parameter space covers Weber numbers We = 2–360, normalized forcing accelerations Γ = 0–4, and frequencies f = 25–200 Hz, with the primary dataset acquired at f = 50 Hz. Using high-speed side-view imaging, we track the front and trailing contact lines for up to 2000 ms and quantify both the normalized wetted length and the net downslope drift. Across all conditions, the droplets remain in an attached deposition regime, and no prompt splashing is detected in the side-view images. Peak spreading occurs during the early inertia-dominated stage and is governed mainly by the Weber number. Varying Γ produces only small changes in the phase-averaged maximum wetted length, indicating that vibration does not substantially amplify inertia-driven spreading. By contrast, vibration strongly modifies the late-time response. Without forcing, the residual footprint relaxes to an effectively pinned state, whereas for vibration, the contact line repeatedly depins and undergoes sustained downslope migration. The resulting drift increases with forcing acceleration and, at fixed Γ, becomes stronger as f is reduced. These findings show that, for oblique impact on a dry incline, vibration acts primarily as a post-impact mobilization mechanism and is therefore captured more effectively by late-time drift than by peak spreading.

papers.title: Transient wake and cross-zone exchange induced by human doorway crossing: A manifold-learning analysis
papers.abstract: Human passage through a doorway generates a strongly transient indoor flow characterized by pressure redistribution, wake formation, and cross-zone contaminant transport. Principal component analysis (PCA), locally linear embedding (LLE), and isometric mapping (ISOMAP) are established dimensionality reduction (DR) methods; however, their physical implications for this class of indoor flows remain unclear. In this study, a dynamic-mesh approach was used to simulate unsteady indoor multi-physics fields generated by a human passing through a doorway between two zones with different initial pressures. Under five controlled conditions, PCA, LLE, and ISOMAP were compared using a common evaluation framework based on field reconstruction and temporal-structure preservation. Both univariate and multivariate representations of pressure, velocity, and contaminant concentration were examined. The results show that the pressure field exhibits a comparatively coherent large-scale structure; therefore, PCA provides the best reconstruction and the strongest preservation of temporal evolution. In contrast, the dominant complexity of velocity and concentration fields is spatially concentrated near the moving body and doorway, regions that contain more localized nonlinear features. LLE achieves the lowest reconstruction errors, but ISOMAP performs best in preserving the temporal characteristics of these nonlinear fields. Thus, local reconstruction fidelity and preservation of global temporal structure represent distinct objectives in DR analysis. Multivariate DR further reveals coupled behavior among pressure, velocity, and concentration. The joint representation captures key transient events. The study provides a physically motivated and case-dependent basis for selecting DR methods for transient indoor flows with moving boundaries and offers an interpretable low-dimensional representation of cross-zone contaminant exchange.

papers.title: Various mathematical models of internal inertia-gravity waves in the nontraditional f -plane approximation
papers.abstract: This paper examines three existing mathematical models that describe the propagation of internal inertia-gravity waves (IIGWs) in a stratified atmosphere under the following approximations: incompressible fluid, compressible fluid, and anelastic gas. It is shown that, only in the compressible fluid approximation, the temperature field is consistent with the heat conduction equation. Therefore, this work proposes three new mathematical models of IIGWs. The first model serves as an alternative to the anelastic gas model, i.e., it excludes the acoustic spectrum, and the temperature disturbance field is consistent with the heat conduction equation. An alternative to the incompressible fluid model is also proposed, in which the temperature field is consistent with the heat conduction equation. Finally, a model is presented that describes IIGWs in the general case of a baroclinic atmosphere. All the proposed models assume an ideal liquid with no viscosity or thermal diffusion. Taking into account the nontraditional component of the Coriolis force is shown to qualitatively change the dispersion relation surface as a function of the wave vector components and introduce asymmetry in the horizontal plane. An analysis of the oscillation frequency isosurface as a function of wavenumbers was conducted. It was found that a nontraditional effect causes the frequency isosurface to rotate clockwise.

papers.title: Critical acceleration effect of supercritical CO2 flow across the pseudo-critical line in a microchannel
papers.abstract: The pressure-driven flow of supercritical CO2 through a planar-slit microchannel is numerically investigated as its thermodynamic trajectory crosses a pseudo-critical line defined by the local maximum of the isobaric specific heat. A fully compressible Navier–Stokes framework is coupled with the Peng–Robinson equation of state and state-dependent thermodynamic and transport properties. The results reveal a localized pseudo-critical response region in which density and thermodynamic properties vary rapidly but continuously, without formation of a liquid–vapor interface or latent-heat transport. Within this region, the approximately linear streamwise pressure decrease is accompanied by a pronounced nonlinear increase in velocity. The local density-gradient magnitude reaches 2330 kg m−4, while the streamwise velocity gradient increases to approximately 8 s−1, substantially exceeding the upstream and downstream values. This localized acceleration enhancement, referred to descriptively as critical acceleration, is associated with the nonlinear coupling among streamwise depressurization, rapid density reduction, strong thermal expansivity, and mass conservation. A localized negative temperature deviation also develops near the pseudo-critical crossing despite the isothermal inlet and wall conditions, reflecting the coupled pressure-dependent real-fluid response and wall heat transfer. Parametric calculations further show that the thermofluid response is strongly dependent on the imposed pressure conditions. Increasing the inlet pressure at fixed outlet pressure shifts the response region downstream and intensifies the density gradient, velocity gradient, temperature depression, and thermodynamic-property variation. Across the investigated cases, the maximum density-gradient magnitude and velocity gradient reach 3194 kg m−4 and 19.1 s−1, respectively, while the peak cp increases to 127.8 kJ kg−1 K−1. These results clarify the continuum-scale coupling between pressure-driven acceleration and strong near-pseudo-critical property variation in supercritical CO2 microchannel flow.

papers.title: Study of transient dual-porosity gas transport during diffusion–desorption in coal particles
papers.abstract: Following desorption, gas migration in coal particles becomes a transient transport process through interacting macropore–micropore systems, with shifts in dominant transport regimes. However, the influence of different macro–micropore pathways on coupled desorption–diffusion remains insufficiently understood. To address this issue, we develop a transient dual-porosity diffusion model considering gas pressure, pore size, porosity, and diffusion mechanisms. A transient gas-diffusion model incorporating mechanical equilibrium and constitutive equations was established to investigate gas migration within coal particles. Research findings show that both dual-porosity series and parallel models reproduce experimental desorption data with satisfactory agreement, although fitting performance varies with coal type and conditions. Compared with the parallel model, the series model exhibits a larger initial macropore diffusion coefficient and stronger temporal decay. In the series model, micropore pressure remains uniform, whereas parallel diffusion proceeds independently in macro- and micropores, producing stronger concentration gradients. In both models, viscous flow dominates macropore transport initially, while Knudsen diffusion becomes more significant at later times. Micropore transport remains predominantly Knudsen-dominated, although larger pore sizes increase viscous-flow contributions. Relative to primary coal, tectonic coal shows faster reductions in gas pressure and diffusivity, with an earlier transition from viscous-flow to Knudsen diffusion. These results demonstrate that dual-porosity pathways and coal-type parameters jointly control transient gas transport, providing a basis for gas-hazard prediction and extraction.

papers.title: Influencing factors and physical mechanism of rheological evolution of oil-based complex fluids at ultralow temperatures
papers.abstract: Extreme low-temperature environments pose significant challenges to fluid physics. It is urgent to maintain good rheological behavior of oil-based complex fluids under extreme, low-temperature conditions. Conventional oil-based fluids suffer from deteriorated rheology under extremely low temperatures and lose the capacity to suspend solid phase particles, but the multi-scale physical mechanisms influencing this rheological behavior have not been fully studied. This creates an unresolved scientific issue. Revealing the multifactor control laws and potential microphysical mechanisms of rheological evolution in oil-based complex fluids is crucial for the development of high-performance fluids. The viscosity and gel strength of the fluid changed significantly at −55 °C, indicating that the colloidal network structure might change at this temperature. This behavior distinguished the cold-induced gel state below −55 °C from the thermal relaxation state above −25 °C. The concentration of ice debris divided the fluid into cross-linking reinforcement and friction thickening zones. This multiscale study revealed the rheological evolution mechanism of oil-based complex fluids, laying the foundation for the rational design of high-performance complex fluids suitable for extreme, low-temperature environments.

papers.title: Estimating the disjoining pressure of liquid nanofilms from molecular dynamics simulations via implicit treatment of the bulk liquid phase
papers.abstract: The commonly adopted constant bulk liquid density approximation for evaluating disjoining pressure (Π) of free liquid nanofilms, although justified by the low compressibility of liquids, can introduce significant errors under strong confinement. Here, we develop a thermodynamically consistent molecular dynamics framework for estimating Π that implicitly accounts for variations in bulk liquid density. The framework couples a surface-tension-based formulation with an equation of state obtained from independent simulations and employs an iterative algorithm to simultaneously determine the bulk liquid density, film thickness, and Π. The method is applied to water and argon nanofilms and benchmarked against conventional constant-density approaches and alternative methods based on chemical potential calculations. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient and thermodynamically rigorous route for evaluating Π without explicit simulations of fully coexisting systems. Incorporating density variations substantially improves the accuracy and thermodynamic consistency of the predicted Π. For water nanofilms, a 3.6% deviation in bulk density can lead to an overestimation of Π by up to 77% at a film thickness of 12 Å, while the effect is weaker but remains non-negligible for argon. The proposed approach also recovers the inverse-cubic scaling of Π with film thickness predicted by Hamaker theory and reduces discrepancies among independent computational methods. These results demonstrate that a self-consistent treatment of bulk thermodynamics is essential for quantitatively reliable evaluation of surface forces in confined fluid systems.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic mechanisms of wall-confined helical propulsion in Newtonian and viscoelastic fluids
papers.abstract: The propulsion of helical microrobots in biological environments is strongly affected by wall confinement and fluid viscoelasticity. However, the coupled influence of these two factors on propulsion mechanisms remains poorly understood. In this study, an OpenFOAM-based non-Newtonian Stokes flow solver is employed to investigate the propulsion characteristics of non-uniform helical microrobots in confined Newtonian and viscoelastic fluids. The effects of wall distance and wall microstructures on the propulsive force, torque, propulsion efficiency, and surrounding flow field are systematically examined. The results reveal a critical confinement threshold at wd/d ≈ 12.3, where wd represents the minimum distance between the tail of the microrobot and the wall surface, and d denotes the initial helix radius of the microrobot; wall-induced hydrodynamic interactions become dominant when wd/d falls below this threshold. Wall confinement produces fundamentally different propulsion responses in the two fluids. In Newtonian fluids, the propulsive force and propulsion efficiency increase as the microrobot approaches the wall owing to enhanced viscous confinement. In contrast, viscoelastic fluids exhibit reduced propulsion performance under strong confinement because fluid elasticity weakens the effective axial momentum transfer. An optimal helical radius ratio of β = 3 is identified for achieving the highest propulsion efficiency in both fluids, where β characterizes the geometric non-uniformity of the helical tail. Rectangular groove structures further enhance propulsion in both fluids, whereas severe confinement increases energy dissipation in Newtonian fluids but improves propulsion efficiency in viscoelastic fluids. Flow-field analysis reveals that fluid elasticity fundamentally alters the confinement-induced flow redistribution, leading to opposite propulsion responses in Newtonian and viscoelastic fluids.

papers.title: Pore-scale investigation of flow-induced particle detachment in unconsolidated sandstone
papers.abstract: Subsurface fluid flow induces particle detachment and alters the petrophysical properties of unconsolidated sandstone. Although particle detachment and changes in hydraulic conductance have been observed, the roles of interparticle cementation and fluid–solid coupling in controlling pore-scale particle detachment have not been quantitatively investigated. In this work, a computational fluid dynamics coupled with the bonded discrete element method was employed to quantify the dynamic process of particle detachment. A pore model of bonded particles was constructed to investigate how flow velocity and cementation strength control particle detachment in unconsolidated sandstone. The results show that a critical velocity exists above which particles start to detach from the pore skeleton. The critical velocity exhibits a linear correlation with cementation strength. An empirical detachment coefficient (De), which is proportional to flow velocity and inversely proportional to cementation strength, was proposed to characterize the detachment of particles. Specifically, three distinct detachment regimes are identified: no detachment (De ≤ 1.67 × 10−3), surface detachment (1.67 × 10−3 < De ≤ 3.33 × 10−3), and pore collapse (De > 3.33 × 10−3). Under surface detachment, the pore skeleton remains largely intact with only surface erosion. When pore collapse occurs, large clusters of particles detach, leading to significant alteration of pore structure. Moreover, the relative change in apparent hydraulic conductance decreases with increasing cementation strength but increases with flow velocity. A stepwise jump in hydraulic conductance is observed during the transition from surface detachment to pore collapse.

papers.title: Film cooling performance of shaped holes in wedge-shaped channels
papers.abstract: This study investigates the adiabatic cooling efficiency of a shaped film cooling hole within a wedge channel. A combined experimental and numerical approach is employed to compare the laterally averaged film cooling effectiveness of the shaped hole and a conventional cylindrical hole under varying pressure ratios and temperature ratios. The experimental results indicate that as the pressure ratio increases, the wall temperature of the test section decreases, while the adiabatic cooling effectiveness increases, with the maximum effectiveness achieved at a pressure ratio of 1.4. In addition, an increase in the temperature ratio leads to a slight reduction in wall temperature, but the temperature ratio has a limited and configuration-dependent influence on the adiabatic cooling effectiveness. For the shaped hole, the averaged cooling effectiveness exhibits a non-monotonic variation and reaches its maximum at (KT = 2.5). Under the tested conditions, the shaped hole consistently outperforms the cylindrical hole in terms of cooling effectiveness. Based on the averaged cooling effectiveness, the maximum relative improvement ratio (φ) of the shaped hole over the cylindrical hole reaches 73.64% at (Kp = 1.4), while the maximum improvement under different temperature ratios reaches 64.86% at (KT = 2.5), respectively. The numerical results were validated against the experimental data using the local ηaw(x/D) distributions. The root mean square error and mean absolute error values for the temperature-ratio cases were 0.264%–0.425% and 0.189%–0.342%, respectively, indicating good quantitative agreement between the simulations and experiments.

papers.title: Transonic buffet control mechanism of the supercritical airfoil with an oscillating morphing surface
papers.abstract: Transonic shock buffet arises from a self-sustained interaction between unsteady shock motion and the boundary layer and remains a fundamental challenge in transonic aerodynamics. Recent advances in morphing-surface technology offer new opportunities to manipulate shock wave–boundary-layer interactions actively through surface deformation and oscillation. This study investigates the control mechanism of an oscillating morphing surface (OMS), with particular emphasis on phase coupling between the OMS and shock motion within the present two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes framework. The results indicate that the flow undergoes a transient OMS interference process before reaching an OMS-buffet stage, in which the shock motion is synchronized with the OMS excitation. When the OMS is deployed at the mean shock position, an excitation frequency of 100 Hz reduces the buffet load by 70.92%. Two OMS-buffet states are identified according to the phase relationship between shock excursion and surface motion. The in-phase OMS-buffet is associated with a substantial reduction in buffet load, whereas the anti-phase OMS-buffet shows no consistent suppression tendency. Dynamic mode decomposition analysis reveals that in-phase and anti-phase modal patterns coexist during the interference process and that the OMS preferentially amplifies the mode whose frequency is closest to the excitation frequency, thereby selecting the resulting OMS-buffet state. The physical mechanisms identified in this work provide a unified interpretation of OMS-based buffet control and guidance for active transonic buffet control strategies.

papers.title: Entropy production driven multi-objective Bayesian optimization—Non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm III collaborative optimization of a biomimetic serrated impeller for a mixed flow pump
papers.abstract: Cavitation-induced irreversible energy loss limits the efficient and stable operation of mixed flow pumps. This study proposes an entropy production driven Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization–Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III) method for designing a biomimetic serrated leading-edge impeller. The prototype impeller's principal hydraulic and structural parameters are retained, with serration height and tooth width as design variables. Three-dimensional numerical simulations are validated using model tests. Entropy production theory quantifies internal energy dissipation, and a multi-objective framework minimizes the total entropy production rate and low-pressure-region volume fraction under constraints of hydraulic efficiency and critical net positive suction pressure. A Kriging surrogate model, the expected hypervolume improvement criterion, and NSGA-III are integrated for global exploration and local refinement. The recommended serrated impeller has a tooth height of 7.78 mm and a tooth width of 4.32 mm. Relative to the prototype, the total entropy production rate decreases from 0.90 to 0.72 W/K (a 20.4% reduction) and low-pressure-region volume fraction from 1.81% to 0.68% (approximately 62.6% reduction), without appreciable hydraulic-performance deterioration. The serrations induce localized leading-edge turbulence modulation that redistributes near-wall momentum and blade loading, suppressing downstream cavity growth, separation, and intense shear. Rear-region entropy production decreases by 32.4%, 2.04 times the added dissipation in the front and middle regions. These results reveal a spatial redistribution mechanism of controlled leading-edge dissipation and dominant rear-region loss suppression, guiding cavitation-resistant, low-loss biomimetic design of mixed flow pumps.

papers.title: Near-wall flow reconstruction in turbulent channel flow using a physics-informed neural network
papers.abstract: Near-wall flow reconstruction from outer-region observations is challenging because the unobserved region contains the transition from viscous- to Reynolds-stress-dominated momentum transport and the buffer-layer maximum in turbulent kinetic energy production. We develop a physics-informed neural network with adaptive asymptotic hard constraints (AAHC-PINN) for a restricted statistical inverse problem in fully developed turbulent channel flow. Only statistics at y+> 30 are observed, while near-wall fields and pressure are withheld and no empirical turbulence closure is prescribed. The AAHC representation imposes the wall-limit values and leading asymptotic orders of the mean velocity and Reynolds stresses, while their amplitudes and wall-normal distributions are inferred from outer-region observations, the unclosed Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, and additional physical constraints. At Reτ= 1000, the mean streamwise velocity and Reynolds-stress components are reconstructed within y+≤ 30 with errors below 5%. The reconstructed fields capture the transition from viscous-dominated to Reynolds-stress-dominated momentum transport and the transfer of kinetic energy from the mean flow to turbulent fluctuations through buffer-layer mean-shear production. The characteristic locations of the momentum-transport transition and production maximum differ from direct numerical simulation by 4.6% and 3.8%, respectively, while the production maximum is underpredicted by 7.5%. Cases at Reτ= 550, 950, and 2000 use the same formulation and settings, showing robustness across the tested range. The results show that the reconstruction recovers both the missing near-wall statistics and their coupled momentum-transport and energy-transfer organization. Under the conditions examined, the characteristic locations of the momentum-transport transition and production maximum are recovered more accurately than the local production intensity.

papers.title: Diffusioosmosis of electrolyte solutions in axisymmetric channels
papers.abstract: We present a theory of fluid flow in long axisymmetric channels induced by salt concentration and pressure drops between their ends. The consideration is restricted to electrostatic diffuse layers that are thin compared to the local radius, but remains valid even when the concentration drop is quite large. We show that the magnitude of the diffusio-osmotic fluid flow rate QDO in a cylinder is the same as in a slit with a thickness equal to the cylinder diameter, whereas channels with variable cross sections can either retard or enhance it, depending on their geometry. The application of a pressure drop Δp≠0 results in an extra contribution QP to the total fluid flow rate Q without affecting QDO. We calculate the curves Δp(Q) for several axisymmetric channels and conclude that they are nearly linear, with slopes that are sensitive to the channel shape. This leads to the possibility of introducing a simple, but rather accurate, cylinder approximation, where the radius of the imaginary cylinder is related to the hydrodynamic resistivity of the real channel and can be easily determined if its geometry is known. We also derive an equation relating the ionic flux with the total fluid flow rate and demonstrate that both the sign and magnitude of the ionic flux can be tuned by using an appropriate channel shape. Our analysis provides a framework for interpreting experimental and numerical data, as well as guiding the design of micro- and nanofluidic devices.

papers.title: Erratum: “Transient compressible flow in a compliant viscoelastic tube” [Phys. Fluids 32 , 112014 (2020)]
A physics-guided permeability prediction equation for digital rocks based on pore network structural parameters
papers.abstract: Permeability is a fundamental property governing fluid transport in porous media and is critical to enhanced oil recovery. Nevertheless, existing methods remain limited by experimental uncertainty, computational cost, and insufficient interpretability. This study proposed an enhanced permeability prediction equation. The equation was developed by combining machine learning with theoretical analysis. The proposed equation outperformed the calibrated Kozeny–Carman (K–C) and baseline models and achieved performance comparable to that of XGBoost. It therefore provides a concise and physically interpretable description of permeability within the adopted pore network modeling framework.

papers.title: Assessment of numerical lift coefficient data for a circular cylinder with application to bladeless turbines
papers.abstract: We assess computed lift coefficient data for flow past a circular cylinder to evaluate their suitability for practical applications. Specifically, we consider lift coefficient data for a circular cylinder over Reynolds numbers from 120 to 8000. The results are obtained from two-dimensional finite element simulations of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations using pressure robust discretizations. We compare the computed lift coefficients with published experimental and numerical results, finding good agreement in some cases but significant disagreement in others. Because lift fluctuations are central to vortex-induced vibration concepts, these data therefore provide input for the analysis and preliminary design of bladeless turbines.

papers.title: Analysis of flow characteristics and backflow suppression in a high-altitude simulation test chamber for thrust-vectoring engines
papers.abstract: A high-temperature overexpanded jet entering a confined altitude simulation test chamber may induce upstream hot-gas recirculation through the coupled effects of jet entrainment, spatial confinement, and pressure recovery; nozzle deflection disrupts flow-field symmetry. A three-dimensional numerical model comprising a thrust-vectoring nozzle, an altitude simulation test chamber, and an exhaust diffuser was established. The numerical method was evaluated using experimental data for an overexpanded nozzle and wall-pressure measurements in the chamber, and was used to investigate deflection-induced changes in the recirculation structure and the momentum-based control mechanisms of secondary jets. At zero deflection, jet entrainment and the adverse pressure gradient produce approximately symmetric recirculation structures on both sides of the primary jet. Nozzle deflection causes asymmetric jet-wall impingement and pressure recovery, concentrating large-scale hot-gas recirculation on the side opposite the impingement wall. The cooling secondary flow supplies fluid for jet entrainment and downstream-directed axial momentum while forming a continuous, low-temperature coflowing layer outside the primary jet, thereby progressively separating the hot jet from the near-wall recirculation pathway. In the deflected configuration, the effectiveness of multi-hole blowing depends on the balance between axial momentum opposing recirculation and radial momentum providing a flow barrier, while the hole arrangement is jointly governed by circumferential coverage continuity and the effective penetration of individual jets. These findings clarify asymmetric hot-gas recirculation and secondary-jet momentum control in a confined chamber and provide a basis for thermal-environment control and blowing-scheme design in altitude simulation test chambers.

papers.title: Numerical study on the near-field characteristics of waves generated by the collapse of a partially immersed axisymmetric granular column into water
papers.abstract: The near-field characteristics of the wave generated by the collapse of a partially immersed axisymmetric granular column into water is studied numerically using an unresolved computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method coupling framework. The numerical approach is thoroughly validated, ensuring reliable resolution of granular–fluid interactions and wave dynamics. Three distinct wave types are identified: cnoidal-like waves, nonlinear transition waves, and nonlinear oscillatory waves. Two distinct wave-generation mechanisms are proposed to elucidate the transition between different wave types. In addition, the energy evolution during wave generation is analyzed, and the influence of the initial conditions is also examined. Finally, an empirical scaling law for the maximum wave amplitude is proposed. Compared with existing formulas, the present formula incorporates both the granular shape parameter and the water-depth parameter and shows good agreement with the numerical results.

papers.title: Spectral observability-based sparse sensing of cylinder-wake and turbulent channel flows
papers.abstract: Sparse sensor placement is central to reconstructing unsteady flow fields from limited measurements. This study develops a spectral-conditioning-based forward sequential sensor placement (FSSP) strategy for sparse reconstruction in a spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) basis. The method is motivated by the frequency-domain reconstruction formulation and a perturbation-bound interpretation of the sampled observation matrices. To obtain a single physical sensor layout over the resolved spectrum, the same row-selection matrix is applied to all frequency-dependent SPOD bases. Sensor locations are then selected sequentially to reduce the summed squared condition numbers of the sampled observation matrices. The method is assessed using two flows with distinct spectral characteristics: a narrowband laminar cylinder wake and a broadband turbulent channel-flow slice. The comparisons include a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) layout obtained by column-pivoted orthogonal–triangular (QR) factorization (POD-QR), a regularized multi-frequency SPOD-D-optimal sensor layout (SPOD-D-opt), and random sensor layouts, all evaluated using a common retained SPOD reconstruction operator to isolate the effect of sensor placement.
