The results show that layout sensitivity is limited once the dominant structures of the narrowband wake are sufficiently sampled, whereas the role of frequency-resolved conditioning is more evident in the broadband channel flow. In the latter case, SPOD-FSSP generally provides better-conditioned observation matrices together with improvements in global and spectral reconstruction metrics. These findings support spectral conditioning as a practical and physically interpretable criterion for sparse sensing of unsteady flows.

papers.title: Lattice Boltzmann simulation of successive droplets impacting sand particles
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional sand printing is a key technology in digital casting, and its forming quality is critically governed by the impact dynamics of binder droplets on sand particles, the investigation of which has been constrained by the predominant focus of existing numerical studies on single-impact events. This study develops a numerical framework based on the color-gradient lattice Boltzmann method, in which a field-inheritance technique is employed to simulate the interfacial dynamics of successive binder droplets impacting sand particles. With this approach, distinctive phenomena arising from successive droplet impact are identified, including coalescence-induced depinning, liquid-film memory, and longitudinal–lateral spreading antagonism. Moreover, the influence of critical parameters, i.e., inter-droplet interval, impact inertia, impact offset, and sand-particle size, on the droplet-impact dynamics is systematically examined, elucidating the underlying mechanisms of residual-film retention, inertia-assisted contact-line escape, edge-throat contact triggering, and scale-dependent transport redistribution. This work provides a microscopic-level pathway for investigating binder-droplet impact dynamics in three-dimensional sand printing.

papers.title: Modeling and simulation of the electrohydrodynamics for dielectric to high-conductivity liquids
papers.abstract: Electrohydrodynamics investigates the fluid motion driven by electric fields. It provides the theoretical foundation for applications such as high-resolution printing and electrospray. However, existing electrohydrodynamic (EHD) models often suffer from unreal charge diffusion across the mixed fluid–fluid interface. This unreal charge leakage can severely affect numerical convergence and solution accuracy, particularly in systems with extremely large conductivity contrasts between the two phases, where the conductivity ratio exceeds 1013. In this study, a new two-phase EHD model is developed to calculate the EHD phenomena, coupling the flow field, electric field, and phase field. A novel transition function framework is proposed to ensure the smooth and rapid change of electric parameters across the interface, thereby suppressing the unreal charge diffusion. Volume charge transport is resolved using the Poisson–Nernst–Planck-derived charge-transport formulation rather than imposing the leaky-dielectric approximation. Three representative cases are studied, including a parallel-plate capacitor, a suspended droplet, and EHD printing. The model demonstrates superior accuracy in calculating static, electrostatic, and dynamic responses. Additionally, the mechanism of unreal charge leakage is revealed. By using the transition function, the unreal charge leakage is effectively suppressed, even with a large conductivity difference between the two phases. Consequently, the model allows the computable relative conductivity to increase by at least five orders of magnitude to 1018 compared to existing models. This first makes the high-fidelity calculation of EHD systems with high relative conductivity feasible. Overall, the developed model proves to be advantageous, with high fidelity and wide applicability to a range of EHD phenomena.

papers.title: A computer-vision approach for bulk flow parameters and Lagrangian bubble motion in millimeter-scale tubes
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid flow in millimeter-scale tubes exhibits transient dynamics at both bulk and individual-bubble scales, which are difficult to measure simultaneously under low-frame-rate imaging. This study develops a computer-vision framework for synchronized measurement of bulk flow parameters and Lagrangian bubble motion in bubbly and slug flows using single-view 30 fps backlit image sequences. Attention-UNet segmentation is combined with a kinematically constrained matching strategy based on foreground-normalized mask overlap and an inertial continuity constraint. The framework extracts a relative image-derived gas-occupancy proxy, global bubble velocity Uglobal, individual-bubble trajectories, projected-area variation, image-derived apparent near-wall clearance, and in-plane nose curvature from the same video stream. Cross-validation yielded a segmentation Dice coefficient of 0.9736. Synthetic-displacement tests gave a mean relative offset error of 0.95%, and the representative type-B uncertainty in individual-bubble velocity was 0.47%. The global bubble-velocity signal contained a dominant low-frequency component whose frequency increased nearly linearly with U¯global (R2=0.984); the fitted slope corresponded to an apparent advective length of 1.52 m, close to the apparatus length and supporting a facility-scale interpretation. At the bubble scale, the higher Weber-number end-member group exhibited lower mean in-plane nose curvature. The framework therefore enables synchronized characterization of millimeter-scale gas–liquid flow at global and bubble-resolved scales using a single low-frame-rate image sequence.

papers.title: Interfacial and rheological changes during foam flow based on two-dimensional (2D) pore-scale modeling
papers.abstract: Foams consist of gas bubbles dispersed in a surfactant stabilized liquid, greatly increasing gas viscosity for subsurface engineering applications. As foam moves through the complex pore geometry of rocks and soils, its bubbles continually change, making their behavior and viscosity difficult to quantify. We develop a new numerical model validated by quasi-two-dimensional microfluidic experiments from Liontas et al. Our method simulates foam propagation incorporating fundamental mechanisms within the detailed geometry of a porous medium. We further propose a workflow using bubble replenishment at the inlet and calculate the foam apparent viscosity when a quasi-steady state is reached. The foam propagation is modeled using a lattice Boltzmann model that couples the momentum transfer for liquid flow and the advection-diffusion equation for the gas phase. We quantify, for the first time, detailed pressure and velocity spatial changes that lead to foam bubbles splitting or wiggling while moving through the complex pore scale geometry. Depending on the injection conditions, we correctly capture foam bubble wiggling or splitting (into multiple bubbles) through pore throats. We describe bubble behavior in a parametric space and ultimately quantify foam rheology. Foam apparent viscosity decreases with increasing capillary number, and the data follow a power law relationship.

papers.title: A two-stage non-intrusive reduced-order model for parametric prediction of liquid-bridge interface evolution in gravure-printing cavities
papers.abstract: Roll-to-roll (R2R) gravure printing transfers functional inks from engraved cavities onto a substrate through the stretching and pinch-off of a confined liquid bridge, whose necking dynamics and final liquid partitioning depend sensitively on the cavity geometry. High-resolution phase-field simulations resolve this geometry-dependent interface evolution, but their cost makes systematic exploration of cavity design space impractical. Here, we develop a non-intrusive, two-stage reduced-order model that predicts the pre-pinch-off interface evolution and resulting liquid-transfer ratio directly from the cavity height and width. In the first stage, Gaussian-process (GP) surrogates predict the pinch-off time and the transfer ratio from the geometry. The predicted pinch-off time defines a normalized time coordinate that aligns the interface snapshots across geometries; in the second stage, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) compresses these snapshots and GP regression reconstructs the modal coefficients. Trained on 18 cavity geometries, the surrogate reproduces the reference interfaces to an overall root-mean-square error of 1.85% under leave-one-out cross-validation, with the error separating in quadrature into a 1.04% POD-truncation floor and a 1.53% coefficient-regression contribution. On five independent held-out test cases, accuracy remains comparable (0.61%–1.19%). The transfer ratios predicted from the reconstructed interface are consistent with both the high-fidelity simulations and the independent scalar GP surrogate. Once trained, the modal-interface prediction for a new geometry requires milliseconds, rather than the hours-to-days cost of a phase-field simulation. These results show that cavity-controlled liquid-bridge breakup and partitioning can be captured by a low-dimensional, geometry-dependent representation, enabling rapid screening of gravure-cavity designs within the explored geometric domain.

papers.title: Effects of wave diffraction around rigid walls with typical geometries on cavitation loads induced by underwater explosions
papers.abstract: Wave diffraction around rigid walls of varying geometries critically affects cavitation and collapse-induced loading during underwater explosions. This study develops a numerical framework integrating Runge–Kutta discontinuous Galerkin discretization, Level Set interface tracking, the ghost fluid method, and an isentropic cavitation model. Validation against representative one- and two-dimensional benchmarks confirms the framework's accuracy and robustness in capturing shock propagation, interface evolution, and cavitation inception, growth, and collapse. The validated model is used to examine the effects of wall thickness, length, and configuration, stand-off distance, and charge depth on cavitation evolution and wall loading. The results show that interactions among incident, reflected, and edge-diffracted waves govern the cyclic inception, expansion, collapse, and regeneration of near-wall cavitation. Increasing wall thickness enhances near-wall confinement, producing more concentrated cavities and higher initial collapse loads, whereas increasing wall length prolongs the low-pressure state, enlarges the cavitation region, and intensifies collapse loading at the wall center. Increasing stand-off distance weakens and delays cavitation, while increasing charge depth suppresses cavity growth and accelerates collapse through elevated hydrostatic pressure. Wall configuration also strongly influences cavitation morphology and loading. The upright conical wall delays collapse but produces a central collapse load comparable to that of the cylindrical wall, whereas the inverted conical wall promotes oblique shock reflection and radial energy dispersion, substantially reducing cavitation severity and concentrated wall loading. These findings elucidate the mechanisms governing near-wall cavitation loads and provide a theoretical basis for the blast-resistant design of typical underwater structures.

papers.title: Erosion characteristics of aluminum and copper under double-excited cavitating waterjets
papers.abstract: Building upon our previous characterization of the cavitation cloud dynamics, this study presents a systematic quantification of the erosion performance of a double-excited cavitating waterjet on aluminum and copper targets. The erosion performance of a double-excited cavitating waterjet, combining active and passive excitation, is investigated across a range of standoff distances using aluminum and copper targets, with single-passive, single-active, and non-excited cavitating waterjets as benchmarks. Erosion behavior is quantified through optimal standoff distance, cumulative mass loss, cumulative erosion rate, instantaneous erosion rate, and surface morphology. Results show that the double-excited cavitating waterjet markedly enhances erosion compared to single- and non-excited configurations. This enhancement is attributed to the combined interaction between pulsed-jet-induced impulsive loading and intensified cavitation-collapse dynamics. For aluminum, the optimal standoff distance is comparable to that of the single-passive cavitating waterjet, whereas for copper, it shifts to shorter distances, reflecting the relative contributions of impulsive loading and cavitation-driven damage. The coupled excitation accelerates the onset of erosion, shortens the incubation and deceleration stages, and sustains higher erosion rates. Surface characterization reveals deeper craters and wider material removal zones under the double-excited cavitating waterjet, confirming enhanced erosion performance. These results demonstrate that combined active–passive excitation provides an effective pathway for process intensification in cavitating waterjet-based material removal.

papers.title: Data-driven surrogate models for forecasting experimentally measured fluid flows
papers.abstract: Data-driven modeling shows significant promise for faster-than-real-time forecasting of fluid flows. For real-world engineering applications (e.g., flow control), models must contend with limited, imperfect, and incomplete experimental measurements. However, most data-driven surrogates have been developed and demonstrated entirely within the computational domain. In this work, we present an analysis of data-driven surrogate models trained to forecast the time evolution of experimentally measured cylinder wakes. Using a dataset of two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry measurements, we train fully convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, Fourier neural operators, and dynamic mode decomposition-based models to forecast the development of experimentally measured velocity fields. To characterize data-driven approaches contending with transient flow features and limited, imperfect observations, the development of predictions over extended forecast horizons is examined at a fixed Reynolds number (Re=590). Next, models are trained at a range of Reynolds numbers (Re=230–2920) to investigate the impact of increasingly turbulent and three-dimensional flow phenomena on forecast quality. Through a triple decomposition of measured and forecast velocity fields, we find that error is dominated by the fluctuating velocity component, with all surrogates exhibiting a decay in estimated planar turbulent kinetic energy. The characteristics of this decay are architecture-dependent. Regardless, we find that the experimentally trained surrogate models can provide meaningful predictions over short time horizons, propagate low-frequency dynamics over longer forecast periods, and achieve faster-than-real-time evaluation in the considered contexts. These results highlight the opportunities and challenges that remain for data-driven fluid dynamics in real-world, real-time engineering applications.

papers.title: The effect of surface roughness on interfacial dynamics and wettability in two-phase microchannel flow
papers.abstract: We investigate the interfacial dynamics of two immiscible fluids flowing within a two-dimensional microchannel with structured wall roughness through numerical simulations. The simulations are performed using a finite-volume approach combined with the volume-of-fluid method to capture the fluid interface. Wall roughness is introduced on one wall of a straight channel in the form of an obstacle array. Three different obstacle shapes are considered: rectangular, triangular, and semi-elliptical. The effects of geometric parameters, including the spacing-to-width ratio (s/d) and height-to-width ratio (h/d), intrinsic contact angle (θC), viscosity ratio, and capillary number (Ca), are examined. The results show that roughness shape strongly influences interfacial behavior. The rectangular shape produces the largest interfacial deformation and promotes greater water entrapment, whereas the triangular shape results in a more stable interface. Reducing s/d increases water trapping and slightly accelerates interface movement, whereas increasing h/d produces a more pronounced influence on the flow. Changes in θC alter the interface curvature and are associated with higher apparent contact angles and more frequent water entrapment within the cavities. The onset of partial water trapping occurs at a local capillary number of approximately 1.1×10−4 for triangular and rectangular elements, whereas semi-elliptical profiles require a nearly fourfold higher threshold. For capillary numbers below 10−3, the static contact angle formulation remains physically valid because deviations of the dynamic contact line are minimal.

papers.title: Wall effect on the wake structure around a heated sphere in steady aiding-buoyancy mixed convection
papers.abstract: The interaction between wall confinement and thermal buoyancy produces complex wake dynamics in mixed convection around heated bodies, particularly in low-Prandtl-number liquid metals where thermal and momentum boundary layers evolve differently. In this study, the wake topology and transport mechanisms around a near-wall heated sphere in steady aiding-buoyancy mixed convection are numerically investigated using Galinstan (Pr=0.025). The results reveal a previously unexplored wake-transition mechanism induced by the competition between buoyancy-driven acceleration and wall-induced confinement. At Re=200, increasing buoyancy strength or reducing wall clearance transforms the wake from large counter-rotating vortices into a suppressed spiral structure and finally into a plane-symmetric wake containing a shear-generated vortex pair near the wall. The maximum and minimum values of local Nusselt number Nu, dimensionless pressure p* and x direction vorticity ωx* along the sphere surface almost monotonically increase with Ri increasing and γ decreasing. Drag composition ratio Cdp/Cdf shows a trend of first decreasing rapidly and then increasing slowly as Ri increases, which becomes more obvious at higher Re. Moreover, their asymmetrical distributions become more pronounced as γ decreases and all undergo significant variation near the lowest region of the sphere. It is found that the average Nusselt number Nu¯ increases monotonically and decreases with Ri and γ increasing, respectively. These findings establish the physical links between wake topology, near-wall shear generation, pressure redistribution, and thermal transport. Empirical correlations for drag and heat transfer are additionally provided as secondary tools for engineering prediction.

papers.title: A graphics processing unit accelerated simplified lattice Boltzmann method on a multi-resolution mesh for incompressible thermal flows
papers.abstract: The simplified lattice Boltzmann method (SLBM), a recent advancement in the lattice Boltzmann community, evolves macroscopic variables directly while preserving numerical stability at high Reynolds numbers. Extending its applicability to multiscale problems, a multi-resolution mesh formulation of SLBM has recently been developed for isothermal hydrodynamic and acoustic flows. In this work, this framework is extended to convective flows involving heat transfer, through a double distribution function formulation that consistently couples the velocity and temperature fields across mesh interfaces of differing resolution. The resulting multi-resolution thermal SLBM is further accelerated through an asynchronous graphics processing unit (GPU)-based parallelization strategy, with the GPU implementation alone yielding speedups of 4.6–11.8× over the corresponding serial multi-resolution computations. The method is applied to three convective heat transfer problems of increasing complexity: natural convection in a differentially heated square cavity across a wide range of Rayleigh numbers, forced convection over a heated square cylinder across a range of Reynolds numbers, and the flow and thermal interaction between two side-by-side heated square cylinders at varying transverse spacing. Beyond validating the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed framework, these studies show how the localized spatial resolution afforded by the multi-resolution mesh makes it computationally affordable to resolve thermal-hydrodynamic coupling that would otherwise require a globally refined mesh—in particular, how the classical wake-interference regimes of closely spaced bluff bodies are reflected in, and in turn reshape, their convective heat transfer response. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach preserves the simplicity, locality, and numerical stability of SLBM while providing a computationally efficient tool for probing convective heat transfer in confined and multiscale wake-interference flows.

papers.title: Coupled effects of silica nanoparticle size and concentration on supercritical CO2–crude oil interfacial tension
papers.abstract: Interfacial tension (IFT) between supercritical CO2 (scCO2) and crude oil governs capillary trapping, mass transfer, and microscopic displacement efficiency, making it a key variable in CO2 enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) and geological CO2 storage. This study systematically investigated how SiO2 nanoparticle concentration and particle size, two coupled formulation parameters, govern scCO2-crude oil IFT. Experiments were performed at 82.2 °C and 15.86 MPa using the pendant-drop method, while minimum miscibility pressure (MMP) was determined through slim-tube experiments. A central composite design combined with response surface methodology was used to evaluate the response over 0.125–1.0 wt. % concentration and 5–100 nm particle size. The base system exhibited an MMP of 25.51 MPa, whereas SiO2 nanofluids reduced MMP to 18.20–21.53 MPa. All MMP values exceeded the IFT measurement pressure, confirming sub-MMP measurement conditions. Across the design space, IFT ranged from 3.79 to 7.38 mN m−1. The quadratic model was highly significant (R2 = 0.9955 and p < 0.0001), accurately capturing the nonlinear combined response. Numerical optimization identified 0.73 wt. % SiO2 and 50 nm as the optimum, predicting an IFT of 3.58 mN m−1. Experimental validation yielded 3.41 ± 0.12 mN m−1, corresponding to a 72.83% reduction relative to the base value of 12.55 ± 0.25 mN m−1. The results indicate that IFT reduction reflects a size-dependent balance among interfacial accessibility, colloidal dispersion, and finite interfacial capacity. These findings provide a physically grounded basis for designing SiO2 nanofluids under reservoir-relevant pressure-temperature conditions while maintaining formulation variables for CO2-EOR and geological CO2 storage.

papers.title: Acoustic characteristics of a ventilation duct elbow with a whale flipper-inspired tubercle guide vane
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic noise generated in ventilation elbows is an important contributor to noise in ship ventilation systems. Inspired by the leading-edge tubercles of humpback whale flippers, tubercle guide vanes are introduced to regulate the internal flow and reduce aerodynamic noise. Experimental measurements are used to validate the numerical flow and acoustic models. The effects of tubercle placement, amplitude, wavelength, and guide vane thickness are subsequently investigated. The results show that leading-edge tubercles redistribute the incoming flow before it develops along the guide vane. The redistribution suppresses local acceleration and alleviates concentrated pressure gradients near the vane entrance, thereby reducing aerodynamic noise. The geometric parameters affect the acoustic response through different flow control mechanisms. Amplitude mainly regulates the intensity of local flow redistribution. Wavelength controls its spatial extent and the interaction between adjacent tubercles. Guide vane thickness influences local flow deflection, together with the resulting velocity and pressure gradients. Effective noise reduction therefore depends on the combined adjustment of the three parameters rather than on the independent optimization of a single parameter. An orthogonal design is further employed to identify a preferred parameter combination. The optimized configuration weakens the local concentration of high-velocity flow and improves downstream pressure recovery. Lower aerodynamic noise is consequently obtained than with the conventional guide vane. The identified relationships among tubercle placement, geometric parameters, local flow regulation, and noise reduction provide a physical basis for the low-noise design of ship ventilation elbows.

papers.title: Normal-inverse-Gaussian description of the velocity-increment cascade in homogeneous isotropic turbulence: Dissipative-boundary closure and the Reynolds dependence of the asymmetry
papers.abstract: Intermittency in turbulence causes some scaling exponents of the longitudinal velocity increment to deviate from Kolmogorov's prediction. Multifractal closures reproduce that deviation accurately, but each fits its parameters to the exponents themselves and leaves the underlying increment distribution unspecified. Using direct numerical simulations of homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Taylor-microscale Reynolds numbers of 433, 611, and 1257, we identify the distribution first. Throughout the inertial range, the increment density is normal-inverse-Gaussian; at the highest Reynolds number, it is preferred over Gaussian, Student-t, and skew-t alternatives at every scale tested. Its parameters are fixed at the dissipative boundary by the kinematic viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the universal velocity-gradient skewness and are carried through the inertial range by the measured second and third moments. The exponents then follow without being fitted, the fourth-order exponent falling 0.10 below the measured value and the higher even orders falling short in the same direction. This is expected of a single-shape density whose tails are too thin for the rare increments that dominate high moments. The density asymmetry weakens as the Reynolds number rises. Compared at matched large-scale sampling volume, the change is carried by the increment flatness and not by the skewness, whose contribution is unresolved in every matched pair over a factor of 2.9 in the Reynolds number, while the scale dependence of the flatness gives an intermittency exponent μ=0.314±0.020. The increment distribution is thus set by measurable small-scale physics, and its asymmetry inherits the Reynolds-number dependence of intermittency.

papers.title: Secondary-flow suppression through transverse energy-transport regulation in a multiphase pump
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid multiphase pumps experience significant performance degradation under high inlet gas volume fraction (IGVF) conditions because the low-density and highly compressible gas phase cannot effectively follow the conventional centrifugal pressurization pathway, thereby inducing phase slip, flow separation, and secondary-flow development. Here, a multi-parameter impeller redesign is proposed to enhance axial gas transport and sustain continuous gas compression. The redesigned pump is evaluated through experimental measurements and numerical simulations, with particular emphasis on the high IGVF of 80%. To elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms, a potential rothalpy gradient (PRG) framework and a secondary-flow indicator (SI) are employed to characterize the competition between PRG-induced transverse energy transport and Coriolis induced rotational constraint. The redesigned impeller maintains superior pressure-rise capability and hydraulic efficiency at elevated IGVFs while promoting continuous gas compression and reducing flow recirculation and vortex-dominated structures. Increasing IGVF does not necessarily result in a monotonic enhancement of secondary flow; instead, it shifts regions with high secondary-flow susceptibility from the impeller inlet toward the passage core and tip-side outlet by modifying the local balance between transverse energy transport and rotational constraint. Impeller redesign mitigates this process by redistributing rotor energy more uniformly and weakening regions characterized by high PRG and SI values.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of aerodynamic mechanisms governing lateral-load fluctuations of a 600 km/h high-temperature superconducting maglev train passing through a double-track tunnel
papers.abstract: When a high-temperature superconducting (HTS) maglev train passes through a double-track tunnel, asymmetric confinement by the U-shaped guideway and tunnel boundaries produces complex pressure variations and wake dynamics that act as unsteady lateral aerodynamic excitations. A refined full-scale three-car train traveling at 600 km/h is simulated using three-dimensional unsteady compressible flow, improved delayed detached-eddy simulation, and a sliding mesh. Proper orthogonal decomposition and dynamic mode decomposition are used to analyze surface pressure, side-to-side pressure differences, and wake dynamics. The results show that (1) under open-line conditions, a side-to-side pressure phase lag produces a low-frequency, large-amplitude pressure difference, and lateral-force fluctuations; (2) in the tunnel, pressure waves mainly modulate the common-mode pressure, whereas lateral force is strongly correlated with differential pressure and increases from the head to the tail car; (3) tunnel confinement produces a tail wake biased toward the tunnel-center side. Interaction between downward flow above the tail car and upward gap flow promotes local low pressure, reduced wall shear stress, and separation near the tail nose, generating a unilateral wake associated with a component near 27 Hz; and (4) the principal dimensional frequency bands remain broadly similar from 400 to 600 km/h, although their energy and Strouhal number vary. Increasing line spacing reduces the persistent lateral bias; at 5.8 m, the mean tail-car lateral force and mean spanwise pressure gradient approach zero, although high-frequency fluctuations remain. These results distinguish the roles of pressure waves and wake asymmetry in the lateral aerodynamic response of HTS maglev trains.

papers.title: Reynolds stress anisotropy and secondary flow prediction in turbulent channel flow over riblets: A comparison of large-eddy simulation with linear and nonlinear Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes closures
papers.abstract: Near-wall Reynolds stress anisotropy and secondary flows play a dominant role in drag reduction over riblets. In this study, a systematic evaluation of the wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity model, the shear-stress transport (SST) k–ω model, and the Wallin–Johansson explicit algebraic Reynolds stress model (WJ-BSL-EARSM) is conducted for turbulent channel flow over riblets under s+=20 and s+=40 regimes, focusing on macroscopic drag variation, secondary flows, and near-wall statistical characteristics. Results demonstrate that large eddy simulation (LES) reproduces pairs of counter-rotating secondary vortices, the lifting and pinning effects on quasi-streamwise vortices, and shear-layer instabilities, with the resolved turbulent kinetic energy ratio exceeding 98.61%, satisfying the Pope criterion threshold (M=kresolved/ktotal≥80%). The standard SST k–ω model fails due to the breakdown of its isotropic assumption, rendering it incapable of responding to the Reynolds normal-stress difference ⟨v′2⟩−⟨w′2⟩, which leads to a failure in predicting drag increase (12.42% lower than direct numerical simulation). In contrast, the non-linear WJ-BSL-EARSM model captures stress anisotropy by virtue of high-order tensor cross-terms, reconstructing Prandtl's second-kind secondary flows and capturing the key physical trend of drag reversing from negative to positive (4.92%). This study reveals how Reynolds stress anisotropy affects drag in riblet flows, clarifies the predictive performance gaps and physical limitations between Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes models and LES, and provides theoretical foundation for turbulent flows over riblet walls.

papers.title: Effects of airfoil thickness on flow control using multiple dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuators in a straight-bladed vertical-axis wind turbine
papers.abstract: This study numerically investigates the influence of airfoil thickness on the effectiveness of flow control using multiple dielectric barrier discharge plasma actuators in a straight-bladed vertical-axis wind turbine. Two-dimensional simulations are performed for five symmetric national advisory committee for aeronautics airfoils: NACA0027, NACA0024, NACA0021, NACA0018, and NACA0015. Multiple plasma actuators are installed on the inner surface of each blade. The use of multiple plasma actuators for flow control effectively suppresses flow separation and improves turbine performance. In particular, for the relatively thick airfoils, the power coefficient is substantially higher under the controlled condition than under the uncontrolled condition, with the NACA0027 airfoil achieving an 18.87% improvement at λ=2.19. In contrast, the improvement in the power coefficient is limited for the thinner airfoils, with the NACA0015 airfoil showing only a 2.41% increase at λ=2.19. Flow-field analysis reveals that, within the range 100°≤θ≤110°, the pressure reduction around the leading edge on the inner surface under the controlled condition contributes substantially to the improvement in turbine performance. This pressure reduction is likely attributable to an increase in near-wall velocity in the same region. Furthermore, the thicker airfoils exhibit greater increases in near-wall velocity and larger pressure reductions, whereas the differences in the velocity and pressure fields between the controlled condition and the uncontrolled condition are limited for the thinner airfoils. These results suggest that the performance improvement achieved by plasma-actuator control depends on airfoil thickness.

papers.title: Study on nonlinear seepage mechanism of water injection coal under the action of threshold pressure gradient
papers.abstract: During the initial stage of water injection into deep, low-permeability gas-bearing coal seams, a significant threshold pressure gradient causes the seepage behavior to deviate from Darcy's linear flow law. Consequently, the pressure gradient of pressure-driven water increases during transport through the porous medium, which restricts the effective infiltration range of water injection. Based on fractal theory and seepage equations, this study develops permeability and threshold pressure gradient models for gas-bearing coal by considering the effects of the boundary layer, gas pressure, surface tension, and contact angle. An influencing-factor analysis was further conducted to clarify the roles of different parameters in the nonlinear seepage process. Moreover, considering the physical and chemical properties of the fluid, a mechanism for permeability enhancement during the initial nonlinear seepage stage of water injection is proposed. The results indicate that the initial threshold pressure gradient during water injection is positively correlated with gas pressure and surface tension, but negatively correlated with pore radius and contact angle. The boundary layer effect reduces the effective flow radius, thereby decreasing coal permeability. After the addition of sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate to the injected water, the surface tension and contact angle are significantly reduced, resulting in a lower threshold pressure gradient, enhanced coal permeability, and a substantially larger water infiltration range. These findings provide a theoretical basis and technical support for optimizing water injection parameters and improving disaster prevention and control in deep, high-gas coal seams.

papers.title: Effect of recirculation-zone regulation on vibration and energy conversion in a double-interference piezoelectric energy harvester
papers.abstract: In wake-induced vibration piezoelectric energy harvesting, the recirculation zone was a critical factor governing wake structure and flow excitation. To reveal the mechanism by which downstream interference column spacing regulates the recirculation zone, wind tunnel tests and two-way fluid–structure interaction simulations were conducted to investigate the influence of recirculation-zone regulation on wake-induced response and output performance. Results demonstrated that the feedback effect of the downstream interference column on the responsive cylinder first increased and then decreased with increasing spacing ratio in the range of 3.5–5.5. At a spacing ratio of 3.5, the maximum vorticity in the recirculation zone increased by 100% compared with the baseline case, because the shorter cylinder gap reduced vortex dissipation during backflow and generated weak gap thrust. When the spacing ratio was 4.5, the moderate cylinder gap enabled full vortex development and minimal dissipation. Thus, the maximum recirculation zone vorticity increased by 150% compared with the baseline, resulting in a maximum displacement of 40.68 mm with a 7.5% improvement over the baseline case. At a spacing ratio of 5.5, the vortices dissipated prematurely and disrupted wake symmetry, generating a displacement 8.7% lower than that of the baseline configuration. As a result, the maximum output voltage 1.18 V was obtained at G* = 4.5 with a 4.4% improvement over the baseline case, while the minimum output voltage was 1.04 V at G* = 5.5 with a 8.7% reduction. This study verified the modulation mechanism of downstream cylinder spacing on the recirculation zone, offering theoretical support for optimization and application.

papers.title: Moving contact line dynamics and detachment mechanism of a discontinuous oil phase in microchannels
papers.abstract: The dynamics of moving contact lines govern the displacement of immiscible fluids on solid surfaces, with broad relevance to diverse industrial processes including enhanced oil recovery, chemical processing, and biomedicine. Accurate simulation of these dynamics is essential for understanding and predicting the associated physical phenomena. This study focused on the moving contact line of a discontinuous oil phase within a microchannel. Based on a pore-scale two-phase flow model coupling the Navier–Stokes equations and the phase-field method, the migration morphology, dynamic evolution of the contact line, and detachment mechanism of the discontinuous oil phase were systematically investigated. By varying capillary number, oil viscosity, surface tension, and surface wettability distribution, the variations of the front and rear contact line velocities, the oil–wall contact area fraction, and the detachment time are analyzed in detail. The results show that the asymmetric evolution of the front and rear contact lines was identified as a key factor governing droplet detachment. Increasing capillary number raises both front and rear contact line velocities, but the rear velocity gains more, leading to a larger velocity difference that characterizes stronger contact-line asymmetry and shorter detachment time. Higher oil viscosity suppresses both velocities, narrows the difference, and prolongs detachment. Higher surface tension weakly inhibits motion and prolongs detachment. Increasing wettability heterogeneity enhances the asymmetry in meniscus deformation and the imbalance of capillary pressure between the front and rear interfaces, thereby accelerating detachment. This pore-scale study reveals droplet detachment dynamics, offering a foundation for residual oil mobilization and microfluidic droplet control.

papers.title: A new data-derived wall damping function for the universal velocity profile
papers.abstract: A recently developed mixing length model of the turbulent shear stress in wall-bounded flows has been used to formulate a universal velocity profile (UVP) that is uniformly valid from the wall to the free stream at all Reynolds numbers and accurately approximates pipe, channel, and boundary layer data, including pressure gradients and roughness. In the current formulation, the wall damping function is a van Driest type decaying exponential that depends on two of the five parameters in the model, including a wall damping length scale. While this formulation provides an accurate fit to velocity data, the approximation to Reynolds shear stress and velocity gradient data is not fully satisfactory. A new wall damping function has been developed where simulation data is used to construct the damping function and the two parameters of the original model are replaced by just a damping length scale. The reduction from five to four parameters makes it much easier to find optimal values using a visual search process. In addition, the Reynolds shear stress and velocity gradient data are reproduced more accurately, as is the velocity data. The optimal model parameters vary relatively little with Reynolds number, enabling the data can be well approximated using averaged parameters. The two wake parameters of the UVP are correlated with a modified Clauser pressure gradient parameter, forming the basis of a boundary layer integral method that can be used to rapidly evaluate the viscous drag of aerodynamic shapes at arbitrary Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Multi-frequency fluid–structure response of a parallelogram-section beam with clearance flow and intermittent compression-front formation
papers.abstract: Time-resolved evidence remains limited for flexible sharp-edged bodies involving finite-clearance flow, structural motion, and compressibility effects. This study investigates an idealized cantilevered parallelogram-section beam at freestream Mach numbers of Ma∞=0.27, 0.34, 0.39, and 0.43. Laser vibrometry and 10 000-frame high-speed Schlieren records are combined with edge tracking, coherent-front statistics, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition. Solid-inclusive and flow-only regions are compared to distinguish structural-boundary signatures from clearance-flow fluctuations. The dominant structural-response frequency increases from approximately 435 to 449 Hz, while the band limited root mean square (RMS) displacement increases from 58.6 to 187.1 nm. Between the two highest conditions, the nominal dynamic pressure increases by 18.9%, but the band limited RMS displacement increases by only 2.6%, suggesting an apparent flattening of the response. At Ma∞=0.43, intermittent coherent front candidates occur downstream of the probe, with a maximum occurrence probability of 0.0965 at approximately 42.2 mm downstream. The boundary-associated response also becomes the leading ordinary POD mode, while the clearance-flow variance is distributed over more spatial modes. A component near 2505–2510 Hz persists under all conditions. Its leading spatial pattern is insensitive to the two segment lengths examined, although its modal contribution is segmentation-dependent. Propagation analyses do not identify a simple traveling or standing disturbance. These results distinguish the frequency-resolved structural and clearance-flow signatures in a flexible finite-clearance configuration.

papers.title: Formation and mode transition in swirling liquid jets with low swirl-based Weber number for biomedical cleaning
papers.abstract: This study investigates the morphology and impingement characteristics of a swirling water jet by numerical simulations. The jet Reynolds number ranges from 750 to 6000. Six flow regimes (straight, pulse, spiral, sheet, screw, and splash) are classified and mapped in terms of the azimuthal Weber number (We) and the swirl number (Sw) at the jet exit. The jet morphology transitions from a helical (m=1) spiral mode to a planar sheet mode as Sw increases under low-We conditions. In the planar sheet regime, the m=2 mode becomes energetically dominant. Flows exhibiting dynamic rotation appear when Sw≥0.4, across multiple flow regimes. Using wall shear stress as an indicator of cleaning, the conventional nonswirling jet (straight) produces high shear stress in a ring-shaped region and forms a stagnation point at the center, resulting in a dead zone of cleaning. In contrast, the spiral and sheet regimes eliminate this stagnation point through dynamic macroscopic rotation driven by the m=1 or m=2 modes while maintaining liquid continuity. This dynamic instability generates spatiotemporally modulated wall shear stress, providing a highly effective mechanism for surface cleaning without significant energy dissipation.

papers.title: Modeling electromechanical coupling behaviors of elastic beams for droplet energy harvesting using the smoothed particle hydrodynamics method
papers.abstract: The complex fluid–structure interaction and electromechanical coupling behaviors of piezoelectric beams under droplet impact pose considerable challenges for conventional grid-based numerical methods, particularly when large droplet deformation and beam vibration occur simultaneously. To address these challenges, a fully coupled fluid–structure–electrical numerical framework is developed based on the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) method. The free-surface droplet is modeled using the weakly compressible SPH approach, while the piezoelectric beam is simulated via the total Lagrangian SPH formulation, into which the piezoelectric constitutive relations are incorporated. A boundary-repulsion contact algorithm is adopted to ensure robust momentum transfer at the fluid–solid interface. The proposed model is capable of reproducing key droplet impact behaviors—including spreading, recoiling, rebounding, and splashing—across a wide range of Weber numbers. Systematic parametric investigations reveal that the output voltage scales approximately linearly with impact velocity and droplet diameter within the tested ranges, and that an optimal beam length exists for maximizing energy density. For fixed–fixed beam configurations, a three-part electrode segmentation strategy with a 1:3:1 ratio is proposed to mitigate charge cancelation and significantly enhance the electrical output. This work provides a reliable and effective numerical tool for the performance evaluation and optimal design of droplet-driven piezoelectric energy harvesters.

papers.title: Pressure fluctuation suppression through attenuation and spatial reorganization of the impeller outlet wake in a centrifugal pump with splitter blade
papers.abstract: Pressure fluctuations induced by impeller-volute interaction affect the stable operation of centrifugal pumps. Splitter blades can effectively suppress pressure fluctuations, but how the internal flow modifications induced by splitter blades are transmitted to the pressure response in the volute remains insufficiently understood. In this work, pressure fluctuations of a centrifugal pump equipped with a baseline impeller and a splitter-blade impeller are investigated experimentally and numerically. Under the design condition, the splitter-blade impeller maintains energy performance comparable to that of the baseline impeller. The dominant frequency of pressure fluctuations is the blade passing frequency (BPF) of 169.17 Hz for both impeller configurations. However, the experimental BPF amplitudes of the splitter-blade pump at four monitoring points decrease by 38.28%, 73.50%, 57.56%, and 47.98%, respectively, while the circumferentially averaged p′rms decreases by 39.45%. The splitter blades reduce the load of the long blades in the mid-to-rear chordwise region, thereby decreasing both the circumferential scale and the local velocity difference of the principal continuous low-speed structure. The onset of pronounced attenuation of the principal low-speed structure shifts inward from the normalized radial coordinate s = 0.83 to s = 0.72. Within 0.83 ≤ s ≤ 1, the total area of the residual velocity deficit regions increases only slightly by approximately 2.6%, whereas their mean deficit intensity decreases by 12.0%. The area occupied by the largest connected structure and its dominance within the overall deficit distribution decrease by 40.2% and 41.6%, respectively. Consequently, the residual velocity deficit changes from a concentrated distribution dominated by one large connected structure to a dispersed distribution composed of multiple localized structures. These results show that the splitter blades suppress pressure fluctuations not by simply reducing the total area of the residual velocity deficit but by accelerating the attenuation and spatial reorganization of the principal low-speed structures, which transforms the concentrated outlet wake into weaker and less coherent structures, thereby reducing the periodic interaction between the wake and the volute tongue.

papers.title: Vortex-reconstruction and source-suppression mechanisms of secondary flows in a compressor cascade induced by a bionic ridge fence
papers.abstract: This study develops a parameterized bionic ridge fence inspired by the dorsal ridge structure of the leatherback turtle and investigates its secondary-flow control mechanisms in a highly loaded compressor cascade. The numerical results reveal two distinct mechanisms. At an incidence angle of 0°, the optimal fence was located at 75% chord length from the leading edge (LE) and 12.5% chord from the suction surface, with a height equal to 20.75% of the incoming boundary-layer thickness. The fence generated additional vortices that separated the passage vortex (PV) and concentrated shedding vortex onto opposite sides of the fence and suppressed their spanwise development. Their interaction, premixing, and dissipation disrupted the original large-scale vortices, redistributed them into smaller-scale structures, and reduced cascade total pressure loss by 1.5%. At an incidence angle of 4°, the optimal fence was located at 50% chord length from the LE and 27.5% chord from the suction surface, with a height equal to 10% of the incoming boundary-layer thickness. The fence acted during the incipient stage of PV development by intercepting and redirecting low-momentum end wall fluid. This weakened the transverse adverse pressure gradient and limited the spanwise lift-up of PV, resulting in a 1.3% reduction in cascade total pressure loss. The results demonstrate that the end wall placement and geometric parameters of the bionic ridge fence significantly influence secondary-flow control effectiveness, providing a physical basis and reference for the further development of passive secondary-flow-control strategies in highly loaded compressor cascades.

papers.title: Cooperative regimes and wake–foil interaction mechanisms of tandem flapping-foil energy harvesters in a confined channel
papers.abstract: Energy-harvesting performance and wake–foil interaction mechanisms of two tandem flapping foils operating within a moderately confined channel are investigated numerically. The numerical model solves the two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations on overset grids and is validated against published single-foil ground-effect and tandem-foil benchmark data. A wide parametric range is considered with the streamwise spacing (L* = 2.5–4.5), inter-foil phase difference (Φ = 0°–180°), and non-dimensional flapping frequency (f * = 0.10–0.30). Two favorable operating regimes with different dominant wake–foil interaction signatures are identified where the downstream foil achieves slightly better energy-harvesting performance compared to the upstream foil. In the compact-spacing regime (L* = 2.5, f * = 0.22–0.25, Φ = 0°), the upstream-shed vorticity is transported toward the suction surface of the downstream foil and overlaps with the locally generated leading-edge vorticity region. This interaction coincides with a mid-chord suction hump that contributes to the downstream-foil lift and efficiency. In the anti-phase large-spacing regime (L* = 4.5, Φ = 180°, f * = 0.2), the upstream-wake vortex passes along the vicinity of the downstream-foil surface and produces a localized pressure perturbation, amplifying lift with minimal pitching-power costs. Moreover, the peak cycle-averaged efficiency of both foils consistently exceeds 60% across all cases near the optimal frequency, markedly above the ceiling reported for unbounded configurations. The findings supply mechanistic guidance for the design of compact, near-wall tandem flapping-foil energy converters in rivers, tidal channels, and other confined hydrodynamic environments.

papers.title: Linear stability of porous–fluid–porous systems under transverse crossflow: Modal and non-modal analysis
papers.abstract: The linear stability of plane Poiseuille flow through a porous–fluid–porous (PFP) system subjected to uniform transverse crossflow is investigated by considering anisotropic and inhomogeneous porous media. The fluid region is bounded by porous layers of finite thickness, with equal suction (injection) at the upper (lower) boundary. The base flow is obtained by coupling the Navier–Stokes equations in the fluid layer with the unsteady Darcy model in the porous layers through the Beavers–Joseph interface conditions. Modal and non-modal stability analyses are performed using a Chebyshev spectral collocation method. The modal analysis for the PFP system reveals four distinct instability regimes governed by crossflow intensity. Relative to the permeable-wall case, weak-to-moderate crossflow promotes instability by enhancing disturbance transport across the porous interfaces, while strong crossflow suppresses perturbation growth and stabilizes the flow. Furthermore, increasing anisotropy stabilizes the PFP flow under weak-to-moderate crossflow, while its influence becomes negligible under strong crossflow. In contrast, inhomogeneous porous exhibits a dual influence: it promotes instability under weak-to-moderate crossflow, but stabilizes under strong crossflow regime. Non-modal analysis reveals significant transient energy amplification below the modal critical Reynolds number due to the non-normality of the linear operator. Analyses of optimal perturbations, frequency response, and energy stability further demonstrate the dominance of spanwise disturbances in transient energy amplification and show that substantial disturbance growth can occur even in modally stable flows. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between transverse crossflow and porous-medium properties, offering valuable insights for the design and control of porous-wall flow systems.

papers.title: Size-dependent aerodynamic interference between adjacent bluff bodies: A two-stage generative adversarial network-super-resolution approach
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of wind-induced interference effects in building groups is essential for wind-resistant design, yet traditional approaches based on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) or wind tunnel tests are prohibitively expensive for large-scale parametric investigations. This study presents a deep learning-aided framework for rapid prediction and analysis of high-resolution wind pressure fields, enabling systematic investigation of aerodynamic interference effects between adjacent non-identical square-sectioned bluff bodies. Given building positions and section sizes as inputs, the framework first predicts a pressure-field image at 128 × 64 resolution using a conditional generative adversarial network. A geometry-conditioned super-resolution network then refines this prediction and reconstructs the pressure-field representation at 512 × 256 resolution using the corresponding high-resolution CFD contour as the supervised target. The model was trained on a dataset comprising 12 758 cases covering size ratios from 0.5 to 2.0 and diverse relative building configurations. Parametric analyses reveal that first, upstream interfering buildings can influence downstream structures at separations of up to 20 times the characteristic building dimension, with surface pressure reductions exceeding 70%. Second, side-by-side arrangements produce the strongest interference effects throughout the flow field, whereas tandem configurations with the interfering building located three times the characteristic building dimension downstream exhibit the weakest effects. Third, the size-dependent variation of interfering building is the dominant parameter governing spatiotemporal evolution of vortex shedding, thereby controlling both the intensity and spatial extent of aerodynamic interference. The proposed framework provides an efficient geometry-conditioned surrogate for high-resolution pressure-field image reconstruction and supports the investigation of size-dependent interference trends within building groups.

papers.title: A self-consistent physics-informed neural network paradigm for sloshing analysis
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a physically driven alternative to conventional computational fluid dynamics, yet their application to sloshing remains largely unexplored. This paper establishes a self-consistent PINN paradigm for two-dimensional linear sloshing that trains exclusively on physical residuals, requiring no reference data. The dynamic free-surface boundary condition is enforced as a hard constraint, which removes it from the loss function and structurally eliminates the gradient imbalance that dominates conventional penalization-based formulations. This single modification reduces the free-surface elevation error from above 6% to below 2%. Validation against analytical solutions, experimental measurements, and computational fluid dynamic simulations across sway, roll, and combined excitation modes yields median steady-state amplitude deviations below one millimeter across all benchmarks. A systematic ablation study covering six hyperparameter categories and 13 variants isolates the influence of each design choice and yields practical tuning guidance. Because the paradigm relies entirely on physics residuals, it generalizes naturally to configurations for which analytical reference data are unavailable.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-driven airfoil aerodynamic design via deep surrogate modeling and evolutionary algorithm
papers.abstract: Airfoil aerodynamic design relies on computationally expensive flow solvers, while aerodynamic performance optimization and target pressure distribution inverse design are treated separately. This study develops a framework combining low-dimensional geometric representation, deep surrogate modeling, and evolutionary search for aerodynamic prediction, constrained optimization, and inverse design. A density-guided principal component analysis strategy constructs the airfoil design space, while a fully connected autoencoder provides a compact representation of the surface pressure distribution. A multi-branch residual surrogate network jointly predicts lift coefficient, drag coefficient, and surface pressure coefficient distribution from airfoil geometry, Mach number, and angle of attack; mean absolute errors are 3.765 × 10−3, 1.178 × 10−4, and 1.399 × 10−2, respectively. The surrogate maintains high accuracy for combinations of unseen airfoil geometries and interpolated inflow conditions, demonstrating predictive coverage within the training parameter range. Each inference requires 0.024 ms, and 6 × 104 aerodynamic evaluations are completed in 20.5 s. Coupled with the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, the surrogate supports two constrained design tasks. Aerodynamic-efficiency optimization improves the lift-to-drag ratio in all 20 cases without reducing lift or increasing drag. Target pressure distribution inverse design reconstructs the prescribed suction peak, low-pressure region, and pressure-recovery process. Independent high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics recalculations of 40 optimized airfoils show close agreement with surrogate predictions. Flow-field analyses reveal localized velocity and pressure changes for efficiency-oriented optimization, whereas inverse design produces broader upper-surface acceleration, increased suction, and modified pressure recovery. These results demonstrate an efficient framework linking airfoil geometry, aerodynamic performance, and distributed flow responses.

papers.title: A deep learning-based surrogate model of nonlinear sloshing subjected to random excitations
papers.abstract: Liquid sloshing under external excitation produces strongly nonlinear free-surface motion that is expensive to simulate and difficult to predict over long times with purely data-driven surrogates, which tend to lose stability during recursive rollout. This study presents a deep learning-based surrogate model for nonlinear sloshing subjected to random excitations using a Lagrangian method. The model partitions the dynamics into an explicitly computed response to external forces and an implicitly learned correction for particle interactions, which reduces the learning burden and improves interpretability while enabling fast and stable rollout. In the tested cases, the accumulated error grows approximately linearly at early steps and then stays within a bounded range around 25 mm. The model applies across coupled multi-degree-of-freedom excitation, different tank geometries and dimensions, and varying filling ratios, while preserving the dominant free-surface dynamics. Further analysis traces this stability to the convolution operator, whose kernel is stored on a fixed grid and evaluated by interpolation. This structure constrains the local perturbation response, yielding a narrow distribution of empirical Lipschitz estimates, with only 7% of the states exceeding the neutral value, compared with 47% for an otherwise identical graph-neural-network baseline using a free multilayer-perceptron kernel. It also reduces the disruption caused by topology switching by more than an order of magnitude, from 0.176 to 0.01. The proposed surrogate offers a fast and reliable route to sloshing prediction and provides a useful reference for building particle-level sloshing surrogates in digital-twin applications.

papers.title: Metric-dependent reversal of magnetoviscous response in ferrofluid–biological fluid mixtures
papers.abstract: Biocompatible ferrofluids have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, particularly in magnetic drug targeting, owing to their magnetically controllable rheological properties. However, the evaluation of magnetoviscous effects (MVEs) in complex biological environments, such as blood, remains challenging, especially when baseline viscosities differ significantly between systems. In this study, the MVE of a starch-coated ferrofluid (FluidMAG-D200) diluted in water, sheep blood, pig blood, and sheep plasma was systematically investigated at low shear rates relevant to microvascular flow. To evaluate the magnetoviscous behavior more clearly, we applied a dual-metric evaluation strategy, which combines conventional analysis of relative viscosity change (ΔηR) with a novel approach based on absolute stress increments. The results reveal that the analysis of ΔηR is strongly influenced by the baseline viscosity of the mixtures and may therefore misrepresent the actual magnitude of magnetically induced structuring. In contrast, absolute stress increments analysis provides a more consistent basis for comparison across systems with differing viscosities. Notably, while water-based mixtures exhibit the highest relative changes, blood-based systems—particularly pig blood mixtures—show larger absolute viscosity increases under magnetic fields. These findings highlight the importance of evaluation methodology in interpreting MVE in complex magnetic fluids. Additionally, shear-dependent differences between blood-based systems suggest a possible influence of red blood cells on field-induced microstructural formation, although direct interactions cannot be conclusively determined within the scope of this study.

papers.title: A partitioned state-exchange physics-informed neural network for bidirectionally coupled particle–fluid systems
papers.abstract: Unresolved particle–fluid systems require coupled prediction of fluid motion, particle dynamics, and interphase momentum exchange. We develop bidirectionally coupled physics-informed neural networks (Bi-PINNs) based on partitioned state exchange. F-PINN reconstructs velocity and pressure fields governed by the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with particle feedback, whereas P-PINN predicts particle velocity and recovers trajectories through differentiable time integration. The subnetworks form a closed loop by exchanging the local background-velocity proxy, particle state, and interphase force. Multiscale temporal Fourier encoding and refined collocation sampling in particle near-field and near-wall regions improve the representation of transient and localized disturbances. Faxén parallel-wall drag correction, annular background-velocity sampling, and discretely normalized Gaussian momentum feedback define the force closure for confined low-Reynolds-number transport. Architecture and sampling analyses show that lower physics losses do not necessarily imply greater predictive accuracy and that balanced regional sampling improves multivariable reconstruction. Verification against computational fluid dynamics solutions based on the same governing equations and closure model shows close agreement for the bulk flow, particle-induced disturbance, particle Reynolds number, and trajectory over 0–1 s. Across six independently trained cases, with the inlet centerline-to-initial-particle velocity ratio α ranging from 0.85 to 1.15, the mean terminal-trajectory relative error is 1.34%, with a maximum of 2.79%. The case-wise L2 relative errors in streamwise velocity and pressure range from 3.52 × 10−4 to 4.64 × 10−2 and from 3.42 × 10−3 to 1.18 × 10−2, respectively. These results demonstrate that the Bi-PINNs framework accurately reconstructs coupled particle–fluid dynamics without labeled data during optimization.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation of oblique backward jet-induced transition over a hypersonic sharp cone
papers.abstract: Direct numerical simulations investigate boundary-layer transition over a Mach-6 sharp cone with annular oblique injection from a backward-facing step. The baseline jet-off condition, weak-jet condition (J=0.168), and strong-jet condition (J=0.5) reveal distinct pathways linking disturbance generation to near-wall response. Comparisons of disturbance frequencies, wavelengths, and wall-normal amplitude profiles with local linear-stability theory support a second-mode-dominated baseline route. Jet injection produces early broadband fluctuations and three-dimensional shear-layer structures characteristic of a separation-mediated bypass-like route. By combining mean reattachment, velocity intermittency, pressure spectra, and sustained wall responses, the analysis distinguishes successive stages of transition. A counterintuitive finding is that transition occurs later under the strong-jet condition than under the weak-jet condition, despite the stronger outer disturbances. The downstream shift is more pronounced for the sustained near-wall response than for the establishment of the turbulent near-wall state. Explicit wall-normal projections of turbulent kinetic energy fluxes associate the earlier sustained near-wall response under the weak-jet condition with earlier wall-directed transport, while the strong-jet condition retains an elevated outer disturbance region farther downstream. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition further characterizes frequency-dependent velocity structures and leading-mode differences with bootstrap uncertainty estimates. Together, these diagnostics identify the downstream coupling between the separated shear layer and the near-wall region as the physical connection between annular injection, transition development, and wall response.

papers.title: Inter-row forcing of cavitation–vortex coupling and vorticity transport in contra-rotating cavitating flow
papers.abstract: This study investigates the unsteady cavitating flow within a contra-rotating two-blade-row configuration to elucidate how strong inter-row wake forcing modulates cavitation–vortex interactions and vorticity transport. A delayed detached eddy simulation framework coupled with a bubble–bubble interaction cavitation model is employed to resolve the phase-dependent evolution of vapor structures, tip vortices, and vorticity source terms. Three representative cavitation numbers, σ = 2.05, 1.09, and 0.71, are analyzed using the relative blade-passing period as the reference timescale. As the cavitation number decreases, vapor accumulation within the clearance shear layer modifies the transverse pressure-gradient forcing and promotes a coherent-to-merged transition between the tip-leakage-vortex (TLV) and tip-separation-vortex cavities in the upstream blade row. Under severe cavitation, pressure reversal near the trailing edge drives cavity shedding and entrains a secondary tip-leakage vortex into a perpendicular cavitating vortex. In the downstream blade row, inter-row wake interference produces circumferentially non-uniform cavitation, local bubble collapse, and severe fragmentation of coherent TLV tubes. The circumferential vorticity budget reveals two distinct pathways. In the upstream row, vortex evolution is governed by intra-passage phase change, where stretching and dilatation jointly control leakage-vortex deformation and reorganization. In the downstream row, inter-row shear and vapor blockage re-organize the stretching and Coriolis-force contributions, thereby promoting vortex breakdown, while bubble collapse enhances the positive dilatation contribution. These results clarify how phase change, shear-layer distortion, and rotating-frame source terms jointly govern cavitating vortex breakdown in confined rotating flows.

papers.title: Post-impact nanodroplets exhibit effective single-exponential relaxation over finite-amplitude displacements
papers.abstract: We use molecular-dynamics simulations in three dimensions and quasi-two dimensions to examine the post-impact relaxation of nanodroplets over a broad range of Weber numbers. After maximum spreading, we show that the contact radius can be summarized by a translated single exponential in the displacement from equilibrium u(t)=R(t)−Req. A two-exponential alternative and a stretched-exponential form are tested explicitly, and neither yields a resolved improvement once the serial correlation of the fit residuals is accounted for. In the present homogeneous, defect-free molecular model, this effective description remains useful over finite-amplitude displacements reaching u/Req≃0.54 at the start of the fitted branch, and the corresponding spreading maximum is u/Req≃0.57. The effective return times fluctuate non-monotonically with We. Relative to the advancing spontaneous-wetting reference, the return is slower on average. Zero-impact wetting and dewetting controls show no resolvable dependence on the direction of contact-line motion, which makes an explanation by advancing–receding asymmetry unlikely, although these controls use a different preparation protocol from the reference and therefore cannot exclude it.

papers.title: Nonunique pore-scale responses of co-current spontaneous imbibition under equivalent macroscopic capillary driving: A quasi three-dimensional lattice Boltzmann study
papers.abstract: Spontaneous imbibition is an important process in many subsurface multiphase-flow applications, yet the pore-scale mechanisms of co-current spontaneous imbibition remain incompletely understood. We employ a quasi three-dimensional (3D) color-gradient multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann method to simulate co-current spontaneous imbibition in regular and complex porous media over a range of viscosity ratios M defined as μnw/μw (nonwetting/wetting). Interfacial tension and contact angle are varied in combinations that maintain a constant σ cos θ. Results show that the final recovery factor varies nonmonotonically with the σ–θ combination, and the ranking of the three cases changes with viscosity ratio and pore structure. Mirzaei time scaling collapses the recovery trajectories onto a common kinetic trend during the main front-propagation stage, and the kinetic similarity does not imply equivalent final states. As the viscosity ratio increases, the displacement front shifts from relatively continuous lateral sweep to selective channel advance. Pore structure further controls branch competition, bypassing, and the distribution of residual nonwetting phase. A Saffman–Taylor-based linear stability interpretation indicates that higher interfacial tension suppresses short-wavelength perturbations, although the resulting displacement pattern remains jointly controlled by wettability and pore accessibility. Analyses of capillary pressure and fluid–fluid interfacial area further show that the in-plane curvature response and interfacial topology remain nonunique even at identical σ cos θ. These findings define the applicability limits of equivalent macroscopic capillary driving and provide a mechanistic basis for structure-specific selection of interfacial parameters and improved continuum-scale closure models.

papers.title: Jet-driven depressurization and thermal homogenization in cryogenic propellant tanks: A multi-scale experimental and numerical study
papers.abstract: Despite extensive studies on spray-bar thermodynamic venting system, the coupled effects of jet axial distribution, circulation flow rate, and subcooling on the dynamic interplay between depressurization and thermal homogenization under partial-fill conditions remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the competition between condensation-driven and mixing-driven mechanisms. An experimental and numerical study is conducted to investigate the two-phase flow dynamics and associated thermal-hydraulic behaviors during jet-induced mixing, depressurization, and temperature homogenization in a cryogenic tank. A numerical framework is established using the volume-of-fluid method combined with the shear stress transport k–ω turbulence model to resolve the interfacial two-phase flow and transport processes. The Eulerian–Lagrangian approach is adopted to track the jet droplet trajectories and to account for droplet–vapor, droplet–droplet, and droplet–wall interactions in the two-phase system. A series of parametric jetting experiments is performed to measure the transient pressure and temperature responses. High-speed flow visualization is used to record the jet-induced two-phase flow structures inside the tank. The model is validated against experimental data. The effects of axial jet distribution, jet flow rate, and jet subcooling on the flow development, depressurization, and thermal homogenization are examined. It is found that jet injection within the vapor-phase zone enhances interfacial mass exchange and improves depressurization efficiency. The thermal field near the tank wall is strongly affected by jet parameters. Higher jet flow rates and temperatures promote vapor-phase condensation, thereby accelerating the pressure decay. This work improves the physical understanding of jet-driven two-phase flow and transport in cryogenic storage systems.

papers.title: Learning periodic shear flow dynamics via physically aligned generative flow model
papers.abstract: The modeling of complex spatiotemporal dynamics has been extensively investigated across diverse physical systems due to its critical role in understanding and predicting time-dependent physical behavior. While several previous studies have shown promising results in addressing the inherent limitations of transient modeling, significant challenges remain in accurately predicting condition-dependent state transitions and controlling accumulated errors. In this study, we propose a deep learning approach for efficient and stable modeling of complex spatiotemporal dynamics. Specifically, the proposed framework aligns the generative process of flow matching with physical temporal evolution, thereby enabling direct modeling of state transitions. Both quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior generative performance, showing improvements of up to 86% in variance-scaled root mean squared error and 46% in structural similarity index measure compared to baseline models. Moreover, we highlight the computational advantage of the proposed framework, achieving high predictive performance while requiring 8–49 times less inference time than the baseline models. The proposed approach not only enables accurate and stable long-horizon generation but also provides a promising framework for efficient modeling of complex spatiotemporal dynamics.

papers.title: Oscillatory dynamics of three-dimensional rigid particles in unsteady Stokes and linear viscoelastic fluids
papers.abstract: We present a numerical study of oscillating three-dimensional rigid particles in both linear viscoelastic and viscous Newtonian fluids. Based on the correspondence principle between unsteady Stokes flow and linear viscoelastic fluids, we establish a unified integral formulation in the frequency domain, which is solved using an accurate boundary integral method. For prescribed oscillatory particle motions, we compute the normal and shear stresses on the particle surfaces, as well as the flow fields in their vicinity. Both axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric motions are investigated for a pair of rigid particles. The flow characteristics are examined under various conditions, including different Weissenberg and frequency numbers, particle separation distances, and particle sizes, highlighting the complexity of stress distributions on the particle surfaces. We observe that the shape of the stress profiles remains unchanged in the case of unsteady Stokes flow as the oscillation frequency changes, whereas in the case of viscoelastic flow, the behavior is quite nonlinear. Traces of swirling motions are observed in the velocity fields near the particles. Remarkably, in three-dimensional flows, we find that for a fixed polar angle, the normal and shear stresses on spherical particle surfaces are proportional to the cosine of the azimuthal angle in spherical coordinates.

papers.title: Dual-cavity-based supersonic combustion stabilization and enhancement actuated by gliding-arc plasma
papers.abstract: In view of the instability characteristics of self-sustained combustion in a Ma 2.5 dual-cavity supersonic combustor, an active control technique based on gliding-arc plasma assistance is used to suppress combustion oscillations. Through analyzing flame spontaneous emissions, Schlieren images, wall pressure taps, and OpenFOAM-based three-dimensional simulations, the flame development characteristics and plasma-assisted combustion (PAC) mechanisms are analyzed. It is found that the gliding-arc plasma continuous assistance at the bottom of the rear cavity forms a stable global flame more rapidly, improving the flame distribution and enhancing the flame spontaneous emission by 10%–24%. In contrast, the enhancement of the gliding-arc plasma assistance in the front cavity ranges from 4% to 14%, with a longer delay time in forming stable combustion.
