The flow mechanism of PAC lies in increasing the turbulence intensity and heat release in local regions within cavities. Thus, the interaction between the mainstream flame and the hot flow is facilitated continuously by the plasma, forming stable resident flames in the vicinity of cavities. During the plasma action, excited species such as N2(C3Πu) and O(1D) act on the local plasma region through thermal and kinetic effects, inducing the continuous formation of initial flames and heat release for temperature rise. Meanwhile, excited species with longer relaxation time, such as N2(v1) and N2(v2), are transported into the mainstream region. Outside the plasma-actuated region, these long-life excited species do not directly engage in the dominant heat-release reactions, but catalytically facilitating the redox reactions via transport effects and kinetic effects, thereby achieving combustion stabilization and enhancement.

papers.title: Experimental deep reinforcement learning control of lift-to-drag optimization on NACA 0015 airfoil using dual synthetic jet
papers.abstract: Dual synthetic jet actuators (DSJAs) offer a promising approach for improving the aerodynamic performance of wind turbine blades, yet effective closed-loop control in physical environments remains challenging. This study improves the NACA 0015 airfoil performance by the DSJA array control of an agent trained through the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) wind tunnel platform (DRLinWT). First, the DSJA is designed, and the location of 12%c from the leading edge is used to train the agent for DSJA array control. An experience-based specialist-to-generalist training strategy is then introduced to improve data reuse and support stable training under multi-wind-velocity conditions. The trained generalist agent can modulate the control voltage of the DSJA array according to the incoming wind velocities, increasing the lift-to-drag ratio by as large as 192.1%. Results show that the improvement of the lift-to-drag ratio by the DSJA array control of the agent is clearly related to the momentum coefficient. When the momentum coefficient is sufficient, the DSJA array can delay large-scale separation and, hence, improve the leading-edge suction, thereby increasing the lift on the airfoil model.

papers.title: Crossflow-induced port reversal and thermal plume interaction in a non-uniform rosette multi-port diffuser
papers.abstract: A non-uniform rosette multi-port diffuser with large thin-walled rectangular side openings provides a flow configuration in which internal riser flow, port-level exchange, and external buoyant plumes are coupled under crossflow. This study combines laboratory observations with validated three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations to investigate buoyant thermal jets discharged from this diffuser under quiescent, moderate-crossflow, and strong-crossflow conditions. The results show that increasing ambient velocity ratio changes the outlet condition from geometry-induced non-uniform discharge to crossflow-controlled redistribution. Under strong crossflow, ambient water intrudes into the riser through the upstream port, producing port-level flow reversal and redirecting the supplied discharge mainly toward the side ports and downstream port. The resulting outlet velocity and temperature fields control the external plume evolution, leading to port-dependent deflection, plume merging and shielding, wake-influenced transport, and lateral thermal core displacement. The thermal impact volume follows a power-law dependence on temperature-rise threshold, while the inclusion of ambient velocity ratio improves the scaling for crossflow cases. These findings demonstrate that the thermal field is governed by coupled internal–external adjustments, rather than by crossflow deflection of independent jets.

papers.title: Scale similarity of sediment concentration in pressurized pipelines under complex terrain conditions
papers.abstract: Sediment deposition in pressurized pipelines under complex terrain conditions poses a serious threat to the safe operation of engineering systems. This study employed a combination of physical model tests and numerical simulations to examine the influence of geometric scale on sediment concentration and deposition characteristics in the descending, horizontal, and ascending sections of the pipeline. The results indicate that the radial sediment concentration decreased by more than 84% in the range of 0 < y/D < 0.3 except for the 1:2 scale. In the descending section, the scale similarity on sediment concentration is primarily controlled by the slope angle, and the scale effect becomes less pronounced with gentler slopes. In the horizontal section, the sediment concentration near the pipe bottom is positively correlated with the geometric scale, and the scale effect is more significant in shorter horizontal sections because of the stronger disturbance induced by the elbow flow field. In the ascending section, the scale effect is jointly governed by the inverted siphon size and elevation difference. At the 1:5 scale, the most severe deposition occurs in the ascending section with a relatively small elevation difference. Both sediment discharge and sediment deposition decrease exponentially with increasing geometric scale.

papers.title: Mechanistic and statistical study of two-phase flow instability in a heat removal pipeline under rolling motion
papers.abstract: Passive residual heat removal systems are influenced by oscillatory inertial forces under marine conditions, making two-phase flow instability more complex than under static conditions. In this study, visualization experiments were conducted to investigate two-phase flow instability in a residual heat removal pipeline under different rolling frequencies and amplitudes. Four instability modes were identified based on their initiation locations and interfacial evolution: cold-side instability, solitary-wave impact instability, global interfacial instability, and vapor-side impact instability. Within the tested conditions, rolling frequency more strongly affected instability transition than amplitude, which mainly affected instability intensity and mode diversity. At the representative condition of 0.3 Hz and 3°, the rolling period was comparable to the characteristic thermal-hydraulic response time, and pronounced phase-locking was observed, with concentrated instability triggering dominated by Mode IV. At this condition, the event count increased by approximately 27% relative to 0.1 Hz, and all recorded peak pressures remained below 1 MPa. At higher rolling frequencies, stronger inertial effects promoted multi-mode instability and complex interfacial evolution. Together, these results identified three response regions characterized by condensation-dominated instability, gravity-constrained synchronized response, and inertia-enhanced multi-mode instability. Non-inertial-frame analysis identified the Coriolis acceleration as the dominant rolling-induced component and quantified the increasing modulation of the pipe-normal effective acceleration, supporting the proposed response-region interpretation.

papers.title: A viscosity-adaptive valveless piezoelectric pump for in vitro debridement
papers.abstract: Valveless piezoelectric pumps offer a compact structure, fast response, and flexible flow regulation, showing promise for portable wound irrigation and debridement devices. However, their viscosity adaptability and debridement performance have rarely been evaluated together, limiting practical application. This study proposes a viscosity-adaptive valveless piezoelectric pump for in vitro wound debridement and compares its performance with a commonly used peristaltic pump. When viscosity increased from 1.0 to 19.0 mPa s, the flow attenuation rate of the piezoelectric pump was 22.7%, lower than the 34.0% of the peristaltic pump. An in vitro cleaning platform consisting of an agar substrate and a carboxymethyl cellulose sodium/activated-carbon-simulated adhesive contamination layer was further established to compare the two pumps at identical average flow rates. Quantitative image analysis showed that the piezoelectric pump consistently achieved lower residual contaminant area ratios at 90, 110, and 130 ml/min. At 110 ml/min, the residual ratios were 1.249% and 5.387% for the piezoelectric and peristaltic pumps, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed pump maintains relatively stable flow under varying viscosities and provides effective contaminant removal under simulated wound-irrigation conditions, highlighting its potential for clinical wound-irrigation devices.

papers.title: Evolution characteristics of thermal fluid after submillisecond pulsed discharge in water
papers.abstract: During submillisecond pulsed discharge in water, local Joule heating produces liquid-phase disturbance, including thermal fluid with appreciable motion. However, the post-pulse evolution of the primary thermal fluid (PTF) and its governing mechanisms remain insufficiently quantified. This study combines high-speed Schlieren imaging with a two-dimensional axisymmetric model coupling current conduction, laminar flow, and heat transfer with temperature-dependent water properties; the measured gap-voltage waveform is imposed as the electrical input. The model is validated against published thermal-fluid velocity and temperature data, with a 4.96% difference in peak axial velocity and a maximum temperature deviation of 1.03 °C. The results identify two stages of PTF evolution. During energy deposition, Joule heating and electric forces establish nonuniform temperature, pressure, and velocity fields. After the pulse, the established pressure gradient and fluid inertia sustain PTF expansion, while heat conduction, viscous dissipation, and momentum exchange progressively weaken the internal disturbance. From 1 to 10 ms, the equivalent PTF volume increases approximately linearly, and its growth rate shows an approximately linear positive correlation with cumulative Joule heating energy density near the pin tip over the investigated voltage range. The negative polarity PTF exhibits stronger internal temperature gradients and disturbances, consistent with more concentrated local Joule heating associated with interfacial charge transfer and current-density distributions near the pin tip. These findings establish quantitative links between energy deposition, polarity, and post-pulse PTF evolution, providing a physical basis for regulating pre-breakdown thermal-fluid behavior in underwater pulsed-discharge systems.

papers.title: SiO2/epoxy superamphiphobic inner-tubing coatings for gas-lift deliquification: Interfacial regulation of water and crude-oil droplet transport and near-wall retention
papers.abstract: Gas-lift deliquification in multiphase wells can be hindered by wall-adhered droplets and persistent liquid films, increasing hydraulic resistance and reducing liquid transport. Here, a SiO2/epoxy superamphiphobic coating was developed to regulate the phase-specific near-wall transport of water and crude-oil droplets under upward gas flow. PFOTS 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyltrichlorosilane (PFOTS) reduced surface energy, while 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane (KH-560) promoted interfacial coupling between SiO2 particles and the epoxy matrix, producing a hierarchical fluorinated surface. The coating exhibited static contact angles of 155° for water and 153° for crude oil, with contact-angle hysteresis below 9°. Experimentally measured advancing and receding contact angles were incorporated into the level set wall-wetting condition to represent macroscopic contact-angle hysteresis. Shear-rate-dependent constitutive models were further introduced for heavy and extra-heavy crude oils to account for non-Newtonian rheology. Simulations showed that the normalized near-wall migration metric for water increased from 1.22% on bare steel to 1.87% on the coated surface, while the recalculated values for heavy and extra-heavy crude oils were 0.98% and 0.81%, respectively. The results indicate that reduced interfacial retention promotes droplet migration, whereas shear-rate-dependent rheological resistance becomes increasingly important in high-viscosity oils. These findings highlight the coupled roles of wall wettability and liquid rheology in near-wall droplet transport. Simultaneous oil–water coexistence, competitive wetting, and emulsification remain outside the present scope.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation of power and wake responses of a tidal stream turbine under prescribed floating-platform motions
papers.abstract: Platform-induced motions can modify rotor loading and wake development in floating tidal-stream turbines, yet the individual roles of different motion components are difficult to isolate in fully coupled wave–current–platform systems. This study formulates a prescribed-motion problem in uniform inflow to examine the effects of surge, heave, pitch, and coupled surge–heave–pitch motions on the power and wake responses of a tidal stream turbine. A large-eddy simulation framework combined with a dynamic actuator line model is used to resolve rotor performance and wake structures. Under the investigated motion conditions, surge dominates rotor-performance unsteadiness, reducing the mean power and thrust coefficients by approximately 7.6% and 8.9%, respectively, relative to the static baseline, while producing pronounced low-frequency fluctuations in both quantities. Blade-resolved analysis indicates that this reduction is associated with repeated large angle-of-attack excursions over the inner blade span and a decrease in the time-averaged lift coefficient, whereas the drag increase remains limited. In contrast, isolated heave and pitch produce weak variations in rotor performance. The wake response shows a different motion dependence. Surge maintains a narrower wake with a larger local peak velocity deficit and earlier loss of organized tip-vortex coherence, whereas heave contributes more strongly to wake-center displacement, wake unsteadiness, and wake spreading. The coupled case retains performance fluctuations closely resembling those of the isolated-surge case, while exhibiting wake-transport features closer to the heave-dominated response. These findings provide a controlled reference for interpreting motion-component effects.

papers.title: Finite-time relaxation of inertial particle clustering in non-equilibrium turbulence
papers.abstract: Inertial particles in turbulence form clusters, which strongly affect particle collisions and transport properties. Clustering models based on statistically stationary turbulence implicitly assume the instantaneous-equilibrium approximation when applied to time-varying non-equilibrium turbulence. However, the validity of this approximation remains unclear. In this study, the temporal response of inertial particle clustering in non-equilibrium turbulence was investigated using direct numerical simulation of homogeneous isotropic turbulence with unsteady forcing. Periodic responses of the flow and clustering intensity were evaluated by varying the forcing period. The flow showed non-equilibrium dissipation scaling for all forcing periods. The relationship between instantaneous energy dissipation rate and clustering intensity showed hysteresis exceeding statistically stationary fluctuations when the forcing period exceeded several large-eddy turnover times. For the particles with the largest inertia, clustering intensity took values of 0.80 and 1.56 times the reference value at the same instantaneous energy dissipation rate. This demonstrates that the instantaneous-equilibrium approximation is not appropriate under such conditions. A linear relaxation model was constructed from transient responses, in which clustering intensity approaches the instantaneous-equilibrium value with a finite relaxation time. The relaxation time scaling was identified as τg=1.0Te(t) St(t)0.40, where Te(t) and St(t) are the instantaneous large-eddy turnover time and Stokes number. The model reduced the maximum relative error from 49% to 10% for the particles with the largest inertia and from 76% to 22% in an independent validation case. These results demonstrate that finite-time relaxation improves prediction accuracy for clustering intensity in the non-equilibrium turbulence considered here.

papers.title: A data-driven approach for morphological characterization and classification of flying inkjet droplets
papers.abstract: We present a data-driven framework for the characterization of flying inkjet droplets based on a compact parametric representation of droplet contours. Starting from a large image database of experimentally generated droplets, the outer contours are extracted and described using elliptic Fourier descriptors, providing an accurate and low-dimensional representation of a wide range of droplet morphologies. The resulting contour coefficients are analyzed to identify a reduced set of characteristic droplet shapes, which are organized into representative morphological families capturing the dominant features observed in the dataset. The Fourier decomposition reveals a natural separation of geometric scales, with low-order modes describing the primary droplet geometry and higher-order modes capturing finer perturbations associated with tail deformation and capillary effects. Building on this representation, a set of physically interpretable morphological fingerprints is introduced, including modal areas, modal orientations, and deformation metrics derived from the Fourier modes. These quantities provide a further reduction of the contour description into a compact morphological parameter space while retaining the principal geometric characteristics of the droplets. Within this reduced space, a distance-based compatibility analysis is used to compare new observations with the representative families, enabling the classification and reconstruction of droplet shapes from a limited number of reference contours. The proposed methodology offers a robust and interpretable framework for reducing, organizing, and analyzing complex droplet morphologies, with potential applications to the study of droplet breakup, satellite formation, and process monitoring in inkjet printing.

papers.title: Clustering dynamics of floating particles on Faraday waves in a brimful rectangular container
papers.abstract: Faraday-wave-assisted particle assembly provides a contact-free, bottom-up route for interfacial manipulation, with broad applications in biofabrication and particulate transport. Existing studies, however, often rely on oversimplified sinusoidal wave representations that conflict with brimful edge constraints and predict only the final clustering position without resolving the full migration process or its parametric dependence. Here, a boundary-consistent framework is developed for floating particles clustering on Faraday waves in a brimful rectangular container. The three-dimensional Faraday wave field with pinned contact lines is obtained by solving the corresponding generalized eigenvalue problem via the Rayleigh–Ritz method and is then coupled with the Maxey–Riley–Gatignol-type equations for a finite-size floater to determine equilibrium clustering locations and time-resolved migration trajectories. The predicted wave field agrees with experiments more closely than prior simplified sinusoidal models, with improved accuracy in the wave frequency. The model is validated against dedicated experiments on Faraday-wave-driven particle assembly, followed by a parametric study on the clustering regime and distinct migration trajectories. The results demonstrate that clustering behavior is governed by the static flotation–capillarity–inertia balance rather than by hydrophilicity alone. The clustering efficiency is found to depend strongly on wave amplitude and particle radius, with an approximately optimal particle-size range that minimizes the assembly time. The framework provides a theoretical basis for arranging objects at prescribed interfacial locations and for forecasting the accumulation pathways of floating debris and microplastics under wave forcing.

papers.title: Staged compression and pneumatic buffering in a tandem-disk aerospike at Mach 2.23
papers.abstract: The interaction between a supersonic freestream and a multi-stage aerospike induces complex shock/shear-layer coupling across sequential recirculating cavities. This study maps the steady-state topological regimes of a tandem-disk (Double Disk) aerospike mounted on a hemisphere-cylinder blunt body at Mach 2.23, using a compressible Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes framework closed by the k-omega shear stress transport model and validated against benchmark experiments. Three regimes are identified and mechanistically quantified through mean-field diagnostics: cavity pressure, shear-layer momentum thickness, and convective Mach number. Below a radial threshold (r2/r1 < 2.0), the secondary shock merges with the terminal reattachment system (Regime I); crossing the threshold pressurizes the primary cavity from P/P∞ ≈ 1.05 to ≈1.6 and decouples the intermediate shock. A forward-biased secondary disk (l2/l1 = 2.0) then traps a compressed vortex (P/P∞ ≈ 1.95) that acts as a pneumatic buffer registered as a monotonically intensifying thrust on the primary-disk back face and restructures the single normal-shock compression into a staged pressure staircase (Regime II). Extending the spike beyond L/D (L:Length of Spike & D: Hemispherical Body Diameter) of 1.0 collapses this buffer: with the convective Mach number above unity at both lengths, shear-layer growth is compressibility-suppressed, and breakdown arises from accumulated growth over the doubled residence length, evidenced by a reversal of the momentum-thickness trajectory (0.668 → 0.551 mm vs 0.613 → 0.733 mm) and buffer decompression (Regime III). In full three-dimensional simulations, the optimal configuration reduces payload drag by 82.8% relative to the bare blunt body (42.8% vs a single aerospike) and net-assembly drag by 46.7%, while suppressing the integrated payload thermal load by 9.1% relative to a single aerospike and demonstrating a load-shifting mechanism that trades sacrificial disk compression and a spatially concentrated heating footprint for superior overall payload protection.

papers.title: Prediction of Reynolds and stokes number behavior of particle-laden turbulent flows using artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: A hybrid machine learning framework is proposed, demonstrated, and assessed for the prediction of inertial particle dynamics in turbulent channel flows. The approach couples a feed-forward artificial neural network, trained on direct numerical simulation (DNS) and Lagrangian particle tracking (LPT) data, with a stochastic Gaussian noise model to reconstruct particle trajectories leading to the prediction of both the mean and fluctuating particle velocity fields. The model extends prior work by incorporating lagged particle velocities, as well as local particle concentrations and concentration gradients, to capture inertial memory effects and by introducing a novel wall-normal-dependent noise generation method to reproduce spatially varying turbulence intensity. The training dataset spans two Reynolds numbers (Reτ=180 and 300), three particle diameters (dP*=0.0025, 0.005, and 0.0075), and three density ratios (ρP*=2.5, 1111.0, and 2041.0), covering a broad range of Stokes numbers (St+=0.028 → 574.03). The hybrid model reproduces the correct qualitative trends for key turbulent transport features, including inertial lag, turbophoresis, and enhanced near-wall velocities for inertial particles, and recovers root-mean-square velocity fluctuations well, particularly for high Stokes number particles. Visual comparisons of particle trajectories further confirm the model's ability to capture large-scale dynamics across particle-laden flow regimes. Validation against DNS-LPT shows good agreement for both first- and second-order statistics. A held-out test at a Reynolds number absent from the training data confirms that the model interpolates across the Reynolds-number range. The framework performs consistently across the range of particle and flow parameters studied and provides a computationally efficient alternative to full-resolution simulations for modeling particle-laden turbulent flows.

papers.title: Experimental and kinetic study of water mist and inert gas inhibitions of premixed hydrogen/air explosions
papers.abstract: Investigating hydrogen explosion inhibition is necessary to ensure the safe utilization of hydrogen fuel energy. The effects of single inhibitors (water mist, N2, and CO2) and the combined water mist with N2 or CO2 on hydrogen/air explosions were investigated using a 21 l semi-confined tube and a reaction kinetics model. The results show that increasing the equivalence ratio from 0.55 to 0.65 and 0.75 under pure hydrogen explosion conditions decreases thermo-diffusive instability (TDI) and inhibits the development of flame wrinkles and cellular structures on the flame front. In contrast, the combined inhibitors enhance TDI and promote the development of cellular structures and flame wrinkling. Compared with the single inhibitors, the combined inhibitors significantly attenuate the hydrogen/air explosion intensity, with the maximum overpressure reduced by 60.5%. The combined inhibitor of water mist + CO2 exhibits higher inhibition performance on the explosion than the combined water mist + N2. Based on the reaction kinetics analysis, the combined inhibitors reduce the rates of multiple elementary reactions in hydrogen/air explosions. As a result, under the water mist + CO2 and water mist + N2 conditions, the total active radical mole fraction [H + O + OH] decreases by 61.8% and 52.6%, respectively. This reduces the laminar flame speed and net heat production of hydrogen explosions.

papers.title: Retraction: “Corrugated airfoils for enhanced low-speed aerodynamics: A bio-inspired review” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 085120 (2025)]
Flow-induced vibrations of a freely oscillating square cylinder in tandem arrangement with a stationary cylinder at low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: The study delivers a detailed analysis of tandem square cylinders by directly bridging these identified gaps to investigate flow-induced vibrations of two tandem square cylinders at a spacing ratio of S/D=5.5 at Reynolds numbers of 100 and 200. First, the vibrations are isolated into two distinct scenarios [case 1—upstream cylinder (UC) free/downstream cylinder (DC) stationary, and case 2—UC stationary/DC free] at a fixed mass ratio of m*=10 and a damping ratio of zero. In case 1, the UC's response amplitude is amplified by roughly three times compared to the single cylinder. It is well documented that an isolated square cylinder at Re=200 is highly susceptible to galloping. However, in the present tandem configuration, i.e., case 1, the physical presence of the stationary DC fundamentally disrupts the wake conditions necessary for this instability, thereby completely suppressing the galloping of the UC. Conversely, in case 2, the presence of the stationary UC significantly delays the onset of galloping in the DC. In both configurations, wake mode transitions strictly coincide with the vortex force becoming anti-phase.

papers.title: Thermal-radiation effects on buoyancy-driven puffing and turbulence statistics in methane pool fires: A large-eddy simulation study
papers.abstract: Buoyancy-driven puffing is a characteristic global hydrodynamic instability of pool fires, but the influence of thermal radiation on the puffing frequency and associated thermal and turbulence statistics remains unclear. Large-eddy simulations are performed for methane pool fires with diameters D = 0.10, 0.30, and 0.50 m, with and without gas radiation represented by the weighted-sum-of-gray-gases model. From consistently processed 10–60 s records, radiation changes the dominant puffing frequency at zD = 1 by no more than 4.7%, and the buoyancy Strouhal numbers of all six simulations remain within 0.44–0.49. In contrast, the peak excess temperature and vertical velocity decrease by 6%–13% and 7%–12%, respectively, while kres and Trms decrease by 12%–22% and 14%–20%. The positive centerline integral of w′T′ over the common probe interval z = 0.05–0.80 m decreases by 15%–28%, indicating weaker vertical turbulent transport of sensible heat. The heightwise maxima of a hydrostatic baroclinic-vorticity-generation proxy and the mean spanwise vorticity change by only 0%–4%. The results indicate a separation between frequency selection and amplitude response: over the present regime, source diameter and gravity continue to set the leading vortex formation and shedding timescale, whereas radiative cooling weakens temperature and density fluctuations, buoyant turbulent transport, and second-order turbulence statistics.

papers.title: Mechanism of cavitation suppression in rotating flows: Modulating vapor evolution via vortex design method
papers.abstract: As a crucial energy equipment, the highly efficient and stable comprehensive hydraulic performance of the mixed-flow pump has made it a focal point of research in the field of fluid engineering. However, cavitation is easily induced due to the complex multi-scenario operating environments, while the complexity of rotating turbulence can exacerbate the cavitation instability. Consequently, a vortex design method based on the potential flow function theory is developed to achieve mesoscale modulation of cavitation inside mixed-flow pumps. Based on current high-precision numerical simulations, primary conclusions are drawn as follows: vortex design strategy significantly enhances the anti-cavitation performance of the pump: compared with the original impeller, the critical net positive suction head for scheme 2 (S2) impeller under the forced vortex design and scheme 3 (S3) impeller under the compound vortex design decreased by 0.33 and 0.47 m, respectively. From the perspective of flow control mechanisms, the decreased blade curvature of S2 effectively reduces the low-pressure region on the suction side, suppressing the disturbance mechanism of vapor on the mainstream and the cavitation development. Furthermore, S3 optimizes the blade leading edge profile and reconstructs the local pressure gradient, not only significantly decelerating the cavitation growth, but also effectively attenuating the turbulent energy dissipation induced by cavitation.

papers.title: Nibbling versus engulfment in a high-speed turbulent boundary layer
papers.abstract: Entrainment in a Mach 4.5 turbulent boundary layer is investigated using direct numerical simulations and a Lagrangian analysis framework. A mass-conservation-based formulation is employed to decompose the total entrained mass flow rate into contributions from nibbling, associated with diffusion and generation of vorticity across the turbulent/non-turbulent interface, and engulfment, associated with the incorporation of irrotational fluid pockets into the turbulent region. While engulfment accounts for the larger fraction of entrainment in both adiabatic and cold-wall cases, nibbling is found to contribute significantly. The relative importance of nibbling increases in the cold-wall case due to enhanced viscous effects associated with steeper velocity and vorticity gradients in the thinner boundary layer. These findings indicate that entrainment in high-speed turbulent boundary layers is governed by a combination of large-scale and small-scale processes, and that the dominance of engulfment is less pronounced than traditionally assumed.

papers.title: Multi-scale wake dynamics around a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 64-618 airfoil at various angles of attack
papers.abstract: This study examines the effect of angle-of-attack, α, on wake dynamics of a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 64-618 airfoil using wall-resolved large-eddy simulation at a chord-based Reynolds number Re = 1.5 × 105. The flow is investigated at α = 0°, 8°, and 12°, corresponding to attached, mildly separated, and near-stall regimes, respectively. This controlled configuration is used to isolate the influence of incidence on separation and wake reorganization of a wind-turbine-relevant blade section. An integrated Eulerian, spectral, modal, and Lagrangian analysis is performed to connect incidence-dependent changes in coherent-structure energetics with finite-time material transport. Mean-flow and turbulence statistics are combined with power spectral density, wavenumber–frequency spectra, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), finite-time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE) fields, and passive-tracer transport. Increasing α moves flow separation upstream, thickens the suction-side shear layer, and produces a progressively wider and more deflected wake. At x/c=2.5, the tracked wake center shifts from y/c ≈−0.018 to 0.127 and 0.269 for α = 0°, 8°, and 12°, respectively. The fundamental spectral peak correspondingly increases from St ≈ 0.49 to 0.55 and 0.67 for α = 8° and 12°, respectively. SPOD associates these frequencies with increasingly compact shear-layer and wake structures, whereas FTLE and passive-tracer analyses reveal concurrent increases in ridge folding, transverse spreading, and cross-wake material exchange. Together, these results establish a direct correspondence between frequency-resolved coherent-structure organization and finite-time material transport as the flow progresses toward near stall. Also, the results provide a unified picture of how separation induces wake reorganization and identifies frequency–space–time targets for reduced-order modeling and flow control in wind-energy applications.

papers.title: From vertical inspiration to tilted mitigation: A computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method study of photovoltaic soiling mechanisms and baffle-based flow control
papers.abstract: Non-uniform dust accumulation reduces the power output of photovoltaic (PV) modules, while their mounting configuration influences particle deposition and removal. In this study, a three-dimensional coupled computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method model is established to investigate particle deposition and resuspension on vertical and tilted modules at particle scale, and an opto-electrical coupled analysis is used to evaluate the effects of dust accumulation on output performance. The results show that the vertical module reduces particle contact through aerodynamic shielding and promotes post-deposition removal under near-wall aerodynamic forces with gravity assistance. At a wind speed of 5 m/s and an effective surface-energy of 0.03 J/m2, the particle residual ratio of the vertical module is 0.154, ∼35.0% lower than the value of 0.237 for the tilted module. The opto-electrical analysis based on extrapolated deposition distributions shows that the high-density band-shaped dust accumulation near the bottom of the tilted module causes photocurrent mismatch and bypass-diode activation, resulting in pronounced power loss, whereas the output degradation of the vertical module is smaller. Based on this, an upstream passive baffle is proposed to suppress dust accumulation near the bottom of the tilted module by shifting the lower-edge stagnation point upward and enhancing the local tangential airflow. Under the same conditions, the baffle reduces the particle residual ratio and maximum deposition density of the tilted module by ∼81.9% and 64.4%, respectively. This study integrates particle-deposition mechanism analysis with local flow regulation and provides a basis for the passive anti-soiling design of desert PV systems.

papers.title: Vortex dynamics and pressure-loss mechanisms in a liquid-metal magnetohydrodynamic generator
papers.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) power generation provides a direct energy-conversion method for electrically conductive fluids and has attracted increasing interest as a compact, low-water-demand energy system. The coupled effects of inlet temperature, magnetic flux density, working-fluid properties, and external load resistance on vortex-flow structure, pressure losses, and electrical response in liquid-metal MHD generators (LMMHDGs) remain insufficiently characterized. A segmented-electrode vortex-type LMMHDG using Galinstan and NaK is evaluated with temperature-dependent properties under a constant-hydraulic-input-power strategy, avoiding unequal hydraulic bases in fixed-inlet-velocity comparisons. The analysis combines vortex-flow visualization, current-density and Lorentz-force fields, local mechanical-pressure and viscous-dissipation diagnostics, pressure-loss decomposition, load-resistance matching, and Stuart-number interpretation. Results reveal organized circumferential vortex flow without pronounced large-scale separation, with viscous dissipation concentrated near the walls and inlet–chamber junction and Lorentz-force braking strongest near the upstream electrode pair. Inlet velocities spanning 1.75–40.5 m s−1 produce Stuart numbers of 0.53–0.77, indicating comparable electromagnetic-to-inertial force balances across different hydraulic conditions. Pressure-loss decomposition reveals that the MHD contribution accounts for 50.11% to 75.62% of the total pressure loss, while the non-MHD contribution ranges from 24.38% to 49.89%. The maximum electrical power output reaches 69.1 W for NaK at 1 T and 373 K under impedance-matching conditions. The highest generator-level hydraulic-to-electric efficiency is 43.95% for NaK at 473 K and 0.5 T under the Panchadar reference resistance. The modeled exergy-loss rate decreases between 293 and 573 K, whereas the hydraulic-input-based exergy-destruction fraction decreases monotonically with increasing temperature. Generator performance depends on both electromagnetic braking and geometry-dependent hydraulic resistance.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of cloud-cavitation control over a Clark-Y hydrofoil using Salvinia -morphology-inspired branched microstructures
papers.abstract: Periodic cloud-cavity shedding causes severe load fluctuations and pressure pulsations, thereby degrading hydrodynamic performance. Branched solid microstructures inspired by the geometry of Salvinia trichomes were introduced onto the suction side of a Clark-Y hydrofoil for passive control. Large-eddy simulations examined their effects on cloud-cavitation evolution, hydrodynamic performance, and vortex–cavitation coupling. Among the three S = 1.0 mm placement cases, the near-trailing-edge configuration (CS3) delivered the most favorable balance of hydrodynamic performance and cavitation suppression. Relative to the unmodified hydrofoil (Clean), CS3 increased the mean lift coefficient by 4.04% and reduced the mean drag coefficient by 4.96%. It also improved the mean lift-to-drag ratio by 9.47% and reduced the mean vapor volume by 52.36%. For geometric comparison, cylindrical-post (CP) and hemispherical-bump (HB) arrays were evaluated in the same downstream region under identical flow and numerical conditions with explicitly documented geometric constraints. Relative to Clean, HB and CP reduced the mean vapor volume by 56.60% and 26.41%, while changing the mean lift-to-drag ratio by +3.08% and −1.18%, respectively. Analyses of near-wall re-entrant-flow velocity and the magnitude of suction-side pressure recovery characterized the hydrodynamic response of CS3 relative to conventional protrusions. Further analyses of velocity vectors, local vapor volume fraction, Q-criterion vortical structures, and vorticity-transport terms clarified the associated vortex–cavitation interactions. Refined-time step Clean, paired-spacing (CS2-S1.2 and CS3-S1.2), and doubled-span Clean and CS3 simulations assessed time step, array-density, and spanwise-domain sensitivity. These findings provide a geometry-based biomimetic approach for controlling cloud cavitation and improving hydrofoil performance.

papers.title: Multifactorial assessment of hemodynamic thresholds in a three-layered elastic stenosed coronary artery
papers.abstract: Hemodynamics controls the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in coronary arteries having stenoses, but the joint effect of stenosis degree, blood viscosity, heart rate, and Reynolds number (Re) on coronary artery dynamics has not been explored using a fluid–structure interaction model. A two-dimensional fluid–structure interaction model of the left anterior descending coronary artery having a hyperelastic three-layered arterial wall was established; wall shear stress (WSS), luminal pressure, radial arterial displacement, and velocity field were calculated at the peak systole, mid-diastole, and late diastole for different stenosis degree (25%–35%), blood viscosity (0.003 65–0.0045 Pa-s), heart rate (60–100 bpm), and Re (50–200). An increase in stenosis degree from 25% to 35% resulted in an increase in peak wall deformation by 7.7% (0.65–0.70 mm) under hemodynamically significant trans-stenotic pressure gradients. A 23% increase in viscosity resulted in a 36% increase in peak wall deformation and a 43% increase in peak WSS, resulting in decreased coronary flow reserve of 25%–30%, which is consistent with the hemodynamic challenge due to polycythemia and diabetic microangiopathy. Heart rate variation exhibited an inverse relationship with wall deformation, governed by the Frank–Starling mechanism: bradycardia (60 bpm) provided a deformation nearly eightfold greater compared to tachycardia (100 bpm) (0.95 mm vs 0.12 mm) while giving 67% more diastolic perfusion time. A Re range of 50–200 encompasses conditions ranging from inward wall displacement at Re = 50 to a peak WSS of 23 Pa at Re = 200. Model-defined parameters for critical stenosis are greater than 30% diameter reduction, hematocrit of more than 45%, and heart rates of 65–80 bpm.

papers.title: Microscopic translational and rotational transport of water in a highly viscous deep eutectic solvent at elevated temperatures
papers.abstract: Understanding how molecular crowding reshapes transport in complex fluids is a central problem in fluid physics, with implications spanning biologically to industrially relevant systems. Using all-atom molecular dynamics, we examine translational and rotational dynamics of water molecules, dispersed at low concentration in a highly viscous glucose-based deep eutectic solvent at 328 and 343 K, and show that this bulk, geometrically unconfined liquid reproduces transport behavior normally associated with nanoconfinement or supercooling. A subtle plateau like feature near 1 ps in the self-intermediate scattering function, together with a coincident shoulder in the translational non-Gaussian parameter, signals transient caging. Rotational non-Gaussian parameters reveal comparable orientational trapping preceding diffusive reorientation. Axis- and rank-resolved analysis shows pronounced anisotropy in first-rank relaxation, while the second-rank calculation is nearly axis-independent. The l(l+1) Debye scaling holds for dipole-axis reorientation but fails for the remaining two perpendicular axes, revealing two coexisting rotational relaxation channels. Power spectra reveal low-frequency collective excitations and librational bands near 450 and 700 cm−1 common to both translational and rotational motion, evidencing coupling mediated by hydrogen motion. Correlation analysis further shows this translation–rotation coupling is strong and axis-selective at first rank but becomes nearly axis-independent at second rank, with dipole-axis coupling to the other rotational axes strengthening from first to second rank interpretation. These results establish rank- and axis-resolved anisotropic transport coupling as a generic signature of crowding-induced dynamical arrest in complex molecular fluids.

papers.title: Gyroid porous trailing-edge modulation of deep-stall wake dynamics and turbulent-energy pathways in a wind-turbine airfoil
papers.abstract: Deep stall of thick wind-turbine airfoils can sustain coherent low-frequency shedding and large sectional-load fluctuations. The additional role of flow through a deterministic porous trailing edge, beyond that of geometric extension, remains unclear. Improved delayed detached-eddy simulations compare a blunt baseline airfoil with an impermeable solid wedge and a same-envelope gyroid insert at Re = 1.02 × 107 and α = 8.5°. The solid extension retains the baseline lift- and drag-spectrum peaks at Stc = 1.018; it lowers the lift fluctuation but increases the drag fluctuation, showing that geometric elongation alone does not reduce both load components. With the gyroid insert, the strongest response moves to Stc = 1.357, and the lift- and drag-spectrum peaks decrease by 72.63% and 54.46%, respectively. The corresponding root mean square values fall from 0.1336 to 0.1046 for lift and from 0.0179 to 0.0152 for drag, while approximately 95% of the displayed short-time Fourier transform power remains below 10 Hz. Across four successive sections, the signed axial mass-flow rate rises from 0.255 to 0.389 kg/s and the axial momentum flux from 6.19 to 9.19 N, while transverse and spanwise velocity fluctuations persist. Positive mean turbulent-kinetic-energy production is distributed over successive passage-scale regions, and the displayed near-wake structures are shorter, more branched, and more strongly inclined in the streamwise direction than in the impermeable cases. For the examined gyroid realization and spanwise-periodic sectional domain, this passage-scale redistribution is consistent with a weaker concentration of the dominant roll-up response.

papers.title: Transient hydrodynamic coefficient analysis of the 3-degree-of-freedom underwater parallel manipulator for polymetallic nodule collection
papers.abstract: The precise collection of deep-sea polymetallic nodules using underwater manipulators has emerged as a novel commercial paradigm, balancing high mining efficiency and low environmental disturbance compared to traditional crawler vehicles. However, executing these operations requires accurate modeling of highly nonlinear hydrodynamic interactions. Existing hydrodynamic models primarily target serial manipulators, leaving the transient hydrodynamics and multi-link coupling effects of underwater parallel manipulator systems (UPMS) insufficiently investigated. To address this, this study proposes a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-driven transient hydrodynamic framework for a 3-degree-of-freedom UPMS. Focusing on a single limb, the hydrodynamic loads are decomposed into drag and added inertia components, and the corresponding transient coefficients are normalized by the dimensionless relative displacement of the limb centroid. Using Box–Behnken design simulations and second-order polynomial regressions, these normalized coefficients are formulated as functions of kinematic and relative configuration parameters. These explicit formulations are then coupled with inverse kinematics to predict the global transient hydrodynamic torques of the UPMS. Parametric scale analyses reveal that while increasing the limb diameter amplifies the absolute transient loads, the normalized coefficients remain scale-invariant with respect to the dimensionless relative displacement. Furthermore, the proposed framework is validated against full-system CFD simulations and physical prototype experiments under a continuous time-varying trajectory, yielding a normalized root mean square error of approximately 12%. This framework reduces the reliance on repetitive, computationally intensive simulations, providing a reliable mathematical foundation for real-time dynamic control and energy optimization of deep-sea operations.

papers.title: Does bulk viscosity govern the compressive-to-rotational dynamical coupling in reflected shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction? A direct numerical simulation (DNS) study
papers.abstract: Bulk viscosity plays a central role in compressible flows by dissipating dilatational motions, yet its impact on reflected shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction has remained largely unexplored. Using high-resolution three-dimensional direct numerical simulations (DNS) at Re=2000 over the range A=μb/μ=0–20, it is shown that increasing bulk viscosity systematically broadens the reflected shock, with the measured shock thickness increasing by factors of approximately 1.7–5.6 relative to the A=0 reference case, thereby weakening density gradients and progressively reducing the volume-integrated baroclinic activity Bbaro, and suppressing baroclinic vorticity generation. The energetic role of bulk viscosity is quantified through the bulk-viscous dissipation, which is found to increase approximately as Db≃0.5A2, and its fractional contribution to the total viscous dissipation, fb≃0.025A, reaching approximately 50% at A=20; the turbulent Mach number and the root mean square velocity divergence (∇·u)rms are found to decrease systematically over the same range, providing an independent measure of the progressive damping of dilatational motion. As a result, the rotational intensity of coherent vortices, quantified by the normalized circulation Γ/Deq2, decreases monotonically, with a corresponding increase in the circulation-based characteristic rotational timescale trot∼Deq2/Γ. A strong correlation is observed between Γ/Deq2 and (∇·u)rms (R=0.979, R2=0.959); this statistical association is interpreted as supporting, rather than by itself establishing, a coupled compressive-to-rotational dynamical mechanism, since a rigorous causal demonstration would require a complete kinetic-energy and vorticity budget that is beyond the scope of the present study. Together, these quantitative diagnostics establish, within the investigated reflected-SWBLI configuration (Re=2000, A=0–20), a coupled dynamical mechanism in which bulk-viscous damping broadens the shock, reduces density gradients and baroclinic activity, suppresses dilatational motions, and modifies the subsequent rotational dynamics of coherent vortices.

papers.title: A tensor-free parallel method for second-order flow-field sensitivities in transonic flow
papers.abstract: Second-order flow-field sensitivities reinforce Newton aerodynamic optimization and Taylor-series-based flow reconstruction. However, their efficient evaluation is difficult because the associated third-order tensor cannot be stored explicitly on engineering-scale meshes. To address this, a tensor-free parallel method is proposed that computes full-field second-order flow-field sensitivities through second-order forward-mode differentiation. It is derived and proved that the entire right-hand side of the tangent equation for the second-order flow-field sensitivity can be written in the standard form required for a single second-order automatic differentiation (AD) sweep. No second- or third-order derivative tensors are formed or stored. This reduces storage complexity from O(N3) to O(N), where N denotes the number of flow-field degrees of freedom. In addition, an outer-vectorized parallel method reduces the number of inner AD sweeps in the construction of the full Hessian from O(n2) to O(n), where n denotes the number of design parameters. The parallelism is based on AD-seed vectorization at the outer differentiation level and does not involve message passing interface or thread-level parallelism. Finally, the proposed methodology is validated for transonic flow over a National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics 0012 airfoil at Mach number Ma=0.8. The full-field second-order sensitivity computation for a geometric deformation parameter costs on the same order as for the first-order case, while the peak memory of the second-order sensitivity computation is 54% of that of the first-order solve.

papers.title: Stationwise separation of local mean-thickness scaling and interfacial-wave statistics in a vertical falling water film
papers.abstract: This study provides dataset-specific evidence separating local mean-thickness scaling from interfacial-wave statistics in the public Falling Film Evaporation Test Rig archive. Eighteen 20 s point records cover six nominal liquid Reynolds numbers, Rel=q/νl=500–1100, at 100, 350, and 600 mm on a vertical water-film surface without countercurrent gas. At Rel=620, the 600-to-100 mm mean-thickness ratio is 1.001, whereas the coefficients of variation are 0.0428 and 0.2029, and the skewness values are −0.044 and 0.591. At Rel=740, the mean ratio is 0.978, and the fluctuation-intensity ratio is 3.54. Six-setting fits of h¯=CRelp give p=0.594, 0.428, and 0.331 at the three stations. The 600 mm exponent is numerically near the laminar reference 1/3, but separate lower- and upper-setting fits give 0.431 and 0.244. This pooled exponent coincides with the largest relative fluctuations and does not identify a Nusselt state. The contribution is a joint characterization of mean scaling and wave statistics in this archived subset, extending an established distinction to these specific records. It does not establish a universal criterion for film development. All station comparisons are descriptive: absent synchronization, one acquisition per station and setting, and an incomplete uncertainty budget preclude causal interpretation or inference across repeat experiments.

papers.title: Disturbance-energy analysis of Widom-line-coupled instability in supercritical binary mixing layers
papers.abstract: Cryogenic propellants in liquid rocket engines are often injected at supercritical pressures, where a mixing layer may cross the Widom line and experience sharp thermodynamic-property variations. These variations can induce an instability distinct from the classical Kelvin–Helmholtz mechanism, but its energy source remains unclear. Here, a compressible multispecies linear stability framework based on the Soave–Redlich–Kwong equation of state is developed for a supercritical liquid-oxygen/methane mixing layer. A positive-definite Chu-type disturbance-energy norm is formulated for binary real-fluid mixtures, comprising kinetic, acoustic, and coupled entropy-composition contributions. The associated thermodynamic coefficient matrix is obtained in the closed form from the Hessian of the internal energy, and the norm recovers the established single-component real-fluid and ideal-gas limits. A reversible disturbance-energy budget is then derived for a steady parallel base flow and decomposed into shear, entropy-gradient, and composition-gradient production. When the Widom line is aligned with the flow inflection point, entropy-gradient production supplies approximately 98% of the net disturbance-energy growth, whereas shear production contributes only about 1%. Parametric analyses show that entropy and composition gradients provide complementary thermodynamic energy pathways, so thermodynamic dominance does not require both gradients to coexist. Under Widom-line misalignment, the peak growth rate varies non-monotonically because of competition between thermodynamic and shear modes, while the disturbance-energy budget remains overwhelmingly dominated by thermodynamic production. The proposed norm provides a quantitative framework for identifying instability mechanisms in supercritical binary mixing layers.

papers.title: Acoustic diffraction and pressure-amplitude recovery behind an air bubble subjected to a collapse-induced pulse
papers.abstract: Understanding the interaction between pressure waves and air bubbles is important for load attenuation by bubble curtains and pressure-wave shielding in water. In this study, numerical simulations and theoretical modeling are combined to examine the interaction between a collapse-induced pressure wave and an air bubble. The results show that the large acoustic-impedance mismatch between the gas and liquid phases causes the air bubble to locally block and scatter the incident pressure wave, leading to the formation of a low-pressure shadow region behind the bubble. As the diffracted and scattered waves recombine downstream, the centerline peak pressure gradually recovers with increasing propagation distance. The classical spherical acoustic scattering model reasonably predicts the pressure-amplitude recovery trend for small and intermediate bubbles; however, more pronounced deviations are observed for larger bubbles, particularly in the recovery rate of the centerline peak pressure. These results clarify the acoustic mechanism by which an isolated air bubble affects the propagation of a collapse-induced pressure wave under the present pulse conditions.

papers.title: Data assimilation of the near-field dynamics of the hydrofoil tip vortex
papers.abstract: Tip vortex cavitation is a critical issue in marine hydrodynamics, yet its prediction is hampered by challenges in capturing the complex, unsteady flow in the hydrofoil near-field. Conventional experimental and numerical methods often struggle to resolve the unsteady structures and the physically consistent pressure–velocity coupling associated with vortex instability. This study applies an established continuous-adjoint data-assimilation (DA) framework to a new hydrofoil-tip-vortex application by assimilating time-resolved tomographic particle image velocimetry measurements into the spatially filtered Navier–Stokes equations. The DA step reconstructs a physics-constrained three-dimensional velocity field; pressure is subsequently estimated from that velocity field by solving a pressure Poisson equation. The flow is examined at angles of attack (AoA) of 5°, 10°, and 15° under non-cavitating conditions. Increasing AoA strengthens the reconstructed vortex, lowers the mean core-pressure estimate, and increases vortex wandering and pressure fluctuations. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD)/extended POD reveals a change from a monopole-like pressure-fluctuation pattern at low AoA toward a dipole-like displacement pattern at higher AoA. These patterns are interpreted as qualitative indicators of pressure-based cavitation susceptibility. The DA framework therefore provides a physics-constrained approach for investigating near-field vortex velocity and pressure dynamics that are difficult to obtain from experiments or under-resolved simulations alone.

papers.title: Investigation on the leading-edge receptivity mechanism of hypersonic boundary layers over a small-bluntness cone
papers.abstract: This study investigates the leading-edge receptivity of a hypersonic boundary layer to freestream entropy waves, under Mach 8 flow over a blunt cone with a nose radius of 0.254 mm. In this configuration, an evanescent wave is generated behind the shock, as confirmed by both disturbance–shock interaction theory and direct numerical simulation. This evanescent wave is identified as the critical external pressure source that excites unstable disturbances within the boundary layer. Specifically, in the leading-edge region, where the shock remains sufficiently close to the wall, the pressure fluctuations associated with the evanescent wave penetrate the boundary layer and excite the slow mode through their interaction with the nonparallel mean flow. The slow mode is subsequently modulated by the external entropy–vorticity wave and eventually undergoes conversion into the rapidly growing second mode near the synchronization point. Systematic parametric studies demonstrate that this mechanism remains qualitatively unchanged under variations in the gas model, wall thermal condition, disturbance frequency, and Reynolds number, with only quantitative changes in the receptivity amplitude, synchronization location, and modal growth rates.

papers.title: A constitutive equation for partially reversible thixotropy fluids
papers.abstract: Classical structural-kinetics models of thixotropy usually assume that the material structure can fully recover after the imposed shear is removed. This assumption is inadequate for colloidal suspensions in which sufficiently strong shear permanently lowers the recoverable structural level. Here, we formulate a partially reversible thixotropic constitutive model by separating two structural variables: the structural state, λ, and the maximum recoverable structural level, λbreak. The variable λ describes the structural level realized under the current shear condition, whereas λbreak records the shear-history-dependent reduction of the maximum recoverable structure. The resulting model reduces to the classical Moore equation when λbreak=1 but predicts a transition to partially reversible behavior when the imposed shear rate exceeds a critical value γ̇c. For a constant shear rate above the critical value γ̇c, the model gives an analytical solution for the evolution of λbreak and a closed-form expression for the maximum recoverable structural level, λbreak,max. Rheological measurements on 4.5 wt. % fumed-silica suspensions, including three-interval thixotropy tests, repeated high-shear cycles, high-shear duration tests, and critical-shear-rate tests, are used to evaluate the model. The experiments show irreversible viscosity loss after high-shear loading, identify a damage threshold near 10 s−1, and show that the experimentally extracted recovery limit is consistent with the analytical prediction. The proposed framework therefore provides a compact constitutive description of thixotropic materials whose structural recovery is limited by irreversible shear-history effects.

papers.title: Effect of polarized light on the swimming behavior of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii in capillary confinement
papers.abstract: As a model unicellular puller microswimmer, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii cells swim along characteristic helical trajectories generated by the beating of their flagella and their interaction with the surrounding fluid. In confined capillaries, these swimming trajectories are further influenced by geometric constraints. While polarization-dependent phototactic responses have been reported in other photosensitive microswimmers, the influence of light polarization on the motility of C. reinhardtii under geometric confinement remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate how light intensity and polarization state modulate this phototactic motion under microscale confinement. By quantitatively analyzing cell trajectories and power spectral densities across illumination conditions (2.5–6 W/m2) and polarization states—linearly polarized parallel (LPP) or perpendicular (LPN) to the capillary axis, and unpolarized light (NP)—we demonstrate that these microalgae exhibit distinct behavioral responses to both light intensity and polarization orientation. Increasing incident intensity modestly enhances swimming speed; however, a distinct behavioral transition occurs for LPN at 3.67 W/m2. At this threshold, LPN illumination induces suppressed axial displacement, elevated transverse reorientation rates, and a non-monotonic shift in dominant oscillation frequency—responses absent for LPP or NP light. Under LPP illumination, the dominant axial oscillation frequency remains nearly stable across all intensity levels. These findings reveal that the eyespot–flagellar system of C. reinhardtii exhibits polarization-sensitive phototaxis, whose expression is amplified by geometric confinement. This mechano-optical coupling provides quantitative insights for light-guided microalgal sorting, bio-hybrid microdevice design, and ecological models of phytoplankton navigation in anisotropic light fields.

papers.title: A continuous method for solving condensation shocks in pure and mixture real gas supersonic flows
papers.abstract: Condensation shocks arise when a vapor expands at supersonic velocity and is driven into the metastable region as pressure and temperature fall, until the homogeneous nucleation limit triggers a phase change resembling a shock-like, discontinuous front. Their prediction is central to vapor-handling devices such as steam turbines, supercritical carbon dioxide compressors, ejectors, and supersonic gas separators, and becomes demanding at high pressures and low temperatures, where real gas effects dominate. This work presents a continuous method for condensation shocks in pure vapors and constant-composition real gas mixtures. In contrast to gas-kinetic descriptions, the proposed approach requires neither droplet nucleation and growth calculations nor transport properties such as thermal conductivity, surface tension, or diffusion coefficients, which are difficult to obtain for high-pressure, metastable mixtures. Instead, the condensation zone is treated as a finite-thickness region across which a prescribed specific entropy profile is imposed, and the flow follows from integrating the one-dimensional mass, momentum, energy, and entropy balances with a multiparameter equation-of-state. The total specific entropy jump closing the model is taken from the Rankine–Hugoniot maximum-entropy solution, either numerically or from a new analytical real-gas weak-shock expression derived here. The condensation-zone thickness and entropy-distribution coefficient are not free parameters; they emerge as the unique solution forcing the downstream state onto the thermodynamic-equilibrium locus. The method is validated against experimental pressure data for steam, pure carbon dioxide, and a carbon dioxide–dry air mixture, reproducing the pressure recovery and shock location within the experimental scatter, whereas the discontinuous solution overestimates the pressure peak.

papers.title: Physics-informed identification and independent numerical verification of conditional modal collapse in active control of lid-driven cavity flow
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks identify distributed actuation for a two-dimensional lid-driven cavity by combining the Navier–Stokes constraints with an objective reducing viscous dissipation at prescribed actuation energy. The control is represented in a truncated spatiotemporal Fourier basis, while a parametric network represents the Reynolds-number dependence over 100≤Re≤1000. At Re=100 and 500, the control concentrates in the stationary second spatial harmonic (91.6% and 92.2% of the energy), the time-dependent contribution below 1.3%. At Re=1000, the second harmonic remains the largest contribution (64.0%), the temporal fraction rising to 32.2%. The branch persists across actuation energy, network capacity, Fourier truncation, and cavity aspect ratio AR=Lx/Ly, but its purity is geometry-dependent: it remains above 91% for AR=1 and 2, whereas it falls to 69.9% at AR=0.5, where the temporal fraction reaches 26.7%. Branches are not unique: independent initializations at Re=500 produce distinct converged branches with comparable objectives, and removing the variance regularization redirects the solution toward a first-harmonic branch. The structure is also conditional on the control representation: a modified-Chebyshev basis produces a temporally dominated branch. Controls are transferred without retraining to an independent multiple-relaxation-time lattice-Boltzmann solver. The Fourier branch is reproduced as a low-dissipation, quasi-stationary flow, with a fluctuating-to-mean-flow kinetic-energy ratio RK<1% at all three Reynolds numbers, whereas the modified-Chebyshev branch fails this criterion. The second-mode-dominated solution is thus a repeatedly recoverable, parameterization- and regime-dependent branch, and systematic branch analysis with independent numerical verification is essential when interpreting control structures from physics-informed optimization.

papers.title: Ionic liquid droplet impact on solid substrates under horizontal electric fields
papers.abstract: Droplet impact under an external electric field is governed by complex electrohydrodynamic couplings. Still, the impact dynamics of ionic liquids (ILs), which exhibit significantly higher electric conductivity than common liquids such as water and ethanol, under electric fields remain largely unexplored. In this study, we experimentally and theoretically investigate the impact dynamics of conductive ionic liquid droplets falling vertically onto a smooth substrate subjected to horizontal direct-current electric fields (up to 10 kV/cm), oriented perpendicular to the vertical impact velocity, over a wide range of Weber numbers (57<We<320). High-speed imaging indicates that the electric field induces pronounced pre-impact prolate deformation (with deformation parameter α up to 0.14), which accelerates the early-stage radial expansion upon contact, yet does not substantially modify the observed impact regimes or the maximum spreading factor within the investigated parameter range. Remarkably, despite this intense initial deformation, the applied field only has a minor effect on the maximum spreading factor (βmax). By incorporating the deformation-induced surface energy and an empirically formulated viscous dissipation term into an energy conservation framework, we propose a semi-empirical model for the maximum spreading factor. The predicted βmax agrees well with the experimental data for all ionic liquids examined in the study, with predictions falling within a ±5% deviation band of the experimental data.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic interference and thrust enhancement of two vertically stacked low-aspect-ratio flapping plates
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic interactions in fish schools are complex and poorly understood. This study numerically investigates the collective performance of two flapping plates arranged in vertically stacked formations. The results indicate that the hydrodynamic performance of the two-plate system strongly depends on both vertical (D1) and longitudinal (D2) spacings. Compared with the isolated flapping plate, two vertically arranged plates achieve significant thrust enhancement, at the cost of increased power consumption, when the vertical and longitudinal spacings are appropriate. Moreover, the thrust augmentation monotonously increases with decreasing D1, which can be described as ΔCTc ∼ D1−5/4, but it linearly increases with the reduction of D2. For the parameters considered in this study (Re = 1000, St = 0.5), the maximum increase in thrust can reach up to 34.4%, and that in efficiency can reach up to 7.6%, both achieved in the case of D1 = D2 = 0.1. Furthermore, vortex interactions between the two vertically arranged plates are analyzed. When the vertical and longitudinal spacings are small, only one set of vortex rings forms in the wake of the two-plate system, which results from vortex merging and vortex reconnection. When the longitudinal spacing is large, distortion and reconnection of vortex rings commonly occur, which result in complex morphologies of vortex rings in the wake of the two-plate system. These results may shed light on the physical mechanisms behind the collective motion of fish schools.

papers.title: Bouncing and spreading dynamics of drops on non-wetting solid surfaces
papers.abstract: This study investigates the dynamics of a drop impacting a superhydrophobic surface. Drops of water and water–glycol mixture are considered with different initial velocities to vary the Weber number and Ohnesorge number. The simulation results are benchmarked against in-house experimental results as well as experimental results available in the open literature. The spreading dynamics of the drops are examined for various values of the Ohnesorge number and Weber number. In addition, the effect of the initial drop shape on spreading and bouncing dynamics is systematically analyzed by considering spherical, oblate, and prolate shaped drops. The simulations reveal that the outcome of the impact is influenced by the initial shape of the drop. The numerical analysis provides insight into the energy budget of the bouncing process, delineating the role of viscous energy dissipation in determining the outcome of impact. The maximum spreading factor is also found to be strongly influenced by the initial shape of the drop over a range of Weber and Ohnesorge numbers. Such effects become more pronounced at smaller values of the Weber number.

papers.title: On the effects of a perforated shroud on turbulence mechanisms in the wake of a cylinder
papers.abstract: The turbulent wake of a circular cylinder fitted with a perforated shroud is investigated experimentally using time-resolved particle image velocimetry to identify the turbulence mechanisms governing passive wake control. While perforated shrouds are widely used to mitigate aerodynamic loading and vortex-induced vibrations, prior studies have primarily focused on global force and wake-integrated quantities and have generally considered configurations outside the design ranges prescribed by the American Society of Mechanical Engineers in the Standard code for Steel Stacks. Perforation ratios of β=0.3 and 0.5, a shroud-to-cylinder diameter ratio of DS/D≈1.1, and a hole-size ratio of DH/D=0.07 and 0.08 are examined at Reynolds numbers of ReD=23×103, 38×103, and 55×103. Full-field velocity data are used to quantify wake recovery, recirculation dynamics, Reynolds shear stress, turbulent kinetic energy, characteristic temporal scales, and second-order structure functions. Increasing the perforation ratio enlarges the recirculation region while reducing Reynolds shear stress and turbulent kinetic energy and accelerating downstream wake recovery. Despite these changes, normalized temporal statistics and second-order structure functions exhibit a strong collapse across Reynolds number, indicating weak Reynolds-number sensitivity of the normalized multiscale wake organization over the range considered. The primary effect of the shroud is, therefore, to redistribute turbulence production and reduce the spatial coherence of dominant wake structures through distributed momentum exchange. These results provide turbulence measurements linking perforated-shroud performance to wake physics and connecting engineering design guidelines with the underlying mechanisms of passive flow modification.

papers.title: Instability of a viscoelastic Oldroyd-B fluid flowing over a slippery inclined plane with an imposed shear
papers.abstract: We investigate both linear and weakly nonlinear stability analyses for the viscoelastic Oldroyd-B fluid falling down an impermeable slippery inclined plane, where a constant shear stress is applied at the fluid surface to take into account the dynamic effect of surrounding airflow. A linearized boundary value problem in terms of the amplitudes of perturbation variables is derived to execute the linear stability analysis. In the linear regime, Deborah number De, slip length α, and applied shear stress τs destabilize surface mode instability by decreasing the critical Reynolds number, while the solvent viscosity ratio β stabilizes it by increasing the critical Reynolds number. However, surface mode instability is stabilized if the external shear stress is applied in the counter-flow direction. Interestingly, we find a critical value of τs(<0) for a given slip length; below this value, the Newtonian fluid is more unstable, while above it, the viscoelastic upper-convected Maxwell fluid is more unstable compared to other fluids. Moreover, we observe the emergence of a purely elastic instability induced by elastic stress, and this instability can be made faster by introducing the slip effect at the solid impermeable plane. On the other hand, the weakly nonlinear stability analysis is performed based on the Benney-type nonlinear surface evolution equation. We find a filtered wave equilibrium solution in both the subcritical and supercritical zones. However, in the case of a purely elastic instability, we observe only a supercritical equilibrium solution. Finally, the nonlinear traveling wave solution exhibits that its amplitude amplifies as the Deborah number, the slip length, and the imposed shear stress rise.

papers.title: Numerical study on the effects of inlet obstacle geometry on detonation wave propagation characteristics in semi-confined straight channels
papers.abstract: In detonation engines and combustion explosions in complex confined spaces, inlet obstacles can strongly influence detonation wave propagation. To clarify the interaction mechanism between detonation waves and inlet obstacles in semi-confined straight channels, numerical simulations were conducted using the OpenFOAM platform. The effects of different inlet obstacle configurations, characterized by the normalized projected obstacle area (A*) and aspect ratio (AR), on detonation propagation were systematically investigated, with emphasis on wave system evolution, cellular structure, and triple point evolution. The results show that inlet obstacles induce a characteristic sequence of diffraction, local decoupling, and re-initiation, followed by gradual reconstruction of the detonation wave. Within the investigated parameter range, increasing A* for the circular obstacles enhances the upstream compression and downstream diffraction effects, resulting in a larger disturbed region and delayed detonation recovery. For the rectangular and square obstacles with the same A*, increasing AR progressively advances re-initiation and recovery and results in a higher overall triple point number. Meanwhile, the diffraction induced decoupling region and the spatial extent of pressure and velocity disturbances are reduced as AR increases, indicating a more localized influence of the obstacle on the detonation flow field. These trends are associated with the reduced extent of interaction between the obstacle and the detonation front at larger AR. Moreover, different obstacle shapes with comparable A* and the same AR can exhibit similar macroscopic recovery characteristics. These findings provide physical insights into the effects of inlet obstacle geometry on detonation propagation and recovery in semi-confined channels.

papers.title: Flow-induced vibrations of a serrated flexible splitter plate
papers.abstract: We experimentally investigate flow-induced vibrations (FIV) of a cantilevered flexible splitter plate with triangular trailing-edge serrations mounted downstream of a circular cylinder. Seven plate configurations, including two non-serrated baseline plates and five serrated plates with varying serration heights, were investigated in a low-speed wind tunnel over a Reynolds number range (based on diameter) of 4×103–5×104. Structural response and wake characteristics were measured via laser displacement sensing, high-speed imaging, and hot-wire anemometry. All plates exhibit three regimes with increasing free-stream velocity: initial excitation, transition, and synchronized response regime inferred from frequency matching. The synchronized response regime is characterized by frequency matching between the plate oscillation and the wake frequency near the second natural frequency of the plate, accompanied by large-amplitude limit-cycle oscillations. Trailing-edge serrations shift the onset of the synchronized response regime to higher reduced velocity and alter the amplitude and frequency response relative to the base plate 1. Increasing serration height modifies the effective length and structural properties of the plate, which together increase the dimensionless root-mean-square displacement by 25.9% and reduce the dimensionless frequency by 14.9% in the synchronized response regime for plate 5 relative to base plate 1 at a reduced velocity of Ur=7.71.
