Flow visualization shows that serrations generate localized vortex formation at the serration gaps, suggesting enhanced wake instability and stronger fluid–structure interaction. These results establish trailing-edge serrations as a passive control parameter for tuning FIV, relevant to energy harvesting, aeroelastic control, and vibration mitigation.

papers.title: Pore-scale simulation of three-phase displacement initialized from large-scale two-phase microfluidic experiments
papers.abstract: Among various mitigation strategies, CO2 geological storage has gained widespread adoption because it both mitigates global warming and enhances oil recovery. Most existing three-phase (oil–water–gas) pore-scale simulations of water-alternating-gas (WAG) displacement rely on artificial initial conditions rather than two-phase experimental results. To bridge this gap, oil–water distributions obtained from microfluidic experiments were digitized to establish initial conditions for three-phase displacement simulation. The single-cycle WAG injection process was then simulated. Pore-scale dynamic mechanisms, including coalescence and split-up, bypass-double displacement, pinch-off, and sandwich-type displacement, were observed and analyzed. The displacement process was divided into four distinct stages, each with different three-phase saturation evolution trends. The computational domain was partitioned into six subregions of equal area to evaluate spatial differences in saturation behavior. Significant spatial heterogeneity was identified during secondary water flooding after the gas flooding stage in the large-scale porous structure.

papers.title: Quantitative evaluation of anti-cavitation performance inside bionic regulating valve based on nonlinear dynamics
papers.abstract: The anti-cavitation performance of regulating valves under high-pressure conditions represents a critical challenge in fluid control systems. Traditional evaluation methods are inherently limited in characterizing the nonlinear dynamic behaviors associated with transient cavitation evolution. In this paper, a bionic regulating valve is designed based on the biologically inspired theory of inventive problem solving, and a dynamic evaluation method for its anti-cavitation performance is proposed based on nonlinear cavitation dynamics. High-speed photography, phase-space reconstruction, confidence ellipsoid analysis, and the maximal Lyapunov exponent are used to characterize the dynamic evolution of the cavitation field. The results show that the shark-skin groove structure significantly suppresses cavitation development, with a maximum reduction in cavitation area of 67.31%, while having little influence on the flow characteristics, with a minimum flow rate difference of 0.7 l/min at 2.0 MPa. The three-dimensional projected-state distributions of both valves exhibit approximately ellipsoidal envelopes, and the principal-axis lengths of the 0.80 and 0.99 confidence ellipsoids are consistently smaller for the bionic regulating valve. Although its maximal Lyapunov exponent is slightly higher at 2.0–2.4 MPa, the pressure-induced increase is substantially weaker at higher pressures, with a 76.6% lower value at 3.0 MPa. These results indicate that the bionic structure suppresses cavitation development, limits phase-space dispersion, and restrains the intensification of nonlinear cavitation dynamics. The proposed nonlinear dynamic indicators provide a new quantitative perspective for evaluating the anti-cavitation performance of regulating valves.

papers.title: Momentum and thermal transport in Casson fluid flow over an unsteady radially stretching sheet: A comparative study of unified and modular physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: This study presents two artificial intelligence-based frameworks, unified physics-informed neural network (UPINN) and modular physics-informed neural network (MPINN), for analyzing boundary-layer flow and heat transfer of a Casson fluid over an unsteady radially stretching sheet. The governing partial differential equations are transformed into nonlinear similarity ordinary differential equations using similarity transformations. The resulting equations and boundary conditions are incorporated into the neural-network loss function through automatic differentiation, enabling a label-free solution strategy. UPINN employs a single network to predict the dependent variables, whereas MPINN uses separate subnetworks for the velocity and temperature fields, consistent with the one-way coupling structure of the governing system. A systematic hyperparameter analysis examines the effects of learning rate, network architecture, and collocation points. The predictions are validated against numerical solutions obtained using the BVP4C solver and show close agreement. Parametric studies investigate the effects of the unsteadiness parameter, Casson parameter, Prandtl number, and suction/injection parameter on the velocity and temperature profiles and wall transport quantities. The results demonstrate that both frameworks produce stable solutions and show close agreement with the reference BVP4C solutions, with differences in loss and relative error across the investigated configurations. The study provides a comparative assessment of unified and modular PINN architectures for the present nonlinear boundary-layer system.

papers.title: Configuration and back-pressure effects on back-propagation pressure suppression in rotating detonation engine intakes: A shape optimization approach
papers.abstract: An automated shape optimization framework coupling a quasi-two-dimensional compressible flow solver with sequential least squares programming is developed to suppress back-propagating pressure waves in rotating detonation engine (RDE) intakes under periodic strong backpressure. A seventh-order Bézier curve parameterizes the streamwise cross-sectional area; the objective minimizes the inlet root mean square (RMS) pressure pulsation. The optimized profile reduces pulsation by 50.22% and peak pressure by 7.19% vs baseline, while mean flow velocity rises from 153.4 to 258.9 m/s. This high-kinetic-energy barrier weakens upstream wavefront propagation. Downstream pressure-boundary analysis reveals nonlinear shape sensitivity: a transition between the two regimes is observed between Pmin = 1.3 and 1.4 atm (the maximum Mach number decreasing from 0.808 to 0.733): monotonic contraction remains effective at the lower trough pressures, whereas at the higher trough pressures, an internal expansion chamber appears and shifts downstream with increasing back pressure and provides an aerodynamic buffer for shock-wave expansion. Three-dimensional reconstruction agrees with the quasi-2D prediction within 0.703% in inlet JRMS and shows that internal expansion cavities act as selective spectral suppressors rather than uniform broadband attenuators. Under matched back-pressure loading, both optimized structures reduce total spectral power near the first contraction by approximately half; however, inlet response is governed by spatial-frequency reconfiguration of the 2884 Hz forced fundamental and its higher harmonics. For the 1.4 atm pair, the optimized structure lowers the fundamental band to 69.88% of baseline, while spectral power above 5 kHz rises to 147.93%, reducing the inlet JRMS by 4.99%; for the 1.6 atm pair, it retains a 16.9% inlet JRMS reduction with inlet total spectral power at 71.24% of the baseline. These fluid-mechanics-based mechanisms provide a quantitative basis for the stability-oriented design of RDE intakes.

papers.title: Carbon dioxide bubble plume dynamics and mass transfer under random waves and comparison to regular waves
papers.abstract: Injecting carbon dioxide (CO2) bubbles into seawater is a potential approach for mitigating the greenhouse effect and climate change. This study conducts a series of physical experiments and a numerical model coupling computational fluid dynamics with CO2 mass transfer to investigate the hydrodynamic and mass transfer characteristics of CO2 bubble plumes under random waves, and a comparative analysis is performed with regular waves. The results showed that the dimensionless velocity half-width and the CO2 mass transfer coefficient (MTC) increase for regular and random waves with increasing wave height and wave period and decrease with increasing still water depth. Under random waves, the CO2 MTC exhibits a nonmonotonic trend with variations in the injection hole diameter and injection angle. In addition, dimensionless parameters of the waves and CO2 bubble plumes are utilized to develop a predictive equation for the CO2 MTC, and the equation is validated using the related data.

papers.title: Modeling dispersion in cementing flows: From vertical to horizontal wells
papers.abstract: Primary cementing often involves a laminar displacement flow of miscible fluids at a high Péclet number (Pe≥107) along an inclined narrow eccentric annulus. As the displacing fluid penetrates ahead of the mean flow in the center of the annular gap, significant dispersion may result. In this study, we explore the impact of dispersion on horizontal well cementing flows in detail by comparing both quantitative and qualitative results obtained from three-dimensional (3D) simulations, the dispersive two-dimensional gap-averaged (D2DGA) model, and the earlier two-dimensional gap-averaged (2DGA) model. Unlike in vertical wells, buoyancy acts transverse to the main flow direction, but surprisingly the 3D and D2DGA models predict very similar flows. Further external verification of the D2DGA approach was provided by comparing with existing experimental results in the literature. Outcomes from both 3D and D2DGA models reveal pronounced dispersive fronts that are largely absent in the 2DGA model. The results suggest that advective dispersion smears the fronts in both 3D and D2DGA models, thereby retarding the growth of fingering instabilities arising from an unfavorable viscosity or density gradients, as found in the 2DGA model results. Consequently, advective dispersion can significantly alter the flow structures and, perhaps remarkably, lead to less fingering-dominated flow patterns.

papers.title: Simulation of wave-induced heave motion of a buoy using solvers based on the Navier–Stokes equations and spectral wave explicit Navier–Stokes equations
papers.abstract: Based on the NS (Navier–Stokes) equations and the SWENSE (Spectral Wave Explicit Navier–Stokes Equations), a domain decomposition potential–viscous-flow coupling solver and a functional decomposition potential–viscous-flow coupling solver using the overset mesh method are established in this paper. In the NS solver, the potential-flow wave field is prescribed using the stream function wave theory, and the viscous-flow wave field is resolved by the NS equations. In the SWENSE solver, the total wave field is decomposed into incident and complementary components. The incident field is obtained from the stream function wave theory, whereas the complementary field is governed by the SWENSE, which are derived by subtracting the Euler equations from the NS equations. A numerical study is conducted to compare the performance of the developed solvers. One regular-wave condition is used for wave-only and buoy-response validation, while additional wave conditions with different wave steepnesses are considered for wave-load assessment. The vertical displacement and wetted height predicted by both solvers agree well with the experimental results. The SWENSE solver reduces the number of mesh cells and computational cost by using a reduced cylindrical domain while maintaining satisfactory accuracy. Under different wave-steepness conditions, the NS- and SWENSE-based simulations provide consistent wave-load predictions, and the horizontal load is more sensitive to wave steepness than the vertical load.

papers.title: A regularized thixotropic yield-stress model for deep-sea ultra-soft sediments
papers.abstract: Deep-sea ultra-soft sediments undergo stress overshoot, post-peak softening, and structural recovery during low-rate shearing. A constitutive description must account for these transient responses as well as the residual-flow resistance. We develop a regularized thixotropic yield-stress model and compare it with direct-shear, ramp-sweep, and rest–restart measurements. A scalar structural variable interpolates between structured and broken-down strength levels. Papanastasiou regularization describes the yielding transition, while recovery and shear-induced breakdown govern the structural evolution. Direct-shear tests give nearly linear peak and residual strength envelopes. Cohesion decreases from 9.07 to 5.40 kPa, while the friction angle remains close to 13.1°. The rheometric coefficients are calibrated to the ramp data with a prescribed recovery ratio. The resulting fit over 0–50 s−1 gives R2 = 0.9963. Using the same parameters, predictions of seven restart peaks give R2 = 0.9780, root mean square error = 92.86 Pa, and mean absolute percentage error = 5.60%. These predictions assume an instantaneous restart and use the same 480 s observation window as measurements. Comparisons with Bingham, Herschel–Bulkley, Casson, regularized Herschel–Bulkley, Houska–Zitny, and Xu-type models show improved agreement across the overshoot and softening regions. The tensorial formulation retains the simple-shear response and provides a constitutive description of sediment resistance during shearing and rest.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of tip-vortex cavitation with a modified cavitation model incorporating the effect of dissolved gas
papers.abstract: Tip-vortex cavitation (TVC) is strongly affected by water-quality conditions, yet dissolved-gas effects remain insufficiently represented in the Schnerr–Sauer (S-S) cavitation model. In this study, a modified cavitation model considering the dissolved gas effect is developed to improve the prediction of TVC. Oxygen species transport is considered in both the liquid and gas phases, and the interfacial exchange of oxygen is described based on Henry's law mass-transfer relation, and the released oxygen partial pressure is incorporated into an effective cavitation threshold within the S-S framework. The model is first verified against a plug-discharge experiment for transient oxygen dissolution and then validated for cavitating flow over a Clark Y-11.7% hydrofoil. It accurately predicts dissolved-oxygen evolution and improves the reproduction of cavity morphology and the dominant lift-frequency response. The model is further applied to TVC over an elliptical NACA 16-020 hydrofoil, where the predictions show close agreement with experimental observations. The results indicate that oxygen exsolution is primarily concentrated near the cavity interface, where it increases the local partial pressure of non-condensable gas, modifies the effective cavitation threshold, thereby promoting downstream cavity persistence under the examined conditions. These findings demonstrate that dissolved gas plays an important physical role in the reliable prediction of TVC.

papers.title: Effects of nozzle geometry on the evolution of three-dimensional twin synthetic jets
papers.abstract: The effects of nozzle geometry on the evolution of three-dimensional in-phase twin synthetic jets issuing into a quiescent medium were investigated using improved delayed detached eddy simulation. Five orifice geometries were examined: circle, square, rectangle (two orientations, aspect ratio of 3), and ellipse (aspect ratio of 3), with a fixed spacing ratio of s/d=2, cross-sectional area, and actuation parameters. The Reynolds number, based on the spatially averaged jet exit velocity, was approximately 120 to ensure the generation of discrete vortex rings in the near field. The results show that nozzle geometry primarily influences the near-field behavior, while the combined jet demonstrates similarity in the far field. Rectangular and elliptical nozzles promote self-induced deformation and axis-switching of individual vortex rings near the exit before merging, thereby enhancing entrainment and shortening potential core lengths. However, within the merging region, the circular and square cases exhibit significantly stronger entrainment driven by axis-switching of the merged vortex rings. The merged rings undergo axis-switching before the combined point in all cases except for the rectangular nozzle with its major axis parallel to the symmetry line, for which axis-switching occurs after the combined point. Circular and square nozzles exhibit similar flow development owing to the rapid corner-induced deformation of the square rings near the exit, while rectangular and elliptical nozzles of similar orientation likewise display comparable behavior.

papers.title: Algebraic estimation of the three-dimensional radial energy spectrum in quasi-homogeneous and wall-bounded turbulence
papers.abstract: Approximating the three-dimensional radial energy spectrum based on one-dimensional directional data is challenging, as experiments and reduced datasets provide limited spatial information. Additionally, spectral analysis is often restricted directionally by rapid spatial variations in flow properties. Classical relations, such as Batchelor's, formally connect one-dimensional and three-dimensional spectra, but their practical application requires numerical differentiation, which heavily amplifies noise in discrete spectral data. In addition, Batchelor's formula relies on the assumption of isotropy. To avoid these limitations, this study assesses a simple algebraic mapping for radial spectrum estimation. The parametrization and validation of the proposed function are based on direct numerical simulation data of Kolmogorov flow. The approximate radial spectrum is compared against the exact spectrum computed from the full three-dimensional velocity field. In addition, the resulting turbulent kinetic energy and dissipation values are also examined. The results show that the approximate spectrum reproduces the energy-containing and intermediate scales well, preserving the total turbulent kinetic energy. Larger discrepancies appear at high wavenumbers, indicating reduced accuracy near the smallest resolved scales. The conversion is extended to wall-bounded flows by introducing a local mapping function dependent on the nondimensional wall distance. Furthermore, the practical utility of the approximation is demonstrated by fitting the data to Pope's model spectrum to extract the integral length scale across the channel height. Overall, the proposed approach provides a simple, robust, and differentiation-free method for radial spectrum approximation.

papers.title: Free-surface response and waveform reconstruction of granular landslide-generated impulse waves in the generation zone under mainstream–tributary confluence conditions
papers.abstract: Landslide-generated impulse waves are a typical secondary hydrodynamic hazard in mountainous river-type reservoirs and exhibit pronounced nonlinear characteristics. However, the mechanisms by which mainstream–tributary confluence flows modulate wave dynamics in the generation region remain insufficiently understood. To elucidate the wave-response characteristics of granular landslide-generated impulse waves under confluence conditions, three-dimensional physical model tests were conducted. Time–frequency analysis, empirical correlations, and free-surface waveform modeling were then combined to investigate wave types, spatial responses, and free-surface evolution in the wave-generation region. The impulse waves were dominated by nonlinear oscillatory and nonlinear transitional waves, with dominant frequencies concentrated at 1–2 Hz. Increasing landslide velocity, relative landslide thickness, and entry angle promoted the transition toward nonlinear transitional waves. The free-surface response exhibited pronounced directionality, with the largest amplitude occurring directly in front of the landslide, followed by the upstream region, and the smallest occurring downstream. Landslide impact primarily controls wave amplitude. At a 30° confluence angle, the discharge ratio has a limited effect on amplitude but modifies the directional crest–trough structure. Predictive formulas were developed for the first-wave amplitude and wave height by incorporating landslide dynamics and flow modulation. A Hann-windowed overlapping local Fourier expansion was further used to construct a free-surface waveform function, which reproduced the measured wave-train evolution well. These results clarify the coupled effects of landslide impact and confluence flow on wave generation and provide a framework for waveform representation, rapid prediction, and hazard assessment in complex river channels.

papers.title: Influence of baffle on fuel sloshing of partially filled fuel tanker semi-trailer: Application for enhancing rollover stability
papers.abstract: Liquid sloshing inside partially filled tanks shifts the fluid center, affecting the rollover stability of fuel tankers during cornering. This study investigates how gasoline filling level, turning radius, and vehicle speed affect rollover stability of a tanker semi-trailer under steady-state turning. Numerical simulations based on computational fluid dynamics and the volume of fluid method are conducted to compare two tanker configurations: a non-compartmentalized tank and one equipped with internal rigid baffles. Results demonstrate that the baffles significantly dampen liquid motion; the longitudinal translation of the fluid center in the compartmentalized tank is reduced by ten times compared to the non-compartmentalized design. Furthermore, the compartmentalized design exhibits superior damping, reaching a steady state of rollover moment significantly faster than the smooth tank, thereby preventing prolonged oscillations that threaten vehicle stability. The baffles increase the rollover lateral acceleration threshold by 31.1% at 50% filling level. The compartmentalized tank maintains rollover stability at higher filling ratios, with acceleration thresholds of 0.223g and 0.236g at 70% and 90% filling levels, respectively, and allows for stable cornering at velocities up to 4.5 m/s. These findings confirm that rigid baffles effectively enhance rollover safety, providing a quantitative basis for evaluating the stability limits of liquid-carrying vehicles.

papers.title: Evaluating k–ω shear stress transport closure model in physics-informed neural network for turbulent channel flow
papers.abstract: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) provides a mesh-free surrogate model that solves the governing partial differential equations (PDEs). In the present study, we develop a PINN for turbulent channel flow utilizing Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations with a k–ω shear stress transport closure model and evaluate the effect of specific dissipation rate (ω) stiffness and numerical simulation data usage on the trained model performance. It is shown that the stiffness of ω near the wall is challenging for the PINN to learn, which can result in large prediction errors in the whole domain. The stiffness has the highest impact on reducing the residual of ω PDE and fitting the boundary condition of ω at the wall. A case study using a two-dimensional converging–diverging channel shows that using 250 interior reference data points (0.25% of simulation mesh points), the relative L2 errors between PINN prediction and RANS result reduce to around 5% for velocity and pressure, around 10% for the turbulent kinetic energy, and around 20% for the specific dissipation rate by removing the ω-PDE residual. Such a result indicates that the ω values in the flow field can be effectively learned from other PDEs and sparse interior reference data with stiff ω values near the wall.

papers.title: Lateral-boundary interference in pack-ice channels of varying width during ship self-propulsion
papers.abstract: Lateral level-ice boundaries in a pack-ice channel constrain pack-ice motion and alter the hull-propeller local hydrodynamic environment, thereby inducing lateral-boundary interference during ship self-propulsion. This study investigates the Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering Container Ship in pack-ice channels of varying width. A coupled computational fluid dynamics–discrete element method is used to simulate self-propulsion at W/B = 1.4, 1.6, 2.0, and 2.5, where W and B denote channel width and ship breadth, respectively, together with an unconstrained condition without lateral level-ice boundaries. The lateral-boundary interference is examined from the perspectives of pack-ice motion, free-surface deformation, stern-flow characteristics, and the resulting propulsion response. Results show that narrower channels restrict the lateral clearing of pack-ice and promote ice accumulation along the hull, which strengthens the interaction among the hull, pack-ice, and lateral level-ice boundaries. As W/B increases, the total resistance coefficient decreases and approaches that of the unconstrained condition. The thrust deduction factor decreases, while the wake fraction increases slightly. A narrower channel shifts the self-propulsion point toward a higher propeller rotational speed. Compared with the unconstrained condition, the rotational speed at W/B = 1.4 increases from 4.80 to 5.77 rps, thrust increases from 22.04 to 37.73 N, and delivered power increases by approximately 110.3%. Propulsive efficiency decreases from 0.790 to 0.651. This study clarifies the influence of pack-ice channel width on lateral-boundary interference during ship self-propulsion and provides guidance for performance prediction and route planning in pack-ice channels.

papers.title: Aeroacoustics of the bogie region of high-speed trains in a tunnel: Dual-mode competition and harmonic enhancement
papers.abstract: To investigate the influence mechanism of the tunnel environment on aerodynamic noise in the bogie region of high-speed trains, numerical simulations based on the Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation model are performed on a simplified cavity-bluff coupled configuration. The flow and acoustic field characteristics under both open-air and tunnel conditions are compared and analyzed. The results show that, under the open-air condition, the flow in the bogie region is dominated by the primary vortex shedding mode originating from axles and rods. Under the tunnel condition, the energy proportion of this primary mode decreases, while a secondary flow mode is excited. This secondary mode originates from the coupling between the tunnel annular cavity mode and the bogie cavity standing-wave mode and generates the second and third harmonics through nonlinear fluid distortion. These mechanisms lead to a concentration of acoustic energy in the mid-to-high frequency range under the tunnel condition, resulting in significant narrowband peaks. Consequently, both the overall surface sound power level and the near-field overall sound pressure level in the bogie region are higher than those under the open-air condition.

papers.title: Direct simulation Monte Carlo based on the vibrationally state-resolved rotational relaxation model
papers.abstract: This study implements a vibrationally state-resolved rotational relaxation model within the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) framework. The model, which employs an exponential correlation function to characterize rotational energy transition probabilities, is integrated via two approaches: (i) the temperature-dependent rotational collision number Zrot(T) is constructed based on a set of pre-calculated vibrationally state-specific rotational relaxation times; (ii) instead of computing Zrot, the probabilities of the rotational–translational energy exchange are calculated directly in accordance with the vibrationally state-resolved rotational relaxation model based on the statistical inelastic cross section theory. Both approaches yield density and temperature profiles in good agreement with experimental normal shock data over Mach number 1.53–12.7, with the approach (i) offering a significant reduction in computational cost compared to the approach (ii). Compared to the classical Parker and Boyd models, both approaches provide improved predictions of rotational relaxation rates at elevated temperatures. Another contribution of this work is the identification of the precise non-equilibrium regimes where the use of the vibrationally state-resolved model becomes essential. The two-dimensional flat-plate simulations reveal that under conditions of strong vibrational non-equilibrium, neglecting vibrational excitation results in systematically underpredicted rotational–translational relaxation rates, leading to substantial differences in the flow field. In such regimes, the vibrationally state-resolved formulation is required to accurately capture the internal energy relaxation dynamics. These findings provide a practical framework for selecting the appropriate level of modeling detail in DSMC simulations of high-enthalpy flows, enabling a balanced trade-off between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency for engineering applications.

papers.title: The interaction noise reduction performance of the wavy leading-edge airfoil in the high and moderate subsonic flow field
papers.abstract: It has been verified that airfoils with a wavy structure can reduce interference noise at inflow velocities below 100 m/s. Limited by the excessive background noise of high-speed wind tunnels, no existing research indicates that wavy-airfoil configurations maintain noise reduction capability for freestream velocities above 100 m/s. This study establishes an efficient implicit lower–upper symmetric Gauss–Seidel transient density-based solver in the OpenFOAM framework. Then, the cylinder-combined airfoil configuration is adopted as the research object for interaction noise, where a cylinder with surface grooves is used to adjust the intensity of the incoming flow disturbance source. The key findings are as follows: Under the inflow condition of 0.6 Ma, the configuration of wavy-leading-edge (WLE) airfoil paired with an upstream grooved cylinder achieves the optimal noise-reduction performance. Compared with the smooth-cylinder/standard-airfoil configuration, it yields noise reductions of 8.94 dB in peak noise and 4.44 dB in overall sound pressure level (OASPL), and these values that are the lowest among the four configurations. The configuration with only an upstream grooved cylinder paired with a downstream standard airfoil achieves noise reductions of 5.83 dB in peak noise and 3.94 dB in OASPL. The wavy-airfoil/smooth-cylinder configuration yields no noise reduction, although it still produces a noticeable spanwise truncation of turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) in the vicinity. Under the inflow condition of 0.4 Ma, the grooves on the upstream cylinder have almost no effect on far-field noise, while the WLE of the downstream airfoil shows a remarkable noise reduction effect. The two configurations incorporating the wavy airfoil both achieve a peak noise reduction exceeding 11 dB and an OASPL reduction of more than 6 dB. Finally, the influence of the wavy airfoil on the flow field in the surrounding region is further analyzed based on the distribution characteristics of TKE in the flow field between the cylinder and the airfoil.

papers.title: Effects of inert gas addition on detonation initiation in a modeled rotating detonation engine
papers.abstract: Due to the unresolved complexity of detonation initiation, which hinders a complete understanding of wave modes, this study investigates inert gas addition in a modeled rotating detonation engine configuration to quantify how the chemical sensitivity of the mixture governs initiation dynamics. High-resolution two-dimensional simulations of hydrogen/air mixtures with inert gas addition are conducted by solving the reactive Navier–Stokes equations with a detailed chemical mechanism. This work shows that forward- and backward-propagating detonation waves originate through different mechanisms, and clarifies how inert gas dilution modifies the hot-spot-driven backward initiation process and thereby controls the initial detonation mode. The results show that with increasing dilution, hot-spot formation near the inner wall is suppressed, causing the propagation mode to transition sequentially from two counter-rotating waves to a single wave and finally to a state without detonation. Two failure routes of the backward-propagating detonation wave are identified. At moderate dilution, a small detonation wave forms from the wall-induced hot spot but decouples into a leading shock and a deflagration wave. At stronger dilution, the hot spot itself is suppressed, so the backward-propagating wave is not initiated. Analysis shows that maximum thermicity is more strongly associated with the observed initiation-mode transitions than induction time within a certain range. The critical mixture exothermicity can therefore serve as a preliminary criterion for determining the existence of the backward-propagating detonation wave under the present conditions. These findings provide a physical basis for using inert gas addition to regulate the initial detonation propagation mode in rotating detonation engines.

papers.title: Modeling the dynamics of surfactant-laden droplets in oscillatory shear flow
papers.abstract: The combination of oscillatory shear and surfactants provides a powerful and versatile strategy for manipulating droplet behavior in microfluidic systems. In this study, the deformation and breakup of clean and surfactant-laden droplets in oscillatory shear are investigated using a hybrid lattice Boltzmann-finite difference method. We first examine the effects of the oscillatory period (controlled by the period-controlling parameter n), the confinement ratio Wc, and the Reynolds number Re on droplet deformation during a steady oscillatory period. Under these influencing parameters, we quantitatively analyze the effects of the phase lag between the maximum wall velocity and the time at which the maximum deformation parameter Df,max occurs and the surfactant distribution along the droplet interface on Df,max. We then investigate the effect of n on the critical effective capillary number Cae,c for droplet breakup in both clean and surfactant-laden systems. The results show that Cae,c decreases as n increases, and that Cae,c is smaller in the clean system than in the surfactant-laden system. These findings not only provide fundamental insights into the interplay between oscillatory shear and surfactants but also offer practical guidelines for applications ranging from microfluidic droplet manipulation and emulsification to enhanced oil recovery, where precise control over droplet deformation and breakup is essential.

papers.title: Mechanism-oriented numerical investigation of dynamic stall control in a vertical-axis wind turbine under real-time pitch control
papers.abstract: Dynamic stall severely limits the aerodynamic efficiency and load characteristics of vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs). Although real-time pitch control has been experimentally demonstrated to be effective, its underlying unsteady flow evolution and physical control mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. This work conducts a mechanism-oriented numerical investigation into VAWTs under real-time pitch control. High-fidelity numerical simulations are performed to investigate the evolution of dynamic stall under real-time pitch control. The high-order central moment of pressure and the modulated location of peak pressure are employed to quantitatively characterize dynamic stall vortex (DSV) initiation and shedding. These results at two representative tip-speed ratios (TSRs) reveal regime-dependent control mechanisms. At the design condition (TSR = 3.2), pitch control moderates dynamic stall by weakening leading-edge separation, extending the positive-torque region, and enhancing downwind power extraction, which raises the cycle-averaged torque coefficient from 0.0719 to 0.1327, representing a substantial increase of approximately 84.6%. At the off-design condition (TSR = 1.5), pitching suppresses deep dynamic stall by reducing effective angle-of-attack overshoot, attenuating DSV development, delaying vortex shedding, and mitigating vortex–blade interactions. The average torque coefficient increases from 0.0260 to 0.1202, corresponding to a 362.3% improvement, with significantly reduced fluctuations. These findings demonstrate that real-time pitch control improves aerodynamic performance by regulating the effective angle of attack and modifying DSV evolution in a regime-dependent manner, thereby improving the physical understanding of dynamic stall control in VAWTs.

papers.title: Near-wall turbulence physics and the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes/large-eddy simulations transition in wall-modeled hybrid simulations
papers.abstract: Near-wall turbulent motions are organized within a thin inner-scaled region, posing a fundamental challenge for hybrid Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes/large-eddy simulation (RANS/LES): the modeled-to-resolved transition must allow these motions to develop while providing sufficient spatial resolution. Here, we investigate this transition from a turbulence-physics perspective using a shear-stress transport-based wall-modeled hybrid RANS/LES framework with a direct numerical simulation (DNS) informed turbulence-resolution measure. At friction Reynolds number Reτ=550, systematic variation of the LES-like transition location shows that moving it from y+ = 14 to 10 progressively improves the near-wall streamwise Reynolds stress, high-wavenumber wall-pressure content, and resolved coherent structures. The DNS peak of streamwise Reynolds stress at y+≈15 provides a physical reference, but the LES-like branch must be established upstream of this peak to allow the resolved turbulence to develop. Complementary RANS-end tests identify two distinct failure modes: insufficient resolved turbulent energy when the RANS branch terminates early, and delayed activation of scale-resolving turbulence when the RANS region extends into the buffer layer. For the cases examined, these results support yRANS+<5 with rk1≤0.5 and yLES+≈10 with rk2=0.2. The same wall-unit-based requirements are then applied at Reτ = 1000 and 2000 without transition-parameter retuning and retain good agreement with DNS. The results show that turbulence resolution and transition location should be treated as coupled physical requirements for wall-modeled hybrid simulations.

papers.title: Cavity disturbance and impact modeling during water entry of a slender object with an inner flow diversion structure
papers.abstract: The interaction of a passive jet guided through an inner flow diversion orifice of a water entry object with the cavity wall is a very interesting phenomenon. It can effectively reduce water entry impact by modifying the flow pattern without relying on external active control. In this study, we experimentally investigate the cavity disturbance, jet behavior, and impact force of a cylinder with a Y-shaped diversion structure impacting a quiescent free surface. The orifice allows part of the incoming liquid to be transformed into inner jets that induce cavity wall disturbance with different modes at different Froude numbers. The jet impact on the cavity wall induces the formation of an unsteady, chaotic cavity. It is worth noting that the stability of cavity development is related to both the Froude number and the diversion angle. We theoretically analyze the impact dynamics of the diversion structure based on added mass modeling and momentum transfer. It indicates that the orifice reduces the growth rate of effective added mass by tuning the momentum exchange path of the frontal liquid. A simplified model based on the dynamic pressure scale and the momentum flux of the internal diversion jet is also established. This model explains the main order of magnitude and variation trend of the peak acceleration difference between the solid model and the diversion model. The results confirm that the force reduction effect is due to the momentum flux release scale of the internal jet rather than the change in dynamic pressure area.

papers.title: Asynchronous transport of heat and silica with fracture-aperture feedback in enhanced geothermal systems
papers.abstract: In enhanced geothermal systems, the differences in propagation timescales between temperature and reactive-solute disturbances, together with their effects on fracture-aperture feedback, remain insufficiently quantified. This study employs a three-dimensional thermo-hydro-mechanical-chemical coupled model and uses the 50% normalized response time to quantitatively characterize the propagation differences between temperature and silica concentration disturbances, followed by an analysis of fracture-aperture evolution and its feedback on transport. The results show that, although the two disturbances propagate along the same preferential fracture pathways, they exhibit distinctly different propagation timescales. As the distance from the injection well increases from 50 to 300 m, the thermo-chemical response lag increases from 2.00 to 26.22 years. This time lag allows low-concentration fluid to continuously drive silica dissolution before the temperature reaches 50% response, with the chemical aperture at all locations reaching more than 98% of its value at 40 years. Fracture-aperture evolution also exhibits pronounced spatial variability: the reduction in mechanical closure is more evident near the injection well, whereas the chemical aperture increases with distance from the injection well. Under fully dynamic fracture-aperture conditions, silica concentration propagation is consistently delayed throughout the 50–300 m range, whereas the effect on temperature propagation changes from retardation near the injection well to enhancement farther downstream, with the feedback direction switching between 150 and 175 m. These results indicate that the separation of propagation timescales between temperature and silica concentration leads to earlier fracture-aperture evolution and subsequently affects heat and solute transport.

papers.title: Investigation on the influence of Mach disk on the impact performance of under-expanded carbon dioxide flash boiling jet
papers.abstract: The kinetic energy and the phase-change refrigeration effect generated during the process of high-pressure liquid carbon dioxide (CO2) sprayed into a lower ambient pressure enable the CO2 jet to be widely applied in the cutting and refrigeration fields. The intense phase-change at the nozzle outlet region induces the generation of a downstream Mach disk, which subsequently affects the jet impact performance. This study comprehensively uses high-speed photography, numerical simulation, and impact experiments to analyze the influence mechanism of the Mach disk structure on the impact performance of the CO2 jet. The experimental results show that the position of the Mach disk is positively correlated with the throat diameter of the nozzle under a constant operation condition. The convergent–divergent nozzle can induce the liquid CO2 to undergo a phase-change inside the nozzle in advance, thereby reducing the static pressure at the nozzle outlet and inhibiting the formation of the Mach disk. For the under-expanded state of a CO2 jet, the liquid mass fraction and velocity of the CO2 downstream of the Mach disk rapidly decrease, the pressure increases, and the temperature first increases and then decreases. When the under-expanded CO2 jet impacts the target plate, a Mach disk structure exists in the free flow field, and a plate shock wave structure forms on the target surface. The distance between the two is a key factor affecting the impact performance of the CO2 jet. In the current research, the Mach disk is located 7.4 mm downstream of the nozzle outlet. The impact performance of the under-expanded CO2 jet within a target distance of less than 10 mm increases as the target distance increases. However, when the target distance exceeds 10 mm, the impact performance of the CO2 jet drops sharply. This indicates that the Mach disk in the free flow field and the plate shock wave in the impact flow field jointly determine the impact performance of the CO2 jet. When the positions of the Mach disk and plate shock wave overlap, the influence of the Mach disk can be ignored regarding the impact performance of the jet, and the impact performance of the jet rapidly decreases after the two separate.

papers.title: Oscillatory Oldroyd-B flow in rigid planar channels: Reciprocal-theorem analysis and effective Womersley scaling
papers.abstract: We apply the Lorentz reciprocal theorem to derive closed-form analytical expressions for the flow rate amplitude in oscillatory, pressure-driven flow of an Oldroyd-B viscoelastic fluid through rigid planar channels. Two dimensionless groups govern the response: the Deborah number De=ωλ and strain amplitude γ0=vc/(ωh0), where vc=h02Δpa/(μℓ) is the Hagen–Poiseuille velocity scale. Their product is the amplitude Weissenberg number Wiamp=Deγ0=λvc/h0; when Wiamp≪1, the Oldroyd-B constitutive law linearizes to the Jeffreys form, characterized by the complex viscosity ratio ξ=(1+iDe)/(1+iβDe). At O(Wo2), the reciprocal theorem gives Qa=(ξ/12)(1−iξWo2/10) for a straight channel, recovering the Newtonian result exactly as De→0. The full arbitrary-Wo solution follows by replacing the real Womersley number Wo with the complex effective value Woeff=Woξ in the standard Newtonian solution; this is algebraically identical to the frequency-response function of Casanellas and Ortiń and is independently verified against a finite-difference solution. The reciprocal-theorem formulation additionally provides a compact O(Wo2) expression and its nonuniform-channel generalization, accurate to within 5% for Wo≲1.5/|ξ|1/2. The positive imaginary part of ξ produces a flow rate phase lead relative to the driving pressure, reflecting elastic energy storage and release by the polymer. For slowly varying channels, rheological and geometric factors separate multiplicatively at O(Wo2), enabling their leading-order effects to be assessed independently. All results apply within the small-amplitude regime Wiamp≪1.

papers.title: Inertial effects on flow dynamics near a moving contact line
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of inertia in moving contact lines using experiments, theoretical analysis, and numerical simulations. Experiments are conducted using a plate immersion configuration over a wide range of Reynolds numbers from O(10−3) to O(10). Flow configurations and quantitative measurements are obtained using high-speed imaging and particle image velocimetry. The streamfunction contours reconstructed from the experimental velocity fields are compared with the viscous modulated wedge solution (viscous-MWS) and inertial-MWS theory. Experimental observations show that the streamfunction contours agree well with viscous predictions at low Reynolds numbers; however, systematic deviations emerge as the Reynolds number increases. The inertial-MWS theory, an inertial extension of the Huh and Scriven framework, accounts for these deviations, but only within a narrow range of Reynolds numbers 10−1<Re<1. At higher Reynolds numbers, inertial theory fails to accurately capture the deviations in the streamfunction contours observed in the experiments. Moreover, simulations conducted using the volume of fluid method support our findings, exhibiting deviations in streamfunction contours consistent with experimental observations. We demonstrate that inertia does not fundamentally alter the underlying flow configuration but instead induces a systematic deviation in the streamfunction contours. At finite Re, the interfacial speed transitions from a nearly constant value in the viscous regime to a monotonic decay along the interface. These findings expose the need for more sophisticated models of moving contact lines.

papers.title: Linear perturbation analysis of flow over a flat plate with an elliptic leading edge
papers.abstract: Linear perturbation analysis is used to investigate the impact of leading-edge geometry on disturbance amplification, and a flat plate is adopted to eliminate other geometric factors, e.g., thickness, camber, etc. The two-dimensional (2D) base flow is first examined across a range of Reynolds numbers (Re) and leading-edge aspect ratios (AR). The threshold for the formation of a laminar separation bubble (LSB) on the AR-Re plane is identified, with the critical AR increasing monotonically with Re. At Re=300, the optimal energy gain exhibits two competing branches: a three-dimensional (3D) steady branch at inflow frequency ω=0 and finite spanwise wavenumber β, and a 2D unsteady branch at β=0 and finite ω. For higher AR with attached base flow, the dominant response is the 3D steady branch, and its optimal perturbation structure and downstream evolution are consistent with the lift-up mechanism, while finite-frequency responses are weaker. For lower AR with an LSB, the dominant response is the 2D unsteady branch, which exhibits strong finite-frequency amplification over a broad frequency range and downstream wave-packet structures concentrated along the separated shear layer, consistent with Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. A transitional regime is identified near AR≈0.6, where the 3D steady and 2D unsteady branches attain comparable gains, and a 3D unsteady mode with mixed features is observed to be the most energetic one. As Re increases, the crossover between the 2D unsteady and 3D steady branches shifts to lower AR. These results demonstrate that the leading-edge geometry dominates the amplification of free-stream disturbance through its influence on leading-edge separation.

papers.title: Shape optimization to suppress the lift oscillation for a stationary cylinder at low Reynolds numbers: A low-cost lift oscillation intensity proxy objective function
papers.abstract: Shape optimization can suppress the lift oscillations generated by the fluid flowing over a stationary cylinder at low Reynolds numbers. By constructing the objective function based on linear stability analysis or resolvent analysis, the calculation of unsteady flow fields in traditional schemes can be avoided. However, additional calculations of the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix or singular value decomposition of the resolvent operator are still required on the basis of the steady-state base flow, resulting in high computational costs of the objective function and affecting the optimization efficiency. To address this, this study proposes a low-cost proxy objective function for the intensity of lift oscillations. By establishing a mathematical relationship between the average resistance and the integral of positive lift in a single cycle, the drag coefficient in the subcritical Reynolds number regime is used as the objective function. Thus, only the steady laminar solution at subcritical Reynolds numbers and the stress integral on the cylinder surface need to be calculated. The class function/shape function transformation technique is selected as the shape parameterization method, and the Adaptive Design of Experiments algorithm is used to optimize the objective function. The results show that through shape optimization, the vortex shedding intensity can be effectively suppressed in two-dimensional flow, reducing the amplitude of the lift coefficient by more than 59%. At the same time, the flow stability is improved, and lift oscillations are completely eliminated within the Reynolds number range of 47–60.

papers.title: Retraction: “Deflection law in trajectory of large caliber conical-nosed projectile at high-speed oblique water entry” [Phys. Fluids 37 , 034126 (2025)]
Numerical investigation of enhanced vortex induced vibration energy harvesting of a circular cylinder using a rotating control rod
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of an upstream rotating control rod on the vortex-induced vibration energy harvesting of a circular cylinder at Reynolds number 10 000, using a combination of a modified direct forcing immersed boundary and a large eddy simulation technique. Specifically, we analyze the effects of the control rod rotation rate, the gap ratio, and the damping ratio on cylinder response, hydrodynamic forces, wake dynamics, and energy harvesting efficiency. The results show that the rotating control rod significantly modifies wake and enhances the vibration response in a wide range of reduced velocity. The optimum energy extraction efficiency occurs at a control rod rotation rate of 1 and a gap ratio of 0.2, achieving a harvesting efficiency of 43%, an improvement of approximately 15% over the passive case, and double the efficiency of a bare cylinder. Moderate control rod rotation promotes coherent vortex shedding and maximizes oscillation amplitude and fluid to structure energy transfer, while higher rotation rates destabilize the wake and reduce energy harvesting performance. Although very low damping produces the highest oscillation amplitudes, the highest harvesting efficiency is obtained at a moderate damping ratio of 0.025–0.05, indicating an optimal balance between vibration response and energy extraction. In general, the upstream rotating control rod greatly enhances vibration response and energy harvesting by manipulating wake interaction and broadening the lock-in region.

papers.title: Fluid-mechanical mechanisms of oblique vehicle water entry through a near-free-surface explosive bubble
papers.abstract: High-speed water entry at small oblique angles is often accompanied by asymmetric nose wetting, transient impact loads, and pitching moments, which may cause trajectory deflection, tail slap, and motion instability. This study proposes an active method for improving water-entry stability by using an underwater explosion near the free surface to generate a bubble before entry. A numerical model of a near-free-surface explosive bubble is first established and validated against experimental observations. The model is then coupled with an oblique water-entry model to examine the effects of the explosive bubble on attitude response and flow-field evolution. The results show that the expanding bubble raises and inclines the local free surface, shortens the initial asymmetric nose-loading interval, and changes the effective entry angle. Passage from water into the bubble then interrupts liquid loading, while re-entry through the opposite bubble interface produces a pitching moment that partly offsets the initial slamming-induced moment. Compared with calm-water entry, the explosive bubble reduces the post-entry pitch-angle variation by 58.8%, the initial peak pitching-moment coefficient by 36.0%, and the main drag coefficient peak by 13.2%. Nose shape changes the same loading sequence. The flat nose gives the smallest pitch-angle variation, but its axial-force peak reaches 30.6 kN, whereas the baseline nose has a smaller axial impact and a larger pitch excursion.

papers.title: Free-surface breaking dynamics and morphology of waves generated by the semi-submerged wedge-shaped body
papers.abstract: The breaking waves at the bow and stern represent a fundamental free-surface phenomenon involving violent interface deformation, air entrainment, and strong two-phase coupling. The temporal evolution and spatial distribution of wave breaking are fundamental to understanding water-air mixing flows around ships. The present study adopts the square stern of high-speed ships as a reference and selects a wedge model as the research object in order to investigate the characteristics of interface breaking and the flow morphology. The free-surface waves around the wedge model were measured using a binocular vision system. A systematic analysis was conducted to investigate the impact of various parameters on the flow patterns in the bow and stern regions. The parameters investigated included draft depth (D), stern width (B), attack angle (α), and draft Froude number FrD=U/gD. The results show that the wave profiles have strong similarity when FrD is chosen as the dominant parameter. The associated parameters of FrD and geometric parameters are found to have a significant influence on the morphological characteristics of the waves.

papers.title: Rotation-enhanced vortex-induced vibration of the elliptic cylinder
papers.abstract: Unlocking the rotational degree of freedom (DOF) fundamentally alters the vortex-induced vibration characteristics of an elliptic cylinder. In this study, the immersed boundary lattice Boltzmann flux solver is applied to investigate multi-DOF fluid–structure interactions of elliptic cylinders with aspect ratios from 1.5 to 2.5. A “high-amplitude, suppressed-force” paradox is identified: releasing the rotational DOF significantly enhances the transverse vibration amplitude and broadens the lock-in bandwidth, while reducing the fluctuating lift. This behavior is attributed to the modified force–motion coupling during the transient growth stage, where weakened acceleration-correlated lift and sustained favorable lift–velocity phasing enable greater hydrodynamic work accumulation. The rotational motion also introduces an alternating imbalance in boundary-vorticity flux between the upper and lower surfaces, modifying the near-body wake organization while retaining the basic 2S shedding mode. For slender cylinders, an ultra-low-frequency response branch emerges beyond conventional lock-in. The loss of effective torsional stiffness indicates a rotational static divergence onset associated with this transition. These findings reveal the role of rotational freedom in energy transfer and stability of multi-DOF fluid–structure interactions.

papers.title: Richtmyer–Meshkov instability on high-temperature non-equilibrium air pairs
papers.abstract: The influence of high-temperature non-equilibrium effects, induced by strong-shock waves, on the Richtmyer–Meshkov instability (RMI) remains less understood. In this study, the RMI at an air interface with an initial temperature difference is numerically investigated for Mach numbers 6.0–8.0 across three thermochemistry models: frozen (FR) flow, thermal non-equilibrium (TN) flow, and thermochemical non-equilibrium (TCN) flow. The vibrational excitation in the TN model and the combined vibrational excitation and chemical reactions in the TCN model cause the interface velocity and the amplitude growth rate to deviate significantly from the FR cases. Particularly, at the strongest shock wave (Ma = 8.0), relative to the FR baseline (2725.0 m/s), the TN and TCN models lower the interface velocity to 2593.8 and 2487.7 m/s, respectively. The amplitude growth rate, initially 130.2 m/s, increases to 144.3 m/s with TN but decreases to 119.6 m/s with TCN. A modified compressible model incorporating an enhanced shock-proximity effect is proposed, which accurately predicts RMI growth in FR, TN, and TCN flows. The suppressed density contrast is the primary mechanism mitigating RMI growth at high Mach numbers in TCN flows. Spectral analysis reveals that fast chemical reactions reduce the asymmetry of the evolved interface. These findings underscore the critical role of TCN in modulating RMI growth in high-enthalpy, strong-shock environments.

papers.title: Scheme for backward-transport acoustic guided modes in water microfluidics
papers.abstract: Backward acoustic guidance, in which phase and time-averaged energy flux have opposite axial directions, offers an additional degree of freedom for acoustofluidic field design. A frequency-general water-immersed transverse waveguide scheme containing locally resonant double-negative (DNG) cells is derived from the linear acoustic equations. The derivation gives an invariant phase–power criterion, B=kzPz<0, where kz is the axial phase constant and Pz is cross section-integrated axial acoustic power. Lorentz parameters are calibrated so that the analytical DNG target reproduces the effective constitutive values used at the representative 1 MHz verification point. An independently rebuilt finite-element model of the 3×3 effective-DNG guide yields a tracked backward branch over 0.99–1.03 MHz: kz<0, Pz>0, and the finite-difference group velocity is positive (184–314 m s−1). A three-level mesh study (6112–33 040 domain elements) changes the representative phase constant by at most 0.38% relative to the fine mesh, and changing the eigenvalue-search shift from 0.30 to 0.55 m−1 changes it by less than 1.2×10−10 rad m−1. In addition, a silicon–polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)–water membrane–cavity unit is specified as a reproducible fluid–structure interaction (FSI) baseline. The results establish a finite-element dispersive branch in the effective-medium guide and provide a physically parameterized route for subsequent unit-cell retrieval and periodic-array analysis.

papers.title: Flow-induced vibration characteristics of a square cylinder with normal slit offset at low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: Flow-induced vibration (FIV) of bluff bodies is a critical fluid–structure interaction problem, with square cylinders susceptible to large amplitude responses due to their sharp corners. The present study numerically investigates the FIV characteristics of a two-dimensional elastically mounted square cylinder with a normal slit at a low Reynolds number of 170. The study covers a parametric set of calculations including six different slit offset positions (−0.3≤δ/D≤+0.3), measured from the geometric center of the cylinder and the effect of slit width (0≤S/D≤0.4) on vibration and frequency responses, and the associated flow dynamics. Furthermore, a range of reduced velocities (3≤Ur≤30) is considered to characterize the vortex-induced vibration (VIV) and galloping responses. The results show that the normal slit induces periodic suction and blowing, thereby modifying the wake dynamics and FIV response. The results suggest that normal slit can suppress or increase the FIV response depending on the slit offset position. Offsetting the slit toward the front stagnation point (δ/D<0) maintains the enhanced VIV response of the centered slit case (δ/D=0) and suppresses galloping, while offsetting it toward the rear stagnation point (δ/D>0) weakens VIV and enhances galloping. In the VIV regime, δ/D<0 sustains strong near-wake vortex formation through enhanced slit-wake interaction, whereas δ/D>0 shifts the vortex formation downstream and reduces the fluctuating lift. For δ/D<0, the response transitions from galloping to the secondary VIV regime. Wavelet analysis further shows that δ/D<0 strengthens wake mode (WM) dominance, whereas δ/D>0 weakens WM dominance and enhances structural mode control, promoting large amplitude galloping.

papers.title: The role of thermodynamic forcing in direct numerical simulations of turbulence–cloud microphysics interactions
papers.abstract: Particle-based direct numerical simulation (DNS) is a promising approach to study microscale turbulence–cloud–aerosol interactions. Such DNS models require external forcing to sustain turbulent fluctuations in the momentum and thermodynamic fields. Although momentum forcing is common in particle-based DNS studies of atmospheric clouds, thermodynamic forcing has not gained enough attention. This study implements external forcing in the thermodynamic fields of temperature and vapor mixing ratio in addition to momentum forcing. The forcing terms are constructed in the Fourier space using a band of low wavenumbers. The turbulent flow of air is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic. Aerosol particles and cloud droplets are tracked in Lagrangian fashion, with processes of condensation, evaporation, activation, and deactivation considered together. The impacts of thermodynamic forcing on entrainment of ambient air into the cloud and subsequent turbulent mixing are examined. It is found that thermodynamic forcing sustains fluctuations in the thermodynamic fields and reduces the mean temperature, water vapor mixing ratio, and supersaturation. Although thermodynamic forcing is applied at large scales only, it influences the energy at all scales by interacting with latent heat change. The probability distributions of forced thermodynamic fields are negatively skewed with kurtosis values larger than three. Further analysis of microphysical properties shows that thermodynamic forcing enhances evaporation and deactivation with broadening of particle size distributions. The activation and deactivation regimes are fluctuation-dominated if thermodynamic forcing is present as opposed to being mean-dominated only when thermodynamic forcing is not applied.

papers.title: Thermal transport enhancement in a crescent-shaped cavity using MoS2–SiC hybrid nanofluid
papers.abstract: Nanofluids are often employed in cavity-based systems, which are common in industrial and electronic applications where efficient convective heat transfer is needed. Among these configurations, crescent-shaped cavities introduce complex flow behavior that can influence thermal performance. Therefore, the present study investigated the flow of a MoS2–SiC hybrid nanofluid inside a crescent-shaped cavity under the influence of a magnetic field. The cavity contains triangular heat sources, and hot and cold walls are used to control the temperature. MoS2 acts as an exothermic element to dissipate heat within the outer layer of the wall, whereas silicon carbide acts as an endothermic element to conduct heat around triangular structures. These nanomaterials combine to provide efficient heat transfer. A mathematical model is developed using momentum, energy, and concentration equations and solved via the finite element method through COMSOL Multiphysics. The effects of the Reynolds number (Re), Hartmann number (Ha), and Peclet number (Pe) on the velocity, temperature, and concentration are also studied. The results show that higher Re strengthens convective flow, leading to stronger vortex structures and enhancing heat transfer. In contrast, a larger value of Ha reduces the fluid velocity and consequently decreases thermal transport. Additionally, the quantitative results include the average Nusselt number (Nuavg), Sherwood number (Shavg) and kinetic energy. Their results revealed that both Nuavg and Shavg increased with increasing Re, resulting in increased heat and mass transfer. However, Pe has a small effect on Nu but significantly increases Sh, as it enhances the concentration gradient. The novelty lies in combining MoS2–SiC hybrid nanofluid with a crescent-shaped cavity and triangular heat-generating elements. The results demonstrate that cavity curvature and internal heat-source geometry can substantially modify the vortex structure and transport characteristics, which are useful for thermal-management applications.

papers.title: Methodological case study on saccular aneurysm initiation mechanisms using patient-specific models
papers.abstract: A computational investigation of the hemodynamic mechanisms underlying saccular aneurysm (SA) initiation at the circle of Willis is presented. The study incorporates 3-dimensional patient-specific and idealized geometries, laminar flow, non-Newtonian blood rheology, fully coupled fluid–structure interaction, and physiologically realistic Windkessel-based boundary conditions. The developed methodology is validated against available experimental and analytical data. By integrating findings from previous studies, the work aims to provide a generalized assessment of aneurysm initiation and the associated hemodynamics. The significance of various parameters is evaluated by analyzing distinct SA at the anterior communicating and middle cerebral arteries. Vascular geometric abnormalities, such as absent or hypoplastic arterial segments, produced anatomical asymmetry and directed high mass flow rates toward the aneurysm ostium, leading to localized flow impingement and widespread wall shear stress regions. Both cases demonstrated elevated oscillatory shear index, large circumferential wall shear stress gradients, and persistently low aneurysm formation indicator, suggesting that these parameters function as supportive hemodynamic markers of aneurysm initiation. In contrast, vorticity and relative residence time exhibited case-dependent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that a combination of vascular abnormalities and characteristic hemodynamic disturbances can be used to identify regions susceptible to aneurysm initiation.

papers.title: High-fidelity and generalizable wake flow prediction in wind farms with a physics-informed domain-adversarial neural network
papers.abstract: With the increasing scale of wind farms, wake effects have become increasingly important for turbine safety and power generation efficiency. Accurate wake modeling for yaw control and layout optimization requires low computational cost, high prediction accuracy, and robust generalization across operating conditions. In this study, a physics-informed domain-adversarial neural network (PI-DANN) is proposed for wind turbine wake prediction. The incompressible Navier–Stokes equations and the vorticity equation are incorporated into the training objective to enforce physical consistency and improve the representation of wake flow structures. Meanwhile, a domain classifier coupled with a gradient reversal layer is introduced to extract condition-invariant flow features and enhance cross-condition generalization. The model is validated against light detection and ranging measurements and computational fluid dynamics simulations under multiple operating conditions. Compared with a fully connected neural network and a domain-adversarial neural network, PI-DANN reduces the prediction error by 15.42% and 2.71%, respectively. This work provides a practical wake modeling framework that supports intelligent control and digital operation of wind farms.

papers.title: Influence of the restitution coefficient on the vortex-induced vibration of a near-wall cylinder experiencing wall collision
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of the restitution coefficient on the coupled vortex-induced vibration (VIV) and wall impact dynamics of a near-wall cylinder with a small gap ratio of 0.1. A two-dimensional fluid–structure interaction (FSI) model is established at Re = 150 for an elastically mounted cylinder undergoing pure transverse motion. Employing an overset grid scheme and a velocity reversal impact model, the structural vibration, impact loads, hydrodynamic forces, and wake evolution are systematically analyzed over a reduced velocity range of 2 ≤ Ur ≤ 14 under three restitution coefficients: b = 0, 0.5, and 1.0. The wall confinement substantially suppresses vortex development on the gap side, leading to two distinct wake regimes: a no-shedding (NS) mode for Ur = 2–5 and a single-sided shedding (SS) mode for Ur = 6–14. The NS–SS transition triggers a sharp increase in the root mean square vibration amplitude at Ur = 6 and forms a well-defined lock-in regime for Ur = 6–12. Continuous cylinder-wall collision occurs within the lock-in range, whereas collision is absent at low reduced velocities (Ur = 2–5) due to insufficient vibration amplitude and at high reduced velocities (Ur = 13–14) owing to the elevated time-averaged equilibrium position and attenuated vibration response. The mean collision force reaches its maximum at Ur = 10. The wall impact process is characterized by gap fluid compression, instantaneous velocity reversal, and inertia-dominated pressure and lift pulses, followed by post-collision high-frequency velocity oscillations and hysteresis. An increase in the restitution coefficient strengthens impact intensity, amplifies high-frequency dynamic responses, and prolongs the hysteresis stage, while exerting a negligible influence on the wake topology and low-frequency VIV characteristics. The studied FSI system presents a typical dual-timescale coupled behavior, where the global dynamic response is dominated by single-sided vortex excitation and weakly modulated by collision-induced nonlinearities.

papers.title: Flow reconfiguration and vorticity transport mechanisms of an active Gurney flap under airfoil dynamic stall
papers.abstract: An active Gurney flap (AGF) strategy based on time-domain phase control is proposed to mitigate wake expansion and performance degradation caused by fixed Gurney flaps in deep stall. For a pitching NACA 0012 airfoil, unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations using an arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian formulation and three-layer nested overset grids are combined with control-volume vorticity-transport analysis. Benchmark and experimental comparisons support numerical fidelity. Among the tested cases, 18°–22° provides a comparatively favorable actuation window. The AGF establishes kinematic phase locking by transiently modifying the trailing-edge Kutta condition and generating a strong trailing-edge secondary vortex. Its upwash lifts the dynamic-stall-vortex core away from the surface, retards downstream convection and dissipation, and promotes vortex residence over the mid-to-aft chord. Consequently, maximum lift increases by 9%, whereas Cycle-averaged aerodynamic damping decreases by only 3.9%. During deep stall, AGF-induced reconstruction of the chordwise pressure gradient suppresses reverse boundary-vorticity generation and increases peak circulation from 1.39 to 1.48. These findings elucidate the vorticity-budget mechanism underlying active trailing-edge control of dynamic stall.

papers.title: Electrophoresis of a polymeric Brinkman droplet in a cylindrical pore
papers.abstract: Electrophoresis of a nondeforming polymeric Brinkman droplet with a constant surface potential in an uncharged cylindrical pore is investigated theoretically. The droplet is modeled as a polymer-containing fluid inclusion whose internal flow is resisted by a Debye–Büeche–Brinkman (DBB) hydrodynamic drag. An analytical relation converting the polymer-induced internal drag into an equivalent Newtonian viscosity is derived. A patched pseudo-spectral method based on Chebyshev polynomials is adopted to solve the coupled electrostatic, ionic-transport, and hydrodynamic equations. The results show that the boundary confinement effect is most profound in narrow pores. In addition to the extra hydrodynamic resistance, the nearby wall squeezes and deforms the electric double layer, thereby enhancing the motion-deterring double-layer polarization. Consequently, a droplet with a thick double layer may undergo mobility reversal and migrate against its usual electrophoretic direction. At low surface potential, increasing the DBB screening parameter suppresses internal circulation and shifts the mobility continuously from the Newtonian-droplet limit toward the rigid-sphere limit. At higher surface potentials, however, the ordering of the mobility curves for different DBB screening parameters reverses across a critical double-layer thickness. A hydrodynamic solidification point is observed where the mobility becomes nearly insensitive to internal hydrodynamic screening and the interior recirculating flow is strongly suppressed, while the translational mobility remains finite. These results provide physical insight into the electrophoretic transport of polymer-containing droplets through confined micro- and nanofluidic channels.

papers.title: Conditional neural field-based reduced order model for dynamic ditching load prediction
papers.abstract: Grid-based neural networks such as convolutional autoencoders are widely used in dimension reduction-based surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics. Recently, the use of coordinate-based approaches like conditional neural fields (CNFs) has emerged. Their independence of the spatial discretization is an advantageous feature and a key motivation for computational fluid dynamic applications. This paper discusses the spatiotemporal prediction of aircraft ditching loads using a CNF approach. The model employs a Fourier feature mapping of input coordinates to capture high frequency content. Based on feature-wise linear modulation, the output is conditioned on a latent vector, which is learned by autodecoding. The model is evaluated using two datasets for the dynamic loads on the fuselage of a German Aerospace Center (DLR) D150 aircraft. The first dataset relates to a single fixed spatial discretization, and the second dataset includes data from different discretizations. On the first dataset, the model is compared to a grid-dependent convolutional autoencoder-based model, and both approaches achieve similar reconstruction accuracy, but the CNF requires significantly fewer parameters. When paired with a long short-term memory network in the latent space, both approaches achieve similar spatiotemporal prediction accuracy. Results for the second dataset demonstrate the ability of the CNF-based approach to reconstruct ditching loads accurately for heterogeneous spatial discretizations. In particular, the model can generalize to discretizations not used for training. This allows for flexible use of training datasets generated for different geometries and/or discretizations and the use of the surrogate model to predict loads for different configurations.

papers.title: Liquid jet plunging into restricted baths: The role of bounding wall
papers.abstract: This study experimentally investigates the influence of bounding wall on jet penetration and bubble entrainment for a viscous liquid jet plunging into a millimeter-scale closed-bottom restricted liquid bath. The entire jet–bath interaction process is divided into an initial impact stage and a continuous shearing stage. During the initial impact stage, wall confinement causes part of the air film that separates the jet from the bath to shift from the liquid–liquid interface to the liquid–solid interface and prolongs the film rupture time. However, the ejected-liquid volume required for film rupture remains nearly insensitive to confinement. In the continuous shearing stage, wall confinement suppresses jet penetration: the penetration depth referenced to the instantaneous rising bath surface decreases substantially, whereas the depth measured relative to the initial quiescent free surface changes only weakly. In an unrestricted bath, the jet-induced cavity grows progressively and develops into a filament structure, whose violent oscillations readily trigger millimeter-sized bubble entrainment. By contrast, the bounding wall strongly constrains cavity development and thereby effectively suppresses bubble entrainment under these confined-injection conditions.

papers.title: Erratum: “On the interaction of Tollmien-Schlichting waves with a wall-embedded Helmholtz resonator” [Phys. Fluids 35 , 034104 (2023)]
Heat transport pathways in local thermal non-equilibrium magneto-convection through anisotropic porous medium
papers.abstract: The proposed study demonstrates an irreversibility analysis of magneto-convection in a square enclosure filled with an anisotropic porous medium under the local thermal non-equilibrium framework under a uniform inclined magnetic field. Distinct energy equations are solved for the solid and fluid phases, coupled through an interphase heat transfer coefficient.
