A novel formulation of Bejan's heat function is derived under the non-equilibrium thermal interaction by combining the fluid and solid-phase energy equations, enabling rigorous visualization of total heat energy pathways within the domain. Numerical solutions are obtained using the finite volume method with the semi-implicit method for pressure linked equations algorithm. The coupled effects of anisotropic properties, fluid–solid thermal interaction, magnetic inclination and porosity are systematically examined. The results demonstrate that permeability anisotropy suppresses buoyancy-driven convection and reduces the average fluid Nusselt number Nuf,avg, whereas enhanced fluid–solid thermal coupling progressively drives the system toward local thermal equilibrium and |Δθ|max tending toward zero at high H. The magnetic field orientation produces a non-monotonic heat transfer response with an optimum inclination around 45°–60° enhancing convective transport. The variation in Nuf,avg over the investigated inclination range is ∼5.2%. The fluid–solid conductivity ratio Γ strongly affects the heat transport pathways with the maximum heat function magnitude |H|max decreasing from 5.714 at Γ=0.1 to 0.806 at Γ=100. Increasing porosity from ϵ=0.1 to 0.7 increases |H|max from 0.404 to 1.0269, demonstrating enhanced energy transport through stronger fluid circulation. The combined effects of anisotropy and magnetic field on thermodynamic irreversibility provide actionable insights for optimizing heat transfer in porous media systems such as solar energy collectors, geothermal reservoirs and heat exchangers.

papers.title: Linear stability analysis of counter-rotating wingtip vortex pair in grid-generated turbulence
papers.abstract: The instability of a counter-rotating wingtip vortex pair developing in grid-generated turbulence at Rec≈1.1×104 is investigated using time-resolved stereoscopic particle image velocimetry and bi-global linear stability analysis. Vortex pairs generated by two finite-span wings are examined under three different freestream turbulence (FST) levels and two wing spacings. After removing vortex wandering, the measured mean vortices are used as base states for stability analysis. The vortex profiles remain approximately self-similar during downstream evolution and are well represented by Batchelor-type vortices. Increasing FST exerts a non-monotonic influence on vortex evolution, strengthening the newly formed vortices in the near wake while accelerating their downstream decay, whereas reduced wing spacing weakens the vortex pair through enhanced mutual induction. The instability spectrum is organized into multiple helical branches, with dominant amplification consistently occurring at intermediate azimuthal wavenumbers. Growth rates exhibit a bandpass dependence on streamwise wavenumber, indicating a preferred axial scale associated with the vortex core and vortex pair interaction. Increasing FST systematically enhances modal amplification and shifts the most unstable disturbances toward higher wavenumbers, implying preferential excitation of smaller-scale instability modes. These results demonstrate that freestream turbulence affects vortex persistence not only through mean flow decay but also through instability amplification and scale selection.

papers.title: Compressible Bell–Plesset effects of Rayleigh–Taylor instability in a finite-thickness cylindrical shell
papers.abstract: The double-shell target is an important pathway toward inertial confinement fusion ignition, and its implosion performance is sensitive to perturbation feedthrough from the outer surface of the inner shell. This feedthrough is governed by compressibility, Bell–Plesset (BP) effects, and double-interface interaction, yet the coupled dynamics remains incompletely described. In this work, the Equal Convergence Ratio Hypothesis (ECRH) is first proposed as a closure, providing an analytical description of the coupled dynamics for a vacuum-bound cylindrical shell. Then, an asymptotic solution is derived via Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin analysis. The hypothesis and solution are validated against numerical solutions and hydrodynamic simulations, showing good agreement during the linear stage. Compared with the incompressible model, the ECRH-based model is simpler yet more accurate. Compared with that in the classical Rayleigh–Taylor instability, the inner perturbation growth is enhanced because BP convergence shortens the effective wavelength. The normalized outer-to-inner feedthrough strength is likewise enhanced. With an initial phase difference, the outer perturbation phase varies monotonically with mode number m and the radius ratio α, whereas the inner phase first approaches and then recedes from the outer phase as m increases. Finally, the competing dependence of the growth rate and of the feedthrough on m determines the most unstable mode for a given shell thickness, which follows the approximate scaling law mαm+1=const: for thicknesses of 10–30 μm, the most unstable mode number is 40–100. This work provides a new theoretical description of the compressible BP effect in cylindrical double-interface instabilities.

papers.title: Onset of pseudo-slug flow in upward-inclined gas–liquid pipe flow governed by liquid-film backflow
papers.abstract: Pseudo-slug flow is a transitional intermittent pattern between stratified and fully developed slug flows, yet its onset mechanism in upward-inclined low-liquid-loading pipes remains unclear. Air–water experiments were performed in a 50 mm inner-diameter transparent pipe at inclination angles of 2°–30°, superficial gas velocities of 2–35 m/s, and superficial liquid velocities of 0.001–0.05 m/s. High-speed visualization, pressure-drop and liquid-holdup measurements, pressure-signal cross correlation, and dye tracing were combined to identify flow patterns and quantify the hydraulic and kinematic responses. The results show that pseudo-slug flow is initiated by liquid-film thickening and local backflow, forming through a mechanism chain of liquid-film reversal, local liquid accumulation, partial blockage, gas penetration, and liquid redistribution. Unlike fully developed slug flow, the pseudo-slug body cannot stably block the pipe cross section; gas continuously penetrates the liquid-rich region, producing a finite-lifetime intermittent structure with weak pressure accumulation, non-periodic motion, and strong spatial instability. Increasing pipe inclination or superficial liquid velocity promotes axial gravitational backflow and shifts the stratified-to-pseudo-slug boundary toward higher gas velocities. Based on this physical picture, a transition model was developed by coupling a stratified-flow two-fluid momentum balance with two liquid-wall shear stress reversal criteria: cross-section-averaged shear reversal and bottom-film shear reversal. The proposed model links pseudo-slug onset to liquid-film backflow and wall shear stress reversal, providing a mechanistic criterion for predicting the stratified-to-pseudo-slug transition boundary.

papers.title: A radial basis function-finite difference method for incompressible Stokes flow on curved surfaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, a novel mesh-free method is developed for solving the unsteady incompressible Stokes equations on curved surfaces. To tackle the numerical challenges arising from complex vector-valued differential operators on surfaces, a polynomial-augmented radial basis function finite difference (RBF-FD) scheme is constructed for surface flow discretization. As a localized mesh-free technique, the RBF-FD method produces sparse differential matrices for approximating surface vector-valued differential operators, which effectively improves computational efficiency for surface Stokes simulations. An implicit fractional-step approach is further adopted for temporal discretization to ensure stable and long-term evolution of surface flow fields. Extensive numerical experiments verify the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method for simulating surface Stokes flows. Beyond pure algorithm development, this work also provides supportive evidence and fundamental references for understanding the hydrodynamic characteristics of curved-surface viscous flows. Through systematic numerical tests, we investigate the interrelations among surface curvature, fluid viscosity, and flow kinetic energy, which reveals how geometric features and physical parameters jointly govern the dynamic behaviors of surface viscous flows.

papers.title: Flow-induced vibration and stability transition in a parallel dual-pipe system with series piecewise stiffness clamps
papers.abstract: Parallel multipipe systems are common in engineering, where coupled vibration between adjacent pipes is one of the primary instabilities. To explore the nonlinear dynamic mechanism of such vibration, this paper proposes a fluid-conveying parallel dual-pipe system constrained by series piecewise stiffness clamps, and the flow-induced vibration and stability of the system are studied. Two types of nonlinear mechanisms are introduced: geometric and constraint nonlinearities, and the fluid–structure interaction and the elastic coupling between the pipes are considered. Numerical results reveal multiple stability transitions triggered by an internal flow. Within a dimensionless parametric framework, nonlinear analyses further demonstrate that the parallel pipe system experiences limit-cycle oscillation, quasi-periodic motion, and chaotic flutter via Hopf bifurcations. Increasing the piecewise stiffness leads to earlier quasi-periodic bifurcation by disrupting single-frequency energy dissipation, while increasing the clearance suppresses the nonlinear effect and causes the system to return from quasi-periodic to periodic motion. At different flow velocities, the mass ratio induces irregular transitions among periodic, quasi-periodic, chaotic, and stable states via the added mass effect. This study integrates the flow-induced energy input mechanism with piecewise stiffness regulation, providing a mechanistic basis for the dynamic design and vibration control of multipipe systems in engineering.

papers.title: An approach for modeling vibration-induced average flows in two-phase systems
papers.abstract: High-frequency vibrations applied to a two-phase fluid system generate steady average flows concentrated near the interface. Direct simulation of these flows is expensive because every vibration period must be resolved, and the number of periods per convective time grows with the frequency. We remove this restriction with an averaged description for the level-set method, obtained by applying the method of multiple scales to the diffuse interface. The averaging is carried out across a transition layer where viscous and vibrational effects balance, so the pulsational flow there is viscous and acquires an out-of-phase component. This flow gives rise to a viscous vibrational stress and a Stokes-drift mass flux. Two exact identities recast the system in Lagrangian-mean variables, in which the velocity that solves the momentum equation also advects the interface. The closed system couples the averaged Navier–Stokes equations, driven by an explicit interfacial vibrational force, to a linear quasi-stationary problem for the pulsation amplitudes. The admissible time step is set by the average flow alone, independent of the vibration frequency. The simulation results are compared with analytical solutions for a vibrated drop and bubble, with a time-resolved simulation of the frozen-wave instability, and with an experiment at high viscosity contrast. The model is shown to predict the structure and the intensity of the generated average flows, which can govern heat and mass transfer in multiphase systems under vibrations. Moreover, since these flows dominate transport whenever buoyancy is absent or weak, their modeling is crucial for materials processing in weightlessness.

papers.title: Moving focused ultrasound reorganizes coupled heat and solute transport near a pulsatile blood vessel
papers.abstract: Near a large vessel, axial convection competes with heat diffusion and the retention of released solute. This study examines how translating a focused-ultrasound source changes the spatial distribution of heating and drug exposure under pulsatile flow. A three-dimensional transient model couples a prescribed moving Gaussian intensity field, attenuation-based heating and radiation force, Carreau–Yasuda blood flow, porous-tissue heat transfer, and temperature-dependent liposome release and free-drug transport. For an 8-mm vessel with a mean inlet speed of 0.020 m s−1, the nominal Reynolds and Womersley numbers are 48.5 and 5.52; and the thermal and free-drug Péclet numbers are 1.21 × 103 and 3.20 × 105. Compared with a static focus, scanning with a 15-mm amplitude increases the tissue volume above 315 K from 32 to 108 mm3 and reduces the peak temperature from 319.1 to 318.2 K. The strongest intensity–drug co-localization occurs near 1 Hz within the sampled frequency range. This response is consistent with competition among focal dwell, revisit, and convective washout: dwell decreases from 1.18 s at 0.25 Hz to 0.074 s at 4 Hz, while mean-flow transit across the 24-mm focal length takes ∼1.20 s. A matched force-on/force-off calculation shows that the prescribed radiation force can materially reorganize lumen flow and scalar transport. Source translation therefore redistributes thermal exposure and solute transport along the vessel–tissue interface. The prescribed acoustic field, fixed scan–cardiac timing, and the 3-s observation window limit the frequency response to the simulated configuration; a phase-independent optimum is not established.

papers.title: Coupled plasma-particle dynamics during low-pressure plasma spraying of 8YSZ on a complex double-airfoil geometry: Effects of gas composition and impingement angle
papers.abstract: Achieving uniform thermal-barrier coating deposition on multi-airfoil turbine components remains challenging because substrate curvature, inter-airfoil confinement, and geometric shadowing strongly affect plasma-jet behavior and particle transport. This study numerically investigates low-pressure plasma spraying of 8YSZ particles onto a double-airfoil geometry using a three-dimensional model coupling compressible turbulent plasma flow, Lagrangian particle motion and heating, and particle deposition behavior. Three representative impingement orientations, including leading-edge interaction (Angle 1 = 0°), mid-airfoil interaction (Angle 2 = 90°), and wake interaction (Angle 3 = 45°), were evaluated using two plasma gas mixtures: 30 SLPM (standard liter per minute) Ar + 60 SLPM He and 30 SLPM Ar + 60 SLPM He + 18 SLPM N2. The results demonstrate that impingement orientation has a stronger influence on predicted deposition behavior than plasma composition. Angle 1 maintained the most coherent plasma momentum and thermal structures, producing global maximum deposition rates of 6.86 and 6.96 μm s−1 for Ar + He and Ar + He + N2, respectively. Angle 2 exhibited strong jet splitting and particle bypass, resulting in maximum deposition rates of 0.37 and 0.34 μm s−1. Angle 3 generated wake recirculation and particle-path convergence, producing the highest local deposition rates of 28.75 and 31.59 μm s−1 but with significant spatial variation. Quantitative analysis of sampling locations confirmed that high local deposition rates do not necessarily indicate improved deposition uniformity. These findings highlight that controlling particle accessibility and impingement orientation is critical for optimizing deposition on complex double-airfoil geometries.

papers.title: Effect of critical-inertia particles on the wake breakdown and downwash suppression of a transonic rotor
papers.abstract: The influence of particle inertia on interphase momentum transfer and coherent wake breakdown for a transonic rotor in a low-density particle-laden flow is investigated using Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation (DDES) coupled with an Eulerian–Lagrangian Discrete Phase Model (DPM). The rotor operates at Matip = 0.94, and five monodisperse particle sizes from 1 to 100 μm are examined. The aerodynamic response depends non-monotonically on the particle Stokes number (St). Among the sampled sizes, the 10 μm case (St = 2.4) produces the strongest wake modulation, whereas the 100 μm ballistic-like case remains close to the clean-flow baseline in the integral loads and vortex circulation. At z/R = 0.4, the normalized plane-integrated particle mass-flux index reaches 5.2 for the 10 μm case, while the normalized tip-vortex circulation decreases from 0.891 in the clean flow to 0.384, a reduction of 56.9%. This wake attenuation is consistent with reduced coherent downwash over the outer rotor region and coincides with a maximum local sectional thrust increase of 34.8% at r/R = 0.85; the corresponding increase in the time-averaged total rotor thrust is 26.4%. The thrust spectrum changes from discrete blade-passage harmonics toward broadband fluctuations, with the broadband level increasing by up to approximately three orders of magnitude. The peak total local entropy generation rate is 978.29 W m−3 K−1; turbulence-related dissipation and interphase drag contribute 52.0% and 33.2%, respectively. These results establish, for the investigated conditions, a mechanism-based relationship among particle relaxation, preferential concentration, wake attenuation, sectional-load redistribution, spectral broadening, and local irreversible dissipation within a unified DDES-DPM framework.

papers.title: A high-order interpolation method for hanging points based on the adaptive Cartesian mesh
papers.abstract: The adaptive mesh refinement technology is widely employed in Cartesian grid methods to improve computational efficiency by refining the mesh only in regions requiring high resolution. However, local refinement introduces hanging points at coarse–fine interfaces, making the construction of accurate and robust interpolation methods a key challenge for high-order numerical discretization. In this work, a third-order hanging-point interpolation framework is developed for both first- and second-type hanging points. For different types of hanging points, we propose (1) the least squares interpolation and (2) multi-stencil interpolation weighted by weighted essentially non-oscillatory and exponential inverse-distance strategies. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves third-order accuracy in smooth regions and maintains good robustness in the presence of shocks and shock interactions. In addition, the proposed interpolation framework is independent of the subsequent reconstruction procedure and can be readily integrated with different schemes for adaptive Cartesian methods.

papers.title: Membrane-mediated hydrodynamic shear transmission to cells
papers.abstract: Hydrodynamic shear regulates cellular remodeling and mechanotransduction, yet externally prescribed wall shear stress does not uniquely specify the mechanical stimulus transmitted through the plasma membrane to the cell interior. Here, we develop a reduced-order multiscale framework in which the plasma membrane functions as a mechanically responsive hydrodynamic transmission layer rather than a passive geometric boundary. An effective interfacial slip condition and a first-order membrane thickness-dependent attenuation relation yield closed-form expressions linking external shear to membrane slip velocity, transmitted intracellular velocity, effective strain, forcing frequency, membrane properties, and cellular geometry. A steady-flow extension distinguishes the membrane-mediated mechanical input from slower cytoskeletal remodeling. Comparison with independent endothelial and epithelial studies conducted under shear stresses of approximately 4–15 dyn cm−2 demonstrates qualitative consistency with rapid subcellular structural responses, slower hour-scale remodeling, and substantial variability among cellular systems exposed to comparable external loading. Because the published studies do not report the membrane parameters required for direct evaluation of the model, these comparisons are presented as literature-constrained consistency tests rather than quantitative validation. The framework provides a testable continuum-mechanics description of hydrodynamic transmission from extracellular flow toward the membrane–cortex region, thereby specifying a mechanical input that may subsequently engage established cellular mechanotransduction pathways.

papers.title: The overset-grid implementation in the multiple-relaxation-time regularized lattice Boltzmann model
papers.abstract: The treatment of moving fluid–solid boundaries represents a pivotal challenge in computational fluid dynamics. To address this, we propose a systematic overset-grid implementation algorithm for moving bodies undergoing large-amplitude, six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) motions, based on an advanced multiple-relaxation-time regularized lattice Boltzmann (MRT-RLB) model. Within this overset-grid framework, flow information between the fixed background Cartesian mesh and the body-attached moving mesh is dynamically exchanged in the overlapping region. Crucially, this exchange is mediated by the interpolation of the density and momentum together with high-order Hermite central moments, which are subsequently transformed into Hermite raw moments to reconstruct the post-collision distribution functions directly through the MRT-RLB collision operator, distinguishing our approach from existing overset methods. Furthermore, a sharp-interface interpolated bounce-back scheme is employed, restricting the geometric treatment of arbitrary fluid–solid interfaces to a single initialization phase owing to the overset-grid strategy. To accommodate long-range 6-DOF motions, a novel numerical treatment is developed to handle the hole boundary nodes of the fixed mesh, offering a fundamental departure from traditional sliding-mesh methods. The accuracy, robustness, and versatility of the proposed algorithm are successfully validated through various two- and three-dimensional numerical examples, demonstrating close agreement with both experimental and numerical benchmarks.

papers.title: A unified lattice Boltzmann finite volume framework: Direct numerical simulation of acoustics and low-Mach-number flows
papers.abstract: The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) has intrinsic mechanisms for stabilizing computation and extraordinarily low acoustic dissipation, while the finite volume method (FVM) applies to nonuniform meshes and ensures conservation naturally. Their advantages complement each other, and many approaches have been proposed to integrate the two methods. However, existing integrations compromise the stability or low-dissipation properties of LBM. This paper proposes a general framework, the unified lattice Boltzmann finite volume scheme (ULBFVS), to unify the two methods, without losing their advantages. On uniform meshes, ULBFVS is mathematically equivalent to LBM, thereby fully preserving its numerical stability and extraordinarily low acoustic dissipation. Moreover, the framework can be naturally extended to nonuniform meshes, inheriting the conservation property and mesh flexibility of FVM. The framework is based on the LBM collision and streaming steps and extends general LBM models to conservative simulations on nonuniform meshes. As an example, the present paper proposes ULBFVS based on the recursive regularized LBM for low-Mach-number flows. Numerical tests validate its good numerical stability, accuracy, and extraordinarily low acoustic dissipation.

papers.title: A multiscale deep learning framework for predicting stratified shear flow instabilities
papers.abstract: Kelvin–Helmholtz (KH) instability in stratified shear flows exhibits strong multiscale dynamics, in which large-scale vortical structures evolve into smaller-scale motions through nonlinear interactions. Accurate prediction of KH dynamics is important for understanding mixing and transport in geophysical and environmental flows. Although high-fidelity simulations such as direct numerical simulation and large eddy simulation (LES) can resolve these dynamics, their computational cost limits their use across a wide range of flow conditions. Data-driven reduced-order models based on convolutional neural network autoencoders (CNN-AEs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks offer a promising alternative but often underrepresent dynamically important fine-scale structures. This study presents a parameter-conditioned multiscale deep learning framework for reduced-order prediction of stratified KH instability. The framework employs a state CNN-AE to capture dominant large-scale flow structures, a difference CNN-AE to learn finer-scale motions, and a parameter-conditioned LSTM to jointly evolve both latent representations using the gradient Richardson number (J) and the shear-to-stratification thickness ratio (R). The model is trained using vorticity and buoyancy fields from two-dimensional LES-like simulations spanning multiple flow configurations and is evaluated on both training and previously unseen test cases. The framework accurately reproduces the evolution of KH billows and preserves fine-scale structures throughout the nonlinear stages of instability development, as assessed through comparisons with the conventional CNN-AE–LSTM framework and LES using statistical metrics and physics-based diagnostics, including perturbation enstrophy, instability growth rates, and kinetic energy spectra. The proposed model also enables long-horizon forecasting from a single early-stage flow snapshot and generalizes successfully to previously unseen (J,R) combinations.

papers.title: Dual-scale and hybrid micropillar architectures for enhanced boiling and capillary transport: A three-dimensional pore-scale study
papers.abstract: Efficient thermal management of high-heat-flux systems requires boiling surfaces capable of sustaining liquid replenishment while limiting vapor accumulation near the heated surface. Conventional single-scale micropillar arrays are constrained by a permeability–capillarity trade-off, where enhanced capillary pumping can restrict liquid transport and vapor removal. In this study, hierarchical dual-scale micropillar architectures are proposed to partially decouple these competing mechanisms. Three-dimensional pore-scale volume of fluid simulations are conducted to investigate liquid–vapor transport, interfacial evolution, and phase-change behavior in monopillar, bipillar, and hybrid pillar configurations over heat fluxes ranging from 10 to 100 W/cm2. The bipillar architecture substantially increases permeability relative to the monopillar geometry while maintaining comparable capillary pressure. However, its larger inter-cluster pores promote localized vapor accumulation at elevated heat fluxes, reducing liquid rewetting and increasing wall superheat. To address this limitation, a hybrid architecture incorporating secondary micropillars within the large pores of the bipillar structure is introduced. The secondary pillars modify the local pore morphology and phase distribution, reducing vapor accumulation and persistent vapor pockets while largely preserving the enhanced liquid-transport characteristics of the bipillar geometry. Consequently, the hybrid structure exhibits lower wall superheat, reduced vapor saturation fluctuations, and more stable phase-change behavior across the investigated range. The predicted heat transfer coefficient increases from approximately 4.8 to 8.9 W/cm2 K between 10 and 100 W/cm2, with the hybrid configuration consistently outperforming the monopillar and bipillar structures. Overall, the results demonstrate that boiling performance in micropillar arrays is governed not only by capillary-driven liquid supply but also by pore-scale vapor management. Under the investigated conditions, the proposed hierarchical architecture suppresses vapor accumulation while preserving favorable hydraulic characteristics, highlighting the potential of multiscale pore designs for improved high-heat-flux boiling performance.

papers.title: Investigation and revision of the viscous torque formula for a non-parallel friction pair with a wedge-shaped oil film
papers.abstract: A hydro-viscous drive clutch transmits torque through viscous shear in the oil film between friction elements. Axisymmetric conical deformation produces a radially varying clearance and limits the accuracy of conventional parallel-disk models. An axisymmetric non-parallel friction-pair model with linearly varying film thickness was derived from the Navier–Stokes equations in cylindrical coordinates. The revised torque expression incorporates the coupling between radial flow and circumferential motion into the local shear formulation and torque integration. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted using single-factor, pairwise-factor, and four-factor three-level L27 designs. Across the four single-factor cases, the revised-model mean errors ranged from 1.44% to 5.57%, compared with 14.83% to 18.10% for the conventional model evaluated at the intermediate film thickness. For the three pairwise cases, the corresponding ranges were 1.32%–5.75% and 14.27%–17.95%, respectively. Analysis of variance of the L27 results showed that angular velocity difference and inclination angle contributed 44.09% and 30.22% of the CFD-torque variation, respectively, whereas flow rate contributed 66.46% of the revised-model error variation. The 27-case mean and maximum errors were 5.474% and 14.282%, respectively. The revised model improves torque prediction for smooth, axisymmetrically coned, continuous liquid films, while high-flow rate conditions remain a limitation.

papers.title: A force-driven reduced-order hybrid temporal network framework for flow field prediction around circular cylinders across Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: Accurate reconstruction of time-resolved cylinder wakes across a wide range of Reynolds numbers (Re) is important for engineering monitoring and structural assessment yet remains challenging with minimal sensing information. This study proposes a force-driven hybrid temporal network (FD-HTNet) framework that reconstructs time-resolved cylinder wake fields from the global lift and drag time series, with Re provided as an operating condition. A shared spatial basis is built through incremental proper orthogonal decomposition, with separate energy-based truncation criteria applied during training and inference. A hybrid temporal predictor combining recurrent encoding and attention-based global aggregation estimates modal-coefficient increments for sequential state updates and field reconstruction. Two-dimensional cylinder-wake simulations over Re=50–1050 validate the framework. The FD-HTNet framework accurately reconstructs dominant wake structures and periodic vortex shedding under both interpolation and near-boundary extrapolation to unseen Re, with an overall relative L2 error of the velocity magnitude below 0.54% in the statistically stationary regime. Shapley additive explanations-based attribution further reveals condition-dependent model reliance on Reynolds-number, force-derived, and temporal features. With compact sensing and low inference cost, FD-HTNet provides a practical data-driven approach for cross-Re wake reconstruction.

papers.title: Interfacial instability transition of stratified two-phase flows driven by gravity and pressure difference in inclined microchannels: A quantitative classification
papers.abstract: Linear stability analysis of stratified gas–liquid flows with fixed Rel = 15 in inclined plane microchannels (with height H̃ ≤ 1 mm) is performed to disclose the instability transition driven by tangential component of gravity (TCG) and pressure difference via numerical solution of the Orr–Sommerfeld equations for all wavenumber disturbances. Combining energy balance theory, five transitioning instabilities are classified quantitatively according to the disturbance energy inputs (DEI) by gravity and interfacial shear stress. Apart from the co-current gas flow, two counter-current [the counter-current gas flow with thinner liquid film (CT-1) and the counter-current gas flow with thicker liquid film (CT-2)] gas flows may exist with different liquid film thicknesses under specific H̃. Special attention is paid to the re-entrant instability of CT-1 flows when Reg approaches its maximum Reg, CT-max. For CT-1 flows, the disturbance work done by the TCG serves as the DEI, which is dissipated by both interfacial shear stress and bulk flow viscosity dissipations, and the residual energy determines whether the disturbance grows. As θ decreases to a critical value θc−c, Reg, CT-max gradually shifts toward the left boundary of the stable flow region, where the DEI is entirely consumed. When θ is smaller than θc−c, continuously increasing gas velocity can strengthen the stabilization and even completely suppress the gravity-driven instability. CT-2 flows are much more unstable than CT-1 under the same Reg, because gravity and interfacial shear stress jointly promote instabilities. Analytical expressions of disturbance work done by gravity and interfacial shear stress for long-wave instabilities are derived to facilitate the instability type identification.

papers.title: Flow mechanism on the air–water mixed wakes of an air lubrication ship: A numerical study
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of ship air-layer drag reduction (ALDR), as a form of ship air lubrication, in reducing frictional resistance. However, research on air distribution around the hull and the influence of air-entrained stern wakes on the wake field remains limited. In this paper, the Euler–Euler two-fluid method integrated with the interfacial area transport equation (IATE) in the open-source platform OpenFOAM is employed to investigate a specially designed oil tanker equipped with an air-layer device. The numerical method is validated by comparison with experimental wake results. The results show that the present method reproduces the mean wake fraction at the propeller disk plane with errors of 6.89% and −9.6% under single-phase and air-entrained conditions, respectively, and captures the main features of the air-entrained stern wake. The air layer beneath the hull exhibits a tendency of cyclic accumulation–instability–reaccumulation, as observed in the present simulations, with maximum thickness in the mid-ship region. At the stern, the air fraction decreases from 4.42% to 0.57% downstream, while the stern separation vortex retains a portion of microbubbles, carrying approximately 0.17% air fraction to the rearmost propeller plane station. After applying ALDR, the high wake fraction region is substantially reduced, and the mean wake fraction at the propeller disk decreases by about 49% compared with the single-phase case. Meanwhile, the streamline pattern transitions from a dual-vortex to a single-core vortex structure. These findings suggest that, within the present numerical framework, ALDR may modify the stern flow vorticity dynamics, providing preliminary insights into the air–water mixed wake characteristics. Quantitative drag reduction effects are not evaluated in this study.

papers.title: A deep learning-assisted dynamical downscaling framework for wind fields over deep-cut canyon bridge sites
papers.abstract: Accurate simulation of the bridge-site wind field is essential for the wind-resistant design of long-span bridges, especially for those crossing deep-cut canyons where the wind environment is strongly influenced by complex terrain. Dynamical downscaling using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is widely adopted to obtain high-resolution wind fields for such bridge sites. In practice, conventional WRF configurations usually require substantial terrain smoothing to maintain numerical stability, leaving bridge elevation wind-field nonuniformity insufficiently resolved. Although grid refinement can improve terrain representation, the strengthened Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) constraint over steep canyon terrain makes stable high-resolution integration more challenging. To address these limitations, this study proposes a deep learning-assisted WRF dynamical downscaling framework for high-resolution wind-field simulation at deep-cut canyon bridge sites. Specifically, stable nested WRF simulations under the conventional configuration are first performed, and their outputs are used to train a deep learning model. The learned nested-domain relationships are then extrapolated to the target high-resolution inner domain to estimate local wind-speed maxima relevant to the CFL condition. From these estimates, the CFL-controlling values are identified and used to optimize the vertical grid spacing and select a stable time step. The framework is validated at a representative bridge site in a deep-cut canyon. Compared to conventional stable WRF simulations, the optimized high-resolution simulation provides a finer representation of bridge-site wind-field characteristics and achieves smaller errors against observed wind speeds. The proposed framework provides an effective solution for stable high-resolution WRF simulation over complex canyon terrain.

papers.title: Non-equilibrium condensation and secondary vortex dynamics of moist air in the high-speed turbo-expander
papers.abstract: The spontaneous condensation of water vapor during rapid expansion of moist air induces strong thermodynamic non-equilibrium effects and influences the vortex structures in the high-speed turbine passage. In this study, a numerical simulation is performed on the high-speed turbine flow passage using an Euler–Euler multiphase framework coupled with classical nucleation theory and droplet growth models, and experimental validation is conducted on a reverse Brayton cycle test rig. The relative deviations between the simulation and experimental results are 2.57% for isentropic efficiency and 4.17% for outlet humidity, respectively. Comparative analysis with dry air conditions reveals that phase-change effects induce a substantial temperature rise of 18.8 K at the outlet relative to the dry air case, accompanied by a maximum liquid mass fraction reaching 0.77%. Entropy generation analysis indicates that the impeller passage is the primary source of irreversible losses, accounting for over 41% of the total. The secondary vortices induced by condensation near the suction surface and the associated local pressure fluctuations are identified as the main loss contributors. The humidity-induced increase in entropy generation follows a power-law relationship, with a critical relative humidity threshold of approximately 30%. Beyond this threshold, the entropy generation increases superlinearly with relative humidity, with an exponent of 1.803. The efficiency loss is linearly correlated with the entropy generation increase. These findings reveal the coupling mechanism between non-equilibrium condensation and vortex dynamics in high-speed turbines.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic and biological controls on dinoflagellate bioluminescence induced by two-dimensional plunging breakers
papers.abstract: Breaking waves generate intense mechanical forcing that can stimulate dinoflagellate bioluminescence, yet how breaker dynamics and biological properties jointly regulate the emitted-light response remains poorly quantified. In this study, we develop a coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian framework for two-dimensional plunging breakers by integrating an adaptive mesh multiphase solver with a reduced phenomenological bioluminescence model. The results show that the macroscopic flash is governed by the spatiotemporal overlap between suprathreshold shear forcing and cell availability, while two-dimensional vortical activity co-evolves with the integrated light response. Across the four simulated wave-steepness cases, both peak intensity and total light yield increase monotonically, although no universal nonlinear scaling is inferred. Variations in Bond number modify interface fragmentation and luminous-cell transport, while the peak response tends toward saturation under the strongest forcing conditions. Biological properties further regulate the signal: higher activation thresholds act as a physiological filter, whereas prescribed shallower near-surface cell distributions enhance the total emitted light under otherwise identical hydrodynamic conditions. These findings clarify the hydrodynamic and biological controls on breaker-induced bioluminescence.

papers.title: Comparison between continuum and molecular dynamics simulations in shock-to-detonation transition
papers.abstract: This study investigates the intricate relationship between shock waves and chemical kinetics, specifically focusing on the role of translational non-equilibrium in shock-induced chemistry during the shock to detonation transition in a reactive gas. Molecular dynamics simulations are employed and compared with continuum descriptions using reactive Euler and Navier–Stokes models for hard spheres. Results reveal a significant impact of translational non-equilibrium on shock amplification rates and the transition to detonation, with an approximately twofold acceleration compared to conventional Euler hydrodynamic models. Notably, a Navier–Stokes model incorporating hard sphere transport properties effectively captures this acceleration, emphasizing its implications for modeling gaseous detonations with finite-rate, collision-controlled chemistry (i.e., reactions whose characteristic time is comparable to the translational relaxation time) and complex pressure wave dynamics. The study concludes that non-equilibrium effects, particularly those associated with molecular hotspots, may lead to corrections in reaction rates and shock dynamics, underscoring the importance of considering diffusive effects for accurate modeling of gaseous detonations.

papers.title: Effects of turbulence and subgrid-scale modeling on transient free-surface dynamics predicted by a coupled volume-of-fluid method and discrete phase model in a gas-blown continuous casting mold
papers.abstract: A transient multiphase model coupling the volume-of-fluid method and discrete phase model was evaluated against a 1:2 gas-blown water-model experiment. Five turbulence configurations—standard k–ε, shear-stress transport k–ω, large-eddy simulation (LES), k–ε-based stress-blended eddy simulation (SBES), and k–ω-based SBES—were compared using jet trajectory, near-surface velocity, wave-height statistics, oil-layer exposure, visible oil entrainment, and computational cost. On the common 1.80 × 106 cell mesh, k–ε-based SBES and LES gave three-point mean absolute relative velocity errors of 8.32% and 10.60%, respectively. SBES required 44.1% of the LES wall-clock time. The SBES velocity RMSE was 0.009 03 m/s. Its mean absolute wave height and temporal standard deviation were 0.79 and 0.59 mm, respectively, compared with 0.87 and 0.61 mm experimentally. LES gave smaller common-mesh errors in both wave-height statistics and exposure variability, whereas SBES gave a slightly smaller mean-exposure error. For visible entrainment, SBES predicted a maximum penetration depth of 107.51 mm vs 110.86 mm experimentally, but mean visible droplet counts were 6 and 3, respectively. Within k–ε-based SBES, the wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity closure was closest to the experimental point estimates in all four retained interfacial statistics. Model performance therefore depends on the observable, and selection should consider complementary measurements and computational cost within the investigated water-model condition.

papers.title: Spectral analysis of wall-pressure fluctuations in electronic expansion valves
papers.abstract: Electronic expansion valves (EEVs) regulate refrigerant mass flow in air-conditioning and refrigeration systems through throttling, during which unsteady cavitating two-phase flows and wall-pressure fluctuations develop. A helical groove can be employed in the downstream pipe as a passive modification of the internal flow. However, how the helical groove modifies the jet motion associated with the wall-pressure fluctuations remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate how a helical groove modifies the asymmetric jet motion associated with the dominant low-frequency wall-pressure fluctuation using volume-of-fluid-based multiphase large-eddy simulations of the configurations with and without the groove. The frequency ranges identified from measured acoustic spectra are used only as reference bands for the simulated wall-pressure analysis. The wall-pressure fluctuations are concentrated in the near-orifice impingement region, where the dominant low-frequency component is associated with the asymmetric lateral motion of the jet. At z/D=0.5, where z and D denote the streamwise coordinate measured from the orifice and the downstream pipe diameter, respectively, the groove reduces the rms jet-center displacement and asymmetric wall-pressure fluctuation by 12.5% and 18.4%, respectively, and their low-frequency band-integrated cross-spectral magnitude by 55.3%. The maximum magnitude-squared coherence below 1 kHz also decreases from 0.559 to 0.395 with the groove. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition further shows that the leading streamwise- and radial-velocity eigenvalues decrease by 27.4% and 29.4%, respectively, while the normalized radial-velocity mode is redistributed from the outer part of the pipe toward the interior. A secondary high-frequency response is observed in connection with fragmented near-wall small-scale motions. These findings support the interpretation that the helical groove reduces the dominant low-frequency wall-pressure fluctuation by weakening the asymmetric jet motion toward the wall and provide a structural description of the associated changes in coherent motion.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics and predictability of sediment plumes from a deep-sea mining vehicle under different source configurations
papers.abstract: Plumes generated by deep-sea mining vehicles are multiphase flows in which hydrodynamic adjustment, entrainment, transport, settling, and particle state evolution act over competing time scales. How source configuration reorganizes these dynamics and their predictability remains unclear. We analyzed 22 stationary collection (SC), mobile collection (MC), and transit (TR) events using temporal analysis, ExtraTrees models, and recursive simulation. The modes represented a fixed collection source, collection combined with motion, and motion without active collection. Approximate velocity to concentration lags were 110 s for SC and MC and 170 s for TR, with broad uncertainty intervals. Particle irregularity decreased in five of six responsive MC events and increased in 10 of 11 TR events in the mapped records. Across withheld events, velocity carried appreciable predictive importance for concentration increments in the moving modes. ExtraTrees reduced velocity root mean square error (RMSE) by 11.1%–17.6% at 30–120 s, while derived flux RMSE decreased by 1.4%–17.5% at 10–120 s. Concentration and particle properties retained persistence as the final predictor, with particle scores influenced by sampling resolution. Recursive validation and initial state tests constrained the 95 scenarios to hypothetical comparisons. Together, the results show that the tested source configurations differ in measured temporal responses and fitted predictive dependence, while recursive scenario trends remain conditional on model validation.

papers.title: Transport regimes in pulsatile stenotic flow
papers.abstract: Pulsatile flow through a stenosed artery generates phase-dependent separation and recirculation that influence nanoparticle transport. This study develops a reduced-order model coupling pulsatile non-Newtonian flow with nanoparticle advection–diffusion, wall deposition, payload release, and dissolved-drug uptake. The model is used to examine the effects of Reynolds number, Womersley number, stenosis severity, and nanoparticle Peclet number on recirculation, particle residence, and transport response. A multidimensional Reynolds–Womersley–stenosis study, together with residence-time and timescale analyses, is used to relate flow structure to transport outcomes. The release–diffusion transport parameter ΠRD provides a compact organization of the simulated transport response but is not interpreted as a universal regime criterion. Numerical-resolution and mass-balance checks are supplemented by comparison with digitized published particle image velocimetry observations. A Q-learning analysis is included as a proof-of-concept downstream application of the reduced-order transport model. The results are interpreted within the assumptions and parameter range of the reduced-order formulation and are not intended as clinically validated predictions.

papers.title: Regulation mechanisms of impeller geometry on hydraulic loss and impeller–volute pressure pulsations in a submersible centrifugal pump
papers.abstract: Flow separation, strong shear, and periodic impeller–volute interaction are major sources of hydraulic loss and pressure pulsations in centrifugal pumps. This study investigates how impeller geometry regulates these phenomena in a submersible centrifugal pump using steady computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations validated against hydraulic-performance measurements of the original prototype, together with transient CFD calculations. Blade outlet width, blade outlet angle, and blade wrap angle were examined, while the entropy-generation-theory-based volumetric energy dissipation rate, including viscous and turbulent contributions, was used to evaluate local hydraulic losses. Response surface methodology and the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II identified a representative design within the prescribed geometric space. The three parameters were changed from 25 mm, 22.6°, and 90° to 26.33 mm, 24.8°, and 102.2°, respectively. Under the design operating condition, the CFD-predicted head increased from 35.92 to 38.32 m, while the CFD-predicted efficiency increased from 62.52% to 66.39%, corresponding to an increase in 3.87 percentage points, or 6.19% relative to the original value. The CFD results over 0.6–1.4 times the design flow rate indicate that the modified geometry is associated with a more continuous pressure-rise process, weaker recirculation and separation, less pronounced outlet-flow distortion, and reduced high-dissipation regions on the blade surfaces, at the impeller outlet, and near the volute tongue. The numerically evaluated integrated dissipation also decreases in both the impeller and the triple-volute casing. The dominant deterministic pressure components occur at the blade-passing frequency of approximately 290 Hz and its harmonics. The numerically predicted amplitudes decrease after modification, particularly near the volute tongue.

papers.title: Effects of eddy-viscosity turbulence models on turbulent transport characteristics and reattachment dynamics in backward-facing step flows
papers.abstract: Separated flow over a backward-facing step involves a separated shear layer, recirculation, and subsequent reattachment, making it a benchmark for assessing turbulence models in strongly separated flows. A Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes solver is employed to investigate the effects of the Spalart–Allmaras (SA), Q–ω, shear-stress transport (SST), and locally source-term-modified SST (SST-m) models on flow evolution and momentum transport. Grid dependence is quantified using Richardson extrapolation and the grid convergence index. Combined with the experimental data of Driver et al., the models are evaluated in terms of flow topology, transport mechanisms, and a normalized multi-quantity error matrix. The SA model responds rapidly to eddy-viscosity transport in the separated shear layer, enhancing shear-layer diffusion and promoting premature momentum transport toward the wall, thereby underpredicting the reattachment length. Its lower complexity reduces computational cost by approximately 45%–48%. The Q–ω model predicts the reattachment length closest to the experiment, with an error of 2.27% but exhibits insufficient suppression of turbulent scales and momentum transport during early separation, resulting in delayed Reynolds shear-stress development and near-wall pressure overshoot. The SST model accurately predicts wall-pressure recovery and skin-friction evolution, while SST-m reduces the reattachment-length error from 5.18% to 3.73% through a local source-term limiter. A normalized root mean square error assessment using Cp, Cf, U, k, and −uv under multiple weighting schemes shows that SST-m maintains a relatively low comprehensive error, indicating consistent predictions across multiple flow quantities. These results clarify the relationship between turbulence-scale and Reynolds-stress transport and the macroscopic processes of separation, recirculation, and reattachment.

papers.title: Dynamics of flexible filaments in granular media
papers.abstract: Interactions between flexible structures and their surrounding media underpin many forms of animal locomotion, from the flapping of wings in air to the undulating propulsion of tails and fins in water. However, the coupling between deformable bodies and granular materials, crucial for movement in sandy environments, remains comparatively understudied. The equations governing flexible structures in viscous fluids do not apply to granular media, where resistive forces depend on motion direction rather than speed. We provide the first experimental validation of a predictive theoretical framework for deformable body dynamics in granular media. In this framework, the shape of the filament arises from a balance between the internal elastic and the anisotropic friction forces. We test the model using experiments in which a filament is actuated through prescribed angular oscillations at its head while fully immersed in a granular medium. Across a wide range of driving amplitudes and filament stiffnesses, we observe characteristic localization of deformation near the driven end, consistent with the highly dissipative, friction-dominated medium. Furthermore, significant coupling between filament motion and surface deformation is observed. Quantitative comparisons between experiments and simulations show improved agreement when surface coupling is included, demonstrating that the framework captures the essential physics governing interactions between oscillating flexible structures and granular substrates. These results provide a foundation for predicting and controlling flexible-body motion in granular environments, with implications for biological locomotion and device design in frictional media.

papers.title: Optimal control of mixing efficiency in a viscous fluid: A Navier–Stokes and advection–diffusion approach
papers.abstract: We study an optimal control problem motivated by the physical process of mixing a soluble substance into a viscous fluid, such as dissolving sugar in coffee by stirring with a spoon. The fluid motion is modeled by the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, while the transport of the dissolved substance is described by an advection–diffusion equation. The control variable represents the imposed stirring action, modeled here as a distributed body force acting throughout the fluid domain. The objective is to achieve fast and efficient homogenization while minimizing the energetic cost of stirring. We first establish the well-posedness of the coupled system under suitable assumptions on the data and the control. Using the direct method of the calculus of variations, we prove the existence of at least one optimal control. Subsequently, we derive first-order necessary optimality conditions through an extended Lagrangian formalism, which yields a coupled system involving the primal state (velocity, pressure, and concentration) and the adjoint states. The gradient of the cost function is explicitly computed, providing the foundation for gradient-based optimization algorithms. Finally, we implement a gradient-based numerical method and validate it on a two-dimensional test case: for a localized concentration blob stirred by a physically bounded distributed force, the optimal control reduces the terminal spatial variance of the concentration by approximately 99% relative to the uncontrolled (purely diffusive) case, and by approximately 96% relative to a constant forcing of comparable energy. The influence of the regularization parameter on the temporal structure of the optimal forcing is also discussed. The proposed framework offers a rigorous and quantitatively validated approach for optimizing mixing processes in various industrial and natural applications.

papers.title: X-CAL: Explaining latent causality in physical space for fluid mechanics
papers.abstract: We combine a β-variational autoencoder (β-VAE), the synergistic–unique–redundant decomposition (SURD) [Martínez-Sánchez et al., “Decomposing causality into its synergistic, unique, and redundant components,” Nat. Commun. 15, 9296 (2024)], and Gradient-SHAP, a SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) attribution method, in X-CAL, a framework for reduced-state causal analysis of turbulent flow. The β-VAE defines a nonlinear latent state, SURD measures directed predictive information among its retained coordinates, and Gradient-SHAP maps those relations back to physical space. Using direct numerical simulation data of the flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder at Reh=2000, we learn a three-coordinate latent state from the two-component mid-span velocity field, identify the dominant positive-lag relations inside that state, and map them to encoder supports and decoder response fields. Percolation of the SHAP fields extracts time-resolved attribution supports that separate upper-, mid-, and lower-wake regions. The interpretation is restricted to this retained three-coordinate velocity-based state: it identifies predictive reduced-state relations and their physical-space traces, not the full causal state of the three-dimensional wake.

papers.title: Transient flows and quasi-dynamic hydraulic coefficients at unpressurized circular pipe confluences
papers.abstract: In one-dimensional (1D) transient simulations of unpressurized drainage networks, confluence junctions are commonly represented using static hydraulic coefficients, which cannot adequately capture their dynamic hydrodynamic behavior. To address this limitation, three-dimensional (3D) simulations validated against experiments were conducted to investigate the flow physics and hydraulic characteristics of circular pipe confluences. The results demonstrate that, beyond the junction angle θ and the discharge ratio q*, the filling ratio y* plays an important role in governing the flow structure. As y* increases, it non-linearly modifies the cross-sectional aspect ratio and increases the submergence of the branch inflow, driving a transition from smooth merging to vigorous rolling with intensified turbulent kinetic energy dissipation. Based on these flow physics insights, a dynamic 1D control volume confluence branch junction model was developed, where the momentum correction and localized head-loss coefficients vary with the transient flow. To complete the model, a database of 150 3D simulations was established, and the control volume boundaries were identified at 0.2, 0.9, and 1.4 pipe diameters upstream, branch, and downstream sections, respectively. Formulas for the quasi-dynamic hydraulic coefficients were then derived as functions of θ, q*, and y*. By incorporating these formulas, the 1D model demonstrated high accuracy for transient flow simulation: reducing the maximum dynamic time warping water-depth alignment error by 68.69% and the peak water-depth relative error from 5% to 0.1% in their respective cases. These results demonstrate that incorporating dynamic junction characteristics enables the proposed 1D model to more accurately represent confluence hydrodynamics in unpressurized circular pipe systems.

papers.title: Molecular dynamics validation of shear-dependent nonlinear slip boundary condition for water
papers.abstract: The classical no-slip boundary condition has long served as a foundational assumption in continuum fluid mechanics; however, it is known to break down in microscale and high-shear flows where interfacial slip becomes significant. Nonlinear slip models proposed by Thompson and Troian, and later generalized by Thalakkottor and Mohseni, demonstrated that slip length is not constant but increases nonlinearly with shear rate. Previous validations of these models have primarily relied on monatomic Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluids, limiting their applicability to realistic liquids. In this study, non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations are performed to investigate the validity of the nonlinear slip boundary condition for transferable intermolecular potential with 3 points water confined by LJ walls. Three liquid–solid interfaces with different wall–water interaction parameters are examined under Couette flow conditions, and published Extended Simple Point Charge water data for graphene nanochannels are analyzed as an independent comparison. The results demonstrate that water exhibits the same nonlinear slip behavior previously observed in simple LJ fluids. In addition, this nonlinear behavior can be described by the same universal scaling relationship proposed by Thompson and Troian. These findings extend the applicability of nonlinear slip models to commonly encountered fluids such as water.

papers.title: Effect of rotor–fuselage spacing on the development of the vortex ring state
papers.abstract: A wind tunnel investigation to assess the impact of rotor–fuselage spacing on the development of the vortex ring state (VRS) and flow topology is presented. Particle Image Velocimetry was utilized to investigate flow mechanisms across a range of rotor–fuselage spacings (xs/R=0.34−1.56) and descent ratios (α=0.0−2.0), which were compared to the isolated rotor configuration. Mean velocity flow field data were utilized to identify coherent flow structures and features within the rotor wake, while flow unsteadiness was quantified through statistical analysis of the velocity fluctuations. For cases of VRS onset, the presence of the fuselage delays the development of the VRS for all rotor–fuselage separation distances tested. Furthermore, at an intermediate rotor–fuselage separation distance, a strong recirculation region between the rotor and fuselage is identified, resulting in a change in the VRS onset boundary. Moreover, at large descent ratios a decoupling between the development of the VRS and rotor–fuselage separation distance is observed.

papers.title: A wake-triggered double-secondary-vortex topology over a multi-element airfoil: A sensitized Reynolds stress model study
papers.abstract: The flow over a 30P30N multi-element airfoil at a Reynolds number of Rec = 1.83 × 104 and an angle of incidence of α = 4° is investigated computationally by employing an eddy-resolving Reynolds stress model within the time accurate unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes framework. This scale-resolving model follows the scale-adaptive simulation concept and is capable of providing a reliable three-dimensional fluctuating flow field. The wake-triggered double-secondary vortices topology, reported in experiments but rarely discussed in numerical simulations, is successfully identified in the boundary layer of the main element. The downstream three-dimensional evolution of these double-secondary vortices and the related wake-induced bypass transition can be comprehensively mapped with the aid of the three-dimensional velocity databases obtained computationally. It is found, among other issues, that the specific topology of the wake-triggered double-secondary vortices is responsible for the unsteady aerodynamic lift.

papers.title: Driving mechanisms for laser ignition of a gaseous oxygen–methane shear-coaxial injector in a rocket combustor
papers.abstract: A statistical investigation was performed on a laser-ignited single element gaseous oxygen–methane shear-coaxial injector in a model rocket combustor. The laser focal point was positioned at 21 discrete locations across a total of 474 ignition tests. Laser energy was deposited during the steady state flow of oxygen and the transient introduction of methane. A point-biserial statistical analysis was performed to ascertain that the ignition outcome had no correlation with changes in inlet conditions. This enabled the study of the ignition transient affected exclusively by laser focal location and the underlying flow field. Two-dimensional velocity statistics of the pre-ignition flow field were obtained using particle image velocimetry. High-speed schlieren and OH* chemiluminescence imaging captured density gradients and heat release during ignition tests. Four distinct mechanisms inherent to the ignition process were investigated: (1) laser energy deposition, (2) hydrodynamic ejection, (3) shear layer mixing, and (4) flame growth. A variety of properties (kernel/ejecta position and velocity, flame location and size, etc.) were extracted from diagnostic images. Phenomena controlling ignition outcome at multiple deposition locations were identified. Near the injector face, plasma-kernel asymmetry and the resulting strength of the hydrodynamic ejecta controlled ignition outcome more strongly. Farther downstream from the injector face, the instantaneous position of the turbulent reactant-jet shear layer relative to the kernel and ejecta were more dominant. Stochastic fluctuations in the pre-ignition recirculation zone and shear layer velocity fields were found to influence shear layer mixing time and flame growth trajectory, affecting test outcome throughout all steps of the ignition process.

papers.title: Phosphorylation-programmed cellulose nanofibers enable sustainable pyrite–serpentine separation via interfacial assembly and steric stabilization
papers.abstract: Regulating mineral surface interactions is essential for achieving particle separation and sustainable resource recovery. However, serpentine-induced hetero-aggregation in sulfide flotation masks valuable mineral surfaces, weakens bubble–particle attachment, and reduces separation selectivity. Herein, phosphorylated cellulose nanofibers (P-CNFs) with controlled phosphorylation degrees were developed as bio-based depressants for sustainable pyrite–serpentine separation. Micro-flotation established a non-monotonic relationship between phosphate content and separation performance, with moderately phosphorylated P-CNF achieving the highest pyrite recovery of 89.33%, whereas insufficient or excessive phosphorylation led to inferior performance. This behavior was governed by phosphorylation-regulated surface chemistry and interfacial adsorption architecture. Increasing phosphorylation introduced more phosphate groups and shifted serpentine surface charge negatively, thereby weakening electrostatic attraction with pyrite. However, higher phosphorylation degrees also reduced cellulose crystallinity and drove the structural evolution of P-CNFs from extended fibrillar networks to shorter particle-like aggregates. On serpentine surfaces, moderate phosphorylation enabled compact assembly of a dense and continuous fibrous adsorption layer, whereas excessive phosphorylation generated discontinuous deposits with lower surface coverage. Direct atomic force microscopy force measurements demonstrated that the optimized P-CNF layer transformed pyrite–serpentine interactions from attraction-dominated to repulsion-dominated by coupling electrostatic double-layer repulsion with long-range steric stabilization, decreasing the adhesion force from 13.00 ± 0.03 to 0.30 ± 0.05 mN m−1. These findings establish a direct structure–interface–performance relationship, demonstrating that adsorption-layer architecture and polymer-mediated steric forces, beyond phosphate-derived mineral affinity, are decisive factors governing cellulose-based depressant performance. This work provides a sustainable interfacial engineering principle for designing bio-based macromolecular reagents for cleaner mineral beneficiation and broader aqueous separation processes.

papers.title: Research on a rotating nonlinear energy sink for vortex-induced vibration energy harvesting: Including a discussion of the application limitations
papers.abstract: Vortex-induced vibration (VIV) technology for fluid flow energy harvesting and continuous power supply for environmental microelectronic devices has attracted extensive research attention. Against this backdrop, this study proposes a rotating nonlinear energy sink (NES) power generation system for cylindrical VIV energy harvesting and establishes a numerical model based on the wake oscillator model that integrates key governing parameters. Numerical results show that the maximum output power of the proposed energy harvesting system under two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) VIV excitation reaches 3.26 W. For single-degree-of-freedom (1-DOF) VIV, the vibration response of the cylinder can be divided into three distinct regions across varying flow velocities: the vibration suppression region, the modulation response region, and the offset response region. Specifically, the periodic oscillatory-unidirectional rotation state in the vibration suppression region exhibits desirable energy harvesting performance and can maintain stable operation over a wide range of flow velocities. Furthermore, this study reveals that the locked steady state under 1-DOF VIV excitation can lead to functional failure of the energy harvesting system across a wide flow velocity range, while the corresponding flow velocity range under 2-DOF VIV excitation enables the system to restore energy harvesting functionality, although the system primarily harvests energy along the weak vibration direction of the cylinder. This study optimizes the structural design of the rotating NES-VIV energy harvesting system, systematically investigates its energy harvesting characteristics under 2-DOF conditions, identifies the limitations of current applications, and proposes corresponding improvement strategies, which can provide valuable reference for future related research and development.

papers.title: A nanoscale flow characterization model based on the apparent boundary layer
papers.abstract: The incompatibility between macroscopic continuum assumptions and microscopic molecular mechanisms remains a key challenge in nanoscale flow modeling. To address this issue, this work introduces the concept of an apparent boundary layer, with its thickness denoted as happ. The model is constructed by combining a short-range interaction viscosity model with a fixed-partition viscosity model under flow conservation constraints. The parameter happ is determined through numerical solution of the resulting implicit equation. After model validation, the flow behavior within a single nanopore is systematically analyzed. The results demonstrate that happ is jointly governed by the geometric scale R, contact angle θ, Hamaker constant AH, and the solid–liquid Lennard-Jones size parameter σLS. The absolute thickness happ increases with R, whereas the dimensionless thickness happ/R exhibits a more intricate dependence: at low AH or high σLS, happ/R increases with R (a larger radius yields a larger dimensionless thickness); conversely, at high AH or low σLS, happ/R decreases with R (a smaller radius yields a larger dimensionless thickness). In contrast, θ primarily modulates happ through boundary viscosity and slip contribution; within the effective mapping range, θ regulates happ nonlinearly but exhibits no pronounced saturation over the studied range. AH and σLS display monotonic variations accompanied by significant saturation: both markedly affect the thickness within their respective effective ranges, yet their regulatory effects diminish rapidly beyond a certain threshold. The synergistic interplay among these three parameters ultimately governs the evolution of happ. The maximum effective mapping range of happ occurs in the parameter regime characterized by high θ, high AH, and low σLS. This model bridges the gap between macroscopic description and microscopic mechanisms in nanofluid flow, offering a theoretical reference for understanding transport phenomena in shale matrix nanopores.

papers.title: An unconditionally stable fully discrete method for Navier–Stokes-type viscoelastic fluid models with tempered kernel
papers.abstract: This paper develops a fully discrete finite element method with first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy for a class of Navier–Stokes-type viscoelastic fluid equations with a tempered power-law memory kernel. The finite element method is employed for spatial discretization, while a first-order convolution quadrature is utilized to approximate the nonlocal memory term, and a semi-implicit scheme is adopted to treat the nonlinear convection term. The proposed method is rigorously analyzed in terms of stability, consistency, and convergence. In particular, stability estimates, truncation error bounds, and optimal L2-norm error estimates for the velocity are established. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to verify the theoretical convergence rates for both manufactured solutions and benchmark problems without available analytical solutions. Furthermore, a two-dimensional 4:1 planar contraction channel is considered to investigate the impact of viscoelastic effects on complex flow dynamics. The numerical results reveal that the elastic stress coefficient and the tempering rate parameter play a crucial role in regulating the evolution of corner vortices and recirculation structures. In particular, the competition between viscous dissipation and elastic stress effects leads to non-monotonic vortex evolution, including vortex suppression and subsequent enlargement with increasing elasticity. These observations demonstrate the capability of the proposed method to capture the characteristic flow behaviors of viscoelastic fluids, including elasticity-induced instability and drag-reduction phenomena.

papers.title: Water–vapor–air three-phase numerical investigation on characteristics of cavitation with air injection
papers.abstract: In fluid machinery, cavitation erosion degrades material strength and causes mass loss, reducing operating efficiency. Recent studies have used high-speed cameras to observe cavitation and the effects of gas injection, but distinguishing the gas–vapor mixture remains difficult, posing a major challenge for research. This study takes a blade as the research object and combines experimental and numerical investigations into the characteristics of air-injected erosion mitigation. The phase structures are resolved using the volume of fluid method, coupled with the large eddy simulation approach to capture the turbulence features using the wall-adapting local eddy-viscosity model handling the sub-grid scale effects. The cavity is composed of vapor–air mixture and pure air, while the mixture is treated as a phase-changing gas handled through the Schnerr–Sauer mass transfer model considering the mixed saturated pressure and the pure air is treated as a non-condensable gas. By simulating the cavitating flow field around the propeller blade and the cavity morphological evolution on the blade surface, the cavitation phenomena distributed on the propeller blade and their formation mechanisms are explored. The influence of different inlet flow rates and air injection rates on the air-injected cavitation characteristics is analyzed. The results indicate that the water–vapor–air three-phase flow model considering the effect of air on the saturated pressure of the gas mixture can well predict the cavitation features consistent with high-speed imaging results and capture the main features of bubble expansion, breakup, and mixing.

papers.title: Competitive interplay of fracture number and aperture in thermo-hydro-mechanical coupled heat extraction from enhanced geothermal systems
papers.abstract: Increasing fracture connectivity and hydraulic conductance can improve fluid circulation in enhanced geothermal systems, while faster reservoir cooling can offset the resulting gains in heat output. This study examines how natural-fracture number and aperture jointly affect this trade-off over time using a two-dimensional coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical model. Thirty-six simulations combine three fracture-network realizations, natural-fracture numbers of 10, 20, and 40, and apertures of 0.10–0.22 mm over 50 years of constant-pressure operation. Fracture apertures remain fixed during each simulation, while matrix porosity and permeability evolve through the adopted constitutive relations. Larger fracture numbers and apertures generally increase mass flow and cumulative gross sensible-heat extraction, but reduce production temperature and advance thermal breakthrough. A 10% loss of the initial reservoir-to-injection temperature difference occurs within 50 years in 23 of the 36 cases. Quadratic response-surface sensitivities show a shift in thermal-power control from aperture at early times to fracture number at later times, with the first crossover occurring between years 17 and 21 across the three realizations. Local matrix permeability also partially recovers during continued cooling in one examined case, without establishing recovery of reservoir-scale thermal performance. Requiring the year-30 production temperature to exceed 150 °C in all three realizations retains nine of the 12 tested number–aperture combinations. These results show that parameter rankings depend on both the performance metric and the operating horizon. Joint assessment of flow, temperature, and cumulative heat provides a basis for temperature-constrained comparison of the tested configurations; economic ranking additionally requires pumping energy and cost estimates.

papers.title: A density-based Euler–Lagrange framework for compressible reacting flows and supersonic sprays in OpenFOAM
papers.abstract: A density-based Euler–Lagrange solver, SprayScramjetFoam, is developed in OpenFOAM to simulate the strongly interacting shock-spray-combustion processes in liquid-fueled supersonic combustors. The framework combines shock-resolving compressible-flow calculations with turbulence-chemistry interactions and Lagrangian spray models accounting for breakup, evaporation, and two-way interphase coupling. A hierarchical validation strategy is employed for shock propagation, supersonic reacting flow, droplet evaporation, and transverse liquid injection. The solver reproduces the principal shock and flame structures, improves droplet-evaporation predictions relative to the native OpenFOAM formulation, and captures the penetration and breakup characteristics of a supersonic transverse liquid jet. The framework is further applied to a kerosene-fueled two-cavity supersonic model combustor, where the predicted flame-stabilization region and streamwise wall-pressure evolution agree with experimental observations.
