The numerical results reveal the interaction among combustion-induced compression, cavity recirculation, spray breakup and transport, evaporation, and fuel-air mixing, which together determine the flame-stabilization behavior. These results demonstrate the reliability of SprayScramjetFoam for investigating gas-liquid flow and combustion processes in liquid-fueled supersonic combustors.

papers.title: Underwater explosion bubble jet criterion considering free surface and rigid bottom
papers.abstract: A commonly adopted method for predicting bubble jet direction is the theoretical criterion developed by Blake based on Kelvin impulse theory. However, its derivation relies on the classical Rayleigh bubble equation, which does not explicitly consider the influence of different boundaries on bubble dynamics. To develop an improved bubble jet criterion considering boundary effects, a series of underwater explosion centrifuge model tests were conducted over a wide range of gravity levels, providing a unique experimental framework for systematically examining bubble pulsation between the free surface and a rigid bottom. For a fixed explosive charge weight and detonation depth, with increasing gravity level, the buoyancy force gradually increases and eventually exceeds the boundary-induced Bjerknes forces, resulting in a transition of the bubble jet direction from vertically downward to upward. When the two forces reach an approximate balance, the bubble exhibits no distinct directional jetting behavior. Furthermore, Zhang's unified bubble equation was adopted for comparison with the experimental results, and the key bubble pulsation parameters showed good agreement. Finally, an improved underwater explosion bubble jet criterion accounting for boundary effects was derived by replacing the classical Rayleigh bubble equation in the Blake criterion with Zhang's unified bubble equation, and its applicability and reliability were further verified through centrifuge model tests. The research findings can provide a theoretical basis for evaluating localized structural damage induced by bubble jets and for improving the protective design of underwater structures.

papers.title: Quantifying the effect of natural ventilation on post-occupancy aerosol exposure in a cruise ship cabin
papers.abstract: Most studies on airborne transmission in transportation systems have focused on exposure during the simultaneous presence of infectors and susceptible occupants, whereas the transport mechanisms of residual aerosols after the infector departs remain insufficiently understood. This study employed validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to investigate the temporal evolution of aerosol concentrations in a cruise ship cabin during and after the presence of an infector, under varying ambient wind directions and natural ventilation configurations. Results show that ambient pressure distribution governs aerosol removal by reorganizing cabin airflow. Under recirculating air-conditioning ventilation, a closed longitudinal circulation continuously redistributes aerosols without forming an effective exhaust pathway, resulting in rapid aerosol accumulation to 4381 ppm after 10 min. In contrast, natural ventilation establishes pressure-driven through-flow transport. Against-wind conditions produce a longitudinal transport pathway, whereas side wind generates a transverse cross-cabin pathway that accelerates aerosol removal. Accordingly, the air change rate increases from 23.39–104.38 h−1 under against-wind conditions to 61.78–333.65 h−1 under side-wind conditions. Furthermore, ventilation effectiveness is governed primarily by the organization of transport pathways rather than the area of ventilation openings. The frontal opening may disrupt the pressure-driven transport pathway by introducing an opposing inflow. These findings reveal how natural ventilation controls aerosol transport in moving enclosures and provide a generalized framework for ventilation design.

papers.title: Density evolution in inhomogeneous fluids from a kinetic Gibbs–Duhem relation
papers.abstract: The classical Gibbs–Duhem relation is restricted to quasistatic thermodynamic processes and does not include kinetic energy contributions. Consequently, its connection to fluid mechanics remains indirect. Here, we derive a kinetic Gibbs–Duhem relation that consistently incorporates kinetic effects, thereby linking thermodynamic and mechanical descriptions of fluid motion. On this basis, we formulate a density evolution equation for inhomogeneous fluids. The proposed equation recovers, as limiting cases, the classical relations for the speed of sound, Bernoulli's equation, and the van der Waals equation of state.

papers.title: Nonlinear displacement dynamics of solid gallium microspheres under traveling surface acoustic waves
papers.abstract: High-precision size sorting of liquid-metal microspheres is of great significance for flexible electronics, biomedicine, and microfluidics. Traveling surface acoustic waves (TSAWs) enable non-contact manipulation under continuous-flow conditions; however, the acoustic response of liquid-metal microspheres, which combine high density and extremely low compressibility, remains unclear, and the competition between acoustic radiation force and acoustic streaming is difficult to decouple. Solid Ga microspheres were used as the primary objects, with polystyrene (PS) and fused silica microspheres as references, while liquid eutectic gallium–indium droplets were limited to dispersion-medium screening and liquid-droplet-model validation. Electro-acoustic-fluid multiphysics simulations and experimental observations were combined to investigate the swirling, patterning, and migration modes of microspheres of different materials and sizes in TSAW fields. The results showed that, in the small-particle-size range, the migration boundary of solid Ga microspheres shifted overall toward smaller sizes. Low-ka analysis and PS-baseline parameter scans showed that the small-size acoustic-radiation-force response was highly sensitive to bulk compressibility. Further analysis showed that Ga microsphere trajectories exhibited an alternating step-like pattern of steep-rise and plateau segments, caused by alternating strengthening and weakening of the acoustic radiation force along the propagation direction due to near-wall diffraction; when a microsphere entered a low-force region, the driving force dropped abruptly, and the lateral motion temporarily slowed. These results provide mechanistic insight into acoustofluidic manipulation of materials with complex properties and quantitative parameters for precise size sorting of liquid-metal microspheres.

papers.title: Reorganization of the horseshoe vortex system by developing scour-hole geometry at a cylindrical pier
papers.abstract: The horseshoe vortex (HSV) system is the principal agent of local scour at bridge piers, yet its response to the geometry it excavates is difficult to measure: during active scour the boundary evolves while the flow is sampled, and the mobile bed obstructs optical access. Here, scour holes generated in mobile-bed tests were laser-scanned from within a transparent pier, digitally reconstructed, scaled, and printed as three-dimensional models, molded and cast in clear resin. The casts, representing bed states after 0–20 h of scour development, enabled repeatable time-resolved particle image velocimetry at a circular pier, with vortex cores tracked in every velocity field. The results show that the developing geometry does not merely amplify the HSV: it relocates and confines it. The primary core descends by 0.125D±0.004D (D, pier diameter), spends 95% of the time below the initial bed level in the 20 h geometry, and maintains a standoff of only 0.06D–0.11D above the local bed as it deepens. The area enclosed by the core trajectory falls by about two-thirds, core circulation strengthens by 28%, mean downflow deepens by 62%, and organized bed-parallel Reynolds shear stress over the slope rises to 1.7–2.9 times its flat-bed value; these percentages are condition-specific, whereas the geometry-relative behavior, with descent tracking the deepening bed at a standoff of order 0.1D and progressive confinement, is robust. The measurements show the scour hole acting as a progressive hydrodynamic organizer of the vortex-system, continually re-seating erosive forcing at the deepening bed; the resulting sediment response is inferred rather than measured.

papers.title: Effects of back pressure and injector geometry on the flashing spray characteristics of nitrous oxide under critical conditions
papers.abstract: Nitrous oxide (N2O) has emerged as a highly promising green propellant for spacecraft attitude and orbit control systems. However, its high-saturation vapor pressure readily triggers violent non-equilibrium flash phase transition during injection, posing significant challenges to injector flow rate prediction and reliable combustion chamber ignition. This study employs the backlight shadowgraphy technique to investigate the effects of back pressure (0.01–1.00 MPa) and plain-orifice injector geometry (orifice diameter, length-to-diameter ratio, L/D) on the flash spray characteristics of N2O under critical conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that the pressure ratio (Rp) is the dominant factor governing the extent of flash. The flash spray field exhibits a pronounced cooling effect, even inducing a gas–liquid–solid phase transition, with lower back pressures resulting in a significant increase in solid particles; L/D has a comparatively weak effect on spray development and discharge characteristics within the investigated range; in contrast, increasing the orifice diameter leads to a power-law decrease in the manifold pressure, which significantly weakens the flashing intensity. Based on the present experimental data, an empirical correlation is established for predicting the flow rate of N2O plain-orifice injectors within the investigated flashing critical flow regime and geometric range. These findings contribute experimental data and a theoretical foundation to fundamental investigations of flash phase-change kinetics in multiphase systems.

papers.title: Effect of high-frequency vibration on silicon melt in a cavity with cold curved bottom and hot horizontal top
papers.abstract: A numerical study of thermovibrational convection in molten silicon confined within a cavity characterized by a curved cold bottom wall and a uniformly heated plane top wall is presented. High-frequency (HF) vibrations are imposed on the system, and their influence on flow structure, symmetry, and intensity is examined under various configurations. Within the framework of the Boussinesq approximation, the governing equations are formulated in a dimensionless streamfunction–temperature form and solved using a spectral collocation method with Gauss–Lobatto–Chebyshev points and Crank–Nicolson time integration. The effects of vibration direction, amplitude, and cavity-bottom curvature are investigated across a wide range of Grashof (Gr) and vibrational Grashof (Grv) numbers. Three distinct situations are analyzed: pure buoyancy-driven convection, purely vibrational flow under microgravity, and the combined state in which HF vibration is applied to buoyant convection. Flow symmetry, pattern, and intensity are found to be highly sensitive to both the bottom deflection parameter and the vibration angle. The obtained results provide insights into the control of convective behavior in low-Prandtl-number melts, with implications for crystal growth and the purification of silicon in photovoltaic technologies.

papers.title: Stimulated saliva in X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia: Rheological comparison with healthy controls and resting saliva
papers.abstract: The lubricating and moisturizing function of laryngeal mucus is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to phonation, yet its direct sampling is invasive. Saliva offers a noninvasively collectable alternative for investigating viscoelastic properties both as a surrogate for laryngeal mucus and with regard to its own role, particularly in ectodermal dysplasia (ED), where dysfunction of certain eccrine glands is associated with reduced salivary flow, characteristic voice quality, and difficulties in chewing/swallowing. A rheological characterization was performed on stimulated saliva (SS) from patients with X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED) and matched healthy controls, and SS was compared with resting saliva (RS) from previous cohorts. SS was measured using a plate–plate rheometer with stress-controlled oscillatory frequency sweeps (f = 1–10 Hz; τ = 0.1 Pa) and strain sweeps (0.01–20 Pa; f = 0.5 Hz). ED saliva tended to exhibit lower storage and loss moduli at low frequencies/low strains, with convergence toward or exceedance of control values at higher frequencies/strains, indicating altered viscoelastic behavior. In healthy controls, pronounced rheological differences between resting and stimulated conditions were observed, whereas these differences were substantially attenuated in ED, most notably in adult males. Strikingly, RS from male XLHED patients closely resembled SS from healthy male controls, suggesting that “resting” saliva collection in XLHED may involve unintended functional stimulation or reflect varying degrees of impairment of the different salivary glands in XLHED. Overall, the data indicate disease- and sex-specific alterations in salivary viscoelasticity, potentially reflecting altered gland-specific secretion and/or macromolecular composition. Conclusions about the molecular basis and functional relevance require compositional, gland-specific, extensional, and tribological validation.

papers.title: Geometric vorticity coupling: A geometric diagnostic of anisotropic nonlinear structure formation
authors: Fabiana Rita do Couto Santos Pereira
papers.abstract: Geometric Vorticity Coupling (GVC) is investigated as a local scalar diagnostic that combines the amplitudes and relative orientation of a density gradient and a rotational velocity field. We evaluate the diagnostic in three-dimensional periodic particle calculations using mass-weighted Eulerian velocity reconstruction, complemented by controlled rotational benchmarks, coarse-graining tests, spectral robustness analyses, density-Hessian environment classification, and amplitude-conditioned angular null models. Decomposing GVC into an amplitude factor and an angular factor shows that its statistical variation is predominantly amplitude-associated in the reconstructed flow. The relation between GVC and its amplitude control has an exponent of 1.0017 ± 0.0003, while coarse graining strongly attenuates both quantities and produces only modest angular reweighting. Their reference spectral-slope difference is 0.019 ± 0.020 and varies from approximately −0.029 to 0.032 across numerical robustness tests, providing no configuration-independent spectral enhancement. At one-cell coarse graining, the filament-to-void mean ratios are 1.386 ± 0.094 for GVC and 1.398 ± 0.099 for its amplitude control, whereas the angular-factor ratio is 0.9881 ± 0.0020; the GVC contrast reverses sign without smoothing, demonstrating scale dependence. Finally, angular enrichment of high-GVC regions relative to unrestricted shuffling is reproduced by an amplitude-conditioned null model, leaving a residual strong-angle fraction of −0.001 794 ± 0.000 474. These results establish GVC as a scale-dependent amplitude–orientation diagnostic: orientation provides local geometric weighting, but the present calculations resolve neither a positive angular enrichment beyond amplitude-conditioned selection nor a robust independent spectral enhancement.

papers.title: Non-equilibrium turbulence generated by a fractal grid in density-stratified fluids
papers.abstract: Turbulence generated by a towed space-filling square fractal grid was investigated in non-stratified, linearly stratified, and two-layer stratified fluids. Six cases were considered, with initial Reynolds numbers ReL0=U0L0/ν of 43 200 and 54 700. For the stratified cases, initial Froude numbers FrL0=U0/(NL0) ranged from 0.93 to 2.36, where U0, L0, N, and ν denote the initial characteristic velocity, the largest mesh size, buoyancy frequency, and kinematic viscosity, respectively. Velocity fields are measured using a two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry system. Under stratification, the horizontal kinetic energy decays faster than in the non-stratified case. Dissipation reconstructed from the two planes, and the resulting Cε=εLu/urms3 (ε: total dissipation rate; Lu: longitudinal integral length scale; and urms: the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) streamwise velocity fluctuations) displays trends consistent with non-equilibrium behavior. The transition from non-stratified to weakly stratified turbulence, identified by the Froude number FrH=urms/NLu and the Reynolds number ReH=urmsLu/ν, occurs near the onset of Lu growth. The energy spectra initially exhibit a clear k−5/3 inertial range and only later steepen toward a −2 slope, indicating a delayed transition to quasi-two-dimensional turbulence. The coupled roles of different initial conditions and stratification in non-equilibrium dissipation mechanism are discussed.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of flow evolution in a V-shaped dual-slot plasma synthetic jet
papers.abstract: Vane-type vortex generators (VGs) suppress flow separation, and single-slot jets can serve as active VGs to emulate the same effect. Therefore, V-shaped dual-slot synthetic jets may also hold promise for similar applications, yet their actuation characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study designs a V-shaped dual-slot plasma synthetic jet actuator and experimentally investigates, under quiescent conditions, the transient evolution and time-averaged (over the pulse window) characteristics of the dual jets across three energy deposition ratios (ε = 0.93, 2.59, and 6.63). The results show that the evolution of the dual jets comprises converging, merging, and combined stages, with the radial velocity profiles at the peak velocity location transitioning from a double-peaked to a single-peaked distribution. Increasing ε accelerates merging and enhances jet penetration; at t/Td = 0.02, the penetration depths for the three cases reach 8.4D0, 10.9D0, and 14.3D0, respectively. Large-scale vortex structures form a merged vortex ring that exhibits an axis-switching tendency under self-induced velocity, consistent with the observed compression of the jet at the long-axis ends and its subsequent splitting in the orthogonal direction. In the time-averaged fluctuation field, the turbulent kinetic energy is more dispersed than the phase-correlated kinetic energy and exhibits far-field merging features. Increasing ε broadens both the instantaneous vorticity and time-averaged fluctuation distributions, and causes the time-averaged streamline topology to degenerate from a standing vortex into a single source point.

papers.title: Coupling effects of two forward-facing triangular bubbles interacting with a planar shock wave
papers.abstract: The study presents numerical simulations of two forward-facing equilateral triangular bubbles under the impact of a planar shock wave to study the induced instabilities, vortex formations, and coupling effects. The simulations are performed using a pressure-based compressible two-phase flow solver, integrated with a coupled level set volume of fluid algorithm to capture the interface, and incorporating a high-resolution total variation diminishing scheme to study shock–interfacial interactions. The evolution of the two bubbles is analyzed by varying the initial separation distance, Atwood number (At), and Mach number (M). Qualitative and quantitative analyses are performed to study the interfacial features, i.e., length, height, upstream and downstream locations of the distorted bubbles, the vortex interactions, baroclinic vorticity produced, and coupling jet formation. The results show that the initial separation distance significantly affects the coupling between the bubbles; a smaller distance leads to stronger coupling, which, in turn, promotes vortex interactions and earlier coupled-jet formation. Furthermore, the effects of varying the Atwood number reveal negligible inter-bubble interaction for a positive Atwood number up to 0.67, even for the smallest separation distance of 2 mm. An increase in the Mach number results in rapid interfacial motion, enhanced vortex structures and interactions, and stronger coupling jet formation. The results highlight the roles of geometric configuration, initial separation distance, Atwood number, and Mach number in determining coupling effects, the growth of interfacial instabilities, and vortex formation in Richtmyer–Meshkov instability studies. A scaling law is further established to quantify the coupling metric dependence on different parameters.

papers.title: Low-dimensional subspace and local dynamical equilibrium in transonic buffet
papers.abstract: The transonic buffet phenomenon over the ONERA OAT15A supercritical airfoil is investigated using two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations with Reynolds Stress Model turbulence closure at M∞=0.73 and α=3.5°. The simulations reproduce the characteristic self-sustained shock oscillation, shock–boundary layer interaction, and periodic aerodynamic response, with a dominant buffet frequency of 166.5 Hz corresponding to St=0.070, consistent with available experimental measurements. Proper Orthogonal Decomposition identifies a dominant conjugate modal pair containing approximately 83% of the total modal energy, highlighting the low-dimensional organization of the principal buffet dynamics. A two-dimensional Koopman representation is subsequently employed to assess the dynamical closure of the dominant modal coordinates, establishing a coherent reduced temporal description of the buffet cycle. Building on this reduced dynamics, a theoretical and mathematical formulation is introduced to interpret the dominant shock-associated motion as a local dynamical equilibrium of the evolving flow state. The formulation provides a complementary description of the established shock–boundary layer feedback by organizing its collective effect through inertial, restoring, and non-conservative contributions. Finally, a two-mode lower-order reconstruction reproduces the dominant flow evolution with a mean normalized error of 4.67%, while the reconstructed lift and drag histories achieve correlation coefficients of 0.998 and 0.976, respectively. The results connect the established low-dimensional structure of transonic buffet with its dynamical closure and a local dynamical-equilibrium interpretation, while demonstrating the effectiveness of the resulting reduced representation.

papers.title: A numerical study of silica sol flow regimes during oil displacement from the models of porous media
papers.abstract: The present work reports the results of a systematic numerical investigation of displacement flows during oil recovery from models of terrigenous and fractured porous media using silica nanoparticle-based nanofluids. In the calculations, nanofluids with a mean particle size of 10 nm were considered, with the mass concentration of particles varied within the range of 0.25–1.0 wt. %. The nanofluid properties required for the simulations were preliminarily determined through experimental studies. The effects of nanoparticle concentration, pore-space structure, capillary number, and displaced oil viscosity on flow regimes and displacement efficiency were examined. A relationship was established between the physicochemical properties of the investigated nanofluids and the oil displacement characteristics in the model porous media. The key factors are identified as improved wettability and reduced interfacial tension upon nanoparticle introduction. It was demonstrated that an increase in nanoparticle concentration leads to a higher oil displacement coefficient for both reservoir models. Moreover, the efficiency of nanofluid application is substantially enhanced with increasing oil viscosity and decreasing capillary number.

papers.title: Bubble dynamics on top of protruding objects observed with x-ray phase-contrast high-speed imaging
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive, qualitative investigation of the complex dynamics of laser-induced cavitation bubbles near rigid, protruding objects with various cross-sectional geometries. We employ a threefold approach that combines synchronized optical videography, high-speed x-ray phase-contrast imaging (at MHz frame rates), and three-dimensional compressible multiphase flow simulations. While conventional optical high-speed imaging is often limited by refraction, which obscures the bubble interior, synchrotron x-ray radiation enables unprecedented visualization of internal structures, including secondary cavitation, splashing, and jetting dynamics. Four distinct geometries are investigated: a cylindrical pillar, a cone, a vertical blade, and a three-point star column. We identify several universal qualitative features of bubbles generated above both axisymmetric and anisotropic columns over normalized stand-off distances D∗ in the range [0.047, 0.79] and normalized object widths β in the range [0.251, 0.893], including configurations where the bubble is generated off-center relative to the column. Results show a clear correlation between bubble dynamics and a specific cross-sectional geometry. Furthermore, effects of small-scale features of the object surfaces, such as roughness and sharpness of edges, can occur. These can play a role in apparent pinning of the gas–liquid interface, flow detachment and vortex formation, and secondary cavitation. The combined experimental–numerical framework allows for precise determination of bubble parameters and provides validation of three-dimensional simulations, demonstrating that geometric asymmetries significantly influence jet formation compared with fully axisymmetric configurations.

papers.title: Impinging atomization regimes and breakup dynamics of a shear-thinning supramolecular gel sheet
papers.abstract: Atomization of non-Newtonian gel fluids is of significant importance in two-phase fluid mechanics. To address the difficulty of liquid-sheet breakup caused by the high viscosity of conventional macromolecular gels, this study focuses on supramolecular gelled kerosene with pronounced shear-thinning characteristics and experimentally investigates its atomization and breakup behavior under impinging-jet conditions using high-speed photography, a laser particle-size analyzer, and image-processing techniques. The evolution of spray morphology, discharge coefficient, droplet-size distribution, and breakup mechanisms is analyzed. The results demonstrate that, compared with conventional macromolecular gelled kerosene, supramolecular gelled kerosene exhibits pronounced post-yield shear-thinning behavior, with a Herschel–Bulkley flow behavior index of n=0.0880 in the stable shear-thinning regime, and can form a well-developed spray even at relatively low injection pressure drops. As the injection pressure drop increases, the discharge coefficient continuously decreases from 0.82 to 0.69, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 15.85%. A generalized Reynolds number applicable to non-Newtonian fluids is introduced to interpret this behavior, indicating the influence of the pronounced shear-thinning characteristics on flow resistance. The droplet-size distribution further reveals a transition of the breakup mechanism from a viscosity-dominated regime to a turbulence-dominated regime. This study reveals the atomization characteristics of supramolecular gels and demonstrates the feasibility of employing supramolecular gels as a novel modification strategy for gelled kerosene propellants. The present findings provide experimental guidance for the design and operating-condition selection of impinging injectors, as well as for spray organization and atomization-distance control in gel-propellant rocket and ramjet propulsion systems.

papers.title: An experimental study of discrete gust interaction with a propeller in axial flight: Asymmetric loading and gust breakdown mechanisms
papers.abstract: Distributed electric propulsion systems in electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft are expected to encounter unsteady inflow conditions in low-altitude flight, yet the interaction between discrete gusts and small-scale propellers remains insufficiently characterized. This study investigates the response of an isolated propeller subjected to a discrete one-minus-cosine like gust generated by a dual-vane gust generator. The propeller was tested at U∞=10 ms−1 and rotational speeds of 5000, 6000, and 7000 RPM, corresponding to advance ratios of J=0.47,0.39, and 0.34, respectively. Hot-wire anemometry and phase-synchronized stereo particle image velocimetry were used to characterize the incident gust and its evolution through the propeller disk, while synchronized six-axis load measurements quantified the corresponding unsteady propeller response. The results show that the propeller-induced swirl velocity redistributes the imposed gust field, locally attenuating the vertical gust velocity on the upstroke side of the disk and amplifying it on the downstroke side. A direct comparison between the measured combined velocity field and a local kinematic reconstruction confirmed that this gust–swirl interaction captures the main asymmetric inflow mechanism, while discrepancies near the blade-root region coincided with the loss of gust coherence observed in the particle image velocimetry fields, indicating gust breakdown and additional unsteady effects. This redistribution produces asymmetric out-of-plane torque responses and alters the induced velocity field in the wake. Increasing the propeller rotation speed from 5000 to 7000 RPM (J=0.47–0.34) reduced the thrust increment induced by the gust, but strengthened the distortion of the gust field, increasing the affected region by approximately 60%. The measurements identify the gust–swirl interaction and subsequent gust breakdown as the mechanism linking discrete-gust ingestion, asymmetric loading, and wake distortion and provide an experimental dataset for modeling unsteady propeller loading in non-uniform inflows.

papers.title: The inverse capillary-rise problem: Conditioning, resolution limits, and the comparability of contact angles
papers.abstract: The height to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube depends on its surface tension and on its contact angle with the wall. Computing the height from a known angle, the forward problem, has been settled for a century: the meniscus-volume correction (r/3)M(θ) is due to Verschaffelt and Dorsey. The relation is now routinely used in reverse, with the surface tension taken from a table and the contact angle inferred from the measured height, but this inverse problem has not been analyzed. We show that it is intrinsically ill-conditioned near complete wetting, derive a closed-form uncertainty for the inferred angle, and use it to determine a resolution floor, below which an apparatus can report only an upper bound, and an optimal tube radius. For water, the floor is 3°–5°, and better length metrology cannot lower it, because the reference surface tension contributes 60%–97% of the variance and the rise height less than 2%. Because authors invert different meniscus treatments, two laboratories measuring the same surface with different tubes can report angles differing by 5° with no experimental error, and the discrepancy grows with radius, mimicking a confinement effect. Re-inferring traceable published values shifts them by up to 6°, and three of eleven admit no solution at all. Benchmarking six treatments against an eleven-point historical dataset identifies Verschaffelt's forgotten second-order term as the most accurate closed form; length and volume observables such as the meniscus height or the footprint of a sessile drop remain well conditioned where the column weight fails.

papers.title: Modeling of dam-break flow with sediment particles over different riverbed forms by coupled level set and volume of fluid-discrete element method
papers.abstract: Modeling dam-break flow involving sediment particles presents a significant challenge in hydraulic engineering and multiphase flow due to complex fluid–solid interactions. To address this, an Eulerian–Lagrangian hybrid model for air–water–particle multiphase flow, termed CLSVOF-DEM (coupled level set and volume of fluid–discrete element method) model, is proposed. Within this framework, the CLSVOF method integrates the level set and volume of fluid approaches, using secondary interface reconstruction to accurately capture the air–water interface. Concurrently, the DEM resolves the contact and collision dynamics of sediment particles. By incorporating various fluid–particle interaction forces directly into the governing equations, the coupled CLSVOF-DEM enables robust fluid–solid interactions. The proposed model is validated and subsequently applied to simulate dam-break flows carrying sediment particles over different riverbed forms. This study reveals the hierarchical governing laws of sediment-laden dam-break flows. The sediment material properties are the primary influencing factor: the massive entrainment of highly mobile Polyvinyl Chloride particles consumes considerable flow kinetic energy, slowing the wavefront propagation by approximately 20% and yielding a bed reworking amplitude roughly three times that of natural sand. Bed topography and downstream tailwater constitute the secondary controlling factors that further modulate the flow morphology and bed deformation.

papers.title: A parametric physics-informed neural network framework for cylinder-induced thermal flows
papers.abstract: Thermal design and monitoring of compact heat exchangers require fields across changing operating conditions, and increasingly from a few embedded sensors, yet each new Reynolds number is a new mesh-based simulation. A physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework is presented for the coupled prediction and inverse recovery of velocity, pressure, temperature, and vorticity fields in laminar forced convection past a heated circular cylinder at Pr=0.71 and Re∈[20,200]. A single Reynolds-number-augmented parametric PINN, implemented in PyTorch and trained once over the full range, predicts unseen Reynolds numbers with relative L2 velocity error εU=0.68% and average Nusselt number deviation below 0.7% from an OpenFOAM finite volume reference, against 3.82% for a Deep Operator Network and 6.54% for a graph neural network, without retraining. Hard boundary condition enforcement through a smooth distance function output transformation, an auxiliary vorticity transport residual, residual adaptive collocation resampling, and gradient normalization loss weighting act synergistically to yield a divergence error of 2.1×10−4 and an 86% cumulative reduction in velocity error over the unaugmented baseline. Promoting the Reynolds number to a co-optimized scalar parameter recovers an unknown Re from ten sparse pressure observations with mean relative error 0.45%. Integral quantities agree with experiment: Nu¯ rises from 3.06 to 9.54 across the range, within 1.6% of classical correlations, and St=0.166 and 0.194 match measurements to within 1%. Conservation metrics on held-out grids confirm constraint satisfaction, and inference is approximately 3000× faster than the finite volume solver, giving a physically consistent surrogate for real-time monitoring of sensor sparse thermal infrastructure.

papers.title: Suppression of low-frequency unsteadiness in shockwave and turbulent boundary-layer interactions with herringbone riblets
papers.abstract: The low-frequency unsteadiness inherent in shockwave/boundary-layer interactions (SWBLIs) poses significant challenges to aircraft structural integrity and flight safety. This study experimentally evaluates the effectiveness of herringbone riblets in controlling the low-frequency unsteadiness of incident shockwave/turbulent boundary-layer interactions at a freestream Mach number of 1.85. High-speed Schlieren visualization, combined with statistical analysis and fast Fourier transform, is employed to characterize the baseline and controlled flows, and dynamic mode decomposition is applied to the baseline flow to independently confirm its dominant frequency. The baseline flow exhibits a dominant separation-shock oscillation frequency of 550 Hz (St = 0.039). Riblet arrays with two wavelengths (Λ = 25 and 10 mm) and a height of merely 0.018δ (δ being the boundary-layer thickness) are applied upstream of the interaction region. Despite their submerged height, the riblets raise the dominant frequency of the separation shockwave to 1326 and 2597 Hz, respectively. Crucially, the absolute low-frequency (0–1 kHz) spectral energy of the shock motion decreases by 34.8% and 53.9%, the total fluctuation energy decreases by 26.9% and 45.5%, and the standard deviation of the tracked shock position decreases by 14.9% and 26.7% for the two configurations. These findings demonstrate that riblets can effectively suppress the low-frequency unsteadiness of SWBLIs. A proposed interpretation attributes these effects to the riblet-induced streamwise vortices, which deform the separation shock and shrink the separation bubble. The present results suggest that herringbone riblets are a promising passive control strategy and merit further in-depth investigation toward future aerospace applications.

papers.title: Under-resolved direct numerical simulation of flat-plate boundary layers at various Reynolds numbers with fully staggered grid
papers.abstract: Under-resolved direct numerical simulation of a flat-plate boundary layer is conducted without a subgrid-scale model for four Reynolds numbers ranging from the order of 105 to 108, using a fully staggered grid system with a high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory convection scheme. The simulation is performed without any turbulence model and with an affordable grid resolution, rather than the extremely fine grid required by a conventional direct numerical method. Three vortex-identification methods are compared, and the λ2-criterion is confirmed to be the most appropriate identifier for the flat-plate boundary layer. All cases generate and sustain near-wall vortical structures from the transition region to the trailing edge. The time-averaged boundary-layer thickness follows the Blasius scaling with the Reynolds number although it is about 20% smaller than the Blasius solution, and the streamwise fluctuation becomes progressively confined to the near-wall region as the Reynolds number increases. The turbulent dissipation rate shows a strong near-wall concentration at high Reynolds number, and the power spectrum of the velocity fluctuation exhibits a broadband decay without a spurious peak. For the shear stress, an empirical model based on the viscous and turbulent dissipation source terms of the averaged energy equation is constructed, which recovers a consistent friction coefficient for wall resolutions from y+ = 1 to 50 and agrees with the International Towing Tank Conference-1957 friction line, demonstrating a practical route for estimating frictional resistance for a wide range of Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: On the dynamics of particles in continuum suspensions. II. Unsteady flow
papers.abstract: Since the pioneering theoretical investigation by Einstein on how suspended particles alter the effective viscosity of a fluid, researchers have worked to develop a general continuum framework for the dynamics of suspensions. Recently, a promising approach has been developed that links the continuum dynamics of the fluid to moments of the force distributions from the suspended particles. These models have primarily considered the dynamics of the particles in a low Reynolds number limit. Here, we show how to modify this approach to include the unsteady motion of the suspended particles. Our results include a more complete description of the inertial terms than was previously derived in other works on the continuum dynamics of suspensions at finite Reynolds number. In addition, we show that the inertial terms can also naturally account for the Brownian motion of the suspended particles. Indeed, our results are not only consistent with the prior classical work on diffusion in suspensions but also provide a direct way to compute the diffusion coefficient that does not rely on independently computing the volume fraction dependence of the hindered settling function and chemical potential. The leading-order dependence of the diffusion coefficient on volume fraction found using this method also agrees with experimental data. Consequently, our results not only provide a way to include some inertial behavior into the continuum dynamics of suspensions but also provide a general means for accounting for the thermal motions of the particles in these suspensions.

papers.title: Experimental and numerical investigation of novel passive fluidic thrust-vectoring aerospike nozzle
papers.abstract: Passive fluidic thrust vectoring is attractive for detonation-based propulsion systems because it requires neither external gas supplies nor moving parts. This paper proposes a novel two-dimensional aerospike nozzle in which a throat-bypass passage is embedded within the central spike: the natural pressure difference across the nozzle drives a secondary jet through the passage, and its aerodynamic interference with the primary flow deflects the thrust vector. The concept is investigated through cold-flow wind tunnel experiments with schlieren diagnostics, complemented by steady compressible Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations over nozzle pressure ratios (NPRs) of 3, 5, 10, and 15. The schlieren images provide qualitative experimental validation: with the upper bypass passage opened, the nozzle jet exhibits pronounced deflection and flow asymmetry at all tested NPRs, and a distinct Mach disk appears on the injection side at NPRs of 10 and 15, whereas the closed-bypass configuration remains symmetric. Validated against published benchmark experiments and the present schlieren images, the simulations reveal the underlying vectoring mechanism: the bypass jet deflects the throat sonic line and attenuates the Coanda-driven wall attachment, and the resulting differential expansion establishes a large-scale wall-pressure asymmetry over the thrust surface. Integrating the numerically predicted wall-pressure distributions yields normal-to-axial force ratios of 0.233, 0.431, and 0.359 at NPRs of 3, 5, and 10, respectively, corresponding to a peak vector angle of approximately 23.3° at an NPR of 5, while the axial-thrust penalty remains below 1.1% and the bypass mass flow fraction below 8%. These results demonstrate the feasibility and control efficiency of the proposed throat-bypass passive vectoring aerospike nozzle and provide a reference for passive thrust-vectoring design in future detonation engines.

papers.title: On characterizing the wake of side-by-side rectangular prisms at low Reynolds numbers
papers.abstract: This study directly solves the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations to investigate the laminar wake dynamics of two identical side-by-side rectangular prisms over ranges of Reynolds numbers, gap ratios, and depth ratios to gain a detailed understanding of bluff-body wake interactions. While canonical side-by-side wake transitions are usually interpreted primarily in terms of Reynolds number and spacing, the present results show that varying prism depth ratio substantially modifies gap-flow acceleration, shear-layer development, mean recirculation, and the resulting flow regimes. Based on the Strouhal number, unsteady vorticity fields, and spectral analysis, the wakes are classified into four principal regimes: steady, merged, separated, and transitional wakes. These regimes contain distinct synchronization sub-states and downstream reorganization patterns. Furthermore, the depth ratio shifts the regime boundaries and alters the transition pathways between canonical wake states. To account for the effect of prism depth ratio on wake development, a corrected Strouhal number scaling is introduced using the local gap velocity and the mean recirculation length and width. This definition links shedding frequency to both the local convective timescale and the shape of the wake formation region. The proposed framework establishes the depth ratio as a key control parameter in the wakes of side-by-side prisms.

papers.title: Experimental study on the development characteristics of the shoulder cavity of an underwater vehicle influenced by the launch tube cover
papers.abstract: The launch tube cover significantly affects the attached cavity. Launch experiments are used to study the vehicle motion and the evolution of the shoulder cavity. Under the launch tube cover condition, the effects of shoulder ventilation, environmental pressure, vehicle exit velocity, and cover opening angle on shoulder cavity evolution are studied. The results suggest that the launch tube cover affects the initial flow field around the shoulder cavity. The cavity and reentrant jet develop more slowly near the launch tube cover. The cavity also separates earlier from the air mass at the launch tube mouth. The measured initial axial acceleration of the vehicle is also lower with the launch tube cover than without it. Afterward, the acceleration curves gradually converge as the vehicle exits the launch tube. At the same time, the cavity near the launch tube cover shows three stages: “attraction-stretching,” “repulsion-compression,” and “secondary attraction.” With ventilation, the influence of the launch tube cover on the shoulder cavity is weakened, and asymmetric shedding at the cavity end becomes less pronounced. In the presence of the launch tube cover, the cavity asymmetry increases significantly as the environmental pressure decreases or the vehicle velocity increases. As the opening angle of the launch tube cover increases, the flow near the launch tube mouth becomes more uniform. The cavity also develops more symmetrically. Furthermore, the cavity tends to form a gourd-like shape, with larger radial dimensions at both ends and a narrower center.

papers.title: Extracting coherent structures in oscillating cylinder wakes by means of image-based proper orthogonal decomposition and independent component analysis
papers.abstract: The extraction of coherent structures from high-speed flow visualization images is challenging because image-based proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) often produces a large number of modes, making the selection of appropriate inputs for subsequent independent component analysis (ICA) difficult. In this study, a multi-feature coupled framework is developed to identify coherent structures and characteristic frequencies in oscillating cylinder wakes from high-speed visualization images. Snapshot POD is first applied to grayscale image sequences to obtain dominant spatial modes and temporal coefficients. A mode-selection criterion combining the energy contribution ratio, dominant frequency energy ratio, and excess kurtosis is then proposed to rank the extracted modes according to their suitability for ICA. The selected modes are subsequently decomposed using FastICA to separate dynamically distinct flow structures. The proposed criterion consistently provides improved ICA performance in the tested 2S and 2P wake regimes, yielding lower spatial correlation and spectral entropy than single-feature selection strategies. For the 2S wake, the method identifies the dominant vortex shedding frequency at 18.7 Hz, together with the second harmonic at 37.4 Hz and the stroboscopic frequency at 49.3 Hz. For the weak 2P wake, the dominant shedding frequency of 11.9 Hz and the stroboscopic frequency of 49.3 Hz are identified. These frequencies and the corresponding flow structures are independently supported by spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and line-averaged grayscale fast Fourier transform analyses. This study provides a new technical approach for extracting complex flow structures and characteristic frequencies under low-cost experimental conditions.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic control of clustering and transport in squirmer–passive suspensions
papers.abstract: This study examines how mixture composition and total concentration affect collective organization and passive-particle diffusion in squirmer–passive suspensions. Lattice Boltzmann simulations are performed for two-dimensional periodic suspensions of equal-sized squirmers and passive particles at a low Reynolds number (Re). Using pure squirmer suspensions as a reference, we investigate the effects of the hydrodynamic mode (β), passive-particle fraction (c), and total area fraction (ψ). At an intermediate area fraction, increasing the passive-particle fraction is associated with more pronounced local ordering in strong puller mixtures, whereas the spatial structure of strong pusher mixtures changes comparatively little. At this area fraction, the relative ranking of passive-particle transport metrics across swimming modes also varies with mixture composition: as the passive-particle fraction increases, the mode yielding the highest metric values changes from neutral squirmers to strong pushers. For strong pushers, the area-fraction-weighted passive diffusivity varies nonmonotonically with the total area fraction and reaches its highest value at the intermediate area fraction among the concentrations examined. These results connect changes in local particle organization with composition- and concentration-dependent transport, showing that the swimming mode, mixture composition, and total concentration jointly influence particle aggregation and passive-particle transport in the two-dimensional suspensions studied.

papers.title: Direct spectral-inversion reconstruction of focused waves on sheared currents for cylinder-load prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the load of a focused wave group on a cylinder in a vertically sheared current requires the incident field to reproduce the focal crest, the current-dependent propagation, and the subsurface kinematics together. Existing wave-on-current focusing relies on four-phase harmonic decomposition, which needs a linearized target spectrum and four realizations per correction. We develop a direct spectral-inversion iteration for reduced-data cases with only an event-centred free-surface segment at one gauge. The target and simulated segments are projected onto a common complex spectrum, and inlet amplitude and phase are corrected using the amplitude ratio and wrapped phase error, with one numerical realization per iteration. A four-step procedure assesses current maintenance, focal-event reconstruction, unfitted subsurface velocities with two- to three-dimensional transfer, and the inertia-dominated cylinder load under no, adverse, and following currents. In the no-current example, five iterations reduce the focus-point root mean square error from 6.4599×10−3 to 4.2769×10−3 m and raise the correlation from 0.9679 to 0.9857. Peak-load errors remain within 8.79%, with focus-window root mean square errors of 1.82–3.19 N. The inlet phase corrections follow the shear-modified dispersion, with opposite signs for adverse and following currents. The only substantial discrepancy, the following-current post-focus force, is associated with an amplitude-dominated residual in the primary and sum-frequency bands that this current carries into the post-focus window, where it acts through pressure; viscous and difference-frequency contributions are negligible. Additional no-current Joint-North-Sea-Wave-Project and Pierson–Moskowitz cases indicate portability to other unimodal spectra. Control of post-focus higher-harmonic content still requires phase decomposition.

papers.title: Novel mixed approximate deconvolution large-eddy simulation models for two-phase flows
papers.abstract: Approximate deconvolution (AD) frameworks for large-eddy simulation offer a promising approach for modeling multiscale interactions in turbulent multiphase flows. However, some conventional formulations exhibit structural inconsistencies, identified in our previous work [Amani et al., Phys. Fluids 36, 085188 (2024)], which can impact the accuracy and robustness of AD-LES. To address this issue, the present study extends a family of structurally consistent AD closures to turbulent two-phase flows. Specifically, we introduce the alternative local dynamic model with kinetic energy equation (A-LDMK), an improved non-equilibrium one-equation mixed eddy-viscosity AD framework. These closures are evaluated through a posteriori analyses of a single-phase turbulent channel flow and a turbulent two-phase gas–liquid mixing layer. The results indicate that the consistent frameworks enhance numerical stability and can sustain energy backscatter under less restrictive stability constraints compared to standard dynamic procedures. Specifically, the proposed A-LDMK provides the most accurate prediction of the multiscale primary atomization cascade in terms of droplet size distribution, compared to the other assessed closures.

papers.title: Biomechanical study of intracranial arterial stenosis based on fractional fluid–structure interaction
papers.abstract: Intracranial arterial stenosis alters local hemodynamics and arterial-wall mechanics; however, the extent to which changes in stenosis geometry and bifurcation configuration alter the coupled fluid-induced wall displacement and stress response remains insufficiently quantified. In this study, a two-way fluid–structure interaction framework incorporating a fractional Maxwell model is developed to characterize the viscoelastic response of the arterial wall. The effects of plaque length, stenosis severity, and bifurcation angle on flow patterns, wall shear stress (WSS), time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS), oscillatory shear stress index, displacement, and von Mises stress are investigated. Increasing plaque length enhances the spatial heterogeneity of TAWSS, producing coexisting high-shear regions near the stenosis and extended low-shear regions downstream. Increasing stenosis severity promotes jet acceleration, flow separation, vortical structures, and oscillatory shear, whereas bifurcation angle has a comparatively limited influence within the investigated range. More importantly, the fluid and solid responses exhibit a distinct spatial mismatch in the representative (plaque length of 5 mm, a bifurcation angle of 45°, and stenosis rate of 70%): the highest regional WSS occurs in middle cerebral artery M1 segment, while the largest wall displacement and von Mises stress are concentrated in the stenotic segment. These results suggest that elevated WSS does not necessarily coincide spatially with the greatest wall displacement or von Mises stress, because the structural response depends on the combined effects of fluid traction, local geometry, boundary constraints, and the assumed viscoelastic constitutive behavior. In addition, increasing α or decreasing β increases the stenotic-wall displacement and alters its temporal persistence, confirming the contribution of fractional viscoelasticity to the predicted structural response.

papers.title: Linking canopy density and submergence level to vegetative drag and flow dynamics in fluvial systems
papers.abstract: Vegetation enhances hydraulic resistance by removing momentum from the flow; however, the effective drag response depends on canopy configuration, including canopy density and submergence. This study examines how the reach-averaged vegetative drag coefficient, CD, varies with vegetation density and submergence ratio for an idealized rigid-stem canopy, correlating the drag coefficient with observed flow patterns. Laboratory experiments were performed in a closed-loop, recirculating flume, utilizing staggered arrays of rigid cylindrical stems to simulate high-stiffness vegetation canopies. Two-dimensional particle image velocimetry measurements were conducted in both vertical and horizontal planes to collect hydrodynamic data and estimate CD from a reach-scale momentum balance with stem Reynolds numbers, Red≈200–800. Velocity fields show that canopy density modifies the spatial distribution of momentum within the patch through vegetative drag, while turbulence statistics vary across the water column and differ between canopy densities and flow regimes. Across all scenarios, CD decreased as Red increased, reflecting the transition from viscous to inertia-dominated flow. Sparse canopies exhibited higher CD than dense arrays due to reduced wake sheltering. Conversely, submerged canopies maintained higher CD than emergent ones because downward vertical momentum flux from the canopy-top mixing layer partially offsets the momentum loss from upstream stem sheltering. Finally, this study identifies a density threshold where the balance shifts between competing sheltering and blockage effects on CD. The results provide new insight into the combined effects of canopy density and submergence on reach-scale drag, with implications for improved parameterization of vegetated flows in hydraulic modeling and river restoration.

papers.title: Three-dimensional deformation and breakup dynamics of an n -decane jet in crossflow
papers.abstract: Primary atomization of liquid jets in crossflow involves coupled aerodynamic loading, interfacial instability, coherent-core breakup, and droplet formation, yet their three-dimensional interactions remain incompletely understood. Three-dimensional simulations of an n-decane jet in subsonic crossflow are performed using the coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid method with large-eddy simulation and adaptive mesh refinement for crossflow velocities of 53–194 m/s. The results indicate that windward pressure loading and lateral and wake shear jointly contribute to jet deformation and breakup. Windward disturbances exhibit acceleration-influenced Rayleigh–Taylor-type characteristics, whereas lateral disturbances show predominantly shear-driven Kelvin–Helmholtz-type behavior. The fluctuation range of the normalized windward interfacial normal displacement increases with jet-normal distance and time. Increasing crossflow velocity suppresses jet-normal penetration while enhancing downstream deflection, cross-stream spreading, and anisotropic core deformation. As the crossflow velocity increases from 100 to 194 m/s, the normalized jet-normal and streamwise coherent-core breakup distances decrease from 6.29 to 3.42 and from 2.71 to 2.10, respectively. Within the statistical window, higher crossflow velocities produce more detached droplets and intensify fragmentation, whereas the Sauter mean diameter (D32) exhibits temporal fluctuations and its time-averaged value varies non-monotonically with crossflow velocity. Overall, increasing crossflow velocity intensifies fragmentation and fine-droplet production, while persistent relatively large fragments sustain a coarse-size tail, resulting in a strongly right-skewed droplet-size distribution.

papers.title: Interfacial instability and failure mechanisms of ferrofluid seals in liquid environments: A ternary phase-field ferrohydrodynamic study
papers.abstract: Ferrofluid sealing in liquid environments involves strongly coupled magnetic, interfacial, and hydrodynamic effects that are difficult to resolve using conventional two-phase models. In this study, a ternary phase-field ferrohydrodynamic framework is developed to simulate the interfacial evolution and failure of an air-ferrofluid-water sealing system. The framework couples magnetic-field-induced stresses, ternary phase-field dynamics, interfacial tension, wetting, shaft rotation, and pressure-driven flow within a unified computational model. Its numerical reliability is systematically examined through mesh independence, time step sensitivity, and phase-field interface-thickness sensitivity. The model is further validated against three benchmark problems involving magnetic deformation of a ferrofluid droplet, a three-phase liquid lens, and the critical sealing pressure of a conventional ferrofluid gas seal, showing good agreement with analytical, experimental, and published numerical results. The validated framework is then applied to investigate steady-state interface morphology, leakage-channel formation, and critical sealing pressure in liquid environments. The results demonstrate that liquid-environment sealing exhibits a distinct failure pathway from gas sealing, characterized by progressive interface deformation, liquid penetration, necking, and continuous leakage-channel formation. Increasing magnetic field intensity enhances sealing stability, whereas shaft rotation promotes interface instability. A dimensionless failure regime map based on the magnetic Bond number, Weber number, and critical pressure Bond number is established to distinguish inertia-dominated, transitional, and magnetically stabilized regimes. The proposed framework provides a computational basis for predicting and optimizing multiphase ferrofluid sealing systems.

papers.title: Simulation of high-speed droplet impact on surfaces considering compressibility and cavitation effects
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of droplet impact on solid surfaces is prevalent in scramjet combustor environments. Accordingly, this paper conducts three-dimensional simulations of spherical water droplets impacting solid surfaces under standard atmospheric pressure in air. The computational model is established based on the finite volume method and the compressible volume of fluid method and is validated against experimental results reported in existing literature. Key phenomena during the impact process including pressure wave propagation, interfacial rarefaction wave reflection, and internal cavitation are analyzed, and the oblique impact cases are further discussed. Results show that water compressibility effects emerge when the impact velocity reaches 50 m/s, corresponding to a density increment above 5%; the critical impact Mach number (relative to the speed of sound in water) for observable internal cavitation falls between 0.063 and 0.069; and steep water-hammer shock waves can persist and maintain a well-defined shock structure propagating all the way to the droplet top interface beyond 110 m/s. For oblique impact with a fixed normal impact velocity of 500 m/s, the tangential flow barely disturbs the pressure field and the pressure distribution remains approximately axisymmetric at impact angles ≥ 30° (defined as the angle between the total velocity vector and the wall), when the impact angle falls to 20°, tangential momentum dominates asymmetric wave evolution and shifts high-pressure zones tangentially; and the maximum wall shear stress is negatively correlated with the impact angle. This research could offer theoretical support for anti-erosion design of scramjet combustors and other power equipment.

papers.title: An extended scattering kernel formalism for multi-scale gas–surface dynamics
papers.abstract: Gas–particle interactions with non-absorbing surfaces are commonly described using the scattering-kernel formalism. In this framework, an operator K maps incident velocity distributions to reflected velocity distributions. The operator is self-adjoint and has norm ||K||=1 in an L2 space weighted by the three-dimensional Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, and must satisfy non-negativity, normalization, and reciprocity. In standard formulations, K represents the aggregate effect of all gas–surface interaction mechanisms through a single operator, without distinguishing the physical scales at which these mechanisms occur. For gas scattering from a rough surface, however, it is advantageous to separate geometric effects associated with distinct roughness scales from the underlying thermochemical processes occurring at the atomic scale. We, therefore, introduce a roughness-based extension of the scattering-kernel formalism, in which a local kernel is successively lifted to larger scales via single- and multi-reflection operators associated with statistically defined surface morphologies. We derive sufficient conditions under which the resulting global kernels preserve reciprocity, normalization, and non-negativity whenever these properties hold for the smallest-scale kernel. We further show that these constructions define operators on the space of scattering kernels and establish the associated multi-scale composition laws that allow independent roughness contributions to be combined recursively. The resulting framework provides a general basis for modeling gas–surface scattering on rough surfaces with arbitrary scale decompositions.

papers.title: Waveform-driven kinetic energy quantification of roll waves: From crest-trough disparity to steady-state and instability indicators
papers.abstract: Roll waves are a unique hydraulic phenomenon arising from overland flow instability, and the kinetic energy carried by the wave body is considered a key factor that contributes to soil erosion. Existing energy analyses often focus solely on total energy, and thus fail to reflect the internal energy distribution within the wave body, making it difficult to capture the direct contribution of crest impact to soil detachment. In this study, we move beyond the conventional total-energy framework and investigate the evolution of the kinetic energy of roll waves. We systematically obtained the waveforms and characteristic parameters of roll waves under different bed slopes and unit discharges using fixed-bed flume experiments and an ultrasonic measurement system. Based on the measured waveform characteristics, we developed separate methods to calculate the kinetic energy of the crest, trough, and entire wave body. The results showed that wave velocity and kinetic energy are notably influenced by bed slope and flow discharge, with the kinetic energy of the crest segment accounting for the dominant proportion of the total kinetic energy of a single wave. The crest-to-trough kinetic energy ratio (Rk) exhibits a power-law decrease with increasing unit discharge, and the ratio tends to converge across different bed slopes. On this basis, Rk is proposed as a post-formation indicator of roll-wave disappearance, and the analysis indicates a threshold of approximately 2.1. In addition, the unit-area kinetic energy of roll waves effectively characterizes the steady-state behavior of the overall kinetic energy when the roll waves are fully developed.

papers.title: Effect of thermophysical properties and injection parameters on microscopic and macroscopic spray characteristics
papers.abstract: Fuel spray characteristics are governed by the injection parameters and the fuel's thermophysical properties. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the effects of these parameters on the macroscopic and microscopic spray characteristics, using diesel, ethanol, and methanol as model liquids that span a wide range of viscosities, surface tensions, and latent heats of vaporization. Experiments were conducted at different fuel injection pressures (FIPs) (600, 900, and 1200 bars) and ambient pressures (1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 bars) to study the effect of injection parameters and ambient gas density. Macroscopic and microscopic spray characteristics were investigated using diffused backlit illumination imaging and Phase Doppler Interferometry, respectively. For all test fuels, liquid penetration length (LPL) increases with increasing FIP and decreases with increasing ambient gas pressure. Diesel, having the highest viscosity and surface tension, showed the greatest sensitivity of LPL and spray area (SA) to changes in FIP, as its penetration relied more strongly on initial jet momentum. Methanol, with the lowest viscosity, surface tension, and density among the test fuels, exhibited the shortest LPL and SA, while ethanol showed a longer LPL and higher SA than methanol. Ethanol exhibited the highest arithmetic mean diameter (AMD) and Sauter mean diameter (SMD) among all test fuels across all FIPs, attributable to its lower vapor pressure and higher latent heat of vaporization, which limited the droplet evaporation despite efficient spray atomization. Increasing FIP from 600 to 1200 bars reduced the AMD of diesel and methanol by 16.2% and 17.4%, respectively, whereas ethanol showed negligible size reduction. Methanol exhibited the smallest AMD among all the test fuels due to extensive secondary spray breakup because of its low viscosity and surface tension; however, its SMD (8.42 μm at 1200 bars) remained comparable to baseline diesel (8.17 μm) due to the presence of larger unevaporated droplets alongside the fine droplet population, attributed to high latent heat of vaporization. Methanol showed the highest average droplet velocity, while diesel showed the lowest. Overall, the results establish that the injection parameters and fuels' thermophysical properties dictate macroscopic and microscopic characteristics of the spray.

papers.title: Bubble dynamics near elastoplastic plates of varying thickness and span
papers.abstract: Bubble collapse near-rigid boundaries has been studied extensively, whereas the dynamics near deformable elastoplastic boundaries remain comparatively unexplored. Bubble collapse near deformable elastoplastic boundaries is controlled by stand-off distance and structural characteristics, yet the transition from compliant to near-rigid behavior has not been resolved within a single experimental framework. Single spark-generated bubbles are examined near fully clamped square aluminum plates using synchronized high-speed imaging and stereo digital image correlation. The tests cover stand-off distances γ = 0.40–2.00, plate thicknesses h = 0.1–5.0 mm, and clamped spans b = 100–150 mm, giving flexural rigidities D = 0.0065–818 N m. For h = 0.3 mm and b = 150 mm, the maximum bubble radius Rmax increased from 30.72 to 42.17 mm and the oscillation period Tosc from 4.925 to 7.325 ms as γ increased from 0.40 to 2.00. At γ = 1.6, increasing h reversed the terminal centroid displacement from −19.7 to +27.6 mm. Four collapse modes are identified as the boundary stiffens, namely, mushroom-shaped, compliant-boundary repulsive, transitional annular, and rigid-wall-like attractive collapse. A dimensionless boundary-compliance parameter β, defined solely by boundary and fluid properties, is proposed as an in-sample empirical coordinate that orders the four modes in a β–γ phase diagram. Attraction was observed below log10β ≈ 5, an annular transition band between about 5 and 7.2 and compliant repulsion above 7.2; these are in-sample empirical ranges for the present matrix, not established thresholds. The full-field deformation records resolved a six-stage response from shock-driven bulging to plastic settling. A phase index Π, defined from the timing of the plate-deflection extrema relative to the bubble pulsation, separates the attractive mode from the repulsion-family modes at Π = 0, showing that collapse direction is strongly associated with the rebound phase of the plate rather than with deformation amplitude alone. These results clarify how stand-off and initial plate compliance correlate with bubble evolution and loading direction on deformable structures; engineering use additionally requires strength, fatigue, and application-specific validation.

papers.title: Effect of the internal cooling structure on film outflow under rotating conditions. I. Crossflow
papers.abstract: This paper experimentally investigates the flow characteristics of two internal cooling configurations (supply plenum and crossflow) under different rotation numbers (Ro = 0, ±0.4, ±0.8) using time-resolved particle image velocimetry. The results indicate that for the supply plenum, the velocity pattern at the film hole inlet remains approximately symmetric under all rotating conditions, and the normal penetration of the coolant jet is largely unaffected by rotation. However, the jet deflects differently in the spanwise direction due to the different directions of the Coriolis force. For the crossflow configuration, the Coriolis force points toward the film hole directly when rotating counterclockwise (Ro < 0), accelerating the coolant jet and causing it to detach. When rotating clockwise (Ro > 0), the Coriolis-induced secondary flow forces the coolant to follow a detour before entering the film hole. Consequently, the flow rate of coolant into the film hole is lower than that under counterclockwise rotation, though still higher than under stationary condition. The normal penetration of the coolant jet is also between the stationary and counterclockwise cases.

papers.title: On the dynamics of particles in continuum suspensions. I. Low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: Recent work by a few different groups has aimed to develop a general continuum framework for describing the dynamics of suspensions. In one method, moments of the force distributions from the suspended particles are ensemble-averaged to derive the effective stress tensor, while a separate method computed the effective stress tensor using the spatial average of a series of spherical Green's functions. Here, we begin by showing the equivalence of these methods. We then focus on the Green's function approach and consider in more detail and generality what this method predicts for the equations of motion for the suspended particles. Specifically, by treating the volume fraction and particle force distributions as slowly varying fields in the vicinity of a suspended particle, we show that this formalism naturally leads to the presence of the divergence of the particle stress tensor in the equation of motion for the particles, consistent with what other authors have found, albeit with a different resistive drag than is often assumed. Furthermore, by considering the pair distribution in the presence of shear, we show that the particle stress contribution to the particle dynamic equation leads to shear-induced hydrodynamic diffusion and particle transport driven by normal stress differences. Consequently, the results presented here expand our Green's function formalism for the dynamics of continuum suspensions to account for the direct effect of the particle-induced stress on the dynamics of the suspended particles, which leads to a more complete description of shear-induced transport in suspensions.

papers.title: Flow mechanisms of lateral–directional control by an all-moving wingtip on a tailless configuration
papers.abstract: All-moving wingtips (AMTs) are attractive for tailless configurations as they provide yawing and rolling moments while preserving low-observable characteristics. However, previous studies have mainly focused on the overall aerodynamic forces and moments under AMT deflections, whereas the underlying flow mechanisms, especially the interaction between the AMT and the adjacent wing, remain insufficiently understood. To establish a fundamental understanding of AMT-induced lateral–directional control mechanisms, this study employs numerical simulations and wind tunnel tests to investigate unilateral AMT deflection, a basic control case in which only the left all-moving wingtip (LAMT) is deflected. The results reveal a distinct transition in the moment-generation mechanism with increasing angle of attack (AoA): at low AoAs, where the flow remains largely attached, LAMT deflection mainly acts as a local aerodynamic blockage and produces yawing and rolling moments on the LAMT itself, with little influence on the adjacent left-wing flow. As the AoA increases and the left-wing leading-edge vortex (LEV) develops, the yawing moment remains dominated by the LAMT contribution, whereas the rolling moment becomes primarily governed by the interaction between LAMT-induced flow structures and the left-wing LEV. The LAMT deflection modifies the breakdown behavior of the left-wing LEV and influences the upper-surface suction on the adjacent wing, thereby generating rolling moment contributions from both the LAMT and the left wing. Depending on AoA, deflection direction, and deflection amplitudes, LAMT-induced interactions can either delay or advance the breakdown of the left-wing LEV.

papers.title: Periodically undulating air–liquid interface on a patterned superhydrophobic surface for drag reduction
papers.abstract: Superhydrophobic surfaces have been widely applied to underwater drag reduction due to their capability of maintaining an air layer, which converts the solid–liquid interface into an air–liquid slip boundary. However, continuous air layers with millimeter-scale thickness are highly unstable and exist only temporarily due to the shear of the liquid flow. Here, a periodically undulating air–liquid interface was formed on a triangular-patterned superhydrophobic aluminum-alloy surface (TSS) fabricated by nanosecond-laser direct writing and hydrophobic treatment. The superhydrophobic and hydrophobic regions exhibited advancing contact angles of approximately 166° and 121°, respectively, while the rolling angle of the superhydrophobic region was approximately 0.8°. This wettability contrast provides a capillary pinning barrier that resists bubble displacement at the three-phase contact line, thereby promoting the formation of a periodically undulating air–liquid interface. The equal-area geometrical analysis identified a favorable full apex-angle range of 45°–65°, within which the equivalent chord length remained close to its maximum, providing favorable geometrical conditions for interfacial confinement. Experimentally, the triangular pattern with a 64° apex angle exhibited comparatively stable bubble morphology and air-layer retention, which is consistent with the theoretically favorable apex-angle range of 45°–65°. At a flow velocity of 2.0 m/s, the 64° TSS maintained an interconnected, periodically undulating air–liquid interface for up to 600 min under continuous water flow, demonstrating long-term air-layer retention. At 3.0 m/s, corresponding to a Reynolds number of 7.2 × 104, the air-layer coverage ratio remained at 25.14% after 90 min. In separate drag measurements under the corresponding air-layer states, the TSS exhibited a measured drag-reduction rate of 14.57% at 0.5 m/s. At 4.0 m/s, the measured drag-reduction rate reached a maximum of 25.71% and subsequently decreased to 9.86% as the retained air layer was progressively depleted. The results demonstrate that rational design of the triangular-patterned superhydrophobic surface can provide long-term air-layer retention together with appreciable underwater drag-reduction performance over the tested flow conditions.

papers.title: Droplet sliding modulated by Marangoni effect on an inclined miscible liquid film
papers.abstract: Droplet sliding is widely exploited in applications such as anti-icing, drug delivery, and microscale printing. Although the effects of surface properties on sliding dynamics have been extensively investigated, the role of interfacial flow and mass transfer at miscible interfaces remains poorly understood.
