papers.abstract: This paper investigates the coupled radial oscillations and translational motions of two encapsulated gas bubbles embedded in a viscoelastic medium. Each bubble comprises a gas core and a finite-thickness viscoelastic shell. The bubble shells and surrounding medium are modeled separately as Kelvin–Voigt-type viscoelastic mediums combining neo-Hookean elasticity with viscous dissipation. Resonance occurs when the driving frequency of the acoustic field matches the bubbles' natural frequency, which causes higher bubble oscillations. The material properties of both the shell and the surrounding medium can increase these oscillations, depending on their relation to the resonance frequency. The shell properties of each bubble significantly affect the surface area of the other bubble, which can be critical to determining the drug payload capacity and diffusion rate. Key parameters, such as acoustic pressure amplitude, initial bubble separation, and resonance, increase the bubble surface area. At resonance, the distance between the bubble centers reaches a minimum, which may cause bubbles to collapse. The bubbles can repel or attract each other depending on shell properties and bubble sizes. The velocity field of the surrounding medium is derived by expanding the velocity potential to the third order in the inverse bubble separation distance. This paper also examines the differences between simplified and higher-order models, highlighting that these differences become particularly pronounced near resonance. Finally, dual-frequency excitation allows bubble expansion and separation to be tuned by redistributing the pressure amplitudes while keeping their sum of squares fixed.

papers.title: Gravity-driven unstable interfacial patterns of two-phase flow in square microchannels
papers.abstract: Gas–liquid two-phase flows in porous media are ubiquitous in numerous hydraulic and environmental applications. However, the mechanisms governing gravity-driven interfacial instability and the associated flow-regime transitions remain insufficiently explored. In this study, we experimentally investigate gravity-driven gas–liquid flow patterns in vertical square microchannels. The experimental results reveal that all observed flow regimes originate from a gravity-driven interfacial instability characterized by the accumulation, acceleration, and subsequent sliding of liquid columns. Five representative flow patterns are identified, namely bubbly, slug, bubbly–slug, falling film, and continuous liquid flows, whose occurrences are governed by the liquid injection rate, fluid properties, and channel dimensions. The liquid injection velocity mediates regime transitions by regulating the bubble length in the microchannel. A flow-pattern phase diagram is established in the space of the Weber number and the Bond number, and the corresponding regime boundaries are determined. These findings provide new insight into gravity-driven two-phase flow in confined pore spaces and provide guidance for predicting and controlling flow patterns in subsurface engineering applications such as geological CO2 sequestration and underground hydrogen storage.

papers.title: Multiscale modeling of shale-gas flow in nanopores with multiple transport mechanisms
papers.abstract: Methane transport in organic shale nanopores is jointly influenced by first adsorption-layer occupancy, surface diffusion, gas slip, and the Knudsen layer. We developed a regularized multiphysics multiple-relaxation-time lattice Boltzmann model that incorporates molecular-scale adsorption properties. The Peng–Robinson equation of state is employed to describe the non-ideality of high-pressure methane. The pore-size- and pressure-dependent adsorbed-phase density obtained from grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations is coupled into the combined bounce-back and full-diffusive boundary condition, while a local mean-free-path correction is introduced to capture the near-wall Knudsen layer. Second-order Hermite regularization is further employed to enhance numerical stability in complex pore geometries and at high Knudsen numbers. Results show that pressure and pore diameter have stronger effects on apparent permeability than temperature. Compared with conventional lattice Boltzmann method, the proposed model exhibits higher sensitivity to nanoscale transport parameters. Apparent permeability increased with both Langmuir parameters, whereas the response to the Langmuir constant b approached saturation. The Real-gas effect becomes increasingly significant with increasing pressure. The Knudsen-layer correction contributes less than adsorption and slip effects but remains non-negligible under rarefied conditions. Gas slip substantially increases apparent permeability and is a major permeability-enhancement mechanism. The proposed model can identify the dominant mechanisms and provide single-phase simulations of gas transport through nanoporous media, thereby establishing a parameter basis for upscaling nanoscale media to larger-scale applications. Quantitative results and insights obtained from 2D structures are subject to limitations and should not be directly compared with 3D core-scale measurements.

papers.title: Transient air-oil two-phase flow and churning losses in splash-lubricated cylindrical roller bearing
papers.abstract: Oil splash lubrication is widely employed in cylindrical roller bearings (CRBs) for high-end rotating machinery. However, intense air-oil two-phase flow under high-speed operation causes remarkable churning power loss and complicates lubrication state assessment, while the transient interface evolution mechanism remains insufficiently validated by systematic quantitative experiments. In this study, a full-scale three-dimensional fluid dynamics model of splash-lubricated CRBs is established using the volume-of-fluid multiphase flow approach. Two quantitative indicators, drag torque and oil splash ratio, are proposed to comprehensively evaluate lubrication performance. A synchronous test platform integrating high-speed flow visualization and high-precision torque measurement is constructed to achieve cross-validation between numerical simulation and experimental results. The influences of inner ring rotational speed, initial oil level, and lubricant viscosity on flow field characteristics and power loss are systematically analyzed. Results show that churning power loss is approximately proportional to the second power of inner ring speed. A suitable oil level is found, reducing power loss by nearly 15% while maintaining effective lubrication. The transient hydrodynamic pressure evolution and inter-roller oil replenishment mechanism during roller entry and exit from the oil sump are further revealed. This work clarifies the flow mechanism at air-oil phase transition, providing solid theoretical and experimental support for low loss lubrication optimization of high-performance CRBs.

papers.title: Pore-scale connectivity evolution during oil–water redistribution induced by pressure release in fractured porous media
papers.abstract: Following stimulation and shut-in, production progressively depletes the pressure stored in a fractured formation, yet the accompanying changes in oil–water connectivity remain poorly quantified. Here, volume-of-fluid simulations are performed in a pore model comprising a sandstone matrix derived from micro-computed tomography and a prescribed fracture network. A finite oil-filled buffer, coupled to the pore domain through an oil-phase mass balance, represents the surrounding pressure-storage region. A constant-pressure outlet represents the production side. The effects of initial pressure differential and wettability are examined. The normalized pressure histories exhibit approximately exponential relaxation. The relaxation times are nearly identical for Δp0 = 0.20–0.50 MPa, whereas the 0.10 MPa case relaxes more slowly. This domain-scale behavior coexists with pressure-dependent connectivity evolution at the pore scale. As the buffer pressure decreases, oil-phase connectivity develops through selective pore-throat activation, interface rearrangement, and reconnection of previously separated oil regions. This evolution is quantified using the buffer–fracture oil-connectivity index, Ibf, and the largest connected oil-cluster fraction, Fo,max. Higher initial pressure differentials accelerate the growth of both metrics and expand the connected oil region. Wettability also influences the amount and distribution of matrix water. Water-wet conditions retain more water in fine pore bodies, whereas oil-wet conditions leave a greater fraction of the remaining water in large pore bodies. These results clarify how pressure depletion, phase connectivity, and water localization evolve together during post-shut-in production.

papers.title: Wide-operating-range propulsive performance and wake kinetic-energy transport of a ship propulsor incorporating a pre-duct and propeller boss cap fins
papers.abstract: Because the propeller advance coefficient varies widely during ship operation, this study numerically investigates the propulsive performance and wake kinetic-energy transport of an integrated propulsor combining a pre-duct with propeller boss cap fins (PBCF) over J = 0.30–1.10. The bare-propeller, PBCF, pre-duct, and integrated configurations were compared. Axial and circumferential resolved mean-flow kinetic-energy fluxes were evaluated over full-wake and near-hub regions, and the combined response was compared with an additive reference derived from the isolated-device responses. The integrated configuration increased the prescribed-inflow thrust–power ratio by 1.67%–6.29%, with the maximum at J = 0.745. Near the design condition, both flux responses remained close to the additive reference. At J = 1.10, only 6%–45% of the axial-flux increase and 15%–20% of the referenced circumferential-flux reduction were retained. The small design-condition deviation resulted mainly from cancelation between positive and negative local responses. At J = 1.10, the negative axial deviation was maintained mainly by the outer slipstream, whereas the positive circumferential deviation arose jointly from the near-hub and outer regions and persisted downstream mainly through the outer region. These results suggest that the pre-duct-modified inflow and propeller wake alter the local flow environment experienced by the PBCF. The attack angle produced the largest parameter-response ranges, reaching about 11.5% and 17% points for thrust–power ratio and axial flux, respectively, at J = 1.10. An outlet-diameter ratio of Dd/Dd,0=0.9 achieves the highest equal-weight score (about 0.70) and is identified as the most balanced candidate within the investigated numerical design space.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic synergy between undulating and caudal fins in a bionic underwater vehicle
papers.abstract: This study investigates the hydrodynamic synergy of a biomimetic underwater vehicle propelled by coordinated undulating fins (dorsal and anal) and a caudal fin. Numerical simulations are conducted to analyze the effects of key kinematic parameters and three propulsion modes on swimming and hydrodynamic performance. Results indicate that higher frequencies and larger amplitudes increase thrust but amplify unsteady hydrodynamic loading, whereas a larger wavelength reduces roll fluctuations, representing a beneficial exception. Phase difference has a negligible influence on mean thrust but strongly affects loading steadiness. The coordinated multi-fin mode (Mode 3) achieves the highest forward speed with a favorable balance of lateral and yaw loading. A positive interaction force of 1.25 N confirms genuine nonlinear synergy, while the 22% circulation amplification and 73% momentum-flux enhancement relative to Mode 2 further support the proposed wake-coupling mechanism. These wake metrics, however, include the direct contribution of the additional active caudal fin and thus cannot alone isolate the nonlinear effect. These findings provide quantitative guidance for designing efficient multi-mode underwater vehicles.

papers.title: Aerodynamic response characteristics of high-speed trains under turbulent crosswind using a train-adapted consistency-improved random flow generation inflow scheme
papers.abstract: Turbulent crosswind produces hazardous low-frequency aerodynamic loads that threaten the lateral stability of high-speed trains (HSTs). Nevertheless, the underlying eddy evolution physics and St-dependent load-amplification mechanisms remain insufficiently quantified under conventional steady uniform inflow conditions. This work establishes the HST-consistency-improved random flow generation (CIRFG) synthetic turbulence framework by coupling the CIRFG algorithm with velocity superposition for HST turbulent crosswind simulations. Unsteady improved delayed-detached-eddy simulations are performed under uniform inflow and 15% turbulence intensity turbulent inflow conditions. The synthetic turbulence undergoes a two-stage streamwise evolution and reaches statistical equilibrium at (x/H ≈ −4) upstream of the train. Incoming turbulence exerts limited influence on time-averaged aerodynamic quantities, with most mean-coefficient deviations below 4% except for the Head Car drag (−11.3%) and Tail Car lateral force (−12.3%). Turbulent inflow substantially amplifies force and moment fluctuations: the Head Car lateral force, drag, and lift root mean square (RMS) rise by 208.6%, 717.1%, and 61.3%, while the corresponding Tail Car increments are 118.1%, 496.5%, and 40.8%. The total train roll and yaw moment RMS increase by 115.3% and 100.4%. Spectral coherence results show strong linear coupling between upstream turbulence and local aerodynamic forces of the head and tail cars within (0.3 < St < 1.5), whereas nearly no detectable coherence is found for integrated total train moments. Turbulence driven load amplification is confined to low-Strouhal-number bands. This study indicates that uniform inflow simulations underestimate low-frequency overturning relevant loads, and HST-CIRFG provides a feasible tool for HST turbulent crosswind research.

papers.title: A dissipative-signed subgrid-scale flux decomposition for local enstrophy transfer in two-dimensional decaying turbulence
papers.abstract: Filtered two-dimensional vorticity transport contains both forward and local reverse subgrid-scale (SGS) enstrophy transfer, which a positive scalar diffusivity cannot represent simultaneously. We develop a neural flux decomposition that retains an explicitly dissipative tensor-diffusive component and adds a bounded sign-indefinite correction supported by resolved gradients. The dissipative component has non-negative local enstrophy transfer, while the correction supplies signed and non-collinear transport. Physical SGS labels are constructed by applying a periodic Gaussian filter to a grid-refined numerical reference. A three-seed 2×2 factorial identifies the signed correction as the dominant reproducible contribution: for the isotropic model, mean a priori transfer correlation increases from 0.483 to 0.933 on the training realization and from 0.465 to 0.934 on an independently phased initial condition. Learned symmetric positive-definite anisotropy provides a smaller, interaction-sensitive increment. Classical and neural closures exhibit distinct local and dynamical rankings. Clark gives the smallest instantaneous SGS-source error, whereas the signed isotropic neural model has the lowest mean free-running vorticity error among the original comparators; substantial late-time drift and a high-error Full realization remain. Fixed 4% sparse observations further constrain drift in extended-time reconstruction to 10 s. Frozen evaluations at two unseen filter widths, two viscosity settings, and one periodically forced flow retain Clark's local transfer advantage but reveal greater wide-filter trajectory sensitivity for Clark and Mixed, alongside a material increase in neural trajectory error. These results establish the role of the signed correction and distinguish local SGS fidelity from closed-loop performance in the tested two-dimensional flows.

papers.title: Multimodal acoustic impedance and piston loading in a locally excited hydraulic-cylinder cavity
papers.abstract: Localized high-frequency inlet excitation in large hydraulic cylinders can generate multidimensional pressure fields that depart from the cross-sectionally uniform behavior assumed in lumped-compliance and one-dimensional water-hammer models. This study develops a closed-form hydroacoustic formulation for multimodal propagation and piston-coupled loading in a finite, rigid-walled cylindrical cavity. The pressure field is expanded in axisymmetric Bessel modes, with modal amplitudes determined from a localized incident volumetric source, complex inlet-end reflection, and a moving rigid piston. The formulation yields the pressure field, source-induced blocked force, acoustic dynamic stiffness, and incident-source-to-piston-velocity transfer function. Axisymmetric finite-element benchmarks show close numerical agreement: at the representative benchmark condition, the fully reflecting case gives full-field and piston-face amplitude errors of 0.4866% and 0.005 74%, respectively, while the median piston-face L2 error over 34 frequency-resolved and position-resolved cases is 0.005 28%. The results distinguish radial cutoff, finite-cavity acoustic resonance, and coupled piston-response resonance. Reflection magnitude governs resonant amplification, reflection phase shifts resonance locations, and piston position modifies modal phase accumulation and acoustic loading. Higher-order modes remain important for local pressure nonuniformity despite their vanishing net-force contribution on an ideal full-face piston, while below-cutoff evanescent components remain influential over finite distances. Sensitivity analyses show that effective sound speed and piston mass mainly shift characteristic frequencies, source localization controls higher-order modal content, and acoustic loss and mechanical damping primarily regulate resonance amplitude and bandwidth. These results provide a physically interpretable framework that links inlet, cavity, and mechanical parameters to multimodal pressure redistribution and the piston-coupled response.

papers.title: Effect of asymmetric swirl induction on swirl-center dynamics and turbulence in a confined swirl flow
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry has been used to investigate the effect of port configuration on bulk flow statistics and turbulence in a confined swirl flow. Three different port configurations were examined to assess the effects of port geometry and combinations on the evolution of swirl flow. The axial variation of the flow field was investigated by velocity measurements in different axial planes. A swirl center analysis was performed to understand the bulk flow fluctuations and orientation in the engine cylinder. The cycle-resolved ensemble flow field was extracted to study the cycle-to-cycle variations in the bulk flow. The in-plane turbulent kinetic energy was estimated using the conventional ensemble averaging method and the window averaging method, and the results were compared. The findings suggested that the characteristics of the port location affected the bulk flow structure. Variations in swirl ratio across port configurations also yielded different levels of cyclic flow variability in the cylinder.

papers.title: Complex-ray extraction of flat-plate leading-edge receptivity with finite-distance corrections
papers.abstract: Leading-edge receptivity converts free-stream forcing into downstream Tollmien–Schlichting waves through the first Lam–Rott mode. We develop a direct asymptotic formulation to control finite-distance bias in the extracted receptivity coefficient. A further Fredholm condition and main-deck matching determine distinct corrections for displacement and wall-shear estimators under common scaling, phase, and normalization conventions. These correction coefficients are evaluated before comparison with computed ray solutions. Seven rays spanning both halves of the dominance sector test the resulting extraction over four common windows. The correction reduces maximum pairwise distances between complex coefficients by factors of 24–60. The maximum corrected displacement–shear difference is approximately 1.67×10−4, while normal-grid and marching changes remain below the predeclared 2.5×10−4 tolerance. The measured remainder decay is consistent with the predicted O(χ−2) order over the tested range. Together, the explicit correction and resolution checks provide reproducible finite-window controls for complex-amplitude extraction in the stated flat-plate problem.

papers.title: Effects of muzzle brake geometry on near field shock evolution and wall force impulse in a cased telescoped ammunition rarefaction wave gun
papers.abstract: A cased telescoped charge configuration and rearward gas ejection in a rarefaction wave gun jointly modify pressure release before and after projectile muzzle exit, producing an underexpanded central jet, multiple lateral jets, and strong shock–wall interactions inside the muzzle brake. To clarify how brake geometry governs transient flow topology and momentum redistribution, a three-dimensional unsteady viscous compressible flow model with two-way data exchange between the interior ballistic and computational fluid dynamics solvers was developed for impact–reaction, reaction, and impact muzzle brakes. The three brakes generated dispersed lateral discharge after pre-expansion, sustained multi-row high-pressure discharge, and concentrated baffle impingement, respectively. The impact–reaction brake produced dispersed side jets and compression waves, whereas the reaction brake yielded a larger lateral discharge fraction and a wider compound wave region. The impact brake formed a concentrated stagnation-pressure zone, strong reflected compression structures, and highly directional jets. Peak axial forces on the principal braking surfaces were 41.61, 57.97, and 110.48 kN, with corresponding impulses of 64.39, 106.42, and 113.92 N s. Although the impact brake produced a peak force 1.91 times that of the reaction brake, its final impulse was only 7.0% higher, demonstrating the combined importance of load magnitude and duration. Rearward gas ejection reduced recoil impulse from 1720.36 to 352.27 N s; adding the three brakes further reduced it to 287.88, 245.85, and 238.35 N s, corresponding to recoil-reduction efficiencies of 83.27%, 85.71%, and 86.15%. These results link brake geometry to shock topology, wall loading, and impulse accumulation.

papers.title: Frequency-selective disturbance amplification in a supersonic cavity-ramp flow
papers.abstract: Supersonic cavity-ramp flows in scramjet combustors exhibit strong frequency-selective amplification under external disturbances, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Based on a steady two-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) base flow, we investigate the forced response using Input–Output analysis, supported by planar unsteady RANS (URANS) simulations and a three-dimensional large-eddy simulation (LES) database. The resolvent gain spectra identify three distinct response branches: a low-frequency branch associated with a modal resonance consistent with an intrinsic global instability; a robust planar intermediate-frequency branch that forms a coherent amplification pathway from the shear layer to the reattachment shock; and a localized high-frequency branch concentrated near the leading-edge shock and upstream shear layer and strongly affected by viscous damping. Planar URANS with periodic forcing shows that the nonlinear two-dimensional response is selectively amplified at the intermediate-frequency branch, confirming its role as the dominant planar amplification mechanism. Additionally, sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition of the spanwise-averaged LES fields recovers coherent structures at all three characteristic frequencies, whose streamwise wavelengths and convection speeds are consistent with the corresponding optimal responses. Overall, the cavity-ramp flow behaves as a frequency-selective amplifier, and the intermediate-frequency branch is its most robust and dominant pathway: the long-range convective growth from the cavity leading edge to the reattachment shock is consistent with a convective, non-resonant amplification mechanism.

papers.title: Cavitating flow evolution and restoring-moment generation mechanisms induced by wraparound fins on underwater vehicles
papers.abstract: The attitude of high-speed underwater vehicles in the pre-exit stage is strongly influenced by cavitating flow structures and nonlinear hydrodynamic loads. Although wraparound fins (WAFs) provide a passive means of generating restoring moments under constrained spatial conditions, the coupling among WAF geometry, cavity evolution, and restoring moment generation remains unclear. This study investigates the restoring-moment response of WAFs under a prescribed fully submerged cavitating condition using computational fluid dynamics simulations and a surrogate-assisted design exploration method. A Gaussian process regression model optimized by a genetic algorithm is developed to characterize the nonlinear relationship between WAF geometric parameters and hydrodynamic responses, and is coupled with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II to identify representative configurations balancing drag and nose-down restoring moment. The results show that WAFs modify tail pressure distribution and cavity structures, changing the pitching-moment response from nose-up to nose-down under the investigated condition. Sensitivity analysis indicates that the wrap angle dominates drag variation, while the deployment and wrap angles jointly control the nose-down restoring moment. Further flow analysis shows that, for the larger WAF configurations, the attached-cavity closure region and pressure center migrate upstream, accompanied by a reduction in the effective moment arm and a diminishing increase in restoring moment. These results support a time-averaged association among cavity closure, pressure redistribution, and restoring-moment response within the present steady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes framework.

papers.title: Sessile analogs of spherical bubbles
papers.abstract: The Letter concerns the shape of spherical bubbles and their transition to sessile analogs on planar surfaces. A theoretical model is proposed, predicting the resting bubble's radius as a function of the initial bubble radius, which agrees well with the experimental data. We found a 26% increase in the characteristic radius for the transformation of a spherical bubble into a sessile counterpart on hydrophilic surfaces for soap bubbles and on hydrophobic surfaces for air bubbles in water. The model also highlights under which conditions significant deviations from the 26%—law can be expected for the transition to sessile analogs.

papers.title: Fluid structure interaction in wind-sensitive structures: Flow mechanisms, coupled modeling, and reduced-order prediction
papers.abstract: Fluid–structure interaction (FSI) in wind-sensitive structures arises from a closed exchange among separated flow, surface traction, structural motion, and wake reorganization. This review compares experiments, numerical methods, reduced-order models, and learned surrogates through the feedback and interface quantities they retain. Mono-directional analysis is distinguished from bi-directional FSI according to whether the computed structural motion is returned to the flow. That distinction determines which pressure phase, wake state, and aerodynamic work can be represented. The synthesis leads to two conclusions. First, agreement in force or response amplitude alone is insufficient near an instability boundary because an error in load–motion phase can reverse the inferred aerodynamic work. Second, neither fine flow field resolution nor a learning architecture guarantees power-consistent transfer across a moving interface; this property must be imposed or verified separately. Experimental methods are therefore assessed through synchronized load, motion, and flow observables, and numerical and learned models through interface consistency, response regime coverage, and uncertainty. These criteria guide model selection for bluff-body vibration, bridge and building response, flexible membranes, and related wind-sensitive systems.

papers.title: Impact force characteristics of outburst flows triggered by dam breach: Insights from flume experiments
papers.abstract: Outburst floods triggered by dam failures are highly destructive, and their impact-force characteristics constitute a key indicator for hazard risk assessment and engineering mitigation. A comprehensive understanding of these characteristics is essential for revealing dam-breach processes and the dynamic evolution of outburst flows. In this study, we systematically investigate the impact-force characteristics of outburst floods through a series of flume experiments conducted under varying inflow discharges, dam-material grain sizes, and downstream channel-bed conditions. The results show that the impact forces of outburst flow are strongly controlled by the evolution process of the dam breach and exhibit a distinct three-stage evolution, characterized by rapid growth, intense fluctuations, and gradual decay. The impact forces can be separated into a mean component and a fluctuating component. Increasing inflow discharge can enhance both the mean impact forces and the intensity of fluctuating forces, and coarsening of the dam material and downstream bed sediments leads to a marked increase in the proportion of high-frequency energy (>30 Hz) in the impact-force spectra, indicating more intense particle-collision processes. A strong temporal correspondence is observed between impact-force fluctuations and seismic power in the time domain, with both signals effectively capturing particle collisions and interactions within the flow, suggesting that impact-force fluctuations can serve as a reliable proxy for sediment transport intensity. This study not only elucidates the multiscale characteristics and governing mechanisms of impact forces during dam failures, but also provides valuable insights for the engineering mitigation and hazard management of outburst floods.

papers.title: Effects of aftbody vortex shedding on forebody vortex oscillation over hemisphere–cylinder bodies
papers.abstract: Previous studies have revealed that the leeward vortices around a hemisphere–cylinder body exhibit low-frequency antisymmetric oscillations at angles of attack (AoAs). The oscillation frequency is around 0.11 at AoAs of 10°–40°, whereas at AoAs of 40°–80°, it drops to 0.06, accompanied by apparent vortex shedding from the aftbody. It remains unclear whether this abrupt frequency drop arises from the interference of the aftbody vortex shedding. In this study, large eddy simulations were employed to evaluate the effects of the vortex shedding on the vortex oscillations over the hemisphere–cylinder bodies at two typical AoAs of 30° and 50° with various fineness ratios. The fluctuation of the sectional side-force coefficient is quantified using the axial distributions of the root mean square (RMS) and Strouhal number St obtained via Fast Fourier Transform. The underlying vortex dynamics are identified using dynamic mode decomposition and mode reconstruction. The results show that even when the aftbody length is reduced to the point where vortex shedding is completely suppressed, the forebody vortex oscillations persist, indicating that the sudden frequency shift at high AoAs is caused by the intrinsic characteristics of the forebody vortices, rather than the aftbody vortex shedding. Furthermore, the amplitude and frequency of the forebody vortex oscillations are almost unaffected by the aftbody length; they slightly decrease when the aftbody is shortened. Similar to the high fineness-ratio model, the RMS increases to a peak over the forebody or mid-body even after the model is shortened; longer bodies exhibit slightly stronger fluctuation intensities. Dominant low-frequency oscillations prevail in the forebody region across all fineness ratios.

papers.title: Molten metal flow and crater evolution during cathode spot retrograde motion
papers.abstract: A three-dimensional hydrodynamic erosion model is established to analyze molten metal flow and cathode surface evolution along a prescribed cathode spot (CS) retrograde motion trajectory under a transverse magnetic field (TMF). The CS trajectory is determined using a statistical model based on the probability density of TMF-driven CS motion, while molten metal flow and crater evolution are simulated using the volume of fluid method with adaptive mesh refinement. The simulations show that pressure drives molten metal redistribution, whereas craters left by extinguished CS disrupt the axisymmetric evolution of newly ignited CS. This asymmetry promotes molten metal jetting and droplet formation on the previous spot side. For the prescribed CS motion trajectory, at 150 mT, cathode erosion remains localized during the first 150 ns, causing adjacent craters to coalesce into deeper composite erosion craters. Increasing the TMF from 150 to 571 mT strengthens the retrograde motion bias in successive CS ignition, producing a more directional erosion trajectory and reducing localized cathode erosion. Comparison with experimental morphologies shows that the model can effectively simulate molten melt flow under a prescribed retrograde motion trajectory of the CS. These results provide a basis for understanding the retrograde motion and evolution mechanisms of vacuum arc CS.

papers.title: An improved total-shear-stress-conserved wall model for large-eddy simulation with subgrid-scale eddy viscosity fluctuation
papers.abstract: The unphysical near-wall turbulent structures observed in wall-modeled large-eddy simulation (WMLES) may lead to the well-known logarithmic-layer mismatch (LLM) and affect the evolution of the flow field. To make the WMLES an effective and practical tool for high-Reynolds number wall-bounded turbulent flows, it is crucial to accurately represent the near-wall turbulent structures. In the present study, by systematically investigating the effect of the subgrid-scale (SGS) eddy viscosity fluctuation (ν¯sgs′) on WMLES, it is revealed that neglecting ν¯sgs′ within the wall model region results in unphysical near-wall turbulent structures as the wall-parallel grid resolution increases. To address this issue, an SGS eddy viscosity modification model based on the instantaneous local momentum equation is proposed, which naturally satisfies the total-shear-stress-conserved constraint while incorporating the effect of ν¯sgs′. The unphysical near-wall turbulent structures are effectively eliminated, with no LLM phenomenon observed in turbulent channel flows at Reτ=550 and 2000. The results also demonstrate the ability of the proposed model to capture very-large-scale motions in the outer layer and their interactions with the inner layer. Furthermore, a preliminary “high-grid resolution” criterion is proposed to determine when ν¯sgs′ should be incorporated in WMLES. Overall, the present study highlights the importance of ν¯sgs′ in WMLES and provides a practical wall model that effectively eliminates unphysical near-wall turbulent structures and avoids the LLM phenomenon.

papers.title: Physics-closure neural surrogates for uncertainty-aware operating-window discovery in generalized-Newtonian slit-die extrusion
papers.abstract: Identifying feasible operating conditions in non-Newtonian extrusion requires repeated solution of nonlinear constitutive and flow rate relations across large design spaces, making exhaustive physics-based screening impractical for time-sensitive operating-window assessment. This study presents a physics-closure neural surrogate for uncertainty-aware operating-window discovery in generalized-Newtonian slit-die extrusion. A deterministic reduced-order solver with temperature-dependent Carreau–Yasuda rheology generates reference wall states. A heterogeneous multi-output neural ensemble predicts wall shear stress, wall viscosity, and wall shear rate from operating variables, material descriptors, and physics-guided features. Pressure drop is reconstructed through the slit momentum balance, and extrudate swell is reconstructed through a prescribed wall-state recovery and residence-to-recovery-timescale closure. Model development, threshold selection, and uncertainty calibration exclude an untouched 20% independent holdout. On this holdout, the ensemble achieves R2=0.9994, 0.9889, and 0.9881 for wall shear stress, viscosity, and shear rate, respectively; momentum-derived pressure and prescribed-closure swell reconstruction achieve R2=0.9996 and 0.9995. Conservative screening combines uncertainty-adjusted physical constraints, feasibility classification, and an aggregate uncertainty criterion. Among 30 000 admissible candidates, 3997 states define the retained operating window. Reference-model recomputation confirms that all 25 highest-ranked and 25 boundary-sensitive candidates remain consistent with the prescribed engineering constraints. Screening 10 000 candidates requires 0.478±0.040 s; linear extrapolation from 250 directly solved states gives an estimated 2.83×104 acceleration. The reported swell and recommendation tests quantify consistency with the prescribed reference model rather than independent experimental validation.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic response and near-wake reorganization of propeller boss cap fins under pre-duct-modified inflow
papers.abstract: The hydrodynamic interaction between multiple energy-saving appendages plays an important role in determining the effectiveness of integrated propulsion systems, while the influence of an upstream flow-modifying device on a downstream wake-control device under realistic ship-wake conditions remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the coupled hydrodynamic characteristics of a propeller–duct–propeller boss cap fin (PBCF) system using unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations. Four propulsion configurations, including ship–propeller, ship–propeller–PBCF, ship–propeller–duct, and ship–propeller–duct–PBCF arrangements, are compared under identical inflow velocity and propeller rotational speed conditions. The numerical method is assessed against available experimental measurements, while grid- and time step-sensitivity analyses are conducted to establish the consistency of the predicted trends. The results demonstrate that the duct modifies the inflow environment experienced by the PBCF and changes the downstream wake evolution. Compared with the duct-only configuration, the combined duct–PBCF arrangement increases the total thrust coefficient by 1.15%, reduces the total torque coefficient by 1.35%, and improves the thrust–power ratio by 2.56% under the investigated condition. Wake kinetic-energy analysis shows that the duct increases the PBCF-induced reduction in the circumferential kinetic-energy ratio by approximately 2.3 times at the near-wake section immediately downstream of the PBCF. The circumferential kinetic-energy flux decreases from 1.20 W in case C to 0.66 W in case D, with 67.5% of this reduction occurring within the inner hub region. These findings demonstrate that the hydrodynamic response of combined energy-saving devices is governed by the interaction between upstream flow modification and downstream wake regulation, providing guidance for the integrated design of stern energy-saving devices.

papers.title: Pore-network reconstruction, energy evolution, and mechanical damage of shale under supercritical CO2–water/brine interactions
papers.abstract: Deep saline aquifers are considered promising sites for large-scale CO2 geological sequestration. However, interactions among supercritical CO2 (ScCO2), pore fluids, and rock minerals may alter shale pore structures and mechanical properties, potentially increasing CO2 leakage risk. In this study, Longmaxi shale was exposed to H2O–ScCO2 and brine–ScCO2 at 90 °C and 12 MPa for 14 days, followed by x-ray diffraction, nuclear magnetic resonance, and uniaxial compressive strength. Both treatments induced mineral dissolution, pore restructuring, and mechanical degradation, with stronger effects under brine–ScCO2 conditions. Dolomite and calcite contents decreased by 42.4%–52.8% and 30.8%–43.1%, respectively, while total porosity increased by 13.2% under H2O–ScCO2 and 18.1% under brine–ScCO2. The increases in the permeation-pore and overall fractal dimensions further indicate enhanced pore-network heterogeneity and geometric complexity, particularly after brine–ScCO2 treatment. Fluid–ScCO2 interactions also altered the pre-failure deformation and crack-evolution processes. Both treatments increased the relative proportions of the crack-closure and stable crack-propagation stages while reducing that of the elastic deformation stage, whereas the unstable crack-growth stage remained nearly unchanged. These changes were more pronounced under brine–ScCO2 conditions. Young's modulus decreased by 7.8% and 11.6%, respectively. Energy analysis revealed a shift from elastic energy storage toward energy dissipation, indicating weakened brittleness and more progressive deformation behavior after treatment. A segmented statistical damage model incorporating porosity related chemical effects and dissipated energy driven mechanical degradation effectively reproduced the initial compaction and pre-peak stress–strain response of chemically altered shale.

papers.title: Large-eddy simulation and time-lagged correlation analysis of aerodynamic interference between tandem 4:1 rectangular cylinders at various spacings
papers.abstract: Large-eddy simulation is applied to study the flow around two tandem 4:1 rectangular cylinders at a Reynolds number of 1.1 × 104 and four gap ratios of 0.4, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0. The inter-cylinder aerodynamic coupling is measured by time-lagged correlation analysis. With the increase in spacing, the shielding effect of the upstream cylinder on the downstream one weakens, and the aerodynamics of the downstream cylinder approach those of a single cylinder. The mean drag on each cylinder remains smaller than that on a single 4:1 cylinder, while the fluctuating lift is larger at gap ratios 2.0 and 4.0. The negative time-lag correlation coefficient of lift remains below −0.7, suggesting a strong inter-cylinder coupling. The drag time series on two cylinders, however, exhibit a strong negative correlation at a small gap ratio of 0.4 and a weak correlation at larger spacings. The mean, fluctuating, and extreme values of pressure on the downstream cylinder are significantly affected by flow interference. At a large gap ratio of 4.0, negative pressure extremes are found near the leading edge of the downstream cylinder. At smaller gap ratios, the upstream wake is trapped in the gap, and the vortex shedding is less significant. At larger gap ratios, strong vortex shedding from both cylinders is observed.

papers.title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent shear layer in an open cavity and its aero-optical effects
papers.abstract: This study conducts direct numerical simulations (DNS) of the subsonic turbulent shear layer in an open cavity using a self-developed heterogeneous parallel solver to investigate its flow features and aero-optical effects. The DNS results show good agreement with the previous theoretical predictions and experimental data. Driven by Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, the shear layer rolls up into large-scale coherent vortices and induces primary and secondary recirculation zones within the cavity. Turbulence intensity is amplified along the shear layer and peaks near the trailing edge. Proper orthogonal decomposition reveals that the oscillatory energy of the shear layer is mainly concentrated in the low-order modes. Dynamic mode decomposition confirms that the unsteady dynamics follow the Rossiter mechanism, with the medium-to-large-scale coherent vortices being significantly enhanced in the mid-rear part of the cavity. Consequently, the wavefront distortion is more severe in the mid-rear cavity and exhibits a strong correlation with local density and pressure fluctuations. The oscillations of the shear layer and optical path difference (OPD) are dominated by the first Rossiter mode in the front and rear parts of the cavity but by the second Rossiter mode in the middle part. The energy of OPD oscillation contains negligible high-frequency components due to the spatial filtering effect of optical path integration, indicating that wavefront distortion is dominated by large-scale structures.

papers.title: DeepONet-assisted DeepMMnet for full-field reconstruction of Rayleigh–Taylor and tilted-rig turbulent mixing
papers.abstract: This study addresses the problem of multi-component turbulent mixing, where traditional numerical methods often suffer from limited generalization capability and inefficient utilization of measurement data. To overcome these limitations, we developed intelligent models tailored for different scenarios. Based on high-fidelity numerical simulation data of Rayleigh–Taylor (RT) mixing, neural operator networks were constructed for the one-dimensional RT turbulent mixing problem and the two-dimensional tilted-rig problem, achieving efficient predictions with relative errors within 5%. For more challenging cases with only sparse mass fraction data, we proposed a deep multi-physical-field neural network (DeepMMnet), which enables accurate reconstruction of the full flow field, including density, velocity, and energy, from limited mass fraction data. Furthermore, predictions under noisy data were investigated to evaluate the robustness of the proposed model under more realistic measurement conditions. For noisy inputs, DeepMMnet successfully reconstructed the full flow field with relative L2 errors below 5%. Overall, the intelligent models developed in this study overcome key limitations of traditional numerical simulation methods and provide new tools and perspectives for accurate simulation and reconstruction of engineering mixing problems.

papers.title: The effect of flow inertia on viscoelastic flow with wall slip through slowly varying channels
papers.abstract: We investigate analytically the steady flow of an isothermal Oldroyd-B fluid through a symmetric channel with slowly varying walls, accounting simultaneously for viscoelasticity, inertia, and wall slip. The dimensionless governing equations are solved using the high-order asymptotic method recently developed by Housiadas and Beris [J. Rheol. 70, 403–417 (2026)], which employs a nondimensional formulation in which all components of the polymer extra-stress tensor are scaled using the same characteristic quantity before applying the perturbation expansion, thereby retaining the ability to capture the extensional-flow characteristics on the channel symmetry plane. The small channel aspect ratio serves as the perturbation parameter, enabling the systematic computation of higher-order corrections beyond those accessible by the conventional lubrication theory. Analytical expressions are derived for the integrated pressure drop required to sustain a prescribed volumetric flow rate. To improve the accuracy and extend the applicability of the asymptotic predictions, the resulting series are represented by diagonal Padé approximants. The analysis evaluates the viscous, inertial, elastic, and coupled inertia–elastic contributions to the pressure drop, showing that the leading inertia–elastic contribution first appears at second order in the aspect-ratio expansion. For both linear and hyperbolic contractions, although inertia and elasticity individually affect the required driving pressure in opposite directions, their coupled interaction increases the pressure drop. The resulting analytical expressions are applicable up to moderate Reynolds and Weissenberg numbers, provided the channel aspect ratio remains sufficiently small, and furnish benchmark solutions for the analysis and validation of numerical simulations.

papers.title: Development and validation of an improved double-multiple streamtube model for predicting performance of H-type straight-bladed vertical axis wind turbines
papers.abstract: H-type straight-bladed vertical axis wind turbines (H-type SB-VAWTs) are a promising concept for deep-sea floating wind power, yet traditional Double-Multiple Streamtube (DMS) models severely overestimate their aerodynamic performance. Existing improved DMS models for SB-VAWTs disagree on the relative contribution of the individual correction terms and generally lack sufficient consideration of the critical three-dimensional (3D) effects. A systematically corrected DMS model is therefore developed by integrating tip/aspect ratio and strut parasitic drag corrections, which act directly on 3D effects, with dynamic stall and flow curvature corrections for unsteady aerodynamic effects. Three-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes computational fluid dynamics simulations are conducted to resolve the 3D flow physics of a floating H-type SB-VAWT prototype, and comprehensive validation is performed across four VAWT cases with different configurations. The results reveal that 3D effects have a universal and decisive impact on H-type SB-VAWTs. The corrected DMS model not only remarkably reduces the prediction error of the power coefficient, but also accurately captures the blade azimuthal load variations. This study provides an efficient and high-precision numerical tool for aerodynamic prediction of H-type SB-VAWTs, supporting the design of offshore floating wind turbine systems.

papers.title: On the validity of the inductionless approximation and a φ–A0 formulation for transient liquid-metal magnetohydrodynamic flows in fusion blankets
papers.abstract: Liquid-metal breeding blankets in fusion reactors operate in strong magnetic fields and may experience rapid electromagnetic forcing during plasma transients. Under normal steady-state reactor operation, the magnetic Reynolds number of the liquid-metal flow in a blanket is much smaller than unity, and the inductionless approximation is well justified. During plasma transients, however, liquid-metal velocities may increase substantially, and a magnetic Reynolds number based on the duct dimension can approach or exceed unity. This work examines whether such liquid-metal flows can nevertheless remain inductionless and develops a reduced φ–A0 formulation for time-dependent imposed magnetic fields, where φ is the electric scalar potential and A0 is the prescribed magnetic vector potential. Analytical and scaling arguments show that, for strong-field flows in which flow-induced magnetic perturbations are controlled by the Hartmann-layer dynamics, the relevant local length scale is the Hartmann-layer thickness rather than the duct dimension. The resulting local magnetic Reynolds number remains well below unity for representative blanket conditions. The analysis further distinguishes the inductionless condition from the quasi-static electromagnetic condition, since sufficiently rapid imposed-field variations may produce magnetic-diffusion or Alfvénic transients even at small local magnetic Reynolds numbers. Within the quasi-static regime, the proposed φ−A0 formulation retains the non-conservative electric field required by Faraday's law without evolving the flow-induced magnetic field. Analytical cross-verification for a two-dimensional rectangular duct with electrically insulating walls yields the same velocity and current-density fields as the corresponding magnetic-field formulation.

papers.title: A unified Eulerian formulation for immersed deformable solids
papers.abstract: An Eulerian methodology is formulated to model the dynamics of immersed, deformable solids using a two-way coupled approach implemented within a unified simulation framework for incompressible viscous flow. A neo-Hookean constitutive model for incompressible hyperelastic materials is used to relate solid deformations to solid stresses, and the divergence of the solid stress tensor is added as a source term to the momentum equation. The resulting unified formulation allows a single Poisson equation for pressure to be solved across both the fluid and solid domains using fast solvers. Due to the modular nature of the formulation, material models other than neo-Hookean can be incorporated. The displacement field associated with the solid domain is evolved using a set of scalar functions that form a dynamic grid, while the boundary of the immersed solid is represented by an additional signed distance function. The motion of the dynamic grid relative to the underlying Cartesian grid is used to determine the deformation gradient tensor. A hyperbolic partial differential equation extrapolation scheme, combined with topology-preserving reinitialization of the solid boundary, propagates the dynamic grid into the fluid domain. The material properties and the corresponding solid and fluid stresses are regularized across a finite-width interface using a continuous Heaviside function. For the parameter ranges examined, the formulation produces stable calculations with systematic grid convergence and permits simulations at stiffness and density contrasts extending beyond those considered in the comparison studies. A preliminary three-dimensional implementation is also demonstrated.

papers.title: Physics-constrained symbolic regression for reduced-order carinal pressure laws in transient endotracheal-tube airflow
papers.abstract: High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) can resolve transient airway flow during mechanical ventilation, but its cost limits parametric exploration and rapid model evaluation. We present a physics-constrained symbolic regression framework that converts transient three-dimensional multiphysics CFD simulations of endotracheal-tube airflow into closed-form reduced-order laws for local carinal pressure. The database spans pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV), volume-controlled ventilation (VCV), oxygen mass fraction, tip-to-carina distance, Murphy-eye orientation, and the transient inlet-flow response. All regressors are expressed as dimensionless variables, so that the search is unit-invariant, and nonlinear operators act only on dimensionally admissible arguments. Separate symbolic searches are performed for pressure-controlled and VCV. The recovered laws are consistent with mode-specific ventilation physics: an inverse quadratic inspiratory phase dependence for PCV and a normalized-time Reynolds number dependence for VCV. The best expressions achieve a coefficient of determination of 0.9993 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 6.98×10−4 for PCV, and a coefficient of determination of 0.9983 and a root mean square error of 1.75×10−3 for VCV, reducing the prediction error by approximately one order of magnitude relative to a multivariate-linear baseline. Multi-seed Pareto screening and dimensionless pressure-regime maps show that the surrogate enables rapid interpolation within the sampled parameter space without rerunning CFD. The framework provides a transparent, scientific machine learning route from multiphysics flow simulations to dimensionally admissible pressure laws for biological fluid mechanics, while remaining limited to the investigated airway geometry and operating conditions.

papers.title: Unsteady loading mechanism of a pre-swirl stator pump-jet propulsor under grid-wake ingestion
papers.abstract: Pump-jet propulsors (PJPs) generally operate in complex inflow environments involving the combined effects of the hull boundary layer, appendage wakes, and ocean turbulence. The resulting fluctuating hydrodynamic loads play an important role in propulsion-system vibration and radiated noise. In this study, a pre-swirl stator PJP under the wake of a 6-in. grid is investigated numerically using large eddy simulation. A comparative investigation based on spectral and coherence analyses is conducted to reveal the distribution characteristics and generation mechanisms of the unsteady forces acting on the PJP subjected to grid-wake ingestion. The results show that grid-wake ingestion substantially enhances the broadband energy of the rotor axial force near the blade-passing frequency (BPF), with the integrated energy in the BPF band increasing by a factor of 15.24. Further analysis suggests that the multi-blade superposition in the middle-to-outer radial region tends to shift from partial cancelation under uniform inflow to coherent reinforcement under grid-wake ingestion, with S7 and S8 real-part cross-spectral contribution ratios reaching +54.72% and +60.00%, respectively. Those lead to a pronounced hump-shaped spectral feature, particularly on the high-frequency side. The present findings provide an interpretation of the unsteady loading mechanism of PJPs under grid-wake conditions from the perspective of energy distribution and coherence, providing guidance for the low-vibration and low-noise design.

papers.title: A physics-constrained multi-scale attention surrogate model for multi-field response prediction in geological CO2 storage
papers.abstract: Geological carbon dioxide (CO2) storage involves coupled fluid-flow and geomechanical processes and is a key technology for carbon mitigation. During storage, pore-pressure perturbations induced by CO2 injection propagate through the reservoir and surrounding formations, alter the effective stress field, and may trigger geomechanical responses such as surface deformation. Conventional hydro-mechanical numerical simulation is computationally expensive and therefore difficult to use for rapid risk assessment. This study proposes a surrogate model that combines bidirectional convolutional long short-term memory (BiConvLSTM), a U-Net architecture, and a multi-scale adaptive spatial attention gate (MASAG), hereafter referred to as BiConvLSTM-UNet-MASAG, together with physics-constrained loss terms to jointly predict the three-dimensional pore-pressure field, the three-dimensional average effective stress field, and surface vertical displacement. A gridded hydro-mechanical model was established using the Generalized Equation-of-State Modeling simulator developed by Computer Modelling Group Ltd. (CMG), and 1000 samples were generated by varying porosity, permeability, and injection rate. On the testing set, the proposed surrogate model achieved field-specific coefficient of determination (R2) values of 0.98, 0.97, and 0.98 for pore pressure, average effective stress, and surface vertical displacement, respectively. The corresponding structural similarity index values for the three-dimensional pore-pressure and effective-stress fields were 0.92 and 0.91. Field-specific comparisons further showed that BiConvLSTM-UNet-MASAG consistently reduced root mean square error and mean absolute error relative to both the baseline BiConvLSTM-UNet and the variant enhanced with a convolutional block attention module across the three prediction tasks. The inference time for one case was 1.3 s, whereas a CMG simulation required 726 min. The model balances multi-field prediction accuracy and computational efficiency while efficiently reproducing coupled pressure, stress, and deformation responses, supporting rapid assessment and monitoring interpretation for geological CO2 storage.

papers.title: Bionic micro-cavitators for underwater vehicles: Cavitation performance and drag reduction
papers.abstract: Natural cavitation has attracted considerable attention as a passive drag reduction technique because it requires neither external gas injection nor additional energy input. To enhance cavitation performance, cavitators are commonly employed; however, the additional drag they introduce may offset the resulting drag reduction benefit. Accordingly, this study proposes bionic micro-cavitators to promote cavity development while limiting the drag penalty relative to traditional designs. Three annular micro-cavitators with circular, triangular, and square meridional profiles were first screened based on drag coefficients and minimum static pressure. Subsequently, inspired by the smooth convex morphology of the dolphin's melon, bionic circular and triangular micro-cavitators were developed. Numerical simulations showed that the bionic circular micro-cavitator provided better cavitation and drag reduction performance than the traditional disk cavitator. At U∞ = 55 m/s, the bionic circular micro-cavitator achieved a maximum drag-reduction rate of approximately 38%, compared with approximately 27% for the traditional disk cavitator. In addition, although it incurred substantially higher pressure drag, the bionic triangular micro-cavitator exhibited the best cavitation performance, achieving full supercavitation at σ = 0.079, higher than σ = 0.055 for the other two cavitators. Experimental observations of cavitation and measurements of drag for the bionic circular micro-cavitator showed qualitative agreement with the numerical predictions. The present work may therefore provide a feasible new approach to cavitator design.

papers.title: Experimental investigation of supersonic impinging jets across overexpanded and underexpanded regimes using schlieren and modal analysis
papers.abstract: This study examined the effects of nozzle geometry, nozzle pressure ratio (NPR), and nozzle-to-wall distance on the flow structure and unsteady dynamics of supersonic free and impinging jets. Jets issuing from convergent and convergent–divergent nozzles were studied using time-resolved Z-type schlieren visualization and snapshot proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). Free-jet measurements established the shock-cell structure, Mach disk, jet boundary, and shear layers, while impinging jets were examined at L/De=1, 2, and 3. The convergent nozzle remained underexpanded throughout the range, whereas the convergent–divergent nozzle transitioned from overexpanded below its design pressure ratio of approximately 7.9 to underexpanded above it. Decreasing L/De shifted the first normal shock upstream, while its normalized width depended more strongly on nozzle geometry and expansion state. At L/De=1, the wall limits development of a complete shock-cell pattern, resulting in a confined near-wall compression region, whereas at L/De=2 and 3, the first Mach disk and near-wall stand-off shock became increasingly distinct. POD showed that increasing NPR broadened the dominant fluctuation structures from localized shock-intersection and impingement-region motions to structures involving the Mach disk, shock-cell system, extended shear layers, and wall jets. The slightly underexpanded convergent–divergent jet at L/De=3 and NPR=9 exhibited the most pronounced breathing-like motion in the stagnation region. The upstream barrel shock and first Mach disk remained comparatively stable, while the stand-off shock, reflected compression waves, stagnation region, and wall jets underwent strongly coupled motion. These results demonstrate that nozzle geometry, expansion regime, and nozzle-to-wall spacing govern the shock organization and coherent dynamics of supersonic impinging jets.

papers.title: Line-tension effect on the equilibrium and stability of a spherical floating particle at a fluid–fluid interface
papers.abstract: A recent matched-asymptotic framework for a spherical particle floating at a fluid–fluid interface reduced the coupled Young equation and vertical force balance to a single nonlinear equation but assumed a constant macroscopic Young angle. We extend the framework to include line tension. A variational derivation places the dimensionless line tension κ=k/(r0σ), the ratio of the line tension k to the product of the sphere radius r0 and the surface tension σ, in the modified Young equation. Because the line-tension energy depends on the filling angle alone and that angle is set by the modified Young equation, the line-tension term drops out of the vertical force balance identically. The coupled system reduces to a single substitution of the constant contact angle by a filling-angle dependent contact angle. Closed-form first-order corrections agree with the numerical solution of the nonlinear asymptotic equilibrium equation with O(κ2) remainders away from the floatability boundary, and the line-tension response of the framework is confirmed independently by a direct numerical solution of the Young–Laplace equation that shares no asymptotic ingredient. The hydrophilic regime is about an order of magnitude more sensitive to κ than the hydrophobic one across the full range of contact angles. The modified Young equation rewrites as a linear regression that recovers k from multi-sphere datasets, and its regression form is shown to be consistent with the original droplet dataset of Klauser and coworkers.

papers.title: Inlet pre-swirl regulation of flow separation in mixed-flow pump passages
papers.abstract: The effects of inlet pre-swirl generated by an adjustable inlet guide vane on flow separation in a mixed-flow pump are investigated numerically under representative off-design conditions. The circumferential velocity and relative flow angle at the impeller inlet are examined to relate changes in inlet-flow matching to the observed separation patterns. At 0.5Qd, positive pre-swirl reduces the incidence mismatch and suppresses flow separation near the impeller shroud, accompanied by a relative efficiency increase of 4.8%, reduced total entropy production, and lower dominant-frequency pressure amplitudes at most monitoring points. At 1.2Qd, negative pre-swirl improves inlet-flow matching near the impeller leading edge and increases the efficiency by 13.4%. However, the reduction in the volume of vortical regions in the impeller is accompanied by an increase in the diffuser. The impeller contribution to turbulent entropy production decreases, whereas entropy production in the diffuser and outlet regions increases. Meanwhile, the dominant-frequency pressure amplitudes at both the impeller inlet and outlet increase. These results associate the suppression of local impeller separation with pre-swirl-induced changes in inlet-flow matching while showing different downstream responses under the two operating conditions. In particular, the high-flow rate results reveal a trade-off in which improved efficiency and improved impeller inlet-flow matching coexist with increased downstream entropy production and pressure fluctuations.

papers.title: Effects of block size and arrangement on downstream grid-generated turbulence structures in open-channel flow
papers.abstract: Block arrays are widely used as laboratory roughness elements, yet how block size and arrangement affect downstream turbulence and momentum transport remains poorly understood. Particle image velocimetry measurements downstream of five beds in subcritical open-channel flow (Re=3.51×104 and Fr=0.08) compare a no-block (NB) reference with four near-cubic block arrays: small aligned (SA), small staggered (SS), large aligned (LA), and large staggered (LS). The approach flow is conditioned by a square-bar turbulence-generating grid, so the study characterizes how a finite block array reorganizes controlled, grid-generated turbulence. All arrays redistribute momentum vertically, producing near-block velocity deficits with faster flow above; block size dominates, larger blocks generating deeper, more intense deficits. Unlike NB, all rough cases sustain predominantly positive Reynolds shear stress across the domain, indicating continuous downward momentum transport attributed to block-generated shear layers and wakes. Turbulent kinetic energy production increases with block size, by 9.0% (SA), 28.6% (SS), 322.2% (LS), and 375.9% (LA) relative to NB. Integral length scales decrease in all rough cases, and quadrant decomposition confirms a shift toward ejection-sweep (Q2–Q4) dominance with geometry-dependent vertical penetration. Sweeps are more frequent near the blocks, but ejections are more energetic and dominate the Reynolds shear stress, even under hole filtering. Within the present conditioned-inflow configuration, block size governs the magnitude and vertical extent of roughness-induced turbulence, while arrangement modulates its spatial organization, guiding block-array design in laboratory open-channel flows.

papers.title: A spectral boundary collocation method for the Rayleigh–Taylor–Birkhoff instability and the collapse of a non-spherical bubble near a rigid wall
papers.abstract: The Rayleigh–Taylor–Birkhoff (RTB) instability of a collapsing bubble is studied by a spectral boundary collocation method (SBCM). The velocity potential is expanded in analytic harmonic bases satisfying the wall condition through the method of images. The interfacial modal amplitudes are obtained with spectral accuracy. The SBCM agrees with the linear Birkhoff–Bell–Plesset theory in growth rate and phase. It agrees with the second- and third-order weakly nonlinear theories for the coupled harmonics and with a reference Eulerian simulation. Beyond the weakly nonlinear range, the perturbation growth is suppressed and the interface evolution saturates nonlinearly. For a bubble near a rigid wall, the computed collapse and migration agree with the electric-spark experiments and with the spherical-bubble theory for large wall distances. The bubble is elongated for γd<2.0, with the aspect ratio reaching κ=0.7 at γd=1.2. The wall markedly modifies the RTB dynamics: it reduces the modal activity of the low-order modes (l=3,4) and delays or suppresses their zero crossings. For the high-order modes (l=5–32), its effect is equivalent to a similar prolongation of the instability process, with the similarity ratio Tcollapsewall/Tcollapsefree. For a rising bubble, the SBCM profiles agree with the boundary-element results and provide a reference for the elastic-mesh-technique frequency.

papers.title: Actuation to ejection transduction via multi-physics coupling and drive-waveform shaping in piezo drop-on-demand inkjet printing
papers.abstract: In piezoelectric drop-on-demand inkjet printing, the drive waveform is converted into the jetting response through deformation of the piezoelectric structure, pressure perturbations in the ink chamber, and nozzle flow. We have developed a dynamic model in the frequency domain that accounts for multi-physics coupling, covering the process from the onset of the drive waveform variation to the first arrival of the meniscus at the nozzle-exit plane. The model is then used to determine how individual frequency components affect meniscus motion along this transfer path. Experiments with a printhead and an equivalent time imaging system examine the effects of some general conditions. The initial jetting velocity generally decreases with increasing rise time and increases with voltage amplitude, whereas the dwell time has a weaker effect over the tested range. The model reproduces the principal experimental trends and relative ordering. Decomposition of the meniscus displacement at the theoretical ejection time into signed harmonic contributions shows that, under the conditions studied, lower-frequency components primarily promote motion toward the nozzle exit, an intermediate band produces cancellation, and contributions from higher-frequency components progressively diminish. Comparisons between furan resin and 95% ethanol show that the initial ejection velocity can be modulated by replacing the linear voltage rise with a piecewise linear rise, and the effect of rise path shaping depends on the liquid properties.

papers.title: Aerodynamic characteristics of dual lock-in regions of vertical vortex-induced vibration in a streamlined box girder
papers.abstract: Streamlined box girders, commonly adopted as the main girder form in long-span bridges, may exhibit multiple vertical vortex-induced vibration (VIV) lock-in regions under specific incoming-flow conditions. In this study, wind tunnel tests, numerical simulations, and higher-order dynamic mode decomposition (HODMD) of the fluctuating-pressure field were combined to examine the aerodynamic characteristics of dual vertical VIV lock-in regions. At an angle of attack of +3°, two distinct vertical lock-in regions were observed over the reduced wind-speed ranges of V = 7.33–9.20 and V = 14.71–20.92. In both regions, the aerodynamic lift is dominated by a primary frequency matching the structural natural frequency, with clear harmonic components also present. HODMD analysis shows that the fluctuating-pressure field is mainly governed by the lock-in fundamental component and its low-order harmonics, with the first mode being dominant and the cumulative contribution of the first three modes exceeding 95% in both regions. In the lower-speed region, the dominant upper-surface separation vortex exhibits a more evident alternating evolution between the upstream and downstream parts. The first-mode pressure fluctuations and the main energy-input regions on the upper surface show segmented distributions. In the higher-speed region, the dominant separation vortex develops more continuously toward the downstream region, accompanied by a more continuous first-mode pressure response and the main energy-input regions concentrated in the middle and downstream parts. These results provide insight into the dominant aerodynamic features of the two lock-in regions of vertical VIV in a streamlined box girder.

papers.title: Effects of forebody deflection on separated vortex pairs over slender bodies
papers.abstract: Morphable forebodies offer a promising flight control strategy for slender-body vehicles, yet the impact of forebody deflection on leeward vortex dynamics remains poorly understood. This study uses particle image velocimetry to investigate vorticity analysis, dynamic mode decomposition, proper orthogonal decomposition, and phase-averaged reconstruction, and we characterize the downstream evolution and unsteady behavior of the leeward vortex pair. Results indicate that the flow remains dominated by forebody vortices. Positive deflection strengthens these vortices, causing regular variations in the time-averaged intensity, position, and scale of the aftbody vortices. However, excessive deflection pushes the forebody vortices away from the aftbody surface, preventing entrainment by the aftbody shear layer and thereby weakening the overall vortex strength. Under most conditions, the dominant Strouhal number (St) remains between 0.09 and 0.12, consistent with the self-sustained oscillations observed in undeflected flows. Notably, at a high angle of attack (30°) and large deflections (20°), a novel dual-frequency oscillation emerges. A low-frequency component (St = 0.04–0.05) appears with higher energy, becoming the dominant oscillation mode. Vortex-core trajectories reveal that this oscillation maintains a periodic alternating pattern relative to the symmetry plane, but with the core positioned further from the body surface. These findings demonstrate that forebody deflection not only governs the time-averaged downstream development of the leeward vortex pair but also fundamentally alters its unsteady dynamics.

papers.title: Metal cation-enhanced low-rank coal flotation using water-in-oil high internal phase emulsion (HIPE) collectors
papers.abstract: To address the low attachment efficiency and high consumption of traditional nonpolar hydrocarbon oil collectors in low-rank coal (LRC) flotation, this study developed metal cation-reinforced water-in-oil (W/O) high internal phase emulsion (HIPE) collectors. The effects of multivalent metal cations (Na+, Ca2+, and Al3+) in the dispersed phase on the droplet size, Zeta potential, rheology, and dynamic stability of HIPEs were systematically investigated. Interfacial micro-interaction forces were quantified via an in situ microbalance system, and flotation parameters were optimized using a Box–Behnken design (BBD). Results showed that higher cation valences significantly reduced the median droplet diameter (reaching 3.673 μm for Al3+) and the absolute Zeta potential, while enhancing apparent viscosity and structural strength. Micromechanical tests confirmed that multivalent cations substantially increased the maximum adhesion force, peaking at 2734.38 μN for the Al3+ system. The 0.1 mol/l AlCl3 system achieved an optimal flotation combustible recovery of 94.81% at a collector dosage of 560 g/t. BBD optimization identified optimal conditions [0.15 m3/(m2 min) aeration rate, 560 g/t collector, and 1000 g/t frother], revealing a highly significant collector–frother interaction. Mechanistically, multivalent cations compress the electrical double layer, reduce interfacial potential, and promote specific adsorption and ion bridging. This macroscopically enhances emulsion stability and microscopically reinforces three-phase contact line anchoring, thereby significantly improving the LRC flotation efficiency. This study provides a profound mechanical insight into the interfacial optimization of coal flotation, establishing a theoretical foundation for the precise design of high-performance emulsion collectors.

papers.title: From crown splash to bell-shaped closure: Dynamics of laser-induced splashing on the liquid metal surface
papers.abstract: This study combines high-speed imaging and multi-physics coupled numerical simulations to investigate the dynamic evolution and topological transition of free-surface splashing of Galinstan induced by nanosecond pulsed lasers. Within laser energies of 0.15–0.45 mJ and pulse durations of 150–350 ns, three sequential splashing regimes are observed experimentally with increasing laser pulse energy: open crown, transitional state, and closed bell-shaped crown. The fully closed crown with a steady central liquid column is reported for the first time in laser-induced liquid metal splashing. A compressible volume of fluid model accounting for vapor recoil pressure is established and validated against experiments. Flow-field analysis reveals that gas-phase recirculation vortices originating from the initial crater and pressure difference across the cavity dominate crown closure. A two-dimensional regime map is constructed using the crater aspect ratio γ* at laser pulse termination and equivalent Weber number We as coordinates. A simplified crater-liquid-film mechanical model is developed based on axisymmetric bell theory, yielding a critical criterion for bell-shaped closure. The theoretically predicted regime boundaries are qualitatively consistent with the experimental regime map. Furthermore, control experiments under oxygen-free environments are also conducted to verify the robustness of the regime map. This study provides mechanistic insights and a quantitative classification framework for topological transitions in laser-triggered liquid metal splashing.

papers.title: A fast deep-learning surrogate with autoencoded boundary feature extraction for supersonic combustion flow field prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning surrogates provide an efficient approach to accelerating computational fluid dynamics simulations.
