However, their application in complex system such as supersonic reacting flows remains challenging because of the strong coupling among heterogeneous boundary information, mesh topology, and thermochemical flow structures. This study proposes an encoder–decoder surrogate, named supersonic combustion flow prediction (SCFP), which reformulates flow field prediction as a boundary conditioned solution operator approximation. Instead of directly regressing the flow field from the original inputs, SCFP encodes the physical boundary conditions and geometric descriptors into a compact latent vector on a low-dimensional feature manifold. A decoder then combines the latent vector with the coordinates of each cell to reconstruct velocity, pressure, temperature, and species fields at each cell. SCFP is evaluated on datasets of three-dimensional supersonic cavity combustors. The results show that encoding multimodal boundary information as a 17-dimensional vector enables a continuous mapping of input parameters from physical space to the feature manifold. Compared with seven benchmark models, SCFP achieved lower relative L2 error and higher correlation coefficients. For each case containing approximately 600 000 cells, the complete three-dimensional flow fields are inferred in less than 10 s. This work demonstrates that organizing multimodal boundary information on a continuous latent manifold improves the prediction accuracy of reacting flows and design space exploration of high-speed propulsion systems.

papers.title: Influence of ultrasonic excitation on a transitional hypersonic boundary layer
papers.abstract: Wind-tunnel experiments are performed to investigate hypersonic boundary-layer transition control using 40 kHz ultrasonic excitation over a sharp 5° half-angle flared cone at Mach 6 under zero angle-of-attack conditions. The unit Reynolds number ranges from 5.65×106 m−1 to 1.13×107 m−1. Wall-pressure fluctuations are acquired by flush-mounted high-frequency pressure transducers for power spectral density and higher-order bicoherence analysis, while infrared thermography quantifies surface aerothermal heating and transition-onset locations. Under 40 kHz ultrasonic actuation, the amplitude of second-mode instability waves is significantly attenuated, and the mean attenuation ratio increases monotonically with unit Reynolds number, reaching 55% reduction of spectral peak amplitude at Re∞=1.13×107m−1. In contrast, low-frequency excitation below 10 kHz yields negligible measurable control efficacy. Auto- and cross-bicoherence analyses demonstrate that ultrasonic excitation suppresses two dominant nonlinear triadic interaction pathways governing laminar–turbulent breakdown: the self-coupling of fundamental second-mode waves, and the difference-frequency amplitude modulation between the second-mode and its first harmonic. The external ultrasonic forcing disrupts quadratic phase locking among instability modes, rather than simply damping broadband disturbance energy. Infrared thermography confirms delayed transition onset and reduced surface aerodynamic heating under ultrasonic excitation. Unlike classical receptivity results where external high-frequency acoustic forcing amplifies second-mode instabilities, the present configuration yields stabilization by targeting post-receptivity nonlinear modal interactions. Limitations of the current study include fixed excitation frequency, transducer location, and driving voltage. This work provides a mechanism-oriented perspective for hypersonic active transition control.

papers.title: An implicit mixed finite element method for solving the Beljadid–Cueto-Felgueroso–Juanes–Richards equation modeling unstable infiltration in porous media
papers.abstract: Unstable infiltration in porous media, characterized by gravity fingering phenomena, cannot be captured by the Richards equation. We propose a robust numerical framework for solving the partial differential equation, developed by Beljadid, Cueto-Felgueroso, and Juanes, which is endowed with an entropy function as an extension of the Richards equation, which we call the Beljadid–Cueto-Felgueroso–Juanes–Richards equation. This equation is able to model unstable infiltration through porous media. Its formulation is based on a second gradient theory by considering a free energy functional as a symmetric expansion of the traditional capillary energy density in Richards' equation. To address the challenges posed by the high-order spatial operator, we develop an implicit mixed finite element method using a second-order temporal discretization. The nonlinearities are addressed using novel techniques based on a Picard–Newton linearization scheme that applies Taylor expansion to linearize the capillary pressure term and Picard iterations for other nonlinear terms. We used a high-performance computing library based on Just-in-time compilation, Automatic differentiation, and Accelerated Linear Algebra, enabling efficient graphics processing unit (GPU) acceleration via vectorized operations. A single GPU showed speed-up factors of up to 55× with respect to a single-core central processing unit (CPU) execution for one-dimensional cases, and of up to 50.4× with respect to a multi-core CPU execution for two-dimensional cases. The numerical model is calibrated, and its validation against experimental data demonstrates good agreement in capturing saturation overshoot. Two-dimensional simulations successfully reproduce fingering patterns across different flux ratios, confirming the robustness and accuracy of the proposed numerical methodology.

papers.title: Vortex-mediated scour mitigation in twisted-flip bucket jets: Dimensionless scaling and interpretable modeling
papers.abstract: High-velocity jets released from high-head spillways can produce severe localized scour under narrow-valley and oblique-channel constraints. This study develops a physics-guided dimensionless framework for predicting the velocity-reduction and scour-mitigation performance of a twisted-flip bucket (T-FB) using physical-model data from the Santuhe Reservoir spillway and complementary computational fluid dynamics results. A composite performance coefficient, Y, combines the impact-point velocity, jet trajectory distance, and maximum scour depth. Dimensional analysis organizes the candidate variables, from which five predictors are retained for the reduced model: the relative tailwater depth ht/W, Froude number Fr, dimensionless discharge Q/gW5, takeoff angle (α), and turning angle (γ). The fitted power-law relationship achieved an in-sample R2 of 0.8471 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0384. Under leave-one-out cross-validation, its RLOOCV2 and RMSE were 0.7285 and 0.0511, respectively, which were comparable to those of the dimensionless ordinary least squares model. Both dimensionless-feature models substantially outperformed the regression model based on the original design variables. Standardized-coefficient analysis identifies Fr and Q* as the two leading predictors under the adopted entropy-weighted objective. The proposed framework provides a scale-consistent and interpretable approach for evaluating T-FB performance within the investigated parameter range.

papers.title: Two-phase flow and water management of Higee hydroxide exchange membrane fuel cells with radial flow fields: A visualization study
papers.abstract: Water flooding and membrane dehydration drastically degrade the power performance and durability of hydroxide exchange membrane fuel cell (HEMFC). This work innovatively adopts a Higee rotating field to modulate gas–liquid two-phase flow for optimized HEMFC water management. Blank field, 8-channel, 12-channel, and 16-channel radial flow fields with equal active area are fabricated via three-dimensional printing. High-speed visualization tests are implemented under Higee level β of 0–6.93 and gas–liquid molar ratios (G/L) ranging from 1 to 10, where two-phase pressure drop, flow patterns, overall liquid coverage, and liquid fraction within radial channels are quantitatively characterized via image binarization. The rotation-induced centrifugal field facilitates liquid expulsion, cuts pressure loss, and broadens the stable operating range for droplet and mist flow regimes. At static state (β = 0), the liquid coverage reduction of the three radial flow fields falls within 33.75% as G/L rises from 1 to 10. At G/L = 10, the radial liquid reduction rate of the 16-channel configuration sharply rises from 22.6% at β = 0.77 to 44.05% at β = 6.93. The radial flow field configuration with optimal water management performance varies with operating conditions: the 12-channel design delivers superior performance at low G/L, the 8-channel design outperforms others at moderate G/L under intense rotation, and the 16-channel structure maintains the minimum liquid holdup at high G/L. This work reveals how β, G/L, and channel number jointly govern water transport, offering quantitative engineering guidance for radial flow field design of Higee-HEMFC.

papers.title: Loading-dependent propeller-wake dynamics under ship- and submarine-type wake inflows
papers.abstract: Two representative axial wake distributions are considered in this study. They are derived from the DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency) Suboff submarine model and the Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering Container Ship (KCS), respectively. Both distributions are imposed as nonuniform inflow conditions on an identical propeller to investigate how hull-wake morphology is converted into downstream propeller-wake dynamics. The DARPA Suboff wake represents a relatively balanced submarine-type inflow, whereas the KCS wake exhibits a pronounced velocity deficit localized within a limited circumferential sector. Four advance coefficients are considered for the evaluation of the integral hydrodynamic response, while J = 0.591 and J = 0.984 are further examined through velocity and vorticity fields, cross-plane wake evolution, Q-criterion structures, the root mean square (RMS) velocity fluctuations, kinetic-energy spectra, and tip-vortex-core vorticity. The KCS wake yields lower thrust and torque coefficients than the Suboff wake, with the reduction increasing with advance coefficient and reaching approximately 30.2% in thrust coefficient (KT) and 28.7% in torque coefficient (KQ) at J = 0.984. In contrast, the amplification of unsteady wake dynamics is more pronounced at J = 0.591. The localized KCS velocity deficit produces azimuthally varying blade loading, leading to directional wake deformation, enhanced RMS fluctuations, stronger low-frequency and noninteger spectral components, and a nonmonotonic evolution of vortex-core vorticity in the affected sector. At J = 0.984, these unsteady responses are substantially weakened despite the larger difference in integral loading between the two inflows. The integral hydrodynamic response becomes more dependent on inflow morphology, whereas the amplification of inflow nonuniformity into unsteady vortex dynamics becomes weaker.

papers.title: Role of step height in aeration performance over a pre-aerated stepped spillway
papers.abstract: This experimental study investigates the effect of step height on the air–water flow properties in a stepped spillway equipped with an upstream aerator ramp. Physical model tests were conducted on a 30° sloping chute with three step heights (0.025, 0.05, and 0.1 m). A double-tip conductivity probe was used to measure the air concentration, bubble frequency, and bubble chord length. The results show that increasing step height increases both the near-bottom air concentration and the cross-sectional mean air concentration. A larger step height also enhances bubble breakup, leading to a higher proportion of small bubbles and an increase in bubble frequency. These findings demonstrate that a larger step height promotes the formation of a denser layer of fine bubbles near the chute bottom, thereby improving cavitation protection.

papers.title: Exact solution to the Riemann problem of porous shallow water equation with discontinuous porosity and bottom topography
papers.abstract: This study addresses the Riemann problem for the porous shallow water equations with discontinuities in both porosity and bed elevation. Elementary waves associated with the two geometric discontinuities are formulated using the generalized Rankine–Hugoniot relation within a path-conservative framework, yielding stationary waves that satisfy mass and energy conservation. A class of monotonic paths is introduced to regularize the discontinuous porosity and topography while preserving the monotonicity of surplus energy along the paths. The existence of such paths provides a key condition for constructing an exact Riemann solver by ensuring the uniqueness of the stationary-wave solution. When the porosity and bottom elevation discontinuities exert opposing effects on the flow, a critical discharge is identified at which the net geometric influence reverses, determining the solution structure in phase space. Based on these results, an exact Riemann solver is developed using the left-state-to-middle-state and right-state-to-middle-state curve framework, capable of capturing all admissible solution structures across the full range of initial conditions. A total of 17 distinct solution types are identified, including 10 wet cases and 7 dry cases, and validated through 13 benchmark examples. Among these, three cases exhibit triple solutions, highlighting the potential non-uniqueness of the Riemann problem under certain initial conditions. The solutions are applicable to quasi-discontinuous geometries, and the non-uniqueness is shown to originate in the local flow state lost during upscaling.

papers.title: Shock wave reflections and blast load distribution in confined and vented cubic rooms
papers.abstract: Internal explosions in rooms produce repeated shock reflections, strong load concentration near edges and corners, and complex overpressure-time histories. However, the relationship between changes induced by venting in reflected-wave propagation and the spatial distributions of peak overpressure and positive impulse remains insufficiently resolved. To address this gap, internal blast tests and high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted in a 2 × 2 × 2 m3 cubic reinforced concrete room. For centered detonation at a charge-weight-to-volume ratio of 12.5 g/m3, the maximum reflected overpressure at the front wall corner was ∼1.53 times that at the opposite back wall corner for a vent-area ratio (VAR) of 0.04. At VAR = 0.16, the difference between maximum reflected overpressures at the two corners decreased to 10.2%, while the positive impulse decreased over most of the wall. CFD results linked this contrast to two concurrent processes: changes in the reflecting boundary redistributed the early reflected peaks, while mass discharge accelerated the subsequent pressure decay. A higher-order image-source method for internal explosions reconstructed the pressure histories using geometrically screened reflection paths. It predicted maximum reflected overpressure and positive impulse with overall mean deviations of 8.7% and 10.9%, respectively, requiring ∼3–4 s per measurement point. Comparisons with a second-order image-source model further indicated that later reflections were more important for accumulated impulse than for maximum reflected overpressure.

papers.title: Splitter-blade suppression of inter-blade vortices for low-load flow stabilization in Francis turbines
papers.abstract: Inter-blade vortices in Francis turbines operating at low load can induce pressure variation and uneven blade loading. This study investigates the use of splitter blades to weaken these vortices by subdividing the runner passages. Global hydraulic-performance predictions from full-passage, sliding-mesh unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) simulations were compared with model-test data for the splitter-blade runner at three operating points; the maximum absolute relative error in dimensionless efficiency and unit discharge was 2.08%. At the representative low-load condition, L* = 0.327, the baseline and splitter-blade runners were compared using Liutex and pressure-variation statistics, cross-passage pressure-gradient intensity, relative velocity, secondary-flow intensity, blade-surface torque, and total-pressure evolution. The splitter blades divided the continuous, large-scale inter-blade vortices into weaker, more localized structures. The maximum central 95% interpercentile range of dimensionless Liutex magnitude decreased from approximately 1.5 to 1.1, a reduction of 26.7%, while regions of high URANS-resolved pressure variation contracted. The redistributed pressure-gradient and relative-velocity fields were accompanied by more localized low-velocity regions and a 23.3% decrease in streamwise-averaged secondary-flow intensity. The splitter blades carried 16.8% of the combined blade-surface torque, redistributing the blade loading. At the same head, the URANS calculations predicted a 0.38% relative decrease in hydraulic efficiency for the splitter-blade runner. These findings quantify the relationship between vortex suppression and hydraulic-performance change, providing an engineering reference for splitter-blade design in Francis turbines intended to operate over a wide load range.

papers.title: Nonlinear coupled confinement in stenosed catheterized arterial flow: Hemodynamic and nanoparticle transport mechanisms
papers.abstract: Stenosis in artery coupled with intravascular catheterization create restrictions for flow of blood. If these happen at the same time, combined influence created by them shall differ largely from effects produced by any of it alone. This research takes into account how does stenosis combined with catheter restrictions combinedly effect pressure drop, wall shear, and nanoparticle transport. Finite-difference scheme has been used to understand steady, axisymmetric flow in a stenosed annular geometry, along with heat and nanoparticle transport applying Buongiorno formulation. Numerical solution is validated for a limiting-case analytical result. Simulations depict that on increasing stenosis severity as well as catheter radius cause a raise in pressure drop and wall shear, along with combined response departing largely from additive stand alone prediction. The maximum reported deviations reach 178.3% for pressure drop and 185.37% for wall shear, showing the significance of considering both geometric restrictions together. Results also showcase Brownian diffusion and thermophoresis effect on nanoparticle distribution in the obstructed flow field.

papers.title: Pressure-driven cross-sectional intensity and local spray-structure velocity responses in a cold non-reacting spray
papers.abstract: In cold non-reacting sprays, it remains unclear how inlet-pressure disturbances manifest in cross-sectional and local responses under limited experimental observations. This study compared the pressure-to-cross-sectional intensity response (PCI), obtained by integrating planar laser-induced fluorescence intensity, with the pressure-to-velocity response (PV), defined from local spray-structure velocity. The PCI amplitude ratio showed nonmonotonic variation across the sampled forcing frequencies, whereas the PV amplitude ratio generally decreased over the sampled range. Along the 32-position PV measurement line, the gain decreased downstream while the relative delay increased. Pressure–velocity coherence remained high, and the delay gradient corresponded to a phase-derived equivalent propagation speed of 42.4 m s−1. Frequency-resolved analysis further showed positive delay gradients across all sampled forcing groups, whereas the normalized gain profiles remained condition-dependent. For pressure-to-response reconstruction, a harmonic-residual (HR) model and a black-box temporal convolutional network (TCN-BlackBox) were evaluated under paired real-only and teacher-guided training with fixed data splits. Teacher-guided training reduced the median wrapped phase error of TCN-BlackBox to 6.82° for PCI and 8.03° for PV. HR retained lower real-only phase errors and showed smaller changes after teacher-guided training. Given the small independent test sets, the reconstruction results are interpreted diagnostically. The measurements distinguish a persistent downstream timing progression in PV from condition-dependent local gain, while prior-assisted phase recovery remains dependent on response representation.

papers.title: Assessment of electrical conductivity and species diffusion models for magnetohydrodynamically controlled nonequilibrium hypersonic flows
papers.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flow control has been proposed as a promising approach for reducing aerodynamic heating and modifying the plasma environment during hypersonic flight. Numerical predictions of these flows, however, remain sensitive to the transport models used for electrical conductivity and species diffusion. In this study, thermochemical nonequilibrium flow over the radio attenuation measurements-C II blunt cone configuration under an externally applied magnetic field is investigated numerically. Several representative electrical conductivity models are compared to quantify their influence on the predicted MHD response. The results show that differences in shock standoff distance depend on both the magnitude and spatial distribution of electrical conductivity. A broader conducting region produces a greater cumulative magnetic braking effect, even when its peak conductivity is relatively low. A global magnetic interaction parameter based on the spatial integration of the magnetic braking force is introduced to characterize this accumulated effect. The influence of species diffusion models is subsequently examined under different magnetic field strengths. Magnetic braking expands the shock layer and increases the transit time available for species transport and chemical reactions. The differences among the diffusion model predictions vary nonmonotonically with magnetic field strength because the dominant effect shifts from accumulated transport history to progressive chemical relaxation. Under the strongest magnetic interaction, further changes are limited as dissociation progresses, species production and consumption become more balanced, and composition gradients weaken. The Gupta model is retained as a species and state-dependent reference, whereas prescribed Lewis and Schmidt numbers should be reassessed when the thermochemical state or magnetic interaction regime differs from their calibration conditions. These findings provide physical and practical guidance for selecting electrical conductivity and species diffusion models in simulations of hypersonic MHD flow control.

papers.title: Bypass ratio effects on spray field evolution in a dual-stream crossflow
papers.abstract: The effect of the outer-bypass stream on the spray field in a dual-stream crossflow is investigated experimentally at temperatures of 300–950 K and bypass ratios of 0.28–0.78, using planar Mie scattering and particle image velocimetry. As the bypass ratio increases, the time-averaged concentration field contracts toward the centerline, and the dimensionless spray area and the unmixedness decrease monotonically at both temperatures. Velocity measurements show that this contraction results from a selective acceleration of the droplets. The streamwise velocity in the upper spray region increases substantially with the bypass ratio, while the vertical component remains nearly unchanged, so the droplets are carried downstream before they can disperse vertically. In the region dominated by the outer-bypass stream, the droplet velocity increment is found to be proportional to the square of the outer-stream velocity, with all operating conditions collapsing onto a single line against the outer-to-inner momentum flux ratio (R2 up to 0.97). This quadratic dependence is consistent with momentum transfer through aerodynamic drag from the outer-stream dynamic pressure. The relation breaks down below y≈2–3 mm, within a vertical interval of about 1 mm, which indicates a fairly sharp lower limit of the outer-bypass influence. A residence-time scaling further relates the mean upper-boundary position to a composite parameter of the temperature ratio and the bypass ratio, collapsing the twelve simulation cases onto a linear correlation with R2≈0.72 and a mean absolute error of about 2.4%.

papers.title: A vertical four-stage low-speed research compressor: Design and experiments
papers.abstract: This paper describes a four-stage, vertical, low-speed research compressor (LSRC) at Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU). The compressor has a casing diameter of 1.5 m and was designed following the Wisler similarity methodology to reproduce the aerodynamics of a rear stage of a modern civil high-pressure compressor. The vertical installation provides an axisymmetric baseline for controlled studies of non-axisymmetric tip clearance. The instrumentation combines interstage five-hole probe traverses, L-shaped probes for intra-passage flow surveys, and an 80-port flush-mounted Kulite array above all four rotor stages. Three experimental campaigns with nine test articles are reported, and repeat runs quantify the uncertainty of efficiency differences. In the first campaign, a single-variable test design isolates rotor and stator contributions to stage loss. In the second campaign, reshaping the stationary end wall of the stator hub cavity raises the design-point efficiency by 1.17 points at the same seal clearance, whereas reducing the seal clearance of the baseline cavity nearly threefold produces no resolved change. In the third campaign, a non-axisymmetric inlet guide vane stagger distribution and a second-harmonic tip clearance distribution on the first rotor reduce the design-point efficiency by 0.55 and 0.63 points, with no resolved change in stall margin. Casing pressure measurements show that the clearance pattern modulates the pressure trough beneath the tip leakage vortex at two cycles per revolution, with an amplitude eight times that of the baseline. These measurements establish the SJTU-LSRC as a multistage platform capable of resolving aerodynamic features that are difficult to isolate in high-speed rigs.

papers.title: Finite-volume residual formulations for Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-constrained physics-informed neural network reconstruction of a hydrofoil tip-clearance flow from two-dimensional three-component particle image velocimetry
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) provides spatially resolved velocity measurements, whereas pressure remains unobserved. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can infer hidden quantities by coupling observations with governing equations, but the effects of residual discretization and internal-face flux organization remain unclear. In this paper, a hydrofoil tip-clearance flow is reconstructed from single-plane two-dimensional three-component PIV using a Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-constrained PINN framework. Pointwise strong-form, independent local finite-volume method (IL-FVM), and shared-face (SF)-FVM residuals are compared. Finite-volume integration is applied to in-plane fluxes, with temporal terms and out-of-plane derivatives evaluated by automatic differentiation. At α = 8° and t = 5 mm, all models yield time-averaged velocity relative L2 differences of 4.0%–4.3% under a common training budget. IL-q1 matches the strong-form baseline in velocity accuracy while reducing training time from 9.7 to 5.1 h. For hidden pressure, IL-q2 agrees most closely with the large-eddy simulation reference, with a mean squared error of 10.0 × 10−3 and a relative L2 difference of 67.9% for the zero-mean time-averaged pressure coefficient. An independent control-volume test shows that SF-q2 reduces continuity and momentum residuals by ∼40% and 32%, respectively, relative to the strong-form baseline. However, improved local physics consistency does not improve velocity or pressure reconstruction and incurs greater computational cost. An additional test at α = 4° and the same tip clearance yields similar velocity errors for Vanilla and IL-q2, with ∼34% less training time for IL-q2. Thus, stronger SF discrete conservation improves local physics consistency without necessarily improving flow reconstruction.

papers.title: Adaptive companion flow based fully parametric design for a Rim-Toroidblade driven thruster (RTDT)
papers.abstract: A fully parametric multidisciplinary optimization framework is developed for a novel Rim-Toroidblade (toroidal blade) Driven Thruster (RTDT), integrating a hubless rim-driven architecture with a closed-loop toroidal blade topology. F-spline parameterization is used for blade geometry, while hydrodynamic and acoustic performances are evaluated using the shear stress transport, k–ω-based improved delayed detached-eddy simulation, transient sliding-mesh method, and Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings (FW–H) acoustic analogy under a prescribed non-uniform Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering Container Ship wake. Sobol sampling combined with smoothing spline analysis of variance identifies the dominant geometric variables, followed by Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II optimization of wake-field efficiency and radiated noise under a thrust constraint. At the design condition, the optimized RTDT increases wake-field efficiency from 0.2193 to 0.5758 and reduces the overall sound pressure level at monitoring position by 11.66 dB. Wake analyses indicate that the RTDT redistributes axial momentum, vorticity, turbulent kinetic energy, and pressure fluctuations toward the outer annular region, weakening the centrally concentrated vortex system. Under approximately thrust-matched conditions, its efficiency exceeds that of the ducted propeller but remains below that of KP505, while exhibiting the lowest predicted acoustic radiation. Overall, the RTDT demonstrates advantages in thrust capacity, wake organization, and hydroacoustic performance, whereas reducing torque demand remains an important direction for further development.

papers.title: An explainable physics-informed neural network prototype for synthetic proppant transport in a two-dimensional fracture domain
papers.abstract: This study examines a single-domain physics-informed neural network (PINN) prototype on a normalized two-dimensional rectangular domain representing a planar fracture cross section. The recovered implementation maps (x,y,t) to (u,v,p,Cp) and penalizes velocity divergence, pressure gradients, and a scalar advection–diffusion–settling residual together with supervised concentration error; it does not enforce the full Navier–Stokes momentum equations. The archived run uses all 5000 generated concentration labels for both training and evaluation and reports an in-sample R2=0.635. To provide independent verification, we add a seeded 3500/750/750 training/validation/test protocol on manufactured analytical u, v, p, and Cp fields with exact forcing. Matched data-only, reported-proxy, and full-residual PINNs use the same corrected 3–64–64–64–4 architecture. On the 750 held-out points, the full-residual PINN gives Cp root mean square error 1.71×10−4, mean absolute percentage error 0.610%, maximum absolute error 9.12×10−4, and R2=0.973. Its relative L2 errors are 0.0228, 0.606, 0.356, and 0.00834 for u, v, p, and Cp, respectively. The full residual improves held-out concentration, horizontal velocity, continuity, and scalar-transport consistency, whereas the data-only model remains better for v and p. SHapley Additive exPlanations, Integrated Gradients, residual maps, and the controlled comparison provide an inspectable synthetic benchmark without implying experimental or high-fidelity fracture validation.

papers.title: Mechanical-energy loss and transfer in patient-specific carotid stenosis under heart-rate-dependent pulsatile inflow: A bidirectional fluid–structure interaction study
papers.abstract: Carotid artery stenosis substantially alters local hemodynamics and can increase blood-flow energy loss (BFEL). How heart-rate-dependent inflow redistributes viscous loss, wall-related net loss, and Reynolds-stress transfer remains unclear. Nine patient-specific carotid models spanning mild, moderate, and severe stenosis were examined using a bidirectional fluid–structure interaction framework. Flow-rate waveforms were converted to inlet velocities using case-specific common carotid artery areas; three-element Windkessel outlet models supported 27 simulations at 67, 100, and 140 beats per minute (bpm). Clinical Doppler ultrasound measurements were compared with predicted external and internal carotid velocity waveforms in one mild-stenosis case. A literature-based reconstructed phantom benchmark additionally assessed outlet-pressure predictions. Molecular viscous dissipation (Eμ), wall-related net energy loss (EW), and shear stress transport (SST)-modeled Reynolds-stress energy transfer (ERS) accounted for 10.14%–82.97%, 3.04%–32.81%, and 0.02%–66.37% of BFEL, respectively. Viscous loss dominated most cases, while BFEL generally increased from (3.0–10.5) × 10−5 J/cycle at 67 bpm to (5.4–17.7) × 10−5 J/cycle at 100 bpm and (7.0–23.0) × 10−5 J/cycle at 140 bpm, reflecting changes in flow magnitude and pulsatile timing. Wall-related loss varied comparatively little, whereas ERS responded strongly under selected conditions. In Case 7 at 140 bpm, ERS/BFEL was 66.37% with baseline SST and 62.52% with transition SST. A separate scale-resolving improved delayed detached-eddy simulation estimated mean-flow-to-fluctuation transfer and turbulence-associated irreversible dissipation at approximately 58.0% and 45.0% of BFEL, respectively. Thus, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes-derived ERS is a model-dependent interscale-transfer metric rather than a physical turbulent-dissipation fraction.

papers.title: Pressure diffusion and gas–water redistribution induced by CO2 pre-injection in tight sandstone
papers.abstract: CO2 pre-injection-assisted hydraulic fracturing offers potential for tight-sandstone stimulation and geological CO2 storage, yet pressure propagation and gas–water redistribution across fracturing, shut-in, and production remain insufficiently understood. An integrated model continuously transfers fracture geometry, pressure, and saturation across these stages within an equivalent gas–water framework. Main hydraulic fractures, the stimulated reservoir volume, and the unstimulated reservoir are represented by an embedded discrete fracture model, a dual-continuum model, and a single-continuum model, respectively. Grid sensitivity was evaluated, production-stage calculations were compared with Computer Modelling Group simulations, and Well JS pressure and water-production histories were matched under imposed gas rates. Two representative treatment schedules were compared, with differences in fluid type, injection rate, and duration considered jointly. The CO2 schedule produced smaller intermediate fractures but comparable final dimensions. Pressure perturbations extended beyond regions of substantial saturation change, while lower near-fracture water saturation persisted into subsequent stages. Shut-in promoted pressure relaxation and gas–water redistribution. During production, gas expansion contributed to pressure support, and cumulative total gas production was approximately 3.3% higher than in the conventional case after 500 d. Increasing CO2 injection volume yielded diminishing production gains, whereas injection rate had limited long-term effects at fixed volume. Shut-in duration produced a small nonmonotonic response, consistent with competing redistribution and pressure-relaxation effects. These results link injection history to subsequent multiphase transport through inherited pressure gradients and phase mobilities.

papers.title: Two-phase flow dynamics of gas jet impingement under reduced boundary layer effects
papers.abstract: Gas jet impingement on liquid pools is a key technology widely used in chemical and metallurgical processes. However, most existing research on this technology is based on jets issuing from straight circular nozzles, in which boundary layer development leads to significant momentum dissipation. In this study, gas jet impingement under reduced boundary layer effects is investigated using a converging variable-cross section nozzle. First, numerical simulations are performed to characterize the flow fields of both the gas jet and the liquid pool and to reveal the underlying impingement mechanism. The simulation results are then validated against experimental data. Next, a theoretical model for predicting the gas–liquid interfacial morphology under a converging variable-cross section nozzle is developed based on the force balance at the stagnation point, and the model constant is determined by nonlinear global optimization using measured interfacial parameters. Furthermore, experiments are conducted to analyze the interfacial morphology at different outlet Reynolds numbers. The results elucidate the coupling mechanism between boundary-layer suppression and interfacial momentum transfer, providing a new theoretical basis for the accurate prediction and active regulation of gas–liquid interfacial morphology in multiphase impact systems.

papers.title: A study of supersonic flow past a plate using a two-fluid turbulence model
papers.abstract: This paper presents a numerical study of supersonic flow past a sharp flat plate at zero incidence using a two-fluid turbulence model written in von Mises variables and solved with an implicit marching finite-difference scheme. Velocity, skin-friction, temperature, and turbulent Prandtl number distributions were obtained for M = 2 and M = 5 with adiabatic (Tw/Tr=1) and cooled (Tw/Tr=0.5 and 0.2) walls, Tr being the recovery temperature, in the range Rex≤3⋅107 (Reθ up to about 2 × 104). Laminar-to-turbulent transition was captured by varying the amplitude of the initial disturbance from 0.05% to 5%. The skin-friction coefficient was compared with the van Driest II correlation, with direct numerical simulation (DNS) data at matched Mach number and wall-temperature ratio, and with the recent skin-friction scaling law of Zhao and Fu. For adiabatic walls, the model agrees with van Driest II within 9% (mean deviation 4%–5%) for 4000≤Reθ≤12 000. For cooled walls, the model predicts a skin friction 11%–21% lower than van Driest II. This reproduces the tendency, found in DNS, of van Driest II to over-predict the skin friction on cold walls but overestimates its magnitude: the model under-predicts the DNS skin friction by 3%–26% (14% on average) for 0.15≤Tw/Tr≤0.5. Besides the skin friction, the two-fluid model describes phenomena that are not described by empirical correlations: the dependence of the transition onset on the intensity of the incoming disturbances and the anisotropy of turbulent heat transfer in a compressible boundary layer, which cannot be represented by models based on the Boussinesq hypothesis. The computed turbulent Prandtl number varies strongly in the transition region and tends to a constant value of 0.855 in the turbulent zone.

papers.title: Transport characteristics of CO2 in coal during cyclic injection-production: Permeability hysteresis and stress sensitivity
papers.abstract: CO2-enhanced coalbed methane recovery (CO2-ECBM) is a vital approach for synergizing deep methane extraction with geological carbon storage. This study characterized the multi-scale pore structure and fractal attributes of coal specimens across various ranks to clarify pore architecture evolution. Subsequently, gas pressure cyclic loading–unloading seepage experiments were conducted to replicate complex stress conditions induced by periodic bottom-hole pressure fluctuations. Results indicate that cyclic stress induces substantial nonlinear hysteresis and irreversible permeability damage, with permeability decreasing by up to 8.53% after 3 cycles. Crucially, this hysteresis is revealed not merely as a mechanical response, but as a manifestation of non-equilibrium fluid–solid interaction, where delayed matrix swelling competes with irreversible micro-fracture compaction. Furthermore, a dynamic seepage prediction model incorporating fractal characteristics, stress, and adsorption was established. The study explicitly articulates the underlying physical contributions by treating the internal swelling coefficient and fracture compressibility as dynamic state variables rather than constants. The model's strong agreement with experimental data validates its ability to capture permeability evolution and hysteresis under cyclic paths, overcoming limitations of traditional steady-state models. Ultimately, this research elucidates the microscopic seepage mechanism driven by stress and adsorption, providing the physical insight that permeability evolution under cyclic loading is governed by the competition between stress-induced fracture compaction and adsorption-induced matrix swelling, both dynamically altered by cumulative damage. This study reveals the permeability evolution mechanism, guiding CO2-ECBM parameter optimization. The proposed dynamic model overcomes traditional limitations, significantly enhancing productivity prediction and carbon storage evaluation under complex stress.

papers.title: Slip effects in gravity currents of power-law fluids
papers.abstract: We investigate the propagation of gravity currents of power-law fluids spreading over a slippery substrate. We develop a one-dimensional lubrication model that incorporates a Navier slip condition at the substrate and accounts for shear-dependent viscosity. The resulting formulation shows that the current dynamics is governed by three independent parameters: the injection exponent, the rheological index, and a slip number quantifying the relative importance of substrate slip with respect to bulk viscous transport. Our analysis identifies two asymptotic spreading regimes: (i) a no-slip limit controlled by bulk viscous deformation, and (ii) a very-slippery limit governed by basal sliding. Each regime is characterized by a distinct scaling law for front propagation. We show that the competition between these two limits is determined by the difference between the corresponding spreading exponents, leading to the emergence of a critical injection condition that governs regime selection. In addition, we introduce a time-dependent regime indicator based on the ratio between slip-driven and viscous fluxes to quantify the transient dynamics. The results demonstrate that the slip number controls the duration of the transition between regimes, whereas the rheological index modulates the rate at which this transition develops. The proposed framework provides a unified interpretation of how injection conditions, fluid rheology, and substrate slipperiness jointly control regime selection and transient evolution. Finally, we apply the model to spreading ice sheets and outlet-glacier lobes, showing that the proposed framework provides a robust approach for identifying the dominant transport mechanisms and the associated dynamical time scales in these environmental flows.

papers.title: Thermodynamic compatibility, holographic property, and wave-function representation of generalized weakly nonlocal self-gravitating non-relativistic fluids
papers.abstract: Two pillars of physics—gravity and quantum mechanics—are usually formulated in entirely separate languages. Surprisingly, both can be expressed in the language of a fluid: a self-gravitating fluid for Newtonian gravity and a quantum-pressure-carrying fluid for the Schrödinger equation. In this work, we show that this resemblance can be understood within a common framework based on how the second law of thermodynamics constrains the class of non-dissipative continua considered here. Using a transparent thermodynamic procedure, we derive the most general fluid model within a chosen constitutive state space involving density, velocity, energy, an internal scalar field, and their spatial gradients. The framework recovers, as special cases, the Euler equations, a restricted family of Korteweg fluids (including the hydrodynamic form of the Schrödinger and Gross–Pitaevskii equations), Newtonian self-gravitating fluids, and the Schrödinger–Newton system. We identify the conditions under which perfect fluids exhibit classical holography: the pressure-tensor divergence can then be represented by the gradient of a scalar potential. Classical holography yields a vorticity transport law that preserves sufficiently regular, initially irrotational flows and, under additional assumptions, enables a single complex-valued Schrödinger-like representation. While gravitational and quantum-hydrodynamic theories were investigated separately in our previous works, the present study develops a substantially more general scalar-internal-variable construction, refines its perfect-fluid analysis, and systematically embeds the earlier models within a unified framework. The framework also identifies a thermodynamically admissible density–gravity coupling that connects classical and quantum self-gravitating fluids, although its stability and observational consequences remain to be explored.

papers.title: Bubbles formation and rising dynamics from a capillary in quiescent liquid under the influence of a nonuniform electric field
papers.abstract: This work investigates the dynamics of gas bubble formation on a capillary immersed in a quiescent liquid under a nonuniform electric field. Ethyl alcohol was used as the working fluid. To create a nonuniform electric field, two electrodes were immersed in the liquid: a stainless-steel capillary through which air was injected, and a copper ring positioned above the capillary. Using a high-speed camera, the bubble formation and rise were filmed at different voltages, gas flow rates, and capillary diameters. It was shown that applying an electric field can significantly reduce the size of the bubble formed. Based on the force balance, the electrostatic force required to form the resulting bubble was estimated. Also, based on the electric field calculated using finite element method magnetics, the integrated electrostatic force acting on the bubble was obtained. It was shown that this force is insufficient to form bubbles of the desired size. This demonstrates the existence of additional mechanisms that reduce the bubble detachment diameter in an electric field. During their rise, the bubbles do not move in a single line, but scatter in different directions. The growth of the vertical velocity component in the presence of a nonuniform electric field and the appearance of the radial velocity component prevent the coalescence of bubbles near the capillary. These effects make it possible to efficiently generate monodisperse gas–liquid mixtures with submillimeter-sized bubbles, thus generating a finely dispersed gas–liquid mixtures.

papers.title: Zero-shot super-resolution reconstruction of turbulent wakes of cylinders and wind farms using physics-embedded generative adversarial networks
papers.abstract: Turbulent wakes are of great significance in the fields of marine structures, while achieving high-fidelity resolution remains computationally expensive. Recent machine learning, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), offers promising solutions for flow field super-resolution (SR). This paper first verifies the applicability of the generalizable SR turbulence reconstruction model [Scale-Oriented Zonal GAN (SoZoGAN)] to turbulent wakes, which are characterized by periodic vortex shedding and turbulent motions. Then, to address the unique dynamic characteristics of the wake, we designed a Filter-Guided SoZoGAN (F-SoZoGAN) framework to further enhance the reconstruction results of the wake. Specifically, the low-resolution wake data are decomposed into large-scale coherent structures and small-scale turbulent fluctuations via Gaussian low-pass filtering, followed by applying SoZoGAN separately to each component for SR reconstruction. The single cylinder wake and the wind farm wake are selected as two typical cases to examine the applicability and robustness of our model. Results demonstrate that both SoZoGAN and F-SoZoGAN can accurately reconstruct key physical quantities in wakes, such as the instantaneous velocity fields, Reynolds stresses, turbulent kinetic energy, wavenumber spectra, and velocity statistics. Compared to SoZoGAN, F-SoZoGAN demonstrates superior performance in terms of instantaneous field errors, wavenumber spectra, velocity statistics, and higher-order moments. Ablation studies further confirm that the combination of scale alignment and filter-based decomposition effectively alleviates the reconstruction challenges caused by multiscale coupling, thereby enhancing the model's accuracy and detail restoration capability. The proposed F-SoZoGAN framework integrates the strengths of physics-based and data-driven approaches, offering a zero-shot transferable solution for efficient and high-fidelity super-resolution reconstruction of complex turbulent wakes.

papers.title: Coupled effects of wall slip and Casson rheology on thermal entrance-region heat transfer
papers.abstract: The present study investigates the internal convective flow of a Casson fluid in a cylindrical duct with a constant wall temperature. The analysis considers the thermal entrance region and hydrodynamically fully developed flow using an extended Graetz framework. The temperature field is derived using an eigenfunction expansion and semi-analytical solutions to the transport equations. Particular attention is given to the physical mechanism by which the Casson rheology and wall slip affect the shear layer at the wall, redistribute viscous dissipation, and consequently govern thermal entrance-region heat transfer. The findings show that increasing the Casson parameter enlarges the unyielded plug region and confines deformation to a thinner shearing layer near the wall, while wall slip changes interfacial momentum transfer. These coupled effects keep wall-normal temperature gradients steeper and delay thermal equilibration in the core fluid, thereby improving heat transfer. Consequently, the mean Nusselt number in the transition region rises about 5.4–6.6, while the local Nusselt number increases from approximately 24 to 38 near the thermal entrance. Viscous dissipation further modifies the thermal field by converting mechanical energy into thermal energy near the wall. It may also produce Nusselt-number singularities when the wall-to-bulk-mean temperature difference approaches zero. The influence of axial conduction decreases beyond the entrance region as convection becomes dominant downstream. The analysis shows that slip-driven Casson flows', thermal boundary-layer growth, and viscous dissipation enhance heat transfer.

papers.title: Wax crystal network percolation control via nanohybrids: The liquid-to-gel transition in natural gas condensate
papers.abstract: The transition of a crystallizing suspension from a flowable liquid to a mechanically percolated gel is a canonical phenomenon in the physics of complex fluids, governed by the interplay of nucleation, crystal growth, and the aggregation of anisotropic crystallites into a space-spanning and load-bearing network. The extent to which growth and aggregation pathways can be perturbed without a corresponding change in nucleation behavior remains incompletely understood in crystallizing wax systems. Here, the silica- and silicate-based nanoparticle (NP)-polymer hybrids of controlled surface chemistry and morphology are used as a probe of these mechanisms in a model natural gas condensate (NGC). Four nanoparticle architectures (spherical, platelet, tubular, and microporous) grafted with an octadecyl acrylate-vinyl acetate copolymer were introduced at fixed surface-area loading, and their effect on crystallization onset, crystal morphology, network connectivity, and the liquid-to-gel transition was tracked using pour-point, cold-finger deposition, optical microscopy, and rheology. Across all nanohybrid architectures, the rheological onset of structure formation (∼30–33 °C) remained essentially unchanged relative to the untreated condensate, while the liquid-to-gel transition was delayed, most strongly for the microporous zeolite-clay hybrid, which lowered the gel temperature from 25 to 10 °C and wax deposition from ∼39 to ∼19 mg g−1 NGC. This pattern is consistent with network percolation, rather than nucleation density, acting as a rate-limiting step governing macroscopic gel strength. Optical microscopy further shows that, among the co-varying particle properties, geometry shows the most consistent association with the degree of lamellar disruption and intercrystal spacing, consistent with adsorption-mediated steric hindrance as the dominant mechanism of network disruption. These findings establish nanohybrid-modified wax crystallization as a model system for probing how additive geometry governs the crossover from a growth-limited to a percolation-limited regime in crystallizing particulate networks.

papers.title: Geometry-induced modal reorganization of shear-layer–wall coupling in a confined supersonic jet
papers.abstract: Low-frequency pressure fluctuations in a confined supersonic free jet-collector system are governed by the coupling between shear-layer vortices and downstream solid boundaries. This study investigates how the collector inlet geometry controls shear-layer–wall interaction and reorganizes the modal structure of jet oscillations. A coupled detached eddy simulation and dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) framework is employed to resolve the unsteady jet evolution, identify coherent pressure modes, and quantify the relative modal contributions of pressure-fluctuation structures. In the baseline configuration, the sharp vertical lip sustains wall-normal impingement of large-scale shear-layer vortices, producing a dominant low-frequency coherent mode at around 47 Hz. The modified inlet configuration, which combines an inlet lip curvature radius of 800 mm and a capture angle of 12°, redirects the incoming shear layer into a smoother tangential guidance path. This weakens vortex–wall impingement, reduces the spatial extent of the high-fluctuation shear-layer–wall interaction region, and is accompanied by a relative increase in smaller-scale, higher-frequency coherent components. The modified configuration preserves the upstream core-flow structure while weakening the collector-induced shear-layer–wall interaction, resulting in a 6.51% reduction in the spatially averaged pressure fluctuation RMS in the core region and a 17.8% decrease in the peak fluctuation near the collector inlet. DMD results show that the relative modal contribution of the original low-frequency mode around 47 Hz decreases from 15.7% to 8.70%, while higher-frequency modes around 77 and 112 Hz become more prominent in the retained DMD spectrum. These findings suggest a geometry-induced modal reorganization pathway for the representative modified configuration examined in this study and provide a physical basis for further parametric studies of collector-inlet design in confined supersonic jet systems.

papers.title: Erratum: “Entropy and shear-parabolic admissibility of algebraic closure models for rarefied gas dynamics beyond one-dimensional calibration” [Phys. Fluids 38 , 086107 (2026)]
Wavenumber-frequency spectrum diagnostic method for aerodynamic instability precursors in confined compressible jets: From spectral precursors to vortex-wave mechanisms
papers.abstract: A confined compressible jet can undergo aerodynamic instability through coupled shear-layer amplification, wave forcing, and pressure-wave redistribution. Conventional single-point pressure spectra cannot distinguish spatial organization from propagation, limiting mechanistic diagnosis. This study combines pressure-array wavenumber-frequency (k − f) spectra with large-eddy-simulation diagnostics to examine operating-condition-dependent spectral reorganization in a generic compressible-gas Laval-tube special valve. Each condition uses a 20-cycle pressure record. The typical and 363.15 K low-frequency conditions each include three independent seed-perturbed realizations. Their realization-mean dominant frequencies are fp = 111.08 ± 0.30 and 94.04 ± 0.44 Hz, respectively; all three values at 363.15 K remain below those of the typical condition, confirming that the frequency depression exceeds the tested seed variability. Increasing pressure drop raises fp to 1165.23 Hz and changes the signed spectral occupancy, accompanied by expanded acceleration, localized Ma > 1, and vorticity footprints. Opening variation reorganizes the downstream response path and produces a nonmonotonic frequency sequence over 40%–100% opening. Across the pressure-drop, opening, and temperature sweeps, the spectral response is interpreted jointly with jet acceleration, compressibility, vorticity, and resolved turbulent-energy redistribution. Conditional phase-velocity estimates are 22.83 ± 0.50 m/s for the typical condition and 33.64 ± 0.44 m/s at 363.15 K. However, only one typical-condition realization and none at 363.15 K passes the complete phase/coherence gate, so an ensemble propagation direction is not assigned. The k–f spectrum therefore provides a physical diagnostic of flow reorganization rather than stand-alone evidence of propagation. Time-resolved pressure-array measurements remain necessary to validate the unsteady diagnostics.

papers.title: Transient compressible flow and acoustic resonance characteristics of high-pressure gas release in a confined pipe system
papers.abstract: The transient release of high-pressure gas into a confined pipe–cavity system involves complex compressible flow and acoustic resonance mechanisms, where the dynamic pressure acting on the cavity is governed by wave propagation, boundary reflection, and sound-speed modulation. This study investigated the time-history characteristics of in-cavity pressure under varying release pressures (50–120 MPa) and temperatures (456–1018 K) using a custom-built high-pressure gas release test system. The pressure signal was found to consist of two physically distinct components: a low-frequency envelope governed by the upstream mass flow rate and mid-to-high-frequency pulsations arising from acoustic modal resonance within the system. Through theoretical analysis combining the one-dimensional wave equation, the temperature-dependent sound-speed relationship, and acoustic impedance mismatch at boundaries, we established that the dominant frequency is quantitatively controlled by the release temperature via the sound speed, with the frequency ratio proportional to the square root of the temperature ratio. Boundary conditions dictate the spectral peak position via the reflection coefficient determined by acoustic impedance: closed ends enhance reflection, yielding higher dominant frequencies (100–200 Hz), whereas open ends dissipate energy, producing lower frequencies (80–150 Hz). A lumped-parameter model was further developed to predict the maximum low-frequency loading rate, with theoretical predictions agreeing well with experimental measurements. These acoustic coupling principles extend beyond borehole applications to general high-pressure gas release systems.

papers.title: Hydroelastic wave scattering by arbitrarily shaped floating plates with localized constraints
papers.abstract: The problem of wave scattering by a floating elastic plate of arbitrary geometry with localized point constraints is investigated, based on the linearized velocity potential theory for fluid and the Kirchhoff–Love plate theory for elastic cover. The fluid domain is divided into free surface and plate-covered regions, and the velocity potentials are constructed using boundary integral equations and vertical eigenfunction expansions. This reduces the three-dimensional problem to a set of two-dimensional equations with unknowns located only along the plate edge and at the constraint points. The formulation can accommodate different plate geometries and arbitrary arrangements of spring supports and power-takeoff units and is validated by comparing with the existing semi-analytical solution for a circular elastic plate and by the generalized optical theorem. The results show that localized constraints do not simply suppress the plate response. Instead, they may modify the hydroelastic modes according to their displacement at the constraint locations, shifting the force maxima and load-cancellation minima to different wavenumbers. For sufficiently stiff springs, the displacement at the constraint points is strongly suppressed, while appreciable deformation can still be observed in other regions. Near a minimum global vertical force, considerable local deformation and wave scattering may persist, which demonstrates that a small resultant wave force can arise from cancellation between spatially distributed contributions rather than from a weak hydroelastic response. These effects are observed for circular and elliptical plates, as well as rectangular plates with rounded or sharp corners.

papers.title: Blockage effect on flow and heat transfer for lead-bismuth eutectic cross-flow past a circular cylinder
papers.abstract: This work numerically investigates the coupled thermal-hydraulic impacts of blockage ratio (β = 0.1–0.8) on lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE) cross-flow past an isothermal circular cylinder. Simulations are performed at a cylinder temperature TC = 773.15 K and a low inlet Reynolds number Rein = 150. Three distinct flow regimes emerge as the blockage ratio grows: symmetric vortex shedding (β ≤ 0.6), steady asymmetric flow (β = 0.7), and asymmetric vortex shedding (β = 0.8). The thermal boundary-layer thickness at the front stagnation point varies nonmonotonically with β. It initially decreases and subsequently increases, attaining its minimum value near β ≈ 0.3, which corresponds to the peak root-mean-square lift coefficient. Meanwhile, the thermal boundary-layer profile evolves from convex at low blockage ratios to concave at high blockage ratios. For low-Pr LBE, the convex-to-concave transition arises from confinement-induced velocity redistribution within the exceptionally thick thermal boundary layer, governed by the competition between centerline stagnation deceleration and gap-side acceleration. Single-property analysis further identifies temperature-dependent specific heat capacity as the dominant contributor to thermal boundary-layer thickening. The present study unveils the unusual evolution mechanism of thermal boundary layers for low-Prandtl-number fluids within confined domains. These results offer fundamental physical insights for the thermal-hydraulic design of confined structures in lead- or LBE-cooled reactor systems.

papers.title: Aeroelastic characteristics of a shear sweep wing during the dynamic morphing process
papers.abstract: Dynamic sweep morphing generates additional aerodynamic loads that depend on motion history and are not captured by conventional aeroelastic models. This paper develops an efficient time-domain aeroelastic framework for a dynamic shear sweep wing by combining a geometrically exact beam model with a hybrid unsteady aerodynamic model. The hybrid aerodynamic model separates the loads due to elastic deformation from those due to dynamic sweep motion. Combining Fourier feature mapping, a Transformer encoder paired with a convolutional neural network decoder reconstructs the aerodynamic response induced by dynamic sweep motion, taking sweep-angle histories and aerodynamic mesh coordinates at each step as inputs. For six independent test cases, the aerodynamic pressure predictions achieve normalized root mean square errors of 0.76%–1.85% and relative L2 errors of 2.39%–9.14%. Aeroelastic results show that the flutter speed under fixed configurations reaches a minimum of 6.7 m/s at Λ=10° and increases to 16.3 m/s at 60°. During forward sweep at rates of −40°/s, −200°/s, and −400°/s, the predicted flutter speeds are 7.2, 7.1, and 7.1 m/s, respectively, slightly larger than the flutter speed for the static wing. During backward sweep, including aerodynamic loads induced by sweep motion reduces the predicted flutter speed from 13.0 to 9.0 m/s at 200°/s and from 16.0 to 11.0 m/s at 400°/s relative to predictions based on loads induced by deformation alone. These results demonstrate the importance of aerodynamic loads generated by sweep motion in predicting the transient stability of dynamically morphing wings.

papers.title: Phase-sensitive vortex switching in acoustic streaming through geometry-induced symmetry breaking of a ring-ended microprobe
papers.abstract: Acoustic streaming in sessile droplets provides an effective approach for microscale transport, however, the mechanism underlying reconfigurable vortex topology remains unclear. In this work, a ring-ended microprobe is developed to introduce geometric symmetry breaking into the near-field acoustic field. Experiments combined with multiphysics simulations suggest that the ring structure enhances vortex controllability not by increasing the local vibration amplitude, but by expanding the effective liquid–solid interfacial vibration region and enhancing acoustic streaming. This enlarged active region strengthens the phase sensitivity of the streaming field and promotes Reynolds stress redistribution, enabling reversible vortex reorientation through phase modulation. The effects of phase difference, excitation frequency, and vibration amplitude ratio are systematically investigated. The results demonstrate that the orthogonal vibration phase difference primarily determines vortex topology, whereas excitation frequency and vibration amplitude mainly regulate streaming intensity. These numerical results are consistent with a potential role of geometry-dependent phase sensitivity in vortex reorientation. The ring geometry appears to induce competing acoustic streaming pathways, potentially bringing the system closer to a bifurcation regime, where small phase perturbations may trigger transitions between different vortex states. These findings indicate a geometry-dependent mechanism for phase-controlled acoustic vortex switching and provide new insights into nonlinear acoustic-flow interactions in confined droplets.

papers.title: Effects of inlet flow distortion on flow characteristics and flow control performance of an afterburner blown diffuser
papers.abstract: The diffuser is critical for efficient combustion in aero-engine afterburners, but inlet flow distortion and structural constraints make flow separation more likely. This study experimentally investigates the effects of inlet velocity peak height (h/H = 1/3, 1/2, and 2/3) and blowing flow ratio (0%–4.88%) on the flow characteristics of a blown diffuser based on boundary-layer blowing active control. A blowing momentum coefficient and quantitative scaling laws are introduced to characterize the control sensitivity. The results show that control effectiveness varies with the inlet velocity peak location. When the velocity peak is located at the passage center (h/H = 1/2), blowing effectively suppresses separation with a wide control window. When the velocity peak is close to the blowing-sidewall (h/H = 1/3), separation is suppressed at low blowing ratios. However, flow separation is induced on the opposite wall at moderate blowing ratios. Consequently, the control window is narrowed. When the velocity peak is near the opposite wall (h/H = 2/3), blowing only converts the large-scale separation vortex into a localized reverse flow region. Flow separation cannot be completely eliminated, and increasing the blowing flow ratio further deteriorates the control performance. Overall, the control window is widest at h/H = 1/2, narrow and prone to abrupt upper-wall separation at h/H = 1/3, and persistently limited at h/H = 2/3. Flow pattern evolution and the underlying physical mechanisms are also analyzed. These findings highlight the necessity of considering inlet distortion in blowing system design to avoid control failure or excessive energy consumption.

papers.title: Microphysics and rheology of magnetic emulsions composed of ferrofluid droplets: Effects of viscosity ratio on magnetic chain dynamics
authors: Marcos Fabrício de Souza Aleixo Filho
papers.abstract: The microstructure and steady-shear rheology of semi-dilute magnetic emulsions composed of ferrofluid droplets are experimentally investigated under uniform magnetic fields. Emulsions with a constant droplet volume fraction of 5% and different droplet-to-matrix viscosity ratios are studied to elucidate the coupled effects of viscosity contrast, magnetic interactions, and shear flow on chain dynamics and rheology. Under an applied magnetic field, magnetized ferrofluid droplets assemble into elongated chain-like aggregates, whose deformation and fragmentation under shear are correlated with the rheological response. The experiments demonstrate that the Mason number, Mn, which quantifies the competition between hydrodynamic and magnetic stresses, provides the governing dimensionless parameter for the evolution of the chain microstructure. A critical Mason number, Mnc separates a regime of stable, field-aligned chains from a regime of flow-induced chain fragmentation and pronounced shear thinning. Importantly, Mnc decreases systematically with increasing viscosity ratio, Mnc=Mnc(λ) demonstrating that chain stability is controlled not only by the balance of magnetic and hydrodynamic stresses but also by the internal hydrodynamics and deformability of the constituent droplets. A scaling analysis further shows that Mn governs the relative magnitude of hydrodynamic and magnetic bending of the chains, with the ratio of the corresponding transverse deflections scaling as δhyd/δmag∼Mn. Thus, the Mason number provides a direct link between the competition of magnetic and hydrodynamic torques at the chain scale and the macroscopic rheological response. These results establish a unified physical framework connecting droplet-scale hydrodynamics, chain-scale deformation and fragmentation, and the macroscopic rheology of magnetic emulsions.

papers.title: Local segregation effects in nominally premixed turbulent lean syngas–air flames
papers.abstract: The effects of preferential diffusion and chemical kinetics on reaction zone structure and combustion characteristics in turbulent premixed syngas–air flames are investigated using direct numerical simulation. Freely propagating statistically planar flames with varying H2/CO composition, equivalence ratio, and turbulence intensity are analyzed within the thin reaction zones regime. The disparity in molecular diffusivities and reaction rates of H2 and CO leads to pronounced segregation of their isosurfaces, resulting in differences in propagation and consumption rates and flame surface wrinkling. Preferential diffusion of H2, characterized by its low Lewis number, promotes rapid transport and consumption within the reaction zone, whereas CO oxidation remains slower and is governed by OH availability. Local equivalence ratio varies non-monotonically across the flame front, with a decrease from the unburned gas side followed by a recovery toward the burned gas region. This behavior is attributed to preferential diffusion induced redistribution of hydrogen-, carbon-, and oxygen-containing species. Flame index analysis indicates a departure from the classical lean-premixed flame structure toward the burned gas side of the flame front. This departure occurs over a wider temperature range for H2 than for CO, reflecting the stronger influence of preferential diffusion on H2 transport. Local segregation modifies the transport–reaction balance experienced by fuel components within a lean-premixed syngas–air flame. The qualitative behavior remains consistent across the conditions considered. The results highlight the limitations of single-scalar modeling approaches and emphasize the need for high-fidelity models that account for preferential diffusion induced equivalence ratio stratification in turbulent premixed syngas–air flames.

papers.title: Permeability of evolving dendritic porous media: Effects of dendrite crystallographic orientation on interdendritic flow
papers.abstract: Dendrite spatial orientation dominates the geometry of liquid channels and interlocking states of dendritic skeletons, yet quantitative correlations between crystallographic orientation and mushy zone seepage performance remain insufficiently clarified. In this study, a phase-field lattice-Boltzmann method is applied to numerically simulate dendrite growth of Mg-6 wt. % Gd alloy under varying dendrite orientations. Three hierarchical simulation frameworks (single dendrite, dual interacting dendrites, and a multi-dendrite network) are constructed to decouple and quantify the independent and synergistic effects of dendrite orientation and solidification conditions (undercooling and flow intensity) on dendritic morphology, solid fraction, fractal dimension, and interdendritic permeability. Results demonstrate that the solid fraction acts as the primary controlling factor of permeability, while the dendrite orientation functions as a secondary critical regulator by modifying channel tortuosity and intergranular interlocking modes. For the dual-dendrite systems, identical orientation induces severe face-to-face dendrite interlocking and yields 15%–20% lower permeability than symmetric staggered orientation; a universal permeability minimum occurs at orientation angles of 25°–35° due to maximized channel tortuosity. In the multi-dendrite networks, uniformly aligned dendrites form dense narrow flow channels with the lowest permeability, while a dispersed orientation distribution optimizes inter-channel connectivity and improves overall seepage capacity. This study clarifies the regulatory role of dendrite orientation on the seepage capacity of the mushy zone and provides a microscopic explanation for the differences in liquid feeding capacity under different grain orientation conditions.

papers.title: Convective and absolute instability of Phan-Thien–Tanner viscoelastic planar jet flows
papers.abstract: The temporal and spatiotemporal linear stability of a viscoelastic planar jet flow is investigated for the linear (LPTT), quadratic (QPTT), and exponential (EPTT) variants of the Phan-Thien–Tanner constitutive model. The baseflow follows a hyperbolic-tangent velocity profile, with viscoelastic base-state stresses computed numerically via a Runge–Kutta marching procedure. The linearized equations are discretized using a Chebyshev pseudospectral collocation method and cast into a generalized eigenvalue problem, whose predictions are verified against high-order numerical simulations with relative differences below 1.43%. For the temporal analysis, the sinuous mode is found to be more unstable than the varicose mode in all cases. The three PTT variants exhibit distinct sensitivities to the extensibility parameter ε, and the slip parameter ξ: increasing ε produces nearly no change in growth rate for the LPTT model, a monotonic decrease for the QPTT model, and a non-monotonic response for the EPTT model, while increasing ξ is consistently destabilizing across all models. Spatiotemporal analysis reveals that both ε and ξ suppress absolute instability, with the EPTT model being the most sensitive to this suppression. The ordering of the models in terms of the extent of the absolutely unstable parameter region is LPTT > QPTT > EPTT models, with the Oldroyd-B model limit (ε=ξ=0) yielding the largest absolutely unstable region, this ordering is explained by the progressively stronger attenuation of base-state elastic stresses by the linear, quadratic, and exponential stress functions, respectively. A critical Weissenberg number map in the β×Wi plane is constructed for each model, providing a theoretical criterion for predicting the convective-to-absolute instability transition in PTT jet flows.

papers.title: Mechanism investigation of flow structures and aero-optical distortions over a turret in subsonic flow
papers.abstract: Aero-optical distortion caused by a hemisphere-on-cylinder turret is investigated at freestream Mach numbers of 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5. An aero-optics framework is established by combining improved delayed detached-eddy simulation, the Gladstone–Dale relation, and geometrical ray tracing. For each Mach number, instantaneous aero-optical distortion is obtained at five angles from the forward to rearward direction. Statistical analysis, spatial correlation, and time-delay dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) are then used to clarify the influence of the intercepted flow structures on the aero-optical distortion. The results show that increasing Mach number strengthens the separated shear layer and wakes around the turret, leading to enhanced aero-optical distortion. Forward beam transmission mainly passes through the boundary layer and accelerated flow and therefore produces relatively weak wavefront distortion. In contrast, rearward beam transmission intersects the separated shear layer and wake, resulting in much stronger time-averaged and peak-to-valley distortions. Spatial correlation analysis indicates that the coherent pattern of the aero-optical distortion is governed mainly by the flow structures crossed by the optical path, while Mach number mainly amplifies the distortion intensity. Time-delay DMD further reveals that the dominant distortion changes from rapidly varying disturbances in the forward direction to low-frequency, long-lived coherent structures in the rearward direction. The findings clarify the connection between subsonic turret flow structures and unsteady aero-optical distortion.

papers.title: High-G coronary hemodynamics: Effects of bifurcation anatomy and acceleration direction
papers.abstract: Repeated high-G exposure is a health risk factor for high-performance fighter pilots, increasing the likelihood of adverse cardiovascular events. Current aviation cardiovascular research primarily focuses on overall cardiac compensation, yet coronary hemodynamics remain incompletely understood. This study aims to investigate the hemodynamic responses of left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCx) arteries with varying bifurcation angles under high-G acceleration. Computational fluid dynamics simulations are carried out for LAD–LCx branch models under high-G conditions with varying magnitudes and directions. High-G effects have been incorporated through an acceleration body-force term and corresponding hydrostatic pressure corrections, with inlet velocity and outlet pressure adjusted for various acceleration levels. The results demonstrate a nonlinear correlation between bifurcation angles and atherosclerosis risk. Under Earth's gravity, the 85° bifurcation exhibits the highest risk in the LAD branch, associated with relatively weaker and less coherent helical flow, pronounced high-velocity core deflection, and increased low time-averaged wall-shear stress (TAWSS) exposure. Under +4 Gz condition, the risk associated with obtuse bifurcations increases markedly, accompanied by weakened helical flow and expanded low-TAWSS regions.
