A 30° reclined posture partially restores helical flow and reduces low-TAWSS exposure to approximately the level observed under +1 Gz. The Gx acceleration strengthens helical flow and increases high-TAWSS exposure near the bifurcation carina. This study reveals that high +Gz amplifies the adverse hemodynamic effects through changes in helical-flow intensity and wall-shear patterns, while seat recline under +Gz reduces the risk of atherosclerosis. Acceleration direction also plays a distinct role, with Gx acceleration increasing the risk of endothelial injury.

papers.title: Mechanisms of shear-layer coherence disruption and aeroacoustic-source redistribution in a high-speed train bogie with square-tooth leading-edge spoilers
papers.abstract: Aerodynamic noise generation in a high-speed train bogie compartment is closely associated with the interaction between the shear layer developing from the cavity leading edge and the wakes generated by the wheelset, brake disks, and bogie frame. This study introduces square-tooth leading-edge spoilers (STLESs) with inclination angles of β = 30°, 60°, and 90° as controlled geometric perturbations to investigate how spanwise modulation alters coherent flow structures, unsteady surface loading, equivalent surface-dipole source-power characteristics, and far-field noise radiation at 400 km/h. Large-eddy simulation is coupled with the permeable Ffowcs Williams–Hawkings analogy, equivalent surface-dipole source-power analysis, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD). The spoiler-free prototype model exhibits pronounced spanwise-coherent pressure fluctuations at the fundamental frequency f0 = 547 Hz and its harmonic 2f0 = 1094 Hz. STLES-30 disrupts this coherent loading, fragments elongated vortical structures within the wheelset–frame interaction region, and reduces the energy contribution of the leading velocity SPOD mode from 35.4% to 28.0%. At 547 Hz, the leading pressure-SPOD eigenvalues associated with the brake disk, axle, and wheel sections decrease by 22.6%, 15.6%, and 3.8%, respectively; at 1094 Hz, the leading eigenvalue decreases by 40.6%, accompanied by a redistribution of modal energy toward higher-order modes. These modifications to the coherent flow and pressure fields weaken the dominant equivalent surface-dipole source contributions at 250, 500, and 1000 Hz and reduce the overall sound pressure level at all 16 standard receivers, with a maximum reduction of 2.2 dB. Larger square-tooth angles induce stronger spanwise modulation but may also introduce additional pronounced peaks in the equivalent source-power spectra. The results indicate that effective passive noise control depends on sufficiently disrupting coherent shear-layer loading while avoiding the formation of new localized strong equivalent source regions.

papers.title: Wind load reduction on heliostat with porous fences: Experimental and large-eddy simulation studies on the effects of height, porosity, and distance
papers.abstract: Porous fences are increasingly adopted for reducing wind loads on heliostats, and their deployment requires quantifying the effects of governing parameters (fence height H, porosity β, and fence-heliostat distance D) under a single and experimentally validated framework. However, the scale separation between the pores and entire fence-heliostat system makes pore-resolving large-eddy simulations (LES) computationally prohibitive, while reduced-scale wind tunnel tests (WTTs) require a dedicated fence model for each configuration. In this study, the fences in LES are represented by the pressure-jump approach, which reproduces the macroscopic windbreak effect without resolving the individual pores. First, this framework is validated against WTTs of a 1:10.5-scale heliostat with two fence heights at elevation angles of 0°–90°, reproducing the measured wake velocity profiles, mean and peak pressure distributions, and force coefficients. Parametric LES covering H = 0.4h–1.2h, β = 25%–76%, and D = 1.5h–12h (h is the torque-tube height) shows that fence height dominates, with the mean-load reduction becoming limited beyond H ≈ 1.0h, while the peak loads continue to decrease and the three parameters exhibit diminishing returns on the mean loads. The porosity effect is observed mainly near the fence: for the 0.4h-high fence, reducing β from 38% to 25% increases the velocity reduction at 1.0h downstream from 42.0% to 51.9%. These differences between porosities become less noticeable beyond about 3h, which indicates that porosity sensitivity weakens with the fence-heliostat distance. The results provide a validated, computationally efficient framework and quantitative criteria for optimizing porous fence deployment in heliostat fields.

papers.title: Physical insights into the wake structure and vortex dynamics of a circular cylinder modified by helical strakes
papers.abstract: The influence of helical strakes on the near-bed junction flow and wake dynamics of a wall-mounted circular cylinder is investigated using improved delayed detached eddy simulation. At a Reynolds number of 7500, the characteristics of flow past a helical straked cylinder with a strake height of 0.2d and a pitch of 10d are examined using a plain cylinder as the reference configuration, where d is the cylinder diameter. The cylinder is vertically positioned at the domain's base, with one of the strakes aligned at 0° to the incoming flow. Results show that the strakes suppress the development of the horseshoe vortex by modifying the near-wall junction flow and promoting asymmetric, three-dimensional vortex structures. The wake becomes increasingly incoherent due to the interaction of the vortical structures from multiple strake-induced separating shear layers. Surface pressure distribution indicates localized flow separation along the edges of the strakes, while wall shear stress is redistributed into localized regions of high and low intensity due to the guided motion of the flow by the strakes. Spectral analysis shows that the strakes shift the spectral energy to a broader range of frequencies. Finally, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition reveals a redistribution of modal energy from the low-order to the higher-order modes, highlighting the role of strakes in disrupting and fragmenting the large-scale coherent wake structures.

papers.title: Kinetic closure of turbulence: Collision-side modeling beyond the filtered Boltzmann equation
papers.abstract: This article extends a recently introduced kinetic closure of turbulence by developing its theoretical framework, operational realizations, and validation. In contrast with filtered Navier–Stokes formulations, filtering the Boltzmann equation retains subgrid transport under the linear streaming operator, so that unresolved physics is concentrated on the collision side. We show that in dilute-gas large-eddy simulation, the main limitation of Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK)-type collision models is not the breakdown of molecular chaos, but the retention of a Markovian collision at a scale where filtering can induce finite temporal correlations in the collision product. In a BGK-type framework, the closure problem is dual: one must infer the filtered fine-grained equilibrium, not computable from filtered moments alone, and model the non-Markovian collision dynamics generated by the collision-product covariance. The present framework makes this dual structure explicit and represents the resulting collision-covariance source term through a BGK-like closure built from the equilibrium commutation residual, with the turbulent relaxation frequency given by a first phenomenological realization. The framework relies on a Chapman–Enskog analysis organized by the reference timescale ratio emerging from the nondimensionalization of the kinetic equation, performed in the classical sense, thereby avoiding artificial turbulent scale separations. We show that the Chapman–Enskog structure is not a pure one-parameter Knudsen scaling: the primary ordering is set by the kinetic-to-macroscopic timescale ratio, while higher moments retain an additional Mach dependence through the mixed scaling of particle velocity. The resulting kinetic closures are validated through lattice Boltzmann simulations and compared with the Smagorinsky model and regularization-based collision models.

papers.title: Unified understanding of parahydrogen thermophysics: Integrating optimization, EOS coupling, and quantum effects
papers.abstract: Parahydrogen (p-H2), the spin isomer of hydrogen residing predominantly in its quantum-mechanical ground state, stands at the frontier of next-generation cryogenic and propulsion technologies. Yet, despite decades of research, notable uncertainties persist in its thermophysical and transport properties; uncertainties that hinder the accurate simulation and design of hydrogen-based systems. In this work, the fundamental transport and interfacial properties of p-H2 are revisited through a synthesis of classical models, modern optimization, and quantum-informed correction. A modified formulation for viscosity, built upon Diller's legacy data and refined via Sequential Least Squares Programming, reduces the absolute average deviation to 0.52%, marking an 18.8% precision gain over the base model. For thermal conductivity, a reconstruction of the Roder–Diller model captures the complex interplay of dense-fluid and critical-region effects, attaining an AAD of 3.09%. Beyond pure-fluid behavior, a new quantum-coupled diffusion model bridges Chapman–Enskog kinetics with the Leachman equation of state, revealing markedly improved predictions for p-H2 interaction with N2, He, O2, and H2O. The surface tension correlation is further reformulated using the updated critical temperature of 32.938 K, preserving subpercent-level accuracy (AAD = 0.23%). Moreover, a set of straightforward correlations for engineering applications is presented for thermal properties of p-H2 in the saturation condition with AAD below 1%.

papers.title: Effects of the initiation timing of water-alternating-gas injection on displacement front evolution and remaining oil mobilization after waterflooding in low-permeability conglomerates
papers.abstract: Low-permeability conglomerate reservoirs exhibit complex pore-throat structures and pronounced flow heterogeneity. During waterflooding, preferential flow pathways develop while oil remains in poorly swept regions. Subsequent water-alternating-gas (CO2-WAG) injection can further mobilize this oil, but the influence of preceding waterflooding on displacement front propagation and remaining oil mobilization remains insufficiently understood. In particular, the development of flow pathways and changes in remaining oil distribution may exert competing effects on subsequent CO2 and water slug propagation. This study investigates how CO2–WAG initiation timing affects pore-scale displacement behavior after waterflooding in low-permeability conglomerates. Core-flooding experiments on three cores monitored by in situ low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) are combined with micro-computed tomography-based three-phase volume-of-fluid (VOF) simulations incorporating CO2 dissolution and interphase mass transfer. The experiments characterize oil recovery and oil-related NMR signal changes, while the simulations examine displacement front propagation, incremental sweep, and remaining oil connectivity under different initiation conditions. The core-flooding experiments show that earlier WAG initiation produces greater incremental oil recovery and larger additional reductions in oil-related NMR signals in the short-T2 range. Axial NMR profiles and MRI maps of a representative core further reveal a wider spatial extent of remaining oil mobilization. The simulations identify competing effects of preceding waterflooding on subsequent WAG displacement. With less-developed flow pathways, CO2 and water slugs have fewer established routes for propagation. As waterflooding continues, preferential pathways become better developed and facilitate slug propagation; however, prolonged waterflooding also directs subsequent flow along established pathways, restricting invasion of adjacent poorly swept pores. At an intermediate waterflooding state, connected pathways support front propagation while allowing injected fluids to reach neighboring oil-bearing regions. This increases incremental sweep and promotes fragmentation and mobilization of connected remaining oil. Further analysis of a representative initiation condition shows that CO2 dissolution into oil is spatially nonuniform and continues during water-slug injection. CO2 dissolution is accompanied by local oil viscosity reduction in the model, while alternating CO2 and water slugs change three-phase occupancy and redistribute remaining oil. The local fluid distributions and oil-related responses vary across pore regions, linking CO2–oil contact and mass transfer to fluid redistribution during alternating injection. Together, these findings reveal how flow pathways and remaining oil distribution established during waterflooding influence subsequent CO2–WAG displacement, providing a pore-scale understanding of displacement front evolution and remaining oil mobilization in low-permeability conglomerates.

papers.title: Effect of superhydrophobic obstacles on the impact dynamics of a shear-thinning droplet
papers.abstract: The present numerical study investigates the effect of obstacle curvature on the impact dynamic of shear-thinning droplets using a 400-ppm xanthan solution. Superhydrophobic obstacles with cube, cylinder, and hemisphere geometries are considered to systematically vary the surface curvature and geometric discontinuity. The morphological evolution, deformation factor, and shape anisotropy ratio are used to characterize the droplet spreading, deformation, and circularity. The effects of obstacle edges and curvature on the flow dynamics are further examined through the pressure and velocity distributions within the droplet and surrounding air. Curvature-sensitive indices (CSISC and CSIDC) are introduced to quantify the influence of single and double curvature on droplet deformation and impact force relative to the flat, zero-curvature obstacle. The results show that obstacle geometry significantly influences the temporal evolution of droplet deformation and impact force. The impact force analysis reveals sustained contact at low inertia, intermittent detachment at intermediate inertia, and rapid detachment at high inertia. The normalized energy budget shows that the surface energy contribution decreases with increasing Weber number, whereas the dissipation energy contribution increases, irrespective of obstacle geometry. The kinetic energy increases more during the receding stage for the hemispherical obstacle due to its smooth curvature, which facilitates droplet retraction. In contrast, the cubic and cylindrical obstacles show a smaller increase due to their corners and geometric constraints.

papers.title: Multi-fidelity numerical investigation of a deflected slipstream blown wing unit for Martian unmanned aerial systems
papers.abstract: A numerical parametric study of a deflected-slipstream (DS) propeller-blown wing is conducted under Martian atmospheric conditions. A multi-fidelity computational fluid dynamics framework, comprising a two-dimensional (2D)-equivalent source-term model, a three-dimensional body-force propeller virtual actuator disk model, and blade-resolved simulations, is used to assess the performance of the different fidelity levels, explore the design space, and identify the underlying flow physics. The different fidelity simulations consistently capture the dominant trends of the lift-to-thrust ratio (L/T), drag-to-thrust ratio (D/T), and resultant force turning angle (θ). A semi-empirical parameter, ε, is introduced to characterize the strength of the slipstream–flap interaction and provides a geometry-based correlate of L/T within the investigated design space, with increasing scatter at large flap deflections. The 2D-equivalent model captures broad parametric trends within the investigated design space while reducing computational cost by up to 105 relative to blade-resolved simulations, supporting rapid preliminary design screening. Across the investigated design space, several configurations achieve L/T values close to or greater than unity, demonstrating strong thrust redirection capability. Control-volume analysis shows that L/T>1 results from the combined effects of slipstream redirection and surrounding-flow entrainment induced by the slipstream–flap interaction. These findings clarify the aerodynamic mechanisms governing DS-blown wing performance and support the concept as a promising lift-augmentation approach for preliminary Martian unmanned aerial systems design.

papers.title: Thermal-fluid model study on high-speed oil-air-lubricated ball bearings with annular flow and thermal elastohydrodynamic lubrication effects
papers.abstract: Thermal and fluid characteristics of lubricants within the bearing cavity are critical to the high-speed performance of rolling bearings in computer numerical control machine-tool motorized spindles. In this study, an oil–air-lubricated angular contact ball bearing is modeled using a thermal-fluid combination framework in which the inlet condition is obtained from a volume of fluid simulation of annular oil–air flow in the supply pipeline, while the rolling element-raceway heat sources are evaluated using a non-Newtonian thermal elastohydrodynamic lubrication (TEHL) shear model. The framework links nozzle geometry, annular-film formation, local TEHL shear stress, friction power loss, and the flow and temperature fields in the bearing cavity. The results show that increasing rotational speed enhances interfacial convection but increases friction heat generation to a greater extent, leading to higher temperatures in both the solid components and the oil–air mixture. Positioning the nozzle near the rolling element and inner raceway contact pair improves oil delivery to the high-shear region and results in the lowest bearing temperature. A multi-nozzle arrangement improves circumferential oil-phase uniformity and suppresses temperature rise, while an intermediate oil-supply speed minimizes the competing effects of insufficient lubrication and viscous churning.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural network analysis of magnetohydrodynamic squeezing flow of hyaluronic acid in periodically oscillating joints
papers.abstract: Synovial fluid ensures smooth joint movement by providing lubrication, primarily through hyaluronic acid (HA). In osteoarthritis (OA), the level of HA decreases, leading to increased friction, inflammation, and impaired joint function. OA is a common global disease that greatly affects patients' daily activities. To compensate for this deficiency and reduce synovial inflammation, viscosupplementation is widely used, in which HA is injected into the joint cavity. The present work analyzes the flow dynamics and thermal characteristics of HA in joint spaces by modeling joint motion as the axisymmetric, oscillatory squeezing flow with thermal transport of an incompressible Maxwell fluid under magnetohydrodynamic effects between two rigid disks. The governing equations are tackled using a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to determine the flow and temperature fields. The PINN model is validated by comparison with the Keller–Box method, showing minimal discrepancy. Error analysis shows that increasing the number of hidden layers and neurons improves solution accuracy. The results reveal that a higher Hartmann number increases the viscosity of HA and dampens fluid motion, whereas increasing the frequency of joint motion leads to a more uniform velocity profile. Elevating Reynolds and Prandtl numbers reduces heat transfer, altering wall temperatures. Higher Hartmann number and porous parameter increase wall shear stress and entropy generation, potentially reducing lubrication efficiency and contributing to cartilage damage in OA. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of PINNs in solving complex partial differential equations and provides theoretical insight into the rheological and thermal behavior of HA relevant to OA therapy.

papers.title: Method for calculating the absolute methane adsorption capacity considering the adsorbed-phase volume: A correction for free-space measurement
papers.abstract: Accurate measurement of methane adsorption is vital for predicting coalbed methane (CBM) reserves, while its volumetric determination depends on the proper partitioning of the calibrated residual space between free methane and the adsorbed phase. The conventional volumetric method often misestimates residual volume by neglecting the space occupied by adsorbed molecules, yielding excess rather than absolute adsorption. To address this, this study proposes a novel method for accurately calculating the absolute methane adsorption capacity—namely, the adsorbed-phase volume method. Based on the micropore-filling model, low-pressure N2 and CO2 adsorption measurements were used to characterize the pore structures of 12 coal samples and quantify their adsorbed-phase volumes, which were subsequently used to correct the helium-calibrated residual volume. The adsorbed-phase volume accounted for 1.58%–5.38% of the experimentally measured residual volume. After correction, the Langmuir volumes derived from absolute adsorption were 1.84–5.18 cm3/g higher than those obtained from excess adsorption, demonstrating that the occupied adsorbed-phase volume measurably affects the gas mass balance in volumetric adsorption measurements. To facilitate the calculation of absolute adsorption, the adsorbed-phase density approach was further simplified by using an effective adsorbed-phase density of 0.36 g/cm3, avoiding the need to determine the adsorbed-phase volume for each individual coal sample. The resulting absolute adsorption values differed from those obtained using the volume-based correction by only 0.82%–4.08%. This study provides a scientific basis for accurate CBM reserve evaluation.

papers.title: Diurnal cycle of the marine atmospheric boundary layer: Implications for rotor wakes
papers.abstract: To elucidate the interaction mechanisms between the wake of large floating offshore wind turbines and the diurnal cycle of the marine atmospheric boundary layer, a fully coupled aero-hydro-mooring-elastic large-eddy simulation model is developed by extending an open-source platform. This strategy reconstructs the atmospheric and oceanic conditions over a typical diurnal cycle and investigates their impacts on the wake evolution of a 15-MW semi-submersible floating offshore wind turbine. The results show that the sea-surface turbulent kinetic energy peaks at 13:20 and 03:10 the following day with values of 1.01 and 1.42 m2/s2, while its minimum occurs at 21:30 at only 10.58% of the preceding daytime peak value. At hub height, the wind speed increases after sunset and decreases after sunrise, accompanied by a clockwise turning induced by the Coriolis force as the flow accelerates. The maximum diurnal differences in the streamwise and spanwise wind speed components reach 2.71 and 3.84 m/s. Across the five representative conditions, the rotor blockage effect is positively correlated with the tip-speed ratio, with the initial maximum and minimum velocity-deficit occurring under the morning and stable conditions. After fitting a power-law function, the negative exponent under stable conditions is only 37.50% of that under convective conditions, with larger exponents indicating slower wake recovery. Benefiting from the additional turbulence induced by cloud circulation, the morning transition exhibits a further reduction in the exponent, reaching the lowest value of −0.68 over the diurnal cycle.

papers.title: Correcting a capillary-number sign pitfall in Kistler dynamic contact-angle modeling of droplet/bubble recoil and receding contact line
papers.abstract: We identified a common implementation pitfall in the Kistler dynamic contact-angle model that replaces the signed capillary number with its magnitude, eliminating the directional dependence required for receding contact-line prediction. We introduce a modified formulation that preserves advancing and receding dynamics while maintaining numerical robustness even at high receding velocities. Validated droplet-impact and bubble-coalescence simulations show that the magnitude-based model mispredicts recoil and suppresses bubble detachment, whereas the modified formulation proposed here accurately captures both phenomena. These findings show that the proposed model provides a physically consistent description of receding contact-line dynamics in volume-of-fluid simulations.

papers.title: Numerical study of CO2-enhanced coalbed methane recovery: Integrating the Span–Wagner and Setzmann–Wagner equations of state with dynamic viscosity
papers.abstract: CO2-enhanced coalbed methane recovery (CO2-ECBM) integrates methane production with geological CO2 storage, offering a promising pathway for the cleaner utilization of coal-associated energy resources. However, the predictive accuracy of existing CO2-ECBM simulations is often limited by simplified descriptions of gas properties, especially under medium- to high-pressure conditions, where CO2 and CH4 exhibit non-ideal behavior, and their viscosities vary with pressure and temperature. In this study, a fully coupled thermo–hydro–mechanical (THM) model is developed by incorporating real-gas thermodynamics and pressure-temperature dependent gas viscosity. The model is validated against published experimental observations and subsequently applied to examine how the evolution of gas thermophysical properties influences methane production, CO2 storage, pressure-temperature responses, and sweep behavior. The results demonstrate that the density and viscosity of CO2 and CH4 are strongly regulated by reservoir pressure and temperature, leading to substantial variations in flow resistance, adsorption–desorption behavior, and thermal feedback during CO2-ECBM. Compared with the proposed model, the conventional approach based on the ideal-gas equation of state and constant gas viscosity underestimates methane recovery and CO2 storage capacity by ∼25% and 50%, respectively. Moreover, this prediction bias is not constant but varies with pressure–temperature conditions and injection parameters, indicating that simplified gas property assumptions may introduce scenario-dependent errors in CO2-ECBM performance assessment. By resolving the dynamic evolution of gas thermophysical properties within a coupled THM framework, this study provides a more physically robust basis for the CO2 injection design, storage capacity evaluation, and cleaner coalbed methane development in deep coal seams.

papers.title: Phase-resolved reduced-order theory for pulsatile flow in sinusoidal-walled channels
papers.abstract: Pulsatile flow in non-uniform channels is commonly characterized by mean pressure drop, flow rate amplitude, or cycle-averaged transport measures. These quantities do not identify when the response occurs within the forcing cycle. We develop a reduced-order, first-harmonic admittance framework for a rigid sinusoidal-walled channel and state its circular-tube specialization separately. The Newtonian branch is anchored by the appropriate unsteady cross-sectional admittance; the generalized-Newtonian and linear viscoelastic branches use, respectively, a regularized tangent viscosity and a Jeffreys/Oldroyd-B complex viscosity. The computational fluid dynamics evidence is restricted to two-dimensional planar channels, for which the parallel-plate kernel is the relevant comparator. Streamwise-periodic OpenFOAM and rheoTool calculations assess frequency, wall-amplitude, rheological, and prescribed-wall-temperature responses without inlet–outlet development effects. We formulate a direct small-waviness correction, phase-extraction convention, and validity indicators. The framework therefore provides phase-resolved observables that can complement, rather than uniquely identify from, mean-flow diagnostics.

papers.title: Two-phase flow simulations of surface waves and turbulence underneath
papers.abstract: The accuracy of global circulation models relies on an understanding of the processes occurring at the coupled atmosphere–ocean interface, which are experimentally challenging to observe. This study numerically examines the interaction between surface waves and turbulence of an underlying countercurrent—with and without additional mean shear—in reference to recent laboratory water channel experiments. Presented results are based on a previously reported hybrid, scale resolving numerical method that resolves both the air and water phases at realistic Reynolds numbers, thereby overcoming the free surface boundary conditions prescribed by single-phase approaches. The procedure is supplemented with a method for generating synthetic turbulence to rapidly develop resolved turbulence within a compact domain. Results confirm the existence of an anti-Stokes flow and reveal that surface waves significantly amplify the streamwise enstrophy near the surface (by a factor of up to 6) and increase the Reynolds normal stresses, while turbulence anisotropy is rebalanced in a way that qualitatively agrees well with rapid distortion theory predictions. Observed phase shifts of enstrophy components are consistent with experimental data, but differ from the results of single-phase approaches. Largely unaffected by the presence of waves, the vertical flux of horizontal momentum is strongly influenced by mean shear. This work also analyzes surface pressure fields and the corresponding drag coefficients, confirming a quadratic wave slope dependence of pressure drag. Overall, the numerical model proves to be a promising approach for future collaborative experimental/numerical studies of turbulent transport processes in the vicinity of the atmosphere–ocean interface.

papers.title: Effect of wall disturbance on unsteady channel flow
papers.abstract: Channel flow driven by unsteady piston motion subject to external disturbances is investigated via two-dimensional numerical simulations. Unlike previous studies that have considered disturbances distributed throughout the flow, we apply disturbance at the channel wall. The piston is prescribed trapezoidal motion with four phases, namely acceleration, uniform velocity, deceleration, and after-stoppage. The evolution of perturbation energy for various wavenumbers, frequencies, and amplitudes of external disturbance is investigated. Using a metric based on perturbation energy, we have identified the most dangerous disturbance. Its wavenumber matches that of the instability reported in earlier works. Comparison of growth rate of perturbation energy with results of linear stability analysis yields good agreement. It is observed that the flow pattern becomes increasingly complex with increase in frequency and decrease in wavenumber of external disturbance. For small wavenumbers, disturbance at one wall results in the formation of vortices near the opposite wall. On the other hand, for large wavenumbers, the flow near the opposite wall remains unaffected. The amplitude of external disturbance is found to have non-monotonic effect on the gain of perturbation energy in the deceleration phase. The gain initially increases and then decreases with increase in amplitude.

papers.title: Pore-scale mechanisms of surfactant-assisted oil displacement revealed by a dipole lattice Boltzmann model
papers.abstract: Surfactant flooding is an important chemical enhanced oil recovery technique because of its ability to reduce oil–water interfacial tension and improve microscopic sweep efficiency. However, the pore-scale mechanisms by which surfactant concentration and injection velocity influence displacement behavior remain poorly understood. Unlike previous pore-scale studies based on idealized pore geometries, this work develops a dipole surfactant model coupled with the multicomponent Shan–Chen lattice Boltzmann method. Simulations are performed on the binarized pore pattern of a heterogeneous microfluidic chip whose geometry is representative of the Xinjiang glutenite reservoir. The model is validated against three independent benchmarks: the static interfacial tension of a droplet, interfacial surfactant adsorption, and droplet deformation under shear flow. The influences of surfactant concentration and injection velocity on displacement efficiency, displacement front stability, and the spatiotemporal evolution of the surfactant concentration field are then systematically investigated. The results show that displacement efficiency varies non-monotonically with surfactant concentration. Among the concentrations tested, c = 0.5% yields the lowest final oil saturation of approximately 21%, whereas at c = 2% the displacement front becomes locally stalled near the middle of the porous section, resulting in a higher final oil saturation of approximately 27%. The dipole orientation field reveals a more heterogeneous interfacial state at the higher concentration, and the adsorption isotherm of the model shows that the adsorption efficiency reaches a maximum and then declines as the surfactant density increases, suggesting that the approach to adsorption saturation may contribute to the reduced displacement efficiency at 2%. Injection velocity has only a limited influence on the ultimate displacement efficiency, with the final oil saturation remaining within 23%–27% over the investigated range. Notably, the mean interfacial dipole magnitude is nearly independent of injection velocity, whereas its spatial variation increases with velocity because newly created interfaces receive less surfactant than persisting ones. Although surfactant concentration and injection velocity act through different physical mechanisms, possibly approaching adsorption saturation and limited surfactant supply to newly created interfaces, both can be interpreted within a common capillary controlled framework in which variations in the local capillary number at individual pore throats govern the transition from channelized invasion to more uniform displacement. Variations in the local capillary number at individual pore throats govern the transition from channelized invasion to more uniform displacement. The dipole orientation field provides complementary pore-scale information beyond saturation curves, offering a physical basis for optimizing surfactant flooding strategies in heterogeneous reservoirs.

papers.title: Experimental study of the impact dynamics of polymeric hollow droplets
papers.abstract: The impact dynamics of hollow droplets, while influential in applications such as coating and spraying, remain less explored than their dense counterparts. This knowledge gap is particularly pronounced for viscoelastic hollow droplets. This study presents an experimental investigation into the impact of hollow Newtonian (water) and viscoelastic (polymeric solution) droplets on a solid surface at different impact velocities and polymer concentrations. We demonstrate two hallmark features of hollow droplet flattening: the formation of a central counter-jet and the final deposition, both associated with the entrapped air bubble. For Newtonian droplets, the counter-jet exhibits rapid growth and breakup due to capillary instabilities. Introducing polymer additives fundamentally alters this behavior: viscoelasticity affects the counter-jet's height and velocity, delays bubble rupture, and inhibits droplet detachment. Crucially, we observe the emergence of beads-on-a-string structures during filament thinning, a signature of the competition between elastic and capillary forces. By systematically varying the polymer concentration and impact velocity, we identify the conditions under which three distinct outcomes occur: deposition, partial deposition, and detachment. Our results show how inertia, viscosity, capillarity, and elasticity together govern the splashing morphology of hollow non-Newtonian droplets.

papers.title: Gradient-inertia classification and rank-one well-posedness for a variational two-fluid natural mode
papers.abstract: Two-fluid models describe dispersed and boiling flows, yet inadequate relative-motion inertia can produce short-wave instability. We classify Galilean-invariant, local first-gradient kinetic corrections that are quadratic in relative velocity for the one-dimensional variational natural mode. Gradient-block semidefiniteness requires κ ≥ 0, μ ≥ 0, and κμ ≥ λ2. At uniform states with nonzero relative flux, strictly positive-definite corrections produce O(|k|) growth, and positive void-fraction-gradient inertia alone produces O(k2) growth. A nontrivial semidefinite correction has bounded high-wavenumber growth if and only if μ > 0 and κμ = λ2. Under phase-conserving kinematics, this rank-one form is material-derivative micro-inertia transported at j − gJ; an explicit transport window determines all-wavenumber spectral stability. An integrating-factor transformation yields elliptic recovery coupled to first-order transport, and energy estimates establish local Hadamard well-posedness for the source-free periodic problem. Spectral propagation and independent real-space integration recover the growth orders and transport window. Published air–water coupling parameters and bubble micro-inertia give a mass crossover wavelength of 15.63 mm at α = 0.05 and Rb = 1 mm. A finite heated water-steam channel couples evaporation to momentum and total energy with positive gradient inertia. Two published inertial families place vapor transport on opposite sides of the frozen source-free stability window, while all 16 channel cases close the heat-normalized energy budget within 5.9 × 10−12. These results guide the selection of gradient structure, transport velocity, and inertial scale and specify their use in conservation-compatible phase-change closures.

papers.title: Dynamical and statistical model for cellular premixed flame propagation in diverging Hele–Shaw channel
papers.abstract: A phenomenological model for the propagation of a cellular premixed flame front in a Hele-Shaw channel is developed. It accounts for the key experimental observations: the formation and dynamics of front cusps, cell shrinking and vanishing, spontaneous cell division induced by the Darrieus–Landau instability, and the unsteady flow of the fresh mixture ahead of the front caused by heat losses to the channel walls. The model incorporates the dynamical and statistical characteristics of the front determined from experiments in a diverging Hele-Shaw channel, including cell shape, amplitude, skewness, growth rate, splitting probability, and the subsequent cusp locations. Simulation results are presented and compared with experimental video recordings for a stoichiometric propane–air flame propagating in a channel with a 20-degree side opening angle and a 4 mm gap. The model is demonstrated to adequately capture the overall flame dynamics and provide a cell size distribution that closely matches the measured data.

papers.title: Instability and tail pitching-down benefit the aerodynamic efficiency of barn owl in equilibrium gliding
papers.abstract: Birds can switch between high maneuverability and enhanced stability via large-scale morphing of their lifting surfaces. While the avian tail serves primarily as an auxiliary lift surface, it is crucial for stability control, lift production, and drag reduction. In this study, we develop a theoretical model that enforces both force and pitch-moment balance to examine how static longitudinal stability modulates tail control and gliding aerodynamic efficiency. We apply this framework to a barn owl (Tyto alba), a naturally unstable glider, using computational fluid dynamics simulations based on reconstructed free-flight geometry. Tail pitch and spread angles, as well as center of gravity location, are virtually manipulated to quantify their effects on aerodynamic forces, pitch-moment, and trimmed gliding performance. Our results show that, for the barn owl model, trimmed states under unstable configurations correspond to a pitch-down tail, whereas stable trimmed flight requires a pitch-up tail. Importantly, moderate static instability combined with tail pitch-down reduces drag and power consumption and improves aerodynamic efficiency compared with stable trimmed conditions. As flight speed increases, the required tail pitch-down angle decreases, indicating reduced instability and relaxed control demand. These findings demonstrate that longitudinal instability is not inherently detrimental for avian gliding; instead, it can form part of an efficient trim strategy. This work provides insight for bird-like micro air vehicles adopting relaxed static stability and active tail control.

papers.title: Petrov–Galerkin variational physics-informed neural network framework for two-dimensional singularly perturbed problems
papers.abstract: This study proposes a Petrov–Galerkin-based variational physics-informed neural network (VPINN) for efficiently solving two-dimensional singularly perturbed problems (SPPs) with one and two small perturbation parameters. The approach employs neural networks to construct the trial solution space, while tensor-product hat functions are adopted as test functions to enforce the variational form. To accurately resolve sharp boundary layers, the variational form is implemented using a Petrov–Galerkin formulation. Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed directly, while the source terms are computed at the collocation points. Computational experiments on standard two-dimensional problems demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accuracy in both the maximum and L2 norms. These results indicate that the Petrov–Galerkin VPINN approach can effectively capture the multiscale features of two-dimensional SPPs.

papers.title: Shock wave attenuation in confined ducts with periodic obstacles: How geometry redistributes shear and bulk viscous dissipation
papers.abstract: How obstacle geometry redistributes shock wave energy dissipation between shear and bulk viscous pathways in confined spaces remains poorly understood, despite its importance for explosion protection and supersonic propulsion systems. Here, we address this gap by simulating shock propagation through a confined duct containing periodic arrays of rectangle, forward-triangle, backward-triangle, and semi-ellipse obstacles using a discrete Boltzmann method. All obstacle configurations reduce the outlet pressure peak and overpressure impulse, with the rectangle array yielding the strongest peak attenuation. Critically, obstacle geometry does not merely enhance total dissipation indiscriminately but selectively regulates dissipation pathways: the forward-triangle array predominantly enhances bulk viscous dissipation, whereas the rectangle array preferentially activates shear dissipation. Instantaneous flow fields reveal the underlying mechanism: forward-triangle obstacles preserve a continuous transmitted shock front and generate repeated local compression to enhance bulk viscous dissipation, while rectangle obstacles truncate the shock front and promote cavity-confined wave reflections to amplify shear dissipation. A key insight is that geometric periodicity alone does not guarantee periodic dissipation in confined geometries; rather, the dominant dissipation pathway is controlled by how the obstacle shape modulates shock front continuity and cavity wave trapping. These findings provide quantitative guidance for tailoring bulk energy dissipation in confined compressible flows through obstacle array design.

papers.title: Axial particle segregation in unevenly rotating fluid-filled cylindrical layer
papers.abstract: The dynamics of a two-phase medium of water and glass beads in unevenly rotating horizontal cylindrical layer is studied experimentally. The rotation rate varies according to the law f=fr[1+ϵ cos(2πfosct)], where fr is the mean rotation rate, which is set so that the centrifugal force of inertia keeps the glass beads in a stable position near the outer boundary of the cylindrical layer. In an unevenly rotating cylindrical layer, the interaction of water with the layer's walls occurs exclusively in thin boundary layers. So, the core of the fluid rotates at a constant rate fr relative to the observer. From the perspective of glass beads, water oscillates azimuthally at a frequency fosc. It is observed that as the oscillation amplitude ϵ increases, a threshold redistribution of the glass beads occurs, resulting in the axisymmetric pattern formation. It is demonstrated that this phenomenon emerges when the viscous stress at the interface becomes large enough (the Shields number exceeds the critical value θcr), the glass beads become mobile and can move within the cylindrical layer. The present paper discusses the results of experiments on the axial segregation of glass beads. It is revealed that axial particle segregation is associated with the initiation of the vortical flows by standing inertial waves. The spatial period of the band formation is determined by the axial wavenumber of the inertial waves that satisfy the resonance condition.

papers.title: Dynamic wetting characteristics of nanoscale water films on regular textured surfaces under periodic vibration
papers.abstract: Smart surfaces with controlled wettability induced by vibrated surfaces have gained growing interest among researchers, owing to their practical applications in keeping dry, self-cleaning, and removing dropwise heat. In this study, we perform molecular dynamics simulations to investigate wetting characteristics of nanoscale water films on regularly structured surfaces induced by periodic vibration. We systematically investigate how vibration amplitude and oscillation period affect dynamic wetting behaviors through free-energy analysis, calculations of the average water molecular velocity, and phase diagram characterization. Detailed energy pathways on vibrated surfaces are calculated via calculated interfacial free energy to reveal the mechanisms underlying wetting dynamics. The free energy profile exhibits multiple energy peaks during the partial-wetting transition, while it eventually stabilizes at a global energy minimum for the full-wetting transition. In total, five wetting outcomes are identified, including the Cassie state, Wenzel state, unstable Wenzel state, reversible switching state, and liquid film rising up. The boundary dividing the highly non-wetting and collapsed regimes obeys the scaling law of Acri/T = constant, where the constant varies with water film thickness, groove aspect ratio (H/W), and Young's contact angle (θY). The effect of H/W and θY on wetting outcomes is studied by observing different phase diagrams. These findings provide natural insights into the wetting dynamics of aqueous water by applying vibration to groove surfaces and supply theoretical references for designing surfaces with controllable wettability.

papers.title: Wake energy redistribution and modal evolution with a pre-duct under self-propulsion
papers.abstract: This study compares hull–propeller and hull–propeller–pre-duct (HPD) configurations at the same model speed and their respective experimentally prescribed self-propulsion rates, relating delivered power to wake-energy organization. The improved delayed detached-eddy simulation based on the shear stress transport model (SST-IDDES) results are analyzed using blade-passage phase, shaft-order frequency, triple decomposition, sectional energy metrics, and area-weighted proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), spectral POD (SPOD), and dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). HPD operates at a 3.85% lower propeller rate and 1.47% lower torque, reducing mean delivered power by 5.25%; its phase-averaged power remains lower throughout the blade-passage cycle. Upstream, HPD reorganizes axial and circumferential inflow. In the wake, it shifts the outer vortical system inward and redistributes vortical structures and the mean slipstream. Computational fluid dynamics results show 14%–17% lower section-averaged circumferential kinetic energy in the near wake, while residual unsteady kinetic energy is higher at all sections. POD requires more modes to capture 90% of fluctuation energy, indicating a broader spatial distribution. SPOD identifies higher band energies at the blade-passing frequency (BPF) and its second harmonic, but a lower leading-mode energy fraction at the representative near-wake section. Downstream, higher harmonics decay rapidly, while resolved low-frequency band energy generally increases and remains higher in HPD within the available 20-revolution record. DMD identifies BPF modes with spatial topologies closely matching the corresponding SPOD modes. These results show that the pre-duct modifies propulsion performance and the phase-resolved and spectral organization of unsteady wake energy, offering a frequency-resolved perspective beyond integral metrics.
